### Of Abbot Joachim

...to consider the gentle animal of Christ <note>original: "dere mite animal Christi," referring to the donkey Christ rode into Jerusalem</note> and seeks the arrogance of a foaming horse: He shows his King, whom he remembers sat upon an ass. folio 180, column 2.

How four crimes bring about beautiful moral lessons. folio 180, column 2.

In the sixth age of the world, first the apostles were sent; second, the martyrs; third, the teachers; fourth, the contemplatives; and the world did not listen to them. For this reason, in the fifth time <note>Joachim’s theology divides history into "ages" (etates) and "times" (tempora) corresponding to the Trinity and the days of creation.</note> others were sent to pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the race of the wicked: so that the hardened and blinded may walk in darkness and not know where they go, until in the sixth time judges are sent against it to remove the memory of Babylon from the earth. folio 181, column 2.

He who loves God more is kindled with greater zeal against transgressors; both because it is more fitting for those whose lives are irreproachable to be zealous, and because they have nothing to fear if a scandal is stirred up against them. folio 181, column 2.

There is great power in the mouths of spiritual men to enact vengeance against transgressors. folio 181, column 2.

What method should be held in correcting a sinner. folio 181, column 2.

It was necessary for the spirit of gentleness to come first in the apostles and other preachers, and finally for the spirit of Elijah and Elisha <note>Helye & Helysei</note> to follow near the end to enact vengeance upon the nations. folio 181, column 2.

The evil person and sinner, having become incorrigible and worse because of a rebuke, begins to persecute and attack the physician. folio 182, column 1.

The reason why the harsh rebuke of the saints is called the "last plague," and why the wrath of God is completed within it. folio 182, column 1.

Many times the impulse of God’s anger is held back by the saints for a certain time, because they pretend to speak harsh words to sinners so that they do not fall into the pit of despair. folio 182, column 1.

Why some holy men speak to sinners humbly and kindly as if to their sick brothers, and others speak with zeal as if to the enemies of God; yet both do well. folio 182.

<column-break/>

Christ first came in a spirit of leniency, but he is to come for judgment as if in a spirit of fire: in the first coming sinners were encouraged, but in the second even the just will be afraid. folio 182, column 1.

Why they are called the last plagues. folio 182, column 1.

Just as the fig tree was expected to bear fruit until the fourth year and in the fifth was to be cut down entirely, so in this fifth age of the church, the <term>carnal church</term> <note>original: "ecclesia carnalis." Joachim used this term to describe the worldly or corrupt element of the Church that would be purged before the Age of the Spirit.</note> must be cut down. folio 182, column 1.

In the "beast" is designated the multitude of infidels persecuting the church of God; in the "image," the doctrine of that beast; and in the "number of his name," the great quantity of vices. folio 182, column 2.

Blessed Augustine, in his book on the Psalms, commends three orders of the faithful: the first of the laity, the second of the clergy, and the third of the monks; where he says he has found none better than those who have made progress in a monastery. folio 182, column 2.

From the <term>lay order</term> victory over the beast is specifically required; from the <term>clerical order</term>, victory over the beast and the image; but from the <term>monastic order</term>, victory over the beast, the image, and the number of his name. folio 182, column 2.

Many in the order of the laity and clergy have kept, and do keep, the perfection of the monastic life; and conversely, many having the monastic habit are far from that perfection which this figure represents. folio 183, column 1.

For what reason a religious person enters the cloister; note on the three vows <note>Poverty, chastity, and obedience.</note>. folio 183, column 1.

He is not a monk who is merely called a monk, just as one is not necessarily a cleric or a Christian simply because he is called a cleric or a Christian. folio 183, column 1.

He who is truly a monk considers nothing to be his own except the "new man" <note>A reference to the Pauline concept of the *novus homo* (Ephesians 4:24), the spiritual self created in God's likeness.</note> who is created according to God, or the operation of the Holy Spirit in which three general strings resonate: Faith, Hope, and Charity. folio 183.

That heart cannot absolutely praise God which is occupied by the images of things and the anxieties of the world. folio 183, column 1.

Without faith, hope, and charity, we are least able to praise God with heart and soul. folio 183, column 1.

In what way spiritual men ought to pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon sinners. folio 184, column 2.

That everyone ought to take care lest they be kindled with an indiscreet zeal against their neighbors and strike down delinquent brothers—only to be struck down themselves by another; but rather, one should learn to have humble mercy for the faults of others as much as one recognizes their own need for mercy. folio 185, column 1.

That many have leather belts <note>original: "zonas pelliceas"</note> around their waists, but few have golden belts <note>original: "zonas aureas"</note> around their chests; that is, many observe the continence of the flesh, but few possess the purity of the mind. folio 185, column 1. <note>This references the description of the angels in Revelation 15:6, contrasting outward asceticism with inward virtue.</note>

How spiritual men who devote themselves to silence, hearing that the people are not converting to repentance, are kindled with zeal and in a time of necessity present themselves, etc. folio 185, column 1.

That Elijah <note>original: "Helyas"</note> designates the order of contemplatives—that is, the hermit-like order. folio 185, column 1.

That the order of hermits established the order of monks. folio 185, column 2.

That the hermit-like order came first, having ready the vials handed to it by the just God; but it did not pour them out itself, but handed them to others to be poured out at the time when sins would be completed. folio 185, column 1.

That the vials <note>The "vials of wrath" from Revelation 16.</note> are the pious traditions of the Fathers, by which they instructed perfect disciples, teaching them to work for justice and be zealous for it, so that their light might shine before men. folio 185, column 2.

That this is true religion in the sight of God: that which both shines outwardly through example and is kindled inwardly by the heat of justice. folio 185, column 2.

That these two—namely, a holy life and zeal for God—are so suited to each other that one cannot please God without the other. folio 185, column 2.

That each individual time from the first to the seventh has within it something that pertains to the pastors and similarly to the other orders; and each order, from the first to the seventh, is distinguished into seven portions. folio 186, column 2.

Why there are said to be seven angels who have gone out of the temple to pour out the seven vials of the wrath of God, when all are of one order and of one power. folio 186, column 2.

That there are six times (but the sixth is double) which are given for repentance to the people of God, in which the elect are struck so that they may profit, and the reprobate so that they may have no excuse for their sin, and so that their completed malice may be revealed in contrast to the charity of those others. folio 186, column 2.

That the primitive church <note>The early Church of the Apostles.</note> which was gathered in Judea from the circumcision <note>Jewish converts.</note> is called "the earth." folio 187, column 1.

That the Gentile people began from Japheth <note>The son of Noah, traditionally viewed as the ancestor of the European/Gentile nations.</note> until Christ. folio 187, column 2.

# Of Abbot Joachim

That the fifth age of the church began with the Emperor Constantine. folio 188, column 2.

That it is human to fall into error, but to persecute Catholics and shed their blood in defense of error is diabolical. folio 188, column 2.

That all chastity and all religious life is vain if it is not founded and solidified in the root of humility, even if by its excellence it seems to transcend the stars of heaven. folio 189, column 1.

That hypocrites, who consider themselves holy and just and worthier than others, are all the more kindled with wrath if they are rebuked by anyone, insofar as they consider the lives of others to be worth nothing. folio 189, column 1.

That those mentioned above, who repute themselves just, are accustomed to complain to those they meet and explain their own life to them, so that they might know that they are being reproved [only] out of the zeal of envy and the malice of hatred. folio 189, column 1.

That carnal <note>Worldly or non-spiritual.</note> men are scandalized when they see disputes and discords among those whom they reputed to be holy and just. folio 189, column 1.

That carnal men seethe and kindle their wrath against those who pursue hypocrites as if they were lost men—those very hypocrites whom they themselves for a long time testified, believed, or preached were holy among men. folio 189, column 2.

That in the fifth age, the general church shone forth—specifically the order of clerics and of conventual <term>religious</term> <note>This refers to members of monastic or mendicant orders living in a community under a Rule.</note>, at the end of which age we now stand. folio 189, column 2.

That the Antichrist has reigned from the beginning of the church in his members <note>Followers or agents who act as the "body" of the Antichrist on earth.</note>. folio 189, column 2.

That bad monks <note>original: "religiosi"</note> are worse than other secular <note>Laypeople living in the world.</note> people, as Augustine says: "I have found none better than those who have progressed in monasteries; and on the contrary, I have found none worse than those who have failed in monasteries." folio 189, column 2.

That such bad monks are immoderately ambitious to rule over their brothers, wherefore the kingdom of God is justly taken away from them. folio 189, column 2.

That ambitious men, when they are rebuked by their equals regarding their religious habit <note>The distinctive clothing of a monastic order.</note>, take it with indignation, not considering that the habit is of no benefit—rather it is a hindrance—if the habit is in discord with one's life. folio 190, column 1.

That hatred blinds the mind; for he who hates his brother is in darkness and has not seen the light. folio 190.

<column-break/>

That when such carnal, ambitious men are prevented by spiritual men and cannot obtain what they desire, they immediately break out into the defamation of those who rebuke them because of the excessive pain of their heart. folio 190, column 1.

That those who, while they are rebuked, endure it patiently and confess they are justly reproved, shortly afterward—if they persevere in patience—find consolation as grace arrives, and having been consoled, they bless the Lord who saves those who hope in Him. folio 190, column 1.

That those who are impatient while being corrected first tear at their correctors with their teeth; then, as impatience and malice grow, they break out even into blasphemies against the Creator. folio 190, column 1.

That he who does not resist lusts and vices from the beginning while there is time for repentance, ends up with multiplied sorrows (because he does not have what he pleases); it happens that the inner parts of his heart are so wounded by the arrows of temptation that his mind is often snatched away to blasphemy against his will, and seeking to find a way to repentance, he cannot. folio 190, column 1.

That they are fools who delay their conversion from day to day; for although Mercy has promised the sinner that in whatever hour he repents with all his heart [he will be forgiven], He has not promised to always give the impulse of repentance to those who sin; wherefore the Lord said: "Strive to enter through the narrow gate; for I say to you: many will seek to enter and will not be able." folio 190, column 1.

That the fifth vial <note>A reference to the "seven vials of wrath" in Revelation 16.</note> of the wrath of God was poured out upon those who seemed to be of the household of God and of the orders of the perfect—namely, of the clerical and <term>religious</term> orders. The sixth vial, however, will be poured out upon the irregular and worldly, such as soldiers and the merchants of the earth. folio 190, column 1.

That the river Euphrates once flowed into that most wealthy ancient Babylon. folio 190, column 2.

That the city of Rome is the "New Babylon" and the prostitute who sits upon the waters—that is, the peoples of the Roman Empire. folio 190, column 2.

That for the "waters to be dried up" means that the armies are weakened so that they cannot resist the kings and the nations of the infidels coming from the rising sun—which is understood literally. folio 190, column 2.

That after the desolation of the Roman Empire re- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "reparabitur" (will be restored) or "revelabitur" (will be revealed).</note>

# Index for the Exposition on the Apocalypse

The Antichrist <note>original: "Antixps"</note> will reveal himself, and he will have in his company an army of lost men and crowds of false clerics and his own so-called prophets. Their purpose is to provoke infidel kings to empty out the kingdom of Christ. This is called the "beast that ascends from the earth" and is referred to as the false prophet. folio 190, column 2.

Concerning how, when the words spoken by John in this chapter are seen to be fulfilled, the coming of the Antichrist will be near; so much so that from 그 hour it is necessary for the elect to be in suspense and prepared for the coming of the Judge, not knowing on what day or hour he may come. folio 191, column 1.

Concerning the example of the flood in the time of Noah brought forward by the Lord, and that saying of the Apostle: "When they shall say peace and security," etc. This is to be understood more as referring to the destruction of Babylon than to the final judgment. folio 191.

Concerning how in the sixth age <term>sixth time</term> <note>Joachim of Fiore divided history into distinct "Ages" or "Times" (tempora) corresponding to the seals and vials of Revelation.</note>, the sixth angel shall generally pour out his vial against all the reprobate, who, having been struck before, shall be wiped out from the earth. And soon the seventh angel follows, himself pouring out his vial upon the elect: note this. folio 191, column 2.

Concerning how the church of the fifth age is called the "seat of God," and the general church which is spiritually called "Jerusalem," which is in conflict with the church of the malignant—namely, Babylon. folio 191, column 2.

Concerning how when God wishes to change the state of the church through the succession of ages, his messengers precede him by some years, either by performing miracles or by making proclamations. This is done so that the sleepy and the lazy might be roused from the sleep of death—that is, from their sins— and so that they and others might understand that the Lord is about to do something new upon the earth. folio 191, column 2.

Why they do not advance [using such] methods, wishing to avenge themselves and Christ against the infidels and recover the Holy Land. folio 192, column 1.

How it shall be given to the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note>; but now it has been given to the infidel nations, and why. folio 192, column 2.

Concerning the usage of Holy Scripture: that often a part of a thing is taken for the whole, and what is done in a part is referred to the whole: note why. folio 192, column 2.

Concerning how, although the events are diverse according to the time, there is nevertheless one will among all the reprobate, just as there is among the elect. 

<column-break/>

For the children of the Jews hear that their fathers rejected Jesus of Nazareth as if he were a deceiver and an enemy of their law; and the zeal of their fathers pleases them, so much so that they themselves crucify him in their will, even though they cannot persecute him in action. folio 192, column 2.

Concerning how God generally, throughout five ages, patiently endured and permitted Babylon to reign in its delights, and allowed the children of Jerusalem to be afflicted by the children of Babylon, until the justice of the former and the iniquity of the latter be fulfilled. folio 193, column 1.

Concerning how in the sixth age there will be no tribulation against the elect from the children of Babylon—that is, from the false Christians who are called such but are not Christians—for they will have already been destroyed. folio 193, column 1.

Concerning carnal men <note>Those focused on worldly rather than spiritual matters.</note> who love the world: they and the things that are of the world cannot patiently endure it when they hear that what they love is seemingly perishing, thinking that nothing is more pleasant than this present life. folio 193, column 2.

Concerning the thief who said to the Lord on the cross: "If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us." He was crucified on the left side of the Lord. folio 193, column 2.

How reprobate Christians blaspheme against Christ, saying: "What necessity was there for him to suffer? For if he is omnipotent, he could have saved us without suffering." folio 194, column 1.

Concerning how it is useful to see and know the damnation of the "Great Harlot" <note>original: *meretricis magne*</note>; for she who does not know what she is to suffer for her errors is easily deceived by the glances of her eyes. folio 194, column 1.

Concerning how the Catholic Fathers said that Rome is this "Great Harlot"—not as regarding the church of the just which is a pilgrim within her, but as regarding the multitude of the reprobate, who blaspheme and attack that same pilgrim church in their midst with their wicked works. folio 194, column 1.

Concerning how, although Rome is principally to be understood as that most famous harlot and Babylon, the location of this harlot is not to be sought in only one kingdom or province, but in the whole Roman Empire—especially among those who have the greater power and will to sin, who lead a luxurious life, and, abounding in delights, rejoice when they have done evil. folio 194, column 1.

# Of Abbot Joachim

Concerning how the **kings of the earth** in this place are understood to be **prelates** <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> to whom the governance of souls has been granted, yet who commit "fornication" with Babylon. folio 194, column 1.

Concerning him who desires the office of a bishop <note>original: "episcopatū"</note> for this purpose alone: that he may be a father to orphans and a judge for widows—he desires a good work. But those who desire it so they may become great, friends of the rich, and kin to the powerful, commit "fornication." folio 194, column 2.

Concerning how the **wine** offered by the harlot is understood as the sweetness of her pleasure; and by the name of **fornication**, all sins committed voluntarily are understood, but principally the vice of Babylonian corruption. folio 194, column 2.

Concerning how the love and heat of luxury reign in the rich of this world. folio 194, column 2.

Concerning how there are **two things** that do not allow a man to see the ruin of the children of this world: namely, earthly anxieties and the literal sense of scripture "which kills." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." Joachim emphasizes spiritual over literal interpretation.</note> folio 194, column 2.

Concerning how **leisure** for reading, **peace**, and **silence** are necessary for you if you wish to understand what you read. folio 194, column 2.

Concerning how, if you always accept what you read exactly as it is written <note>original: "vt legis"</note>, a fleshly understanding will often lead you into absurdity; for it is the Spirit who gives life, but the flesh profits nothing. <note>original: "spiritus est qui viuificat: caro aūt nō pdest qcq̃z"</note> folio 194.

Concerning how, in this sixth part, the discourse is so mixed that some things must be understood according to the **letter** and some according to **allegory**; note the reason why. folio 195, column 1.

Concerning how, in this sixth part of the book and in the **sixth age** <term>sixth time</term>, hidden mysteries shall be opened to the elect, and the book shall be clearly opened; for the appointed time spoken of by Daniel has arrived, where he said that the words would be closed and sealed until the appointed time. folio 195, column 1.

Concerning how where there is an abundance of wealth, there is an enormity of vices. folio 195, column 1.

Concerning how when the children of Jerusalem offend in word or deed, they feel great shame and seek to hide their guilt before God and men, lest perhaps men be scandalized and sin, or God in his indignation punish them; they hide it, however, by performing penance. The children of Babylon, conversely, do the opposite. folio 195, column 1.

Concerning how not only the city of Rome is to be considered **Babylon**, but the entire multitude of impious men born according to the flesh. folio 195, column 2.

<column-break/>

Concerning the **beast which was and is not**: this is the infidel people of the **sect of Muhammad** <note>original: "mahumeth"</note>. As for the phrase "was and is not," this is to be ascribed to the sixth age of the Church, during which—Babylon (that is, the harlot herself) having been struck first—the beast itself shall be overcome by Christ (that is, by the faithful). And it is said "it is not" because its ferocity must cease for a time, as it were, while Christ prevails with his soldiers; and after a little while, that which was thought to be slain shall rise up; note the reason. folio 196, column 1.

Concerning how **carnal men**, seeing the infidel people fighting against Christians once again, will be scandalized, saying: "If this Christ were the Son of God as he is said to be, the persecution by the infidels which was recently settled would never rise again in such power; but it appears that he can do nothing." folio 196, column 1.

Concerning the **seven kings** written of here: the first was **Herod** with his successors; the second was **Nero** and his successors; the third was **Constantius**; the fourth was **Muhammad** <note>original: "Mahumeth"</note> or rather **Chosroes** <note>original: "Losdroe," likely referring to the Persian King Chosroes II</note> with his successors. folio 196, column 2.

Concerning how the **fifth king** is he who first began to harass the Church in the western regions over the **investiture of churches** <term>investiture controversy</term> <note>A 11th-12th century conflict between popes and monarchs over who had the right to appoint (invest) church officials.</note>, because of which cause many schisms and tribulations have arisen in the Church of God from 그 time, along with his successors. folio 196, column 2.

Concerning how the **sixth king** is he of whom it is said: "And one is" <note>A quote from Revelation 17:10: "five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come."</note>; in his time the revelation is to be clearly opened, and **New Babylon** (that is, Rome) is to be struck by this same king and his accomplices. folio 196, column 2.

Concerning how after the striking of Babylon, the **seventh head** of the beast shall be killed, as if unto death; and tranquility and breathing room shall be given to the Church of Christ, with the empire of Babylon failing entirely. folio 196, column 2.

Concerning how the aforesaid beast shall rise as if from death, ascending from the abyss to carry out yet one more persecution, as if in the **eighth place**; and immediately it shall go into destruction, never to rise again. folio 196, column 2.

# Index to the Commentary on the Apocalypse

Concerning the doubt whether those ten Kings <note>In the Book of Revelation, ten kings receive power along with the Beast.</note> joining with some great King reigning over the beast will strike Babylon together; and afterward, he will reign who shall humble three of those kings <note>A reference to the "Little Horn" of Daniel 7, traditionally associated with the Antichrist.</note> to wage war against Christ. folio 197, column 1.

Concerning how the waters must first be dried up—meaning the peoples or the armies of the Christians—otherwise the impious and unfaithful kings cannot come against the faithful. folio 197, column 2.

Concerning the coming of the infidels who all hate the Christians with one mind, and especially the Roman Empire, so that they might make the harlot <note>The "Whore of Babylon," whom Joachim identifies here with the corrupt elements of Rome.</note> desolate of her children and her substance and kill them by the edge of the sword. folio 197, column 2.

Concerning how, in the said tribulation caused by the infidels, there will be one single persecution involving all Christians in 그날; but not one single outcome: for some through it will be crowned with martyrdom; others, recognizing their own guilt and that they deserve to suffer these things, will obtain pardon and live. Others, blaspheming Christ and saying: "If this were the son of God whom we worship, he would not allow us to be handed over into the hands of his enemies," shall be removed from the earth. folio 197, column 2.

Concerning how Rome is that great city and the new Babylon and the harlot, in which city the holy city Jerusalem also lives as a pilgrim. <note>Joachim uses the image of Jerusalem "pilgriming" within Babylon to describe the true, spiritual Church existing within the corrupt institutional structure.</note> folio 198.

Concerning how not only those good or evil people who live in Rome are understood to be under tribulation, but all who belong to its empire, even though it is divided and torn into parts: namely, the empire of the Latin language principally. folio 198, column 1.

Concerning how some, holding in contempt the exposition of the holy fathers—namely Augustine and Jerome—regarding what was said about Rome, cling to that word of the blessed Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great.</note> who says he heard that the blessed Benedict <note>Saint Benedict of Nursia.</note> prophesied that Rome would not be destroyed by infidels, but, exhausted by earthquakes, would wither away within itself. This is indeed true regarding the walls, but not regarding the inhabitants, against whom an angry God threatens so many and such great evils. folio 198, column 1.

Concerning the angels who are said to go out from the temple:

<column-break/>

these are the preachers and holy men of the conventual orders <note>Religious orders living in community, such as monks or friars.</note>; however, those who are said to have descended from heaven are the solitaries and contemplatives. folio 198, column 2.

Concerning the angels pouring out the bowls of the wrath of God who go out from the temple: that is, from the conventual order. folio 198, column 2.

Concerning how the kings of the earth are understood here as the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials.</note> of the churches, some of whom—indeed many—commit "fornication" with Babylon. folio 198, column 2.

Concerning the merchants of the earth who have become rich from the delights of Babylon: these are the false priests and hypocrites who gape after temporal profits and seek to please the rich of this world with deceitful words, extracting alms from them so that they themselves might become wealthy and live henceforth in luxury. folio 198, column 2.

Concerning how God tolerates sinners and the children of Babylon even though they continually persecute the elect. But when the sinner "sets his mouth against heaven"—namely, by blaspheming whenever any adversity happens to him—God can no longer endure it. folio 199, column 1.

Concerning how the Lord does not always command us to pray for our enemies, especially if they are enemies of God; but only for a time, that is, up to the time appointed for penance; for when the time of judgment comes, one must pray no longer. folio 199.

Concerning how the merchants of the earth are priests: brute animals who "eat the sins of the people" <note>A common medieval critique of priests who profited from hearing confessions or performing funerals without spiritual care.</note> and who sell prayers and masses for money, making the house of prayer a shop of business and a public marketplace, etc. folio 200, column 2.

Concerning the merchandise of gold and silver, precious stones, pearls, fine linen, purple, and similar things spiritually understood: these have been committed to the priests and the clergy not to be exchanged for carnal things, but for spiritual things—that is, for the souls of the faithful and for good works. folio 201, column 1.

Concerning how the gold of wisdom and the silver of eloquence have been committed by God to some for the benefit of the Church; but nevertheless, because of this, they [do not value] the elect of God (who are often held in contempt)...

->dd<-

That they [the clergy] do not seek what they ought to build, but rather seek to cling to the wealthy of this world, speaking pleasing things to them so that they might be honored by them and seek greater profit. folio 201, column 1.

That the divine sacraments, represented by pearls and precious stones, have been entrusted to many for the salvation of the living and the dead, but they do not wish to give them to anyone unless they either receive something or hope to receive something. <note>Joachim is here critiquing simony—the practice of selling sacred things or church offices.</note> folio 201, column 1.

That because such great wickedness remains principally in the fornicating city—that is, Rome—it therefore pertains to the just examination of the Heavenly Judge that that great harlot, who provokes others to her crimes, should be judged first; while those who were seduced by her are reserved for mourning, seeing their joy taken away from them. folio 201, column 1.

That carnal minds cannot easily forget those things which they have loved most, especially since they have no consolation from heaven, or think the joys of heaven to be nothing compared to earthly things; for the "animal man" <note>original: "animalis homo." A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:14, describing one who lacks spiritual perception.</note> does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. folio 201, column 1, column 2.

That the lust of the throat <note>Gluttony.</note> remains chiefly and principally in the "rich fruits and drinks" in which Babylon delights. folio 201, column 2.

That not only are many bishops and priests entangled in the business of Babylon so that they may become wealthy, but even many abbots, monks, and other religious persons. folio 202, column 1.

That by "pilots" are understood the leaders of monasteries, and the "ships" are the monasteries of those same religious orders. <note>In the imagery of Revelation 18, the "shipmasters" weep for Babylon; Joachim interprets these as church leaders.</note> folio 202, column 1.

That all these carnal people who love Babylon herself, seeing her destruction and that of other most noble cities, and seeing them left without inhabitants, will mourn and weep most bitterly because they loved them in a temporal and carnal way. folio 202, column 1.

That carnal men do not know how to think of anything except the glory of the flesh; and if they read in the canonical books, they understand less, or are unable to trust those who do understand fully. folio 202, column 1.

<column-break/>

That just as pouring oil upon the head signifies joy, so dust signifies sadness. folio 202, column 1.

That King Theodosius <note>Likely a reference to the legend of Theodoric the Great, who was said to have been cast into the volcano of Lipari as punishment for his treatment of Pope John I.</note> was miraculously cast into the "pot of Vulcan" by Pope John. folio 202, column 2.

That just as the children of Judah, rescued from the chains of that ancient Babylon and returned to their homeland, sang a song of joy; so too we, when God has struck our rival—namely, the New Babylon—will sing "Alleluia" <note>A Hebrew expression meaning "Praise the Lord," used here as a song of victory.</note>; not because she herself falls, but because (by her falling) liberty is left to us. folio 203, column 1.

That just as great joy was made four times by the people of Judah returning from Babylon, so "Alleluia" will be sung four times by the elect in the Church after the ruin of the harlot. folio 203, column 1.

That immediately after the ruin of the New Babylon, there will be such great joy for the elect of God as has not been since the days of the Emperor Constantine. <note>Joachim views the era of Constantine as the beginning of the Church's earthly peace, but believes an even greater spiritual era is coming.</note> folio 203, column 1.

That just as when the "Sixth Seal" began, the Babylonian metropolis of the Chaldeans was struck by the Medes, the captivity of the Jews was ended, and the Temple was rebuilt; so also now, as the "Sixth Age" begins, the New Babylon will be struck and the elect will be set free. folio 203, column 2.

That the first "Alleluia" will be sung by the elect in the Church because of the death of the adulteress; and the second "Alleluia" because of the liberation of the Church, which was persecuted and oppressed by that same adulteress—namely, Babylon. folio 203, column 2.

That in this book, the "four living creatures" designate four spiritual orders; and the seat or throne of God designates the General Church. <note>The "four living creatures" appear in Revelation 4; Joachim often links them to different ranks or eras of the Church.</note> folio 204, column 1.

That the aforementioned four orders do not receive into themselves anyone except the perfected and proven members of the true General Church; and the "common life" <note>original: "vita communis." This refers to the shared, monastic-style living of the clergy.</note> is so tempered by the holy Fathers that it accepts the perfected in a way that does not exclude "little ones" in Christ, so that both the strong and the weak may be present. folio 204, column 1.

That the said "common life" has a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit: it has contemplatives in cloisters, workers in ministries, and those to be instructed in schools. folio 204, column 1.

# Index for the Commentary on the Apocalypse

<margin>A</margin> They began commonly: namely, the preaching [life] signified in Peter, and the contemplative [life] signified in John. folio 204, column 2.
<margin>D</margin> For an angel to "read" <note>original: "dicere" (to speak/say) - the indexer interprets this as an act of explaining/exposing the text.</note> is to narrate by explaining; however, for a listener to "write" is to retain something by memory in the volume of the heart. folio 205, column 2.
<margin>D</margin> Blessed John, in this book, carries the character <note>original: "typum"</note> of pious listeners. folio 206, column 1.
<margin>D</margin> It is of greater merit to believe what is not known than to seek understanding in Scripture through which one might arrive at faith. folio 206, column 1.
<margin>D</margin> Concerning the fifth week of Lent, which we call the week "of the Passion," the Greeks call it the sixth; note what this signifies mystically. folio 206, column 1.
<margin>D</margin> The institutions of the Greeks are understood mystically in many ways among the Latins. folio 206, column 1.
<margin>D</margin> In Quinquagesima <note>The Sunday before Ash Wednesday, traditionally the start of the pre-Lenten season.</note>, the abstinence of the Greeks solemnly begins; how it designates the double tribulation of the sixth age. folio 206, column 1.
<margin>D</margin> In the sixth age <note>original: "i. 6. tpe" (in the sixth time/age).</note> there will be a double tribulation. folio 208.

<margin>D</margin> Concerning the two last heads of the dragon that will battle against the faithful: the first will be that king who sits upon the beast ascending from the sea; the second, truly, upon the beast ascending from the earth, that is, the false prophet. folio 207, column 1.
<margin>D</margin> It is doubted by some whether Christ will come personally before the Day of Judgment to fight against the aforementioned nations on behalf of His elect, or not; he [the author] holds that He will. folio 207, column 1.
<margin>D</margin> Blessed Augustine confesses that he does not know whether the resurrection of the dead will be near the beginning of that time called the Day of Judgment, or at the end. folio 207, column 2.
<margin>D</margin> By the angel who stands in the sun, in this place is understood the prophet Elijah <note>original: "Helyas"</note>, to whom was given the property of the contemplative life. folio 209, column 1.

# Abbot Joachim

**How the opinion of those who say a period of time remains after the fall of the Antichrist is true. folio 210, column 2**

It seems the text of this book <note>original: "huius libri" (this book), referring to the commentary on the Apocalypse</note> intends that, once the sixth age has begun, the devil will bring forth the Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims</note> against the Christian empire, and Babylon <note>The indexer likely refers to the corrupt "earthly city" or institutional corruption</note> is to be handed into their hands to be judged and destroyed by them; and finally, after many evils inflicted upon the faithful, they too are to be overcome by the faithful. folio 220, column 1

After the aforementioned battle is finished, there will be peace in the Church of God, which, once briefly completed, the dragon will again rouse the beast that appeared dead—namely, the pagans—and he will add false prophets to them for assistance; and once again they will fight more strongly against the faithful of Christ, and finally they will be overcome by the soldiers of Christ. The beast and the false prophet will be sent into the lake (of fire), and the devil will be imprisoned by Christ until the time when the rest are converted to the Lord. folio 210, column 2

Once that battle is completed, there will be great peace in the Church of Christ, such as has not been since the beginning of the world, the limit and end of which will be at the judgment of God. folio 210, column 2

Finally, when that peace is finished, the devil, having gone out from prison, will lead Gog and his army with him and engage in a third battle, much more grave than the first two; after which, all those who came with him having been punished, the devil himself will be delivered after everyone else into the lake of fire. folio 210, column 2

These three battles of yours will (perhaps) be so close together that the Antichrist could be present at all of them, especially the second and third. Note this. folio 210, column 2

Some have thought, on the occasion of this passage where it says the devil is to be imprisoned for a thousand years, that the seventh age ought to be extended for a thousand years; this falsehood is destroyed by Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, who argued against literal "millenarianism," suggesting the 1,000 years represented the entire duration of the Church</note>. folio 211, column 1

What certain carnal men have said—that the Lord Jesus with his saints is to indulge in carnal feasts for a thousand years after the general resurrection—is entirely contrary to the faith and erroneous. folio 211, column 1

<column-break/>

The kingdom is taken from the devil at that time when the divine spirit begins to reign in the human race, whom we say is that angel who descends from heaven to seize the wicked spirit. folio 211, column 1

The "abyss" here designates the unbelieving people. folio 211, column 2

For the devil to have the "key of the abyss" signifies having a certain power to carry out his works among the unbelieving people; while the devil has this for a time, he uses it poorly; the Holy Spirit will most notably have it by right of victory, taking the kingdom and power away from him. folio 211, column 2

Such a key and power to open the pit of the abyss and produce "beasts and creeping things of the earth" from it is given to the devil because of the sins of those impious men who confess they know God but deny Him by their deeds. folio 211, column 2

For the Angel to have a "great chain" in his hand is the virtue of concord which the Holy Spirit possesses to keep the hearts of the faithful in the bond of peace; and this is the only chain by which the Devil is held shackled so that he cannot find a way to enter to do harm and pour out his power as he is accustomed. folio 211, column 2

The time of Satan's imprisonment, designated as a thousand years, is understood as being from the resurrection of the Lord until the time of his release. folio 211, column 2

Satan, during the time of his imprisonment, is enclosed by God in the hearts of the Scythian <note>original: "fithicarum," a common misspelling of "Scythicarum"</note> peoples—namely, the Tartars <note>The Mongols, whom medieval Europeans often identified with the apocalyptic tribes of Gog and Magog</note>—against his will, because he is not permitted to lead the said peoples against the faithful until the appointed time. folio 211, column 2

After the fall of the seventh head of the Dragon there will be peace; and after the peace, the persecution designated by the "tail of the Dragon"—namely, Gog with his army of Scythian peoples; meanwhile, however, before the aforementioned final battle, all unbelievers—both Jews and Gentiles—will be converted to Christ. folio 212, column 1

# Works of Abbot Joachim

...clarification against his own affairs. folio 214, column 1 <note>original: "illustratione aduersus sui res"</note>

That the blessed Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> says the Lord will come in person to destroy the Antichrist, even though Scripture records that he will come in fire; and that the blessed Peter says fire will consume Gog and his army. folio 214, column 1

That if Scripture spoke openly about the coming of the Son of God—giving us its order just as it does many other things—the Lord would not have said, "Of that hour no one knows but the Father," etc. And therefore, because the divine authorities seem almost to contradict one another, we are equally distressed in this matter: we are dulled, overwhelmed, and we fail. folio 214, column 1

That it is not to be understood that the sins for which the elect were judged in this life by the **vicars of Christ** <term>vicarijs Christi: the clergy or priests acting as earthly representatives</term> and which were forgiven, are to be brought up again on the day of judgment; rather, they shall bring forward their good deeds to the confusion of the wicked. folio 214, column 2

That here, and in the fourth part of the book, by the name **"death"** we should understand the "false prophet" of the **Saracens** <note>original: "sarracenorum"; a medieval term for Muslims, whom Joachim often integrated into his apocalyptic timeline</note>; and by the name **"hell"** we should understand that eleventh king who is to reign at the end of that same kingdom, about whom we have spoken so much. folio 215, column 1

That if some "descend alive into hell and the lake of fire" (as is said here), it is not to be believed that they do not die like everyone else; but rather that their bodies will be more quickly constrained by pains, they will give birth to the wicked souls assigned to punishments, and their bodies will be corrupted just like others, so that they may rise from death with the rest to receive the evils they committed. folio 215, column 1

That the **first resurrection** is more blessed than the second resurrection, and the **second death** more unhappy than the first death; because the first resurrection pertains to the glory of the saints, and the second death to the eternal punishments of the rejected. folio 215, column 2

That once the impious have been thrust back into hell, a **new heaven and a new earth** will appear. folio 215, column 2

That just as a river, always flowing from its source and from a higher place, descends to the lowlands and yet is always where it flows and from where it emanates; so that **heavenly Jerusalem**, always remaining in heaven, descends through humility: see how. folio 217, column 1

That the **twelve precious stones** signify the twelve apostles, who are the twelve foundations: and see how the virtues are fitted to them. folio 225, column 1

That he who proposes to build a city first finds a place in which, by digging, he may lay the foundations; second, he builds the walls; third, he establishes the gates and the houses are built. folio 225, column 2

That in the likeness of an earthly city, that most noble and heavenly city is founded: in the first place, the people of **Israel** were chosen as the foundation, so that the preparation for this most noble city might be made in them; second, at the coming of the Lord, the **twelve apostles** were chosen to be in the foundation of the city; and after them, their "children and grandchildren" in faith from among the Gentile people. folio 226, column 1

# Index to the Exposition on the Apocalypse

...ten: since neither Moses nor Christ chose more than seventy-two: and here twice seventy-two. folio 226, column 1.

The twelve pearls seen at the gates of the city will be the preachers of Gospel truth at the time when Israel will be converted to the Lord; when Elijah <note>The prophet expected to return before the Great Day of the Lord</note> is also to come to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children: and they will cling to the twelve gates just as the seventy-two disciples clung to the twelve apostles of Jesus Christ. folio 226, column 1.

Why rather in five parts of the city than in six or seven? The author says it is because he has more fully assigned the reason in his work *The Psaltery of Ten Strings* <term>original: "psalterij decem chordarum"; one of Joachim of Fiore's three main books, using the ten-stringed harp as a map of the Trinity</term>. folio 226, column 2.

Furthermore, other gates of the city are written as being on the east, others on the west, others on the south or midday, and others on the north: this refers to the grace of graces; note the individual virtues for each. folio 226, column 2.

It belongs to the spiritual man to teach the spiritual understanding of Holy Scripture, and not to the animalistic man <note>original: "virum animalem"; referring to those who only understand things on a physical or literal level</note>; for the latter is only able to teach the surface of the letter. folio 227, column 1.

In the six ages of the world, an end will be imposed on the Babylonian kingdom <note>representing the world of sin or the corrupt earthly city</note>; once it is destroyed, whatever is lacking in the structure of Jerusalem and the calling of all the people destined to be in it will be perfected in the seventh age; so that in the future age which is to come—as if it were the eighth—all things belonging to them may appear completed. folio 227, column 1.

In that same seventh age, in the holy Church, the depths of God's mercy will be opened and will be manifest to everyone; and this will not be in the darkness of ignorance, as it has been until now, but in the fullness of understanding. folio 227, column 1.

Then there will no longer be disgrace or shame for the Church of the saints, as there once was, but rather beauty, loftiness, and majesty; because the nations converted to Christ the King will bring their glory and honor into that most bright city, so that they themselves might share in its glory; and they will prostrate themselves humbly at the feet of the saints, begging them to be mindful of them in their prayers. folio 227, column 1.

<column-break/>

The third person of the Trinity is not always to be understood by the name **"spirit"**; rather, it is sometimes used for the gift of the Holy Spirit, as in the case of Elisha <note>original: "Helly scoz", referring to Elisha, the successor of Elijah</note> when he says: "I pray that your spirit may be double within me." folio 227, column 2.

Christ is the **tree of life**: simple in himself but manifold in his branches or even in his offshoots. folio 227, column 2.

Without works of piety, faith is dead and teaching is useless. folio 228, column 2.

Regarding this word: **"I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end"** <note>original: "Ego sum. A. z ω i. pncipium z finis"</note>; this repetition is made three times in this book, so that we may understand that we must arrive at the full knowledge of truth through three solemn steps, just as the revelation of the Holy Spirit was made in three turns and three ways: namely, in the dove, the breathing, and the fire <note>referring to the different biblical manifestations of the Spirit: at Jesus' baptism, when Christ breathed on the Apostles, and at Pentecost</note>. folio 228, column 2.

The robes with which we are clothed are the **works of justice**, which nevertheless are often stained, as if by the blood of the dead, while among the good works we perform, we daily commit many evils by which they are polluted. folio 229, column 1.

Christ, insofar as he is man, is called a **star**, but insofar as he is God, he is called the **sun**; and just as the morning star precedes the coming of the sun, so the revelation and manifestation of his humanity preceded the showing of his majesty; for Jesus Christ is true Man and true God. folio 229, column 1.

Blessed John, knowing that animalistic men <note>unspiritual men who lack deeper insight</note> would be scandalized by the words of this book, not understanding the high mysteries and deep meanings within it, and might think it a work of piety to add to or take away from the text in some places, protests, etc. folio 229, column 2.

The author asks pardon from the Lord if, in some places, he has presumed to speak otherwise than the Lord himself willed or found pleasing; for he knows that only the fear and love of God compelled him to presume this, giving thanks to Him because, having traversed so many and such great seas, He has brought him safely to port. folio 229, column 2.

# Abbot Joachim

The author beseeches the faithful, saying: "I also entreat you, the faithful, that just as I have taken up the labor of so great a burden for your salvation, desiring to give you a sign so that you may flee from the face of the bow <note>A biblical metaphor, likely from Psalm 60:4, referring to escaping the coming judgment or divine wrath</note>, so you also should stretch out your hands to me in support; so that if I have erred as a human being in this or my other small works <term>original: "opusculis"; refers to Joachim's various shorter treatises and essays</term> (though I am not aware of any such error in my conscience), may He who is good grant me forgiveness." folio 230, column 1.

The author wrote this work by the mandate of the Roman Church and with its permission; he submits himself to its authority in all things. folio 230.

<column-break/>

If any sayings in this work should perhaps seem poorly expressed, and because of this could be twisted by rivals into an illicit understanding, let the defender of truth seek diligently in his other small works, and he will find sufficient clarification. folio 230, column 1.

**Here ends the Index of the eighth and final part of this work by Abbot Joachim.**

# The Life and Authenticity of Abbot Joachim

<margin>
Question.
</margin>
What is known regarding the death of Abbot Joachim?
He died in the year of our Lord 1202, on the 30th day of March, at the age of 72. He was buried first in the Monastery of Fiore <note>The mother house of the Florense Order, San Giovanni in Fiore, located in the mountains of Calabria</note>. Work is now being done by the grace of almighty God so that he may be transferred from that same place to the Cathedral Church of Cosenza, where, because of the miracles he performs there, he is more and more revered and honored by all every day. This is especially true of the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord Archbishop of Cosenza, who is working hard so that he may be enrolled in the number of the Saints by the Holy Apostolic See <note>Joachim of Fiore has long been the subject of a canonization cause; while not officially canonized by the Vatican, he is often referred to as "Beatus" (Blessed) in the region of Calabria</note>.

<margin>
Question.
</margin>
Is the author of his works certain?
Certainly: for he himself wrote the work whose title is the <term>Psaltery of Ten Strings</term> <note>original: "Psalterium decem chordarum"; one of Joachim’s three primary works, which uses the musical instrument as a symbolic framework for the Holy Trinity</note>, in which he says that he is the author of all his books, which he names there. He also desires that all his writings be under the correction of Holy Mother Church and the Holy Apostolic See, as is evident in his Letter, which is found at the beginning of the aforementioned book, and also at the end of the <term>Exposition on the Apocalypse</term> <note>original: "Expositio in Apocalypsim"; his most famous work, interpreting history through the lens of the Book of Revelation</note>.

<margin>
Question.
</margin>
What of the Prophecy that is said to be his?
That Prophecy which is said to be his is not his own, but belongs to someone else who composed it under his name <note>This refers to the "Pseudo-Joachimite" literature—a large body of prophetic texts produced by later followers and attributed to Joachim to lend them authority</note>, as is evident from his genuine works, in which no such thing is found.

It also serves as a bibliographical defense, distinguishing his authentic theological works from the "Pseudo-Joachimite" prophecies that were falsely attributed to him.</summary>

# Prologus

Indeed, let his labor in these matters be presented in every way to the mastery of the **Apostolic See** <note>The "Apostolic See" refers to the office of the Pope in Rome</note>. I ask on behalf of Almighty God: my abbots and priors and the rest of my brothers who fear the Lord: and I command with the authority I seem to possess: that as long as they have the present writing or a copy with them, let them take the works I have produced so far as if they were my **testament**; and if it happens that I write anything new until the day of my death: as quickly as they can, let them collect everything, leaving the copies in safe custody, and present them to the apostolic examination. They shall receive on my behalf correction from that same See, and they shall explain my devotion and faith concerning it: and that I am always prepared to hold what that See has established or shall establish. I shall defend no opinion of mine against its holy faith, believing entirely what it believes, and receiving correction from it in both conduct and doctrine, rejecting those whom it rejects, and accepting those whom it accepts. I believe firmly that the gates of hell cannot prevail against it; and even if it happens to be disturbed for a time and tossed by storms, its faith shall not fail until the end of the age.

->**CONFIRMATION**<-
I, Abbot Joachim, have made this writing and confirmed it with my own hand in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1200 <note>The Latin text reads "M. C.", which is an abbreviation for 1200 in this context</note>. And I confess that I hold to it as it is contained herein.

->**SUBSCRIPTION**<-
I, brother Joachim, Abbot of Fiore.

¶ A brief admonition or command of the Supreme Pontiff that he should finish the exposition of the Apocalypse as quickly as possible and present himself to the Pontiff.

Clement, Bishop, servant of the servants of God. To his beloved son Joachim, Abbot of **Curazzo** <note>original: "de curatio"; Curazzo was the Cistercian abbey where Joachim first served as abbot before founding his own order at Fiore</note>, greeting and apostolic blessing. The rule of the canon and the duty of evangelical charity persuade us that in all our acts, we should strive for this: that according to the testimony of the Gospel truth, our good works may shine before men, so that they may take from them the material and example for progress. Therefore, since you are said to have begun the **Exposition on the Apocalypse** and the **Book of Concordance** <note>original: "opus concordie"; a work comparing the "concords" or parallels between the Old and New Testaments</note> at the command and encouragement of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory, and later to have composed them under the authority of his successor, the Lord Pope Urban: we warn and exhort your charity in the Lord, commanding through this apostolic writing: that you strive to put the desired and proper end to your labors in this part (the grace of the Lord following you), and to complete and diligently correct that work for the benefit of your neighbors. Come to us as soon as the opportunity arises, so that you may present them to the discussion and judgment of the Apostolic See. For if you should wish to keep them hidden, look out with diligent care lest you incur the offense of the Supreme Father of the house concerning the **talent of knowledge** entrusted to you, which you must satisfy. Given at the Lateran, on the sixth of the Ides of June, in the first year of our Pontificate.

<column-break/>

¶ Here begins the prologue of the Lord Joachim, Abbot of Fiore, in the exposition of the book of the Apocalypse.

With what great zeal Catholic and orthodox men have striven to instruct the newly arisen Church with humble precepts! While she was still lying in the cradles of the faith, they nourished her with a drink of milk. Their works, which have flowed down to us through the course of time, bear witness to this, being made fruitful by the breasts of heavenly teachings. Indeed, it was necessary for them at that time to teach such things (the Holy Spirit suggesting it) and to write things that would suit the **infancy of the Hebrews** <note>Joachim refers here to the early Church being like a nursing infant</note> and the little ones who were inexperienced in **solid food** <note>A reference to Hebrews 5:12-14, where milk represents basic teachings and solid food represents deeper mysteries</note>. This was so that she would not rush to ascend to high mysteries before she had learned, being more fully educated in the lowest things, to agree with the humble.

But when they saw her grown up and ready for marriage, they began to show her greater **sacraments** <note>original: "sacramenta"; here meaning "mysteries" or "sacred secrets"</note> through which, having been exercised for a long time, she might experience the sweetness of solid and perfect food. Leaving behind the word of the beginning of Christ’s instructions, she was carried toward perfection. Finally, they showed her the gifts of spiritual ointments, precious garments of various designs and immense beauty, earrings and bracelets, and everything that pertains to adornment. There is no further need for such a great abundance of gifts already sent; nor is there anything she should expect from us—being of the least merit and time—except perhaps that her **Bridegroom** might be shown to her more clearly than usual. He is that soul-beloved heavenly Bridegroom, to whom she has sought to cling with such great effort since her infancy.

# On the Apocalypse

<margin>
Song of Solomon 1
Genesis 24
</margin>
Finally, Rebecca—the mother of Jacob, to whom ministerial gifts were given as a symbol <note>original: "i typo", meaning a prophetic symbol or "type"</note> of this holy Church—received those gifts from Abraham's servant. This servant represents the teachers of the Church. We do not read that Rebecca received new gifts near the end of the journey when the servant returned to his master Isaac, nor from the servant who led her, nor from anyone else. Instead, she received only the sight of the Bridegroom, whom she had previously known only by hearing. Guided by that same servant, she contemplated him; then, she descended from the twisted animal <note>The "twisted animal" refers to the camel Rebecca rode, which medieval commentators often allegorized as representing the burdensome or "crooked" nature of the old life or the Gentiles</note> she had been riding to be clothed in the cloak of her beauty, and she entered into the tent with her spouse, who exulted in his grain <note>original: "farre". This refers to the provision or the "bread" of the bridal chamber</note>.

<margin>
Genesis 24
</margin>
We, too, rightly follow the last footsteps of this servant if we take care to demonstrate the truth (which is in the Spirit) to her whom Rebecca represents. Thus, being diligently instructed, she may learn to forget the things that are on earth and to grasp and hold that for which she has run until now.

<margin>
Psalm 45
Revelation 19
Matthew 25
</margin>
She must forget her own people and her father's house; and because the time of the wedding is flourishing, she must cover herself—according to the voice of this book—in fine linen, bright and white. Thus, with lamps prepared and lit, she may deserve to enter the wedding with the Bridegroom. For the King of Heaven cannot desire her beauty unless she herself desires the Bridegroom's chamber; for there is no legitimate marriage in which one party does not consent. Wherefore the Lord himself

<margin>
Matthew 10
</margin>
says in the Gospel: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me." If this is so—indeed, because it is so—the beauty of the bride's loveliness is of no use unless she scorns her people and her homeland for the sake of the Bridegroom. Surely, if she does not love the Bridegroom, or if another who is not the Bridegroom is loved by her, she must be persuaded by all means to avoid such great infamy, lest (heaven forbid) she be proved unworthy of the royal bed. But with what words could anyone persuade her to leave present things for future ones? To desert the known for the unknown? To leave the parents and neighbors she knows for a Bridegroom and a homeland whose glory she does not know? Just as she has no experience of it, she might think it impossible—especially since she does not think the time of the wedding is near. This is no small labor that falls upon us in these days! But who is fit for these things? Perhaps one who could do it scorns the task; while one who desires it

<column-break/>

does not know how. One who possesses refined speech lacks knowledge; to the one granted knowledge, the ability to speak appropriately is denied. Thus, no one is fit. But are all equally excused? He who does not know has a reason not to be held accountable—either a full or partial excuse. But for those to whom it is given to know, even in part, there is no confidence of excuse. Do I say this to claim the title of knowledge for myself? Not at all. I profess myself completely insufficient in one respect [speech], yet I fear judgment in the other [knowledge]. For even if I would be foolish to believe I am knowledgeable, I would be lying to excuse myself by saying I don't know what I am bound to speak. I will speak, therefore, as best I can; if I cannot speak, I will signal with gestures: the joys of the world have failed, tribulations are imminent, and the Kingdom of Heaven is at the doors! Even if in rustic and unpolished speech, I believe I can prove this with certain and necessary evidence—provided that He is present who mocks those who are over-confident and makes the tongues of infants eloquent when it pleases Him.

<margin>
Judith 6
Wisdom 10
</margin>
Therefore, not trusting in what is mine (which I do not have), but in the kindness of Christ, I have taken up the task of explaining the Apocalypse—which Blessed John wrote while exiled on the island of Patmos—not out of my own presumption, but by the authority of the Roman Pontiff. From the sequence of this book, as I believe, it can be clearly proved what I said before: that there are things worthy of praise which can inspire the Bride and the children of the Kingdom to contempt for the world. They can hear the voice of the Lord saying to them: "Look up and lift up your heads, for your redemption is drawing near." However, so that we might more easily be raised up to contemplate such high mysteries (while we still remain on the ground), it is necessary to gather the entire subject matter of the book into a summary. Because the things we are approaching are unusual, we need a more extensive and multifaceted discourse to unlock the door of the book. This is why, contrary to the usual practice of the elders, I have written not just a preface but a small book, consulting the reader's benefit rather than custom. I am not ignorant of how difficult it is to consider the excellence of these sacraments <note>In this context, "sacraments" refers to the sacred mysteries or hidden meanings within the text</note> according to the fullness of the Scriptures, or to expand the narrow mind to contemplate them as if in the blink of an eye...

<margin>
Luke 21

<meta>This page continues the prologue of Joachim of Fiore’s commentary. # Prologue

...so many and such secret mysteries which have been gathered—as if into a summary of a book—in the Book of Revelation. Therefore, as we strive to enter that spiritual house, in which the understanding of the Scriptures is locked away behind many bars, let us not approach it without the keys of the mysteries. Otherwise (God forbid), that which is said to some through the prophet might happen to us:

<margin>Isaiah 29</margin>
"The vision of all things will be to you like the words of a sealed book. When they give it to one who is learned, they say: 'Read this.' And he will respond: 'I cannot, for it is sealed.'" <note>original: "signatus est enim." This passage from Isaiah 29:11 serves as a classic medieval justification for why even scholars might fail to understand prophecy without divine aid.</note> For the angel predicted to Daniel that the words would be closed and sealed until the end of the world—but only until a predetermined time: until the time of the Angel of Philadelphia. This refers to that order signified in Christ, to whom it is said:

<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
<margin>Revelation 3</margin>
"These things says the Holy One, the True One, who has the key of David; who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens. I know your works; behold, I have set before you an open door which no one can shut, because you have little strength." If those who, according to the Savior's voice, know how to judge the face of the sky and the earth <note>A reference to Matthew 16:3, where Jesus rebukes those who can predict the weather but cannot recognize the "signs of the times."</note> either do not recognize or do not believe the signs of the times, it is not for me to judge them. The word of God is sharp and more piercing than any two-edged sword, and it is the word that judges them; its voice is fitting and exceedingly terrible. In that same book of Daniel, it follows, saying:

<margin>Hebrews 4</margin>
<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
"Many shall be chosen and made white, and shall be tested as if by fire; the impious shall act impiously, and none of the impious shall understand; but the learned shall understand." Hence, Truth <note>The "Truth" (Veritas) is a common medieval title for Christ himself.</note> says through itself:

<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
"I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones." Hence, it also says through the Apostle:

<margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin>
"And if our Gospel is hidden, it is hidden to those who are perishing, in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ—who is the image of God—should not shine." And lest anyone should accuse him of vanity—for he said that he indeed understood the words of God while others were ignorant—he soon gave an evident sign of his humility when he first added and said:

<margin>2 Corinthians 4</margin>
"For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord." For it is as if he were saying more clearly: "If I wish to glory, I will not be foolish, for I shall speak the truth."

<margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin>
For he who speaks the truth is the one who preaches Christ; he who speaks the truth is humble, because he understands that he has nothing of his own. And therefore, he does not speak so that he may be seen by men and glory in his own knowledge. Rather, he speaks because truth and charity are flourishing, according to what he says elsewhere: "If I preach the Gospel, I have no glory; for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel." Therefore, the disciples of truth do not preach themselves, but Christ Jesus, because they do not seek the things that are their own, but the things of Jesus Christ.

<margin>Philippians 2</margin>
But those who seek what is their own cannot find the truth, as Truth itself testifies, saying among other things to the unbelieving Jews:

<margin>John 5</margin>
"How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another, and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?" It is clear, therefore, that he who seeks his own glory cannot believe; and he who cannot believe is unable to understand, because the darkness of unbelief blinds the eyes of his mind, and he is not permitted to find the door even by groping around. But to those who spurn their own glory, it is granted by the Lord that they may believe; He grants that, by believing, they may be able to understand. 

For their sake, we shall take care to make known what God has granted in this introductory booklet, which is like a preamble to the exposition of the whole book. We do this so that we may sail all the more securely through the unknown paths of this sea, just as those who remain for a while in the harbor sit and calculate the necessary costs. Therefore, I advise the reader who thirsts for the milk of this book: let him trust that he will receive a full understanding from it if he meditates upon it intently and entirely without the noise of voices, and if he does not find it tedious to read through this introductory manual at the same time, in which the subject matter of the entire book is contained.

<column-break/>

->End of the prologue.<- <note>original: "Explicit prologus"</note>

### Here begins the preface, or the introductory book, for the interpretation of the Apocalypse. Chapter 1.

<margin>The vision of the books of the Old Testament</margin>
The entire forests of histories that shade the Old Testament are divided into five portions, of which one is general and four are specific. # On the Apocalypse

A 3

This history presents the patriarchs first, the judges second, the kings third, and then the chronicles; it possesses a single narrative thread, but diverse writers, because death prevented them from remaining for long. There is, however, a group of four histories: the first is titled Job; the second, Tobit; the third, Judith; the fourth, Esther. These are "the wheel" and "the faces." And although two of these <note>Referring to Tobit and Judith.</note> are judged less canonical among the Hebrews (as Jerome says), they indicate this status to the Hebrews, but not to the Church, to which the Spirit gives testimony. In place of these four histories, four Gospels were given, not without a demonstration of harmony and the protection of spiritual understanding.

There is one thing among the rest that must be considered with distinct reason: that the first Evangelist and the last—namely Matthew and John—are apostles of Jesus Christ and they report things seen rather than heard. The two in the middle, Mark and Luke, are not apostles but disciples of the apostles, and they describe things heard rather than seen. Just as among us—if it were left to human judgment—one would say that those things written by the apostles as eyewitnesses are of greater authority than those written by the disciples of the apostles as things heard rather than seen; so too the elders of the Jews gave greater authority to the first and last of the four histories (namely Job and Esther) than to the two middle ones (Tobit and Judith).

But the observer of secret speech <note>Likely referring to the Holy Spirit or the inspired author.</note> by no means said these were inferior, for he perceives in them a spiritual and mystical understanding. For never would such clear mysteries illuminate those histories if the "finger of God" <note>A common metaphor for the Holy Spirit.</note> had not written them as He did the others. Just as the four Gospels were given in place of those four histories—as if they were "wheels in the middle of wheels"—so the Book of Revelation was given for general history. Certainly, it is itself like a wheel within a wheel; I mean that wheel which first appeared upon the earth, so that the prophecy might be fully completed which says:

"And the appearance of the wheels and their work was like a wheel in the middle of a wheel." <note>original: "quasi si sit rota in medio rote." This is a reference to Ezekiel 1:16, a central image in Joachim's theology representing how the New Testament (the inner wheel) is contained within the Old Testament (the outer wheel).</note>

Therefore, the first and greater wheel is that general history—or rather, the collection of histories and books—which extends in succession from Adam all the way to Ezra, after which the writers of the sacred page are known to have "sabbatized" <note>orig: "sabbatizasse." To sabbatize here means to rest or cease writing; Joachim refers to the period after Ezra when the Old Testament canon was considered closed by the Jews.</note>. Truly, for this outer wheel, this Book of Revelation was made the inner wheel, reaching to the end of the age and passing through by revealing the hidden mysteries that lay concealed in that first wheel. For this reason, it is not undeservedly called the "Apocalypse" <note>From the Greek *apokalypsis*, meaning "unveiling" or "revelation."</note>, because it uncovers hidden things and reveals secrets. For it is the key to the old writings, the knowledge of future things, the opening of sealed things, and the detection of secrets.

Great and singular is the prerogative of this volume, because the Spirit of God is great, who speaks openly in it with His own voices. For the fact that the number seven possesses this entire book shows that it is intimate with Him who is the giver of the sevenfold gifts. Nor is it a wonder if it is written by the "chamberlain of heaven" <note>original: "celi camerario." A poetic title for John the Apostle, highlighting his intimacy with God.</note>—the one who, while reclining upon the breast of the Lord, was granted to contemplate secret mysteries and to drink more abundantly from the torrent of the Holy Spirit. 

<margin>John 21</margin>
This was so he might prove that what had proceeded from the mouth of Truth as a general promise was fulfilled in himself more specially, saying: 

<margin>John 7</margin>
"Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly." <note>John 7:37-38.</note> 

If we hold—as is both pious and Catholic to do—that the Holy Spirit is the love of Christ proceeding from the Father and that same Son, what else should we understand when John records that he was the "beloved of Christ," except to testify that he drew the streams of grace more abundantly from the heart of Christ? Therefore, what he himself drank, he has at last offered as a drink to the elect: namely, the living water which he himself had drunk from the fountain of life. 

For living waters are the spiritual scriptures—not those depicted with ink and pen on paper, but those engraved in the book of the human heart by the power of the Holy Spirit. Such waters, divinely inspired, flow indefatigably from the well of the heart; once the stone has been moved aside, the Lord’s flocks are watered from them. They water not the acres of the earth, but often the meadows of parched minds, and they fertilize the hearts of thirsting men with a bounty of fruit. And while this is true of all [scripture], what shall I say of the prerogative of this book? In it, the rush of the heavenly river gladdens the city of God, surging with the fullness of seven channels to water all the earth. In these days, it has flowed more abundantly to us from the belly of John. 

<margin>Psalm 46</margin>
"Blessed," it says, "is he who reads and he who hears the words of this prophecy and keeps those things which are written in it." <note>Revelation 1:3.</note> For this is not just any prophecy, but (if we are truly wise) the prophecy of all other prophecies, seeing as it includes all, or nearly all, into one; and because it [continues...]
