# The Abbot’s Book of Exposition

...is: it encompasses and opens. For other prophecies brought forth either few or obscure things, touching upon the scope of peoples and wars as a <term>type</term><note>A "type" is a person, event, or thing in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament or the future of the Church.</note> of future events. This work generally unlocks hidden things: it makes known secrets, looses the bonds of the seals, and illuminates the shadows. That is wonderful, but another thing is more wonderful: it follows the battles of the Church so summarily and in sequence; it distinguishes the orders and wars through the courses of time in such a way that it does not disagree with the ancients—showing that whatever preceded in figure among the Hebrew people must be fulfilled in the Church of Christ. Nor was it done in a confused order, so that first things are written last and last things first (through which the reader might lose confidence because of the difficulty created for him); rather, he should not doubt that they were written to follow one another just as they were to occur in future times. This is done, however, in such a way that he distinguishes the individual parts as we will show below, and a recapitulation is made in each part. Because, however, even that which is clear is less clear to one who does not know the subject matter of the book, I consider that the reader needs no small preface. Indeed (as I have already said), it is not so much a preface as a book, through which the door may be unlocked and all that is in the house may lie open: namely, that he may first see where he is going, so that he does not later proceed through unknown places.

### On the Opening of the Letter and the Book. Chapter 2.

Therefore, all the historical books—of which we made mention above in the figure of the wheels—in which mystical deeds were written from the beginning of time until John the Baptist, were collected under a certain general book wrapped in seven seals. In the victory <note>original: "palma," literally the palm of victory.</note> of its opening, no one was found worthy (as John testifies in this book) except he who, overcoming the kingdom of death by dying, trampled the strength of the lion by rising again. "Behold," he says, "the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered to open the book and to loose its seven seals." To the dying and rising Lord alone, therefore, was it granted to open the mysteries of this book, so great and so secret; because, namely, with Christ dying, the power of the "letter" <note>The "letter" refers to the literal, historical meaning of the text, which Joachim believes "kills" if not understood through the Spirit.</note> which killed perished, and the spiritual understanding which gives life lived. For this book was like a tomb sealed on all sides, in which Life lay dead, lest the light of life shine upon the dead. But when Christ, who is Life, rose from the dead, the vital understanding which 

<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>

<column-break/>

was hiding came forth, and proceeded from the monument of Scripture like the appearance of a certain flower. The Apostle [Paul] disputes about these things in the Epistle to the Romans, and among the many things he wrote while discussing law and grace, he commends in words why the victory of the Lion or the resurrection of Life is required for the opening of the book. Regarding these same matters, he says: "We are buried together with Christ through baptism into death: so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life." And because the oldness of the letter pertained to death, but the newness of the spirit pertained to life, after some interjected words he followed up, saying: "But now we are loosed from the law of death in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter." And after some other things: "For what was impossible for the law, in which we were weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh for the sake of sin, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit." 

For who is it who rose from the dead through the power of the spirit, if not he who, because of the weakness of the flesh, is shown to be like a lamb as if slain? For if the weakness of the slaughtered sheep denotes the infirmity of the flesh, what does the insuperable strength of the lion designate if not the majesty of the triumphant spirit? Hence it is that Samson, that strong man, as long as the spirit of strength was present in him, overcame the strength of the lion; but when he fell into sin through love of the flesh, he was deprived of the power of the spirit so that he could not resist his enemies a second or third time. Therefore, since in the death of Christ the ancient weakness of the flesh was weakened (so to speak) and the oldness of the ancient letter received its consummation, while in the resurrection the newness of the spirit and the strength of faith arose—rightly is the opening of the book attributed to the victory of the lion; rightly is the loosening of the seals attributed to the life of Christ. For then "he opened the sense of the disciples so that they might understand the scriptures." Therefore Christ, who is the teacher of all, opens the book; he opens what was bound and looses the seals. For so, as we have already said regarding the angel of Philadelphia, it is written of him among other things: "These things says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens." For as we have already said, the Old Testament, from the patriarch Abraham until Christ, was wrapped in seven seals: because seven spiritual battles, distinct in their times and figures, are read as having been written and completed under that same testament; in these, the wars of the Church and the spiritual battles and labors of the saints are signified.

### On the Seven Seals and Their Opening. Chapter 3.

But we seek the loosening of the seven seals in vain unless we first mark the seals themselves that have sealed the book. And indeed, the book itself was sealed with seven seals, but there is something of interest that ought to be noted. Five of them are certainly uniform. The sixth and seventh are dissimilar: for five are simple, the sixth is double, and the seventh "keeps the Sabbath" <note>Joachim suggests the seventh seal represents a period of rest or peace, mirroring the seventh day of creation (the Sabbath) when God rested.</note>. Therefore, in the six seals, some labor is designated. Thus, the six seals are six general wars from the time of Moses until the death of Ezra; some believe that these were completed in six periods by the prophet Malachi and written down in the sacred books by the prophets. The first of these wars was that of the Egyptians. The second, of the Canaanites. The third, of the Syrians. The fourth, of the Assyrians. The fifth, of the Chaldeans. The sixth, which we said would be double, was likewise of the Assyrians and the Macedonians. For the sixth conflict is contained in the history of Judith. The seventh is contained in the history of Esther. Now, Holofernes was an Assyrian. Haman, who was also an Agagite, was a Macedonian by nation. Some, however, have handed down doubtfully that the history of Ezra was composed before the history of Esther. Since this is an opinion and not an assertion because of the two Artaxerxes—one of whom is believed to have reigned after the other—I do not know whether we should yield to their opinion: namely, to believe it happened in the time of the later Artaxerxes, and not rather in the time of the first, under whom Ezra also lived. For the Scripture plainly says that Mordecai was among the number of captives whom Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had transported with Jeconiah, king of Judah; and according to the calculation of years from the Babylonian migration to the last Artaxerxes, they say more than two hundred years passed. It would seem absurd enough for a man of two hundred years to be considered fit to serve in the king’s palace and to have a niece who was a young girl, the daughter of his brother.

But this is because of Ezra the <term>hystoriographum</term><note>A historian or writer of sacred history.</note>, whom I said was the last among the writers of ancient histories. I say "histories" not of just any kind, but the authentic ones. For the books of the Maccabees are outside the canon <note>Joachim is referring to the "Hebrew Canon." While the Books of Maccabees are in the Catholic Bible today, medieval scholars often noted their different status compared to the older books of the prophets.</note>. If, however, this history must be accepted, and it pleases the reader more this way, the sequence of times and the order of wars is not offended in any way. For even if Ezra and Mordecai were contemporaries, the history of Ezra could have begun first, which is altogether true; for beginning from Cyrus, he compiled the things that happened through the times until the end of his days. Therefore, we must allow something regarding the "letter of the law that kills," so that the "spirit that gives life" is not extinguished in us <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, a central theme for Joachim: looking past literal dates to find the spiritual meaning.</note>. Whether we place the end in the death of Ezra (whom some, as I said, hand down as being the prophet Malachi), or in the death of Nehemiah who was joined to him, or in Zerubbabel who built the temple for the Lord, or in Esther—let the end be established piously and simply; for even if we do not doubt they were contemporaries, we do not know which of them died first and which later. Yet, what is said about Malachi (who prophesied concerning John the Baptist) being Ezra himself, is a minor opinion, not an assertion. Let us place the end of the sixth seal, if it pleases, in him who was the last of the twelve prophets; after Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied under Darius the Persian, he is known to have prophesied in the old age of Zerubbabel. Furthermore, regarding what pertains to the sixth seal: under one sixth time (as I have said), two final tribulations were brought about almost at the same time—one under Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians <note>In the Book of Judith, Nebuchadnezzar is described as King of the Assyrians ruling from Nineveh.</note>, and the other under Artaxerxes, who reigned over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces. Just as the children of Israel, coming up out of Egypt, were commanded to gather the manna sent to them from heaven—each person gathering one <term>omer</term><note>An omer is an ancient Hebrew unit of dry measure, roughly 2 liters.</note> for each of the five days of every week—but on the sixth day they gathered a double portion, that is, two omers at once (one for the sixth day and the other for the Sabbath day, on which it was not lawful to work); so in the sixth time, the war was doubled, acting as a double nourishment.

It is set down in the book <note>The Book of Revelation/Apocalypse.</note>, one indeed for the sixth time: another for the seventh, in which the Sabbath rest was given to that ancient people. Thus also, from that place where it deals with the kingdom of the beast which is to strike Babylon, until that place where "Alleluia" is sung by the saints, it must be understood as that night in which Christ was betrayed. But one must not therefore be confident in that peace: because the revived temptation of the beast itself will darken it, with that other temptation added which will be made through the other beast ascending from the land.

Now it is ready to speak of the harmony of the two testaments, or even of the harmony of the three works which, in the three states of the world, began to shine one after another; so that while we weigh how similar things respond to their like, we can better investigate the intention of the author, the more we perceive the new to agree with the old, and to harmonize as if subsisting from the same things. ### Chapter 5. On the Three States of the World.

The first of the three states of which we have spoken was under the time of the Law, when the people of the Lord were still, for the time, a small child serving under the elements of this world, not being able to attain the liberty of the spirit, until he should come who says: *If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.*
<margin>John 8.</margin>
The second state was under the Gospel and remains until now, in liberty indeed with respect to the past, but not in liberty with respect to the future. The time which will be from now until the consummation of the age is ascribed to the Son: because what was designated in Christ born according to the flesh must be more fully consummated in him according to the spirit. The future age which will be after the resurrection is to be ascribed to the Holy Spirit: because there, not only our souls—which are by nature more subtle—but even our bodies will be spiritual, and a temple of the Holy Spirit; when all the corruptions of the flesh have been consumed, the same Spirit alone shall reign in them. In the assignment of the first mystery, the time of the Gospel was given to the Holy Spirit. In the assignment of the second, the time of spiritual understanding. # The Abbot’s Book of Exposition

The first course of time: must be begun from the patriarch Jacob and ended in Christ. The second, from Christ until the end of the age, when Christ is to come again in glory to perform judgment. However, the initiation of the first was made in Abraham; the initiation of the second in Zachary, the father of John. But indeed, because the New Testament is genuine and, as it were, twofold—insofar as not only did the Son appear in the flesh, but also the Holy Spirit deigned to be revealed to men in the dove and the fire—the Son was not sent alone to redeem the world, but also the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him, to complete what he himself had begun. This time, which is called the <term>Time of Grace</term> <note>Joachim refers to the era beginning with Christ’s incarnation as the "tempus gratiae," contrasted with the era of the Law.</note>, is distinguished into two portions of time, which is entirely necessary. We find in the three "states" certain great works of the Lord distinguished by their own properties, in which a concordance ought to be assigned on both sides, while preserving the higher understanding and that first assignment which harmonizes the two Testaments as if on equal footing. For the Son and the Holy Spirit are not something greater than the Father alone, nor is the Son alone or the Holy Spirit alone something less; and therefore there is a simple relationship of the New Testament to the Old, and an equal relationship of the second state to the first, and of the third to the second. Hence it is that both the two Testaments which Scripture commemorates, and the works of the three states—which are equally great in each—look toward a simple similarity on this side and that. In the first distinction, the <term>concordance</term> <note>Joachim’s "concordia" is his signature method: finding precise historical parallels between the Old Testament (the era of the Father) and the New Testament (the era of the Son).</note> is to be assigned as follows.

The time of the **first seal**: from the patriarch Jacob until Moses and Joshua.
The time of the **second**: from Moses and Joshua until Samuel and David.
The time of the **third**: from Samuel and David until Elijah and Elisha.
The time of the **fourth**: from Elijah and Elisha until Isaiah and Hezekiah.
The time of the **fifth**: from Isaiah and Hezekiah until the Babylonian Exile.
The time of the **sixth**: from the Babylonian Exile until the death of Esther or Malachi the prophet.
The time of the **seventh**: from the death of Malachi until Zachary, the father of John the Baptist.

These are in the Old Testament; in the New, however, they are as follows.

These are either those which occurred then for the faith in the one God, who is the creator of all, or those which occur now for the name of Christ, who is true and one God with the Father, through whom all things were made, which the faithful are read to have endured. Likewise, in the time of the first opening, under which—with the Old Testament terminated in the fathers— the New was begun, there rose up again on behalf of the fathers a new and spiritual Israel. This new Israel would enter into a new struggle for the sake of the Spirit against the "New Egyptians," the Jews. This was initiated by the "New Moses," who is the most faithful lawgiver and the Lord of all the prophets. Just as in that first conflict, while the children of Israel remained silent, Moses the servant of the Lord fought and conquered; so also here, while the elect—who were sweating under the burden of the Law and the "letter" and were oppressed by empty labor—remained silent, Christ Jesus alone would fight and conquer. He would snatch them with a strong and extended hand from the superstition of the literal sense and the servitude of the Law. ...powers are shown below, and nonetheless those things which must be fulfilled in the children in their own times: so that in his works both the new and the old may be brought together into a single sum. From this matter something wonderful happens: just as he himself is everywhere, so in many places of Scripture he is found to be the one responding to so many fathers of the first testament. And yet, in the sequence of <term>concordance</term> <note>Joachim’s "concordia" is a method of matching people and events from the Old Testament with those in the New Testament to show a divine pattern in history.</note>, he responds only to the patriarch Jacob. For just as Jacob fathered twelve patriarchs in the Old Testament, so he who is the true Israel procreated the same number of apostles in the New. The exception is that in the former, it was flesh propagated from flesh; in the latter, it was spirit from spirit—as Truth itself testifies when it says: <margin>John 3</margin> *That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.* Therefore, Jesus Christ does not reject Moses in this concordance any more than he rejects the patriarch Jacob; rather, he proves that any of the others held his <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows someone or something in the New Testament.</note> according to the specific place and time. Just as the first apostles correspond to the twelve patriarchs, so Paul and Barnabas, the last of the apostles, correspond to Moses and Aaron. For just as Moses and Aaron preceded the children of Israel as they were about to depart from Egypt and proceed into the land of the Canaanites, so Paul and <margin>Acts 13</margin> Barnabas preceded the faithful people as they were about to exit the unbelieving synagogue and pass over to the provinces of the pagans. Moses fought for the liberty of Israel; Paul also fought. The former fought so that the servitude of making bricks might cease; the latter, so that the servile Law, which consisted in the works of the flesh, might cease. And both, having conquered the enemies prostrated by God, triumphed. Nor is it a wonder: for who was fighting in them, if not he of <margin>Psalm 23</margin> whom it is said in the Psalms: *The Lord, strong and mighty in battle*? And of whom it is said through John in <margin>Apocalypse 6</margin> this book: *When he had opened one of the seven seals, I heard one of the four living creatures saying as if with a voice of thunder: "Come and <margin>Apocalypse 6</margin> see." And I saw, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering so that he might conquer.* The first seal, therefore, continued until the death of Joshua and that entire generation <margin>Joshua, last chapter</margin> which had gone out from Egypt among the fathers; yet the second seal began from the crossing of the Jordan.

But why is there one man for these two? Because the fathers were prohibited by the debt of death from remaining longer in this life. And therefore it was necessary for the children to fill the place of the fathers, so that what the fathers had fulfilled less might be completed in the children. It is not only because of this, however, but also because of other enigmas of figures about which we shall speak in their proper places, as God grants. ### Chapter 7: On the second assignment of concordance.

Now something must be said concerning the concordance of the *three works*—that is, concerning that concordance which consists of the **three states** <note>Joachim's "Three Status" or Ages of the world correspond to the Father (Old Testament), the Son (New Testament), and the Holy Spirit (a coming age of spiritual understanding and monastic peace).</note>. ...to represent Manasseh; in the last, however, Ephraim. And according to this, the first time is to be attributed to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit. I say "until the present" according to the beginning of the third status, not according to the end of the second. For between the beginning of the third status and the end of the second, the times of two generations pass, as it were, in common, so that the prophetic word might be fulfilled in them: *Until the new things are born, you shall eat the old.* <note>original: "Donec nascant noua: vetera comedetis"; this refers to the transitional period where the old era and the new era overlap.</note> Wherever we say "until the present," let it be understood as if the entire time of these generations—whose end we seem to have nearly reached—is taken for the end of the second status and the beginning of the third. And whether we say "until the year 1200 of the incarnation of the Lord" <note>original: "M.CC. icarnatiōis dñi"; Joachim famously focused on the year 1200 as a significant prophetic milestone.</note>, in which the end of forty generations occurs, or "until the present," or "until the time of the fullness of the Gentiles" or "the conversion of Israel," do not think it is different. For "the end" in the Divine Page <note>A medieval term for the Bible.</note> is accustomed to being accepted in both a broad and a strict sense. Thus, sometimes the entire sixth age, which began with Christ, is called the "end of the world"; at other times, it refers to that final day in which the Lord shall come for the extreme judgment. If the entire sixth age is called the "end of the world," how much more can one, two, or three generations be called the "end," whether of the first status, the second, or the third? Therefore, the time of the first status, which by the property of the mystery is attributed to the Father, was from Abraham until John the Baptist. The time of the second, which is attributed to the Son, is from John the Baptist until the present. But because Zacharias, John the Baptist, and the man Christ Jesus retain the figure of the Trinity—just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did—so we must begin commonly from the three of them, as if the whole time of them should be taken for one generation and as one beginning. ### Chapter 8: Concerning the Antichrist and the Dragon, and his heads and members.

<margin>Revelation 12</margin>

A red dragon having seven heads and ten horns; and his tail swept away a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth.* <note>Quoting Revelation 12:3-4.</note> This Dragon is the Devil. His body consists of all the reprobate <note>The "reprobate" refers to those rejected by God or the wicked throughout history.</note>. His heads are those who take the lead among 
<margin>The First Head</margin>
the reprobate; those who, surpassing even those they rule over, lead the way and excel in evil. The first head of this dragon, through which he poured out his venom, was **Herod**. For through him, the dragon 
<margin>John 2</margin>
sought to devour the newborn Christ; and because he could not take Him, he killed the innocents. Along with him, however, are to be included all the kings of the region of the Jews whom he left as successors to his kingdom and his crimes in the persecution of Christ. 

<column-break/>

<margin>The Second Head</margin>
The **Second Head** was **Nero**, the murderer of the princes of the apostles. And along with him are to be included all his successors who persecuted the Church of God up until Julian the Apostate. 
<margin>The Third Head</margin>
The **Third Head** of the dragon was **Constantius the Arian**, <note>Constantius II, a 4th-century Emperor who supported Arianism, a doctrine the Church deemed heretical.</note> who, along with his successors (I mean successors in his treachery, not necessarily in his throne), afflicted the Church until the times of the Saracens. 
<margin>The Fourth Head</margin>
The **Fourth Head** of the dragon was **Chosroes**, <note>Khosrow II, the Persian King who captured the "True Cross" in 614 AD.</note> King of the Persians, whose kingdom after a few years was given into the hands of the Saracens, and in him the sect of **Muhammad** was confirmed; which, in the time of Chosroes himself, was being established in the regions of 
<margin>The Fifth Head</margin>
Arabia. The **Fifth Head** of the dragon was one of the kings of the **New Babylon** <note>Joachim often used "New Babylon" to refer to the Islamic Caliphate centered in Baghdad.</note> who, wishing to sit upon the mountain of the testament and appear like the Most High, inflicted many persecutions upon the Church for this reason. 
<margin>The Sixth Head; Daniel 7</margin>
The **Sixth Head** of the dragon is the one of whom it is said in Daniel: *Another king shall rise after them, and he shall be more powerful than the former ones.* However, I think the beginning of the sixth head was taken from this King of the Turks named **Saladin**, who recently began to trample the Holy City; and who, because our sins required it, has grown thick upon the necks of Christians beyond what we imagined. But as for what John says in the sixth part: 
<margin>Revelation 17</margin>
*And there are seven kings: five have fallen, and one is, and the other has not yet come,* the speech is to be understood as if it were addressed to us who are speaking here and now, as if the prophecy had been established in the **sixth time**. It is a marvel, because in this very time it was to be opened to the faithful. For only in the sixth time, and in the sixth vision of his book, 
<margin>Revelation 13</margin>
does the angel instruct Daniel, teaching that mystery of the beast having ten horns; and only in the sixth time and the sixth part of the book does the angel speak to the blessed John, teaching him in the same way the mystery of the beast having ten horns. Thus they should weigh, understand, and reflect together: those whom Daniel and John—men dedicated to God and distinguished by their purity—designate, are granted by the Lord to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of God in this sixth time, and to know...

### On the general parts of the Apocalypse. Chapter 9.

The general parts of the book which pertain to the <term>Second State</term><note>Joachim's "Second State" or Age (Status) corresponds to the era of the New Testament and the Son, spanning from the first coming of Christ to the dawn of the Age of the Spirit.</note> are six, and these parts are distinguished by certain chapters; so that in each of the five parts, besides other things that precede in them, they seem to have seven divisions, although in the fourth part the divisions themselves are not so

<column-break/>

manifest as in the other parts; which nevertheless can be considered and discerned by certain changes, each by its own properties. 

¶ Furthermore, the sixth part, which is established to be double, is not distinguished in the same way as the others by times or seven chapters; yet even it does not lack its own sevenfold nature. For it is established that for the beast which is to reign especially in the sixth time, it is said to have seven heads, and to be those seven kings of whom it is said: *Five <margin>Apocalypse 17</margin> have fallen, and one is, and one has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain a short time.* There are, therefore, six parts of the book and as many times pertaining to the Second State, in the consummation of which—the great harlot who sits upon many waters having first been judged—the <margin>Apocalypse 19</margin> beast shall be captured, and with it the false prophet, so that they may be sent together into the lake of fire. Then also the devil, who is the author of such great evil, is to be shut in the abyss, so that he may no longer seduce the nations until the final times of the <term>Third State</term><note>The Age of the Holy Spirit, a future era of monastic peace and spiritual understanding on earth before the literal end of the world.</note>; and let there be peace and rest in the Church of Christ. 

From that place where these things are written, the seventh part of the book will begin, which alone contains the time of the Third State. And because the spiritual church will begin there and have its own time—which tends toward the One which is necessary for contemplatives—it is not necessary that divisions be made concerning many things. Instead, it remains whole and entire in the contemplation of God, looking continually toward its King until the end of the age. In six parts of the book, therefore, the Second State is contained. In one—that is, in the seventh—is the Third State. And through these, in another way, those six parts are contained under one, as if mother Leah with her seven children. Under the other, the seventh stands alone, as if her sister Rachel with her only son Joseph; for Rachel had no other in her life, because as soon as she gave birth to the second <note>Benjamin.</note>, she died. Therefore, the five parts of the book pertain to the five sons; that is, to those orders which are signified by them. <margin>Genesis 35</margin> 

¶ Furthermore, the seventh part pertains to Joseph alone, whom alone Rachel bore in the land of her birth; and because of this, for nearly seven years and until the end of Rachel's life, he was an only son, so that unity...

Indeed, the eighth part of the book—which in another categorization is called the third—begins from that place where it is said: *I saw a great and white throne, and one sitting upon it, from whose sight the earth and the heaven fled; and no place was found for them.* <note>original: "Vidi thronū magnum & candidum..."; Revelation 20:11.</note> However, so that one may understand more fully what has been said concerning the eight parts of the book, the entire book must be distinguished into three divisions. According to this, one division pertains to the second state, following the character of the literal sense which is veiled in various enigmas. The second division pertains to the third state. The third pertains to the world to come, which will be the eternal kingdom on that blessed day of which the Psalmist says:
<margin>Psalm 83</margin>
*One day in your courts is better than thousands.* <note>Psalm 84:10 in modern bibles; 83 in the Vulgate.</note> The first division, which pertains to the second state, is divided into six general parts as we have already said; truly, each of these six has its own <term>septenary</term> <note>A grouping of seven things, such as the seven seals, trumpets, or vials.</note>, just as each of the six weeks of the Lenten season is concluded by a count of seven days. Since things are so, it is clear that in respect to these six times which pertain to the second state, a seventh time must be spoken of, which will belong to the third state; and in respect to the six parts of the book pertaining to the second state, that seventh part must be spoken of which we predicted would pertain to the third. Not only in respect to the six times of the second state is that time of the third state to be considered the seventh, but also in respect to the six ages of the world, of which five had passed when Christ came into the world. The sixth, having begun from that same time, continues in labor until these times of ours, in which the second state is in its final throes and the third, which will be the <term>Sabbath</term> <note>A period of spiritual rest and contemplation on earth before the end of time.</note>, has been initiated. Because all the scripture of the New Testament partly pertains to the second state in such a way that it does not pass into the third—such as that which
<margin>John 21</margin>
the Lord says to Peter: *Follow me*—so it partly pertains to the third in such a way that it is not referred to the second, like those things written in the seventh part of the book concerning the coming of Gog and the final
<margin>Apocalypse 20</margin>

judgment and similar things. Part of it pertains to the second state in such a way that it is nonetheless referred to the third. We must make such a distinction between those scriptures which touch upon what the prophets specifically say regarding the second state, and those which properly touch the third, and those which commonly touch both. Thus, let it refer to the second state so that it is nonetheless referred to the third; yet let us never refer to the second state that which specifically touches the third, nor refer to the third that which properly touches the second. But that which by a single impulse touches both should be referred to the second state such that it is nonetheless referred to the third. For example: there is a shared account in the Gospel regarding Elizabeth and Mary, because one conceived a son by her husband in her old age against all hope, and the other, while still a young girl, conceived by the Holy Spirit. And there is no doubt that Elizabeth designates the <term>Church of Preachers</term> and Mary the <term>Church of Contemplatives</term>; of these, one indeed preceded in conception, while the other followed. Because these two holy women were born between the Old and New Testaments, in the first understanding, Elizabeth signifies the Synagogue and Mary signifies the Church converted from the Gentiles to the living God. In the second understanding, Elizabeth signifies the Church of the second state, and Mary the Church of the third, because *not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal <note>original: "animale"; referring to the natural or physical soul/life.</note>; then that which is spiritual.* <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> Similarly, the mysteries of the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist.</note> and of Christ are to be understood. Likewise, the apostles Peter and John (the author of this book). Therefore, Elizabeth, John the Baptist, and the apostle Peter do not cross the boundary of the second state. But Mary, Christ, and John the Evangelist remain in the second state in such a way that they are much more harmoniously accepted in the third. Indeed, that scripture which was published among the Gentiles—like this book—does not have within itself what can be referred to the first state, but refers either simply to the second—such as the things written about the beast having seven heads and ten horns and the battles of the holy martyrs—or simply to the third state, such as those things written in the seventh part, or commonly to both, such as those things concerning the seven churches.

### Example of the Ancients. Chapter 10.

But perhaps the Truth will satisfy us in this very matter if we weigh the examples of the ancients, noting that just as Hagar the handmaid signifies the Synagogue which belonged to the first state, and Sarah signifies the Church which belonged to the second, so Leah signifies the Church which pertains to the second, and Rachel signifies the Church pertaining to the third. <note>Joachim uses the two wives of Jacob, Leah (active) and Rachel (contemplative), to represent different stages of the Church's development.</note> Since these things are so, it is pleasing to consider that Sarah sometimes has a place in the first state, especially in that history where Isaac is said to have introduced Rebecca into the tent of his mother and to have loved her so much that it tempered the grief that had happened from his mother's death. Hagar, however, has a place in the second state, which was given to the free woman; according to this, there is no place for her after a son was born to the father from the free mother, for the handmaid and all her sons were expelled—namely, the Jews who chose to be followers of the righteousness <note>original: "iustitie"</note> which is in the Law rather than lovers of grace. In that same way, Rachel, and the mother of the Lord, and even the Lord Jesus himself and John the Evangelist (whose book this is), have a place in the mysteries in the second state, but more so in the third. Leah, however, and Elizabeth, and her son John [the Baptist], and Peter, have their place in the second state in such a way that they do not have it in this manner in the third. The fruit of this understanding <note>original: "intellectus"</note> is this: since the first understanding properly pertains to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit, it is necessary that the first pertains to the first state and the second to the second, so that the Father is understood as the one sending and the Son as the one sent. And because the Son is not sent by the Father alone, but truly with him the Holy Spirit, it is necessary that the understanding which pertains to the Holy Spirit has a place in the second state, so that he may be understood as being sent at the same time. Certainly, according to this mode of understanding, neither does the understanding which pertains to the Father have a place in the second state, nor does the understanding which pertains to the Son have a place in the third; for neither is the Father understood to be sent with the Son when the Father is said to send the Son, nor is the Son sent with the Holy Spirit when it is said that the same Son sends the Holy Spirit—even if the Father should come...

<margin>John 14</margin> ...it can be said with the Son: and the Son with the Holy Spirit, the Truth itself testifying when it says: *If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.* <note>John 14:23</note> And these things are indeed so.

### Concerning another understanding. Chapter 11.

But if we turn to another understanding: we find that things take place in one way in the second and third state which are known to belong properly to the first; and things have a place in the first and third which properly belong to the second. There is no doubt that this must also be understood regarding those things which belong to the third state. This, however, differs between one and the other: for the latter cannot be taken as "properly" as that which <margin>Gen. 16</margin> was said above. For behold, we said that the **rejected handmaid** <note>Hagar, the mother of Ishmael, whom Joachim uses to represent the "servitude" of the Old Testament Law.</note> properly designates what belongs to the first state: and yet those who live carnally in the second and third states are reckoned as the handmaid’s sons. For he who does this (says <margin>John 8</margin> the Lord) "is a slave to sin." We said that **Leah** and certain others designate those who properly belong to the second state <note>Leah, the first wife of Jacob, traditionally represents the "Active Life" of the Church/Clergy.</note>: and yet those who preached the word of life in the first state were reckoned in Leah. Similarly, those in the third state also, because many are to be taught toward the knowledge of Him. We said that **Rachel** and certain others designate those who properly belong to the third state <note>Rachel, the beloved wife of Jacob, represents the "Contemplative Life" of the Monks and the upcoming Age of the Spirit.</note>: and yet in the first and second states there were found men of contemplation who, by the merit of their lives, were designated even then in Rachel. It remains, therefore, that these and similar things should be understood according to "more or less." If the fruit of knowledge is sought from these understandings, it is that which we have been taught by the holy fathers to believe and hold firmly: namely, to hold unshakably that the Son and Holy Spirit are in the Father; the Father and Holy Spirit are in the Son; and both the Father and the Son are in the Holy Spirit. And these three together are one God. All of present life, which contains within itself the three states of the world, is designated together in **Hagar**. But the future life is designated in **Sarah**. Similarly, Leah is set in comparison to Rachel. So too in Rachel: when she is set in comparison to Benja-

We must not be forced to keep silent rather than speak if it were not permitted to talk in this way, as has been the custom in the Divine Scriptures from ancient times. For if, because we say the **Synagogue** of the Jews is rejected, we were to include the whole multitude of Israel under this word, we would also prove the patriarchs and prophets to be rejected. ### Concerning the double understanding of the distinction. Chapter 12.

Because our discourse concerned the distinction of the first book of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, there is a double reason for its understanding: one by which its words are to be interpreted in a direct course through their proper times up to the place where it deals with the Judgment; the other by which a distinction must be made between the sixth and seventh portions, so that a difference is made between the second and third states. It is pleasing to seek a special fruit in this very thing: so that we who already know our God through faith may be able to hasten toward the hope of contemplating His highness, as much as He Himself shall grant. It is clear to all Christians who firmly hold the Catholic faith that there are three persons in the Trinity which is God: of whom one is unbegotten, another is begotten; and one of them is from no one, while the other is from the Father alone. But there is also another person who proceeds from the Father and the Son: who, just as the Son works with the Father, so He Himself also works with the Father and the Son. For a mystical exposition occurs when greater things are understood through the smallest, or many things through the few, whether in a good or bad sense; as when God is understood in the King of Jerusalem, or the devil in the King of Babylon. Here, however, where something is said openly about the devil himself, it is not something that should be reflected mystically onto some other person in the future—especially since there is no one greater in wickedness than the devil who could be designated by him. Rather, what is said of him must be understood as such. And if there are some things there that need a special understanding, such as the "chain" with which he is said to be captured, let one not think it is an evil thing; other things are cloaked in certain hidden obscurities so that they do not become cheapened by being revealed entirely before their time. Nor should it be believed that Scripture is obscure only where it is wrapped in mystical figures, or manifest only where literal understanding is ready at hand (as it seems to some); but often there is much more in the literal than in the spiritual sense. # Joachim’s Introduction to the Apocalypse

On the contrary, another <note>likely referring to James 2:24-26</note> says that a person is justified by works alone, proceeding to say: *Faith without works is dead.* These words were to be understood according to the letter, yet they are quite hidden in themselves and nearly difficult to understand. The Psalmist says in a psalm:
<margin>Psalm 111</margin>
*Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.* And the Lord in the Gospel commands, saying: *Fear him who can*
<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
*destroy soul and body in Gehenna.* John,
<margin>John 4</margin>
however, seems to feel the opposite, saying: *He who fears is not perfected in love; but*
<margin>1 John 4</margin>
*perfect love casts out fear.* The Lord says in the Gospel: *Look at the birds of the heaven: and do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat or what shall we drink or what shall we wear?"* And: *Work: not for the food*
<margin>John 6:9; 2 Thessalonians 3</margin>
*which perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life.* But the Apostle <note>Paul</note> commands the faithful to work for their bread, saying: *He who does not work, let him not eat.* Truly, these things are given for the sake of example, so that no one thinks the scripture is easy to understand, or that difficulty is found only in allegorical <note>symbolic or metaphorical</note> senses. On the contrary, we suffer greater difficulty regarding the bare words themselves which are written prophetically, so much so that it seems especially
<margin>Psalm 17</margin>
written of them: *Dark water in the clouds of the air.* For what can be clearer than: *They gave*
<margin>Psalm 68</margin>

And yet, because the Psalm did not say, "They will give gall for Christ's food and in his thirst they will give him vinegar," but spoke of Christ in the first person <note>original: "in persona propria"</note> and in the past tense rather than the future, who would have understood this before it was fulfilled in
<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
Christ? Therefore, it should not be thought that there are not many things difficult to understand in the letter itself—I mean those things of another kind where it is the spirit, not that of which the Apostle says: *The letter kills* <note>original: "Litera occidit"; 2 Corinthians 3:6</note>. This is undoubtedly because the letter is not the truth itself, but only a figure <note>a representation or sign</note> of the truth; nor should one attend to what is read, but to what it signifies. But that which is not a figure but truth is to be taken just as it is read, provided there is nothing there that needs explanation—lest perhaps it be understood not as it is, but differently than the matter requires, like that:
<margin>John 14</margin>
*If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice, because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.* Truly, if indeed the Father is greater than him, it is not 

<column-break/>

according to Christ being God, but according to him being man. In order for this to be understood, one should vigilantly observe that there are three general modes by which God speaks in the scriptures, as is clearly shown in this book <note>The Apocalypse</note> as in others. For he speaks either **historically**, as in Genesis and the Books of Kings, and in all books whatsoever that are written as history—in which category of speech the four Gospels and the Book of Acts of the Apostles are also to be accepted, even if there are some things in them excluded from this rule—or he speaks in the **revelation of images**, such as that wheel which appeared to Ezekiel, or the beasts shown to Daniel; or he speaks in the **simplicity of truth**, such as: *Behold the days come, says the Lord, and I will raise up to David a righteous branch.* And:
<margin>Ezekiel 1; Daniel 4; Jeremiah 23</margin>
*Behold the Lord my God shall come, and all his saints with him*; and other things which were pronounced by the prophetic spirit, not under a mist of mysteries, but openly. According to these three modes, then, John speaks in the Apocalypse. He speaks **historically** there when he says of himself: *I was on the island called Patmos* and *What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches which are in Asia.* He speaks in the 
<margin>Apocalypse 10</margin>
**revelations of images**, as when it is said: *I saw an open door in heaven and behold a throne was set in it*—and the other things that follow there—and *when he had opened one of the seven seals, behold a white horse, and he who sat upon it was given a crown, and he went out conquering to conquer*; and *I saw seven angels prepared to sound the trumpets*; and *I saw and behold a red dragon*; and *I saw a beast ascending from the sea.* And things similar to these which are in **simple truth**, such as: *Satan shall be loosed from his prison.* Since these things are so, we must have such discernment in these three modes in this book: that in the images shown up to the end of the "sixth time" <note>the sixth period of history</note>, we understand the struggles of the **second state** <note>the Age of the Son/the Church</note>. In the prophetic words, which are brought forth literally in the seventh part, let us understand those things pertaining to that **third state** <note>the Age of the Holy Spirit</note> in which there will not be, as until now, dark enigmas; rather, it is the state in which we shall begin to see more clearly and, as it were, face to face.

In those things which are spoken of as history, certain double works <note>original: "opera quedā duplicia"</note> pertain to both states, because two mystic understandings can be found in the historical words of the New Testament, according to what was said above. Thus, from these things written in this summary—and from others that could be written—it is most clearly evident that liberty is granted in that Sabbath, which is God’s own, for the sake of acknowledging the truth. Just as it is said by the Apostle: *There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God.*

<margin>Hebrews 4</margin>
Nor should it be troubling that in the eighth part, that heavenly city called Jerusalem is narrated as being constructed of precious stones and pure gold. Or that a fountain of living water is said to flow into that city, and the tree of life is said to be planted on either bank of the river.

<margin>Revelation 21, 22</margin>
For in the eighth part of the book, neither a typical <note>symbolic</note> nor a historical understanding properly applies, but only the **anagogical** <term>anagogical: an interpretation that detects a spiritual or heavenly meaning, looking toward the end of time or the afterlife</term>, which contemplates celestial things alone. Nor does John speak there through figures regarding that city as if to hide the understanding of them in obscure enigmas, but rather so that through the noble images of visible things—by which such glorious things are said of her—the mind of the reader may be snatched up into love for her.

### Chapter 14: On the Difference between Sabbaths

Because in those things we have written so far, mention has been made of Sabbaths—and will occur more frequently in what is to be written—I think it worthwhile to discuss with diligent scrutiny what the difference is between one Sabbath and another. This is to ensure that, because they are diverse (both the Sabbaths themselves and the diverse mysteries of the Sabbaths), one occurring thing does not obscure the understanding of another. As often happens in similar matters, a mind occupied with many things might wander in different directions and foolishly mistake one thing for another. There are, therefore, several kinds of Sabbaths. For there is a **historical Sabbath**, a **moral Sabbath**, a **tropological Sabbath**, a **contemplative Sabbath**, and an **anagogical Sabbath**.

The **historical Sabbath** is when someone, after daily labor, returns to contemplation at least on feast days. The **moral Sabbath** is when someone, having left behind the vanity of the world, offers themselves entirely to serve God in mind and body. The **tropological Sabbath** <term>tropological: a moral or figurative interpretation of a text</term> is when, after

<column-break/>

the labors of learning the letter <note>the literal text</note>, someone is raised up to a spiritual understanding. The **contemplative Sabbath** is when, after the exercise of the active life, someone is led to the contemplative life. The **anagogical Sabbath** is also when the animal body is sown <note>a reference to burial/death</note> so that the soul may be refreshed until, its own Sabbath having been completed, it receives a spiritual body. Of this Sabbath the Apostle says: *He who has entered into his rest, he also has rested from his works, just as God did from his own.*

<margin>Hebrews 4</margin>

There is, however, another Sabbath which is called **typical** <note>symbolic/foreshadowing</note>, having several types, which is shown from the figures of the Old Testament in the New. This is when, namely, a Sabbath is understood to exist in each of the periods of the "sixth age" until the sixth period. This means that in each of the six periods, God has given peace to His Church so that it might rest at intervals of time from its labors. For just as each of the weeks of Lent is known to have a Sabbath, so it was given to each period of the Church to have its own Sabbath, lest a prolonged affliction should bring about despair. Furthermore, concerning this Sabbath, the Apostle says to the Hebrews: *There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God.*

<margin>Hebrews 4</margin>

Nor should one be troubled by the different kinds of Sabbaths, which might run through various interpretations according to the customary use and solemn understanding of the Scriptures. Yet in another way, three Sabbaths can be assigned, the third of which is that which we have said is to come in the third state of the world <note>Joachim's "Age of the Holy Spirit"</note>. The first of these was before the Law; the second was under the Law; the third is under Grace. Before the Law, there was a Sabbath for the four hundred and thirty years that the children of Israel remained in Egypt—that is, from the time their fathers entered Egypt until Moses.

<margin>Genesis 46, Exodus 3</margin>

The second Sabbath under the Law was when the histories and prophets ceased, namely from the days of Malachi the prophet until John the Baptist. Truly, the third Sabbath under Grace is to come from the time when the devil shall be imprisoned so that he may no longer seduce the nations, until the end of the world. And what is written of the first of the three literally by a certain wise man: *While all things were in quiet silence* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 18:14</note>—which nevertheless in spirit must be understood of the second—is not absurdly asked, whether the second also...

<margin>Revelation 20</margin>

<meta>This page continues the introductory section of Joachim of Fiore's Exposition on the Apocalypse. Having previously discussed the symbolic meanings of the New Testament, Joachim now elaborates on the concept of "Sabbath silences"—historical periods where the scriptural record falls silent or pauses between major revelations—as a way to structure the three great ages of the world.</meta>

->**Joachim’s Introduction to the Apocalypse**<-

...whether the second and third Sabbath had silence; and where; and what kind of silence each possessed. If we begin to count the deeds of the fathers and the course of times and years through each individual father, starting from Adam, we find in them a number of years and a continuous narration of deeds until the righteous man Joseph, who died in Egypt, at which point the histories and computations of years fail. For from that time until Moses, nothing is written of any of the grandsons of Jacob regarding how old he was when he fathered this or that person. Even if a number of years for the life of Levi and his son and grandson seems to be written, the chronology of the chronicles cannot be assigned through it, except what is handed down confusedly and as if in a summary: that the dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years. <margin>Exodus 6</margin> But neither are the works of anyone written, as was accustomed to happen before and as happened in the following time from Moses until Ezra; so that this time was a Sabbath, testifying to silence as much as to rest. In the same way, from Zerubbabel <note>A leader of the Jewish people who led the first group of captives back from Babylon</note> and Nehemiah until John the Baptist, the sum of years is not distinguished either through the chronicles of kings or the genealogy of the fathers. Nor are the deeds of any written until John the Baptist in the manner they were written before, except for the Books of the Maccabees, which, according to the testimony of Saint Jerome, are "outside the canon" <note>original: *extra canonem*; meaning they were not included in the official Hebrew Bible</note>, until the Word of Almighty God should come from the royal seats. <margin>Jerome</margin> He calls, therefore, the time of the first silence a Sabbath in respect to those times which were before the Law until Joseph, who ruled in the land of Egypt. <margin>Genesis 41</margin> The second, in respect to those which passed under the Law and the Prophets until Malachi the prophet. The third, in respect to the new things which have passed until now under Grace, and which are carried out in hardships and groans until the end of the sixth time. Just as the judgment of Sodom preceded the first silence, and the judgment of the first Babylon (which was the metropolis of the Chaldeans) preceded the second, <margin>Genesis 19, Daniel 5</margin> so the new silence precedes the judgment of the New Babylon, which John took care to note in the sixth part of this book. And it must be noted that in every state, Almighty God consoles His people, so that through the good things we perceive in time,

**¶ On the seven portions of the year, the sixth of which is from the fiftieth day <note>Likely referring to a liturgical period of fifty days before Easter</note> until Easter; the seventh from Easter to Pentecost. Page 15.**

That sacred time called the Paschal season <note>The season of Easter</note>—namely, from the holy day of Easter until Pentecost—comprises the seventh portion of the entire year, with fifteen days excepted which were given as a supplement and an abundance to the fifty-day period. This is according to the seventy elders <note>The seventy leaders who accompanied Moses partway up Mount Sinai</note> mentioned in Holy Scripture; <margin>Exodus 24</margin> and yet two others were added for a specific reason, as it is the custom of Divine Scripture that even the smallest parts fall into the mysteries of the portions. Now, if the time of fasting <note>Lent</note> is considered in the sixth portion of the year, and the time of Paschal feasting in the seventh, it is clear that just as the time of fasting designates the sixth age of the world, so the time of feasting, which is called the Paschal Sabbath, looks toward that third Sabbath. This third one is more glorious than the two previous ones, as those two served it in mysteries. For just as five fifty-day periods precede the sixth (which is assigned to fasting above all others), so five ages of the world preceded the sixth age as if in feasts of the flesh. But that sixth age itself is assigned to sacred fasts. One of these, belonging to the second state, is designated in the Sabbath of the Easter Vigil; the other, belonging to the third, in the Sabbath of the Pentecost Vigil. These alone, as far as I can see, should not be called simply Sabbaths, but with an addition: "Sabbaths of Sabbaths." Truly, this book, throughout its six parts, extends and keeps its pace within the limits of the second state, so that starting from the Resurrection of the Lord, it reaches until the end of that state, returning again and again to its own beginning. Finally, in each of the five parts, a "recapitulation" <note>A method of interpretation where the same historical period is retold several times to reveal different spiritual meanings</note> is made, and the course of each is directed toward the end of the second state. These recapitulations are not to be understood as applying to the whole, but according to a part; thus the times of the second state are to be held generally in each part, yet specifically each part or order is fitted to its own proper time: the first to the first, the second to the second, and so on for the rest. Finally, even in the last parts, there are some things that require recapitulation. But we attribute this more specifically to the five parts here because the recapitulation in them is more manifest. For the rest, the six parts generally relate to the struggles of labor. But the seventh part is distinct and separate from the six parts of the book, although the number of years of Satan’s imprisonment seems to belong in part to the times of the second state. For he was not all imprisoned at once, but through each of the five times of the second...

->### Joachim’s Introduction to the Apocalypse<-

In each state, each individual head of the dragon <note>original: "draconis caput"; refers to the seven-headed dragon of Revelation 12, which Joachim interpreted as a series of historical persecutors of the Church</note> has been defeated; and in the sixth period, two are defeated at once. ### On the division of the eight parts of the book of Revelation. Chapter 16.

<margin>Daniel 7</margin>
<margin>Revelation 9</margin>
First, it was stated above that there are seven parts of the book, representing as many periods from the arrival of the Savior until the final judgment. In the first part, it treats the **prelates** <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops</note> who took up the first war of that time. In the second part, it treats the **martyrs**. In the third, the **doctors** <note>In this context, "doctors" refers to great teachers and theologians of the early Church</note>. In the fourth, the **virgins** <note>Those dedicated to a life of purity and monasticism</note>. In the fifth, the **general Church**. Indeed, those four orders held a conflict against four specific beasts—I mean those beasts which the prophet Daniel says he saw in a vision <note>See Daniel 7:3-7</note>—while the Church, which is the New Jerusalem, fought against Babylon itself. As shown in the sixth part of the book, this "New Babylon" is to be judged in the sixth period. After her (as we have already said), the Beast and the False Prophet must be judged, who will rise up against Christ more audaciously than usual at the very turning point of the sixth period. Then, with the devil imprisoned, there will be a Sabbath for the people of God. Near the end of this Sabbath, the devil will be released again from his prison and will seduce the nations which are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog. Finally, the devil will be cast into the lake of fire, and there will be the general judgment and the resurrection of the dead. Once these things are accomplished, there will be no further worldly times, but one eternal day. No longer will the kings of the earth reign, but the Lord of hosts alone will be King. There will no longer be cities of the nations as there have been until now, but only the City of God: our mother Jerusalem. The eighth part of the book will follow the glory of her brightness, according to what was shown to John when he was invited to contemplate the glory of her brightness by one of the seven angels who held the seven bowls of the wrath of God. For he says this about it: *One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues came and spoke with me, saying: "Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb."* And immediately he added: *And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, having the glory of God*—and the rest that follows there.

### What is general and what is special to each order of saints. Chapter 17.

<margin>Revelation 21</margin>

Let us suppose that the people of **Jerusalem** had a battle against the **Arabs**, and it was their specific duty to fight in the first month, with support given to them by all the peoples listed below, so that they themselves might provide help to each of the others during their respective months as they were able. # John’s Introduction to the Apocalypse

...to be exercised in the flesh: for others, the exercises were to be more in the spirit than in the flesh. For God gave priests to the Church as ears <note>The transcription reads 'aurea' (golden), but contextually this is likely 'aures' (ears) to complete the five senses mentioned later.</note> for shaping and teaching: and disciples in the doctrine of His Gospel. Deacons are like the mouth for evangelizing what they have learned from the priests. Bishops are like the hands who, with the strength of true faith, defend the flock entrusted to them from the tearing of wild beasts: <margin>Titus 2</margin> because of this, they are likened to the patriarch Judah, who was the strongest among his brothers. Virgins are like the eyes who sit contemplating the things of God: awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our savior Jesus Christ. He also gave the clergy as the nose to run toward the scent of His ointments: under which the entire multitude of the faithful is contained: a creature nonetheless created for the praise and glory of the Most High God, for the honor of Holy Mother Church, and for the completion of the body of Christ. To these five orders belong the four Gospels and the book of the Acts of the Apostles, <margin>Acts 1</margin> which begins thus: "The first account I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day in which he was taken up, giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he chose." For so that the blessed Luke might show that those four works of Christ were signified in four decades of days, he added and said: "To whom he also presented himself alive with many proofs, appearing to them throughout forty days." Again, to show that in the fifth time and fifth work the completion is given by the Holy Spirit to those things which Jesus began to do and teach, after a few words he added and said: "And when the days of Pentecost were completed: suddenly there came a sound from heaven like a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole <margin>Acts 1</margin> house where they were sitting." Thus, the Nativity is ascribed to the priests, whom Paul signifies; the Passion to the deacons, who are also evangelists, whom Stephen signifies; the Resurrection to the bishops, whom Peter signifies; the Ascension to the contemplatives, whom John designates; and the coming of the Holy Spirit upon them to those serving in life: the significance in the Church of the disciples of Christ, upon whom on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit fell—

Or do only those who do this reach the kingdom of God? (By no means!) For this reason, the Son of God came in the flesh: so that <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> "all flesh shall see the salvation of God alike." Now, therefore, regarding these orders, nothing in this way belongs to the book of the Apocalypse: because they had their own historical books in which they could be instructed, not only according to the mystical understanding which is common to both them and others, but also according to the surface of the letter and historical morality, which requires the outer man no less than the inner. Furthermore, this book of the mystery <note>original: "sacramenti," meaning a sacred secret or mystery</note>, full of spiritual things, was given primarily to spiritual men who say farewell to the cares of the world: who do not wish to have a lasting inheritance here, but seek the things to come. It deals with the seven orders designated in the seven tribes of Israel and in the seven churches which are in Asia, just as those five orders were designated in the five larger tribes and as many churches. Moreover, five barley loaves are set before those five—that is, the five books written above which are historical, and in which spiritual fruit lies hidden under the husk. But for these [spiritual men], there are seven wheat loaves—that is, the seven parts of this book, which sound nothing historical like those others, but almost everything understood in them is spirit and life. # Explanation of the Book

We must carefully consider that five of the seven orders noted in this book <note>original: "libro isto", referring to the Apocalypse or the author’s commentary on it</note> have a great affinity with the five previously written orders. Therefore, we must discuss this diligently, lest the spirit be extinguished in the flesh, and lest—heaven forbid—the higher understanding be swallowed up by the lower. There is a difference between them, however: in that first comparison <note>referring to the life of Christ</note>, the first position is Birth, the second is the Passion, the third is Resurrection, the fourth is Ascension, and the fifth is the Coming of the Holy Spirit.

In this current arrangement, it is not so. Instead, the first is Resurrection, the second is the Passion, the third is Birth, the fourth is Ascension, and the fifth, sixth, and seventh involve the giving of the Holy Spirit. Why in the fifth, sixth, and seventh? Because the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles on three occasions: first when they believed in Christ, second on the day of Easter, and third on the day of Pentecost. It was given first to precede, second to cooperate, and third to perfect. For whoever does not receive the Holy Spirit in this way cannot be a perfect Christian. For this reason, I speak of three gifts—not three Spirits, because the Spirit is indeed one—but three gifts. In the same way, a child is anointed once with oil before being baptized; once baptized, they are anointed with chrism by the hand of the baptizer; and once more by the hand of the bishop.

Although there are seven orders to which this book generally pertains, there are five among them that belong properly to the "second state" <note>A term often used by the theologian Joachim of Fiore to describe the Age of the Son/the Church</note>: namely, the Apostles, the Martyrs, the Doctors <note>Teachers of the faith</note>, the Virgins, and those who are called "Regulars" because of their communal life <note>Monks or clergy living under a religious rule</note>. These orders are not to be ranked with those we wrote of above, but rather above them; for those others, as we have said, gave and renounced themselves and their belongings freely for the Lord. The first of these is symbolized by the Lion, the second by the Calf, the third by the Man, the fourth by the Eagle <note>The four "living creatures" of Revelation 4:7</note>, and the fifth by the Throne of God. These five orders, which are known to have shone through the five ages of the Church, belong properly to the second state. The two that follow—the sixth and the seventh—although they (like the preceding ones) belong to the second state, their brightness is nonetheless obscured by the new things that come after them. This is so that once the old 

<column-break/>

way of speaking is set aside, the impulse of the Spirit may direct itself toward the new rather than the old. And so it is. Nevertheless, these numbers—five and seven—can be assigned within the Book of Revelation alone, as if the five senses of the body and the seven virtues of the soul were thought to come together in one perfect man. But we understand this better if we consider the great deeds performed in mystery by two of Christ's apostles.

->Of the active life symbolized by Peter and of the contemplative life symbolized by John. Chapter 19.<-

Peter and John are known to have held a great prerogative in mysteries compared to their fellow apostles. For the first signifies the active life, while the second notes the contemplative life. This is because the one followed the Lord by taking up his cross <note>referring to Peter's martyrdom</note>, while the other, after struggling long in the body, reached his end in peace <note>referring to the tradition that John the Evangelist died of old age</note>. And because the five senses of the body pertain to action, while the seven virtues of the soul pertain to contemplation, it was fitting that Peter, the elder, should preside over five churches, and John, the younger, over seven, so that in these twelve, the foundations of all others might consist. 

Regarding John, we have certain authority. Regarding Peter, however, we must investigate whether such authority can be found. From the beginning, Peter presided over Jerusalem and built the church there, which has a harmony with the tribe of Reuben. Next, he presided over the church of Antioch, which harmonizes with the tribe of Gad. Then over the Roman church, which accords with the tribe of Judah. Furthermore, he did not preside over Alexandria in person, but sent his disciple there <note>Saint Mark</note> to found and rule it in his stead, nurturing it to be exalted among the primary churches. 

When a portion of the Romans followed Augustus and a "New Rome" was propagated among the people at Constantinople—so that in ancient times this "New Rome" was spoken of as the daughter of Rome and a partner in the Empire—it seemed right to the leaders of the churches, and was even established in councils, that the Church of Constantinople should be exalted among the principal churches. It was to be the second rank <note>original: "secunda parma", likely meaning second place or shield/honor</note> after Rome among the four remaining sees, as a partner and sharer in the Holy Roman Church. Therefore, the Roman Church is like a second Jerusalem, and like a second Jerusalem, it is the seat of God, in the center and circumference of which were seen the four living creatures of which John speaks in this book.
