### John’s Introduction to the Apocalypse
### L 2

The first was like a lion; the second living creature was like a calf; the third living creature had a face like a man; and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle. <note>These are the four "living creatures" from Revelation 4:7, often used in Christian art to represent the four Evangelists, but here used to represent different stages or centers of the Church.</note> Finally, the primitive church was likened to the strongest animal, the lion, because in it the holy apostles were strong in faith; through them, it pleased Almighty God to conquer the whole world. The church of Antioch was likened to the second animal, that is, the calf, because in it the disciples were first called "Christians," ready to obey whatever the apostles might command. <note>In biblical symbolism, the calf or ox often represents sacrifice and patient service.</note> The church of Alexandria was likened to the third animal, that is, the human being, because great teachers were found there in ancient times, even before any of their own teachers had become famous in the Latin church. <note>Alexandria was famous for its Catechetical School and scholars like Origen and Clement.</note> That Eastern church which was later named after the royal city of Constantinople is likened to the fourth animal, that is, the eagle; for that church was contained within its boundaries, to which Paul said from the beginning—not without a hidden mystery—"I am jealous for you with a divine jealousy; for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." <margin>2 Corinthians 11</margin> <note>The original text cites 2 Cor 10, but the quote is from 11:2.</note> That the wings of a flying eagle belong to the virgin churches is testified by John in this book <margin>Revelation 12</margin> in the fourth part of it, in which he specifically deals with virgins; speaking through some things concerning the woman clothed with the sun, he added and said: "And there were given to the woman two wings like those of an eagle." And this indeed concerns the five great and famous churches of which <margin>Isaiah 19</margin> we have already spoken, as is said through Isaiah: "There shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan." Furthermore, the seven churches to which John writes in this book, of whom it was specifically written through the <margin>Isaiah 4</margin> prophet Isaiah: "Seven women shall take hold of one man," designate those spiritual orders who are separated from the fellowship of the world. Just as those five churches which Peter is known to have founded—either by himself or through others—designate those five general orders we wrote of above (namely, that these five principal churches belonging to Peter designate five general orders devoted to the Passion), so the seven belonging to John designate seven special orders assigned to the religious life. It remains for us to inquire who these orders are, and whether they are thought to have any similarity to those five, and whether they agree with each other in the same way that the physical senses agree with

<column-break/>

the virtues of the soul. First, therefore, we must discuss what we deferred shortly before: whether the number seven is silently understood within the number five, especially since five and seven arise from twelve, and yet they by no means meet as equals; for in order to meet as equals, seven would require seven. In this matter, the mystery of the faith of the twelve apostles would be disturbed if Paul and Barnabas—set apart for the Gospel of the Gentiles—had not been gathered into that same sacred number by the unity of God. Thus, not only can five and seven be distinguished in the fact that twelve were chosen from the beginning, but also seven and seven in the fact that two apostles were added. <margin>Acts 13</margin> In the same way, joined to the twelve patriarchs were two grandsons, the sons of Joseph, to whom it is read that the birthright lost by Reuben was given. Therefore, the number five is to be ascribed not only to the first state (to which the five barley loaves are rightly attributed) but also to the second; however, the number seven is silently understood beneath it, so that there is both a difference within unity and harmony within unity. For even the senses of the body, as we have said, are five; yet under the name of "touch," the walking of the feet and the work of marriage are contained. In the same way, there are five general orders, and yet under the fifth general order (which is designated in the seat of God), the orders of the continent <note>Those practicing celibacy or self-restraint.</note> and the laity consist. It is clear, then, that the five orders that seem to belong to Peter—which in another sense are seven—have a great deal of harmony with these seven orders belonging to John, so that where the former lead, the latter follow to some extent, just as John says of himself: "Peter, turning, saw that disciple following whom Jesus loved." <margin>John 21</margin> So also that heavenly city Jerusalem is shown to have five general parts, but yet under the fifth part... equally contained... For the city itself is set in a square, as John says, and it is described as having three gates in each of its parts. Of these, the eastern part belongs to the lion, which designates the pastors; the northern to the calf, designating the deacons; the western to the man, designating the teachers; the southern to the eagle, designating the contemplatives; the body of the city and the dove, which is the church...

### The Abbot’s Exposition of the Books
### L 2

...expresses the order of clerics: under which, however, are contained two inferior orders: namely, the continent <note>Those who abstain from marriage, but are not necessarily monks.</note> and the married. This city is one, and its proper name is Jerusalem; yet while it remains in its earthly pilgrimage, it is known by the name "Church." For even that which was once called the Synagogue was called Jerusalem, just as that church which is to be in the third state <term>status: one of the three great ages of history in this author’s theology, corresponding to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term> of the world. Nor is it a wonder if each is called Jerusalem individually and yet all three are together one Jerusalem, since we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person of the Deity to be God and Lord, and yet we are forbidden by the Catholic religion to speak of three Gods or three Lords.

The first Jerusalem, which was called the Synagogue, is designated in Sarah—I do not speak of the rejected ones whom Hagar <note>In the Book of Genesis, Hagar was the handmaid of Sarah; here she represents those outside the spiritual promise.</note> designates, but of the elect whom Sarah signifies; and this is true when she is considered in relation to Rebecca. For when Sarah is considered in relation to Hagar, then Hagar designates the synagogue of the rejected, and Sarah the Church called from the nations. But when Sarah is placed in relation to Rebecca, then Sarah signifies the Synagogue—not in regard to the rejected, but in regard to the elect. Rebecca, who was brought into the tent of Sarah, signifies the Gentile Church which was established through the Lord, who is the heir of the kingdom. And so the first Jerusalem, which was called the Synagogue, was designated in Sarah; the second, which is called the Church, was designated in Rebecca; the third, which is more blessed, was designated in Rachel. <note>The author uses the three wives of the patriarchs—Sarah (wife of Abraham), Rebecca (wife of Isaac), and Rachel (wife of Jacob)—to represent three stages of religious history.</note> The first was joined to the Father through fear; the second was coupled to the Son through humility; the third was united to the Holy Spirit through devotion. Nevertheless, what is joined to one person is joined to all three at once, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, and the three peoples are one people. 

The first Jerusalem was built in the first state; the second in the second; the third in the third. However, the third of these, which is to be built in the third state of the world, began to be built at the same time as the second, from the very beginning of that second state; for these two are themselves one. Because the cause of the Son and the Holy Spirit is not the same in this regard: that the Holy Spirit should be from the Son alone in the same way the Son is from the Father alone; rather, the Spirit is also from the Father just as the Son is. Because of this, at the beginning of the second state, both were sent together. Therefore, so that the same Spirit who is with the Son might be shown to proceed from the Father, once the work of the first state was completed (which is specifically ascribed to the Father himself for the sake of the mystery), it was necessary to begin another work which would be ascribed to the same Spirit for a similar mystery. And it was nonetheless necessary—indeed, much more clearly for that time—to begin another work which would be ascribed to the Son, so that both might be shown to be sent together by the Father. I said "much more clearly" because the work which specifically pertains to the Holy Spirit will have its clarity in the third state, just as the work ascribed to the Son has its clarity, as we have already said, in the second.

This work of which we speak is the human race: one indeed in nature, but distinct in its own orders just as in the Trinity. For the first order is of the married, created in the image of the Father. The second is of the clerics, instituted in the image of the Son. The third is of the monks, in the likeness of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, the order of the married is from no other order, and was instituted for this: that it ought to procreate children. The order of clerics does not exist from itself, but was propagated from the order of the married alone by the origin of the flesh; yet it was not instituted for procreating children of the flesh, but for evangelizing the Word of God, just as Christ himself, in whose image it was instituted. The order of monks proceeds from both; for if people from the married order join by mutual consent, they are received into the monastic life, and those from the clerics are received into it much more freely. We say this order also "proceeds" well because, as if given to another or sent out, it even physically departs from its own places to dwell where it was not before—just like the patriarch Jacob, who for a similar mystery departed from his own house to seek wives and children for himself in a foreign region. The order of the married was constituted from the beginning, and it persevered alone, or as if alone, throughout the entire time of the first...

state: <note>original: "statu"</note> that is, from Adam until Christ. For although those other two orders <note>The orders of clerics and monks.</note> existed during that time, they were held enclosed under the shadow of the literal Law and were bound by the tie of marriage just like everyone else. However, once the first state ended and the second began, the orders of clerics and monks soon commenced; there is no doubt that this occurred in the primitive Church, which preserved both the ecclesiastical life through preaching and the monastic order through a communal life. Furthermore, there was such a great union of these two orders in this second state that there were neither clerics who did not live communally like monks, nor monks to whom the duties of clerics were not committed.

Since the one man Jacob took two wives, namely Leah and Rachel, it appears that the order of monks—which we said pertains to John according to its symbolic meaning—is twofold. This is because of the two lives it pursues, namely the **active** and the **contemplative**, and because of the two understandings: one of which belongs to the second state, and the other to the third. For the symbolic meaning of Peter is to be understood in the second state in such a way that it never passes into the third, as we have already said. But the symbolic meaning of John is to be understood in the second state in such a way that it resounds much more worthily in the third. 

Therefore, just as Isaac had only one wife, Rebecca, but Jacob had first Leah and then her sister Rachel, so in the second state of the world, the general Church of clerics is joined in a kind of marriage to Christ, while the twofold Church of monks is joined to the Holy Spirit. This is arranged so that the part pertaining to Leah <note>Symbolizing the active, working life.</note> would bring forth its fruit in the second state, while the part pertaining to Rachel <note>Symbolizing the quiet, contemplative life.</note> would bring it forth in the third. For this reason, the prophet says three things: *In that time, a man shall nourish a young cow or two sheep, and from the abundance of milk he shall eat butter.* <margin>Isaiah 7</margin>

Therefore, Rebecca—the mother of Jacob who was joined in marriage to Isaac—signifies the general Church joined to Christ. But Leah and Rachel, who were joined together to the one man Jacob, designate those two special churches which are joined more closely to the Holy Spirit through the bond of charity and unity. Whence it is also said by the Psalmist: *Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell as one; like the oil upon the head that runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.* <margin>Psalm 131 <note>This is Psalm 133 in modern Bibles.</note></margin> But why are there two together? Because after the resurrection of the Lord, the Holy Spirit was given twice to the apostles; because Elisha asked to have a double portion of Elijah’s spirit; because one life is active and the other contemplative; and because there are two precepts of charity: the love of neighbor and the love of God.

### On the Designation of the Fathers. Chapter 20.

<margin>Acts 4</margin>

It was brought about in a wondrous way in the second state that the life signified by Rebecca is seen to belong properly to Christ. However, the two lives designated by Leah and Rachel belong properly to the Holy Spirit. To the general Church, signified by Rebecca, belong five general orders according to the number of churches we said belong to Peter: that is, **prelates, deacons, priests, virgins, and common clerics**. According to these five orders, the four Gospels and the book of the Acts of the Apostles are to be understood. To the two special churches signified by Leah and Rachel belong the numbers six and seven together: six regarding the labor of the active life, and seven regarding the rest of the contemplative life. For Leah gave birth only to six males; and Joshua, who was of the seed of Rachel, divided the inheritance among seven spiritual tribes. 

Nevertheless, to the six sons of Leah was added a daughter, Dinah, to complete the number seven, because of the sevenfold number of churches to which John writes. Truly, at the same time that Rachel conceived, her sister Leah began to grow weak in childbirth; for with the decline of the second state, the exercise of the active life will pass away across the six ages of the world, and the fruit of the contemplative life will begin to grow strong. And because the contemplative life is of greater happiness—or rather, because the initiation of the third state begins from the sixth period of the second state—it appears that in that same sixth period, as well as in the seventh, the likeness of Zebulun and Dinah <note>Sons of Leah.</note> fails, while Joseph and Benjamin <note>Sons of Rachel.</note> remain. 

To understand what is being said, it is helpful to assign the sons of Jacob to specific orders. The second was in Antioch, where the disciples were first called "Christians"...

And it was nonetheless necessary—indeed, for the time, much more clearly—that another work begin which would be ascribed to the Son, so that both might be shown to be sent together from the Father. I said "much more clearly" because the work that specifically pertains to the Holy Spirit will have its clarity in the third state, just as the work ascribed to the Son has its clarity in the second state, as we have already said. 

Now, this work of which we speak is the human race: one indeed in nature, but distinct in its own orders, as if in a trinity. The third is that of the monks, in the likeness of the Holy Spirit. For the order of the married is from no other order, and was instituted for this: that it must procreate children. The order of the clerics is not from itself, but was propagated from the order of the married alone by the origin of the flesh; yet it was not instituted to procreate children of the flesh, but to evangelize the Word of God, just as Christ himself was, in whose image it was instituted. 

The order of monks proceeds from both: because if they come from the married, they are received into the monastic life by mutual consent, and from the clerics they are received into it much more freely. We have said that this order also "proceeds" well because, as if given to another or sent out, it even departs corporally from its own places to dwell where it was not before—just like the patriarch Jacob, who for a similar mystical reason departed from his own house to seek wives and children for himself in a foreign region. ### The Exposition of the Abbot's Book

[The previous section] expresses the order of the clerics, under which two inferior orders are contained: namely, the continent <note>Those who are celibate but not monks, such as secular priests.</note> and the married. However, there is not just one city, and its proper name is **Jerusalem**. Yet, while it remains in its earthly pilgrimage, it is known by the name **Church**. For even that which was once called the **Synagogue** was called Jerusalem, just as is that Church which is to come in the third state of the second age. It is no wonder if each is called Jerusalem individually and yet all three together are one Jerusalem; for we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person of the Deity to be God and Lord, yet we are forbidden by the Catholic religion from saying there are three Gods or three Lords.

The first Jerusalem, which is called the Synagogue, is designated in **Sarah**. I do not speak of the reprobate, whom **Hagar** designates, but of the elect, whom Sarah signifies; and this is when Sarah is viewed in relation to **Rebecca**. For when she is viewed in relation to Hagar, then Hagar designates the synagogue of the reprobate, while Sarah designates the Church called from the Gentiles. But when Sarah is placed in relation to Rebecca, then Sarah signifies the Synagogue—not regarding the reprobate, but regarding the elect. Rebecca, who was brought into Sarah’s tent, signifies the Gentile Church, which was established by the Lord who is the heir of the kingdom.

Therefore:
*   The **first Jerusalem**, called the Synagogue, is designated in **Sarah**.
*   The **second**, called the Church, is designated in **Rebecca**.
*   The **third**, which is more blessed, is designated in **Rachel**.

The first was joined to the Father through fear; the second was coupled to the Son through humility; the third was united to the Holy Spirit through devotion. Nevertheless, what is joined to one Person is joined to all three together, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, and the three peoples are one people. The first Jerusalem was built in the first state; the second in the second; the third in the third. However, the third of these, which is to be built in the third state of the world, began to be built alongside the second from the very beginning of the second state. Indeed, those two are one together. In a great way, therefore, it was arranged in the second state that the life signified in Rebecca would seem to pertain properly to Christ. ### Concerning other mysteries of the sons of Jacob.
<margin>Chapter 21.</margin>

When he dealt above with the sons of Leah and Rachel according to the order of their birth and according to that understanding which pertains to the Second State <note>The "Second State" refers to the era of the New Testament and the literal Church.</note>, we find the last of Jacob's children to be the sons of Rachel: namely, Joseph and Benjamin. But when they entered the promised land, which was said to flow with milk and honey, those who appeared to be the last were found to be the first. Thus, in the place of Joseph his father, Joshua <note>The Latin uses "Iosue" for Joshua; the author links him to Joseph because Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim, Joseph's son.</note> ruled over the people; and he himself divided the land by a measuring line for the seven tribes who had not yet received an inheritance, and the first lot fell to the tribe of Benjamin. In a wonderful way, the one man John <note>Saint John the Apostle.</note> has a concord with two—namely, Joseph and Joshua. For just as Joseph was one of the twelve patriarchs, so John was one of the twelve apostles. And just as Joshua rose up in place of Joseph in his tribe and divided the inheritance among the seven tribes, so John divided the spiritual inheritance among the seven churches <note>A reference to the seven churches of Asia in the Book of Revelation.</note>, as we have already said. Nor is it strange if one John has a concord with Joseph and Joshua; for in these mysteries, the one tribe of Joseph is generally to be understood from the beginning to the end as if Joseph himself were present in it. The same applies to the others. However, it is certain that there is a reason for this great and sublime mystery. These are indeed deep secrets; yet for a man skilled and devoted to wisdom, they are quite necessary for the strengthening of faith. For we know that after Joseph, who ruled in Egypt, Moses was born there, who struck Egypt with every plague and led the children of Israel out of it. Joshua the son of Nun succeeded him (that is, Moses) to water and build upon what he himself had planted. Moreover, Moses designates the Son of God, who was born in the synagogue of the Jews, which is spiritually called "Egypt," and from which he led out the true children of Israel. Truly, Joseph, who preceded Moses in Egypt, signifies the Holy Spirit, in that he proceeds from the Father and first spoke through the prophets, announcing the coming of Christ in the flesh, and afterwards, descending to the Virgin, worked the incarnation of that same Son. That Joshua, who rose up in the tribe of Joseph as his own, finally received wisdom and teaching from Moses which he was to announce to the children of Israel, signifies that which the same Son says concerning the Holy Spirit: *For he will not speak on his own; but whatever he hears he will speak... and he will glorify me, for he will take of what is mine and announce it to you.* <note>original: "Non. n. loquet a semetipso: sed quicunque audiet loquet: & ille me clarificabit quia de meo accipiet & annuntiabit vobis." A quote from John 16:13-14.</note> Because of the secret of this sacred faith and pious profession, it pleased him who made all things according to the counsel of his will to store all these things in the sacred books and to seal them with worthy and manifold mysteries until the appointed time, so that these things would not perhaps be thought newly invented, but rather hidden and covered until the time of light and revelation arrived. Therefore, in the type of the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father, Joseph was exalted in the land of Egypt and solved the dreams of Pharaoh. In the type of the only-begotten Son of God, who descended from the heavens and was incarnated of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, Moses was born in Egypt; and he himself led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt and led them through the desert for forty years, seeking to introduce them into the land flowing with milk and honey. So that Moses might be born in Egypt, everything Joseph had in Egypt was the cause; for unless Joseph had ruled in Egypt, Jacob and his sons would not have gone to dwell there—although both events were predestined and came to effect by the Lord's disposal. But Moses, who led the people out of Egypt, died (and indeed for the sins of the people) and in a certain way failed on the way; he himself did not introduce the people into the land flowing with milk and honey, but Joshua the son of Nun did, who was from the tribe of Joseph. This is because, Christ having died for the sins of the people, the Paraclete <term>Paraclete</term><note>A title for the Holy Spirit, meaning "Advocate" or "Comforter."</note> Holy Spirit was sent and is still being sent to go before the faithful and introduce them truly into the land flowing with milk and honey, and to divide it among the seven tribes by a measuring line. That Joseph preceded from the beginning and Moses followed signifies the mystery of the Lord's incarnation, according to which the Holy Spirit is the beginning of the Son just as of all creatures, and according to what was said of Christ: that he was conceived of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. But when the ministry of labor was finished, it says Moses went up alone onto the mountain, and sent Joshua to go before the people and introduce them into the land of promise:

# Joachim’s Introduction to the Apocalypse

<margin>John 16</margin>
This signifies what the Lord says concerning himself and the Holy Spirit: "Unless I go away, the Counselor <note>Original: "paraclitus." This term refers to the Holy Spirit as an advocate, comforter, or helper.</note> will not come to 
<margin>John 14</margin>
you; but if I go, I will send him to you." And also: "But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit himself, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." For that land flowing with milk and honey was spoken of for no other reason than that one might understand what the Lord says 
<margin>John 16</margin>

For when he comes to the Church of Christ—which was once barren and empty—he soon makes her fruitful by his grace and causes her to flow with a double hope of doctrine: one which nourishes the little ones, the other which provides a taste for the mature. <margin>Psalm 30</margin>

To show that Joshua held the place of his father Joseph in this mystery, he held a similarity to his very name and, reaching the 
<margin>Genesis 50</margin>

And lest any doubt of faith should arise in the heart of the reader from this, or lest one think the Spirit who proceeds from the Father is different from the Spirit who proceeds from the Son, the similarity of the mystery is compressed in the New Testament; and there is given one man, John, who holds an equal cause of concord to both—that is, to Joseph and Joshua—so that what was shown there through those two, he shows here through one, which is completed in such an order.

### That Peter, Paul, and John carry the mystery of the Trinity. Chapter 22.

John was chosen by Christ from the beginning and was held as great among the first apostles, as he was the one whom the Lord loved more spiritually. Paul was the last of all the apostles, and as he himself says, the "least of the apostles." Yet he who was last by vocation was found at the end to be first in grace with Peter, the 

<column-break/>

prince of the apostles. Paul, called by lot to preach to the Gentiles, preached in Asia and laid there the foundation of the faith. When he departed from that same province, John arrived and built upon Paul’s foundation. And John did this because Paul—as he himself bears witness—did not wish to do it, lest he should be seen to be building upon 
<margin>Romans 15</margin>
another’s foundation. For he says this in the Epistle to the Romans: "Thus I have preached this Gospel, not where Christ was named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation." But if Paul does not wish to build upon the foundation of the prior apostles (of whom John was one), and yet John builds upon the foundation of Paul, either a mark of pride seems to fall upon Paul because he was deceptive, or the sentiment of Paul himself is true when he says: 
<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
"The letter kills, but the spirit gives life." For if you seek the reason according to the literal surface, it would seem more expedient for Paul to build upon the foundation of John and the other apostles who heard the Lord from the beginning and solemnly received the Holy Spirit, rather than for John to build upon the foundation of Paul, who was the least of all the apostles and called last by lot. And the "letter" indeed seems to want this; but because the reality is otherwise, the letter kills and does not give life; it destroys and does not build. But the Spirit does not act thus, but rather approves what was done. He demonstrates that it was necessary and faithful. For where John worked from the beginning with Peter, who was the father of the entire Church, because there was no mention of Paul, it signifies the Spirit of the Lord speaking through the prophets; and the Spirit of the Lord was fittingly noted by the people of the Jews, because there was no fitting confession of the Son of God among those same people. Whence it is said through the prophet: 
<margin>Isaiah 53</margin>
"Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" And he shall grow up, he says, like a tender plant before him and like a root out of thirsty ground. Therefore, although that carnal people understood the truth neither concerning the Spirit of God nor concerning the Son, nevertheless in the divine Scriptures there was frequent and fitting mention of the Holy Spirit, but rare and hidden mention of the Son. Why is this? Because concealment mostly belongs to humility, while revelation belongs to liberty. And humility properly pertains to the Son, while liberty pertains to the Holy Spirit. For both are shown in the divine Scriptures. # The Abbot’s Book of Explanations

Paul was chosen as the last of the sons of the humble: he who was baptized by the least of the disciples, and was made an apostle and preacher of the church. Who else does this "least" one signify—this Paul who, having completed his ministry of preaching, was found 

<margin>Philippians 2</margin>
in Rome sitting with the first apostle <note>St. Peter</note>—except him who "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in human form"? Who else, except him who was suddenly found as a small child in Bethlehem and placed in a manger? At the end, he speaks 

<margin>Revelation 3</margin>
in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> and says: "I sit with my Father on his throne." Now, the fact that a multitude of nations was converted to God through Paul's preaching signified that through the Gospel of Christ, the nations who previously did not know the living and true God were to be converted, just as indeed happened. And that as Paul was departing from Ephesus, John arrived and built upon Paul’s foundation: this signifies the coming of the Holy Spirit, about 

<margin>John 8</margin>
whom Christ said: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; however, when 

<margin>Galatians 2</margin>
he, the Spirit of Truth, comes, he will teach you all truth." <note>Note: While the margin notes John 8, the quote is from John 16:12-13.</note> Therefore, the fact that Paul went up to Jerusalem at the beginning to confer his Gospel with his predecessors, the apostles, signifies the humility of the Son of God, who was found by his mother in the temple among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And that John followed Paul in the preaching of Asia signifies the truth of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Lord says: 

<margin>John 16</margin>
"For he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you." For John received something from the doctrine of Paul to confirm those who had believed through his word. This was because Paul, when he was in Jerusalem with James and Peter, did not dare to cast aside circumcision on account of those among the Jews who had believed and were zealous for the Law; so much so that Paul said of him <note>Peter</note> and his fellow apostles that they had not walked uprightly toward the truth of the Gospel. 

<margin>Galatians 2</margin>
Afterward, following Paul—who had already labored long for this cause and endured many temptations—he [John] freely preached the grace of the Gospel of Christ.

<column-break/>

Thus, in the one person of John, there was shown mystically in the New Testament what had previously been shown in two men: namely, Joseph and Joshua. This is also to be observed in other scriptures. It should not seem absurd that one man, John, should have a concordance <note>a mystical or historical harmony</note> with two others, for a teacher speaks one way to perfected disciples who are men in both sense and age, and another way to those who are imperfect and established in the beginning of their education. For it is necessary to divide parts into syllables for those beginners; to those others, one does not speak in that way, just as a child is judged by his speech. Hence, the apostle said to some: 

<margin>Hebrews 6, Isaiah 10</margin>
"Leaving behind the initial talk of Christ—that is, the elementary word of Christ—let us be carried toward perfection." And the prophet: "The Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth." Therefore, the seven churches also have a double cause 

<margin>Romans 9</margin>
for comparison regarding their concordance. For in that understanding which pertains to the "second state" <note>The Age of the Son/the Church</note>, the Church of Ephesus agrees in its mysteries with Reuben; the Church of Smyrna with Simeon; the Church of Pergamum with Levi; the Church of Thyatira with Judah and with Rachel. When this same Judah was born, the sister <note>Rachel</note> envied Leah and said to Jacob: "Give me children, otherwise I shall die"—or rather, she is linked with Bilhah, her handmaid, who conceived and gave birth upon her knees. For because Rachel could not have children of her own, she gave her handmaid to her husband so that she might see herself having children through her. For as we have already said, Rachel’s handmaid signifies the flesh of the soul seeking God, which is consecrated to God in virginity and chastity. Many, provoked by her example, are born as if from the handmaid of the barren mother, Rachel. Why from a handmaid? Because those who emulate virginity but do not emulate the contemplative life are indeed joined to the contemplatives by the likeness of purity and chastity; but because they do not reach that purity of which it is said: "Blessed 

<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," they can be called sons of Rachel's handmaid, but they cannot be called sons of Rachel. Therefore, those who had this grace from the beginning of the church were reckoned as being in Rachel, who for that reason was without children: because those who possess this grace were few. For the time had not yet come when this grace would reach many; because in the "third state" of the world, in the power and operation of the Holy Spirit, it was to be revealed so that in him all perfection may receive its consummation.

# John’s Introductory Book on the Apocalypse

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> For he himself is the love of God. And it is written of love <note>original: "charitate"</note> that it "thinks no evil"; because of this, "perfect love casts out fear." Therefore, the church of Thyatira possesses a certain harmony <note>original: "concordiam," a technical term for a mystical historical parallel</note> with Judah; it also has a harmony with Rachel's maidservant <note>Bilhah</note>. ¶ Furthermore, the church of Sardis is linked to the remaining sons of Leah and the maidservants alike: who altogether with Dinah were seven in number. The church of Philadelphia, which is the sixth in number, is linked to Joseph. The church of Laodicea is linked to Benjamin. This arrangement belongs to the understanding of the **second state** <note>The Age of the Son, or the current era of the Church</note>. However, in the understanding which pertains to the **third state** <note>The Age of the Holy Spirit, which Joachim believed was coming</note>, it is as follows: From the sixth period of the second state, the third state must begin, along with a **new order** which is created in the image of the Holy Spirit, signified in Joseph and John the Evangelist. Because just as the Holy Spirit has seven gifts, so too that order will have seven spiritual orders proceeding from it. One, namely, is joined to it just as the church of Ephesus was to Saint John. The other six on either side—following the likeness of the lampstand which Moses made in the wilderness—assign a harmony of Ephesus to Benjamin, to whom the first lot fell when Joshua gave the seven lots to the seven tribes so that they might divide their inheritance. 

The harmony <margin>Joshua 21</margin> of Smyrna belongs to the tribe of Simeon; the harmony of Pergamum to the tribe of Zebulun; the harmony of Thyatira to the tribe of Issachar; the harmony of Sardis to the tribe of Asher. The harmony <margin>Joshua 2</margin> of Philadelphia belongs to the tribe of Naphtali; the harmony of Laodicea to the tribe of Dan. This is the end of the third state; and this is the assignment of the seven churches according to that understanding which pertains to the third state: that is, from the time when Israel shall be converted to the Lord, once the "fullness of the Gentiles" has been completed (about which <margin>Romans 11</margin> Paul speaks in his letter to the Romans) until the end of the age. Therefore, in the second state, something is found according to its meaning to pertain commonly to both the Son and the Holy Spirit: that is, the significance of Rebecca, who was the wife of Isaac, and the significance of Leah and Rachel, who were the wives of Jacob. In the third state, however, only that remains which pertains to the Holy Spirit: that is, the significance of Rachel and Joseph and Joshua <margin>Joshua 18</margin> and the seven tribes to whom he himself divided the inheritance. But lest it seem obscure to anyone what has been said concerning the second and third states, let us frequently take the mysteries of Peter and John as an example. ¶ During the time of the second state, to which the **active life** properly belongs, the **contemplative life** was given in part; however, in the time of the third state, to which the contemplative life will properly belong, the active life should not be applied.

### Chapter 24.

That Peter and John (whom we mentioned above) have a relationship of mystery to one another is confirmed by frequent authority which grants faith, and the opening of that authority grants understanding. For Luke the Evangelist says of them in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles: "Peter and John were going up to the temple at the ninth hour, the hour <margin>Acts 3</margin> of prayer." And when the apostles had heard that Samaria had received the word of God, it says "they sent Peter and John to them." And in the Gospel something similar is found: indeed, the Lord is described as having sent Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal for him. By this, we are to understand that because we find those two apostles joined in mystery, they signify something great; although they differ according to the diversity of places (about which there is no room to discuss at length, as I am hurrying toward the end of this summary). 

However, it is appropriate here to set down and explain that which pertains more directly to the matter. Namely, from that place where it is written that the Lord said to Peter: "Follow me." But Peter, seeing <margin>John 21</margin> that disciple whom Jesus loved following them, questioned him and said: "But what about him?" The Lord answered both of them and said: "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me." This is because, in the feeding of the sheep, Peter succeeded in the place of Christ. But John was loved by Christ more than the others. In this place, Peter designates that which relates to Christ: namely, a life of labor, which he deigned to undergo for us. John, however, designates the quiet life <note>The contemplative life</note> which pertains to the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, John were to succeed in faith upon the death of Peter (that is, if John were called at the time Peter passed away), it would be clearly understood that the second state pertains absolutely to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit. But because they were called by the Lord by lot almost at the same time—and perhaps on the same day and at the same hour—namely, Peter and John; and yet they did not pass from this world to God at the same time, but first...

# The Abbot’s Book of Exposition

...Peter indeed: but long after him, John. It is clear that the **second state** <note>The Age of the Son, spanning from Christ to Joachim’s own time</note>—which is designated by the course of Peter—pertains not only to the life of Peter, but also to the life of John. However, the **third state** <note>The Age of the Holy Spirit, which Joachim believed would be a time of monastic peace and spiritual understanding</note> pertains truly to the life of John. If you seek the light of understanding, it is clear, and it is most necessary for our faith: namely, that we are taught to grasp a certain sacred mystery. That is, that two are sent by the One: namely, the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent from the Father. But from the Son, only one is sent: that is, the Holy Spirit; and it is none other than the Holy Spirit himself who is sent and proceeds from the Father. Since this is the case, it is not absurd to ask why the second spiritual state is ascribed to the Son, so that the fullness of grace is understood to be in the Son—just as it is in the Holy Spirit—lest it be thought (heaven forbid!) that the Son could do nothing without the help of the Holy Spirit’s grace. But it must be noted that as long as John remained with Peter, he seemed to yield to him in all things as to his elder. Thus, while John was standing by, Peter spoke to the lame man and said: <margin>Acts 3</margin> "Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, I give to you." While John was standing by, he rebuked Simon Magus and said: "May your money perish with you." Why say more? Read through the Acts of the Apostles in order and you will find that Peter preached as the leader: he condemned Ananias and Sapphira with a sentence of death; he healed a vast multitude of the sick by the mere touch of his shadow; he escaped the hands of the raging Herod not without a miracle; he raised Tabitha from the dead; and he called Cornelius and those with him to the faith of Christ after revelations were sent to both sides. These things we read specifically about Peter in the book of the Acts of the Apostles. But of John, nothing is said, except what is said in common of all <margin>Acts 5</margin> the apostles: "And by the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people." It was as if John were waiting and saying: "My time has not yet come; meanwhile I must yield to Peter, whose proper time it is now." But the days will come when Peter himself shall be called from this world to God, and then I shall begin to fulfill the course of my ministry. And indeed, after the death of Peter, we read that John preached in Asia: namely, to the seven churches that were in it. He described this book <note>Revelation</note> and the Gospel more excellently than the others; and according to what is handed down in that scripture written about his life, God worked great

<column-break/>

signs and wonders through him there. Therefore, although they were called at the same time and sent out to preach together with the rest—namely, Peter and John—because John (as the younger) was seen to defer to Peter while he was alive, it is clear enough through this mystery what faith requires in reality: namely, that the **second state** belongs in common to the Son and the Holy Spirit, yet more properly to the Son than to the Holy Spirit. This is seen in Rachel and Leah, who were joined in marriage to Jacob within the same span of time, yet both were not made mothers at once. First, within the course of seven years, Leah the firstborn was made a mother; then Rachel conceived and gave birth, even into the second period. Therefore, just as the **first state** <note>The Age of the Father/Old Testament</note> is properly ascribed to God the Father; the **second** belongs in common to the Son and the Holy Spirit, yet more properly to the Son; and the **third** to one of them, that is, the Holy Spirit. Thus, the understanding of the second state is common to both the **active** and **contemplative** lives <term>active and contemplative: the "active" life involves external works and preaching (Peter), while the "contemplative" life involves internal prayer and mystical vision (John)</term>; it is common to the six and the seven <note>Joachim links the "six" to the days of creation/work and "seven" to the Sabbath/rest</note>; common to the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet it fits the active life more than the contemplative; the six more than the seven; and the Son more properly than the Holy Spirit. But the understanding of the third state belongs properly to the Holy Spirit, because "that which is spiritual is not first, but that which is physical <note>original: "animale," often translated as "soulish" or "natural"</note>; then that which is spiritual." <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> For the physical pertains to the **active life**, which the Son of God deigned to undergo for our salvation. But the **spiritual** pertains to the **contemplative life**, which is proper to the Holy Spirit, as the Scripture witnesses when it <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> says: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." And it was very useful for that [active life] to withdraw so that this [contemplative life] might follow happily. In this matter, one should consider diligently that the greatest discernment must be used in the scripture of testimony to distinguish between those words which can refer to the second state alone, and those which pertain to both together—that is, to the second and the third. For those words which pertain to the active life refer absolutely to the second state; but those which pertain to the contemplative life refer to both the second and third together, although they refer more properly to the third. For the property of the third state is contemplation, just as action is the property of the second. Therefore, if this word which was spoken by Saint Luke in the Acts of the Apostles: <margin>Acts 1</margin> "But you shall be baptized..."

### John’s Introductory Work on the Apocalypse

"You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now" <note>original: "baptizabimini spū sancto nō post multos hos dies," quoting Acts 1:5</note> and that which is joined to it: "You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the end of the earth." <note>original: "Eritis mihi testes in hierusalem..." quoting Acts 1:8</note> If we weigh these discretely, we find that the first of these—which is contemplative—pertains to both states. The second—which is active—pertains to the second state only. For certainly, preaching is a matter of action, while being baptized by the Spirit is a matter of contemplation; for in the former there is labor, but in the latter there is rest. 

Therefore, in the forty days in which the Lord showed himself alive to his disciples through many proofs—appearing to them for forty days and speaking of the kingdom of God—we recognize the light of the time of the second state. For then it is necessary that what follows be universally fulfilled: "You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the end of the earth." 

<margin>Acts 1</margin>

For it is necessary that these things be fulfilled at the end of the second state; that end, indeed, must be called the beginning of the third. It is designated by forty [days] in a certain respect—or even by fifty days—or even by the entire time in which Christ and the apostles preached in the world, specifically up until the passion <note>the martyrdoms</note> of the apostles Peter and Paul, who individually in their own works designate the second state. 

However, when we take the time of the third state universally as the forty or fifty days of the time called "Easter-tide" <note>original: "paschale," the season from Easter to Pentecost</note>—just as we take the time of the second state as the days of Lent <note>original: "quadragesime"</note>—this understanding is more appropriate than the one written before. Then indeed we say that what is promised regarding the outpouring of the Holy Spirit is to be fulfilled more broadly and perfectly at the end of the second age. 

But yet, that which follows: "And you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the end of the earth"—and many things that follow in the same book—have no place in this part of the mystery. For in that blessed life which will follow after the end of the age, just as there will be no time for marriage, so there will be no preaching. For in the resurrection, as the Lord says: "they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God in heaven," and they will be children of God, since they are children of the resurrection. 

<margin>Acts 1</margin>

<margin>Matthew 22</margin>

This rule of interpretation, laboriously

<column-break/>

sought out and so fruitfully discussed, is such that one would hope in vain to assign the tropes <term>tropes: "thropos" here refers to the figurative or spiritual senses of scripture</term> of the Scriptures without it. These tropes, poured out with diverse properties, run through various points, not only in this book [the Apocalypse] of which we specifically speak, but also in every sacred page of both the Old and New Testaments. 

Wherefore it befits the spiritual man to be attentive to this very thing: to vigilantly attend to what should be taken in what respect, how, and when. At the same time, he should study to consider what differs between words and words in the divine page. Thus, when the beginning of this book is ascribed to the beginning of the second state, he should not doubt that there is something in it that pertains individually to both lives; and when the beginning of the third state is established as the beginning of that same book, setting aside all those things that pertain to the active life, he should study to hold only those things that pertain to the contemplative. 

And these indeed are simple and few, because Martha (as the Lord says) "is anxious and troubled about many things." 

<margin>Luke 10</margin>

But for Mary, "not many things, but one is necessary." <note>Joachim compares the active life of the Church to Martha and the contemplative life of the future age to Mary.</note> Thence it is that in the series of this book, six parts indeed are ascribed specifically to the second state; but the seventh part alone to the third state, and the eighth alone to the future life <note>the eternal life after history</note>. For here [in the second state] there is multiplicity, but there [in the third] there is simplicity. Indeed, the active life is occupied with many things and runs toward diverse ends. But the contemplative life is in one thing only: which is to gaze continually upon the living God. 

Wherever, therefore, in Divine Scripture, there is a discourse about two men or two women, it ought to be rightly understood by us as designating these two lives—which the saints of God often commemorate. We must confess that the second state pertains to both, just as it pertains to Peter and John equally; but to the third state, only one pertains, which belongs to John. This is according to the fact that after Peter suffered, John alone was left. 

From this matter, it is also clearly weighed: that whether it is Christ Jesus when he is placed in respect to John the Baptist, or John the Evangelist when he is placed in respect to Peter, they have a place in the second state in such a way that they belong more properly to the third. John the Baptist and Peter, however, are not in both the second and third states together, but in the second only. Therefore, every...

...Scripture: or almost all of it: which, according to the spiritual understanding <term>spiritual understanding: a deeper, non-literal interpretation of the Bible used to find prophetic meaning</term>, properly regards Christ; it is properly to be completed in the second state <term>second state: the Age of the Son, the period of the Church from the time of Christ until Joachim's own era</term>. This is because Christ willed to become human, to preach, to be afflicted, and to suffer, so that he might rescue us from such a miserable condition. And because the man Christ Jesus carries the type <note>original: "typum gerit," meaning he serves as a prophetic model</note> of the Holy Spirit—just as John the Baptist did for Christ—we ought to assign all things written about John the Baptist according to the letter <note>original: "ad literam," the literal historical meaning</note> within the limit of the second state in the Spirit. But those things written about Christ we assign to the second and third, though more properly to the third. For the third state (as we have often said) more properly belongs to the Holy Spirit; thus, whatever is written about the labor and preaching of Christ should be referred to the second state rather than the third, especially when something regarding him occurs in relation to the Holy Spirit.

### Summary of all things that have been said in this book. Chapter 25.

<margin>Revelation 16</margin>
To bring together what has been said scatteringly into a summary: we ought to maintain five orders <note>original: "ordines," referring to specific ranks or groups of people in the Church</note> contained in the five parts of the book in a general sense. We should also assign in a specific sense <note>original: "in specie"</note> seven others designated in the seven churches, to which this book is specially destined; and nevertheless six periods of time <note>original: "sex tempora"</note> spent in labor, of which the sixth is double because two churches are contained in it at once. Furthermore, the seventh period will be in rest, and the eighth in the homeland <term>homeland: "patria" in Latin, a standard medieval term for Heaven</term>. If all these things are diligently noted, there will be no difficulty (with God's help) in understanding why this book encompasses five general orders in its five parts, or six periods of labor; or why, in the seven divisions of the first part, it treats the seven churches as a type <note>a symbolic representation</note> of seven special orders belonging properly to the Holy Spirit, just as the general ones belong to Christ. For that which is "general" seems as if corporeal and animal <note>original: "corporale et animale," meaning physical and related to the basic biological soul</note>; that which is "special" is as if incorporeal and spiritual. And while the former is more easily known, the latter is not so easy to understand. Unless all these things are cautiously discussed, it is difficult to examine them in the "head" <note>Christ</note> or the members of the body <note>the Church</note>. Because of this, I seem to have drawn out a longer period of time in this little book to track down and untie the knots of the mysteries, lest necessity should then force us to survey unexperienced shores when, with the golden sails set, it is not permitted to turn away from the sandbanks <note>original: "syrtibus," referring to the treacherous Syrtis shoals off the coast of Africa</note>.

### On the parts of the book.

The first part of the book, in which mention was made of the Lord’s Day and the angels, is ascribed to the pastors of the seven churches. The second, in which it treats the Lamb who was slain and the seven openings of the seals, is ascribed to the martyrs. The third, in which it treats the angel offering incense before the golden altar and the seven angels sounding the trumpets, is ascribed to the doctors <term>doctors: "doctores," the learned teachers and theologians of the Church</term>. The fourth, in which it treats the woman clothed with the sun and her son, and the 144,000 who were not defiled with women, is ascribed to the virgins. The fifth, in which it treats the temple of the tabernacle and the sea of glass mixed with fire, and the seven angels coming out of it, is ascribed to the general Church. Because these five orders indeed do battle in mortal flesh, yet do not fight in a carnal <note>physical or worldly</note> way, it is not in vain that each of them is described as having seven periods of time—since it is clearer than light that six periods are given to those struggling in labor, and the seventh as a Sabbath, so that they may rest as God did from His works. To state briefly what this book encompasses more broadly: what do we say Babylon is, if not the kingdom of the devil which is in hell? And what is Jerusalem, if not the kingdom of God which is in heaven? There are therefore two contrary kings: Almighty God and the devil; one who is called the king of the South <note>original: "austri"</note> and the other who is called the king of the North <note>original: "aquilonis"</note>. Similarly, there are two cities: one Jerusalem, which is the kingdom of God, and the other Babylon, which is the kingdom of the devil (though they call it a "kingdom" improperly <note>original: "abusive," meaning the word is used incorrectly since a true kingdom belongs only to God</note>, for whatever is an adversary to the true kingdom). Jerusalem has four animals—that is, four orders of soldiers—who fight for her; and she nonetheless prevails as much as she can, because each of the orders (as we wrote above) has its own time. Babylon also has four beasts who fight for her, which at the command of God will rise up at the last against her, "because there is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord" <note>original: "non est pax impijs dicit dñs," quoting Isaiah 48:22</note>.

<meta>This page continues Abbot Joachim of Fiore’s exploration of biblical interpretation. Having established that historical figures can have multiple meanings, he now distinguishes between mere "opinion" based on external appearances and true "spiritual understanding" granted by the Holy Spirit. This leads into a discussion on why certain biblical mysteries—like the fate of the bodies of Moses and the Virgin Mary—remain hidden from us.</meta>

### Books of the Abbot's Exposition

...he says: or if something is presumed, it should not be called understanding, but merely an opinion of some kind—for instance, where it is said: "In the days of **Antipas**, my witness" <note>original: "In diebus antiphas testis meus" (Revelation 2:13). Antipas was a martyr of the early church, but little was known of him in the Middle Ages.</note> and "I will give to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days" <margin>Revelation 11</margin> and similar passages. For if it is asked according to the letter <note>The "literal" or historical meaning of the text.</note> who this **Antipas** was, it is entirely unknown; and if someone says that those two prophets written of in this book are **Enoch** and **Elijah**, <note>A common medieval tradition held that the "Two Witnesses" of Revelation were these two Old Testament figures who never died.</note> he may say so by way of opinion based on certain external conjectures. He does not say this by understanding and asserting, because what those two signify can be stated not through a doubtful opinion, but through a certain understanding. It is one thing to compare one thing to another; it is quite another to state what this or that actually is. 

For example: let us suppose there is a man who has never seen ships nor learned their names. If he were led by chance to the shore and saw small vessels passing nearby, while large ships were driven by the winds through the deep sea, it would be easy for him to say: "These small vessels are similar to those others, though unequal in size." But to name each one, to say where they were built, where they came from, or where they are going—this he cannot understand unless he hears it from someone who tells him. 

So it is regarding the "face of the letter" <note>The literal, surface meaning of the text.</note>: only the writer himself, if he were present, or someone else who saw or wrote about the same thing, could know. Perhaps that writer would record what the other remains silent about—as often happens in the Gospel. Where something might lead to doubt, he should simply be questioned. However, in allegorical matters, <note><term>allegorical</term>: A method of interpretation where people and events in the Bible represent deeper spiritual or prophetic truths.</note> it is not so; rather, "the Spirit blows where it wills" <margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin> and "divides its own to each as it wills." <note>original: "spūs vbi vult spirat: & diuidit de suo singulis prout vult." A combination of John 3:8 and 1 Corinthians 12:11.</note> For just as it is not to be doubted that it was the divine will for the **Word of God** to become incarnate, to speak to men in the language of the flesh, and to teach his disciples first with his own mouth—and then in the course of time to send the **Holy Spirit** who, without the help of human teaching, would teach them not the shadow of the truth found in the letter, but the truth itself which is in the spirit—so it is His will that in recognizing the letter of both Testaments, we should presume nothing except what is written by the accounts of others or by opinion. Instead, we should venerate only the mastery of those who wrote it, unless perhaps what is added can be proven from elsewhere. But in spiritual

<column-break/>

understanding, in which the truth lies, honor and glory must be shown to the **Holy Spirit** alone, who, having put to flight the darkness of ignorance, teaches His chosen ones every certainty of the truth.

### Why the Lord wished to hide the body of his mother Mary. Chapter 27.

If, therefore, we are constrained by the letter when men demand from us what Scripture does not say—as if someone were to ask: "What became of the body of **Moses**? Of the body of the **Lord’s mother**? Of the body of **John**?"—what else should we answer but that we do not know? And if perhaps someone reproaches us, saying, "If you do not know these things, where is your understanding?" let him understand it himself if he can! For this reason, God wished to hide these very things from His chosen ones: so that in this very concealment which was made for a time, we might have an understanding quite worthy of relating. 

For example: He who in the beginning created man, forming him from the mud of the earth, "breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." <note>Genesis 2:7.</note> Therefore, one man consisted of two things: that is, of the visible and the invisible; that is, of the flesh and the <term>rational soul</term>. <note>The "rational soul" (anima rationalis) was the part of the human being believed to possess intellect and immortality.</note> But when men began to die and return to the dust of the earth from which they were taken, many who saw this were greatly afraid, thinking there was no "breath of life" and no life of the soul after the destruction of the flesh. 

Because it was to happen that He would come who was to redeem the human race and teach the sons of men that there is life of the soul after the death of the flesh, He wished to demonstrate this very thing through mysteries and express it through signs—so that in His Gospel, not only words but also the signs of His works might bear witness. We have said there are two parts: the flesh and the soul; one visible, the other invisible; one which receives the end of life through death, the other which lives after the death of the flesh and remains without end. In the likeness of these, then, two and two were chosen by the Lord, of whom one would be seen to die, and the other would not be seen, but would be thought to remain—in a <term>type</term>, <note>A "type" is a person or event in history that foreshadows or symbolizes a later spiritual reality.</note> namely, of the flesh and the soul. The first of these dies; the second lives. The first is dissolved into the dust of the earth; the second is left and remains forever. Therefore, there were chosen...

# John’s Introduction to the Apocalypse

**D 1**

...two for the governance of the people: namely, **Aaron** and **Moses**. One who designates the body—the first one <note>Aaron</note>—because the body was formed before the soul; the other who designates the soul, which is called the "breath of life" <note>original: "spiraculum vite" (Genesis 2:7)</note>. And **Aaron** rightly represents the body, since he was chosen to speak to the people; **Moses** represents the soul, who spoke to God. For when we wish to speak to humans, we cannot speak to them except through the tongue of the flesh; but to God, who is not flesh but spirit, we seek to speak with the mouth in vain unless we also speak with the mind. 

Now, **Aaron** was seen to have died <note>original: "occubuisse," literally "to have fallen" or "lain down" in death</note>, but **Moses** was not seen to die; rather, he disappeared while still living, as if to show that he remained alive. This is because the body, which **Aaron** signifies, is turned into the dust of the earth and ceases to be as it was before. But the soul, which **Moses** designates, lives in itself even after the death of the flesh; remaining in its own place, it waits to take back what it laid down in life. 

Lest the meaning signified in these two should seem insufficient, other witnesses were brought forward to designate the same thing. For **Elizabeth** and **Mary** were joined to designate this very point: the first is believed to have "fallen asleep" <note>died</note> clearly, like other humans; but concerning the second, regarding her passing—how she departed from this world and what became of her sacred body—there is no certainty. Two apostles were also joined to designate this same thing: namely, **Peter** and **John**, 
<margin>John 21</margin>
in that place where it was said to **Peter** by the Lord: "Follow me." And when that same **Peter** asked about **John**, it was added: "If I want him to remain until I come," which pertains to the fact that a saying went out among the brothers that this disciple would not die. And these things were indeed predicted by the Lord, who knows all things before they happen; or rather, who knows which thing stands for what, and who knows how to predict what he himself foreknew he would do. For just as **Simon Peter** was older than **John**, so he first completed his course through the palm of martyrdom. **John**, however, as tradition hands down, descended into his tomb alive and unharmed; yet, when sought, he did not appear, just like the Mother of the Lord and **Moses**, as if God had taken him. from the flesh, just as our Lord says: "He is not

But now let those who complain about their ignorance of the "letter" <note>The literal, surface-level meaning of the Bible.</note> consider and learn that this ignorance itself is sometimes a path to wisdom. When certain things are kept from us by God's will, such great floods of wisdom and knowledge flow from the "abyss" of this non-knowing. Let them know that the saying of the Psalmist is true: 
<margin>Psalm 138</margin>
"As is its darkness, so is its light" <note>original: "Sicut tenebre eius ita et lumen eius" (Psalm 139:12). Joachim suggests that even what is hidden in Scripture has a divine purpose.</note>. It is good, therefore, to be ignorant of some things according to the "surface of the letter which kills," so that the "spirit which lives" may be established and the intellect may be brought to life. 

This <term>spiritual intellect</term><note>The deeper, non-literal meaning of the Bible revealed by the Holy Spirit.</note>, like the Holy Spirit, is simple in substance but rich in gifts. Just as the Spirit is one and the same, yet there are many divisions of His graces, so too is the spiritual intellect one, yet its forms are many. There are four general categories of it that proceed from the single fountain of the literal text: **Typic**, **Historical**, **Moral**, and **Allegorical**. The **Typic** is divided into seven species gathered under that one name as if in a bundle. The **Allegorical** is divided into three: namely, **Tropological**, **Contemplative**, and **Anagogical**. 

Thus, there are five general "understandings" distinguished by their own names, and seven special species. 
The first of the five understandings is called **Historical**. 
The second is **Moral**. 
The third is **Tropological**. 
The fourth is **Contemplative**. 
The fifth is **Anagogical**. 

1. The <term>Historical understanding</term><note>Finding spiritual parallels in historical events or people.</note> is the likeness of a visible thing to an invisible one: for example, a certain virgin of Christ <note>the Church</note> is designated in the "free woman" <note>Sarah</note>, and a married woman in the "slave woman" <note>Hagar</note>. 
2. The <term>Moral understanding</term><note>Applying the text to the internal life and struggle of the individual soul.</note> is the likeness of a visible thing to an invisible one according to a part, or according to the whole: as when the slave woman signifies the flesh which gave birth in servitude, and the free woman signifies the mind—provided it is free—which rejoices in spiritual leisure and rest. 
3. The <term>Tropological understanding</term><note>original: "tropologica," often used for moral instruction, but here Joachim links it specifically to the "doctrine" of letter vs. spirit.</note> is that which pertains to doctrine: as when the slave woman signifies the "letter" <margin>Galatians 4</margin> and the free woman signifies "spiritual understanding." 
4. The <term>Contemplative understanding</term><note>Focusing on the internal spiritual experience and the different ways of living the faith.</note> is that which pertains especially to the gifts of the Holy Spirit: as when the slave woman signifies the "active life" and the free woman the "contemplative life"; or the slave woman signifies "servile fear" and the free woman the "grace of the Holy Spirit," which is the love of God and neighbor—because in the former there is slavery, but in the latter there is...

...liberty. **Anagogical** <term>anagogical: from the Greek for "leading upward," this level of interpretation focuses on the ultimate spiritual reality of heaven and the afterlife</term> understanding is that which pertains to the heavenly homeland, or sometimes to God himself. For example, the handmaid [Hagar] signifies the earthly homeland, while the free woman [Sarah] signifies that Jerusalem which is above, who is our mother. It is called **historical** understanding because it is not far from the history, but walks entirely near it and according to it. It is called **moral** because it shapes our character. It is called **tropological** <term>tropological: from the Greek 'tropos' (way/turn) and 'logos' (word); the interpretation that provides a moral or ethical lesson</term> because it encompasses the manners of the speeches of God. For *tropos* in Greek is "manner" or "way" in Latin, and *logos* is "discourse." Thus, it is tropological because it encompasses and distinguishes the manner of God’s words. It is called **contemplative** because it makes one contemplate the invisible things of God, as the Apostle says: *While we contemplate not the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen.* It is called **anagogical** because it is superior to the others, dealing with God himself or with that heavenly homeland where those predestined for life—all these labors having ceased—shall remain in peace without end or failing.

Indeed, the seven typical understandings are to be referred to the various states of the world, about which we have spoken sufficiently in the second book of the *Psaltery of Ten Strings* <note>Joachim of Fiore’s *Psaltarium decem chordarum*, a work explaining his theology of the Trinity through the metaphor of a ten-stringed instrument</note>, just as we did regarding the five described above. We showed what suits the first three, what suits the following three, and what suits the last—and what is more necessary, why this or that is so, and what the benefit is. These things regarding the diversity of mysteries have been said summarily and briefly, lest anyone think that what appears diverse is actually contrary; for truth is by no means subject to the mysteries, but the mysteries are subject to the truth. Nor should we be concerned about the diversity of the paths, provided that the different ways lead to the one city.

Therefore, the Revelation of Christ is the work of truth; because the things he himself was going to do in the fullness of time, the divinely inspired prophets spoke of.
