->D 3<-
<meta>catchword: where</meta>

[This revelation] completes all those things which were predicted by the prophets or prefigured in the works of the patriarchs. And he well added: *Which God gave him to make known to his servants what must soon take place* <note>original: "Quam dedit illi deus palam facere servis suis quae oportet fieri cito"</note>; because Christ came into the world around the final hour. This revelation, however, was not made manifest at the moment it was shown to Saint John, nor when it began at the Lord’s resurrection; rather, it is made manifest in the Church during the "sixth age" <term>sixth age: in Joachim's theology, the history of the world is divided into ages; the sixth age is the time of the New Testament leading toward a final era of spiritual peace</term>, the beginnings of which we now hold. This is seen, for instance, in the hand of that angel who was seen descending from heaven, where the book that was once closed is now shown to be open. But to whom is it permitted for this revelation to be made? Surely not to the children of this world, to whom the Lord says under the figure of Jerusalem: <margin>Luke 19</margin> *In this your day, the things that are for your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes.* Is it for those who hide pearls and tear apart those who offer them? Not at all. "Not to them," he says, but to **his servants**; not to those, but to the ones to whom he had already said: <margin>Matthew 13</margin> *To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God; but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.* Thus, he does not reveal the secrets of the sacred mysteries to everyone who seems to hear the word of God, but only to his elect. For some hear unto judgment, so that they have no excuse; others hear unto salvation, so that by hearing they may believe, and by believing they may perform what is good, and by performing it they may attain eternal life. It follows:

<margin>Text 2</margin>
### And he signified it, sending his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever he saw.

## It should be noted that in this book the name "angel" is hardly ever introduced simply, as if the name "angel" did not designate some holy person, or an order, or something pertaining to the matter in a mystical sense. For it is the custom of the Holy Scriptures that men sent by God are called "angels," <margin>Matthew 11, Malachi 3</margin> just as John the Baptist, of whom it is said: *Behold, I send my angel,* and Elijah the prophet, in whose spirit John preceded the Son of God, and who himself shall come as a forerunner at the end, to turn the hearts of the fathers 

<column-break/>

to the children before the great day of the Lord comes. <margin>Malachi 4, Luke 1</margin> Not only these, who are of such high standing that among those born of women none are believed to be greater, but even the ministers of the altar themselves are called "angels of God," as the prophet attests: <margin>Malachi 2</margin> *The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.* Therefore, in this place, "angel" designates spiritual teachers and those announcing heavenly sacraments. Indeed, it signifies the living Spirit of God who speaks His words through them. Saint John, however, represents the "order of contemplatives" <term>order of contemplatives: for Joachim, this refers to a future or current group of monks and spiritual people who perceive the deeper, hidden meanings of Scripture</term> to whom it is given—as we have already mentioned—to know the mysteries of the Word of God. Therefore, the angel speaks to John so that John may write down what he has heard for the others. For what spiritual teachers indicate to perfect disciples—or indeed what the Author, the Spirit Himself, pours into the God-fearing person—these perfect disciples then present to the crowds of the faithful. This is because the Holy Spirit is the teacher of spiritual men, and spiritual men are the teachers of those who seek to understand spiritual words through the gift of that same Spirit. Rightly, then, as a model of a teacher, it is added concerning John: <margin>Revelation 1</margin> *Who bore witness to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever he saw.* For while the disciples of truth preach the words of life to men, they "bear witness to the word of God"—that is, to the Son—because He is true God begotten of true God before all ages; and they bear "testimony of Jesus Christ," because He is true man born of a Virgin mother in time. He who bore witness, he says, to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever he saw. One who bears witness without knowing is either a liar or a flatterer. God does not approve of such witnesses but rejects them; for he who speaks of what he knows he does not know calls upon a conscious witness against himself, even if what he says is true. For it is better for an ignorant person to hear the witness along with others than to bear witness when he has not been called, lest by refusing to be a disciple of truth, he becomes a teacher of error to the detriment of his own soul. Therefore, the disciples of truth do not bear witness regarding things they do not know, but rather things they learn reverently, either by reading or by hearing from the mouths of spiritual men who announce these things to them, or certainly things they receive from the Spirit himself, who blows where [he wills].

He emphasizes that the revelation is intended only for the "servants of God" who can understand its spiritual mysteries.</summary>

<margin>Luke 11</margin> But blessed are those who, even as they are taught, hear the word of God and keep it. <note>original: "Beati autem sunt & ipsi: qui vel ipsis docentibus audiunt verbum dei & custodiunt illud"</note> Hence, it is added here:

<margin>Revelation 1:3</margin> ¶ Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written in it; for the time is near.

### Lesson

Reading pertains to the literate; hearing pertains to the unlearned <term>unlearned: original 'idiotas', referring to those who cannot read but can listen to the text read aloud</term>. Whether, therefore, one hears or one reads the words of this prophecy, let him rejoice that he is blessed in this; in this let him think himself happy: if he keeps those things which are written in it. For if anyone, according to the opinion of James: is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man considering his natural face in a mirror. <margin>James 1</margin> Truly, "prophecy" is what this book is called: not only specifically like certain others, but also generally; because whatever the great volumes of the prophets brought forth dispersedly and at length, the Spirit has compressed into the sum of this book of prophecy, according to what Isaiah, the distinguished among prophets, <margin>Isaiah 10; Romans 9</margin> mentioned in the prophecy of his work, saying: *The Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.* <note>original: "Verbum breuiatum faciet dominus super terram"</note> In the observation of commands, however, the delay of rewards is often a great hindrance. Lest, therefore, the observer should grow weary through the long duration of this life, John <margin>Apocalypse 1</margin> exhorts them here toward such great blessedness when he says: *Blessed is he who reads and who hears the words of this prophecy and keeps those things which are written in it; for the time is near.* <margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> Concerning this shortness of time, Paul says: *We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come*; and John himself, whose book this is, says: <margin>1 John 2</margin> *As you have heard that Antichrist comes, now many Antichrists have arisen; from which we know that it is the last hour.* John says this for this reason: so that the more the last day approaches, the more we may know that false Christs and false prophets are multiplying in the world; and so great a necessity lies upon us to cautiously "redeem the evil days," because sometimes we encounter those who are more false, who on account of a feigned appearance of religion are esteemed as truthful. In this matter, another thing is to be feared, which generates a danger of shipwreck regarding the faith: that while we encounter many false ones

<column-break/>

whom we think are truthful, we begin to hold both the good and the bad (indifferently) as suspect; and often we believe those to be liars who adhere more closely to God. And surely it is necessary that the simple suffer ruin through various precipices, while (with everyone suspected) they do not know from whom they should seek sound counsel. Such are these days, such as those which follow closely, of which the Savior says: <margin>Luke 17</margin> *Days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man.* The Apostle foresaw these days when he said: <margin>2 Timothy 3</margin> *In the last days perilous times will come, when they will not endure sound doctrine.* But in a crisis of such great necessity, I think no protection is better than for each person to continually commend himself in prayer to his almighty God with the great groan of compunction <term>compunction: a feeling of deep regret or remorse for sins, often accompanied by a desire for spiritual change</term>, saying: <margin>Psalm 12</margin> *Enlighten my eyes lest I ever sleep in death, lest my enemy say, "I have prevailed against him."* It should be noted in this work that up to the present place, Blessed John has maintained a sort of introductory style, indicating the name of the book and the cause, but also the fruit for the reader, the hearer, and the worker alike; and thus he wishes grace and peace to the seven churches, to whom he also explains the manner of the vision and the order in which it was revealed to him, concluding this in a high place where he begins to narrate the very words he had heard and seen to each church, saying: *And to the angel of the church of Ephesus, write.* Therefore, so that we also may place a certain point of departure in this work with the author, we make the first distinction in this place, so that we may take up the life-giving words from the greeting with another beginning.

# First Commentary on the Apocalypse of John #

->D 4<-

<margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> ...as Moses said in his final book: *He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the children of Israel.* <note>original: "Constituit terminos gentiu iuxta numeru filioru israel." This refers to the idea that the structure of the world and the Church is mirrored in the twelve tribes.</note> We have learned by the authority of Divine Scripture <margin>Genesis 49; Exodus 1</margin> that there were twelve sons of Israel. Therefore, so that the prophetic word might be fulfilled in us—or rather, so that the subsequent Testament <note>The New Testament</note> might agree with the prior one <note>The Old Testament</note>—it was necessary that twelve churches be founded in the New Testament in the same order that the twelve tribes of Israel are read to have been distributed in the obtaining of their possessions.

Indeed, Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh were assigned to the eastern side <term>eastern side: original 'plagam orientalem'</term> before the crossing of the Jordan River; the remaining part of Manasseh, along with Ephraim and Judah, were stationed on the other side of the river. And indeed, these five tribes, which seemed the greatest among the rest, were located in their possessions by a certain mediating boundary. The seven remaining tribes, who had not yet received an inheritance, received their command last, where they might divide the land among themselves by lot. The lot fell to Benjamin, who was the youngest and possessed the greatest grace, though he was the last; this is so that those who rejoice in great things may learn to embrace the smallest, and those who desire and ambition to be first may willingly consent to the humble.

But the order of the narrative itself demands that we first deal with the five primary tribes, so that while we grant to each of the first ones their due, we may pass more orderly to the harmony of those that follow. Reuben was the firstborn of Leah <margin>Genesis 29</margin>; Gad stood as the first among the sons of the handmaids; Manasseh and Ephraim, the twin offspring of Joseph (who was himself the firstborn of Rachel), were given the birthright among their uncles, so that they might inherit the grace which Reuben lost. Reuben lost his through incest <note>original: "incestus amisit," referring to Reuben sleeping with his father's concubine, Bilhah</note>, violating the chastity of his father's bed. Scripture also commends Judah <margin>Genesis 30</margin>, saying he was the strongest among his brothers, for which reason he received the leadership over all.

We have, therefore, five principal tribes from the Old Testament; we also have five principal churches from the New. The first of all these is Jerusalem; the second is Antioch; the third is Alexandria; the fourth is Constantinople; the fifth is Rome. Each is known to have flourished in such an order. Although the Roman Church excels in dignity on account of Peter, the first leader who founded it, and although Mark was sent by Peter from the city of Rome to the city of Alexandria, and though it is handed down that the Church of Constantinople received the honor of its patriarchate last, nonetheless, Rome is to be written at the end. This is because the other four, running their course in some way, failed along the way <note>This refers to the Eastern Patriarchates falling under Islamic rule or theological error in the author's view</note>, while Rome's final times were dearer in the purity of the faith. Because these churches were to be preferred over others, the prophet Isaiah foresaw them in the spirit. <margin>Isaiah 19</margin> *In that day,* he said, *there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan and swearing by the Lord of hosts; one shall be called the City of the Sun.*

<column-break/>

Just as Reuben was the firstborn of Israel, so the Church of Jerusalem was, so to speak, the firstborn of Christ. But just as the firstborn Reuben defiled his father's couch and lost his birthright, so the Church of Jerusalem—by interpreting the Scripture perversely and appearing to "Judaize" <term>Judaize: 'iudaizare', meaning to maintain Jewish legal customs instead of following Christian grace</term> the faithful through a carnal seed—justly lost the birthright that was owed to it. The birthright was given to Manasseh and Ephraim: that is, to the churches of Alexandria and Constantinople. Thus, Reuben is adapted to Jerusalem, Gad to Antioch, Manasseh to Alexandria, Ephraim to Constantinople, and Judah to the Holy Roman Church. But the Lord rejected <margin>Psalm 77</margin> the tabernacle of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim; instead, he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved. What this signifies is evident enough.

But just as Ephraim was preferred over Manasseh although Manasseh preceded him in birth, so the Church of Constantinople was preferred over Alexandria in the course of time, even though Alexandria was anciently written as first after the Roman Church. And just as Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh received their inheritance on the eastern side, while the other half-tribe with Ephraim and Judah was situated on the other side of the river, so the churches of Jerusalem, Antioch, and Alexandria were founded within the boundaries of the eastern region—that is, in the borders of that people from whom the faith began to arise among the patriarchs and prophets. Truly, from the great river Euphrates unto the river of Egypt, around whose borders these churches are situated, the possession was promised to the children of Israel, some of whom are known to have lived within those boundaries for some time. But what is designated in this place by the Jordan River except the grace of baptism and the Passion of Christ? The fact that Reuben and Gad and...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical mapping of the Twelve Tribes of Israel to the history of the Christian Church and the ages of the world. ### Part of the Exposition ###

The half-tribe of Manasseh, crossing the river Jordan at the command of Moses to do battle, preceded the remaining tribes. It is clear that these represent the faithful from the circumcision <note>The "circumcision" refers to the early Jewish converts to Christianity</note> who believed that the Law of Moses must be observed and that reverence must be shown to the words of the Law. Yet, being washed by the grace of baptism, they went out to preach to the Gentiles and endured the great agonies of torture for the name of Christ. On the other side, however, is the "son"—that is, among the nations of the Gentiles, where nothing of Judaism was practiced. Here, one part of Manasseh, along with Ephraim and the tribe of Judah, are known to have received vast possessions, representing the Church of Constantinople and the Roman Church. Nor should it be thought different that we say the Church of Alexandria is assimilated to the half-tribe of Manasseh, while the Church of Constantinople is the whole of Ephraim and the other half-tribe of Manasseh. For it is not read that the half-tribe of Manasseh which crossed the Jordan was divided from Ephraim, but rather received its possession together with it. Thus, the five greater tribes are known to correspond with the five principal churches <term>principal churches: the five Patriarchates of Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem</term>, just as the seven remaining tribes correspond with the seven churches in Asia, to whom this book was specifically sent, as is said in the following: *What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches which are in Asia: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.* <margin>Revelation 1</margin> These churches—by the dignity of their founders, the faith of their mysteries, the authority of their antiquity, and their number—along with the five named above, were made venerable so that the Scripture might be fulfilled and its meaning understood: *He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the children of Israel.* <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> For when the seven Asian churches are joined to the first five, exactly twelve churches are found to correspond individually to the twelve tribes. ¶ It is pleasing, however, to look upon these things in a broader way and to direct the sharp gaze of our eyes toward a spiritual understanding, so that we may show how these things, which we have learned agree so clearly, come together into one mystical sense. In Reuben is designated the first age of the world, beginning from the first parent <note>Adam</note>, to which the birth of the righteous Noah—or according to some, the flood—

<column-break/>

which occurred under him, gave an end. From Noah until Abraham followed the second age, designated in Gad. To this, the third age was joined: that is, from Abraham until David, designated in Manasseh, which appeared clearly distinct in two parts, since in that age the Lawgiver <note>Moses</note> appeared in the midst of the Jordan. Furthermore, the fourth age from David until Jechoniah <note>The Babylonian Captivity</note> is designated in Ephraim, which was succeeded by the fifth age, designated in Judah: from the migration to Babylon until Christ, or rather until the end of the primitive Church, in which the Law and circumcision reached their fulfillment. For Jesus Christ was made the mediator between the Law and Grace in such a way that he joined both Testaments in himself. Like a cornerstone, he coupled the two walls coming from different directions into one, dissolving the enmities of both, as the Apostle says <margin>Ephesians 2</margin>, and reconciling the two peoples in himself, according to what the angels are read to have sung at his birth: *Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.* <margin>Luke 2</margin> Rightly, however, is the first generation of the world, which began from the first parent, designated in the tribe of Reuben <margin>Genesis 49</margin>; for just as Reuben by right lost his birthright because he defiled his father’s bed, so the first man, falling in Paradise, lost the honor of his primacy which he had poorly guarded. These birthrights were then given to the sons of Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of a righteous father <note>Joseph</note>, as is read in the Book of Chronicles. For indeed the glory of the patriarchate, which would have befitted the first man had he not sinned, was given to Abraham and David, so that they might deserve to be called the fathers of Christ. <margin>Genesis 22; Psalm 131</margin> This is not because the first man is not also the father of Christ—since the entire human race is propagated from him—but because to these others the promise was made by the Lord through the grace of faith: namely, that in the seed of Abraham all nations would be blessed, and that the Lord would set the fruit of David's womb upon his throne. Rightly is Abraham with his offspring designated in Manasseh, which is interpreted as "oblivion" <note>original: "obliuio" or "forgetting"</note>; for to him it was first said by the Lord: *Go forth from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house* <margin>Genesis 12</margin>; so that there might be seen prefigured in him what was later said through the mouth of David to Holy Mother Church: *Hear, O daughter, and forget your people and your father's house.* <margin>Psalm 44</margin>

He uses the fall of Reuben to explain Adam's loss of primacy and the name "Manasseh" (forgetting) to explain Abraham's departure from his homeland.</summary>

# Explanation of the Parts #

The half-tribe of Manasseh, <note>original: "dimidia tribus" – the OCR "midia" is a fragment of "dimidia."</note> crossing the river Jordan at the command of Moses to do battle, preceded the remaining tribes. It is clear that this refers to the faithful of the circumcision <note>The "faithful of the circumcision" refers to the early Jewish Christians.</note> who believed that the Law of Moses must be observed and that reverence must be shown to the words of the Law; yet, having been filled with the grace of baptism, they preached to the Gentiles and endured the great agonies of torture for the name of Christ. But on the other side is the son: that is, in the nation of the Gentiles, where nothing of Judaism was practiced. Here, one part of Manasseh, along with Ephraim and the tribe of Judah, are known to have received large possessions, representing the Church of Constantinople and the Church of Rome. Nor should it be thought dissimilar that we compare the half-tribe of Manasseh to the Church of Alexandria, while the whole tribe of Ephraim and the other half-tribe of Manasseh are likened to the Church of Constantinople. For it is not read that the half-tribe of Manasseh that crossed the Jordan was divided from Ephraim, but rather received its possession together with it. Thus, the five greater tribes are known to correspond with the five principal churches, <note>The "Pentarchy" or five major episcopal sees of early Christianity: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem.</note> just as the seven remaining tribes correspond with the seven churches <margin>Revelation 1</margin> that were in Asia, to whom this book was specifically sent, as is said in the following: "What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches which are in Asia: to Ephesus, to Smyrna, to Pergamum, to Thyatira, to Sardis, to Philadelphia, and to Laodicea." <note>original: "Quod vides scribe in libro..." — Revelation 1:11.</note> These churches—through the dignity of their founder, the faith of their mysteries, the authority of their antiquity, and their number—along with the five noted above, were made venerable so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> says: "He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel." <note>original: "Constituit terminos gentiū..." — Deuteronomy 32:8.</note> For when the seven Asian churches are joined to the five primary churches, exactly twelve churches are found, which correspond individually to the twelve tribes. ¶ Now it is pleasing to look upon these things in a broader way, and to direct the sharp edge of our internal light toward a spiritual understanding, so that we may show how these things, which we have learned to agree so clearly, converge into one mystical sense. In Reuben is designated the first age of the world, beginning from the first parent [Adam], to which the birth of the righteous Noah, or the Flood according to some,

<column-break/>

which happened under him, gave an end. From Noah <note>original: "Moe" – an OCR error for "Noe" (Noah).</note> until Abraham, the second age followed, designated in Gad. To this, a third age was joined: that is, from Abraham until David, designated in Manasseh itself, which appeared clearly divided into two parts, as the legislator <note>Moses</note> stood between them at the Jordan. Furthermore, the fourth age, from David until <margin>Joshua 13</margin> Jeconiah, <note>Jeconiah was a king of Judah exiled to Babylon; his reign marks the transition to the Captivity.</note> is designated in Ephraim. The fifth age also followed, designated in Judah: from the Babylonian transmigration until Christ, or rather until the end of the primitive Church, in which the Law and circumcision reached their fulfillment. For Christ Jesus was made the mediator between the Law and Grace, so that he might join both testaments in himself; like a cornerstone, <note>original: "lapis angularis"</note> he coupled the two walls coming from opposite directions into one, dissolving—as the Apostle says—the <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> enmities of both and reconciling the two peoples in himself. This is according to what the angels are read to have sung at his birth: "Glory to God in the highest, <margin>Luke 2</margin> and on earth peace to men of good will." <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis deo..." — Luke 2:14.</note> Rightly, however, the first generation of the world, which began from the first parent, is designated in the tribe of Reuben; for just as Reuben by right lost his birthright because he defiled his father's bed, so the first man [Adam], falling in Paradise, lost the honor of his primacy which he had poorly guarded. These <margin>Genesis 49</margin> birthrights were given to the sons of Manasseh and Ephraim—that is, the sons of a righteous father—as is read in Chronicles. <note>original: "paralipomenon" — 1 Chronicles 5:1.</note> Because, undoubtedly, the glory of the patriarchate—which would have befitted the first man had he not sinned—was given to Abraham and David, so that they deserved to be called and were the fathers of Christ. Not that the first man is not the father of Christ, since from him the entire race of men was generally propagated, but because to these others the promise was made by the Lord through the grace of faith: namely, that in the seed of Abraham all nations should be blessed, and <margin>Genesis 22; Psalm 131</margin> that the Lord would place the fruit of David's womb upon his throne. It is well that Abraham and his offspring are designated <margin>Genesis 12</margin> in Manasseh, which is interpreted as "forgetfulness" <note>original: "obliuio" — A traditional etymology of the name Manasseh (from the Hebrew 'nashah', to forget).</note>; for to him it was first said by the Lord: "Go out from your land and from your kin and from your father's house," so that he might seem to prefigure what was once said through the mouth of David to Holy Mother Church: "Hear, O daughter, and <margin>Genesis 12; Psalm 44</margin>

### Joachim's First Book on the Apocalypse ###

<margin>Romans 8</margin>
"Look, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house." <note>original: "vide z inclina aurem tuam..." – This is a quote from Psalm 45:10, though the margin notes Romans 8, likely reflecting a thematic connection to the "body of sin" mentioned in that chapter.</note> For as long as we live in sin, we remain as if in our own land; that is, we remain in the body of sin. Whence it is also said by the Apostle: "But those who are in the flesh cannot please God." <note>Romans 8:8</note> We depart, as it were, from our own land when we turn away from evil works. It is well designated also in **Abraham**, who was with his offspring; for to him and his descendants the promise was made concerning **Christ**, saying: <margin>Psalm 131</margin> "Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne." <note>Psalm 132:11 (131 in the Vulgate). The author links the promise made to David back to Abraham’s lineage.</note> But although both Abraham and **David** are outstanding in such wondrous dignity—that, as I have already said, they deserved to be called and were the fathers of Christ—yet that prophetic word was fulfilled in them which the patriarch **Jacob** spoke when blessing his grandsons: he preferred the younger **Ephraim** over the firstborn brother **Manasseh**. <margin>Genesis 48</margin> For **Matthew** the Evangelist, writing the genealogy of Christ, by no means placed Abraham (who was first) before David; rather, he preferred David to Abraham, saying: <margin>Matthew 1</margin> "**The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.**" And indeed, Abraham was a patriarch only; but David was that which is more worthy: both patriarch and king. And rightly also **Reuben**, **Gad**, and the half-tribe of Manasseh received the rewards of their labors on the eastern side [of the Jordan]; <margin>Joshua 13</margin> for those first generations of the world—from **Adam** to **Noah**, from Noah to Abraham, and from Abraham to **Moses**—lived, as it were, like two and a half tribes without the Law. They were adjacent to the origin of the world as if on the eastern side; that is, in the first ages in which they lived without the Law, they are known to have received the rewards of spiritual mansions, just as the other ranks of the righteous (who do not cease to serve as soldiers through the true and catholic faith until the present time) are known to have received them. Thus, it would seem that the gift of private grace was never lacking to those desiring to be saved in any span of time. Therefore, in the river **Jordan**, the streams of the Divine Law are to be understood. These streams of the Law were crossed by the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, armed and ready for battle, preceding the remaining tribes; for all those in those times who are believed to have had knowledge of the Almighty God, unencumbered by the weight of the Law and without the burden of the commandments, fought against

the opposing ranks. Even then, they were pleasing to Almighty God through faith and grace, for no mortal can ever reconcile himself to God through the mere servitude of the Law. Nevertheless, some works which were written in their own time and commanded by the Lawgiver [Moses] among the words of the Law are read to have been observed by those ancient fathers: such as the sacrifice of the lamb in **Abel**, abstinence from blood in Noah, circumcision in Abraham, the taking of a deceased brother's wife in **Judah**, and whatever similar things are found. <margin>Genesis 4</margin> Therefore, from Moses until Christ, the remaining half-tribe of Manasseh, as well as Ephraim and Judah, received their inheritance as if from this side of the river; for just as God Almighty willed there to be two ages and a half before the Law, so He willed there to be two and a half under the Law. <note>The author is dividing human history into precise "ages" (aetates) that correspond to the 5.5 tribes that settled in or near the Promised Land, totaling the "six ages" of the world.</note> Indeed, He established seven distinctions of times from the beginning of the second state until the beginning of the third; specifically in this sixth age, according to what this book teaches. This was done so that the integrity of the number twelve might be preserved, as well as the perfection of the numbers five and seven, and any others that might be present. This is why the Lord, when about to feed the people by the miracle of faith, by no means deigned to satisfy the crowds with twelve loaves at once, but first with five barley loaves, and finally with seven others. For without doubt, the Only-begotten of God the Father first opened the five books of Moses—or rather those five types of histories of which we made mention in the work *The Harmony* <note>original: "ope concordie" – referring to Joachim of Fiore's *Concordia Novi et Veteris Testamenti* (The Harmony of the New and Old Testaments).</note>—to the people who were still hungry. Then, He set out the mystical books of the New Testament, explained by His ministers, as a more refined food against loathing for those who were already satisfied and full. Therefore, we exhort the faithful to exert themselves to taste these spiritual banquets. Let us receive with a joyful mind and not without thanksgiving those things which He abundantly sets before us, His unworthy servants, near the end of the world. Thus, we who—due to a stomach corrupted by long sickness—scorn harder foods, may be brought to salvation as if by certain liquid foods. But lest it perhaps seem unequal to anyone that we say the sixth age of this world is to be divided into seven distinctions of ages, let him see that those [earlier] ages were given to only a few faithful; but this one age, which is the sixth, God has consecrated for the salvation of many nations, so that what was worked in them through long...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of history, moving from the distribution of the biblical tribes to the era of the "fullness of the Gentiles." ## Part of the Exposition by the Abbot ##

...the unity of times: so that in these, the multitude of the fullness of the Gentiles might be fulfilled. For this is like the great King **Artaxerxes** <note>The Persian king from the Book of Esther, used here as an allegory for God.</note> who prepared a special feast for his princes and nobles for a long time; and finally, for seven days, he solemnly invited all the people of his city to a universal feast. This signifies that Almighty God first revealed the gifts of His grace to the patriarchs and prophets—the few elect of those times—but when the **fullness of time** arrived, He called the fullness of the Gentiles without delay to that great feast of the **Lamb**. And rightly was the span of this common feast restricted within the limit of seven days, because, as it is written in this book: <margin>Apocalypse 10</margin> *When the seventh angel begins to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God shall be finished.* Therefore, that which generally concerns the five tribes was completed from the beginning of time until **Christ**. Indeed, in those same five tribes, the entire lineage of the elect of those times is to be understood, who by faith and good works deserved to inherit the kingdom of eternal blessedness. After these, the crowds of the elect—designated in those seven tribes—depart one after another without ceasing to possess their eternal inheritance, until the time of the **conversion of the Jews**.

To these crowds of the elect, under the figure of the **Seven Churches**, the blessed **John the Evangelist** predicts the things that were to come; in a brief volume but with an expansive mystery, he encompasses them through a manifold kind of sacrament. This, therefore, is the reason why the beloved disciple of Christ, with the divine Spirit teaching him, wished to build seven churches. This is why he directed the sacred mysteries to the seven churches by writing to them. But it is not without a mystery that these same churches are said to be in **Asia**. For "Asia" is interpreted as **exaltation** <note>original: "elatio" – Medieval scholars often used etymological symbolism; here, Asia represents the pride or "lifting up" of the worldly powers.</note>; and truly this world lifts itself up with continuous exaltation over the elect. Whence it is also said by the Psalmist: <margin>Psalm 92</margin> *The floods have lifted up their waves; the Lord is wonderful on high.* <note>Psalm 93:3-4 in modern bibles, 92 in the Vulgate.</note> Indeed, the "exaltations of the sea" are changeable, because animal-like men admire the glory of this world. But if they admire this, what will they say when the glory of the heavens is revealed? Yet Christ endures the exaltation of this age for a time, so that the

<column-break/>

elect might be able to sustain it. He suffered under **Pontius Pilate**, leaving us (as **Peter** says) an example, so that we might follow in His footsteps. And this indeed it is necessary to do if we wish to come quickly to the glory of heaven; but because we can do nothing without Him, John prays that **grace** and **peace** be sent to us, so that He who can do all things might work all that He wills in us. For there follows:

> Grace to you and peace from Him who is, and who was, and who is to come.

<margin>John 14</margin>
### Concerning Grace
It is written: *Grace for grace He has given us.* But concerning peace: *My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you.* But what kind of peace? Not (He says) as the world gives, do I give to you. For the world also gives peace to its lovers. But Christ does not give to His own in a similar way. For the former glory in great things, while the latter glory in small things. The former in high things, the latter in the lowest; the former in the prosperity of this life, the latter in adversity—knowing that <margin>Romans 5</margin> *tribulation works patience, and patience hope.* Therefore, the peace of the former is in delights, but the peace of the latter is in virtues. For what vices work in the former, virtues work in the latter (if I may say so). For even if the former rejoice in things that are outside, the latter much more rejoice in things that are within; and what the former thought was to be possessed through vain pride, the latter hold more strongly and happily through **humility**.

Therefore, Christ grants grace to the elect, and He also grants peace; for those whom He anticipates by inspiring them to work, He provides help to persevere in the good of peace. For frequently we begin what is good with joy and fervor, but nevertheless, that which is written is difficult: <margin>Matthew 10</margin> *He who perseveres to the end shall be saved.* It is necessary, therefore, that peace follows the grace that goes before; so that what had previously seemed harsh might become mild by the gentleness of helping grace. Otherwise, if grace does not go before, the vice of our corrupt nature resists. For we were, as the Apostle says, <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> *by nature children of wrath*; or the labor of the mind alone would be contrary if the Spirit of peace did not assist. For a person is not called "peaceful" simply because he lives without scandal when all things are as he likes and are permitted; rather, he is truly called peaceful who <margin>Psalm 119</margin> perseveres in a time of scandal.

# John, First Part in the Apocalypse #

...harvested. This is that peace which the prophet David, speaking in the person of **Christ**, declares he has kept when he says: <note>original: "Cum his qui oderat pacem: era pacificus cum loquebar illis: ipugnabant me gratis."</note> *With those who hated peace, I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.* Therefore, **John** prays that this grace and this peace be given to the seven churches—not from a mortal man, who has nothing of himself, but from Him "who is, and who was, and who is to come." The **Divine Majesty** claimed this <term>substantive word</term> <note>Referring to the verb "to be" used as a name, signifying essential existence.</note> for His eternal name, just as He speaks for Himself in the Book of **Exodus**, saying: <margin>Exodus 3</margin> *Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: "He who is" has sent me to you.* For He who alone possesses unchangeable being—the blessed and powerful God from whom everything that exists received its existence—rightly claims this name for Himself. He alone is from eternity, so that all changeable things should fear when He proclaims His essence. And because we also who are called humans—or however we exist—possess our existence as a temporal gift from God, He added "and who was" to distinguish the divine essence from the human. For He Himself was when we were not; but now He is, and we exist through Him. <margin>Psalm 99</margin> *He indeed made us, and not we ourselves.* But even this is not enough for us, unless He is to come; unless He comes in glory to fulfill the promise, so that we may see Him as He is, and in that longed-for sight be reformed into His likeness. This is the testimony of **John**, whose book this is. For he himself says in his epistle: <margin>1 John 3</margin> *We know that when He appears we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is.* Now, the "coming" and "appearance" of the Lord are to be understood in this place in the same way as that which is read in the **Gospel**: <margin>1 John 3</margin> <note>The text likely meant John 14:23 as per the margin note below.</note> <margin>John 14</margin> *If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.* But how do the Father and the Son come to those who love them, when they are never absent? It is because often God remains in a person through the presence of His divinity, yet is not yet in them through inhabiting grace; then God is said to "come" to a man when He visits him with His presence and touches his heart. And since this visitation of the Lord—by which He now secretly prepares His elect—will at the end, when He comes for judgment, visibly pour over them an even greater abundance of grace. Correcty then it is not said "who comes," but "who is to come." Although if, for the sake of the supreme

<column-break/>

unity of the Persons, these three attributes <note>Who is, who was, who is to come.</note> can be applied equally to the whole **Trinity** at once, nevertheless in this place, each should be understood specifically: as if it were said of the **Father** "who was" working in the first state; of the **Son** "who is" cooperating in the second; of the **Holy Spirit** "who is to come" in the third, to bring all things to completion. Furthermore, it should be noted that He does not say "Who is, and who was [fuit], and who will be," but "Who is, and who was [erat], and who is to come," <note>The author distinguishes between the perfect tense (fuit - "has been") and the imperfect (erat - "was/was being") to emphasize continuous, eternal existence over a fixed point in time.</note> lest He should seem to limit God within time. By this, His eternity might be thought capable of being interrupted by the intervals of different times, whereas His eternity is entirely simultaneous and boundless. Since to Him nothing of the past has flowed away, and nothing of the future is yet to be; what human frailty can believe, it cannot fully describe. Although—to use an illustration of a dissimilar thing—the human mind is known to have received this in its nature: that it can exist through memory in past things and, without leaving present things, sometimes grasp future ones, so that it rejoices not only in what it possesses but even in those things it hopes to have. How much more in the divine nature, which always is that which it is? To Him nothing can happen by the change of times; those two times which cannot be present for us—namely the past and the future—are together for Him, so that for Him nothing is past, nothing is future. For whatever has passed seems to have flowed away from us; whatever is future, we cannot yet grasp. It is also impossible for us to return to past time, or even to anticipate the future, so that we might possess those three times together. And yet the soul, created more subtly in the **image of God**, is known to retain these three in memory, just as the physical eye gazes not only upon those things which are near, but often upon both near and far things at once. Just as man was created in the image of God, yet cannot be equal to Him who shaped and formed him, so that which the human memory holds by imagining, God possesses essentially all at once, as He who alone rema...

<meta>This page continues the Trinitarian exposition of the greeting in Revelation. The previous page discussed the name of God as "He who is." This page moves to the significance of the "Seven Spirits" and the unity of the Holy Spirit through the analogy of the sun and a fruiting tree.</meta>

# Part of the Exposition #

...is great: He alone is eternal, through whom all things were made; through whom exists and has been whatever was and is. Therefore, **Saint John** says, he is not "He who was" in the sense of someone who existed at some point and then ceased to be; rather, he positioned it without limit as "He who was." Nor does he say "He who is to be" or "He who shall be," but "He who is to come." This is because a thing is rightly said to "be about to be" when it does not yet exist; but **God** both was and is, and in the future, He is "to come." Furthermore, this is spoken in the singular number and not the plural, just as that saying of **Paul** where it is said:

<margin>Romans 11</margin>
*From him, and through him, and in him.* <note>original: "Ab ipso & per ipm̄ & in ipso"</note> By these words, the <term>Divine Persons</term> <note>The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> can be distinguished by faith and intellect, yet they cannot be divided from themselves, because they are one. Just as light and heat cannot be divided from that fiery substance called the sun: the substance itself is not the ray that touches the earth, but the ray comes from the substance; likewise, the ray is not the heat, but the heat comes from the ray. And yet, we do not say there are three suns, but one sun. These things concerning that supreme nature from which all good things proceed now follow.

<margin>Text 5</margin>
> And from the seven spirits who are in the sight of his throne.

<margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin>
**It seems** very strange what is meant by this saying: *And from the seven spirits who are in the sight of his throne.* It would be much more miraculous if the **Apostle Paul** did not say in his letter to the Corinthians: *There are varieties of graces, but the same Spirit.* For we know that there are <term>seven gifts</term> <note>Traditional gifts of the Holy Spirit: Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Fortitude, Knowledge, Piety, and Fear of the Lord.</note>—doubtless of the **Holy Spirit**—and those are the very gifts which are called here the "seven spirits." Concerning these gifts—as with others which are infinite in number—there are certainly authorities among the Fathers stating they are not the **Holy Spirit** Himself, but "divisions of His gifts," according to what is added in that same letter regarding their effects: *But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as He wills.* For a weak and needy nature could not otherwise rejoice; a nature which of itself has nothing other than a miserable existence, even if it is a "good" of some kind, since this too must be true: *God saw everything he had made, and they were very good.* All things He made are "very good," certainly in their own kind and according to Him who made them, who, as Scripture testifies, made all things in **Wisdom**. Finally, He made the mute elements, which neither live nor feel;

<column-break/>

He made the brute animals, which live and feel but do not discern. He made spirits <note>Referring to angels and human souls.</note> which live, feel, and discern; but if they are without the gifts of the **Holy Spirit**, they cannot be blessed—indeed, they cannot be so without the Gift which He is Himself, through which all gifts are poured in. As there are many leaves and branches of a tree, but only one tree. And we see proceeding from the tops of the trees certain "gifts," as it were, which serve as food for the hungry: that is, the abundance of fruit which proceeds from them. In these, there is no empty figure of that "desirable fruit" which the **Apostle** commends when he says: *But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, patience, goodness.* <note>original: "fructus autem spiritus: est charitas: gaudiuz: pax: lōganimitas: patiētia: bonitas"</note> And these indeed concern those virtues without which salvation cannot exist, among which <term>Charity</term> <note>From the Latin 'caritas,' meaning selfless, divine love.</note>—the virtue which Scripture commends so greatly and without which others are of no use—holds the primacy. But the remaining gifts of the **Spirit** are rather for ornament and beauty, and for some spiritual utility for the **Church**. For thus the **Apostle** says among other things: *To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for utility.* And he added: *To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,* and things similar to these. For the same **Spirit** flows into the <term>City of God</term> <note>A common metaphor for the Church or the community of believers.</note> and, among His other gifts, traverses the whole as if through seven channels, giving some special gift to each troop of the elect, and one gift which is common to all; so that the diverse kinds of gifts preserve beauty, and the unity of love excludes the foulness of envy. Moreover, these special gifts are called the "seven spirits" and "seven lamps," or even "the seven eyes of the Lord sent out into all the earth." For while the **Spirit** "breathes where He wills," He pours those gifts into human minds as He wills, making them shine like lanterns in a dark place and making known through them the paths of life to men, so that they may walk in the paths of **God's** commandments. Therefore, although there is one **Spirit** to whom <term>Charity</term> properly belongs—which also properly retains His name, and because of which that same **Spirit** is called the "Gift" of the Father and the Son—there are nonetheless other gifts, the number of which is...

<margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 11</margin>

# First Part of the Exposition on the Apocalypse #

<margin>Augustine, 15 *On the Trinity*</margin>
...infinite, among which, as we have already said, are the seven special spirits: which are called the "seven eyes of the Lord" and the "seven spirits." For both are found in the divine scriptures, as **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> says: both the "Gift" (in the singular) and the "Gifts" (in the plural), just as if it were said: "There is one body, but many members." This is the same example the **Apostle** <note>Referring to Saint Paul.</note>
<margin>Luke 24</margin>
took up. Certainly, when the **Lord** was about to ascend into heaven, he promised the **Holy Spirit** himself to the apostles, saying: *Behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you.* Furthermore, the **Apostle** did not write "gift" in the singular, but "gifts."
<margin>Ephesians 4, Psalm 67</margin>
For he says: *Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.* From these and other places in the scriptures, it is clearly shown that there are many gifts of the **Holy Spirit**, and among them the "seven special ones" which are named here as the "seven spirits." These were given to men in the same way as they belong to Him whose gifts they are—except that He possesses them as **God**, whereas we possess them not as God, but as his spiritual gifts.
<margin>1 John 4</margin>
Indeed, it is according to these gifts that **John** says: *He has given to us of his Spirit.* And 
<margin>Joel 2</margin>
the **Lord** himself says in **Joel**: *I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.* For it is one thing when it is said, *Through the Holy Spirit who was given to us,*
<margin>Romans 5, 1 John 4</margin>
and another when he says, *He has given to us of his Spirit.* In the former, the reference is to the **Spirit** himself; in the latter, to one of his gifts. And when He was about to bless us through the **Holy Spirit** who was given to us,
<margin>Romans 5</margin>
He promised, saying: *The charity of God is poured out in our hearts.* For just as through those seven gifts the "word of wisdom" and the like are infused into us,
<margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin>
so through that Gift which is He himself—who is the <term>Charity of God</term> <note>original: "charitas dei"; in this context, it refers to the divine love that defines the Holy Spirit's nature.</note>—charity is diffused in our hearts. This is because He is infused through each individual gift, being the one who performs every work in the heart of man according to his own likeness. For He himself is Charity, and therefore He pours out charity. Similarly, in the spiritual gifts, He works something according to their own likeness: as in the "spirit of wisdom," he works the "word of wisdom"; and in the "spirit of knowledge," the "word of knowledge"; and so on with the rest. Therefore, the **Spirit of God** is great and his gifts are ineffable. Who is as great as God? These gifts are not God himself, but are His gifts. For He himself is **God**, proceeding from the **Father** and the **Son** from eternity; yet these graces of His are given in time by Him to bless the human and angelic creatures whom He 

<column-break/>

created. For this "pouring out" and "infusion" did not begin from eternity. Rather, it began from the moment there were "vessels of mercy" to receive it, of whom it is said: 
<margin>John 7</margin>
*He who thirsts, let him come and drink, and from his belly shall flow rivers of living water.* He does not say "river," but "rivers," because His gifts, as we said, are many. Those angelic spirits experienced the inexpressible glory of these gifts; they were able to have them in their knowledge to a greater degree because they were created more "spiritually" in the image of the **Holy Spirit** than men are. In contrast, human parents and their children possess the image of **God the Father** and the **Son** in a special way, because the former beget and the latter are begotten. To this extent, the fathers of the **Old Testament**, in that they were "fore-speakers" <note>Prophets who spoke before the fulfillment of the promise.</note>, attained a certain image of the **Father**; and the sons of the **New Testament**, who are properly called "sons of men," attained the image of the **Son**. But the **Angels**, who are neither fathers nor sons, reflect the image of the **Holy Spirit**, who is neither begetter nor begotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son. In this, we should not consider it a mystery without form: that just as faithful men are called "voices," so those angelic powers are called "virtues" in the divine pages. This is because, just as "voices" relate to the **Word** <note>The Son.</note>, so "spiritual virtues" relate to the **Love of the Spirit**. 
<margin>Tobit 12</margin>
Hence, in the **Book of Tobit**, **Raphael** speaking to **Tobias** said that he was "one of the seven angels who stand before the Lord," as if to say that the "seven gifts of the spirit" are seen to be conferred more specially upon them than others. And in truth, both they and all others are full of these gifts, which is why they are believed to be sent to help the elect. 
<margin>Luke 22</margin>
According to this, when the **Son of God** was in his Passion, an angel is described as having appeared to him—not because He himself was in need, for He alone has power that neither man nor angel possesses, but so that those who hope in the **living God** might believe that help is sent to them from above, so they can overcome the threats of executioners and all the torments applied to them. Therefore, we should not believe that those seven angels stand before God because they have any good of their own which they might send to others; just as no man should be believed to have anything of himself. Nevertheless, it is not in vain to believe that they have the grace of the "supreme spirits"—that is, love and help.

<summary>This page explains the theological distinction between the Holy Spirit as a person of the Trinity and the "Seven Gifts" of the Spirit, using the roles of angels and humans as analogies for the different persons of the Trinity.</summary>

We seek and desire: since we know how good a thing it is: the love of God: which in both angels and humans comes from God: so that even God himself requires it from angels and humans: as is said through John: "Let us love God, because he first loved us." <note>original: "Diligamus nos deum: quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos." <margin>Isaiah 11</margin>

<margin>Revelation 4</margin>

### And from Jesus Christ who is the faithful witness.

It would seem to be **more appropriate** that Jesus Christ be written of first, before the seven spirits (that is, the gifts of the Spirit): since he is surely God: whereas those are not God, but gifts of God: the divisions of graces which were given to angels and humans. But it would be rightly asked here: if Christ were not God and man: if the scripture speaks anything of him according to that which he is as God: if he had not <term>emptied himself</term> <note>original: "exinanisset" - a reference to the 'Kenosis' or the act of Christ setting aside his divine glory to become human.</note> taking the form of a servant. # John’s First Commentary on the Apocalypse

### Page 32

...rites: and a little later: "And from Jesus Christ who is the faithful witness." <note>original: "Et a iesu xpo qui est testis fidelis" - quoting Revelation 1:5.</note> It is clear that this speech refers to his human nature, according to which the same Son was made lower not only than the Father and the Holy Spirit, but he even willed to be made a little lower than the angels, just as it is written: <term>You have made him a little lower than your angels, Lord.</term> <note>original: "Minorasti eum paulominus ab angelis tuis domine."</note>

<margin>Psalm 8</margin>
The Apostle [Paul] reveals how this is to be understood when he says: <term>We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.</term> <note>original: "Eum qui modico quam angeli minoratus est..." quoting Hebrews 2:9.</note> But what kind of grace can the Son of God give us, in whom there is a man? For no one has what he did not receive. Therefore, he himself also received something to give to us. He received it, I say, just as it is written:

<margin>Hebrews 2</margin>
<margin>Psalm 67</margin>
<term>You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive: you have received gifts among men.</term> <note>original: "Ascendisti in altum cepisti captivitatem: accepisti dona in hominibus." quoting Psalm 68:18.</note> And he says well: "You received gifts among men," because he did not receive them then for himself, but for us. He himself gave through himself, and received for us. For he also ascended on high for this reason: so that from the raised Head, gifts might be poured out through the members of his body. Wherefore John also says:

<margin>John 7</margin>
<term>The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.</term> <note>original: "Spiritus nondum erat datus: quia iesus nondum erat glorificatus." quoting John 7:39.</note> But we must still consider more carefully what we touched upon in passing regarding the two great works of God, so that we may more fittingly repeat here what was omitted there. Among the other things which the Holy Spirit has worked for his own praise, there are two great works in which there could be no regret, because they were and are so good that nothing in created things was closer to God, nothing so dear to God, and nothing so necessary to humans. The first of these was the creation of the **new man**, who was created according to God. The second: the working of **virtues**, about which the Apostle says: <term>One and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills.</term> <note>original: "Haec omnia operatur unus atque idem spiritus diuidens prout vult." quoting 1 Corinthians 12:11.</note> Now, I have called this the "second" work in terms of the fullness of his gift, not in terms of a private outpouring; for even before then, these gifts had been given to the prophets—not all to everyone, but certain ones to certain people according to the measure of the Giver. I have called it "second" in relation to humans, not in relation to angelic creatures, especially since there was a great reason for the mystery: so that the **contemplative life** 

<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 12</margin>

<column-break/>

in the angelic creature, and the **active life** in humans might come first, and finally that which preceded in the angels might follow here in humans; so that in one sense it is first, and in another it is not first, but later. Therefore, as far as it concerns those whom the wave of sacred baptism has washed, that work of the **new man** came first, followed by the outpouring of his graces. In the first work, the Word was made the Son of Man. In the second, humans are made children of God.

<margin>Romans 8</margin>
For we cannot be children of God in any other way except by receiving the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle testifies when he says: <term>God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, in which we cry out, "Abba, Father."</term> <note>original: "Misit deus spiritum filij sui in corda nostra: in quo clamamus abba pater." quoting Galatians 4:6 and Romans 8:15.</note> For the Spirit is not given to anyone to whom his virtues are not also given; because unless he himself prepared a home for himself by adorning it with his virtues, it cannot be worthy enough to deserve to have such an inhabitant. Just as it is the greatest concern of a bridegroom to adorn his bride with jewels, so it was Christ's concern to decorate with virtues that beloved Church which he joined to himself, "not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing." <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:27.</note> O, what an exchange the Lord Jesus made with us! He took our weakness and gave us his virtue. He was humbled even to us, so that he might lift us up above ourselves and make us his co-heirs. O, how great is what he showed us in exchange for the small and meager thing he took from us! Finally, let us match each thing one by one:
* He took the sight of eyes from our nature: and gave us the **Spirit of Wisdom**, through which the eyes of the mind are enlightened.
* He took hearing: and gave us the **Spirit of Understanding**, which opens the inner ears.
* He took the sense of smell: and gave us the **Spirit of Counsel**, in which spiritual discernment remains.
* He took speech: and gave us the **Spirit of Knowledge**—since, of course, knowledge of worldly things is learned through the tongue.
* He took from us hands: and gave us the **Spirit of Fortitude**. For in the "arm of the flesh," human strength is recognized.
* He also took feet: and gave us the **Spirit of Piety**. The Spirit of Piety is likened to the walking of feet because he who wishes to spend the work of piety in ministering to a neighbor must, like Martha, go here and there...

**Vocabulary:** Jesus Christ, Holy Spirit, Baptism, Church, Virtues, Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Fortitude, Knowledge, Piety, Martha.

# The Explanation of the Parts

### Page 32

<margin>Psalm 118</margin>
...that it may spread. He received from us a mortal body bound to infirmity and suffering in the likeness of sin, and in return, he gave to us the spirit of fear, of which it is written: <term>Pierce my flesh with your fear.</term> <note>original: "Confige timore tuo carnes meas" - Psalm 119:120 (numbered as 118 in the Vulgate). The author suggests that healthy fear of God protects the soul just as fear of pain protects the body.</note> For a human is greatly afraid for his body to be wounded, so much so that the stronger limbs will put themselves in the way to protect it. Finally, if it were necessary to choose between two things, one would rather suffer the loss of a single limb than have his whole body in danger—not because he prefers to live miserably, but because death is naturally feared by all flesh. But perhaps this is free from the gift of grace: that from the substance of our flesh he received blood, without which life cannot remain in the body; the Lamb gave us another gift in place of blood: namely, <term>brotherly charity</term>, without the participation of which no one can be saved. Ultimately, however great those gifts are which are designated in the seven spirits, the Apostle shows that they are worth nothing without charity when he says:

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
<term>If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.</term> <note>original: "Si linguis hominum loquar & angelorum..."</note> We must come to that which is highest and foremost, the completion of the whole divine gift. He received what belongs to man—a living soul—in exchange for which he gave us a <term>life-giving spirit</term>; <note>original: "spiritum vivificantem" - see 1 Corinthians 15:45.</note> that is, charity itself, by which we love God. This is not because there are two charities or two spirits, but because there are different effects by which we love God and man: we love God by always exulting in Him, but we mostly love men by having mercy on them, insofar as they are miserable and pitiable—which properly belongs to brotherly love. It appears clearly, therefore, that what he gave us is to be preferred over what he received from us. For this reason, the seven spirits are written of first, and then followed by the man Christ Jesus, <term>who is the faithful witness and the firstborn of the dead.</term> <note>original: "testis fidelis & primogenitus mortuorum" - Revelation 1:5.</note> These sacred works were signified in Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of Joseph, one of whom is interpreted as "forgetfulness" and the other as "fruitfulness." <note>Manasseh means "causing to forget" and Ephraim means "fruitful" in Hebrew.</note> For when holy Joseph brought them to his father so that he might bless them among his brothers, he placed the firstborn at the right hand and the younger

<margin>Genesis 2, 1 Corinthians 15</margin>
<margin>Genesis 41</margin>
<margin>Genesis 48</margin>

<column-break/>

at the left hand, so that the firstborn might obtain the firstborn's blessing according to the order of birth. But Jacob, who foresaw the future in the spirit, <term>crossing his hands</term>, <note>original: "cancellatis manibus" - Jacob crossed his arms to form an 'X' shape, a gesture often seen by medieval commentators as a sign of the Cross.</note> blessed them both in such a way that he placed his right hand on the younger and his left on the firstborn. When Joseph saw this, he took it poorly and tried to move his father's hands so that the right would touch the firstborn. But the father, as one with foreknowledge of the future, refused to comply, saying: "I know, my son, I know. This one indeed shall become a people and be multiplied, but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall grow into nations." In this place, Jacob designates the person of God the Father, and Joseph designates the Holy Spirit. Truly, Manasseh represents Christ Jesus according to his humanity, not according to his divinity; whereas Ephraim represents the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Manasseh was born first, then Ephraim, because Christ was first born according to the flesh—who taught the elect to consign the Law of Moses to "forgetfulness"—and then the gifts of grace were given to the Church so that they might "bear fruit" in righteousness. Thus it happened that Christ Jesus, as the firstborn and holding the primacy, was placed at the right hand, while the Church was placed at the left. For in her—that is, in the Church—those gifts were fulfilled which were designated by the "tongues." To her, as I have already said, were given the gifts of grace to bear fruit for God, after the grain of wheat had died—which, while still living in the flesh, seemed to remain alone. Christ was therefore placed as the firstborn at the right hand of the Father, and the Church, as the lesser and younger, at the left; because the Son preached to the Jewish people, who were as if at the right hand of God, but the primitive Church (or that apostolic army) was sent to the Gentile people, who until then had stood at the left. And behold, those people who were the flesh of Christ were found under the left hand. But the Gentile, who was on the left, was moved under the right hand, being given the birthright that the Jewish people lost. That people, I say, was found under the right hand; they were joined to Christ not by the closeness of flesh (like those of the seed of Abraham), but solely by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, which was poured out upon faithful souls and does not cease to bear fruit even unto the present day.

<margin>Genesis 48</margin>

"It is true," he says, "it is true." The Lord was accustomed to use this word <note>The Hebrew word "Amen," meaning "certainly" or "truly."</note> in the Gospel. There is this difference, however: the Lord himself used it at the beginning of his speech, but we are accustomed to use this word at the end. # First Part on the Apocalypse
## E 2
<meta>catchword: mus</meta>

so that he may impose an end upon those things which he began: an end not of destruction, but of consummation <note>The author distinguishes between an "end" that destroys and an "end" that perfects or completes (consummation).</note>. Because truly, it is not only he himself who does this, but also the Father and the Holy Spirit. Although he does so manifestly and visibly, the others do so invisibly and secretly. Rightly, after he says: **The Lord God says**, he added: **Who is, and who was, and who is to come**, so that it may be understood as spoken concerning the whole Trinity together. For the Father is the beginning, the Son is the beginning, and the Holy Spirit is the beginning; yet they are not three beginnings, but one beginning. However, so that the faithful people might acknowledge the three persons to be God, he willed there to be three beginnings belonging to their own specific times: the first of which pertains especially to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit. These three, if we are sound in wisdom, are designated in the letter **A**, which is a triangular element and is written first among the others, not only in Greek but also in Latin. Indeed, in the beginning of our teaching, this foundation of faith must be laid. But because it is not easy to know all things that belong to the articles of faith, many things follow in his doctrine, of whose fullness the Christian religion is known to be in need; concerning which it was said by the Lord: <margin>John 16</margin> **I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; but when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.** <note>original: "Multa habeo vobis dicere..."</note> It is as if he were to say: "Because my Father first taught that he is God; yet it is not enough for the world to know the Father unless it knows the Son and the Holy Spirit. And if I have revealed many things to men so that the world may acknowledge me, and all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father, it is nevertheless necessary for him to come—he who proceeds from the Father and me—so that he himself may be known by the world, and the chosen people may know the whole truth." This means knowing not only the Father or only the Son, but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together: that is, the whole Trinity equally. Thus, having acknowledged the truth, which is God, they themselves may likewise rest from their labors. For it is not enough for the world to know the Father alone unless it knows the Son and the Holy Spirit; nor is it enough to know all three persons unless one also believes one of them to be unbegotten, another begotten, and another proceeding; unless one believes each to be true God; unless one believes

<column-break/>

the three persons to be co-eternal and co-equal to themselves; unless one believes the Son to be begotten from the Father alone, and the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son <note>This refers to the "Filioque" doctrine, a major theological point in the Western Church stating the Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son.</note>. Therefore, with many things preceding which pertain to the knowledge of the persons—namely the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—there follows one thing in which is the end of faith and the consummation of truth: namely, the knowledge of the one essence; that is, that we understand the three persons to be one God. For where the end is, there also is the consummation. This consummation is therefore placed in the advent of the Holy Spirit, because he himself is the communion of the Father and the Son; he is the bond of unity. And therefore, he who knows that he proceeds from the Father and the Son understands the highest and ineffable unity of the three persons. For in no way could he himself proceed from both unless the Father and the Son were one; nor could he proceed from them without end if he were not one with them from whom he proceeds without ceasing. If, therefore, we believe the Father is the beginning, the Son is the beginning, and the Holy Spirit is the beginning—the Father perfect God, the Son perfect God, and the Holy Spirit perfect God—which that triangular letter <note>The letter A (Alpha), which the author views as a triangle representing the three-in-one nature of the Trinity.</note> is shown to designate, what remains except that we understand those three to be one God? This fact of faith is designated in the round **O**, since just as the Trinity is designated by the triangular element, so Unity is designated by the round element which is **O**. This is the end of faith for the salvation of every believer. For if we do not understand little by little that there are three, how can we understand those three together to be one? Otherwise, those who so accept the "one" of the essence of the three persons as to say it is some distinct and proper "one"—speaking of it as some single thing—they do so as if we believed: "God the Father is one, God the Son is one, God the Holy Spirit is one," as if there were some fourth thing that is the divine substance. They worship an idol, not God, for our faith does not receive some fourth thing, but only the three persons who are signified in **A**. If this is so, what did it pertain to the mystery of faith that, having said **"I am Alpha,"** he should add **"and Omega,"** <note>The text uses the Latin 'O' to stand for the Greek 'Omega' to maintain the geometric symbolism of the circle.</note> unless because it is not enough for us to believe God is truly triune, unless we believe him whom we believe to be triune is [one].

<summary>This page provides a symbolic interpretation of "Alpha and Omega," using the shape of the letter A (a triangle) to represent the Trinity and the letter O (a circle) to represent God's Unity. The author argues that true faith requires acknowledging both the distinct persons of the Trinity and their single, undivided essence.</summary>
