...such an understanding: one which threatens such great evils to the wicked and promises such immense rewards to the elect? Wherefore it is soon added: **What you see, write in a book, and send it to the seven churches which are in Asia.** The fact that the seven churches to which John writes are said to be in Asia—although it can be understood in the geographical sense mentioned previously—this name can also be taken in a good sense to mean "elevation" <note>original: "elatio". Medieval scholars often used the etymology of "Asia" to mean "elevation" or spiritual height</note>, just as pride <margin>Isaiah 6</margin> is used in the words of the prophet Isaiah: "It shall be said to you, you shall eat the strength of the nations, and you shall boast in their glory." What the saints see, they write in a book, because whatever they understand through meditation, they store by imprinting it on the book of the human heart with the pen of their tongue. He sends it to the seven churches in Asia because, through those who are capable of retaining the words of God more vividly, it is delegated as if by a letter to all the lineages of the elect, who are represented by those seven churches. The Apostle <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> showed himself to be writing in such a book when he spoke to those to whom he had committed the word of God, saying: "You are our letter, written in your hearts, known and read by all men; being manifested that you are the letter of Christ, ministered by us, and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; not on stone tablets, but on the fleshy tablets of the heart." In such a book Moses wrote the words of the Law to send them to the children of Israel, when he spoke more secretly to his brother Aaron, so that he, who was eloquent, might recount them to the whole multitude. Therefore, what the saints see, they write in a book, because they send it to the seven churches in Asia; they explain the mystery of the secret which they penetrate within to those seven orders <note>referring to the different ranks or types of people within the Church</note> who are designated in the seven churches listed below that were in Asia. Because the names of these places correspond specifically to the works of each order when investigated, the author did not wish to remain silent regarding their expression, but having said: "What you see, write in a book and send to the seven churches which are in Asia," he immediately added:

<margin>To them</margin> ¶ Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.

¶ Ephesus is interpreted as "fall" <note>original: "lapsus"</note>; Smyrna as "myrrh"; Pergamum as "dividing the horns" <note>original: "diuidens cornua"</note>; Thyatira as "illuminated"; Sardis as "the beginning of beauty"; Philadelphia as "saving the inheritance"; and Laodicea as "vomit" <note>This harsh interpretation stems from the biblical text where Christ threatens to spit the lukewarm church out of his mouth</note> or "beloved tribe." Interpretations of names of this kind apply to each order individually. How they apply, however, I will for now refrain from pursuing, so that we may explain them more fruitfully when we come to their specific sections in the text. It follows:

### And I turned to see <margin>Chapter 1:12</margin> the voice that spoke with me: and having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands.

¶ A physical voice is not visible to the eyes but is heard by the ears; but the voice which resonates without the noise of speech in the inner chambers of human hearts is both seen and heard by the spiritual eyes of the mind. We "turn" to see the voice that speaks with us because, while we perceive a small thing from sacred scripture when illustrated by grace, we are soon invited by the doorkeeper and turn to the study of reading, so that we may contemplate those things that are above us. ### Part of the Explanation

...its founder, the differences of the dwellings, and of him who sanctifies and gladdens them. Because the great works of God—which were to take place from the first coming of the Lord until the last—were written under a hidden enigma in this volume: so that it is to be believed that it can suffice for the fullness of knowledge, if anyone is sufficient to penetrate the secrets of this voice. "And being turned," he says, "I saw seven golden lampstands" <note>original: "septē cādelabra aurea"</note>. What in the time of Moses is represented by one lampstand is here, in this present place, represented by seven lampstands. Nor should it be wondered at. For each of the churches has these seven orders <note>Refers to the seven ranks of clergy or spiritual gifts</note> which will be dealt with in their proper places. To sufficiently untie the knot of this question, a rational cause may suffice: since indeed that lampstand shaft [in the Tabernacle] is read to have had one main stem but seven branches <note>original: "calamos", literally "reeds" or "stems"</note>, so that that single shaft was sufficient to hold seven lamps. These lampstands here, however, while nothing of that sort is said about them, are in no way believed to be multiple in that same way, but are rather believed to be "simple" or individual. They are said to be golden because the hearts of the righteous are pure, which Christ sanctifies by the bounty of grace to dwell within them. For he who is the Truth of God abhors all falsehood; he who is the Son of the simple Parent <note>A reference to God the Father as being without complexity or division</note> abhors all pretense. He dwells among them, as is shown subsequently.

<margin>Chapter 1:13</margin>
**And in the midst of the seven golden lampstands, one like the Son of Man, clothed in a robe reaching to the feet.**

But what do we say he intended, when the only-begotten Son of God—whom John beholds in majesty—is called not "the Son of Man" but "like the Son of Man"? Is it not because (placed in the kingdom of his divinity) he excels with such clarity, and shines over the angels with such glory of majesty—he who for a time had been made lower than the angels for the sake of men—that just as his humanity once concealed the glory of his divinity, so now the lowliness of his humanity, emptied by the glory of his majesty and the splendor of supreme light, seems as if absorbed? For as he once emptied himself <margin>Philippians 2</margin> taking the form of a servant, so now that very servant form has been emptied by the majesty of glory, so that no suspicion remains by which he might be believed to be less than the true Son of God. Whence also it is said by the Apostle: "And if we have known Christ <margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin> according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer." Nevertheless, it can—and indeed should—be understood in another way why he does not say "the Son of Man" but "like the Son of Man." The Apostle, speaking of the body of Christ, which is the Church—which is us—after he had said many things specifically about individual members, added and said: "Until we all meet into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ." <margin>Ephesians 4</margin> If therefore the members of Christ are described by Paul—not simply to be understood as those physical limbs with which he was born for us from the Virgin, but the hosts of righteous men who are designated in his carnal shadows <note>original: "in tenebris eius carnalibus". This likely refers to the human, mortal state of the Church on earth</note>—it is clear that he whom John saw in the spirit is not to be understood simply as the Son of Man himself, but he whom the Son of Man himself designates in humility: namely, Jesus Christ, who is the head of all together with his members. Thus, it is not he alone, but he with his members: that is, the head and the body together. He is also rightly shown to be clothed in a <term>podere: a long robe reaching to the feet, specifically the ceremonial garment of the Jewish High Priest</term>, because he also put on flesh for us, having been "made flesh," so that we, receiving that same flesh in an ineffable mystery, are clothed in the same "new man." Truly, because he himself is our righteousness, of which it is also read: "Let your priests <margin>Psalm 131</margin> be clothed with righteousness." Therefore, in the garment reaching to the feet, his virginal flesh is designated, in which he was made a priest forever for the salvation of the world; so that he who once offered himself for us might offer an eternal sacrifice of praise for us in his living and rising body. For that it is a sacrifice worthy of God, God himself teaches when he says: "A sacrifice of praise shall honor me." And let him be, according to the voice of this John in his epistle, our advocate with the Father and the propitiation for our sins. This kind of garment is said to be a linen tunic, which was permitted to be used only by the priests, the sons of Aaron (from whose lineage, in part, Christ was born), undoubtedly as a <term>type: a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of Christ</term> of that same priest of whom it is said in the Book of Psalms: "The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order <margin>Psalm 109</margin> of Melchizedek." It follows:

**And girt about the breasts with a golden belt.** <margin>Chapter 1:13</margin>

# John [the Apostle's] First [Vision] in the Apocalypse

f 2

<margin>John 13</margin>
The **girding of the golden belt** <note>original: "zōe auree", from the Greek *zone*</note> **at the chest** signifies the internal protection of chastity, because the mind of the spiritual man must be tightened, lest the flow of luxury dissolve it through impure and illicit thoughts. For this purpose, indeed, the Head [Christ] went before so that the members [the Church] might follow. This is possible if it is asked of Him with confidence; for He says: "Without me you can do nothing." <note>John 15:5</note> "It was fitting for us to have such a high priest," says the Apostle, "who was innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners." <note>Hebrews 7:26</note> Such a one, he says, and so beautiful: who would possess a virginal body and know nothing of the foulness of the stain of internal corruption; just as among the many things He spoke to the apostles as they were dining, the Truth—which He is—bore witness to Himself, saying: "For the prince of this world comes, and in me he has nothing." <note>John 14:30</note>

But this, as we have already said, was written not so much for His sake as for ours: so that [it might show] what kind of life a priest's should be. I do not mean the life of one who, according to the voice of the prophet, is given to the outer court to eat the sins of the people there; but of him who is led toward the inner places to "taste how sweet the Lord is," <note>Psalm 34:8</note> showing by example more silently than with words. It should be known that there is a double protection of chastity. One of these is designated in the belt of Christ; it is also described that John the Baptist had a belt. Therefore, both had a belt—the servant and the Lord—but the former had a leathern one, the latter a golden one; the former around the loins, the latter at the chest.

In a similar way, both are read to have eaten honey: but John ate wild honey, while Christ ate domestic honey. This is well understood silently, since it is not recorded that Christ's honey was wild. Nor should the difference in the other [food] be believed to be devoid of mysteries: since John is read to have eaten locusts, while Christ is read to have eaten roasted fish. If we consider the distance between the belts and the foods to refer to the times of the Jews and the Gentiles, the reason is clear. Indeed, earthly justice is emptied and fails where heavenly justice is revealed. Even that great Moses hid his face where He who descended from heaven speaks with a revealed face. Wherefore John himself, than whom there was none greater among those born of women, knowing the dispensation of the mystery entrusted to him, signaled that he himself represented the justice of the Law which is of the earth, while Christ represented spiritual justice which is from heaven. "He who is of the earth," he says, "speaks of the earth; but he who

<column-break/>

comes from heaven is above all." <note>John 3:31</note> Therefore, in John's belt or food, the justice of the Old Testament is designated. In the belt or food of Christ Jesus, the justice of the New Testament which descends from heaven is designated; although in these same things we can assign two lives of the Church: namely, the **active** and the **contemplative**. Of these, the one that comes first in time is unequal in merit; the other which follows is preferred in dignity. For however much John was of perfection, compared to Christ, he appears imperfect. And so all his mysteries demonstrate this lack of total sight.

To have a **leathern belt around the loins** is, therefore, for the weak—and would that it were not lacking in those to whom it is said: "Let your loins be girded." <note>Luke 12:35</note> But for all the perfect, and especially monks, it is to have **golden belts at the chest**. For to the former, it is something if they keep the body undefiled; to the latter [monks], it is almost nothing unless they also have purity of heart. The food of the locust suffices for the former, which signifies rare and interrupted reading <note>The author compares the locust's hopping flight to someone who only studies or prays occasionally</note>; for the latter [the perfect], continual reading is necessary, which the fish signifies, being a creature nourished in the water. 

Rightly, then, the locust signifies interrupted reading or meditation, while the fish signifies continuous study; because the locust, lifted from the earth, soon fails in its flight; but the fish travels untiringly through the waters of the sea. Likewise, wild honey signifies any sort of delight in divine worship; but domestic honey signifies not just any delight, but that which is perfect and whole. For truly, he alone understands how great is the multitude of the sweetness of his God, who leaves himself behind through an ecstasy of the mind, and, having despised all things that are of the world, desires only heavenly things. 

Moreover, those two things are well joined together: namely, the locust and the wild honey, or even the fish and the honeycomb; because there are two special types of understanding around which the faithful soul ought to be occupied. Namely, the **knowledge of external things** which is below, and the **wisdom of internal things** which is from above, and which descends from the heavens like a honey-flowing dew. The first of these specifically pertains to the Son, who deigned to take on flesh. The second pertains to the Holy Spirit, who did not do so, but on the day of Pentecost, a sound being made suddenly from heaven, descended upon those who were dwelling as one. In truth, like the ointment from the head which...

### Abb: Part of the Exposition

[The oil] descends upon the beard: the beard of Aaron: and like the dew of Hermon which descends upon Mount Zion. <note>A reference to Psalm 133, where the oil on Aaron’s beard symbolizes the unity of the Church and the flow of divine grace from the head (Christ) to the members (the faithful).</note> Why is the first [attribute] referred to the Son, who is properly called the Wisdom of the Father? It is said because of the assumed form of our mortality. Whenever two such things are placed together, one of which is greater than the other: that which is lesser and more lowly refers to Christ, who has within himself [a human nature] to which it can be referred. That which is more worthy and clear refers to the Holy Spirit. Hence that saying: "Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him. But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the one to come." <note>Matthew 12:32. The author is explaining how Christ’s human nature allows for "lesser" descriptions, whereas the Holy Spirit is described in purely divine terms.</note> For the Son cannot <margin>John 16</margin> be thought of as lesser because of this, insofar as he is God; since he himself says of the Holy Spirit: "He will glorify me, because he will receive of mine." <note>John 16:14</note> But clearly this could be thought of concerning the Spirit himself, if he had accepted human substance more than the Son. For the Holy Spirit would be thought lesser than the Son by the very fact that he could not say of the Son what the Son himself can say of the Spirit: "He will glorify me because he will receive of mine." And why could the Holy Spirit not say this? <margin>John 7</margin> Because he is the Truth and everyone, as the Lord says, "who seeks the glory of him who sent him, this one is truthful." <note>John 7:18</note> For the Son is not from the substance of the Holy Spirit, but rather the Holy Spirit is from the substance of the Father and the Son. <note>This reflects the "Filioque" doctrine, the belief that the Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son.</note> Because he is indeed of the substance of the Father and the Son in such a way that he is not lesser than them, it pleased the Son to take upon himself in the mysteries a lower part—not everywhere, but in some places—not so that he himself should be thought lesser (which would be a disparagement to the Spirit if he proceeded from one lesser than himself), but so that he might be believed to be equal to the same Son. He also prefers the fish to the locust in value and mystery, because the locust resides only on the earth, which is the lower element, and can hardly be moved a little from the earth unless forced, soon to fall back again; and this occurs on dry land, not in water. For those who have neither knowledge of the Holy Scriptures nor the habit of reading them are vehemently weighed down by earthly desires, and if they are ever compelled to rise, they cannot stay on high for long, because they do not have the persistence of the Scriptures to sustain them on high.

<column-break/>

In the same way, regarding belts, there is a very great difference. For what lies between leather belts <note>original: "zonas pelliceas"</note> and golden belts <note>original: "zonas aureas"</note> is the difference between the chastity of the body and that of the mind. In the former, the outer man—in the latter, the inner man—is kept immune from carnal enticements. In the former, free will operates with the help of God; in the latter, God himself is the operator, who is the creator of all. The golden belt, therefore, is the virtue of internal purity, a firm and unshaken spiritual purpose of chastity. However, the leather belt is unlike this in its endurance, color, and value. For the leather one quickly fails and is consumed by age in a short time; the golden one is preserved longer in its newness, because the nature of gold is incorruptible. The leather one is unsightly and cheap; the golden one is precious among the things of the world and of a dearer price. Thus, however great bodily righteousness may be, compared to spiritual righteousness, it becomes cheap, because one can lack the spiritual [glory]; for he who rejoices in the chastity of the mind, which is glory in the purity of the flesh, cannot fail to have the bodily. But if someone who, guarding the initial goods, burns with all his strength for those things which are ahead; even if he departs from this light before he arrives at that toward which he tends, one must not despair. For what he did not receive in this life, he will attain in the other. Because he did not look back once the journey was undertaken, and as much as was in him, he did not stop but proceeded in haste, seeking though imperfect to receive what is more perfect; and while still weighed down by the mass of the flesh, he sought to anticipate the times of his perfection. God is just and good to receive such a person, whose nature it is not so much to accept works as to accept faith. But he who so serves in the body that he fixes his step, thinking it enough for himself that he is continent in the flesh alone—undervaluing spiritual righteousness and purity of heart—is a fool. For he is not worthy to perceive that which is perpetual, and he must necessarily lose that in which he vainly glories. Therefore, "bodily exercise is of little use; spiritual exercise is useful for all things," <note>1 Timothy 4:8</note> having the promise of the life that now is and that which is to come. For the Lord does not say, "Blessed are those <margin>Matthew 5</margin> who are pure in body," but "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." <note>Matthew 5:8</note> In leather, therefore, there is no splendor; in gold there is, because for them to see their God...

It emphasizes that while physical chastity is good, internal "purity of heart" is the ultimate goal that leads to seeing God.</summary>

[It] is granted: to those who are protected with golden belts around their chests: who are drawn by the brightness of the wisdom on which they feed to contemplate and preserve heavenly things: and as if by royal power, they cast away impure thoughts from themselves. If he speaks of the value of the belts, the reason is clear: one uses a leather belt only out of necessity, but a golden belt by choice. This is because it is one thing to resist passion out of fear of physical punishment <note>original: "timore pene corporali"</note>, and another to diligently embrace the goal of spiritual purity with all the strength of the mind out of a love for glory. However, for this to be done more strongly—since a manly strength is indeed necessary—it is required that the mind be occupied with holy meditations worthy of God so that these virtues can be maintained courageously and vigorously. Otherwise, it is inevitable that a person will fall: one who presumes they can act strongly and stand by their vow while their "inner head" has been shaved.

<margin>Judges 16</margin>
What does "with a shaved head" mean, and why did I say it? To wage war against luxury <note>In this context, "luxury" (luxuria) refers specifically to lust or lack of self-restraint.</note> with a "shaved head" is to take up the purpose of internal chastity—which is no small labor—without the meditation of the Holy Scriptures. Even an unlearned person <note>original: "idiota"; referring here to someone who cannot read the Bible themselves.</note> is not strong enough to do this unless this gift is granted to them at least in part; for even if they do not know how to read the silent letters, they nevertheless do not cease to ruminate within themselves, constantly and silently, on what they hear from the teachers.

<margin>Samson</margin>
### On the Fall of Samson.
I made mention of the "shaved head" because the sad mystery of Samson—though it serves as a necessary example—provoked me to this. In his head, which was consecrated to the Lord, we read there were seven locks of hair. While he was a Nazirite <term>Nazirite: A person in the Hebrew Bible consecrated to God by a vow, which included not cutting their hair.</term> of the Lord, as a symbol <note>original: "in typo"</note> of any faithful person who lives a life of purposeful self-restraint, the Spirit of the Lord rested upon him. In the sight of that Spirit, bonds were broken, enemies were put to flight, and the snares of rivals were considered as nothing. But when his hair was shaved, the Spirit departed from him, and the soldier was overcome; for he became weak just like other men. These things were written not so we would believe that the Spirit of strength actually lived in those hairs, or that the invisible Spirit takes delight in unfeeling things, but because those locks designated the virtues through which the grace of the Holy Spirit is perceived and felt by human minds. In these seven

<column-break/>

locks, the seven virtues of the soul which are granted to us by nature are designated. Within these virtues—as if they were honey in waxen vessels—rest the seven gifts of the Spirit <note>A reference to the gifts from Isaiah 11:2: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord.</note>, without which human fragility can perhaps do nothing. These are rightly compared to locks of hair <note>original: "crinibus"</note> because the expression of each is so complex and intertwined; so many things occur to those meditating upon them that the tongue can scarcely express them, and the pen can scarcely comprehend them in writing. 

Therefore, the head of Samson consecrated to the Lord designates the mind of a self-controlled person. As long as he guards those natural goods which were themselves given freely, he inherits the gifts of the Holy Spirit like a good host. Samson was attacked by a harlot; so too is the mind attacked daily by the "flesh of sin" <note>original: "carne peccati"</note>, in the mass of sinners, corrupted in that first sinner and deserter of justice [Adam]. For even if a person has paid the debt of eternal death in baptism, they are not immediately freed from all punishments and the stings of luxury, because the flesh still lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. 

Grace is given first so that we may *will* the good, and then so that we may *be able* to do what we will. Yet the "importunate Eve" <note>The author uses Eve here as an allegory for the lower, sensory part of the human soul which was "seduced by the serpent."</note> does not cease to stimulate the man’s mind and attack it with flatteries. First, she arrives by suggestion, occupying the mind with vain thoughts—though they are simple and seemingly without deceit, not yet showing anything dishonest, impure, or indecent. For example, it might occur to the mind to think that a woman is beautiful with a simple heart, not yet suspecting anything that would delight or excite shameful movements. These are the first bonds of Samson; these are the first ties of the wicked woman that must be avoided. These ties, I say, must be avoided—even if they can be broken quickly and easily—lest the "woman" grow accustomed and presume to do greater things. Secondly, if the first are neglected, a second set of bonds is applied, which are worse than the first to the same degree that the rigor of the mind is softened and weakened by them. Indeed, after the simple suggestion, an impure thought...

...[it] is admitted. If that [seed] is alone with the soul, it indeed infects it but does not succeed, because the soul is still strong and threatens the seed, manfully contradicting its cursed prayers. Therefore, these chains are also broken, because spiritual strength still stands by the soldier who is fighting. But if the miserable man assents to the soothing seed, if the soul, softened and weary, is joined to carnal delight, if it not only fails to resist the foul tickling but agrees to it, then the hair is woven together with a certain cord <note>original: "licio" (the OCR says "lirio"), referring to the thread or cord used to weave Samson's hair into the loom in Judges 16:13.</note> and, bound by it, a nail is driven into the ground of the earthly mind. This is because when good thoughts are mixed with bad, a certain "nail of desire" fixes its root in that earthly soul. Unless he pulls it out first with all his might, he can no longer act as bravely as he did the first and second times, because—his hair of holy thoughts being damaged—the Spirit assists him only in part, not in full. Hence, in the two previous battles, the Spirit is described as being present from the moment he woke from sleep; here, however, it is not from the beginning, but only after the nail has been pulled from the heart of the earth. Certainly, in the fourth war, his hair is no longer woven with a cord but is read to be shaved off, because of which he could not stand. For when depraved delight prevails to such an extent that it excludes holy and God-worthy thoughts from the heart of the sleeping soldier, the miserable man is blinded by the Philistines and carried into Gaza. He is deprived of the freedom of his will, so that he is no longer allowed to do what he pleases; for those who would snatch him away are ready, but there is no one ready to rescue him. But because we have taken up the sad mystery of Samson—presented as a type <note>In theology, a "type" is a historical figure or event that foreshadows something else, usually Christ or the Christian life.</note> of miserable men—to be explained by the occasion of his hair, let that physical fall of Samson move us terribly so we may fear the ruin of perfect men. Let us now return with joy, with the steps of the mind, to our new Samson <note>Referring to Christ</note>, whose head and hair are white, and take his triumphal glory as an example. For it follows:

### ¶ But his head and his hair were white like white wool and like snow.

¶ Why are his head and hair said to be white? Except because the only-begotten of God is holy and innocent? Because he is the head of the Church, for from him all the members of his whole body are drenched in a wave of holiness; his thoughts are pure, and his judgments are true and justified in themselves. Hence, it is said through the prophet in the person of God the Father: "For my ways are not your ways, nor are my thoughts your thoughts. For as the heavens are exalted from the earth, so are my ways exalted from your ways, and my thoughts from your thoughts" <note>Isaiah 55:8–9</note>. "Like white wool," he says, "and like snow." Some things are white by nature, and some by accident <note>The author uses "accident" in the philosophical sense: something that is not part of the essential nature of a thing but is added to it, like paint on a wall or a tan on a person.</note>. Naturally, like white wool and snow; accidentally, like a whitewashed wall. Therefore, because Almighty God is just by nature, but man is just by accident, in saying that the Lord's hair is white, he used natural whiteness as an example, so that Almighty God might be believed to be just by nature, and not by accident like a man. Indeed, even if Christ <note>original: "xps"</note> is a man, "no one is supremely good except God alone" <note>Matthew 19:17</note>—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—this Trinity alone is one God. Now, if the seven locks of Samson signify the natural virtues of each one of us, what do we understand by the hair of Christ, which is white, if not the gifts of the Holy Spirit? Or if whatever is described in this place is to be referred to his humanity for the sake of example, and not to the Divine Majesty (which is to be admired rather than imitated), but should rather be ascribed to the human nature in which he became the leader of our journey—nonetheless, his justice is shown to be like white wool or snow. This is because it did not come from the goodness of a changeable nature, but from the power of the unchangeable Godhead, so that such great perfection of spiritual justice was inseparably in him. This is attested by the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> who says: "The first Adam was made into a living soul; the second Adam into a life-giving spirit" <note>1 Corinthians 15:45</note>. And again: "The first man was of the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly" <note>1 Corinthians 15:47</note>. But if natural virtues rather than spiritual graces are to be understood by his white hair, it is clear that through these same means the gifts of the Spirit rest in him, as already long...

-># The First Part of John in the Apocalypse<-

<margin>Isaiah 11.</margin>
...[as had been] said before: the holy Isaiah had predicted it. *A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.* <note>original: "Egredietur virga de radice iesse..." This is a famous prophecy of the Messiah's lineage and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note> Therefore, it must be considered with vigilance: that just as the soul was created in the image of God and bears the likeness of the Trinity which is God, so too the seven natural virtues within the soul hold the image of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. For as the Trinity, who is God, inhabits the soul of a just man by presiding over it, so the seven gifts of the Spirit rest within the natural virtues of the soul as likes within likes; it follows:

<margin>John 14.</margin>
<margin>Table 20</margin>
**And his eyes were like a flame of fire, and his feet were like fine brass, as if in a furnace of burning fire.** <note>Revelation 1:14-15. The "fine brass" is the Latin *aurichalcum*, a brilliant ancient alloy.</note>
If Samson, having lost his hair, also lost his eyes, it follows that our Samson <note>Referring to Christ as the "true Samson" who destroys the power of death.</note>, whose head and hair are white, should have eyes like a flame of fire. In the eyes, the **contemplative life** is designated; in the feet, the **active life** (the steps of work) is shown. Therefore, in both lives of Christ, he was set ablaze by the fire of the Holy Spirit. For the grace of the Holy Spirit is diffused not only in those members called to leisure and quiet, so that they may stand in the sight of their God in contemplation; but also in those who are assigned to outward ministries, although there is as much difference between the two lives as there is between feet like fine brass in a glowing forge and eyes like a flame of fire. For just as it is one thing to be like a flame of fire, and another to be like a thing remaining in the fire, so the grace of the Holy Spirit is present differently in the active life than in the contemplative life. Just as the uncircumscribed Spirit (who is God and Charity) rests differently in the body of a just man than in the soul, which is spirit. For although the bodies of the just are temples of the Holy Spirit, the bodies do not know God; rather, the souls do. For according to the words of the holy Pope Gregory <note>Gregory the Great, a foundational theologian for medieval thought.</note>: I do not say that the souls of the elect are a thing similar to the bodies, but dissimilar;

<column-break/>

the Spirit of Almighty God vivifies them by pouring into them. Therefore, the eyes of Christ are like a flame of fire, and his feet are like fine brass as in a furnace of burning fire, because both those who receive the grace of contemplation through his gift are flooded with the light of wisdom and set ablaze by the fire of charity; and those who have received the gift of patience through the same Spirit, through the innumerable afflictions which they sustain by suffering, become purer, as if they were gold in a furnace. Because there are some who pant for the contemplative life, yet this proceeds not from charity but from vanity—which according to Moses is to have a "white spot" in the eye <note>original: "albuginem habere in oculo." This refers to Leviticus 21:20, where a physical blemish disqualified a priest; here it is interpreted as a spiritual blemish of pride or vanity.</note>—the example of Christ's eyes demonstrates what the eye of intention ought to be: the flaming vision of those who hasten to this grace at the Lord’s invitation. For it says: *And his eyes were like a flame of fire.* But the proof of the active life is found in temptation, as is said by a certain wise man: *The furnace proves the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation proves just men.* <note>original: "Vasa figuli probat fornax." A quote from Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 27:6.</note> Whence it is also said by the Apostle: *Fire shall prove what sort of work each man's is.* <note>1 Corinthians 3:13.</note> And why is this? Because some, while they glory vainly in the work they do, build not gold, or silver, or precious stones, but wood, iron, and stubble, which cannot stand for long; therefore they must be examined in the future forge—those who pass from this life without the lash, yet not without the cause for the lash. For it belongs to a just judgment that He who did not spare his only innocent Son should scourge every adopted son he receives who is liable to the lash. In this way, therefore, the feet of Christ shine, having been examined in the forge of tribulation; yet, so that they may be able to endure it, they have this strength from nowhere else but the virtue of heaven. For as the soul has nothing of itself, so even if some natural goods were given to it, they are like extinguished lamps and need light, so that through the fire of the Holy Spirit which descends from heaven, it may suffice to tolerate the fire that examines. For how is it believed that Lawrence could have sustained that fire <note>referring to St. Lawrence the Martyr, who was famously killed on a gridiron.</note>, unless from the fire of the Holy Spirit which filled his inner parts...

Whether, therefore, we follow the Lord with Peter <note>Representing the active life of service.</note>, or we are free for contemplation with John <note>Representing the contemplative life of prayer and study.</note>—whether, I say, we hold to that life which is ascribed to the body of Christ and designated by the **feet**, or that life which better fits the **eyes** of His mind—it is the same. For the eye, which is the light of the body, bears His likeness, because the God whom the soul contemplates is surely Light. Both are a gift of God; both are grace. For just as it is through Him that we are able to be like a flame of fire by contemplating heavenly things, so it is also from Him that we are able to sustain pressures and undergo suffering for the love of truth. 

Moreover, because our nature was corrupted in our first parent <note>Referring to Adam and Original Sin.</note>, just as pure gold is turned into **mountain copper** <term>aurichalcum: a bright, gold-colored alloy of copper and zinc, often translated as "fine brass" or "bronze" in Bibles</term>, so Christ (for the sake of likeness) and we (for the sake of the truth of the flesh of sin) must be refined in the **furnace of tribulation** so that we can return to that ancient purity. <margin>Table 21</margin>
### And his voice was like the voice of many waters.

The voice of Christ is like the voice of many waters because, just as many rains sound together with a multifaceted harmony, so too—though there are so many utterances of divine authority and so many commentators of the sacred volumes (separated from one another) in whom Christ speaks—they nevertheless all agree in one sentence of truth and one speech of love, which is the fulfillment of the commandments. Furthermore, just as the sound of flooding rain or the rush of rivers over high precipices toward lower places is heard from a great distance, so the preaching of Christ has been heard to the ends of the earth. Hence, it is said of the holy preachers through the Psalmist: 
<margin>Psalm 18.</margin>
*Their sound has gone out into all the earth: and their words unto the ends of the world.* <note>original: "In omnez terrā exiuit sonus eorum..." - Psalm 18:5 in the Vulgate (Psalm 19 in modern Bibles).</note>
<margin>Psalm 67.</margin>
This is that "voluntary rain" which God set apart for his inheritance, of which it is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews through the Apostle: 
<margin>Hebrews 6.</margin>
*The earth, drinking the rain that often falls upon it and bringing forth herbs useful to those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God; but that which brings forth thorns and briars is rejected and is near to a curse, whose end is to be burned.* <note>Hebrews 6:7-8.</note> Truly, the "earth" which, having received the rain, brings forth thorns instead of herbs is near to a curse; for whoever, having received the preaching of Christ, neglects to bring forth the fruit of justice, it remains that they shall be more severely judged in the end concerning the rain of the Word they received. ### And his face was like the sun shining in its strength.

Each of us knows a person by the appearance of their face. Therefore, so that you do not doubt that Jesus Christ—whose members we are—is the only-begotten Son of God, consider his face in the brightness of the sun. For the face of Christ was seen not as that of Moses once was, having the likeness of the moon <note>In medieval theology, Moses and the Old Law were often compared to the moon, which only reflects light, whereas Christ is the sun, the source of light.</note>, but rather in the likeness of the greater light; so that he might be shown to be the one of whom the Psalmist says: *In the sun he has set his tabernacle, and he comes forth like a bridegroom from his chamber.* <note>Psalm 19:4-5 (Vulgate Psalm 18). The "chamber" was often interpreted as the Virgin's womb.</note> For this is the hope which he showed on the mountain, when he was seen by the three apostles between Moses and Elijah. And when did this happen? After six days, it says. Why after six days? Because that sixth day, on which Jesus took the three disciples and ascended the mountain, designates nothing other than the **sixth age** of the Church <note>Medieval thinkers divided history into six ages; the sixth age began with Christ and was believed to be the final era of the world.</note>. Nor does the splendor of his face signify anything other than the open and manifest knowledge of the Scriptures. Hence, in that same mystery, under the sixth angel sounding the trumpet, one angel was seen to descend from heaven who is said to have a face bright in the manner of the sun, and an open book in his hand; surely this is because the Gospel truth then illuminates those who contemplate it like the sun, when that book which had been partially closed is opened in its entirety—and when that which was spoken by the Apostle begins to be fulfilled: *But when that which is*

<margin>Exodus 34</margin>
<margin>Psalm 18</margin>
<margin>Matthew 17</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>

<column-break/>

*perfect comes, that which is partial shall be done away.* <note>1 Corinthians 13:10. The author links the "perfect" state with the "open book" of final revelation.</note> And that other saying: *Going from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.* <note>2 Corinthians 3:18.</note> And it is well that this happens on the sixth day, by which the sixth age of the Church is designated (as we have already said); for surely all perfection is displayed at the end of the struggle, just as it is said by the Apostle: *Christ is the end of the law for salvation to everyone who believes.* <note>Romans 10:4.</note> And concerning charity, it is said by the Psalmist: *I have seen the end of all perfection; your commandment is exceeding broad.* <note>Psalm 119:96 (Vulgate Psalm 118).</note> Hence, in this place, after the other things written above were sent before, mention is made last of the splendor of the Lord’s countenance. This is because: after the modest light which he poured out upon the earth through his members—whether through those who work in worldly matters for the sustenance of the needy and suffer many pressures and inconveniences for the name of Christ (who for this reason are designated as the **feet** of Christ), or whether through those who, like the **eyes** of Christ, contemplate celestial lights—that which pertains properly and, as it were, specially to himself, he indicates through himself. This happens when he fulfills in us that which he promised through the Prophet, saying: *Behold, I myself will seek my sheep.* <note>Ezekiel 34:11.</note> For the sheep are, as it were, fed by others when pastors are chosen among the people to teach the subordinate churches. But when he clarifies the Gospel truth through his Spirit, it is to fulfill the prophecy which says: *After those days, I will put my law in their inward parts and write it in their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people; and a man shall no longer teach his neighbor or his brother, saying: Know the Lord. For all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest.* <note>Jeremiah 31:33-34. The author suggests that in the final age, believers will have a direct, internal experience of God.</note> It is as if the Lord no longer seeks his sheep through others, but through himself; and he truly visits them just as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep. And because God is wonderful in his saints, and far more wonderful in his majesty, it is necessary that anyone who is deemed worthy to see such great glory should cast himself down; for surely earthly height is confounded when the loftiness of the heavens is opened. Whence it is immediately added:

<margin>Romans 10</margin>
<margin>Psalm 118</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 34</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 31</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the vision of Christ in the Book of Revelation. # Part of the Exposition

**And I fell at his feet as though dead.** <note>original: "Et cecidi ad pedes eius tanquam mortuus." — Revelation 1:17.</note>

Why did he fall as though dead? Because he who previously perceived these things <note>The "he" here refers to John the Apostle, the traditional author of Revelation.</note> presumed that he stood at the very peak of righteousness—as a disciple of Christ and one beloved above all others. But when he was drenched in the light of divine clarity and the splendor of justice, he came to despise whatever he had previously found pleasing in himself. Thus, he is said to have fallen at the Lord's feet "as though dead," because the human mind never judges its own darkness better than when it recognizes the truth in the light of divine wisdom and that justice which comes from heaven. For this reason, the blessed Job—who had raised so many objections against God as judge while speaking in the persona of those being tempted—fell silent once he heard the voice of the Lord, saying:

<margin>Job 42</margin>
> With the hearing of the ear I have heard you: but now my eye sees you. Therefore, I reprehend myself and do penance in embers and ash. <note>Job 42:5-6. Job transitions from arguing his own innocence to recognizing God's absolute sovereignty.</note>

Therefore, just as the blessed Job, before he heard the voice of the Lord, seemed to stand firmly in the rigor of his own persistence as if he possessed some measure of justice, yet was shut out and overcome by the Lord once he heard His voice in a failing response; so too are those who are now ignorant of the equity of judgment, and because of this, they complain against it either with their voice or in their soul. On that day which is known to the Lord, they shall be poured out and fall down. I say "on that day" which shall be between the lashes of punishment and the time of rest—as if between the dead and the living, between the sadness of suffering and the joy of consolation.

The "time of lashes" signifies the course of the "second state" <note>The author uses a medieval framework of "states" or "ages" of the world to explain history. The second state is often associated with labor and trial.</note> represented by Job's suffering. The "time of consolation" signifies the "third state," which will be in leisure and quiet once the days of labor are completed. Moreover, the fact that he earned the right to hear the voice of the Lord between both times and recognized the justice of hidden judgments is to be referred to that clarity of the True Sun, which gloriously shone upon the three apostles on the "sixth day," as I have already mentioned.

<margin>Matthew 17</margin>
Therefore, the contemplator of heavenly things falls as though dead at the feet of Christ when, having recognized the law of truth, he is overcome by the light and becomes terrified—realizing how perverse and impious it was to have wished to penetrate hidden judgments before the proper time. For why does the Almighty God, who is just and pious, 

<column-break/>

so often afflict the innocent with many calamities? Should we not rather hold with uncorrupted faith that God is altogether unable to do anything except what is just? Nor would He wish His chosen ones to undergo the discipline of judgment without cause, while the reprobate (whom God does not take care of in the same way) perish through their own fault. For it is written in the Book of Psalms:

<margin>Psalm 24</margin>
> All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. <note>Vulgate Psalm 24:10; modern Psalm 25:10.</note>

<margin>Psalm 84</margin>
And again:
> Mercy and truth have met each other: justice and peace have kissed. <note>Vulgate Psalm 84:11; modern Psalm 85:10.</note>

<margin>Psalm 88</margin>
And once more:
> Mercy and truth shall go before your face. <note>Vulgate Psalm 88:15; modern Psalm 89:14.</note>

Indeed, mercy and truth precede the face of the Lord because Almighty God exercises the human race with these two virtues until His face is gradually revealed, just as it is written elsewhere:

<margin>Psalm 74</margin>
> Lift not up your horn on high: speak not iniquity against God. For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains: for God is the judge. One he humbles, and another he exalts: for in the hand of the Lord there is a cup of pure wine full of mixture. and he has poured it out from this to that: but the dregs thereof are not emptied: all the sinners of the earth shall drink. <note>Vulgate Psalm 74:5-9; modern Psalm 75:4-8. The "cup" is a common biblical metaphor for God's judgment or the portion assigned to a person.</note>

For men either "lift up their horn" by opposing Him from the "East"—questioning His judgment and saying: "Why did Almighty God exercise such strict judgments at the dawn of time, so that He immediately committed the sinning angels to eternal punishment and chastised the original world with a terrible judgment, addicted to blindness?" Or they oppose from the "West": "Why, near the end of the world, does He permit a whirlpool of nations to inundate the faithful people?" Or even from the "desert mountains": "Why does He leave so many thousands of men in blindness?"

Thus men speak iniquity against God, not knowing the equity of His judgment. Namely, that God is not to be rebuked from the East, nor the West, nor the desert mountains, for the very reason that He is the Judge. Whether He humbles one or exalts another, whether He offers a cup of wine to the just or punishes the just with the sentence of the dregs, He does this through no fire of cruelty or fury, but either by the vengeance of just zeal or the instruction of justice. For He either lashes His sons so that He may restore them to salvation, or He is about to justly punish the impious who now [live] unjustly... <note>original: "fi-" — likely "finiunt" or "faciunt", continuing the thought that the wicked are currently acting out their will.</note>

<summary>This page explores the theme of divine justice by comparing John's vision in Revelation to Job's submission to God. It argues that God's judgments, though often mysterious and appearing as "lashes" or suffering, are always rooted in a perfect balance of mercy and truth.</summary>

# John Primasius on Revelation

<margin>Psalm 145</margin>...follow others: For He executes judgment for those who suffer injustice. Therefore, observing these twofold judgments—those that were just, are just, and shall be—the contemplator of heavenly things <note>referring to John the Evangelist</note> falls prostrate, trembling from the weight of his own complaint; he is seen to fall specifically where he was most moved in judgment. For this reason, the feet of the Lord, which are the lower parts of the body, are worthy of greater honor even from those who fly at higher altitudes. For they have endured greater punishments for the name of Christ. <margin>a. Acts 6. Blessed Stephen.</margin> What part of the body, indeed, is attributed to Blessed Stephen if not the feet? For he, with his companions, was appointed to serve at tables <note>The first deacons were chosen to handle the physical service of the community, acting as the "feet" or support of the early Church.</note>; and yet, because he ran swiftly and outran others toward his suffering, he was found first among the others in grace. Those who are in peace consider the venerable sufferings of those martyrs; judging themselves unworthy—I do not say of the crown, but of life itself—they prostrate themselves before those same holy martyrs, that they might deserve to follow after salvation through their merits. But He who said to Peter, "Follow me," did not say the same of John, but rather: "I wish him to remain thus until I come." <margin>John 21</margin> He reveals the abundance of His goodness toward those whom John himself signifies, when He touches that same beloved disciple with His right hand and exhorts him not to fear. For there follows:

<margin>Chapter 25</margin> **> And he laid his right hand upon me, saying: Fear not. I am the first and the last, and I was dead, and behold I am living for ever and ever.** <note>Revelation 1:17-18.</note>

<margin>John 14</margin> ¶ It is as if He were saying: "Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid; in my Father's kingdom there are many mansions." I, who prepared a place of peace for the martyrs, have nonetheless prepared a mansion for the <term>virgins</term><note>In this context, "virgins" refers to those who live a life of dedicated celibacy and spiritual purity, often contrasted with the "red" martyrdom of blood.</note>. And as I have given the martyrs purple crowns from their passion, I have also prepared for you white crowns from the constant and perpetual triumph of chastity. I wished to touch those others as if they were soldiers with my left hand, so that they might endure the death I suffered for them, laying down their own lives for my servants (that I might win them over). But you, as beloved sons and chamberlains of the heavenly court, I do not wish to grieve; therefore, I touch you not with the left, but with the right hand. And the more closely I count you among my friends, the more I commit to you the

<column-break/>

hidden <term>sacraments</term><note>Here, "sacraments" (sacramenta) refers to divine mysteries or hidden truths of the faith.</note>. For I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends <margin>John 15</margin>; nor do I impose the burden of a painful passion upon you as if you were subjects, because I have made known to you all the pious things I have heard from my Father. And because I know that the souls of the elect are moved by the poverty of justice, I promise them gentler things than those I commanded for their servants. He manifests the cause of this state by saying: **I am the first and the last, and I was dead, and behold I am living.** What does it mean, "I am the first and the last," if not that which he adds next: **And I was dead, and behold I am living**? It is as if he were saying: The first order is that of the martyrs; the last <note>original: "novissimus" - can mean last or most recent</note> is that of the virgins. But I am entirely present in both. I worked there; I rest here. Therefore, it is not fitting for you to be anxious about this matter, for I, who disposed myself to grant you peace freely in this final time, am the same one who gave patience to the battling army so that they could triumph over their enemies. Therefore, you cannot be reproached by my martyrs, who have learned best and remember that they have nothing which they did not receive, and could do nothing on their own. Therefore, the phrase "I have done" or "I am doing" contains a great mystery within it. ¶ I was dead for an hour, but now I live; so that I, who deigned to die for the ungodly, might have companions in my passion. And I, who live forever, might have those who, for a time, hold the mystery of life, so that they too might live together with those who suffered for my name. And I gave those martyrs a greater occasion for joy because of my passion; but to these others, I give joy because of the life-giving Holy Spirit, who did not assume the clay of a human body nor anything of that kind in which he might endure the sadness of passion. ¶ Therefore, because of those who suffered, a number of forty days <note>Lent</note> precedes the sacred day of the divine Passion. ¶ Because of these others who will follow in quiet, another 40 days <note>The season of Eastertide</note> follow in solemn joy; undoubtedly in memory of those 40 days the Lord showed himself alive to his disciples, appearing to them frequently and speaking of the kingdom of God <margin>Acts 1</margin>. And because those forty days—and one week which is called the <term>fiftieth</term><note>The "Quinquagesima" or the 50-day period of Easter concluding at Pentecost.</note>—precede any affliction, so that from the beginning of it until the Saturday of the Easter Vigil, 49 days run together in affliction.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the vision of the glorified Christ from Revelation 1. Having previously discussed the "feet" of Christ as symbols of the martyrs, the author now transitions to the "eyes" and the "right hand," contrasting the active suffering of martyrs with the contemplative life represented by the Apostle John.</meta>

Ten days follow the Ascension of the Lord: so that from the holy day of Easter until the eve of Pentecost, he may spend the same number of days in joyful celebration. If, therefore, in the Passion of Christ the persecution of the martyrs is signified, but in His Resurrection the happiness of the living in Christ is designated, it is clear why the Lord Jesus said to the disciple whom He loved: "Do not be afraid: I am the first and the last; and I was dead, and behold, I am alive" <note>original: "noli timere: ego sum primus & nouissimus: & fui mortuus & ecce sum viuens"</note>. He is working, you see, through both these times and those: no less with the last than with the first, so that He might be the Lord of both the dead and the living, rendering to each according to their works. 

Nor should it trouble anyone that we said the contemplators of the true light are designated in the eyes of Christ—as if it were not an equal comparison that we say this is designated in John. For it is one thing what is given to some in part, and another what is granted to many as a whole. This is especially true since many virgins, wishing to make known to this world the truth which they deserved to contemplate with the eyes of the mind, followed Christ even through the labor of martyrdom; they studied to be incorporated more closely as His "eyes." Yet, this good is not a little different from that which was granted to the blessed John, of whom it was said to the Vicar of Christ <note>Referring to Peter</note>: "I wish him to remain thus until I come." <margin>John 21</margin> <margin>E. 26</margin> It follows:

### And I have the keys of death and of hell.

The keys of death and of hell which the Lord Christ says He has, are the legal rights of the ancient enemy <note>The devil</note> which he held over the human race from the beginning of the world. This began from that time when, through the woman he seduced, he overcame our first parent Adam in Paradise to usurp the forbidden thing; having overcome him, he made him subject to death, and finally snatched him away into hell. For his power prevailed to such an extent that there was scarcely anyone in the human race who was permitted to go out, once it happened that they entered in. 

Therefore, as long as the devil—who is the father of all perdition and damnation—held these keys, he snatched the sons of Adam indiscriminately, damning the impious and accusing the elect. But once, out of the greed of his own malice, he killed the Savior of the world—in whom he found nothing of his own—that unjust judge immediately lost his rights of destruction. The keys were given to Christ, who also conquered him, so that it is no longer permitted for the devil to devour whom he wills, but only those whom the most high Judge permits him to devour by His just judgment. 

Hence it is said through the prophet: "In that time it shall not be said: 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge'; but he who eats the sour grape, his own teeth shall be set on edge." <margin>Jeremiah 31, Ezekiel 18</margin> <note>This scriptural reference argues that individuals are now responsible for their own sins, rather than being automatically damned by the "original sin" of their ancestors.</note> In this way, Jesus Christ is said to have the keys of death and of hell, not so that the gates of death might be opened to swallow the innocent, but so that they might remain closed for many years, just as it is written in the sixth part of this book concerning the author of death: "I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand: and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him." <margin>Revelation 20</margin> And a little later: "And he cast him into the abyss, and closed and sealed it over him." 

And because two great persecutors with their armies were to come—one of whom is called Death, the other Hell—who were to carry out the greatest slaughter of the righteous in their times, it is necessary that they be similarly imprisoned and delivered in the "sixth age" <note>A theological division of history; the sixth age began with Christ</note> into the lake of fire. Indeed, at the time when the father of lies is to be imprisoned, this speech of the Lord saying, "I have the keys of death and of hell," can be appropriately referred to the time of that victory. For He shall close the mouth of the one so that he cannot persist, and the mouth of the other so that he may not swallow those who have been killed. Peace is granted on all sides to the faithful, and the adversaries of the Jews and Gentiles are subjected to the scepter of Christ, who must dominate and reign until He puts all His enemies under His feet. <margin>Psalm 109</margin> <note>Psalm 110:1 in modern bibles</note> 

It is as if it were said: "Because the time of battle is now finished, and the number of those who were to follow me by taking up the cross and were to be crowned with the glory of martyrdom is complete, the gates of hell are from now on closed and sealed; and the keys of their power have been delivered to me, so that it is no longer permitted for the devil and his members to go out to do..."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Christ’s words in Revelation 1:17-18. The previous page established that Christ is the Lord of both the dead (martyrs) and the living (contemplatives). Here, the author explores why Christ claims the "keys of death and hell" and contrasts the public deaths of figures like Peter and Moses with the mysterious "passing" of John and Mary.</meta>

# First Part of John’s Apocalypse

...to do battle with my elect until the appointed time: and therefore it is not necessary for you to be anxious about the penalty of death: but rather to rejoice in the enjoyment of the kingdom: because you will no longer serve me in the death of the flesh—which is to offer a sacrifice to God for sin—but in the life of justice: which is to me a sweet and in every way most pleasing **holocaust** <note>The word "holocaust" here refers to a "burnt offering," a sacrifice completely consumed by fire, symbolizing total devotion.</note>. And these things are indeed fitting enough. But He who says: *I have the keys* <note>original: "Habeo claues"</note>: and does not rather say that the gates of death and hell are obstructed or barred by walls: indicates that there will be a time in which, by the just judgment of almighty God, those same gates must be opened. This is to say: when after the time of the **Sabbath** <note>The "Sabbath" here refers to a period of spiritual rest or a specific age of the Church.</note>—which was indeed initiated by the passion of the Lord, but confirmed for the people of the saints after the ruin of that seventh king who is written of in this volume—which is designated by the Sabbath in the thousand years in which the saints of God alone are promised to reign with <margin>Revelation 17</margin> Christ: Satan shall be released again from his prison: and he shall go out and seduce the nations which are over the four corners of the earth: **Gog and Magog** <note>Traditional biblical names for the enemies of God's people who appear in the final battle.</note>. It does not, therefore, pertain to those whom John, the beloved of Christ, designates to be anxious about the labor of the struggle: but rather about the gift of contemplation which they received from Him: so that they may write what they have seen: both what is, and what must happen after these things. For because it was granted to the blessed John—or rather to that **order** <note>The author uses "order" to mean a specific group or "class" of people in church history, specifically the contemplatives.</note> which is signified by him—as we have already said, to begin from the start of the **second state** and to remain until the end of the **third** <note>The author follows a "Three Ages" theology: the age of the Father (Law), the Son (Grace/Action), and the Spirit (Contemplation/Monastic life).</note>: his gaze is directed by the Lord's bounty toward both of these states, so that he may write all the things he saw: namely, those things which then were, as well as those which were to come. That is: both those pertaining to the second state, as well as those pertaining to the third, and even to the heavenly homeland and the future life. For such things were committed to Saint John to write: such as were not committed even to Peter, the prince of the apostles—to whom it was said by the Lord, *Follow me*—nor to any of the twelve apostles who followed Christ in His passion. But <margin>John 21</margin> this was not from the beginning: but after all the brothers had fallen asleep in the Lord: this mystery is **very much like the Lamb** <note>original: "admodum agnus"; this may be a scribal error for "admodum magnum" (very great), but as written it suggests the mystery is characterized by the nature of the Lamb of God.</note>, and must be weighed by diligent and frequent scrutiny. For the just and pious Lord, who is Wisdom itself, does nothing outside the order of wisdom <margin>Psalm 103</margin>: but as it is written: *In wisdom*—

<column-break/>

—*you have made all things, O Lord: the earth is filled with your possession.* For as I recall having already said in the preface of this work: **Aaron and Moses** were associated together as one: so that they were brothers in flesh and faith: but the first of these died openly: while the second, without the people knowing, was taken from their midst. He associated in mysteries **Elizabeth and Mary**: but the first of these is believed to have failed by a common death: while regarding the most holy body of the Mother of God, what was done is unknown to this day: and it remains a matter of wonder among many who do not know the cause of the mystery. He nonetheless associated **Peter and John**: but Peter, the elder, died openly: while John, descending alive into his tomb, left a great hesitation for his descendants as to what was done with him afterward. Therefore, since it is established that the former of these died openly as a **type** <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future spiritual reality.</note> of Christ: the younger ones, as a type of the **living Spirit**, disappeared as if they had not died. This is either because *the letter kills, but the spirit gives life*: or because in the Holy Spirit, perpetual life is promised to us, as the apostle says: *If <margin>Romans 8:2, col. 3</margin> the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you: He who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of His Spirit dwelling in you.* Or it is because Christ deigned to die for the human race in the human flesh which He assumed: while the Holy Spirit neither assumed that in which He could die, nor could He die since He did not assume it. How fittingly, then, it was said to that disciple who designates the "junior order": *Do not fear, I am the first and the last: and I was dead and behold I am living forever and ever: and I have the keys of death and hell.* Who, being sufficient to weigh this, will prudently recognize it? And because John has that same relationship in this place to Christ—or even in that place where it was said to him by the same Lord hanging on the cross regarding His virgin mother: <margin>John 19</margin> *Behold your mother*: so that he himself might succeed Him in filial obedience, he who was loved by Him above the others—which he has toward Peter in many mysteries: it is clear that in Christ Jesus the **leader of the army of the elect** is designated; in John, the one who is to follow is designated in Christ. That is, he who through act—

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Revelation 1, focusing on the significance of the "ten days" following the Ascension and moving into a deep theological explanation of Christ’s authority over death and hell. It builds on the previous distinction between the "dead" (martyrs) and the "living" (contemplatives like John).</meta>

->Abb. Part of the Exposition<-

Ten days also follow the **Ascension of the Lord**: just as from the holy day of **Easter** until the vigil of **Pentecost**: may the days of the same number pass in joy. If, therefore, in the passion of Christ the persecution of the martyrs is signified, while in his resurrection the happiness of those living in Christ is designated: it is clear why the Lord Jesus said to the disciple whom he loved: *Do not be afraid; I am the first and the last: and I was dead, and behold, I am living.* <note>original: "noli timere: ego sum primus & nouissimus: & fui mortuus & ecce sum viuens"</note> Working, that is, for the sake of time, through these things and those: no less with the last than with the first: so that he may be the Lord of the dead and the living, rendering to each according to their works. Nor should it be troubling that in the eyes of Christ the contemplators of the true light are said to be signified, as if it were not an equal comparison when we say this same thing is signified in John: because one thing is that which is given to some in part, and another that which is granted to many in the whole. This is especially true since many virgins, wishing to make known to this world the truth which they merited to contemplate with the eyes of the mind, also followed Christ through the labor of **martyrdom**: they studied to be more closely incorporated as his "eyes." Yet, this good is not a little different from that which was granted to the blessed John, concerning whom it was said to the **Vicar of Christ** <note>The "Vicar of Christ" here refers to Saint Peter.</note>: *If I wish him to remain until I come.* <note>original: "Sic eum volo manere donec veniaz." A reference to John 21:22, where Jesus speaks of John's destiny.</note> It follows:

### And I have the keys of death and hell.

The **keys of death and hell** <note>original: "claues mortis & inferni"</note> which the Lord Christ says he possesses are the "rights" of the **ancient enemy** <note>The "ancient enemy" is a traditional medieval title for the Devil or Satan.</note> which he held over the human race from the beginning of the world. This dates from that time when, through the woman whom he seduced, he overcame **Adam**, our first parent, in Paradise so that he might usurp the forbidden thing: and having overcome him, he made him subject to death, and finally snatched him away into hell. For his power prevailed to such an extent that there was scarcely anyone in the human race who was permitted not to enter the gates of the underworld: and no one who was permitted to go out, once it happened that they entered. On the contrary, the devil—who is the father of all perdition and damnation—held these keys; he snatched the sons of Adam indifferently, damning the impious and accusing the elect. But from the moment that, in the greed of his malice, he killed the **Savior of the world**—in whom he found nothing of his own—that unjust judge immediately lost the rights of destroying. Those keys were given to Christ, who also conquered him, so that it is no longer permitted for the devil to devour whom he wills, but only those whom the most equitable Judge permits him to devour by his just judgment. Whence it is also said through the prophet: *In that time it shall not be said: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge: but he who eats the sour grape, his own teeth shall be set on edge.* <note>A combined reference to Jeremiah 31:29 and Ezekiel 18:2.</note> In this way, therefore, Christ Jesus is said to have the keys of death and hell: not so that the gates of death might be opened to swallow the innocent, but so that they might remain closed for many years, just as it is written in the sixth part of this book concerning the author of death: *I saw an angel coming down from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand: and he apprehended the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him.* <note>Revelation 20:1-2.</note> And a little later: *And he sent him into the abyss, and closed it, and sealed it over him.* And because two great persecutors with their armies were to come—one of whom is called **Death**, the other **Hell**—who were to perform the greatest slaughter of the righteous in their own times, it is necessary for them to be similarly imprisoned and handed over in the **sixth age** to the lake of fire: namely, at the time when the "father of lies" is to be imprisoned. Not inconveniently, this speech of the Lord saying, *I have the keys of death and hell*, can be referred to the time of that victory: because he shall close the mouth of the one so that it cannot reach out, and the other so that it may not swallow those who have been killed. Peace is given on every side to the faithful round about, and the adversaries of the **Jews and Gentiles** are subjected to the scepter of Christ, whom it behoves to dominate and reign until he puts all his enemies under his feet. <note>original: "donec ponat omnes inimicos suos sub pedibus suis" (Psalm 110:1 / 1 Corinthians 15:25).</note> It is as if it were said: Because now the time of battle has passed, and the number of those who followed me by taking up the cross and are to be crowned with the glory of martyrdom is complete, the gates of hell are henceforth closed and sealed, and the keys of their power are handed to me, so that it is no longer permitted for the devil and his members to go out to do...
