### First [Vision] of John in the Apocalypse

...doing battle with my chosen ones until the appointed time: and therefore you ought not be anxious about the penalty of death, but rather to rejoice in the enjoyment of the kingdom: because you shall no longer serve me in the death of the flesh—which is to offer to God a sacrifice for sin—but in the life of justice: which is to me a sweet and through all things most pleasing burnt offering <term>holocaustum: a religious sacrifice where the offering is completely consumed by fire, symbolizing total devotion</term>. And these things are indeed fitting enough. But because he says, *I have the keys* <note>original: "Habeo claues"</note>, and not rather that the gates of death and hell are hidden or barred with walls, it indicates that there will be a time in which, by the just judgment of almighty God, those same gates must be opened. This is to say: when after the time of the Sabbath—initiated indeed by the passion of the Lord, but confirmed for the people of the saints after the ruin of that seventh king who is written of in this volume <margin>Revelation 17</margin>—which Sabbath is designated in the thousand years in which the holy ones of God alone are promised to reign with Christ—Satan shall be released again from his prison, and shall go out and seduce the nations which are upon the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog. Therefore, it does not pertain to those whom John, the beloved of Christ, designates to be anxious about the labor of the struggle, but about the gift of contemplation which they received from him: so that they may write the things they have seen, and the things that are, and the things that must happen after these. For because it was granted to the blessed John—or rather to that order <note>The author uses "order" here to refer to a specific group or era of people in Church history who embody John’s contemplative spirit.</note> which is signified through him—to begin, as we have already said, from the start of the second state <note>This refers to the "Second Age" of history, associated with the Son/New Testament.</note> and to remain until the end of the third <note>The "Third Age," associated with the Holy Spirit and a more spiritual, contemplative Church.</note>: his gaze is directed, by the Lord's bounty, toward both of those states, so that he may write all that he saw: namely, both those things which then were and those which were to be. That is: both those pertaining to the second state, and those pertaining to the third, and even to the heavenly homeland and the future life. For such things were committed to be written by Saint John as were not committed to Peter, the prince of the apostles, to whom it was said by the Lord, *Follow me* <margin>John 21</margin>, nor to any of the twelve apostles who followed Christ in his passion. But this mystery was not [revealed] from the beginning, but after all the brothers had "fallen asleep" in the Lord: and it must be weighed by a frequent and diligent searching of the spirit. For the just and pious Lord, because he is Wisdom itself, does nothing outside the order of wisdom: but just as it is written: *In wisdom* <margin>Psalm 103/104</margin>

<column-break/>

*you have made all things, O Lord: the earth is filled with your possession.* <note>original: "Oia in sapientia fecisti dñe: repleta est terra possessione tua"</note> For as I recall having already said in the preface to this work: He associated Aaron and Moses together as one, so that they might be brothers in flesh and faith: but the first of these died openly, while the second was taken from their midst without the people knowing. He associated Elizabeth and Mary in mysteries: but the first of these is believed to have failed by common death, while what became of the most holy body of the Mother of God is unknown to this day—and it remains a cause of wonder among many who do not know the reason for the mystery. He likewise associated Peter and John: but Peter the elder died openly; while John, descending alive into his tomb, left a great hesitation to his posterity as to what happened to him afterward. Since, therefore, the former of these pairs are confessed to have died openly as a type <note>A "type" is a biblical person or event that foreshadows a future reality.</note> of the [mortal] Christ, while the younger ones, as a type of the living spirit, disappeared as if they did not die: either because *the letter kills, but the spirit gives life* <margin>Romans 8, 2 Corinthians 3</margin> <note>original: "littera occidit: spiritus autē viuificat"</note>, or because in the Holy Spirit perpetual life is promised to us, as the Apostle says: *If the spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his spirit dwelling in you* <note>original: "Si spiritus eius qui suscitauit Jesum a mortuis habitat in vobis... viuificabit & mortalia corpora vestra"</note>; or because Christ deigned to die for the human race in the human flesh which he assumed, while the Holy Spirit neither assumed that in which he could die, nor could he die while he did not assume [flesh]. Therefore, to that disciple who designates the younger order, it was clearly said: *Do not be afraid; I am the first and the last, and I was dead, and behold, I am living forever and ever: and I have the keys of death and hell.* Anyone who is capable of weighing this will acknowledge it prudently. And because John has that very revelation in this place toward Christ—or even in that place where it was said to him by the same Lord hanging on the cross concerning his Virgin Mother: *Behold your mother* <margin>John 19</margin> <note>original: "Ecce mater tua"</note>: namely, so that he who loved him above the others might succeed him in filial obedience—the relationship he has to Peter in many mysteries makes it clear that in Christ Jesus the preceding army of the chosen is designated, and in John the one who is to follow. Namely, in Christ, who through action...

->Abbot’s Part: An Explanation<-

...and a laborious life in the time of the second state <note>Joachim of Fiore’s theology divided history into three "states": the Father (Old Testament), the Son (the Church of the martyrs/clergy), and the Holy Spirit (a future era of spiritual understanding/monks).</note>, they are crowned with martyrdom: while those in John, who by contemplating heavenly things, shall rest in peace during the time of the third state. Thus, the summer of the age to come, which the children of the kingdom expect, is anticipated not only by the beauty of the rose <note>The rose is a traditional symbol for the blood of martyrs.</note>, but also by the beauty of the lilies <note>The lily symbolizes the purity of virgins and contemplatives.</note>. Nevertheless, because Peter was never in the office of apostleship without John, but John was without Peter—because John remained in this life for a long time after him—since Peter first migrated from this life through the battle of suffering <term>passionis: refers here specifically to the "Passion" or suffering of martyrdom</term>, it is clear that this second state produced not only an exceeding multitude of holy martyrs, but also an infinite crowd of holy <margin>Revelation 7</margin> virgins. For as in the second part of the book, one hundred and forty-four thousand martyrs are recorded to be sealed: so in the fourth part one hundred and forty-four thousand virgins were seen upon <margin>Revelation 14</margin> Mount Zion: of whom it is said: *I saw upon Mount Zion a Lamb standing: and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads.* And a little after: *These are they who were not defiled with women: for they are virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes.* Therefore, it is clear in all ways that these two orders are necessary to him who made them: especially since in the first of them [the martyrs] there is a clear and manifest likeness of the Son; just as in the second [the contemplatives] there is a likeness of the Holy Spirit. This order, which John designates, ought not to fear because it is immune from the whip of suffering; for it does not happen out of its own imperfection that it seems to be without the crown of martyrs, but by the will of the supreme Arbiter, who works and disposes all things according to the counsel of his own will. For he who gave to the martyrs the power to prevail in faith, himself bestowed upon the confessors the power to understand the truth of God’s secrets. And because they behold not only the present things which are at hand, but also the past and the future understood through those things which are written. And since each one receives as much as he is to spend upon his fellow servants from him who distributes the talents: it is rightly said in the person of John to those same contemplators of truth:

> Write therefore the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which must be done hereafter.

<column-break/>

¶ For it is as if he were saying: Since on account of two principal virtues without which the kingdom of God cannot be obtained—namely, the servitude of humility and the liberty of love—two orders of the righteous are necessary: it is not safe hereafter for those who belong to the second order to be disturbed by the penalty of instilling the spirit of servitude again in fear, but rather by the description of the glory which has been shown to you for the sake of persuading love; because the time hereafter will be of love and joy, in which perfect charity casts out fear <margin>John 8</margin> <note>The margin likely refers to the Gospel of John, but the quote "perfect charity casts out fear" is from 1 John 4:18.</note>. But the words of God must be written and marked in the book not so much with ink and pen on the skins of dead bodies <note>A reference to parchment, which is made from animal hides.</note>, but with the pen of the human tongue in the hearts of living souls: so that while they perceive those things which have passed, and those which are, and those which are to come, they may grow cool toward the love of the present world; and each one may progress in his own order as much as the merits of each are clearly seen. Truly, the blessed John saw in the spirit what had been done before him in the Old Testament; he saw what was done in his own time; he saw what was to be until the end of the world. He saw indeed among the ancients the sealed book; he saw in his days the Lamb slain, and the Lion rising from the dead: and he wrote that in human hearts: because he took care to preach to the churches subject to him that very thing which he had been granted to see. He also saw and wrote that the seals were to be loosed in seven times: and those things which were veiled under the husk of the letter <note>original: "sub cortice littere". This refers to the "spiritual" meaning hidden beneath the literal, "fleshy" words of scripture.</note> in those same seals; which also, as was said to him, were quickly to be completed: Because a thousand years before your eyes <margin>Psalm 89</margin> <note>Psalm 90:4 in modern numbering.</note> are as a day that has passed. In the same way, the spiritual contemplators see with spiritual eyes what has been completed in the church of God from the advent of the Lord until the present: they see both what is present and what is to come: and they certainly take care to write them with the pen of the tongue in the hearts of their listeners: so that men may not die in their sins, but rather be converted and live. It follows:

### [The First Chapter of John in the Apocalypse]

...which you saw in my right hand and the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches. <note>The text is quoting Revelation 1:20.</note>

¶ What is said in this place concerning the explanation of the stars is not a mere allegorical speech, but rather a kind of introduction to mystical language. It acts as an explanation of the vision, holding the integrity of the truth of allegorical speech in hidden things. Thus <margin>Genesis 41</margin> Joseph, interpreting the dreams of Pharaoh, said that the seven thin ears of corn and the seven lean cows would be seven years of famine that would consume the seven years of plenty. In this interpretation, if one should not consider it a purely allegorical understanding, it is because Joseph explained the king’s dream in such an allegorical way. For the first seven years in this work designate the seven noted ages of the Hebrews, in which—as in seven ages—the seven seals of the book were completed, and the grains of the sacred words were collected into heaps. But the seven years of famine signify the seven ecclesiastical times <note>The "seven ages of the Church," a common theme in medieval apocalyptic thought.</note> to which the individual parts of this book are assigned—except that the sixth part includes two together in one. This is because the seventh part is secluded from this law, and it alone corresponds to these six parts as Rachel corresponds to Leah <note>original: "Rachel Lye." Leah represents the active life, while Rachel represents the contemplative life.</note> on equal terms. Therefore, in these seven times, the sacred storehouses of the prophetic books are prepared; and the wheat of the Word, long hidden, fills the hearts of the hungry peoples until the days of famine pass, and the ancient abundance, longed for by all people, returns. Moreover, when Joseph stores up the grain and bestows it by dividing the provisions, whom else should we believe he represents but the order of models? He is the one who looses what is bound, and through the Holy Spirit who dwells within him—or rather, the Holy Spirit through them—divides spiritual nourishment for hungry and afflicted souls. Thus, in this place, the mystery of the stars and the golden lampstands must not be observed simply as it is spoken, as if the mystery were completed in those seven bishops and their churches;

<column-break/>

but rather in those orders <note>The "orders" (ranks or groups) of the faithful, such as monks, clergy, and laity.</note> which are designated in those same bishops (whom He also calls angels) and in their churches. But why is Christ said to have seven stars in his right hand? The reason for this is what we discussed above when we dealt with Christ's right hand being placed upon John: namely, that just as the left side looks toward Peter (pertaining to the prelates of five churches), so the leaders of the seven churches (pertaining to John) were seen to stand at the right. And why is this? Because Christ Jesus, by the most humble dispensation of His kindness, took the left part for Himself to provide to the human race an example of true and most sincere humility. He demonstrated through many clear signs that the gift of liberty and grace, in which we must be made free, is to be attributed to the Holy Spirit. This is not to say the Son frees us any less (far be such a thought from the hearts of the elect!), since He Himself says <margin>John 8</margin>: *If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.* Rather, it is because the same Spirit by whom we are made free is the love of the Father and the Son, by which they love us; and therefore, because they love us, they grant freedom, just as it is said by the Apostle <margin>Galatians 4, Romans 8, Philippians 2</margin>: *God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father.* And again: *You did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry: Abba, Father.*

¶ In this matter, it is useful to note something else worthy of memory and report: the Son of God, who is properly called Wisdom, assumed the form of a servant in which He might endure weariness and labor. But the Holy Spirit, who is called the Charity <note>original: "charitas," meaning divine love.</note> of God, did not assume it. This is because we are distressed, afflicted, and labored in learning wisdom; but in loving what is pleasing to love, we endure no afflictions or distresses. It was fitting, therefore, for the goodness of God to labor with us where we labor, so that through His labor of freedom, we might finally come to liberty ourselves. And because there are five senses of the body (as we have already said) in which mortal man exercises himself in the study of action, but seven gifts of the Spirit by which the inner man is made spiritual, the five principal...

### [The Explanation of the Parts]

...of the church: about which we made mention near the beginning of this book: [these] are to be attributed to the only-begotten Son of God. But the seven things of which he treats here are attributed to the Holy Spirit: because even the Word of the Father deigned to be incarnated, so that through His five works, by cleansing us from the corruption of our first parent <note>Adam</note>, He might heal us; and the Holy Spirit, coming not in flesh but in fire, by infusing the gift of the sevenfold grace, might fill the hearts of His elect. Someone may ask us to state what the five works of Christ are: let him seek this from the writers of the Gospel, and especially from Saint Luke, who followed all things in order, as he himself asserts; and who, after he described the Gospel of Jesus Christ, joined the Acts of the Apostles to the same Gospel in a summary.

<margin>The five works of Christ</margin>
The first work of Christ was the Nativity; the second, the Passion; the third, the Resurrection; the fourth, the Ascension; and indeed, the fifth work is the manifestation of the tongues and the sending of the Holy Spirit. Truly, for this reason He was sent by the Son: so that He might bear witness to Him, and that all might honor the Son just as they honor the Father. For this reason, as I have already said, the four books of the Gospels of Christ and the book of the Acts of the Apostles are to be ascribed to these five works, because among that people called the "Circumcision" <note>Referring to the Jewish people of the first century.</note>, these five works were visibly completed: whether the Nativity by which He was born; or the Passion by which He suffered; or the Resurrection by which He rose from the dead; or His Ascension into heaven; or the arrival of the Holy Spirit sent by the Son in tongues of fire as He had previously promised. Truly, as the blessed

<margin>Gregory</margin>
Pope Gregory says: "The tongue has a great affinity with the Word." Therefore, He was demonstrated in tongues of fire to show Himself to be the Spirit of Truth—that is, the Spirit of Him by whom He was sent. And because He announced nothing other than what He had received from Christ, the Word of the Father, who, when He promised Him to the apostles, said:

<margin>John 15</margin>
> "When the Paraclete <note>original: *paraclitus*; the Helper or Comforter.</note> comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of Truth, who proceeds from the Father..."

He immediately added and said:

<margin>John 16</margin>
> "He will glorify me, because He will receive from what is mine and announce it to you."

Therefore, not only the four works which are special and are known to correspond to the four living creatures <note>The lion, ox, man, and eagle from the Apocalypse, traditionally representing the four Evangelists.</note>—according to the state which most specially belongs to Christ—are to be ascribed [to Him]; but also this arrival of the Holy

<column-break/>

Spirit, who gladdens the City of God. By the fact that He was shown in the form of tongues and sent in the name of the Son—especially since He made them eloquent for preaching and sharp for speaking—all of this is to be ascribed to the property of the Word. Just as it is the property of the Spirit to breathe where He wills, even without the hearing of ears or the vision of eyes; indeed, all the more perfectly, the more sight is absent from the eyes and hearing from the ears. But because the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God, neither is the Son without the Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit without the Son, just as the Father works nothing without them. And yet, because they are truly three persons, some of those things which they work together have more the image of the Father, some of the Son, and some of the Holy Spirit. Certain things are more specially attributed to the Father, such as power, fear, and faith; certain to the Son, as humility, truth, and wisdom; certain to the Holy Spirit, as charity, joy, and liberty. Although each of these belongs to all three, and all alike belong to each individual. In another way, therefore, it was brought about that the Holy Spirit should appear in tongues to teach what the apostles of Christ did not know, so that He might show Himself to be the Spirit of Truth—because Christ is the Truth. To demonstrate that the work of teaching <term>magisterium: the office of authority or teaching in the church</term> belonged to Him, forming His elect to the custody of humility, after those things He had foretold concerning the Father, He subsequently added concerning Himself, saying: "And do not be called masters, for your Master is one, Christ." Therefore, the property of preaching belongs to the incarnate Word, yet the Holy Spirit assists Him, as one who was sent from heaven by the one Father with Him to bear witness to the truth; although the property of the Holy Spirit seeks silence more than speech, and by no means forces Himself upon us by shouting, but inspires us by being silent. For who does not know that the office of preaching has been conferred by right upon the clergy—which pertains to the "second lamp" <note>original: *secundam lpaz*; likely referring to the second era of the church or the second person of the Trinity.</note>—but that silence is appropriate for monks, which looks toward the beauty of Rachel <note>The biblical Rachel represents the contemplative, silent life of a monk, while Leah represents the active life of a preacher.</note>? He is quite far from the household of faith who does not know that spiritual gifts cannot be perfectly possessed by anyone without the tranquility of silence. For who can dictate even a few letters amidst the noise of words, when the intellect is scattered among many things?

-># John’s First [Commentary] on the Apocalypse<-

From this we see why the blessed John merited to contemplate the secrets of this book at that time: because he had been removed from the noise of the crowds and banished to a solitary place. This was to teach those who are spiritual and who long to taste the abundance <note>original: "ubera", literally "breasts," a common metaphor for the nourishing richness of divine grace</note> of spiritual gifts that it is necessary to be removed from the bustle of the people. The further they depart by fleeing from worldly cares, the closer they become to God through silence. And indeed, concerning those five senses which are external, human instruction is necessary—either so that one may exercise them in good works, or so that they may study to vigilantly abstain from evil. Just as this is a task of no small labor, so too it is granted as a gift not to be looked down upon. However, concerning those seven gifts—with which the seven spirits of this book are known to agree—the industry of the human tongue is not so much required as the grace of the Holy Spirit. Since He is an invisible and simple substance, once the noise of the voice is removed from every side, and without the obstacle of any difficulty, He breathes invisibly where He wills and works whatever He pleases without the help of the human tongue. Nor was the cause of this mystery to be valued so lightly as to pass by untouched without a mystical example; rather, because it is of greater glory, it has been gathered together in the Gospel oracles under even more sublime figures, so that through those things which were wonderfully done, we might be able to contemplate what happens daily <margin>Luke 1</margin> in the Church of Christ, being instructed by that same Spirit. Saint Elizabeth was a sterile woman, even though she knew and had a husband. Mary was a fertile virgin, and yet she was unknown to a man. In both, therefore, according to human standards, conception was hopeless: surely because one was sterile, and the other <margin>Matthew 19</margin> had not known a man from whom she might conceive. But what does the Truth <note>A title often used for Christ</note> say? "What is impossible," He says, "with men is possible with God." <note>original: "Que impossibilia sunt apud homines: possibilia sunt apud deum."</note> Therefore, the woman who was known—and long known—by a husband conceived from a man, but through God. The unknown virgin also conceived, not from a man or through a man, but by the mediation of an angel who announced that very thing from the Spirit. Recognize now in Zacharias the order of preachers, and in Elizabeth the churches of the listeners. Understand in Joseph the spiritual men who

<column-break/>

are set over the assemblies of the righteous; and in Mary, understand that spiritual Church itself, sequestered from the world. The "Elizabeth-part" of the Church is praised if it hears the word of God gladly and attends to it frequently. The "Mary-part" is praised if it continually keeps silence in the "chamber of the cloister," <note>original: "claustri thalamo," referring to the private, inner life of a monastery or the soul's private devotion</note> devoting itself to prayers and psalms, speaking to itself and to its God, seeking in divine readings to grasp that "one thing" <margin>Luke 10</margin> of which the Lord says: "Furthermore, one thing is necessary." <note>original: "Porro unum est necessarium." This refers to Jesus's praise of Mary of Bethany, who sat at his feet while her sister Martha was busy.</note> Yet she herself also waits for a spiritual angel to speak to her—that is, a spiritual preacher who speaks wisdom among the perfect. These are surely mystical and spiritual discourses, not historical and carnal ones; they are certainly not for those who do not understand, but <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> are suited for "little ones in Christ." Indeed, the carnal man <note>original: "animalis homo," often translated as the "natural" or "soulish" man who lacks spiritual perception.</note> does not understand the things of the Spirit of God; and because of this, those things which the saints contemplate—who are often lifted up into the "third heaven"—they do not dare to speak to carnal people, lest they perhaps become weak, be distressed, and fall away. Therefore, Mary's speech should be like Gabriel's, but it must be entirely of the Spirit <margin>Luke 1</margin>. He said: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you." <note>original: "Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te & virtus altissimi obumbravit tibi."</note> Do not say, "I have no teacher who can explain to me every single thing I read"; where the Spirit is the teacher, a small spark of the word grows to an immense size. <margin>John 1</margin> And because "the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us," He who was invisible due to the simplicity of His nature deigned to become visible through the assumption of a human substance. He willed to sound forth through visible men by the mystery of the voice, so that those who were unable to penetrate the secrets of the Divinity by contemplation might be snatched up to sublime things by visible examples. But spiritual men are not like this—not so—but rather, the purer their hearts are, the more they intellectually fix the sharp gaze of their spiritual eyes upon the Creator of all things through the invisible works of God which are closer to them. However, so that they may be able to do this, the seven gifts of the Spirit are necessary for them. These are divided among individuals as He wills by that one Spirit, who is God, and who was poured out into the hearts of the faithful on the day of Pentecost, because He is Himself the emanation of the Father and the Son.

<margin>John 8</margin>
saying: "If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink: and rivers of living water shall flow from his heart." <note>original: "de ventre eius", literally "from his belly," a biblical idiom for the innermost being</note> ¶ In this matter, something ought to be noted with vigilance: namely, that the blessed John—who often serves as a type <note>a symbolic figure or representative</note> of the Holy Spirit—departed from the primitive Church (in which the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out) and presided over the seven churches which are in Asia. He is known to have rested in the city of Ephesus after the course of his struggle was completed, just as Peter rested in Rome. If it was necessary for Peter to participate in the gift of the Holy Spirit in this way, how much more so for John, who was loved by Christ above the rest? This was to show the bond of unity that exists between the Son and the Holy Spirit. Spiritually, Christ Jesus was seen to rest in those who followed the humbler path <note>referring to the active life of service and leadership represented by Peter</note>; but the Holy Spirit rests in those who rejoice in freedom—those who are known to have chosen the "better part" for themselves by leaving behind the world and its business so they might be free for divine service.

<margin>Luke 10</margin>
However, since those five churches were made the special inheritance of Christ, how can the seven churches discussed here be seen as belonging to the Holy Spirit? By reason, Christ loves the former, but the Holy Spirit loves these latter much more closely. Yet, because "charity does not seek its own," but rather what belongs to another, Christ is declared to love that disciple more closely who was, as it were, the Holy Spirit’s own, when it is said:

<margin>John 21</margin>
"That disciple whom Jesus loved." And the Holy Spirit wished to descend first into that Church which was committed to Peter, the vicar of Christ: namely, the Church of Jerusalem, which Christ presided over from the beginning and which Christ himself committed to Peter, saying: "Feed my sheep." <margin>John 2</margin>

Thus, Christ Jesus embraced him who was like the Holy Spirit’s own; while the Holy Spirit honored him who was like Christ Jesus’s own, infusing him more abundantly with the sweetness of his charity, so that he might love the Lord and Master more than the other fellow apostles. So it was with the two sons of Joseph: the first of whom designates the Latins, and the second the Greeks. This is because John, the younger, was sent to the Greeks; and Peter, the elder, being the first apostle, was sent to the Latins. According to this, the firstborn, Manasseh, is to be attributed by a certain property to the Son, and Ephraim to the Holy Spirit. They were weighed in a friendly contention between Israel <note>Jacob</note> and Joseph: so that the one whom Joseph tried to prefer, Jacob (foreknowing things to come) placed second in his blessing, and vice versa. Although Manasseh was by no means moved from his place, nor was Ephraim transferred from his place and moved to the right, rather, the one who stood on the right was touched by the left hand, and the one who remained on the left was touched by the right hand. Thus, with neither of the fathers yielding entirely to the other, both appeared as the first and, in turn, the inferior, as if from an equal standing. ->### First [Exposition] on John in the Apocalypse<-

Joseph signifies that he tried to honor that people more, who seemed to belong to Jesus Christ by the right of the firstborn. But the Father, whom Jacob signifies, wished to remain "unconquered" <note>original: "invictus", playing on the name Israel, "he who strives with God"</note> regarding this: lest the special people should seem inferior in two ways, and so that the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Son, should not be thought by some to be lesser than the Father and the Son. Therefore, although the only-begotten Son of God, seeking the glory of the Holy Spirit, may elevate His special ministers with the prerogative of His love, let the Holy Spirit in turn diligently bestow honor and glory upon that same only-begotten Son. Yet I would say that the part which Christ, as was said before, "bore unconquered" is to be esteemed the happier part; the prudent and careful reader will clearly understand this from what has been written and what may still be written. But why should greater glory be attributed to that part which the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit as the "Comforter" or "Advocate"</note> brought forth? This happiness, and to whom it is to be preferred, is not [found] except in that the people rejoice in being loved more, even if he who is loved less is honored more; this is clearly seen in things that frequently happen. However, the judgment of the ambitious is deceived in this matter because they are entirely ignorant of the power of love, without which even all her magnificence does not suffice for a queen. And what should be said of this? The wife of a soldier, beloved by her husband, considers herself—and is—happier than the wife of a king whom the king does not love, even if she complains of no loss in her glory; unless perhaps she is a harlot and does not herself love the one by whom she scorns to be loved, having her own secret lovers with whom she wretchedly thinks herself happy. If this is so, even in this way the reasoning is not hindered, since even if she considers a depraved love to be happiness, she nonetheless considers *love* to be happiness, and that there is no happiness, but only misery, where love is absent. Wherefore I would say the part of John, who is loved more by Christ, is happier than the part of Peter, who is loved less—if he himself loves more. Yet Peter's part is also happy because, even if not loved equally, he is still loved; and what the distance of love lacks, the prerogative of glory and the majesty of honor supplies. Finally, the scepter is given to Leah, to whom

<column-break/>

the beauty of Rachel is denied: so that what she has less in love, she may supply in offspring. <note>Referring to the biblical sisters; Rachel was loved by Jacob for her beauty, but Leah was more fruitful in bearing the tribes of Israel.</note> Because the understanding of mysteries <note>original: "archanorum", secret or divine mysteries</note> is granted to that part which pertains to the beloved John, the discourse concerning the special orders belonging to him has run ahead. However, the discussion of the "five greater" ones—who are preferred in time and power—is postponed, so that they may be shown to be subject to God, as the first are last and the last are first, and so that all the world may learn to be subject to God, and no flesh may glory in His sight. The Primitive Church is signified by what the **lion** represents: namely, the order of the **prelates** <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops</note>. The Church of Antioch is signified by the **calf**: namely, the order of **martyrs**. The Church of Alexandria is signified by the **human**: namely, the order of **confessors** <note>Those who suffered for the faith but were not killed</note>, who are specifically to be called **doctors** <note>Teachers of church doctrine</note>. The Church of Constantinople is signified by the **eagle**: namely, the order of **holy virgins**. The Roman Church is signified by the **throne**: representing the general **church of the just**, which consolidates the various dwellings within itself in the bond of unity and peace. In the fact that John was "in the Spirit on the Lord's day," he contemplated the only-begotten of God the Father, who is the prince of pastors in the glory of majesty; this sufficiently shows that the order of the vision is to be referred to the day of the Lord's resurrection and to the **order of pastors**, which is first. Indeed, the Lord's resurrection is attributed to the pastors (who must be "lions" in the strength of their faith), just as the Passion or baptism is attributed to the **martyrs**, the Birth to the **doctors**, the Ascension to the **contemplatives**, and the coming of the Holy Spirit to those **fervent in charity**. But if we must deal with the special orders: behold, in this first part of the book, they are designated by the type of the seven churches, so that 
<margin>Matthew 20</margin>
the "first shall be last and the last shall be first" <note>A reference to Matthew 20:16, suggesting a reversal of historical importance</note>. This is especially true since in this vision a prerogative of love is ascribed to them because of Saint John, who was given to them as if as their own; or rather, because of the Holy Spirit, who rests in them more specially, just as was designated in the seven locks of hair of Samson. Therefore, that which pertains to the flesh began from the Church of the Circumcision <note>The early Jewish-Christian community</note>—that is, from that 
<margin>Judges 16</margin>
people who lived according to the flesh. But that which pertains to the Holy Spirit began from the Church of the Gentiles, where nothing was done according to the law of the flesh, but everything, in a certain way, according to the law of the Spirit. This is the principal church: that Church of the Ephesians, which is known to have flourished first in Asia after Antioch—that is, after that church in which the faithful from the circumcision frequently quarreled over Judaism. Which

<column-break/>

in the Ephesian church and the remaining six is read to have hardly ever happened. Therefore, we must then deal with these churches and with those things signified through them: how the Holy Spirit had predicted the future to them through the things that were written, fulfilling the promise of the Lord saying: "For he 
<margin>John 16</margin>
will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come." <note>A quote from the Gospel of John regarding the Holy Spirit (the Paraclete)</note> Since not all religious orders run with one mind or equally, let each person weigh from these things which are written and described—by a man, indeed, but from the Holy Spirit—which of the seven churches is worthy of praise or of reproach. Note what was said: **Five parts** of the book are to be attributed to the **five general churches** pertaining to Peter; **seven portions** of the first part are to be attributed to the **seven special [churches]** pertaining to John. And yet, there is a certain similarity between the general and the special: for just as in the first part of the book it treats of all prelates, so in the first portion of the first part it treats of certain prelates; and just as in the second part of the book it treats of all martyrs, so in the second portion of the first part it treats of certain martyrs; and so on for the others—except that in the general parts a general number is held, while in the special parts a sevenfold number is held. But if we wish to follow those things brought forth concerning the **sixth time** <note>original: "sexto tempore", referring to the sixth age of the world or church history</note>, when the splendor of the face of the Lord was discussed, we are truly compelled to pass over to the **third state** <note>A key concept in Joachite theology referring to the coming Age of the Holy Spirit</note>. However, we are barely able to assign anything yet regarding its understanding: because how the future order itself (which will exist in the remnants of the Jews and the Gentiles in the likeness of the present Church) is to be distinguished, we cannot assign now, any more than the things that have been done in this Church of the Gentiles from the time of the Apostles until now could be assigned by the doctors of the Primitive Church. I see only this to be noted concerning the aforesaid churches according to the understanding pertaining to the **third state**: that just as the life of Peter pertains only to the second state, but the life of John to the second and third, so the understanding of the five churches and the five general parts of the book is to be directed only to the second state. But the understanding of the seven churches and the seven portions of the first part belongs to the **second and third [states]**.

<meta>This page continues the symbolic analysis of the five major episcopal sees and their relationship to the "Four Living Creatures" of the Apocalypse. It transitions into a discussion of the seven churches of Asia and the distinction between the "State of Peter" (the present Church) and the "State of John" (the coming age of spiritual understanding).</meta>

->### Abbot’s Part of the Exposition<-

...the Church of Constantinople; and in the fifth, the Roman Church. By these five, we understand four things: namely, the four <term>living creatures</term><note>Refers to the lion, ox, man, and eagle from Revelation 4, traditionally symbols of the Evangelists but here applied to historical "orders" of the Church.</note> and the throne of God. Their meaning is as follows: The **Primitive Church** is signified by the **Lion**, representing the order of **prelates** <note>original: "prelatorum"</note>. The **Church of Antioch** is signified by the **Calf**, representing the order of **martyrs**. The **Church of Alexandria** is signified by the **Man**, representing the order of **confessors**, who are specifically called **doctors** <note>The "doctors" were the great teachers and theologians of the early Church.</note>. The **Church of Constantinople** is signified by the **Eagle**, representing the order of **holy virgins**. The **Church of Rome** is signified by the **Throne** (or Seat), representing the general **Church of the Just**, which consolidates various dwellings within itself through the bond of unity and peace. Because John was "in the spirit on the Lord’s day" and beheld the only-begotten Son of God the Father—the Prince of Pastors in the glory of His majesty—this sufficiently shows that the order of the vision refers back to the day of the Lord’s Resurrection and to the **Order of Pastors**, which is first. Indeed, the Lord’s Resurrection is attributed to the pastors, who must be "lions" in the strength of their faith; just as the Passion or Baptism is attributed to the martyrs, the Nativity to the doctors, the Ascension to the contemplatives, and the coming of the Holy Spirit to those fervent in charity. But if we must speak of specific orders, behold, in this first part of the book, they are designated under the <margin>Matthew 20</margin> figure of the **seven churches**, so that "the first shall be last and the last first." This is especially true since, in this vision, a prerogative of love is ascribed to them because of **Saint John**, who was given to them as if he were their own; or rather, because of the **Holy Spirit**, who rests in them more specifically, just as was <margin>Judges 16</margin> signified by the **seven locks of hair** on Samson’s head. Therefore, that which pertains to the flesh began with the Church of the Circumcision—that is, from that people who lived according to the flesh. But that which pertains to the Holy Spirit began with the **Church of the Gentiles**, where nothing was done according to the law of the flesh, but everything, in a sense, according to the law of the Spirit. This is the principal church: that **Church of the Ephesians**, which is known to have flourished first in Asia after the Church of Antioch—that is, after that church in which those of the circumcision frequently argued about Judaism. This

<column-break/>

was a conflict that is recorded as having scarcely ever happened in the **Church of Ephesus** and the other six. I see only this one thing to be noted regarding the aforementioned churches according to the understanding pertaining to the Third State: just as the life of **Peter** pertains only to the **Second State**, but the life of **John** pertains to both the **Second and Third**, so the understanding of the **five churches** and the five general parts of the book is to be directed only toward the **Second State**. But the understanding of the **seven churches** and the seven portions of the first part belongs to both the **Second and the Third**.

### Concerning the Angel of Ephesus. Chapter 2.
**And to the angel of the church of Ephesus write: These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.**

The only-begotten Son of God, speaking of himself as if of another, suggests that the entire Church of the elect is to be placed at his right hand, saying: *He shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.* And since he himself says in another place: *Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,* it is not absurd to ask why he says he holds only the **stars** in his right hand and not also the **seven lampstands**, or why he claims to walk in the midst of the **golden lampstands** and not also among the stars. 

In the riddle of this question, we must follow the custom of the Scriptures, which demonstrates that one and the same thing often produces diverse understandings, just as the "wheels" of the Scriptures <note>A reference to the "wheels within wheels" in the vision of the prophet Ezekiel, symbolizing the complex, moving layers of biblical meaning.</note> move according to the impulse of the Spirit. For one must judge specifics in one way and generalities in another. It is one thing when a single person is written of, another when a second is joined to him; it is different when that which is joined is of lesser value or dignity, and different when it is of greater. It is different when a "simple" thing is paired with another "simple" thing, and different when a "simple" thing is related to a "multiple" thing. 

We sense something specific and mystical is designated when God speaks to **Moses** alone on Mount Horeb. But if **Aaron** is joined to that same Moses, the understanding immediately shifts from that matter to another. In the same way, if we deal with **Sarah** without **Hagar**, Sarah alone can designate something beyond what she signifies when she is placed in relation to Hagar. But when Hagar is associated with Sarah, the mystery immediately changes—yet it is not the same as when Hagar is removed and **Rebecca** is substituted. This is how it works with two "simple" things <note>In this context, "simple" refers to individual persons or singular symbols.</note>. 

However, we speak of the "simple" and the "multiple" when two things are placed together where one refers to a person and the other to a multitude—such as the **Pastor and the Flock** in the Old Testament, where one usually designates **Christ** and the other the **Church**. If someone cannot understand this rule of mysteries, I do not know if anyone can satisfy him regarding the individual places where these changes occur. But he who does not grasp this yet is curious should first learn to believe what he hears, so that in his own time he may reach full understanding.

# Joachim: Part One on the Apocalypse
## Page 52
-> B 4 <-

For who does not know that silver, compared to bronze and tin, is a precious metal? But if gold is placed beside it, it ceases to be precious; this is clearly shown in this passage. So too, in comparison to the reprobate <note>The "reprobate" refers to those rejected by God or destined for damnation, contrasting with the "elect."</note>, the whole assembly of the elect are said to be placed at the right hand of almighty God. Nevertheless, no mention is made of them in this place, but only of the **seven stars**, in which it is clearly shown how great is the glory of the good prelates <note>Prelates: high-ranking church officials or leaders, such as bishops.</note>, even if some, on account of "decayed members" <note>A metaphor for corrupt individuals within the church hierarchy.</note>, are rebuked more harshly for a time. 

Therefore, the seven stars are not said to be held in **Christ's** right hand as if they alone, and not the whole community of the elect, were to be placed at God's right hand; rather, there is a specific rational cause why this is said of them particularly. Among the four living creatures <note>A reference to the vision in Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4. Traditionally, these represent the four Evangelists, but here they represent different "orders" of the faithful.</note>, the **lion** is written as the first according to John, and it is clear that the order of pastors <note>The clergy or shepherds of the church.</note> is signified by it. But when Ezekiel spoke of these same living creatures, he said: *The face of a man and the face of a lion were on the right side of those four; the face of a calf was on the left; and the face of an eagle was above those four.* 

We know, furthermore, that the order of pastors pertains to the Lord's **resurrection**, which is why the holy Apostles were called witnesses of the resurrection. The **martyrs**, however, pertain to the **passion** <note>The "Passion" refers to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note>, because they themselves, by enduring punishments, earned the right to be called witnesses of the Lord's passion. For in Latin, a "witness" is interpreted as a *martyr* <note>The English word "martyr" comes from the Greek word for "witness."</note>. It was not said by the prophet that "the face of a man and the face of a lion were on the right side of those four, and the face of a calf on the left" because the birth and resurrection are joyful, while the shame of the passion is sad and obscure. Rather, it is not inappropriate that the order which is the minister of the Lord's resurrection, and which is joined to that same resurrection by a certain affinity of mysteries, is said to be held in the Lord's right hand. 

And it should be noted that to **hold** something is greater than to **have** it; for that which is had is often lost, but what is held cannot easily be lost. Whence the Truth <note>Christ refers to himself as "the Truth" in John 14:6.</note> says through himself: *My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from my Father's hand.* Therefore, the Lord holds the seven stars in his right hand, so that they would not fall <column-break/> <margin>Psalm 74</margin> among the company of the reprobate; for unless the Lord held some by strengthening them, the entire fabric of the churches would lie open to ruin, just as it is said by the voice of the Lord himself through the Psalmist: *The earth is dissolved and all who dwell in it; I have strengthened its pillars.* <note>Original: "ego confirmavi columnas eius," from Psalm 75:3 (Vulgate 74:4).</note>

Yet, above, they were said to be "had" and not "held," because both can certainly be understood as the same thing. For the Lord **holds** that which he **has**, because he preserves those things which are his own, just as he himself professes to his Father, saying: *Those whom you gave to me I have guarded, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition.* <note>Referring to Judas Iscariot (John 17:12).</note> And these things are indeed said of the seven stars, which are also called the **seven horns of the Lamb**, because in them he winnows <note>To "winnow" here means to separate the wheat from the chaff—the good from the bad—among the nations.</note> the nations and kingdoms.

What then shall we say of the **lampstands**, which are not said to be at Christ's right hand like the stars, but among which the Lord Christ is described as walking? Are they not also at the right hand in that respect, seeing as they are the spiritual children of John, who are designated by the lampstands? Indeed, they too are at the right hand; but why it is omitted here is a mystery of great weight. 

Finally, if we weigh it correctly, to have the stars at the right hand belongs to **Majesty**; but to walk among the lampstands belongs to **Humility**. For Christ is so great in glory that those who are great are said to be held in his right hand; and yet he is so small in humility that he deigns to stand and walk in the choir of the "little ones." For—if I may use a small example for a great one—one hardly ever finds in Divine Scripture that something stands at someone's right hand without that person being preferred at whose side they are described as standing. Such is that which is said to the Son by the Psalmist: *The Queen stood at your right hand in clothing of gold, surrounded by variety.* <note>Psalm 45:9. In medieval commentary, the Queen often represents the Church.</note> And he shall indeed place the **sheep** on his right hand, but the **goats** on his left. 

But to remain or walk in the midst is a mark of humility, as the true Master himself who descended from heaven teaches us; when his disciples were contending for precedence, he showed himself as an example of the humility for which he had come, saying: *I am in your midst as one who serves.* <note>Luke 22:27.</note> Therefore, let the "great" exult, whom such a prerogative of glory illustrates by honoring them; but let the "little ones" rejoice no less, with whom and in whom Christ walks, so that they too may follow wherever he goes, **running**. <note>The final word "running" corresponds to the catchword "currentes" on the original page.</note>

### Here begins the section on the Angel of Ephesus. Chapter 2.
**And to the angel of the church of Ephesus write: These things says he who has the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.**

When the only-begotten Son of God—speaking of himself as if of another—suggests that the entire church of the elect is to be placed at his right hand, saying: *He shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left* <note>original: "Statuet quidem oves a dextris suis: edos autem a sinistris"; quoting Matthew 25:33.</note>; and when he himself says in another place: *Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them* <note>original: "Ubi duo vel tres congregati sunt in nomine meo: ibi sum in medio eorum"; quoting Matthew 18:20.</note>; why then is it not absurd that he says he holds the stars alone in his right hand and not also the seven lampstands? Or why does he claim to walk in the midst of the golden lampstands and not also among the stars? 

In the riddle of this question, we must emulate the custom of the Scriptures, which demonstrates that one and the same thing often produces different understandings, just as the "wheels" of the Scriptures move according to the impulse of the Spirit. For one must judge differently concerning specific things than general things. It is one thing when a person is written of as alone; another when a second is joined; another when that which is joined is of lesser value or dignity; another when it is greater; another when it is simple paired with simple; and another when simple and multiple are placed in relation. 

For the Spirit acts specifically concerning one alone, as when God spoke to **Moses** alone on Mount Horeb; we feel that something special and mystical is designated there. But when **Aaron** is joined to that same Moses, the understanding immediately shifts from that matter to another. In the same way, if we speak of **Sarah** without **Hagar**, Sarah alone can designate something even beyond what she signifies when she is placed in respect to Hagar. But when Hagar is associated with the same Sarah, the mystery immediately changes—yet it is not the same as when Hagar is removed and **Rebecca** is substituted. This is how it works with two "simple" <note>In this context, "simple" refers to a single individual or figure acting as a symbol.</note> things. 

However, there is a discourse concerning the "simple" and "multiple"—as when two are placed together, one of which refers to a single person and the other to a multitude—such as the **pastor and the flock** in the Old Testament, where one usually designates Christ and the other designates the Church. If someone cannot understand this rule of mysteries, I do not know if anyone can satisfy him regarding the individual places where this change occurs. But he who does not grasp this and is scrupulous: let him first learn to believe what he has heard, so that in his own time he may arrive at understanding.

Since the only-begotten Son of God—speaking of himself as if of another—suggests that the entire church of the elect is to be placed at his right hand, saying: *He will set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left;* <note>Matthew 25:33.</note> and since he himself says in another place: *Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them:* <note>Matthew 18:20.</note> it is not unreasonable to ask why he says he holds only the stars in his right hand and not also the seven lampstands, or why he claims to walk in the midst of the golden lampstands and not also among the stars. But in the riddle of this question, we must follow the custom of the Scriptures, which demonstrates that one and the same thing often brings forth various understandings, just as the "wheels" of the Scriptures move according to the impulse of the Spirit <note>A reference to the moving wheels in the vision of Ezekiel 1.</note>. For we must judge individual cases differently from general ones. Furthermore, it is one thing when a person is written of alone, another when a second is joined; another when that which is joined is of lesser value or dignity, and another when it is of greater; it is one thing when a simple <note>In this context, 'simple' means a single element or person.</note> thing is paired with another simple thing, and another when a simple thing and a multiple thing are placed in relation. For when God spoke alone on Mount Horeb, we perceive something special and mystical being designated. But if Aaron is joined to the same Moses, our understanding immediately moves from that matter to another. In the same way, if we speak of Sarah without Hagar, Sarah alone can designate something even beyond what she signifies when she is placed in respect to Hagar. But when Hagar is associated with the same Sarah, the first changes the mystery—but not in the same way as when Hagar is removed and Rebecca is substituted. This is true of two simple things. We speak of the simple and the multiple when two things are placed together where one refers to a person and the other to a multitude—such as the shepherd and the flock in the Old Testament, where one often designates Christ and the other the Church. I do not know if anyone can satisfy a person who cannot understand this rule of mysteries regarding the individual places where this change occurs. However, he who does not grasp this and is hesitant should first learn to believe what he has heard, so that he may in his own time reach understanding.

<column-break/>

<margin>Matthew 25</margin>
<margin>Exodus 3</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening vision of the Apocalypse (Revelation), specifically focusing on the meaning of the seven stars and seven lampstands. ->First Commentary of John on the Apocalypse<-
B 4

For who does not know that silver, compared to copper and tin, is a precious metal? But if gold is placed beside it, the silver ceases to be seen as precious; this principle is made clear in this section. So too, in comparison to the reprobate <note>Those rejected or excluded from salvation.</note>, the entire host of the elect is said to be placed at the right hand of Almighty God. However, no mention is made of the general host in this passage; instead, the text speaks only of the **seven stars**. In these stars, it is clearly shown how great the glory of good prelates <note>Church leaders or bishops.</note> is, even if some are rebuked harshly for a time because of "rotten members" <note>Corrupt subordinates or sinful individuals within their care.</note>. Therefore, the seven stars are not said to be held in Christ's right hand as if they alone—and not the entire company of the elect—are to be placed at God's right hand. Rather, there is a specific reason why this is said specifically about them. Among the four living creatures described by John, the **lion** is written first; and it is manifest that the order of pastors is signified by it. But when <margin>Ezekiel 1</margin> Ezekiel spoke of these same creatures, he said: *the face of a man and the face of a lion were on the right side of the four; but the face of a calf was on the left; and the face of an eagle was above the four.* We know, furthermore, that the order of pastors pertains to the Lord’s Resurrection—which is why the holy apostles are called "witnesses of the Resurrection"—while the martyrs pertain to the Passion. For they, by enduring punishments, earned the right to be called witnesses of the Lord’s Passion. Indeed, in Latin, the word "martyr" is interpreted as "witness." This was said by the prophet: *The face of a man and the face of a lion were on the right of the four, but the face of a calf on the left,* because birth and resurrection are joyful events. But the shame of the Passion is sad and obscure. It is not unfitting, then, that the order which serves as the minister of the Lord’s Resurrection, and which is joined to that same Resurrection by a certain affinity of mysteries, is said to be held in the right hand of the Almighty. And it should be noted that to be **held** is something greater than simply to be **had**; for that which is merely "had" is often lost, but what is "held" cannot easily be lost. Hence, Truth itself <note>A common medieval title for Christ, referring to John 14:6.</note> says: *My Father, who gave them to me,* <margin>John 10</margin> *is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father’s hand.* Therefore, the Lord holds the seven stars in his right hand, so that they do not fall away to the left

<column-break/>

hand of the reprobate. For unless the Lord held certain people back from the crowd of the wicked, the entire fabric of the churches would lie open to ruin, just as is said by the voice of the Lord through the Psalmist: *The earth is melted, and all who dwell* <margin>Psalm 74</margin> *therein; I have strengthened its pillars.* Nevertheless, earlier they were said to be "had" rather than "held," though both terms can certainly be understood as the same thing. For the Lord "holds" what he "has," because he preserves those things which are his own, just as he professes to his Father, saying: *Those whom you gave* <margin>John 17</margin> *to me I have guarded, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition.* And these things are said concerning the seven stars, which are also called "seven against the host" because in them he winnows the nations and kingdoms. <margin>Apocalypse 5</margin> What then shall we say of the **lampstands**, which are not said to be at Christ’s right hand like the stars, but among which Christ the Lord is described as walking? Are they not also at the right hand, specifically in respect to John, whose "special sons" are those designated by the lampstands? Indeed, they too are at the right hand, but why this is omitted here is a matter of great weight. Finally, if we weigh it correctly, to "have the stars at the right hand" belongs to majesty; but to "walk among the lampstands" belongs to **humility**. For Christ is so great in glory that those who are great are said to be held in his right hand, and yet he is so small in humility that he deigns to stand and walk in the choir of the lowly. For—to take a small point as an exception—one hardly ever finds in Divine Scripture someone standing at the right hand of another where the person they are standing by is not preferred. Such is that which is said to the Son through the Psalmist: <margin>Psalm 44</margin> *The Queen stood at your right hand in a golden vesture, surrounded by variety.* And indeed, he will place the sheep at his right hand, <margin>Matthew 25</margin> but the goats on the left. But to remain or walk in the midst is a mark of humility, as the true Master himself taught when he descended from heaven; when his disciples were contending for leadership, he showed himself as an example of the humility for which he had come, saying: <margin>Luke 22</margin> *I am in the midst of you as one who serves.* Therefore, let the great exult, whom such a prerogative of glory illustrates by honoring them; and let the little ones rejoice no less, with whom and in whom Christ walks, so that they too may follow him wherever he goes, running after him.

<summary>This page explores the symbolic distinction between Christ holding the seven stars (prelates/leaders) in his right hand and walking among the seven lampstands (the churches/the humble). It argues that the right hand represents the majesty of the Resurrection, while walking in the midst represents Christ's humility and his presence among common believers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the vision of Christ from the Book of Revelation. The previous page established that the "seven stars" held in Christ’s right hand represent the prelates (church leaders) who are set apart for a high degree of glory, while the "lampstands" represent the wider body of the faithful. ->Exposition of the Abbot, Part of the Commentary<-

...into the fragrance of his ointments <note>A reference to Song of Songs 1:3, signifying the drawing of the faithful toward Christ.</note>. Indeed, the great should fear; it must be said that they should tremble rather than rejoice in comparison to those among whom Christ walks humbly. For in the former position, he holds the place of a judge, making the worldly powers tremble before his face; but here, walking among the crowds of the humble, he sets aside his majesty. This is why, when the holy John said earlier, **And he had seven stars in his right hand**, it was immediately added: **And from his mouth went a sharp two-edged sword.** This is so that each person might strive to fear in proportion to the high rank in which they are placed. Conversely, the humble may act with all the more confidence because they have more willingly chosen to be "cast down" in the house of their God, as the Scripture testifies:
<margin>Psalm 114</margin>
*The Lord preserves the little ones; I was humbled and he delivered me.* <note>Psalm 116:6 in modern bibles; the author uses the Vulgate numbering.</note> Thus, when the disciples thought the children coming to him should be turned away, he—who had come for this very purpose, to choose the weak things of the world—took it poorly.
<margin>Matthew 19</margin>
*Let the little ones come to me,* he said, *for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.* Therefore, the text does not say "he who walks among the stars" or "he who remains among the lampstands," but **he who holds the seven stars in his right hand and who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.** This is to demonstrate that he stands still with the stars (which he holds at his right hand) and walks among the lampstands. As I have already said, one position belongs to the one presiding <note>The leader/judge</note>, the other to the one serving. For standing and sitting belong to the master; going and returning belong to the disciple. Even that Centurion, who did not wish for the Lord to labor by walking to his house, found an example from the things he knew about himself. In order that the power of such great majesty
<margin>Matthew 8</margin>
should not have to be fatigued for the sake of men, he humbly refused, saying: *Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one "Go," and he goes; and to another "Come," and he comes.* But he who came not to be served, but to serve, did not disdain to walk among his servants, and to be with them as 
<margin>Luke 22</margin>
one of them, just as he himself testified concerning himself, saying: *I am among you as one who serves.* Therefore, he does not demand from us what he himself did not provide; nor did he ever fail to love, nor will he ever fail to love, that which he was seen to love in time.

<column-break/>

He certainly always loves the "little ones," for he was made a little one himself for their sake; and that which he loves from eternity, he revealed in time.
<margin>Psalm 137</margin>
*The Lord is indeed high, but he regards the humble.* <note>Psalm 138:6.</note> *He puts down the mighty from their seat and has exalted the humble.* 
<margin>Luke 1</margin>
But how does he exalt the humble if he finds it displeasing to be proud? Is it permitted for those whom he himself places on high to be proud? Far from it! 
<margin>Luke 22</margin>
For he said: *He who wishes to be greater among you, let him become like the younger; and he who is the leader, like the one who serves.* If this is so, whom among the multitude of the elect should I call more blessed than those who are more humble—not so much by the necessity of their faults, but by the love of virtue? For why should subordinates envy their prelates <note>Ecclesiastical superiors</note>, when it is more pleasant to remain privately with the King in humble clothing than to sit in glory with him on a solemn feast day? While the latter is in some sense more glorious, the former is more pleasant. Even the great men of the world are often envious of their social inferiors who always assist kings, considering those subordinates more blessed than themselves because they enjoy greater freedom in the presence of princes. Here we must question Peter, the first of the apostles; we must question him about himself and about his fellow disciple whom Jesus loved. We must ask whether Peter believed the other to be happier than himself when he urged him to ask the Lord who it was that would betray him—a question Peter judged himself unworthy to ask on his own. For I believe that Peter could have envied John for the "prerogative of sweetness" with which he was loved by Christ; but John could never have envied the primacy or power of Peter. For love is sufficient by itself without the addition of honor, whereas honor is by no means sufficient without the seasoning of love. Furthermore, although both the stars and the lampstands are counted as part of John's vision, there is nevertheless the same difference between the stars and the lampstands as there is between Peter and John. And if only the stars (and not also the lampstands) are said to be in the right hand of Christ, it is according to the way the **man** and the **lion** are said to be on the right. The **eagle**, however, is above; though in respect to the eagle which is above, even the man or the lion are seen to be on the left.

# John’s First Book on the Apocalypse

...are to be believed: namely that Peter is likened to the lion: who, having taken up the cross, imitated Christ <note>original: "imitatus est Christum"</note>. [Then there is] the eagle, John, of whom the Lord says: *I will that he remain until I come* <note>John 21:22</note>. For just as if I were to speak of Peter and Stephen: Peter is on the right, who is likened to the lion. Stephen, who is like the calf, is on the left; specifically because the former [Peter] survived a long time, while the latter [Stephen], as soon as he believed, ran ahead [to martyrdom]. And yet he who is on the right, Peter, when compared to Stephen—but also in respect to the disciple whom Jesus loved [John]—appears to be on the left, because he [Peter] was left behind in the world after Him. 

Thus the seven stars, which in respect to that order designated in Peter are written to be on the right, must be considered to be on the left in respect to the lampstands among which Christ walks. This is because the care of ruling <term>regiminis: the administrative and pastoral duties of a bishop</term> keeps them away from the pursuit of contemplation. And although they are less [distracted] than those given to the waves of the sea, they themselves are nonetheless frequently compelled to endure the cares of lawsuits and the "left-hand" <note>In medieval symbolism, the "right" represents spiritual contemplation, while the "left" represents necessary but worldly action</note> concerns of the active life because of the needs of governance. For who does not know that greater cares weigh upon the assembly of bishops than upon the superiors of monasteries? And yet those who are known to have chosen the right-hand part for themselves, in respect to those who are free for reading, are reckoned in the "left-hand" part of Martha. 
<margin>Luke 10</margin>
But for me, I am with Mary, of whom it is said: *Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.*

¶ These things having been said generally regarding the stars and lampstands, it is permitted to move from these occupations to the spiritual contemplation of the seven stars. Nor should I omit that common opinion of the philosophers, who said that from such an innumerable multitude of stars, only seven heavenly bodies <note>original: "sydera"</note> were to be set apart, because alone, beyond the law of all others, they appear to have wandering paths. I speak of those seven heavenly bodies which they name "planets," about which such wicked things have been written by the philosophers of this world that it was considered unlawful for Catholic men to speak of them, lest they seem to support in any way their detestable treachery—except for the sun, and moon, and stars, and even some named specifically, as divine Scripture records in the book of Job. 
<margin>Job 38</margin>
Surely, we are to understand something other than the objects themselves through these names. However, to wish to announce what will happen to anyone through the contemplation of the sun and stars is a type of divination <term>auguriandi genus: the practice of foretelling the future through signs</term>.

<column-break/>

The prophet Isaiah testifies to this, who under the appearance of Babylon and Egypt detests worldly princes, saying: 
<margin>Isaiah 47</margin>
"Let the astrologers <note>original: "augures celi"</note> of the heaven who contemplate the stars announce to you, so that they may predict the future for you from them, what the Lord of hosts has thought concerning you." If this was damnable then and an enemy to the Catholic faith, when Christ had not yet enlightened the world which lay long in darkness, how much more impious is it now to wish to presume such an art? Now the light shines in the world, and the light that has risen in the darkness for the righteous reveals the hidden things of darkness 
<margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin>
and discloses the counsels of hearts. But they say: "It is not a sin, because this art is based on nature." How is this proved? "Because," they say, "we many times predict things to come." But if it is not a type of divination simply because they predict the future, then it is not a sin to practice divination by the Crow and the Raven and other birds of the sky. For those who are accustomed to study such arts also sometimes predict various outcomes of things by conjecture and opinion, as if prophesying. 

But although they predict many true things about the future, it is nonetheless a type of divination by which they so predict the future. This is something which not only the faith of Christ abhors, but even the Law and the Prophets condemned while it was yet night and darkness. And if God occasionally allows such desperate men to predict some future things to test (as it is written in the Law) the constancy of the chosen ones—just as he once allowed the Magicians Jannes and Jambres 
<margin>Exodus 7, 8</margin>
to resist Moses and perform similar miracles, and will allow the "Son of Perdition" <note>The Antichrist</note> and false prophets to perform great and unheard-of signs, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error— 
<margin>Matthew 24</margin>
nonetheless, these things happen because of those who darken the true light with their errors. By using their "fantastic intellect" <note>The faculty of the mind that deals with images and appearances rather than spiritual truths</note> poorly, they are corrupted; where they ought to have drawn out the light of spiritual understanding, they instead breed for themselves the smoke of ignorance. We, therefore, say that the sun, moon, and stars are good creatures made by a truly good Creator, usefully brought forth for the sake of humans. To them it was given not only to have the duty of shining upon the earth, but also—what is greater—the great and fitting sacrament <note>In this context, a "sacrament" refers to a visible sign of an invisible spiritual reality</note> of signifying the invisible light. For the higher a thing is among physical objects...
