### Abbots: Part of the Exposition

They seem to be placed in the heavens to give light to all who are in the world: through that internal light which is true. They are shown here in a clearer and more familiar image of brightness, so that through visible light we might be able to contemplate the invisible light which is within us, or above us. I speak of that light of which John says: **It was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world.** <margin>John 1</margin> For to take an example from the greater heavenly body: who does not know that in that place the **Sun** signifies Christ? To you it was said: *The sun knows its setting.* <margin>Psalm 103</margin> And *the sun has risen and they are gathered together.* The **Moon**, however, of which it is said there: *He made the moon for seasons,* designates the **Church**. Furthermore, where the same Psalm speaks to the almighty God, saying: *I will see your heavens, the works of your fingers: the moon and the stars which you have founded* <margin>Psalm 8</margin>—who does not see that he [the Psalmist] omitted the sun for this reason: because he understood another Moon and other Stars according to the fact that He to whom he spoke was Himself the Sun? 

Therefore, the **Moon** designates the Church, and the **Stars** designate the multitude of the elect. Because the Son of God is both God and man, He willed to be signified not only by the Sun, but also by a **Star**, just as it says of Him through the Magi: *We have seen his star in the East.* <margin>Matthew 2</margin> And Balaam: *A star shall rise out of Jacob.* <margin>Numbers 24</margin> Thus it is clearly evident that not only the Sun but also the Star sometimes signifies Christ; yet it is a very small thing for him that inanimate and irrational creatures are likened to Him; rather, He prefers rational humans whom He created in His own image and likeness. Because humans are of such great dignity that they are called (and are) "children of God," the almighty God willed to display not only the greater light [the Sun] after His own likeness, but also the innumerable troops of stars: the great, the middling, and the small, and those which can scarcely be discerned except as a tiny spark of brightness. What He intended to designate in these, the Apostle makes manifest when he says: **There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead.** <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> In this significance, who else is to be understood as the **Sun** except Jesus Christ? And who else as the **Moon** except the glorious Queen of the world <note>The Virgin Mary</note>, who in the beauty of her vir-

<column-break/>

-ginity deserved to conceive and bring forth the true Sun? Who are the **Greater Stars** except the patriarchs and prophets, the holy apostles, martyrs, and confessors, who were given like pillars of the world to carry the fabric of the house of the Lord, and like the precious lights of heaven to illuminate the churches? And who are the **Middling Stars** except those who have done many good things, yet have not reached the merits of those whom we called great and first, and who were like the great stars? Who, then, are the **Smallest Stars**, which can scarcely be distinguished from nothing, except those who were snatched from the very jaws of death by the hope of mercy alone, and who are known to have had no [good] works at all, but were saved in Christ Jesus through the leading of penitence—so that they might praise His name because He is good, because His mercy endures forever? <margin>Psalm 117</margin> 

Therefore, those who despair of themselves are foolish, however much they may be liars and impious, unwilling to understand so that they might act well. However, the Sun and Moon do not signify this everywhere, but clearly do so in this aforementioned comparison of the Apostle. In other places, the "lesser light" [the Moon] has various and manifold relations, and according to the places where it is written, it receives different interpretations. For sometimes the Sun is Christ and the Moon is designated as **Moses**, just as it is written mystically of these two lights in Genesis: *God made two great lights: a greater light to rule the day, and a lesser light to rule the night.* <margin>Genesis 1</margin> The greater light was made to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, because *day unto day utters speech, and night unto night shows knowledge.* <margin>Psalm 18</margin> For Christ is the **Day**, and those who belong to Christ are the day; but **Moses** is the **Night**, who is a man and not God; and as far as was in him, he was night and not day, because no one has anything that he has not received. He is "night" nonetheless [as a symbol for] the **Synagogue**, to whom he [Moses] showed the knowledge of the Law which he himself wrote. 

[These symbols] designate: 
In the Sun: **Wisdom** <note>original: "sapientia"</note> | In the Moon: **Knowledge** <note>original: "scientia"</note> 
In the Sun: The **Contemplative Life** | In the Moon: The **Active Life**
In the Sun: The **Spirit** | In the Moon: The **Flesh**
In the Sun: The **Contemplative Church** | In the Moon: The **Preaching Church**
In the Sun: The **Future Life** | In the Moon: The **Present Life** 
...and if there are any others in this [vein].

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the heavens in the First Commentary on the Apocalypse. Having previously discussed the Sun and Moon as symbols for Christ and the Church, the author now turns to the "seven stars" held in Christ's right hand, identifying them with the seven planets of classical astronomy and seven key figures in salvation history.</meta>

# John’s First Commentary on the Apocalypse

...method: which we cautiously suppress in this place, so that we may hasten toward that which our impulse tends. Finally, the discourse concerns the **seven stars** which Christ holds in his right hand. On this occasion, we are prompted to dispute somewhat concerning those seven stars which are called **planets** by the philosophers <note>original: "phis" (physici). In the Middle Ages, "physicists" were natural philosophers who studied the physical world.</note>; so that what is burned into the destruction of guilt for those who savor earthly things might, with the Spirit as our guide, lead us to salvation. But because two of the seven planets—the **Sun** and the **Moon**—are said to be more brilliant than the rest, and because of the diversity of places in which something is written about them, they are involved in various enigmas of mystery by the impulse of the Spirit which runs through diverse paths. It pleases us first to treat the seven together generally, so that we may finally be able to contemplate the high and venerable mysteries of those lights more specifically and abundantly.

There are, as I have already said, seven stars which are called **planets**, known for the "uncertain" courses they hold—I say "uncertain" with respect to those stars which are fixed in the **firmament** <note>The "firmament" refers to the sphere of fixed stars which appeared to move together, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note>; not that they are uncertain in themselves, for they serve the law of their own nature. The deluded pagans of old thought these were gods, and according to them, these are their proper names: **Saturn, Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, the Moon, and the Sun.** The divine Scripture frequently commemorates the names of these two—namely, the Sun and the Moon—but in the divine pages, hardly anything is ever found written of the others; instead, the poets of the pagans discovered them, or certainly those who were the authors of the **astronomical art**. 

But this is nothing to us. For our discourse is not about names, but about realities. If you ask about them—what they have that is dissimilar from other stars so that their mysteries are special—I do not need to labor over this, because the world knew this before Christ was born of the Virgin. For the faithful and the unfaithful alike confess that these are not stars fixed in the firmament with the others, but each performs its own course. This thing especially forced the pagans into error. But we, who are enlightened by the grace of Christ, do not say that the stars of heaven are living bodies <note>A common ancient and medieval debate: whether stars were "animate" beings with souls or merely physical objects.</note>, but rather that they are prepared for the mystery of the living. We understand them also because they shine outwardly, providing us with a more splendid service of mysteries, because they bear the **type** <note>A "type" is a person or thing in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament or the spiritual life.</note> of the human race, which will one day be like the splendor of the firmament, and like 

<column-break/>

<margin>Basil, 13</margin>
stars for all eternity. Because when we think of the multitude of stars, which there is no doubt designate the elect men, the **seven stars**—disjoined from the rest and distinct by such a great gap—do not occur without a rational order. By this very fact, we are advised to understand the ranks of those to be saved within the multitude of stars. For we are compelled to consider what the distinction of the seven planets means, especially since the **number seven** <note>original: "septenarius numerus"</note> is of such great perfection that it can hardly, if ever, be without a perfect mystery. 

We seek therefore by faith, with reason helping, and we find in the ranks of the elect seven certain men who, by a certain property in the mysteries, are segregated from the multitude of others—not because they excel all the saints in dignity, but because the cause of their mystery and the special depth of their sacrament is unique. 

The first of these is **Adam**: I say in age, not in dignity, because on account of the fault of disobedience he lost his birthright. The second is **Noah**. The third, **Abraham**. The fourth, **Moses**. The fifth, **David**. The sixth, **John the Baptist**. The seventh, **Elijah**. I have called **Elijah** the seventh, not because he was born after John, but because he is to come after John himself at the end of the age <note>Referring to the prophecy in Malachi that Elijah would return before the Day of the Lord.</note>. These seven great and named men Almighty God sent into the world at various intervals of time, so that they might perform, as it were, certain **new courses** of the precepts of God. In 
<margin>Malachi 4</margin>
them, the true philosophers—according to what this book teaches—can search out the sacred mysteries, and perceive how far the carnal philosophers of this world are from the truth. 

For who does not know that those [carnal philosophers] use comparisons and subject the specific kingdoms of the world to individual planets? This is among their other deceptions, by which they deceive the senseless, thinking that the power and will of God—and His mercy and judgment—vary according to the change of the **hours**. As if a "good hour" could protect the proud from the wrath of the judge, or a "bad hour" could impede or subject the work of the just man to chance? But how far their conjectures—or rather their inventions and madness—fall from the truth, the truth of God will show, when what is rational...

### Abbot’s Part of the Explanation

...the meaning of the star: it will appear in the end. To take an example from this: just as the brightness of the stars is hidden and completely disappears at the rising of the sun, so the wisdom of the world perishes where even the smallest portion of the wisdom of God is shown. Now, therefore, insofar as He—who is the wisdom and the Word of the Father—has granted it, let us show what these planets signify: first indeed spiritually, then generally. In this part, we follow their own "prudence," which must be destroyed so that it might perish by its own blows and incline toward its fall.

They say that the star they name **Saturn** is of a cold nature and completes its course over long spaces of time. And we have in our own heaven—which is revealed more to the eyes of the mind than of the body—the first-formed <note>original: "protoplaustum." A common theological term for Adam as the first created human.</note> **Adam**, whom we read was in paradise. We read that both he and the other men of the first age endured beyond the measure of modern men by seven times and more, and that he exceeded the others in the length of that original age. The star they name **Venus**, they say, is of a temperate quality. We can quite worthily liken this to the righteous **Noah**, who, because of his temperance and justice, was saved in the flood of waters and took care to restore the loss of all flesh within the protection of the Ark. The star they call **Jupiter**, they have preferred above all others by some madness of their art; we, not without cause, proclaim him to be **Abraham**, the father of all believers. For from him arose the assembly of the patriarchs; from him the prophets and apostles and the only-begotten Son of God in the flesh—to such an extent that the faithful Apostle is inspired <note>original: "spoletur," likely a scribal error for "inspiretur" or "loquitur."</note> to say: *If you are Christ’s, then you are the seed of Abraham.* <margin>Galatians 6</margin> Furthermore, I do not know what they found that would lead them to attribute the authority of knowledge to the planet they call **Mercury**; but we, not in vain, believe the holy **Moses** to be a "vessel of knowledge," inasmuch as we have learned that he delivered the knowledge of the Law to the people of the Jews. And to whom they gave the art of war—**Mars**—we, not absurdly, feel that **King David** was warlike beyond all others. These five planets having been run through as if in preparation, we must come to the Moon and the Sun, concerning which there is a common reason for speaking:

<column-break/>

The reason for speaking of the **Moon** and the **Sun**, I say, is because there is a very common connection between **John the Baptist** and **Elijah** <note>original: "Helyas." The Latin form of the Greek name for the prophet Elijah.</note>. For one is the precursor of the Judge <note>Elijah was traditionally expected to return before the Final Judgment.</note>, and the other, by being born and dying, was made the forerunner of the Redeemer. Thus, one would not be reached by the fire of Elijah before the water (so to speak) of John separated the chosen from the reprobate. I do not say this because I feel water or fire to be anything other than what they are in the Sacrament of the Altar, but I refer to that which is understood spiritually and mystically through water and fire. From this, we must gather the reasons for accepting these mysteries: not that one is as good as or better than the other, or more or less, but according to how even through less clear things, more excellent goods are sometimes designated—just as sometimes good is designated through evil, and contraries through good. For although John the Baptist is likened to the Moon and Elijah to the Sun, we do not proclaim that Elijah is greater than John the Baptist, than whom "there has not been a greater among those born of women." <margin>Malachi 4</margin> <margin>Matthew 11</margin> But because John was baptizing near water, running before the great work of God's mercy, that Elijah punished the unjust in the fire of judgment, demonstrating the future severity and adversity of the judgment; for as it was said, he is the precursor of the Judge, while John preceded the Redeemer who was to die in the flesh. We can, however, consider Elijah greater than John, not in terms of his person, but in terms of the dignity of his office: for the latter ran before the Humble One, while the former runs before the Exalted One; the latter before Him who suffered in the flesh, the former before Him who will reign in the glory of the Godhead. For John was the last of all the great men who were propagated through the birth of the flesh from women since Abraham; but Elijah, after many who have been reborn of the Spirit, is to come at the end of the age to complete his own course. Thus we have in John the humble, and in Elijah the severe and terrible. We have in John one who did not know the judgment <note>Referencing John's questioning of Jesus from prison.</note>, and in Elijah the person of a man who did not know [death]; for while John, imprisoned by Herod, endured even to the shedding of his blood, Elijah—when sought in like manner by an impious king—being moved by the most burning zeal, consumed the soldiers sent against him with the fire of judgment. <margin>4 Kings <note>In the Vulgate, 4 Kings is modern 2 Kings.</note></margin> <margin>2 Kings 1</margin> We also have in the water of John the moisture of the Moon, and in the fire of Elijah the dry...

### First Part on the Apocalypse

...of the sun: one of these designates mercy, the other judgment. Nevertheless, in John, who died, we see the waning of the moon; in Elijah, who deferred death, we see the perseverance of the sun. This is because the **active life**, designated by John, fails and ceases to be along with the flesh; the **contemplative life**, <note>In medieval theology, the "Active Life" refers to outward works of charity and preaching, while the "Contemplative Life" refers to the interior focus on God. John the Baptist is often the model for the former, and Elijah for the latter.</note> designated by Elijah, knows no such loss. Why then are there such different qualities in men of the same spirit? Or how is this true: that John came in the spirit and power of Elijah? It must be noted that the Spirit is one, but his actions are diverse. There was one zeal in both, and the same patience; but it was fitting for one to demonstrate zeal and the other patience, according to the requirements of the time.

What is more "one" than the Son and the Holy Spirit, in whom there is no diversity of nature or will, but always one and the same substance? And yet the Son came in such a way as to be present in the flesh, and he alone deigned to die for those who were dying or dead. The Holy Spirit, however, came in such a way that he did not assume that in which he could die, or in which he might ever happen to die; for he is not God and man together, like Jesus Christ, but God only, just like the Father, with whom he always shares the same living and understanding. For only the Son, as the Catholic faith holds, was incarnate; only he was crucified, died, and was buried. And even if he was not sent alone, but with him came the Holy Spirit—who is with him, in him, and from him—it was so that what the Son began by acting, the Spirit might complete. The foundation that Christ laid, the Spirit would firm up by bringing it to perfection.

For this reason, John received power in water, but Elijah in fire. This is because, first, the multitude of preachers was permitted to preach in the **water of wisdom**—which is the word of God—and second, another crowd of teachers is to follow in the **fire of the Holy Spirit**, so that the last might perfect what the first began. Thus, a single joy of happiness may encompass both groups, so that those who sow and those who reap may rejoice together.

One might be moved by the fact that Elijah, who is to come later, preceded John by appearing [at the Transfiguration], unless we understand what John said of Christ and himself: "He who comes after me was made before me, because he was prior to me." And unless the grace of the Holy Spirit—of whom John says: <margin>John 1</margin> "The Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified"—preceded the birth of the Holy Virgin. For the angel who performed the office of such a great <margin>John 7</margin> embassy said of him: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall

<column-break/>

overshadow you." See how the gift of the Spirit preceded the man Christ Jesus, who for this reason is said to be conceived of the Holy Spirit. According to his nature as God, he demonstrates that he always is what he is when he says: <margin>Luke 1</margin> "Before Abraham was, **I am**," and "Clarify me, Father, with yourself, with the clarity I had with you before the world was made."

If this is so—or rather, because it is so—how should we understand what John says in the person of Christ concerning the Holy Spirit: "Because he was prior to me"? <margin>John 8</margin> And what Christ himself says of himself and the Holy Spirit: "Whoever speaks a word against the Son of <margin>John 12</margin> Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the future"? Is it not because he, who was born for this purpose to provide an example of humility, was not speaking with that voice by which he was eternal God—in which he was equal to the Holy Spirit—but from that voice by which he was a man within time? <margin>Luke 12, John 7</margin> Otherwise, because he is Truth and cannot deny himself, he promised that he would give that same Spirit to his disciples—not indeed in the time of his humility, but in the time of his glory. As John says: "The Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified."

Why was this? So that men might learn to hide the grace given to them during the time of their "childhood" and "adolescence" <note>Metaphors for the early or immature stages of spiritual development or the Church's history.</note>, lest they seem to glory in the gift received before the proper time, and while they are puffed up outwardly by the gift, they become empty of glory within. For if he waited for the proper time—he who was born of the Father without time and possesses all things with the Father by the authority of nature—how much more should one not glory before the proper time, especially when he did not possess what he did not receive?

For this reason, it was not absurdly said by John: <margin>John 7</margin> "The Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified." But otherwise, if the Spirit had not been given, how do we confess of him in the Creed <note>original: "symbolo." Referring to the Nicene Creed.</note> that "he spoke through the prophets"? Was it because he did not work such things in them as he does in those to whom he suggests a chaste and spiritual life? Those who are so filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit that they no longer seek wives, children, houses, fields, vineyards, or any worldly possessions? The Holy Spirit was indeed in the prophets before Christ Jesus was born of the Virgin, but he was not then "given" in the way he was to be given in his own time. And therefore, he was later said to be "sent" and to "come," he who...

### Part of the Exposition

...had been accustomed to come to the prophets before: but not in that way which came later; nor indeed so solemnly. Jesus Christ therefore came in the **likeness of the moon**: humble, gentle, and mild. The Holy Spirit followed in the **likeness of the sun**: strong, terrifying, and manifest. Thus, those things which were carried out differently in John and Elijah were partially fulfilled in the Son and the Holy Spirit, and are to be fully completed in the whole. This is not because the only-begotten Son of God is different from the Holy Spirit according to his nature as God, being equal to the Father; rather, it is because he willed to receive into himself what he did not previously have—so that he could be "unequal" <note>The author is using "unequal" here not to deny the Trinity's equality, but to describe the voluntary "emptying" or *kenosis* of Christ, who took on human limitations that the Holy Spirit did not.</note> to the Holy Spirit according to his goodness, not by malice, but by a voluntary humility, not by the pride of elation. However, these things are not so contrary as they seem to be diverse in themselves; for the one Son himself decreed to appear different from himself, as did the one Spirit in the forms of the dove and the fire. For what is simpler than a dove, which in the origin of its creation was produced from water? And what in this world is more terrifying than fire? It is superfluous to raise a question about fire signifying the gift of the Holy Spirit, and water signifying the wisdom of God, which is Christ Jesus, since the Lord says of the Holy Spirit:

<margin>Luke 12</margin>
"I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it be kindled?" <note>original: "Igne veni mittere in terram: & quid volo nisi ut accendatur?"</note> And the Psalmist says of the Son of God:

<margin>Ps. 35</margin>
"With you, O Lord, is the fountain of life." <note>original: "Apud te domine est fons vite." This is Psalm 36:9 in modern numbering.</note> What then? Are the Son and the Holy Spirit divided between themselves because the Son is more frequently designated by water and the Holy Spirit by fire? And where does it stand that the flame of the bush and the sun signify the Word of the Father, and that Truth itself <note>"Truth itself" is a common medieval title for Jesus.</note> says of the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive: "Let him who thirsts come and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly"? If this is so, it remains that both metaphors must be accepted according to a certain distinction of the Persons; for the Son willed something for himself which the Spirit did not will for himself. If the Spirit had willed it, he would have made it happen: namely, to be born as a man from a woman, to be nourished by milk, to move among men, and to be made visible upon the earth. This the Son clearly willed for himself; but the Holy Spirit did not will this for himself. Yet the will of the Son and the Holy Spirit is not diverse, because the Son willed himself to be incarnated and did not will the Spirit to be incarnated; and the Spirit willed the Son to be incarnated and did not will himself to be incarnated.

<column-break/>

Therefore, there is one will in both: even in this, that one willed for himself what both willed for him. For God wills nothing that is not just and which he does not do in wisdom, as the Scripture testifies, saying:

<margin>Ps. 103</margin>
"In wisdom you have made all things, O Lord." <note>original: "Omnia in sapientia fecisti domine." Psalm 104:24 in modern numbering.</note> It is clear, then, that it was done in wisdom that the Son alone was humbled, and alone deigned to die for men by assuming flesh and descending to the lower regions. And because the nature of water is heavy and seeks low places, while fire, because of its lightness, runs back to higher places, why is it that the Son is more frequently likened to water and the Spirit more often to fire? It is because the Son "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" <note>A reference to the *Carmen Christi* in Philippians 2.</note>—which the Holy Spirit did not do. Regarding the Holy Spirit, it is said:

<margin>2 Cor. 3</margin>
"Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty"; and of whom the Apostle likewise says:

<margin>Rom. 8</margin>
"You have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which you cry out: Abba, Father." Did he not remain in the majesty of his glory without assuming flesh, in no way humbled in the manner the Son was? But if the Son alone, remaining in himself what he was, assumed what he was not, it is clear that he himself sought the lower things more, intending to ascend on high with those for whom he descended. Through this, the rational cause is evident why the Son is more likened to water, and the Spirit more to fire. Although the Holy Spirit himself assumed the form of a dove, I would not say in vain that he is likened to flowing water, as the Evangelist Luke says of him:

<margin>Luke 3</margin>
"The Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form like a dove." But if the same Spirit is shown to have assumed a bodily creature, in what way is a greater humility demonstrated in the Son than in the Spirit? It is in this: that man is born for labor, but a bird for flying; and because the Word of the Father was made flesh, assuming our **clay** <note>original: "limum nostrum," referring to the dust/mud of the earth from which Adam was formed.</note> into the unity of his person. The Holy Spirit, however, did not assume the dove in order to *become* a dove, but to show that he is a simple nature in it. Because he is spirit and not body, he cannot appear to bodily eyes.

<margin>Job 5</margin>
<margin>John 14</margin>
"I," says the Lord, "will ask..."

### Commentary on the Gospel of John

...the Father, and he will give you another Advocate <note>original: *paraclitum*; a term meaning "one called alongside" to help, often translated as Counselor, Comforter, or Advocate</note> to be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him; but you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you. Because, therefore, the Holy Spirit was also humbled <note>The author suggests the Spirit's "humility" is shown by his quiet presence in the sacraments and the soul, similar to water</note>, he is not inappropriately designated by water; and because the Son was exalted to the glory of the Father, he himself is also appropriately designated three times over in the fiery sun, just as it is said of him through the prophet <margin>Habakkuk 3</margin>: "The sun was lifted up; the moon stood in its order." For the only-begotten of God the Father, consisting of and in two natures, did not wish to reveal both natures at the same time, because it would not have been suitable for our miserable state. Instead, he first revealed what was designated by the moon, and then what was designated by the sun. For what is meant by the moon—which is called the "lesser light" and is illuminated by the sun, yet itself illuminates those looking upon it—if not the human and mortal nature assumed into the unity of the [divine] person? And what is meant by the sun, if not the divinity which does not receive its essence from elsewhere, since it is truly that very "light which illuminates every man coming into the world" <margin>John 1</margin>? Now, if Christ is the true light and the Holy Spirit is the true light, they are undoubtedly both one light together. Why then is the "fullness of truth" promised at the coming of the Advocate by Christ the Light, as if the Advocate who proceeds were something greater than the one who sends and gives him? It is simply because the Spirit himself is the **heat** of the true sun which illuminates the world. We see that this visible sun illuminates in one way through the "lesser light" <note>the moon</note> while remaining hidden in itself, and in another way by its own direct presence, when its heat is made manifest upon the earth. For if something is perceived of the sun's light through the lesser light without the touch of heat, the whole is necessarily revealed when its heat is felt. Who does not see how clear it is that the "fullness of light" should not be attributed to heat in such a way as if heat achieved this without a ray of light? Rather, it is because some form of light can exist where heat is not present, but it cannot be **perfect** light except where heat is present. Or, if you were to say that heat is devoid of the power of light, that would not be true; for fire is usually ignited <note>original: *ignis solet accendi*</note> from the sun's focus,

<column-break/>

and there is no doubt that this is in the likeness of that fire which appeared to the apostles on the day of Pentecost and illuminated the hearts of those who had previously believed in Jesus. According to this, therefore: while the only-begotten of God exhorted the apostles through "tongues of flesh" as a man, he exhibited light to his subjects as if through a "lesser light" <note>the moon/humanity</note>. But when he sent the Holy Spirit whom he had promised, he also exhibited himself as manifest; for where the Holy Spirit is present, the whole divinity is somehow made manifest. As the Truth <note>Christ</note> says of himself: "If anyone loves me, <margin>John 14</margin> he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." And again, speaking of how he appears manifest in the heart of one who loves him, he says: "He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and will manifest myself to him." <margin>John 14</margin> Therefore, the Holy Spirit does not teach all truth without the Son; rather, the Truth itself—which is Christ—is fully manifested to no one except the one to whom the Holy Spirit comes. For this reason, the Son himself says of the Spirit: "He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you." <margin>John 16</margin> Therefore, since the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit is one and the same, whether the human nature of Christ stands in relation to the Word of the Father (which was made flesh) or to the Holy Spirit, nothing prevents both from being accepted. It pleased God that both could stand together wonderfully, and the mysteries of the two prophets <note>John the Baptist and Elijah</note> aptly suit both. For whether human nature is understood in John and divine nature in Elijah, or the man Christ Jesus in John and the Holy Spirit in Elijah, how beautifully the mention of Elijah is made in the third book of Kings <margin>1 Kings 17</margin> without the name of a father, or a mother, or a recorded genealogy! This was done so that, according to what the Apostle says of Melchizedek <margin>Hebrews 7</margin>, he might be shown as a likeness of the Son of God, who was always the Word—even if he became man in time. Wherefore, it was not absurd that the one who was to precede the Judge <note>Elijah</note> went before the precursor of the Redeemer <note>John the Baptist</note>; for he who appeared as a true man at the end of time was the eternal God before all ages, and before he was born from...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "missions" of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Having established the Sun and Moon as metaphors for divinity and humanity, the author now distinguishes how the Son (as water/moon) and the Holy Spirit (as fire/sun) manifest their shared divine will through different modes of humility and majesty.</meta>

# Abbreviation of the Part of the Exposition

[He] was accustomed to come to the prophets before, but not in the same way as afterwards, nor so solemnly. Therefore, **Jesus Christ** came in the likeness of the moon: humble, gentle, and mild; the **Holy Spirit** followed in the likeness of the sun: strong, terrible <note>original: *terribilis*; in this context meaning "awe-inspiring" or "overwhelming," rather than "bad"</note>, and manifest. Thus, the things which were carried out differently in John [the Baptist] and Elijah were partially completed in the Son and the Holy Spirit, and are to be completed in their entirety. This is not because the only-begotten Son of God <note>original: *unigenitus dei filius*</note> is different from the Holy Spirit according to his nature as God—for he is equal to the Father—but because he willed to take upon himself what he did not previously have, so that he might be "unequal" in relation to the Holy Spirit: not by malice, but by goodness; not by the pride of elation, but by voluntary humility. 

Yet, these things which seem diverse in themselves are not so contrary that the one Son could not decree to appear differently, just as the one Spirit appeared both as a dove and as fire. For what is simpler than a dove, which was produced from water at the beginning of its creation? And what in this world is more terrible than fire? It is unnecessary to raise a question about fire signifying the gift of the Holy Spirit, or water signifying the **Wisdom of God**—which is **Jesus Christ**—since the Lord says of the Holy Spirit:
<margin>Luke 12</margin>
"I have come to send fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it be kindled?" And the Psalmist says of the Son of God:
<margin>Psalm 35</margin>
"With you, O Lord, is the fountain of life." What then? Are the Son and the Holy Spirit divided between themselves because the Son is more frequently designated by water and the Holy Spirit by fire? And what of the burning bush and the sun, which signify the Word of the Father? Or what the Truth itself <note>A common title for Jesus</note> says of the Spirit, whom 
<margin>John 7</margin>
those believing in him were to receive: "Let anyone who is thirsty come and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly"? 

If this is so, it remains that both symbols must be accepted according to a certain distinction of the **Persons** <note>The distinct identities of the Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit)</note>. This is because the Son willed something for himself which the Holy Spirit did not will for himself; for if he had willed it, he would have made it happen. Specifically, the Son willed to be born as a man from a woman, to be nourished by milk, to live among men, and to become visible upon the earth. The Son clearly willed this for himself, but the Holy Spirit did not will this for himself. Nevertheless, the will of the Son and the Holy Spirit is not diverse, because the Son willed that he himself be **incarnated** and willed that the Holy Spirit not be incarnated; and the Holy Spirit willed that the Son be incarnated and willed that he himself not be incarnated. Therefore, there is one will in both, even though one willed for himself what both willed [together for him]. For God wills nothing that is not just and that is not done in **wisdom**, as the Scripture testifies:
<margin>Psalm 103</margin>
"In wisdom you have made all things, O Lord." 

It is clear, then, that it was done in wisdom that only the Son was humbled; he alone, by assuming flesh, deigned to die for men and descend to the lower world. And because the nature of water is heavy and seeks low places, while fire by its lightness returns to the heights, why is the Son more frequently likened to water and the Holy Spirit more often to fire? Is it not because the Son "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" <note>A reference to Philippians 2:7, describing the *Kenosis* or self-emptying of Christ</note>—which the Holy Spirit did not do? Of the Holy Spirit, it is said:
<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
"Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." And again, the Apostle says:
<margin>Romans 8</margin>
"You did not receive a spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry out: Abba, Father." The Spirit was by no means humbled in the same way as the Son, but remained in the majesty of his glory without assuming flesh. 

For if the Son alone, remaining in himself what he was, assumed what he was not, it is clear that he himself sought the lowlier things, intending to ascend on high with those for whom he descended. Through this, the rational cause is plain as to why the Son is likened more to water and the Holy Spirit more to fire. Even though I might say the Holy Spirit was not without reason likened to flowing water when he took the form of a dove, as 
<margin>Luke 3</margin>
Luke the Evangelist says of him: "The Holy Spirit descended in a bodily shape like a dove." For if the same Spirit is shown to have assumed a bodily creature, in what way is a greater humility demonstrated in the Son than in the Spirit? Only in this: that 
<margin>Job 5</margin>
"man is born to labor, and the bird to fly." And also because the Word of the Father became flesh, assuming our "clay" into the unity of his person; but the Holy Spirit did not assume the dove in order to *become* a dove, but rather to show that his nature is simple <note>In theology, "simple" means pure, undivided, and non-material</note>. Because he is spirit and not body, he cannot appear to the eyes of the body. 
<margin>John 14</margin>

# John’s First [Epistle] in the Apocalypse [Commentary]

the Father & he will give you another **Paraclete** <note>original: *paraclitum*; a Greek-derived term meaning "advocate" or "comforter," used here for the Holy Spirit</note>: that he may remain with you forever: the **Spirit of Truth**: whom the world cannot receive: because it has not seen him nor known him: but you shall know him: because he shall remain with you & shall be in you. Because therefore the **Holy Spirit** was humbled: not incongruously he himself is also designated by water: and because the **Son** was exalted to the Father’s glory: not incongruously he himself is also designated three times by the fiery sun: just as it is said of him through the <margin>Habakkuk 3</margin> prophet: *The sun was raised: and the moon stood in its order.* For the **Only-Begotten** of God the Father, consisting of and in two natures, did not wish to make both natures public at the same time: because it was not expedient for our misery: but first indeed that which is designated in the moon: then that which is designated in the sun. Indeed, through the moon—which is called the "lesser light" and is illuminated by the sun—is meant our human and mortal nature assumed into the unity of his person. But what is meant by the sun, except **Divinity**, which does not have what it is from elsewhere: since it is surely the **True Light** itself which illuminates every man coming into the <margin>John 1</margin> world? Now, if he is the True Light: and the Holy Spirit is the True [Light]: then surely both are one light together. Why then is the "fullness of truth" promised in the coming of the Paraclete by the light of **Christ**: as if the Paraclete who proceeds might have more power than he who sends and gives him? Unless it is because the Spirit himself is the **heat** of the true sun which illuminates the world. We see that this visible sun illuminates in one way through the "lesser light" <note>the moon</note> while remaining hidden in itself: and in another way in its own presence: for its heat is manifest upon the earth. For if something of the sun's light is perceived through the lesser light without the touch of heat: it is necessary that the whole be revealed when its heat is felt. Who does not see what is clear: that the "fullness of light" is not attributed to heat in such a way that the heat accomplishes this without a ray: but rather that light can be of any sort where heat is not present: but it cannot be perfect except where heat is present? Or if you say that heat is separate from the power of light: it is not true: because from it, fire is seen and usually

According to this, therefore: while the Only-Begotten of God exhorted the apostles through "tongues of flesh" as a man, he exhibited light to his subjects as if through a "lesser light" <note>the moon</note>. But when he sent the Holy Spirit whom he had promised: he also exhibited himself as manifest: because where the Holy Spirit is present: the whole **Divinity** is somehow manifest: just as the **Truth** <note>Christ</note> says of himself: *If anyone loves me* <margin>John 14</margin> *he will keep my word: and my Father will love him and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.* And again, speaking of himself, that he may appear manifest in the heart of the one who loves him, he says: *He who loves me: shall be loved by my Father: and I will love him and will manifest myself to him.* Therefore the <margin>John 14</margin> Holy Spirit does not teach all truth without the Son: but because the Truth itself—which is **Christ**—is fully manifested to no one: except to him to whom the Holy Spirit comes. For this reason the Son himself says of him: *He will glorify me because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you.* Therefore, <margin>John 16</margin> since the divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is one and the same: whether the humanity of Christ has a relationship to the Word of the Father which was made flesh: or to the Holy Spirit: it certainly does not prevent both from being accepted: because it pleased him for it to happen in this way: so that both can stand miraculously: and the mysteries of two prophets may aptly suit both. For whether human nature is understood in **John [the Baptist]** and divine nature in **Elijah**: or the man **Christ Jesus** in John and the **Holy Spirit** in Elijah: it is beautifully commemorated in the book of <margin>1 Kings 17</margin> Kings <note>original: *3. reguz*; 1 Kings in modern Bibles, 3 Kings in the Vulgate</note> that the mention of Elijah was made without the name of a father: or mother: or a following genealogy: so that, according to what the apostle says of **Melchizedek**, he might be shown to be "assimilated to the Son of God": who was always indeed the **Word**: even if he became man in <margin>Hebrews 7</margin> time. # Abbot’s Part of the Exposition

<margin>Exodus 3</margin> ...from the **virgin**: he was revealed in the flame of the bush to his servant **Moses**: and to all the holy prophets who spoke of him: who again at the end of the age shall come manifestly: to render to each <margin>Matthew 16</margin> according to his works: Therefore it is not without mystery: that the course of the **sun** is twelve times longer than the course of the **moon**: or that **Elijah** <note>original: *Helyas*</note> remains in the life of the flesh for the space of so many years: while **John** [the Baptist] indeed [remained] under a circuit of nearly thirty years: and was completed in under one month: because the work of the **Incarnate Word**: received its completion under a brief space of years and without the monthly cycles of suffering <note>original: *sine mestruis passionis*; the author contrasts the short, linear life of Christ with the repetitive, cyclical nature of human time and suffering</note>: but the essence of the **Creator** remains from eternity unto eternity: that which is: concluding and circumscribing all things which are below: and as if the most serene splendor of the sun: it does not incur the costs of old age. For he decreed to exhibit each of them to himself in such a way as he—either as **Redeemer** or **Judge**: either in his first coming or to be exhibited in his second coming: first indeed in water: that he might cleanse and justify the penitent: second in a flame of fire: that he might consume the remnants of the impious. For **John** precedes by deeds more than by voice: so that he himself might be in a certain way the **voice**: which precedes the **Word**: just as the prophet **Isaiah** long before <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> predicted concerning him: which also John himself, not being ignorant of the mystery: responded to those who questioned him: saying. *I am the voice of one crying in the desert, prepare the way of the Lord.* Therefore also **Elijah**, who is to precede the coming **Judge**: was not incongruously <margin>Matthew 3</margin> sent ahead: to anticipate the fiery judgment so that—how great he is who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world through fire—he might intimate more silently through deeds than by voice: Finally, after the late manifestation of Elijah: the most strict **Judge** shall come in fire: who in **Deuteronomy** terribly <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> threatened saying. *A fire is kindled in my fury and shall burn even to the lowest hell: and it shall devour the earth with its growth and shall burn the foundations of the mountains.* And concerning <margin>Psalm 49</margin> whom it is said through the **Psalmist**. *God shall come manifestly: our God and he shall not keep silence: a fire shall burn in his sight and a mighty tempest round about him.* And enough has been said of these things for this place.

<column-break/>

But this must not be overlooked, that when the **seven stars** <note>original: *syderibus*; here referring to the seven "planets" of the ancient world: the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> written above were treated in common: according to how they are assigned to the individual acting days: it was by no means begun from the first day: which among us is called the **Lord's day** <note>Sunday</note>: but from the **Sabbath** and in retrograde order until reaching the first. Nor let anyone think it idle: or accidental: that the first things were made last: and the last things first: because not first (as the **Apostle** says:) that which is spiritual: but that which is animal <note>original: *aiale* / *animale*; meaning natural or of the physical soul, as opposed to the spirit</note>: then that which is spiritual: But if from the <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> extremes we begin, following the authority of the Lord saying. *The first shall be last and the last first*: we ourselves find **Elijah**, by the dignity of so great a mystery: to hold the first <margin>In [the] de[cree?]</margin> place in this part: more glorious than those past: just as also the **sun** among the Gentiles [is] in the days of the week: in the second place **John the Baptist**: the third **David**: the fourth **Moses**: the fifth **Abraham**: the sixth **Noah**: the seventh **Adam**: according to the order of the five stars <note>the five planets excluding the Sun and Moon</note>: which are fitted to the individual days. How this was done: I think it a matter more for wonder than for expression: since indeed not even in those very errors could men so err: as not to give testimony—even against their will—to the **truth**: and not only faithful men by adhering to God bear testimony: but even those who savor of earthly things: by receding from the living and true God. For what if the Lord wished through the mouths of those ignorant of the truth: either to bring forth the truth itself: or at least an image of the truth? For who is more detestable than **Caiaphas** <note>the High Priest who condemned Jesus, but unwittingly prophesied that one man should die for the people</note> who is described as having prophesied so many true things concerning the death of Christ? So also that great poet **Virgil**, not knowing that the heavenly offspring was **Jesus Christ**: and that the time was near that he should be born of a **virgin**: while bringing forth words as if invented: wonderfully promised the truth saying. <margin>Virgil</margin> *Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven.* <note>original: *Jam noua pgenies celo demittitur alto*; a famous line from Virgil’s Fourth Eclogue, which medieval Christians believed was a pagan prophecy of the birth of Christ</note> So also in the **order of the planets**: it was done by the wondrous providence of God: so that by erring in a certain way the Gentiles might not err: and by lying they might express the truth: because even if the opinion of the gods was false: whom they feigned to be planets: they nevertheless held the figure of true things, not knowing what they were doing: As much as it seems to me, the cause of the mystery was hidden: and a sign of things to come, namely a presage.

<margin>Genesis 2</margin>
Moreover, because he broke the command and tasted the forbidden wood, he himself died along with the entire guilt he committed, and he punished those whom he begat in sin with an equal penalty. After him, **Noah** received the law—a good and righteous man. Many years had passed from the beginning, during which it is said that no mortal had ever received a general precept. He commanded that the Lord be praised through it, which has been done from that time until the present day. He also received a mandate from the Lord to shepherd his people Israel, and that his throne should be over them forever. **John the Baptist** was also sent in the sixth age of the world before the face of the coming Lord, to baptize in water and to preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. **Elijah** <note>original: *Helyas*</note> is also to come, as was said above, to precede the Judge who will come at the end in a flame of fire, and he shall precede him with a spiritual baptism. # The Part of the Explanation

...us in the contagion of sin: the first wall <note>original: *paries*; here used as a metaphor for the origin or source of the human lineage</note> of the human race. He was not created in such a way that his act of procreation would make us guilty; rather, he made himself so by abandoning the command and transgressing the law which had been divinely given to him: namely, that he should not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. But because he tasted the forbidden tree by breaking the command, he himself died along with all the guilt he committed, and he subjected those whom he fathered in sin to an equal penalty. After him, **Noah** received the law—a good and righteous man. Many years had passed from the beginning, during which it is said that no mortal had ever received a general precept. He himself received a law similar to the first law which **Adam** transgressed: namely, that neither he nor his offspring should eat flesh with the blood. **Abraham** followed, a man of faith; he was the first among the patriarchs, but the third from Adam to receive a mandate. For he was the first of all to be circumcised, and so that his entire posterity would be subject to the same mandate, he received the command. Fourth from Adam followed **Moses**. He wrote the law in its fullness and taught the people its ceremonies. He also established, among other things, the duties of the Levites—being himself a man of the tribe of Levi—and which sacrifices should be used to appease the Lord. **David** succeeded him, the fifth in this order from Adam; and since he was the <term>Anointed of the Lord<span>original: *Christus Domini*; while "Christ" usually refers to Jesus, the author here uses the term in its literal sense to describe David as the divinely anointed king.</span></term>, he fashioned the instrument of the Holy Spirit, the ten-stringed psalter and the book of Psalms. He commanded that the Lord be praised in it, which has been done from that time until the present day. He also received a mandate from the Lord to feed his people Israel, and that his throne should be over them forever. **John the Baptist** was also sent in the sixth age of the world before the face of the coming Lord to baptize in water and to preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. **Elijah** is also to come, as has already been said above, to precede the Judge who will come at the end in a flame of fire, and he himself will precede the spiritual baptism. Regarding this baptism, surely, the promise was made to us in the Spirit by the 

<column-break/>

<margin>Acts 1</margin>
Lord where he says: "John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now." And when the days of Pentecost were completed (he says), all the disciples were together in the same place, and there appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire, and it sat upon each one of them. It must not be thought, however, that what the Lord had promised concerning the Holy Spirit was fulfilled in a general sense on that day, just as that which had been shown to the prophet regarding the four living creatures <note>A reference to the vision in Ezekiel, often associated with the four Evangelists</note> in the birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension of the Lord was not limited to those events. For these works themselves were mysteries and signs of things to come, just like the other works of the Savior which are contained in the four Gospels. Therefore, what the fire signifies was not fulfilled in a general sense on that day of Pentecost, just as what the water signifies was not fulfilled on the day the Lord was baptized, nor what was designated by the dove which, in a similar way, was taken from the water. But just as the likeness of the Red Sea, in which the Egyptians died, was fulfilled in the second state, so the likeness of the water of the Jordan, in which Christ was baptized, is fulfilled in the third. The likeness of the fire of Elijah, however, is to be fulfilled in the future life. Because in this time in which Christ came into the world, these three mysteries seek to be assigned, we ought to remember that the same Spirit who descended in bodily form like a dove upon the Lord baptized in water, was also given to the holy apostles on the day of the Lord's resurrection through the <term>insufflation<span>The act of breathing upon someone, symbolizing the transmission of the Spirit (from John 20:22).</span></term> which happens through the air; and on the day of Pentecost, he appeared in the likeness of fire. Thus, just as air is placed above water and fire above air, so through intervals of time the grace of the Holy Spirit would increase, which must be completed by such increments. In the first coming of the Lord, which John preceded in water, the grace signified by the water and the dove was given generally, since the dove comes from the water. Around the beginning of the third state—which is near, or rather, present—it is necessary that the grace signified by the air be given to the faithful, and that many mysteries shown to the apostles on the day of Easter be fulfilled. But on that last day, in which there will be the general and final resurrection of the dead, that grace which is signified in fire is to be revealed. We say this, however, so that

# First John on the Apocalypse
->D 2<-

...let us show that it was sacred: because on the day of Pentecost, fire was sent from heaven above the apostles and the other disciples who were with them. This was done on the last day of the festival to show what will come upon all the righteous on the last day. However, we read that at other times the Holy Spirit descended even without visible fire, such as upon the crowd gathered with **Cornelius** <note>A Roman centurion and early Gentile convert mentioned in Acts 10</note>; of which it is said: *While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word, and they spoke in tongues and magnified God.* The same happened to those twelve men whom **Paul** baptized, who had already been baptized in the baptism of John.

Because the Spirit being sent in fire is a sacred mystery, it is to be understood as a sacred thing rather than a physical object. One Evangelist records that **John [the Baptist]** said of himself and of **Christ**: *I baptize you with water; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.* Another Evangelist did not add *and with fire*, but only *the Holy Spirit*. In this context, water signifies the Word, while fire designates the Holy Spirit. Why is water never omitted, while fire is sometimes omitted? Perhaps because the **Word** <note>original: *Verbum*; the second person of the Trinity</note> was made flesh in such a way that it always remains in the flesh and is truly visible to men. The Holy Spirit, however, assumed the forms of a dove and fire only so that, once the mystery was performed, it ceased to appear to human sight.

Truly, human flesh, propagated from flesh, carries the image of the Word of God, just as that dove which appeared was an image of the Holy Spirit. Since the Word was made flesh, it never ceases to be man; but the Holy Spirit was not "made" a dove, nor is he called a dove, nor did he remain a dove. Thus, this one—the Son—is visible through the things that were made visible by the invisible and eternal God. The other is invisible because of invisible creatures. Thus, one God sanctifies all things: that is, both the visible and the invisible. Visible things are sanctified through the Son; invisible things through the Holy Spirit. Yet the visible is not without the Son, nor the invisible without the Holy Spirit, because the Word and the Holy Spirit are one God with the Father. But because only the Son took on our clay <note>original: *limum*; a reference to the dust/earth from which man was made in Genesis</note>, the Holy Spirit did not take on a nature that could be said to "be" his essence in the way the Son did. Having specifically touched upon these things regarding **John** and **Elijah** as types <note>original: *typo*; a historical person or event that foreshadows a later one</note> of the Son and the Holy Spirit, it is now pleasing to speak generally of their properties and the prescribed writings.

<margin>Genesis 2</margin>
<margin>Romans 13</margin>
<margin>Genesis 9</margin>
<margin>Genesis 9</margin>
<margin>Apocalypse 16</margin>
<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
<margin>Psalm 49</margin>
<margin>Romans 6</margin>

...and to show how they are <unclear>demonstrated</unclear> in the seven mandates which were established to illustrate the fullness of justice. In the first precept given to **Adam**, the concupiscence of the eyes and the throat <note>original: *gulae*; gluttony</note> was specifically forbidden. In the second, given to **Noah**, homicide was forbidden. In the third, given to **Abraham**, the wantonness of the flesh was forbidden.

Indeed, the forbidden fruit designated the desire of the throat, from which the Lord prohibits us through the Apostle, saying: *Make no provision for the flesh in its desires.* That the prohibition of eating blood designates homicide is clearly demonstrated by the text itself. For when the Lord said to Noah: *I have given you all things even as the green herbs, except that you shall not eat flesh with the blood,* he immediately added: *I will require the blood of your souls from the hand of every beast; and from the hand of man, from the hand of a man’s brother, I will require the soul of man. Whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed.*

The wantonness of the flesh is designated in the foreskin, as the shame of that nakedness teaches us, which is recognized as most evident in that part of the flesh. Hence, in this book [of Revelation], regarding the sixth angel pouring out the seven bowls, the Lord himself speaks, saying: *Behold, I come as a thief; blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame.*

In these three precepts, every illicit desire of our outer man is inhibited. But because it is not enough to stop doing evil unless a worthy fruit of repentance follows the crimes already committed, three other mandates follow. In these, contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction of work are designated. Contrition of heart is shown in the sacrifice of **Moses**; confession of mouth in the **Psalms of David**; and satisfaction of work in the baptism of **John**. Regarding the first, it is written in the Book of Psalms: *A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.* Regarding the second, it says in the same volume: *The sacrifice of praise shall honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.* Regarding the third, which is the satisfaction of work—that is, the mortification of the flesh—it is said by the Apostle...

### Exposition, Part 2
->C ii<-

You have been buried together with Christ through baptism into death. It should be known, however, that there is a twofold contrition <note>original: *contritio*; a state of deep remorse for sin</note> of the heart: a twofold confession of the mouth: and a twofold satisfaction of work. The contrition of the heart is twofold because we must groan not only for the evils we have committed, but also for the neglect of good; for the former, because we incur death; for the latter, because we are deprived of eternal glory and happiness. There is also a twofold confession of the mouth, according to what has been said regarding contrition. For there is a confession of sins, and there is also a confession of justice <note>original: *iustitia*; here meaning a declaration of God’s righteousness or praise</note>; whether when we punish our own faults by accusing them, or when we praise God's justice by confessing it. Concerning the confession of sin, it is written:
<margin>Psalm 31</margin>
*I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.* Concerning the confession of justice, there is no speech worthy of reporting it, since from almost this entire book, a certain abyss of confessions breaks forth. *I will confess to you, Lord,* it says,
<margin>Psalm 110</margin>
*with my whole heart; and I will confess to your name,*
<margin>Psalm 135</margin>
*because it is good. And confess to the Lord because he is good,* and things similar to these. James the Apostle also, in his epistle, manifests how much the confession of sins is worth when he says: *Confess your sins to one another.* The confession
<margin>Job 5</margin>
of praise is also expressed by the Savior himself when he says: *I confess to you, Father, Lord*
<margin>Matthew 2</margin>
*of heaven and earth.* It is established, therefore, that there is a twofold confession of the mouth, and both pertain to the praise of God, though one more properly than the other. That marvelous thief hanging on the cross handed this down to us by his example, so that each of us may know how and in what order to break forth into the praise of the Creator; he reverently exhibited the one so as not to deny the other. For he offered the first thing first, as if a sacrifice for sin, when, accusing his own fault, he also rebuked his blaspheming companion and said:
<margin>Luke 23</margin>
*Do you not fear God, you who are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive what is worthy of our deeds.* And because a burnt offering <note>original: *holocaustum*; a sacrifice completely consumed by fire</note> is often joined to a sacrifice for sin, he immediately followed by saying: *But this man has done nothing wrong.* Therefore, both are a confession, and both are praise; for we praise the Creator not only when we call Him just, but also when we acknowledge our own faults, for which 

<column-break/>

we are justly judged. For we by no means confess and believe Him to be just if we suspect Him (may it be far from us!) to be cruel, or to exercise an unjust judgment against man. Whence it is also said through
<margin>1 John 1</margin>
John: *If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word*
<margin>Romans 3</margin>
*is not in us.* And the Apostle says: *God is truthful, but every man is a liar,*
<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
just as it is written: *That you may be justified in your words and overcome when you are judged.* But if God is truthful and every man a liar, this is what John says: *If we say we have no sin, we make him a liar,* unless the Truth <note>referring to Christ as the personification of Truth</note> who cannot lie says this truthfully? But if we ourselves say that we are liars, in a certain wondrous and ineffable <note>indescribable</note> way, by the very fact that we say we are liars, we are no longer liars; for we begin to be helpers of the truth against ourselves, who are truthfully liars and guilty. For while we pursue the fault of our lie by being severe against ourselves, we are no longer who we were—ministers of falsehood—but true disciples of truth. Thus it may be said of us, as Truth itself said of that good and humble man: *Behold, truly an Israelite in*
<margin>John 1</margin>
*whom there is no guile.* But why is this? Is it because we are not sinners, or because he who heard this word from the mouth of Truth had no stain of sin? Not at all. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Latin Church Father</note>, who vigilantly explains this passage of the Gospel, does not understand it this way, nor does anyone who is of sound mind and a Catholic. But for this reason there was no guile in him: because, recognizing himself to be a sinner, he daily confessed his sins to the Lord, saying continually
<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
with the prophet: *To you alone have I sinned and done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and overcome when you are judged.* Therefore, a sinful man ought to acknowledge the truth if he does not wish to be empty of eternal salvation, and he should humbly profess his own fault and truthfully proclaim God’s justice as it is. But there still remains for whoever has time: the satisfaction of work <note>original: *satisfactio operis*; making amends through good deeds</note>. It remains for him to exercise himself in good work, so that he does not seem to have only the leaves of words while holding the works of piety in low esteem, but rather let him study as much as he can to produce worthy [fruits].

->### John’s First Part on the Apocalypse<-

->D 3<-

...the fruits of penance. For just as there is a twofold compunction <note>original: *compunctio*; literally a "piercing" of the heart by sorrow for sin</note> of the heart and a twofold confession of the mouth, so there is a twofold satisfaction of work designated in the baptism of John. For the sacrament of baptism, which is perfected in water, designates the true mortification <note>original: *mortificatio*; the "putting to death" of sinful desires</note> of the flesh of sin and likewise the renewal of the old life. Therefore, just as the burial and mortification of the flesh of sin is designated in the fact that the person to be baptized is submerged in the sacred font (if I may put it that way), so in the fact that the baptized person rises from the washing of the font, there is the renewal of the inner man following the stripping away of the "old man" <note>A reference to Adam and the fallen human nature</note> who sinned in Paradise, as the Apostle witnesses when he says:

<margin>Romans 6</margin>
*For we are buried together with him through baptism into death; that as Christ is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life.* Therefore, when we follow Christ by taking up the cross and afflicting our bodies—in which we previously lived uselessly—so that the "body of sin" might be destroyed, we are certainly performing that work which the immersion into the waters designates. 

<column-break/>

<margin>Colossians 3</margin>
But when, by doing good, we exult in the Lord, seeking and savoring the things that are above where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God, then we perform that work which the burnt offering <note>original: *holocaustum*; a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire</note> once designated as a victim; this is the sacrament demonstrated by the one rising from the water and living after the funeral of burial. Thus, in this sixfold observation of the commandment, all purification is completed: namely, of both the body and the mind, and of the "outer man" who, having changed his old skin (so to speak), is renewed in Christ, as well as that "breath of life" <note>original: *spiraculum vite*; the soul or spirit</note> which is within. Although the soul itself is stained not so much by actions as by impure thoughts, the grace of Jesus Christ diligently cleanses it through the three things that are written, so that it may be prepared to receive the celestial fire. And certainly, as something already cleansed—yet still needing to be cleansed until it attains that blessedness—it may grasp that of which it is said:

<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
*Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* This wonderful perfection, designated in the burning of the fire and the ascent of the victim, is granted only at the seventh degree; and certainly to those who have been exercised for a long time and established in the labors of the virtues. For those are truly considered worthy before God to receive the perfect liberty of the Holy Spirit who subject themselves to every servitude for the love of God; and they attain the grace of contemplation on the "seventh day," as it were, because they have carried the burdens of the active life through the cycles of the "six days." Rightly, therefore, was it said of Elijah as a type <note>A "type" is a historical figure or event that foreshadows a future spiritual reality</note> of the Holy Spirit:

<margin>Matthew 17</margin>
*Elijah indeed shall come and shall restore all things*; because when that Spirit of Truth comes (he says), *he will teach you all truth.*

<margin>John 16</margin>
But because, on the occasion of discussing the "seven stars," we seem to have deviated from the straight course of our journey (though not into entirely barren land), and like those seeking pastures for the flock, we have passed through trackless places into the interior of the desert; it is pleasing now, even if late, to return to the path, so that the wave of the word may flow back into its own proper channel. *These things,* he says, *says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks.* Who is this who says these things? Jesus, the Son of God. But why, when about to speak to the first church, does he mention the seven angels and as many churches, unless it is to suppress the pride of that same first church to which he writes? He does this lest, glorifying itself in the dignity of its primacy, it should extol itself by boasting over the others. For just as the proud, by seeking private glory, separate themselves from those they deem lesser, so the Author of Peace, loving community, joins all things together in unity by embracing them; so that while he remembers all together, he works the salvation of all equally, preserving the first from "swelling" <note>original: *tumore*; here meaning the puffing up of pride</note> and the last from the malice of hatred, joining them all together in one covenant of peace. It follows:

<margin>Revelation 2</margin>
> I know your works, and your labor, and your patience.

For God "to know" is to approve, or to be mindful of Himself, and to show Himself mindful through His own people. Wherefore He even deigned to tell His servant Moses that he had found favor in His eyes: *I have known you by name,* He said.

<margin>Exodus 33</margin>
On the other hand, He declares that He does not "know" the reprobate whose works are wicked. Just as, when coming to judgment, He threatened that He would answer some, even after many miracles, saying:

<margin>Matthew 7</margin>
*Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, I know not who you are.* Therefore, He is ignorant of who those people are; but He diligently recognizes His own elect, just as He says of Himself in the Gospel:

<margin>John 13</margin>
*I know whom I have chosen.*

->Part of the Abbot's Exposition<-

in another place: *And I know my sheep, and mine know me.* <note>original: "Et agnosco oues meas & cognoscunt me mee."</note> In this way, the only-begotten Son of God knows the works, the labor, and the patience of the saints, and he approves and commends their good work. As he says through the Psalmist: *The Lord knows the way
<margin>Psalm 1</margin>
of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly shall perish.* We can, however, take this simply to mean that this was said for the sake of those who neglect God's commands, thinking that God does not care about 
<margin>Matthew 16</margin>
