<margin>Psalm 13</margin>
see if there were any that did understand, or seek God.* For this reason, it is said of certain people: *And they said, the Lord shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob understand.*
<margin>Psalm 93
Psalm 72</margin>
And elsewhere: *And they said, how does God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?* Therefore, God’s "knowing" does not always signify approval; sometimes it means this, but other times it shows that He is aware of those who think He is ignorant of something. This is also why it is
<margin>Revelation 3</margin>
said to the church of Sardis: *I know your works, that you have a name that you live, and you are dead.* Most people, however, think "patience" <note>original: *patientia*; meaning endurance or long-suffering</note> consists in tolerating the faithlessness of wicked men. But the meaning of the present passage makes clear that it is a virtue, not a vice, for one to be unable to suffer the wicked—indeed, to be able to "suffer" them would be a detestable vice—when it adds:

<margin>Book 3</margin>
### AND because you cannot endure the wicked, and you have tested those who say they are apostles and are not, and you have found them to be liars; and you have patience, and you have endured for my name's sake, and have not grown weary.

¶ In this place, he seems to utter two contrary and almost repugnant words. In one and the same man or order, he commends both patience and impatience at the same time, when he says: *You have patience, and you cannot endure the wicked.* Yet they are not contrary, even if they seem to be. For who would persecute the saints if the good tolerated errors? Why do those who are unequal <note>meaning those weaker in faith or position</note> endure, except because they fear suffering persecution? And because the first of the churches of Asia was, as it were, 

<column-break/>

strong for enduring the dangers posed by the false apostles <note>original: *pseudo apostolos*</note> who were preaching circumcision, it applied itself with all its strength. Rightly, in the person of the first "angel" <note>The "angel" of the church is traditionally interpreted as its bishop or leader</note>, it is commended for both impatience and patience, as well as for the observation of justice, when it is said: *You cannot endure the wicked, and you have not grown weary.* That there were false apostles at that time who preached things contrary to the faith, the Apostle makes clear in his letter to the 
<margin>Galatians 6</margin>
Galatians when he says: *As many as desire to please in the flesh, they compel you to be circumcised, only that they might not suffer the persecution of the cross of Christ. For neither do they themselves who are circumcised 
<margin>Titus 1</margin>
keep the law; but they want you to be circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh.* Writing also about these men to Titus: *There are* (he says) *many disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision; whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for the sake of filthy lucre.* Therefore, the faithful who were the first from among the Gentiles to believe, by resisting such false apostles, were usefully proven to be both patient and "impatient." They were patient regarding the scandals they suffered for this cause; they were impatient because they could not endure those whom they had proven to be liars. Or certainly, what he says—*You cannot endure the wicked*—must be referred to the zeal <note>original: *zelum*; a holy passion for the truth</note> with which they rebuked sinners. But what he added—*And you have tested those who say they are apostles and are not, and have found them liars*—refers to the caution of prudence. For surely no one can be a true preacher if they lack either of these: that is, if one preserves the faith but allows the briars of vice to grow, or if one fights bravely against vice but is defiled by the impiety of error. But frequently, one who has both becomes lukewarm in the fervor of charity, and almost approaches nothingness; because when the iniquity of a few men abounds, 
<margin>Matthew 24</margin>
the charity of many grows cold (as the Lord says). It is not a great thing to have charity in 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 27</margin>
prosperous times, unless one remains strong in adversity; as the scripture witnesses which says: *The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous men.* Hence Truth <note>meaning Christ</note> says through itself: 
<margin>Matthew</margin>
*He that shall persevere unto the end, he shall [be saved].*

# First Book on the Apocalypse
<sig>D 4</sig>

he will be saved. But that church <note>The Church in Ephesus</note> was not destined to persevere in its first love <note>original: *charitate prima*; a reference to the zeal and devotion of the early Christian community</note>, as is shown in the Acts <margin>Acts 20</margin> of the Apostles. There, Paul says to the elders of the Ephesians: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the church of God, which he purchased with his own blood." And he immediately adds: "I know that after my departure, ravenous wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock. And from among your own selves shall arise men speaking perverse things, to lead away disciples after them." Since, therefore, it did not persevere in the heat of love which it had conceived when Paul was preaching, it is rightly praised for its beginning but rebuked for its end when it is said:

<margin>2:4</margin> **"But I have a few things against you, because you have left your first love."**

He does not say "because you have left love," but "your *first* love." To fall away in some part is to decline from the highest and greatest good toward a lesser one; for the "holy living creatures" <note>A reference to the four living creatures in Ezekiel's vision</note> did not turn back as they moved, but each one walked straight forward. Therefore, it is soon added:

<margin>2:5</margin> **"Be mindful, therefore, from whence you are fallen."**

It is as if it were openly said: "The good that you do should not comfort you so much that you judge it sufficient for yourself; rather, be more afflicted by your fall. For the good you do is less acceptable in my sight unless you strive to return to that degree of grace from which you fell through sloth." In this matter, it is necessary <margin>Psalm 74</margin> to pay diligent attention and to fear greatly what is said through the Psalmist: *God is the judge; he humbles this one and exalts that one.* For he deserted the people of the Jews who were raised up in pride; that famous city in which the Jews gloried, <margin>Isaiah 27</margin> he humbled even to the earth, just as Isaiah had predicted: *The Lord has bowed down those who dwell on high; the lofty city he shall humble; he shall humble it even to the ground, he shall pull it down even to the dust. The foot of the poor shall tread it down: the steps of the needy.* As we have heard these things, so have we seen them. Truly, that lioness which 

<column-break/>

Daniel describes <margin>Daniel 7</margin>—which, like the others he saw, was raised up high as if with eagle's wings—was cast down from her pride by God’s command and placed under the feet of the Romans. The Romans did not know the riches of God's goodness until that time, and the Gentile people, who were until then "needy" <note>spiritually poor or lacking the Covenant</note>, entered into their faith. Those who remained of the Jewish people were truly humbled even to the dust. But was the "wild olive" <note>The Gentiles</note> to be spared, when he did not spare the "natural olive" <note>The Jews</note>? For the Church of the Circumcision, which was founded in Jerusalem, was left behind by Peter, the prince of the apostles, because of the favorable omen of ancient pride; the Lord provided something more glorious for him in Rome. Likewise, Paul was taken away by a just but hidden judgment of God from that church <note>Ephesus</note> which he had previously founded, and was destined for Rome, where he took up his dwelling along with the apostle Peter. We do not say that this threat was fully completed at that time while John was still alive—except perhaps in part—but we say it because, as it appeared after the death <note>original: *dormitionez*; literally "falling asleep"</note> of Saint John, that Eastern church was reduced to nothing. The lampstand <note>original: *candelabro*; symbolizing the presence and grace of the church</note> was removed from there and given to other cities. This is that terrible and strict punishment <margin>Matthew 20. Luke 1.</margin> of a just God, by which the sinning angels in heaven were condemned from the beginning, and the original world was deleted by the flooding Deluge as an example (as Peter says) for those who would act impiously. This is the reason why the first are made last and the last first; why the hungry are filled with good things and the rich are sent away empty; why those who think they are nothing are found to be something, and those who think they are something are found to be nothing. This is the reason <margin>Romans 9. 1 Cor. 2.</margin> why God chose Jacob the younger and rejected the firstborn Esau; why God chose the base things of the world to confound the strong; why he calls those things which are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that all the world may become subject to God, and no flesh should glory in his sight. <margin>1 Cor. 1.</margin> For this is why, when Saul was rejected, Samuel was sent to choose from the sons of Jesse; yet Samuel was not permitted to anoint the firstborn, for the Lord said: "Look not on his face, nor on the height of his stature..."

In the same way, in the book of the Acts of the Apostles <margin>Acts 1</margin>, Joseph, who was surnamed the Just, is listed first; and yet, so that he might be in the number of the apostles, it says: "the lot fell upon Matthias." Therefore, the nine apostles, together with that blessed Joseph surnamed the Just, designate those ten tribes that were deported from the three tribes mentioned above. Truly, those same three tribes <note>represent</note> James and Cephas and John; while Barnabas represents the nation of the Greeks, and Paul represents the least of the Latins. <note>original: "minimūs latinorum"</note> Moreover, the apostles signify this together with the holy women and Mary the mother of Jesus: insofar as the churches are designated in the women, and the prelates of the churches are designated in the apostles. Since these things are so, why is it that, omitting the nine apostles, the Apostle <note>Paul</note> makes mention of only three <note>James, Peter, John</note>? It is because, while those nine tribes (one of which was doubled) were far from the fatherland, the promise of God was fulfilled in the three remaining tribes, and in them, the gifts of the Holy Spirit were poured out from the beginning, and likewise upon the Greeks...

...were the Latins <note>The author uses "Latini" here to refer to the Western/Gentile converts</note> converted to the Lord? What then do we say: that those three apostles <note>James, Peter, and John</note> had, as it were, grown lukewarm in grace, as Paul testifies? It is rather that the faithful among the circumcision <note>Jewish converts to Christianity</note>, being zealous for the Law, began to fall away from grace. Indeed, when all the strong were being weakened and growing lukewarm in this regard—fearing those many thousands who had believed—all the brothers (as they testified when Paul came to them) were zealous for the Law. In this matter, we must consider that the sentiment of the same Paul is true, where he says: **the letter kills, but the spirit gives life** <note>original: "littera occidit: spiritus aut viuificat"; quoting 2 Corinthians 3:6</note>. For we read that Paul, out of fear of causing a scandal, acted according to the ritual <note>Jewish custom</note>, even though he boasts that he rebuked Peter, in whose actions he was joining himself. But what shall we say of that which is added: **so that even Barnabas was led into that hypocrisy**? <note>original: "simulationem"; referring to the incident in Galatians 2:13 where Peter and Barnabas stopped eating with Gentiles</note> Was it as if the sin of Barnabas was more serious than that of Peter, the first of the apostles? And for this reason, it was said by Paul: **So that even Barnabas was led into that hypocrisy.** Indeed, it seemed more serious and more unbearable to God's elect that the error of Jewish superstition grew strong among the Gentile people than it did among the Jewish people themselves, where it could not be easily rooted out due to ancient, long-standing habit.

<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
where he says: **The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.** <note>original: "littera occidit: spiritus aũt viuificat"</note> For we read that Paul, out of fear of causing a scandal, performed certain acts according to the ritual <note>Paul followed Jewish purification rites in Jerusalem to appease the local believers</note>, he who boasted of having rebuked Peter—the very one Peter had joined in those actions. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Revelation, specifically interpreting the relationship between the apostles Peter and Paul through the lens of Old Testament figures Saul and David. It explains the historical and spiritual transition of the Church's center from the East (Ephesus and Jerusalem) to Rome.</meta>

### Part of the Exposition

...the holy ones <note>original: "scōs," abbreviation for "sanctos"</note>: not so much with oil as with the Holy Spirit. The former [oil] is for the protection of bodies; the latter [the Spirit] is for the kingdom of souls. After the kingdom was transferred to David and to the tribe of Judah, and the ten tribes withdrew from the house of David and chose Jeroboam the son of Nebat as their king, only the tribe of Benjamin clung to the tribe of David. Its name was suppressed and as if deleted, so that although there were two tribes, it is recorded in the Book of Kings that only the tribe of Judah remained for the house of David. 

We know that something similar happened in the Church if we consider that the deeds of Paul and Peter were similar in some respect to the deeds of Saul and David. For Peter—to whom the Lord said: "Feed my sheep" <note>John 21:17</note> and for whom He had prefigured a place of royal priesthood at Rome—remained for some time in Jerusalem by his own administration, presiding over the churches of the circumcision <note>Jewish converts</note> which were propagated as far as Antioch. In that city, indeed, no small dispute arose concerning the Law and grace; not secretly as in Galatia, but openly before the Gentiles and Jews, as if placed on the border, since it distinguished between the boundaries of the Jews and the Gentiles. 

But Paul, sent with Barnabas from that same city by the Holy Spirit, reached Ephesus by preaching and advancing in the faith of Christ. He stayed there continuously for two years, disputing and persuading concerning the kingdom of God, so that all who dwelt in Asia heard the word of God, both Jews and Gentiles. And so it happened that Paul reigned among the Gentiles before Peter, just as Saul of the tribe of Benjamin reigned before David of the tribe of Judah. And yet, according to the ancestral law, David was greater than Saul, because Judah, the father of David, preceded Benjamin, the father of Saul, in birth. Thus, if considered prudently, even in this way a similarity of harmony is not lacking. Peter followed Paul and was enthroned at Rome, and there the kingdom of the "strong-handed" David <note>The name David was traditionally interpreted as "strong of hand"</note> was raised up in the spirit. Paul was then removed from Ephesus, proceeding "bound in the spirit" <note>Acts 20:22</note> as if about to die in the flesh, and was joined at Rome to Peter, the first of the apostles. Thus, just as the glory which by right was owed to Jerusalem—when Reuben lost his birthright—was transferred to Rome with Peter, so

<column-break/>

too the lampstand of Ephesus is transferred to Rome with Paul. Or, to speak more truly, it follows Paul; so that just as after the death of Saul the tribe of Benjamin was united to the tribe of Judah—and so strongly united that when others departed, it remained insolubly bound to it—so that grace which was bestowed on Asia from the beginning, together with that which had been given to Jerusalem for the fruitfulness of justice, is known to have arrived in one Latin people <note>The Romans</note> according to both lives <note>likely referring to the contemplative and active lives, or the Jewish and Gentile missions</note>. 

Certainly, this very thing was designated in Saul when his daughter [Michal] was joined in marriage to David. It was as if, when the men failed (as gathered from the end of his line), his humbled posterity migrated, as it were, to the other tribe. Lest it should happen to be proud again, it was deprived of the succession of its lineage—not so that the tribe itself should fail, which began to be joined to the tribe of Judah, but so that nothing of the royal stock remained in it except the "lame and weak" <note>a reference to Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson</note> who could have resisted the supreme Judge. 

This is why Paul did not have his own successor in Rome, but was received equally with Peter in the one See of Peter, so that the word of Christ might be fulfilled which He had spoken: **I have other sheep which are not of this fold; and those I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.** <note>John 10:16</note> Rather, it was to reveal that great mystery by which we believe Christ the King is the true Son of the highest King, yet we believe both together to be one King, just as there is one Lord and one God. 

However, when He says: **Otherwise, I am coming to you** <note>Revelation 2:5</note>, it must be referred to the time of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor, r. 284–305 AD</note>, who, residing in the eastern parts, afflicted those regions beyond measure and reduced the entire practice of religion to desolation. In a similar way, Almighty God showed Himself "coming" to Sodom when He said: **The cry of the Sodomites and Gomorrahites is multiplied, and their sin is become exceedingly grievous; I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry that has come to me, or if it is not so, that I may know.** <note>Genesis 18:20-21</note> This is His hidden coming, with which He threatens in another place of this book, saying: **Behold, I come like a thief.** <note>Revelation 16:15</note> And of which it is said in a similar way by the Apostle: **The day of the Lord shall so come as a thief in the night.** <note>1 Thessalonians 5:2</note> Regarding this day of the thief...

### The First Part of the Apocalypse

<margin>Isaiah 13</margin>
The coming of the Lord is spoken of by the prophet: *Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, to lay the earth in solitude and to crush its sinners from it.* <note>Isaiah 13:9. The author interprets this "day of the Lord" as a specific judgment on a corrupt city.</note> Truly, this refers to the general plague upon Babylon, which is solemnly written about in the sixth part of this book. However, this [current judgment] is specific, and according to its part, just as that 

<margin>Matthew 24</margin>
most specific judgment which is read in the Gospel: *The lord of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and an hour he does not know, and will cut him asunder, and place his part with the hypocrites.* <note>Matthew 24:50-51</note> Because no good thing is left unrewarded—even among those who sin gravely—God also commends the good of this angel <note>The "Angel" of the Church refers to its bishop or spiritual leader.</note>, which he vigilantly preserved despite the loss of his initial charity. For it is added:

<margin>Revelation 2:6</margin>
> But this good thing you have: that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.

It is said that the author of this heresy was Nicholas, who is described as having been one of the seven deacons. <note>Nicholas was one of the seven chosen to serve the early Church in Acts 6:5. Early traditions often debated whether he truly started this sect or if his name was misused.</note> It is said that this Nicholas had a beautiful wife; because he did not understand the virtue of chastity, he loved her with a passionate and slippery devotion. When he was accused of the jealousy he had for her, he is said to have offered her up to those who wished to abuse her. In this way, his followers multiplied, and he became the "heresiarch" <note>A leader of a heretical sect.</note> of this crime. Therefore, the hatred of these deeds is best commended to those who are jealous for chastity. For the excess of luxury is so foul and so horrible that it is hated by those known to have chosen a chaste life—or even those who, having wives, are as if they had none, holding them for the sake of children rather than lust, and preserving themselves from fornication not so much by the zeal of desire as by the hatred of unspeakable crime. Moreover, the Angel of the Church of Ephesus is praised for having this good quality because, having been instructed from the beginning by the doctrine of Paul, he learned with what affection a man ought to love his wife, and that it is not permitted to depart from a wife without a certain cause, nor to leave her to another. Therefore, if he is rebuked for a cooling of his charitable fire, he is nevertheless praised in that part where he was praiseworthy, so that he might not despair over his fault but rather perform penance for his fall. But he who for a long time on account of the good he

<column-break/>

possesses is expected to repent, if he is expected so that he might have more but does not convert, then even what he seems to have is removed from him. This was done so that what is specifically said in the New Testament might be shown to have been designated by mystical things in the Old Testament. Since 

<margin>Genesis 30</margin>

### Abbot: Part of the Exposition

<margin>Saint Sylvester</margin>
Pope <note>original: "pa," an abbreviation for "Papa"</note> Sylvester obtained the solemn power of the entire royal priesthood. But up until that time, that illustrious inheritance of Peter was buried under bushes and thorns, so that he could not freely use the power handed down to him, because the Roman princes <note>Meaning the pagan Roman Emperors before Constantine.</note> opposed it and sought to erase the name of Christ forever from the earth. Indeed, because the province of Asia is far distant from the city of Rome, the Christian religion there could not at first offend the minds of the emperors in the same way; for things seen nearby disturb differently than things heard from afar. 

Therefore, two were chosen from the Old Testament and two from the New: Joshua from the tribe of Joseph and Caleb born of the tribe of Judah; John the Younger, who corresponds with Joshua the Younger; and along with him Peter the Elder, who has a wondrous harmony with Caleb the Elder. Just as from the beginning of the entry of the children of Israel into the land of Canaan, Joshua, who was of the tribe of Joseph, held the leadership among the whole of that people—even though Caleb was so great in the sight of the Lord that, being angry against the leaders who spoke ill of the land, <margin>Numbers 14</margin> He spoke saying: *My servant Caleb, who is full of a kind spirit and has followed me, I will lead into this land which he scouted, and his seed shall possess it* <note>Numbers 14:24</note>—likewise here, blessed Peter received the promise of possessing the inheritance of the Lord. 

Yet because eleven churches were founded among the Greek people, in which faith flourished from the start while the Western Church (called the Latin Church) was not yet permitted to raise its head, Saint John was seen at that time to have a greater title of prerogative in the leadership of the Church, as so many Greek churches followed him as Christ's apostle. For because he preached the name of Christ freely there, which was not permitted here in Rome due to fear of the emperors, and because John survived for a long time after the death of the Prince of the Apostles [Peter] along with his other co-apostles, it was not without reason that all the churches obeyed such a great apostle of Christ; for after his brothers were taken from this light, he alone survived of them all. And so it happened that, just as in that time Joshua, who was of the house of Joseph, held the leadership among the children of Israel, so among the Easterners

<column-break/>

in that humble time, Saint John [held leadership], who was seen to belong to that church which in succeeding times was called the Constantinopolitan. If one asks about its lateness—why it did not have its own name from the beginning like the others—the cause is certainly this: that He who had pre-chosen them willed Peter to be the elder over the others and John to be the younger, joining and uniting them in equality of honor, so that those who are in the middle might not be scandalized, but that, with the torches of jealousy extinguished everywhere, they might rest in pleasantness. 

Nor was this regarding the glory of the patriarchate, which was given to that same royal city [Constantinople] in the course of time. But the other churches to which Paul writes—the Corinthians, the Thessalonians, and others to whom he sends epistles—were considered as being of the family of Ephraim. But the Tabernacle of Joseph was rejected, <margin>Psalm 76</margin> <margin>Psalm 77</margin> <note>The author cites Psalms 77 and 78 according to the Vulgate numbering. These verses describe God rejecting the tent of Ephraim/Joseph in favor of Judah and Mount Zion.</note> just as the Kingdom of Benjamin was, which was the first among the seven; and the tribe of Judah was chosen for the kingdom and for the temple of the Lord. 

But because the house of David, to whom the height of the kingdom was given, forgot the benefit it had received and sinned before the Lord its God, the leadership was likewise given to Ephraim, <margin>3 Kings</margin> <note>Referencing 1 Kings 12 (3 Regum in the Latin Vulgate), where Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim leads the rebellion against David's grandson.</note> and that tribe was taken up again under its own lordship, of which it had been said: *He rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim.* And Jeroboam the son of Nebat was appointed king over it, and after him Samaria was built as a royal city, in which the kings of Israel reigned together, just as the kings of Judah did in Jerusalem. 

In the same way it happened in the Church, if we carefully weigh the order of historical events. Finally, in the days of Constantine Augustus, the Roman Church—which is the second Jerusalem—obtained a privilege from the same Augustus so that, just as it had been truly given to her by the Lord, she might be the head of the faithful and the mother of all Christians. But after the seats of the impious were established in the city of Byzantium, it became in a wondrous way like a second Samaria in the tribe of Ephraim, which would itself be a head—not of all, but of many churches—those, I say, which in some way have been separated until the present from the Roman Church. And which are those that were so separated? Alexandria, Jerusalem, Antioch, and the six churches of Asia of which we speak.

And in it is the truest likeness of Ephraim, who alone, besides the tribe of Judah, followed in the likeness of sons; who alone, having received the Kingdom, was moved by rivalry. For just as envy arose between Judah and Ephraim because of the kingdom, so too between the Roman and Constantinopolitan churches. <margin>Galatians 3</margin>
In certain matters, he [Paul] rebuked them, saying: "Are you so foolish: that having begun with the spirit, you are now being perfected by the flesh?" <note>Referring to the Galatians who returned to Jewish legalism after accepting the Gospel.</note> But why does this one [the Spirit speaking to Ephesus] not rebuke them for receiving false apostles, but on the contrary, praises them for not receiving them? It is clear that he is not rebuking them concerning the letter of the first testament which was in circumcision, but concerning the letter of the new testament, which <margin>1 Timothy 3, Titus 1</margin> was itself to be understood spiritually. For as the Apostle says: "the husband of one wife," one should not understand this literally, as the Greeks wish, but rather in the spirit, so that he understands his "wife" to be no other than the very Church over which he is said to preside—and other things similar to this. Therefore, there is a difference between both types of followers: for the closer the understanding is to the spiritual letter, the less one sins; and the further one is distant from it, the more such a person is consumed in the corruption of the flesh. For concerning those who were circumcising, the Apostle shows more clearly how worthy they were of <unclear>attu</unclear> <margin>Philippians 3</margin> when he says: "Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision." <note>The "concision" or "mutilation" was Paul's derogatory term for those insisting on physical circumcision.</note> However, those who were caught between the flesh and the spirit are deservedly praised in part and blamed in part, so that they may understand that a space for repentance has been given to them for their salvation, and that the ruin of their dogmas is not imminent. All these things, as we have heard, so we have seen: for just as Holy Scripture has testified concerning future things, so the experience of events proves them more clearly than light regarding the past. But because it is not enough merely to have ears of the mind, and to set one’s heart to understand, the following is rightly added:

<margin>Luke 8</margin>
> HE who has ears for hearing: let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

He calls "ears for hearing" a teachable heart <note>original: "precordia docibilia"</note>, to distinguish them from those who, hearing, do <margin>Luke 8</margin> not hear, and seeing, do not understand. Just as Truth itself [Christ] spoke to those to whom it was given to hear and understand, saying: "To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God: but to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand." These two young pigeons represent two works of the Holy Spirit. One is the Incarnation of Christ; the other is the outpouring of charity <note>Love or divine grace.</note>. One pigeon is the Bridegroom of the Church, who is Christ Jesus. The other is the Bride of Christ herself, which is called the Church. Because the prelates of the churches carry out the role of Christ on earth, Christ speaks to them in the Holy Scriptures so they may know what they ought to do and how they should arrange the burdens and progress of those subject to them. For it is fitting for rectors to teach and instruct the subject churches, and to impart to their subjects with the greatest effort what they themselves receive from the one Master. Thus, as if through certain funnels, the wine of doctrine may be poured into the hearts of those thirsting for the Word of God, and the meadows of the souls of the faithful may be irrigated. For in the former, a man speaks as a man; in the latter, it is not a man who speaks but the Spirit of the living God. <meta>This page continues the spiritual exposition of the Apocalypse, moving from the distinction between the "letter" and the "spirit" to an allegorical interpretation of church roles, using the biblical figures of Zechariah, Elizabeth, Mary, and various Old Testament patriarchs to define the relationship between Christ, the Holy Spirit, and the Church hierarchy.</meta>

# First Part of John in the Apocalypse

<margin>Acts 10</margin>
...they heard the word. And this indeed happens for the most part. Just as Elizabeth received [conceived] through the action of her husband, and Mary received [the Word] through the angel speaking. Though we read that Mary received through the angel and Elizabeth through her husband, there is a difference in the nature of these things: for the priest Zechariah signifies the priests of the church who, like mute elements—that is, historical narratives—teach the soulish churches <note>original: "animales ecclesias" — churches focused on the physical or literal level of understanding rather than the spiritual.</note> subject to them. This type of doctrine, owing to their weakness and carnality, is compared to marital assistance. The angel, however, signifies spiritual men who teach spiritual things spiritually, "Comparing spiritual things with spiritual" <note>original: "Spiritualia spiritualibus comparantes" — a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:13.</note>.

For (to skip over the rest), what else does it seem to be to treat the literal account of Abraham’s two wives, of Rebecca—how she was very beautiful and how Isaac was with her—of Rachel and Leah, of Tamar who conceived by her father-in-law, or of the wife of Potiphar the Eunuch <note>Potiphar is described as a "eunuch" in the Latin Vulgate (eunuchi Pharaonis).</note> who fell in love with Joseph, and other such things? What, I ask, is it to treat such matters except to receive certain "voluptuous seeds" in the mind, if the spirit does not resist them manfully? But if the spirit speaks in a spiritual person, it pours into them a spiritual understanding—water effectively converted into wine. Then it is no longer a man who seems to speak about these deeds, but an angel. For while that which was tasted carnally in the literal sense is approached by fire coming down from heaven, the spirit devours it all. This is that fire which descended from heaven and consumed the flesh, the water, and the dust in the sight of those standing by <note>A reference to Elijah's sacrifice in 1 Kings 18.</note>. For this reason, these men are not undeservedly called "angels," as they preside over spiritual assemblies—provided they are such as the mysteries declare they ought to be.

But for us, each one of them carries the image of Christ in themselves, while the seven churches represent the seven spiritual graces. Truly, the *Messiah* (which is translated as "Christ") is shown to have a masculine name, and *Rua* <note>The Hebrew word "Ruach" meaning Spirit, which is grammatically feminine.</note> (which is translated as "Spirit") a feminine name. This is not because gender is to be considered in God, but because striking with a rod belongs to the man, while showing the affection of sweetness belongs to the woman. The first of these is spiritually ascribed to Christ, the second to the Holy Spirit. That is why Christ speaks to the angels [the leaders], while the Spirit speaks to the churches.

<column-break/>

For it is the role of those acting [the leaders] to commend to memory the words of Christ written in the books, so that they know what they ought to do in teaching. And it is the role of those who plant <note>Referring to those who nurture the spiritual growth of the congregation.</note> to conceive a spiritual understanding in those same words. Thus, they should strive not only to pay attention to what they hear, but also to what he, whose temples they are, suggests, as the Lord says: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; but when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth" <note>John 16:12-13.</note>. Although the Son speaks to both and the Holy Spirit speaks to both—namely to the pastors and the churches—nevertheless, because of the difference in the similarity between pastors and churches, first and more specifically the Pastor speaks to the pastors, and then the Dove (if I may say so) speaks with his voices to the doves. I think it is worth the effort to examine this more diligently.

We said above that the two young doves signify Christ and the church. But because of other words interjected, it was not set forth as clearly as it ought to have been: just as the more express image of Christ is in the pastors, so the likeness of the Holy Spirit is in the church. This is undoubtedly because of the multitude of gifts contained under one spirit. For there is one King and one Queen; but of this Queen, the children are innumerable. Nor was any other virgin chosen to be both mother and bride of Christ except one; yet the church, which is spiritually joined to him, is not one single person. There is one mother, but many children; one dove, but many eggs. For there is one Spirit of God, which in Hebrew (as I have said) is called *Rua*, but his gifts are many, divided among individuals. In each of the churches, this likeness is expressed: he is called an "egg" who is second after the prelate and set over the others. Considering the necessity or utility of each brother, he distributes to each as there is need. For there is one leader, but many brothers; one spirit, but many gifts.

The one who is first [the leader] carries the likeness of the Father; the one who is second carries the likeness of the Mother. Hence, Isaac and Rebecca mystically signify that the former corrects the erring with his mouth, while the latter raises up the exasperated with maternal leniency so they are not offended and fall by the rod of the father. And indeed, to give judgment belongs to the prelate; while the one who...

<margin>John 14</margin>
...is present after him: in the souls of the subjects, suggest the patience of discipline: so that in the one, the likeness of the Son may shine forth, and in the other, the image of the Holy Spirit. The author is contrasting the external teaching of Christ with the internal illumination of the Spirit.</note>. For it is as if it were said: "Even if the precepts I have proposed to you now as Lord and Master seem harsh to you, he, when he comes, will show how necessary they are for salvation." Moreover, Christ speaks well at the beginning of each chapter, but the Holy Spirit speaks at the end: because Christ was sent first to teach the apostles, and secondly the Holy Spirit was sent to speak to all the faithful. Yet he speaks nothing other than what Christ spoke, but in a similar way, so that he who is written here may aptly understand: "Thus says the Son of God," and "He who has ears for hearing, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches" <note>A reference to the repeated refrain in Revelation 2 and 3.</note>. Not only for this reason, but also because of the beginning of the **second status** <note>This refers to the "Three Ages" theory popularized by Joachim of Fiore: the Age of the Father (Old Testament), the Son (New Testament/Church), and the Holy Spirit (a future age of spiritual understanding).</note>, in which Christ spoke aptly to the preachers of life; and because of the end of that same second status and the beginning of the **third**, in which the Holy Spirit will show his voices more fully and perfectly, and will suggest by the truth those things which are of God to those who are contemplating. Therefore, wherever this word occurs in this first part, let it suffice that we have explained it once in this chapter. It follows:

<margin>A. 9.</margin>
### ¶ To the one who overcomes, I will give to eat of the tree of life: which is in the paradise of my God.
<note>Revelation 2:7.</note>

While the doctors of the churches speak many things in various places of the Holy Scriptures according to their own estimation, that particular kind of exposition is more customarily practiced by them when the individual parts of the word are proven to pertain to the matter, and the following parts respond to those preceding. Therefore, to the affirmation of the preceding sentence is joined what we have just heard: *To the one who overcomes, I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.* But in this matter, the reader must consider how great is the weight of

<column-break/>

this book; for while it touches upon a small word, it comprehends the fullness of history. For, in order to show to whom specifically and about which church he was speaking spiritually, he invites us, by the occasion of the "tree of life," to the history of the **first-formed** <note>original: "protoplausti" — referring to Adam and Eve, the first created humans.</note>, in which he declares the departure of the primitive church in a mystery. Certainly, since Adam—an earthly man and an inhabitant of paradise—was placed between the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and the tree of life, he designated that primitive assembly of those circumcised in the faith of Christ. They were placed between Moses and Christ, between the Law and Grace, between the taste of death and of life. Lest, after the grace of baptism, they should have tasted again of the fruit of the Mosaic law—which is the "spirit of servitude"—instead of the true tree of life, which is the Incarnate Word and the heavenly bread. The Teacher of the Gentiles <note>The Apostle Paul.</note> explains something in them through the divine volumes understood spiritually, and he took up an argument <unclear>parmusap</unclear> <note>This word is obscure in the original Latin; it may be a corruption of a term regarding the "table" of the apostles or their shared understanding.</note> against the apostles regarding this (if indeed he was wise). Therefore, not without the cause of judgment were both expelled from paradise. Both? Was that people in paradise? They certainly were. But perhaps they possessed less happiness than the former? Far from it! For who is so foolish that he would dare to compare the tree of life to the Only-Begotten of God? Or the wood of paradise to the disciples of Christ? Or the river of pleasure to the torrent of the Holy Spirit, which had also flowed over them?

<margin>Genesis 2</margin>
"The Lord," it says, "had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning." What is "from the beginning"? From that time when he came to redeem the world, according to what had been pre-ordained in the foreknowledge of God. Therefore, the paradise was the **primitive church**: the very same as the tabernacle, in which there was also the lampstand from the beginning. But why "of pleasure"? Because she was inebriated by the abundance of the house of the Lord, so that others also might be inebriated by her and by the torrent of the pleasure of the love of God, by which she was most sweetly given to drink. Finally, pleasure joins a wife to a husband. From where, then, is the church the wife of Christ, except because she tasted the immensity of the sweetness proceeding from him? Her soul clung to him, so that she might say: "Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your ointments" <note>Canticle of Canticles (Song of Solomon) 1:3-4.</note>. Man was placed there when the Lord had formed him—that is, that great multitude from the circumcision of believers <note>This refers to the first Christians who were originally Jewish and followed the Law of Moses.</note> which was formed through faith, the word, and the love of God in baptism, so that he might grow into a "perfect man," reaching the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.

<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>
Furthermore, there were in this church some who were stronger, like **Adam**; some who were weaker, like **Eve**; and some who were shifty <note>original: "versipelles," literally "skin-changers," a term used for the cunning or deceptive.</note>, like the **serpent**. Those who were stronger in faith, following the example of Adam, were nonetheless still bound by carnal love. Those following the example of Eve were not only carnal but also weak in faith. Those following the serpent were malicious, treacherous, and unjust—enemies of the cross of Christ and friends of those who crucified him. Therefore, because they were joined by race, by law, and by their native land, that ancient enemy who once entered the serpent and persuaded Eve to eat from the forbidden tree entered once again into the "synagogue of Satan" <note>A term from Revelation 2:9 and 3:9, used here to describe those who opposed the spiritual transition from the Law to the Gospel.</note> to deceive the simple and the carnal. If you ask what he said, consider the words of the serpent.

<margin>Genesis 3</margin>
"Why," he said, "did God command you not to eat from every tree in paradise?" To him the woman replied: "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat of it or touch it, lest we die." "Why," the Jews say, "do you not observe the law which the patriarchs, prophets, and all the righteous kept? If the law is bad, why did the prophets observe it? Why did your apostles and all the elders venerate it, walking in all its commandments?" "Granted," they say, "that Christ is the son of Mary. Why did he himself wish to be circumcised if circumcision was not to be observed?" It is certain, therefore, that what Paul writes is false, even though he prophesies as if on behalf of God, saying:

<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>

This is because the divine substance is invisible; yet, those to whom the angels are recorded to have appeared nonetheless professed that they had seen God. Although through this, the name of "God" seems to have been transferred to the creature by the "Father of Lies," because he added: "You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil." Finally, even Moses, who agrees with Paul, was called "god" by title <note>original: "nuncupatiue," meaning having the name or title without the underlying essence.</note>, and all the priests of the Church are named "gods" in the same way, as the Scripture attests: "God stood in the synagogue of the gods."

<margin>Psalm 81</margin>
Therefore, he who was called to the "seed of words" and was appointed by the Lord as the teacher of all the churches—and especially the churches of Asia—so that by a certain spiritual prerogative of doctrine he seemed to carry the role of the Only-Begotten God <note>Christ</note> speaking within him: he could not without reason be called "god" by title, just as Moses was. Thus, that word ought to have been ascribed to him in a mystical sense, for he forbade the following of the "letter that kills," in which (according to the same Apostle) is the knowledge of good and evil. This is especially true since, as I recall having written elsewhere, mysteries are to be understood in such a way that they sometimes overflow from the head <note>Christ or the leaders</note> to the members. Thus, Eve was deceived by the serpent; her husband was deceived through Eve; the weaker were deceived by the impious; and the strong and courageous were deceived by the weak. They seized the forbidden apple; they ate the "fruit of the flesh," in which death resided from the beginning. They repeated the forbidden sacrifice of the Law; they tasted the "corpse-meat" and the deadly banquet. And what happened then? The eyes of both were opened, and they saw their own shame. For, as it says, both were naked and were not ashamed.

<margin>Genesis 3</margin>
If they were naked, why were they not ashamed? Because they did not know that they were naturally naked and subject to shame. I say this mystically, not historically; for the understanding of the "letter" is one thing, and the "spiritual" understanding is another. In the spiritual sense, evil is often designated through the good, and something good through the bad. # Exposition of the Apocalypse: Part 2
## Signature: Z
-> Catchword: cause <-

[The person] does not see [it]: because he fears to bring the evil conceived in his mind into effect. Although he is naked in the sight of God—who sees the inner parts of the heart more than the outer appearance—the carnal mind still does not know that it is naked within itself, because it fears only outward losses <note>The author is explaining that "nakedness" in a spiritual sense is a lack of internal virtue, which a person focused only on physical reality cannot perceive.</note>. But when the bonds and reins of fear are cut, and he approaches the commission of a deed, overcome by the flesh, then for the first time—having returned to himself (albeit fruitlessly)—he begins to understand his own confusion, which he had first neglected by undervaluing it. 

Thus Eve was naked of interior good when she abstained from what was forbidden not out of a love for justice, but only out of a fear of punishment. In the same way, that people <note>Referring to the Israelites or the "Synagogue" in this allegory.</note>, unrefined in faith, did not understand the shames of their carnality which they were accustomed to keep; they did not know what they lacked, nor did they know they were naked, except after the light was extinguished—that is, only when they lost the freedom of grace and consolation. But what wonder is it if a carnal people who, according to the Apostle, still had need of **milk and not solid food** <note>original: "lacte opus erat et non solido cibo"; a reference to Hebrews 5:12</note>, could not see their own nakedness? For it is written: <margin>Hebrews 5</margin> **Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he hath been compared to senseless beasts, and made like to them.** <margin>Psalm 48</margin> <note>This is Psalm 49 in modern Bibles.</note> 

Therefore, when the Jewish people began to seize forbidden things and—contrary to the opinion of the Teacher of the Gentiles <note>The "Teacher of the Gentiles" is a traditional title for St. Paul.</note>—became [merely] zealots of the Law, they were deprived of the virtues and signs that the Apostles were working among them. Thus, confused and ashamed, they were compelled, even against their will, to acknowledge their own foulness, and to see what kind of "fruit" came from the tree to which they studied to adhere so strongly, while they persecuted those who were zealots of grace and excluded them from their borders. <margin>1 Kings 3</margin> <note>The author cites the story of Eli from the book of Kings/Samuel.</note> This was also well-signified in Eli of Shiloh, who could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished; for surely that people, once illuminated and now blind, first realized they were stripped of grace only when they lost that which they had neglected to venerate while they had it. And would that even now, in their confusion, they would depart from that tree, so that after their fall they might shrink from the deadly wood! But they have added evil upon 

<column-break/>

evil, hiding themselves in the tree, from which it was not only forbidden for them to eat, but even to touch; departing from the sight of the Most High so that they might not find the place of mercy. For they did not know the gift of confession and the grace of penance; therefore they perished. Finally, they despaired and were swallowed up; they took on the "brow of a harlot" and refused to be converted. 

This is what usually happens to the incestuous and to adulterers: fearing that they might come to public notice, they wish they had not committed the crime, yet they do not cease to repeat the very thing they condemn in themselves; for while sin dominates them, they find it more pleasing to lie down than to rise up, and they cannot abstain. As if "at the breeze after midday," they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise <note>original: "ad auram post meridiem"; a literal translation of the Vulgate Genesis 3:8, often interpreted as a time of judgment.</note> after they were deprived of the gift of grace. This happened when Paul himself—whom they had despaired of, and through whose mouth Christ had spoken to them without his own name, as if in passing—wrote to them. And indeed, he was "passing" to the Gentiles and withdrawing from them, most miserably writing to them of their own ruin and turning away, saying: **For whereas for the time you ought to be masters, you have need to be taught again what are the first elements of the words of God: and you are become such as have need of milk, and not of solid food.** <margin>Hebrews 5</margin> 

And after a few words: **It is impossible for those who were once illuminated, have tasted also the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, have moreover tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, and are fallen away: to be renewed again to penance, crucifying again to themselves the Son of God, and making him a mockery.** <margin>Genesis 3</margin> <note>This is a direct quote from Hebrews 6:4-6.</note> For they were accustomed to making **loincloths** <note>original: "pizomata"; from the Greek 'perizomata', referring to the fig-leaf aprons of Adam and Eve.</note> from fig leaves for themselves, hiding themselves in that same tree—which the Jews do not cease to do even to this day. Whenever any Christian reproaches them for their carnalities, they "sew together"—I say, even to the present—the words of the prophets and the Law; they cloak themselves under the word of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, saying that it is not permitted for them to leave the ceremonies of their fathers or to depart from the Law which the Lord commanded to Moses. But as for the fact that Almighty God is described as walking "at the breeze after midday," this seems to express the cause of their fault, by which...

<margin>John 13</margin>
...the favor of grace turns in time and the midday of justice declines toward the sunset. Or certainly, the only-begotten Son of God who says: *He who receives whomever I send receives me* <note>original: "Qui recipit si quem misero me recipit"</note>, is said to walk in the breezes after midday—that is, between the sixth and ninth hour. This is the time in which he sustained the burning of the sun for our sins. For while a man is raised up through the swelling of pride against Almighty God, it is as if the mildness of the world is dissipated by the heat of concupiscence <note>The "heat of concupiscence" refers to intense worldly or sinful desires that overwhelm spiritual peace.</note>. And as if finding no shade of a tree—that is, a righteous man—under which he might lay his head, the preacher who is sent by the Lord is greatly afflicted. Through this, meditating in his heart, he walks here and there, returning to the mildness of divine consolation. And what 
<margin>Luke 10</margin>

<margin>1 Kings 19</margin>
people of whom Adam bears the type <note>In medieval exegesis, "type" means a person or event that foreshadows or represents another; here, Adam represents the Jewish people who rejected Christ.</note>. Hence it is that Elijah rested under the shade of a juniper tree, fleeing from the face of Jezebel, with whom 
<margin>Genesis 18</margin>
he found no rest. Hence Abraham, when the angels came to him in the heat of the day, humbly and suppliantly prayed that they might turn aside to him, and reverently invited them to rest under the tree. Therefore, this man [Abraham], who designates the Gentiles, invited the angels to rest under the tree—and in the angels, God himself—whom Adam, who designates the Jewish people, neglected to invite. Rightly, then, after midday—that is, in the heat of the day—the Lord is said to walk in paradise in the afternoon breeze. For while the proud man does not receive the words of him whom [the Lord] himself sends, the preacher returns to the divine consolation which is in the love of God and the Church, so that the heat of his soul, which the sterility of the listener brought forth, might be extinguished by the mildness of the Holy Spirit, who knows the hearts of men. Because truly, neither does that following true love rest, nor can he who is often wounded soften from the rigor of his heat; he seeks at least to show the ruin to the wretched one, who, unwilling to yield to him, lost the peak of happiness. The Lord speaks

For that people could not fail to recognize their own nakedness, stripped and distanced from grace, remembering the many works which the Holy Spirit had performed among them—so much so that even those who did not wish to receive sacred baptism confessed and said: *What shall we do to these men? For indeed a known sign has been made through them 
<margin>Acts 4</margin>
and we cannot deny it.* When, therefore—the dew in which Gideon's fleece had been commanded <note>Referring to the miracle of the fleece in Judges 6, often used to symbolize grace falling on the faithful.</note> failing in them in spirit—they could not fail to recognize their loss; but they were unwilling to acknowledge this alone: that on account of the death-bearing eating of the Law, they were irrecoverably deprived of the fruit of grace, which is the tree of life. And rightly the Lord is described not as standing but walking, because among the just to whom he comes, he makes a dwelling through mercy, but from the delinquents [he departs] through judgment; and if he approaches, he recedes. He approaches them so that he may reveal the guilt of their offense; but he passes away from them so that it may become known what the merit of the fault is. For if, as before when they had not sinned, they felt him present and pleasing to them, they would either pretend they had not sinned at all, or think they had sinned venially <note>that is, committed only a minor, forgivable sin</note>, and through this believe it was permitted for them to transgress, since they would not feel the punishment for their crimes. Therefore Adam and Eve were expelled from the paradise of pleasure. The unhappy Jews were expelled from the Church of the saints and led to the lake of misery and the filth of dregs <note>original: "lutum fecis," meaning the sludge or residue at the bottom of a container; a metaphor for spiritual degradation.</note>, so that at least in this way they might learn not to blaspheme. *Behold,* he says,

<margin>Isaiah 6</margin>

What does it mean for Christ to say "as one of us," except that he willed to be one of the mortals so that he might be one of the "created gods" <note>In medieval theology, "gods" often refers to the saints or the righteous who are transformed by God's grace, a concept known as theosis or deification.</note>, he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is the creator of all gods? Who, then, are these gods of whom Christ became one, if not the prophets, the apostles, and all the saints of whom he is the firstborn? How is he the firstborn? Except that he is the *firstborn of the dead*. And of which "dead"? Except those of whom it is said in the psalm: *I said, you are gods and all sons of the Most High*? <margin>Psalm 48</margin> <margin>Psalm 81</margin> We know that to holy men, and especially to the doctors of the churches, the gifts of the Spirit were brought for use: from these, some were made teachers by the grace of knowing and discerning between good and evil, and discussing the difference between the letter and the spirit, between the Law and Grace. Because of this, they read the Law of Moses most frequently—yet this is not profitable for those who think "carnally" <note>"Carnally" (carnaliter) refers to a literal or worldly interpretation of the Bible, as opposed to a spiritual or symbolic one.</note>, who follow only the surface of the letter and the historical meaning. These people, being ignorant of God's gift, think they can reach the fullness of knowledge by human study; whereas knowledge is rather granted by God to those who strengthen their hearts by grace, who desire to please God through faith more than they desire to know the letter of the Law. Therefore, for those who use the words of the Law in such a way that they transfer them to a carnal understanding, it is better for them to unlearn rather than learn the Law; it is better for them to be ignorant of something than to be like "gods knowing good and evil." And because that proud people <note>Referring to the Israelites who rejected the Gospel.</note> sinned by turning aside—preferring the knowledge and observation of the Law over Grace—they deservedly were stripped of Grace, and it is said of them through a rebuke: *Behold, Adam has become like one of us:* <margin>Genesis 3</margin>

For he who trusts that he can enter the kingdom of humility by knowing "high things" is actually distanced from it; he runs into darkness in the very place where he suspects the path of light to be. Thus, as a type <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic precursor to something in the New Testament.</note> of this, it was said to Thomas, who was for a time unbelieving, through a rebuke: *Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.* <margin>John 20</margin> Do you seek proof? The very hardness of the Jews is a witness. But when they are converted to God, he will take away the veil.* <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> Surely you have heard what the Apostle says about faith? *When they are converted to God,* he says, *he will take away the veil.* Why? Because he who does not believe does not understand, and he who is hard of heart toward believing is made even harder toward understanding. If you ask what that voice means when it says, *Behold, Adam has become like one of us* and so forth: it means nothing else than what was written by the Apostle: that a man is surely saved through faith, and through faith he arrives at the knowledge of the scriptures; but he is deprived of the gift of grace who strives to arrive at faith through the Law. For it happens sometimes—not without the fear of the Lord—that someone might reach an understanding of the faith through much labor and the study of reading; but because he offended God through unbelief and pride (so that he did not believe when he was ignorant), he is not worthy to believe when he is led to understanding. They are therefore deprived of the fruit of the Tree of Life who gloried in the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil. For he who relies on knowledge more than grace, even if he is allowed to know many things, is nevertheless deprived of participation in the gift of grace. But because it was of great value then... to remain easily in righteousness: the Word of God is for the faithful in general indeed all: but specifically for those to whom false apostles came, seeking to turn them away from the faith which is in the spirit and the freedom of grace: as often happened in Asia in the time of the Apostles: and he exhorts them to persevere in the gift of grace when he says: *To the one who conquers, I will give to eat of the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God.* <note>original: "Vincenti dabo edere de ligno vite quod est in paradiso dei mei." - Revelation 2:7.</note> For it is as if it were said: Those who glory in the Law of Moses—which is not the power of faith, but an occasion for sin, a sterile and unproductive knowledge of good and evil alone—will remain empty; but those who are solidified in the root of faith will cling to me, so that, fed by the tree of life, they may live and rejoice forever. ### Here begins the section on the angel of Smyrna.

<margin>2:10</margin> **A**nd to the angel of the church of Smyrna write: These things says the First and the Last, who was dead and is alive.

<column-break/>

Through each individual species of this book and special "stations"—if I may call them that—one must pause for a little while and apply the memory, lest anything be brought forth carelessly in a specific case that might seem to disagree with the general rule already so often proposed. It had to be said at the beginning of the book: and lest it perhaps slip from the eyes of the mind, it must be repeated again and again: that there are seven special times prefigured in this sacred volume; likewise seven "orders" <note>Medieval theologians often categorized the history of the Church into different groups or "orders," such as the Apostles, Martyrs, and Monks.</note> of which we have begun to treat in the present, pertaining to the spirit; and five others pertaining to the body. Because there cannot be concord where there is no union or unity, these orders fit together in a wonderful way, so that when some rejoice, others rejoice with them; and when some suffer, others suffer with them. The first of the five orders was that of the Apostles; the second was of the Martyrs, because the first had a special conflict against the Jews for the "spirit" against the "letter." The second was against the pagans, for the word of the cross against the worship of idols: though both groups fought against both for both causes. Just as the first order, leading a life of renunciation and being entirely free from the cares of the world, could not help but share in the temptations of the Apostles which they suffered for the spirit and grace against the letter and circumcision; so also the second order could not be exempt from the labors of the martyrs. For although it is a light thing <note>The author uses "lightness" (leuitas) here ironically or comparatively to describe the monk's life of silence vs. the martyr's physical death.</note> to evangelize Jesus and follow the footsteps of his passions, or for monks to devote themselves to silence and prayer, they themselves could not be exempt from sorrow, since they too would drink the cup of Christ; which indeed they cried out indefinitely, if rarely by voices, then certainly by their character and habit. They were often seized and led along with the preachers to trial: so that the "part of John" <note>John here represents the contemplative or monastic life, while Peter represents the active or apostolic life.</note> might aptly seem to have drawn something from Peter; because of which it was said to him and his brother by the Prince of Martyrs: *You shall indeed drink*

<margin>Matthew 20</margin> *of my cup.* For it was not as Peter and Andrew, who, having taken up their cross, followed the Lord; so on the contrary James and John, who were called "Sons of Thunder," both slept in peace together, but one of them fell by the sword, while the other, having completed his course, groaned at a peaceful end. Why is this? Because since the contemplative life is proper to the angels,

<meta>This page continues the allegorical exposition of the Book of Revelation, specifically focusing on the message to the Church in Smyrna. The author uses the names of the Apostles and the etymology of "Smyrna" to explain the necessity of suffering and the certainty of the resurrection.</meta>

### Part of the Exposition

Just as the active works of the sons of men are categorized, so this cannot be ascribed to any one holy order in the same way that the **active life** is ascribed to some: because the former must be understood according to the whole, while the latter according to a part. For it was not given to that order which is designated by **Peter and Andrew** <note>In medieval exegesis, Peter and Andrew often represent the "active life" of labor and struggle.</note> to strive perfectly in the agony of contest in the same way as it was given to those designated by **James and John** to live entirely without struggle. For each is a man; each is mortal. But it was given to the one who is stronger for the fight to patiently bear the burden and heat of the day; to the one who is more delicate, it was given to rest, at least in part. Because of this, even if the latter suffers less than the former, it was still granted to him to undergo the **Passion**. For what is it to "drink the cup" <note>A reference to Matthew 20:22, where Jesus asks James and John if they can drink the cup of his suffering.</note> if not to feel the bitterness of the Passion? To this bitterness, the name of the city is well-suited: which in Greek is called **Smyrna**, but in Latin is interpreted as **myrrh** <note>original: "myrrha"</note>; for since myrrh is bitter, it protects the flesh from rot, just as the bitterness of suffering extinguishes fleshly desires. **"These things,"** he says, **"says the First and the Last, who was dead and lives."** <note>Revelation 2:8.</note> For whom was it more fitting to set an example for those about to die than He who was dead for a time and lives forever? Or what else is the very strength of all patience but to arrive at the joys of true life through death? **"These things,"** he says, **"says the First and the Last, who was dead and lives."** About to say "who was dead and lives," he first stated: **"These things says the First and the Last."** For if He himself is the First and He himself is the Last, undoubtedly because He both lived before death and lives after death, it follows that those who first live in Him and die with Him shall rise again from the dead and live without end with Him. For He who was able—by the power of His eternity by which He always was—to create the first man from the mud of the earth <margin>Gen. 2</margin> and breathe into his face the breath of life, is also able to rouse the bodies of the sons of **Adam** from the dust and restore to them on the last day the souls they received. For it is not that He who could create the earth from nothing could not create the first man except from the earth; rather, He did so that mortals might believe it possible at the end of time, since they do not doubt the Almighty was able to do it at the beginning.

<column-break/>

For if He willed and was able to form the body of Adam, who was the father of all, from the mud of the earth, why should He not be able in the same way to reform the bodies of the children of Adam from the earth? You were once the dust of the earth and you began to exist, though you were not. Indeed, in Adam, we were all dust from the beginning; and can God not restore that which has returned to dust into its first form, so that you begin to exist as you once were? Or is it because the **Word of God** was present then, through whom these things were made, but now He has ceased to exist so that He no longer performs similar works? **O foolish hearts of men and slow to believe** <note>A reference to Jesus’s rebuke to the disciples on the road to Emmaus in Luke 24:25.</note> in all that the prophets have spoken. Was it not necessary for the human race to suffer these things on account of the evil of pride, and thus through the death of the flesh to reach eternal life? For the Almighty willed to exercise this judgment upon the human race, not to destroy His work, but to show it the height of His greatness and to instill the fear of discipline; so that man would not think of high things, knowing that He who was powerful enough to form him was not powerless to reform him—not only to restore what was dissolved, but even in restoring it, to change it for the better. For He is the **First** and He is the **Last**. He is the First to give life to the human race, and again at death; He is the Last to provide life to those coming from death. The First to form **natural bodies** <note>original: "corpora animalia" - literally "soul-animated bodies" or physical, mortal bodies.</note>, the Last to reform and change those same bodies so that they begin to be **spiritual**. <margin>1. Cor. 15</margin> For He will change them—not all of them, but those He wills. **For we shall all rise again** <margin>1. Cor. 15</margin> **but we shall not all be changed.** Therefore, we must not only hope that the Last will return to us what the First had given, but also that He will make glorious what was previously <margin>1. Cor. 15</margin> ignoble, as the Apostle bears witness, saying: *It is sown a natural body, it shall rise a spiritual body.* If this is so, we should not only flee from death, but hasten toward it by all means, so that through temporal death we may come to life, and through temptations to glory. ->Joa. Prima In Apo.<-
3 4
<meta>catchword: council [original: cilium]</meta>

...such an exchange could [hardly] be earned, so that it would seem entirely uncertain to all mortals, if he whom the Jews killed were not already living in heaven; he of whom the Holy Spirit speaks in this place and says: *These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives.* <note>original: "Hec dicit primus & nouissimus qui fuit mortuus & viuit" — Revelation 2:8</note> For it cannot seem harsh that we are commanded to despise death, and it would be much more and beyond our strength if the promise of rising again, to be hoped for by all mortals, did not follow. Therefore, he who claims he was dead subsequently adds that he is alive, so that the hope of life might lift up and strengthen those whom the fear of death might crush by terrifying them; so that while the reward of the battle was at hand for the combatants, they might undergo the burden of the fight secure and undaunted. 

For if a temporary hope of safety makes some people more steadfast in enduring tortures, how much more does the hope of eternal life strengthen the minds of God’s chosen ones, so that they might despise whatever can be pleasurable in the moment of this life and count as nothing everything that is bitter? Yet many, though they know they must die, say they are willing to be beheaded for the name of Christ, but nevertheless blush with shame when they are helped to suffer something sad—as if the sufferings of this time could be worthy compared to the future glory that will be revealed in us <margin>Romans 8</margin>, or as if it were a great thing to pass from pleasure to pleasure, and not rather to pass through fire and water and so arrive at a place of refuge. For the Lord does not say: "He who wishes to follow me, let him take up his cross for one day," but *let him take up his cross daily and follow me.* <margin>Luke 9</margin> Nor does the apostle say that one must enter the kingdom of God through only one tribulation, but through many; <margin>2 Timothy 2:11</margin> nor that anyone is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules. Hence it is added:

¶ **I know your tribulation and your poverty; but you are rich.**

¶ "Tribulation" refers to the pressure [of persecution], and "poverty" to temporal hunger. In both, the holy martyrs sustained losses; in both, a struggle. For just now they endured chains and prisons and various torments in their bodies, but they were also stripped of the wages of their goods which they seemed to possess for daily use in time. This was so that, as if hemmed in on all sides, they might fail in their torments; and while no comfort seemed to remain for them, they might obey sacrilegious orders. It was necessary, therefore, for them to know that their temporal goods had not been taken away from them, but carried away to the mansions of heavenly treasures, so that they might receive security from true and eternal riches in proportion to how they despised temporal and worldly wealth for the sake of Christ and the Gospel. He says, **I know your tribulation and your poverty; but you are rich.** 

If rich, how poor? If poor, how rich? But he says, *they have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands.* <margin>Psalm 75 [76:5]</margin> *The rich have lacked and suffered hunger.* <margin>Psalm 33 [34:10]</margin> But it is not so for the poor of Christ who have left all for the Lord; not so. For he says: *everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.* <margin>Matthew 19</margin> But where is this? Is it on earth where Christ wished to be poor? Certainly, even if a proportional retribution follows in this life—since we see some people, constrained more by the necessity of penury rather than by will, flee to the community of the righteous so that they might abound in temporal goods which they lacked in their own homes—nevertheless, retribution is not to be expected in this life, nor should we rejoice in such a turnaround, but rather in those eternal riches which are in heaven. To these the apostle teaches that we ought to sigh when he says: *If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God; mind the things that are above, not the things upon the earth.* <margin>Colossians 3</margin> But perhaps those heavenly riches are earned by poverty alone, and not also by the blasphemies and curses with which the apostles rejoiced to be affected when they went away glad from the coun-

the perfect ones, renouncing the world, are delivered into the power of Satan so that he might test them according to his will, interrogating them through punishments and torments. For if none of them were to clash with the Devil, the author of deceit would have an occasion to reproach them regarding their holy leisure <note>original: "sancto otto suo"; likely meaning their state of peaceful devotion</note>, as if they had not dared to do battle with him. And if no one escaped his hand, he would ascribe this to the power of his own strength, as if he were so powerful in malice that no one could pass by his face immune. It is well said that the power given to the Devil is restricted to "ten days," because twelve generations of years passed from Christ until Julian the Apostate <note>Julian (reigned 361–363 AD) was the last polytheistic Roman emperor, known as "the Apostate" for rejecting Christianity.</note>. Two of these had already passed when this book was written, but ten—or nearly ten—followed afterward. <margin>Matthew 10</margin>

It means nothing else than that those who conquer for God through the triumph of a precious death arrive at true life. That very life becomes for them a crown of glory; in order to preserve it in the kingdom, they lost it while in exile <note>Life on earth is often described in medieval theology as an "exile" from our true home in heaven.</note>. <margin>Text 17</margin>

<column-break/>

What is the second death? It is that by which the soul is tortured after the death of the flesh, and through which body and soul are lost eternally in Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. Do not fear those who kill the body, says the Lord, but are not able to kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. For it is good to undergo the first death with the triumph of victory rather than to escape it—even if one wishes to, it is not permitted—so that the second death may be avoided. If one wishes, that is possible. It is better to avoid the second death than to avoid the first death for an hour—which cannot be avoided anyway—only to be harmed by the second death, which anyone can avoid if they wish. It is good, I say, to despise what is brief and transitory in this present life, and to endure this light and momentary tribulation, rather than to be harmed by the second death. As it is written below, the second death is the lake of fire <note>original: "stagnus ignis"</note> into which all the impious are to be plunged, along with those who are not found written in the book of life.
