Just as the branches recognize their root and the streams recognize their source through a prick <note>original: "punctionem," suggesting the sharp "pricking" of the conscience or the "piercing" of the Word</note>, so each person may reach perfection by the grace distributed to them, provided they watchfully attend to the source from which it remains for them. We often see the heads of households and those to whom the management of domestic affairs is entrusted arranging different things for different people. Regarding things that pertain to individuals, they deal with each of them separately and, as it were, individually. So also those who take up the rudders of kingdoms, when they wish to please diverse people, strive to become "all things to all men" as much as possible, and to be with individuals as they themselves are. For they do not dispute with soldiers about the institutes of laws, nor with philosophers about military skill, but separately with these and those about their own matters. # Joa. Prima In Apo.
### Page 70

...the Spirit of the Lord in the form of a dove; or when the same Lord breathed into the faces of the apostles and said to them: "Receive the Holy Spirit"; or when, on the day of Pentecost, it suddenly came from heaven <margin>Acts 2</margin> like a rushing, violent wind, and there appeared to the apostles divided tongues like fire, and it sat upon each of them. This was so that each of the faithful might understand that they are cleansed in the name of the Holy Trinity, and that no one can come to perfect cleansing who does not believe that grace is given to them not by the Father alone, but rather by the entire Trinity together. Because when grace increases for a second time, a person still has <margin>Job 9</margin> that which needs purging, even if they have already been partially cleansed. It is rightly said through the holy man: "He himself consumes <note>original: "presumit"; in the context of the Vulgate Job 9:22, this suggests taking away or destroying</note> both the just and the wicked." This does not refer to the one who is already perfectly cleansed—<margin>James 3</margin> which rarely or never happens to anyone in this life—especially since Saint James says: "In many things we all offend." Rather, it refers to the one who is just in such a way that there remains in him something to be further justified, so that the just man may become even more just. The just man is not consumed in that part where he is just, but in that part where he is less just; though this may be understood in other ways, it carries the same meaning. There are many men—which should not be said without a groan—who are so subjected to impiety that their desire for pleasure serves as their law. As the Scripture says, "they rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things." Against such people, the faithful teacher must have an unsheathed sword and strike those of this kind with direct blows, so that those who do not perceive their own impieties by themselves may at least weigh them when compelled; or certainly, that the word of God may stand as a testimony against them, so that the truth of God may abound in this very thing, and they may have no excuse for their sins. There are also some who vigilantly guard themselves against evil works as much as they can, seeking to reach the heights of perfection as far as human frailty allows. But when they see men entangled in many crimes, they are lifted up with pride, like that Pharisee of whom we read boasting in the Gospel. Unless they are helped by Him who is able, they lose whatever perfection they thought they possessed. Because of the innate changeability of this kind of nature, it is difficult

<column-break/>

for a doer of good to lack the evil of boasting. Through this, if he becomes insolent, he falls into the crime of confusion—unless he is restrained from the impulse of pride by either sharp words or by scourges <note>original: "flagella"; referring to divine discipline or trials</note>, while preserving the authority of God, for whom all things are possible. For who would dare to say: "Why does God take the just man to task by scourging him?" Is not the Lord rather "just in all his ways and holy in all his works"? <margin>Psalm 144</margin> Finally, it is for this reason that the skilled physician uses the iron of the incision in two ways: for sometimes he cuts away rotten flesh to provide a remedy, and at other times, when signs of future corruption break out even in healthy flesh, he opens a vein to reduce the blood; or certainly, he cuts those laboring from the <term>disease of the stone<note>original: "morbo calculi"; likely referring to bladder or kidney stones, a common and painful ailment in the Middle Ages.</note></term> near the thigh, even when there is no rot in the flesh, lest perhaps a terminal illness follows him and he be seized by the sleep of death. Therefore, because God consumes both the just and the impious by scourging both, he is not undeservedly said to have a sword sharp on both sides. In another place, this is called the "flaming and turning sword." It is meant to strike from every side everyone who takes up the office of preaching. ¶ For what is meant by the <term>Cherubim<note>original: "Cherubin"; often interpreted in medieval theology as "fullness of knowledge."</note></term>, which is interpreted as the "fullness of knowledge," if not the teachers of the Church? And what is meant by the flaming and turning sword, if not the sword of the spirit, which is the Word of God? This sword is placed in the hand of the teacher so that no one may enter the interior paradise unless through him, and so that they may be allowed to taste of the tree of life, which is the fruit of the spirit and the grace of Jesus Christ—unless perhaps someone is among those designated by the Cherubim. If an earthly man is not permitted to enter without him, what do we call the teacher of the Church but the gatekeeper of paradise? And what is the Word of God but the gate through which, if anyone enters, he is saved and finds the pastures of eternal life? The Word is rightly compared to a turning sword and, as it were, to a round shape, because it mangles the sinner from every side; it devours and consumes from every side. For nothing is left untouched by it in which a sinful man might be permitted to live carnally or mortally, while the Word stands continually free to cut down all types of vices and is ready to slay all crimes. This, therefore, is the flaming and turning sword; this is the Word itself.

# Abb. Part of the Exposition
### Page 70

A two-edged sword <note>original: "romphea," a large, ancient sword</note> sharp on both sides, cutting down sterile trees on one side, and on the other, more bitingly, those that bring forth bad fruit. This is the rule which a teacher <note>original: "doctor"</note> of the church must use on the right and on the left, so that in both directions he may appear to be a true imitator of the judgment of the True Master. For this reason, the Lord began to speak of Himself to the angel <note>In Revelation, "angels" of the churches are often interpreted as their bishops or leaders.</note> of Pergamum in this way: so that they might strive to present themselves as such teachers of the church as they know their Master to be. Thus, they should not only rebuke those who are "mute dogs" <note>original: "canes muti," a reference to Isaiah 56:10, describing leaders who fail to warn their people</note> unable to bark, but they should also much more harshly reprove those who, among the Catholic <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox Christian faith.</note> words they speak, put forward things that are false and unworthy. For on one hand, this order is rebuked for being negligent, while on the other, it is commended when it is said:

<margin>Isaiah 56</margin>
<margin>Revelation 2</margin>
"I know where you dwell, where the throne of Satan is; and you hold fast to my name, and you did not deny my faith."

However, that he has been negligent in another area is shown when he adds: "But I have a few things against you: because you have there those who hold the doctrine of Balaam <note>A biblical figure who led the Israelites into sin through deception.</note>, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication." It is written of the Devil in the book of Job: "He beholds every high thing, and he is king over all the children of pride." For in this matter, it must be carefully considered that just as the choir of the humble is the throne of Christ, so the assembly of the proud is called the throne of the Devil. Because, according to the voice of Paul, "knowledge by itself does not build up, but puffs up," and Satan himself—the rival of knowledge—is called the "outstretched and protecting Cherub" in the prophet; who are those who are more properly called the "throne of Satan," if not those who aspire to the vanity of the teaching office without the gift of grace? These are they who, according to the voice of the Lord, love "greetings in the marketplace" and seek "to be called Rabbi by men." While they do not wish to be seen as disciples, they become teachers of error. Such was that Scribe who asked the Lord, saying: "Master, I will follow you wherever you go," who also immediately heard the sentence of truth according to what was necessary for him: "Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of

<margin>Job 41</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 8</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 28</margin>
<margin>Matthew 23</margin>
<margin>Matthew 8</margin>
<margin>Luke 9</margin>

man has nowhere to lay his head." For truly, proud minds are the nests of demons—namely, the throne of Satan and his attendants—just as the hearts of the carnal are the holes of foxes. This refers to other impure spirits who, being of a more serious <note>or "heavier"</note> nature compared to others, are known to burden the hearts of carnal men, so much so that many of them are said to be driven to extremes even by physical agitation. How this can happen by the just (but hidden) judgment of God is uncertain, except that through the power of God, one believes it can happen to those whom He permits to be handed over to demons because of their sins. We read that even good angels, having taken on bodies, have not only appeared to men but even helped them in their presence. There is a distinction among the impure spirits: some are designated by foxes, others by birds. It is the nature of the former to rest in the darkness of the lustful, and the latter to boast boastfully and vainly among the proud. In this matter, we might wonder with what severity of judgment it was done that a just and pious God permitted some priests of the church—who strove to follow, prefer, and assert the truth—to nevertheless wander so enormously astray. But the cause of judgment is certain: as with that Scribe of whom we speak, who seemed to want to follow the Lord, but was rejected by the same just Lord—who says, "Him who comes to me I will not cast out"—by a just judgment. This was because he wanted to follow not as a disciple, but as one who was swollen with pride, wordy, arrogant, and puffed up, not knowing what is written: "He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house; he who speaks wicked things did not direct his path in the sight of my eyes." Such are those Scribes established within the Holy Church who, puffed up by the vanity of the age and the knowledge of the world, arrogantly usurp for themselves the teaching office of a wicked dogma. Their proud minds are the nests of birds and the thrones of malignant spirits, "wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight." Among their number were Arius, Eunomius, and Macedonius <note>Arius, Eunomius, and Macedonius were early Christian leaders whose teachings on the Trinity were condemned as heretical by the Church councils.</note> and their followers, who, not knowing the King of the humble, became the throne of Satan, and being ignorant of the Author of Light, [continued...]

# John's First [Book] on the Apocalypse
### Page 71

They clung to the prince of darkness: in whose time there were distinguished teachers: Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and many other orthodox [fathers] keeping the communion of the faith unshaken; to whom, in the person of the angel of Pergamum, that which was written above is addressed. For their commendation and praise, it was said by the Prince of Teachers: "I know where you dwell, where the seat of Satan is, and you hold fast to my name, and you have not denied my faith." It follows:

<margin>Chapter 2</margin>
And in those days Antipas, my faithful witness, who was killed among you where Satan dwells.

This martyr Antipas is believed to be a certain person who completed his course <note>original: "peregerit cursum suum," an idiom for finishing one's life or mission, often used of martyrs</note> at the city of Pergamum, or near the city; of whom, even if we read nothing certain according to the letter <note>original: "ad litteram," meaning a literal historical account</note>, nevertheless in him those martyrs are signified who were killed by Arian tyrants for the Catholic <note>original: "fide catholica," meaning the universal, orthodox faith held by the early Church</note> faith, and were afflicted with various kinds of punishments for the glory of the indivisible Trinity. This, however, is in a marvelous way reflected back to the praise of the teachers, who were able to hold the name of Christ in the day of such a great struggle, not terrified by the threats of judges, nor by the threat of being driven to punishments, choosing [this] rather than to allow the name of their Redeemer to be annulled. Whence also "Pergamum"—which in our language is interpreted as "dividing their horns" <note>This is a medieval interpretive etymology, likely attempting to link the name of the city to the Greek or Latin roots for 'dividing' and 'horns' to fit the allegorical theme of defeating heretics.</note>—was well-named, so that the great prudence of the teachers of Christ in dividing the horns of the heretics might be made known through the name of the city: not so much that they themselves might escape punishments, but that the faith of Almighty God might remain unhurt. For to omit other things, which would be long to recall to memory, the Arian heresy had produced as it were three discordant horns; by whose dissension it came about that the teachers of Christ could [prevail] against those dividing the churches of the malignant and frustrating the council of vanity. For Macedonius was not in agreement with Eunomius in all things, nor did they themselves feel the same as Arius; who nevertheless, so that they too might err and establish their own heresies as principal ones, took their occasion from Arius. These were therefore three horns of one beast, but yet unlike and disagreeing with one another. However, just as in the time of the Jews the Pharisees

<column-break/>

and Sadducees were enemies to each other, yet they are read to have breathed together in persecuting Christ; so also these [heretics] did not cling to each other, but yet for the subverting of the orthodox faith, they offered each other a plan and the help of deceit. But just as Paul, that distinguished teacher, wisely dividing the horns of those same Pharisees and Sadducees, escaped through the split <note>A reference to Acts 23:6-10, where Paul cleverly set the Pharisees and Sadducees against each other to avoid condemnation</note>; so also these [teachers], although there the sign was given, here the cause of the sign is completed: for in such a way Paul divided the horns of the Pharisees and Sadducees that I might specifically say it should be understood that we place the Arians on one side and the Sabellian heretics on the other. The former [Sabellians] stubbornly attempted to keep a certain unity which they had fashioned for themselves from their own hearts, denying the persons of the Trinity in the Godhead; the others [Arians] denied that the Word of God and the Holy Spirit are one God with the Father, though they did not deny that they were something great and above the common race of men or the nature of angels. Finally, the Sadducees reject the prophets, deny the resurrection, and disavow the angel and the spirit. The Pharisees, on the contrary, read the prophets, but they do not concede that the great prophet whom the Lord promised through Moses is the King of Glory. They also proclaim with a living voice that there are celestial spirits, but the Spirit of Almighty God, of whom there is frequent mention in the divine page, they do not acknowledge to be God and Lord. They preach that their dead must rise again; but yet the witnesses of truth, who say that the Author of Life has risen from the dead, they vehemently attack as if they had spoken falsely. Therefore, the Sadducees preached as it were one person, who by not receiving the prophet or the spirit, denied the Son of God and the Holy Spirit—into whose detestable treachery the Sabellian heretics fell—and the Pharisees announced as it were three divided and unequal persons, who indeed felt about the prophets and spirits according to the universal <note>original: "catholice," here meaning "generally" or "traditionally"</note> view, but yet denied that he who is truly the Prophet, or the Holy Spirit, is equal to God, as if foreshadowing the Arians. Therefore, the Catholic teachers divided as it were two horns, when walking between Arius and Sabellius, [avoiding] the danger of Scylla on one side and Charybdis on the other... <note>Scylla and Charybdis are mythical sea monsters representing two equally dangerous options; here, the author uses them to represent the two opposite heresies of Arianism and Sabellianism.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the commendation of the Church of Pergamum and its teachers for resisting heresy. It allegorizes the city's name to describe how Church Fathers like Augustine and Jerome "divided the horns" of discordant heretical groups, comparing Arians and Sabellians to the Pharisees and Sadducees of the New Testament.</summary>

# Exposition of the Part
### Page 71

...they are known to have avoided the pit <note>original: "baratrum," often used to describe a hellish abyss or a fatal error</note> of heresy: holding against Sabellius, but not as Sabellius did, who claimed the Godhead was only one person; and against Arius, but not as Arius did, who claimed the Trinity was three separate ranks. They avoided Sabellius, who denies the distinct Persons, and Arius, who preaches divisions and inequality within the Trinity. But because not everyone who feeds sheep is a shepherd of sheep, nor is every tiller of a vineyard its owner, a harsh rebuke follows, both for those and against those who are mere hirelings—either because they correct the wicked less than they ought, or because they themselves are of such a character that they deserve to be rebuked more harshly. For it is added:

<margin>Revelation 2:14-15</margin>
¶ "But I have a few things against you, because you have there those holding the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed to idols and to commit fornication; so you also have those holding the doctrine of the Nicolaitans."

¶ There are two types of error that frequently trouble the Church: one in the doctrine of faith, the other in the preservation of morals. Of these, holy men tolerate the one against the faith for no necessary reason, because it is not fitting; the other they often endure and often carry, and if only their patience did not exceed a just measure. And regarding those who have fallen away from the faith and are alienated from the body of the Church, there is nothing for which the Catholic teachers can be blamed, if after a first and second admonition they are able to return to the bosom of the mother Church from which they fell; but they refuse, and put off from day to day being converted to the truth of the faith, because it is written: 

<margin>Psalm 57</margin>
"Their rage is according to the likeness of a serpent, like the deaf asp that stops its ears." <note>This refers to Psalm 58:4 in modern Bibles; the author compares stubborn heretics to a snake that refuses to listen to the charmer.</note> And 

<margin>Titus 3</margin>
the Apostle says: "Avoid a heretical man after a first and second correction, knowing that he who is of this sort is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment." Therefore, the angel of Pergamum is not rebuked concerning such heretics as these for having some in his church who hold the 

<margin>Titus 1</margin>
doctrine of Balaam, but rather concerning those who believe rightly, yet attack the right faith with wicked works, according to that which is written: "They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny Him."

<column-break/>

For Balaam, while preaching true and catholic <note>original: "catholica," meaning universal or orthodox truths about God</note> things about God, did not walk rightly before God, for he was corrupted by greed. For he taught Balak, as John writes in this place, to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel: to eat forbidden things and to commit fornication. And why was this? Because Balak compelled him, or rather because greed blinded him. For he knew his own guilt, nor was he able to excuse himself with any cover; and therefore (as if unwilling, yet willing) he was led to teach this crime. In this same way, greedy teachers and those who desire to become rich fall into the snare of the devil: so that the truth which they judge ought to be kept, they abandon, being overcome by greed; and that which (as their conscience bears witness) they said was to be held a little while before, they subvert without delay, oppressed by the weight of desire. Similarly, Nicolas, who was chosen in the number of the ministers <note>This refers to Nicolas, one of the seven deacons appointed in Acts 6:5</note>, is said to have introduced a wicked custom of behavior, exposing (as we have already said) his own wife to those who wished to have relations with her. Although Luke does not record this in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, nor do any of those who are known to have published the canonical scripture at that time; rather, it is established only by the report of ancient tradition from the elders, and perhaps by the occasion of this passage, in which the doctrine of the Nicolaitans is shown to be similar to the doctrine of Balaam. Indeed, one does not read that the Church in its third period had Nicolaitan heretics; especially since the same thing signifies another thing rather than itself, the Nicolaitans are not to be understood in this place as the actual Nicolaitan heretics, but for those who, still remaining in the faith, have dared to teach wicked things: either by magnifying mercy beyond what is expedient and thinning out judgment, or by ignoring and counting both as nothing. It is certain that the carnal hearts of men often invent such things. Holy men fear to uproot the vast multitude of such people, lest worse things happen, and lest perhaps the merciful God might look upon them and release them from the snares of the devil by which they are held captive. For who does not know what wandering and disordered movements a carnal mind brings forth, even if it is learned and sufficiently imbued with the liberal arts? For it seeks to know something for the defense of its faction. It seeks how it might excuse that which it does not wish to lack; and when it cannot find what it desires, it falls into sin either through hope or through despair.

The author argues that while open heresy is easily identified, the "thinning out of judgment" by those within the Church is a more complex danger for its leaders.</summary>

# First Letter of John in the Apocalypse
### Page 72

<margin>Numbers 24</margin>
...so as to teach himself to sin prudently: and weeping in tears, he accuses himself. He said (it says) the man whose eye is stopped up: he said, the hearer of the words of God, who has gazed upon the vision of the Almighty: who falls, and so his eyes are opened. <note>original: "obturatus est oculus... qui visionem omnipotentis intuitus est," a reference to the prophecy of Balaam in Numbers 24:3-4</note> And a little later: He said, the hearer of the words of God, who knows the doctrine of the Most High, and sees the visions of the Almighty, who falling has his eyes open. For it is as if he were saying: I do not stray from the path of rectitude out of ignorance, like most heretics; but knowingly and prudently, I put my hand into the fire. For it is not because I perceive falsely that I desert the truth, but because a wicked will is within me, I willingly leave the path of light. Hence it is that the doctrine of Balaam, which he spoke in the apocalypse, is accepted into the catalog of scriptures, precisely because it is universal and faithful. <note>The author distinguishes between Balaam's true prophecies and his wicked personal advice</note> However, that which is rebuked here was hidden, and is not expressed in manifest words: because those of this sort dogmatize contrary things more secretly than openly, not so much so that they believe what they teach to be true, but so that they may satisfy their own allurements. It follows:

<margin>T. 23</margin>
> "Repent likewise; or else I will come to you quickly and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth." <note>Revelation 2:16</note>

¶ This was said previously regarding what had been told to the angel of Ephesus concerning the word of repentance. But because he does not say "let them repent," but "repent" <note>original: "age," the singular imperative addressed to the 'angel' or bishop</note>, and "or else I will come to you quickly and fight against *them*," he suggests the great mystery of the unity of the Church, and that the virtue of charity is great and singular. For it is asked, not absurdly: What does the groaning of the righteous benefit sinners? And what harm does the perdition of the miserable bring upon the righteous, who neglect the safety of those who are lost? For it is said to him: "Repent," he who holds the likeness of the righteous; yet he threatens judgment against those who sin without him. How the groaning of the righteous may dissolve the crimes of the delinquent is fully witnessed by <term>Moses</term> <note>The OCR reads "Adorph," but the context of interceding for the people indicates Moyses (Moses)</note>, who obtained pardon for the delinquent people as often as he, afflicted and pitying, entreated the Lord for them. That the ruin of the miserable pertains to the harm of the church is shown by the very disfigurement of a mangled body, and the mutual concern of the members, which protect one another by standing in the way. For what did it profit the Jews that a man called from the Gentiles is gathered into the sum of the elect? It would have been better for them if they had remained in the faith, rather than that their fall should become the salvation of the Gentiles.

<column-break/>

What if God converted their fault into the salvation of others? Can they therefore have a just complaint, since the Lord did not compel them to sin, but rather helped them so that they might be saved? Yet Almighty God willed to work the salvation of others from their just death, using evil things well, as He is supremely good—not by necessity, but by will; not because He could not save His elect otherwise, but so that He might show the riches of His glory in the vessels of mercy. <margin>Romans 9</margin> But regarding these things, elsewhere. This, however, is clearly evident: that the losses of the Lord’s flock frequently redound upon the pastors, and the ruin of the children produces grief in the parents, especially if it is by their fault that the children depart from the truth. You ask: what fault? The relaxation of discipline. <note>original: "Remissio disciplinae," referring to a leader's failure to correct subordinates</note> For examples of the ancients are not lacking by which it can be sufficiently proven: both that salvation comes to subjects through the burning of zeal, and danger through the softness of patience. For we read that <term>Phinehas</term> <note>Phinehas (Phinees) was the grandson of Aaron who stopped a plague by executing an Israelite man and Midianite woman for their public sin (Numbers 25)</note> pleased God with zeal, lest the Lord himself consume the delinquents in His fury; and that <term>Eli</term> <note>Eli (Hely) was the High Priest who failed to restrain his wicked sons, leading to his own death and the loss of the Ark (1 Samuel 4)</note> provoked God by his patience, so that he deserved ruin both for himself and for his posterity. Since therefore the pastor is the father and the physician of the people—and he who is a father loves his children, and he who is a pastor loves his sheep—he who loves deserts with pain that which he used to possess with delight. What is it that is said to the pastor, that he should perform penance over the sins of his subjects, except that it is so much more necessary for the pastor who wishes to obtain pardon for a delinquent people to prick himself by afflicting himself, and to impute the fault to himself and his own neglect? For the guilt of a crime is heavier where the people subject to it are not kept in rectitude. For so great (as I have already said) is the virtue of charity, so great is grace, that it can even overcome the sins of others. Every Christian is bound to have this by common mandate, but a pastor is bound by the necessity of the governance he has undertaken; so much so that if he neglects to bestow this, he incurs the loss of the flock committed to him, and does not escape that terrible sentence of the Lord, which says: "But I will require his blood at your hand." <margin>Numbers 25</margin> <margin>Ezekiel 3</margin> No less does that strike terror which is pronounced in the present sentence: "If not, I will come to you quickly and fight against them with the sword of my mouth." If (He says) you do not perform penance, I will come to you quickly and fight against them. When any earthly power is moved in spirit against its subjects and wishes to punish some of them with lashes, the parents of those people are usually moved to anger against them as well, so that this word is frequent in the mouth of those moved by anger: "If I come there, if I go there." But the severity of the strictness remains in this word so much more as the [judgment is] greater...

# Commentary on the Apocalypse
### Part of the Exposition

...it is the man who says this, and it is unbecoming of him: that for any slight cause he should move from the height of his position. "If not," he says, "I will come to you quickly, and I will fight against them with the **sword of my mouth**." <note>original: "gladio oris mei," referencing Revelation 2:16</note> This coming of the Lord is very terrible; it does not display a physical presence, in which Christ is to judge [at the end of time], but an invisible majesty, by which he judges all things as God and renders to each according to their works. For when Christ tolerates a transgressor and does not rebuke him, he demonstrates himself to be, as it were, far away, and seemingly ignorant of the judgment. But when he exercises the severity of judgment upon a sinful people, he is soon said to "come" to the sinner, immediately scrutinizing and judging their deeds, and discussing them as if he were seeing for the first time what is being done. Therefore, it is as if he were saying: "I, who by the long-suffering of my patience show myself to be far from sinners—unless that for which I feign indifference intervenes—will quickly show myself to be present through judgment." And "with the sword of my mouth"—that is, by the word of judgment, with which I judge the sinners of the earth—I will contend with them. When they are presented before me for the sentence of death, they will learn that I was present during their faults, but without the fruit of repentance, because they now feign indifference while there is still time to repent. For this is the meaning of that:

<margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin>
**Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts.** But lest anyone, thinking the day of death is far off, should set a limit for their own repentance, saying: "When I have grown old, I will perform my penance," and "when I am already decrepit, I will be converted with my whole heart," Almighty God willed both the day of a man’s death and the end of the world to be uncertain. Yet, lest one should wickedly flatter oneself in ignorance and perish, how very near it is is demonstrated in another place when it is said: **Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to everyone according to their works.** <note>original: "Ecce venio cito," from Revelation 22:12</note> Wherefore, even here saying "I come," he added "quickly," lest one should think a delay ought to be made in performing penance. It should be noted, however, that the <term>Doctors of the Church</term> <note>The "Doctors" or "Teachers" refer to the authoritative theologians and bishops of the early Church who defined doctrine.</note> are called the "mouth of the Lord" in Scripture, just as his word is a **sword sharpened on both sides**; which sword, indeed, is given to these same teachers to carry out vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples. So that those who, having been

<column-break/>

waited upon for a long time, despise and look down upon the spirit of gentleness, may—when the spirit of zeal is kindled against them—be handed over to Satan by a sentence of judgment. Thus they may learn how grave and illicit it is to "fornicate" <note>In this context, spiritual fornication refers to idolatry or heresy.</note>, being bound by the chain of <term>anathema</term> <note>A formal curse by a council or the Church, excommunicating a person and cutting them off from the community.</note> and sequestered from the threshold of the Holy Church. For the strict Judge who speaks to the saints is not to be believed absent from the synods of the Fathers, since he himself says:

<margin>Matthew 18</margin>
**Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.** Nor is anything decreed there by anyone according to the truth without his authority. Nor is anyone other than he himself to be believed to have stirred them up to the vengeance of the wicked, fighting through them and in them, and remaining continually with them even until the end of the age. For it is not recorded that such celebrated <term>synods</term> <note>Ecclesiastical councils or assemblies convened to decide on matters of doctrine or discipline.</note> occurred in the Church previously as those in the time of the Doctors, from the **Council of Nicaea** onwards, in which errors were corrected and useful statutes were established to be kept. It follows:

<margin>Revelation 2:24</margin>
->**He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.**<-

Truly, what is said to one is said to all. For who is so perfect in words that he does not sometimes, when speaking to the powers of the world, speak more softly than he ought—either to gain favor or to avoid anger? But even if he is so perfect that he does not stumble in doctrine, he still ought not to appear without bitterness in the sight of Almighty God, because he knows many of his leaders constantly sin in such a matter. Wherefore, by the voice of Almighty God, it was said to the man who was clothed in linen: **Mark a "Tau" upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and grieve over all the abominations that are done in the midst of Jerusalem.** <note>original: "Signa thau super frontem," referencing Ezekiel 9:4. In the ancient Hebrew alphabet, the letter Tau was written as a cross.</note> When this was done, the Lord’s command was given to the other men to kill all the men of the city, except those who had the letter **Tau** written on their foreheads. For to groan and grieve over the ruin of the Church is to carry the cross in the mind. Not without reason, then, is the sign of the letter Tau impressed on the foreheads of those who must [grieve] over the crime of the city, so that the passing plague might fear them—those whom God knows...

It emphasizes that the "sword of the mouth" represents divine judgment delivered by Church Doctors and warns against delaying repentance, using the biblical sign of the 'Tau' as a mark of those who truly mourn for the Church's failings.</summary>

# First [Commentary] on the Apocalypse
### Chapter 2

...God knows how to rescue the pious from temptation, and those who set the fear of the Lord before their sight and judge themselves, so that they might not be judged more harshly by the Lord. Woe, therefore, to him whose heart is hardened so that he is unable to fear, since the avengers of crimes are ready to strike him. Happy is he to whom it is given to have the fear of the Lord before his sight, and to fight legitimately against vices. Catholic doctrine commends such a person's life, and the sincerity of their life and the rectitude of their faith commend their doctrine; for they shall attain rewards from the Lord that are all the greater as they are found to be prudent and vigorous while contending in the struggle. Wherefore, he soon adds:

<margin>v. 25</margin>
¶ To the victor, I will give **hidden manna**. <note>original: "Vincenti dabo manna absconditum," referencing Revelation 2:17</note>

¶ This is a sufficiently just recompense. For just as it was said to those for whom there was a conflict between the law and grace, or between the flesh and the spirit: *To the victor I will give to eat from the tree of life*—that is, from the grace of Jesus Christ, who is the tree of life; and as it was said to those for whom there was a conflict of suffering: *He who overcomes shall not be harmed by the second death*, and *be faithful unto death and I will give you the crown of life*; so in this place, where he speaks to teachers, the **hidden manna** is promised to the victor. By this, the sweetness of the interior word is to be understood, of which it is said by the Psalmist:

<margin>Psalm 31</margin>
> How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you! <note>Psalm 31:19 (Vulgate 30:20)</note>

Do you ask what this sweetness is? It is the manna itself and the **living bread**, of which the Bread Himself who came down from heaven spoke to the murmuring and unbelieving Jews,

<margin>John 6</margin>
saying: "It was not Moses who gave you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven." He himself, therefore, is the **hidden manna**; He, I say, is Christ Jesus, who is the Word and the Wisdom of the Father. He inebriates the minds of good teachers by the flowing torrent of his pleasure, just as it is proper for him to be called "Master," because he is the river of Paradise

<margin>Genesis 2</margin>
watering the entire surface of the earth. For this very reason, he is called the doctrine and wisdom of the Father. This can also be understood as the gift of the Holy Spirit, since it is infused so secretly

<column-break/>

into the just man that it only becomes known to the one to whom it is given—just like the **new name** written on the stone, which is indeed added next.

<margin>v. 26</margin>
¶ And I will give him a **white stone**, and on the stone a **new name** written, which no one knows except the one who receives it. <note>Revelation 2:17</note>

¶ When the Apostle spoke regarding certain figures of the Old Testament, and had come to explaining the **rock** from which, when Moses struck it, the most abundant waters flowed, he said:

<margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin>
> And the rock was Christ. <note>original: "Petra autem erat christus"</note>

Furthermore, that same rock was rejected by the Jews, but chosen and pre-elected by the Lord. To Simon, who confessed and said, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," He responded regarding both Himself and Simon:

<margin>Matthew 16</margin>
> You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.

Why was he called Peter <note>The name Peter (*Petrus*) is derived from the word for rock (*petra*).</note>? Because he was strong like a rock. But from where did this come? Surely from nowhere else than from a participation in the grace that is in that most firm Rock. To participate in such great grace, and to worthily receive the Body of Christ, is to inherit the gift of this **precious stone**. How great its beauty and glory are is demonstrated by its very whiteness. We know, indeed, that red roses pertain to the suffering of the martyrs, while white lilies pertain to the purity of virgins; for the color red signifies the shedding of blood, and white signifies the purity of chastity. In this matter, something great seems to be hinted at in the fact that a **white stone** is promised to the victor. For although there are some who, by receiving the Body of Christ unworthily, eat and drink judgment upon themselves, only the victors are those to whom the beauty of the **new man** is promised, so that they may be like Him, as John says: *For we shall see him as he is.* Thus it was appropriately said: *And on the stone a name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it*; for no one knows how great a dignity it is to be called a "Christian" by Christ, except the one to whom it is given to know and understand. This is the special property of those who have conquered the lusts of the world, who have prostrated the hidden adversary in war, who from the...

### Here begins the section on the angel of Thyatira.

<margin>Rev. 2:18</margin> **And to the angel of the church of Thyatira, write.**

The **Virginal Order** <note>In medieval theology, the "Virginal Order" refers specifically to those dedicated to a life of celibacy and contemplation, often within a monastic setting.</note>, which is fourth in the number of holy orders, is recognized to have flourished in the fourth age of the Church. Yet, in this place, the discourse is not about those virgins who remain in a lay habit and in their own homes—who will themselves receive a worthy reward for the gift of their virginity—but rather about those who, having changed their habit <note>The "habit" refers to the distinctive clothing worn by monks and nuns to signify their withdrawal from secular life.</note> in both mind and body, are holy contemplatives, gazing upon the face of the Bridegroom through the gift of God, into whom even the angels long to look. How great their glory is is made known by the name **Thyatira**. For "Thyatira" is interpreted as **enlightened**, or **inflamed**, or **a living sacrifice**, or **transforming into a sacrifice**. <note>original Latin interpretations: "illuminata," "inflammata," "vivens hostia," "transserens in hostiam." These are traditional medieval etymologies rather than modern linguistic ones.</note> All of this is proven to befit that sacred order because of the abundance of gifts conferred upon it. For, as I recall explaining at the threshold of this work: just as the order of **Prelates** <note>leaders of the church</note> reflects the rising Lord, and the **Obedient** <note>those who suffer or obey unto death</note> reflect the dying Lord, and the **Doctors** <note>teachers</note> reflect Him proceeding from the womb [at His birth], so the order of **Contemplatives** bears the likeness of Him ascending into heaven. Thus, they appear to be more kindled with fire and illustrated with light than the other three orders. For His birth seems to have something in common with the **earth**, because through it He showed that He had taken on our clay [flesh]. His death and burial have something in common with **water**, because we are buried

<column-break/>

with Christ through baptism into death. Wherefore, the sacrament of baptism, which the Church preserves annually, is established to be celebrated solemnly on the day following the Lord’s Passion. His resurrection also has something in common with **air**, because the subtlety of transparent air signifies a spiritual creature, and without the drawing in of air, we cannot live in the flesh. Also, His ascension into heaven has something in common with **fire**, because heaven is fiery and full of lights, so that it illuminates the dark regions of the three elements that are below it by its radiance.

And it should be noted that the **earth** bears a likeness to the human body; **water** to the soul; **air** to angelic spirits; and **fire** to the divine nature. In this matter, it is worth considering that neither earth, nor water, nor air illuminates the present world, but only fire; for it is the **divine nature** alone which illuminates every person coming into this world. <note>Referencing John 1:9</note> Although this light illuminates some minds even among those stationed in the depths, like those who are entangled in carnal works and yet perceive something of that light by the Lord's dispensation—as Balaam saw some things—nonetheless, the "sea" of this world, with those who are intent on worldly laws and resolving legal cases, sometimes returns to itself and opens its internal eyes. Some "fly through the air," like those who are intent on allegorical teachings. Yet none do so as perfectly as those who, transcending human and angelic nature, open the eyes of their mind to contemplate God Himself. This is properly the characteristic of those designated in the **fourth church**, because even the great lights of heaven which illuminate the world were created on the **fourth day** of the world's creation.

It is, therefore, quite appropriate to the matter that the **virginal church**, which is fourth in its order, received the name Thyatira (meaning **enlightened** or **inflamed**), because the happiness of contemplation belongs more properly to her. For just as the moon is illuminated by the brightness of the sun, so are contemplatives illuminated by the vision of God. In this mystery, "Thyatira" is also interpreted as **a living sacrifice** or **transforming into a sacrifice**, since it is well known that just as the order of martyrs made themselves a sacrifice by dying, so the order of contemplative virgins—whatever they are or can be—offered themselves as a burnt offering to their God by living justly and piously. Thus, for the rest of their life, they no longer live for themselves, but for Christ, having their members ready for a **good work**, and not for the use of transgression... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

Song of Songs 3:6.</note> From the desert, he says, because the desert is the place of those who contemplate, just as it is said more significantly in the fourth part of this book: **And there were given to the woman two wings of a great eagle, that she might fly into the desert unto her place.** <note>Revelation 12:14</note> It is as if to "ascend like a pillar of smoke from the aromatics of myrrh and frankincense" means to be unceasingly affected by two kinds of compunction <note>In medieval theology, "compunction" refers to a "piercing" of the heart—either by sorrow for sins or by a burning desire for God.</note> and to pass over to higher things through constant sighs. But since the fourth order is properly that of virgins, over whom mothers take precedence rather than fathers, why is it that in the type of the angel the letter is written to men and not to women? It is because the care of virgins is usually committed to spiritual men—just as the mother of the Lord was committed to that virgin disciple <note>The Apostle John, often referred to as "the virgin" because of his traditional celibacy.</note> whom Jesus loved—for the reason that woman is of a weaker nature and is by no means sufficient for herself without the help of a man. Nevertheless, this fourth order is common to both women and men; not indeed as wives and husbands, but as virgins in both sexes. This is what the Lord Jesus—as I have just recalled—took care to designate by a worthy and happy mystery when he commended his virgin mother to the virgin disciple, saying to that same venerable mother concerning that same chaste disciple whom he loved above the others: **Woman, behold your son**; and to the disciple: **Behold your mother.** <margin>John 19</margin> Therefore, this order is illustrious in both sexes and eminent in both. But since it was begun by the virgin mother of Christ, the prerogative of this order is rightly attributed to the female sex, so that they might not seem despised among the others because of their sex, since in dignity this order is greatest and honored among the most eminent. Just as when the text dealt with the martyrs, mention was made of the mind of Christ for the sake of understanding, and when it dealt with the teachers, mention was made of the sword sharp on both sides <note>The "rumphea," the two-edged sword of the Word of God.</note>—by which is understood the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God—so it is not without a rational cause that the words we have just heard were spoken in this place to the virgins: **These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire.** For it is fitting for each order to have an example from their King, who is the true Teacher, so that while each one gazes upon his instructor, he may be reformed into the likeness of Him who is "all in all." For there are many who abound in their own sense and presume upon their own spirit; they envy the contemplative life, which is granted only to free and pure minds that are burning with charity. When they presume to usurp a grace not given to them, instead of the clarity of the true light, they incur the foulness of "whiteness" in their eyes. <note>original: "albugini." This refers to a medical condition like a cataract or white spot on the cornea, used here as a metaphor for spiritual blindness or pride.</note> Therefore, lest those who are such contemplators should glory in themselves, the form of true contemplation is suggested when it is said: **These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire.** This is indeed the true form, the manifest tradition of the speculative life: it will either be burning and bright, or it will be nothing or false. Because to whom it is not given to see clearly and to love ardently, it is better for him, according to the sentence of Truth, **to enter into life with one eye, than having two eyes to be cast into the Gehenna of fire.** <margin>Matthew 18</margin> It is necessary, therefore, for wisdom to shine, and—what is even greater—for the fire of charity to be set ablaze in anyone who exists as an emulator of this rare way of life. <margin>T. 27</margin>
## And to the angel of the church of Thyatira, write.

The Virginal Order, which is fourth in the number of the holy orders, is recognized to have shone forth in the fourth age of the Church. Yet in this place, the discourse is not about those virgins who remain in a lay habit and in their own homes—who will themselves receive the gift of their virginity with a worthy reward—but about those who, having changed their habit in mind and body, are holy contemplatives <note>original: "contemplantes"</note> by the gift of God, seeking the face of the Bridegroom into whom the angels desire to look. How great their glory is is made known by the name "Thyatira." For Thyatira is interpreted as: "illuminated," or "inflamed," or "a living victim" <note>original: "vivens hostia"</note>, or "transformed into a victim." All of this is proven to suit that sacred order because of the abundance of gifts bestowed upon it. For as I recall explaining most clearly at the gateway of this work: just as the order of leaders represents the rising Lord, and the order of martyrs represents the obedience of the dying Lord, and the order of teachers represents Him proceeding from the womb, so the order of contemplatives bears the likeness of Him ascending into heaven; thus, more than the other three, it is seen to be kindled with fire and illustrated with light. For the birth of Christ is seen to have something in common with the earth, because through it He showed Himself to have assumed our clay. Death and burial have something in common with water, because we...

<column-break/>

...are buried with Christ through baptism into death. Hence the sacrament of baptism, which the Church keeps annually, was solemnly established to be celebrated on the day following the Passion of the Lord. <note>This refers to the Easter Vigil on Holy Saturday, the traditional time for baptisms.</note> The Resurrection also has something in common with the air, because the subtlety of clear air signifies a spiritual creature, and without the drawing in of air, we cannot live in the flesh. His death and ascension into heaven have something in common with fire, because heaven is fiery and full of lights, such that it illuminates the dark regions of the three elements below with its radiation. And it should be noted that the earth bears the likeness of the human body; water, of the soul; air, of the angelic spirit; and fire, of the divine. 

In this matter, it is worth considering that not the earth, nor water, nor air illuminates the present world, but only fire; because the divine nature alone is what illuminates every man coming into this world. Yet, even if it illuminates some in mind who are situated among the lower things, when those who are involved in carnal works receive something of that light by the Lord's dispensation—just as Balaam <note>A biblical figure who, though not of Israel, was granted a divine vision of the future (Numbers 24).</note> saw the sea of this world—or when those who are intent on worldly laws and deciding cases sometimes return to themselves and open their inner eyes; or some who "fly through the air," such as those intent on allegorical teachings; yet none perceive it as perfectly as those who open the eyes of their mind to contemplate God Himself, transcending human and angelic nature. This properly belongs to those designated in this fourth church, because the great lights of heaven, which illuminate the world, were created on the fourth day of the world. 

It is therefore quite fitting to the subject that the virginal church, which is fourth in its order, received the name of Thyatira, meaning "inflamed" or "illuminated"; for the happiness of contemplation belongs more properly to it. For as the moon is illuminated by the brightness of the sun, so the church of contemplatives is illuminated by the vision of God Himself. Nor is it devoid of a harmonious mystery that it is interpreted as "a living victim" or "transformed into a victim," since it is certain that just as the order of martyrs made a sacrifice of themselves in dying, so also the order of contemplative virgins—whatever it is or can be—has offered itself as a whole burnt offering <term>holocaustum</term> <note>In a biblical context, a 'holocaust' is a religious sacrifice that is completely consumed by fire, symbolizing total devotion.</note> to its God by living justly and piously; so that what lives of the remainder may no longer live for itself, but for Christ, having its members for good work, and not for the use of transgression...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the fourth "order" of the Church—the Virginal Order—associated with the Church of Thyatira. Having previously discussed the eyes of Christ as symbols of contemplation, the author now moves to the feet of Christ to explore the relationship between the "active life" of service and the "contemplative life" of prayer.</meta>

->Exposition of the Parts<-
<note>original: "Abb. Pars Exponis"</note>

to work that which is good. Indeed, since that happy life <note>referring to the perfect happiness of heaven</note> is given to no mortal established in this pilgrimage <note>The "pilgrimage" is a common medieval metaphor for earthly life as a journey toward heaven</note> except in part, whoever presumes he has received the grace of freedom ought to show a certain judgment of his freedom through pious works. Hence, the text immediately adds: **And his feet were like fine brass.** <note>original: "auricalco." This refers to *orichalcum*, a brilliant, gold-like alloy of copper and zinc mentioned in Revelation 1:15.</note> Truly, we are led to various places by our feet. With our eyes, when we please and are allowed, we contemplate those things that please the soul. The utility of the feet is in movement; the freedom of the eyes is in stillness. Therefore, those who are moved more toward the work of justice are more profitable, while those who are moved less <margin>Luke 10</margin> see more clearly. You ask for an example?

There was a sister of Martha named Mary, who, sitting at the Lord's feet, heard His word. Martha, however, was busy with frequent ministry <note>the work of serving and hospitality</note>. One, therefore, sat so that she might hear and see the light; the other ran about so that she might do what frequent ministry required. Action, therefore, pertains to the feet, and contemplation to the eyes; thus, in the eyes of Christ, the perfection of contemplation is designated, while in the feet, the work of action. **But because the active life is also, in its own kind, bright and useful for salvation—as the same Lord whose feet are like fine brass says:** <margin>Matthew 5</margin> "Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works." Yet it is not bright in the same way as the contemplative life. Because the former is done in the body and the latter in the spirit, the feet of the Lord (whose eyes are like flames) are rightly said to be like fine brass. For fire is burning, bright, and intangible; brass, while bright, is less bright than fire and is tangible. For the contemplative life is a simple good, because the Spirit we have received from God is He who searches all things, even the depths of God. <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> By the very fact that the charity of God is poured out in our hearts, we are set on fire to contemplate Him whom we love; and by contemplating, we are set on fire much more in our love for Him. The active life is not like this, but is either a manifestation of love or its nourishment. For I do not necessarily work by the same act by which I love, nor do I necessarily love by the same act by which I work; but because I love, it pleases me to work, and because I work, I am proven to love; as the Apostle bears witness: <margin>1 John 3</margin> "Little children, let us not love in word, but in deed and in truth."

<column-break/>

Therefore, works also have their light, but not such that it can be equated to that spiritual light, just as the body cannot be equated to the spirit. It is as if fine brass were placed beneath fire, or silver beneath gold, or the night-light of the moon beneath the sun; though He who created both neither despises nor rejects either, for He knows why He subjected the handmaid to the mistress <note>A traditional allegory: the active life (handmaid) serves the contemplative life (mistress)</note>. For although the contemplative life should always be in the will, the active life must not be despised; for if Rachel was more pleasing in appearance, Leah was laborious and <margin>Genesis 29</margin> more fruitful in children. <note>In medieval theology, the two wives of Jacob represented the two lives: Rachel the contemplative, Leah the active</note>. And because he served his father-in-law for seven years for Rachel, he unknowingly found Leah imposed upon him. Hence, it is added here:

### **I know your works, and charity, and faith, and service, and patience; and your last works are more than the first.** <margin>Rev. 2:19</margin>

Blessed Paul, wishing to show Christians the way of salvation—especially for those who looked toward circumcision or uncircumcision—said to certain ones: <margin>Galatians 5</margin> "In Christ Jesus, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything, but faith which works through charity." If, therefore, that faith is valid in Christ which works through charity—but that which is without charity, as the same Paul witnesses, is nothing, even if it could move mountains; and again, faith without works is dead—rightly are these three commemorated together in the praise of this church: namely, works, charity, and faith. For one cannot please God without the others, except where there is no time for working. As for what is added, **"And service,"** <note>original: "ministeriū"</note> it is specific, not general. For we read in the Acts of the Apostles that seven deacons were appointed to minister to the saints, just as Martha was busy with frequent ministry. But there is also a spiritual ministry of which the Lord says: "Father, I will that where I am, there my servant <note>original: "minister"</note> may also be." <margin>John 12</margin> According to which the Apostle also says: "Let a man so account of us as the ministers of Christ and dispensers of the mysteries of God." <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> Whether it be that or this, it refers to action, not contemplation; and it is recognized as pertaining more to the spiritual fathers (represented by the angel) than to the subjects (represented by the church). For we know that those very fathers and abbots were said to have great vigilance of concern so that they might win over many; they had those who ministered to these people, whom they were able to snatch from the jaws of the dragon, <note>original: "fauce draconis"</note> not only with spiritual feasts...

<margin>Luke 21</margin>

For He Himself says this, who had already said in the Gospel: *In your patience you shall possess your souls.* <note>original: "In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras." ### But I have something against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat food sacrificed to idols.

<margin>T. 30</margin> <note>Likely a reference to Thyatira or a specific section in a source text.</note>

For in the time of the fourth seal, <note>Joachim of Fiore divided history into "seals" or eras. At that same time of the "fourth opening," there were found in the religion of the Greek people most proven men, inhabitants of the desert. Some of these, who had gone before in imitation of Elijah, were already beginning to dry up; but others, who had followed in imitation of Elisha, began to become the fathers of monks and virgins, whose imitation has reached even to the Latins. <note>Joachim is tracing the movement of the monastic ideal from the Greek East (Elijah/Desert Fathers) to the Latin West.</note> For just as the prophet Elijah fled from the people of Israel because of the impurities of their inventions and came to a widow woman who was in Sarepta of the Sidonians, so that perfection of the monastic life, which flourished in the first age among the Greeks, was transferred to the Latins when errors multiplied among the Greeks in the time of the fourth church, until the time of their visitation should come. Indeed, that the woman Jezebel was among them in that time in spirit, not in the letter, he demonstrates to us...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the message to the Church of Thyatira from the Book of Revelation, specifically focusing on the rebuke concerning "Jezebel." # Abbot’s Part of the Exposition

...we say firmly to him who rebukes the angel <note>In this context, the "angel" refers to the bishop or leader of the local church at Thyatira.</note> of Thyatira, saying: *I have something against you: because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants.* <note>original: "Habeo aliquid aduersum te: qz pmittis mulierem iezabel que se dicit propheten docere & seducere seruos meos." quoting Revelation 2:20.</note> Since it is certain in every way that the historical Jezebel perished in the days of Jehu, another Jezebel must surely be sought, of whom that ancient harlot held the image. Although this Jezebel designates false religious women who, under the appearance and habit of religion, deceive the servants of Christ by alluring them with deceitful words and drawing them in with the nods of their eyes—of whose kind were those <margin>1 Timothy 5</margin> about whom the Apostle says: *When they have grown wanton in luxury, they want to marry in God.* <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 5:11-12 regarding younger widows who lose their spiritual focus.</note> It seems, however, that this should rather be understood as a specific type of adultery: that is, the adultery about which the Psalmist says: *You have destroyed all <margin>Psalm 72</margin> who fornicate away from you.* <note>Psalm 72:27 in the Vulgate; Psalm 73 in modern translations.</note> For this fornication is to wander from the truth, and by wandering, to recede from the living and true God, who rests in simple minds and those who follow the truth. And because, just as in the tribes of Israel a certain collection of errors was found in the days of Elijah, so in the time of this "angel" in the Greek churches—with great heresiarchs leading them from the days of Sabellius <note>Sabellius (3rd century) taught "Modalism," the idea that the Father, Son, and Spirit are just roles or "modes" of one person, rather than three distinct persons.</note> and Origen <note>Origen (c. 185–253) was a hugely influential theologian whose works later became controversial and were eventually condemned as heretical in some aspects.</note>—that <margin>Origen</margin> party of heretics, which deceived the unwary under the appearance of religion, was called "Jezebel." For just as she deceived many under the guise of prophecy, so also this party protected itself with "the arrows of the powerful," <note>Referring to sophisticated but misleading arguments or worldly influence.</note> not by the reason of words but by a show of a "perfect way," as many of the Greeks do even to the present day. And although all heretics have the "ears of an asp," <note>A biblical metaphor for being willfully deaf to the truth.</note> it is proven that their women are far worse, by the example of Jezebel herself, and Athaliah, and Herodias, and other similar women. Especially <margin>Ecclesiasticus 25</margin> since the wise man says: *There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and no malice above the malice of a woman.* <note>Quoting Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 25:22-26.</note> And indeed, regarding those who were outside the church, it mattered nothing to the angel or the case; for he who recedes from the sheepfold by breaking the bonds of unity cannot be restrained by the pastor of the church, because, having been condemned by his own judgment, he does not recognize

<column-break/>

the pastor’s sentence. But for those who were inside, and showed themselves to be inside by their profession and their habit <note>The "habit" refers to religious clothing or an outward lifestyle of a monk or nun.</note>, yet through the audacity of presumption and the greed for empty glory taught false things as true and illicit things as licit—merely those who were in charge of them were to be rebuked. This is especially so since the Apostle says that the power of teaching is not to be given to women, because "the woman," he says, <margin>1 Timothy 2</margin> "was seduced, but the man was not seduced." <note>1 Timothy 2:14.</note> Therefore, by the woman Jezebel, those wicked women were not to be understood who publicly departed from the church due to some error, but those who simulated being Catholics in the presence of Catholics, and by lurking in secret plots, drew the simple and unarmed into error. Not without merit are those who are seduced by them silently accused of "fornication" and "eating things sacrificed to idols," because to depart from the Catholic faith and adhere to a soul or a church corrupted by heretical depravity is to fornicate; and to participate with them in food and drink is as if one eats what is offered to idols. Whether this was said of spiritual fornication or of bodily fornication—which is no less displeasing to God, especially in those who are bound by a vow of chastity—or, as is more likely believed, of both together: the prelates <note>Church authorities or superiors.</note> are rebuked for their crime. For a leader should only cease from the correction of the wicked when, due to abounding iniquity, it is no longer safe for him to live among them, as the Lord says: *If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.* <margin>Matthew 10</margin> Otherwise, if the depravity of the subjects is capable of being corrected, the rod must not be spared. This is taught by the downfall of Eli of Shiloh, who, because he would not amend the wicked deeds of his sons with worthy chastisement—though he was long expected and warned by Him who is a patient payer—at last suffered a fitting vengeance upon himself and his entire house. Or it might be believed that a simulated religion and the outward appearance of finery were sufficient in the sight of the Most High, with all the debts of vice hidden from man being forgiven and feigned goods rewarded.

# First Part of John on the Apocalypse
<page-num>77</page-num>

<margin>Job 41.
Psalm 124.
Psalm 91.</margin>...from the snare of the hunters: saved from the night terror and from the noonday demon. <note>The author quotes Psalm 91:3-6, traditionally interpreted as God's protection against spiritual dangers.</note> Just as they enter, they say: *I will not put upon you any other burden.* <note>original: "Non mittam super vos aliud pondus." A quote from Revelation 2:24.</note> Who are those who say this? They are those who do not attend to the manner of the precept and the moderation of divine dispensation. Martha was busy about her frequent ministry; Mary sat at the feet of Jesus: and, being freed from the cares of the world, she listened intently to His word. Each has her own burden: both Martha and Mary. And then Martha asked of the Lord that He might impose another burden upon her <note>A reference to Luke 10:40, where Martha asks Jesus to tell Mary to help her with the chores.</note>. Peter was chosen to follow the Lord; John to contemplate the mysteries of the heavens and to write those very things down diligently. And then Peter thought that he should have John as a companion in his passion <note>Peter's suffering/martyrdom.</note>, even though John was not to be his companion in the description of the books. This was a sign of a great mystery and an indication of things to come. For the Lord foreknew that those devoted to **action** would be moved against those who are vacant for **contemplation** and rest—as if it were not equally heavy to stand by as it is to act manfully. Therefore, they think this is just and say it must be imposed: namely, that the burden of martyrdom belongs to them, and the Lord should not spare the others in the moment of passion. It is as if they do not see it as a fair judgment that while some are destined for battle, others, serving in leisure, should remain in tranquility. And in saying this, they show they do not know the "weight" of the hope, patience, and long-suffering of those contemplatives, and that it is no less heavy for human nature to be "vacant" for God than to do something physically—to sit in one place rather than to run about working through various actions. But the Lord, who knows all things, rebukes Martha concerning her sister, and Peter for moving the question about his fellow disciple. He speaks to that order which is designated in John and Mary, saying: *As they say, I will not put upon you another burden; but that which you have, hold fast until I come.* <note>original: "Quod habetis, teneate donec veniam." quoting Revelation 2:25.</note> Why does He speak to this order, saying, "that which you have, hold fast until I come"? Or concerning that disciple whom Jesus loved: *So I wish him to remain until I come*? <note>Quoting John 21:22.</note> Except that the contemplative life is made contemporary to the active life, yet in such a way that the active life precedes in some of its parts, and the contemplative follows. For the birth of Peter preceded

<column-break/>

the birth of John; yet the birth of John did not wait for the death of Peter, but he himself was born while Peter was still surviving. He who, like Peter, had preceded in birth, so he himself remained alone in this life after Peter. So, in this way, the ecclesiastical order designated in Peter—who was chosen for the battle of martyrdom—preceded, according to a certain order, the order of <term>monastics</term> <note>original: "monachorum." Refers to those living a life of secluded prayer and contemplation.</note> which John designates. Which ecclesiastical order, having at last accepted its cross, is to follow Christ, stretching out its hands so that He may gird and lead it where it does not wish to go. But that part of the elect which is designated in John will be left behind, to which the whole succession of Peter must pass once that laborious part designated in Peter has failed, and tranquility is given everywhere to the lovers of Christ. For in that time, there shall be one Lord, and His name shall be one, as is said through another prophet: *Behold, I will take the children of Israel from the midst of the nations to which I have dispersed them, and I will gather them from every side and lead them to their own soil; and I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and there shall be one king commanding all, and they shall no longer be two nations, nor shall they be divided any longer into two kingdoms.* <note>A translation of Ezekiel 37:21-22.</note> It follows:

<margin>Ezekiel 37</margin>

<margin>T. 33</margin>> **He who overcomes and keeps my works until the end, I will give him power over the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron; and they shall be broken like a potter’s vessel.** <note>Revelation 2:26-27.</note>

It is clear that in the fourth age of the world Elijah <note>original: "Helyas."</note> was revealed, and in the sixth, John; and again in the seventh age, Elijah will appear. This is a great sacrament <note>In this context, "sacramentum" means a sacred mystery or hidden truth.</note>; I think it has already been mentioned in this work. After Moses—who in this part of the mystery signifies the Father—Elijah was revealed, who regarding this mystery designates the Holy Spirit. After John the Baptist, who signifies the Son, Elijah is to be revealed again, because one and the same Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Thus, after the active life, the contemplative life shone forth; both in the fourth—specifically the ecclesiastical time—and it will shine again in the seventh.

### He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

¶ Let a man diligently examine himself and reprove himself: and let him watchfully attend to whether he is blessed in every part: lest perhaps he fall, being destitute in some part of himself: and thinking himself to be something, he be reduced to nothing: while he permits some vice to reign within himself, even if his works are great and worthy of praise, for which he expects a reward that is not empty. For so great is the equity of the judge, and so great the mercy of the redeemer, that he does not dismiss the unconfessed sins of one who had time but neglected them because of his well-performed works; nor, because of those things for which a repentant man judges himself by accusing himself, does he omit to reward him for his labors. For if he were held to reward anyone by right of debt, surely he who once slipped would have fallen into ruin. But because the reward itself, which a free man hopes for for his labor, is not a debt but a gift, he who worthily repents can recover what he lost and be restored to his first dignity: just as David and Peter and many others: who even after great crimes held their former honors: so that they themselves might know how to be indulgent to the wandering flock, and to recount the depths of the mercy of their God, in which "the sunrise from on high has visited us" <note>original: "oriens ex alto" from Luke 1:78</note>.

...of the heavenly homeland might be found in him: in which homeland—namely <note>original: "v3" for videlicet</note>—various kinds of flowers, as it were, make the dwellings of the saints pleasant and beautiful, and the varied beauty of precious stones adorns the universal walls of that city.
