And after a few verses: "And the structure of its wall was of jasper stone: but the city itself was of pure gold like clear glass: the foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone" <note>Revelation 21:18-19</note>. 

But clarification <note>original: "Luz" likely for "Lux" or "Lucidatio"</note> stands from the opinion of Peter, who says the elect of God are **living stones** <note>1 Peter 2:5</note>; the buildings of that city are the fellowship of just men, who by faith and works have pleased God. For what is meant by the variety of colors implanted in precious stones, if not the diverse gifts of graces, which are given specially to each and every one, so that nothing is lacking in beauty, nothing in grace? Indeed, does not that queen of the heavens <note>A reference to the Church as the Bride</note> who stands at the right hand of the lamb appear beautiful, surrounded in gilded clothing with variety <note>original: "varietate"</note> in the sight of him who loves her? 

For it is not given to every one of the saints to have that entire variety; rather, it is given to each one by one Spirit, dividing His own gift to each as He wills: so that each person might study to love his neighbors as much as he possesses in all of them all the things which he does not have in himself. For it is so given to each to have what he has, that he who possesses it should rejoice that he has received it not so much for himself as for his neighbors; nor should he estimate it as given to himself alone, but in himself for others; nor should he think himself to belong to himself, but to be the eternal possession of others. "Do you not know," he says, "that our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God, and you are not your own?" <note>1 Corinthians 6:19</note>. If we are not our own, we surely belong to Him who bought us—and to those whom He commands. Where then is this law regularly enacted 

<margin>1 Corinthians 9</margin>

<column-break/>

if not in **Sardis**? Where is the question of this mandate established, if not in the "beginning of beauty," in the **college of monks**? For who lives in that state if he lives for himself and not for his neighbors? 

For just as the beauty of a precious stone is useless and idle unless it fulfills its part in a structure according to its quality and measure—nor does it render any appearance of decor, however industriously it may be polished by the sculptor, unless it is fitly joined to the joints of other stones—so in the monasteries <note>original: "cenobijs"</note> of monks, whatever grace is in a man is idle if he loves only himself, who seeks only those things which are his own, and thinks little of the common and useful salvation of the many. 

And indeed, that such monks—if they are even to be called monks and not rather **false monks** <note>original: "pseudo monachi"</note>—exist in monasteries, there is no doubt. Concerning them, nothing pertains to him who guards the little ones gathered into one; for those whose way of life is crooked cannot be counted among the golden lampstands. 

On the contrary, concerning the true unity of brothers, it is said through the Psalmist: "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity. Like the ointment on the head" <note>Psalm 133:1-2</note>. In which head, if not in Christ? For to Him it is said concerning this ointment through the Psalmist: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows" <note>Psalm 45:7</note>. This ointment, poured out from the head, which is Christ, followed that good which is written in the Acts of the Apostles: "And of the multitude of believers, there was **one heart and one soul**: nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them" <note>Acts 4:32</note>. 

Where therefore such unity exists, there that most precious ointment is poured out; and there those principal gifts follow through the pouring. For where there is charity, what good can be lacking? Indeed, where charity is not, even that which someone seems to have shall be taken away from him. Because the nurturer of charity is unity, the virtue of unity is rightly imposed upon monks: for where there is no unity, charity cannot exist. For as a small fire is made great in a collection of wood, so in the unity of souls and hearts, love grows unto immensity. Conversely, just as in the division of wood...

<margin>Psalm 44</margin>
<margin>Acts 4</margin>

# John’s First Part on the Apocalypse

...fire dies out which once lived: so too in dissension and discord, love is extinguished and becomes empty. And although all the rules of the holy fathers prefer unity above any other spiritual virtues, almighty God nevertheless willed that certain perfect men should lead the way, who would do the will of their God in various ways; especially that those four orders should lead, who are designated by the **four living creatures** <note>The "four living creatures" from Revelation 4:6–8, often associated with the four Gospels or specific types of religious life</note>, until the time should come that pertains to the throne of God, which designates an innumerable multitude of the elect. This is the time of the **fifth angel**, which is the subject of this chapter.

But alas! How prone to evil is our nature, corrupted in the **first-formed** <note>original: "protoplasto," a Greek-derived term for Adam, the first created human</note> of the human race. "It is time for acting, O Lord," says a certain one, "they have destroyed your law." <margin>Psalm 118</margin> Just as if two different men, differing in character and discipline—one of them being a transgressor—were at odds with each other, and such discord remained between them for many years, so that the more one of them promised and offered dearer things each year, the more the other (as if turned to madness) would inflict greater fights and insults upon the one who loved and soothed him in vain; so it is between the goodness of God and the depravity of the human race. A constant and invincible dispute remains until the appointed end, so that through every increase of the gifts bestowed upon us by God, we, having become worse, return evil for good. Yet even when we do these things, our malice cannot overcome the goodness of the most high God; for though sin abounds, His bounty of grace abounds and superabounds from day to day. Nor, while His grace abounds, does our iniquity cease to abound on the contrary, until that blessed time comes in which He must conquer and reign until He puts His enemies as a footstool for His feet. 

In the meantime, that which is said by the voice of the Lord Himself through the Psalmist must be fulfilled: "In return for my love, they detracted me." <margin>Psalm 108</margin> And in the prophet Isaiah, making a complaint over his vineyard: "I expected," he says, "that it would produce grapes, and it produced **wild grapes**." <note>original: "labruscas," referring to sour, uncultivated grapes</note> <margin>Isaiah 5</margin> Wherefore also to this angel, for whom such gifts were prepared and in part bestowed—because he did not prepare himself to give thanks 

<column-break/>

for the benefits he had received, nor did he vigilantly show himself worthy in his service—the One who has the **seven spirits and the seven stars** began to speak with the voice of harsh rebuke, saying: **"I know your works: that you have a name that you live, but you are dead."** 

But if he is said to be dead, it must be asked more diligently: why does he have a name that he lives? For not all who are dead have a name that they live; rather, this sentence encompasses only the **hypocrite**. For those who are bound by worldly business and live in a secular manner cannot have such a vain name, so that even those who live among them are often judged to be dead by resemblance, since they do not differ in garment and clothing from those who truly die. 

But whoever has changed his garment and clothing—which is given for no other reason, and assumed for no other reason, than for the sake of [spiritual] life (unless perhaps by the ministers of the devil, who often transform themselves into angels of light to deceive the unwary)—and yet lives differently than his clothing and profession suggests: such a person is certainly condemned by this sentence which says: **"You have a name that you live, and you are dead."** 

Such were the hypocritical Pharisees, who were called "the divided ones" <note>The author provides a common medieval etymology for "Pharisee," suggesting they were "divided" or "separated" by their hypocrisy</note>; the Lord commands the apostles to abstain and beware of their doctrine and teaching when He says: "Take heed and beware of the doctrine of the Pharisees, which is **hypocrisy**." <margin>Matthew 16</margin> For nothing is more detestable before the Lord than hypocrisy; nothing more cursed than feigned justice, which is always rooted in lies and robbery, and which simulates by **tonsure** <note>The practice of shaving the top of the head as a sign of religious devotion</note> and **habit** <note>The distinctive clothing of a monk or friar</note> to be what it is not. 

For it is written: "You will destroy all who speak a lie." <margin>Psalm 5</margin> Whence the Savior also says to those same Pharisees: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! Who are like **whitewashed tombs**, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but within are full of dead men's bones and all filth; so you also outwardly appear just to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity." <margin>Matthew 23</margin> Behold what kind of "name of life" this is, to which the truth of the matter is not subject. "The joy of the hypocrite," he says, "is like a mere point <note>meaning a fleeting moment</note>. If he raises his head even to the clouds, he shall perish in the end like a dung-heap." <margin>Job 20</margin> Indeed, who is more of a hypocrite than...

The author uses a series of biblical metaphors, including Isaiah's wild grapes and the whitewashed tombs of the Pharisees, to emphasize that external religious appearance without internal love is spiritual death.</summary>

# Part of the Exposition

...guilty of deceit: for who is he who wears the monastic habit but lives an "irregular" life? <note>original: "habitū... irregulariter"; "regular" refers to living according to a religious Rule, like that of St. Benedict</note>. They have a reputation for being alive among those who are worldly and think according to the flesh; people who only know how to judge a person by the outward things they see. They are unable to "dig through the wall" and see the idols that are hidden within <note>A reference to Ezekiel 8:8-12, where the prophet is shown the secret sins of leaders</note>. Because of this, they are deceived and deluded: they praise and exalt these wretched men, in whom there is no true cause for praise or glory, hoping that through the merits of such men they might be granted forgiveness for their own sins. Yet the souls of these hypocrites, once the life of the flesh is ended, descend with the dead to the underworld.

But if there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents <margin>Luke 15</margin>, how much sadness do you think there is over a righteous man who turns away from justice? It is made clear by what follows that through a shepherd’s negligence, a soul may sometimes turn away from justice, yet by his vigilance, that person—who was about to die—might be saved from the destruction of death.

<margin>Ezekiel 8</margin>
<margin>Luke 15</margin>
<margin>Revelation 3</margin>
**Be watchful, and strengthen the things that remain, which were about to die.**

<margin>Ezekiel 34</margin>
People wonder at this statement—those who think that by God’s predestination, free will is stripped of its own power, as if the laziness of a sluggish shepherd does no harm to the chosen flock, and the vigilance of a studious and concerned one provides no benefit. If this were so, shepherds would be rebuked in vain by the Prince of Shepherds, who says: "You have not sought that which was lost." From this sentence, it is clearly gathered that by the zeal of a pious shepherd, sheep are saved, and by the sloth of a lazy one, they perish. Many who are among the "elect" <term>The Elect: those chosen by God for salvation</term> live while committing a deadly crime; yet because they are chosen, even if they perish in the eyes of their earthly shepherds, they do not perish to Christ, who says: "I will seek that which was lost, and I will bring back that which was cast away; I will bind up that which was broken, and I will strengthen that which was weak." And further: "I myself will search for my sheep, and I will visit them as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep."

If He had also said, "I will raise that which was dead," the question would not be disputed, for He once raised Lazarus in the flesh after he had been dead four days; likewise, He daily grants life to sinners. And He does this for none other than the elect—those whom He predestined to life from eternity. Therefore, we should not listen to those who think the elect of God cannot sin mortally through their own negligence or that of their shepherds...

<column-break/>

...but this is in every way undeniable: none of the elect can be held by death forever, for our Leader <note>Christ</note> strikes the jaw of the **Leviathan** <margin>Job 40</margin> <note>The biblical sea monster, representing the Devil or the power of death</note> and strikes the prey from his faws, leading the captive out from the middle of the belly of hell. Therefore, it is not in vain that this angel is commanded to strengthen those things that were about to die—either because the Lord is powerful enough to raise those whose souls are buried in sin, or because not only those specific things that were dying, but indeed all the elect would perish, if heavenly piety did not come to their aid through mercy.

However, we do not know what this angel did after hearing this correction. God rebukes not only those who are to be corrected to show them salvation, but even the incorrigible, to demonstrate the truth of His judgment. For He always rebukes and warns the sheep who are perishing so that they might not perish; and yet they cannot be saved because they refuse to be converted. By the just but hidden judgment of God, they continue to be hardened for the worse, going from sin to sin all the days of their lives. Nevertheless, we read that some "reprobates" <term>Reprobate: those rejected by God or hardened in sin</term> were partially corrected, and at the insistence of righteous men toward the end of their lives, some performed penance and were less cruel thereafter than in times past.

But whether this angel accepted the correction—and if he did, whether he produced worthy fruits of repentance—does not appear. Nevertheless, the fall of those who came before clearly suggests a warning. Just as it was said to them that they should repent, and yet they either did not repent or did not do so worthily (as the sentences carried out against them testify), so too for this one, who earned a rebuke before them, it is to be feared which sentence he might be struck with; for his hour has not yet come, and it seems delayed until the present time. And it should be known that the first order, once the time of the second order had begun, was punished in this world for its fault. The third was punished when the fourth began, and the fourth when the fifth began; in this way, one order does not fall away before another arises, so that the earth is not desolated and every living soul does not perish. Do you seek an example? The legal institutions of the Old Law <note>The "legalia instituta" refer to the Jewish ceremonial and religious laws</note> are sufficient to prove this; they were not abolished in the early church before the New Testament...

->### John’s First Book on the Apocalypse<-

<margin>Leviticus 25</margin>
...might establish fear among the nations. Do you ask for authority? The Scripture says: "Until the new are born, you shall eat the old" <note>original: "Donec nascantur noua: comedetis vetera"; a reference to the transition from the Old Covenant to the New, or the old self to the new</note>. Therefore, a sinful man should not rejoice, nor should he think little of his sins just because the severity of vengeance is delayed. For the greater the window of mercy granted for the correction of a fault, the stricter the sentence will be for punishing the proud. Therefore, if every one of those people is to be judged by the Lord for their failings, and if another order was established to follow in their place, there is no doubt that as the ruin of the "fifth order" <note>The "fifth order" likely refers to the fifth period of church history or the fifth "angel" of the Apocalypse</note> approaches, another will be raised up to take its place and receive the promise which the former, by its own conduct, was not worthy to hold.

It should be noted that he does not say: "I find no good in your works," or "you have no works," but rather: **I do not find your works full.** Even hypocrites have works which they show off to other people, but they do not have them "before God." Although they have lamps which they light, they do not take oil in their vessels along with their lamps <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25</note>. In the same way, a nutshell is often empty of its meaty kernel, yet in its outward appearance, it lies, pretending to be completely full. Likewise, the sad stalk of a poorly grown crop pretends to be something far better than it is, until the careful inquiry of the farmer reveals its true nature. And as it is written

<margin>1 Samuel 16</margin>
in the first book of Samuel: "Man sees the things that appear, but the Lord looks at the heart." After saying, "I do not find your works full," he immediately adds: **before my God.** Hence it is also said by the Apostle: "He who glories,

<margin>1 Corinthians 1</margin>
let him glory in the Lord." For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends. For this reason, Truth itself spoke to certain people who were exalting themselves because of their empty and

<margin>Luke 16</margin>
vain works, saying: "You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among men is an abomination before God." For I do not find your works full before my God. Truly, humility is the nurse of love and the root of affection.

He who could taste with the "palate of the heart" <note>A common medieval metaphor for spiritual discernment</note> would know how sweet it is to say: *My God*. In Hebrew, this is said as *Eloi*. Because the "first angel" <note>Lucifer/Satan</note> refused to say this, being corrupted and losing the joy of internal gladness, he lost his place. In one sense, the word

<column-break/>

"God" demonstrates the humility of the one calling upon Him; in the other word, "my," it demonstrates the integrity of love. For the charity of a subordinate <note>original: "subditi"; referring to a monk or a layperson under authority</note> can only be true if it is rooted in humility; otherwise, such "love" is judged to be nothing more than a proud liberty. The cause for love is not the same in a subordinate as it is in a prelate <note>original: "prælato"; a high-ranking church official like an abbot or bishop</note>, or in a friend versus one who is not a friend. Therefore, it is enough for a prelate to love his subordinate, but it is not enough for a subordinate to love his prelate as an equal or a peer; for such love does not proceed from virtue, but merely from nature. Thus, the subordinate often despises the superior and is rejected by a just judgment. The virtue of love in subordinates is this: that when they are lashed <note>meaning disciplined or corrected</note> out of love, they do not grumble; when insulted, they do not repay the injury. And why is this? Certainly, because they recognize judgment and love equity. For true judgment consists in this: that the servant be subject to the master, and the son to his father; that they love discipline and acknowledge their fault. 

But who is fit for these things? There is only one who is just and who justifies the ungodly: Christ Jesus, the only-begotten of God, who is the innocent and spotless Lamb who takes away and blots out the sins of the world. He was made obedient to the Father even unto death; when lashed like a sheep, He remained silent; when crucified, He gave thanks. For this reason, He is the Lamb of God, the Leader of the journey, the Teacher of the sons of men, and is called "Truth"—even though the Father is also Truth. He did not seek His own glory, but the glory of Him who sent Him, showing us the way of salvation through humility and patience, so that each of us, when corrected, may learn to bless the Lord, and when constrained by lashes, may humbly cry out:

<margin>Psalm 21; Matthew 26</margin>
**My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?** Let the one who is lashed say this from the soul, so that he may inherit that name and acquire God for himself as an eternal possession—lest perhaps God say to him at the end: "You are not mine, and therefore I am not your God,"

<margin><insert>Sermon</insert></margin>
because you did not know the time of your visitation. For what is the "time of our visitation" except this time in which He, who was and is God blessed above all things, took upon Himself our form, so that He might say with us

<margin>Psalm 117</margin>
what is fitting for us to say: "You are my God, and I will confess to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you." That one who was

<margin>John 8</margin>
created first among all things <note>Lucifer</note>, and who became a murderer through envy, did not wish to say this; he did not stand in the truth, but spoke through defiance.

...guilty of deceit: because he who wears the habit of a regular <note>original: "regularem habitum"; referring to someone living under a religious Rule, such as a monk or priest</note> lives irregularly <note>outside the requirements of the Rule</note>? For they have a reputation for being alive among those who are carnal and think in a fleshly way: those who do not know how to consider a person except by the outward things they see; who are unable to dig through the wall <margin>Ezekiel 8</margin> and look upon the idols that are within. Because of this, they are deceived and deluded: they praise and extol those miserable men in whom there is no cause for praise or glory, hoping that by the merits of those men, the pardon for their own sins might be granted to them. Yet the souls of these leaders, once the life of the flesh has ended, descend with the dead to the lower regions <note>original: "inferna"; hell or the underworld</note>. 

But if there is joy in heaven over a sinner who performs penance <margin>Luke 15</margin>, how much sorrow do you think there is over a righteous man who turns away from righteousness? He makes it manifest that, through the negligence of a pastor, someone may sometimes depart from justice, yet through that same pastor’s vigilance, one who was about to die can be saved from the destruction of death, when he adds:

<margin>T. 3.</margin>
**Be watchful, and strengthen the things that remain, which were ready to die.**

<margin>Ezekiel 34</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel 34</margin>
He <note>The author</note> wonders at those who think that, by the predestination of God, free will is deprived of its own law—as if the laziness of a sluggish pastor does no harm to the chosen flock, or the study and solicitude of a vigilant one provides no benefit. If this were so, pastors would be rebuked in vain by the Prince of Pastors <note>Christ</note>, who says: *That which was lost you have not sought.* From this statement, it is clearly gathered that through the diligence of a pious pastor, the sheep are saved, and through the laziness of a sluggish one, they perish—even many who are among the "elect" <note>the chosen</note>, while they are living in deadly sin. Yet, because they are the elect, even if they perish in the eyes of the pastors, they do not perish to Christ, who says: *I will seek that which was lost, and bring back that which was driven away, and I will bind up that which was broken, and I will strengthen that which was weak.* And further on: *I myself will seek my sheep, and will visit them, as a shepherd visits his flock in the day when he shall be in the midst of his sheep that were scattered.* He who said, "I will raise up that which was dead," showed this when he once raised Lazarus from the flesh after four days; He daily provides life to sinners—and certainly to no others than the elect, whom He predestined to life from eternity. 

Therefore, we should not listen to those who think that the elect of God cannot sin mortally through their own negligence or that of their pastors. Yet this remains undeniably true: none of the elect can be permanently held by death, for our Leader <note>Christ</note> strikes the jaw of Leviathan <margin>Job 40</margin> and knocks the prey from his fangs, leading the captive out from the midst of the belly of the underworld. Therefore, it is not in vain that this angel <note>the leader of the church</note> is commanded to strengthen those things that were about to die—either because the Lord is powerful enough to raise the buried even after the death of the soul, or because not only these things, but all the elect would perish if divine piety did not come to their aid through mercy. Although we do not know what this angel did after hearing the correction, we know that God rebukes not only those who are to be corrected to offer them salvation, but also the incorrigible to demonstrate the truth of His judgment. For God always rebukes and warns those who are going to perish so that they might not perish; yet they cannot be saved because they refuse to be converted. By the just but hidden judgment of God, they proceed from bad to worse, going from sin to sin all the days of their lives. Although we read that some reprobates were partially corrected and, near the end of their lives, performed some penance according to the justice of righteous men, and were thereafter less cruel than in times past. 

However, it is not clear whether this angel accepted the correction and performed worthy fruits of penance. Nevertheless, the fall of those who came before clearly hints at the situation: just as it was said to them that they should perform penance, yet it appears either they did not do so, or they did so unworthily (judging by the sentences carried out), so it is to be feared for this one who earned a rebuke before them. Although the sentence seems delayed, his hour has not yet come. And it should be known that the first order <note>the first period of the Church</note>, once the time of the second order had begun, was punished physically for its fault. The third was punished when the fourth began; the fourth when the fifth began; so that one order does not fall before another rises, lest the earth be made desolate and every living soul perish. Do you seek an example? The institutes of the Law <note>the Old Testament laws</note> are sufficient to prove this: they were not abolished in the primitive Church until the New Testament...

"Until," He says, "the new things are born, you shall eat the old." <note>original: "Donec nascantur noua: comedetis vetera"; a reference to Leviticus 25:22 regarding the harvest cycles, used here allegorically for spiritual transition</note> Therefore, a sinful man ought not to become cheerful, as if the severity of vengeance were of little weight just because it is delayed. For the greater the space of indulgence given for the amendment of a fault, the more severe will be the sentence for rewarding the proud. Therefore, if each one of them is to be judged by the Lord for his own sins, and another order was followed which was established for him, there is no doubt that—as the ruin of the **fifth order** <note>The "fifth order" refers to the Church of Sardis, the fifth of the seven churches of Revelation</note> approaches—another shall be raised up in its place, and shall receive the promise which this one is not worthy to pursue.

¶ It must be noted that He does not say, "I find no good in your works," or "you have no works," but: **I find not your works full.** For even hypocrites have works which they show to men, but they do not have them before God. For even if they have lamps which they light, they nevertheless do not take oil in their vessels along with their lamps <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25</note>. In this way, a nutshell is often empty of the richness of the kernel, yet in its outward appearance, it lies, claiming to be entirely full. So too, the wretched stalk of a poorly grown crop pretends to be something far different from what it is, until the investigation of a diligent farmer reveals its true nature. And because it is written 
<margin>1 Samuel 16</margin> in the first volume of Samuel: "Man sees those things which appear, but God looks upon the heart," therefore, to the phrase **I find not your works full,** 
<margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin> there is immediately added: **before my God.** Whence it is also said by the Apostle: "He who glories, let him glory in the Lord." For it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends. Hence Truth itself <note>A common medieval title for Christ</note> speaks to certain people who were extolling themselves because of their empty and 
<margin>Luke 16</margin> vain works, saying: "You are they who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for that which is high to men is an abomination before God." For **I find not your works full before my God.** Truly, humility is the nurse of love and the root of affection.

¶ Oh, that one might feel in the **palate of the heart** <term>palato cordis: a medieval metaphor for spiritual discernment or the "taste" for divine truths</term> what sweetness it is to say: *My God*. In Hebrew, this is called *Eloi* <note>original: "heloi"</note>. The first angel <note>Referring to Lucifer/Satan</note> refused to say this; deprived of the joy of internal gladness, he lost it. In a marvelous way, in one of these 

<column-break/>

words, which is "God," he demonstrates the humility of the one who invokes Him; in the other, which is "My," he shows the integrity of love. For the charity of a subject cannot be true if it lacks the root of humility, nor does he judge such a love to be anything other than a proud liberty. For the cause is not equal in a subject and a **prelate** <term>prelato: a high-ranking church official or superior in a monastery</term>, nor in a friend and a non-friend. And therefore, it is enough for a prelate to love his subject, but it is not enough for a subject to love his prelate merely as a peer or an equal; for such love proceeds not from virtue, but from nature. Whence it is that he often despises his superior and, by a just judgment, is rejected. 

Therefore, the virtue of love in subjects is this: that when they are scourged for the sake of love, they do not murmur; when injured, they do not return the injury. And why is this? Certainly because they recognize the judgment and love equity. For it is a true judgment for a servant to be subject to his lord, and a son to his father: to love discipline and to acknowledge fault. But who is fit for these things? One alone is just and the justifier of the impious: the only-begotten of God, Christ Jesus, who is the innocent and spotless lamb, taking away and blotting out the sins of the world. He was made obedient to the Father even unto death; when scourged, he was silent like a sheep; when crucified, he gave thanks. From this He is the Lamb of God; from this the leader of the journey; from this the teacher of the sons of men; from this He is called the Truth—even though the Father is also Truth—because He did not seek His own glory, but the glory of Him who sent Him, showing us the way of salvation in humility and patience. Thus, each one of us, when corrected, should know how to bless the Lord, and when hemmed in by scourges, to cry out humbly:

<margin>Psalm 21; Matthew 26</margin> **My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?** <note>original: "Deus meus: deus meus: vt quid dereliquisti me?"</note> Let the one who is scourged say this from his soul, so that he may be able to inherit this name and acquire it for himself as an eternal possession. Otherwise, the Lord might say to him at the end: "You are not mine, and I am not your God," 
<margin><insert>Servant</insert></margin> because you did not know the time of your visitation. 

For what is the **time of our visitation** <note>The moment when God offers grace or calls a soul to account</note>, if not this time in which He, who was and is God blessed above all things, took upon Himself the form of a servant <note>original: "formam sui" corrected by the insert "servus"</note> among all, so that He might say with us what was fitting for us to say: 
<margin>Psalm 117</margin> "You are my God and I will confess to you; you are my God and I will exalt you." He who was 
<margin>John</margin> first created among all <note>Lucifer</note> refused to say this, and because he was made a murderer through envy, he did not stand in the truth, but spoke out of defiance.

It emphasizes that true love is rooted in humility, modeled by Christ’s submission to the Father, and contrasts this with the pride of the fallen angel.</summary>

->### Abbot’s Expository Part<-

<margin>Isaiah 14</margin>
**"I will ascend into heaven: above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne."** <note>original: "In celum ascendam: sup astra celi exaltabo solium meum"; a reference to the pride of Lucifer, here applied to hypocrites</note> And because all hypocrites seek glory, the further someone recedes from the truth, the closer they become to a lie. The Lord, rebuking that "angel" <note>The "angel" refers to the bishop or leader of the Church of Sardis</note> whose works are not full—because they are vain, because they are empty, because they are to be despised—immediately added: **"before my God,"** <note>Revelation 3:2</note> so that the leader might feel, stimulated by a silent objection, how far he has receded from this Good by desiring earthly things. For whoever wishes to be among those of whom it is said:
<margin>Psalm 32</margin>
**"Blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God,"** <note>Psalm 32:12</note> must not work for what is good out of a desire for vain praise, nor so that he might be seen by men, but for the sake of obtaining an eternal inheritance, which is to possess God Himself and His Spirit, which has been given to us. There follows:
<margin>A. 4</margin>
**"Remember then how you received and heard; keep it, and repent."** <note>Revelation 3:3</note>
Since the Holy Scripture says that nothing on earth happens without a cause, do we think it happened by chance, or by the whim of human will, that a man to whom so many miracles bore witness should write a Rule for monks <note>Referring to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the foundational document for Western monasticism</note> and command it to be kept? As if he had dared to say by his own authority: "Let the disciple follow the Rule as a teacher, nor let him rashly deviate from it," or that he should arrange the Canonical Hours <note>The set times for daily prayer</note> according to his own judgment in a way other than the Roman Church was accustomed to? But if he spoke not from himself, but from the Holy Spirit who spoke within him, who does not know that those who—while serving under that same Rule—have broken its stricter precepts are rash and corrupters of the truth? They are "tithing mint and dill" according to the voice of the Lord, while abandoning the weightier matters of the law <note>A reference to Matthew 23:23, accusing the monks of focusing on trivialities while ignoring core spiritual duties</note>. But it is clearly manifest to the whole world that many monasteries were founded under the name of the Blessed Benedict during the **fifth course** of ecclesiastical time <note>The author correlates the seven churches of Revelation with seven historical ages of the Church; the "fifth" is the age of Sardis</note>. These endure even to the present time, yet in them several chapters of the Rule have been so swallowed up as if Saint Benedict had never issued them—especially regarding manual labor and abstinence from food and drink. This is known to have happened because, while they

<column-break/>

wished to be rich under a Rule of poverty, they became delicate and tender; they became weak and infirm; they became those who
<margin>Hebrews 5</margin>
have **need of milk, not solid food.** <note>Hebrews 5:12</note> And it is no wonder. For who was ever able to maintain a life of poverty and a resolution of chastity amidst riches and luxuries, where food is plentiful? I am silent regarding the fact that many monasteries are located within cities and villages, and things are at hand which entice the minds of monks. For some—oh, the sorrow!—they pluck out the eyes of the captives and lead them into the treasury. I am silent regarding that most unspeakable crime, whose fierce cry reaches even to heaven.
<margin>Genesis 19</margin>
Do even those men think themselves to be clean who, defiling themselves with their own hands (which is a sin even to speak of), become adulterers? For he is said to have committed adultery in his heart who has
<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
looked at a woman to lust after her. Therefore, even if there is a difference between various kinds of filth and uncleanness which arise from idleness and the delights of the flesh—and the more gravely one is defiled, the more strictly he is to be punished in the future—nevertheless, anyone who, once associated with the company of the servants of God, persists unhappily in the ultimate form of adultery is made a stranger to the **white garments.** <note>The "white garments" promised to the faithful in Sardis (Rev 3:4-5)</note> But why did this evil happen to the **fifth order** <note>The era of the Church represented by Sardis</note> except that it did not keep in mind how it "received and heard"—namely, that **idleness is the enemy of the soul**? They are not truly monks unless they live by the labor of their own hands; they should all abstain from the eating of meat, except for those who are entirely weak and sick; two cooked side-dishes <term>pulmenta: secondary dishes of vegetables or legumes served with bread</term> daily should suffice for the brothers, and this on account of the infirmities of different men; they may use wine (which is not for monks at all) in such a way that we never drink to the point of drunkenness or satiety; it is not permitted for monks to have any private property; it is not expedient to complain about the color or coarseness of clothing, but rather to use such as can be found in the provinces where they live, or whatever can be bought more cheaply; apart from cowls, tunics, stockings, and shoes, no other clothing should be issued; and he <note>Benedict</note> removed garments of fur and linen from the borders of the monks, especially since the Lord says: <note>The text cuts off here, likely leading to a quote from the Gospels about simple clothing</note>

The author laments that monks have abandoned manual labor, poverty, and dietary discipline for a life of urban luxury and moral decay.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the message to the Church in Sardis from the Book of Revelation. The previous page discussed the pride of hypocrites and the importance of working for God's glory rather than human praise. This page specifically applies these lessons to the corruption of monastic life and clarifies the nature of the "Day of the Lord."</meta>

<margin>Matthew 11</margin> **"Behold, those who are clothed in soft garments are in the houses of kings."** <note>original: "Ecce qui mollibus induunt in domibus regum sunt"; a reminder that the religious life should be one of austerity, not luxury</note> These things, and others like them, the monastic order received to be observed from the father and leader of monks, Benedict <note>Saint Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547 AD), the founder of Western monasticism</note>. Yet in certain monasteries, these rules are so stifled that it is as if they were not even commands. They treat them as minor suggestions, though these things which are merely advice for the laity <note>non-clergy believers</note> are actually matters of a solemn vow for monks. By the debt of their promise, and even by the very appearance of their habit <note>the distinctive clothing of a religious order</note>, they are bound to keep them, lest they be seen to damnably usurp a habit that is not their own. They preach one way of life by their appearance, but confess another by their deeds. But lest those who wish to repent might think the path to mercy is closed to them because they are accused of defiling their holy habit, it is shown that they may satisfy God through worthy repentance when it is said: **"Remember then how you received and heard; keep it, and repent."** But often, when a thing begins badly, it ends badly; a person not only neglects to weep for past sins but commits worse ones day by day. Hence it is said through the prophet: <margin>Isaiah 26</margin> **"Let us have mercy on the wicked, yet he will not learn to do justice."** The goodness of God is abundant so that He may forgive sins, yet men do not even blush at their own ways enough to convert and live. Thus, in the book of Job, regarding such negligent people, it is said in the person of a scorner: <margin>Job 24</margin> **"God gave him a place for repentance, and he abused it in pride."** But <margin>Psalm 7</margin> what does the Scripture say? **"Unless you be converted, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready."** Therefore, the following is added:

<margin>1 Thess. 5</margin> ### If therefore you will not watch, I will come to you as a thief, and you shall not know what hour I will come to you.

Concerning this sudden coming of the Lord, the Apostle says in the epistle to the Thessalonians: <margin>1 Thess.</margin> **"The day of the Lord shall come as a thief in the night."** And the Lord himself said: **"The lord of that servant will come in a day in which** <margin>Luke 12</margin> **he does not hope, and at an hour that he does not know, and shall separate him, and shall appoint him his portion with the hypocrites."** But regarding this, what should we think? Is this said about that coming of the Lord which will be on the Last Day, or about some special coming of His by which He shows Himself present to a human sinner through the distinction of His zeal? For the "coming of the Lord"

<column-break/>

is not always to be understood as that final coming which will be manifest at the end of the age. Often it refers to a temporal judgment that occurs in the days of the Lord's wrath and at the time of vengeance, as is clearly gathered from what was said to the first "angel" <note>the leader of the first of the seven churches</note>. Since it is certain that the mystery of that first angel touches the first period of the Church, He surely would not have said to him, "Otherwise I will come to you," if the "coming of the Lord" were spoken of only regarding the final coming. However, the time of the fifth angel <note>the Church of Sardis</note> draws very near to that time which is called the Last Day—and also to that time in which the Great Prostitute <note>a figure from Revelation 17 often interpreted as a corrupt system or city</note> who sits upon the waters is to be judged temporally, when all hypocrites shall be surrendered from the earth. The closeness of these two events makes us hesitate in this part, not knowing whether it should be understood according to the letter or according to the spirit. Some are deceived by the word "mystically" when they hear people speaking of the Last Day, not realizing that a "day" is something more than an "hour," just as a week or a month is more than a day, or a year more than a month. Yet John, speaking of the entire final age in which many days and years have already passed, calls it the "last hour," saying: **"Little children, it is the last hour."** <note>1 John 2:18</note> If, therefore, the "last time" can be understood by the "last hour," how much more so by the "last day"? Lest anyone think me reckless in this matter or distant from the understanding of the Fathers who spoke of the Last Day, I wish to bring forward in this place the opinion of Augustine. In his book *The City of God*, he discussed the Last Day, examining many opinions and asserting many truths by the authority of the Scriptures and purity of intellect. He said: "What the whole Church of the true God holds in its profession is that Christ will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead. This we call the last day of divine judgment, that is, the last time. For it is uncertain over how many days this judgment may extend; but according to the custom of the Holy Scriptures, no one who has read those writings—however carelessly—is ignorant that the word 'day' is usually put for 'time'." If, therefore, the "day" which is called the Judgment, in which Christ is to come to judge the living and the dead, is understood as the last time...

It argues that "day" in Scripture often refers to an era or "time," rather than a single 24-hour period, citing Saint Augustine to support this interpretation of the final judgment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the message to the Church in Sardis from the Book of Revelation. The previous page discussed the corruption of monastic life and the need for repentance. This page shifts to the symbolic interpretation of the raven and the dove to explain who will be saved during the coming judgment and why purity—specifically chastity—is required for the monastic order to walk with Christ.</meta>

### Part of the Exposition

...it must be [said]: ended by an uncertain number of days. Who knows if that sad time will be joy for the pious? For in it, the saints will obtain the kingdom, even while the Lord has not yet descended, but His arrival is nevertheless near. And if this is at the end of this second state <note>referring to a stage in the history of the Church</note>, while the last two angels remain—that is, the two orders designated by them—wherefore it is said to the angel of Philadelphia: **"Behold, I come quickly."** And to the angel of Laodicea: **"Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him and dine with him, and he with me."** <note>original: "Ecce venio cito... Ecce sto ad ostium et pulso..."</note>

<margin>Matthew 24</margin>
Because the Lord, speaking in the Gospel about the hour of His revelation using the example of the flood which occurred in the days of Noah, predicted that all the wicked are to be uprooted from the earth, it is pleasing to notice carefully that it was not for nothing that the names of so many other birds and animals saved in the ark were omitted, and such famous mention was made only of the raven and the dove. Nor was it for nothing that he first sent out the raven, which did not return to the ark, and then sent out the dove, which would return and bring back the sign of peace. Just as the laity <note>non-clergy believers</note> are understood through the land animals and the clergy through the fish of the sea, so religious men <note>monks and those under holy vows</note> are understood through the birds of the sky. Among these birds, some are designated by the specific names of the raven and the dove, not without some hidden meaning. I pass over the differences of the orders <note>the various monastic rules</note>, in which either the greed of the raven or the simplicity of the dove is noted. In one and the same order, if they are noted separately, both are found according to their parts. For what should those who live simply and love the brilliance of purity be called, if not doves? Their simplicity is proposed everywhere as an example for spiritual men to imitate. That there have been such men in the monastic order, even if rare and few, is made clear by what follows:

<margin>Revelation 3:4</margin>
> **"But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments: and they walk with me in white because they are worthy."** <note>original: "Sed habes pauca nomina in sardis qui non inquinauerunt vestimenta sua..."</note>

<column-break/>

Behold, these are the white doves, washed with milk, sprinkled with hyssop <note>a plant used in biblical rituals for purification</note> and cleansed, washed more diligently and made whiter than snow. And for such men, multiplied in spirit, a "seed" will be left upon the earth, symbolized by the dove whose blessed seed shall be multiplied by the Lord upon the earth. But the others, symbolized by the raven—even those who seem to stand tall—will not escape the judgment of the Most High, until that most foul seed is deleted from the earth. Therefore, even if there are many in this fifth order <note>likely referring to the fifth age of the Church symbolized by Sardis</note> who do not know the time of their consolation, the Lord will nevertheless be consoled in his remnants. Of whom it is said: **"You have those few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments: and they walk with me in white: because they are worthy."** They have garments, but they are defiled; though they may seem to have many works of justice, they do not carefully guard the purity of <term>chastity</term> <note>Latin: "castitas"; the commentator places heavy emphasis on sexual purity as the defining "white garment" of the monk</note>. But those who keep their good works pure before their God are truly worthy to walk with the same Lord in white. But why are they worthy? Because they have fought worthily and lawfully against the impulses of lust. For if no one is crowned unless he has fought lawfully <margin>2 Timothy 2</margin>, it is clear that everyone who fights lawfully is crowned by the Lord and is esteemed worthy by the Lord to become His imitator—whether by shedding error in the struggle of a warlike military service, or by striving for purity in the vow of chastity. Hence it is added:

<margin>Revelation 3:5</margin>
> **"He who overcomes shall thus be clothed in white garments; and I will not blot out his name from the book of life; and I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels."** <note>original: "Qui vicerit: sic vestietur vestimentis albis..."</note>

What else is it to say "he who overcomes" but "he who has fought lawfully"? What is it to say "shall thus be clothed" but that the glory of things past becomes the certainty of things to future? What else is "I will not blot out his name from the book of life" but that the names of certain monks who renounce this world are written in the book of life, even if they seem to be for a time...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the message to the Church in Sardis from the Book of Revelation. The previous page discussed the symbolic meaning of the raven and the dove in Noah's Ark, representing those who fall away from the faith and those who return to the peace of the Church. This page explores the "Book of Life" and why some names are recorded while others are blotted out.</meta>

### John Primasius on the Apocalypse
L 2

...the losses caused by a neglected way of life are blotted out from the book of the living. For thus it is written concerning certain people: <margin>Psalm 68</margin> *Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous.* <note>original: "Deleantur de libro viventium"</note> Indeed, one is blotted out from the book of life and not written with the righteous if, though invited to life and appearing for a time to stand and flourish among the faithful people, he does not persevere. This is so that he might reach that state of which Peter speaks: *Brethren, be even more diligent to make your call sure through good works.* <margin>2 Peter 1</margin> For what are we to understand by "the book" in this place, if not the very memory of the Lord, of which it is said: <margin>Psalm 111</margin> *The righteous shall be in eternal memory.*? And it is well said that they shall be in "eternal" memory; for those who do not persevere to reach true righteousness—which cannot be corrupted—may indeed be held in temporal memory, but by no means in eternal memory, as they are those who believe for a time, but in the time of temptation, they fall away. <margin>Luke 8</margin> Furthermore, by the "names" written in the book, we should understand the specific recognition of the elect, by which they become known to the heavenly Bridegroom. To some, He will say at the end, "I do not know you." But to His servant Moses, He spoke differently, <margin>Exodus 33</margin> saying: *I know you by name.* Truly, the "name" of a righteous person is the brightening <note>or manifestation</note> of their life. For this reason, only those are said to be "named" who are great and possess something worthy of fame and deserving of praise, according to what is read of certain men: <margin>Psalm 18</margin> *Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.* This, therefore, is why certain names are said to be held in Sardis, and why the names of the righteous are said to be written in heaven: because just as a man among men is called "named" not simply because he is a human being, but because he has become great, so too no one should be believed to have a "name" before God merely because he is called a Christian, but because he is innocent, God-fearing, and just. Indeed, the most certain reason for names being written in the book of life is that each individual has his own gift from God—one in this way, another in that—as the Apostle said to those <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> to whom he directed his letters: *You are our epistle, written in our hearts, which is known and read by all, manifested by us*

<column-break/>

*and written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone, but on the fleshy tablets of the heart.* You ask what these things signify? Surely they mean exactly what has been said: that the words of God are to be written in the book of our heart, not with ink to form letters, but by the Spirit of the living God, so that we may know they have been given to us by God. Moreover, the specific gift that each one receives functions for any righteous man like a "proper name," so that he may be <margin>Exodus 33</margin> known by name, just as it was said to Moses by the Lord: *I know you by name.* For indeed, several names of the righteous are known to designate something pertaining to the reality of their character. Furthermore, the common gift, which is the love of God <note>charitas</note>, creates a common name for the whole community of the righteous, so that they are called "citizens of Jerusalem"—as many as are elected by the Lord and preordained for life. This distinguishes them from those who are not. Similarly, the common cause of nature gives a universal surname to the "sons of Adam," so that each individual is called a "man," to distinguish them from those living things that lack reason, such as sheep, oxen, and the beasts of the field. However, it is not a common name, but a proper one—such as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Peter, Paul, and John—that gives a person greater recognition; a specific grace, more than a common one, makes a person truly "named." Rightly then, he whose name is held written in the book of life is made manifest, with Christ confessing him both before God the Father and before His angels. For by this very act, each of the faithful acquires an eternal name for himself and becomes "named" in that heavenly court of angels. In this court, he fights and conquers in a battle against invisible enemies, even when visible conflict is lacking. From this, he is made manifest to the invisible Father and the holy angels much more than if he were enduring physical blows and wounds to his body—for that is a physical and visible thing, while this is an invisible and spiritual struggle. And since angels are invisible and incorporeal, we are made known, kin, and companions to the companies of angels more through that battle in which we fight against unclean angels with spiritual weapons. And because the man Christ Jesus, who was made the mediator between God and men, is just as He is—truly God with God, and man with men—so also...

<vocab>Book of life, election, divine love, Jerusalem, Moses, Christ Jesus, spiritual warfare</vocab>

<summary>This page explains the "Book of Life" as God's eternal memory, where the names of the righteous are recorded based on their perseverance and individual spiritual gifts. It contrasts the "common name" of humanity with the "proper name" of the elect, who are recognized by God through their spiritual struggle against invisible evil.</summary>

### The Interpretation of the Revelation
L 2

...with the angelic spirits as far as his spirit is concerned, which is called the soul <note>original: "anima"</note>: he has something in common with them, so that he may join all things in himself and be the very boundary of peace: just as he is between God and men, so let him be established between men and angels. It is clear that whoever he may be, who in this portion of grace is made an imitator of Him by following Him, cannot be unknown to God—who loves the purity of chastity—nor to those angelic spirits, to whom an unpolluted and innocent life is most dear; because that very likeness of purity is a confession of love, and a certain eternal knowledge: the innocence of life. It follows:

<margin>chapter 8</margin>
¶ **He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.**
¶ Because many, while they have the time, think little of hearing the voice of the Spirit and of striving manfully for eternal life: again and again they are rebuked by God; again and again they are warned that they should hear. In this, having been so often corrected and admonished, they despise His lordship so that they might have no excuse for their own stubbornness, when He who waits patiently and is now despised shall appear at the end to judge the present age.

->**Here ends the section concerning the angel of Sardis.**<-
->**Here begins the section concerning the angel of Philadelphia.**<-

<margin>chapter 9</margin>
¶ **And to the angel of the church of Philadelphia write: These things says the Holy One and the True One, who has the key of David; who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens. I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door which no one can shut.**

¶ Because the previous threat, which was made to the angel of Sardis by rebuking negligent and lazy monks, terrified us, it was altogether opportune—and as much fitting for divine goodness as it is expedient for our fragility—that He should temper the rigor which He had previously shown out of severity. Here, out of the goodness of His clemency, He gives a pledge of promise to those desiring to be saved. In this way, He gave the harsh Law through Moses, which at length He

<column-break/>

himself, upon coming, took care to mitigate; so that He who had commanded the woman caught in adultery to be stoned might Himself calm the ignorant stone-throwers by correcting them. Why is this? Because the time of children is one thing, and that of the elderly another; and just as it is right to correct children with the austerity of the rod, so it is healthy to grant liberty to men: so that the adoption [as sons] may follow the spirit of fear, and the liberty of sons follow the weariness of servants. Nor is it a wonder if in this angel, who is the sixth, such great liberty is preached; since a certain renewal of the age is at hand in the days of this angel. Concerning this—if not many things, yet not obscure ones—we have touched upon in the preface, saying that all justice must be consumed in three states. <note>The "three states" refers to a medieval theological concept (often associated with Joachim of Fiore) dividing history into the Age of the Father/Law, the Son/Gospel, and the Spirit/Grace.</note> The third of these, which is the last, begins from this sixth angel, as is revealed by many testimonies of the Scriptures if they are understood inwardly; of which some are to be written below so that you may understand what I say. For indeed, the second state, which began from John the Baptist and is signified in him—just as the third state, which we have already gathered from the end of the second, ought to begin from these times—is signified in Elijah; or even, what is greater, in Christ Jesus. Although in the spiritual people who belong to the third state, it was necessary for something to precede, just as something preceded in the people of the second state in a mystical way. One of these was signified in the mother of the precursor of the Lord <note>Elizabeth, mother of John the Baptist</note>, the other in the mother of the Lord himself. John preceded Him, because by the mother of John, John himself, and the mother of the Lord, the Lord himself, preceded in being born into this world. Moreover, the mother of John designates the primitive Church, whose son is the people of the Gentiles in faith; for by the right of that Church we are called sons, she who bore us through her Gospel in Christ Jesus; just as it is said by the Apostle to certain ones who had believed at his word: <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> *In Christ Jesus through my Gospel, I have begotten you.* And because the dignity of the primitive Church, over which Peter is described as presiding from the beginning, was translated to Rome with the same Blessed Peter and his colleague Paul, so that it might be called and be the mother of all: Elizabeth signifies nothing less than that same holy Church of the Latins, which was founded at Rome, and was, as it were, translated there from Jerusalem with the same Peter. But if in that aged Elizabeth the primitive or principal Church is designated, what else do we say should be understood in John the Baptist, but the faithful people, whom she carries in her sacred womb...

# First [Commentary] of John on the Apocalypse
L 3
<meta>catchword: when now</meta>

the church: Which is to say: the church even to the present day suffers in the pain of labor, until, under the approaching crisis, she brings forth that same elect people and sends them out toward heaven: meeting as a 

<margin>Ephesians 4</margin>

**perfect man** in the **measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.** <note>original: "perfectum in mensuram etatis plenitudinis christi"</note> But when will this be? When that unbelieving people—whom the priest Zacharias signifies <note>Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist, was struck mute for his unbelief until his son was born.</note>—from whom this holy woman once took her start among the chosen branches, shall receive the office of the tongue which it lost long ago: to bless the almighty Lord and 

<margin>Luke 1</margin>

to say with a full mouth: **Blessed be the Lord God of Israel because he has visited and made redemption for his people.** <note>The "Benedictus," the song of Zacharias from the Gospel of Luke.</note> But also, in this, Elizabeth preceded Mary by five months; then in the sixth month the Virgin herself conceived. And this indeed is Elizabeth: though she was in her old age, she nevertheless preceded the Virgin’s conception by a space of six months. But you ask: what does the Virgin signify, she who followed by conceiving and giving birth? She signifies the Church that **knows no man**: <note>A reference to Mary’s virginity, here symbolizing a Church free from worldly corruption.</note> which grows strong in the silence of the wilderness, where there are no studies of letters nor teachers of ecclesiastical institutions, but a simplicity of life—yet an honorable one—and sobriety, and charity from a pure heart and a faith that is not feigned. For her—that is, the Church: so chaste, so sober, so spiritual—no dispensation was ever made, nor was it permitted, nor will it be permitted, that in her a man should have a wife or a wife a husband. This is frequently tolerated and granted by dispensation in the church of the clergy <note>original: "ecclesia clericorum"</note>—which Elizabeth designates—and in the Greek church, where it was established by public law; <note>A reference to the Eastern Orthodox tradition allowing married priests, unlike the Roman Catholic requirement for celibacy.</note> but so that she might serve God in mind and body, she bound herself by a vow of chastity and sobriety. And this [spiritual church] was indeed small from the beginning, and remained in a state of barrenness until a certain fullness of time; for they were very few in comparison to those who live otherwise, who would rise up to the same service in the very bosom of the Lord, even if He had many outward zealots in a false habit.

<margin>Namely</margin>

But when the sixth month arrived—that is, the sixth time of the church in which it was necessary for the **sixth seal** to be opened—Almighty God visited the Virgin, just as He had once visited the aged woman. This is because that church which Elizabeth designates took its origin from Saint Sarah, whose conception was in her old age: that is, in the days of Elizabeth herself. 

<margin>Daniel 8</margin>

But the end [of that age] is in that most wicked king, concerning whom it is written in the prophet Daniel: that beyond what can be believed, he shall lay all things waste. But it is not so in

<column-break/>

the church of the faithful: she who passes daily out of this world among the chosen branches will not fail in that king; rather, what was designated in Elizabeth shall be consumed, while what was designated in Mary shall remain until the end. For once Elizabeth was always in labor and anxiety, and she will be so until the time of that king who shall work the works of his father more abundantly than all others. Nevertheless, where labor abounds, leisure <note>original: "otium," referring here to holy rest or contemplation.</note> shall superabound. For the days of the laborious Martha shall pass, and the blessed time of the quiet Mary shall arrive. Even that aged Elizabeth, having been fulfilled, shall pass away, and the holy Virgin shall be strengthened in the Lord her God: carrying within her holy womb that which she conceived by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the **contemplative church** designated in Mary, the mother of the Lord, was begun by the glorious Virgin herself. For this reason, many monks in all their monasteries are known to have taken up her holy name by tradition, so that they might show themselves to belong to that church which the holy Virgin, the mother of the Lord, herself designates. Moreover, just as that carnal synagogue, which is designated in Hagar, is known to have had two different times—namely, a time of barrenness and a time in which she bore sons: one before the Law, the other under the Law—and just as Sarah (who is here designated by Elizabeth) had one time under the Law and another under grace, until these very days in which the **third state of the world** <note>original: "tertius status seculi," a central concept in Joachite theology referring to a future Age of the Holy Spirit.</note> ought to begin or rather become clear; so too the spiritual church, which is designated in Mary, is noted to have had her time of barrenness from the birth of the glorious Virgin until the present, and her time of fruitfulness from these days until the consummation of the age. Thus the Synagogue began from the start of the original age; she conceived from the days of Hagar (who also signifies the Synagogue) and she labored in birth in the days of Antiochus. The Church began—which was first designated by Sarah and most recently by Elizabeth—from the days of Sarah herself; she conceived from the days of Elizabeth, and she herself is about to give birth soon under the pressure of that king who is often written of in this work. But the spiritual Church, which Mary designates, 

<margin>Truly now near to the Lord</margin>

began from her days: she is about to conceive soon—if she has not already conceived—and is about to give birth in the days of **Gog**, <note>A biblical figure associated with the final apocalyptic battle.</note> when the consummation of the age will be entirely imminent.

### Part of the Exposition
<meta>Catchword: and of Trachonit-</meta>

<margin>because</margin>
In order that we might more clearly behold these very things that have been said, we must consider again and again the aforementioned mystery of Mary, in which she was told by the angel announcing that a son would be born to her: **“And behold, your kinsman Elizabeth has herself conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who is called barren; because no word shall be impossible with God.”** <note>original: "Et ecce helysabeth cognata tua z ipsa concepit filium in senectute sua: z hic mensis est sextus illi que vocatur sterilis: quia non erit impossibile apud deum omne verbum." — Luke 1:36-37</note> This designates, as we have already said, the **sixth time** of the Church within the sixth month. In this time, it was necessary for the spiritual Church to conceive—without doubt a certain new spiritual understanding—or even children of promise and a spiritual offspring from the past; this is the very order that Jesus designates. 

This order, which is lovable and illustrious above many others that preceded it, is to be initiated within the limit of the **second state** <note>The author uses a "Three States" model of history: the Father (Old Testament), the Son (Church age), and the Holy Spirit (a future age of spiritual monks).</note>—that is, in the sixth time—if indeed it has not already been initiated in some people, which is not yet clear to me, because beginnings are always obscure and held in contempt. It is, however, to be multiplied and expanded in that **third state** of the world which is to come in the final time. Truly, from the sixth month of Elizabeth’s conception until the end of the ninth month in which she gave birth to the boy—that is, from the first month of Mary’s conception until the end of the third—that entire span of time was common to both pregnant women. This was so that the womb of the old woman, once the months were complete, might decrease in swelling from the burden she had long carried, and the womb of the new mother, consecrated to a divine birth, might be filled more and more with the swelling of the Holy Spirit. 

For this reason, the blessed mother herself is described as having remained with Elizabeth during the whole space of those days, not without the cause of a great mystery: so that the spiritual Church might learn to serve the general Church until the time of her own labor is completed. 

And these things are concerning the conception of the mothers. However, so that we may be led toward perfection once the infancy of Christ is left behind, **John the Baptist** was sent before the face of Christ to baptize in water for the remission of sins and to preach the coming of one stronger than himself, who would baptize in the Spirit. Just as after his resurrection, the Lord spoke to his disciples, saying: **“John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”** <note>original: "Joannes quidem baptizavit aqua: vos autem baptizabimini spiritu sancto non post multos hos dies." — Acts 1:5</note> Furthermore, John’s belt—as we have already written above in this work—was made of leather; Christ’s was golden. John’s was worn around the loins, while Christ's is recorded as being held at the breasts. John was also clothed in camel's hair, but Christ was seen dressed in a *podere* <note>term: podere (from Greek *podērēs*), a priestly garment reaching down to the feet.</note>, or certainly, as is read elsewhere, in white garments. John ate locusts and wild honey; Christ, after his resurrection, ate fish and a honeycomb. 

Whence also Mark the Evangelist—or rather the Holy Spirit through him—says quite fittingly: **“The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my messenger who shall prepare your way before your face.”** <note>original: "Initium evangelij iesu christi filij dei sicut scriptum est in Esaia propheta. Ecce mitto angelum meum qui preparabit viam ante faciem tuam." — Mark 1:1-2</note> For John indeed prepares the way; Christ comes. John begins; Christ fulfills. John preaches in the desert; Christ preaches in the cities. 

Therefore, the testimony of Mark saying, **“As it is written in Isaiah the prophet,”** should not yet be referred to what he subsequently added: **“Behold, I send my messenger,”** but rather to the work that was begun by John. The beginning of this work was touched upon by the prophet Malachi, who is brought in so that **“by the mouth of two witnesses every word may stand.”** <note>original: "ut in ore duorum testium stet omne verbum" — Deuteronomy 19:15 / Matthew 18:16</note> However, he was not named for this reason: because the "beginning of the gospel" is not exactly as Malachi says, but as Isaiah testified. For he (that is, Malachi)—or rather the Lord through him—spoke only recently of a messenger and a way to be prepared for the Lord in what he said: **“Behold, I send my messenger who shall prepare the way before your face.”** 

Isaiah, however, setting aside the order of the sending, transferred himself to the beginning of the Gospel, saying: **“The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”** <note>original: "Vox clamantis in deserto parate viam domini: rectas facite semitas dei nostri." — Isaiah 40:3</note> For Malachi foretold that a messenger was to be sent before the face of Christ. Isaiah points to him as if he were present and preaching. One of these pertains to his birth, according to what John says: **“There was a man sent from God whose name was John.”** <note>original: "fuit homo missus a deo cui nomen erat ioannes." — John 1:6</note> The other pertains to the start of the Gospel, of which Luke says: **“In the fifteenth year of the empire of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother was tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene...”** <note>original: "anno quintodecimo imperij tyberij cesaris procurante pontio pilato iudeam: tetrarcha autem galilee herode Philippo autem fratre eius tetrarcha ituree z traconitidis regionis: z lisania abiline" — Luke 3:1</note>
