# First [Book] of John In the Apocalypse
L 4

...tetrarch, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John, the son of Zechariah, in the desert. Where it is also immediately added: "And he came into all the region of the Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins; as it is written <margin>Isaiah 40</margin> in the book of the sermons of Isaiah the prophet: *The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.*" <note>original: "Uox clamantis in deserto parate viā dn̄i: rectas facite semitas eius." — Luke 3:4 quoting Isaiah 40:3</note> Behold, this was the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, just as the prophet Isaiah says. For the beginning was in John, the consummation in Christ; the beginning in the flesh, the consummation in the spirit. 

Truly, this same John preceded the birth of Christ by five months; since indeed Christ himself was born in the seventh month from the birth of John. This is surely because that "order" <note>Referring to a specific group or monastic "order" of people whom the author believes will represent the spiritual peak of the Church.</note> which he signifies was to be born in the **sixth time** of the Church. This is just as we have written elsewhere regarding Joseph, Samuel, Solomon, and John (the author of this book), and other holy men whose names are in the book of life. This order shall indeed take its beginning from the sixth time of the **second state** (as I have already said); but it shall achieve its increase more fully in the time of the **third state**. 

These mysteries are exceedingly great and must be weighed with diligent scrutiny. And although they have been discussed above, it should not seem burdensome if, for the sake of the place and the cause, we imitate the apostle <margin>Philippians 3</margin> who says: **"To write the same things to you is not troublesome to me, and for you it is necessary."** <note>original: "Eadē vobis scribere mihi qdē nō pigruz: vobis aūt necessariū." — Phil 3:1</note> Certainly, John the Baptist preceded the Lord in his birth; he preceded him in preaching and baptizing. Yet, because the birth—and I do not say only the birth, but also the preaching and baptism—of both were so different, it was undoubtedly for the sake of a great mystery to be fulfilled in the two states of the world. 

Do you wish to know why this is so? Read the gospels and the Acts of the Apostles; note the dissonance of the **letter which kills**, and weigh the necessary spiritual understanding. For certainly the holy apostles were already baptized in Christ and had already received the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of water; Truth itself had already borne witness to them, saying: **"You are washed."** They had already received the gift of the Holy Spirit on Easter day when Christ was taken up from them; and yet, on the same day he ascended into heaven, they heard the Lord promising

<column-break/>

to them the gift of the Spirit, saying: **"John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now."** <margin>Acts 1</margin> This was said, I say, on that day when the Lord ascended into heaven, as if they themselves had not also been baptized in water, and as if they had not already received the Holy Spirit. 

It is as if grace had been denied only to those who were obedient to John, when we know that even before then, so many were made safe by grace—great and illustrious men, the patriarchs and prophets through whom the same Spirit spoke. He made them all safe from the sin of our father’s transgression, not by the sacrament of baptism, but rather by a **hidden grace**, just as is said by the voice of Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: **"Why do you tempt God to place a yoke upon the neck of the disciples <margin>Acts 15</margin> which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear, but through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe we are saved just as they?"** 

But what shall we say to this? Must we turn back to the spirit where the letter fails? Yes, it is so. For if we seek this truth, we find that the letter becomes empty in every way; because in the Old Testament, certain people were baptized with the Holy Spirit through hidden grace, and in the New, the baptism of water remains even until now, the Lord saying: **"Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."** <margin>John 3; Acts 1</margin> 

How is it, then, that he says: "John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit," when the baptism of water is still necessary? It is because that which John signifies in the **second state** was to be enacted through Christ, and that which the Lord designates was to be consummated in the **third state** through the Holy Spirit. This was to fulfill what he himself said: **"I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. <margin>John 16</margin> But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth."** 

Finally, Zechariah, the father of John, designates the fathers of the **first state**; just as John designates the chosen sons belonging to the ecclesiastical time (which is properly of the second state); and just as the man Christ Jesus designates those spiritual men whom the grace of the Holy Spirit makes to despise the world and those things which are...

The author is describing the "Third State" of the world—a future era of spiritual perfection—and how the conversion of the Jewish people fits into this divine timeline.</meta>

<margin>Romans 11</margin>
...of the world belonging to the **third state** of the age: in which, once the fullness of the Gentiles is complete, all Israel shall be saved. <note>original: "omnis israel salvus fiet" — Romans 11:26</note> Nor should that opinion held by many disturb you—namely, that for the conversion of Israel, only a very short time remains. Yet no writer has dared to fix a specific limit or end to this time, because of the most hidden and ambiguous voices of the mysteries, which do not always allow themselves to be fully investigated. This is especially true since now a thousand
<margin>1 John 2</margin>
years and more have passed since John was heard to say: "Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that Antichrist is coming, so now many Antichrists have appeared; by this we know it is the last hour." <note>original: "filioli nouissima hora est" — 1 John 2:18</note> For who at that time could read those things and not believe the times of the Antichrist were already pressing? However, a man full of God could not be deceived; nor did he say this falsely to cause terror, as some dream. Rather, he said it because **Peter** signifies the elect of the **second state**, while **John** signifies the elect of the **third state**. This is seen in what the Lord said to Peter:
<margin>John 21</margin>
"Follow me"; but concerning John: "If I will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?" He speaks here in the person of that "order" <note>A specific group of spiritual people expected to arise in the future.</note> which the Church of Philadelphia signifies; and he says what we were meant to say—indeed, he taught it to his own as children, saying: "Little children, it is the last hour." This last hour is like the twelfth hour, because that eleventh hour was the one in which the Gentiles were called to the faith. Whether the span of this last hour is longer than men think or not, the state itself will nonetheless have its portion in the remnants of the Jews and the Gentiles who have been left in blindness until now. For even if the span of that time is short, it will be more abundant than the others in the gift of grace, so that the harvests of many years are gathered into one. For that generation will be powerful in work and word, as the anointing of God will teach them concerning all things, just as
<margin>John 2</margin>
the same John says to those in the spirit: "You have received an anointing from the Holy One and you know all things." And a little later: "You have no need for anyone to teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about all things." <note>1 John 2:20-27</note> Certainly, to those to whom he seemed to say this literally, they were ignorant of many things as men, by the testimony of
<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
his fellow apostle Paul, who speaks in the person of the men of that state (of which he and Peter were ministers), saying: "Now we know in

<column-break/>

part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away." Therefore, this word is not to be referred to those to whom the letters seemed to be sent, but rather to that "order" for whom he and they together displayed the mystery of significance. Specifically, it refers to how when the apostle Peter was assigned to his passion to follow the Lord, this John alone of the fellow disciples was left behind to designate that order which this angel of Philadelphia designates in this place, to whom it is also said:

<margin>T. 10</margin>
### These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David; who opens and no one shuts; who shuts and no one opens.

<margin>1 John 2</margin>
Behold those to whom it was said by John: "You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things, and you have no need for another to teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about all things." And lest we be forced to say what this **key of David** is, let it be known to all to whom it is given to know and taste even a little: it is the secret and free jubilation of the Psalms. This properly pertains to the **Holy Spirit**, just as the study of reading pertains to the **Word** [the Son], and the work of hands to the **Father**. For indeed, many are the testimonies of the scriptures that what was made is said to be made by God the Father, and all that was made was made through his Word. Among these is that saying: "From him and through him,"
<margin>Romans 11</margin>
and that which is similar. Truly, that which is added—"and in him"—pertains to the Holy Spirit without doubt. For just as all things are *from* the Father and all things are *through* the Son, so also *in* the Holy Spirit, which is the Love <note>original: "charitas"</note> of God, all things must be brought to completion. For the Lord has done all things that he willed, and certainly his will is Love. He loved the good things he made; and for the sake of those he loved, he made those things which were not to be loved for their own sake—not in the state they were by nature, but in the state where they departed from the path of truth by misusing their judgment.
<margin>John 12</margin>
Certainly, because this name "all" <note>original: "omne"</note> which is used often does not encompass everything it seems to sound like, as in: "If I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself." And through him it pleased him
<margin>Romans 11</margin>
to reconcile all things in himself. So that here it is said only of the elect things: "From him, and through him, and in him are all things." Nor is it in vain, since besides those things which are blessed or to be blessed, the rest are counted as nothing...

### On the First Epistle of John [and] On the Apocalypse ###

...all things must be weighed. Since it is certain that God shares His wisdom with His chosen ones and bestows the perfection of all grace through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the reason for the saying is clear: *From him, and through him, and in him are all things.* <note>original: "Ab ipso: & per ipsum & in ipso sunt oia" — Romans 11:36</note> Doubtless this is because by the **word of the Lord** <margin>Psalm 32</margin> the heavens were made firm, and all their power comes from the **breath of His mouth**. For God spoke long ago to our fathers through the prophets; most recently, in these days, He has spoken to us through His **Son**, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the ages. <margin>Hebrews 1</margin> But the Son, in the same way, promised that He would speak to His chosen ones through the **Holy Spirit**, saying (among other things) to those who had been with Him from the beginning: "I have spoken these things <margin>John 14</margin> to you while staying with you; but the **Paraclete**, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, He will teach you all things, and will suggest to you everything I have said to you." And again: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; <margin>John 16</margin> however, when that **Spirit of Truth** comes, He will teach you all truth." Where all truth comes to be known, there indeed is the final consummation. Therefore, these three things belong to the Three Persons equally; yet it seems that according to a certain order, **reading** pertains to the Son, while **jubilation** <note>In this context, "jubilation" refers to the wordless, joyful singing of the heart during prayer.</note> pertains to the Holy Spirit. This is because the fear of God demands true service; the mastery of Christ demands subjection to His doctrine; and the joy of the Holy Spirit demands the rhythmic dance of jubilation. Finally, one can seek wisdom if they fear punishment; but one cannot sing and praise unless they love. Often, one who does not love still sings, but he sings for himself, not for God. And if he does it by force, he sings neither for himself nor for God; indeed, if it does not proceed from the heart, he does not sing at all, because he does not truly rejoice in the Lord, but only appears to rejoice. Therefore, whoever is saddened by a "bad sadness"—that is, a sadness that is not according to God—should, according to the voice of James, <margin>James 1</margin> sing with a calm mind. And whoever seeks wisdom should love God and ask in faith, and it shall be given to him sufficiently, just as He Himself says: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach." Hence the Psalmist, to whom this concluding thought belongs, wishing to show that the perfection of doctrine can be obtained through **psalmody**, professes and says: "But I will always <margin>Psalm 70</margin> hope and will add to all your praise; my mouth will announce your justice, and your salvation all the day." And when he was asked about the fruit he had gained from this, he added: "Because I did not know literature <note>original: "litteraturam" — referring to human learning or formal academic study.</note>, I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember your justice alone. God, you have taught me from my youth, and even until now I will announce your wonders." This is what it means to possess this virtue: the constant jubilation of the Psalms. The blessed Pope Gregory also <margin>Gregory</margin> testifies to this, saying: "The voice of psalmody, when performed with the heart's intention, prepares a path to the heart for the Almighty God, so that He may pour into the intent mind either the mysteries of prophecy or the grace of compunction." This, therefore, is the **Key of David**; it is the opening of the prophets: namely, the intent, devoted, and constant jubilation of psalmody, free from the wound of vanity, and planted for God's sake. Through this, a way is prepared for the Lord to descend into the heart and, by setting it on fire with His grace, make it understand the secrets of God. The prophet Elisha is a witness to this: when he <margin>4 Kings 3</margin> did not know how to answer the king who was questioning him, he began to sing before the Lord, so that by what he did once, many might learn from his example what ought to be done daily. For it is written in the same book: "A sacrifice of praise shall honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God." <margin>Psalm 49</margin> And rightly is this the **key** which Christ holds. To David, who was the Anointed of the Lord, it was first granted; for unless someone is granted enough of the divine anointing to make them a praiser of the Lord, God may remain with them temporarily, but cannot remain eternally. For whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him; <margin>1 John 4</margin> but from the one who does not remain in charity, the truth recedes, just as it did from the proud Saul. In such a person, there remains only anger and a sluggishness of mind, which perhaps is not absurdly called "an evil spirit from God." That was the spirit that troubled Saul. For the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul <margin>1 Samuel 16</margin> and was directed toward David; and an evil spirit from God began to trouble Saul himself, which David often drove away by singing psalms with his hand, not without a miracle. This is what we mentioned above: "Is anyone among you sad? <margin>James 5</margin> Let him pray with a calm mind and sing psalms." For the virtue of psalmody is so praiseworthy—or rather, the virtue of Him who is called upon through it—that it not only keeps a healthy person in joy, but also strengthens and heals the one who is crushed in heart. By giving comfort to the heart, it cures the bitterness of the mind. Hence, in a certain place, the Psalmist himself said: "You have turned my mourning into <margin>Psalm 29</margin> joy for me; you have cut off my sackcloth and cir/"

### Abb. Part of the Exposition ###

...you have clothed me with gladness: so that my glory may sing to you: and I may not be filled with regret: O Lord my God, I will confess to you forever. <gloss>Psalm 29</gloss> <note>original: "cundedisti me letitia... dñe deus meus in eternum pfitebor tibi." This is Psalm 30:11-12 in modern bibles.</note> If indeed it was foreknown and preordained by God that this good thing in the human race—this very **spiritual anointing**—should be perfected, it was not unfittingly given as a gift of grace to that man who, through **material anointing**, was anticipated in the blessing of sweetness. This was done so that the work might not seem to exist because of grace, but rather grace because of the work (which is false). For anointing does not come because the praise of the just man precedes it; rather, praise follows the anointing and is preserved by it, lest it depart from an ungrateful man through the evil of pride.

But we ought to examine even more subtly: why was the privilege of this **key** <note>The "Key of David" mentioned in Revelation 3:7, symbolizing authority over spiritual understanding.</note> given to King David more than to any other? It is clearly gathered from those things handed down to us in the Holy Scriptures that the entire history of the Hebrews, from the patriarch **Abraham** until the **Babylonian exile**, is distinct in three characteristics.

The first indeed preceded in the **patriarchs**.
The second followed in the **judges**.
The third succeeded in the **kings**.

Although the holy patriarchs and the venerable judges were men of great worth (though not all of them), the **mystic anointing** was nonetheless conferred only upon the kings. It was given first to Saul; but because he did not remain in the grace given to him by obeying the voice of the Lord, the Spirit was directed toward **David**. <margin>1 Samuel 16</margin> Whether it is because the Spirit of the Lord was directed into David, or because kings signify the <term>prelates</term> <note>Ecclesiastical leaders or "superiors" in the spiritual hierarchy.</note> of the **Third Status** in this mystery—for whom it is said in Daniel: <margin>Daniel 7</margin> "The kingdom which is under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High"—just as judges signify the leaders of the second status, and patriarchs the leaders of the first.

Who does not see how appropriately it was given to the first of the kings of Judah and Jerusalem to compose the **ten-stringed psaltery** and the book of Psalms? This book properly belongs to the **Holy Spirit**, who speaks spiritual words and sings through it. In the first state of the world, the focus of the Fathers was to narrate the great works of the Lord begun at the origin of the world. In the second, the focus of the "Sons" was to seek the **mystic wisdom** of the kings and the mysteries hidden from the generations of the ages. Since they have learned that in both Testaments God made all things in wisdom, what remains for us now but

<column-break/>

to sing psalms and rejoice in Him, praising Him whose works are great, whose wisdom is manifold, and whose mercy is abundant? For He comes to us, as it were, as the **Father** when we believe Him to be the author of all things through the things that have been made: the Creator of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible, celestial, terrestrial, and infernal. Recognizing His power, we are shaken by a vehement fear, perceiving and attending to that which we heard in the Psalm: "Come and see the works of God: He is terrible in His counsels <margin>Psalm 65</margin> <note>Modern Psalm 66:5.</note> over the sons of men."

As the **Son**, He truly comes to us when we venerate the doctrine of His words, for He is the Wisdom of the Father. But the **Holy Spirit** is said to come to our hearts and rest there when we taste how sweet <gloss>He had come</gloss> the sweetness of His love is, so that it pleases us more to sing psalms than to be silent from the praise of God. For He who can never be absent, since He is everywhere, is in no way distant from anyone by the presence of His majesty. However, He is said to depart from us when we, by the merit of our iniquity, distance ourselves from the knowledge of Him.

For when we harden our hearts so that we do not fear the Father, then the Father is said to be far from us, because He is not near us through **inhabiting grace**. When our sense is dulled so that, being blunted, it cannot understand God or see with the mind's eye the **Wisdom of God**—that is, that true light which enlightens every man coming into this world—then the Only-Begotten Son of God is said to be distant and to depart from us; <margin>John 1</margin> not because He is not in us by the presence of His divinity, but because He is not with us by inhabiting grace. But also, when the soul is blinded so that it cannot love, then surely the **Holy Spirit**, who is the charity of God, is said to depart from whoever it may be; not because He is not there by the presence of His divinity, but because He is far from him by inhabiting grace.

There are therefore three things by which God, who is one and one <note>Likely referring to the Unity in Trinity.</note>, is said to approach us: **Fear, Wisdom, and Charity**. And there are three things through which these three remain in us: **Labor, Reading, and Jubilation** (Singing). For if you wish to have fear, do not be idle; for idleness despises punishment, knows not judgment, is ignorant of groaning, and thinks little of fury. For he who does not experience humble miseries, lest...

### On the First Epistle of John and the Apocalypse ###

...knows how it is expedient to meditate on eternal things. Why, therefore, should you exhaust yourself in labor so that you are never found idle in your day, as far as your strength allows, except when you are either reading, or chanting the psalms, or humbly praying to your God? But if you wish to be wise with that wisdom which is from heaven—or rather, if you wish that wisdom itself not to desert you—devote yourself humbly to reading and insist upon constant meditation, except when chanting and praying, which is to be more at leisure for God and to perfectly persist in wisdom. If, however, you desire to have the **charity** <note>original: "charitatez" — in a medieval context, this refers to 'Caritas', the highest form of divine love.</note> of God, love **psalmody** <note>The practice of singing or chanting the Psalms.</note> before all things and above all things. Yet do this so that you are not seen by men, nor for any other reason than for the glory of God, for giving thanks, and for praises for all His benefits and mercies. Therefore, he who chants the psalms in this way is more blessed than he who merely reads; for the former finds everything in this one act, although those other two <note>Reading and meditation.</note> are not to be thought little of, especially since one arrives at the former through them. It is not, therefore, in vain that **John**, who signifies the elect of the **Third State**, so greatly preaches charity, saying to those to whom he wrote, whom he also calls "children":

<margin>1 John 2</margin>
*You have no need that anyone teach you; but as his anointing teaches you concerning all things.* <note>1 John 2:27</note> This is that **spiritual anointing** which drove the Lord into the desert after He was baptized by John—or rather, it is that anointing of which the Lord says:

<margin>Matthew 4; Acts 1</margin>
*But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.* For the same Lord was baptized by John in water when He was beginning to be about thirty years of age, in the year (as is thought) when John began to preach and baptize: namely, in the fifteenth year of the impious Tiberius Caesar. He who had come for this purpose in the spirit perhaps preceded Him by five months, just as John preceded Him in his mother's conception and birth—a reason which seems fit enough to approve. For the five months by which John is thought to have preceded Christ in baptizing designate the **five ecclesiastical ages** <note>The author is likely referring to a specific chronological system of five periods of the Church's history preceding the era of the Spirit.</note> about which we treated above, just as the five months during which **Elizabeth** hid herself before she was to conceive the mother of God. For that John was handed over <note>Arrested.</note> once Jesus was baptized signifies almost exactly what was said at the beginning of this work concerning the two sisters <note>Referring to Leah and Rachel from Genesis, often used as types for the Active and Contemplative lives.</note>: namely, that the one would be weakened in childbirth, and now, when

<column-break/>

the child was given to **Rachel**. This also relates to what was said of the mother of John and the mother of the Lord under a similar covering of the **sacrament** <note>In this context, 'sacramentum' means a sacred mystery or symbolic hidden meaning.</note>: namely, that the labor of preaching ceases where God begins to be the teacher of teachers. Hence, it is written through the prophet:

<margin>Jeremiah 31</margin>
*Behold, the days come, says the Lord, and I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not according to the pact which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—a pact which they made void, and I ruled over them, says the Lord. But this shall be the pact which I will make with the house of Israel: After those days, says the Lord, I will give my law in their bowels, and I will write it in their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And a man shall no longer teach his neighbor or his brother, saying: "Know the Lord," for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord; for I will be merciful to their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.*

Nevertheless, we do not deny that in that Third State there will be teachers designated in Christ, of whom it is also said to Daniel by the angel:

<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
*Those who instruct many in justice shall be like the splendor of the firmament, and like stars for perpetual eternities.* But because the mysteries will then be naked and open, there will be no labor for those teachers in teaching, nor for the perfected disciples in retaining, for they will be **men teachable by God**. Thus, the labor of doctrine shall pass away, and the liberty of loving shall remain. The Apostle teaches this most aptly in his epistle to the Corinthians regarding the **letter and the spirit**, and regarding the late conversion of the Jews, saying thus:

<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
*Until this very day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over the hearts of the Jews; but when they shall have been converted to God, the veil shall be taken away.* And because this very thing is a state of servitude—namely, to remain under the veil and under the letter, since a servant does not know what his master is doing—while liberty is to be freed from the veil and to know all things which a son hears from his father, he added and said: *But the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.* Where he also immediately added:

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
*But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with an unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by [the Spirit of the Lord].*

## First Exposition on John ##

...he knows how it is fitting to think on eternal things. Why then do you avoid labor, so that you are never found idle on that day, as much as your strength allows? Except, of course, when you either read, or sing psalms, or humbly pray to your God. If indeed you wish to be wise—with that wisdom which is from heaven—or rather, if you wish that wisdom itself never deserts you: devote yourself humbly to reading, and persist in constant meditation; except when you are singing psalms and praying, which is to be even more "at leisure" for God <note>The author uses "vacare," meaning to be free from worldly labor to focus on the divine</note> and to perfectly persist in wisdom. If, however, you desire to have the charity of God: love **psalm-singing** <term>psalmodia: the act of singing or reciting the Psalms as a spiritual discipline</term> before and above all things. Yet, do so in such a way that you are not seen by men, and say nothing except for the glory of God, for the giving of thanks, and for praise for all His benefits and mercies. He is more blessed, therefore, who sings psalms in this way than he who reads; for the former finds everything in this one act, even though those other two <note>reading and meditation</note> are not to be held in small regard, especially since one arrives at the former through them. It is not in vain, therefore, that John—who signifies the elect of the **third state** <note>In the theology of Joachim of Fiore, the "Third State" is the coming Age of the Holy Spirit, characterized by love and spiritual understanding</note>—so greatly preaches charity, saying to those to whom he wrote, whom he also calls "sons": <margin>1 John 2</margin> *You have no need for anyone to teach you, but as His anointing teaches you about all things.* This is that spiritual anointing which drove the Lord, after He was baptized by John, into the desert; or rather, it is that anointing of which the Lord says: <margin>Matthew 4; Acts 1</margin> *But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.* For that same Lord was baptized <margin>Luke 3</margin> by John in water when He was beginning to be about thirty years old: in the year, as it is thought, in which John began to preach and baptize: namely, the fifteenth year of the impious Tiberius Caesar. Just as John came in the spirit to this end, he perhaps preceded Him in baptizing by five months, just as he did in his mother's conception and in his own birth; a reason which seems appropriate enough to approve. For the five months in which it is thought John preceded Christ in baptizing designate the five ecclesiastical periods <note>A reference to the ages of the Church or world history</note> which were treated above; just as the five months in which Elizabeth hid herself before she was to conceive the mother of God <note>Elizabeth was actually the mother of John the Baptist; the author is drawing a mystical parallel between the two pregnancies</note>. For the fact that John was handed over <note>arrested</note> after Jesus was baptized signifies almost the same thing as was said at the beginning of this work concerning the two sisters: namely, the sister weakened in childbirth, and now, when the child

<column-break/>

was given and conceived by Rachel <note>Rachel and Leah represent the contemplative and active lives; Rachel finally conceiving marks the transition to the contemplative age</note>; and that which was said of the mother of John and the mother of the Lord, under a similar covering of a sacrament: undoubtedly, that the labor of preaching fails where God begins to be the teacher of teachers. Whence it is also written through the prophet: <margin>Jeremiah 31</margin> *Behold, the days come, says the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah: not according to the pact which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; a pact which they made void, though I was their master, says the Lord. But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel. After those days, says the Lord, I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their hearts: and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And a man shall no longer teach his neighbor, and a man his brother, saying: "Know the Lord": for all shall know me, from the least of them even to the greatest, says the Lord: for I will be merciful to their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.* Nor do we therefore deny that in that **third state** there will be teachers designated in Christ, of whom it is also said to Daniel by the angel: <margin>Daniel 12</margin> *Those who instruct many unto justice shall be as the brightness of the firmament, and as stars for all eternity.* But because the mysteries will now be naked and open, there will be no labor for those teachers in teaching, nor for the perfected disciples in retaining what they learn; because they will be men "taught by God." Thus the labor of doctrine shall pass away, and the liberty of loving shall remain; which the Apostle teaches most aptly in his epistle to the Corinthians concerning the letter and the spirit, and concerning the late conversion of the Jews, saying: <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> *Until this very day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over the hearts of the Jews; but when they have turned to God, the veil shall be taken away.* And because this is the very nature of servitude—namely, to remain under a veil and under the "letter," since a servant does not know what his master is doing—while liberty is to be freed from the veil and to know all things which a son hears from his father, he added and said: *Now the Lord is the Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.* Where he also immediately adds: <margin>Ibid.</margin> *But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.*

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the "Third State" or Age of the Spirit, specifically interpreting the "Key of David" mentioned in the message to the Church of Philadelphia (Revelation 3:7). ->### First [Exposition] of John on the Apocalypse###<-

For what purpose did he come who has the Key of David? Surely to teach and to sing psalms; to heal the broken in spirit and the afflicted in heart; to enlighten those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death; to direct our feet into the way of peace. For he alone <margin>Luke 1</margin> was conceived without fault, and therefore he alone is worthy to sing psalms and chants—he who came into the world without sin, so that it is permitted to no other except him whom he himself justifies and glorifies. Hence, through the psalm, <margin>Psalm 49</margin> he says this very thing: "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justices and take my testament into your mouth?" <note>original: "quare tu enarras iustitias meas..." This refers to the idea that only the pure are fit to speak God's word.</note> If, however, Christ alone is without sin, then he alone, I say, has the **Key of David**. It is rightly said of him alone: "He closes and no one opens; he opens and no one closes," because the judgment is his: to judge the hearts of men who do not recognize the time of their visitation. You shall take from them joy and gladness, so that they do not recognize the glory of God; yet it is his role through mercy to give gladness to the penitent, to heal the brokenhearted, and to bind up their wounds.

<margin>Psalm 146</margin> And so, the **Key** of David is spiritual psalmody <term>psalmodia: the act of singing or reciting the Psalms as a spiritual discipline</term>, given freely—not to everyone, but to those who are designated in "David" <note>This refers to those belonging to the spiritual lineage of David or the coming "Age of the Spirit."</note>, so that they may sing and make melody in their hearts to the Lord, and confess to him because he is good, because his mercy endures forever. If, <margin>Psalm 117</margin> however, you still ask what kind of jubilation this ought to be to be of such great efficacy, first examine what the reading of the holy scriptures intends. At the same time, consider that it profits nothing or very little for those who do not meditate upon it; yet it benefits much and is profitable for those meditating toward the knowledge of truth, toward the notice of God's secrets, and toward perceiving the light—which is Christ—enlightening every man coming into this world. <margin>John 1</margin> When someone has looked upon this rightly, they would understand in the same way that psalmody profits nothing or very little for those who do not rejoice in their God, nor strive to have a portion with those to whom it is said: "Rejoice, you just, in the Lord; praise <margin>Psalm 32</margin> befits the upright." Since joy pertains to the Holy Spirit in the same way that meditation pertains to the Son—who is the Wisdom of the Father—what remains to be understood by the "Key of David" except spiritual gladness itself? By this very thing, it kindles the hearts of men, warms them, affects them, and illuminates them, fulfilling in them that promise 

<column-break/>

of the Lord saying: "But when that Spirit of Truth comes, he will teach you all truth." <margin>John 16</margin> Although both are joy and both are wisdom, it is not without reason that one is ascribed to the one and the other to the other. Specifically, because the Son, through the "form of a servant" <note>A reference to Philippians 2:7, describing Christ's humanity</note> which he took on, and that passion which he endured for the salvation of the world, taught us the way of wisdom. But the Holy Spirit, wishing us to be free from the form of a servant and the reproach of the cross, showed that we too must be liberated; he caused us to exult in joy and to glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. Hence the apostle says: "If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ <margin>Romans 8, Romans 4</margin> from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you." Truth and joy were made there, certainly for the wise, and here is the full knowledge of truth: because through that passion of Christ we were liberated from the slavery of sin, and through the illumination of the Holy Spirit shown to the holy apostles, we were made servants of justice. 

The **Key of David**, therefore, is the effect of spiritual grace, which calls its worker to itself, kindling a person to love God and illuminating them to know all truth. For indeed, he who loves and is loved, and he who is loved and loves, is a friend. Moreover, he who is a friend is introduced inside so that he may see the hidden secrets which servants are not permitted to behold. Hence the bride in the Song of Songs says: "The king introduced me into the wine <margin>Song of Songs 2</margin> cellar; he set charity in order within me." Because in the **Third State** of the world <term>status: the Age of the Spirit, following the Ages of the Father and the Son</term>—which is designated in "kings" according to that threefold similarity we used above regarding regions—this grace of which we speak is to be revealed. This key is rightly said to be "of David" and to be "held by Christ," because it belongs to the one to whom it is given in such a way that it cannot be theirs unless it is given by Christ. Thus it belongs to the recipient, but it belongs much more to him by whom it is given, just as the other gifts of the Spirit. Moreover, the Lord promises that an "open door" has been given before the Angel of Philadelphia—that is, to that order which is signified by him—and so clearly opened that no one can close it, just as it was given to Joseph.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the Apocalypse, specifically focusing on the "Key of David" and the "Open Door" promised to the Church of Philadelphia. The author moves from the spiritual meaning of the Psalms to the interpretation of mysteries and the struggle against those who block the understanding of Scripture.</meta>

### Part of the Abbot’s Exposition ###

<margin>to close the door</margin> To **close the door** <note>In the context of Revelation 3:7, "He who opens and no one shuts."</note> in Egypt is to solve hidden mysteries and to interpret the dreams of the king; so too for Daniel in Babylon, because he himself designated the same order in a similar mystical way. For there are some who seek to close this door, scorning prophecy and "extinguishing the spirit," <note>A reference to 1 Thessalonians 5:19: "Do not quench the Spirit."</note> so that they alone may seem to be masters among the people; by using the occasion of teaching, they seek to exercise lordship over men. These men were well-represented by those experts in the law <term>legisperiti: scholars of the Mosaic Law often criticized in the Gospels for prioritizing legalism over spirit</term> to whom it was said by the Lord: <margin>Luke 11</margin> "Woe to you, experts in the law, for you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering, you hindered."

But there is another way the impious are accustomed to **close the door** of the Scriptures, which this passage demands we consider more closely. For sacred Scripture often opens itself to the faithful, yet not entirely, but only in part; we do not yet see "face to face," but as if "through a mirror, in an enigma." <note>original: "per speculum in enigmate" — a famous phrase from 1 Corinthians 13:12 referring to our limited earthly understanding of divine truth.</note> <margin>they sit before the face</margin> The faithful, especially those burdened with the office of pastoral care, cannot remain silent, but each must speak what he feels. It often happens that while a teacher is speaking and falling into very difficult questions, <margin>what he wants</margin> a sinner stands against him who, resisting his words with dialectical arguments, **closes the door** that seemed open, making dark what was lucid and obscure what was clear. <margin>the difficulty of the question where Moses...</margin>

Regarding this, the Apostle said to Timothy: <margin>2 Timothy 2</margin> "Avoid profane and empty babbling, for they lead much toward impiety, and their speech spreads like a cancer." And in the preceding letter: <margin>1 Timothy 6</margin> "If anyone teaches otherwise and does not acquiesce to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine which is according to piety, he is proud, knowing nothing, but languishing about questions and battles of words, from which arise envy, contention, blasphemy, evil suspicions, and the conflicts of men corrupt in mind." It is implied here: <margin>but why</margin> he is to be scorned, lest he ever seem wise to himself if someone should answer him according to his own foolishness. For ecclesiastical histories testify that scandals have often arisen in the Church of Christ because of such pestilential men.

But what did holy men do when this happened? They ran to their weapons, as holy men do—famed in faith and robust. "And if we cannot," they said, "overcome with words, let us dispute with **signs** <note>signis: here meaning miracles or divine wonders.</note>." Indeed, <margin>Bernard</margin> the **Blessed Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux**, <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a major mystic and leader of the Cistercian order.</note> who in our days uniquely illustrated the Church with his life, miracles, and knowledge, was sent against certain heretics by the Supreme Pontiff who then presided over the Church of Christ. When, after a long delay, he profited nothing by disputing, venerable men testify that he "ran to these weapons" [of miracles]. Therefore, it was not to be said to them, or of them, that they had "little power," <note>Referring to Rev 3:8: "I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word."</note> for they were so founded in faith that they did not fear to presume such things.

But for us, who are weak and do not dare to presume such things—and because we are closer to the "Angel of Philadelphia" of this time <note>In Joachite theology, the "Angel of Philadelphia" represents the leaders of the sixth age of the Church, a time of transition and spiritual trial.</note>—precisely because we have followed that prerogative of faith less, this smallest thing is necessary for us: that we might be able to resist in the "evil day" <margin>Ephesians 6</margin> by confronting false Christs and false prophets who perform lying signs. Thus, while retaining power, we may extinguish all the fiery darts of the enemy.

For let it not be a burden to remember what I recall explaining long ago in the *Book of Concordance*. <margin>Book of Concordance</margin> <note>original: "ope pcordie" referring to Joachim of Fiore’s work *Liber de Concordia Novi et Veteris Testamenti*.</note> When the forty days were completed in which the Lord remained in the desert, <margin>Matthew 4</margin> he was tempted by the Devil to perform a **sign**. But He, who had come to give an example to his subjects and not to seek his own glory, deigned to answer his tempter with what he foreknew would be useful for his members when they were tempted by the members of the Devil during the time of this "Sixth Angel": <margin>Matthew 4</margin> "Man does not live by bread alone," he said, "but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God."

This testimony is taken from Moses, <margin>Deuteronomy 8</margin> being partly "bound" and partly "loosed." <note>A common medieval term for interpreting scripture literally (bound) or spiritually (loosed).</note> For Moses said this regarding the literal manna that the people ate in the desert; yet he said it so that every man might know that man does not live by bread—or by manna—alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Doubtless, that physical manna designated the **Word** of which we speak, the Word for which we ask the Lord in prayer, saying: <margin>Matthew 6</margin> "**Give us this day our daily bread.**"

Truly, at the beginning of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, their food was bread; but when the bread failed, manna was given from heaven. **Bread** designates the "work of miracles," which was given at the dawn of the Church to confirm the hearts of believers and to draw unbelievers to the faith. However, after the Church took root, this was to be removed from the hearts of the elect, lest they seem to be like those to whom it was said by the Lord: <margin>John 4</margin> "Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe." Instead, the **celestial manna**, which is the Word of God for the sustaining of life, was to be substituted...

### First Exposition on the Apocalypse ###

<margin>John 10</margin> ...is it said? and so on. Where is it that those who did not see, believed? <note>A reference to John 20:29: "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed."</note> And this is what the faithful know, and concerning this they act faithfully. Yet he is not far off who—through himself and through his members—is coming to tempt the faithful, throwing up the same challenge that he threw at the Head of the faithful <note>Christ</note>, saying: "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread." <margin>Matthew 4</margin> It is just as if he were saying to His body <note>the Church</note>: "If you are the people of God, show us miracles. If you are the elect of God, make it so that stones are turned into bread; that is, show us a sign that is certain and evident, so that your faith does not appear to be in vain according to those things you say your apostles and predecessors once performed." 

Indeed, to say nothing of the things that are to come and to be proven in their own days, let us speak of those things which are present: the certain signs of things to come. Who does not know the heretics of this time, who are called Patarenes? <margin>The Patarene Sect</margin> <term>Patarenes: a medieval religious movement often accused of heresy, similar to the Cathars, who advocated for extreme poverty and criticized the wealth of the Church.</term> Their most abominable sect is said to have grown beyond measure in various parts of the world; they claim the apostolic life for themselves and call us heretics and strangers to the faith. Indeed, as those testify who were perhaps tempted by them but escaped their cunning, they are accustomed to oppose those they desire to deceive with this: "If the faith of these people who call themselves Christians is true, where are the signs that they preach their predecessors performed until now? Why can they not do themselves what they say their fathers did? It remains that they are proven either to speak falsely or to hold a false faith, because they do not show in action that which they preach others have done." 

And so they speak. But to those for whom there seems to be little strength to respond, a door has nonetheless been opened. <margin>Matthew 4</margin> It cannot be shameful or indecent to respond with what they know their Lord responded: "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." For what else <margin>Colossians 1</margin> should be answered to the sons of darkness, and especially to those who are going to perform signs and wonders to seduce, if possible, even the elect? Indeed, it is a gift not to be undervalued: that a door has been opened for us in such a time of necessity to recognize, as the Apostle says, the "mystery which has been hidden for ages and generations." <note>original: "mysterium quod fuit absconditum a seculis et generationibus"</note> Let us not envy those whose signs and wonders we cannot imitate. For even if to Peter, the first of the apostles, was given the prerogative of faith to perform signs as a "type" <note>a symbolic prophetic model</note> of those who were given as the foundations of the Church, the "key of knowledge" <note>original: "clavis scientie"</note> given to Paul, the last of the apostles, is not to be undervalued. He is undoubtedly a type of those who were to be given at the end to support the Church. Surely, even if those were great to whom it was given to serve an abundance of bread to the hungry, those "least ones" are not to be despised to whom it has been granted, 

<column-break/>

by the specific nature of their gift, to provide water to the thirsty. For He who distributes gifts by dividing them according to the variety of times knows what is expedient for these people or those. Thus, according to the time, one must estimate what He has provided to someone; and that thing is to be judged more dear for the time which is useful, rather than that which is more sublime. 

This is why God Himself testifies that this angel, having only a little strength, has kept His word of patience. Yet He did not wish to reward him with an increase of strength, but rather with the opening of a door; for He foreknew that this, rather than the other, would benefit him through the course of time. "Behold," He says, "I have set before you an open door which no one can shut, because you have a little strength, and you have kept my word and have not denied my name." <note>A direct quote from Revelation 3:8.</note> "Because of this," He says, "I have given an open door before you, because I have given you grace for grace." For He Himself gives that which He may receive; He Himself receives justly, that He may mercifully reward. Happy is he to whom such a great moneylender is a debtor, who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach. <margin>James 1</margin> Because of this it is also said: "A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, they will pour into your lap." <margin>Luke 6</margin> Behold how great is the kindness, how great the mercy of our King! He who is a debtor to Himself, by a prior gift, makes it so that He Himself becomes a debtor to the one whom He owes nothing, rejoicing and exulting in the progress of His servants. 

"In return for the fact," He says, "that you kept my word which you received from me, and did not deny my name in the strength which I gave you in part: behold, I have given you an open door which no one can shut, removing the stone from the door of the tomb <note>original: "hostio monumenti"</note> so that you may see and understand the truth." However, it does not seem to me that "door" <note>original: "hostium" — a medieval spelling of "ostium"</note> should be understood in this place in the same way as in that place where it is said: "Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips," <margin>Psalm 140</margin> <note>Psalm 141:3 in modern numbering.</note> in which the wood itself that closes and opens is understood. Instead, it should be understood by the name of "door" as the opening itself which was closed by the stone—that is, the "surface of the letter" <note>original: "superficie litterae" — the literal, historical meaning of the Biblical text as opposed to its spiritual meaning.</note> which was exceedingly heavy and weighty, so much so that it refused to be moved from its place until that "new Jacob" came. He alone moved the millstone from the mouth of the well <margin>Genesis 29</margin> at the arrival of the time of witness, and gave drink to his sheep, concerning whom it is written through Isaiah: "The needy and poor seek water and there is none, their tongue is parched with thirst. I the Lord will hear them; the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will give rivers on the high mountains and fountains in the midst of the fields." <margin>Isaiah 41</margin> Therefore, what is there called the "mouth of the well," and here in the Gospel the "door of the tomb," must be understood in this book as the "open door." <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Letter to the Church of Philadelphia in Revelation 3, moving from the challenge of faith without signs to the promise of the "open door" and the conversion of enemies in the "sixth time" of church history.</meta>

->Abbreviated Part of the Exposition<-

the opening of the door itself is what is being discussed: that which is closed and opened. In this place, we say that by the "door" nothing else is to be understood but the entrance to spiritual understanding. This understanding was once obstructed by the heavy weight of the "letter" <note>original: "pondere littere"; a reference to the literal or surface-level reading of scripture that obscures spiritual truth</note> so that it could not be understood; yet it begins to be opened to man when the Lord removes that weight from the door of the tomb. <note>An analogy to the stone rolled away from Christ's tomb, signifying the revelation of hidden truths.</note> Moreover, the Lord says that He has offered this to the "angel of Philadelphia"—that is, to that order of the Church signified by it. This is not because such understanding was not granted to the holy teachers in earlier times, but because it was not granted so solemnly and manifesty as it shall be in the sixth time, <note>Joachimist theology often divided history into seven "times" or ages; the sixth age was believed to be a period of spiritual renewal and the opening of the scriptures.</note> when all the seals shall be opened. To this Church, He also promises something great when He says:

<margin>Theme 12</margin>
**B**ehold, I will give to you those of the Synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews and are not, but they lie. Behold, I will make them come and bow down before your feet, and they shall know that I have loved you. <note>Revelation 3:9</note>

<margin>Here regarding the <unclear>wicked</unclear> Roman name</margin>
These words were explained in part above. Just as at the coming of the Lord a remnant of the Jews was preserved so that, illuminated by the grace of Christ, they might provoke the unfaithful nations to faith and subject the wicked Roman [power] (in which the "Prince of the North" <note>original: "princeps aquilonis"; a biblical figure often associated with the Antichrist or an enemy of God's people</note> reigned) to the scepter of Christ; so now, from the Christian people who are called "Gentile," it was fitting that a remnant of blessing should remain. Through these, the "Synagogue of Satan"—which falsely claims to confess the Lord—may begin in large part to be converted. Falling down in their sight, they shall be overcome and say: "Truly, this is the right faith which the professors of Christ preach and announce." They did not hope in vain, nor did they keep the word handed down to them for nothing, nor did they endure insults for the faith and name of the Crucified One without cause. Regarding what He says—*And they shall know that I have loved you*—this is sufficiently shown in what we said was signified in Joseph (who was certainly loved by his father above all his brothers) and in John the Evangelist (to whom this book belongs, and who was loved by Christ above the other apostles). Furthermore, the one who contemplates is loved more than the one who works <note>A common medieval distinction between the "active life" (Martha) and the "contemplative life" (Mary).</note> because the contemplative has chosen that part which the Lord desires us to reach. He wishes us to lack the other [active labor] so that we may arrive at rest. Indeed, He greatly comforts these people and strengthens them with a promise; but He no less terrifies others by what is added in the same place.

<column-break/>

<margin>Theme 13</margin>
**B**ecause, He says, you have kept the word of my patience, I will also keep you from the hour of temptation which is to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth. <note>Revelation 3:10</note>

Therefore, He says, I love you: because you have kept the word of my patience and have acted manfully against the vices of the flesh and spirit, against detractors and deceivers, and against the spiritual wickedness of the enemy. Truly, to be bound in solitude and to be held by the "chain of Christ"—not being carried away—is similar to that punishment which this holy John patiently endured, being banished to the island called Patmos, according to what he himself says earlier: *I, John, your brother and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus, was on the island called Patmos for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.* <note>Revelation 1:9</note> Nevertheless, it is necessary in another way for this "angel" to keep the word of patience: that is, for the sake of the truth which he is bound to announce, even though many do not believe but contradict that same truth. As the Lord said: *If the world hates you, know that it hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.* <note>John 15:18-19</note> And a little later: *The servant is not greater than his lord; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will keep yours also. But all these things they will do to you for my name's sake, because they do not know Him who sent me.* <note>John 15:20-21</note> But why is this? Because the flesh and the spirit, the world and heaven, pleasure and penance do not agree with each other. Whence also, to his brothers who did not yet believe in Him and were urging Him to go to the feast day, He replied, saying: *The world cannot hate you; but it hates me, because I bear witness of it, that its works are evil.* <note>John 7:7</note> Therefore, he who wishes to be loved by God, it is necessary that...

### <margin>Chapter 17</margin> And he shall go out no more.

For indeed, before the victory, many enter who must be expelled after a little while. But after that true victory, he who enters once has nothing more to fear. This is the "specific fishing" mentioned earlier; the first <margin>Luke 5</margin> suffered no small loss because the net was torn, but concerning the second, the Gospel says: <margin>John 21</margin> **"Though there were so many, the net was not torn."** <note>A comparison between the first miraculous catch of fish in Luke (where nets broke, symbolizing the Church on earth) and the second in John (where they did not, symbolizing the Church in heaven).</note> Here also Solomon is mentioned; for in respect to Saul, the first king, and David his father who was anointed king after him, the three statuses of the kingdom are designated (which we mentioned before). To the same <margin>1 Chronicles 22</margin> King David, it was said by the Lord: **"The son who shall be born to you shall be a man of great quiet; for I will make him rest from all his enemies round about: and for this reason he shall be called 'Peaceful' <term>Peaceful: the meaning of the name 'Solomon' (Shlomo) in Hebrew</term>: and I will give peace and leisure in Israel all his days. He shall build a house for my name: and he shall be a son to me: and I will be a father to him: and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever."** Great is this reward promised to the victor, and no smaller is that which he adds immediately after.

### <margin>Chapter 18</margin> And I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from my God, and my new name.

That the Only-begotten of God the Father calls his Father "my God" is a dispensation <term>dispensation: the divine plan or arrangement of God's dealings with humanity, specifically regarding the Incarnation</term> of the mortality he assumed (as I have often said). <margin>Psalm 88</margin> Whence also in the Book of Psalms, speaking of the same incarnate Son: **"He shall cry out to me: You are my Father: my God and the protector of my salvation."**

<column-break/>

**"And I will make him my firstborn, high above the kings of the earth."** In this is his humanity; <margin>Psalm 115</margin> for **"all men are liars"** <note>original: "omnis autem homo mendax"; a quote from Psalm 116:11, used here to contrast human frailty with Christ's truth</note>, because he, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, <margin>Philippians 2</margin> taking the form of a servant. Thus, in another way, he could be called "less than the Father." We, however, with puffed-up pride, extend ourselves beyond ourselves incessantly, desiring to ascribe to ourselves that "good" which nature denied us. Does it not seem to you that we, since we are not "higher," seek after whatever we can, endlessly ascribing peaks and honors to ourselves? And do we not try to usurp or steal even what our merits deny us? But if it delights one to stand in the lowest place, and we affect the most humble position (which is rare), this must be known to be in us through the goodness of God. For he willed to become a man among men so that he might, in his mercy, cure the disease of our swelling pride, opposing it with the medicine of his own humility. Therefore, let it delight us also to confess with a humble heart and say with Blessed Thomas: <margin>John 20</margin> **"My Lord and my God!"** This looks toward the glory of God more than "my equal" or "my peer," which would belong more to our own glory—except when it delights us to say this from the affection of love. 

But as for the name of the Father, and his own new name, and the name of the supreme city, New Jerusalem, which he promises to write upon the victor: what else can we understand but that which is written in the fourth Psalm: <margin>Psalm 4</margin> **"The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us; you have given gladness in my heart"**? There are three names he promises to write: the name of the Father, the name of the Mother, and the name of the Son. <note>The author identifies the "New Jerusalem" as the "Mother," following the tradition of Galatians 4:26.</note> Why is it strange if he sometimes prescribes a Mother for himself, he who willed to have a Mother in his humanity? He looked to no other thing than what the law commanded: <margin>Exodus 20</margin> **"Honor your father and your mother."** And this also is for the judgment and confusion of our pride, because we do not wish to reverently pay to the Divine Majesty what God himself, having been made human, did not disdain to pay to our lowliness. For he did this for all of us, regarding his most chaste mother. Her name has been magnified so that **"his praise reaches to the ends of the earth"** <margin>Psalm 47</margin>, so that by his goodness he might conquer and overcome the evil of our pride, humbling himself for us both in deed and word. In this place, he prescribes for himself that heavenly city, which was once a pilgrim on earth for a long time. I speak of that city of which the Psalmist says: <margin>Psalm 84</margin> **"Her foundation is in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob. Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God."** and a little later: **"Shall not Zion say, 'A man, and a man was born in her: and the Most High himself founded her'?"**

# Abbreviated Part of the Exposition
<margin>Luke 2</margin>
What is this? Is anything greater than what is unfolded below: that he was subject to Joseph and Mary? <margin>Matthew 18</margin> Or that he wished to be baptized by John the Baptist? <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> Or that he did not blush to wash the feet of his disciples? It is always a mark of the good that he who is the Supreme Good demonstrated the way of humility; just as, conversely, we who were by nature "children of wrath" always stand in need of the example of his teaching so that we might stand in the truth. This is the cause of Mary <note>likely referring here to the Church or the contemplative soul personified as Mary</note>: that she should never wish to oppose the form she once assumed, so that at last she might learn to show honor to the elect among themselves. And that the lesser should consider the <margin>Romans 12</margin> greater in some respect: that is, **not to be high-minded, but always to consent to the humble.** For even to this day, men strive over their titles, each seeking to prefer his own name in writing and to demand honor from one another. Nor do they blush, after such great humility from God, to dispute so stubbornly over vain and fleeting honors. If they still know how to do these things after so many examples of Christ's gentleness, what would happen if the humility of God did not oppose such a severe plague? He wished his name to be subscribed, therefore, on account of those who, envying their elders, fall into spite and are corrupted by the plague of hatred, becoming murderers. <margin>1 John 3</margin> According to that saying of John: **Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer;** and no murderer has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. After this, it seems necessary to ask: what can the inscription of the name of the Heavenly City confer upon the victor, since the Creator alone is the Supreme Good, of whose participation the rational creature stands in need? As it is <margin>James 1</margin> written: **Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning.** But it should be noted that God the Father is never read as being "born" or "sent," nor "incarnate" or "given," because he alone <margin>The Son is said to be both born and sent.</margin> is from no one else. But the Son is said to be both "born" and "incarnate," and the Holy Spirit is said to be both "given" and "sent." For the Son, who was God begotten before all ages, wished to become man at the end of the ages; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son from eternity, wished to be given in time to that heavenly city, Jerusalem, so that he might be said to belong to the one to whom he is given. Thus, that City is one spirit with him, just as the <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> Apostle says: **He who clings to the Lord is one spirit.** For if the Word and the man are one Christ, and the Holy Spirit with the Church is one spirit, there can be no doubt that the creature stands in need not only of the grace and communion of God, but also of the man Christ Jesus (who is God and man, one Christ) and of that heavenly city Jerusalem, which is common to angels and men; because he who proceeds from God and the City itself are one spirit.

<column-break/>

For if that Spirit which proceeds in God is given to the heavenly city, how can anyone have him if he is deprived of communion with that City? It is necessary, therefore, for him to remain in the Church who wishes to participate in the gift of God—that gift, I say, which is the Holy Spirit, which is granted to the Church alone. Since he must necessarily profess the Catholic Church <note>meaning the "universal" or whole Church</note> who professes the name of the Father, he does so so that he might have written upon himself the name of the **New Jerusalem**, which is interpreted as the <term>vision of peace</term>. For no one can have true and perpetual peace unless he is granted the gift of spiritual grace, so that his soul may be called either the Mother or the Spouse of Christ. That is, so that he may be marked with that name in which an immensity of love is demonstrated; because "fear" (as John says) "has torment," and he who fears is not perfect in charity, but **perfect charity casts out fear.** <margin>1 John 4</margin> He who is a victor, therefore, has the name of the Father written upon him when, through the reverence of holiness, he is esteemed as a "father" by his subordinates, according to that word of the <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> Apostle: **Though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, through my Gospel, I have begotten you.** He also has the name of the Mother, according to what is said by the same [Apostle]: <margin>Galatians 4</margin> **My little children, for whom I labor in birth again, until Christ be formed in you.** He also has the name of the Spouse, when through the sweetness of love he is joined to that heavenly Bridegroom. And these two names indeed pertain to Jerusalem, which is called both the "Mother of all the elect" and the "Spouse of Christ." And because that <margin>Galatians 4</margin> other Jerusalem, which serves with her children, grows old and fails because of the merit of her servitude, this one is called the **New Jerusalem** to distinguish her from that Jerusalem which is consumed by age. This is undoubtedly because of the gift of the Holy Spirit which she received from the Lord, through which it is granted to her to be able to persist always in "newness," according to what is written in the eighth part of this book: **He who sits on the throne said: "Behold, I make all things new."** Furthermore, the name of Jesus Christ is called "New" to differentiate it from the "Old [Man]" who is corrupted according to the desires of error, just as it is said by the <margin>Ephesians 4</margin> Apostle: **Put off, according to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error... and be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God is created in justice and the holiness of truth.** But if it is asked what this name is...

# First [Letter] of John on the Apocalypse
Z 3

<margin>Romans 8</margin>...the name of the Lord, which is new? It is the very name of Christ, from whom we are also named Christians; when, being reborn in that font of baptism, we receive the spirit of adoption, through whom we are made sons and heirs: indeed heirs of God, and co-heirs with Christ. Christ Jesus, therefore, writes the present name upon the victor: just as that great patriarch Abraham was first honored with a name—which is to be called by "Abba, Father" <note>Abraham's name change in Genesis 17 signifies a new status, just as the believer's name change signifies adoption by God the Father.</note>—there is no doubt that by the example of a good work, others are formed to perform justice; according to which even Saint Benedict, abbot and father, deserved to be named; nor [is it] otherwise for those who walk in his footsteps. He also writes upon him the name Jerusalem: when, either through the sweetness of love, where the mind exceeds itself, the soul becomes worthy of God so as to be called the bride of Christ; or through the zeal of doctrine, which she keeps in her heart so as to nourish children with milk, she is named a mother; for that celestial city is called both bride and mother. Bride indeed (as we have already said) of Christ; but mother of those who are reborn in Christ through the Spirit. But the Lord also writes his "new name" upon the victor, when he himself is called the "anointed of the Lord" <note>original: "christus domini"</note> and a "Christian," according to that which is written: <margin>Psalm 104</margin> **Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not harm my prophets.** <note>Psalm 105:15 in modern bibles; 104 in the Vulgate. "Anointed ones" is "christos" in Latin.</note> But if this inscription of the Lord, which is promised to be made upon him who has conquered, designates the Spirit of the living God—which truly is the case. Who is he who proceeds with these inscriptions here, unless he to whom it is given to understand God the Father, and so to understand as to believe Him to be the Father, and to love Him as a Father and only Father; and the heavenly Jerusalem as a mother, on account of the motherly grace that is in her, and on account of Him who dwells in her towers, of whom even just men are said to be temples; and the only-begotten Son of God as a true bridegroom and brother? What is happier than this inscription? And indeed, you often read these things, often speak them, often hear them; but let the Spirit of Jesus suggest nothing to you unless you firmly believe that it is so, and understand how great a blessedness it is for you to be an heir of God and a co-heir with Christ. It is as if you never read it, because you ascribe this to others, not to yourself. Yet it is no wonder. For who would dare to ascribe this to himself—or rather, who would not rejoice, but that he is able—except he who strives legitimately so that he may conquer? For although all these things are given to the faithful in the sacraments, one cannot hold them unless he strives to fulfill in his conduct what the likeness of the sacrament teaches must be held. For to what end are you baptized in Christ if you disdain to be clean? To what end are you buried [with him] if you delight to live in sins? To what end do you approach the body of Christ which for you was handed

<column-break/>

over, if you do not wish to die for Christ when necessity demands? For what do you receive the holy chrism <note>Consecrated oil used in baptism and confirmation.</note> if you do not wish to be tempered from wine <note>A metaphor for spiritual sobriety and avoiding the "intoxication" of worldly desires.</note>? Therefore, the sacraments do not profit those who abuse them, but those who live as the sacraments signify. When, therefore, a faithful man is led this far—that he is proven by faith, instructed in war, and learned through temptations—he receives the gift of God more abundantly, so that by loving he may understand what is to be loved, and by understanding he may love what he now fully understands. Then indeed he bears the name of God present, and the name of the Son, and the name of the heavenly city Jerusalem perfectly and inextricably written in his mind. This is perfect justice here, and consummate joy. It is not foreign to human sight, nor so strange that it cannot be grasped. For men are accustomed to exult in all the names of those dear to them, so that the more they love them, the more they delight to frequent those names (in their conversations); namely of fathers and mothers, of their children’s children, and of any of their dear ones. But if it should happen that any of them should die prematurely by the debt of death, not only do they not wish to remember their names, but they even take care that they be quickly erased from their minds. Why this? Because great joy has been turned into sorrow, and copious sweetness into an abundance of bitterness. But even if this is naturally present in almost all mortals, it happens even more to those who, amid the misery of the present age, live happily. For those whose life is miserable, death is estimated to be happier than life; since someone who does not have much to rejoice in cannot have cause to be too sad. But if anyone is so destitute and poor that he never had a relative or friend in whom he could have been glad, could he therefore lack examples by which he might be instructed and informed to emulate blessedness? Where would his piety grasp exultation, if some prince of the world were suddenly to adopt him as a son, so that he would be his heir and a co-heir with his children? What if he whose life was unworthy and of a servile condition, were called with messengers and much preparation to his palace with signs of joy? He would wait cheerfully, receive gladly, and once received, place him as a free man among his free children. And behold, the Emperor of Heaven has sent to us a true witness who would say no[t]...

### John’s First Vision in the Apocalypse
