...to you just as it is, he might make the truth of the matter certain. But perhaps that name of Christ wearies you: which he willed to have because of the likeness of the flesh of sin, and because of our sins: so that he might be called the Crucified. If this wearies one who is reaching toward life, then the sick man is wearied by the medicine by which he is led to health. Nevertheless, even if it wearies, both must be handled patiently: because through that which causes torment, one arrives at that which soothes the torment. Therefore, you ought not to shudder at the old name, when through it one arrives at the new: because if there were no death of men, there would be no resurrection of the dead. Those who live badly, however, are admonished so that they may be able to live well with him who says: *I am the resurrection and the life: he who believes in me, even if he were dead, shall live* <note>original Latin: "Ego suz resurrectio & vita q credit in me et si mortuus fuerit viuet"</note>: for this is the new name: **resurrection and life.** For he is not the God of the dead, but of the living. For the "name of the dead" is taken from our old parent <note>This refers to Adam, representing fallen humanity and mortality.</note>: but the "name of the living" is from the new man, who is created according to God. He willed to be a partaker of our old nature for this reason: so that he might mercifully lead us, having been liberated from that same misery, to his own newness. 

And it should be noted that the Church of Christ is compared to a sleeping **Turtle-dove**: which, once the winter cold has passed, wakes up as if from the sleep of death and is stirred: and emerging renewed from its hidden dwellings, it appears manifest before the eyes of those watching. Just so, the Church lives in the soul, and even if she sleeps in the body, she lays aside the old garment so that she may be clothed in the new. But he who considers this kind of newness—or, let us say better, these innovations—and meditates on how great a dance of joy it is (not without the joy of hope), has already received the gift of that charity which, through its own perfection, casts out fear. But such a person certainly knows how great this reward is which he promises to the victor. For this is (as I have said) the **grace of the Holy Spirit**: which is promised to all the saints indeed, but especially to this order, which is designated in Joseph, and John, and in the angel of the church of Philadelphia: to whom it is given in the spirit to know hidden sacraments, and to search out even the deep things of God more than is customary. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Seven Churches of Revelation. While the previous page discussed the "new name" of the resurrection and the Church as a "turtle-dove," this page begins the exposition on the seventh and final church: Laodicea. The author continues to use complex tribal allegories—linking the tribes of Israel to different stages of church history—to explain the spiritual state of the believers.</meta>

### Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

¶ Here begins the section concerning the angel of Laodicea.

<margin>Lesson 1</margin>
**And to the angel of the church of Laodicea write: These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of the creation of God.**

Laodicea is interpreted as "vomit" or "lovable tribe." <note>original Latin: "Laoditia interpretat vomitus: siue tribus amabilis." The author is using medieval etymology to connect the name to Revelation 3:16, where God threatens to "spit" or "vomit" the lukewarm out of his mouth.</note> Both meanings, however, apply to this church, in which the end of the preceding state and the beginning of the following state are found. Indeed, the beginning is in this church just as it was in the preceding one, because these two churches are written as a conclusion to the others and are compressed within a single sixth period of time. <note>In the author's historical-theological framework, the history of the Church is divided into distinct ages or "states."</note> This corresponds to the end of the third state, much like the tribes of Naphtali and Dan. According to the beginning, it corresponds to when Joseph and Benjamin appear; what is last in the second state is first in the third state, so that it is both an end and a beginning. It is the end of the second and the beginning of the third. If this is so, it is worth considering how the tribe of Benjamin—which corresponds to the church of Laodicea through a spiritual harmony—was in one respect chosen and beloved, but in another respect hateful and rejected. This is similar to how King David is read to have responded to the proud daughter of Saul (who was of the tribe of Benjamin), <margin>2 Samuel 6</margin> <note>The margin says "2. re. 9" referring to the medieval numbering of the Books of Kings, which included Samuel. The passage describes Michal's scorn for David dancing before the Ark.</note> saying: *As the Lord lives, who chose me rather than your father and all his house, and commanded me to be ruler over the people of the Lord in Israel: I will play before the Lord, and I will be made even more undignified than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes; and with the maidservants of whom you spoke, I shall appear more glorious.* Furthermore, in the days of the Judges, the tribe of Benjamin became exceedingly hateful because of its crimes, for which it was besieged by Israel <margin>Judges 20</margin> and crushed violently, consumed almost to the point of extinction and desolation. Therefore, the Lord appeared to have "vomited" this tribe in two ways: first, when he delivered it to be crushed by the other tribes for its crimes; and second, when not long after, though raising it up, he took away from it the scepter of the kingdom and the grounds for its pride. And because, as it is written concerning this angel, *those whom the Lord loves, he rebukes and chastises,* the Lord did not wish to deliver the tribe entirely into the hands of the nations or remove it completely from his face,

<column-break/>

as he did with the ten tribes of Israel. Instead, he associated it with the tribe of Judah, connecting them in an unbreakable knot until the coming of his Christ. Just as he did with the tribes of Judah and Levi to which it had adhered, he often liberated it from the hand of enemies, preserving it and leading it back to its cities. And since the power of the kingdom was given only to these tribes—namely Judah, Joseph, and Benjamin—who were the first among the tribes that crossed the Jordan to receive their inheritance, what does it mean that Benjamin was joined to Joseph (his brother from the same womb) and also joined to the tribe of Judah with such great affinity? It means that when these tribes act together in a certain way, the tribe of Judah—from which Christ was born—signifies God the Father, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on <margin>Ephesians 3</margin> earth is named. The tribe of Benjamin, which was the smallest among the remaining tribes but nonetheless royal, signifies Him who was *made a little lower than the angels* <margin>Psalm 8</margin> <note>This refers to Jesus Christ, particularly in his humanity and humiliation.</note>. The tribe of Joseph, which was also royal, signifies the Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son. For a time, two tribes appeared to reign separately—that is, the tribes of Judah and Benjamin—but at last they became one kingdom and one tribe. Thus, Scripture says that only the tribe of Judah remained for the house of David, although it is clearly evident from what follows that Benjamin had remained alongside Judah. How the tribe of Joseph—or rather, the ten tribes which were later called Israel—is seen to proceed from the kingdom of Judah and Benjamin refers to the ten principal gifts of God. These are the seven special gifts <note>The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord.</note> and those three general gifts of which the Apostle says: *And now abide faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.* <margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> According to this, at the beginning of the second state, Paul was sent (as we have said) to Ephesus, and Peter to Rome; it was as if Benjamin and Judah were in Saul and David. Finally, Paul was joined to Peter, leaving Ephesus, so that there might be *one sheepfold and one shepherd.* Then Saint John, who was another Joseph, departed with his tribes into the regions of the Greeks. Although many and very grave errors were found among them, there was no lack of spiritual and perfect men among them in whom John’s chastity and the gift of grace might be propagated.

# John’s First Commentary on the Apocalypse

<margin>1 Peter 2</margin>
...spiritual. Therefore, Benjamin the younger preceded his elder brother of the same womb in the kingdom; likewise, Paul, though younger in Christ, preceded the elder John. Or were the holy apostles perhaps not kings, to whom the governance of souls was universally given? Is it not the voice of Peter that says to the elect: *But you are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood* <note>original: "Vos autem genus electum: regale sacerdotium"</note>; and the voice of the same chosen generation which says: *You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God and Father*? <note>original: "Fecisti nos deo & patri regnum & sacerdotes"</note> It is clear, however, that the blessed John both preceded and followed Paul. Indeed, he preceded him in Jerusalem in faith and in the apostolate; but he followed him in Ephesus in preaching and grace. This is according to how the tribe of Joseph preceded Benjamin from the beginning in birth and glory. If indeed from the beginning, since Joseph himself was a prince and lord in the kingdom of Pharaoh—and even among <margin>Genesis 37</margin> his own brothers, as he had seen through a dream—he obtained the princedom. Nevertheless, Joshua the son of Nun, who was one of his descendants <note>Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim, a son of Joseph.</note>, was made prince of the entire people. But as days succeeded days and the cycles of years rolled on, the tribe of his brother Benjamin followed in royal dignity <note>A reference to Saul, the first king of Israel, who was from the tribe of Benjamin.</note>. Then again, when that dignity ceased among the ten tribes after a certain number of years had passed, Joseph <note>Representing the northern kingdom of Israel, often called "Ephraim" or "Joseph."</note> received the height of the kingdom among those same tribes. I say these things so that we may know the difference between the order designated in the tribe of Joseph and the church of Philadelphia, and the order designated in Benjamin and the church of Laodicea; for certainly (as I have often said now), that which is in Joseph is designated in the church of Philadelphia, and that which is in the tribe of Benjamin is designated in the church of Laodicea. As much as is granted to be understood, to that order designated in Joseph and the angel of Philadelphia, that part of doctrine is to be referred which is superior and pertains to divine things. To that order designated in Benjamin and the angel of Laodicea, that part is referred which is inferior and pertains to human things. The first of these shone forth in John; the following in the apostle Paul. But because the inferior part, by which morals are instructed, is temporal and not eternal, as soon as the time of the inferior doctrine pertaining to action is completed, it is necessary that a 

<column-break/>

Hence, one thing is designated in John and another in Paul, where under the name of John both of these orders are to be accepted—just as if under one "Joseph" both Manasseh and Ephraim were accepted together. They also signify something of this together: that Joseph and Benjamin exist because of the different impulses of the Spirit which bring forth various understandings. Therefore, when this understanding occurs, then the two churches of the sixth time <note>Philadelphia and Laodicea</note> are not to be likened to Joseph and Benjamin, but rather to Ephraim and Manasseh—namely, the two brothers, sons of Joseph, in whom the tribe itself was doubled. But when one deals specifically with the second state, then Joseph and Benjamin are to be accepted under one "sixth time," and they are understood to signify what the churches often written about designate. The cause of this change is that which we have often noted. For we have said that the second state, according to those things it signifies, pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, although more properly to the Son, who also worked openly in it; but the third state pertains properly to the Holy Spirit. And through this, when one deals specifically with the second state, in the understanding of that second state, Rachel (who signifies the spiritual life) is to be accepted with Leah <note>Leah represents the active life, while Rachel represents the contemplative life.</note>. # Part of the Exposition

Leah alone with her children is to be understood in the second [state] <note>The "second state" refers to the Age of the Son, or the era of the Church from Christ until the author's near-future.</note>. Rachel alone with hers is to be understood in the third. <margin>Daniel 8, 7, 12.</margin>
more aptly in the book of the prophet Daniel. Therefore, just as Benjamin was the last of all the brothers and was born at the time when his father was already returning to his own people: so, according to that understanding which pertains to the second state, both he and the church of Laodicea designate those final orders of the second state. These are either as if in the crossing to the promised land—a land flowing with milk and honey—by which is understood the blessedness of that state of the church, in whose days there will be an abundance of peace and a wealth of spiritual doctrine until the consummation of the age. Nor should it be troubling that Rachel is said to have been in peril during childbirth: for if the mother is said to die, the children live. But even if that religious order fails in some respect—that which is designated by Rachel—there remains nonetheless that which Joseph designates, and that which the seven tribes signify, of which Benjamin was made the first. Nor is this a contradiction, since the religious order of the second state is designated in each of the twin sisters <note>original: "vtraque sorore gemina." Referring to Leah and Rachel as two aspects of the Church's historical progression.</note>. Since there are two states, they are ascribed equally to the two women: the first offspring of Rachel <note>Joseph.</note> regards the end of the second state; the second <note>Benjamin.</note> the end of the third, whose labor will be in the days of Gog. In this understanding, therefore, the time of Rachel is in the third state, and the labor is in the days of Gog. But in the written time <note>The literal historical timeline.</note>, Rachel's time is shared with Leah, and her labor is at the end of the second state. # First [Part] of John on the Apocalypse

...had hidden in the scriptures until now; it has appeared to us, because of which many have wandered from the faith, for it did not appear clearly enough to be true, at least to the multitude of His elect. <margin>John 15</margin>

For just as the time of the Lord’s birth designates either the beginning of the second state or the beginning of the third, so the time of His passion and resurrection looks back, by way of a likeness, to the end of the second state or even the end of the third. In those ends, the Lord is to give us the spirit of liberty and peace, according to what was designated on the day of Easter and Pentecost in the twofold gift of the Spirit. Therefore, in that time it did not appear clearly enough how exceedingly faithful He was in His promises, because there were very few to whom the gifts of the Spirit were given to recognize all truth; especially since His promise was made in sacraments <note>The author distinguishes between the ritual "sacraments" of the current age and the full "truth" to be revealed in the next.</note> rather than being fulfilled in words in their own times. Yet men believed these things, even if they seemed to tremble as if at an ambiguous vision until now, fearing lest it were some phantom or a lying spirit within them. <margin>Mark 6, Matthew 14, Luke 24</margin>

<margin>Luke 21</margin> 
promised was true; and that His words were unshakable and immovable, concerning which He had said: "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away." And although the Lord is faithful in all His words, He clearly shows in the letter all that He promised before, whether in open speech or in hidden and secret mysteries. Yet that is the highest cause of His promise by which He demonstrates Himself to be, above all, a faithful witness, when He who was promised provides testimony to Him—doubtless by coming and fulfilling the promises and teaching the faithful all truth. ### Abbot’s Explanatory Part

...will begin to be consummated: which has been completed in only a few men, and not without sacramental signs. For the sacramental signs were: the dove, the breathing of the Spirit, fire, and other similar things. In the same way, the days or times in which these things were done are intended to designate something great. Truly, the **thirtieth year** designates the end of the first state <note>In this historical scheme, the "First State" is the Age of the Father or the Old Testament law.</note>; of which end it is said by the Apostle:
<margin>Galatians 4</margin>
"But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law." For how else could we be redeemed from the servitude of the law, unless we receive Him in baptism, who descended in bodily form like a **dove** upon Christ? Regarding this, it is said by the Apostle:
<margin>Galatians 4</margin>
"You have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry out: Abba, Father." Therefore, whether it be John the Baptist, or the water, or the man Christ Jesus who was baptized in it, or the dove that descended upon him—all were shown to designate something, so that through manifest and visible things, we might be able to contemplate invisible and spiritual things. For John designates the teachers of the **letter**; the water designates the outward doctrine which is properly called "the letter." Those baptized by John designate those who learn the canonical scripture according to the truth of the letter, like children still in Christ. Yet from their number comes forth **One** who baptizes in the spirit; to whom the Spirit also provides testimony by descending upon him. For unless the Holy Spirit first descends into a man to make him spiritual, he cannot have a **spiritual understanding**, which is signified in the air <note>original: "aura" — The author links the "breathing" or movement of air with the movement of the Spirit and the intellect.</note>. Therefore, Christ Jesus signifies spiritual men, to whom it has been given by the Holy Spirit to baptize in the spirit—that is, to cleanse the hearts of men with spiritual doctrine and to wipe away unclean thoughts from their minds, as the Lord said: "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them."
<margin>John 20</margin>
But from where does this come? Surely not from themselves? Not at all. But from Him who established the times, giving both darkness and light in their proper seasons. For He gave the **time before the law**, which was like thick darkness and the gloom of night. Then the **time under the law**, which was like the light of the stars. Then the **time that followed until now**, beginning from John

<column-break/>

the Baptist, which is like the light of the moon, because of that
<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
which the Apostle says: "We see now through a mirror, in an enigma." Finally, the **time which is to come**, which shall be like the light of the sun. However, when one speaks simply of the two Testaments, then the Old Testament is to be understood as the moon and the New as the sun; because the Law of Moses presided over the former like the moon, while the Gospel of Christ presides over the latter like the sun. Therefore, a man ought not to wonder if something is promised in one time that was denied in times past; for it pertains to the glory of the Most High God to increase the gifts of grace and to grant to the newest what was denied to the first. This is so that no one may exalt himself because of the honor of his priority, but rather might strive for the good found in the surpassing riches of those who come after. But we also must take the greatest care lest we receive the grace of God in vain and turn our hearts away from the law of God, failing to recognize the time of our visitation. For it is we and our children
<margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin>
upon whom the ends of these ages have come, so that the promises of God might be fulfilled in us—promises which were designated on the holy day of **Easter** through many and immense mysteries. For it is necessary for Christ Jesus to fulfill in the elect of this time what He took care to designate on the day of His resurrection (when the day had already declined toward night) through the **breathing** <note>original: "insufflationem" — Referring to John 20:22, where Jesus breathes on the disciples to give them the Holy Spirit.</note> which He performed. He did this so that we might know the things given to us by God, lest we think any of these things pertaining to God happened by chance. And certainly, this is not a sterile matter, since the Gospel of the Kingdom is still to be preached in all the world. Therefore, our faithful and true witness will fulfill what He promised in that sacrament; He will yet breathe invisibly upon the hearts of the faithful to give a **voice of power** to His voice, and to form spiritual understandings in the trumpets of the scriptures. Thus, as the heralds of Christ blow through them, their sound shall go out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.
<margin>Psalm 18</margin>
Indeed, on the day of Easter when this was done, Truth itself, which had come forth from the tomb on that same day, appeared to His disciples, **opening their senses** so that they might understand the scriptures.

### John’s First [Vision] in the Apocalypse

...understanding which pertains to the third state: or in that which pertains to the second. Not only was this evil found among the Jewish people, but something much worse—the extinguishing of the spirit. For in the death of Christ, they sinned against the **Son of Man** <note>original: "in filium hominis"</note>; here, they sinned against the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "in spiritum sanctum"</note>, so that they find no forgiveness for this guilt, neither in this age nor in the future. For if they had not extinguished the spirit which teaches all things that are true—and which always and everywhere bears witness to the truth—they would have been led to the knowledge of the truth and would have repented, just as those who were stung to the heart at the word of Peter and repented of the sin of their ignorance. But the evil they worked outwardly was a sign of a greater evil they had conceived within: namely, to extinguish the **spiritual understanding** <term>spiritualis intellectus: the deeper, mystical meaning of scripture beyond the literal words</term> and to bury it in the **old letter** <note>The "letter" refers to the literal, surface-level adherence to the Old Testament Law without recognizing its fulfillment in Christ.</note>, so that its voice would no longer be heard in their streets, nor would it have any further place in their possessions. They therefore killed Christ and buried Him in a tomb; they also killed the spiritual understanding, veiling it under the letter of the Old Testament so that they might be permitted to live according to the flesh—which they continue to do to the best of their ability even to the present day. But even though the unfaithful Jews did this, Christ Jesus was not left in hell, nor was the Holy One of the Lord given over to see corruption. Roused as if from the sleep of death, He rose from the tomb; He appeared not to all the people, but to witnesses preordained by God—to those who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead, tasting in that food the mystical and spiritual nourishment which He had promised them while He was still with them, before He suffered and was raised from the dead. In the same way, the spiritual understanding—which they extinguished and buried in the "heart of the letter" (which was of the circumcision)—rose very early in the morning while it was still dark. It appeared in the letters of Paul, who alone set himself against everyone to establish the spiritual understanding, which the faithless Jews always longed to extinguish, unwilling for it to reign over them because it was contrary to their desires and works. It appeared, however (as I have already said), not to all the people, but to witnesses preordained by God: to Mary Magdalene and to others whom the Scripture commemorates.

<column-break/>

<margin>Luke 24</margin>
In this, observe vigilantly: that the more the day itself declined toward evening, the more His appearance became both more solemn and more manifest. For it is believed that He first appeared to Mary, then to the two disciples going to the village which was sixty stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of distance; sixty stadia is roughly seven miles.</note> from Jerusalem. He joined them on the way and spoke with them, yet they did not recognize Him until evening. But after their eyes were opened so that they recognized Him, they returned as quickly as possible to Jerusalem to announce to the brothers what had happened, and how they had recognized Him in the **breaking of the bread** <note>original: "fractione panis"</note>. Meanwhile, while these things were being done, He appeared to Simon, and finally to all the apostles. However, the order of the Gospels must not be confused, so that one may be explained through the other; for the spiritual and mystical understanding looks not so much at the letter as at the power, and at that which is signified more than the signifier itself. Therefore, the two disciples to whom Christ joined Himself on the road signify the **Greeks and the Hebrews**, who daily disputing about the truth (which is in the spirit) indeed see it, but do not recognize it; they are often burning in spirit, but they fail in faith. But when the course of time designated by the "sixty stadia" is completed, their eyes will be opened and they will recognize that truth in the breaking of the bread. And when they return to the Church of Peter to announce their understanding to the faithful, they will find the disciples gathered together saying: "The Lord has truly risen and appeared to Simon." For it was necessary for the spiritual understanding to appear without doubt to the **Latins** <note>The author uses "Latins" to refer to the Western, Latin-speaking Church, symbolized here by Simon Peter.</note> designated in Simon, rather than to the Greeks and Hebrews, who doubted for a long time, and from whose eyes it immediately vanishes and passes away so that they might return to themselves and to the unity of the Church. But to the Latins, it appears truly and without any hesitation, just as the present day of the world proves. Now, therefore, let him who believes, believe; let him who knows, know; let him whom it pleases, be pleased; let him whom it does not please, be displeased. Let the entire Church which is counted by the Christian profession know that the time and hour is now entirely at hand in which all who thirst for the truth may touch it, believe it, handle it, and feel it; so that having returned, they may rejoice and be glad when they find that which was sought. And if perhaps they still do not believe...

### Part of the Exposition

...and they will wonder for joy: let them bring something for him to eat in their presence <note>A reference to Luke 24:41–43, where the resurrected Jesus eats to prove his physical reality to the disciples.</note>; let them touch and see the harmony of flesh and bone: of the Old Testament and the New. For the spiritual words spoken through the spirit of prophecy—which cannot be fully proven until they are seen to be fulfilled—do not yet possess the harmony of the two testaments, but simply announce what is to come. A person who does not know whether a spirit is from God might doubt those words. But here, where nothing is said except what is written—where everything agrees so marvelously as if it were one, like flesh and bone—what room for doubt can there be? It has often been said, and must often be said again: just as the Old Testament was given in the **image of the Father**, so too the New Testament was given in the **likeness of the Son**. And just as the Old Testament contained a **mystical understanding** <term>mysticus intellectus: the hidden, allegorical meaning of the Hebrew Bible</term> which properly belongs to the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father; so too in the scripture of the New Testament—which on its surface relates specifically to the Son—there belongs an internal **spiritual understanding** which properly relates to the same Spirit proceeding from the Son. 

Just as that spiritual understanding, after its clarification, found many stings against itself—the false apostles, the Pharisees, and the Sadducees—so too now it will find those far worse: false prophets and the **beast** <note>original: "bestiam"</note>, specifically the one that will rise from the earth. Truth will be killed in that day and cast down to the ground, so that no one may buy or sell unless they bear the mark of the beast. But though killed, it will live again; it will rise again in glory. While we cannot fully know this now, those who are destined to see it will know. Therefore, Christ’s "late breathing" <note>original: "insufflatio christi serotina," referring to John 20:22 when Jesus breathed on the disciples after the Resurrection.</note> refers to that future time; the power of this act is shown when it is said: *Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained.* Truly, 그 revelation which occurred in the form of fire on the holy day of Pentecost is to be expected at the consummation of the age, according to the principle that all things must be solemnly completed in three states. Nevertheless, just as at the end of the first state, that which was shown in the form of a dove—in that most sweet and beautiful dove in whom the Only-Begotten of God was initiated when the Holy Spirit descended upon him—so too now, at the end of the second state, it is necessary to purify in the likeness of the dove, not so much in 

<margin>John 20</margin>

<column-break/>

one person as in the other Church of the Just. Even there, through the "Son of that Dove" <note>This likely refers to Christ or the spiritual offspring of the Church.</note>, a large crowd of disciples was gathered; a little later, they departed from "Egypt" and passed through the "Red Sea" in spirit through the death of Christ. On the fiftieth day of their departure, they received the law—not from a mountain, but from heaven; not written with ink on stone tablets, but impressed in a marvelous way by the Spirit of the living God upon the "fleshy tablets of the heart" <note>original: "tabulis cordis carnalibus," a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:3.</note>. For in the first state, there was also another "dove" <note>A symbol here for a maternal figure of grace or the synagogue.</note> who gave birth to **Jacob**, while **Esau** was considered a stranger; she, like the Mother of the Lord, bears the likeness of Mother Grace. 

Now, twelve sons were fathered by Jacob, just as twelve were fathered in the spirit by Christ Jesus. Those sons remained in Egypt for a number of years, just as these remained in the synagogue of the Jews until the time of their visitation arrived. Therefore, in both instances, the "temptation of the desert" followed. In the likeness of Christ, Jacob held the role in begetting the people, while **Moses** held it in leading them out of Egypt until they reached Mount Sinai. Afterward, **Paul** was substituted in the place of Christ to "fill up what was lacking in the sufferings of Christ" <note>See Colossians 1:24.</note> and to be a guide for the faithful people in the "desert of the Gentiles." However, that people fell and was consumed in the desert; not one <unclear>reached</unclear> the end to cross the Jordan and see the good things of Jerusalem, except for two men <note>Caleb and Joshua, the only two of the original generation to enter the Promised Land.</note>. Likewise, so it was for the people who believed from among the Jews. But **Joshua son of Nun** entered that land, leading into it a new people born in the desert. Into this land, **John the Evangelist** enters with those who believed from among the Gentiles. For the "land flowing with milk and honey" is the transplantation of the Church, which cannot be possessed as it should be except in an abundance of peace. 

According to this—as I judge—very few of this current people will remain who began to leave the land of Egypt (that is, the society of those who live according to the flesh), because they do not walk before His face but return in their <margin>mind</margin> to Egypt. But their children, who will be fathered in Christ through the **Eternal Gospel** <term>euangelium eternum: the final, spiritual understanding of scripture that Joachim of Fiore believed would characterize the Third Age</term>—which exists in the spirit, since the gospel in the literal letter is temporal, not eternal—these children shall truly enter the good land. They shall enter the land flowing with milk and honey and possess a fertile and lovely land, which is displeasing to the men of this generation who remember the "flesh-pots" <note>original: "ollarum carnium," a reference to the meat the Israelites missed after leaving Egypt (Exodus 16:3).</note> they were accustomed to eat.

# John First in the Apocalypse

...in Egypt. Now, the first of these were from the Greek people (as I have already said); from them, a new people had to be created, as if in the transition of Benjamin <note>The tribe of Benjamin, from which Paul descended, often symbolizes a bridge or transition in medieval exegesis.</note> or even the apostle Paul, because he himself was healed on his journey. Yet, although he was overtaken by his passion <note>original: "passione preventus," likely referring to his martyrdom or his suffering for Christ</note>, he did not lead that people into the region of peace; rather, it was Saint John who followed him into Asia. And indeed, that people entered the kingdom of peace because they believed in the Lord their God, even though this occurred as a symbolic figure. 

However, those who wavered between the Law and Grace—like those Greeks to whom <margin>Galatians 4</margin> the Apostle says: *Now that you have come to know God (or rather to be known by God), how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, which you want to serve all over again?*—were cast out as reprobates from the memory of the Lord. This happened because they dared to prefer the "letter that kills" over the Spirit, obeying false apostles rather than the apostles of Christ, from whom they had received the words of life freely just a little while before. 

The spirit of prophecy foresaw the ends of these people in the future; to them, in the person of a single angel <note>The "angel" or bishop of the church of Laodicea in Revelation 3:14-16.</note>, it is said generally: *Because you are now neither cold nor hot, but are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth.* These things were said so that Christ might show himself to be the "faithful witness," who allows us to prove by experience what he promised through words or mysteries. This is true even if, in this current time, few things are given to us to understand; they will be given in the first <margin>John 16</margin> <note>original: "in primo," likely referring to the "first" or highest level of understanding</note> so that the word of Jesus may be fulfilled: *When that Spirit of Truth comes, he will teach you all truth.* For if the fullness of his inspiration is to be expected now, how much more when he fulfills what is signified by fire? 

Therefore, the true Christ Jesus is spoken of in these two final angels because he is always faithful and true. He chose to name himself "faithful and true" there, where he will show himself to be faithful in the testimonies of truth that harmonize so wonderfully with one another. This is seen either in the witnesses he sends ahead to preach—whether of good or evil things to come which are to be expected—or in those things which are quickly brought to light in their own time. What was expressed under an obscure riddle in the Scripture of Truth will begin to break forth as if proceeding from a womb, appearing to those who could not believe with their carnal hearts when they merely heard it. And lest they should look down on themselves, thinking they are placed at the very end <note>original: "in cauda," literally "in the tail," meaning the last or least significant part</note>...

<column-break/>

...he showed that he himself is the "beginning of the creation of God," just as it is said through James: <margin>James 1</margin> *Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of beginning <note>original: "initium aliquod," often translated as "firstfruits"</note> of his creatures.* This is indeed what we said above: Paul, the last of the apostles, became the first among the Gentiles. Whence he also writes to some, saying: <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> *In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I have fathered you.* Therefore, let them not be ashamed in the house of the Lord because he writes "last" of the others; nor, out of shame, should they despise themselves or cease to wickedly envy those greater than them. 

Let them look to him who is the "beginning of the creation of God," who in the latest of times was prophesied to be the lowliest of all. Isaiah the prophet <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> says of him: *He has no form or majesty, and we saw <gloss>appearance</gloss> him, and there was no beauty; and we desired him, despised and the last of men.* Finally, he is called the "Amen" and the "Faithful and True Witness" in this place for this reason: while every rational creature, by a certain natural law of its own excellence, lusts after high things—so that no living thing is justified before God unless justification is granted by him—the only-begotten Son of God alone desired to hold a humble and despised place among men. 

He did this either to show himself as that "Truth which has sprung out of the earth," or to show men the way by which one comes to God: that is, that power which is perfected in weakness. Moreover, he himself demonstrates in the Gospel why he is specifically called "Amen" and "Faithful and True Witness" in this passage, when he says: <margin>John 7</margin> *He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is truthful.* For we know that whoever seeks what is his own in offering testimony is rejected by that very testimony; by seeking his own interest, he is proven by just judgment to be a liar rather than a truth-teller. But he who seeks the things of others <note>meaning the glory of God or the benefit of the neighbor</note> gains the trust of his listeners; he is not driven by ambitious greed, but the love of truth alone compels him to bear witness to the truth. Now, if a man is proven to be a truth-teller because he faithfully seeks what belongs to others, how much more is he who neglects his own rights so that the rights of another may be preserved? 

The Truth itself did this, emptying itself and taking the form of a servant. But we, who were by nature children of wrath like the rest—and according to the Psalmist: <margin>Psalm 115</margin> *Every man is a liar*—are nonetheless freed from the slavery of sin by the grace of the Holy Spirit and the institution of the Lord Jesus Christ...

### Part of the Exposition

...the sacrament of baptism: because we do not suddenly receive the whole effect of the thing itself all at once, which we seem to receive in the sacrament. That is to say: that after baptism itself, it might be possible for us to remain entirely clean from all fault, just as we were before sin; since John—who wrote this book—says: <margin>1 John 1</margin> *If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.* As if by a certain natural impulse, we run back—even if unwillingly—to the imitation of our ancient parents <note>Referring to Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden.</note> who desired to be like gods, knowing good and evil. For who is so holy and so perfect, situated in the shipwreck of this temporal life, <margin>Genesis 3</margin> who can say with confidence: "I have nothing to fear from any vice"? This is especially true of the vice of ambition and excellence, since we read that a contention arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be the greatest. <margin>Luke 22</margin> And what is even more pressing: the apostle Paul said (who, as he himself says elsewhere, had already received the first fruits of the Spirit like the rest of his fellow apostles): <margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin> *Lest the greatness of the revelations should puff me up, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan, to buffet me.* For if a thorn in the flesh was given to Paul so that he would not be puffed up, who—no matter their level of holiness—would dare to presume they have been freed from the struggle against this Demon? Rather, should one not fear all the more, the more one rejoices in progressing in virtues? Indeed, if such a person is puffed up, a fall is to be feared, as the Scripture testifies: <margin>Proverbs 16</margin> *The heart is exalted before a fall.* However, he who grieves that he is the least must fear falling into "sloth," which is to be lukewarm. Not only is such a person negligent and lazy in emulating charity, but through the hidden poison of envy—which often touches the hearts of the milder sort—that which was written in the book of Job might happen to him: <margin>Job 5</margin> *Anger kills the foolish, and envy slays the little one.* For the one who is foolish is killed by anger, because while he does not know how to reflect on why something is done, or was done, or when it was not done well (which he himself does not perceive), he is vehemently ignited against the author of the deed; and, as if he had some just cause, he is inflamed by the torches of anger. But the "little one" is slain by envy: because he does not know how to weigh 

<column-break/>

what great joys are prepared for the Lord's "little ones." While he grieves that he is small in respect to others, he is deprived of brotherly charity and is strangled by the snare of envy. It also happens sometimes that those of this sort, when invited to a wedding feast, enter joyfully, thinking nothing of their place—whether the first or the last—at the table. But when it comes to the order of seating, and they see themselves suddenly placed in the last spot, the "servant of joy" <note>The initial feeling of happiness or spiritual zeal.</note> that was in them upon entering is turned into lukewarmness by the sadness arising from their shame. Thus, they are neither sad unto penance (because they do not consider themselves to be "outside") nor are they joyful in doing what is good, recognizing themselves to be placed in the final spot (even if they appear to work under compulsion on the surface). Truly, this happens to them because they do not pay attention to the fact that Abel, the younger, was chosen rather than Cain <note>original: "Layz," a scribal error or variant for Cain.</note>; nor Isaac rather than Ishmael; nor Jacob rather than Esau; nor that Joseph and even Benjamin were loved by their father above all their elder brothers. <margin>Genesis 48</margin> Nor do they notice that the same Joseph, the younger among ten, was appointed by the Lord his God as the leader of his elder brothers; nor that the portion of Benjamin, the youngest of all, even though he sat in the last place, exceeded the shares of his brothers fivefold. They also ignore what the Lord says in the Gospel: *Many who are first shall be last, and the last shall be first.* <margin>Matthew 20</margin> Because, therefore, there will be many in this designated order in the Angel of Laodicea (the last of the seven angels) who, weighing the excellence of others, will despise themselves and become lukewarm concerning the faith, the whole community is rebuked in the "type" <note>A symbolic figure or representative individual.</note> of one angel, on behalf of those who will be like that, when it is said:

> ¶ I know your works: that you are neither <margin>Revelation 3 <note>The OCR lists "Ap. 20" (Apocalypse 20), but this quote is from Revelation 3:15.</note></margin> cold nor hot.

¶ He is "hot" who rejoices in the Lord through His mercy. He is "cold" who is saddened within himself for his sins. Therefore, he who rejoices in the Lord rejoices well. He who understands himself to be a pilgrim <note>A common medieval metaphor for a soul traveling through the world toward heaven.</note> is rightly saddened. For who is more of a pilgrim than he who, through the evil works he has done, has departed far from his God, feeding and guarding pigs in a far-off country? <note>A reference to the Parable of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15.</note> But when does he grieve well, if not when, having returned to himself...

<meta>This page continues the moral analysis of the Church of Laodicea. Having established that even the greatest apostles struggled with pride, the author now examines the state of "lukewarmness" through the lens of the Prodigal Son's repentance and the psychological traps of envy and self-deception that lead a believer to be "vomited out" of the divine memory.</meta>

# John’s First Commentary on the Apocalypse
-> n <-
<meta>catchword: whoever</meta>

<margin>Luke 15</margin> **Whoever** he is, he says with a great groan in his heart: *How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance, but I perish here with hunger?* <note>original: "Quanti mercēnarij..." This is the turning point of the Parable of the Prodigal Son, where he realizes his spiritual poverty.</note> And such sorrow indeed is often accustomed to happen to those who are not yet turned away from the vanity of the world toward a religious life; which, though it is not yet sufficiently fruitful in terms of glory, is nevertheless useful and accepted by the Lord in terms of salvation. For even if it is not yet the kind of sorrow that merits a crown, it is nevertheless the kind that pursues pardon. However, for those who are so "cold" before their conversion, it is entirely following that, once turned, they should grow warm—unless a cause emerges from their location, or a preoccupation with promotion. Indeed, it is not easy for this to happen; on the contrary, it is quite difficult for it *not* to happen. That very preoccupation <margin>Luke 22</margin> is demonstrated among the apostles of Christ in the dispute that arose among them as to which of them seemed to be the greatest. But what comes of it? Pride for the greater, and for the lesser, lukewarmness <note>original: "tepiditas"</note> on account of envy. And if that greater one does not descend, he is near to ruin, as the Scripture testifies which says: <margin>Proverbs 16</margin> *The heart shall be exalted before ruin.* <note>Proverbs 16:18: "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall."</note> But if the lesser one does not ascend in his soul so that he may become free, it is necessary that he be cast out from the memory of the Lord and separated from the fellowship and society of the just. Hence, it is added here:

<margin>Theme 22</margin> **And because you are neither hot nor cold, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth.**

A person is accustomed to vomit up lukewarm water and half-raw food when the stomach is unable to hold what nature finds abhorrent. In the same way, one who is neither sorrowful unto penance nor joyful in the service of God—being, as it were, one who is not fit for salvation—is removed from the memory of the Lord. This is what it means to be blotted out of the Book of Life; for even if such a person was once "inside" through the calling of grace, they are nonetheless cast "outside" through the laziness of their life. And it is no wonder. For he who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, seduces himself. Often, those who are of this sort count up the external good deeds they perform, and they frequently look—unwillingly—at the poverty of the wretched and the neediness of the guilty. While they perceive those others to be sterile, they consider themselves to be fertile. Thus, they are rendered not only blameworthy because they are actually nothing, but also because they boast that they are what they are not, saying they are rich and wealthy when they are actually poor, miserable, blind, and naked. Whence it is added:

<column-break/>

<margin>Theme 22</margin> **Because you say, "I am rich and wealthy and I need nothing," and you do not know that you are wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.**

One is "wretched and miserable" who is indeed far from his own happiness, but nonetheless does not recognize himself to be wretched and a stranger to joy. One is "poor and needy" who is empty and void of good works. One is "blind" who does not see the true light—that is, who does not perceive the Word of God. One is "naked" who does not possess justice <note>In this context, "justice" (iustitia) refers to righteousness or being in a right relationship with God.</note>, as the Scripture testifies which says: <margin>Psalm 131</margin> *Let your priests be clothed with justice.* It is natural (as I have already said) for inferiors to envy their superiors and to show themselves off before others so that they do not seem unequal to them. Since they claim to be what they are not, they are nevertheless ashamed to act as they truly are, lest they seem to lose their status through their own poverty; but those who used to be considered the "first" begin with shame to hold the "last place." For he who wishes to ascend to a higher grade must first descend. Unless someone humbles himself to serve his King faithfully, he hopes in vain to receive rewards and honors from Him. But if someone claims to be from the beginning what he was meant to be only at the end, is it not a confusion for him to incline himself to a humble life when, just a moment before, he was pretending to be great? Thus, envy gives birth to a lie, the lie to ostentation, and ostentation to confusion. And where there is confusion, there is sadness. Because no one willingly wants to be confused, the person who is confused works hard to appear joyful so that they do not incur further shame. But because one cannot truly be joyful if they have no rightful cause for joy, it happens to such a person that they become neither hot nor cold, but are made lukewarm. This is precisely because they say, "I am rich and wealthy and need nothing," while being wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. And rightly is the one who labors under envy proved to be ignorant of his own poverty and blindness; for no vice dulls the interior understanding worse than this one, especially when there is always present that vain appetite for glory. This appetite, no less than envy, distances a man from his own senses, so that he not only says he is what he is not, but even believes it, to such an extent that...

<meta>This page continues the moral analysis of the Church of Laodicea, specifically focusing on the dangers of pride and the refusal to accept a humble station. The author compares those who fall from grace due to envy—like the tribe of Dan or Judas Iscariot—with the "little ones" praised in the Psalms. It transitions into a commentary on Revelation 3:18, where Christ advises the lukewarm church to buy "gold tried by fire."</meta>

# Part of the Exposition
-> n <-

When he sees someone honored more, he does not attribute it to the merit of the one to whom honor is paid, but to himself—believing that because it was not paid to him, he is being disparaged. And so it happens that a proud and blind mind, ignoring itself, both desires honor above all others and, in order to reach that honor, blushes to be humbled along with the rest. In this matter, one ought to weigh carefully that Dan—who was the last of the tribes among the seven in receiving the inheritance—became an apostate before the others from his God; and Judas, the last of the apostles, from the choir of apostles; and Nicholas, who is written last among the seven deacons, from the order of deacons. <note>The author uses these biblical figures (the tribe of Dan, Judas Iscariot, and Nicholas the Deacon) as warnings that those ranked "last" often fall into apostasy because they cannot endure their humble position.</note> Thus it is clearly understood that they received their "last lot" with indignation and refused to stand humbly in their own rank. For they were not among those "little ones" of whom we made mention above, of whose number was he who said: <margin>Psalm 83</margin> *I have chosen to be an abject in the house of my God, rather than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners.* <note>original: "Elegi abiectus eē..." from Psalm 84:10 in modern numbering.</note> Nor were they of those of whom the same Psalmist says: <margin>Psalm 114</margin> *The Lord is the keeper of little ones.* Instead, they are of those of whom the Apostle says: <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> *Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal, and walking according to the ways of man?* <note>original: "Cū sit inter vos zelus..."</note> Nor should one wonder at this: that after such glorious and praise-worthy things were said concerning the angel of Philadelphia—in whom the third state is initiated—such harsh things follow concerning the angel of Laodicea. For just as the praise of the former pertains to the beginning of the third state, so the rebuke of the latter pertains to the end of the second; so that in this turning point of time, light and darkness appear to be mixed together. This is well-signified in the Saturday of the Easter Vigil, in which first the *Alleluia* is sung for the beginning of joys, and soon there follows the *Tract* for the completion of mourning. <note>The "Tract" is a type of chant used in the liturgy during penitential times or funerals, contrasted here with the joyful Alleluia.</note> Certainly, even if the beginnings of this "angel" <note>In the Apocalypse, the "angels" of the seven churches represent their leaders or spiritual states.</note> are found in darkness, there can nevertheless follow a good end, especially where he who is miserable is concerned; for it depends not on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy. Therefore, this order invites one who was previously poor and naked to the true and eternal riches, so that he may truly say what was once said falsely, and that a "change of the right hand of the Most High" might be made for him. For there follows:

<margin>A. 23</margin>
### I advise you to buy from me gold fired in the flame, tested so that you may become wealthy; and be clothed in white garments, so that the shame of your nakedness does not appear.

¶ It should be noted that if the Lord shows that he prefers one to be either cold or hot when he says, *I wish you were cold or hot,* he nevertheless does not intend for one who is already lukewarm to return to coldness. For he who has begun to walk before His face, He does not permit to return again to the cares of the world, nor to look back at the works which he abandoned of his own will. It was indeed better for him to remain where he was than to come from the coldness of the world to lukewarmness; but nevertheless, once he has begun, to stand still in such a state is damnable. To return is miserable; only to hasten toward where he began to go is blessed. In a wonderful way, those who are like this are burdened; for they are sometimes bound by certain "ropes of laws" by the words of their own mouth, so that they neither dare to stand lukewarm where they are, nor are they permitted to return to the life of the world; but, willy-nilly, they must be either entirely happy or entirely miserable and useless. 

Or if, by chance, this kind of conversion was not made out of a previous "coldness," but as some are accustomed to do (as we have learned), seizing the sacred signs of religion solely from the impulse of temptation—those who are of this sort ought to be terrified when they understand this. Realizing they are not free from the servitude of the Lord, they should change their minds even if they do not change their habit <note>The "habit" refers to the distinctive clothing of a monk or religious brother.</note>; and fearing that they presumed to take up the habit of liberty when not called by the Lord, they should hasten with prayers and hymns to knock at the door of God’s mercy. Thus, their presumptuous boldness may be converted into faith, and the grace of God may abound where sin abounded. And this applies to those who are drawn neither by fear nor love, but are tossed and carried away by the impulse of some temptation, rather tempting God with those who fell in the desert than acting faithfully and fighting with those who, like Joshua and Caleb, crossed the Jordan. For Almighty God is often accustomed to show the riches of His goodness even in these cases, making a "hidden calling" out of what was thought to be a temptation of the enemy. 

As for those who are led to the service of God by a good impulse: they are to be rebuked especially in this part if, having changed their habit, they do not change their character—if they do not pass from the servitude of fear to the liberty of charity, without which all religion is mere ostentation. For charity itself is the sum of the states and the first among the remaining virtues; he who possesses it needs nothing, hates no one, and envies no one, because he possesses every good in it—especially that which this angel is admonished to receive. For it is that very fire proceeding from this "fired gold"—that is, from the fiery word of the Lord, of which the Psalmist says: <margin>Psalm 118</margin> *Thy word is exceedingly refined by fire, and thy servant hath loved it.* <note>original: "Ignitū eloquiū tuū..." Psalm 119:140 in modern numbering.</note> For gold is seen to pertain to wisdom, and fire to charity; so that just as from a ray of the sun comes heat, so from wisdom...

<vocab>angel: the spiritual leader or essence of a church mentioned in Revelation; Laodicea: the seventh church of the Apocalypse, criticized for being "lukewarm"; Philadelphia: the sixth church, praised for its endurance; fired gold: "aurum ignitum," a metaphor for divine wisdom purified by suffering or love; carnal: focused on worldly or fleshly desires rather than the spirit; Psalmist: King David, the traditional author of the Psalms; Joshua and Caleb: the only two Israelites of the original generation allowed to enter the Promised Land due to their faith; charity: "charitas," the highest form of Christian love; wisdom: "sapientia," spiritual insight.</vocab>

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual dangers of envy and pride in the religious life, using the "lukewarm" Church of Laodicea as a primary example. # First Commentary of John on the Apocalypse
-> n 2 <-

...we bind together with preceding charity. For this is the "gold tried by fire" and the "desirable treasure resting in the mouth of the wise." <note>The author is quoting Proverbs 21:20 and connecting it to the "gold" mentioned in Revelation 3:18.</note> This is the bright commandment of the Lord,
<margin>Psalm 18</margin>
illuminating the eyes. This is the white garment to cover the shame of our nakedness: I speak of wisdom—not of the world, but that which is from God—which cannot "puff up" as the knowledge of the world does, because within it is the charity that builds up. Both, however, are gifts of God; it is grace, not acquired by works, nor bought with a weight of gold, but given freely by God alone to those who thirst. But if this is so, why does the Lord say to this angel: "I advise you to buy from me gold tried by fire, so that you may become rich"? Is the grace of the Lord believed to be bought in such a way? But such a purchase will not be an injustice if the quality of the price is revealed. For what kind of price that is,
<margin>John 1</margin>
John manifests when he says: *Grace for grace he gave to us.* <note>original: "Gratiam pro gratia," from John 1:16. The author argues that we "buy" higher grace by using the smaller grace already given to us.</note> Behold, you have a fitting price with which to buy what cannot be bought otherwise: because through such lesser grace, which was entrusted to you and which, being well-preserved, has become your own, he gives you grace you did not have. This is so that
<margin>Matthew 13</margin>
it may be as it is written: *He who has, more shall be given to him; and he who has not, even what he seems to have shall be taken away.* So too in the Gospel, we are commanded to trade, so that as we trade with the money we have received, the fruit of the received grace may increase and grow. Nor is this trading only among men; it is much more worthy before God. For just as when we preach to men, we acquire the gain of souls among them, so when we exceed in mind toward God, we merit the gift of the Holy Spirit more abundantly. All this (as I said) is through grace, because
<margin>John 1</margin>
*grace for grace he gave to us.* Thus, that strict but pious moneylender <note>A metaphorical reference to God, who demands a "return" on the spiritual gifts He lends to humanity.</note> allows the poor man to buy gold from Him; but he buys it with a price, not of works, and certainly inspired by Him—knowing that just as what is sold is nothing other than Himself, so the price of the purchase cannot be had except from Him. Therefore, whoever is sincere and whole in faith, whoever is a despiser of the world and an heir of the kingdom, whoever desires to possess the happy fatherland and is occupied with the mysteries of Christ, let him desert this world. Although bound here in exile, he lives as a pilgrim away from Christ; but let him kneel daily over his sojourn, and let him humbly ask a blessing from the Lord,
<margin>Psalm 122</margin>
saying constantly with the Psalmist: *As the eyes of the handmaid are on the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes to the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.* And when, after long prayer, he perceives himself as not yet heard, let him
<margin>Psalm 12</margin>
insist vehemently and say: *How long, O Lord, will you forget me to the end? How long will you turn your face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, and sorrow in my*

<column-break/>

*heart through the day?* And also: *Arise, why do you*
<margin>Psalm 43</margin>
*sleep, O Lord? Arise and do not reject us to the end.* For such an apt correction designates nothing else than the cry of Almighty God and the manifest heat of love, by which he desires those whom he loves to come to perfection. Therefore, no one can despair when faced with the object of a very sharp rebuke, where such great and fitting worthiness of consolation follows—where it is clear that the cause of this scolding is love, not anger; the zeal of charity, not the fire of fury. For that which follows is:

### Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise.
<margin>Chapter 24</margin>

For it is as if he were saying: "If I judged you as one cast off and a bastard, unworthy and reprobate, I would patiently endure your iniquities for a time, so that I might condemn you with the other reprobates in a single sentence. But because, like the patriarch Jacob loved the young Benjamin, so I pursue you—born in the old age of the world—with the prerogative of love. I do not suffer you to perish like the many to whom
<margin>Psalm 94</margin>
I swore in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest; indeed, because of the heat of my love, I do not allow you to remain lukewarm." <note>The author links the "lukewarm" state of the Laodiceans to God's refusal to let them stay in that dangerous middle ground.</note> It is not, therefore, much for me to rebuke for their iniquity those whom I say I hate, like Esau and certain others; but rather those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise.

### Be zealous, therefore (he says), and do penance.
<margin>Chapter 25</margin>

To be zealous for the good among the good belongs to the servants of charity. For just as being "zealous" toward the wicked is the heat of envy, not of love, so to be zealous for the just in God is of love, not envy. The Apostle demonstrates that he has this zeal (emulation) toward some when he says:
<margin>2 Corinthians 11</margin>
*I am jealous of you with the jealousy of God.* Indeed, this emulation—by which Jacob was emulated by Esau <note>The author uses the story of Jacob and Esau to represent the relationship between the Church (Gentiles) and the Synagogue (Jews).</note> among the Jewish and Gentile people—Paul teaches to be fulfilled, saying of it among other things in the
<margin>Romans 11</margin>
Epistle to the Romans: *Their offense is salvation to the Gentiles, that they might be jealous of them.* But this "jealousy" is the zeal of the love of God, by which each of the just strives to please the Father with good works, the more he sees Him offended by His first-born. Thus, he does not think he sins if he claims the birthright for himself through better works; for what the former loses by a just judgment, the latter can merit and receive without fault. If the former did not obtain it by the price of merit, the latter succeeds to it as a gift of grace without crime. For that which belongs to no one...

...is: possession falls under the rule of law. How much more so is that which is given to someone by the one who possesses it by right? Therefore, this angel <note>In the context of the Seven Churches of Revelation, the "angel" refers to the bishop or the spiritual leader of the church at Laodicea.</note> is commanded to be zealous and to do penance. This is so that the one whom the sluggishness of the times had proved to be lukewarm—bearing the past mark of disgrace because he seemed to be wasteful—might strive to grieve with the zeal of a new conversion as much as he had previously sought after vanity. For he is truly zealous and performs penance who, considering himself called by lot to that better part which he had neglected, rouses himself to greater exercises. He does this all the more as he recognizes that he has neglected the superior gifts of love. It follows:

<margin>Section 26</margin>
**Behold, I stand at the door and knock: if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him and sup with him, and he with me.**

O wondrous arrangement of God’s providence! Once, the entrance to eternity was closed; the gate of life was barred with stone and blocked with bolts, so that if anyone seemed to wish to enter, he would fail at the entrance. Because of the resistance of the law’s severity, a rejection was faced at the threshold. But from the days of John the
<margin>Matthew 11; Romans 5</margin>
Baptist, it is not so; rather, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. <note>original: "regnum celorum vim patitur: et violenti diripiunt illud." This refers to Matthew 11:12, suggesting that heaven is now accessible to those who seek it with spiritual intensity.</note> For where sin abounded, grace abounded even more. And what further? Do you think a limit has been placed there upon the goodness of the Lord? Far from it. Rather, the more that wickedness abounds, the more the mercy of God overflows. Behold, from the time of John the Baptist, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. And this indeed is a gift of great clemency. But here, grace overflows more and more: so that it is not only open to the violent, but he himself who ought to be knocked upon, knocks; and he invites the sleepers so that the door may be opened to him. Now, to "knock" belongs to the Lord: either to rouse our hearts by secret inspirations, or to invite us to the prize by clear revelations and promises. To "open," however, is our part: when the hardness of our mind is shattered, we open the inner chambers of the heart to the embrace of his love. And because a crowd of the pious cannot be lacking—those who, at the end of this second state, feel the time of the wedding has arrived—the Bride of Christ herself speaks in the Song of Songs. <note>original: "Canticis Canticorum," the biblical book Song of Solomon.</note> There, Christ knocks at the door so that he may manifest himself to the one opening for the knocker, when he says: *The voice of my beloved
<margin>Song of Solomon 5</margin>
knocking: Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled.* And after

<column-break/>

a little: *I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.* <note>original: "Messui hostium meum apui dilecto meo." The author is quoting Song of Solomon 5:6.</note> Moreover, the bridegroom knocks and the bride opens when she cannot deny him who then loves them with diligence—at least when she is overcome by the vehemence of charity, or provoked by the splendor of his golden robe. For our hardness is placed like a door between God and us, so that it seems the Almighty is not able to come to our hearts, or cannot perform any work (he who can do all things), according to that which is written of him in the Gospel:
<margin>Matthew 13</margin>
*He could not do many miracles there*—that is, in Nazareth—*because of their unbelief.* Therefore, when at his voice we prepare a soul of pierced devotion, then we certainly move the obstacle of the door away from the path of our mind, so that he may come to the upper room of our heart to dine with us. Hence, it is also said by the Psalmist: *Today if you hear his voice, do
<margin>Psalm 95</margin>
not harden your hearts.* <note>The OCR reads "Psalm 99," but the text refers to Psalm 95:8.</note> For he hears his voice and does not harden his heart who, as soon as he perceives the truth, is pierced by his voice. Thus, breaking forth into voices of praise, he may offer to the one who is hungry the food which the Physician has prepared; and he may offer the drink of tears from the pupils of his eyes to the same. For God rejoices in such courses; he is appeased by such gifts and sacrifices, as the Psalmist David says of him: *A sacrifice to God is a
<margin>Psalm 51</margin>
troubled spirit; a broken and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.* <note>original: "Sacrificium deo spiritus contribulatus," Psalm 51:17.</note> And he rightly promises to "sup" [eat dinner] in this place rather than to "lunch," because a bridegroom is accustomed to depart from his wife after lunch to go out to his works; but after supper, the man never leaves, but both rest together. O how happy is the supper in which such feasts are prepared! They are certainly not fleshly and slippery, but heavenly and spiritual. A happy supper, I say, and a happy bed, in which the Father and the Physician rest with their children without any stain. Let it be pleasing, therefore, that with all hardness and sloth of heart removed, we open to the one knocking with a joyful and exulting soul. Let us either run to meet him as he comes at the evening hour, like Leah; or, what is greater, let us snatch him up with Rachel, so that he may rest with us continually. Let us say to him daily in our prayers what those two disciples said with whom
<margin>Luke 24</margin>
he walked on the way: *Stay with us, for it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent.* And what further? Let it be pleasing to us to remain with him, because he is with us, so that we may recognize him in the breaking of the bread. Finally, the time of this angel also touches upon harmony. For "morning" designates the time of that day of the Lord's resurrection. "Evening" is this time, in which he promised that he would sup with us. It follows.

### First Part of John on the Apocalypse
n 3

<margin>Section 27</margin> **To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, even as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne.**

¶ To sit upon a throne is to rest from labor. For as God finished his works in six days and rested on the seventh, it was a sign that in the seventh age <note>In medieval theology, history was often divided into "Seven Ages." The Seventh Age represents the eternal rest of the saints.</note> he himself would rest and cause his elect to rest from the labors of this world. He would give them rest and peace, and furthermore, the authority to execute judgment upon his enemies. For there is a time for patience and a time for judgment. Moreover, the fact that Christ suffered on the sixth day signifies the span of patience to be offered until the sixth age. For the number six <note>original: "senarius numerus." In medieval numerology, six was considered a "perfect number" because it is the sum of its divisors (1+2+3), often representing the perfection of work.</note> is most perfect regarding work and perfect obedience even unto death. For what more is to be expected? Or what greater patience should be shown to the wicked so that they might be converted and live? Otherwise, one cuts oneself off from mercy by a just judgment and falls into condemnation. For what do we say it means that the victor is promised to sit with Christ, except that to sit on a throne belongs to those who judge? And he who bravely overcomes his sins is made a judge of the iniquitous. 

Thus Elijah <note>original: "Helyas"</note>, who is to come at the time of judgment, was taken up into the fiery chariot into the aerial heaven—both as a "type" or symbol of Christ ascending into heaven, and as a type of this specific order of the elect chosen for the final trial. In former times, he punished the wicked with a terrible judgment, so that in this very act the generations of future times might perceive that those who suffer persecutions for the name of Christ will be the future judges of those who judge them unjustly, and of all others who despise the words of life. They shall execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes upon the peoples. Wherefore, also through a certain <margin>Daniel 7</margin> angel, it is said to Daniel: *The judgment shall sit, that power may be taken away*—it is understood to be the power of that king who is to reign—*and he shall perish even unto the end; but the kingdom which is under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings shall serve and obey him.* Regarding this, a similar mention is made in the seventh part of this book, where John says of that judgment and the seats of the just: *I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given to them.* This will be the time of this "order," which is the last in the second state, to whom it is said: *To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, even as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne.* 

This is as if it were more aptly said: "Just as I entered into my glory through the shame of the Passion, so it is necessary for him who wishes to reign with me to enter the kingdom of God through many labors and groans." Yet because there are many who hearing do not hear, and seeing do not <margin>Luke 8</margin> see, and understanding do not understand, that which was spoken uniformly through all the angels <note>In this context, "angels" refers to the messengers/bishops of the seven churches.</note> is added here in the conclusion.

¶ He who has ears for hearing, <margin>Section 28</margin> let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

¶ This verse has been repeated seven times so that no one may excuse themselves through ignorance or through the negligence of the one inviting them. The rewards have been heard; the promises have been made clear. But a limit has also been set that cannot be passed. Therefore, let him who has ears hear, and let him attend diligently to what is said to each of the churches, so that he may progress within himself through each step of the churches, ascending from virtue to virtue, until he sees the God of gods in Zion.

¶ **Here ends the exposition of the first part of the Book of Revelation.**

¶ **Here begins the exposition of the second part of the Book of Revelation.**

<column-break/>

But now...
