<meta>This page transitions from the first part of the book—the letters to the seven churches—to the second major vision. It begins the commentary on Revelation chapter 4, focusing on the opening of the "door" in heaven and the symbolic meaning of the "book" with seven seals.</meta>

Part of the Explanation

<margin>Revelation 4, Part 1</margin>
In this second section, the focus is more specifically on the martyrs, although the prophetic word is directed toward various ranks of the elect. Thus says Saint John:

### After these things I saw: and behold, a door was opened in heaven.

¶ After the first vision, he beholds the second, because the second rank of martyrs is nearly equal to the apostolic dignity. Great and sublime are the proclamations of this vision, for it is of great happiness to serve in the heavenly fatherland. "After these things," he says, "I saw and behold, a door was opened in heaven." Many mysteries are contained under the name of "heaven," according to what the diversity of the Scriptures requires. Here, however, by the "heaven" which John saw, the mystery <term>sacramentum; here meaning a sacred mystery or hidden truth</term> of Sacred Scripture is understood; for heaven is so called from "concealing," because the understanding of the sacred page is veiled by mysteries. <note>original: "celum a celando dicitur." A popular medieval etymology, though scientifically incorrect, suggesting the word for heaven (caelum) comes from the word for hiding (celare).</note> Someone might say the "door" of this heaven is Christ Jesus, who demonstrates in the Gospel that he is the door of Scripture when he says:

<margin>John 10</margin>
**I am the door.** He more clearly reveals the reason why he says "door" when he adds: **If anyone enters through me, he will go in and go out and find pasture.** He will "go in" by contemplating so that he may "go out" by preaching; and whereby he fills faithful souls by feeding them, he may find the pastures of the Holy Scriptures. What then of the Jew remaining outside, who thinks he understands the law of Moses? Let him knock at the door by faith, and at heaven with his mind, and let him say where the light is, where the spirit of life is. Let him come to Christ, and the veil shall be taken away. Nevertheless, in this place, by "door," the entrance of spiritual understanding is to be understood, because it was blocked as if by the weight of the letter <note>original: "mole literae." This refers to the literal or surface-level reading of the text, which can hide its deeper spiritual meaning.</note>, lest anyone should enter purely into its inner chambers, as the Cherubim forbade this 

<margin>Genesis 3</margin>
with the flaming sword, which was appointed by the Lord to guard the way to the tree of life in paradise. For before Christ was raised from the dead, the entrance to the Scriptures was closed (as I have already said). But when Christ rose, the firstfruits of those who sleep,

<margin>1 Corinthians 15; Mark 16</margin>
the angel descended from heaven, and the stone was moved away from the door of the tomb; surely because when the opportune time arrived, the Holy Spirit was sent to men, and from the heart of the letter, spiritual and life-giving understanding ascended. And rightly 

<margin>John 20</margin>
Christ entered to his disciples while the doors were closed, because with the mysteries not yet broken open, he displayed the faith of his resurrection. But the doors afterward

<column-break/>

<margin>Luke 24</margin>
a little later he opened, when he opened their minds so they might understand the Scriptures. Wherefore it is said in what follows: "I saw in the right hand of him who sat on the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals." Concerning its opening: when he who shows these things <note>referring to John the Apostle</note> despairs—not without a mystery—he is comforted by one of the elders, who says: "Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, to open the book and to loosen its seven seals." Therefore, the heaven and the book are the same thing: the single but multifaceted volume of the Holy Scriptures. Its door he alone has opened, who is the strongest lion of the tribe of Judah, in whose figure <term>typo; a historical person or event serving as a prophetic symbol</term> that strong man 

<margin>Judges 16</margin>
Samson carried away the gates from the city of the Philistines; namely, when the tyrant <note>referring to death or the devil</note> was overcome and he rose from the dead. There, then, is the loosening of mysteries, where the greatest strength of faith is found; for indeed, as has been handed down to us by the holy and Catholic fathers—who piously and soundly examine the face of faith and Scripture—we do not come to faith through understanding, but rather we come to understanding through the constancy of faith. For he gives us "grace for grace," just as the Psalmist testifies, saying: **I believed, therefore I have spoken.** 

<margin>Psalm 115</margin>
Hence, from the beginning of our redemption, it was not a crowd of the wise who were chosen, who might come to faith through the skill of letters, but unlearned fishermen and peasants, the kind this world was accustomed to despise; so that they might lay the foundations of faith not with words taught by human wisdom, but with unheard-of signs and miracles, lest the preaching of Christ be thought empty and void. The Apostle disputes about these things in a certain one of his epistles; let him who knows how to do so hasten to its fountains and drink. 

<margin>1 Corinthians 1</margin>
Moreover, how "heaven" and "book" are to be understood under the same mystery is also clearly suggested by this: the book itself which John saw was sealed with seven seals, and the secrets of this heaven (which is called the firmament) are said to be hidden by the circles of the seven planets. <note>Medieval science viewed the cosmos as a series of concentric spheres or "circles" for the seven known planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn), which the author correlates here to the seven seals of the book.</note> It follows:

<margin>Topic 2</margin>
### And the first voice which I heard was as it were of a trumpet speaking with me, saying: Come up hither, and I will show thee things which must be done hereafter.

¶ It is established that the instrument of the trumpet was invented for this: so that when something must be sounded solemnly, it might be able to sound further and be heard by many. Therefore, the proclamations of the new witness are compared to the sound of a trumpet, because "their sound has gone out into all the earth, and to the ends of the world..."

The author compares the "heaven" of John's vision to the "book" of Scripture, both being repositories of divine mystery accessible through faith rather than human wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fourth chapter of the Book of Revelation. The previous page discussed the "door opened in heaven," identifying it with Christ and the opening of the mysteries of Sacred Scripture. This page moves into the call for John to "ascend" and his vision of the divine throne.</meta>

<page-num>100</page-num>
<header>John’s Second Vision in the Apocalypse</header>
<sig>m 4</sig>

<margin>Isaiah 58</margin>The words of those who preach across the earth. Whence it is said through the prophet: **Cry aloud, do not cease: lift up your voice like a trumpet.** <note>original: "Clama ne cesses: quasi tuba exulta voce tua"</note> Because if the trumpet is indeed raised by the voice of the preacher, the voice of Christ clearly proclaims the Gospel. And he says, **the first voice which I heard.** If it is "first" here, there are others following. If it is first, it indicates something fundamental: that we should perceive this before we come to the others. And what is that? He says, **Ascend here.** Why? Because **the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.** <note>original: "littera occidit: spiritus autem vivificat" (2 Corinthians 3:6). This is a foundational rule of medieval biblical interpretation, distinguishing between the literal surface meaning and the deeper spiritual truth.</note> Therefore, whoever wishes to see the works of God and contemplate heavenly things—having left behind the works of the flesh which, according to the literal voice, are "below"—let him immediately ascend into the spirit, even to the "third heaven." There, like Paul, he may be able to hear **secret words** <note>original: "archana verba"</note> which, because of their excellence, it is not permitted for a man to speak. Indeed, so that John might show what kind of "ascent" was being discussed, he himself immediately reveals it when he adds the explanation:

<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 12</margin>
<margin>Chapter 3</margin>### Immediately I was in the spirit.
For those things are in the spirit, not in the letter: whoever, by contemplating heavenly things, grazes upon the sacred paths of spiritual figures. For the eye of the mind is not fixed on those things which it reads carnally, but on those things which are discerned by looking spiritually. But it should be noted carefully that he says: **what must take place after these things.** He says "after these things" because those legions of saints who are written about in the following passages were not yet in reality then; for they were then shown in a mystery. Nor were they such as they were at the time of the vision, but such as they will be on the last day. For he was seeing in the spirit not only those saints who were then resting in the kingdom of God, but also those who were to be in the future world. Whether, therefore, it was the few things that had preceded or the many things that followed in mercy, he saw them all as if gathered together and brought to a sum, as if under a single glance of the eye. For it follows:

<margin>Chapter 4</margin>### And behold, a throne was set in heaven: and upon the throne, one sitting.
We said above (and since the place requires it, I do not mind repeating it) that in the usage of the volume of Scriptures, the name of "heaven" designates the Church. Seeking, however, what this "heaven" brings to us or what it contains, we find contained in its secrets the glory of the holy mother Church and of him who presides in her, which surpasses all understanding. But also contained are certain orders of spirits remaining in the circuit, as well as the white-robed men presiding over them, whose venerable praises Saint John delayed opening with words, yet

<column-break/>

took care to make known through certain mysteries. That noble throne, therefore, over which the immense King presides, is the glorious and happy holy mother Church. For the "throne of God" is not always or everywhere to be understood as those angelic ranks called "Thrones"; for concerning Christ who was to be born of a Virgin, it was said to the same Virgin by the angel Gabriel: **The Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David.** <note>original: "sedem David patris sui"</note> And the Lord himself said to his disciples: **You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.** <note>original: "sedebitis et vos super sedes duodecim"</note> Because, however, through the images of the figures—which he forbids the contemplator of heavenly things from seeing in this place—they are intricately veiled <note>The OCR "oedefanemoza itricate" is likely "enigmatibus intricata," meaning "entangled in riddles."</note> as if by a certain barrier, I wish to pause for a moment. I wish to stand here so that, as the mysteries of this place are many and manifold, we may be able to investigate them almost word by word, as each requires. And because after other things written to designate the King of the highest good in images, **twenty-four seats** are also written to be in the circuit of the throne, and as many **elders** sitting upon them, we cannot speak fully of the first throne unless we also pass through the other seats. By the necessity of reason, we are compelled to blend these words so that we can examine one through the other. Indeed, in everything concerning the principal throne, we can speak appropriately of him who resides upon it only if we do not remain silent about the others. While we speak of the principal throne and the one sitting upon it, it is necessary that we also touch upon the other seats of the sons and the elders residing upon them. Therefore, in the first throne, the principal Church is designated, although the "holy assembly" <note>The OCR "byzanagogen" is likely "visio magna" (great vision) or a corruption of "synagogam" (assembly/synagogue).</note> may be called the "throne of God"—that heavenly city which is written about at the end of this book, to whose walls the twenty-four seats are known to belong. We shall speak in what follows concerning the perfection and glory of all these, which God himself has given. Regarding the one "sitting upon the throne," some think the person of Christ Jesus should be understood, who promises he will sit upon the throne of David. But they could say this better if he were said to preside for God the Father, as is said to the angel of Laodicea: **Even as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne.** For it is clearly shown that God the Father is to be understood, since after some things it is added: **And I saw: and behold, in the midst of the throne, and of the four animals and the elders, a Lamb standing as if slain, having seven horns and seven eyes.** <note>Revelation 5:6. The author uses this later passage to prove that the one "sitting" on the throne in chapter 4 is the Father, because the Lamb (Christ) appears as a separate figure "in the midst" of the throne later.</note>

seven: who are the **seven spirits of God sent into all the earth: and he came and took from the right hand of the one sitting on the throne: the book.** <note>original: "septem spiritus dei missi in oēm terram: et venit et accepit de dextera sedentis in throno: librum"</note> This is what Saint John says: **I saw a lamb as if slain having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth; and he came and took the book from the right hand of the one sitting on the throne.** <note>Revelation 5:6-7</note> This must be referred to that day on which the same Lord was crucified by the Jews. For the "slain lamb" came when he rose from the dead. He received the book from the right hand of the one sitting <margin>Matthew 28</margin> on the throne when (as he himself says) **all power was given to him in heaven and on earth,** <note>original: "data est sibi ois potestas in celo et in terra"</note> so that in his name <margin>Philippians 2</margin> **every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.** <note>original: "oē genu flectat: celestium: terrestrium: et infernorū"</note> Indeed, he began to open the book itself when he opened the understanding <term>understanding: "sensum," referring to the internal capacity to perceive spiritual truths</term> of his disciples so that they might understand the scriptures. But more on this in what follows. <margin>Luke 24</margin> Furthermore, if we diligently seek who he is who sits upon the seat and is said to be like those stones in appearance, it is clearly recognized that he is to be understood as the unbegotten Father together with his only-begotten Son.

### <margin>Apocalypse 4:3</margin> And he who sat was (he says) like the appearance of a Jasper stone and a Sardine stone.

¶ And so that the image of the third person might also be expressed—that is, the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both—he immediately followed this by saying:

### <margin>Apocalypse 4:3</margin> And there was a rainbow round about the throne, like an emerald to the sight.

¶ In writing of the similarities to these three precious stones, he shows us the great mystery of the Holy Trinity. For Jasper is of a green color; the Sardine is of a blood-red color; and the Emerald is itself also of a green color, but one that surpasses the greenness of the Jasper. Moreover, it is said that wine and oil reach <note>original: "pervenire," likely meaning "benefit" or "interact with" in a lapidary/medicinal sense</note> the nature of this stone, so that it is reported to improve from them. Now, we know that greenness is the life of trees and plants. Blood is the life of sensible bodies, such as humans and cattle. For a limb withers if it does not grow strong with blood. Hence, not without reason is the blood of animals considered as their life in Genesis, because it is the spirit <note>Here "spirit" refers to the "spirit of life" or "breath," not the Holy Spirit.</note> which gives life to the body; yet we see that 

<column-break/>

the spirit cannot remain in the flesh without blood, and the limbs of the body wither if their veins of blood are cut. Furthermore, plants and trees draw their greenness from water, which is the primary liquid; thus those two things which the same John mentions in his epistle are aptly understood: namely, water and blood, <margin>1 John 5</margin> which two, along with the spirit, are shown to be one. Therefore, in the greenness of the Jasper, the person of God the Father is designated, who is the Beginning in the Trinity. Certainly, in the count of precious stones, Jasper is written as the first of all. But in the blood-red color of the Sardine stone, the only-begotten Son of God is aptly designated; who, though he was true God before the ages of the world, willed to become man at the end of the ages. <margin>Titus</margin> Surely in the color of the Emerald, which especially excels in greenness, that person of the Holy Trinity is designated who is called the **life-giving spirit**; <note>original: "vivificans spiritus"</note> this is because through him human hearts—and without doubt, also bodies—are given life, as the Apostle says: **The first Adam was made into a living soul; <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> the second Adam into a life-giving spirit.** And in another place: **If the Spirit of him who raised <margin>Romans 8</margin> Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you.** Hence it is also said in the Creed of the Fathers: *I believe also in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of Life.* <note>original: "Credo et in spūm sanctum dñm et viuificātēm" from the Nicene Creed.</note> And if Christ says of himself in the Gospel: **As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son <margin>John 5</margin> gives life to whom he will,** why is this name "Giver of Life" attributed to the Holy Spirit as if by a certain property? It is because our inner man is then truly given life when he receives the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that he may remain with him (as the Truth says) forever. For, to touch briefly upon those things which come to mind at present: what (I ask) is the life of the soul if it is empty of wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear—and what is greater than these: faith, hope, joy, and love? Would it not have been better for that soul if it had not been created? And all these things come from the Holy Spirit. Indeed, God gave of his Spirit to those not yet having these gifts, as John says in his epistle (the author of this book): **He has given us of his Spirit.** <margin>1 John 3</margin>

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the Book of Revelation, specifically interpreting the vision of God’s throne from Chapter 4. ### John’s Commentary on the Apocalypse

...twice over. For to use a comparison of things that are not identical but distinct: just as the soul is to the body, so the Holy Spirit fills and gives life to the soul. The color of the **Emerald** <term>Emerald: "Smaragdus," a bright green gemstone</term> is more vivid and lively than the color of **Jasper**, and it is considerably more beautiful; just as the consistency of oil or balsam—which signifies the anointing of the Holy Spirit—is more precious than the consistency of water or wine, in which the Father and the Son are signified. This is so that because the same Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he should not be thought to be lesser in majesty than the Father or the Son.

But perhaps someone might say: "Since the three persons of the Godhead itself are equal, and there is no difference among the three, it would seem more appropriate if their significance were matched to things of equal value." To this, it is answered: if one did not proceed from another, there would be no reason to believe one was prior and another posterior, and the promoters of heresies would have no opportunity to assert their falsehoods. But because one is from the other, clearer comparisons are often given to the Son than to the Father, and clearer ones to the Holy Spirit than to the Son. This is lest anyone should think the Son is inferior to the eternal Father, or the Holy Spirit inferior and unequal to that same Son.

For this reason, the only-begotten Son of God is called the "Wisdom of the Father," <note>original: "sapientia patris"</note> lest anyone should think him to have been born suddenly, or like a human son educated by his father’s diligence. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is called "Goodness" and "the Love of God," lest anyone should think him to be joined to the divine substance by anything other than free goodness. This, then, is the reason why the likeness of **Jasper** is attributed to the Father, the **Sardine stone** <term>Sardine: likely a "Sardius" or carnelian, a deep red stone</term> to the Son, and the much more precious stone—the **Emerald**—to the Holy Spirit. This is why the virtue of charity <note>charity: in this context, "divine love"</note> is preferred above all virtues.

However, the fact that the Emerald is not mentioned simply (as were the Jasper and Sardine), but is mentioned with the inclusion of a **rainbow** <term>rainbow: "iris," the multicolored arc</term> must not be passed over in silence. We must ask why the person of the Holy Spirit is designated by a rainbow, or why that same rainbow is said to be around the throne. *And there was a rainbow,* it says, *around the throne, like an emerald to look upon.* <note>Revelation 4:3</note> If we carefully note the appearance of this rainbow which we see in the clouds, we weigh the fact that there are three colors in it: one green (of which silent mention is made here by the designation of the Emerald), another blue or airy, and the third 

<column-break/>

red. Why does one arch have three colors, if not because grace is given to man first so that he may believe, second so that he may have the strength to act, and third so that, being perfected in the love of God, he himself may rest from his labors?

Hence it is that the Holy Spirit appeared first in the form of a **dove**, second in the **breathing of air**, and third in **fire**. But why this? Because, proceeding from the Father and the Son, he also blows where he wills and divides his own gifts to each person according to his own judgment. To show that he proceeds from the Father, he makes those whom he touches simply (so to speak) free so that they are able to believe. And to show that he proceeds from the Son, he makes those to whom he offers help ready for every good work, and especially for preaching the word of God. And to show himself as the author of life and the distributor of graces, he fills those who have been proven in every good work with the gifts of his goodness, so that he may show them to be spiritual in all things.

As for the statement that this rainbow is "around the throne," it is similar to what is sung in the Psalm:

<margin>Psalm 124</margin>
> **Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion: he who dwells in Jerusalem shall never be moved. The mountains are round about her: and the Lord is round about his people, from this time forth and forever.** <note>original: "Qui cōfidunt in dñō sicut mons syon..." referring to Psalm 125 (124 in the Vulgate)</note>

For in the circuit of **Jerusalem**—that is, Mother Church, which is called the seat of the Lord—there are said to be "mountains" in this place; for unless defenders run to and fro around the city for its protection and guard, the city could not remain in the quiet of peace. Hence it says in the Song of Songs:

<margin>Song of Songs 3</margin>
> **Behold the bed of Solomon. Sixty valiant men surround it, of the most valiant of Israel: all holding swords and most expert in war: every man's sword upon his thigh because of fears in the night.** <note>original: "En lectulum Salomonis..."</note>

The "bed of Solomon" is the same as the holy seat of God: that is, **Mother Church**. In her circuit, therefore, sixty defenders run to and fro, who study to keep her from nightly fear; for the holy **martyrs** carried out spiritual wars for her guardianship, voluntarily handing themselves over to death and offering themselves to the torturers, lest the children of darkness should ever plunder her if she did not have soldiers fighting in her fortifications. Who are also rightly seen...

->## Abbreviated Part of the Exposition<-

...the most brave men are shown to be sixty in number; for the perfection of the number six <note>In medieval mathematics, six was called a "perfect number" because it equals the sum of its divisors (1, 2, and 3). Here, it symbolizes the completeness and moral perfection of the martyrs.</note> requires none but the strong and the perfect, so that they might conquer through the "palm of patience" until the end of the war, and by the strength of faith, they might lay low the enemies of the holy Church by their persistence. For that which the Lord had promised to the holy Church of martyrs through the prophet was fulfilled in the holy martyrs:

<margin>Isaiah 54</margin>
**"I will make your bulwarks of jasper."** <note>original: "Dabo Jaspidez ppugnacula tua." A reference to Isaiah 54:12, where God promises to rebuild Jerusalem with precious stones.</note> Indeed, the strength of faith signified by the jasper was bestowed upon the holy martyrs; the prerogative of this stone was given to the Apostle Peter—namely, because he is the first foundation of the entire Church after Christ. For it is written thus in the final part of this volume <note>The "volume" refers to the Book of Revelation.</note>, in which the heavenly city is discussed: **"The wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the twelve names of the twelve apostles and the Lamb."** And a little later: **"The foundations of its wall were adorned with every precious stone. The first foundation: Jasper."** <note>original: "Jaspis"</note> Concerning this stone, jasper, he had already spoken above: **"And the structure of its wall was of jasper stone; but the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass."**

Behold, the mysteries now begin to be declared. Jasper is the beginning of the foundations, because the faith of Peter—who is first among the apostles—is the firm foundation and origin of the virtues. But from where does Peter—who is the shepherd and guardian of the Church—have this, if not from Him who is the Father of all and the caretaker of all things? **"Blessed,"** He said, **"are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven."** <margin>Matthew 16</margin> Therefore, God the Father gave to Peter the strength of faith so that he might be the foundation of the Church. He also provided this same strength to the martyrs, so that by fighting manfully with Peter, they might lead the triumphal troops of war; thus, those who assisted such a leader in military service might possess glory in heaven together with him.

Hence it is that Blessed Peter, with his fellow apostles, chose seven deacons for himself, of whom Stephen was the first. Having taken up the banner of the cross, Stephen preceded that same leader of the war in battle, so that Blessed Stephen might see where the crowd was to go, and Peter, by encouraging the weak, might help them toward the palm of victory and inspire the spirit of triumph. Therefore, the power of faith that was in Peter was propagated into the deacons appointed by him as helpers in the coming struggle, so that those who deserved to hear from Christ, **"Follow me,"** <margin>John 21</margin> might also assist as the first fight-

<column-break/>

-ers. And he who would take up the war against many would have in his company not a few warriors. **"All of them,"** therefore, **"holding swords and most learned in war."** <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 3:8, describing the guards of Solomon's litter.</note>

<margin>Genesis 3; Ephesians 6</margin>
They certainly held the **"sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God"**; they held the resistance of faith, because he taught them that nothing was to be feared and nothing was to be doubted, as they were those from whose heads not even a hair would perish. Correctifiably, therefore, the stone of the first foundation is recognized to have excelled in the structure of the wall, because the strength of faith bestowed upon Peter prevailed as it was propagated among the holy martyrs. Everywhere, then, "Jasper" is written first, because it is found in the first order of faith. If it signifies God the Father, He is the first person of the Trinity. If it signifies the Apostle Peter, he holds the primacy among the apostles. If it signifies the crowd of martyrs, they preached the Church.

Therefore, the most brave men who surround the litter of Solomon <note>Solomon's "litter" or "couch" (Song of Solomon 3:7) was traditionally interpreted by medieval commentators as a symbol for the Church or the resting place of Christ.</note> are the holy martyrs, as they are the ones who defend the Church from "nighttime fear." They are the promised bulwarks of the holy Church; they are the fortified mountains for the guardianship of Jerusalem, of which it is said: **"Mountains are round about her."** <margin>Psalm 124; Psalm 127</margin> And as it is written elsewhere: **"Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain."** Fittingly, it follows immediately: **"And the Lord is round about his people."** Therefore, both the Lord and the mountains are said to be around Jerusalem, because the merciful Lord deigned to pasture His flock Himself in such a way that He nevertheless roused an army of shepherds for its guardianship. Whence also here, after he said: **"And there was a rainbow round about the throne, like an emerald to look upon,"** <margin>Revelation 4</margin> there was immediately added:

> **"And round about the throne were twenty-four seats: and upon the thrones I saw twenty-four elders sitting, clothed in white garments; and they had on their heads crowns of gold."**

Although in the order of the description it speaks of the seats before the elders, we have thought it appropriate to treat the elders before the thrones. Concerning these, different people have said different things. Indeed, there have not been lacking those who said one thing or another. However, there is a common opinion that they represent the twelve patriarchs and as many apostles. We know some were sons of Jacob according to the flesh, while others—the first sons of Christ—have the Spirit; both were fathers of the chosen people. Concerning the twelve apostles, however, they concede <note>original: "concedunt"</note> without any contradiction, because <note>original: "quia"</note> their life and number with the authority [concord]...

Isaac had two sons, but one was chosen, while the other was reprobate. Jacob had twelve sons, but of these, one was sold for his innocence, while the others were the sellers of their brother out of malice." However, this is so that just as a comparison of the patriarch Jacob to Christ is not rightly made, so too no comparison should be estimated between the former [sons] and the latter [apostles]. But if the twelve patriarchs do not hold leadership among the elect of that people because they are not equal to the Apostles, then neither should the patriarch Jacob be believed to be great in the kingdom of God. Yet toward Christ, whose

son he is in this regard, he is unequal in merit and dignity. Nay rather, if the Apostles are great because He who begat them is great, and the glory of their birth is great because of their origin, then the twelve patriarchs are not equal to the Apostles because Jacob is not equal to Christ, nor is the birth by which those [patriarchs] were born of Jacob equal to that birth by which the Apostles were born of Him. Yet it does not follow that they were not great in their own kind, even if they were not equal to the Apostles in life; for neither are those great patriarchs—namely, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whose faith Christ was granted—read to have held the apostolic life, and yet they are not lesser, even though they are read to have had wives and many riches <note>The author contrasts the Old Testament patriarchs, who lived in the world, with the Apostles, who practiced "apostolic poverty" and celibacy.</note>. Nevertheless, the hours of the night also, to which the moon provided light, are good; for even if a child heir does not differ from a servant, yet he is an heir himself, and God belongs to all, just as he does to those whom full age claims for liberty. <note>This metaphor compares the Patriarchs to the "night" (the time before Christ's coming) and the Apostles to the "day." Since these things are so, it seems that these twelve men belong to the number of the elders, were it not for the fact that they are blamed for the wicked sale of their brother. And those [the patriarchs] indeed changed what they had wickedly conceived into a lighter offense: namely, selling the innocent man without the staining of their hands, whom they had previously said they would kill. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the identity of the twenty-four elders from the Book of Revelation. The author is weighing the merits of the twelve Patriarchs (the sons of Jacob), who sold their brother Joseph into slavery, against the standard of holiness required for such high heavenly office. ### Part of the Exposition

...is cleansed from his crime by repentance as if whitened beyond snow <note>original: "dealbatus super nivem" — a reference to Psalm 51:7, "wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow."</note>: let him dare to cry out confidently, saying: "I will teach the unjust your ways: and the wicked shall be converted to you." <note>Psalm 51:13. The author argues that a forgiven sinner like David has the right to teach others.</note> But we read of his [David's] repentance: and the scourges with which he was corrected: and the forgiveness of his sin. Of those others [the Patriarchs], however, we nowhere read of their repentance, for it is found in no scripture: unless perhaps I might say that this could have sufficed: that being terrified in Egypt they reproached themselves, saying: <margin>Genesis 50</margin> "Justly do we suffer these things: because we sinned against our brother, seeing the anguish of his soul while he entreated us: and we did not hear." <margin>Genesis 42</margin> For that was a confession of repentance; yet Scripture does not explicitly say that this sufficed for them to bear the "fruit of repentance." Nevertheless, there is no doubt that they could obtain full <term>indulgence</term> <note>In this context, "indulgence" (indulgentia) refers to the full remission or pardon of sins by God.</note> through this profession, as it is certain they acknowledged their fault and repented of the crime. Indeed, every sinner begins to be just by the very fact that he confesses the judge's sentence to be just. 

Although perhaps not incongruously, we believe it was done by the just judgment of God that the Egyptians should oppress their <term>seed</term> <note>Their descendants, the Israelites.</note> with servitude because their fathers sold a just man to a foreign nation. Nor does it differ from the same logic that their stay was extended for four hundred years, and they are liberated from Egyptian servitude in the fourth generation. <margin>Genesis 15</margin> This agrees with that sentence which the Lord made manifest through Moses when he says: "I am a strong and jealous God: who visits the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons, unto the third and fourth generation." <margin>Exodus 20</margin> For even that great crime of David is read to have overflowed onto his offspring because of his sins, with the son born to him of the adulteress being killed first. <note>A reference to the death of the child born from David's affair with Bathsheba as a divine punishment (2 Samuel 12).</note> Thus here, the Lord is both lovable and terrible: he both indulges more fully with mercy and yet does not dismiss the sins of the delinquent without the scrutiny of vengeance. Thus, through the grace of **baptism**, original sin is dissolved; and yet the penalty of death, which man deserved for it, is not deleted. But concerning this, we shall speak elsewhere. 

However, the discourse was about the patriarchs: whether they are able to be worthy of that so great honor before God—they who out of malice sold an innocent and simple brother—because it could be justly asked (as we have already said): if David, so great a prophet, could not have risen after his fall; if Peter, even after his several denials; and Paul, after homicide, had not come to the height of glory. It remains, therefore, that we should believe those whose names in this book of **Revelation** are so clearly written—where twelve thousand of the holy are written to be <term>sealed</term> <note>Marked by God as His own.</note> for each tribe—do reign with the living God; because, as Truth itself says: "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living." <margin>Matthew 22</margin>

<column-break/>

Whether these men themselves truly belong to the number of the twenty-four **Elders** is not indeed an assertion of absolute authority, but can be a matter of opinion; although I am not ignorant that many points occur which resist this opinion. Among these is the fact that since spiritual battle is not fought with a material spear but with the "sword of the spirit," which is the word of God, <margin>Ephesians 6</margin> it seems quite absurd that so great a prerogative of glory should be believed to have been conferred on those men who are not read to have contended even unto death for justice... unless perhaps someone should dare to deny that some even then fell for the profession of truth, and that pious men were not lacking in the Old Testament who were crowned with **martyrdom** for the defense of justice. 

But who would dare to deny what Christ says, or treat as a doubt what Truth itself professes? "Woe," he says, "to you scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites: because you build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the just: and you say: 'If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.'" <margin>Matthew 23</margin> Therefore, you are witnesses to yourselves that you are the sons of those who killed the prophets. And after a few words, he says: "That there may come upon you all the just blood which has been poured out upon the earth, from the blood of Abel the just unto the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar." 

This point is even more vital in this second part where the martyrs are discussed: clearly, those twenty-four seats upon which the **Elders** preside designate the chosen legions of holy martyrs; nor are they any others than those of whom it is said in what follows: "I heard the number of the sealed, one hundred and forty-four thousand from every tribe of the children of Israel. From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed. From the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand sealed," etc. And if there are any others who belong to these seats, it would be quite absurd...

# Joachim’s Second Book on the Apocalypse

...it seems: that they should be believed to be the princes of the holy martyrs: who gave no example of martyrdom or virginity to posterity: even if they could have been great in another way: especially since in all the time of the Old Testament, up to the time when this book was published by the blessed John, no consideration of ancient history suggests there were so many thousands of saints from that people who died for the name of God or for justice, from whom twelve out of the twenty-four seats could have been filled. Again, it is shown that this number is to be gathered at the opening of the sixth seal: namely, at that time when we believe that which the apostle says must be fulfilled: <margin>Romans 11</margin> "When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved." <note>A reference to Paul’s prophecy that the Jewish people will eventually convert to Christianity.</note> And nothing of this pertains to the Old Testament, unless someone says perhaps that at that time this sum total is to be gathered from every tribe of the children of Israel: when likewise the people of the Jews shall be converted to God. But if this is held by right, how is that to be understood which is immediately added below: "After these things I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from all nations and tribes and peoples and languages: standing before the throne in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and palms in their hands." <note>Revelation 7:9. The author is comparing the specific number of the 144,000 Israelites with the countless multitude of all nations.</note> Especially since regarding both peoples, the Truth <note>The "Truth" refers to Christ himself.</note> says: <margin>Matthew 20</margin> "The first shall be last, and the last first"? In which matter it seems better to me—according to what is said to the Gentiles by the apostle: "If you are Christ’s, then you are the seed of Abraham"—that by the twelve patriarchs we should understand the twelve apostles: whose children are the holy martyrs, who suffered for the name of Christ from the time of the holy apostles themselves until the opening of the sixth seal and the times of the Antichrist. However, the other twelve elders are to be chosen from the Gentile people at the time when Elijah is to come: just as the twelve apostles were chosen from the Jewish people at the time when John the Baptist came. So that just as through the twelve apostles and their co-helpers the Gentiles were called, so through those twelve the entire multitude of the children of Israel may enter: and they may be truly the "first who were last" and the "last who were first." <margin>Matthew 20</margin> Moreover, this seems to be intended by that triple designation of princes which was made around the beginning of the time that preceded under the Law: where after the twelve

<column-break/>

patriarchs who descended into Egypt: twelve princes were chosen from each of the tribes: who themselves were laid low in the desert: <note>Referring to the generation of Israelites who died in the wilderness because of their lack of faith.</note> and finally, another twelve were designated: to whom it was given to enter the land of promise: and to possess as an inheritance the land flowing with milk and honey. For indeed, the twelve patriarchs who died in Egypt designate all the patriarchs of that people who, before Christ rose from the dead, were completed under the Old Testament. The twelve who were laid low in the desert designate the twelve apostles with their successors: who also receive their completion under this second state: <term>second state</term> <note>Joachim of Fiore divided history into three "states" or ages: the Age of the Father (Old Testament), the Age of the Son (the Church/New Testament), and the approaching Age of the Holy Spirit.</note> nor do they survive to reach temporally that rest which is to come in the seventh age of the world because of sins. Truly, just as Moses himself with the elders of Israel died in the desert because of the sins of the people: so Christ with the holy apostles and martyrs sustained passion because of the sins of the human race: so that God, appeased by such sacrifices, might spare the remnant of his people. Thence it is that for those who were first, being laid low in the desert, the last twelve with the children of those who had fallen entered that land flowing (as it is said) with milk and honey: because when they are completed or in part consumed at the end of this second state—those who, abhorring new things, still emulate the old and ancient: as if it were now permitted for the prelates of the churches to live according to the flesh just as it seemed permitted to the patriarchs and prophets. Only those are about to enter into that rest, which is to be revealed in the third state of the age: who, having spurned the oldness of the <term>letter</term>, have learned to walk in the newness of the spirit. <note>Joachim emphasizes a transition from a literal, carnal understanding of scripture ("the letter") to a spiritual, contemplative one ("the spirit").</note> Therefore, that the twelve elders are the twelve apostles, there is no doubt. But whether the remaining twelve are twelve future men—whether it be an understanding or an opinion—I leave to the judgment of the reader. And of these things, enough has been said. But is it because it is written that twenty-four elders sit upon twenty-four thrones in the likeness of Him who sits upon the throne, that these twenty-four men are believed to be greater than all other saints? If this is so, what shall we say of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: the fathers of the patriarchs, and...

### Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

...of the apostles: What shall we say of Moses and Samuel, David and Elijah? What of John the Baptist, of whom it is written that among those born of women, none greater has arisen? What of the Mother of the Lord, whom we believe to have been exalted not only above holy men, but even above the angelic powers? But this question is easily solved if we understand that there are different ranks of dignity in the house of Almighty God, just as the Lord said:

<margin>John 14</margin>
"In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places." <note>original: "In domo patris mei mansiones multe sunt."</note> But we shall speak of this in what follows. First, however, we must consider how great is the glory of our fathers and how much the shared brilliance of their light illuminates us. For truly, if we are children of God, as we ought to be, and if we know ourselves to be children of one Father, there can be no private ownership in that City where the bond of supreme charity makes all things common. For look, the aforementioned elders are described as being clothed in white garments; and yet John testifies that he saw not only them, but an infinite or innumerable crowd of saints clothed in white robes. They are described as having golden crowns on their heads; and yet the Apostle Paul makes it clear that all the saints are to be crowned with glory and honor when he says: "No one is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules." 

<margin>2 Timothy 2</margin>
For if no one is crowned unless they compete lawfully, it is clear that whoever does compete lawfully is crowned with the crown of victory. Since this is so, why is it that only these twenty-four men are seen wearing crowns, unless it is because their glory is shared by all the elect? We must understand, therefore, that others among the elect <note>The Latin "plecti" in the OCR is likely a scribal error for "electi" (the chosen or the elect).</note> have also succeeded by right of inheritance to the glory and honor with which the holy elders are seen to be decorated. For just as there are different orders and honors in the kingdoms of men, so it is manifest that in the kingdom of heaven there are many ranks in which some are placed above others. If you look for faith among the apostles themselves, Peter excels. If you look for knowledge, Paul stands first. If you look for the grace of divine contemplation, John is preferred. Therefore, to recognize the ranks of heavenly powers, the consideration of earthly things provides no small help. Many people under one king enjoy the gift of high office, but not all are decorated with the same honor or the same glory.

<column-break/>

Indeed, this rank distinguishes some, while that rank distinguishes others. But He who shines in all things is the Lord of all alone. Royal custom requires that after the king, the princes of the people should be honored, who are stationed one by one throughout various places to govern those subject to them. Thus, the glory of the king is more highly proclaimed by everyone because one man specifically rules over many princes in the kingdom. We also see individual princes, who are called by specific names according to the diversity of their provinces, decorated by the gift of their king and presiding over their own courts in the likeness of royalty. So in the court of King Ahasuerus <note>Ahasuerus is the Latin name for the Persian King Xerxes from the Book of Esther.</note>, seven princes sat with the king, whose counsel he used in all matters:

<margin>Esther 1</margin>
so much so that not even Queen Vashti could escape the sentence they gave against her, which resulted in her being deprived of the king's bed and glory, once a remedy was provided. If, therefore, the great men of the kings of the earth, having their own courts in their cities, judge the common people subject to them, they are supported by a certain private glory among the rest, while the royal likeness of glory makes them bright and sublime. But the majesty of the brightness of the royal and principal court is seen to be so great that honor is shown to it not only by the lesser courts below, but even by the great men themselves; for that which clings more familiarly to the king's side excels all the king's subjects in power. So also in the kingdom of God—which is the <term>Holy Mother Church</term> <note>A traditional personification of the Christian Church as a nurturing mother.</note>, which triumphs gloriously through different parts of the world, sending her branches even to the sea—divine providence is known to have established its order. He gives her new children in place of the fathers, whom He has appointed as princes over all the earth: namely, the pastors of the churches. But among these, He makes one face more exalted than all others, inasmuch as it alone out of all is called the "City of Cities." This is the Roman Church, over which the Vicar of the Most High God presides <note>The "Vicar" refers to the Pope.</note>, having around him many episcopal churches. Some of these are more exalted than the rest, in the likeness of that supreme Seat which has twenty-four seats around it, so that through those things which are ordained in the temporal Church, we may understand the order and reason of the Eternal City. For as it was said to Moses concerning the Tabernacle of the Lord and the things that were to be prepared in it: "See that [you make them according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain]."

### John's Second [Exposition] on the Apocalypse

"...do everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain." <note>original: "facias secundum exemplar quod ostensum est tibi in monte." A reference to Exodus 25:40 and Hebrews 8:5, suggesting that earthly worship and structures should mirror heavenly realities.</note> So also in this present time, according to the pattern that the blessed John saw in heaven, the tabernacle of God has been ordered—which is the Holy Roman Church. While he who sits above the seat [the Pope] presides honorably over the principal Church as the universal prelate, the metropolitans <note>Metropolitans are high-ranking bishops, usually archbishops, who oversee an ecclesiastical province.</note> judge throughout individual kingdoms or provinces, following the likeness of the twenty-four elders sitting on their seats. Each of them has his own seat and wears a mitre in place of a crown upon his head. In this ecclesiastical mystery, that which was asked above is especially declared and found to be true: namely, that there are many in the kingdom of God who are not only equal to the twenty-four elders but even surpass them. For indeed, even if the sons of a great king share in the principalities assigned to them by their father, nevertheless the queen who gave them birth is their mother and the lady over all; honor and filial subjection are owed to her by everyone. Finally, if we look closely at the Church itself, we see a greater power attributed to the bishops than to others. For these are they who receive the power of binding and loosing from the Roman Pontiff <term>Roman Pontiff</term> <note>The Pope</note>, participating in the sacred anointing, name, ornament, and power. 

<margin>Likewise, the Roman Church—which is joined, as if in marriage, to the one Pontiff—excels in dignity and a certain special prerogative. I do not mean over the subject peoples, but rather that, with the exception of the Roman Pontiff who presides over it, it stands above all other prelates.</margin> 

Nor have these things been said merely for the sake of an example, nor fruitlessly, I think; for while we remain in this pilgrimage, it is necessary for us to grasp heavenly things through earthly ones, and high things through the lowly. For it was asked whether the twenty-four elders are preferred above all the elect; and certainly, from what has been said, it is clearer than light that many in that multitude of saints are equal to these elders, and even (if I may say so) greater in majestic <note>The OCR reads "mannali," likely a scribal error for "magnali" (great/majestic).</note> dignity. Such are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—the fathers of the prophets, the apostles, and all believers. 

<margin>Exodus 33</margin> 

David, whose son was named Christ; Moses, who spoke to the Lord just as a friend is accustomed to speak to a friend; Elijah and John the Baptist, one of whom was the precursor to the Judge, while the other ran before and pointed out the Redeemer with his finger; and

<column-break/>

above all others, the Mother of the Lord, whom we believe to have been exalted not only above holy men but even above angels, archangels, and all the orders of angels. Since this is so, what do we say those special things mean? For we must not imagine that in that homeland there are seats of gold or silver, or golden crowns adorned with precious stones; rather, we must consider only what is understood through them. For that heavenly city is the seat of God, which is established and built from "living stones"—that is, from that multitude of saints about which it is written further down: "After this I saw a great multitude which no one could number." <note>Revelation 7:9</note> Certainly, the twenty-four seats that belong to the walls of that city are those special and holy groups of saints comprised of a certain number. Of these it is said: "I heard the number of those who were sealed, one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel." <note>Revelation 7:4</note> And those of whom it is said in the fourth part: "I saw the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads." <note>Revelation 14:1</note> And this must be understood in the order of the vision: that those seats in the circuit of the Throne are not to be imagined as all being arranged one after another around the Throne, but rather twelve (so to speak) within twelve, like a wall and an outer wall <term>antemurale</term> <note>A defensive fore-wall or rampart.</note>. Furthermore, as regards the general joy and gladness of all, one must consider more attentively how great the simplicity is in that city, and how common to all is whatever exists there. You have heard that God the Father sits upon the throne, and in the circuit of that throne are twenty-four seats, and upon them as many elders. This was mentioned in terms of earthly high-status and those things in which men rejoice—lest you perceive something else in your mind. But it is not so. Do you wish to know that it is not so? Behold, you have God the Father sitting on the throne of majesty, and twenty-four elders presiding honorably on their thrones. And what shall we say of the Lamb, who is described as being "in the midst of the throne"? For although we have said he sits with the Father, it is proven from other places, lest anyone think him separate from the Father. In this place, however, he is described not as sitting on a seat, but as being "in the middle of the seat," so that those who "walk in great matters" <note>A reference to Psalm 131:1.</note> may diligently learn how great is the height and virtue of humility; and by learning, they may unlearn being lifted up to the heights, so that they may be joined in unity to their Head, who willed to be in the lowest place. For was he not in the lowest place, he who [took on] a most humble body...

There, he who is a little one is great, and he who is great is little; for no one can be arrogant where humility dwells, nor can anything be discordant or out of tune where charity reigns. Christ does not despise his mother, he who is King and Lord of all; nor does Peter, the prince of the apostles, despise Paul, who labored more than all others. No such thing is to be imagined in the kingdom of God—as if one cannot be exalted unless another is brought low. We often see this happen in the kingdoms of this world due to the immense narrowness of this world, or rather due to a lack of charity, which alone knows how to make all its things common and to possess the things of others as its own. I say it will not be so in that heavenly court, because true humility knows nothing of this, and charity tramples all such things. For there, even if the fathers are honored along with the Father, the sons and grandsons are nevertheless more closely loved along with the Son. There, even if the due honor is shown to the patriarchs and apostles as if to certain senators of heaven, the crowd of the righteous following the Lamb nevertheless—singing sweetly on their harps <margin>Revelation 5</margin>—sing a new song before the throne of God, which was not even given to the elders themselves; for each one there receives his own reward according to his labor, and according to the grace given to each, by the judgment of him who gives to all and divides to each as he wills. Moreover (as I have already said), there is so great a prerogative of the first seat that the prerogative of the Queen <note>Here, the "Queen" represents the Church or the Virgin Mary.</note> is greater than all the principalities of her husband. ### John’s Second [Part] on the Apocalypse

#### D

Many cohorts of the perfect have been ordained by God for Mother Church, so that from there, many might rest in that place. Among them, some stood bravely in battle even unto death. The <margin>Psalm 124</margin> Psalmist, as we have already remembered, calls these seats "mountains" when he says: *Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved forever, the mountains are around it.* <note>The author uses the Latin Vulgate numbering; this is Psalm 125 in modern Bibles.</note> He says, "the mountains are around it." What are the mountains around it, if not the twenty-four seats around the throne? For Zion itself is the throne, and it is the one whose mountains are around it: that is, the seats around the throne. Concerning these seats, it is likewise <margin>Psalm 121</margin> said by the same prophet: *There the seats sat in judgment.* <note>Psalm 122:5. The author emphasizes that the "seats" themselves are personified as those who judge.</note> Indeed, the seats sit in judgment because not only these twenty-four men who were seen sitting upon the seats, but also those very legions of saints who are called "seats" or "thrones," will sit together to judge the impious in the judgment. This is according to the words of Christ himself, who is the <term>Truth</term> <note>original: "veritas". A common title for Christ in medieval exegesis, emphasizing his role as the ultimate reality and judge.</note>: *He who overcomes shall sit with me on my throne, just as I also overcame and sat with my Father on his throne.* But now, in the faith of Christ, let us lift our minds somewhat into the heights; and wherever the breeze of this discourse leads us, let us follow to search into the depths of such a great mystery. He in whom we hope assists us, for we do not presume upon our own prudence, but upon the goodness of his generosity. Let us see, then, what these seats are, and what these legions of the ranks are. From that most clear stock which the Lord chose from the beginning—namely Abraham—the twelve patriarchs Isaac and Jacob were descended, and from them, that people who are called Israel. And because it was not in vain that Almighty God gave the law to that people, nor without purpose that he chose that nation to be his inheritance, Saint John says he heard, in this very part we are now treating, the number of those who were sealed: *One hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel.* And he added: *From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed,* and so on for the others. Some say this finite number should be taken for an infinite one. But in every way, this is improbable. If,

<column-break/>

indeed, an infinite number did not follow the finite one, this could perhaps be thought without absurdity. But because he immediately added: *After this I saw a great multitude which no one could number,* I do not know by what understanding the first group, which he described under a finite number, could be said to be taken for an infinite one. If we hold that the number of the twelve apostles is finite, what if God wished to comprehend many more under a finite and perfect number? If this number is not true, then neither is the number of the twelve apostles written in the foundations of the city true according to the letter, but only that which is designated by it; nor would the other twelve be true, about whom we disputed above. But if the number of the sealed is not true—distinct by thousands and summed up in one hundred and forty-four—then the number of the elders is not true either, being fixed at twenty-four. But because the number of the twenty-four elders is true, the one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed must also be true. It is pleasing, as far as it is permitted, to consider the great mystery of this number; so that while we hold the measure of the finite number, we may also learn to venerate the wisdom of God in those things which exceed human reason beyond measure, singing in our hearts with the <margin>Psalm 103</margin> Psalmist: *How magnificent are your works, O Lord; you have made all things in wisdom.* <note>Psalm 104:24.</note> After he reported twelve thousand assigned to each individual father, he added something concerning those who could not be numbered by man, saying: "from such and such a tribe, so many thousands were sealed," and then he added: *After this I saw a great multitude which no one could number.* But from where do we confess this great multitude descended? Was it from the twelve tribes of Israel, like those one hundred and forty-four thousand? Though I would not say that even these [the 144,000] should be understood according to the flesh—that is, as if they were all simply the literal sons of the patriarchs. But this will be treated in its own place. Now let us look at the number. Among other things that are most notably to be observed regarding this number, this occurs first of all to be considered: that if each of the twelve thousands is divided in two, we find twenty-four perfect and complete legions, such that for each of the elders who sit upon the seats...

# Second Book of Joachim on the Apocalypse

It is a wondrous thing, because in the working of other good deeds, the Holy Spirit exhibits Himself as if only partially touched by this person or that; yet, in the working of charity, He pours Himself entirely, in a certain manner, into the hearts of the elect. Truly, those other gifts are for all the elect for their salvation, but these special gifts are for the varied utility of the Church. Thus, they are said to burn before the throne because they are given to those for the benefit of the Church, so that they might truly shine like lamps in a dark place <note>A reference to 2 Peter 1:19, comparing prophecy to a lamp in a dark room.</note> until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness. It follows:

<margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin>
<margin>Chapter 10</margin>
**And in the sight of the throne [was] as it were a sea of glass, like crystal.**

The Church of God is built up and advances in two ways: either through those to whom the manifestation of the Spirit is given for utility, or through those who attend to themselves and to doctrine, so that what is drawn from the sea of glass—that is, from the sacred volume of the Holy Scriptures—makes those who drink it provident and those upon whom it is poured circumspect. Therefore, in the sea of glass, the sacred volume of the Scriptures is designated; it remains continually in the sight of the Church so that the elect of God may contemplate the appearance of their own faces in it, to recognize what sort of person each one is. Not only for this reason, however, but also so they may be able to understand the invisible things of God, doubtless "through a mirror in an enigma" <note>original: "per speculum in enigmate." This famous phrase from 1 Corinthians 13:12 refers to seeing a reflection of divine truth indirectly while on earth.</note> and as if through glass, which is transparent. For we cannot say that glass or calm water lacks the likeness of the "letter" <note>The "letter" refers to the literal, surface-level meaning of the Bible as opposed to its spiritual meaning.</note>, since it is established that in glass or water, truth is known through an image, so much so that a man can observe his own face to see what he is like. And it is well said that the sea itself, which is called "glassy," is also "like crystal": both because it is transparent like glass, and because crystal is said to be frozen water. Unless crystal is melted, it presents the appearance of a hard stone rather than a liquid. Hence, the "letter" is said to kill <note>original: "litera occidere dicta est." A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note>, because some things commanded according to the literal sense are quite terrible and strike a certain chill, as when

<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>

<column-break/>

it commands a delinquent to be punished without mercy. Hence it is also said by the Psalmist: "He sends His crystal like morsels; who shall stand before the face of His cold?" <note>original: "Mittit crystallum suum sicut bucellas ante faciem frigoris eius quis sustinebit?" From Psalm 147:17.</note> For the Lord sent His crystal like morsels because the precepts of the Law are hard and exceedingly icy; when understood according to the literal sense, they seemed unbearable. But what follows there? "He shall send out His word, and shall melt them: His spirit shall blow, and the waters shall run." That is, the Lord sent His Word and melted that ice; His Spirit blew, and the waters flowed. This is because the Son of God, having been sent into the world, tempered the precepts of the Law. By explaining them spiritually, He changed them in a certain way into liquid; and what the faithful were not yet able to carry, the same Spirit, sent from the Father and the Son, fulfilled. As if waters flow from the crystal—whose cold was previously unbearable—the cold words of the Law grow warm with the heat of the Holy Spirit. Thus, those things which previously seemed to destroy anything green and growing were at last turned into warmth to nourish them by His tempering. It follows:

<margin>Psalm 147</margin>

**And in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne, were four living creatures having six wings, full of eyes before and behind. And the first living creature was like a lion. And the second living creature was like a calf. And the third living creature had a face as it were of a man. And the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle. And the four living creatures had each of them six wings; and round about and within they are full of eyes.**

<margin>Chapter 14</margin>

--- Page 338 ---
<meta>This page continues the exposition of Revelation Chapter 4. Having previously discussed the sea of glass and the seven lamps of fire, the author now transitions to interpreting the "four living creatures" (the Lion, Calf, Man, and Eagle) that surround the throne, identifying them with specific roles and historical orders within the Church.</meta>

->### Abbot’s Expository Part<-

...to lead. It is the duty of **Deacons** to provide support by assisting pastors and to preserve the virtue of obedience even until the moment of death. It is the duty of **Teachers** <note>original: "Doctorum"</note> to water the faithful with the rain of Christ’s doctrine and to drench the hearts of the people with the trickling of words. It is the duty of **Contemplatives** to rest in their portion and to sigh for the joys of the light above, to abhor the darkness of the world, and to behold the face of their Creator with the purified eyes of the mind.

Of these, two—the **lion** and the **calf**—run about battling outside; truly, the **man** and the **eagle** rest by contemplating internal things. The former are therefore outside; the latter are inside; and for this reason, the living creatures are described as remaining both "inside and outside." <note>A reference to Revelation 4:8, where the creatures are described as being "full of eyes within" and around the throne.</note> This is because the former are "outside" in such a way that they do not desert internal things, and the latter are "inside" in such a way that they spend themselves for the salvation of their brothers.

What was said spiritually of two must be understood of all four living creatures together: that "in the midst and around the throne were four living creatures having six wings, full of eyes in front and behind." Generally, then, this is said of all four, not just two, because both the active and contemplative lives are common to all. Specifically, however, exterior things are ascribed to the first two, and interior things to the remaining two—although, most spiritually, interior things and, as it were, high heavenly matters pertain to the **eagle**. In comparison to the eagle, the third living creature <note>the Man</note> is reckoned among the exterior ones along with the first two, because the eagle excels every winged animal in its flight. 

Nor is it without the fruit of reason that the perfection of the contemplative life is designated sometimes in secret and intimate things, and sometimes in height; for in spiritual matters, these two are joined, and one cannot be found without the other. What is as subtle as a spirit? And what is as high as the exalted Lord, who presides over all creatures? But what is being said will shine forth better if we examine the natures of the individual animals—not indeed of those in whom the Truth resides <note>i.e., the heavenly archetypes</note>, but of those which are below and serve as types.

The **Lion**, the strongest of beasts, fears the onset of no one. The **Ox** <note>original: "Bos," though earlier "Vitulus" (calf)</note> is the most patient in enduring labor and is the only one among the four accustomed to be offered in sacrifice. **Man**, capable of reason and a sharer in wisdom, alone knows how to discern between good and evil. The **Eagle**, a traveler and inhabitant of the upper air, is said to gaze at the sun with unblinking eyes <note>A common medieval bestiary belief was that eagles could stare directly into the sun to prove their nobility or rejuvenate themselves.</note> and is esteemed to leave every feathered kind below itself.

<column-break/>

These things have been said briefly regarding the natures of each animal so that through them we might investigate the gifts of grace nearest to each of the orders, without which no one can seize the palm of justice.

1.  **First** is the fortitude of faith, which the strength of the **lion** designates.
2.  **Second** is patience, designated by the endurance <note>original: "intolerantia," here meaning the capacity to bear burdens or suffering</note> of the **calf**.
3.  **Third** is the purity of doctrine founded in humility, which reason and infirmity <note>the human condition</note> together designate in the **man**.
4.  **Fourth** is the contemplation of God, which the flight of the **eagle** designates, according to that which is written in the fourth part concerning the "woman clothed with the sun," to whom "two wings, as if of an eagle, were given" <note>Revelation 12:1 and 12:14</note> so that she might fly (it says) into her place in the desert, that she might be nourished there for a time, and times, and half a time.

This first gift—fortitude—suits the **Apostles** of faith; for they truly, like brave lions, feared the onset of no one. Through them, the kingdoms of the Gentiles were subdued and handed over into perpetual servitude to the living God who sent them.

The second gift, which is called patience, spiritually suits the **Martyrs**, 
<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
of whom it is said to Almighty God through the Psalmist: *Deal favorably, O Lord, in thy good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built up. Then shalt thou accept the sacrifice of justice, oblations and whole burnt offerings: then shall they lay calves upon thy altar.* <note>Psalm 51:18-19 in modern numbering. The "calves" or "young bulls" represent the sacrifice of the martyrs.</note>

The third is the virtue of humility, attributed to the holy **Confessors**. <note>"Confessors" are saints who suffered for the faith or lived lives of great virtue but were not martyred.</note> To them it was granted to pour out streams of the Scriptures, so that the meadows of hearts, watered by their doctrine and example, might persist in the greenness they first received when the root of faith was planted by the Apostles. This gift is rightly joined to the virtue of humility because there is no doctrine—or at least no true doctrine—that lacks the virtue of humility, as the 
<margin>James 4; Psalm 103</margin>
Apostle James attests when he says: *God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.* And the Psalmist says: *Who sends forth springs in the valleys.* <note>Psalm 104:10. Valleys represent the humble.</note>

The fourth gift is contemplation, which, in order to be fruitful in a person, rests upon the foundation of hope. For in vain does one attribute the gift of contemplation to oneself whose mind is not set on fire by the grace of hope for the love of God. This gift is specifically given to **Virgins**, so that to Christ, to whom they were once [betrothed]...

Each animal represents a specific virtue—fortitude, patience, humility/doctrine, and contemplation—necessary for the Church's spiritual structure.</summary>
