### John’s Second Commentary on the Apocalypse
D 3

...so they may persevere purely into the ages. Clear reasoning compels us to explain these things in this way: specifically, the custom of the Church, which everywhere calls these four orders solemn. Generally, however, we say that the order of **pastors** is designated in the **lion**. In the **calf**, the order of **deacons**. Priests, who are also **teachers**, are represented in the **man**. In the **eagle**, the order of **contemplatives**. The purity of this understanding depends on two obstacles: first, because what is common to all is also specific to individuals; and second, because necessity often changes these orders when they are being administered. Therefore, virtue must be weighed more heavily than necessity, and the gift more than the administration. For whoever possesses the strength of faith is rightly to be called a **lion**, even if he does not hold the office of a prelate <note>A "prelate" refers to a high-ranking member of the clergy, like a bishop or abbot.</note>. Whoever is truly patient is called a **calf**, even if he has not been ordained as a deacon. He who has attained the gift of understanding is truly to be regarded as a **man**, even if he does not hold the office of preaching. He who has attained the grace of contemplating is to be called an **eagle**, even if he remains bodily among men. Furthermore,

<margin>Ezekiel 1</margin>

as the prophet Ezekiel says, each of the animals has within itself the faces of all four, so that the faces of the lion, the man, the calf, and the eagle are held by the lion alone, and so on for the others. From this it happens that some participate so indifferently in the gifts of others that, in the darkness of this life, it is unknown which animal they most resemble. For example, if we speak of martyrdom, both Peter and Paul, as well as Stephen, might seem able to be called "calves," because they suffered for the faith. However, Stephen alone is known to have this by the property of his office <note>Stephen was one of the first seven deacons; the calf represents the sacrificial service of the diaconate.</note>; Peter and Paul do not have it as their primary property, but as if through those other "faces." For Peter’s primary property is that of the **lion**, and Paul’s is that of the **man**, just as Stephen’s is the **calf** and John’s is the **eagle**. But a question arises regarding the four Evangelists who wrote the Holy Gospel in a four-part volume: how are they themselves to be understood in this mystery? That is, whether only in their description <note>Meaning the way they wrote their books.</note> or also in their reception of the gifts of grace. I estimate they are likened to the four animals more in their description than in their personal reception of gifts, except for John the Evangelist. Otherwise, Luke would have needed

<column-break/>

to be crowned with martyrdom more than Mark, since it is established that the likeness of the **calf** is given to Luke, but that of the **lion** to Mark. Nor would I say Mark is likened to the lion undeservedly; it is because he wrote his Gospel from the mouth of Peter, to whose faith strength was granted. Thus, Mark acted as if in the place of Peter—who was in a sense the king of the churches—filling his role by writing from his mouth that which was necessary to describe. He wrote, however, with brevity, passing over the series of historical narration, desiring only to include those things which would strengthen the defenses of faith. This mode of evangelizing is especially fitting for **pastors**, who, because they are entangled in ecclesiastical business, cannot find leisure for long reading. Thus, passing over other things that are perhaps less necessary for this purpose, they touch briefly upon those things that strengthen faith. Truly, the Gospel of Luke is rightly attributed to **deacons**, who write the series of historical truth in an orderly fashion. He describes Jesus Christ himself—whom Matthew calls King and whom the Magi are shown to adore—as being placed among teachers and taking the turn of the disciples. He adds that Christ was subject to his parents (which is characteristic of ministers/servants) and that he held the office of those who recite the Gospel among the people when, taking the book of the prophet Isaiah, he deigned to read from it himself. All of this, if we are wise, pertains to deacons. For the office of the **deacon** is to minister and to announce the Gospel by preaching to the people—namely, to preach Jesus crucified, as is profitable for the "little ones." The Gospel of Matthew, therefore, fits **priests**—that is, the masters of the deacons—because it is the role of **teachers** to explain the Holy Scriptures, correct vices, and compose morals. Matthew teaches that the Lord did this in his Gospel, from that place where it is written: *Unless your justice abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven* <note>Matthew 5:20</note>, all the way to that place where he says: *Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them shall be likened to a wise man who built his house upon a rock* <note>Matthew 7:24</note>. And it is well that in the description of the animals, the calf is placed before the man; for unless the deacon first reads the literal text, the teacher has nothing to explain.

<margin>Luke 4</margin>

<margin>Matthew 5</margin>

It argues that while individuals may share many spiritual gifts, each office and Gospel has a primary character—such as Mark's Lion-like strength or Luke's Calf-like service.</summary>

### Exposition of the Parts
->Part of the Exposition<-

...spiritually he is unknown. The Gospel of **John**, however, is suited to the **contemplatives**, who shows those seeking him that the true light, which illuminates every person coming into this world, can be contemplated as worthily as it is openly. He says: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God* <note>original: "In principio erat verbū z verbum erat apud deum: z deus erat verbū." John 1:1</note>. And a little later: *That was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world* <note>original: "Erat lux vera que illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum." John 1:9</note>. Behold how clearly the Gospels of each writer agree with the individual animals; it is not without the reason of a mystery that these four writers were given.

To the order of **Pastors** <note>The Latin 'pastorum' refers to the shepherds or leaders of the church.</note>, the first of whom is **Peter**, the Gospel of **Mark** is given. To the **Deacons**, the first of whom is **Stephen**, the Gospel of **Luke**. To the **Teachers** <note>original: "Doctorum," referring to those who teach doctrine.</note>, whose prince is **Paul**, the Gospel of **Matthew**. To the **Virgins**, whose mistress is the **Blessed Virgin Mary**, the Gospel of **John**. 

Furthermore, **Mark** was given to **Peter** and **John** to **Mary**; the former as to the father of the Church, the latter as to the mother, not only of the Church, but of God <note>This reflects the tradition that Mark was Peter's interpreter and John cared for Mary after the Crucifixion.</note>. Now, the glory of the **Resurrection** pertains to the **Lion**, while the sublimity of the **Ascension** pertains to the **Eagle**. Because these two events were glorious, Mark and John seem to have received them as a ministry of the Gospel. 

However, because the **Passion** and **Birth** are matters of humility rather than honor, we nowhere read that **Paul** and **Stephen** had "ministers" in this regard; rather, they had them as equals: **Paul** with **Matthew**, and **Stephen** with **Luke**. This is because Christ Jesus, having become a true man for the sake of men, sought equality rather than preeminence. When the hour of his Passion was near, he wished to serve rather than be served, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Truly, when he rose from the dead, he clearly showed himself to be God and Lord, and even more so when he ascended into heaven. For this reason, **Mark** was given to **Peter** and **John** to **Mary** in the service of the Gospel. The last of these, John, is one of the great and primary disciples of the Savior. Therefore, what the two "inferior" creatures <note>Referring to the Man and the Calf, associated with Christ's earthly life and suffering.</note> suggest by their signs is close to himself, but what 

<column-break/>

the two remaining creatures suggest is "above" himself—one being an indication of goodness, the other of majesty. For those who preach that Christ was born and suffered assert that he was truly **man**; those who teach his rising and ascending into heaven teach that he is truly **God** and **Lord**. 

Therefore, the **Birth** and **Passion** of the Lord are designated in the **Man** and the **Calf**; in the **Lion** and the **Eagle**, the **Resurrection** and **Ascension**. In them are also designated those four gifts we wrote of above, and also the four frequently mentioned orders: the order of **Pastors** in the **Lion** (the first of whom is **Peter**); the **Teachers** in the **Man** (the first of whom is **Paul**); the **Deacons** in the **Calf** (the first of whom is **Stephen**); and the **Contemplatives** in the **Eagle** (the first of whom is the **Virgin Mary**). 

The four **Evangelists** designate four kinds of preachers in this regard, who received the firstfruits of the Spirit to instruct these four orders. They act in the role of the mystery of the Son of God, so that by preaching, they might intimate to the other preachers how they ought to live, and so that they might propagate among the multitude of the common people what they themselves received in their own hearts. 

For example, the Evangelist **Mark** designates the first Apostles as witnesses of the Lord's **Resurrection**, who laid the first foundations of faith after the Lord. **Luke** designates the first **Deacons**, one of whom—**Philip**—the Evangelist himself names; they left their example to posterity in both words and deeds. **Matthew** signifies the first **Teachers**, namely **Paul** and his companions, who were sent to preach to the Gentiles while the number of the twelve Apostles still remained in Judea. From their fountain all those who received the office of Teacher after the Apostles have drunk and still drink. **John** designates the **Virgins** of both sexes who were in the primitive Church, from whom the example of virginity has been derived for those who followed. 

Having said these things briefly concerning the four Evangelists, so that we might not seem to have passed them over in silence, let us now look at the other features of the animals, which are six wings each <note>Referring to the "six wings" mentioned in Revelation 4:8.</note>. The mystery of the Scriptures is manifold and complex...

### John, Part Second, on the Apocalypse
### D 4

Just as one form changes into another—as if liquid wax is being reshaped—we stated above that in the four living creatures <note>The "four animals" or living creatures described in Revelation 4, traditionally the Lion, Calf, Man, and Eagle.</note>, four works of Christ and four corresponding orders are undoubtedly designated in a symbolic way. Morally, they also represent the four virtues: humility, patience, 
<margin>Ezekiel 1</margin>
faith, and hope. These the prophet Ezekiel calls "wings," saying: *Each had four faces, and each had four wings.* <note>original: "Quatuor facies vni: & quatuor pennæ vni." Ezekiel 1:6</note> Indeed, each had four faces just as each had four wings because it is certain that each person possesses four types of knowledge and likewise the four virtues written above. Furthermore, the Seraphim are described as having six wings, designating something similar in those same wings, except that two virtues have been added to the four designated wings. For so it is written concerning them 
<margin>Isaiah 6</margin>
in the prophet Isaiah: *With two wings they covered His face, and with two they covered His feet, and with two they flew.* <note>original: "Duabus alis velabant faciem eius: & duabus velabant pedes eius & duabus volabat." Isaiah 6:2</note> Similarly, here too the animals are described as having six wings each. But how those wings are arranged is not expressed; nevertheless, there is no doubt that they are arranged just like the wings of the Seraphim. Furthermore, the two wings with which the feet are veiled are understood to likewise veil the bodies of the animals. Whence it is said in that other place: *Two wings 
<margin>Ezekiel 1</margin>
of each were joined together, and two covered their bodies.* <note>original: "Due pennæ singulorum iungebantur: & due: tegebant eorum corpora." Ezekiel 1:11</note> Therefore, the two wings with which the bodies are veiled are **penance** and **mercy**, by which the shame of our nakedness—that is, the foulness of our sins—is covered. Whence it is also said through the Psalmist: *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins 
<margin>Psalm 31</margin>
are covered.* <note>original: "Beati quorū remissæ sunt iniquitates: & quorum tecta sunt peccata." Psalm 32:1 in modern Bibles.</note> Truly, not a few authorities testify that this blessedness persists through penance and mercy. Concerning penance, Peter says in the 
<margin>Acts 3</margin>
Acts of the Apostles: *Repent and be converted, so that your sins may be wiped away.* <note>original: "Penitemini & conuertimini: vt deleantur peccata vestra." Acts 3:19</note> Concerning mercy, Truth itself <note>A common medieval title for Christ.</note> says: *Blessed are the 
<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.* <note>original: "Beati misericordes quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur." Matthew 5:7</note> The two wings with which the faces are covered are **humility** and **patience**; with these, holy people are accustomed to cover the "justice" designated in the face, lest whatever they do justly be lost through a vain desire for praise. The two wings with which they fly are **faith** and **hope**, through which every holy animal is raised to the heights. These are those six wings which these holy animals are described as having. Ezekiel omitted two of them, doubtless because faith and hope can be understood silently beneath the four; for he who is humble and patient, and likewise repentant and merciful, possesses those other two virtues without a doubt. But enough has been said of these things for this place.

Symbolically, I estimate that the six wings—which together total twenty-four—designate those who are called the "seats of the elders." Because they transcend other saints by the prerogative of their gifts, they lift others up toward sublime things by their own example, so that those who could not stand in the heights by themselves are carried by the strength and, as it were, the lightness of these elders. For we read in the passions of the martyrs <note>Historical accounts of the deaths of Christian martyrs.</note> that some, having been snatched away to punishments, reached the point of collapse, but were then comforted by other saints who excelled in the constancy of faith; thus they overcame the tortures of the executioners and remained unconquered until their final breath. What then shall we call those martyrs, if not the "wings" of the others—they who both acted courageously themselves and held others up so they would not fall? And what shall we call those hermits <note>referring to the Desert Fathers or monastic recluses.</note> if not "wings," who by word and example instructed the weaker and younger brothers, carrying them through prayer so that they might bear them along to perfection? 

In this matter, one must also carefully consider that there are twenty-four elders and the same number of seats; that is, twenty-four legions of saints. If we divide these into four parts, six elders and as many seats are ascribed to each of the animals. Thus, in the **lion** we receive those strong in faith; in the **calf**, those robust in patience; in the **man**, those endowed with knowledge; and in the **eagle**, those suspended in contemplation. Therefore, the elders are joined to the seats, and the seats to the animals by participation, just as the animals are joined to the throne of God, so that the whole may be bound together by the highest bond of unity. Unless perhaps someone says that the seats are distinct from the animals, and the animals themselves pertain to the greatest seat—

<column-break/>

### Abbot’s Part of the Exposition
### 106

...to remain: for they say especially that the seats <note>These are the twenty-four thrones of the elders mentioned in Revelation 4:4.</note> are in a circle around the throne, while the living creatures are in the middle and in the circle. Thus, just as we understand the twenty-four seats to represent as many legions, so we understand the throne and the living creatures to represent that great crowd which no one could number.

<margin>Revelation 7</margin>
But the living creatures are written to be full of eyes "before and behind" because they prudently avoid carnal desires that war against the soul, and they wisely distinguish the works of justice that are to be done from the works of darkness. For they see the good things that must be done so clearly that, looking behind them, they also carefully attend to the evils that must be lamented. In this way, they pass through to internal things with a spiritual effort, yet they never hand over their past sins to oblivion. For each person ought to remember their past faults as much as they confidently presume to be able to do good and avoid evil in the future. For one must lean on past faults as if on certain roots, lest by chance a breeze of pride agitates the worker, causing them to fall from a higher place because they trusted themselves to stand more firmly. One ought to consider even small and minor offenses as great, because the burden of sins is weighed not by human judgment, but by divine judgment. In that judgment, we often read that things thought to be heavy were easily dismissed, while things hoped to be light and minimal remained unbreakable bonds because of the stain of pride.

<margin>2 Samuel 11</margin>
For who would not consider David's double fault—namely, adultery and homicide—to be worse than the sin of Saul, who spared the herds of oxen and sheep against the word of the prophet, thinking it was a good thing not to kill them? For He who had commanded through Moses that one must not commit adultery or kill, Himself commanded through Samuel that whatever belonged to Amalek should be destroyed, from man even to beast.

<margin>Exodus 20</margin>
<margin>1 Samuel 15</margin>
Both men were found to be resistant to the voice of the Lord, and yet God did not take pity on Saul even though Samuel prayed for him. But He spared David immediately at that hour, doubtless because obstinacy destroyed the former while humility saved the latter; making excuses made Saul guilty of a greater fault, while a prompt confession freed David from death. For as soon as he recognized his fault and confessed that he had sinned, the prophet said: "Do not fear; the Lord has transferred your sin." <note>original: "transtulit dominus peccatum tuum." 2 Samuel 12:13.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>2 Samuel 12</margin>
Therefore, whoever judges himself innocent has no "eyes behind" him; for if he knew how to fully consider his own origin, his beginning took its start from a fault. He would carefully recognize that David’s confession is true, which says:

<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
> I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me. <note>Psalm 51:5 in modern Bibles. The author uses this to explain "original sin" or the inherent fallen state of humanity.</note>

Even if other sins were lacking—which is quite difficult—he would acknowledge this. Truly, the holy living creatures are said to have eyes both "before and behind" because they incessantly think about doing good, they wipe away past faults with pious tears, they strive to guard themselves against future evils, and they study to obtain forgiveness for the past. But it is not enough for us to weigh the pits into which we might fall or have already fallen—which is understood to apply to the greater crimes—unless we also scrutinize the virtues and vices of the "inner man" with vigilant discussion. This is so that no virtue is missing (without which the others cannot stand), and so the tempter does not stealthily send in vices through some opening. Rightly then, after what was said about "before and behind," it was added: *And the four living creatures had six wings each, and in the circle and within they are full of eyes.* One must distinguish very carefully what is meant by "before and behind" and what by "within and in the circle," and what the difference is between them. For it is one thing to have eyes before and behind, and another in the circle and within. In the former, a healthy memory is necessary; in the latter, circumspection and vigilance. By the former, committed sins are mourned and future ones avoided. By the latter, spiritual vices that are hidden within are identified and discussed, and a person industriously stands guard so that the hidden enemies who walk "in the circle" do not find some unfortified entrance to the mind. By the former, past things are contemplated and future things avoided. By the latter, the spiritual wars that are presently imminent, both inside and out, are revealed and avoided. The Psalmist showed that he saw this when he said:

<margin>Psalm 76</margin>
> I thought of ancient days and I had eternal years in my mind. <note>Psalm 77:5 in modern Bibles.</note>

He was supplicating the Lord for this, so that He might purify him internally and externally...

The text contrasts the biblical figures of David and Saul to illustrate how humility and confession lead to forgiveness, while pride and excuses lead to ruin.</summary>

### John’s Second Part on the Apocalypse
### 109

...that he might deign to cleanse; saying in his prayers and professions: *Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, <margin>Psalm 18</margin> and spare your servant from the sins of others.* <note>original: "Ab occultis meis munda me domine... et ab alienis parce servo tuo." This is a quote from Psalm 19:12-13 in modern numbering.</note> Therefore, the four living creatures possess these perfections through which they are deemed worthy of the praise of God and of dwelling in his house, <margin>Psalm 83</margin> according to that word of the Psalmist: *Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever.* <note>Psalm 84:4</note> Hence, the following is added:

<margin>Rev. 4:8</margin> **And they had no rest day and night, saying: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.**

<margin>Isaiah 6</margin> This is also written concerning the Seraphim. It says: *They cried out to one another: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.* But what is designated by "day" except peace, and what by "night" except tribulation? It is no great thing for a person to praise God during the "day," unless he also praises Him in the "night," according to the words of that holy man <note>referring to Job</note>: *The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased God, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord.* <note>Job 1:21</note> For this reason, it is also said through the Psalmist: *In the nights lift up your hands in the sanctuary and bless the Lord.* <margin>Psalm 133</margin> He does not say this only for the "day" when prosperous and desired things succeed, but also for the "nights" when darkness and miseries become terrifying. Thus, the holy living creatures do not cease to invoke the God who is Three and One, neither in day nor in night; because neither in prosperity nor in adversity do they rest from the worthy and perpetual profession of the Holy Trinity and Unity. For the phrase "they had no rest" was not set down as a punishment, but according to that saying of the prophet Isaiah: <margin>Isaiah 62</margin> *For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest.* As for the phrase *Who was, and who is, and who is to come,* let it suffice that we have explained this in the earlier part of the book. It follows:

<margin>Rev. 4:9-11</margin> **And when those four living creatures gave glory, and honor, and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sits on the throne, and they adored him who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the throne, saying: Worthy are you, our Lord God, to receive glory, and honor, and blessing, and power, because you created all things, and by your will they were created.**

If we refer these words to the birth of the Church, the reasoning does not seem sufficiently clear, because the four orders <note>The different ranks of the faithful described earlier.</note> which we wrote of above were not yet complete, seeing as they were still in their beginning at that time; furthermore, how the twenty-four elders adored before the one sitting on the throne is obscure, unless perhaps a part is taken for the whole. But it is more correctly referred to the final time, when all things shall be consumed, or certainly to the course of this present time, under which the four living creatures labor and suffer many dangers for the faith of their God. Furthermore, the **twenty-four elders** can be understood as the great high priests <note>The term "pontifices" here refers to the highest-ranking bishops of the early Church.</note>: such as the Patriarchs of **Antioch**, **Alexandria**, **Constantinople**, and also the five **Metropolitans**, <note>A Metropolitan is a bishop who has authority over an entire ecclesiastical province.</note> because they are seen to keep the place on earth of those who were seen sitting in glory upon the twenty-four thrones. The twenty-four elders fall down at the voice of the living creatures praising God, and they praise and magnify Him who lives forever and ever. This is because when the great leaders of the Christians, who preside over all the orders of the Church, see those same holy orders so strengthened in the faith that they do not keep silent from the praise of the Creator in neither prosperity nor adversity, they rejoice in their hearts and ascribe the entire work to God the Creator, who works all things in all people. Therefore, they place their crowns before the throne <margin>1 Cor. 15</margin> saying: *Worthy are you, Lord, to receive glory, and honor, and power, and blessing, because you created all things, and by your will they were made.* For they do not extol themselves as if they were to receive a reward out of debt, nor do they think themselves crowned with glory and honor or worthy of praise by their own merit, but they attribute everything to God, by whom and for whom all things were made. For this is what is said by the voice of Truth: *When...*

<column-break/>

### Abbot: Part of the Exposition
### 110

<margin>Luke 17</margin>
...when you have done all the acts of righteousness commanded of you, say: *We are useless servants.* <note>original: "Serui inutiles sumus." From Luke 17:10.</note> In contrast, those who refuse to lay their crowns at the feet of the Lord are those who attribute their righteousness to themselves. Because of this, they do not offer praise and thanks to God for the gifts they have received, but instead expect a reward for their works as if it were a debt owed to them for their own natural goodness. However, holy men do not act this way; instead, they say: *You have performed all our works in us.* <note>original: "omnia opera nostra operatus est nobis." From Isaiah 26:12.</note>

<margin>Isaiah 26</margin>
Having set forth these things in the manner of a preface for this second part, the author now comes to the sequence of events. He reveals through marvelous riddles how these living creatures succeeded by fighting through six periods of time, and how the scroll that was rolled up was opened during their battles. He adds:

<margin>Chapter 5. A. 1.</margin>
**AND I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals.**

This book which John saw is the single, general volume of Holy Scripture, containing within itself all the histories produced by the holy prophets under the Old Testament. The book was seen in the right hand of God because in it, things that are prosperous and worthy of praise are announced to the chosen, according to that word of the Apostle:

<margin>Romans 8</margin>
*We know that for those who love God, all things work together for good.* <note>Romans 8:28</note> The book was seen in the right hand of God because through it, the salvation of the world came to be known. This is why it is also said through Moses: *In his right hand is a fiery law.* <note>Deuteronomy 33:2</note> It is written **within and without** because it shows one thing according to the **letter** <term>literal meaning: the historical or surface-level events described</term> and displays another according to **allegory** <term>allegorical meaning: the deeper spiritual or symbolic truth</term>. On the "outside," it speaks to the little ones (the spiritually immature); on the "inside," it speaks to the grown. On the outside, it speaks by instructing the body; on the inside, by shaping the soul in faith. But who could understand this unless Christ revealed it through his works? To set aside other examples: it would have been enough for a teacher of the Law to find Ezekiel’s writings and the four living creatures described in them to see what we have said above, were it not that Christ—by being born, suffering, rising, and ascending into heaven—manifested those sacred orders (designated by the four creatures) not so much by the teaching of a hollow voice, but by the power of the event itself. For what was the prophet showing when he wrote of these four living creatures in mystical terms? Was it that which was present then—except perhaps in part? I say no: it was that which was to come. And how was it to come? Just as Christ was going to accomplish it.

<column-break/>

Who, therefore, could understand this unless Christ showed it by doing it himself? To include what is most relevant to the matter: who could perceive, by guessing with a spirit of understanding, the **wheel within a wheel** <note>original: "rotam infra rotam." A reference to the vision in Ezekiel 1:16.</note>—representing the Old and New Testaments—unless Christ, coming into the world, had completed the New Testament? Yet this book was noted to be written within and without just as the wheel within a wheel was shown to that same prophet, because (as I have already said) the "outer wheel" is shown as history to the little ones, while the "inner wheel" is revealed to the perfect. According to this, the Church commends two lives: the **active** and the **contemplative**. Of these, the one which is exterior is taught more by examples than by simple words; the other is taught by meditation on the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, when we speak to simple people <note>original: "idiotis," referring to the unlearned or laypeople.</note> who are not yet able to grasp spiritual things, we set before them the righteousness of the Fathers which the Old Testament displays. We do this so that they—observing what preceded in those men—might hasten to fulfill the heavenly mandate, rather than thinking it is something to be held onto only in a simple, heard sense. We set before them, I say, the examples of the Fathers; we set before them their lives: namely, the innocence of Abel, the obedience of Abraham, the simplicity of Jacob, the patience of Job, and similar things. This is so that those who cannot grasp high and great things may at least be nourished by those things which are lower and suitable for "little ones." Truly, more spiritual and "internal" words are suitable for contemplative perfection, because (as it is said) *the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one.*

<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>
But we can pursue these and similar things now because, with the book largely uncovered, the "inner wheel" now recurs to the "outer" parts. Before the passion of Christ, however, it was sealed with seven seals, and the way into this wheel was open to no man, since this privilege was reserved for the Lord who died and rose again. Hence, it is added immediately:

<margin>A. 2.</margin>
**AND I saw a strong angel, proclaiming with a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and loosen its seals? And no one could** <note>The text cuts off here at "pote" (could/was able), to be completed as "poterat" on the next page.</note>

It emphasizes that these spiritual depths remained sealed and incomprehensible until Christ's life, death, and resurrection "unlocked" them.</summary>

# Joachim's Second Book on the Apocalypse
## 110

...[was found] in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth to open the scroll, nor to look upon it. <note>original: "in coelo: neq; in terra: neq; subtus terram aperire librũ: neq; respicere illum." This is a continuation of the previous page's discussion of Revelation 5:3.</note>

<margin>Luke 3</margin>
I believe this "strong angel" is John the Baptist, who said regarding this very mystery: *One mightier than I is coming after me, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.* <note>original: "Veniet fortior me post me: cuius ego non sum dignus vt soluam corrigiam calciamentorum eius." From Luke 3:16.</note> For spiritual understanding lies hidden within the literal "sandal." John was indeed a "strong angel" because he was sent to run ahead of the "Strength of God." <note>A play on the name "Gabriel" or the nature of Christ as the power of God.</note> And yet, he confesses himself unequal to the task of loosening the mysteries, because this privilege (as we have already said) was reserved for Christ. 

And "no one," he says, "was able to open the scroll." Not the legal expert endowed with literal knowledge; not any of the poets learned in worldly wisdom; not the souls of the dead dwelling in the underworld, who are said to predict the future through a <term>spirit of divination</term> <note>original: "spiritum phytonicum," referring to the Pythia or the witch of Endor; the author suggests these are often demons in disguise.</note>—if indeed the souls themselves answer and not rather demons transformed into their likeness—none of these were able to open the mysteries of the Scriptures. For God alone is the one who can do all things; He alone retains and distributes to everyone as He wills. 

The reason this privilege was not given to the ancient fathers is that God had decreed to come through Himself, and to teach those He Himself had created, so that He might testify by both His teaching and His works that He is the author of light. In the meantime, Holy Scripture was overshadowed by a certain gloom; as we read in Exodus, it was covered by a cloud of obscurity. *When Moses,* it says, *had ascended to the Lord on the mountain, a cloud covered the mountain, and the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, covering it with a cloud for six days; and on the seventh day He called him from the midst of the darkness.* <note>Referencing Exodus 24:15-16.</note> Just as the Lord covered Mount Sinai with darkness for six days and called Moses on the seventh from the midst of the cloud, so too what He willed to remain hidden through six "days" or periods of time <note>Joachim of Fiore's famous theology of history, dividing time into distinct ages or "status."</note> is revealed in the seventh period, as the elect enter through faith into the inner mysteries, so that the truth which lay hidden for so long may clearly shine forth.

<column-break/>

This has been fulfilled in this time, which—with respect to the preceding ages, as we have clearly shown in our *Work on Concordance* <note>original: "opere concordiæ," referring to Joachim's treatise "The Harmony of the Old and New Testaments."</note>—can be called both the sixth and the seventh. It will be completed perfectly and clearer than light when the seventh angel begins to sound his trumpet. 

Therefore, from the coming of the Savior, Divine Scripture began to be opened for us, and for the most part it is now accessible; but for the Jews, it remains obscure and covered by a veil. As it is said of Scripture by the Psalmist: *Dark water in the clouds of the air.* <margin>Ps. 17, Ps. 103</margin> And again: *Stretching out the heaven like a skin, you who cover its upper parts with waters.* <note>Psalm 104:2-3 (Vulgate 103).</note> Almighty God stretched out the heaven like a skin when He commanded those things which could be understood literally to the faithful of the Old Testament through the prophets. For who does not know that the prophets taught the people of God many things according to the "letter"—concerning the instruction of morals, the love of God and neighbor, and various works of piety? In these matters, if the literal sense is discarded, one goes astray. 

Therefore, the heaven is stretched out like a skin when simple things are told to simple people. And yet, its "upper parts" are covered with waters because, while the first elect of that time were to observe certain things according to the letter, the greater mysteries remained unknown until the pre-appointed times. 

According to the <term>anagoge</term> <note>The spiritual or "upward" interpretation of Scripture leading toward heavenly realities.</note>, many things still lie hidden from men dwelling on earth, which are known only to the angels and the souls of the saints already established in the heavenly homeland. But to us who are below, they are concealed until the day fully dawns. Indeed, even if the prophets understood many things, they did not all understand everything; rather, each was given more or less according to the measure and pleasure of the Giver. For David, who produced such wonders in the Psalter, did not know whether he himself would build the house for the Lord; and Elisha, who was accustomed to having the spirit of prophecy, perceived that the Shunammite woman was indeed sad, but he did not know the cause of her sadness because the Lord hid it from him. 

Therefore, neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth was anyone found who, by opening the scroll, could loosen its seals, because the gift of understanding was not given to any of the saints, nor even...

# The Abbot's Expository Part

[It was not given] to the angels who are in heaven, nor to any of the philosophers educated in worldly knowledge, nor to the spirits of the dead or to demons, to reveal the secrets of the scriptures. This remained hidden until He came who was to suffer according to the letter and rise again with spiritual understanding. <note>The author contrasts the physical suffering of Christ (the "letter" or literal event) with the spiritual meaning of His resurrection.</note> If the Jews had recognized Him, they never would have crucified the King of Glory. For this reason, when Daniel asked what the meaning of the words was, <margin>Daniel 12</margin> the angel did not dare to explain what he requested, but said, "Go, Daniel, for the words are closed and sealed." It follows:

<margin>A. 3.</margin> **And I wept much, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll, or to look upon it.**

He who sees and does not understand, sees nothing; or if he does see, it is often for the sake of judgment, so that he may have no excuse. For this reason, when the disciples asked why He spoke to the crowds in parables, <margin>Luke 8</margin> He replied: *That seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear, nor understand.* <note>original: "Ut videntes non videant & audientes non audiant: neq; intelligant." From Luke 8:10.</note>

Now John (as we have said) represents the <term>Church of contemplatives</term>. <note>A group within the Church focused on deep prayer and mystical understanding of scripture, rather than just outward ritual.</note> Therefore, John’s weeping is to be understood as the sorrow of that very Church. For not just anyone can say, "My eyes are always toward the Lord." Just as a person is rightly called "contemplative," so too can they be called "understanding." It is one thing to believe in God and have the eyes of the mind ready for constant contemplation of Him; it is quite another to know Him and all His secrets that lie hidden in the depths of the scriptures. The former He gives to many, but the latter He gives only to a few and on appointed days. Thus, the Church of Christ wept at times when she did not understand the hidden mysteries, because many heretics rising from her midst were attacking the Catholic faith. First, the <term>Judaizers</term> <note>Early Christians who insisted that followers of Christ must still follow the full Mosaic Law, such as circumcision and dietary restrictions.</note> strove to lead the faithful back to observing the Law of Moses; and because there were very few who understood the scriptures spiritually, they did not know how to respond to their adversaries when faced with this difficulty. Similarly, in the time that followed, heresies began to sprout up here and there, tearing the unity of the Church apart, because even if they felt a mystical understanding existed, they were not yet able to grasp it as they should. Indeed, this is recognized as the chief cause of error. For whoever

<column-break/>

embraces the <term>letter that kills</term> <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." It refers to a strictly literal reading of scripture that misses the divine intent.</note> and argues that mystical words must be understood according to the simple literal meaning, immediately begins to be a heretic; just as, on the other hand, are those who pointlessly invent mysteries where there is only literal truth. Some, indeed, err in the text of the letter, and others in spiritual understanding, because they do not possess the spirit of discernment—straying, as it were, into opposite types of wrongdoing. For he who walks in darkness does not know where he is going, and whether he turns to the right or to the left, he stumbles. To add something more fitting regarding this grief, the record of Church history clearly declares how much bitter sorrow it gave to the faithful of Christ. <margin>John 19</margin> We read that because of this, many philosophers came to the Council of Nicaea, tossing about the simplicity of the Holy Church with the "horns of pride" and attacking the Catholic faith with <term>dialectical arguments</term>. <note>Formal logic and philosophical debate used to challenge traditional doctrines.</note> From there, taking the opportunity, other sects of heretics proceeded from that one heresy, and in all these things was the grief of the Church. But to show the faithful that the victory must be fulfilled, which the Elder uses to comfort John, suddenly eminent teachers shone forth in the Church of Christ. <margin>Doctors of the Church</margin> Finally, at almost the same time, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and other great teachers shone out together. All of them, drinking from the fountain of the book which Christ opened, began to water the parched hearts of the people, wiping away the tears of Holy Mother Church with many labors. The Elder therefore foretold to John what we now rejoice to see largely completed: that the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, just as the waters cover the sea. But from where does this come? Surely from that which is promised in this place. For it follows:

<margin>A. 4.</margin> **And one of the elders said to me: "Do not weep. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered to open the scroll and its seven seals."**

If John the Evangelist represents the Church of the righteous, who is this Elder who spoke here, if not John himself? He is one of those renowned elders who wrote down these very things we are speaking of for the instruction and consolation of the Church; and not he alone, but all those to whom...

This sorrow was relieved when Christ, the Lion of Judah, enabled the great Church Fathers like Augustine and Jerome to "open the scroll" through spiritual understanding.</summary>

# Joachim’s Second Part on the Apocalypse

It was given to know this: that they are to be understood equally with him. And it should be noted that the sacred mysteries do not reach their completion as suddenly as they can be spoken; indeed, many things are described at once in the book which were fulfilled over the course of many centuries. Therefore, just as the whole book was not opened all at once, but through seven periods of time, so the mourning of the church is gradually removed, and its comfort grows as if by specific increments. One might ask regarding the opening of the scroll: why is the lamb who was slain described as the "lion of the tribe of Judah" and the "conqueror of death," unless the explanation of this point had already been given at the start of this work? For there, if I am not mistaken, we discussed the lion and the lamb, the death and life of Christ, and the tomb and his rising from it—which he performed for our sake. Do not be reluctant to turn back the pages and reread what was previously written; it is much better to do that than to burden this volume with repetitions. Now, Christ is called the "Root of David" because he was born of the seed of David and was great among kings. But why the "root" of David and not a "branch" or the "crown"? <note>The author uses "vertex" (crown/top) to represent the highest or most visible part of a tree, contrasting it with the hidden but foundational root.</note> This is because there are two births for men—not indeed for all, but for those who are reborn in Christ. The first of these, which is carnal, is represented in the root; the spiritual birth is designated in the branches. For we see the roots of certain trees sprout, and shoots rise from them as the earth is broken here and there; similarly, the birth of Christ's flesh, which took its origin from the earth, is designated in the root of David. This is why, concerning the birth of the Virgin from the lineage of Judah,

<margin>Isaiah 11.</margin>
it is said by the prophet: *A rod shall come out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from his root.* <note>original: "Egredietur virga de radice Jesse: et flos de radice eius ascendet." See Isaiah 11:1.</note> And 

<margin>Isaiah 53.</margin>
again, the same prophet says of Christ—that he was to be born of a virgin before the Father: *He shall ascend* (he says) *like a sapling before him, and like a root from thirsty ground.* <note>original: "Ascendet... sicut virgultum coram eo: et sicut radix de terra sitienti." From Isaiah 53:2.</note> According to this, therefore, Christ is called the "Root of David," because the life of the tree is in the root, from which (as we said) the shoots are produced. Indeed, the Root of David, one of the precious roots, sprouted and became the "true vine," to which the Holy Spirit afterwards attached innumerable branches. He himself is the Root of David, who lives and reigns in the house of Jacob forever, as is said by the prophet 

<margin>Isaiah 9.</margin>
*Upon the throne of David, and over his kingdom*

<column-break/>

*he shall sit.* And the angel said to Mary: *The Lord God will give him the seat of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob, and of his kingdom there will be no end.* <note>original: "Dabit illi dominus deus sedem David patris sui: et regnabit in domo Jacob: et regni eius non erit finis." From Luke 1:32-33.</note> This mention of the king and the kingdom is quite fitting, because the lion is the strongest and, in a sense, the king of beasts. Strong is the lion, strong is Judah, strong is David; and therefore royal power is ascribed to them. For Christ the strong rose from the dead and entered the powers of his kingdom through the victory of his passion. Did he not say himself: *Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?* <note>original: "Haec oportuit pati christum: et sic intrare in gloriam suam?" From Luke 24:26.</note> And again: *All power is given to me in heaven and on earth.* It follows:

For just as we say, *Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,* so they also professed he would come, saying, *Blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord.* This is why he says of himself in the Gospel: *Blessed are the eyes that see what you see: for I tell you that many kings and prophets wanted to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.* <note>original: "Beati oculi qui vident que vos videtis..." Christ was in the middle of these. But why "in the middle of the throne"? Because the throne itself is generally made up of the two testaments. Thus, in the middle of the throne and the four living creatures and the elders, the Lamb of God was seen as if slain, because he himself is (as the apostle says) our peace.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Revelation 5, moving from the identity of the Lion of Judah and the Root of David to the appearance of the Lamb "as if slain." It explains why Christ is depicted both as a Lion and a Lamb, emphasizing his dual nature as the victorious King and the humble servant.</meta>

### Abbot’s Part of the Exposition

<margin>Ephesians 2</margin>...our peace, who has made both one, breaking down the middle wall of partition <note>original: "medium parietem solvens macerie"</note>, so that he might create the two in himself and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, slaying the enmity in himself. Therefore, the Old Testament also pertains in some way to the four living creatures and the throne of God, insofar as the man Christ Jesus was seen in the midst of the throne and the four living creatures. However, even if this word refers only to the New Testament, Christ nevertheless stands in the midst of the throne, the creatures, and the elders. For, as we have already said in the preceding book, to sit above belongs to sublimity, while to stand in the middle belongs to humility.

Hence, he who is the King of the humble and of little ones, when he wished to show his disciples a master-class in humility, called a certain little child and set him in the midst, saying: "Unless you are converted and become <margin>Matthew 18</margin> like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever, therefore, humbles himself like this little child, he is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven." He did this and spoke regarding the child whom he placed in the midst of the disciples, yet he did not think it sufficient unless <margin>Luke 22</margin> he also said of himself: "But I am in the midst of you, not as one who reclines at the table, but as one who serves." 

Therefore, just as he is called a "Lamb" for the sake of humility—and what is more, "as if slain"—so he is said to be in the midst of the throne, the four creatures, and the elders for the sake of humility. For he himself is the form of justice for all, and the example of humility for everyone. It should be noted, however, that while he is called a "Lion" when rising from the dead and going to the gates of hell, he is called a "Lamb," not a Lion, here. "I saw," he says, "a Lamb as if slain." 

Intending to describe the sequence of the opening <note>The opening of the seven seals of the scroll.</note>, the author directed the eyes of the mind to the beginning: "The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered." But because Christ would not rise unless he first underwent death, the author looks at the beginning in another way. "I saw," he says, "a Lamb as if slain." Why "as if slain" and not simply "slain"? Because a death that cannot hold the dead in corruption is not to be called "death," but rather "as if death"—not the permanence of death, but a transition from this world to the Father.

<margin>Revelation 5:6</margin> **And I saw** (he says) **a Lamb standing as if slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.**

<column-break/>

The seven horns of the Lamb are the seven angels of the churches. These are not necessarily those who presided over those specific churches <note>Referring to the seven historical churches of Asia Minor.</note>, but others designated through them—unless, perhaps, they are those seven men sent through the seven periods of time, of whom mention was made in the first part. 

What the seven eyes are, he himself opens when he adds: "Which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth." Indeed, the seven spirits of the Lord are sent into all the earth because the grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured out over the whole world, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit are found in all the churches of the elect of God. For the Spirit <margin>Wisdom 1</margin> of the Lord has filled the world with a manifold division of graces, and this Spirit, which contains all things, has knowledge of the voice. 

And rightly, as he opens the book, he is described as having seven eyes, because through each of the seven seals, individual "eyes" are necessary, so to speak, so that the gifts of grace may reach the various ranks of believers according to their specific needs. For a certain fitness of character is required: 

*   **Fortitude** for the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials or leaders.</note>
*   **Knowledge** for the deacons
*   **Understanding** for the doctors <note>Teachers and theologians.</note>
*   **Wisdom** for the contemplatives
*   **Counsel** for the conventuals <note>Those living in religious communities.</note>
*   **Piety** for those who show mercy to the poor
*   **Fear** for those bound in marriage.

It follows:

<margin>Revelation 5:7</margin> **And he came and took the book from the right hand of him who sat.**

The Lamb went; the Lion came. The Lamb went from life; the Lion came from death. He went by dying for the dead; he came by rising for the dead. Why the book was seen in the right hand of God has been stated above. Furthermore, the Lamb who was slain, changed into a Lion through the glory of his resurrection, came and took the book from the right hand of the one sitting, when he explained that those things written in the Law and the Prophets were fulfilled or to be fulfilled in himself. "And beginning," it says, <margin>Luke 24</margin> "from Moses and the prophets, he interpreted the scriptures to them." 

From that time, therefore, the opening of the book began. From that time, the loosening of the seals was initiated—on that very day when he rose from the dead and opened the minds of his disciples so they might understand the scriptures. However, although signs preceded to loosen the hearts of those who saw in faith and to confirm the "pillars of the earth" which had melted and flowed away in sins—for even then Jannes and Mambres <note>Traditional names for the Egyptian sorcerers who opposed Moses.</note> performed signs through <margin>Exodus 7</margin> incantations...

It also maps the seven spirits of God as specific spiritual gifts distributed among different orders of the Church, such as prelates, teachers, and the married.</summary>

->### Joachim’s Second Book on the Apocalypse<-

...was, and he was about to do very many of their deeds; yet a doubt <note>original: "scrupulus"</note> could not be lacking if one saw only those outward signs and did not rather consider the interior things through spiritual understanding. For this <margin>John 16</margin> is that which was said: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of Truth comes, he will teach you all truth." And he (he says) will bear witness of me. Much more, therefore, was the truth of our faith declared in the mysteries, with the Holy Spirit rendering testimony to Christ in them, than in those great miracles which he showed to the Jews, after which even they themselves wavered in faith. Wherefore he soon adds:

<margin>Revelation 5</margin> "And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps and golden bowls full of incense <note>original: "odoramentorum," literally "fragrants" or "incense"</note>, which are the prayers of the saints. And they sang a new song, saying: 'You are worthy, O Lord our God, to take the book and to open its seals; for you were slain, and have redeemed us to God in your blood out of every tribe, and tongue, and people, and nation; and have made us a kingdom and priests to our God.'"

The four living creatures (that is, all the saints) and the twenty-four elders (who are the established fathers and leaders) recognized the Lamb to be the true Son of God, and that he was not slain by any necessity of his own sin, but for the salvation of the world. And it should be noted that the understanding which pertains to the beginning of the "second state" <note>Joachim's theology divided history into "states" or "ages"</note> is not always to be taken in its entirety, but in part; but that which pertains to the beginning of the "third state" is to be taken in its entirety. And for this reason (as I have already said), that praise must not be thought of as something sudden—as if that whole multitude, designated by the elders and the living creatures, was present at the very time Christ rose from the dead—especially since they say in their profession: <margin>Isaiah 9</margin> "You have redeemed us to God in your blood, out of every tribe, and tongue, and people, and nation."

<column-break/>

But what was heard there once by John must be fulfilled from the time Christ rose from the dead until the end, when even the rebellious Jews themselves shall say with us: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." Now, divine praise is designated by the harps, while preaching is designated by the bowls <margin>Matthew 23</margin>. And because one part of the saints is appointed to professing and another part to preaching—though both groups may do both—what else follows the opening of the book, except that we receive from it how we ought to profess the Lord and how we ought to announce him to the peoples? For in these two ways we profess the Lord: either when we reverently praise him in the churches, or when we faithfully preach him to the peoples. Of the first profession, it is said through the Psalmist: <margin>Psalm 32</margin> "Praise the Lord with the harp; sing to him with the psaltery of ten strings." Of the second, Truth itself says: "He who confesses me <margin>Mark 8</margin> before men, him will I also confess before my Father." If perhaps in private prayer we offer a sweet odor to our God, and not also in solemn preaching? "We are," says the Apostle, "the good odor of God in every place." <margin>2 Corinthians 2</margin> Therefore, even when we profess him before men, we scatter the odor of his praises; because he whom the contemplatives praise in private prayer, the preachers together praise in solemn profession. Whether it be the former or the latter, all his saints together with one voice praise the Savior of the world, saying: "You are worthy, Lord, to open the book," knowing that he alone is worthy to open the hidden mysteries, who alone is the Word and the Wisdom of the Father. And they sang (it says) a "new song." The saints sing a new song because all things that Christ did in the world are new. A new king, a new song, a new doctrine, new commandments. Therefore, he who wishes to have the new things should strive to be without the old. He who wishes to put on the "new man" who is created according to God, let him strive to be stripped of the "old man," who is corrupted day <margin>Ephesians 4</margin> by day according to the desires of this life. But let us hear how sweet this new song is to the throats of the friends of God, because it is sweet to walk in the newness of the spirit and not in the "letter" <note>referring to the literal vs. spiritual interpretation of the law</note>. "You are worthy," they say, "O Lord God, to take the book and open its seals, because you were slain and have redeemed us to God in your blood, out of every tribe, and tongue, and people, and nation; and have made us a kingdom and priests to our God." "Therefore," they say, "you are worthy to open the book, because you were slain."

->### The Abbot’s Exposition: Part Two<-

For it is as if the Lord killed the letter <note>original: "litteram," referring to the literal or "fleshly" interpretation of the Law</note> with himself: since indeed he willed to be killed in time in his body, which he took from the Virgin, so that he might kill the oldness of the letter; and he rose from the dead in a spiritual body, so that as many of us as have put on the "new man" who is created according to God might walk in the newness of the spirit. For this is that which the apostle had earlier sent ahead in the same place, saying:
<margin>Romans 7</margin>
"A woman, while her husband lives, shall be called an adulteress if she is with another man; but if her husband dies, she shall be freed from the law of the husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man."
<margin>Romans 7</margin>
"Therefore you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another who rose from the dead." He says this, and a little later he added the point we just mentioned, saying: "So that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter." In this way, therefore, we were redeemed in the blood of Christ so that we might not be servants, but free. Nor should we think as the carnal Jews do, who still grow foul in the oldness of the letter and the servitude of the law, believing redemption comes only from the Hebrew people or only from the royal and levitical tribes; but from every tribe, and tongue, and people, and nation, we have been made a kingdom and priests for our God. Now, who are those who say these things? Is it not the four living creatures? It now appears clearly that what previously seemed obscure—namely, the four living creatures—designates the orders of the saints. For surely four individual men cannot be meant here? How indeed does the following follow?

<margin>Lesson 9</margin>
> And they shall reign upon the earth.

Since this is not the voice of those who say, "And you have made us a kingdom and priests to our God," but of the blessed John who wrote these things himself. So also in his Gospel, the voice with which he spoke to his disciples he turned toward them, so that they themselves seem to speak, when he says:
<margin>John 21</margin> <note>The text says John 12, but refers to the famous ending of John 21:24</note>
"This is 그 disciple who gives testimony of these things, and we know that his testimony is true." For the priests of the Lord reign and shall yet reign upon the earth, because under their power many thousands of men are subjected, who obey them for the love of Christ in all subjection; and they shall obey more perfectly toward the end, when the stone shown to Daniel <note>Referring to the stone in Daniel 2:35 that becomes a mountain and fills the earth</note> shall fill the entire
<margin>Daniel</margin>

<column-break/>

surface of the earth. Certainly, when the blessed John described this vision of his, the enemies of Christ held the Roman Empire. But so that Almighty God might make us certain of heavenly things, he even subjected the empire of this world by bowing it beneath the feet of his saints. For who of the faithful would say he is ignorant that the universal and Roman Pontiff is the Vicar of the Emperor of Heaven? What if the children of this world often raise themselves against him, so that they may fall; let them be lifted up even to the heavens, so that they may descend even to the depths? Indeed, the Son of Man goes as it is written of him. Woe to that man by whom he shall be betrayed. Surely if he dies, he rises; if he falls, he is raised up; if he is submerged, he is elevated. For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous. Nor will he forsake his Church until the end, nor desert his members until the consummation of the age. It follows:

<margin>Lesson</margin>
> And I saw and I heard the voice of many angels around the throne, and of the living creatures, and of the elders; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing."

To remain "in a circle" <note>original: "in circuitu," around or in the perimeter</note> is understood in two ways. For those who run to and fro for defense on this side and that remain in the circle in one way. In another way, those who cannot see the inner things. Therefore, Pastors and Deacons are said to run "around" the throne—that is, the spiritual Church—because they confidently oppose themselves to the jaws of wolves on behalf of those who are free for contemplation. But the Laity and the unlearned <term>unlearned: "idiote," referring to those without specialized theological training</term> are said to remain "around" the throne, and the living creatures, and the elders; because those who are accustomed to travel by the broad and spacious way, and as if through the streets of towns, cannot remain in the height of contemplation. Thus, therefore, the Pastors and Deacons are appointed for the guardianship...

### John’s Second Part on the Apocalypse

...the guardianship of the city: so that they may have the **spiritual** and **celibate** within, and the **carnal** and **secular** without. Thus, while they live spiritually, they conduct themselves spiritually as those who are perfect; yet when they are among those who are "animal" <note>original: "animales," referring to those guided by natural instincts rather than the Holy Spirit</note>, they show a certain appearance of carnality—not out of an affection of the soul, but out of compassion—so that they might better win them over. Therefore, these thousands of angels designate an infinite multitude of laypeople who, according to their own small measure, imitate illustrious and perfect men in the praise of their Savior. 

And what do they say? They say: **"Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing."** It should be noted that in the previous chapter, the saints glorify God the Father, saying: "Worthy are you, our Lord God, to receive glory, and honor, and power, and blessing, because you created all things, and by your will they were made." But here they say: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing." 

The Father is called worthy because he himself created; the Son is called worthy not only because he created, but also because by dying he redeemed. <note>original: "Nihil enim nobis nasci profuit, nisi redimi profuisset." This famous phrase is also found in the Exsultet, the Latin hymn sung during the Easter Vigil.</note> **For it would have profited us nothing to be born, unless it had profited us to be redeemed.** In the first instance, power is praised; here, humility. There, excellence; here, mercy. 

Furthermore, the Son is said to "receive" these things here, just as the Father was, not because he did not always possess them within himself, but because in the hearts of carnal men—who look only upon the **"form of a servant"** <note>A reference to Philippians 2:7, describing Christ's humanity</note>—he is not esteemed or believed to be what he truly is. Because of this, he still endures the tongues of blasphemers who say he is a mere man, the son not of a virgin, but of Joseph. It is as if he did not possess all these things among those who did not believe him to be God, the power of God, the wisdom of God, the strength and splendor of God, full of glory, honor, and blessing. 
<margin>John 5</margin>
For this reason, being ignorant, they crucified him; for if they had known, they would never have crucified the King of Glory. 
<margin>John 8</margin>
Moreover, they were unable to know him through faith because, as Truth itself says, they neglected the glory that comes from God alone while receiving glory from one another. 

<column-break/>

"I," he said, "honor my Father, and you dishonor me." And what does he say to the Father? 
<margin>John 17</margin>
"Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was made." The Son asks from the Father not a foreign glory, but his own, which was denied to him by unbelievers, and which is shown here as having been granted by the faithful. 

But from where does this come? Surely from the **opening of the book**. 
<margin>Luke 24</margin>
Indeed, in the **breaking of bread** which took place in the evening, the Lord was recognized by his disciples; likewise, once the book was opened, an innumerable multitude of Christians was converted to the praise of Christ, so that he might receive fully from the elect that which he seemed to have lost among the faithless Jews. Wherefore it follows immediately:
<margin>Rev. 5:13</margin>
> **And every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and in the sea, and all that are in them, I heard all saying to him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb: Blessing, and honor, and glory, and power, for ever and ever.**

The sentiment of Paul agrees with this vision of John, where he says in the Epistle to the Philippians: 
<margin>Phil. 2</margin>
**"Christ became obedient for us to the Father even unto death, even death on a cross; for which cause God also has exalted him and given him a name which is above every name. That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father."** 

Truly, because every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea, and all things in them, are said to have returned blessing, glory, honor, and power to the Father and the Son, we can perhaps understand "in heaven" to be the **celestial paradise**; "upon the earth," the **earthly paradise**; "under the earth," the **lower hell**; and "in the sea," the **upper hell**. For no one doubts that there is a celestial paradise where Christ remains with his saints, and an earthly paradise from which our first parent was cast out because of the guilt of his sin. In this [earthly] paradise, the souls of the faithful who have paid the debt of their sins remain until the day of judgment...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fifth chapter of the Book of Revelation, specifically focusing on the universal chorus of praise. It concludes the discussion on the different realms of existence and the various states of the faithful before beginning the commentary on Chapter 6 and the opening of the first seal.</meta>

<margin>Psalm 85</margin>
...it is perhaps not incongruously thought by many that there are two states. The Psalmist testifies that there is both a lower and an upper hell <note>original: "infernum," which in medieval thought could refer to any place of separation from God, including the hardships of the earthly world</note> when he says: **"O Lord, you have rescued my soul from the lower hell."** <note>Psalm 85:13, or 86:13 in modern Bibles</note> By saying his soul was freed from the "lower hell," he demonstrates by silence that there is also an "upper hell." Therefore, the upper hell is this present world, which never ceases to fluctuate like the inconsistent sea. The lower hell, however, is that place whose mouths lie open through various parts of the world—especially in the island of Sicily with its boiling fires—so that those who might not believe what they hear might at least be terrified by what they see. 

Within this world, there are four kinds of people according to these distances of places. For there are many who are known to belong to the principal seat, or to the "four living creatures" <note>the *animalia* of Revelation, often interpreted as the four Evangelists or perfect Christians</note>; though they still remain in the body upon the earth, they nevertheless reign in the heavens with their minds. They despise all earthly things and desire with total devotion to please God alone. 

Then there are some who wish to please God, yet they are unwilling to leave their wives and children for God's sake. These undoubtedly dwell "upon the earth," for if they see heaven with their eyes, they are nonetheless more like inhabitants and cultivators of the earth in their actions and way of life. 

And there are some who are execrably given over to the allurements of the flesh and other works of darkness, so that they remember neither the kingdom of heaven nor the punishments of hell. Instead, they rejoice—as Solomon says—when they have done evil and exult in the worst things. These are surely "under the earth," as if in a dark lake where the stars of heaven cannot shine. Indeed, they are those of whom the Truth says: **"The light came into the world, and men loved darkness more than the light."** <note>John 3:19</note> 

There are also many who, because they freely pursue the honors of the world, are carried everywhere by the waves of this world. These are reckoned to be "in the sea." Yet, if they fear Him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna <note>hell</note>, though they are overcome by the storms of temptations, they often suffer shipwreck. 

Although some of these are good and some are evil, they all nevertheless glorify God and his Christ in the "open book"—at least by being unable to deny the goodness of God by the manifest reason of truth, and unable to entirely hide or excuse their own malice. Or certainly, they are all called by the name of Christian, and if not all in their hearts, they all sound it out together with their lips. This can be properly understood of those who, though they were already counted among those who had "descended into the lake" <note>a metaphor for death or damnation</note>, suddenly prostrate themselves before the Lord and rise from death.

<column-break/>

And therefore, he <note>the Psalmist</note> says he was freed from the "lower hell" because he was rescued from the mortal crime into which he had fallen. And rightly: **(The four living creatures respond, "Amen.")** Because whether some are provoked to praise by the love of God, or others by the fear of punishment, holy men nevertheless—both by signs and by mysteries—affirm it to be true: namely, that blessing, honor, glory, and power belong to Him alone. For as much as it lies within Him, He wants no one to perish, but wants everyone to come to the knowledge of Himself. 

<margin>1 Timothy 2</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 48</margin>

To speak more briefly, according to the reason that more closely aligns with the truth: every creature is heard praising the "open book" because it now recognizes the mysteries of God through the Lord’s revelation. It perceives that all things were created for the praise of God, and nothing in all that God created is idle or superfluous. Thus, God is more praiseworthy in the hearts of the elect, since He overlooks the sins of reprobate men with much prior kindness, and finally, by His just judgment, eternally punishes those who did not turn toward justice. Furthermore: **(The twenty-four elders fell on their faces and worshiped.)** Because those who (as we have said) possess the place of the elders—rejoicing in the progress of those committed to them—prostrated themselves on their faces and worshiped when they heard the name of Christ glorified and His praise announced to the ends of the earth. They attribute nothing to their own preaching, but in all things they exalt the Almighty, who works all things in all people.

### On the opening of the first seal. Chapter 6.

> **AND when the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals, I heard one of the four living creatures saying as if with a voice of thunder: "Come and see."**

<margin>Text 1</margin>
Although there seems to be a difference between the four living creatures and the elders, it is manifest that the "first living creature" (whom we have called the pastor) began with the Apostles. For just as the kings of the earth can be called "princes," yet it does not follow that all who are called "princes" are also kings, so the holy Apostles could be called "bishops" or "pastors," yet not all bishops or pastors are Apostles. 

Therefore, at the opening of the first seal, the first of the four living creatures speaks as if with the voice of thunder. This is because when the bishops and the rest of Christ's disciples preached the Resurrection, a certain terrible sound was made throughout the world, according to what the Psalmist predicted: **"Their voice went out into all the earth."** 

<margin>Psalm 18</margin>

<term>infernus</term> — hell or the lower world; in this text, it is divided into "upper" (this world) and "lower" (the place of punishment).
<term>quatuor animalia</term> — the four living creatures from Revelation 4-5, interpreted here as the Apostles or leaders of the Church.
<term>viginti quatuor seniores</term> — the twenty-four elders who represent the patriarchs and apostles, or the perfected saints.

<term>septem sigilla</term> — the seven seals of the scroll in Revelation, representing the hidden mysteries of God's plan.
