<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Revelation, moving from the vision of the heavenly court to the actual opening of the first two seals in Chapter 6. The author interprets these seals as stages of Church history, using Old Testament figures like Samson and Gideon as "types" or foreshadowing of Christ and the martyrs.</meta>

...their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world <note>original: "sonus eorũ: ⁊ in fines orbis terre verba eorum," quoting Psalm 19:4, often applied to the Apostles</note>. As was noted earlier in the preface: at the time of His resurrection, the Lord first opened the seal that the great patriarchs—Isaac, Jacob, and the twelve sons of Jacob—had held. This was the same seal held by Moses, the greatest of the prophets, which involved the great conflict with the Egyptians, the crossing of the Red Sea, and the wilderness; as well as the deeds of Joshua and Caleb, and whatever is narrated as having happened in their times. All of this was hidden under the "veil of the letter" <note>This refers to the "literal" or surface meaning of the Old Testament, which the author believes was a coded message for the coming of Christ</note>. From the days of Zechariah and John the Baptist until the death of Saint John the Evangelist, Christ exhibited these things as revealed, giving new things in place of the old. He did this to show that He is that "precious stone" of which the prophet sang, saying: <margin>Psalm 117</margin> **"The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner."** But who announced these things to the Church? Was it not the first living creature, who is heard here saying, "Come and see"? Finally, the first living creature calls John to see, because the apostolic order invites contemplators to consider the victory of Jesus Christ. For there follows:

<margin>Law 2</margin>
### And behold, a white horse, and he who sat upon it was given a crown: and he went out conquering that he might conquer.

The white horse over which Christ presides is the primitive <note>the earliest or original</note> Church; it is the first army of the elect. He who sits upon the white horse is Christ, the King of Justice, to whom the Father gave glory along with the crown of justice—according to His nature as a man, not His nature as God. He truly "went out conquering," so that He might conquer when He rose from the dead, inasmuch as He had prostrated the prince of this world by His dying. In both ways, indeed, Christ conquered; in both ways He threw down and afflicted His enemies: whether when, as a "type" <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note> of Samson, He crushed that fortified structure of the enemy (that is, the kingdom of the flesh) by dying; or when, as another type of Samson, He destroyed the gates of hell by rising again. The elder manifests the victory of the rising Lord when he says: **"Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered."** The Lord Himself foretold the victory of His suffering to His disciples <margin>John 16</margin> before He suffered, saying: **"In the world you will indeed have pressure; but rejoice, for I have overcome the world."** These...

<column-break/>

...He comforted, strengthening His disciples for the crown of victory as well. **"Fear not,"** He said, **"little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom."** For just as the seed of Israel overcame the Egyptians who had afflicted them for a long time, and obtained their inheritance after the Canaanite peoples were destroyed, so the faithful people overcame Jewish unbelief <note>original: "iudaicam perfidiam," a common medieval term for those who did not accept the new Christian faith</note> and, having conquered the worshipers of idols, obtained the Roman Empire. The former victory pertains to this first seal, the latter to the second. For both were victories, even if the causes were different: either the unbelieving Jews, invincible in heart, fell in war; or the Gentiles, more uplifted toward grace, left their idols behind and were converted to the <margin>1 Peter 2</margin> **"Pastor and Bishop of their souls."** The first of these, as I said, pertains to the first seal; the second pertains to the second seal, of which the following discourse is ready.

### Concerning the opening of the second seal.
<margin>Text 3</margin>
### And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the voice of the second living creature saying: "Come and see." And I saw.

After those great first struggles, which were veiled by the first seal, the second struggles followed under the second seal. These are the things contained in the books of Joshua and Judges, and represented in some part by the prophet Samuel as a "type." There is no doubt that this refers to the ecclesiastical war that took place after the triumph of the Apostles and the primitive Church, lasting until the times of the blessed Pope Sylvester and the Emperor Constantine. Truly, in that era, the struggles of Gideon were fulfilled: when the dew of spiritual grace was spread over the floor of the world, while the "fleece" of Jewish carnality was left in dryness, as it remains today. There, finally, you might see the soldiers of Gideon—or rather, the martyrs of Christ—willingly giving up their "earthen vessels" (their bodies) to death, and sounding the trumpets of Gospel speech. Although they were small in number, Christ's chosen soldiers triumphed, protected by the mystery of the Trinity. Because they did not fear temporal death, they pursued the refreshment of eternal life. When, therefore, the faithful had completed the struggles described above, our "kernel" <note>Christ, the core of the scripture</note> opened the minds of His disciples so they might understand the scriptures <margin>Luke 24</margin> and laid open the secret of the second seal. Regarding this, the second living creature invites John to see, because the order of holy martyrs (which is second after the first) contemplates...

### Part of the Exposition

...he hastens to behold the triumph of his own martyrdom. For indeed, that showing does not pertain to words, but to deeds; for by suffering, the living creatures <note>The "living creatures" are the four beings surrounding God's throne, often associated with the four Gospels or, as here, orders of the Church</note> taught more than by speaking. But to see the martyrs is to follow in the footsteps of the saints: so that while we read their deeds, we may follow what is to be emulated, and so forth.

<margin>Text 4</margin>
**And behold, a red horse, and to him who sat upon it, it was given that he should take peace from the earth, and that men should kill one another; and a great sword was given to him.**

<margin>Zechariah 1; Matthew 10</margin>
In Zechariah the prophet, the red horse is to be taken in a good sense. And the Lord himself testified concerning himself, saying: "I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword" <note>original: "Nō veni pacē mittē in terrā sz gladiū," quoting Matthew 10:34</note>. Because of this, it might be doubted by some who should be understood as the rider of this horse, to whom it is given to take peace from the earth, and moreover a great sword. We think, however, from the comparison with what follows, that in this red horse the priests of the pagans or the princes of the world are designated; or in the rider, that red dragon who was a murderer from the beginning, and who rejoices desperately in the slaughter of the dying. Sacred Scripture commemorates that the sword of Goliath was great, because the power of the devil is great for bringing death upon the innocent. However, because the black horse follows the red, and the pale horse follows the black, each horse having its own rider: I believe that in this rider to whom the great sword was given, the Roman Emperor should be understood. To him, in truth, a great sword had been given to conquer the world and to disturb the power of men walking in their own errors. For just as the only-begotten Son of God triumphs everywhere in His members <note>The "members" of Christ are the faithful who make up the Church</note>, so also the devil is born in his own members, attributing to himself as victory whatever iniquity they work perversely. Thus, the Roman emperors are to be understood in this rider, yet in such a way that the devil is understood to work within those same emperors, for he encourages both them and the other princes of the world to battle. Furthermore, the red horse itself is properly understood as the Roman army, which was truly red and blood-stained on account of the constant and long-lasting shedding of blood. For the color red signifies homicide, which is why the author of evils is called a "red dragon." Similarly, the beast that

<column-break/>

came out of the abyss is recorded as being of a scarlet color. How much blood of the saints did the Roman emperors pour out, one after another—especially Diocletian and Maximian <note>Emperors known for the "Great Persecution" of Christians in the early 4th century</note>—that anyone could fully say or describe? Were these and similar deeds not done, without doubt, to fulfill that which is in the Psalm: "They have poured out the blood of your servants round about Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them" <note>original: "Effuderūt sāguinē seruoꝝ tuoꝝ in circuitu hierlm ⁊ non erat q̄ sepelire," quoting Psalm 79:3</note>? Then truly was fulfilled in the Church that which was prefigured by the harmony of that second period: the wars of the sons of Jacob, which pertain especially to the Book of Judges, from the days or the death of Joshua until the times of King David. When this second seal was completed, the third seal began.

<margin>Psalm 78</margin>

->Concerning the opening of the third seal.<-

<margin>Text 5</margin>
**And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: "Come and see." And I saw, and behold, a black horse, and he who sat upon it had a pair of scales in his hand.**

The four living creatures, as we have often said, are four orders of the perfect: the apostles, the martyrs, the confessors or teachers, and the virgins. Therefore, the first battle of Christ was of the apostles; the second, of the martyrs; the third, of the teachers; the fourth, of the hermits and virgins. And the first battle was held with the Jews; the second, with the pagans; the third, with the Arians <note>Arians were followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father—a doctrine the Church deemed a major heresy</note>, of whom there is now speech. Therefore, in the black horse, the clergy of the wandering Arians is to be understood, over whom presided bishops who were proud and estranged from the faith; they were black in appearance because they were masters of error and darkness. For were they not masters of darkness, who sought to obscure the true Light that illuminates this world with their own depraved dogmas? But what is meant by the scales <note>original: "staterā"</note> except the disputation of the letter of Scripture, upon which heretics are accustomed to pose deceitful questions? For in a scale, one recognizes what has more or what has less. And the knowledge of a teacher, which is weighed in such a scale of the letter, is very easily proved; for since they do not have the Spirit, they are "killed by the letter." But those who are spiritual perceive which sense gives life and which kills; and because of this, when they encounter something that seems different from the faith, they understand that there is a mystery hidden and lying within the enigma, which is not foreign to the right faith; because of which they are not moved by what they find.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Revelation, specifically focusing on the opening of the third seal (the black horse). ### John's Second Book on the Apocalypse

...they hear one thing and watchfully attend to another. The disputation of heretics is like a scale; for in it, whoever has more <note>meaning more intellectual wit or cunning</note> overcomes the one who understands less. But what kind of weight a Catholic ought to possess is made manifest by what follows, when it says:

<margin>Revelation 6 <note>The original margin notes Leviticus 6, but the text is quoting Revelation 6:6</note></margin>
**And I heard, as it were, a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: "Two pounds of wheat for a denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and the oil."**

<margin>Psalm 61</margin>
Behold the weight of knowledge; behold the fitting measure of understanding. Wherever the heretic wishes to go, you must weigh these things; keep these measures. "The sons of men are vain," it says, "and the sons of men are liars in their scales, so that they might deceive even themselves out of vanity." <note>A reference to Psalm 62:9, which is Psalm 61 in the Latin Vulgate</note>. It is as if they use a certain scale—or rather they do not use it, but abuse it—in their philosophical disputations, so that they may most easily be turned from the truth to falsehood. For we read that many philosophers came to the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The first ecumenical council in 325 AD, which addressed the Arian heresy</note> to attack the Catholic faith with the cunning of the dialectical art <note>the art of logical argument</note>. But wherever the philosopher goes, I focus on the scale: you, hold your weight; you, preserve the number you have heard. For it is not our part to listen to their voice; it is not our part to argue with logical speeches, but to perceive through the contemplation of faith what the voice brought to us contains, which said: **"Two pounds of wheat for a denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and the oil."** I will say it briefly: the two pounds of wheat pertain to the two Testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments</note>, just as the three two-pound measures of barley pertain to those six laborious ages which are designated in six days or years: that is, from **Abraham** to **John the Baptist**. For each of these times is known to have had two "weeks" of generations <note>A reference to the genealogical divisions in the Gospel of Matthew</note>; thus, it is not simply three measures of barley, but "three two-pound measures" of barley said to be given for a denarius. For the **denarius** <note>a Roman silver coin</note> represents a perfect and whole number. Therefore, to give two pounds of wheat or three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius is the mystery of the two Testaments, or the six ages in which all "servile works" <note>tasks of the law or physical labor</note> are commanded to be brought to a healthy and perfect understanding. There is a difference, however, between wheat and barley: for wheat is for humans, but barley is for beasts of burden. And indeed, the **historical** understanding, which is suitable for "animal-like" men <note>those focused on the physical or literal</note>, is found in the barley;

<column-break/>

but the **typical** <note>or allegorical</note> understanding, which is designated for spiritual men, is in the wheat—just as the **moral** sense is in the wine, and the **anagogical** or **contemplative** sense is in the oil. There are, therefore, four living creatures and four faces of a single wheel, because there are four general ways of understanding the Holy Scriptures. The first of these is **typical**; the second, **historical**; the third, **moral**; the fourth, **contemplative**. And indeed, according to time, the historical is first, just as **Stephen** was the first martyr; but nevertheless, because the typical understanding suits the first living creature (that is, the **Lion**), the second, which is called historical, suits the second (that is, the **Calf**). The third, called moral, fits the third (the **Man**); and the fourth, called contemplative, belongs to the fourth (the **Eagle**). Correctly, mention was made not first of the barley, but of the wheat. For the first understanding <note>typical</note> suits the **Apostles**; the second <note>historical</note> the **Martyrs**; the third <note>moral</note> the **Doctors** <note>the Great Teachers of the Church</note>; and the fourth the **Contemplatives**. Therefore, that voice was heard among the four living creatures because what was said about the four understandings pertains to the four living creatures. Lest it seem absurd to anyone what was said about the priority of the typical understanding, let him see who asks this: that the Apostles (to whom this understanding belongs) preached to that people <note>the Jews</note> whose faith was already founded in history through Moses and the Prophets. The Martyrs, however, preached to the pagans, who—except for some of the Greeks who since the time of **King Ptolemy** had the translation of the **Septuagint** <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>—knew neither the Law nor the Prophets. And these things are so. Nevertheless, in the literal text itself, four specific types are to be noted. One is designated in the barley, another in the wheat, another in the wine, and another in the oil. This is because some things written there are for the building up of **faith**, some for the institution of **works**, just as others are for the composition of **morals**, and many more for the perfection of **charity** and the **contemplation** of heavenly things. Of these, the wise preacher correctly exchanges two—the wheat and the barley—at a perfect price, so that the wine and oil are not harmed. He provides a perfect response concerning those things written for the building up of faith and for physical exercise (which is useful in a small way), so that these two are never established in such a way that those things written about morals and contemplation are harmed. There is no doubt that this could happen if those first two were said to be sufficient such that the other two were despised. This is something a discreet preacher must guard against, not only in the literal face of the text, but also...

# Abbot's Part of the Exposition

in those spiritual understandings which proceed from the single fountain of the Letter. For there are, as I have already said, four general understandings designated by the four winds of heaven, which follow the Spirit wherever it goes, just like those four wheels shown to the prophet Ezekiel; nor is there any doubt that this is the Spirit of whom the Apostle says:

<margin>Ezekiel 1; 2 Corinthians 3</margin>
**The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.** This first understanding, which is called **typological** <note>original: "typica"; an interpretive method where Old Testament events are seen as "types" or symbols foreshadowing New Testament truths</note>, so connects the two Testaments together, just as those two women who married Abraham were joined together in a mystery, as the holy Apostle says of them. For these are the two Testaments, or rather like the two **cherubim** which overshadowed the ark of the covenant of the Lord, or surely like the two **seraphim** who cried out to one another with one voice, saying: **Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty; the heavens and the earth are full of His glory.** For it is as if the two seraphim agree in one voice: while the seraphim themselves cry out that which was under the Old Testament, the living creatures in the New Testament resonate the same thing, crying out likewise: **Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.** These, therefore, are the **two pounds of wheat** which were heard among the four living creatures. If the wretched **Arius** <note>A 4th-century priest whose teachings (Arianism) claimed that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; he was condemned at the Council of Nicaea</note> had recognized these well, he would never have preached that the Son of God is less than His Father, nor that the Holy Spirit is less or unequal to the One from whom He proceeds. Therefore, he who does not wish to err from the Catholic faith should beware lest, by the instinct of some wicked teacher, he desert the faith handed down to him in the two Testaments; and let him rather hear Paul saying: **Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be anathema.** So much for the two pounds of wheat. What of the **three two-pound measures of barley**? Just as the typological understanding is designated by the wheat—which comes to spiritual men who possess full discretion between the letter and the spirit—so the **historical understanding**, which is written in the second place after the typological, is designated by the barley. This is because barley is more suitable for those to whom the Apostle says: **As infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food**, and to whom he preached only **Jesus Christ, and Him crucified.** And it is fitting that Christ crucified suffered on the **sixth day**; for we must by no means provoke animalistic men <note>original: "animales hoies"; those who live by their physical senses rather than spiritual intellect</note>, who cannot perceive the things of the Spirit of God, toward idleness by our exhortation, but toward labor. We know that saying of the holy man: **Idleness without letters is death and the burial of a living man.** <note>A famous quote by the Roman philosopher Seneca the Younger, often used by medieval Christian writers to encourage study</note>. Therefore, the six pounds of barley

<margin>Galatians 4; Exodus 25; Isaiah 6; Galatians 1; 1 Corinthians 3</margin>

<column-break/>

specifically carry the type of that doctrine which simply instructs the listeners toward the perfection of labor; undoubtedly because God perfected His works in **six days**, and for the same number of days or years He commanded the people of Israel to exercise themselves in their works. But why does he not say "six pounds," but rather "**three two-pound measures**" <note>original: "tres bilibres"</note>? It is because it is certain that our work is perfected before the most high God when, in the very good work we do, we hold firmly to the **faith of the Trinity**, offering—so to speak—a sacrifice to the Lord unto the third time to the honor of the Triune God. In each turn, we offer one young dove as a burnt offering and another for sin. It is for this reason that the seraphim cover their bodies with two wings, their faces with two, and fly with two. This is why the **forty-two generations** are described in doubled weeks <note>original: "geminatis hebdomadibus"; referring to the three sets of fourteen (2x7) generations</note> concerning the Lord: from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ are fourteen generations. And fittingly, the number six is also contained within the number three, because, as James says, **faith without works is dead.** Therefore, both the two pounds of wheat and the six two-pound measures of barley are useful in this way to those striving for salvation—provided they do not **harm the wine and the oil.** As we have already said, these designate the **moral** and **contemplative** understandings; for those former things cannot please God without these latter ones. Indeed, just as faith is found in the typological understanding, and works—or what is greater, patience—are in the historical, so **humility** is found in the moral, and in the contemplative, **hope** (which leads to our homeland) is solidified. He who thus walks the paths of this sea is safe from the waves threatening his death; for being accompanied here and there—indeed, from all four sides—by the grace of Christ, no breeze of heretics can harm him, and no terrible beast of the sea can swallow or crush him; for he to whom the Lord is a helper shall not fear what man may do to him.

<margin>Ezekiel 1; Matthew 1; James 2; Psalm 117</margin>

->On the opening of the fourth seal.<-

### AND when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: "Come and see."

<margin>Revelation 7 <note>This refers to the sequence of the seals in Revelation 6</note></margin>

The **fourth living creature**, as we have already said, represents the order of **hermits and virgins**. Concerning this order, we shall treat more fully and appropriately in the fourth part. For just as the first part speaks properly of the **Pastors**, the second part (which is being treated now) of the **Martyrs**, and the third of the **Doctors**, so the fourth part treats of the **Virgins**.

Joachim [of Fiore], Second [Part] on the Apocalypse
D 4

of the hermits. And just as the apostolic order of its own time announced the battle it endured from the faithless Jews—as did the martyrs from the pagans and the doctors from the heretics—so also the hermitic order of the fourth time <note>Joachim of Fiore divided history into "times" or periods; the fourth time here refers to the era of the fourth seal</note> indicates the pressures of its own time, which the "midday plague" <note>original: "plaga meridiana"; a reference to Psalm 91:6, often interpreted in the Middle Ages as the threat from the Islamic South</note> especially inflicted, in which that very order specifically dwelled. This is shown when it says: **"Come and see,"** for surely it could not be hidden from the faithful of Christ what was so solemnly enacted in the fourth time of the Church. For there follows:

<margin>Lesson 8</margin>
### And behold, a pale horse, and he who sat upon him, his name was Death, and Hell followed him.

Rightly is it a pale horse upon which Death presides; rightly a pale horse which possesses the color of the dead. For pale is the color of the dead, and through this, in the color pale, envy and hatred are designated. Therefore, that race of men which is designated in the pale horse is recognized by its color for its malice and wickedness. For a King, out of wisdom, detects hidden mysteries. Moreover, we know that under the fourth seal, as a type of the fourth ecclesiastical war, the fourth tribulation followed under the Old Testament <margin>4 Kings 17</margin> when, namely, after the wars of the predecessors, the proud kings of the Assyrians depopulated the people who were called Israel. Leaving only the tribe of Judah with Levi and Benjamin, they translated the ten tribes to the Assyrians. The opening of this seal was then fulfilled in the Church when the most wicked nation of the **Hagarenes** <note>original: "agarenorum"; a medieval term for Saracens or Muslims, claiming descent from Hagar</note>, drawn from the scabbard of its habitation, devastated the primary churches of the Greeks. We shall speak a few things of them here, as they will occur to be repeated in other places. I think it worth remembering in this present <margin>Daniel 7</margin> place that those four beasts which the holy Daniel describes himself as having seen in a vision of the night designate these four battles—except that in the first seal, so that mention of Christ might be made, the first of the beasts was suppressed. But the fourth beast, which was terrible and unlike the others, begins from the opening of the fourth seal and endures through succession until the times of the sixth seal. Therefore, the pale horse upon which Death presides designates that which the fourth beast does: that is, that cruel nation whose detestable offspring we grieve to have occupied the breadth of the earth. For who could so rightly be called **Death** as that lost man **Muhammad** <note>original: "maometh"</note>, who was made the cause of death for so many thousands

<column-break/>

of men? Certainly, who this **Hell** is who followed him is clearly recognized from the vision of Daniel itself. For afterward, what he had <margin>Daniel 7</margin> seen and heard concerning the four beasts, he wished to learn diligently concerning the fourth beast, which was very different from all the others and exceedingly terrible. Its teeth and claws were of iron. It devoured and crushed, and the rest it trampled with its feet. And concerning the ten horns it had on its head, and concerning the other which had sprung up before which three horns fell; and concerning that horn which had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and was larger than the others. "I looked, and behold, that horn made war against the saints and prevailed over them." Behold how great this one shall be, if he is not already present, who will preside over this worst of beasts in the end! And who is here surnamed **Hell** by John, unless perhaps by the name of **Death** we are to understand Muhammad with his successors, and by the name of **Hell**, the leader of another sect of men <note>original: "heresiarcha"; a leader of a heresy</note> proceeding from that same first sect of the Saracens? This is he who is commonly called **the silent Meses** <note>original: "meses mutus"; likely a reference to a specific Almohad leader or a polemical figure associated with North African Islamic movements</note>, who reigns powerfully in his successors in the parts of Africa and Mauritania.

### Concerning the opening of the fifth seal.

### And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar of God the souls of those slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held.
<margin>Text 9</margin>

If in the four often-mentioned living creatures, four special orders are to be understood, what can we say the **altar of God** refers to if not the Roman Church? For after the four times of those four orders had passed, both in the clergy and in the monks, was it not strengthened in the Lord its God, and did it not flourish beyond others in the fifth time among the Latins? And indeed, this Church was illustrious within itself and to those who knew it from the beginning; but during all the time in which the Emperors of Constantinople ruled in Rome, both they themselves and the bishops of that same city strove to obscure and subvert the clarity of that Church which it received from Christ—not by reason, but by tyranny. But as the first persecution was stirred up in Judea, the second in Rome, and the third in Greece...

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the fourth seal and the fourth "living creature." Joachim is drawing parallels between the historical persecutions of the Old Testament (the Assyrians) and the contemporary threats facing the Church, specifically identifying the rise of Islamic forces in Arabia, North Africa, and Spain as the fulfillment of the fourth seal’s "pale horse."</meta>

->Illustration: Part of the Exposition<-

The fourth [persecution] was in Arabia; likewise, the fifth persecution arose in Mauritania and in the Spanish lands. For there were, and are even to this day, remnants of Christians there under the faith and protection of the holy Roman Church; from whom, as has often been related to us, many were killed by those Saracens <note>original: "sarracenis"; a medieval term for Muslims</note>, leaving a great groan of sorrow for the neighboring faithful. However, in this persecution, it was not said that such or such an animal lived. **"Come and see"**: because just as the fourth living creature—that is, the hermitic order—was propagated in various types of monks, so also the fourth beast <note>Referring to the fourth beast of Daniel's vision</note> is found in various sects of wicked men. <margin>Daniel 7</margin> Whence Daniel also says: *It was unlike the other beasts which I had seen before.* Therefore, as much as I am able to grasp in this fourth time—in which the persecution of this fourth beast began from the opening of the fourth seal—it nevertheless persists in its tyranny even into the fifth and sixth times. And what was said of it in the fourth part: *I saw one of its heads as if it were killed unto death, and its sword-wound was healed* <note>original: "plaga gladij eius curata est"; a reference to the Beast of the Sea in Revelation 13:3, here linked to the fourth seal</note>, we see being fulfilled daily in that race. For that which seemed at one time to have fallen, we now see raised up, even transcending the summits of the highest hills and mountains. For that kingdom of the Assyrians, through which the fourth persecution was completed upon the people of Israel, persisted in its rigor until the time of the sixth seal; so that in the days of Holofernes <note>The general of Nebuchadnezzar in the Book of Judith</note>, the great leader of the Assyrian military, it is said that the same king of the Assyrians exceeded even the limits of human nature in his arrogance of pride, proclaiming himself the sole king, and also the god and lord of the entire earth. But to insert something by way of example concerning the persecution of the faithful, it was recently heard from the reports of certain men who asserted they were nearly present, that "Meselmutus" <note>original: "meselmutū"; likely a Latinization of a specific Muslim ruler or a corruption of the term for "Muslims" (Maslamah/Mussulman)</note> had gathered the Christians who were in his land and killed many of them together out of hatred for the Christian name. Concerning these, if it is true, it cannot be doubted that they themselves experienced the crown of martyrdom; for they were killed on account of the word of God and on account of the testimony which they held, even if they were killed against their will. For it is clearly evident that they would not have been killed if, before they came to that final moment—concerning which there was undoubtedly fear—they had wished to deny the name of the Lord so that they might escape. And this can rightly be felt concerning those who, situated under such a lordship, preserve the faith not without fear of danger. But concerning those who are in peace,

<column-break/>

and enjoy their liberty in its entirety, where there is no suspicion or fear that they ought to suffer for the Christian name: if they are suddenly handed over for their sins and slaughtered by the sword without any interrogation regarding the name of Christ, the cause is not entirely similar. For it is one thing for an enemy to rise against an enemy to obtain a worldly kingdom; it is another for simple people, held in servitude, to be slaughtered by the "sons of darkness" <note>A common medieval term for non-believers or enemies of the Church</note> out of hatred for the Christian name, precisely because they are identified by that Christian name. Nevertheless, if they are good people and are suddenly oppressed by unbelievers out of hatred for the name of Christ, like the innocent martyrs, they cannot be excluded from the reward of martyrdom. Furthermore, even if we judge that what is written under the sixth opening concerning the "crowd of innocents crying out to the Lord under the throne of God" can be fulfilled through this kingdom of wicked men, nevertheless all the innocents who die for the truth in the bosom of Mother Church (unless they are of the number of those who belong to the four living creatures) are to be accepted under the fellowship of those [martyrs]; although others are to follow them under the sixth opening so that the perfect number may be completed. That follows:

> **And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: "How long, Holy and True, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who inhabit the earth?" And white robes were given to each of them. And it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers, who were to be killed just as they were, should be completed.** <margin>Apocalypse 10</margin> <note>Though the margin says 10, this quote is from Revelation 6:10-11</note>

A very wondrous difference is shown to exist between the four living creatures and these martyrs. For we read that the blessed Stephen the Protomartyr <note>The "First Martyr," stoned to death in the Book of Acts</note> not only did not seek vengeance from the Lord for his adversaries, but even prayed for the enemies who were stoning him. These, however, not only do not pray [for their enemies], but even demand vengeance for their blood. As far as it is given to me to understand, there are two kinds of the just noted in this book: those whom <margin>Acts 6</margin>

# Joachim’s Second Book on the Apocalypse

### On the Cry of the Innocents

...men, indeed, some are like the brave: they do not so much endure wars as they compel them to end; others neither seek nor want them, but nevertheless, if battles occur, they persevere unconquered in the struggle. Others, I say, presuming upon grace, do not wish to wait for the conflict within the city walls; but girded with the spiritual sword, they voluntarily throw themselves into the fight. Others adhere to their God with a heart so whole and perfect, yet they have not attained this particular gift of faith <note>Joachim refers here to the "gift" of being able to endure suffering with joy or stoicism</note>. For because they are lovers of peace and innocence, and endowed with such purity of mind and simplicity that they are considered children in malice, it happens sometimes that just as they do not know how to inflict punishment on others, so they cannot bear it with equanimity.

Who, however, even if they cannot bear it calmly, still do not wish to resist their enemies or avenge themselves with their own hands—even if they were able; instead, out of great piety, they groan, shedding many tears. For such is the vow of children; such is the natural weakness of widows and virgins. They love God; they love their neighbor; they harm no one; they persecute no one; instead, they most willingly help those they can. Some of them possess only this "imperfection": that they cannot endure evils with joy. And because they are less fit for battle and less suited for the contest, their very simplicity makes them exceedingly pitiable. 

And what then? *Judgment without mercy <margin>James 2</margin> to him who has not shown mercy.* For those who touch them are to be punished all the more harshly, the more unkindly they treat them; natural compassion itself accuses the attacker. For who does not know that he is more cruel who persecutes a widow than he who oppresses a man; he who opposes a poor person than he who offends a tyrant; he who brings war upon an orphan than he who shows enmity to the powerful? Hence, it is written in the Psalms <margin>Psalm 67; Psalm 9</margin> concerning such as these: *They shall be troubled before the face of him who is the father of orphans and the judge of widows.* And in another place: *To you, Lord, the poor man is left; you will be the helper of the orphan; break the arm of the sinner and the malicious.* We speak of a thing known to all, and which we often experience and have experienced. When the poor man is pursued by the rich, and the ward by the powerful; when the widow is oppressed by the judge,

<column-break/>

or the foreigner by the inhabitant: that wretched and weak party is accustomed to resort to the weapons of groaning and mourning, for there is no one to resist and fight for them, except the *father of orphans <margin>Psalm 67</margin> and judge of widows.* Hence it is also written in the Law: *You shall not harm the widow and the ward; if you <margin>Psalm 23</margin> <note>Though the margin cites Psalm 23, the text quotes Exodus 22:22-24</note> hurt them, they will cry out to me, and I will hear their cry, and my fury will be kindled, and I will strike you with the sword.* 

Thus, although <margin>Psalm 145</margin> God is merciful, he takes pity on all those suffering injury—namely, all those who hope in him; and in a wondrous way, he is moved by pious tears to bring vengeance, even though those tears are not shed by them for the purpose of harming their oppressors, but only so that the Lord might snatch them from the power of the proud. Indeed, and often without any [vengeful] regard. For not everyone who weeps does so to obtain something, but some because they fear and grieve; others because they are moved by piety and burn with love. *"Let me be,"* someone says, *"that I may lament <margin>Job 10</margin> my sorrow a little while."* Or do we believe perhaps that a mother hopes for anything [specific] when she weeps over the death of her sons? Therefore, these saints do not weep so that their tormentors may perish, but because the pressure of suffering itself compels them; otherwise, they would not be innocent. 

Although I might also say that the innocent cry out and demand vengeance from a just God in another way, which can be proven by sacred authority. It can be ambiguous to no one that the first of the innocents who was killed through envy was the righteous Abel. We do not read <margin>Genesis 4</margin> of his tears during his suffering—perhaps because he had no time for lamentation—however, we know the "voice of vengeance" from Scripture, and what that voice was is expressed not by a human voice, but by the divine. For when the impious Cain <note>original: "Caym"</note> strove to hide himself with a lie, he heard: *Behold, the voice of your brother Abel's blood cries out to me from the ground.* <margin>Genesis 4</margin> Just as the voice of the blood of righteous Abel cried out from the ground, so these saints—who were killed without cause for the sake of the word of God and the testimony they held—whether they be children or old men, rightly demand vengeance by the voice of their blood from their God; who then, so that they might endure in peace, received an answer and gifts. *And white robes,* it says, *were given to each of them; and it was told to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until...* <note>Joachim is quoting Revelation 6:11 regarding the martyrs under the altar</note>

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual and legal standing of "weak" victims of persecution—widows, orphans, and the simple—arguing that their tears and blood act as a powerful cry for divine justice. Joachim links the suffering of the martyrs under the fifth seal to the biblical precedent of Abel's blood crying out from the earth.</summary>

**Abbot’s Part of the Exposition**

...their fellow servants and their brothers, who were to be killed just as they were, should be fulfilled. <note>original: "compleatur serui eorum..." — This refers to Revelation 6:11, where the martyrs are told to rest until the full number of their fellow sufferers is reached.</note> In each of the white robes, the joy of souls is designated. Therefore, God, being just, delays carrying out the judgment because that pitiful and pious voice received consolation through the gift of the white robes. For what does it matter if God allows His chosen ones to suffer something sad for a brief hour? Do they not pass from death to life, and from mourning to joy?

It is certain, however, that after the fifth seal—at the very end of which we now stand—the battle of the martyrs still remains. This is so that the total number of saints may be fulfilled, which is currently lacking in the count of martyrs. For this battle will occur in the following opening of the seal, in which it is necessary to fulfill whatever remains of the affliction, so that those spoken of here may be killed and crowned with martyrdom: *Until their fellow servants and their brothers, who are to be killed just as they were, should be fulfilled.*

But it might seem contradictory to someone—if perhaps they were less vigilant in noting what we wrote at the start as a precaution—why four living creatures <note>The "animalia" or four living creatures (Lion, Ox, Man, Eagle) from Revelation 4 and 6.</note> are introduced through the first four seals in this second part, since this second part properly belongs to the second of the three living creatures. Therefore, let the reader look vigilantly at the preface of this work, and they will sufficiently recognize how this is to be understood.

### On the opening of the sixth seal.

<margin>Chapter 11.</margin>
**And I saw when he had opened the sixth seal. And behold, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood.**

Weigh these words well, miserable Babylon; <note>In Joachim’s thought, "Babylon" often represents the corrupt, worldly element within the Church or the city of Rome itself.</note> for behold, your desolation approaches. Lay aside your golden finery and take up lamentation, for behold, your greatest ruin is coming. It was predicted ages ago; it was written down by the prophets; it was announced to you from the days of old. You did not take it to heart, nor did you believe those telling these things to you, but you always walked proudly in your riches. Your fury was not merely against man, nor was your indignation against the sons of men, but against the King of Heavens, whose bed you have defiled. You have raised your horn against the King of Heaven, against the Prince of Strength, against the san-

<column-break/>

-ctuary of His kingdom. Therefore, this burden is against you; this is set aside and laid out for you who live in the day of the Lord's indignation and the visitation of His Christ. You yourself shall drink the very dregs of the cup from which you gave Jerusalem to drink. For it is necessary that you receive in the sixth seal what you inflicted in the fifth. You shall receive weight for weight, and double for your "goods" and your gifts. 

But perhaps you do not know yourself, and you attribute what is read to another; or certainly you have not read it, or you did not read the gift diligently; for in this day of yours, things were for your peace, but now they are hidden from your eyes. But will it be permitted to drowse at the sound of such great thunder? Do you think you understand, or do you recognize yourself in what you now read? Read vigilantly in the works of the Fathers; if you do not know the testimonies of Peter and John, read, I say, in the works of Jerome and Augustine; <margin>Augustine, Jerome</margin> and what is written about you, or what you have been, can be revealed to you through their opinions. 

To express it to you briefly and conclude in a single sentence: whoever attacks the Church of Peter <note>The institutional or Roman Church.</note> with their conduct and their power, mixes themselves among the children of Babylon. And what is dealt with further regarding those calamities in the sixth part of the book is dealt with here specifically—namely, in the sixth chapter and discourse of this one part. Therefore, let them hear, whether they want to or not; let the children of the great harlot hear what they are about to experience before they go and do not return to the land of shadows, covered in the mist of death. <margin>Job 10</margin> Let them hear, I say; let the false Christians hear, by whose occasion it happens that true Christians are crowned with martyrdom. For the very kings who are to strike the harlot so that she may be cleansed from the face of the earth are themselves (as shown in the sixth part) going to fight with the Lamb; and the Lamb will overcome them in His members, who will also fill up what is lacking in His sufferings. 

**And** (he says) **there was a great earthquake.** What is this earthquake? Is it one of the unfeeling elements? No, I say, but of human hearts. For a great fear will rush upon the hearts of those who sleep their sleep; upon those who have pursued earthly things, according to that word of the Apostle: *When they shall say, peace and security, then sudden destruction will come upon them like the labor pains of a woman with child, and they shall not escape.* <margin>1 Thessalonians 5</margin> But who will believe me as I say these things?

### Joachim’s Second Book on the Apocalypse

Tell us, I pray, holy Joel: what will this earthquake be, so great, so terrible, and so unusual? What will be this sudden fear that John describes? I believe it is the same one you wrote about, which you announced so many centuries ago, saying:
<margin>Joel 2</margin>
Blow the trumpet in Zion; wail on my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the earth be troubled, for the day of the Lord is coming, for the day of darkness and gloom is near: a day of clouds and whirlwinds, like the morning spread over the mountains. <note>original: "dies tenebrarum et caliginis... quasi mane expansum super montes"</note> And lest anyone should think he said these things regarding the final day of judgment, he added and said: A people numerous and strong; there has not been the like from the beginning, and after it there shall be none, through the years of generation and generation. Before its face is a devouring fire, and after it a burning flame. The land is like a garden of pleasure before it, and after it a desert solitude; nor is there anyone who may escape it. And after a few words: At its face the earth trembled, the heavens were moved; the sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their splendor. Alas! How harsh, how heavy, how powerful, how immense that earthquake will be is clearly shown in these words of Joel. We could bring forth these same words from another prophet, but we fittingly postpone them for now, so that we may treat them more appropriately in the sixth part of the book. 

Truly, regarding that word I spoke about the day of the final judgment, I earnestly ask the pious listener to be mindful, both in this place and in others, wherever I happen to speak of it. For I want them to know that "the last day" and "the day of judgment" are understood in two ways. For it is understood in a **broad sense** <note>original: "largo modo"</note> for a certain uncertain period of time, as 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine aptly asserts in the book *The City of God*; and it is understood in a **strict sense** <note>original: "stricto modo"</note> concerning the conclusion of time itself, when all mysteries are completed. The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life. If, therefore, it is understood in the broad sense, whatever is said in this manner can be referred without hesitation to the "newest day"—that is, to the extreme, ultimate, and final time. 
<margin>1 Corinthians 10</margin>
Of this kind of speech is also that which the apostle said: *We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come.* And John, whose book 
<margin>1 John 2</margin>
this is, said: *Little children, it is the last hour.* Indeed, it must not be passed over in silence that so powerful 

<column-break/>

and so sudden will be the storm of that sixth plague, that—as if yielding to God, though undoubtedly driven by the contrary malice of humanity—the light of evangelical preaching shall turn black, and the doctrine of Mother Church shall grow pale with terror. And what is more to be feared in these things: the stars of heaven also shall fall to the earth, because many who were thought to be vigorous and exceptional teachers shall be cast down. And the sun (he says) became black like sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood. 
<margin>Revelation 12</margin>
And the stars of heaven fell upon the earth, as a fig tree drops its unripe figs when it is moved by a wind.

When the sun and moon are described together, they signify different things depending on the context. For sometimes Christ is in the sun, and Moses in the moon. Sometimes Christ is in the sun, and the Church in the moon; sometimes Elijah is in the sun, and John the Baptist in the moon. Indeed (as we have written elsewhere), John, who clearly arose from the tribe of Levi, designates the **order of the clergy** <note>The secular priesthood or administrative branch of the Church.</note>, especially since John himself was sent by God to baptize in water, which properly pertains to the priests of the Church. Elijah, whose lineage is uncertain, foretells the **order of the contemplatives** <note>The monastic orders focused on prayer and meditation.</note> to be signified by the moon—that which is signified by John; while that which is signified by the sun is signified by Elijah: this is clear enough and perceived by a sound intellect. 

Moreover, he designates through John, as through the moon, the church of the clergy, because of the "waning" of the active life; but through Elijah, as through the sun, the monastic order, because of the clarity and constancy of the contemplative life, which does not perish with the laying down of the flesh but is increased. Finally, because of this mystery, the throne of the only-begotten God is likewise compared to the sun and the moon, with David saying as if about himself: 
<margin>Psalm 88</margin>
though there is no doubt it is in the person of Christ: *And his throne is like the sun in my sight, and like the moon perfected forever.* Because, clearly, that part which gasps for the celestial splendors of the contemplative life burns with heat; while that which is compelled by the love of neighbors to follow earthly matters grows cold through a certain compassionate mercy. For "coldness" is not always to be taken in a bad sense, but sometimes in a good one: because just as it sometimes signifies the malice of the mind, so also sometimes...

He uses the sun and moon as symbols to contrast the active life of the clergy with the contemplative life of the monastic orders.</summary>

### Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

...which signifies the fear of the Lord. Indeed, the priests of the Church hold the form of sailors in this world: and it is necessary that they should often feel fear, for the wind of storms rises against them without ceasing. This is symbolized in the fear of Peter and his companions when, while the Lord was sleeping, the little boat was tossed by the waves, and they woke the Lord, saying: "Lord, save us, we are perishing."

<margin>Matthew 8</margin>
Thus, it is clearly evident: that the order of <term>contemplatives</term> <note>Those dedicated to prayer and meditation rather than active worldly work.</note> is signified by the sun, while the Church of <term>preachers</term> is signified by the moon. For the former pours out the light of wisdom upon this world, and the latter the light of knowledge. But alas! How terrible are those days of which the Lord speaks: *The sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood.*

<margin>Joel 2</margin>
For this is that very prophecy: *The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.* In darkness and blackness, sorrow and the blinding of the mind are signified; in the sackcloth of hair, the affliction of the heart is shown. But what is signified by the color of blood, if not spite and hatred? But perhaps the <term>sloth</term> <note>original: "accidia." This refers to a specific type of spiritual apathy or "noonday devil" that plagued monks.</note> of the mind, which is signified by the black color, is followed by blindness, and the venom of hatred and the spite of envy do not also accompany it?

<margin>1 John 2</margin>
<note>The original OCR reads 1 John 12, but this is a citation of 1 John 2:11.</note>
You have this clearly in the epistle of John, who wrote this book. *He who hates his brother,* he says, *is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and knows not where he goes, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.* Therefore, whether it is the sloth of the mind—which is contrary to the contemplatives—or that most unhappy spite of hatred—which, through the plague of ambition, infects the minds of the clergy—they simultaneously blind the hearts of wandering men and, in like manner, harden the souls of the wretched. Whence also, in the sixth part of the book, a great earthquake was followed by great hail: because surely (though it must not be said without a groan) that terror will not be followed by devoted contrition, but by a hardening of the heart. Nor is it a wonder. For the cause of a preceding fault is usually the punishment for the crime that follows. For Almighty God would never permit so many evils to come upon us unless our own malice deserved it. Therefore, it is handled by the just judgment of the Almighty: that where we run voluntarily, there we are confined by His sentence. Indeed, to include something more specific regarding the merit of our punishment: behold, even now

<column-break/>

there is a little light, and what peace remains among us. All things are peaceful for those residing in the cloisters; all is tranquil. For peace is a friend to their way of life, and tranquility is desired; for a joyful devotion cannot be stirred up in sorrow. Since, therefore, the blessing of peace still favors those who love that life, why is it that we perceive them to labor so greatly under the spirit of sloth? Why do they only find pleasure when they are drawn toward some fleeting things, passing into a "blindness of the eyes" <note>original: "lippitudinem oculorum," a metaphor for spiritual dim-sightedness or worldly distraction.</note> under the pretext of obedience? Even if some are drawn from the height of contemplation to action—as if from the glory of the sun to the calamity of the night—they are so joined to that action in their hearts that if the judgment of the pastor or the convent ever decides they should rest, absolved from the burden of the ministry assigned to them, they immediately rise up against the father of the monastery and those who gave the counsel. They begin to persecute and hate those whom they ought to love more. And so it happens that while they are forced to remain in the "happier life" <note>Monastic retirement.</note> against their will, the very beauty of the contemplative life takes on the paleness of a kind of sackcloth, which even their physical dullness demonstrates.

The prophet Jeremiah deplored this kind of darkness among monks when he lamented in the person of Jerusalem, saying: *The Nazarenes were whiter than snow, purer than milk, more ruddy than old ivory, more beautiful than sapphire: their skin is turned black.*

<margin>Iren.</margin>
For a Nazarene <note>Here used to mean a monk or one consecrated to God.</note> is whiter than snow and purer than milk when he who approaches to observe the contemplative life remains in that same clarity and serenity of mind. But like an extinguished coal, his skin is made black when, because he is forced to abstain from worldly cares, he walks about saddened and openly demonstrates the malice conceived in secret. God's judgment is therefore just and His severity is fair: so that he who is made sad without cause may run into that which truly makes him sad; and he who considers his neighbors to be rivals may fall into the hands of rivals. Thus the sun becomes black, like a sackcloth of hair, when that illustrious order—which ought to be joyful and bright—becomes darkened.

<meta>This page continues Joachim of Fiore’s interpretation of the Sixth Seal in the Book of Revelation. This page explores the internal decay of these groups, using the metaphors of tarnished gold and the "sackcloth" mentioned in the biblical text.</meta>

### Joachim’s Second Book on the Apocalypse
<meta>catchword: follows.</meta>

...bright with splendor and purity: but when contrary events happen against his holy vow, he is made sad and dark according to the desert of his own wickedness. For peace labors much for such a man and he profits by it; but while he is too occupied in outward things for the rewards of the flesh, he begins to become a stranger to the study of the spiritual life. It is necessary for him to imitate the life of the penitents in the mourning of sadness, just as much as it is necessary that he should stumble in many things while following worldly affairs. Hence, it is said through the same prophet: *How the gold has become dim, the finest color is changed, the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street!* <margin>Lamentations 4</margin> <note>original: "Quo obscuratum est aurum..." Joachim is quoting Lamentations, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, to describe the decline of the monastic order.</note> The gold becomes dim when the splendor of the <term>contemplative life</term> <note>A life focused on prayer and study rather than active ministry.</note> in the monastic order vanishes. The finest color is also changed when those who were positioned to watch for heavenly things begin to gape after earthly gains. The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street when those who ought to have held the narrow path—by which one goes to life—both for themselves and for others, are instead scattered through the broad ways that <margin>Proverbs 26</margin> lead to perdition. 

Indeed, in the <term>tabernacle of the Lord</term>, <note>The portable dwelling place of God in the Old Testament, used here as a metaphor for the Church.</note> not only are scarlet and fine linen necessary, but also curtains of <term>sackcloth</term> <note>original: "saga cilicina." Coarse cloth made of goat's hair, used for protection or mourning.</note> to protect all precious things from dust. But if everything in his thicket consists of curtains of sackcloth, for what use are the curtains themselves hung outside, if there is nothing in the tabernacle that is rightly protected by them? The body of a man is good, but only if the soul is within it; the habitation of a house is good, but only if the inhabitant is not missing. Otherwise, if the house is merely a house, and the inhabitant is not an inhabitant but merely like a house, it remains that not only is he who ought to have been the inhabitant nothing, but even the house itself is useful for nothing, as it lacks the fulfillment of its purpose. Therefore, both are good, provided that each of the two remains in its proper order. For it is not because the feet and the eyes are members of one body that the feet, like the eyes, can pass through dust unharmed; nor because the sons of a king and the sons of a king's servants are men of one nature that both are equally suited for servile work. For indeed, only servants are servants, and only the free are free. So it is that the contemplative life ought to be serene and transparent, even if there are some among the elect removed from this perfection who fulfill the duty of their own calling. For this reason,

<column-break/>

incorporeal things seem vain to them. It is clear enough that the clarity of the sun is turned into the deformity of sackcloth; and that this happens (as our sins demand) is proven in these days by suitable evidence. But why is this? Because there is a time of mercy and a time of judgment; a time of indulgence and a time of wrath. *The just man* (says the prophet) <margin>Isaiah 57</margin> *perishes, and there is no one who understands; and men of mercy are gathered away, and there is no one who considers it.* Or I might say it another way: after the gathering of the just, there remains a certain imitation as far as the outward form is concerned, a sort of propagation of the perfect life, and yet even this is obscure and as black as a funeral sackcloth. 

But we also see the life of the <term>clergy</term>, <note>The secular priests and church officials who live "in the world" rather than in monasteries.</note> which at first used to pour out the rays of its light upon the people—alas!—turned into blood. For there is nothing spiritual in it, nothing of the heavens, but almost the whole thing is slippery, the whole thing is carnal, the whole thing is "flesh and blood," and an emptying out of the spirit. Where are the strifes, where the scandals, where the brawls, where the envies, where the jealousies? Are they not in the church of the clergy? Are they not among those who ought to have given the light of their examples to the subject peoples? Finally, we see even the stars of heaven falling without number to the earth, whether through the ruin of heretical depravity or (as in most cases) by a lapse of the flesh. 

And it is no wonder. For our Counselor has withdrawn further from us, provoked by the multitude of our inventions. He has abandoned us according to the desires of our hearts, and each one of us walks <margin>Psalm 80</margin> in the wickedness of his own heart. We have received <margin>Jeremiah 31</margin> from Him a <term>bill of divorce</term> <note>original: "libellum repudij." A legal reference to God casting off His people due to their spiritual adultery.</note> and we follow the paths of our own hearts, until our cry ascends into heaven and His indignation is fulfilled. For it is written: *Because iniquity shall abound,* <margin>Matthew 24</margin> *the charity of many shall grow cold.* Therefore, all these evils will occur together, worse than usual: there will be battles without and fears within, for the Lord says: *Brother shall deliver brother to death, and children shall rise up against parents and put them to death.* <margin>Mark 13</margin> What is more fearful than this time, in which the foundations of the earth are to be moved by fear? There will be consolation neither in the sun, nor in the moon, nor in the stars, since all things will be disturbed and each thing removed from its proper state. And indeed, in all these things *his anger is not turned away,* <margin>Isaiah 5</margin> *but his hand is stretched out still.* For there follows:

<summary>Joachim interprets the darkening of the sun and the moon as the moral and spiritual decay of the monks and the clergy, respectively. He laments that those who should be spiritual leaders have become obsessed with worldly gain and carnal strife, signaling the approach of a time of judgment.</summary>

### Part of the Exposition
<meta>Catchword at bottom right: perfectione. Marginalia in cursive hand.</meta>

<margin>Chapter 13</margin>
**And the heaven receded like a scrolled-up book.** <note>original: "Et cœlum recessit sicut liber inuolutus." Revelation 6:14.</note>

¶ This is an unusual comparison, but not one unfamiliar to knowledge. An open book is present; one rolled up recedes. For just as certain shining stars, the very elements of the letters <note>meaning the individual characters of the alphabet</note> are present in an open volume. For while they are clearly seen by the eyes of readers, they pour out the light of wisdom and knowledge into human hearts as if from certain vessels of light. But when the book is rolled up, it is not present; for it is not present for its purpose, even if it is essentially there where it was before. 

But if heaven has the true likeness of a book, how much more does the Church, which is called by the name of "heaven"? Both of them possess, as it were, stars: the elect, just as the sacred <term>apices</term> <note>The tips or marks of letters; Joachim compares the saints to the very strokes of the pen in God's book.</note> in a book serve to illuminate the dwellings of the faithful. This she has done in all the days she was permitted to scatter her light, until the time of night and the power of darkness arrives, in which it is necessary for all the "beasts of the forest" to pass through. Indeed, in that day of the repeated <term>Passion of the Lord</term> <note>Joachim refers to a coming time of suffering for the Church that mirrors Christ’s crucifixion.</note>—which I judge has already begun in some part—it will not be permitted for the bells to give their sounds, nor to sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land, until the shadows of the night and the gloom of darkness pass away. 

Therefore, in that night the light will be hidden; and since a rolled-up book does not reveal what it contains within, so the entire Church of the saints will be hidden. For thus the elect of God will keep their wisdom to themselves, such as it is, so that they will not dare to preach publicly while the darkness prevails. Not because the faithful souls will cease to encourage one another more secretly, but because they will not dare to preach publicly. Hence, concerning the beast that ascends from the earth, which John also calls the False Prophet, it is written in the fourth part of the book, in the sixth chapter: *He will bring it about that no one can sell or buy, except he who has the mark of the name of the beast.* <note>original: "Faciet vt neqs possit vẽdere: aut emere..." Revelation 13:17.</note> For the "sellers" in the Church are the preachers; the "buyers" are the listeners. For those sell precious stones; these give what they can here, and they buy with that price received for free what cannot be earned by the price of gold. But in that dark day, it will not be permitted for those who do not keep the law of the beast to sell or buy; because to preach, or to receive a preacher with impunity at that time, will not be permitted except to those who are not afraid to publicly confess themselves as disciples of the beast. Whence it is added here:

<column-break/>

<margin>Chapter 14</margin>
**And the mountains and islands were moved from their places.** <note>Revelation 6:14.</note>

¶ "Mountains" in this place designate monasteries. "Islands" designate the episcopal churches, which are situated as if in the middle of waves, as John says in this book: *Many waters are many peoples.* <note>original: "Aquæ multæ: sunt populi multi"</note> Moreover, the mountains and islands will be moved from their places because, after the quiet monks and the clergy have been driven away, they will either be utterly destroyed so that they no longer exist, or—except for those designated in <term>Noah’s ark</term> <note>A symbol for the remnant of the Church that survives the tribulation.</note>—they will not be permitted to use their own laws. It follows:

<margin>Chapter 15</margin>
**And the kings of the earth, and the princes, and the tribunes, and the strong, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and in the rocks of the mountains; and they said to the mountains and the rocks: "Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of their wrath has come, and who will be able to stand?"** <note>Revelation 6:15-17.</note>

¶ These words are spoken because they wish to imply this: that every rank of person is to be struck with such immense fear that they flee to the caves and rocks of the mountains to be hidden from the face of him who sits upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb. He indicates how intolerable that terror will be with most fitting words. Indeed, the Lord used words of this kind against the daughters of Jerusalem when he was being led to the cross while they were weeping and lamenting. *Daughters of Jerusalem,* he said, *do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children; for behold, the days will come in which they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that did not bear, and the breasts that did not nurse. Then you will begin to say to the mountains and the rocks...* <note>original: "Filie hierusalem nolite flere super me..." quoting Luke 23:28-30.</note> 

We can, however, take "caves" to mean the secret rooms of the monks that will remain, and "the rocks of the mountains" to mean spiritual men, strong in the perfection of faith, to whom [the faithful] will flee...

<summary>Joachim interprets the Sixth Seal's cosmic disturbances as the suppression of the Church's public ministry and the physical destruction or displacement of monasteries (mountains) and bishoprics (islands). He explains that during the coming tribulation, spiritual teaching will become a "hidden" or "scrolled-up" book, available only in secret.</summary>

# Second Book of Joachim on the Apocalypse

...many are about to receive penance, clearly understanding the judgment of Almighty God, and that truly the just God sits upon the throne to judge with equity. The Lamb, who is despised in the day of peace because of his patience, will know that he must one day take vengeance upon his enemies who return his contempt for him. For this is that saying:
<margin>Luke 19</margin>
<note>original: "In hac die tua que ad pacem tibi..."</note> "In this your day, the things that belong to your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes: for the days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a trench, and encompass you, and hem you in on every side, and beat you to the ground, and your children who are within you. And they will not leave in you one stone upon another that is not destroyed, because you did not know the time of your visitation." <note>Luke 19:42-44. Joachim applies Jesus's lament over Jerusalem to the corrupt Church of his own time.</note> Now, the "Day of the Lord" (as I have already said) is not always to be understood as the final Day of Judgment; this is proven not only from this passage, but also from many other places in the Scriptures that agree on this point, among which is this:
<margin>Isaiah 13</margin>
"Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, and wrath, and fury, to lay the land desolate, and to crush the sinners out of it." <note>Isaiah 13:9.</note> Therefore, that "great Day of the Lord" will also be the beginning of that time which is called the Day of Judgment, in which that great harlot **Babylon** <note>In Joachim’s thought, Babylon represents the "carnal" or corrupt institutional Church and the worldly society it inhabits.</note> is to be judged, even in this present life. For as it is clearly shown in the sixth part of the book, which deals with her ruin, the kings of the earth—gathered together as one—will rise up against her. Although they themselves are evil and do not know what they are doing, they nevertheless carry out the just vengeance of Almighty God, purging the Lord's vineyard of thorns, the threshing floors of chaff, the oil from its dregs, and the harvest of the Lord's field from tares. And because it is written of these same kings that they will fight with the Lamb, and be defeated by the Lamb and his elect, there is no doubt that many thousands of saints are to be crowned with martyrdom, in order to fulfill the number of the elect which is written below, and of whom it was said to the martyrs mentioned above: "Wait a little while longer until your fellow servants and your brothers, who are to be killed as you were, are complete." <note>Revelation 6:11.</note> As far as it seems to me, first judgment must be done 

<column-break/>

concerning **Babylon**: that is, concerning the profane multitude of people who call themselves Christians and are not, but are the **Synagogue of Satan**. <note>original: "synagoga Sathane"</note> Shortly thereafter, when the nations see that victory has been given to them, they will attribute it to their own abominable law and to their "false apostle" **Muhammad**, <note>original: "Maometh"</note> as if he were truly sent from heaven. They will begin to interrogate Christians with punishments, tear them apart with torments, and compel them to cross over to their own rite by denying the name of Christ. This will be suggested especially by the **false prophets** who will emerge from the Christian people, just as the present age proves every day. But the Lamb will fight in their minds and will overcome those nations. Once a most evident sign has been given, that savage storm will cease, so that the remaining infidel nations at the four corners of the earth will not dare to cross their boundaries to swallow up the remnants of God's elect, having recognized, without doubt, the manifest power of Christ which will work in his elect, until his servants are marked on their foreheads. For so it says in the following verses:

<margin>Chapter 7, verses 1 & 6</margin>
> **After these things I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that the winds should not blow on the earth, nor on the sea, nor on any tree.** <note>Revelation 7:1.</note>

I believe these angels, to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, are of that kind of which the Psalmist speaks: <note>original: "Misit in eis..."</note> "He sent among them"—that is, among the Egyptians—"the wrath of his indignation: indignation, and wrath, and tribulation, sent through evil angels." <note>Psalm 78:49.</note> I believe the **four winds of heaven**, which are held by these angels so that they do not blow upon the earth, nor the sea, nor any tree, are **four spiritual intelligences**. <note>original: "quatuor spāles intelligentias"</note> By their teaching, the Christian people (signified by the "earth" and the "trees") are accustomed to be supported, and the bitterness of the sea—that is, the wrath of the pagan people—is turned into sweetness. For power will be given for a time to the four angels to harm the earth, the sea, and the trees, before this prohibition is made, because power will be granted against the powers that are [currently] preventing them. <unclear>preventing</unclear>

His "loud cry" is his clear and open preaching, and his prohibition is his authoritative power. He shall therefore "ascend"—whoever he may be—"from the rising of the sun," because, so that the fall of this present life may not be feared, he will preach the resurrection of all the just in the riches of the <term>True Sun</term> <note>Christ, the "Sun of Justice."</note> (of whom the Psalmist speaks):

->Joachim’s Second [Book] on the Apocalypse<-
