The breakfast which was celebrated in the morning—having first enclosed, without doubt, a multitude of fish—signifies the joy that will follow the tribulation of this night. <note>Joachim refers to the breakfast by the Sea of Galilee in John 21, interpreting the "night" as the time of persecution and the "morning" as the subsequent era of peace and joy.</note> Once that joy is truly completed, soon that great battle will begin, which is more clearly declared in the sixth part of the book, when it says: *I saw the beast and the kings of the earth prepared to make war with him who sat upon the horse and with his army.* <note>original: "Vidi bestiam..." citing Revelation 19:19.</note> Moreover, this very thing is designated in Peter, to whom, as soon as that same breakfast was finished, it was said by the Lord: *Follow me.* And after a few words: *When you were younger, you girded yourself; but when you are old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.* <note>original: "Cum esses iunior..." citing John 21:18.</note> Therefore, what was said: *Until we sign the servants of our God on their foreheads* [Revelation 7:3], is as if it were said: "Even if it is necessary that the great tribulation follow, which the passion of Christ designates, yet there is still a place of mercy for those wishing to repent; space is still to be given for calling both Jews and Gentiles to the faith, so that, marked with the sign of Christ and armed with the armor of light, they may be able to resist in the evil day and fulfill those things which are lacking in the sufferings of Christ [Colossians 1:24]." This is just as it was completed in the six continuous years after the Babylonian exile, which seemed to be lacking in the construction of the temple of the Lord. <margin>3 Esdras 6</margin> <note>Joachim refers to the rebuilding of the Second Temple as a historical "type" or pattern for the spiritual building of the Church.</note> So now too, under the sixth opening, let the order of holy martyrs receive its completion. Therefore, on that day which will be in the middle between both tribulations, many of the Jews and Gentiles will be signed with the <term>seal of the Holy Trinity</term> <note>original: "signaculo sancte trinitatis." Joachim often links the sealing of the 144,000 to a specific historical moment of conversion and spiritual marking before the final Antichrist appears.</note> to complete that number of holy martyrs which is written below, and that glorious multitude whose number is infinite. For it follows:

<margin>Text 3</margin>
*And I heard the number of those who were sealed, a hundred and forty-four thousand out of every tribe of the children of Israel.*

Concerning this number of the sealed, we made mention earlier when treating the seats and the elders, and we are nonetheless going to treat these

more fully in the fourth part, because in it, concerning the equal number of virgins, it is said: *I saw the Lamb standing above Mount Zion, and with him a hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.* <note>Revelation 14:1.</note> But to speak briefly of what must be treated more copiously there: the total sum of the signed martyrs is collected under this number because the walls of the heavenly city of Jerusalem are described as being a hundred and forty-four cubits [Revelation 21:17]; the perfection of this number is great and illustrious. # The Abbot's Part of the Exposition

<column-break/>

...an innumerable multitude <note>continuing from the previous page's discussion of the "great multitude" in Revelation 7:9</note> slaughtered for the name of Christ: this is weighed not only from this vision of John, but also from the Old Testament, as David says to them in the book <margin>Psalm 139 <note>original: "ps. 138"</note></margin> of Psalms: *Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their authority is greatly strengthened. I will count them, and they shall be multiplied more than the sand.* <note>original: "Nimis honorati sunt..."</note> Indeed, they are written to have appeared in white robes, just as it says in the following verses: *They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.* <note>original: "Lauerūt stolas suas..." citing Revelation 7:14</note> Moreover, they stand continually in the sight of the throne, assisting in the presence of the Supreme King and in the eyes of the heavenly citizens, who watch them struggle so manfully in this life; because of this, their blessed names are recorded as written in heaven. By the eternal memory of that city—and indeed of its Creator—those names are never deleted by any change of time or overshadowing of circumstance. <margin>Psalm 112 <note>original: "ps. 111"</note></margin> Whence, in the person of one just man, it was said generally of all: *The just shall be in everlasting memory; he shall not fear an evil report.* <note>original: "In memoria eterna..."</note> So here the blessed martyrs assist, as eagerly as they do happily, in the sight of the throne and in the sight <margin>John 12</margin> of that Lamb, who speaks concerning all of them as if in the person of one, saying: *I will, Father, that where I am, there also my servant may be.* <note>original: "Volo pater vt vbi ego sum..." citing John 12:26</note> (They truly cry out with a great voice, saying: *Salvation to our God who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb.*) Because they have preached openly in the whole world, saying that salvation is in God the Father alone, and in His only Son who saves all <margin>Acts 4</margin> freely and does not reproach; nor is there any name in which we must be saved, except that of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. <note>Joachim expands the quote from Acts 4:12 to include the full Trinity.</note> Not only now, but even forever, they do not cease to offer this praise to their Creator, for they do not credit themselves for being victors, but rather God the Father and His Son who provided the victory <margin>Psalm 84 <note>original: "ps. 83"</note></margin> to them. For this is the meaning of: *Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; <margin>L. 4. <note>likely a reference to the fourth book of this commentary or a specific lection</note></margin> they will praise you forever and ever.* It follows:

AND all the angels stood around the throne and the elders and the four living creatures; and they fell 

<column-break/>

on their faces and worshiped God, saying: *Amen. Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving; honor and power and strength to our God forever and ever, amen.*

In this place, "all the angels" are to be understood as all those chosen humans who, even if they are not numbered among the five orders <note>Joachim often categorizes the church into "orders" such as monks, clergy, and laity; here he suggests a hierarchy in the afterlife.</note> who belong more specifically to the City, nevertheless belong to the suburbs and villages, in which (as someone said) *Alleluia* shall be sung. It is not that there is any distinction of walls there, but rather a great difference in spiritual gifts according to merits. Therefore, all who have earned the right to reach the heavenly kingdoms, aided by the merits of the saints, praise God in common. And whatever good or happiness they perceive in themselves, they attribute it entirely to the Creator. 

And it should be noted that the crowd of martyrs praises first, while the crowd of the other elect responds: *Amen.* And they immediately join in their praise, because the holy martyrs were the first to conquer, and so they were the first to return praise to the Lord. And as their praises reached the knowledge of the people, they began to have many imitators and fellow-workers in the word of life, confirming by their own testimony what the martyrs had foretold by going before them. For when they saw the ranks of the elect and the patience of the saints, and understood that the "salvation" of men in this life is vain—and that only that is true salvation for which the holy martyrs of God despised the joys of mortal life—and that their dead bodies shone forth so gloriously with many signs of miracles, being struck in heart and mind, they all responded together: *Amen.* 

"It is true," they say. "It is true that there is no true salvation except in God alone, who crowns His servants in heaven; and for those who trust in His mercy, He makes them famous and illustrious even in the present age." Let us also, therefore, praise Him and honor Him, <margin>Judith 13? <note>original: "Judi. 6"</note></margin> saying: *Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving; honor and power and strength to our God forever and ever, amen.*

### The Second Part Explained
<note>The heading "Abb. Pars Exponis" refers to the Abbot (Joachim) providing his Exposition or explanation.</note>

...is called to labor, as his imitator says to his unique sons of God: He who deigned <margin>Luke 12</margin> to take up this very servitude within Himself. *I say to you, my friends: do not be terrified of those who kill the body, and after these things have no more that they can do.* <note>original: "Dico vobis amicis meis: ne terreamini..." citing Luke 12:4</note> Behold what kind of servitude and what kind of labor lies upon the holy martyrs in the day of battle: for such is the fear of servitude, even if they are lords of all and heirs in Christ. And not without merit was this order begun by the blessed Stephen, who was appointed by the apostles with his companions to serve the church. For to serve is the task of the young, while to sit is the task of the elders; of these two, the former belongs to the active life, and the latter to the happiness of rest. But lest anyone be scandalized by these things, let him consider that this part was given to Christ Jesus, who came to serve, not to be served. That other part <note>The "sitting" or contemplative rest</note> was given to his mother, of whom it is never read—from the moment she gave birth to the Son—that she served anyone. Yet Christ Jesus served both his mother, his foster-father, and his disciples, so that no one should think himself despised because he serves others; rather, advancing more and more in virtue, he should believe that saying of the Savior to be true, where he <margin>Luke 14</margin> says: *He who humbles himself shall be exalted.* <note>original: "Qui se humiliat exaltabitur."</note> But since there is no matter for action in the heavenly homeland, and since John says at the end of the book that he saw no temple in that city, and asserts that its gates are open by day, and there is no night in it, it is asked what he means here. Why does John say the holy martyrs serve the almighty God day and night in His temple, as if he were writing something contrary to himself? But it must be known that in the first state of this world, a likeness of the **altar** was shown in the people of the Jews; in the second, a likeness of the **temple** in the people called the Gentiles; in the third, a likeness of **Jerusalem** in the people of both Jews and Gentiles. And because this voice does not refer to that future time in which Jerusalem must be perfected, but to this present time in which the temple of God—which is the Church of the Gentiles—receives its completion. In this time, truly, the "living stones" are hammered outside the city, and the night of tribulation is mixed with the light of joy. It is said

<column-break/>

of the holy martyrs that they serve Him night and day in His temple, not indeed after the end of the world when servitude and the night of sorrow shall cease, but in all this present time while the building of the temple persists and the purgatorial fire afflicts some. For it is just that they who were in turmoil here while they lived in the flesh should find rest after death. Therefore, they receive a double gift of joy—those who preserve themselves in such a way for the service of Christ—because both here, in the succession of the heirs of blood, they serve God day and night (that is, in prosperity and in adversity) in the ministry of His temple, so that through them those who must be shaped may be formed in patience. Hence, He who sits on the throne dwells over them; and just as the Lord said, like a hen over her chicks, keeping and protecting them continually from the greed of the hawks; and having finished their sorrows within themselves, they acquire the seat of blessedness and rest. ### Concerning the opening of the seventh seal.
<margin>Chapter 8, Lesson 1</margin>
**And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.**

<margin>Luke 23</margin>
When the Evangelist Luke speaks of the passion of Christ, and makes mention of the holy women who were watching the place of his burial, he added: *And on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.* <note>original: "Et sabbato quidem siluerunt secundum mandatum."</note> The silence of the sacred Sabbath is the silence of the <term>contemplative life</term> <note>A life dedicated to prayer and meditation rather than external work.</note>. For the saints are silent once the <term>mysteries</term> <note>The hidden spiritual meanings or sacraments of the faith.</note> are completed, so that they may hear what the Lord God speaks within them, knowing that temporal things pass away so that eternal things may follow. So it is also in the Old Testament: where the book of <term>Ezra</term> <note>original: "Esdre." Referring to the rebuilding of the Temple and Jerusalem.</note> deals with the restoration of Jerusalem, soon the <term>canonical histories</term> <note>The historical narrative books of the Bible.</note> fall silent, and nearly all the prophetic books and volumes of deeds <term>keep the Sabbath</term> <note>original: "sabbatizant," meaning they cease their activity or narrative.</note>. No one appeared who might succeed in continuing to produce books up to that time, because the blessed time was near in which the Lord was going to do a new thing upon the earth. Thus, in the New Testament as well, it is necessary for the sacred mysteries to "keep the Sabbath" when they have been completed through the <term>concordance</term> <note>The harmony or parallel relationship between the Old and New Testaments.</note> of what was done in the Old Testament, each having been given its own individual opening. And because the hearts of men are hard toward believing and vehemently obstinate toward faith, in order to rebuke the impiety of wicked men, a certain angel (under the sounding of the sixth trumpet) is described as having sworn an oath: *that time should be no more,* but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God should be finished. Therefore, there will also be silence in heaven now, because the time for explaining the scriptures will be completed, and this kind of labor will cease in the Christian church, though it does not cease to preach in another way. Moreover, I think that "half an hour" refers to that time which is called in the scriptures "half a time." This is essentially a "seventh" time in respect to the three <term>times</term> <note>Referring to the prophetic "time, times, and half a time" from Daniel and Revelation.</note> which are divided into six "half-times"—whether according to literal truth as six months, or according to a <term>typological</term> <note>Seeking symbolic patterns where Old Testament events foreshadow New Testament ones.</note> understanding, that seventh time which is designated by the final six months.

### Father [Abbot] Part of the Exposition

...was what the Lord had commanded: and behold, in the circuit of the seventh day, the walls of Jericho fell. What, then, do those seven priests with their trumpets signify? They signify these seven angels with the seven trumpets that were given to them. For indeed, the priests of God are called the "angels" <note>The Latin *angelus* means both "angel" and "messenger."</note> of the Lord, as witnessed by the prophet Malachi, who says:
<margin>Malachi 2</margin>
*The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth: for he is the messenger <note>original: "angelus"</note> of the Lord of hosts.* Therefore, whether it be the seven angels in this vision [of Revelation] or the seven priests in the Book of Joshua, they designate the <term>doctors</term> <note>Teachers or theologians of the Church.</note> of the New Testament who are the heralds of truth among the people.
<margin>Joshua 6</margin>
For truly, it is their proper duty to sound the trumpets: that is, to proclaim spiritual words with a loud voice—words emerging from the <term>narrowness of the letter</term> <note>This refers to moving beyond a literal, surface-level reading of the Bible to find its deeper spiritual meaning.</note> which are symbolized by the trumpets—to awaken the sluggish hearts of men as if from sleep, and to encourage those trembling in their suffering toward the prize of victory.

Moreover, in a marvelous way, the very order of those fighting was indicated in very few words; so much so that in a brief speech, nearly the whole sum of the book is touched upon in preparation. For behold, the army went before; the priests followed with trumpets, and the Ark followed them. But the common people also followed the Ark, by which the general order of the Church is designated. Nor is there any doubt that the leaders of the people preceded that same army, even if mention of them does not seem to be made in that same place; this was so that, once the first <term>seal</term> had largely passed, they might appear to have arrived at the time of the second seal. For in the entire first part of this book, nothing is specifically treated except the leaders of the people, who are the <term>prelates</term> <note>High-ranking clergy like bishops or abbots.</note> of the churches. Nor in the second or third parts is there mention of anything except the army of holy martyrs; nor in the third part, except for the angels sounding trumpets and their afflictions. Truly, in the fourth part of the book, the principal mention is made of the Ark of the Lord's Covenant, which designates the "church of virgins"; just as in the fifth part, mention is made of the temple of the tabernacle, which represents the multitude of chosen men among the people who follow the Ark of the Lord.

Consider these things, wise reader, and weigh

<column-break/>

how weighty is the mystery that is so frequent in Divine Scripture, and so solemn and renowned in the canonical books. Since mention was made of the ruin of Jericho among other things, it is pleasing to scrutinize the mysteries of this ruin, so that from those things done in one week, we may contemplate what has been done or remains to be done in the <term>Sixth Age</term> <note>In medieval theology, the "Sixth Age" is the current era of history, beginning with the birth of Christ and ending with the Last Judgment.</note> of the world. For six days, the priests of the Lord go around the city once a day and return to the camp; this signifies that through each of the seven periods which pass in labor until the opening of the sixth seal, the teachers of the Holy Church have predicted the ruin of the world, and yet the world still persists in its stability. It is as if, while the walls remain in their solidity each day, the priests return to the camp, since the teachers are not yet able to show in the present what they predict. Even those who predict the ruin of the world are compelled, like all others, to submit their necks to the burden of this present life. But on the seventh day, they did not go around the city once or twice, but they did the same seven times over; and they did this with a solemn blast, and in that very seventh circuit—in which the sacred number seven was completed—the walls of Jericho fell. This signifies that under the seventh angel sounding the trumpet, the teachers of the Holy Church will predict with one voice that the destruction of the worldly kingdom is at hand; and they will cry out more urgently and more frequently than usual, just as a rooster cries out more insistently when positioned at the dawn.

Nor should it be disturbing that in the preceding part of the book, under the opening of the seventh seal, it is narrated that "silence was made in heaven." That was said regarding the historical preaching, according to which the Gospel of Christ is announced to the world in six laborious times, but in the seventh there will be rest. This [present passage], however, pertains to spiritual understanding, which was indeed partially declared in those six times among spiritual men, but according to its fullness, it will not be manifest except in the seventh—namely, when the enemies of the cross of Christ convert to Him, the truth of the spirit having been recognized. This will no doubt happen through the preaching of those of whom it is said in Daniel:
<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
*Those who are learned among the people shall instruct many.* And it should be noted that the walls of Jericho did not fall...

# Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

...is what the Lord had commanded: and behold, on the seventh circuit of the seventh day, the walls of Jericho collapsed. What, then, do those seven priests with their trumpets signify? They signify these seven angels with the seven trumpets given to them. Indeed, the priests of God are called the "angels" of the Lord, as the prophet Malachi testifies, saying:
<margin>Malachi 2</margin>
*The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the messenger <note>original: "angelus," which means both "angel" and "messenger."</note> of the Lord of hosts.* Therefore, whether it be the seven angels in this vision or the seven priests in the Book of Joshua, they represent the **teachers of the New Testament** who are the heralds of the truth among the people.
<margin>Joshua 6</margin>
Clearly, it is their specific duty to sound the trumpets; that is, to bring forth spiritual words with a loud voice. These words certainly emerge from the <term>narrowness of the letter</term> <note>The "straits" or "narrowness of the letter" refers to the literal, surface-level reading of the Bible, which the author believes must be expanded into spiritual understanding.</note>, which is signified by the trumpets, to rouse the sluggish hearts of men as if from sleep, and to exhort those trembling in the face of suffering toward the prize of victory.

In a marvelous way, the very order of the combatants is revealed in very few words, so that in a brief speech, nearly the whole sum of the book is touched upon in readiness. For behold, the priests with their trumpets follow the preceding army, and the Ark follows them. But the common people also follow the Ark, by which the general order of the faithful is designated. There is no doubt that the leaders of the people preceded this same army, even if they are not mentioned in that place, so that—having mostly passed through the first seal—they might be seen to have arrived by the time of the second seal. For in the entire first part of this book, nothing is treated specifically except the leaders of the people, who are the prelates of the churches. Nor is anything treated in the second part except the army of the holy martyrs; nor in the third part except the angels sounding the trumpets and those standing by them. Indeed, in the fourth part of the book, the primary mention is made of the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord, which signifies the **Church of virgins**; just as in the fifth part, mention is made of the temple of the tabernacle, which designates the multitude of the elect among the people following the Ark of the Lord. 
Consider these things, wise reader, and weigh carefully 

<column-break/>

how much weight this mystery carries, which is so frequent in Divine Scripture, and so solemn and renowned in the canonical books. Because mention was made of the ruin of Jericho among other things, it is pleasing to scrutinize the mysteries of this ruin, so that from the things that were done in one week, we can contemplate what was done—or is to be done—in the <term>Sixth Age of the world</term> <note>Medieval scholars divided history into seven "ages"; the Sixth Age was considered the current era, beginning with Christ and ending with the Apocalypse.</note>. For six days, the priests of the Lord circled the city once a day and returned to the camp. This signifies that through the seven individual periods that pass in labor until the opening of the sixth seal, the teachers of the Holy Church have predicted the ruin of the world—and yet, the world still endures in its stability. It is as if, while the walls remain in their solidity each day, the priests return to the camp, because the teachers are not yet able to show the reality of what they predict. Those who predict the ruin of the world are also compelled, like everyone else, to submit their necks to the burden of this present life. 

On the seventh day, however, they did not circle the city once or twice, but they did it seven times over, and this was done with a solemn blast. In that seventh circuit, in which the sacred number of seven was completed, the walls of Jericho fell. This signifies that under the seventh angel sounding the trumpet, the teachers of the Holy Church will preach with one voice that the destruction of the worldly kingdom is at hand. This will happen with such constant urgency that, like a **rooster at dawn**, they will cry out more insistently and more frequently than usual. 

Nor should it disturb anyone that in the preceding part of the book, it is said that "silence was made in heaven" upon the opening of the seventh seal. That silence refers to the end of <term>historical preaching</term> <note>The "literal" or "historical" proclamation of the Gospel to the world.</note>, according to which the Gospel of Christ is announced to the laboring world in six time-periods, while in the seventh there will be rest. But this sounding of the trumpet refers to **spiritual understanding**. While this was partially declared in spiritual men during those six times, it will not be fully manifest until the seventh, when even the enemies of the cross of Christ will be converted to Him, having recognized the truth of the Spirit. This will undoubtedly occur through the preaching of those of whom it is said in Daniel:
<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
*The learned among the people shall teach many.* And it should be noted that the walls of Jericho did not fall...

The obscurity of the letter <note>The "obscurity of the letter" refers to a strictly literal reading of the Bible without spiritual or allegorical insight.</note> overshadows like a cloud, so much so that the teachers of the Church, represented by Moses, cannot meanwhile see the face of God <note>original: "filia dei," likely a transcription error for "faciem dei" (the face of God), given the context of Moses on Sinai.</note> except through a mirror dimly. But on the seventh day, the <margin>Exodus 24 <note>OCR says "Exo. 2," but the narrative of Sinai is in chapter 24.</note></margin> Lord called Moses from the midst of the darkness and invited him to behold the light, which is He himself.

Truly, he wanders from the truth who does not understand the scriptures and the power of God; he who, not knowing the paths of God's mysteries, is ignorant of whence he comes or where he goes. Hence, to certain heretics, Truth itself <margin>Matthew 22</margin> says: *You err, knowing neither the scriptures nor the power of God.* 

Therefore, it is clear that ignorance is the mother of error. Hence, the angel is said to stand before the golden altar because Christ suffered in the sight of that church—the church which, even before the same Christ came into the world, remained in the faith of the one God and in his profession through the Law and circumcision. Hence, to that same church 

<margin>Psalm 79</margin>

For it was necessary for him to be lifted up on the cross so that he might be seen by all, and so that the "serpentine bite" <note>An allusion to the Bronze Serpent in Numbers 21, symbolizing how Christ's death heals the "bite" of sin.</note> which was killing the unwary might be healed by his power. Therefore, the angel stood before the altar, and the **incense** given to him by many he solemnly offered to God the Father; for the vows and sighs of all the righteous are gathered together in him universally, so that he himself might offer them in the sight of the Most High. For those who wish to pour out their prayers before the royal majesty desire to find such an **advocate** <term>advocatus: one who pleads the cause of another, specifically Christ as the mediator</term> who, by the merit of his own goodness, may be heard by the King, and whose face the King will not turn away from the things he asks to obtain. But why "upon the altar"? Because not only did the passion of Christ benefit us in knocking upon the ears of divine mercy for our sins, but also the faith and merits of the preceding righteous ones, whose names are written in the **Book of Life** and whose works were deemed worthy in the sight of the Lord. Furthermore, their suffrages <note>Intercessory prayers</note> and prayers also benefit us—not because Christ is not sufficient for all things, but because having become man for our salvation, he willed to have godly men as companions in the work of piety. For Christ does not intercede for us alone, as if he alone obtains what others do not deserve; nor is he our only advocate with the Father. Rather, the cohorts of all the righteous who have preceded us into the kingdom of God are with him and through him. Otherwise, if this were not so, the entire church would be deceived and in error (God forbid!), which daily and confidently requests the suffrages of the saints, so that they who are already counted among the friends of God may intercede for us to the Lord our God. ...that heavenly homeland <note>original: "patria illa"</note> in the same way that they are able to show the first fruits of love in this exile: because it belongs more to those who are compassionate to the wretched, who still, in some part, feel the same suffering. However, righteous men offer incense as if upon the altar: just as they are kindled in the fire of the altar together with those who are appointed to intercede for the people, the saints of God pray for them. These saints have already been stripped of the weight of the flesh, so that they themselves might intercede for the people before Almighty God; they know that they can obtain what they ask for all the more easily because, kindled by the fire of God’s charity, they have been made one spirit with Him. Finally, the offering of incense, which could not by its own power be resolved into the scent of smoke, is snatched upward by the power of the fire (which is of a lighter nature) and raised on high like a certain light mist. So it is that while the faithful prayer of those who both love their neighbors and are still weighed down by the mass of the flesh is joined to the prayer of those who, now established in the fullness of liberty, burn more perfectly with the love of God: it happens that both prayers reach the merciful God together, and one is heard through the other, as the two begin to be one. Therefore, the altar contributes something; they bring forth incense, but nothing happens without the mystery of the angel, nothing without the work of Jesus: because <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth. ### Chapter 4.
### ¶ And the smoke of the incense of the prayers of the saints ascended from the hand of the angel before God.

Nor did he require intervals of time to offer the prayers of individuals; rather, he who can do all things did this once, entering through himself once into the eternal holy places, having found <margin>Hebrews 9</margin> redemption. Therefore, the smoke of the incense is said to ascend in the sight of God from the hand of the angel because, through the work of piety and justice which Christ performed, it was brought about that the prayer of the wretched (who could merit nothing through themselves) might reach the sight of God—all others being at rest, and one man opposing himself on behalf of many. -># Explanation of the Parts<-

...that Christ should suffer and so enter into his glory? For on that day he entered into his glory: and soon the promise which he received, he poured out upon his elect with a pouring out even more fully on the day of Pentecost. Christ was indeed glorified twice during that same time: first when, rising from the underworld, he came to those above <note>original: "superos"; a classical term for the living or the inhabitants of the upper world, here referring to Christ’s return to his disciples on earth after the Resurrection.</note>; and secondly, when he returned to heaven in the sight of his own followers. And first, while he was still on earth, he gave them the Spirit as if from the earth; secondly, when he resided in heaven, he sent Him more fully and solemnly as if from heaven. 

But why not before? Why only after Christ was glorified? It was because he did not wish to do this in the time of his humility, lest he should seem to seek his own glory before he fulfilled the ministry of humility for which he had come into this world. This is contrary to those who wish to be glorified before the proper time, being unwilling to be imitators of Christ's patience through the enduring of sufferings. For if he had shown his omnipotence beforehand, how would he have endured the reproach of the passion? Since if men had known him, they would never have crucified the King of Glory. <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> Therefore, those who wish to be seen as holy before they actually are, make it apparent that they are unwilling to be reviled and despised by men as Christ was, but rather wish to be glorified and extolled, so that they might show themselves to be members of that one <margin>2 Thessalonians 2</margin> of whom Paul says: *Who is extolled and opposes himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped, showing himself as if he were God.* 

Those of this sort abuse the authority of the Lord’s saying: *That they may see your good works,* not attending to the fact that the Lord does not say, "And they may glorify you," but <margin>Matthew 5</margin> *glorify your Father who is in heaven.* Nor do they remember that sentence spoken through the Psalmist: *The Lord will scatter the bones of those who please men;* <margin>Psalm 52</margin> *they are put to shame, because God has despised them.* Lest they pretend they cannot grasp the difference between these sayings, these sentences are not contrary to each other as they think; rather, it is when they have performed all righteousness before God alone for nearly thirty years <note>A reference to the "Hidden Life" of Jesus before his public ministry began at age thirty.</note>—that is, until they are founded and rooted in all humility. 

<column-break/>

Indeed, for nearly thirty years the same Lord hid his glory; then let them know it is permitted to show their works to men—and this not suddenly, but little by little, just as the same true Teacher did who descended from heaven—so that men may see their good works and glorify their Father who is in heaven. 

But even then, let them take the greatest care that they do not think themselves—or show themselves—to have anything they have not received. Instead, let them strive to imitate the man Christ Jesus, to whom it was said by the Psalmist: *You have ascended on high, you have led captivity captive; you have received gifts among men;* <margin>Psalm 67</margin> and of whom it was <margin>Acts 2</margin> said by Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: *Exalted by the right hand of God, and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, he has poured out this which you see and hear.* 

In this way the Son is said to receive something from the Father, even insofar as he is God, just as he himself says of the Holy Spirit: <margin>John 16</margin> *He shall receive of mine and shall announce it to you.* But insofar as he is man, he is said to have received the gifts of the Holy Spirit in a far different way: for the purpose of pouring them out into his members <note>In this context, "members" refers to the "members of the Church," which is considered the Body of Christ.</note>. This is not because he did not already have what he might give—since he was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb, and indeed always had Him in himself as his own Spirit—but so that the Divinity might be understood as the author of the gift, which <margin>James 1</margin> *gives to all abundantly and upbraideth not.* 

For if, according to his divinity, he says he has what he has from his Father because he is from Him, how much more according to his humanity was he to be said to have received this or that from the Father? This shows the weakness of our nature which he took from his mother, but without excluding the authority of glory, by which he himself as God can do all things with the Father. For so great is the authority of the Father that the Son is believed to have nothing which he does not have from the Father; yet so great is the equality of the Son that all things which the Father has belong equally to the Son and to the Father. Why then is the Son said to have received the promise from the Father in time, unless so that in...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on Christ's glorification. It explains that although Christ as God already possessed all spiritual gifts, he "received" them as a man to provide a model for human humility and to distribute those gifts to his followers. The previous page ended with a warning against those who seek glory before they have practiced the patience of Christ.</meta>

->### John: Third Part on the Apostle <note>Original: "Joa. Tertia In Apo." Likely referring to a third volume or section of a commentary on the Johannine writings or the Epistles.</note><-

...understands that he remains always in the heavens: that which he deigned to do once on earth for our salvation? And not only that: but also so that mortal man may recognize, by the example of so great a teacher, with what reverence he ought to regard the height of his own honor, lest he should ever fall, being puffed up by the evil of ingratitude; and following him who fell from heaven, he should suffer a similar ruin through pride. What, says the Apostle, <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> do you have that you did not receive? And if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not? For this is what he did who did not stand in the truth: and therefore <margin>John 8</margin> from a good Angel, he was made the Devil and Satan, wishing to obtain by tyranny what he refused to possess with humility. Therefore, just as the only-begotten Son of God did not wish to be baptized for himself, but for us; nor for himself did he see <margin>John 1</margin> the Holy Spirit coming upon him, but for us; nor for himself did he undergo the cross, or rise from the dead, but for us; so he is not said to have received this promise from the Father for himself, but for us, for whom he received it. He did this so that we might know in what order and by what steps we must go from virtue to virtue, receiving the gifts of the Spirit in each stage, until we ourselves, having been lifted up on high, are able to pour out the words of life from him and through him to the disciples of truth, and to bestow spiritual doctrine upon those who love unity. For when any of the faithful are baptized in Christ, they then begin to have that which was signified in the Dove. Indeed, at the beginning of the world, doves, just like other birds, proceeded from the substance of water. Therefore, the Dove—or the water—signifies the simple doctrine that befits the simple and those who are still infants in Christ. This is the doctrine by which those who are little ones in Christ are instructed—not indeed in spiritual words, but according to the truth of the history <note>Historical or literal interpretation of scripture, as opposed to allegorical or spiritual meaning.</note>. But when they begin to be men and fit for spiritual doctrine, according to the mode of that teaching which is called typical or moral, then they begin to have that great gift which was signified in the

<column-break/>

breathing upon by the Lord <margin>John 20</margin> <note>original: "insufflatione"; referring to Jesus breathing on the disciples to give them the Holy Spirit.</note> which was done for the Apostles on the day of Easter. But when, forsaking themselves, they are caught up above themselves to contemplate heavenly things, so that they begin to perceive in the spirit something of the fire of God’s love—and those very things which they are granted to feel, they are permitted to speak worthily to those prepared for it—then, like glowing sparks, they go out from them, by which the hearts of the listeners are set on fire. This happens because it is not they themselves who speak, but the Spirit of Jesus who speaks his own words in them. For it is not you, he says, <margin>Matthew 10</margin> who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. This very thing was proven in the words of Peter, of whom it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: <margin>Acts 10</margin> While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all those who heard his word. This, therefore, is the reason for the mystery: why our Lord Jesus Christ was said to have received the Holy Spirit at certain fixed times, though he always had Him within himself. Inasmuch as he was the <term>Mediator</term> <note>One who acts as a bridge between two parties; here, between God and humanity.</note> between God and men, he, as a man for the sake of men, seemed to ask from God the Father that which he himself, as God, possessed with the same Father before all ages. To speak of something from human experience: if the son of any King had some <term>uterine brothers</term> <note>Brothers shared through the mother but not the father.</note> on his mother's side, who were not related to him on the Father's side, that son could not communicate the father's substance to them without the will and permission of the Father, nor could he make them <term>co-heirs</term> <note>Joint inheritors.</note> in the father’s possession. But if, moved by the piety of his own flesh, he desired to make them his co-heirs, he would ask the Father to grant to him, for his brothers, what he himself possessed by hereditary right. He would count as his own whatever he received for them. Therefore the Son asked for his brothers, and he received what he asked for them: namely, that the Father should grant to him, in the person of his brothers, what he held in himself by hereditary right, counting it (as I have already said) as being given to himself.

<margin>Counting/Reputing</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Christ’s reception of gifts from the Father, specifically addressing the distinction between the eternal and temporal "receiving" of the Holy Spirit. It transitions from the theological nature of this gift to the imagery of the golden censer and the fire of the altar found in the Book of Revelation.</meta>

### John’s Second Volume on the Apocalypse <note>Original: "Joa. Scda In Apo." This likely refers to a commentary by a writer named John (possibly John Gerson or similar) on the Apocalypse, also known as the Book of Revelation.</note>

<margin>ps. 67.</margin> It was said: **"You have received gifts among men."** <note>Psalm 68:18 in modern Bibles. The author is debating whether Christ received these gifts eternally as God or temporally as a man.</note> This may be understood as an eternal reception. However, some do not wish to accept this as a temporal reception, because the Holy Spirit was given, and not a man. Others wish to accept it as temporal because the only-begotten Son of God is both God and man. They do not realize that when the reason for speaking is similar, the manner of speaking should be similar. Therefore, if that first statement refers to an eternal reception, so does this one. If the first is temporal, so is this. However, if both are said regarding a temporal reception—which is more truly believed, since this cannot seem to stand simply regarding the Holy Spirit—let us confess that both were spoken in the way we said above: namely, that we should believe it was said neither for the Son nor for the Spirit, but for those on whose behalf each received it. Or perhaps this refers to the **golden censer**, which the angel is said to have received and filled with the fire of the altar and sent to the earth. Here, too, it is quite properly asked: why does it not say absolutely that he was filled "with fire," but rather "with the fire of the altar"? It is as if the gift of the Holy Spirit belonged to another, and not to him from whom that same Spirit and all good things proceed. But to confess more truly: it belongs both to him who gave it and to him to whom it was given. For truly, the altar to which the fire was given belongs to him who gave the fire; and through this, that which was given belongs to the giver, and that to which it was given becomes the possession of the one from whom it received. The Father gives to the Son, and the **Bridegroom** to the **Bride**; and yet what is given to them remains with the one by whom it is given, because he does not give to strangers, but to his own. Both the thing given and those to whom it was given are in the power of the one who gave. And yet, the Father or the Bridegroom wishes it to be called theirs rather than his own, so that the received gifts may foster the love of the receiver, and all love may burn within the affections of the Giver through the gifts. Therefore, this divine fire which the Son of God sent into the world belongs to the altar in which it is both preserved and kindled. The infusion of the Holy Spirit, which took place under the Old Testament in the patriarchs and prophets, was not emptied out at the coming of the Lord, but increased; not 

<margin>Luc. 12</margin> abolished, but amplified. **"I have come,"** he says, **"to cast fire upon the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?"** <note>Luke 12:49. The "fire" is traditionally interpreted as the Holy Spirit or the fire of Christian charity.</note>

<column-break/>

Rather, this fire is the spiritual words flaming with **charity** <term>charitas</term> <note>Christian love or divine grace.</note>; and for this reason, we read that fiery tongues appeared to the holy apostles. Indeed, this fire not only burns but also 
<margin>Actu. 2 Ro. 5</margin> shines, because the charity of God, which is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us, not only kindles us in the love of God and neighbor, but also illuminates us so that we may know the things that have been given to us by God. These "tongues" were hidden in the altar because the spiritual understandings lay hidden in the hearts and books of the prophets before the coming of the Lord. As we said in the first part of the book, the Lord first opened these to us on the day of Easter, when he opened the sense of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. But if those first utterances of God were entrusted to the faithful number of the righteous, and spiritual words lay hidden within them, it is clear that from the doctrine given to the holy prophets, something was taken and sent into the earth—not according to the "letter that kills," but according to the "spirit that gives life." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, distinguishing between literal and spiritual interpretation.</note> Thus, the Lord took 
<margin>1. cor. 3.</margin> from the spirit of **Moses** and gave it to the elders of Israel, and upon receiving it, they began to prophesy and be made teachers among the people. So too was **Joshua**, son of Nun, 
<margin>Nu. 11. deu. 34</margin> filled with the spirit of wisdom, because Moses laid his hands upon him; just as the spirit of **Elijah** rested upon **Elisha**, and he was made a prophet in Israel. Therefore, when spiritual doctrine was sent into the earth—that is, into human hearts, which are said to be like "good and excellent soil"—there were made thunders, and voices, and lightnings, and an earthquake. For thus it is said in the following:

There were lightnings, because they began to flash with miracles. There was an earthquake, because the hearts of men were moved by this; and seeing so many signs and so many miracles, they were compelled to fear. ### Concerning the first angel sounding the trumpet.

<margin>Chapter 8</margin>

<margin>1 Corinthians 1</margin>
The first of the seven angels was **Paul** with his companions: who was sent (as he himself says) not to baptize, but to evangelize. Just as the holy deacons—who are also called "evangelists" <note>Original: "euangeliste." In the early church, this term often referred specifically to traveling preachers or those who assisted the Apostles.</note> because of the Gospel of Christ—suffered many trials; so the holy doctors <note>Teachers or theologians of the church.</note> endured many injuries for the sake of mystical doctrine. This was due to the Jews who were unwilling to obey that sentence of Paul where it is said: <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> **"The letter kills, but the spirit gives life."** <note>Original: "littera occidit: spiritus autem viuificat." This is a central theme of the author: the conflict between a literal, legalistic reading of the Law and a "spiritual" Christian interpretation.</note> For Stephen was stoned by the Jews because he preached Christ as the Son of God; and Paul was captured

<column-break/>

by those same Jews who accused him (those who were of the "circumcision" <note>A term used to describe Jewish Christians who believed that Gentile converts must still follow the Law of Moses.</note>) not so much because he said Christ was the Son of God, but because he preached to the Jews as well as the Gentiles a departure from the way things were done by **Moses**. Because of this, he seemed burdensome in all things not only to the unbelievers, but even to those who had believed from among the Jews, especially those who were of the sect of the Pharisees. Whoever wishes can read in the Acts of the Apostles, and from the things spoken by the elders, he will recognize the truth. For the Jews could not calmly bear that another sense should be introduced into the letter of the Law and the Prophets; nor could those who had believed in Jesus from among the Jews.

Therefore, when the first angel sounded the trumpet, **"there was hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was cast onto the earth"**: because when the Apostle Paul taught that the Law of Moses was not to be kept according to the letter, but according to the spirit, and showed that spiritual understanding announced more to the Gentiles, there arose the "hail" of hardness, mixed with the "fire" of zeal, and the "gore" <note>Original: "cruore." Often implies the blood of a wound or slaughter, here used to describe the "blood of hatred."</note> of hatred: and it was cast into the heart of the Synagogue <note>In this context, the author uses "Synagogue" to represent the Jewish community or the old religious order that rejected Paul's message.</note>: which, always seeking and loving earthly things, savored only the joys of the earth.

It happened, therefore, that a "third part" as it were of that same Synagogue—composed of those who had already believed—returned to Judaism, thinking themselves to be damned in every way if they deserted the Law. This was similar to what happened to those who were scandalized by the word of the Lord and went back, saying: <margin>John 6</margin> **"This is a hard saying, and who can hear it?"** <note>Original: "Durus est hic sermo: & qs poterit eum audire?" Referring to the disciples who left Jesus after the Bread of Life discourse.</note> Hear what Paul said of this zeal: <margin>Romans 10</margin> **"I bear witness for them,"** (he says) **"that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the law of God."** 

In this way, therefore, the "third part" of the Synagogue—and also some of those who seemed to be "fruitful trees" <note>A reference to the "third part of the trees" being burnt in the Revelation text.</note> and teachers of others among the people, but who became false apostles—and all who were carnally wise fell away entirely; and neglecting the gift of God which they had received in baptism, they lapsed back into Judaism. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the first trumpet of the Apocalypse (Revelation 8:7). Having identified the first angel as the Apostle Paul, the author now interprets the "third part" of the earth and trees that were burned, categorizing different types of believers and their susceptibility to error.</meta>

# John: Third Part on the Apocalypse

It is almost said of the angels: **a third part**: as if it seemed ordained by God that a third part of believers should be led into error. May this be far from the hearts of the faithful. It is not to be understood in that way; rather, it is exactly as the word says it is understood. There are three kinds of the baptized: as if they were **Shem, Ham, and Japheth** <note>The three sons of Noah, used here as allegorical types for different groups within the Church.</note>. These the holy mother Church contains within her womb. The first kind of these is the **wise**; the second is those who think <margin>Matthew 23</margin> they know what they do not know—so that they are called "Rabbi" by men, according to the voice of the Lord, loving the first seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace; the third kind is the **simple**. And indeed, those who have followed the gift of wisdom from God are guarded by Him who sends them. But those who are simple and fear God, walk confidently and securely, for they walk simply in the commands of the Lord, recognizing themselves to be <margin>Job 1</margin> of that number of whom it is said: *The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were feeding beside them.* <note>The author uses this image from Job to represent the simple, hardworking faithful.</note> But those who are in the middle, like **Ham**, while they are ashamed to be seen as ignorant, they do not fear to teach others things they themselves do not know, and to show men (as they think) the way of life, through which they themselves have not known how to enter. And so they are deceived and they deceive: **blind leaders of the blind**, as the Lord says. *If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.* Concerning such proud men, the Lord <margin>Matthew 15</margin> complains through the Prophet, saying: *They ran, and I did not send them.* For they <margin>Jeremiah 23</margin> run and are not sent, whoever—apart from the gift of heavenly grace—do not receive the mystery of doctrine <margin>Philippians 2</margin> but usurp it, seeking the things that are their own, not those of Jesus Christ. Therefore, those who perceive the gift of the Spirit—acting more out of the necessity of the stewardship entrusted to them than from a desire for empty glory—announce the words of life to men; protected by the Spirit of God, they cannot err mortally, or if they do err, they are recalled to the way without delay. For He who grants the gift of glory for the benefit of many, He Himself guards the humble <margin>Romans 11</margin> to whom He bestows His gifts, and He will snatch them from the snares set by the impious along the way. But also the simple, who judge themselves to be 

<column-break/>

what they are, and do not wish at all to "savor high things" <note>A reference to Romans 12:16, "Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate."</note> but to consent to the humble, cannot be eradicated from the solidity of the faith in which they were once founded; for they are taught to believe their elders more—from whom they received the word of faith—than to presume anything by themselves so as to teach others. But those who, lest they seem [ignorant], do not wish to be disciples of the saints, and so that they may seem to be what they are not, impudently presume to teach what they themselves do not know: in as much as they refuse to be students of truth out of shame, they become masters of error out of the fear in their souls. This is therefore the **third part** of men which always and everywhere falls away into error, and being torn from the womb of its mother, while it knows no truths to put forward, it speaks falsehoods. As if, therefore, a **third part of the earth** and a **third part of the trees** was burnt under the first angel. Because many of those who had believed from <term>the circumcision</term> <note>referring to Jewish converts to Christianity</note> erred from the faith, and some who seemed to know something became <term>false apostles</term> <note>original: "pseudoapostoli"</note>. And it should be noted that he does not say "a third part of the green grass," as he says "a third part of the earth" and "a third part of the trees," but **all green grass was burnt**. This is because, while among those who seemed to be spiritual some part fell into error, those who were entirely carnal and believed, all alike went backward with the same ease; for they had believed in the Savior only by following others. For those who do not believe because they understand the word, but because they see others converted who were thought to be of great name among their people—if by chance any of those are moved from their status, all fall alike with them. Just as when a foundation is destroyed, the whole structure collapses unhappily together. Thus, as if a third part of the earth and a third part of the trees were burnt with the **entirety of the green grass** at the touch of fire: because a not-small part of those who seemed to be something ceased to stand in the greenness of faith due to the burning of a false zeal, and the greatest multitude of those who were carnally wise came to a failing, as if they were a species of grass.

# Abbreviated Part of the Exposition

->On the second angel sounding the trumpet.<-

<margin>Chapter 9</margin>
**And the second angel sounded the trumpet.**

This makes a distinction for the second course of time and the second group of teachers. For the teachers of the first time were the Apostles; the teachers of the second time stood alongside the holy martyrs. Just as false apostles went out from the Apostolic Church to attack apostolic liberty—whom Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, resisted along with his helpers—so too from among the seven deacons <note>original: "septem dyaconibus"; referring to the seven men chosen by the Apostles in Acts 6 to serve the early Church.</note> went out the Nicolaitans, who would defile the preaching of the second period with heretical depravity. Therefore, Saint John says:

<margin>Chapter 10</margin>
**The second angel sounded the trumpet: and as it were a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea: and the third part of the sea became blood: and the third part of those creatures died, which had life in the sea; and the third part of the ships was destroyed.**

Just as the Synagogue is signified by the "earth," so the "sea" signifies the Gentile world. I believe this "great mountain" was Nicolaus, one of the first seven deacons, who, being inflamed (as it is said) with the zeal of his own malice, is recorded to have produced such a notorious heresy. Mention was made of this abominable heresy, which is to be detested in every way, regarding the angel of the first church <note>referring to the Church of Ephesus in Revelation 2:6.</note>, where the Lord says: *This you have that is good: that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.* Similarly, regarding the church of Pergamum: *I have a few things against you: because you have there those who hold the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication; so you also have those who hold the doctrine of the Nicolaitans.* "The third part of the sea became blood"—this is understood to be from his doctrine; because a great multitude of men who had some spark of faith from hearing their voice (of whom it is said, *their sound went out into all the earth* <note>original: "in omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum"; a quote from Psalm 19:4, traditionally applied to the spread of the Gospel.</note>, that

<margin>Psalm 18</margin>

<column-break/>

is: those men who had either already begun to believe the truth, or perhaps would have believed if this new treachery, deceived through Nicolaus, had not hindered them) died from the faith of Christ. Thus, though they began with the spirit, they were consumed by the flesh; and following flesh and blood, they utterly lost the kingdom of life. As for what the "third part" signifies, let it suffice that we explained it once regarding the first angel. Truly, because it is told that a third part of the sea became blood, a third part of the creatures in the sea died, and a third part of the ships perished, it indicates that by that carnal doctrine, not only were many believers absorbed, but even several churches perished by the hidden judgment of God.

->On the third angel sounding the trumpet.<-

<margin>Chapter 11</margin>
**And the third angel sounded the trumpet: and a great star fell from heaven, burning as it were a torch: and it fell on the third part of the rivers, and upon the fountains of waters.**

As in the work of concord—since that was the place for a full arrangement—the third succession of teachers, which followed in the third (and, as it were, improper) course of time, is recognized to have begun from the times of the Emperor Constantine. Now, in his days, there was a certain priest of Alexandria named Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336) was a priest whose teachings—Arianism—claimed that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father. This led to the First Council of Nicaea.</note>. Because of the outward respectability of his character which he seemed to maintain in the Church, he was thought by the clergy to be one of the "great lights of heaven." Indeed, he showed the light of his works to men and, by the established example of his life, he provided no small benefit for walking in the way of the Lord. But because he did not have eyes within, but was only raised up outwardly by the arrogance of pride, he desired to be seen as great, ignoring that which is written: *Before a fall, the heart is exalted.*

<margin>Proverbs</margin>

Finally, from pride and license came the appetite for vain glory, and from the appetite for vain glory one goes toward obstinacy and hardness of heart. Furthermore, from hardness of heart is born evil zeal and a fury of indignation against the correctors and teachers of the Church, so that more...

...it may be more pleasing to fall with false and deceitful honor than to stand with shame and modesty, if it should happen that one is surpassed. According to this, it happened to that miserable man <note>The "miserable man" refers to Arius (c. 250–336 AD), whose teachings on the nature of Christ led to the first major schism in the Christian Church.</note> at the correction of the holy man Alexander, the bishop of Alexandria, as he was unwilling to satisfy his teacher and to receive discipline willingly. Finally, inflamed with anger and a zeal of bitterness, vehemently kindled—because he could not bear the injury done to him with equanimity—he hardened his heart upon a stone to defend his error, until there happened to him <margin>Psalm 57 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 58:3-5.</note></margin> and his accomplices that which the Psalmist had predicted of them long ago: *The sinners are alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; and they have been made far off. Their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent, like the deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of the charmers, and of the wizard who is charmed by a wise man.* And it fell (he says) into the third part of the rivers and into the fountains of water: because an innumerable crowd of bishops and priests was infected by that pestiferous error, so that from where the water of wisdom and knowledge used to flow out before (when they were still Catholics), a lethal drink began to go out, which would offer death to those drinking rather than life. For it follows:

<margin>Chapter 12</margin> **And the name of the star is called Wormwood: and the third part of the waters became wormwood: and many men died of the waters because they were made bitter.**

From its very origin, the church has sustained many and fierce heretics; yet none brought it to such bitterness as the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note>; none made the maternal bowels so bitter. For it was not as some others who came into sects only from the outside and not from within, so that as they departed from the womb—that is, from her who had given birth to them in Christ through the sacrament of baptism—they gave the church space for rest; but suddenly within the bosom of the church itself, one who was thought to be a son was found to be a stranger. How much bitterness that caused, those who suffer similar things are truly able to know.

<column-break/>

For what did he say, who wept for those for whom he was in labor again? *Who,* he says, *is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized,* <margin>2 Corinthians 11</margin> *and I am not burned?* Rightly, therefore, it is said: *And the name of the star he called Wormwood*, because wormwood turns sweet waters fit for drinking into bitterness. This is because Arius, unlike Nicolaus <note>Nicolaus was mentioned on the previous page as the founder of the Nicolaitans.</note>, did not gather infidel nations into sects, but rather did so among the Christian people—a people who were of great price, that is, already redeemed by the blood of Christ. As if he were a basilisk <note>original: "Regulus"; literally "little king," a common medieval term for the venomous basilisk serpent, thought to kill with a glance or breath.</note>, he poured out poisons. And it was made (it says) a third part of the waters into wormwood, and many men died of the waters, because they were made bitter. By the name of "waters," the volumes of the Scriptures are designated; then because the Scriptures themselves cannot be read by themselves <margin><gloss>Heretics because</gloss></margin>, nor can they reach the knowledge of men unless there is someone to teach and show them, not absurdly do they understand the "sweet waters" to be the teachers of the church. This is because that too is true which is written in this book: *The many waters are many peoples.* But just as the Apostle calls the law of Moses "Moses," saying: <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> *Whenever Moses is read, a veil is placed before the eyes of the Jews,* so also under the appearance of "teachers," their "doctrines" are also understood. This goes so far that what is said mystically of the teachers is understood of their doctrines, some of which are true and faithful, while others are pestiferous and corrupt—not because the doctrines are simply evil in themselves, but because the men are evil and treacherous who infect them. Arius infected, as it were, a third part of the waters and turned them into the flavor of wormwood when, through his error, the priests and bishops adhering to him were corrupted. This reached the point that from the mouths of those who seemed to be leaders of the people and teachers of the church, there did not go out the water of wisdom and knowledge as was hoped, but rather error; not the sweetness of honey, but the bitterness of wormwood. For what can be sweeter to the human <margin><gloss>it can</gloss> John 3</margin> race than what the Lord says in the Gospel? *God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son?* And that which John says, whose book this is: <margin>1 John 4</margin> *Let us love God, because he first loved us, and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins.*

<summary>This page interprets the third trumpet of Revelation (the star Wormwood) as a prophecy of the Arian heresy. It identifies Arius as the falling star that turned the "waters" of Christian doctrine and its teachers into bitter poison, causing spiritual death within the Church.</summary>

Abbreviated Part of the Exposition

But what can be more bitter than the doctrine of Arius: who preached that our Savior Jesus Christ—who is the hope of all Christians and the life of believers—was not true God just as the Father is, but was like an earthly prince and merely great among the "sons of adoption"? <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, "adopted" by God, rather than being of the same eternal substance as God the Father. This "Adoptionism" was condemned as heresy.</note> If this were true, then surely all Christians and those who believe in him would be cursed, for it is written: *Cursed is the man* <margin>Jeremiah 17</margin> *who trusts in man.* Furthermore, we would hope in vain for that which the Son himself says: *If the Son* <margin>John 8</margin> *sets you free, you will be free indeed.* It would also be in vain what the Apostle says: *God sent the spirit of his Son into our hearts, in which we cry out: Abba, Father.* <note>original: "abba pater". This is an Aramaic and Latin phrase meaning "Father, Father," used to show an intimate relationship with God.</note> For from where do all these things come to us, <margin>Romans 8</margin> unless it is because Christ is the true Son of God—not an adopted one like the others—and that he truly took on our nature, so that having been made one in him and with him, we might be sons and heirs through him: indeed, heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ? If, however, it is <margin>Romans 8</margin> sweet for men to be free and to be heirs of God, it is surely bitter to be servants and strangers to the living and true God—to be deprived of and lacking that most sweet "honey-sweetness" which the elect of Christ suck abundantly from the rock, and that spiritual oil of which the Apostle says: *You have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry out: Abba, Father.* Furthermore, the Arians, feeling contrary to this, taught that only the Father was the true God and true Lord, emptying out the joy of our hope which is in the true Son of God; who, through the taking up of our nature and the gift of the Holy Spirit, absolved us from the reproach of our perdition. Many people, paying attention to them, unhappily received their pestiferous doctrines as if from the elders of the people, so much so that, separated from the sound faith, they formed sects to generally persecute the Church of the Catholics, thinking they could overcome with arms those whom they could not conquer with reason. The persecution by the Arians endured even until the times of the Saracens <note>The author is likely referring to the ongoing religious conflicts in North Africa and Spain, where Arianism persisted among Vandal and Visigothic rulers until they were eventually conquered by Islamic forces (Saracens).</note> so that as some [persecutions] succeeded others, there was never a time when the palm of martyrdom was idle for the Church. Indeed, because of this, we read of many who were afflicted with heavy punishments by Arian kings and bishops, and many who, having lost their temporal life, were crowned with glorious martyrdom.

<column-break/>

### ¶ Of the fourth angel sounding the trumpet.

<margin>Chapter 13 <note>This likely refers to a chapter in the commentary book itself, as the biblical text is Revelation 8:12.</note></margin>
**A**nd the fourth angel sounded his trumpet: and the third part of the sun was struck, and the third part of the moon, and the third part of the stars, so that a third part of them was darkened, and the day did not shine for a third part, and the night likewise.

<margin>In the Book of Harmony</margin>
**I**n the work *The Harmony* <note>Referring to the "Concordia Novi et Veteris Testamenti" (Harmony of the New and Old Testaments) by Joachim of Fiore, a famous 12th-century theologian.</note>—which looks at things by similarity—when that book dealt with the seven original days [of Creation] and reached the fourth day, it was said that the sun, the moon, and the stars signify the hermits and the virgins. These are the ones who, walking through the high paths of contemplation, showed the light of their perfection to the faithful people. For on the fourth day, Almighty God made the sun, the moon, and the stars. Also, in the fourth place in this third part of the book—and in the section on the seven angels pouring out the seven bowls of the wrath of God—mention is made of the sun, the moon, and the stars. However, this is done more solemnly in the fourth part of this Book, where among the other things written there, something more specific and significant is said of these same lights: *A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.* <note>Revelation 12:1.</note> In that woman, the holy church of virgins is specifically designated; for though she took her beginning from the mother of Christ, she is known to have shone forth in the fourth period of the Church. But alas, how swift to do harm is the craftsman of deceit and the master of errors! The higher the rank he sees, the more he exercises the malice of his heart to tempt the godly. For behold, the third part of the sun, the third part of the moon, and the third part of the stars are said to be struck; nor is there any doubt...

# John, Third Part on the Apocalypse
-> R 2 <-

...at the suggestion of that very one who also expelled the first man from Paradise <note>referring to the Devil</note>: but by whom it was struck, or why he struck it, is not expressed. We know that the southern region—which the hermitic and virginal orders inhabited more specifically—was occupied not long after the death of the blessed Pope Gregory: first by the Persian people, and then by the King of the Arabs. For during those same times, that famous heresy of the Saracens <note>original: "Sarracenorum heresis"; the medieval term for Islam</note> erupted upon the earth like a vein of corrupt water. Through it, a multitude of people living in the desert was torn away from the Christian faith by wicked warnings and vice, especially in the region of the Thebaid and Egypt <note>The Thebaid in Egypt was the traditional birthplace of Christian monasticism</note>, where the greatest number of that order lived. This heresy, through the craftiness of diabolical fraud, follows that law (I call it sacrilegious) which Muhammad <note>original: "Mahometh"</note> established. It is contrary to the vow of virgins and those who profess a chaste life because he taught that the highest joy and highest good is sensuality <note>original: "luxuriam"; here meaning carnal or sexual indulgence</note>, promising it even after the end of the world to his followers. The Jew did not have this in his law; the Philosophers of the nations did not pass this on to their listeners; neither did the Sabellian, nor the Arian heretic. But who knows how few virgins could stand firm in their purpose during that pressure? Even if they were prostituted in body, might they at least remain uncorrupted in mind and faith? But because it is not narrated that the whole (God forbid!) but only a third part was struck, it is clear that the just God allowed only those hermits and virgins to be overcome in that hour of their temptation who were laboring under the disease of hypocrisy. They showed one thing in appearance but carried another in their heart. Their detestable offspring was designated in the first part, in the woman Jezebel and her children, as the Lord said regarding her to the angel of the church of Thyatira—which is the fourth in the number of the others: *I have this against you, that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication and eat food sacrificed to idols.* <note>Revelation 2:20</note> Therefore, this third part is said to have been struck; struck

<column-break/>

completely from its clarity. The remaining two parts, however (that is, the prudent and the simple), suffered no harm. It follows:

<margin>E. 14.</margin>
> And I saw and heard the voice of an Eagle flying through the middle of heaven, saying with a great voice: "Woe, woe, woe to the inhabitants of the earth because of the remaining voices of the three Angels who are about to sound their trumpets." <note>Revelation 8:13</note>

If the voice of this Eagle <note>original: "Agle/Aquilae"</note> was heard during the time of this fourth Angel, I believe this Eagle to be the blessed Pope Gregory. He is known to have written so freely and so much about the end of the world and the pressures of the final age; he flew higher than others through the paths of allegories, as if through the arduous ways of heaven. No other is found like him who testified in his works that such calamitous times had drawn near. As for those who raise objections about these matters, we have addressed them in the work on "Concordance" <note>likely referring to the author's *Concordia Novi et Veteris Testamenti* (Harmony of the New and Old Testaments)</note>. For the fact that what he predicted did not happen quickly does not mean it did not happen because he was deceived; rather, God’s mercy tempered the judgment he was going to execute, so that a time of peace might be granted for many days, and he might make the time for gain shorter. Furthermore, one should not look simply at the fact that "woes" <note>original: "ve"</note> are promised to the men who dwell on the earth—that is, those who savor earthly things and follow earthly pursuits—from the voices of the three angels as if it happens by chance. Rather, it is by the truth of judgment: because they refuse to obey the teachers of truth, it is a just and fair judgment that they should fall (by God’s permission) into the operation of error and believe the lie which they loved. But now we must come to the fifth Angel, to whom the first "woe" is ascribed. Let us observe what happened in his time, not without a groan of the heart—especially since in our days all things seem to have been poured out, so much so that even before the first "woe" has been led to its end, we feel other "woes" approaching by evident signs. It follows.
