### Abbot’s Part of the Exposition
<meta>catchword: gie</meta>

...just as he proclaimed the good news through his servants the prophets. For why do you think it is contrary to the truth if so many heralds <note>original: *Precones*</note> precede the arrival of such a great Judge? Do not even the kings of the world, who decide to visit their kingdoms, appoint precursors to prepare the ways for them—one after another—so that all things necessary for their sustenance might be found ready? If a King were to send many messengers, one after the other, to announce the proximity of his arrival, and he were believed by the first and the second, but the rest (who ought to be believed even more) were contradicted by everyone as witnesses of a lie and reproached by many—in this same way, in these final times, the children of this world are unable to hear anything regarding the proximity of that Day. They think that those who believed the Apostles on this matter were deceived, and they guard themselves as if to avoid being similarly misled.

<margin>2 Peter 3</margin>
The Blessed Apostle Peter foresaw this, and just as he himself predicted it would happen, so we see it being fulfilled daily. "In the last days," he says, "scoffers will come in deception, walking according to their own desires <note>original: *consolationes*, likely a variation of *concupiscentias* or desires/comforts</note> and saying: 'Where is the promise or his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation.'" Therefore, this Angel—who was sent, as it were, uniquely to inspire faith—swears an oath so that the unbelieving might be converted to God; if in any way they might wake from the sleep of death upon hearing him, so that that Day does not find them unawares.

<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
And under the sixth seal—which was established at the time of the Babylonian exile—Daniel saw a certain man dressed in linen standing over the waters of the river, raising his right and left hands to heaven and swearing by Him who lives forever that "for a time, times, and half a time" <note>A symbolic period in apocalyptic literature, often interpreted as three and a half years</note> all the mysteries shown to Daniel himself regarding the last days would be fulfilled. In the water of the river over which the man stood, and in the water of the sea upon which the Angel placed his foot, there is one and the same mystery—except that there, through the water of the river, the literal sense <note>original: *littera*</note> of both Testaments is designated; here, on the land, the letter of the Old Testament; on the sea, the letter of the New. And though no mention is made in Daniel regarding a right and left foot, it is said of the man himself who was dressed in linen that he raised his right and left hands to heaven. To raise two hands to heaven, which naturally hang downward, represents the sense of the letter of the two testaments—which often seem to speak of lowly things—being transferred to higher things through a change to spiritual understanding. For these two testaments are like the hands of the Teachers <note>original: *Doctorum*, referring to the Doctors of the Church or authoritative theologians</note>, with which each resists his enemies; so too do the teachers of the Church defend themselves from the enemies of the faith with the protection of the two testaments. Indeed, because that man in the prophet Daniel is said to have raised both his hands to heaven—namely, the right and the left—it signifies that the understanding of spiritual teachers rises up from the literal text of the two testaments and is elevated to higher things.

<column-break/>

For the "inner man" also [raises] his hands—which he exercises concerning the literal text and spiritual intelligence—while he seeks so that he may find, and while he knocks so that it may be opened to him. Indeed, it is while he shows the ways of light to be in heaven, and while he shows the paths of equity to be in the spirit. For he swears for this purpose to those who swear: to demonstrate that he speaks and keeps the truth. Now, full truth is in the spirit; in the literal text <note>original: *littera*</note> it is not full, but partial. Therefore, to swear is, as it were, to make it plain that there is truth—whether it be in the letter of the Old Testament in part, or in the letter of the New Testament more fully, or in the spiritual understanding, in which the fullness of truth is universally contained. Thus, the things which the Angel commemorates—on the land, and in the sea, and in heaven—are designated in the oath. Nor is this different from the trinity <note>original: *trias*</note> found in that land where Elijah built the altar: in the water poured over it, and in the fire sent from heaven.

### Joachim’s Third Book on the Apocalypse

...we are accustomed to call "living water" <note>original: *aquam vivam*</note>; yet it is more like fire than water, for the New Testament is worthier than the Old, and much closer to eternal life. However, spiritual understanding is worthier and more blessed than both. Why then does this Angel place his feet upon the land and the sea, while lifting his hand toward heaven? He appears to be touching the mystery of the Trinity in his own person. He is shown to suggest nothing else to us than that one spirit of understanding proceeds from both testaments. By those things which we see in harmony here below, we may securely and fearlessly search out the heavenly sacraments. Paul attests to this in <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> when he says: "The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." And because the teachers of that time—which (as we have often said) is near—would not boldly introduce anything as if dreaming or divining, but only what can be proven by the mouth of two witnesses (or rather, from the two testaments), this same Angel is said to swear an oath. Truly, he swears who does not doubt what he says, and who brings forth testimony to create faith in his words. For to say "God is my witness" or "Truth is my witness," and similar phrases, is to swear. But why does he who swears in this way make mention of the God of heaven, the earth, the sea, and those things within them? It is because in the three peoples or <term>orders</term> <note>The "three orders" are a central theme in medieval theology: the married/laypeople, the clergy, and the monks.</note>, the testimonies of truth resonate in a wonderful and harmonious way. The first of these is like the earth, the second like the sea, and the third like the heaven or the air. Therefore, he who swears by Him who made all these things swears appropriately, because he swears by the Creator of all. By listing them distinctly—heaven, earth, sea, and all within them—he proves that what he says is true, so that "by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established." Finally, to the order of the <term>married</term> <note>original: *conjugatorum*; referring to the laypeople</note>, whose characteristic belongs to the first state, the land animals are compared. To the <term>clergy</term>, whose characteristic belongs to the second state, the fish of the sea are compared; for just as the life of fish is water, so the life of good clerics is the knowledge of the Holy Scriptures. To the <term>contemplatives</term> <note>monks and mystics</note>, whose characteristic belongs to the third state, the birds of heaven are compared, because they enjoy, as it were, a higher breath and the most healthful air. The Angel therefore swears by Him who

<column-break/>

created these three, and at the same time these three are commemorated in the oath, so that we may know that this triad has been so ordained by the Lord that even if we remain silent, they provide testimony to the truth. And what does he swear? "That time shall be no more," but in the days of the voice of the seventh Angel (understand: the one who is in the first rank), the mystery of God shall be consumed. And how so? "As he proclaimed," he says, "through his servants the Prophets." Since this is the case, and a limit has been given that cannot be passed, why still strike roots in this world and build towers that will fall in the first [age]? Or is it hoped that the time of the seventh age will last longer? But "it is not for us to know" <note>An allusion to Acts 1:7</note>; it is not for this time to investigate. For just as God worked greater things in the brief span of this sixth age than in the five preceding ages of the world, so it is possible even now for many times to be fulfilled in a few days. Just as the time of the sixth age is brief compared to the five preceding it (from the beginning until Christ), so the time of the seventh may be brief compared to the years of the sixth age—yet in its works, nothing shall be unequal, nothing less. Let it be as God has willed, and as He Himself ordained from eternity, He who "works all things in all people according to the counsel of His will." For us, however, it should be enough to despise the world because <margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin> "the figure of this world is passing away." Before we enter into that rest, we must pass through fire and water so that, as if through the pain of the <term>Preparation Day</term> <note>original: *parasceuen*; the day before the Sabbath, specifically Good Friday</note>, those who are worthy may arrive at the Paschal feast. But what is it that he says: "Time shall be no more"? Does it mean that after this word and the Angel's oath, there will be no more time at all? Far from it. But "at the voice of the seventh Angel, when the trumpet begins to sound, the time of the mysteries of God shall be finished," just as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets. How did he proclaim it through his servants the prophets? I omit the others who made mention of the seventh day, but first, regarding this, <unclear>Moses</unclear> <note>original: *effdor les*, likely a corruption of *Moyses*</note> says: "Thus the heavens and the earth were <margin>Genesis 2</margin> finished, and all their array; and God rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. And he blessed the day..."

<summary>The Angel’s oath signifies that the "mystery of God" is reaching its fulfillment across three human orders (lay, clergy, and monks). The text explains that the transition to the final, seventh age of the world is imminent, urging readers to prioritize spiritual readiness over worldly stability.</summary>

### Part of the Exposition

...the seventh day, and He sanctified it: because in it He ceased from all His work, which God created so that He might do it. Behold, in this way time shall cease after the seventh Angel begins to sound the trumpet: not indeed the time of the Sabbath <note>original: *Sabbatum*. Here referring to the eternal rest or a future age of peace.</note> which is to come after the voice of the seventh Angel, but the time of affliction and labor which has been completed generally in the six ages of the world, or in another way, in the six portions of this sixth age. Finally, after this time, a time will come—as the Angel says to <margin>Daniel 12</margin> Daniel—such as has not been from the time when men began to be on the earth. This is surely the time of the seventh Angel, which the Lord will bless, giving in it peace and joy to those who wait for Him. 

In this matter, it should be noted more carefully that the time of the seventh Angel, of which this discourse treats, does not belong to that Sabbath which is the seventh time in relation to the six ages of the world, but to the seventh portion of this <term>second state</term> <note>Joachim of Fiore famously divided history into three "states" (status): the Age of the Father (Old Testament), the Age of the Son (New Testament/Church), and the Age of the Holy Spirit (a future age of spiritual understanding). This "second state" refers to the current era of the Church.</note>, in which the times of the mysteries of God must be consummated. Since we believe that one cannot reach that great rest except through the great labor of the sixth time—just as under the shadow of the former testament, for the sake of the Sabbath rest that followed on every sixth day, month, or year, labor was increased in <term>typology</term> <note>original: *in typo*. A theological method where Old Testament events are seen as "types" or foreshadowing of New Testament realities.</note>—there is no doubt that this applies to those who must still "sow in tears" so that they may "reap in joy." After those things which Saint John had said concerning the oath of the Angel, the following is added:

<margin>Rev. 10:8–10</margin> **And the voice which I heard again speaking with me from heaven, saying: "Go and take the open book from the hand of the Angel standing upon the sea and upon the land." And I went to the Angel, saying to him that he should give me the book. And he said to me: "Take and devour it; and it will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the book from the hand of the Angel and devoured it. And it was in my mouth sweet as honey. And when I had devoured it, my belly was made bitter.**

<column-break/>

That <term>order</term> <note>Joachim uses "order" (ordo) to refer to specific groups of people, often monks or spiritual leaders, who fulfill prophetic roles in history.</note> which is signified by John is about to hear the voice from heaven saying to it: "Go and take the book from the hand of the Angel standing upon the land and upon the sea." For if there were no other voice in Holy Scripture that commanded this very thing, this voice itself which descended from the great heaven (that is, from this book of the Apocalypse) would suffice, as would that which says this very thing in the prophet <margin>Ezekiel 3</margin> Ezekiel. Moreover, that "order" itself will go to the Angel when, having recognized the truth of God, it will reverently assist the messengers of truth. 

It will take the open book from the hand of the Angel and "devour" it when it perceives through faith that which those messengers spiritually perceive and explain. It will preserve this in the "belly of memory," according to what is written of the Mother of the Lord in a similar mystery: <margin>Luke 2</margin> "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Now the mouth and the belly often feel things contrary to one another, so much so that sometimes what delights the mouth in eating, the belly retains with pain and twisting. That the words of the Lord are sweet to those who love Him, the <margin>Psalm 118</margin> Psalmist indicates when he says: "How sweet are Your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" 

But if they are sweet in the mouth, why are some of them so bitter in the belly? For it cannot be said of all His words that they are both sweet in the mouth and bitter in the belly, but of certain ones—that is, those words which pertain to labor and the bitterness of passion. For these are bitter in the belly, yet sweet in the end; because although there is delight in the knowledge of truth, there is nonetheless groaning and affliction of spirit in the experience of labor. Therefore, if that which occurs first because of the opening of the book delights, it is nonetheless bitter... <meta>Catchword: [pro]pter (because/on account of)</meta>

# John, Third [Book] on the Apocalypse

What follows is very important because of the suffering [passion] of the church. It should not be thought that the <term>contemplative</term> <note>original: *premplantiu*, likely a transcription error for *contemplativam*. <margin>John 8</margin>

<margin>John 15</margin>

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
Ezekiel. But the order itself will go to the Angel when, having recognized the truth of God, it reverently assists the messengers of truth. Indeed, he will receive the open book from the hand of the Angel and devour it when he perceives by faith that which they [the messengers] spiritually perceive and, in perceiving, explain; he shall preserve it in the "belly" of his memory, according to what is written of the Mother of the Lord in a similar mystery:

<margin>Luke</margin>
"But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Now, the mouth and the belly often feel contrary things, so much so that sometimes what delights the mouth in eating, the belly retains with pain and twisting. That the words of the Lord are sweet to those who love him, 

<margin>Psalm 119</margin>
the Psalmist indicates when he says: "How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey to my mouth!" <note>Original: *super mel ori meo*.</note> But if they are sweet in the mouth, why are some of them so bitter in the belly? For it cannot be said of all his words that they are sweet in the mouth and bitter in the belly, but of certain ones—that is, those words which pertain to labor and the bitterness of suffering [the Passion]. For these are bitter in the belly, even if they are pleasant in the mouth; because even if there is delight in the knowledge of truth, there is nonetheless groaning and affliction of spirit in the experience of labor. Therefore, although that which occurs first because of the opening of the book delights, it is nevertheless bitter...

### John: Third Part on the Apocalypse

The Greek clergy, along with its children, will be cast out: because it has been given over to the nations. This is because it is not constrained under the measure of the reed and the discipline of the Pastor <note>Referring to the authority of the Pope in Rome</note>, so that all people might learn to be subject to God and obey him in all things whom He himself has commanded. For because they abandoned the Temple of God—which was founded in Rome upon living stones—from which all peoples ought to receive the truth of pure and orthodox doctrine, and not leavened bread <note>original: "panem fermentatum." A reference to the "Azymite" controversy; the Greek Church used leavened bread for the Eucharist, while the Latin Church used unleavened bread</note>, they chose instead to be in the outer court. This court the bishops constructed for themselves in Constantinople, outside the perimeter of the temple. They chose to have those whom they themselves selected as Kings and as the pastors of their souls. We already see that they have been largely given over to the nations, and that they are to be given over to even worse fates. This is made clear by that prophecy which I just mentioned above regarding the type <note>A "type" is a biblical person or event that foreshadows a future reality</note> of the ten Tribes of Israel, when it is said:

<margin>Isaiah 8</margin>
"Because this people has rejected the waters of Shiloah that flow in silence, and has instead taken up Rezin and the son of Remaliah; therefore, behold, the Lord will bring up against them the waters of the River, strong and many: the King of the Assyrians and all his glory. And he shall rise over all its channels and flow over all its banks." This was spoken according to the literal letter concerning the people of Israel, who were to be delivered into the hands of the Assyrians for their sins. Yet, it stands as a figure for those things which many Greek churches have suffered and continue to suffer even now. For just as the Assyrians devastated those tribes, so have the Arabs—who are also called Saracens—devastated many of their churches. And because the Tribe of Judah at that time—or the Latin Church in this time—does not fear to add sin to sin and to commit its own crimes, it is said here of the nations to whom the court outside the temple was given: "they shall trample the Holy City for forty-two months." And in that same place, something similar and no less terrifying is added under the same mystery.

<margin>Isaiah 8</margin>
And what is that? "And it shall go," he says, "running through Judah and passing through until it comes to the neck. And the stretching out of its wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Emmanuel." This shall come to pass in the days of that eleventh King

<column-break/>

who is written about in the prophet Daniel <margin>Daniel 12</margin>: he who is to reign for a time, and times, and half a time <note>A traditional prophetic period of three and a half years, often associated with the reign of the Antichrist</note>. Therefore, both the church of the Greeks is to be given to the nations for its sins, and the Latin church is to be trampled by the nations for forty-two months. Mark what he says: "Measure the temple of God," and immediately he added, "and those who worship in it." Even the remnants of the Greeks who flee to the Roman church are undoubtedly to be included in the number of those worshipping, according to what was said by the Lord to Elijah: <margin>1 Kings 19</margin> "I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed their knees before Baal." However, how the remnants of the Greeks ought to follow the Latins in the knowledge of the truth—and how some of them may even pass into the meaning of those designated in John—can be shown even through mystical words. Indeed, the same John says in his Gospel <margin>John 20</margin> that Mary Magdalene went to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and found that the body of Jesus had been taken away. She went and reported this to Peter and to that disciple whom Jesus loved—namely, to John himself, the disciple who also wrote these things. At her word, they both began to run together, namely Peter and John, to come to the tomb. And so it happened: John ran ahead more quickly and arrived first at the tomb, yet he did not enter. Peter followed him and entered first; thus the first became last, and the last became first. All these things and those that follow are read every year during the week of Easter. But many listen to them externally, failing to attend to what they contain within. Because the time approaches for the mysteries of these things to be fulfilled, they are perhaps more usefully opened now—if any were not open until the present—lest perhaps the farmer think that the thorny fields ought to be despised, from which the Lord expects fruit in his own time. Therefore, if we are free to apply these words of the Gospel to the significance of Peter and John alone, setting aside the mystery of Mary Magdalene, we can understand the people of the Jews in John—who arrived first but entered the tomb later—for they were the first to receive the Old Testament...

# Abb. Part of the Exposition

...the law of the gentiles: and yet, one is not permitted to enter into its internal understanding until the end of the world. However, if three people are brought together as one—namely Peter, John, and Mary Magdalene (as the Gospel reading seems to suggest)—then Mary Magdalene, who came to the tomb in the morning while it was still dark, represents the **Synagogue of the Jews**. She arrived first at the knowledge of the first testament <note>The Old Testament</note> while the darkness of ignorance was still upon the world. This Synagogue, through its chosen branches, eventually recognized that Christ was the Son of God. She saw that He was rejected by His own people but honored and chosen by the Gentiles. By looking more closely into the "tomb" of the Holy Scriptures, she realized that the literal text was empty once the truth—which resides in the spiritual understanding—had been taken from it. Thus, one of them aptly says: *The letter kills, but the spirit gives life* <note>original: "Littera occidit: spiritus autem viuificat" — 2 Corinthians 3:6</note>.

<margin>2 Corinthians 3; Romans 9</margin> *For not all who are of Israel are Israelites; nor are they all children because they are the seed of Abraham; but "In Isaac your seed shall be called."* <note>Romans 9:6-7</note> This means it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise who are counted as the seed. The Apostle Paul said these and similar things along with the other believers from the "circumcision" <note>Jewish converts to Christianity</note>. He showed through many arguments that the "tomb of the letter" was empty in itself, and that the truth of spiritual understanding—which the Jews had killed and buried as if in a pit in the ground to establish a fleshly understanding and a law of the flesh—had been raised from that very letter and transferred to the spiritual sons. By God's will, it happened that through the preaching of that Church of the circumcision, the Gentiles who were predestined for life heard with the ears of their hearts. They ran eagerly toward the knowledge of the first testament to recognize the great thing that God had revealed as truth. Indeed, it is clear that no mention is made of Mary Magdalene after the coming of the Holy Spirit, and that Peter was sent specifically to the **Latin people**, and John to the **Greeks**. Thus, one received his burial in Rome and the other in Ephesus. Therefore, just as Mary represents the Synagogue of the Jews, Peter represents the Latin people and John the Greek people. These two heard the news gladly and ran swiftly together to the tomb. John, however, ran faster and reached it first, yet he did not enter. This is because the Greek ran faster to learn the surface of the letter of the first testament, yet he has not reached its internal understanding even until our own times. If he had reached it, he would certainly have joined himself completely to the Latin people (who have already entered with Peter); indeed, he would be with us in truth, as **one fold and one Shepherd**. To set other matters aside, why was the Jewish people chosen first to worship the one God, followed by these two others near the end of the ages? Is it not because there is one person of the Trinity who is from no one and sends no one <note>God the Father</note>, while there are two who are from the One and are sent by the One?

<margin>Ephesians</margin> If the Jewish people, who were chosen in the patriarchs, carry the "type" <note>A prophetic symbol or pattern</note> of that Person from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named <note>The Father</note>, then of which Person do we say the **Latins** carry the type? To whom was the Vicar of Christ given, if not to the Son himself? It is the Son who is said to have met Peter himself and said, *"I am coming to Rome to be crucified again,"* <note>A reference to the "Quo Vadis" legend regarding St. Peter's martyrdom</note> and who gave to Peter the universal power of binding and loosing over all who are called by the Christian name. Truly, the fact that Blessed John was given to the **Greek people**—from whom the religious life of the perfect Monks began—carries the type of that **Spirit** who seeks and loves spiritual sons: those who walk according to the Spirit and hate the luxury of the world and the lusts of the flesh. If this is so, why is it that the Greeks have not yet been able to believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son? <note>The "Filioque" controversy: the Western Church teaches the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son; the Eastern Church historically teaches the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son</note>. It is because they humbly accepted doctrine from the Jewish people (who carry the mystery of God the Father), but they now scorn to humbly receive it from the Latins (who in this regard bear the likeness of the Son). Just as the same Spirit is said to "receive from the Son" what he announces, so should the Greek people, who once received doctrine from the Hebrew, receive it in the same way...

### John, Part Three: On the Apocalypse

...similarly from the Latin? This is plainly a mystery: if the Greeks had understood it, they would have already entered the tomb with us <note>The "tomb" here represents the deep, spiritual understanding of the Holy Scriptures</note>, knowing that God is not a God of dissension, but of peace. But because John <note>John here represents a specific type of spiritual contemplative</note> did not yet know the scripture—that it was necessary for Christ to rise from the dead—it is no wonder if the Greeks still do not know that the letter is dead where the spirit lives. And they will worship at the altar that was founded in Rome; then the hand of the Lord will be with them. 

Next, Mary Magdalene, who stands outside, represents the **Synagogue**—that is, those who follow external things. She will bow down from her prideful arrogance and look into the tomb; there she will see two angels, which signify the harmony of the fathers of the two testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments</note>. She will understand the voice of those rebuking her, as if they were saying: "Woman, what do you seek? Why do you <margin>John 20</margin> weep?" For she is surely a woman, and not a man, who seeks the Spirit in a tomb—who weeps among the dead for Him who lives forever. 

Mary also sees the Lord and hears Him saying this very thing to her, yet she thinks He is the **Gardener**. This is because when the Synagogue begins to understand the truth with the eyes of her heart opened, she will indeed see it, but she will not recognize it; her eyes will still be held shut, oppressed by the mist of her own unbelief. It was the same for those two who spoke with Him on the road <note>The disciples on the road to Emmaus</note>; their eyes were held so that they did not recognize whom they saw, even though their hearts burned within them. 

But to make what is being said clearer, three types of people should be noted in this regard: 
1. Others who neither see nor recognize. 
2. Others who see but do not recognize. 
3. Others who see and recognize. 

Those who neither see nor recognize are those who in no way perceive the truth that the spirit is life-giving; that is, they neither perceive the truth in what they read, nor do they know how to attribute what was written to its proper subject. Those who see but do not recognize are those who indeed perceive a spiritual 

<column-break/>

understanding, yet they do not yet perceive to whom it should be attributed. But those who see and recognize are those who both perceive the spiritual understanding and foresee what should be attributed to whom. 

Therefore, when Mary neither saw the Lord nor recognized Him, it refers to the time of the Jews' total blindness. When she saw Him but did not recognize Him, it refers to the—so to speak—penultimate time. They will indeed perceive a spiritual understanding, but they will not understand whether they ought to walk according to it and believe in it from then on. 

When she saw Him and recognized Him, she called Him "Rabbi" <note>original: "Rabbi" — Teacher</note>. This refers to the time of their conversion when, the veil having been lifted from their eyes, they will understand that the true mastery is in the spirit. They will recognize what the Apostle meant when he said: *The letter kills, but the spirit <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> gives life* <note>original: "Littera occidit: spiritus autem viuificat"</note>. 

So, while Mary thinks the one she sees is the Gardener, she asks him if he is the one who took away the Lord she lost. Through the things she reads as fulfilled in Christ, the Synagogue cannot deny that the Lord Jesus was some great man; yet she does not believe Him to be the Christ <note>The Messiah</note>. Instead, she views Him as one of the <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> Prophets—like one of those sent to "plant and water," but not as God Himself who "gives the increase." 

And because the entire multitude of the faithful testifies that He is the Messiah whom the Jews expect, the Synagogue—acting with a certain womanly emotion—interpellates and complains to the Spirit (whom she sees but does not yet recognize) as if He were the one who took away the name of the Messiah. "Lord," <margin>John 20</margin> she says, "if you have carried Him away, tell me, and I will take Him away." For just as Mary thinks the one she takes for a Gardener has taken away her Lord, by that time the Synagogue will have turned away from her prideful arrogance to such an extent that, while she may not yet believe the Lord Jesus is the Messiah, she will consider Him such a great Prophet that she believes the truth has been hidden from her as a punishment for despising Him. And so, to show her the Lord reigning as the Gardener...

It categorizes three levels of spiritual perception and explains why the Jews (and Greeks) historically struggled to see the "spirit" behind the "letter" of scripture.</summary>

# Abbot’s Part: Exposition

...Does Mary, in asking for the truth to be shown to her, represent the **Synagogue**? <note>In medieval exegesis, the "Synagogue" refers to the Jewish people or their religious establishment, often personified as a woman in contrast to the "Church."</note> Indeed she does, when she does not yet believe him to be the Truth itself, but regards him as if he were merely a great and singular herald of the truth. This applies to the **Clergy** up to that time. However, when she is called by her own name, "Mary," she recognizes the Lord and calls him "Master." For when the Lord inspires the affection of his grace into the Synagogue—which is symbolized by knowing her by name—they immediately turn to the universal Master. With the veil removed from their eyes, <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:14-16, suggesting that a "veil" covers the hearts of those who read the Old Testament without Christ.</note> she instantly recognizes her Savior. I say she recognizes the Savior because she recognizes the truth, yet not yet as it truly is, but as the Jews think it to be: namely, that the Savior is a mere man and an adopted son of God. 

This is why, after this recognition, she is forbidden to touch the Lord’s feet until he goes to the disciples and professes that he is ascending to his Father. For the Synagogue is by no means admitted to the fellowship of Christ by merely believing him to be the "Son of David" <note>A messianic title focusing on earthly kingship</note>; she must profess him to be the true Son of God, the Blessed One who comes in the name of the Lord. <margin>Psalm 118; Matthew 23</margin> Mary did this literally, just as the Lord commanded. The Synagogue, once turned to the Lord, will also do this in spirit. Therefore, the remnant of the **Greeks**, having recognized the truth which is in the spirit, will be converted to the unity of the Church. And the remnant of the **Jews** will likewise be converted to the Lord, according to what is written in the Gospel concerning the two blind men who serve as a "type" <term>type: a person or event in the Bible that foreshadows a future reality</term> for both peoples. As they—that is, Christ and his disciples—were leaving Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting by <margin>Matthew 20</margin> the road heard that Jesus was passing by, and they cried out, saying: "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!" And Jesus stood still (it says) and called them, saying: "What do you want me to do for you?" They said to him: "Lord, let our eyes be opened." Jesus, having compassion on them, touched their eyes; and immediately they saw perfectly and followed him. This is Matthew’s account. Luke, however, narrates that <margin>Luke 18</margin> there was not two, but only one blind man, adding something about **Zacchaeus**, who was himself blind in his mind—not indeed after the Lord entered Jericho, but before he arrived there. But what of this? Do we say the 

<column-break/>

**Evangelists** disagreed? Or do we think, as the Jews blasphemously claim, that they were deceived? Far from it! Rather, He who knows all things before they happen wished to perform certain acts that were similar in some respects yet different in others. This was so that men might learn that the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> Yet the meaning was not the same for both accounts, because spiritual understanding presented each according to a different perspective. Furthermore, what was written by Matthew was omitted by Luke, and vice versa. For if both had written the same thing, it might be assumed in the spirit that this refers not to two, but to four peoples. But since it must be understood as referring to two peoples—that is, the **Greek** and the **Hebrew**—Luke writes what will happen to these same peoples in part before the **Antichrist** is revealed. Matthew, however, writes what will happen generally after the Antichrist's ruin, when Christ Jesus shall have abolished every <margin>Through man</margin> sovereignty and power, with all his enemies subjected under his feet. For he must reign <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> until he subjects to himself the Jews and many others who have hitherto blasphemed his name, so that they may say together with us: "Blessed <margin>Matthew 21</margin> is he who comes in the name of the Lord." 

Indeed, Jesus went out and walked through Jericho. <margin>Luke 19</margin> This means the word of truth went out from the Church and passed through so that it might reach the Synagogue of the Jews. For the name **Jericho** is interpreted as "The Moon." <note>original: "Luna"</note> The Synagogue of the Jews is like the Moon because of the knowledge of the Law which once shone within her, and because just as the moon suffers monthly cycles, so has the Synagogue suffered her own changes. The blind man sitting by the road begging represents the Greek people. Though they do not have eyes fit for spiritual understanding, they possess this much good: they stand by "the Way" <note>The "Way" is a common early Christian term for the faith itself</note> by professing Christ, seeking the truth, and crying out: "**Kyrie eleison**." <note>original: "Kyrieleyson." This is Greek for "Lord, have mercy."</note> Which is to say: "Lord, have mercy." Many of the **Latins**, however, rebuke them and tell them to be silent, for they despise them because of the blindness of their hearts, not knowing that where sin abounds, grace often superabounds. <margin>Romans 5</margin> But it shall soon come to pass that they see the truth which is in the spirit, and the truth shall set them free from the blindness of their hearts, and make them follow Him, so that they may arrive at Jericho together with Him.

### Third Part of Joachim on the Apocalypse

This mystery, however, will be completed within a portion of the Greek people <note>The author is likely referring to the Eastern Orthodox Christians and their eventual reconciliation with the Roman Church</note> before the Jewish people are converted to God. For as soon as a part of the Greeks perceives the truth, that portion of the Jews symbolized by **Zacchaeus** will also receive the same truth in the "lodging of their heart" and will be subject to Him according to His will. For he shall descend quickly from the sycamore-fig tree <note>original: "ficcomori"</note>. He will immediately leave behind the carnal works of the Law <note>The "carnal works" refer to the literal, ritualistic observance of the Old Testament Law without spiritual interpretation</note> which, for the most part, do not manifest the truth but only point to it from afar; he does this so that, having been humbled, he may take hold of the grace which he does not deserve to have through his own works. This is according to the Gospel of **Luke**.

As for what is handed down according to **Matthew**—the two blind men given sight by Christ after He departed from **Jericho** with His disciples—this refers to the fullness of the Greeks and the Hebrews. To this fullness the generation of spiritual understanding will finally arrive, having departed from the "Synagogue of the Jews" (that is, from that tribe which is called **Judah**, from which Christ was also born according to the flesh). This tribe once remained alone with the **House of David** when the ten tribes, which were specifically called **Israel**, were separated from it. For since it is established that those ten tribes were translated to the East, while this one alone was called Judah—captured by the Roman army and sent to the western parts of the world—

<margin>Concerning the tribe of Judah first.</margin>

when the divine word arrives there, so that having finally departed from it, it may reach the furthest ends of the earth. In this present passage, we believe it necessary to link these things concerning the Greeks and the Jews, so that we may understand that the decree concerning the "court which is outside the temple" <note>Referring to Revelation 11:2</note> was given according to a specific time and a specific part; however, those who flee to the bosom of Mother Church are reckoned among those who "worship in the temple." 

As for that command given specifically to the **Order** designated by **John** to "measure the temple of God and the altar," it seems this refers to the beginning of that very order. Namely, that order is to be found within the **Latin Church**, so that each may bear fruit among that people who are now reckoned to be in the "outer court," and who, in many mysteries, are designated by this same John.

<column-break/>

For it was not without mystical cause that the **Blessed John**, having been tried at Rome, was cast into a vat of boiling oil, and yet, coming out of it alive, was returned to **Ephesus** from whence he had been brought. I believe this was done for no other reason than that we should understand that the **Monastic Order**—which John designates—passed from the Greeks to the Latins. Yet, while staying with them for some time, this order will be "baptized by the Holy Spirit" so that it may live in Christ, and it shall return to that people from whom it came to us, remaining among that same people until the end.

The **reed** <note>original: "calamus," meaning both a measuring rod and a writing pen</note> which was given to John signifies a learned tongue, as the **Psalmist** says:

<margin>Psalm 44</margin>

*My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly.* <note>Psalm 45:1 in modern Bibles; Joachim uses the Vulgate numbering Psalm 44</note>

Indeed, this "reed" is said to be very much like a **rod** <note>original: "virge"</note>; for just as untamed beasts are restrained by the harshness of a rod, so the hard hearts of men are corrected by the discipline of the tongue. Let the temple, the altar, and those worshiping in it be measured; but the court which is outside the temple shall be cast out. This is because those who refuse to be the temple of God and the altar—which pertains to those who strive to enter through the **narrow way**

<margin>Luke 13</margin>

that leads to life—or at least to be among the number of those who humbly worship within it, even if they seem to adhere to the Catholic Church through faith (as if they were the "outer court" to the temple), they nevertheless belong to the examination of the strict judgment. They are to be cast out so that those who remain of them may learn, with a humbled heart, to love **unity**, and to learn that there can be no salvation where there is jealousy and contempt. For the Lord did not say to **Peter**: "Upon this rock I will build my *churches*," 

<margin>Matthew 16</margin>

but "my *church*." Nor did He say, "Feed this flock or that flock," but it was said to him generally: "Feed my sheep." Therefore, those who voluntarily depart from the unity of the Church are—by the just judgment of Almighty God—either given over or to be given over to the gentiles, so that in their remnants

<margin>Isaiah 20</margin>

the Lord may prepare their faces. Just as it was said to **Elijah** (as we have already mentioned) regarding the archetype of these same Greeks: 

<margin>3 Kings 19</margin>

*I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed their knees before Baal.* <note>3 Kings 19:18 in the Vulgate, 1 Kings 19:18 in modern Bibles</note> And these things are indeed said concerning the Church of the Greeks, which, in receding from the structure of the temple...

### Abbot's Part of the Exposition

...in which Christ dwells: it was turned into a courtyard through the schism: walking in the sins <margin>1 Kings 12</margin> of **Jeroboam** the son of **Nebat**, who made **Israel** to sin, and persevering even unto the present in its own inventions. Nevertheless, because **Jerusalem** itself (on account of the sacred mysteries once performed within it) was called the holy city, yet was not immune from crimes, it could not be entirely exempt from the "cup of the Lord's fury" <note>The "cup of fury" is a common biblical metaphor for divine judgment; see Jeremiah 25:15</note>; but it was delivered, and even it was given to the nations to be trampled by them for a time, according to what was said in its own type, and here also terribly said concerning the **Latin Church**: *And they shall trample the holy city for forty-two months* <note>original: "Et ciuitatem sanctam calcabunt mensibus quadraginta duobus"; this refers to Revelation 11:2</note>. This is also suggested in the book of **Psalms**, when it is said: *They divided my garments among them, and for my vesture they cast lots* <note>Psalm 22:18 (Psalm 21 in the Vulgate)</note>. Truly, the "garments" of the Lord are said to be the four patriarchal churches <note>The four ancient seats of Christian authority: Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem</note>. But that one "vesture," of which it was singularly said, *And for my vesture they cast lots*, is the **Roman Church** itself. Although the heretics were not permitted to tear it into parts, it is known that they have often pressed on so as to possess it as an inheritance. This is also well shown to have been fulfilled in the passion of the Lord, to designate that which we have just brought forward, where it is said: *The soldiers therefore, when they had crucified him, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat. Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout. They said therefore among themselves: Let us not cut it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be.* <note>John 19:23-24</note> And this indeed (as I have already said according to the letter) was fulfilled in the passion of **Christ**; yet it is to be mystically fulfilled in the passion of His body, which is the Church. Four of these churches (as is clear from the end) have already been reckoned into the "outer courtyard." But the fifth, which is the **Latin Church**, in which are the temple and the altar, is reckoned into the "holy city," which nonetheless shall itself be trampled by the nations for forty-two months, just as is said through **Luke** in the Gospel: *And Jerusalem shall be trodden down by <margin>Latin Church. Luke 21, Psalm 21, Roman Church. John 19, Luke 21</margin>*

<column-break/>

*the nations, until the times of the nations be fulfilled* <note>original: "Et Hierusalem calcabitur a gentibus: donec compleantur tempora nationum"; Luke 21:24</note>. Indeed, the **Latin Church** is to be understood in **Jerusalem**, just as the **Church of the Greeks** is understood in **Samaria**. And because, as the prophet **Ezekiel** reproaches them, both have sinned against the Lord their God, it was just that both be given into the hands of the nations, though in a dissimilar manner. For one, because of the weight of its faults, was delivered to perpetual oblivion. The other, though chastised, was not put to death, as if having obtained mercy. And that one (that is) the **Church of the Greeks**, it is announced, will be given to the nations in the type of the courtyard which is outside the temple, without any fixed boundary. But this one [the Latin Church], which as far as faith is concerned is a holy virgin, is said not to be given to the nations (God forbid!), but to be trampled by them for forty-two months. This is to say, according to **Luke**: *Until the times of the nations are fulfilled*. This is the time of that "eleventh king" who is written of in **Daniel**, under whom I think another king also shall reign, who is written of immediately in the following vision, concerning whom it is written among other things: *A king of bold countenance and understanding dark sentences shall rise, and his power shall be strengthened, but not by his own force; and he shall lay waste all things beyond belief* <note>original: "Surget rex impudens facie... vniuersa vastabit"; referring to the "Little Horn" or Antichrist figure in Daniel 8:23-24</note>. Now I judge these two to be contemporaries and equally in agreement in the persecution of the just, just as **Pilate** and **Herod** (who although they were previously enemies to one another) were made friends, and came together for the death of **Christ**. So, I say, the nations and the **false prophets** shall come together as one, with their two Kings: one of whom, who shall be of the nations, was designated in **Pilate**. The other, who shall be of the heretics, in **Herod**, who both killed **John the Baptist** with the sword and did not rescue **Christ** when He was sent to him, but mocked Him. It follows: <margin>Latin and Greek Church. Ezekiel 23, Luke 21, Daniel 8, Two kings.</margin>

### Third Part on the Apocalypse
->T 2<-

...twelve hundred and sixty [days]: clothed in sackcloth. These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing in the sight of the Lord of the earth. And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire shall come out of their mouth and devour their enemies. And if anyone wishes to injure them, in this manner must he be killed. These have the power to shut the heavens so that it does not rain during the days of their prophecy; and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague as often as they wish. <note>These verses (Revelation 11:3-6) describe the miraculous powers of the "Two Witnesses" who preach before the end of the age.</note>

Concerning these two witnesses, many people have said many things, and different people have said different things. And because some of them were men of great authority, and what they wrote concerning these same witnesses has already spread through almost the entire world and is read very often in the church of the saints, it seems good to me at least to bring the opinions of the most renowned Fathers into the open. I do this lest, if we say anything in so solemn a matter against the opinion of our elders, we might seem to be "wise in our own conceits." <note>original: "prudentes esse coram nobismetipsis"; a reference to Romans 12:16, warning against intellectual pride.</note> Nevertheless, it does not seem entirely forbidden for a junior to show his own opinion where various people say various things. For even **Paul**, the last of the apostles, not only taught the faithful <margin>Galatians 2</margin> things that others were not teaching, but even dared to say that **Peter**, the first of the apostles, <margin>Jerome</margin> had not walked rightly according to the truth of the Gospel. When Saint **Jerome** was asked about **Enoch** and **Elijah**, he was questioned by the inquirer as if **John** had openly written their names in the Book of Revelation, even though **John** himself did not write this. Whether it was that first person who questioned **Jerome** about them, or someone else, the idea was so turned

<column-break/>

into common use that the opinion passed not only into the understanding of the common folk, but even into the solemn authority of the Great Fathers, by whose doctrine the Church is enlightened even to this day. Regarding the assertion of this matter, I wonder greatly: does this happen because of some hidden mystery, or solely because of a presumption based on the fact that these two men are reported to be still alive? <note>According to biblical tradition, Enoch was "taken" by God (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah was carried to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11), leading to the belief that they never died and would return.</note> I do not know. One thing I say: it can be proved neither by spiritual nor historical understanding that those whom **John** writes about are **Enoch** and **Elijah**. This is especially true since the words that seem to create some presumption on that part do not seem to touch upon **Enoch** and **Elijah**, but rather **Moses** and **Elijah**. These two appeared together (with the Lord mediating and three apostles watching) on the mountain, when a cloud slipped down from heaven and the Father's voice was heard saying: *This is my beloved Son; listen to Him.* <note>This refers to the Transfiguration (Matthew 17), where Moses and Elijah appeared with Jesus.</note> But if one of them whom the text of the reading seems to touch upon—that is, **Moses**—is recorded to have died, then either an understanding other than the historical one must be sought, or we seem to fall into most difficult and unsolvable questions. Although **Jerome** did not contradict the one who questioned him as to whether **Enoch** and **Elijah** were to die according to the Apocalypse of **John**, he nevertheless asserted that it should be understood in the spirit rather than according to the letter, saying: "Concerning **Enoch** and **Elijah**, whom the Apocalypse reports will come and will die, this is not the time for discussion; for that entire book must either be understood spiritually, as we estimate, or if we follow a carnal <note>In this context, "carnal" means a literal or physical interpretation as opposed to a symbolic or mystical one.</note> interpretation, we must acquiesce to Jewish fables: such as that **Jerusalem** should be built again, and sacrifices offered in the Temple, and that, the spiritual worship having been changed, carnal ceremonies should prevail." Therefore, according to **Jerome**, what is seen to be said here concerning **Elijah** and his companion is not to be understood carnally according to the letter, but spiritually. But if spiritually and not carnally, then in such a way...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly investigation into the "Two Witnesses" of Revelation 11. Having established that these figures possess miraculous powers over the weather and the elements, the author now addresses the historical and theological debate over their identities—specifically whether they are Elijah and Enoch (as tradition holds) or Elijah and Moses (as the textual evidence of their miracles suggests).</meta>

### Part of the Exposition
->T 2<-

<margin>Matthew 17</margin>
Where John came in the spirit and power of Elijah: <note>referring to John the Baptist as a precursor</note> two others are to come; or, in them, two spiritual orders are to be understood who will fight with the beast that will ascend from the abyss. So that one of these may be understood as Elijah according to the letter—both the words which seem to have spread from his history and the promise of the Lord saying, "Elijah indeed is coming and will restore all things" <note>original: "Helyas qdem venturus est: & restituet oia"</note>—creates a great

<margin>1 Kings 17</margin>
presumption. If indeed for three years and six months the prophet Elijah bound the waters from heaven, and at the word of his mouth, enemies were burned by fire sent from heaven... But also

<margin>2 Kings 1</margin>
here it is reported that these two prophets will preach for three and a half years, and it is added shortly after that they have the power to shut the sky so it does not rain during the days of their prophecy. Because of these words, I say, there is a presumption that one of these would be Elijah, especially because he is alive and promised by the Lord to be revealed to the world before the great

<margin>Malachi 4</margin>
day of the Lord comes, and he "turns the hearts of fathers to their children, and the hearts of children to their fathers" <note>quoting the prophecy of Elijah's return in Malachi 4:6</note>. "Lest perhaps I come," He says, "and strike the earth with a curse." Regarding Enoch, however: that he is the companion of Elijah, or that he will come with him, there is no mention—neither literally nor spiritually, neither openly nor in riddles. It is only presumed because, since he was a good and just man before God, he alone out of all was translated <note>term: <term>translation</term> refers to being taken up into heaven by God without experiencing physical death</note>; and it is believed he was translated for this purpose: so that he, like Elijah,

<margin>2 Kings 2</margin>
might bear witness to the truth. Since, therefore, Moses is described as having died like other men, while Enoch did not die but was translated alive, it was as if it were alien

<margin>Genesis 5</margin>
to human sense that part of those words could touch upon Moses, whom scripture records as dead and buried, even if his grave is hidden.

<margin>Deuteronomy 34</margin>
Rather, it was readier to presume—even without examining the wording—that he was Enoch, who alone is alive like Elijah and preserved by the Lord where He himself established. From which fact

<margin>Pope Gregory</margin>
it came to pass that even the holy Pope Gregory clearly asserts that Enoch will come along with Elijah, saying thus: "With Enoch and Elijah preaching, many of those who then

<column-break/>

remained in unbelief among the Jews will return to the knowledge of the truth." Both of these are named

<margin>Zechariah</margin>

### Abbot's Part of the Exposition

<margin>
Moses is to come.

...as we noted above) it is estimated: because if three were reserved together for this purpose—to be sent by the Lord near the end of the world—it would neither be foreign to a great and venerable mystery, nor different from what is written in this book. For if we diligently consider these three men: in Enoch, who was from those ancient patriarchs <note>The "patriarchs" were the early biblical fathers before the time of the Law given to Moses</note> who lived before the Law, there is the **likeness of the Father**. In Moses, who was the lawgiver and teacher of the people of Israel, there is the **likeness of the Son**. In Elijah <note>original: "Helya"</note>, who was the initiator of the eremitic <note>The "eremitic life" refers to the life of a hermit or solitary monk</note> and special life, there is the **likeness of the Holy Spirit**. 

However, Scripture says of Moses alone that he died, because only the Son died for a time in the flesh—who nevertheless himself lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and reigns with them forever and ever. But if God (who can do all things) so decreed and so willed, what if Moses had fallen asleep for a time and a little while later risen from the tomb? He would be destined to die again at a predefined time, just as none of those who were raised by the Lord before He suffered—nor even those raised after His resurrection by the apostles or other saints—were raised so as not to die again, but are to be raised again with the others on the last day. 

For if Lazarus and all the others who lived in this way after death died twice, so that they might rise twice, why could Moses not have been called from the sepulcher in the same way, destined to die again? This would serve as a cause for the mystery and satisfy the debt of the human condition <note>The "debt of the human condition" is a traditional phrase for the necessity of death</note>. Thus, the Scripture that confesses him to be dead would be true, and the opinion of those who contend that he is alive even to the present would not be a false one. 

Because perhaps Moses and Elijah are to come together, and Enoch with them—or rather Moses and Elijah with him—the opinion of those who say Enoch and Elijah will preach and suffer may be true, even if Moses is present. This would fulfill what the Apostle says: <margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away" <note>original: "Ex parte enim cognoscimus: & ex parte prophetamus..."</note>. For what if the Almighty God decreed that these three

<column-break/>

themselves be sent to bear witness to the truth? For the Lord says: "In the mouth of two or three witnesses, every word shall stand" <note>original: "In ore duorum aut trium testium: stat omne verbum"</note>. It is presumed, then, that three such men will exist in their own time. Whether they are the ones being discussed, or others, I do not know; God knows. 

This is suggested by that passage of this book where, under the name of **three angels**, three great preachers are described who are to be revealed at the end of this "second state." One of them is to receive the "eternal gospel" to announce it to those living on earth; another is to follow and say: "Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen"; and the third is to say: "If anyone worships the beast and its image, he shall drink of the wine of God's wrath." 

Furthermore, earlier in this work, mention was made of one angel having an open book in his hand, and then of two men, for whose sake all these things were said. Also, that passage in Daniel (which we mentioned above) seems to point to this in a wondrous way where Daniel himself says he saw a certain man above the water of the river, and two others remaining with him, one on this side and the other on that. Therefore, whether it is those men or others, I do not know; God knows. 

Nevertheless, the passages themselves demonstrate that it is not in vain that three men are to be sent by the Lord to bear witness to the truth under the opening of the sixth seal. For it is certain that for the sake of a specific mystery, three great patriarchs were chosen by the Lord at the beginning of the "first state": namely, **Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob**. Three others were said to be like them at the beginning of the "second state": **Zechariah, John the Baptist, and the man Christ Jesus**. Except that one of these three, by His own condescension alone, willed to be as one of His servants to complete the mysteries of the kingdom of God, just as He answered John the Baptist when John was afraid to baptize Him: "Let it be so now; for thus it becomes us to fulfill all righteousness" <note>original: "Sine modo: ita nos oportet implere omnem iustitiam" (Matthew 3:15)</note>. For just as Zechariah preceded alone, and John the Baptist and the man Christ Jesus followed together, so also here: one of the three is seen to go before, and two follow together, both of whom...

# Part of the Exposition
<meta>The header "Abb. Pars Exponis" likely refers to an abbreviation for "Abbreviated Part of the Exposition."</meta>

...those who are to rise from the dead: they will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and they will not taste death. He takes this testimony from the exposition of Theodore of Heraclea <note>original: "Theodozi eracleate"; a 4th-century bishop and biblical commentator</note>. After some words that are added below, he reports that Apollinaris <note>Apollinaris of Laodicea, whose views on the nature of Christ were later deemed heretical, though his commentaries remained influential</note> felt the same way, saying: Apollinaris (though in different words) asserted the same things as Theodore: that some are not to die, but are to be snatched from this present life into the future one, so that with changed and glorified bodies they may be with Christ—which we now believe regarding Enoch and Elijah <note>original: "Helya"</note>.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
Behold, here Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> says: that it is asked by some whether there are those who will not die, but with changed and glorified bodies will be with Christ (which he says he believes) regarding Enoch and Elijah. Therefore, what is written here about the two witnesses—who are thought to be Enoch and Elijah—he says is to be understood in the spirit, not in the letter <note>Jerome is advocating for a metaphorical or allegorical reading rather than a strictly literal one</note>. If this is so, and two others are to be killed by the beast, it follows that they are someone other than Enoch and Elijah. But because the holy fathers do not agree on this point, but different men have felt different things, I think that he who hid the word from the prophet Elisha <note>original: "helyseo propheta"</note> wished this to remain hidden until the appointed time: so that whatever might be said by these or those is more of an opinion that can be mistaken than certain knowledge or understanding—which, if it is true, cannot be mistaken.

<margin>Concordance</margin>
<margin>Note well</margin>
<margin>Gregory</margin>
For if (as Saint Gregory says <note>Pope Gregory the Great, known for his influential writings on morality and ministry</note>) even prophets are mistaken, what wonder if the opinion of those who are not prophets is mistaken? For the same teacher says to Peter the Deacon: "Why do you wonder if we are mistaken, who are not prophets? Or has it slipped the mind that David, who was accustomed to having the spirit of prophecy, gave sentence against the innocent son of Jonathan when he heard the words of a lying boy?" <note>This refers to a biblical story where King David was deceived into punishing Mephibosheth based on a servant's lie</note>. I say this for this reason: that if it is true that Enoch and Elijah are to be killed, the opinion of those who thought they would not die is mistaken. And if they themselves are not to die, but others who are Enoch and Elijah in spirit—or rather (as we wrote above) Moses and Elijah—then the opinion of the other side must be mistaken, because both cannot be true;

<column-break/>

And these things were indeed said in the discussion of the "letter that kills" <note>A reference to the Pauline concept that a strictly literal interpretation of scripture ("the letter") can be spiritually deadening compared to the "Spirit" that gives life</note>, the understanding of which is ambiguous and dark in many places. But what follows: *And the spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters*—we must rise with it from the depth of the letter and go into the heights, where the lights of heaven shine, leaving hidden counsels or judgments to the Lord (who knows all things). Let these men therefore be according to their reputation, whom God himself knows better. 

But according to the typical <term>Typical: A method of interpretation where people or events in the Bible (types) foreshadow later realities</term> understanding, we must consider what they signify. We know that Moses was a Levite and a shepherd of the people of Israel; Elijah was a solitary man having neither children nor a wife. The former therefore signifies the order of clerics; the latter the order of monks. The forty-two months in which they preach, clothed in sackcloth, signify as many generations in which, by both words and examples, they cry out saying: "Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near." 

But the nations, under the number of those years, trample the holy city; because although not in whole but in part, as long as this space of time lasts—designated as three and a half years—power is always given to the unfaithful to trample the faithful, though not in the same way as in the days of the Antichrist. But we see that the court which is outside the temple has been given to the nations for many years (as we said above). As for what is less complete, it is to be feared lest it be quickly completed; because in all these things the fury of the Lord is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. These two orders, in the figure of the two men, are called the "two olive trees" and the "two lampstands": because they burn with the oil of charity and shine with the brilliance of wisdom. One of these is proven to suit monks more specifically, and the other to suit clerics. But what follows concerning the two men standing in the sight of the Lord of the earth—soon why not...

### Joachim’s Third Book on the Apocalypse
<note>original: "Joa. Tertia In Apo."; likely referring to Joachim of Fiore’s *Expositio in Apocalypsim*</note>

...the scripture said: **In the sight of the Lord of heaven.** Christ is to be understood here as the Lord. For it seems he could be called the "god of the earth" or the "prince of the world," who is destined to rule because of the sins of men, represented by that eleventh horn which Daniel writes about: <note>original: "in cornu illo undecimo"; referring to the "Little Horn" of Daniel 7, often associated with the Antichrist</note> because he may change times and laws, which are delivered into his hand for a time, times, and half a time. For it is necessary that there stand—whether two men according to the letter, or the remnants of two religious orders—in his presence, just as Moses and Aaron stood before Pharaoh, who was the lord of the land of Egypt, and as Peter and Paul stood before Nero, who was the emperor of the whole world, to offer testimony to the truth, just as these witnesses are to do. Yet, it appears in the prophet Zechariah that this word was spoken concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, who is also (as we believe) for a similar reason of mystery called in this book the "prince of the kings of the earth." This is surely because, as a true man, he was made the Lord of men, just as God the Father speaks to him in the second Psalm, saying: *Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.* And Isaiah says: *Send the lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth.*

If this is so, why was it said of these men in the prophet Zechariah: *These are the two sons of oil* <note>original: "filii olei"; a Hebrew idiom for "the anointed ones"</note>—that is, of splendor—*who assist the ruler of the whole earth*, and in this book: *These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing in the sight of the Lord of the earth*? It is because from the time those men are to come, it is necessary for our Lord Jesus Christ to reign over the whole earth, until he puts his enemies under his feet. For this reason, it is said that they stand in the sight of the Lord of the earth: because they will come and go before his face for this purpose, to announce that the time has arrived in which it is necessary for the Son of God to reign over the whole earth. For they must preach for the sake of the elect, and announce the words of life to men, so that their light may shine before men, and they will strike <note>original: "impingent"; likely meaning to make an impression or to strike/anoint</note> the hearts of the chosen men by anointing them with the oil of spiritual doctrine.

<margin>
Daniel 12
Zechariah 4
Psalm 2
Isaiah 16
Zechariah 4
</margin>

<column-break/>

On account of the reprobate <note>those rejected by God</note>, however, they are to "bind the water in heaven" when they perceive it is necessary, and also to "turn the water into blood" and "strike the earth with every plague." But how is this so? Is it according to the literal truth? Not at all. Rather, to "close the heaven" so that it does not rain in the days of their prophecy means to hide spiritual words in the hearts of the elect, and to forbid them from daring to speak spiritual words to carnal men who cannot grasp or perceive them. As the Lord said: *Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not scatter your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you to pieces.*

And not only for this reason, but also because those who once despised the words of God are not worthy to hear them; as the Lord said to the prophet Isaiah: *Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them.* Whence also concerning the synagogue of the Jews—indeed, even in spirit concerning the Church—the Lord makes a complaint that he expected it to produce fruit, but it produced wild grapes. He threatened it with this among other things, saying: *I will tear down its wall, and it shall be trampled, and I will make it a wasteland. It shall not be pruned, nor shall it be dug, and briers and thorns shall grow in it. And I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.* 

For the Lord, as it were, commands the clouds not to rain upon an evil and adulterous generation; because when holy men see that they profit nothing in their preaching, they leave behind the "sons of Belial" <note>a biblical term for wicked or worthless people</note> and withdraw themselves to leisure and quiet, lest perhaps they fail to win those people and lose themselves. There are, moreover, some who "adulterate the word of God," who do not seek to know so that they may act, but so that they may be seen by men. From these, the secrets of heaven (that is, the mysteries of the kingdom of God) are rightly to be hidden, so that the "voluntary rain" which God set aside for his inheritance does not come upon them; instead, the mystery itself must be shown to them like a rolled-up book, so that...

### Part of the Exposition
<note>original: "Abb. Pars Exponis"</note>

<margin>Luke 8.</margin> ...that "seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear." Even if they are seen to draw the waters of the rivers of Egypt—so that they may boast in the knowledge of this world, or the knowledge of the **letter that kills** <note>original: "littere que occidit"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life"</note>—they soon feel the holy ones of God coming against them to turn those very waters into blood. By doing so, they show that what these worldly men believe to be life-giving is actually deadly and infected with poison. Oh, how often have worldly men composed little books just to be seen by others! Yet, when these works are brought into the hands of the righteous, they condemn them, showing that the "drink of death" is within them; for in those books, it was flesh and blood speaking, not the Spirit of God. They also "strike the earth with every plague" because, by revealing the plagues of the world, they strike and shake the earthly and carnal hearts of men—plagues which those men cannot see for themselves because they have a veil before their eyes. Indeed, because carnal men do not feel these plagues unless they are revealed by the witnesses, it is not for nothing that the witnesses are said to "strike the earth with every plague." By announcing and showing these plagues, they strike those earthly hearts as if with the rod of their tongue. Thus, the people are tormented by the sight of them, either because the witnesses "withhold the drops of dew" so that it does not rain during the days of their prophecy, or because they reveal that the understanding many people think is useful is actually carnal. They show it is not a drink of salvation, but death and perdition to all who use it. For this reason—even if they are hated at all times—when iniquity abounds, they will be hated much more by many. Many will rise against them in debates over the **Scriptures**, but they will not prevail, because "fire will go out of their mouths" to destroy and consume their enemies. But what kind of fire? Is it material? Far from it. It is the fire of spiritual intelligence, which destroys and consumes carnal understanding. For although they may hide this spiritual intelligence (which descends from heaven) from the children of this world, whenever the **sons of Belial** <note>A biblical term for wicked or worthless men; here refers to those opposing the spiritual truth</note> rise against them in the interpretation of the **Scriptures**, it is necessary that the witnesses speak to them in the power of the Spirit. They do this so that their enemies do not mock them as if they were defeated, but are instead put to shame, being overcome by the power of the Spirit. And it should be known that "rain" signifies that doctrine which waters the hearts of listeners to bring forth fruit; "fire" signifies those stinging words which consume the vices of the flesh by setting them ablaze. Therefore, the saints withhold the one (the rain), but by no means the other (the fire). This is because they hide the teachings that could build up the apostate people because of their sins, but they speak openly of those things which convict them of their evil deeds. Moreover, "when they have finished their testimony"—that is, when they have completed the work of their ministry among the false Christians—the **beast that ascends from the abyss** will make war against them. For so it is said in the following verses:

> And when they shall have finished their testimony, the beast that ascendeth out of the abyss shall make war against them, and shall overcome them, and kill them.

WHO this **Beast** is, and what the **abyss** is from which it ascends, will be discussed at length and in detail in the fourth and sixth parts of this work. However, to speak briefly: it is the multitude of unbelievers who have persecuted the **Church** of God from the time of the Lord’s Passion until the **Antichrist**. Truly, if according to the literal sense there are two individuals who will do these things—or even more if they represent two religious orders—this beast which kills them is to be understood as that **fourth beast** which **Daniel** describes. That is, a fierce and beastly nation gathered into an army, which shall come forth from the "navel of nations" <note>likely referring to a central gathering point of hostile forces or a specific geopolitical origin of the Antichrist's army</note>. To this beast, power will be given over the holy city (as has been said) because of the sins of men, for "a time, and times, and half a time" <note>A prophetic period usually interpreted as three and a half years</note>. That beast, I say, will make war against the saints of the Most High, with **false prophets** assisting it. It will overcome them with lying signs, or even by the fraud of demons and the cleverness of words. That his wrath rages not only against two men, but indeed against many, is demonstrated in the fourth part of Book I...
