# John’s Third Part on the Apocalypse
<note>original: "Joa. Tertia In Apo." refers to a commentary on the third section of the Book of Revelation.</note>

...is said of him. **And he will make war against the holy ones and overcome them.** <note>Revelation 13:7</note> **And power was given to him over every tribe, and people, and tongue, and nation; and all who dwell upon the earth worshipped it—those whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world.** **If anyone has ears for hearing, let him hear.** **He who leads into captivity, goes into captivity.** **He who kills with the sword, must himself be killed by the sword.** <note>Revelation 13:8-10</note> Hence also concerning that **eleventh horn** <note>original: "cornu illo undecimo"; referring to the Antichrist in Daniel 7</note> (that is, concerning that king who will be the head of this beast when the nations are to trample the holy city), it is written in Daniel: <margin>Dan.</margin> **And I saw that the horn made war against the holy ones and prevailed against them, until the Ancient of Days came, and gave judgment to the holy ones of the Most High, and the time arrived, and the holy ones obtained the kingdom.** <note>Daniel 7:21-22</note> Therefore, the holy ones will die at his command, just as the leaders of the apostles <note>Peter and Paul</note> were killed at the command of **Nero**. It should be noted what he says: *When they have finished their testimony.* For the Devil does not receive power over the righteous whenever he wishes, to wipe from the earth those who announce the words of life; rather, he receives it when the Lord wishes to call them from the present age so that he may return to them the prize of their reward for their labors. <margin>T. 3.</margin> If, however, this beast is to reign for **three and a half years** (as the common opinion holds), and during that same span of time the holy men are to preach with two men going before them as their leaders, what else is to be understood except that near the end of his reign he will make war against the holy ones? He will begin by disputing the faith of Christ, so that he may drag those whom he sees are his subjects into treachery. For it is not always the concern of the unfaithful to destroy the laws of men; but sometimes they do so, and especially when—given peace on all sides—they are lifted up in pride. Therefore, he will first apply himself to striking **Babylon**, which has resisted him for a long time, and afterward he will raise the **horn of his insolence** <margin>Dan.</margin> against God, as is said more clearly in the sixth part: **These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, because He is Lord**

<column-break/>

**of lords and King of kings, and those who are with Him are called, elect, and faithful.** <note>Revelation 17:14</note> Why does he say "with the Lamb" and not rather "with the Lion"? Because the victory of the Lamb is in death, and those conquer more gloriously who die for the sake of justice. It follows: <margin>T. 4.</margin>

> **And their bodies shall lie in the streets of the great city, which is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.** <note>Revelation 11:8</note>

If it is true according to the **letter** <note>original: "ad litteraz"; meaning a literal historical interpretation</note> what is written about the two men—namely, that there are two above all others who are to be killed by the beast that ascends from the abyss—it seems likely that they are to be killed in that city in which their Lord was also crucified <note>Jerusalem</note>. Nevertheless, what he says about "the streets of the great city" does not seem to support that same understanding. For Jerusalem is perhaps never read of as being called "the great city"; rather, **Nineveh** and **Babylon** are called "great cities," doubtless because "many are called, but few are chosen." <margin>Dan. 8</margin> Again, that city which is called Jerusalem is not called **Sodom and Egypt** spiritually because of its stones and walls, but because of the **carnal people** <note>those focused on worldly/fleshly desires rather than the spirit</note> who once inhabited it. It remains, therefore, that by the "great city" which is called spiritually Sodom and Egypt, we understand the **kingdom of this world**. Its "streets" are those men who have chosen for themselves the **wide paths** leading to destruction, in which will lie the dead bodies of the blessed men. These men, having the spiritual understanding of the Old and New Testaments, will die in themselves when the preachers of truth are killed by the beast and truth is "thrown down to the ground" (according to Daniel). This applies generally and according to what can be referred to in the spirit to all holy ones who are to be killed in that great crisis. But if we must speak specifically of those two witnesses, let us admit that by a **participation in treachery**, whatever nation the holy ones are to be destroyed in is called the "great city"; and by that same participation, it is said to be the place "where also their Lord..."

# Part I of the Exposition
<note>original: "Abb. Pars I Exponis"; likely referring to an "Abbreviation" or summary of the first part of an Exposition on Revelation.</note>

...where their Lord was crucified: because there is one city for all the reprobate <note>Those rejected by God or condemned</note>; or perhaps, what seems more pertinent to the matter and can be understood in the same sense: that the Jews are to be gathered into Jerusalem, that earthly city in which their fathers lived with their sons, by that **eleventh king** <note>The Antichrist, as described in Daniel 7:24</note> about whom we have written more in this book. In his sight, the servants of God are to be killed by the **beast**, so that among the other evils he will commit, he may proclaim himself the savior of the Jews. This is most strongly suggested by that passage in Daniel: **The sons of the transgressors of your people shall be lifted up to fulfill the vision, and they shall fall.** <note>Daniel 11:14; original: "Filij preuaricatorum populi tui..."</note> If it happens this way, it seems it can occur even according to the literal letter: so that just as once in that city and among that people their Lord lay dead, so also now in the same city and among the same people the bodies of his servants may lie, **filling up what is lacking in his sufferings**. <note>A reference to Colossians 1:24</note> Whether these things happen in that city or another, it is not far from the simple truth, because this adverb "where" in the Divine Page often signifies not so much a physical location as a people who were once in a place, or a similarity to that same people. It follows:

<margin>Topic 5</margin>
**And they of the tribes, and peoples, and tongues, and nations shall see their bodies for three days and a half: and they shall not suffer them to be put in monuments. And the inhabitants of the earth shall rejoice over them and make merry: and shall send gifts one to another; because these two prophets tormented them that dwelt upon the earth. And after three days and a half, the spirit of life from God entered into them: and they stood upon their feet; and great fear fell upon them that saw them.** <note>Revelation 11:9-11</note>

<column-break/>

If according to a **typological** <term>typological: a method of interpretation where historical persons or events are seen as symbols or "types" of spiritual or future realities</term> understanding we take the **three and a half years** as the whole time this **Beast** will reign—that is, from the coming of the Lord until the time of his ruin and downfall—it remains that in the **three and a half days**, shorter spans of time are designated, after which the kingdom which is under all heaven will be given to the people of the holy ones of the Most High. Meanwhile, however, the entrance to this monument remains closed because of what was written by the Lord to the three disciples, which is certainly to be understood in the spirit: <margin>Matthew</margin> **Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man rises from the dead.** <note>Matthew 17:9</note> For just as his death designates the extinction of truth, so his resurrection designates its **vivification** <note>The act of bringing back to life</note>; it is undoubtedly on account of the spirit who gives life, just as those many bodies of the dead who had slept and were raised designate many testimonies of truth which, by God's inspiration, will be awakened from sleep. But because when the time of war is completed, the time of judgment will begin—which, however, is established to be initiated earlier—it is entirely necessary that the **resurrection of the dead** follow. And this is indeed true of all the holy ones. Regarding the **two men**, I think this must be observed in every way: if it is true that there are two who are to be killed by the beast, surely those two, after three and a half days, will rise from the dead. For what if, just as their Lord was killed and on the third day rose from the dead with many others, so also these two—for the sake of those who will rejoice over their death—will rise from the dead after three and a half days, even if the final resurrection of the dead does not happen then? As for what he says: **They shall see from the tribes and peoples and tongues and nations their bodies for three days and a half, and they shall not suffer them to be put in monuments**—whether the speech refers to those two, or generally to all the holy ones who are to be killed in that same storm, it is doubtful...

### John’s Third [Exposition] on the Apocalypse

It is not unlikely that the languages of different nations will gather for that spectacle, just as usually happens in some royal city. That is to say: people flowing there from various parts, of different languages and customs, will be gathered there, seeking (as is the custom) to win the favor of the earthly power, loving the glory of men more than the glory of God. For this reason, they will not allow the bodies of the saints to be placed in tombs, so that while they show themselves cruel toward them in death, they may be more closely loved by those who killed them. 

<margin>Mark 13</margin>
Thus, when Truth itself <note>A common title for Christ in medieval theology</note> was questioned by the disciples about those times, He responded with this among other things, saying: **But brother shall betray brother to death, and the father his son; and children shall rise up against parents, and shall work their death.** <note>Mark 13:12</note> And why is this? Because it is easier to persuade men who savor earthly things of what pleases the flesh than what pleases the spirit. Men are more prone to believe those promising clemency than those who threaten judgment—especially since carnal men, to whom sin is shown, think the judgment threatened by the saints is unjust for the very reason that they think the commandments given are impossible for a human to observe. For they say: "If no one can have anything unless it is given to him from above, then either it is false that they preach God as merciful (He who demands what He does not give), or they themselves are false witnesses of God, because they confess a strict judgment exists even where neither a good will nor the possibility to act supports the person." And while they devise such things as wickedly as they do deceitfully, the words of the preachers act upon them like thorns fixed in the heart, so that their preaching is a torment to them, and their threat of judgment is a labor and an affliction of the spirit.

<margin>Mark 6</margin>
So were the words of John [the Baptist] troublesome to King Herod, and especially to Herodias; so was the preaching of Christ to the impious Pharisees. If these evil men, often unable to bear the words of the good, seek by all means to kill them, how much more must we believe they will rejoice and exult in their death when they are killed by others without any scandal or infamy to themselves? Hence, in the present chapter, concerning the lovers of this life whose way of life is on the earth, that which we have heard is said: **And they that dwell on the earth shall rejoice over them and make merry, and shall send gifts one to another; because these two prophets tormented them that dwelt on the earth.** <note>Revelation 11:10</note> For this is that saying: **But you shall be sorrowful,**

<margin>John 16</margin>
**but the world shall rejoice.** <note>John 16:20</note> Yet it is no wonder. For if "soulish" <note>term: "animales homines" (soulish or natural men), referring to those directed by basic human instincts rather than the Holy Spirit</note> men were saddened by the danger of the cross and the striking down of the faith, they would rightly be saddened by the power of the beast and the kingdom and victory of him who enters the contest against Christ. But those who are made happy by the earthly prosperity preached by the "pseudo-christs" <note>False messiahs or false anointed ones</note> must necessarily hate those who hold this world as an exile, and join themselves in spirit to those who announce and defend it. Therefore, deceived men, whose way of life is on the earth, thinking that peace was given by divine power, will rejoice and be glad with one another. But those who have a healthy heart will mourn and weep, and will frequently torment the lovers of the world—even if they are unwilling to hear—by announcing to them the judgment that is near and the torments of hell. These torments are to receive them in the end because of their impieties; for though they knew God, they did not worship Him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, according to

<margin>Romans 1</margin>
those nations we spoke of above. Because of this, their foolish heart is darkened, so that they worship and serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is God blessed forever, amen. <note>original: "qui est benedictus deus in secula amen"; referencing Romans 1:21-25</note> Truly, what is said in the same place concerning the resurrection of those who are to be killed by the beast—**the spirit of life from God shall enter into them, and they stood upon their feet**—must be confessed as having been said because as soon as the spirits of the just are released from the prison-house <note>term: "ergastulo" (workhouse or slave prison); used here metaphorically for the body or the state of death</note>, they go to God who gave them. Once they are filled to the full with the gift of the Holy Spirit, their bodies (which were previously known to be merely "soulish") shall become spiritual by the power of that Spirit which is from God. They shall no longer have the possibility of falling as before, but shall remain indefatigable without end. Hence it is said through the prophet: **But they that hope in the Lord shall**

<margin>Isaiah 40</margin>
**renew their strength; they shall take wings as eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall fly and not faint.** <note>Isaiah 40:31</note> And what follows: **And great fear fell upon them who saw them.**

# John’s Third Part on the Apocalypse

...it is not surprising that the languages of various nations should gather at that spectacle, just as usually happens in some royal city: where, as men flow there from different parts with diverse languages and customs, they congregate to seek (as is the custom) to win the favor of earthly power, **loving the glory of men more than the glory of God.** <note>A reference to John 12:43. The author suggests the crowd gathers out of political sycophancy rather than just curiosity.</note> For this reason, they will not allow the bodies of the saints to be placed in tombs, so that they may be more closely loved by those who killed them, by displaying their cruelty even in the death of the witnesses.

<margin>Mark 13</margin>
Thus, Truth itself <note>A common medieval title for Jesus Christ (the "Truth").</note> when questioned by the disciples about those times, responded among other things, saying: **"Brother shall deliver up brother to death, and the father his son; and children shall rise up against their parents and shall put them to death."** <note>Mark 13:12.</note> And why is this? Because it is easier to persuade men who savor earthly things of what pleases the flesh than what pleases the spirit. Men are more prone to believe those promising mercy than those who threaten judgment—especially since carnal men, to whom their own sin is shown, consider the judgment the saints threaten to be unjust. They think it is impossible for a human to observe what God commands. For they say: "If no one can have anything unless it is given to him from above, then either it is false that they preach a merciful God who demands what he does not give, or they themselves are false witnesses of God, because they claim there is a strict judgment even where there is neither a good will nor the possibility of fulfilling the law." When they craft such wicked and lying arguments, the words of the preachers become like thorns fixed in their hearts, so that their preaching is a torment to them, and the threat of judgment is a labor and affliction of the spirit.

<margin>Mark 6</margin>
So were the words of John troublesome to King Herod, and especially to Herodias; so was the preaching of Christ to the impious Pharisees. If these evil men, unable to bear the words of the good, sought in every way to kill them, how much more must we believe they will rejoice and exult in their death, when they are killed by others as if without scandal or infamy to themselves? Hence, in the present chapter, concerning the lovers of this life whose "conversation" <note>In the sense of "way of life" or "citizenship" (from the Latin *conversatio*).</note> is on the earth, it is said: **"And those who dwell on the earth shall rejoice over them and be glad, and shall send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell on the earth."** <note>Revelation 11:10.</note> For this is that saying: **"You shall be sorrowful, but the world shall rejoice."** <note>John 16:20.</note> Nor is it a wonder. For if "animal" <note>From the Latin *animalis*, meaning "soulish" or "natural" as opposed to "spiritual."</note> men were saddened by the peril of the cross and the striking down of faith, they would rightly be saddened by the power of the Beast, and by the reign and victory of him who begins the struggle against Christ. But since they are made happy by earthly prosperity (which the false christs preach), they must necessarily hate those who are exiled from this prosperity, and join themselves in spirit to those who announce and defend it. Thus, deceived men whose life is on the earth, thinking that peace was given by God, will rejoice and be glad with one another. But those who have a healthy heart will mourn and weep; and even against their will, the lovers of the world will often torment themselves when these saints announce the judgment that is near, and the torments of hell which are to receive them in the end for their impieties. For though they knew God, they did not worship Him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, fashioning those things we mentioned above. Because of this, their foolish heart is darkened, so that they worship and serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is God blessed forever, amen. <note>A paraphrase of Romans 1:21-25.</note> Indeed, what is said in the same place about the resurrection of those to be killed by the Beast—that **"the spirit of life entered into them, and they stood upon their feet"**—must be confessed to be said because as soon as the spirits of the just are released from the prison-house of the body, they go to God who gave them. Once they are filled to the full with the gift of the Holy Spirit, the bodies which they are known to have previously received as "animal" bodies shall, by the power of that Spirit which is from God, become spiritual. They shall no longer have the capacity to fall as before, but shall remain indefatigable without end. Hence it is said through the prophet: **"But those who hope in the Lord shall change their strength; they shall take wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary, they shall fly and not faint."** <note>Isaiah 40:31.</note> As for what follows: **"And great fear fell upon those who saw them."**

# The Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

This is how it should be understood: as it is said, "excepted," that (as is the custom of the prophets) the past tense is put here in place of the future. It follows:

<margin>Amos 6</margin>
**"And in that hour a great earthquake occurred: and the tenth part of the city fell: and there were slain in the earthquake names of men, seven thousand."** <note>original: "Et in illa hora factus est terremotus magnus..."</note>

In the hour when the glory of the saints shall be made manifest, a great earthquake will happen. This is because the hearts of those seeing or hearing this will be struck and begin to waver within themselves; some will reprove themselves for their own unbelief, while others, falling into despair, will become worse, to the point that they themselves fall and ruin many others by separating them from the faith. For this reason, it is not without merit that this "city," whose tenth part fell in the earthquake, should be understood as the Holy Church, which cannot fall so long as it stands in faith. Hence it is said by the Apostle: **"He who stands, let him see to it that he does not fall."** <note>1 Corinthians 10:12. The author is navigating the paradox of how the "Church" can fall if it is divinely protected.</note> 

But if this designates the Church that stands in faith, how can a part of it be said to "fall" during the glorification of the righteous? It is because many of the clergy <note>The author identifies the "tenth part" specifically with the clergy, who were often symbolized by the number ten in medieval numerology.</note> who seemed to stand will be unbelieving of the saints' words when the struggle arrives. And though they may not insult them openly like the rest, they will nevertheless secretly disparage them—just as some disparaged and insulted their own Lord, saying: **"Aha! You who would destroy the temple of God and in three days rebuild it!"** <note>Matthew 27:40.</note> Some of these people were later struck with remorse and did penance for their guilt; but others, despairing of themselves, did worse things, pursuing the apostles from city to city and persevering in their iniquities until the end. Therefore, some will "fall" in that hour upon seeing the sign, because, being stung by their conscience, they will lose hope. 

That some of the clergy are to fall on that day is shown in the vision of Daniel, when it is said: **"And some of the learned shall fall."** <note>Daniel 11:35.</note> But if many of those who are the "walls of the city" <note>A metaphor for the leaders and teachers of the Church.</note> shall collapse, what will become of the multitude of the laity who "do not know their right hand from their left" <note>Jonah 4:11. A biblical idiom for the spiritually uneducated or innocent.</note> and think nothing of heavenly things in comparison to earthly ones? For this reason, "seven thousand names of men" are said to have died in that same earthquake. This represents the countless multitude of the laity who are considered Christians in name and are thought to remain in the faith, but who—deceived by those clergy who will be on the side of the Antichrist—will be extinguished from the faith. They will say that what was seen or heard concerning the glorification of the saints was done through the art and operation of the Devil; and they will say that one should rather believe the signs which the Antichrist and the false prophets will perform, claiming that he is the Christ and that the others were true prophets. 

For the people then will be, in truth, like a second Egypt: those men will be like Moses and Aaron, while the false prophets will be like Jannes and Mambres <note>Jannes and Jambres (here Mambres) were the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses, mentioned in 2 Timothy 3:8.</note>, at whose signs the heart of Pharaoh and the hearts of the Egyptians were hardened. Something similar is even now happening in the world: for all who preach the truth are like Moses, while those who protect error and resist the truth are like Jannes and Mambres. Yet, both then and now, the hearts of the "Egyptians" do not cease to be hardened through them, until the army of Pharaoh is drowned in the sea. And so it is for those. But Almighty God will prepare the faces of his remaining people, looking upon the earth and making it tremble with a "good fear"—even those who did not sin out of malice, but with a simple mind, like those whom Absalom led unknowingly into Sabaon. <note>Referencing 2 Samuel 15:11, where 200 men followed Absalom "in their simplicity," not knowing he was rebelling against King David.</note> For it follows:

...[through the] cunning of [falsehood] and when lies resist the truth: yet in the glorification of the righteous, even he will rise as if from the dead, so that for the rest they may give glory to the God of heaven, and a sacrifice may be made to Him just as in the days of old. Or surely it was said in this place because it is written: "that the remnant shall turn to the Lord with their whole heart." <note>Isaiah 10:21-22 is often the source for this "remnant" theology in medieval commentaries.</note> It follows:

<margin>Chapter 8</margin>

He calls it the "third woe" because it is what will happen under the seventh angel, since the first was completed under the fifth angel and the second under the sixth angel. The third will be completed under the seventh angel, according to what was foretold by the voice of the eagle flying through the midst of heaven, crying out with a loud voice and saying: **"Woe, woe, woe to the inhabitants of the earth,"** regarding the voices of the three angels who were about to sound their trumpets. This is because the saints in the Church will rejoice over the good things the Lord is about to do, and they will announce His glory to one another, shouting for joy rather than teaching, observing that what we now hold by faith must be fulfilled: that our Lord Jesus Christ must reign until He puts all His enemies under His feet, and that the kingdom <margin>Daniel 7</margin> under the whole heaven must be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all kings shall serve and obey Him.

# The Abbot’s Part of the Exposition

As if not attending to our prayers: the fool says in his heart: **there is no God**; <note>original: "nō est deus" from Psalm 14:1 (Vulgate Ps. 13)</note> the stupid man says: **the Lord shall not see: nor shall the God of Jacob understand**; <note>Psalm 94:7 (Vulgate Ps. 93)</note> and it is said among the nations: **where is their God?** <note>Psalm 115:2 (Vulgate Ps. 113)</note> But what does the apostle say? **Jesus Christ yesterday and today: the same, and forever.** <note>Hebrews 13:8</note> Or if, because of the mystery of the Divine Persons, it was said: **you who are: and who were**; it is clear what the Only-Begotten of God himself says: **My Father works even until now: and I work**; <note>John 5:17</note> and that just as God the Father showed His glory, when—after the kingdom of the Assyrians and Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians</note> was destroyed—He stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of the Persians, who would grant liberty to the children of Judah and command the temple to be founded which the Chaldeans had destroyed; so the Only-Begotten Son of God will show His greatness, working even as His Father does, so that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Therefore, when they say: **you who are: and who were**; they seem to have spoken to the Father and the Son, especially since it was said above: **the kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our God and of His Christ: and He shall reign for ever and ever, amen.** But why only to these two: does the Father work anything without the Son, or the Son with the Father without the Holy Spirit? Far be it. Rather, they say this to the Father and the Son because they see that the laborious times are completed, in which the Father and the Son showed their patience; and that the time of liberty is truly at hand, which by a certain mystical property pertains to the Holy Spirit, who is the love of the Father and the Son (as the apostle bears witness) who says: **Where the spirit of the Lord is: there is liberty.** <note>2 Corinthians 3:17</note> Furthermore, what they say: **And the nations were angry: and your wrath has come**; they clearly demonstrate to be the time of just judgment: not according to that time in which He feigned not to avenge the humble, so that He might instruct them in patience: but according to what was signified in the days of Elijah <note>original: "Helye"</note>, who judged and punished the sinners of the land, rendering to each according to his works. <note>1 Kings 18 and 2 Kings 1</note> And what they say: **And the time for the dead to be judged and to give the reward to your servants: the prophets: and the saints: and those who fear your name: and for destroying those who corrupt the earth**; this is to be referred to that time in which the beast and the false prophet shall be sent into the pool of fire burning with sulfur: and to the third

### Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

<margin>Psalm 30</margin>
**...in the secret of your face from the disturbance of men. You shall protect them in your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.** <note>original: "In abscondito faciei tue...". A quote from Psalm 31:21 (Psalm 30 in the Vulgate), suggesting God's protection for the contemplative soul.</note> It is well said that the Ark is described as remaining **under the wings of the Cherubim**, for the Cherubim signify the teachers of the holy Church, who are established in the fullness of knowledge for the defense of the faith. Indeed, the Catholic teachers are given for the protection of the Church, so that the "erroneous water" vomited out by the dragon might not subvert her—since there is no one to protect her or oppose the dragon with all their strength. Therefore, the **Temple** signifies the Old Testament, which rejoiced in physical offspring; whereas the **Ark** signifies the New Testament, whose glory is chastity and virginity. For the former was given according to the flesh, the latter according to the spirit. The children of the former were carnal; the children of the latter are spiritual. The Ark was small then, and the Temple was great, because in those days there were very few lovers of virginity and many lovers of marriage. Accordingly, **Peninnah** <note>The rival wife of Elkanah in the book of Samuel, representing the "fruitful" Old Law.</note> then had many children, while the barren woman remained so until the time came when she deserved to say: **"Let old things depart from your mouth, for the Lord is a God of knowledge."** <margin>1 Samuel 2</margin> And a little later: **"Until the barren woman has borne many; and she who had many children has grown weak."** <note>1 Samuel 2:3, 5. In medieval exegesis, the barren Hannah represents the Church/New Testament, and the fruitful Peninnah represents the Old Law.</note> Isaiah also says this: **"Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who do not travail; for many are the children of the desolate one, more than she who has a husband."** <margin>Isaiah 54</margin> Thus, here the Ark of the Covenant has grown strong—I do not say into a temple, but into a city. For she herself is the **Heavenly Jerusalem**, whose temple is heaven itself, or rather God himself, of whose greatness there is no end.

Therefore, **the temple of God was opened in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple.** <note>Revelation 11:19. The Latin text uses "Aptum," a common scribal variant or OCR error for "Apertum" (opened).</note> This dates from that day or time when the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom, when the tombs were opened and living men came out and appeared to many. This signifies that the scrolls of the prophets began to be opened, from which spiritual understandings emerged; these appeared not to everyone, but to "many"—that is, to witnesses preordained by God. It is also fitting that this refers to that most sacred monument from which 

<column-break/>

the most holy flesh of Christ emerged incorrupt. This itself signifies the virginal life in like manner, as it is spiritual and angelic, and knows no corruption (as the Lord says). <margin>Matthew</margin> **"In the resurrection, they shall neither marry nor be given in marriage, but shall be as the angels of God in heaven; and they shall be the children of God, being children of the resurrection."** <note>Matthew 22:30 and Luke 20:36.</note> Therefore, in that day, the temple of God was opened in heaven and the ark of the covenant was seen; the Old Testament was opened in the Church and grace appeared; the tomb of the "letter" <note>The literal or surface-level meaning of scripture.</note> was opened and spiritual intelligence appeared. What the corruptible and carnal life had signified was opened, and it was found to have signified the incorrupt and spiritual life. Indeed, all the legal precepts given in the ministry—whether concerning animal bodies, or stones and metals, or trees and herbs and such things—all these were nothing but shadows and patterns of things to come.

It must be noted above all else that those things said in this fourth part regard the state of the whole Church in general, but the fourth state specifically. For although from the Lord's resurrection, and especially from his ascension, the glory of virginity and chastity and the happiness of the contemplative life were clearly opened to the faithful, they did not shine forth in the same way as they did in the fourth time. ### Exposition, Part [Two]
<sig>U 2</sig>

...he thinks that he is ignorant in part: while he scorns to learn what is true, being asked perhaps by others, he is forced to introduce what is false. For he is not truthful who says the truth in part and the false in part, but he who speaks entirely or in part what is true, so that he might guard himself in every way from the crime of falsehood. This, however, those people cannot do who, while they understand something according to a part, rejoice as if they had reached its fullness. Therefore, this woman clothed with the sun both generally designates the universal Catholic Church and—in the eighth order of the parts of this book—the church of blessed virgins, and in the series of the fourth part, the church of teachers (<term>doctors</term>). Furthermore, according to the prerogative of grace, she designates that glorious Queen of Heaven who, being an undefiled virgin, gave birth to the King of Glory. It is for this reason that some of her mysteries concern the mother, some the daughters, some the sacred company of teachers, and some the general church of the perfect. But so that we may follow what is specific according to the order of the parts: while the holy virgins of God have adhered to the Queen of Virgins, they have become one chaste virgin with her and one glorious queen with her. Of which queen indeed it is said in the <term>Song of Songs</term>: <note>The author uses the Song of Songs (Canticles) as a primary tool for interpreting the beauty and hierarchy of the Church.</note> **One is my dove, my perfect**

<margin>Song of Songs 6</margin>
**one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her that bore her. The daughters of Zion saw her and declared her most blessed: the queens and concubines, and they praised her.** Who are these daughters of Zion, and queens, and concubines who praised her? Surely those of whom he had written previously, saying: **There are sixty queens, and eighty**

<margin>Song of Songs 6</margin>
**concubines, and of young maidens there is no number.** For to these things written before he added that which we have just heard: *One is my dove, my perfect one,* and the rest that follows. Now, the opinion of many is that "concubines" are not to be understood in a good sense; but most certainly and without doubt, they are to be understood in a good sense here, since they are included in such a perfect number. For they designate those souls who, after a sin of the flesh or sexual union, turn to Christ with their whole souls with the greatest sweetness of chaste love. These are included in the number eighty because

<column-break/>

this sacred number designates the excellence of <term>contemplation</term> <note>Contemplation refers to a high state of prayerful focus on God, often contrasted with the "active" life of labor.</note> which is found in the perfection of love, because it pertains to eternal life. It is for this reason that the Son of God, on the day of His resurrection, 

<margin>John</margin>
first appeared to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had cast out seven demons. The sixty queens, however, are those happy souls who, enduring the struggle of a great contest for the faith of Christ, merited the palm of victory. For the number seventy <note>original: "Septagenarius." The text mentions sixty queens but then explains the number seventy (septagenarius). This may be a scribal error for sixty (sexagenarius), which medieval writers often associated with active work and the fulfillment of the Law.</note> designates the perfection of labor. The young maidens, of whom there is no number, are those faithful souls who are indeed ignorant of the power of contemplation, but nevertheless, so that they may be able to strive toward it, labor under the discipline of spiritual mothers. 

<margin>Psalms</margin>
Truly, that virgin who hides herself in the secret of the Lord’s face, devoting herself to the praises of Christ and prayers, who forgets her people 

<margin>Psalms</margin>
and her father's house and suspends herself entirely in contemplation of Him, even if she is not a martyr, she excels the martyr in this regard. I think also that those who are such do not wish to be called to Christ through martyrdom for this reason: so that He might show that He has a certain sweetness of love in them more specially—as in His own mother and Saint John, who is the author of this book. Therefore, those who are such are taken into the company of Mary, so that the church of virgins itself, being more specially chosen, may be named the daughter of Mary, so that she may happily merit to hear from her son: 

<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
**One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her that bore her. The daughters of Zion saw her and declared her most blessed: the queens and concubines, and they praised her.** In the praise of which most happy dove, something quite appropriate to the present passage is soon introduced 

<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
when it is added: **Who is she that cometh forth as the morning rising, fair as the moon, bright as the sun, terrible as an army set in array?** <note>original: "Que est ista que pgreditur quasi aurora psurgens: pulchra vt luna: electa vt sol: terribilis vt castrorū acies ordinata?" (Song of Songs 6:9)</note> How these words apply generally to the Holy Church has been sufficiently explained by the Fathers. ->### John, Fourth Part on Revelation<-
<sig>U 3</sig>

...God: let us at least follow up on this briefly. Behold what the <term>wedding song</term> <note>The Song of Songs, often interpreted as a marriage between God and the Church.</note> says concerning the Church: *“Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun.”* The Bridegroom’s secretary <note>St. John the Apostle, who recorded the Book of Revelation.</note> declares this in a similar sign when he says: *“A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun and the moon under her feet.”* Heaven is divine Scripture, in which all things that are written are shown to be signs for the purpose of signifying something; they were written so that they might designate something further. 

For it should not be wearisome to usefully repeat those things we have already touched upon: why is it that **Elijah**, contrary to the custom of the fathers, refused to have a wife and children, and—about to contemplate the things of God—withdrew into the desert, and finally ascended into heaven in a fiery chariot through a whirlwind? Or why is it that the sons of the prophets leading a <term>cenobitic life</term> <note>A communal form of monasticism.</note> in Jericho appointed **Elisha**, the successor of Elijah, as a father for themselves? Is it not because of that which we see fulfilled in thousands of men in the Church? 

For if we lift the eyes of our mind to the "heaven" of the Holy Scriptures to contemplate this sign—and to know what it demonstrates to us by its signifying—we will find that **Elijah** designates Christ ascending into heaven. In **Elisha**, we find the apostolic order upon whom the Spirit of Christ rested. In the church gathered in **Jericho**, we see the primitive Church, which was established under the hand of the apostles. That Church, which was then in Jericho (that is, in the <term>circumcision</term> <note>Referring to the Jewish converts.</note>), failed like the moon; it could not remain there but immediately passed over to the desert of the Jordan (that is, to the Gentile people). 

Again: because the common crowd—who suffer like the monthly moon and attack the church of spiritual people with their depraved morals—the sons of the prophets leave Jericho and flee into the desert. For because the perfect cannot possess the perfection of the solitary life within the city, as many as desire that perfection are transferred by the Spirit of Jesus into the desert, so that they may endure the battles and temptations of the Devil there. For no one shall be crowned unless they have competed according to the rules. It is written: *“Jesus was led into the desert by the Spirit to be tempted by the Devil.”* For who are those who suffer greater pains, cries, temptations, and birth-pangs than those who lead the solitary and communal life in the wilderness?

<margin>2 Kings 2</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 4</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 2</margin>
<margin>Matthew 4</margin>

<column-break/>

Whoever, therefore, is led by the Spirit of God to strip themselves of earthly resources—whom else do they put on but Christ Jesus? He is the eternal **Sun of Justice** who illuminates every man coming into this world. We also, the Bride of Christ, have the moon under our feet because she [the Church] tramples the flesh and the glory of the world under her like dust, subjecting it to service and action so that the handmaid [the flesh] is not raised up against the mistress [the soul]. 

We also have on our head a crown of twelve stars; that is, the five and seven virtues by which she shines, being crowned. For it is of no use to trample temporal things unless eternal things are acquired. For example: you have trampled the moon, you have put on the sun; it remains that you be crowned with virtues. You have fought against impure touch and the lust of the eyes. You have fought against the allurements of words that dishonor chaste hearing, against indecent smells, and depraved speech, by which the carnal mind is soothed at every moment. You must hold these senses not for your detriment, but as an aid to virtue. 

As if with five stars or precious stones, you have adorned the circle of your crown with virtues of this kind. These, certainly, even if they are not spiritual in themselves, are transferred to spiritual use by the help of grace. For when you exercise your hands and arms not for seductive embraces but for good work, you have acquired a star for yourself in the battle through your good deed. When you "circumcise" your eyes—so that you do not look at a woman to lust after her, but rather apply them to the Holy Scriptures—you have added another star, as it were, to the circle of your crown. When you withdraw your ears from idle words and incline them to the word of God, you acquire a third star. When you restrain your mouth from evil speech and voluptuous taste, and instead pronounce the words of God by reading, praying, or preaching; and when you scorn meretricious scents and those things which look toward the luxury of the world, and instead patiently endure the foul odors of the sick—the fourth and fifth stars occupy [the crown]...

# Abbot, Part of the Exposition
<meta>catchword: might be able</meta>

...thinks: since he is ignorant in part: while he scorns to learn what is true: requested perhaps by others, he is forced to insert what is false. For he is not truthful who says the truth in part and falsehood in part: but he who speaks entirely or in part what is true, so that he guards himself in every way from the crime of falsehood; which nevertheless those cannot do who, while they understand something in part, rejoice that they have reached its fullness. Therefore, this **woman clothed with the sun** both generally designates the universal Church of the Catholics: and in the eighth order of the parts of the book, the church of the blessed virgins: and in the series of the fourth part, the church of the doctors <note>Teachers or theologians of the Church.</note>: and by the prerogative of grace, that glorious queen of heaven, who while she was an unspotted virgin, gave birth to the King of Glory. Hence it is that some of her mysteries touch the mother; some the daughters; some the sacred crowd of doctors; some the general church of the perfect. However, so that we may follow more specifically what is proper according to the order of the parts: while the sacred virgins of God joined the queen of virgins, they became one chaste virgin with her and one glorious queen with her. Of which queen, surely, it is said in the **Song of Songs**: <margin>Song of Songs 6</margin> *“One is my dove, my perfect one: she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her. The daughters of Zion saw her and declared her most blessed: the queens and concubines, and they praised her.”* Who are these daughters of Zion, and the queens, and the concubines who praised her? Surely those of whom he had written before, saying: <margin>Song of Songs 6</margin> *“There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and of young maidens there was no number.”* To these things already written, he added what we have just heard: *“One is my dove, my perfect one,”* and the rest that follow. The opinion of many holds that the "concubines" <note>original: "concubinas"; in this medieval allegorical context, this refers to those who turned to a religious life after having been married or having sinned, rather than remaining virgins.</note> are not to be taken in a good sense: but most certainly and without doubt, here they are to be taken in a good sense, as they are contained in such a perfect number. For they designate those souls who, after the sin or union of the flesh, are converted to Christ with all their souls in the greatest sweetness of chaste love. Who are therefore encompassed by the number eighty, because

<column-break/>

this sacred number designates the excellence of <term>contemplation</term> <note>A state of deep, wordless prayer and focus on God.</note> which is in the perfection of love, because it pertains to eternal life. Hence it is that the Son of God on the day of His resurrection appeared first to **Mary Magdalene**, <margin>John</margin> from whom He had cast out seven demons. But the sixty queens are those happy souls who, enduring the struggle of the great contest for the faith of Christ, earned the palm of victory. For the number sixty designates the perfection of labor. But the young maidens, of whom there is no number, are those faithful souls who are indeed ignorant of the virtue of contemplation, but nevertheless, so that they might be able to strive toward it, they labor under the discipline of spiritual mothers. Truly, that virgin who hides herself in the secret of the Lord’s face <margin>Psalm 31</margin> devoting herself to the praises of Christ and prayers: who forgets her people and her father’s house <margin>Psalm 45</margin> and suspends herself entirely in His contemplation: even if she is not a martyr, she surpasses the martyr in this respect. I also think that those who are such do not wish to be summoned to Christ through martyrdom, so that He may demonstrate that He has a certain more special sweetness of love in them: as in His mother and **Saint John**, whose book this is. Therefore, those who are such are taken into the company of Mary: so that the church of virgins itself, more specially chosen, may be called the daughter of Mary: so that she may happily deserve to hear from her son: *“One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her. The daughters of Zion saw her and declared her most blessed: the queens and concubines, and they praised her.”* In praise of this most happy dove, something quite suitable to the present place is soon introduced, when it is added: <margin>Canticle 6</margin> *“Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array?”* How these words generally apply to the holy Church has been sufficiently cleared up by the Fathers. But because the impulse of the Spirit leads us to declare the glory of the virgin, and of those contemplating God in the secret of the wilderness—not because we ourselves wish it, but because the place demands it—we believe it is enough if, with His favor...

# John, Fourth Part on the Apocalypse
**U 3**
<meta>catchword: tines</meta>

...to God: at least let us follow through briefly. Behold what the **wedding song** <note>original: "epythalamus"; referring to the Song of Songs.</note> says of the church: **“Beautiful as the moon, choice as the sun”** <note>Song of Songs 6:10</note>. The secretary of the bridegroom <note>Likely referring to John the Apostle as the recorder of divine mysteries.</note> declares this in a similar sign when he says: **“A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet.”** Heaven is the divine scripture, in which all things that are written are shown to be signs for the purpose of signifying; they are written precisely because they are meant to designate something. For so that it may not be tiresome to usefully repeat those things we have already touched upon: why is it that Elijah, contrary to the custom of the fathers, refused to have a wife and children and departed into the desert to contemplate
<margin>2 Kings 2</margin>
the things of God, and finally ascended into heaven in a fiery chariot through a whirlwind? Or why is it that the sons of the prophets,
<margin>2 Kings 4</margin>
leading a **communal monastic life** <term>cenobiticam vitam: A form of monasticism where monks live together in a community rather than as hermits.</term> in Jericho, set Elisha, the successor of Elijah, over themselves as a father, unless it be for that which we see fulfilled in thousands of people in the Church? For if we lift the eyes of our mind to the heaven of the holy scriptures to contemplate this sign—and so that we may know, if it is a sign, what it demonstrates to us by its signifying—we find that **Christ** ascending into heaven is designated in **Elijah**; in **Elisha**, we find the apostolic order upon whom the spirit of Christ rested; and in the church gathered in Jericho, we find the **primitive church**, which was established under the hand of the apostles. This church, because it was built in Jericho (that is, in the **circumcision** <note>Jericho is used here as a symbol for the Jewish people or the Old Law.</note>), which waned like the moon, could not remain there, but immediately passed over to the desert of the Jordan (that is, to the Gentile people). Again: because the common folk—who suffer like the monthly moon and attack the church of spiritual people with their perverse habits—the
<margin>2 Kings 2</margin>
sons of the prophets leave Jericho and flee into the desert. For because the perfect cannot possess the perfection of the solitary life in the city, all who desire that perfection are transferred by the spirit of Jesus into the desert; and certainly so that they may endure the battles and temptations of the Devil there, because no one will be crowned unless
<margin>Matthew 4</margin>
he has competed lawfully. **“Jesus was led,”** it says, **“into the desert by the spirit, to be tempted by the Devil.”** For who are they who suffer greater pains, cries, temptations, and labors of childbirth than those who lead a solitary and communal life in the wilderness?

<column-break/>

Whoever, therefore, is led by the spirit of God so that
<margin>Romans 8</margin>
they strip themselves of earthly resources, whom else do they put on but Jesus Christ, who is the **sun**
<margin>John 1</margin>
of eternal justice illuminating every person coming into this world? We also, as the bride of Christ, have the moon under our feet, because she treads upon the flesh and the glory of the world like a kind of dust, subjecting it to servitude and action, so that the handmaid <note>The flesh/worldly glory.</note> may not be raised up against the mistress <note>The soul/spiritual life.</note>. We also have on our head a **crown of twelve stars**, that is, of the five and seven virtues, by which the church shines crowned; for it is of little use to trample on temporal things unless eternal ones are acquired. For example: You have trampled the moon, you have put on the sun; it remains that you be crowned with virtues. You have fought against unchaste touch and the lust of the eyes. You have fought against the allurements of words which dishonor chaste hearing, against unseemly smell and perverse speech, by which the carnal mind is bound at every moment; you have done this so that you might possess these senses not for your detriment, but as an aid to virtue. As if with **five stars** or precious stones, you have adorned the circle of your crown with virtues of this kind, which are certainly not spiritual by themselves, yet by the help of heavenly grace, they are transferred to the glory of spiritual things. For while you exercise your hands and arms not for seductive embraces but for good work, you have acquired a star for yourself in the battle from your good work. While you
<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
circumcise your eyes so that you do not see a woman to lust after her, but rather apply them to the holy scriptures, you have added another star to the circle of your crown. While you withdraw your ears from idle words and incline them to the word of God, you acquire a third star for yourself. While you keep your mouth from evil speech and voluptuous taste, and rather pronounce the words of God by reading, praying, or preaching. While you scorn meretricious scents and those things which pertain to the luxury of the age, and patiently endure the stenches of the sick: the fourth and fifth [stars] occupy [the places of] your crown...

# Abbreviated Part of the Exposition
### Page 122

...you have completed. For those virtues known to belong to the back of the head <note>original: "occiput"</note> are considered the least and of lesser value in comparison to the other seven stars, which adorn the front part of the head from ear to ear. Of these, the first is **repentance**, the second **mercy**, the third **patience**, the fourth **humility**, the fifth **faith**, the sixth **hope**, and the seventh **charity** <note>In this context, "charity" refers to *caritas*, or divine love.</note>.

**The fear of the Lord** works repentance; the **spirit of piety** works mercy; the **spirit of knowledge** works patience; the **spirit of counsel** works humility; the **spirit of fortitude** works faith; the **spirit of understanding** works hope; and the **spirit of wisdom** works charity. Charity, therefore, is the root and mother of all virtues. She is indeed the **Seraph** <note>original: "Seraphin"</note> who illuminates and ignites the minds of the elect. To her, six wings—representing the six virtues written above—are connected: 1. repentance and 2. mercy; 3. patience and 4. humility; 5. faith and 6. hope. These are the six virtues without which no one comes to charity.

For the two wings with which the body is covered are **repentance** and **mercy**, by which the sins of chosen men are shielded. The two with which the face is covered are **patience** and **humility**, by which they hide their own righteousness to avoid the trap of vainglory. The two with which they fly are **faith** and **hope**, which are the virtues the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> places before the others. In the seventh place is **charity**, which is the greatest, designated in the Seraph itself. For "Seraph" is interpreted as **"a fire"** <note>original: "incendium"; a reference to the Hebrew etymology of Seraphim as "the burning ones."</note>, because charity sets on fire the hearts it fills with the love of God and neighbor.

Let the Catholic man place these things in his heart and diligently depict this image of the spiritual man. Let him know that he cannot be perfect—indeed, he cannot even be saved—if any of these virtues are missing. But he is truly holy and whole who is made perfect in these seven virtues. For without repentance, one cannot be saved, because he who denies he is a sinner is a liar; and he who recognizes himself as a sinner must necessarily repent and groan. Furthermore, he does not receive mercy who does not show it to others; for he who does not forgive his neighbor expects in vain from the righteous Lord

<column-break/>

the forgiveness of his own crimes. And what shall I say of patience, since it is written: *“In your patience you shall possess your souls”* <note>Luke 21:19</note>? And what of humility, which is itself the root and foundation of the virtues? Concerning faith, hope, and charity—without which no Christian religion exists—all the sacred pages, and especially the New Testament, provide a demonstration. For it is necessary that he who desires to be saved should repent, forgive, and be patient and humble; and before all things he must be founded in faith and hope, and above all else, firmly grounded in charity.

These, then, are the seven stars that adorn the front part of the head, and their arrangement is as follows: In the middle of the forehead remains **charity**, which is the root of all virtues. After this, on either side, are **faith** and **hope**; then **patience** and **humility**; and finally, as if by the ears, **repentance** and **mercy** remain. These are sufficient for the perfect man; they are sufficient for the virgin’s crown. These are the twelve stars with which all those who, placed in this exile <note>A common medieval metaphor for life on Earth as an exile from Heaven.</note>, rely on such great virtues are decorated in the heavenly kingdom.

And this indeed concerns individuals. Furthermore, regarding what pertains to the glory of the **Virginal Church**, we must speak of the moon, the sun, and the stars. For our **wedding song** <note>original: "ephythalamus"; referring to the Song of Songs.</note> (which we mentioned above) is known to take the "moon" in a positive sense. Even if that which is designated by the moon has less perfection, it is not therefore to be taken in a bad sense. For just because the moon designates the flesh, or the carnal people, or the state of this world, it does not mean the people or the world are evil, for it is written: *“God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good”* <note>Genesis 1:31</note>. For creatures themselves are not evil, even if the vices by which they are corrupted are evil; otherwise, the glory of the resurrection is promised to us in vain, and we would hope in vain to receive back the bodies we lay down on the last day. Therefore, he who says, *“Beautiful as the moon, choice as the sun, terrible as an army set in array”* <note>Song of Songs 6:10</note>, does not intend to designate anything sinister by the moon here.

It also defends the goodness of the physical world and the body by interpreting the "moon" as a positive, albeit lesser, celestial sign.</summary>

# Joachim on the Apocalypse, Book Four
### Page 138

<margin>Luke</margin> [sh]ined: but in the moon is seen the beauty of virginal flesh; in the sun, spiritual clarity; and in the battle-line of the camps, the orderly arrangement of virtues. In the moon, therefore, is designated the chaste humility of the simple brothers—specifically those who, led by the spirit, obey spiritual men for the sake of God. In the sun is the justice of the "perfect" <note>In medieval theology, the "perfect" often refers to those in the highest state of spiritual life, such as monks or contemplatives.</note>, which is set ablaze by the fire of charity. In the orderly battle-line of the camps is the virtue of brotherly love. Truly, in this book the likeness is quite clear—even if slightly different—according to which the spiritual Church is designated in the Woman Clothed with the Sun. In the moon, she is like **Martha** <note>Martha represents the "active life" of service and ministry.</note>: the subordinate part of the ministers. In the crown of twelve stars are the spiritual fathers, whom the multitude of brothers obey. Their archetype was **Elisha** <note>original: "Helyseus"</note>, who once presided over the multitude of brothers in Jericho. This is why the Blessed **Benedict** <note>St. Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), the father of Western monasticism.</note>—whom Elisha mirrors from the very beginning—placed abbots of that same number over the twelve monasteries he built. He did this to show that the perfection of this number is fulfilled in the monastic life. It is clear that the perfection of this life belonged to the **fourth age** <note>Joachim of Fiore divided history into "ages" or "times"; the fourth age here likely refers to the era of the great monastic founders.</note>, for Blessed Benedict truly shone in the fourth age, even though his institution preceded the fifth age, for which it would be even more beneficial. Therefore, the spiritual fathers are at the head; the weaker ones are at the feet; and those in the middle are suspended in contemplation between both lives. Those at the head hold the place of Christ; the middle contemplatives take the part of **Mary** <note>Mary of Bethany, representing the "contemplative life."</note>; and the obedient ones at the feet fulfill the service of **Martha**. Even in the female sex, these three types are commended. But why is it that the **Ark of the Covenant** was seen first, and then the Woman Clothed with the Sun, if not because the signs of the Old Testament agree with the signs of the New Testament? Surely in that Ark, the tablets of the testament, **Aaron’s rod** which had budded, and the manna were kept inside. These were a type <note>A "type" is a person or thing in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note>—without a doubt—of the Only-begotten God whom the Virgin guarded in her womb, and who did not depart from her sacred breast even after birth. For He is the Word of God, who is most highly commended

<column-break/>

in such things; He is the rod of power which the Lord sent out of Zion; He is the "hidden manna" for those who love Him. Therefore, the first person of that Church—whom this woman signifies—was the Virgin who gave birth to the Son of God. The **Dragon** believed he would devour Him, but he could not, because He was caught up to God and to His throne. For He was not only a man (as the Devil estimated from the beginning), but He who is true man and true God—the same whom the Father begot from eternity and the Virgin gave birth to in time. Truly, on that day when the Lord suffered, the holy mother Church—Mary, that is, along with her Apostles and the faithful—sustained no small amount of bitterness, just as the Son of God himself predicted and attested when He said: *"A woman, when she is in labor, has sorrow because her hour has come."* Let no one, therefore, think that Mary was exempt from the pain of birth; for she who brought forth the boy without physical pain, spiritually labored for Him once He had become a man. Thus, Christ emerged from the narrow straits of the ecclesiastical womb and reached His kingdom. The Dragon believed he could swallow Him up like the others at the hour of His "birth"—that is, in the hour when, by dying, He paid the debt of Adam—if only He were not (as the Dragon doubted) the true Son of God. For there follows:

# Abbot's Part of the Exposition
### T.j.

...of the beast: which is the dragon’s. But because it is written below: *And there are seven kings* <note>Revelation 17:10</note>, it clearly shows that the seven heads of the beast designate that sevenfold multitude of false ones <note>original: "pſeudoorum," likely referring to false prophets or pseudo-apostles who mimic the sevenfold Spirit of God in a perverted way</note>. Truly, the heads of the dragon are seven kings who, because they act in the dragon's stead, can be called not only "heads" in a simple sense, but even "heads of heads." For just as a certain episcopal church is called the "head" of its subordinate churches, and yet the bishop is the head of that specific church, so it is in the multitude of the unfaithful who go toward perdition: those peoples who boldly fought against the Church in their malice became "heads," and even more so the kings who presided over those same peoples are called the "heads of the dragon." The "body" of the dragon, however, is the innumerable multitude of all the reprobate. This is the only difference: although the beast has seven heads and the dragon likewise, the heads of the dragon—according to this understanding—are not to be distinguished one-by-one by the individual heads of the beast. Rather, they come by another way and a different path, which we shall discuss in the sixth part of this book, where there will be a more appropriate place for this, as the Lord grants. Therefore, the seven heads are the seven names of tyrants who have succeeded one another against the Church throughout the ages. The ten horns, however, are ten kings who (as the angel says below) are yet to reign. Truly, the "tail" is the final tyrant who (as the prophet Ezekiel testifies) is to come at the end of the age. <margin>Gog. Ezekiel 38</margin> What the "third part" signifies was stated in the third part of this work. It should also be noted what is said here: *On his heads were seven diadems* <note>Revelation 12:3</note>, and later concerning the horns of the beast: *And upon his horns, ten diadems* <note>Revelation 13:1</note>. But if we take their diadems to mean nothing other than royal pride, it clearly gives us to understand that the "heads of the dragon" are to be understood as kings, not peoples; whereas the "heads of the beast" are peoples, not kings. And therefore, when he says *Upon the heads of the dragon, seven diadems*, he surely intended the seven kings to be understood by the heads—just as he described the ten horns of the beast as wearing diadems to show that those ten were kings. Or rather, "as if" they were kings; for they are truly kings who are not subverters, but rulers of the faithful. Whence it is said below: *The ten horns which you saw on the beast are ten kings, who have not yet received a kingdom, but they shall receive power as kings for one hour after the beast* <note>Revelation 17:12</note>. However, one must be careful above all else: when you hear of the "woman clothed with the sun," and the "son of the woman," the "dragon," and the "beast," and similar things—especially when the parts are divided into species—do not think of them as something momentary or as being entirely completed all at once. Rather, see them as a work, whether good or evil, which indeed begins once, but is only consummated after a long time. Therefore, do not imagine that the dragon was at the beginning exactly as he is described in this book, but rather as he was destined to become through the ages. For it would not be understood as "prophecy" if it only predicted past and present things, and not rather the future. If, however, one asks who these seven heads of the dragon are, or who they are thought to be, we have sufficiently arranged this in the summary <term>summa: a condensed overview or systematic handbook</term> of this book. But soon the "sign of all" was seen in heaven: because those who are bent downward, so that they look only at the "earth" of the literal letter, cannot see spiritual mysteries. But those who look back toward "heaven" perceive that all these things are "signs"—doubtless because they were written in the canonical books to signify something. It follows:

<column-break/>

But if he had fully grasped those things which were written about this, he would by no means have sought to discover whether this was so or not by such crafty arguments. Therefore, the mystery of the Lord's Incarnation was not revealed to him in its entirety—he who [wondered] if He were the Son of God...

# Joachim’s Fourth [Part] on the Apocalypse
### 157

...doubting: he introduces the testimony of scripture: as if he were waiting to see if he were not the Christ: he hastened to snatch him to torments as one contrary to himself. If indeed he clearly recognized him to be the son of God, he would have desisted from his persecution—if, however, his malice would have allowed him to desist. But in whatever way it was done, we know this clearly: that he entered into the heart of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot <note>original: "Jude Symonis Schariothis"</note>, and led him to the height of his damnation, even to the torments of the Passion. Why was this? So that he might devour him just as he devoured the others. **He stood** (it says) **before the woman.** What is meant by "he stood before the woman"? He stood *against* the woman—that is, against the Church. For those who wish to act against people passing by, or those desiring to do something, prepare themselves before them to resist them. But what do you think you are doing, oh unhappy one? You are able to kill Christ (by his own permission) because he is man; yet you cannot hold him, because he is God. For a lion was sent to kill the prophet, but he was not permitted to devour his corpse <note>A reference to 1 Kings 13, where a lion kills a disobedient prophet but does not eat the body or the donkey</note>. You did not fear to kill Christ; but you destroyed yourself—not the Lord—once again with that spear. You thought to swallow the son of the laboring Church, but you were not permitted to do this; because when you were cast down and defeated, he was snatched up to God and to his throne. If you ask why the Church of the apostles is called the mother of Christ, ask the son of God, Christ himself. For when someone said to him: *Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you,* he immediately responded and said: *Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?* And extending his hands toward his disciples, he said: *Behold my mother and my brothers.* <note>Matthew 12:47-49</note> But what of the labor that is mentioned? When the moment of his Passion was imminent (as I have already said), he testified to this among other things, saying: *A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come.* <note>John 16:21</note> Thus the Church is the mother of Christ; and she who bore him in the flesh is from the Church; and therefore in Mary, who is the primary person <note>or "first persona"</note> of the Church, the son of the Church, Christ, is also born corporally. And because all the faithful

<column-break/>

are one body in Christ, we too are all his sons in Christ—of whom Christ is the Son—according to that word of the apostle: *If you are Christ’s, then you are the seed of Abraham.* <note>Galatians 3:29</note> But one thing pertains to the head, and another to the members in a certain respect; one thing pertains to labor, and another looks toward glory. For that we are sons of the virgin and sons of God—if indeed we are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ—is the house of God and our happiness. Yet that the woman is said to "labor" is indeed a gift of God: to be able to act patiently in birth; and yet in this very thing the Church merits something for which she may be crowned. In a wonderful way—and as if by opposites—these two things agree in her: **virgin** and **childbirth**, so that two kinds of perfection might be shown to come together as one: namely, to have the perfection of justice, and yet to be scourged for justice as if for injustice. I shall say something, then, according to the flesh. If she is a virgin, why is she tortured in labor? Or if she gives birth, how is she a virgin? But clearly both are required from the Church: that she should be both a virgin and one who gives birth, so that there may be fulfilled in her that great mystery of Mary, who both carried a son in her womb and did not lose the glory of virginity. Mary therefore bore her only-begotten son; looking at him at last hanging on the cross, she labored—together with the Church of the apostles—not without groaning; yet he was born in another kingdom and made the firstborn of the dead. Truly, according to the symbolic <note>original: "typicum"</note> understanding, just as the Church of the teachers <note>original: "ecclesia doctorum"</note> is designated in the woman, so in the son of the woman is designated the army of all the righteous who are to reign with Christ and sit with him in judgment (as the Lord himself says in this book): *To him who overcomes, I will give to sit on my throne, just as I also overcame and sat down.* <note>Revelation 3:21</note> For Christ ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, so that—having been raised on high—he might endure as a terrible judge for the one who, as a dragon, thought to devour him at birth. These things concern the son of the woman. What of the woman herself?

The author argues that the "labor pains" of the Church represent the suffering of the righteous, which leads to their eventual glory and role in divine judgment.</summary>
