# Part of the Abbot's Exposition
### 157

<margin>Chapter 4</margin>
**And the woman** (it says) **fled into the wilderness: where she had a place prepared by God: so that there he might nourish her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.** <note>This period of 1260 days is a key prophetic timeframe in the Book of Revelation, which Joachim of Fiore famously interpreted as representing a specific era of Church history.</note>

¶ What this number signifies is clearly declared in the book which we published specifically regarding it and according to it. <note>Joachim is likely referring to his work *The Harmony of the Old and New Testaments*.</note> However, what the woman’s flight into the wilderness means will be discussed in the repetition <note>Joachim often uses "repetition" to refer to the way Revelation circles back to the same historical events from different perspectives.</note>. For it is better demonstrated there than here. Indeed, this very thing is written twice, though with different words, with that "great battle" placed in between—the battle in which the Dragon was cast down. As we shall show below, that battle belonged to the holy martyrs. For it is said of them, not of the angels: **And they overcame him because of the blood of the Lamb, and because of the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives even unto death.** 

This repetition is not without its mystery; the fact that the battle of the martyrs is placed in the middle of the account of the Woman is for a great mystical reason. For there are two kinds of flowers that Scripture commends above all others: **roses**, which designate the holy martyrs, and **lilies**, which designate the sacred virgins because of the whiteness of their chastity. If you ask where salvation proceeded from, **virginity** is found <note>referring to the Virgin Mary</note>. If you ask upon what Mother Church was founded, **martyrdom** is found. Indeed, the Virgin preceded the martyrs, and the martyrs have followed the virgins. 

In this way, our City <note>the New Jerusalem or the perfected Church</note> provides peace to all her children, because in her there is one peace for all and a common joy for everyone. Inasmuch as the virgins are "registered" among the martyrs, and the martyrs among the virgins, in that vision of supreme peace, he who is last shall be first, and the first shall be last. This is just as the Only-Begotten Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found, in turn, to be "registered" to one another in the mysteries. 

Among these is that which Christ says through the prophet: **"Behold, now the Lord and his Spirit have sent me."** <note>original: "Ecce nunc misit me dominus & spiritus eius" (Isaiah 48:16)</note> Afterward, He speaks of the same Spirit through Himself, saying: **"He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you."** <note>John 16:14</note> Certainly, if a likeness for this matter is sought, the life of contemplative virgins seems to look properly toward the Holy Spirit—which is why those who live chastely are called "spiritual"—while the triumph of the martyrs is properly referred to Christ. 

Therefore, it is no wonder if virginity, though first preferred over martyrdom, is in the second instance placed after it, and vice versa. There remains a sign so great and evident that it is not from men, but directed from heaven. For the holy martyrs have the Only-Begotten Son of God, who was made "a little lower than the angels" <note>Psalm 8:5</note>, and who voluntarily humbled Himself to the Holy Spirit so that it might be said of Him: **"He was conceived by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary."** Yet, after His passion, He received honor from that same Spirit, just as He had promised, according to what we said above: *He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine.* 

It was necessary, then, for the holy Virgin first to become the mother of all holy martyrs, and then for the holy martyrs to go before the companies of virgins. This ensures that in this part of the mystery, the martyrs would not disagree in any way with the Son of God, nor the virgins with the Holy Spirit. Indeed, such is the simplicity among the saints in that City that they believe one another to be greater than themselves; such is the fire of charity that they attribute dignity to others rather than themselves—indeed, they even desire it for them. 

The holy martyrs also belong by a certain property to the Son of God, and the virgins to the Virgin Mother—not by a difference of sex, but of virtue. For truly, the strength of the male is the proper beauty of the woman. Since these things are so, what does the Son do when He is being brought forth? Does He not grieve, but only the Mother who gives birth? On the contrary: because this is clear, for no one doubts that the martyrs endured torments after Christ. That other matter comes much more into question—

# John: Fourth Part on the Apocalypse
### 156

...comes. Why is the woman said to be tormented <note>original: "cruciari"</note>, she who certainly did not die through martyrdom, but paid the debt of the flesh through a peaceful and tranquil end? But alas! Who could know how much pain tormented the soul of the Virgin when she saw her own son hanging on the cross—affected by the bitterness of gall, given vinegar to drink, and subject to various other insults—to whom she was not permitted to give even water to drink, nor to show any kind of service (as is usually done for anyone who is dying). Anyone who would weigh these and similar things with a pious mind would think her torment greater in weight than even that of Christ; for surely Christ was tormented in that flesh (which is a heavier burden), but she was tormented in her mind. Even if He grieved, He nevertheless fulfilled it willingly, for which purpose He had also come; yet the inner bowels of her piety <note>The "viscera" or "bowels" was a common medieval metaphor for the deepest seat of emotion and compassion.</note> did not allow her to feel the same thing without agony. 

Therefore, he who is born is tormented, but this happens only once; the mother, however, is tormented and groans through each of her offspring. Correcty, then, the torment is ascribed to the Church for her suffering children; because while they suffer for themselves individually, she (as I have already said) is tormented and groans through each one—and frequently the mother herself imitates those children over whom she weeps. There is also another kind of birth: that which the Apostle <note>Paul</note> describes and ascribes to himself when he says to those whom he had fathered for Christ and who had nearly fallen away: **My little children, for whom I labor in birth again until Christ is formed in you.** But in that case, children are birthed through the labor of preaching in the bosom of the sweating Church; here, they are birthed by passing from the world to the fatherland <note>The "fatherland" (patria) refers to Heaven.</note>. There they are birthed through faith; here through blood. There so that they may take up the cross of Christ; here so that they may attain the reward of the cross they have carried. And because the minds of the holy Virgins are in the heavens—and although they live on earth, they lead the life of that city which is above—they themselves are also tormented in the sufferings of the holy <term>Martyrs</term> <note>original: "Martyrum"; those who bear witness by death.</note>. They are able to weigh this all the more because the martyrs are with them; and the more they love, the more they grieve. And because a pious love shows them to be true mothers, to these same mothers in the king-

<column-break/>

-dom of God they are born, their passion having been released. This is surely because the latter pass over to that place through love where the former already are; and the latter come to that place after death where the former rest even before death through contemplation. 

It must be noted, however, and scrutinized with the utmost discussion, that Christ, while placed on the cross, gave another son to His mother in His place: namely, John the Evangelist. In him were designated not those who pass from this world through martyrdom, but those whom we mentioned above; to whom that saying surely refers which was spoken by Christ to Simon <note>Peter</note> concerning John: **So I will that he remain until I come.** Not only that, but also what the mother of James and John requested from the Lord—namely, that her two sons should sit, one at His right hand and the other at His left—pertains not a little to this matter. For surely the order of <term>Martyrs</term>, signified in James, bore the left hand of passion; and the order of those who contemplate <note>The "contemplative" life, often associated with monks and virgins.</note> is placed at the right hand of Christ. But the place compels us to look upon the battle of the <term>Martyrs</term>, not unmindful of that sentiment (expressed in the special parts of the book) where we have often said that general things are touched upon, and that there is nothing special in the parts without the generalities.

### Abb. Part of the Exposition

Properly, a host of angels is sent to the aid of virgins, because virginity is a relative and a friend to the angels. Listen diligently, O virgin of Christ; listen attentively, O soldier of Christ. For he <note>Likely referring to God or the spiritual struggle itself</note> does not seek out the idle for a struggle of such great weight; he does not approve of the lazy or the lukewarm, but of those who are strong in battle and fervent in faith. A battle took place in the church of the saints <note>original: "ecclesia sanctorum"</note>, which is very often called "heaven" and the "kingdom of heaven." Now, the holy Church is called "heaven" because it stands on high in comparison to the synagogue <note>The author uses "synagogue" here as a historical/theological contrast to the Church, common in medieval exegesis</note>, which desires only earthly things, and in comparison to those men who, although they received the sign of the heavenly man in baptism, nevertheless follow the earthly man rather than the heavenly one. 

Yet the battle took place "in heaven" because the enemy who attacks the faithful is hidden, and the mystery for which the battle is fought is also hidden. The Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> surely encouraged the faithful toward this battle and instructed them to conduct themselves prudently when he said: *Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers of the air, the darkness of these times, and against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places* <note>original: "Non est nobis colluctatio aduersus carnem & sanguinem..." quoting Ephesians 6:12</note>. But was the enemy only invisible? Were the henchmen of that enemy not also invisible, attacking the visible soldiers of Christ? Observe diligently the order of the battles and the soldiers, how the ranks of Christ are directed against the depraved ranks, whether for the chastity of the body or for the integrity of the faith preserved in the heart. 

Michael is the prince of the heavenly army appointed by the Lord. The Devil usurped for himself a kingdom over the evil angels. There, just as they are invisible, they also battle invisibly. But what follows was not said concerning the angels: *And they overcame him by the word of their testimony, and they loved not their lives unto death* <note>original: "Et ipsi vicerunt eum..." quoting Revelation 12:11</note>. This, I say, was not said of angels, but of the martyrs, who in truth did not love their lives even unto death, according to the voice of Truth saying: *He who hates his life in this world keeps it for eternal life* <note>quoting John 12:25</note>. What then do we say this means—that in the battle of the angels, the martyrs are credited with the victory—unless it is that good angels assist good men, and evil ones goad the wicked so that they may fall more deeply? Therefore, there was another in the Church of Christ besides Michael, a prince appointed by the Lord: namely, Peter and his successors, as the present day of this age still proves. Concerning him, this was also shown to be written (which I remember having explained in the *Work of Harmony* <note>original: "opere concordie," likely referring to Joachim of Fiore’s 'Concordia Novi et Veteris Testamenti'</note>): *At that time shall Michael rise up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people* <note>quoting Daniel 12:1</note>. 

Nevertheless, in the synagogue of Satan, Herod the Great held the leadership, acting there in the place of the dragon. Leaving the succession at last to his son Herod, he ultimately deserved to have the princes of the Romans as successors. For when the Tetrarch Herod, the slayer of James, was removed by an unhappy death, the most wicked Emperor Nero soon took up the blade, lest he who had escaped unharmed through the blood-stained gates of Herod should escape the hands of Nero unpunished. Therefore, Michael was the prelate of the angels, fighting in Peter, the prince of Christians. And the Devil was the prince of demons, fighting in Herod, the prelate of the Jews. See in these battles the fourfold crowds of combatants, the terrible clashes of those resisting through the years. Truly a great battle. Truly a singular contest, in which the unfaithful fight with the faithful, and the heavenly spirits battle with the ministers of hell.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Apocalypse, specifically interpreting the spiritual battle in heaven (Revelation 12) through the lens of the Old Testament Book of Job. It explains how Satan's role as "accuser" was revoked through the victory of Christ and the martyrs.</meta>

### John [the Fourth?] on the Apocalypse

<margin>Job 1</margin> before the Lord: Satan was also present among them. If the assembly of the sons of God is believed to be the Church of the holy ones—since the Church is said to be "heaven"—and Satan is described as having been present among the sons of God, then it is certainly shown that Satan held a place in heaven while he had not yet been cast out from the human race. This was because the logic (so to speak) of his own legal right, which he was obliged to seek out, demanded it. In that one man alone <note>Referring to Christ</note> he found nothing to search for; he who was born and remained without sin, and who could truly say: <margin>John</margin> *For the prince of this world comes, and in me he has nothing.* <note>original: "Venit enim princeps mundi huius..." John 14:30</note> And because he did not fear to lay hands upon him in whom nothing of his own existed, just like <margin>Kings</margin> Goliath, whom David killed, he was struck down by his own blade. 

It says he was present among them—that is, among the sons of God—even Satan. But for what purpose? Was it to praise the Creator of all good things alongside the others? <margin>No.</margin> For what then? To detract from faith, and to accuse the works of the elect. It says it was so he might accuse them before the sight of God, using that wondrous type of accusation by which he sought to cloud the simplicity of holy Job. This is why the Only-Begotten of God, at the approaching time of his Passion, said to Peter: *Behold, Satan has desired you, that he may sift you like wheat.* <note>Luke 22:31</note> Therefore, just as the Devil sought out Holy Job, so he sought out the holy apostles and holy martyrs, to sift them like wheat and find something in them to object to, so that he might show everyone to be worthy of rejection. 

And just as (with God’s permission) he struck Job from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, so he expended almost every kind of torment upon the holy martyrs. But because (by the Lord’s grace) they were proven by the fire of tribulation and found to be in their torments purer than refined gold, by the just judgment of God that cruel dragon was cast down to the earth. That ancient enemy was hurled down from on high, so that no place was found for him in heaven any longer, because after this he could by no means stand present in the sight of the Lord to accuse the elect as he did before—those who not only gave <margin>Job</margin> "skin for skin" <note>Job 2:4</note> but most willingly gave even themselves. For what more could they do for the testing of their faith than to lay down their lives to gain Christ? Who then shall bring an accusation against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is there to condemn? 

But what kind of justice is this? Is it like the justice of the Law, in which he who performed it lived by it? Far from it. Rather, it is the kind of justice that can descend from heaven: namely, faith that works through charity. However, there are many within the holy Church who worship and venerate the Lord for the reason that they see themselves prospering in all their affairs, because the prosperity of this life smiles upon them in everything pleasant. And indeed, it is necessary to give thanks to the Creator for temporal benefits, especially since nothing is worse than ingratitude among men or before God; yet that thanksgiving is far removed from the thanksgiving offered for spiritual gifts and the kingdom of God—as far as the east is from the west. Such worship of God is judged to be of little use. For he who worships and fears God only because God imparts temporal goods to him does not worship God truly, but as if deceitfully. For if those things fail for which he was worshiping God, and spiritual apathy <term>accidia: a state of spiritual listlessness, boredom, or "sloth" regarding divine things, common in medieval moral theology</term> supervenes, his devotion is changed. All that thanksgiving—as if from a dried-up spring from which it used to flow—breathes its last, because he was offering it for carnal things rather than spiritual gifts. 

The ancient enemy, understanding this perfectly, based the beginning of his accusation on this, saying: <margin>Job</margin> *Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not hedged him in, and his house, and all his substance round about? You have blessed the works of his hands, and his possession has increased on the earth. But stretch out your hand a little, and touch all that he possesses, and see if he does not curse you to your face.* <note>Job 1:9-11</note> And there are some who, in the loss of temporal things—especially children—are driven by a spirit of blasphemy against the judgment of the Almighty (may God keep this far from the hearts of the faithful!). But fearing lest they provoke the wrath of God against themselves, they are afraid to pour out into speech the poison conceived in the heart. It is certain that they incur the judgment of vengeance, those who do not pour out the evil they have conceived...

### [Abbreviated] Part of the Exposition

...they [obey] because they fear: and they are restrained only by the threats of punishment, rather than being tempered by the sweetness of love. For those of this kind are accustomed sometimes to force themselves to appear as if they are offering thanks in prosperity, while in the loss of things, they pay back God with the same fear of punishment. And so it happens that while they already lie low in the eyes of the Heavenly Spectator because of the bitterness of their minds, they still seem to stand firm through patience in the sight of men. Therefore, by this second kind of accusation, the Devil <margin>Job</margin> strove to cloud the righteousness of holy Job when he said: *Skin for skin; and all that a man has, he will give for his life.* <note>original: "Pellem pro pelle..." Job 2:4. This is a famous and difficult idiom; the Devil suggests Job is only patient because his own body hasn't been touched yet.</note> But it may be asked: what did that hidden adversary want for himself in those words? Why would he accuse secret hearts in the presence of the Searcher of internal minds, as if God could not know the truth unless the Devil had reported it?

But this is easily clear to our understanding if we vigilantly weigh the pride of a haughty mind. For when we wish to more harshly rebuke those who despise justice, we set before them the lives of obedient brothers as a contrast. Thus, those who cannot be overcome by words or warnings may be shamed when convicted by comparisons to others—so that they might either correct themselves if they are correctable, or, if they are incorrigible, they may be silenced. But it does not always happen this way. It does not; for where the life of the good makes progress, the wickedness of the reprobate grows beyond measure. For instead of their wickedness being overcome by the comparison to the good, they soon fashion derogatory words and insults against them, and pervert with sinister slanders whatever those good men suffer for the sake of justice. Why, then, does God commend the righteousness of the holy man in the presence of the "Father of Lies," <note>Referring to the Devil</note> except to confound his pride by reproach? For the Devil, having abandoned the grace of simplicity, chose to be the author of all wickedness. But to him who had fallen by deserting the truth in every way, and who was therefore incorrigible, the Devil leapt forward to accuse the one whom such great authority

<column-break/>

had commended. He did this so that while he revealed the infamy of another, he might excuse his own; and while he contended to prove that no one is truly righteous, he might absolve himself from the singular mark of his own treachery. For as long as he does not allow his own confusion to be reproached, he not only destroys (as far as he is concerned) the goodness of the creature—which is from God—by detracting from it, but in this very act he is convicted of indirectly insulting the Creator. He implies that God made such a creature who, even if he wanted to, could never stand in the path of truth—as if it were impossible for God to give righteousness to a creature to whom He gave existence, or to make one just to whom He was able to grant the gift of being a creature. Therefore the Devil said: *Skin for skin; and all that a man has, he will give for his life.* This is as if it were said: "Job does not endure patiently because he fears God with a son's love <note>Theologians distinguish between 'filial fear' (love of a child for a parent) and 'servile fear' (dread of a slave for a master).</note>, nor does he keep silent from blasphemy because he purely loves his Maker, but he restrains himself from cursing only so that You do not punish him more harshly as a blasphemer. Otherwise, put forth Your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and you will see if he does not bless You to Your face." <note>The word "bless" here is a biblical euphemism for "curse."</note> "If it is not as I say," he says, "the proof is at hand. Begin to afflict and torture him, and then his innocence will appear." Therefore the righteous man is handed over to the wicked, the God-fearing to the unjust—not so that the Lord might test his faith (for to Him all things are naked and open), but so that the righteous man’s merits might advance through his trials, and the Devil’s lie might be proven by the evidence of facts. Indeed, because the Devil is not worthy of divine inspiration—such that he would voluntarily confess himself a liar as a humble man would, or turn from a lie by the mere word of God once he has been hardened—it pertained to the glory of the true God to raise up a soldier against the enemy. Thus, once the enemy was overcome in the field, he would depart defeated and confounded by the very experience of the truth, after the victory of such a great battle had been won. For what then? Was God boasting in His creature as if he were innocent of his own power? Far from it. But He boasted because He was able to make that creature...

# John's Fourth Vision in the Apocalypse

...the guilty one: if he had stood in the truth by confessing his own meagerness and poverty. But because he—who is the father of lies—scorned to do this, he became one who feared no one; and he attempted to attribute this very thing <note>referring to his own fallen state</note> to a corrupted nature rather than to his own choice, which he by no means used well, but voluntarily abused. For the property of truth is this: to recognize that there is no good except from God alone, and that with Him, who is the highest truth, there is no iniquity. If you recognize and confess this, you are close to receiving the gift that you cannot have from yourself. But you cannot have even that good except from God. 

From where, then, does judgment come? Because both angel and man had this [truth] and lost it—by being proud, certainly. But the former [the angel] lost it irretrievably; the latter [man] for a time. Since this is so, what wonder is it, O apostate spirit, if you did not receive the spirit of love? For to receive this, you did not stand in the truth. Truly (as the Savior says): *He was a murderer from the beginning* <note>original: "Ille homicida erat ab initio" (John 8:44)</note> because he who hates is a murderer. He was (he says) a murderer, and he did not stand in the truth because, infected by the bruise of hatred, he refused to acknowledge his own guilt and to blame himself for the fact that he began to be evil. Instead, by thinking things contrary to the truth, he became the **Devil** and **Satan**. 

Therefore, every good is from God: from God comes the grace of love and the gift of justice; but so that the reprobate <note>those who are rejected or unrepentant</note> do not receive this, they refuse it through the wickedness of their own choice. Because the elect of God recognize that they have by no means received such good from themselves but from the Giver of all good things, the Devil strives in vain to accuse those whom God justifies. For the love of God even surpasses **Gehenna** <term>Gehenna: a historical term for Hell, derived from a valley outside Jerusalem</term>, if it had been permitted to enter it for a time. For love conquers all things; it endures all things. For how else would the Apostle show that love is the cause of victory, saying: *Who shall bring an accusation against the elect of God?* <note>original: "Quis accusabit aduersus electos dei?" (Romans 8:33)</note> Immediately he followed this by saying: *Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?* <note>original: "Quis igitur nos separabit a charitate Christi..." (Romans 8:35)</note> And so that he might impress this very point more firmly upon our hearts by the authority of the elders, he added: *As it is written: For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.* <note>original: "Sicut scriptum est. Propter te mortificamur tota die..." (Psalm 44:22 / Romans 8:36)</note> Behold how the witnesses of the truth agree with one another! What the Apostle says—"Who shall bring an accusation against the elect of God?" and "for your sake we are being put to death all day long"—is what John reveals he heard when he says:

<column-break/>

<margin>Revelation 12:10-12</margin>
> And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying: "Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of His Christ have come, because the accuser of our brothers—who accused them in the sight of our God day and night—has been cast out. And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives even unto death. Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them." <note>original: "Et audiui vocem magnam in cælo..."</note>

<margin>Genesis 4</margin> <note>The author likely references Genesis 4 here to compare the blood of the martyrs to the blood of Abel, which "cried out" from the ground.</note>
If a limit was set by the just God upon this great battle—which took place in the church of God in the days of **Emperor Constantine** <note>Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD), the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity, ending the era of state-led persecution</note>—then this voice of the saints' exultation must certainly be referred to his time. For both those who conquered were crowned with glory and honor, and those holy ones who remained, encouraged by his [the enemy's] ruin, began to fight more strongly against him. 

Furthermore, Saint **John** heard a "loud voice" in heaven because men of contemplation—those who could understand how great a fear it is to fight with the author of evils—perceived that a great joy of the righteous had been created in the church of God concerning the victory of the saints and **Martyrs** and the ruin of **Satan**, as they confessed to the Lord and said:

# Part of the Exposition

**Now salvation and power have come for our God, and the authority of his Christ: for the accuser of our brothers has been cast out, who accused them before our God day and night.** <note>original: "Nunc facta est salus & virtus deo nostro..." (Revelation 12:10)</note> What does "day and night" mean? It means in times of prosperity and in times of adversity. This salvation and power of our God and the authority of His Christ is said to have been accomplished, as it were, from the time of **Constantine** <note>Emperor Constantine the Great (reigned 306–337 AD), who legalized Christianity</note>; specifically, when the accuser of God's chosen ones was cast out. From that time on, the Church began to be organized for the salvation and strength of many, and the **vicar of Christ Jesus** <note>The Pope or the leadership of the Church acting as Christ's representative</note> began to have free power to enact justice among the nations and corrections among the peoples. 

Because of this, the heavens rejoiced, as did those who dwell in them. Peace was given to the ranks of the saints, providing a kind of "sabbath" rest from that most atrocious temptation of the **Devil**, through which he had hostiley sought to claim his ancient rights even over holy men. The ranks of the holy martyrs rejoiced in their triumph, and those who were ready to follow them into death rejoiced in the peace. **Rejoice** (he says) **O heavens, and you who dwell in them.** Rejoice, you cohorts of holy martyrs, and you who desire to reach their glory through the palm of martyrdom. For those who conquered the enemy became, as it were, "heavens," and those who contemplated their triumphal victories became "dwellers of the heavens," seeing that it was possible to become like one of them in the struggle they so ardently desired. 

Therefore, the accusation of the Devil—which was first defeated through the patience of **Job**—signified the accusation that was later overcome by the victory of the martyrs; for they gave up not only temporal goods but even their very souls and lives willingly for the Catholic faith. Hence, that ancient enemy was cast out of heaven so that he would no longer be permitted to stand among the sons of God to claim rights over them as he used to do—he who even presumed to assault the God of heaven Himself to see if he had any right over Him. 

And he was **cast down** (he says) **to the earth**—that is, into those who savor earthly things and lust after earthly things. It cannot be said of these people that the Devil does not have much influence over them, just as he does over the unfaithful people signified by the **sea**. For it belongs to the just judgment of God that, while those who are upright of heart are snatched from the Devil’s jaws, he is permitted to demand his "rights" over all others. Thus it is added:

> **Woe to the earth and the sea: because the Devil has come down to you having great wrath, knowing that he has but a short time.** <note>Revelation 12:12</note>

Because he was defeated by the martyrs and suffered the beginning of his ruin at their hands, he certainly realized that his time was short, and the reign of his kingdom was merely momentary. Therefore, he began to act more cruelly toward his own followers after being defeated by the saints. He seeks out those who obey him—treating them as if they were "talents" or payments of wickedness—so that he might recover in them what he grieves to have lost in the saints, making them twice the children of hell than they were before. Nevertheless, because the humility of the resting Church seemed closer to the "earth," he presumed to attempt a third battle against her.

***

### Here ends the second distinction. Here begins the third distinction.

> **And after the dragon saw that he was cast down to the earth, he pursued the woman who brought forth the male child.** <note>Revelation 12:13</note>

After the Devil saw that he had lost the opportunity to accuse the holy martyrs and defame their faith (having been defeated in battle), he prepared new kinds of weapons to violate the simplicity of the faith held by the Church. He who previously thirsted for the blood of the saints—once he saw himself laid low by the shedding of that blood—trusted that he could overthrow the faithful through another kind of persecution, targeting them as people less skilled and unlearned in knowledge. For under the time of Constantine, while the Church was triumphing, the blasphemous **Arian heresy** <note>The belief proposed by Arius that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal or one in substance with God the Father</note> soon rose up in opposition. The **cunning enemy**, having been defeated in faith...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the twelfth chapter of Revelation (the Apocalypse), specifically focusing on the flight of the Woman (the Church) from the Dragon (the Devil) and her refuge in the wilderness. ### John’s Fourth Part on the Apocalypse

...the crafty enemy desired: to dissolve the solidity of faith; he turned his vows toward war. But what are you doing, O impious one? What are you composing, you inventor of deceit? The Lord has moved to snatch the humble from your jaws through spiritual doctrine—He who was able to make the strong in faith invincible in their torments. For it follows:

<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
**And two wings of a great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the desert, to her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, away from the face of the Serpent.** <note>original: "Et datæ sūt mulieri duæ alæ aquilæ magnæ..." (Revelation 12:14)</note>

Whether here as the wings of an eagle, or in the Psalms as the wings of a dove, these symbolize the grace of contemplation. Indeed, the Psalmist had long ago predicted this in the person of the Church fleeing from the face of the dragon: <margin>Psalms</margin> **"Who will give me wings like a dove? And I will fly away and find rest?"** <note>Psalm 55:6</note> **"Behold,"** he says, **"I have fled far away, and I stayed in the wilderness, waiting for Him who saves me from the faint-heartedness of spirit and the storm."** <note>Psalm 55:7-8</note> There are two wings given to the woman, by which she herself can be raised on high and flee from the sight of the dragon; for there are two virtues especially necessary above all others for those who desire to know the truth: namely, **Wisdom** which is from above, and the **Charity** <note>Divine Love</note> of God. One of these—Wisdom—is ascribed by a certain property of mystery to **Christ**, whom the Apostle calls "the power of God and the wisdom of God." <note>1 Corinthians 1:24</note> The other—Charity—is ascribed to the **Holy Spirit**, of whom the Apostle says, "God is love." Without these two virtues, there can be no perfection of contemplation; for just as the brightness of the sun and its heat allow the cultivator of the land to work well, so these two gifts are necessary for the contemplative. These wings of contemplation, therefore, were given to the Church of Christ, so that she might fly higher by contemplating heavenly things and, by fleeing from the cares of the world, might avoid the suggestions of the devil. As for the fact that she fled into the desert or into solitude: although to remain in the desert means to rest from worldly works, according to the words of the Psalmist:

<column-break/>

**"Be still and see that the Lord is sweet,"** <note>Psalm 46:10 / Psalm 34:8. Original: "Vacate & videte..."</note> nevertheless, in the truth of those times, many chose the **hermitic life** <note>The life of a hermit or monk living in isolation</note>, deciding it was better to live with beasts in the woods than to participate with the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arianism, a major early Christian heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ</note> in the marketplace. Likewise **Elijah** <margin>Elijah</margin> <note>original: "Helyas"</note> in the times of the kings, when he saw the people of Israel devoted to error for a "time, and times, and half a time," <note>A symbolic period of 3.5 years or 42 months representing a time of trial</note> withdrew himself from their sight. He received food for his flesh first from ravens and then from a widow woman. Because he was a prefiguration of the virginal and hermitic life—in the number of years, in his flight, in the duration of his solitude, and in his food—we perceive through this concordant middle ground that the mystery of Elijah and this woman is the same. It is fittingly said that either the woman or Elijah remained in solitude for forty-two months, because in those same months the entire "time of the dragon" is designated, in which all mysteries will reach their consummation. To "flee" is to be deprived of the society of secular men, both in spirit and in body, with all haste. But where does she flee? He says: **Into her place.** He had already intimated this same thing above in other words, saying: "And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, that they might feed her there for one thousand two hundred and sixty days." What then is this "place" believed to be? Even if we should understand it simply as those hiding places in the woods where a few dwelt individually or even collectively, there were nevertheless many—especially women—who remained within the enclosures of cities, where they preserved a chaste and contemplative life and held the integrity of the faith inviolably. This "place" in which the woman rests is therefore a spiritual one: it is **contemplative religion**. It keeps minds sober from the face of the Serpent and refreshes souls devoted to Christ with spiritual nourishment. For to see the "face of the serpent" is to gaze into the wicked doctrine of the reprobate with one's heart. For everyone is known by their face. The serpent, however, lurks in hidden places so that he may strike unexpectedly the one who walks incautiously along the path. So also the Devil, lurking in the hearts of the reprobate, then reveals his face...

### Part of the Exposition

...when he brings a long-hidden error out into the open and reveals it. Therefore, the chosen ones <note>The "elect" or faithful believers.</note> fear to look too closely at this face of the serpent, lest they be deceived by its appearance and drawn into imitating it. They flee, as it were, into the desert when they vigilantly hide themselves in the secret of their hearts and in the hidden depths of Holy Scripture. For Holy Scripture is like the face of Christ; in it, all who dread looking upon the face of the serpent modestly hide themselves by contemplating heavenly things. Hence, it is also written in the Psalms regarding such people: *You shall hide them in the secret of your face from the disturbance of men; you shall protect them in the secret of your tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.* <note>Psalm 31:20 (Vulgate 30:21). The author uses this to show how scripture protects the mind from confusing arguments.</note> For what "contradiction of tongues" is more detestable than the doctrine of heretics? But the chosen are hidden in the secret of the Lord’s face: because while they focus the intent of their heart’s meditation on the divine appearance, they are ignorant of what is happening outside, as if it were not happening at all. They are protected, as it were, in the tabernacle of the Lord from the contradiction of tongues; for while they vigilantly focus on sacred readings, they despise the noise of the heretics’ cruelty as if it were the crackling of burning thorns. And because the cruel dragon is further inflamed the more he grieves over the insults inflicted upon him from every side, he pursues the woman fleeing into the wilderness with <term>Arian wickedness</term> <note>Arianism was a 4th-century theological movement that denied the full divinity of Christ. It caused massive divisions and persecutions within the early Church.</note>: so that she, who refused to return willingly, might be snatched toward sin by violence. For it follows:

<margin>T. 11</margin>
**And the serpent cast out of his mouth water like a flood after the woman, that he might cause her to be carried away by the flood.** <note>Revelation 12:15.</note>

Not all water is a flood, but the water of a flood is violent. Thus, while there are many kinds of men, not all were heretics capable of using force; but as for the perfidy of the Arians, the multiple authority of the holy fathers testifies with how much violence they persecuted the Catholics. The books of ecclesiastical history especially recount this in order: it cannot be told in a brief or 

<column-break/>

simple discourse with how much tempestuous force it drove the holy universal church toward errors. It follows:

<margin>T. 1</margin>
**But (it says) the earth helped the woman: and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed up the flood which the dragon cast out of his mouth.** <note>Revelation 12:16.</note>

If by the "heaven" which is above, the Church of the saints is designated, then not incongruously by the "earth" is understood the assembly of sinful men. It often happens as is written in the Book of Wisdom: *The just man is delivered from distress, and the wicked shall be given in his place.* <note>Proverbs 11:8. In the Middle Ages, Proverbs was often grouped with the "Books of Wisdom."</note> For it is fixed, and manifest clearer than light: that many errors are better avoided by the good because the reprobate (by their blasphemy) have made the good attentive. Moreover, we often recognize the fault of others immediately and in the moment, and recognizing it, we avoid it; we could by no means avoid this ourselves if we did not first blame this very thing by judging it in others. For often, by the fall of another, a person is struck with fear, and what he rebukes in another, he himself hastens to avoid.

**Here ends the third distinction. Here begins the fourth distinction.**

<margin>T.</margin>
**And the dragon was angry with the woman: and went to make war with the rest of her seed, who keep the commandments of God, and have the testimony of Jesus Christ.** <note>Revelation 12:17.</note>

Note that it says: *He went to make war with the rest of her seed.* The "seed of the woman" is He who was snatched up to God and to His throne: namely, Christ with His martyrs. For He himself (as I have already mentioned above) says to the angel of Laodicea: *To him who overcomes I will grant to sit with me on my throne: as I also have overcome, and have sat down with my Father on His throne.* <note>Revelation 3:21.</note> Why then is it now said that the dragon went to make war with the "rest" of the woman's seed, unless because the seed of the woman is twofold (as I said), and one part indeed preceded to glory—that is, the assembly of martyrs, whose head

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Apocalypse, moving into Chapter 13. It transitions from the Dragon’s pursuit of the Woman (the Church) to the emergence of the Beast from the sea. The author specifically links the "fourth age" of the Church to the rise of monasticism and the spiritual battles faced by those dedicated to prayer.</meta>

<margin>
The Order 
of Monks. 
The Southern 
part.
</margin>
Christ remained on earth in another form: designated in John the Evangelist as the **order of holy monks of the fourth time**. <note>The author divides church history into "times" or ages; the fourth age is here associated with the rise of monastic life.</note> They occupy the **southern part** especially, where the heat is greatest for those who dwell there. <note>In medieval allegory, the "South" often represents the "heat" of the Holy Spirit or the intensity of divine contemplation.</note> These are those holy men whose total number is gathered in the following passage (as John says): **I saw a lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.** Therefore, the **first war** was against the one whom the woman brought forth <note>Christ</note>. The **second** was the war of Michael and his angels. The **third** was against the woman herself <note>The early Church</note>. The **fourth** is against those who are of the seed of the woman. The first war involved Christ and the apostles; the second, the martyrs; the third, the "professors" or confessors of the Church; the fourth, those to whom it is given to be free for prayers and psalms <note>The monks and contemplatives</note>. Do you perceive, wise reader, how subtle this book is? In it, nothing can be assigned to a specific group without it also relating to the general whole. But enough has been said of these things above. Truly, the dragon goes forth again to do battle with those who are of the seed of the woman. Let us hear what he did. It follows:

<margin>
Chapter 13, 
verse 1.
</margin>
### And he came and stood upon the sand of the sea.
### And I saw a beast rising from the sea, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon its horns, ten crowns.

The **sand of the sea** is sterile land; at one moment it is flooded by the waters of the sea, and at another, it grows hot from the burning sun. This signifies those men who are caught in the middle: they do not seem to be entirely unfaithful, yet they do not adhere to Christian piety with total purity of faith. <note>These are "lukewarm" or "half-way" Christians who lack stability.</note> Upon these men the devil stood, and he saw a beast rising from the sea. This is because false Christians—those who have withdrawn from the bosom of Mother Church by consenting to the devil and his hollow displays—show the examples of their own depravity (with which they infected the Church) to the infidels. This encourages the infidels to persecute the Christian Church even more fiercely. The devil saw this because, through the cunning of his own wickedness, he sensed it beforehand. To take a few examples from many: the Jews could hardly ever have found an opportunity to capture 

<column-break/>

Christ, unless that disciple <note>Judas Iscariot</note> into whom Satan entered had betrayed him. The Emperor Nero would hardly ever have disturbed the apostles, unless that treacherous Simon <note>Simon Magus, a sorcerer often depicted as an arch-enemy of Peter</note> had driven him to it. Constantine the Arian <note>original: "Constantinus arrianus". This likely refers to Constantius II, the son of Constantine the Great, who favored Arianism, or it is a general critique of imperial interference.</note> would hardly ever have taken up arms against the pious, unless impious bishops had provoked him to presume such a thing. Therefore, the Devil stands upon the sand of the sea and sees a beast rising from the sea: for while he discerns that he reigns in these same reprobate Christians, he has no doubt that a multitude of infidels from his own kingdom will join him to bring aid against Christ. It should be noted that the prophet Daniel saw the meaning of this beast divided into **four beasts**. Although we have mentioned them earlier in this work, the subject requires that we speak of them again here. Daniel says: **The four winds of heaven fought in the great sea, and behold, four great beasts came up from the sea, different from one another.** It has often been said in this book that the name "heaven" signifies the Church or Divine Scripture. Likewise, no one can doubt that the "great sea" designates this world. The **four winds of heaven** are four specific types of understanding, corresponding to the four Gospels. The first is called **typical** <note>allegorical/symbolic</note>, the second **historical** <note>literal</note>, the third **moral**, and the fourth **contemplative**. The first is specially suited to shepherds <note>pastors/bishops</note>, the second to deacons, the third to teachers, and the fourth to virgins and hermits. Why? Because the first teaches ecclesiastical works, which were long ago designated in the scriptures and the works of the Fathers; by these, the shepherds of the Church prove that the profession of the Christian faith is true and faithful. The second <note>the historical</note> feeds those faithful whom it receives—who are like infants in Christ—with the "milk" of the examples of the ancients. The third rules the student who is more advanced and already tending toward higher things; it instructs one's character, composes one's actions, and reveals the deceptions of vices which sometimes pretend to be virtues. In all these things, one receives appropriate figures from the deeds of the past, so that through things done in the flesh, one may understand what happens daily in the spirit. Thus, we should strive all the more to labor in the virtues, treading down vices with vigilance, so that our effort is not in vain.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Apocalypse, specifically interpreting the spiritual meaning of the "four winds" and the "four beasts" from the visions of Daniel and John. It builds on the previous page's categorization of the four orders of the Church (Apostles, Martyrs, Confessors/Doctors, and Monks/Virgins).</meta>

### Part of the Explanation

we understand: that for the sake of human salvation alone, the spirit of almighty God has seen fit to ordain. The **fourth understanding**, which is called **contemplative**, taking for itself wings like an eagle in the form of earthly things, deals with heavenly matters. This understanding, above all, teaches us to despise earthly things, to love heavenly ones, to scorn temporal things, and to long for eternal ones. These are those four spiritual understandings which, like the four <margin>Genesis</margin> rivers of paradise, water the hearts of those who have faith in God. However, because contrary powers lie hidden in this world—just as certain winds of heaven are known to fight upon fluctuating waters—the **four winds of heaven** fight in the "great sea." These are four specific spiritual insights by which this world is attacked, so that men might learn to despise earthly things. Concerning these understandings and the "four living creatures" together, it is written in the <margin>Ezekiel</margin> prophet Ezekiel: *Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went; they did not turn back when they walked.* <note>original: "Ubi erat impetus spiritus illuc gradiebantur"</note>

But how did these four winds of heaven fight in the great sea? Indeed, how did they *not* fight, when they disturbed the whole world? For the sea is troubled when the heavens bring forth winds, and the world is likewise troubled when the saints preach the words of God, because those words are contrary to the works and desires of the worldly. It is fitting that there are four Evangelists who wrote the Gospels, because there are (as I have said) four **orders of preachers** who rely on those four understandings: the **Apostles**, the **Martyrs**, the **Confessors** <note>Those who "confess" the faith through teaching and living, rather than death; often called "Doctors" of the Church.</note>, and the **Virgins**. 

But perhaps the virgins and hermits do not preach the word of God because (as some say) they are "dead to the world"? I say that they do indeed preach, and they preach well: for what they cry out with their voices, they demonstrate through their conduct. To say nothing of other things, they preach—if not to others—at least to themselves and to their disciples, whose holy legions have prevailed in monasteries and filled the breadth of the world. Now, therefore, these four orders are designated by the "four living creatures," from whose mouths, as if from the secrets of the heavens, four spirits of the winds went forth to fight in the sea of this age to gather schools of fish. But it happened that as they struggled, not 

<column-break/>

only were many fish caught and pulled out of the sea, but also **great beasts** came out from it to devour the multitude of fish that the saints had captured. 

The **first beast** is the Synagogue of the Jews; the **second**, the Pagans; the **third**, the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, an early Christian priest whose teachings on the nature of Christ were declared heretical.</note>; the **fourth**, the <term>Hagarenes</term> <note>A medieval term for Muslims/Saracens, referring to their perceived descent from Hagar.</note>. While the **Evangelists** (who are called "dragons" by another name—or rather, the true dragons, the holy martyrs who were obedient unto death) were breathing, a bear from the **Pagan** people came out against them. While the **Doctors** (who are also called Confessors) were breathing, a leopard from the sect of the **Arians** came out against them. While the **Hermits** were breathing, the **fourth beast** came out against them, unlike the others: from the fierce race of the **Saracens**. 

To this, Daniel says: *The first beast was like a lioness.* John designated this in that one beast which he saw when he said: *And its mouth was like the mouth of a lion.* And what Daniel says: *The second beast like a bear,* John demonstrated when he said: *And its feet were like the feet of a bear.* And what Daniel adds: *The third beast like a leopard,* John intimated when he said: *And the beast which you saw was like a leopard.* And what Daniel says: *Behold, a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong,* and a little later added, *And it had ten horns,* etc., John appropriately assigns to the ten horns and the head which he saw "as if slain," and a little later, "raised from the dead." 

Furthermore, that one beast which John saw is described as having **seven heads** at once, because those four beasts which Daniel describes are known to have seven heads in total; specifically, because the third beast is said to have four heads <note>1 (lion) + 1 (bear) + 4 (leopard) + 1 (fourth beast) = 7 heads total.</note>. But we understand these things better if we do not shrink from repeating and explaining what we have touched upon in summary. The **Sea** (or the Abyss) signifies the present world; and when it is described in relation to the earth, it signifies the **unbelieving people**. From this world, or unbelieving people, diverse sects of men have gone out in their own times, which in their beastly ferocity...

...persecute the Church with [cruelty]. However, these wings were quickly torn from the lioness when that same beast was handed over to the Roman army; soon those two sects—and any others there were—perished. Hence it is well added: *And it stood upon the earth like a man*; <note>Daniel 7:4</note> because it which previously (as if it were not itself born from the mass of sinners) detested the Gentiles, was finally handed over to the power of the Romans, and recognized that it was of the same nature and misery as other men, having been so atrociously chastised, even if not yet recalled to faith in God. As for what follows: *And its heart was given to it*; this has not been fulfilled even to the present day, because it has not been granted to them even until now to know Him who suffered for their salvation and that of the whole world—unless perhaps it was said ironically. "Its heart": as if to say a hard heart, because they have always been *stiff-necked* <note>Exodus 33:3</note> and indomitable in heart, even if not in the same way as from that time until the present day.

The **second beast**, however, like a **bear**, represented the most savage multitude of the **pagans**. <margin>The Second Beast.</margin> And not without reason was it said to it: *Arise, devour much flesh*; <note>Daniel 7:5</note> since an infinite multitude of saints was destroyed by the pagans, according to what the Psalmist had predicted long before, saying: <margin>Psalms</margin> *O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins. and the worshippers of idols: who raged more boldly than the other infidels in the slaughter of the saints.

Thus they erred in four ways regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit. Thus the third beast, divided into four heads and as many wings, tore at the Catholic Church until the **fourth beast** should succeed it, which would surpass the other three beasts in beastly cruelty. <margin>The Fourth Beast.</margin> And the fourth beast (it says) was *terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong; it had great iron teeth, devouring and breaking in pieces, and trampling the rest with its feet.* It was unlike the other beasts which he had seen before, and it had **ten horns**.

And further on: *I approached one of those standing by and asked him the truth about all these things. And he told me: "These great beasts are four kingdoms that shall rise out of the earth. It was so monstrous that it was thought to be truly not of men, but of some terrible beast. This is especially true since its error does not seem to be protected by any human reason, but is defended only by the detestable madness of lying and the tyrannical power of arms. How much it has grown strong in a short time and how quickly it has advanced in its malice is beyond doubt because of our sins. The desolation of the churches of **Syria** and **Phoenicia**, as well as **Palestine** and **Egypt**, and also **Africa**, **Mauretania**, and the islands of the sea, bears witness to this. In these places, the name of Christ has been abolished, and the detestable tradition of Muhammad himself is preached as if he were a "great prophet of the Lord" and a "herald of the Most High." Alas, if **Antichrist** will do such great evils, then how many has this man already done in his lie? For just as **Moses**, the lawgiver, preceded Christ a long time before, so this bringer of lies has prepared the paths for the Antichrist.

But let it not seem to anyone that the monstrosity of this beast is similar to that of the other beasts. The **Jews** indeed fought against the faith of Christ, but nevertheless, while they were resisting and unwilling, churches were built in Jerusalem; and not many days later they were absorbed by the **Romans**, so that from then on, as far as they were concerned, both the persecution of the churches and their kingdom came to an end. The **Pagans** fought against Christ, but they were defeated daily by His soldiers, so that in the days of **Pope Sylvester** <note>Pope from 314–335 AD, traditionally credited with the conversion of Emperor Constantine.</note>, they almost surrendered their weapons and assigned the scepter of the empire to that same Vicar of Christ. The **Goths**, **Vandals**, and **Lombards**, and other Arian heretics, were partly wiped out by the army of the Romans and partly converted to the Catholic faith. But this **fourth beast** was indomitable, so that it appeared for 

<column-break/>

a time to be humbled and as if dead; yet how it has been magnified again and prepared to devour is more to be feared than to be expressed. This, therefore, is that beast which Saint Daniel calls "exceedingly terrible." **John** <note>The author of the Book of Revelation.</note> indeed encompasses both this beast and the three others under one beast having seven heads and ten horns on one of them. But more on this in what follows. 

Now we see the battle. We said above that the fourth time pertains to **virgins and hermits** (that is, to those holy men whom Saint John says are of the "seed of the woman"). We said that after the red dragon was defeated in three battles, he went away bitter in his indignation to wage war with those same holy men who are of the seed of the woman, *who keep* (he says) *the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus.* <note>Revelation 12:17</note> Then, by the occasion of one beast which the dragon saw ascending from the sea, those four beasts which the prophet Daniel had seen before were brought into the midst. It is as if he were saying: The red and envious dragon, knowing that not only those saints are to be crowned with honor and glory who exposed themselves to torturers for God’s sake, or at least stood firm in faith when captured by infidels, but also those who would lead a solitary life and be exalted by the victory of chastity—he could not look with straight eyes upon the fact that the wilderness was sending a new kind of martyr to the Kingdom. Instead, he directed the Jews against the Apostles, the Pagans against the martyrs, and the Arians against the Catholics into war. A medieval term for Muslims, referring to their perceived descent from Hagar, the handmaid of Abraham.</note>, more monstrous than the others. ### John, Fourth Part on the Apocalypse

[X 4]

...terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong: it had great iron teeth, devouring and breaking in pieces, and trampling the rest with its feet. <note>original: "terribilis atq; mirabilis & fortis nimis" — This is a description of the fourth beast in Daniel 7:7.</note> And when it was explained to him by the angel: *These great beasts are four kingdoms that shall rise from the earth*; after these were set in place, he added and said: *After these things, I wanted to learn diligently about the fourth beast, which was very different from all the others, and exceedingly terrible. It had great iron teeth, devouring and breaking in pieces, and trampling the rest with its feet.* From these words, it is clearly gathered that the ferocities of the other beasts that preceded it were nothing in comparison to this one, which succeeded in the fourth place. And therefore, Saint John—who understood the entire persecution of the Church, which is known to have begun from the first persecutor, Herod, as being contained within one great beast having seven heads and diverse body parts—nevertheless, in the fourth part of this book and in the fourth chapter of that fourth part, began to speak of it. He did so partly because through this beast, the Devil attacked those solitary men living in the midday desert, <note>A reference to the "Noonday Devil" or the spiritual trials faced by the Desert Fathers in the Egyptian wilderness.</note> and partly because through this beast, he is going to do such things <margin>fourth</margin> as he has already partially done—things he was not permitted to do in other times, not even when he was allowed to tear the holy martyrs with blows. Indeed, he says: *Upon its horns, ten diadems.* In the sixth part of this book, the angel explained this, saying: the ten horns of the beast are to be understood as ten future kings (that is) at that extremity of the sorrowful time, when the kingdom of the beast shall end. Having briefly touched upon these four beasts which Daniel saw, we must return to the order of the exposition. It follows:

<margin>D. 2.</margin>
> And upon its heads, names of blasphemy.

Even a name that is contrary to the Christian name can be called a "name of blasphemy." For whatever is done or said to the injury of the Creator is blasphemy; it blasphemes the holy name of the Lord through its own self, while it does not believe Him to be the One who is. Hence, even that thief [on the cross] is said to have blasphemed, because he said to Christ hanging on the cross: *If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us.* <note>Luke 23:39</note> Or certainly, so that the sons of the Devil may make a name for themselves, they draw sects of lost men after them; for that reason, the beast is described as having the name of blasphemy upon its heads. These names are called "names of blasphemy" because, when the proud make a name for themselves, the name of the humble King <note>Referring to Jesus Christ, the "humble King."</note> is blasphemed; naturally, because the humble one is held as nothing wherever the proud man reigns. It follows:

### Abbot, Part of the Exposition

Daniel himself had written concerning the ten horns: that he had seen a small horn emerge from the midst of them, and that three of the horns were plucked out at its appearance. Regarding this horn, he adds after the aforementioned things: *Behold, there were eyes, like the eyes of a man, in that horn, and a mouth speaking great things.* <note>original: "ingentia" — meaning enormous or monstrous things, typically interpreted as blasphemies.</note> And after some other things: *I beheld, and lo, that horn made war against the saints, and prevailed against them.* And again concerning it, the angel who interpreted the vision said: *The ten horns which you saw in the beast are ten kings of that kingdom. And another shall rise after them, and he shall be more powerful than the ones before him, and he shall humble three kings, and he shall speak words against the Most High, and he shall wear out the saints of the Most High, and he shall think that he can change times and laws; and they shall be delivered into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.* <note>Daniel 7:8-25. "A time, times, and half a time" is a prophetic period often interpreted as three and a half years.</note> 

And indeed, we mentioned this in the preceding part—that is, under the sounding of the sixth angel’s trumpet—on account of the saints who are to be killed by this beast. Nevertheless, it had to be repeated now for the sake of those things written in this place, so that from the mouth of two witnesses <note>A reference to the legal principle that truth is established by two witnesses; here, Daniel and John.</note> a single truth might shine forth. For what John says is nothing other than: *And there was given to him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies,* which matches what Daniel says of that horn—that is, of that king who is to reign over the beast: *And there was given to him a mouth speaking great things.* Nor is what John says different—*And power was given to him to act for forty-two months*—from what Daniel says: *He shall think that he can change times and laws, and they shall be delivered into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.* <note>Forty-two months is equal to three and a half years, aligning with Daniel's "time, times, and half a time."</note> Finally, what John says—*And it was given to him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them*—is the very thing Daniel expresses when he says: *And behold, that horn made war against the saints, and prevailed against them.* 

The only difference is that John attributes this to that multitude which is called the "Beast," while Daniel attributes it to that wicked king who is to reign within it. This is because there will be one single will belonging to him and his army: to wipe the name of Christians from the earth. Truly, this occurs at the end of that kingdom which he designates in the beast. Furthermore, what John says—*I saw one of the heads of the beast as if it were slain to death, and his death-wound was healed*—

<column-break/>

it was not said because he did not see the other heads slain, but because he saw this one alone "as if slain to death," and that after the striking, it was healed of its death-wound. For the beast itself lives as long as even one of its heads lives. And because all the heads appeared dead, it seemed as though the beast were entirely dead. Nevertheless, it is not so, for he demonstrates something else at the end. For the others are truly dead, but one was not dead, but only *as if* dead. 

For who has ever heard, from that time when the Jews were crushed by the hands of the Romans for the defense of their Law, that they have raised arms against Christians? What pagan kingdom has fought against Christians for the worship of idols after the death of Julian? <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman emperor who attempted to suppress Christianity.</note> Who has perceived the Goths, the Vandals, and the Lombards—once children of error—finally returning to the Catholic faith from the rigor of their ancient perfidy? <note>original: "perfidie" — used here in the medieval sense of "false belief" or "unbelief." These Germanic tribes were originally Arian Christians (considered heretics) or pagans before converting to Catholicism.</note> Yet the perfidy of the Saracens, <note>A common medieval term for Muslims.</note> having once begun so many years ago, persists in evil; it does not cease to attack the Christian name everywhere with all its strength. 

O, how many thousands of Christians have been given into their hands, and how many, and with what varied torments, do they torture them out of hatred for the Crucified One! This head has not been able to die until the present; it lives even now, to still work the death of many, and to perfect the works of its King as long as it lives. But why did John claim to have seen it *as if* dead? Perhaps it is because it will happen that Christians prevail against it—by preaching more than by fighting—until it almost fails, only to return to its former ferocity with renewed strength. But this is not yet completed; in a short space of time, both could be fulfilled. 

Yet perhaps there will be someone who thinks it was completed by material arms, by no means thinking that those things which happened in the Church some years ago should be disregarded. For in the year 1015 of the Lord’s Incarnation (as it is said), a wonderful sign appeared in the heights of the air: namely, countless stars running about everywhere, just as if they were traversing aerial paths in the manner of birds. Following this sign, at the exhortation <margin>It seems to Christians</margin> <margin>In the year 1015, Pope Urban</margin> <note>While the text mentions 1015 and Pope Urban, Urban II's famous call for the First Crusade was in 1095. The author may be referencing a specific local tradition or a different chronological system.</note> 

<summary>The author compares the apocalyptic prophecies of Daniel and John, identifying the "little horn" and the "Beast" as the same persecuting power. He argues that while other ancient enemies like the Jews and Goths have been subdued or converted, the "Saracens" represent the head of the beast that refuses to die, continuing to persecute Christians.</summary>

# Fourth Part of John on the Apocalypse

...the decree of Pope Urban <note>Pope Urban II, who initiated the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095.</note>: Christians from everywhere, being moved, decided to go across the sea to liberate the Holy Sepulcher; and so it was done. Indeed, after this, such great boldness was given to the Christians that the multitude of pagans already seemed to be nullified and, as it were, reduced to nothing (with Christ prevailing). For, to condense many things into one: the Saracens who were in Egypt paid tribute to the Christians who had attacked the overseas parts; and those who possessed Asia <note>Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> paid it to the people of Constantinople. Africa and the nearby cities, captured by the King of Sicily <note>Likely referring to the Norman conquests under Roger II or his successors.</note>, began to have Christian settlers. The Kings of the Spains <note>The various Christian kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula involved in the Reconquista.</note> often triumphed over their enemies. Who, then, seeing the Christians glorified by so many victories over that indomitable nation, would not safely judge the head of the beast to be dead? 

But if anyone were able to look around with a healthy mind: we see in this day, however small the peace, the nations around us swell like the sea, and the head which was as if dead, restored to its former health, ready on every side to strike down victims, ready on every side to kill and devour; it has become what the Lord foreknew would be done through it. If, indeed (as we said above), it is not yet complete, it is possible for it to be completed in another order without delay. However, the spiritual sense seems to agree more with this opinion: namely, that it is not yet complete, but must be completed in another and more solemn order without delay. As for what follows: **And the whole earth followed the beast in wonder.** Although it is to be fulfilled in its own day, there are already many who wonder and begin to waver, as it were, saying: "What kind of judgment is this believed to be, that such a multitude of men are adverse to the faith, and that they are permitted to prevail so much against the Christian people? Do you think so many thousands of men are to be damned like a single man? Do you think God permits them to grow into such infinity without cause?" Saying these things, the wretched have fallen from the faith, not knowing that which is written:

<margin>Psalm</margin>
> How magnificent are your works, O Lord: your thoughts are made very deep. The senseless man shall not know: and the fool shall not understand these things. <note>Psalm 92:5-6 (Vulgate 91:6-7).</note>

<column-break/>

When sinners have sprung up like grass: and all who work iniquity have appeared: that they may perish forever and ever: but you, O Lord, are the Most High forever. Fools truly do not know this, those who wonder after the beast and desert the faith of Christ, bowing themselves to the beastly power, and passing over to its uncleanness, making themselves heirs of its perfidy. Up to this point, this has happened in part. But it is also to happen in the first sense, so that this itself may be completed in its entirety: namely, **and the whole earth followed the beast in wonder: and they worshiped the dragon who gave power to the beast, those who pant after earthly desires; and they worshiped the beast, saying: "Who is like the beast, and who will be able to fight with it?"** 

<margin>Concerning the eleventh horn.</margin>
<margin>Daniel</margin>

For I believe for no other reason did John, speaking of the ten horns, omit that eleventh horn about which Daniel spoke such terrible things, except to give it to be clearly understood that it will not be so much a man who will do those great evils, but the author of evils himself: the Red Dragon, who is the Devil and Satan. He will primarily dwell in that king, as if in his own temple and the idol of his kingdom; or rather, using him as the quiver of his dwelling place, so that speaking great things through his mouth, there is no one who can stand before his face. And rightly does Daniel introduce a wicked man, while John introduces the Devil, lest anyone think that the king himself will do those terrible things by his own power and not rather through the power of the Devil who will be in him; or lest anyone estimate that the Devil himself is to be visibly manifested in his own nature and worshiped by the sons of this world, and not rather in that iniquitous king, who will be a fabricator of truth and a simulator of justice. 

But to return to the order of the exposition of the discourse: **The whole earth (as John says) followed the beast in wonder:** because the multitude of those who savor earthly things and lust after earthly things will acquiesce to the commands and will of the infidels, leaving the true faith which is in Christ Jesus, and receiving the traditions of impious men in place of the law of God. **And they worshiped (he says) the dragon.**
