->Part of the Abbreviated Explanation<-

Similarly, if sinners placed in temporal distress sustain it patiently, just as gold is purified in a furnace, they cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not. But those who do not wish to be purified here from their vices by the **word of the cross** <note>original: *verbum crucis*, referring to the message of Christ's sacrifice in 1 Corinthians 1:18</note> will burn forever, and their iniquity will not cease. For one whose heart is wicked always thinks of evil, and when placed under the lash <note>original: *flagellis*, literally "whips" or "scourges"</note>, he sends forth not the scent of spices but the smoke of stinking sulfur. For the good, when they are afflicted, bless the Lord, and that blessing is aromatic smoke. But the others, when they are afflicted, murmur and blaspheme, and their blasphemy rises like the smoke of sulfur or the stench of rotting flesh. Therefore, the smoke of their torments shall ascend forever and ever, because the torments will not benefit them for correction, but they will burn always in hell and remain in their perverse will without end. Wherefore it is soon added: *They have no rest day or night, who worshipped the beast and its image, and if anyone has received the mark of its name.* "Day and night" is used to mean "continuously," as if it were said: "always." It is not that there is a succession of time in that world <note>the afterlife</note>, but because we who are placed in this life are accustomed to expressing evils that are continuous in this way—as with acute fevers, which grant no space for rest and are mitigated by no interruption either by day or by night. Indeed, to express their perdition, the spirit of prophecy often brings forward familiar evils as an example, so that through the small things we know, we may learn to judge the greater. It follows:

<margin>Chapter 14</margin>
**Here is the patience of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.**

It is as if he said: Let men not marvel at the severity of the judgment, nor let it seem unjust that Almighty God permits so monstrous a beast to reign, so that those who are His own may be tested. For although an occasion for greater punishment is thereby given to the reprobate, from there the elect shall deserve the palm of victory. The sixth day <note>Friday, specifically Good Friday</note> was sad

<column-break/>

for the apostles for a time, on which Christ suffered; but yet He Himself, through that same passion, rested from all suffering, and together with the glory of the passion, entered paradise not without the palm of victory. I would call the thief <note>the "Good Thief" crucified with Jesus</note> a partner in the passion because, although the cause was not the same—for his was different before his confession—yet after his confession, the penalty owed for his crimes was immediately turned into virtue. Therefore it is necessary—it is necessary—to cross through the **brook of Cedron** <note>original: *torrentem Cedron*, the Kidron Valley Jesus crossed before His arrest</note> on the sixth day, whoever desires to reach the Sabbath <note>the eternal day of rest</note>. That this is established by authority and solid in truth, the following distinction truly and clearly demonstrates.

**Here ends the sixth distinction. Here begins the seventh distinction.**

<margin>Chapter 14</margin>
**And I heard a voice from heaven saying: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth now, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labors; for their works follow them."**

In these words, I find nothing more fitting to say than the words themselves. He is dull indeed who does not understand these words. Concerning this blessedness and so great a sweetness of rest, the Apostle speaks among other things he discussed in the Epistle to the Hebrews: *We who have believed shall enter into rest*, just as God said: *As I have sworn in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest.* <margin>Hebrews, Psalms</margin> And with certain things interposed in the explanation of this word, he added and said: *If Joshua had given them rest, he would never have spoken of another day after this.* Therefore, he says, *there remains a Sabbath-rest* <note>original: *sabbatismus*</note> *for the people of God.* And he added: *For he who has entered into his rest, he also has rested from his works, just as God did from His.* Where it is also immediately joined: *Let us hasten therefore to enter into that rest.* Therefore, what the Apostle feels in that place concerning the Sabbath, John feels in this place—or rather, the Holy Spirit feels.

In which, namely, on the last day, when all the mysteries and labors of the saints are finished, what remains now except the harvest and the vintage? For it follows:

I recall that I have said quite often—and still I am compelled to repeat the same thing in its proper places—that I do not wish to seem to be what I am not, by feigning something out of my own presumption. For they themselves "saw in part" and "prophesied in part," and we still see "in part," and even this through a **glass darkly** <note>original: *speculum in enigmate*, a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12</note>, even if it is necessary for that part of the vision to grow larger as time goes on. For it is one thing to see many things; it is another to see all. A city is seen in one way when it is still a day’s journey away; in another way when one comes to the gate; and in another when one proceeds inside. Therefore we, who are "at the gate," can indeed speak of many things which once were hidden in whole or in part; but we do not speak as those who will be inside and will see **eye to eye**, when those things which are written in this chapter begin to be fulfilled. Certainly, what is written about the harvest and the vintage in this "seventh distinction" is so clear that there can be no doubt about what they signify. <meta>This page continues the interpretation of the Apocalypse (Revelation), focusing on the dual judgment of the "Harvest" and the "Vintage." The previous page discussed the arrival of spiritual men—the Orders of Monks and Hermits—who act as precursors to the final judgment. This page explains why two distinct symbols of gathering (wheat and grapes) are used to describe the end of the world.</meta>

->### Part of the Explanation###<-

brothers. In whatever way this occurs, it is well that two men should be sent together: if, indeed, they are truly men. One comes in a spirit of gentleness to command the gathering of the harvest <note>The "harvest" represents the collection of the righteous (the wheat).</note>; the other in a spirit of zeal to command the completion of the vintage <note>The "vintage" or grape harvest represents the gathering of the wicked for judgment.</note>. For even up to that moment of time, there will be some predestined for life and others foreknown for death. If only the chosen people were to remain in the world, the text would not speak of the vintage of the earth, but only of the harvest. But because the good will not be alone, the vintage will occur alongside the harvest.

If you ask what the harvest signifies, hear the Lord speaking in the Gospel: "The harvest is the end of the age" <note>original: "Messis autem: consummatio seculi." See Matthew 13:39.</note>. Nor should one think this differs from the word of Truth itself, which says: "Do you not say that there are yet four months, and then the harvest comes? But see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest" <note>See John 4:35.</note>. Just as the harvest of the circumcised people <note>The Jewish people of the Old Testament.</note> came after forty generations from Abraham were completed, so now, after forty generations <note>A reference to the medieval "theology of history" which divided time into eras of forty generations each.</note>, there will be a harvest of those who have been called—and will yet be called—into the faith. Their late harvest occurs at the end of the age.

Concerning this late harvest and vintage—and how both pertain to the Day of Judgment—the Holy Prophet
<margin>Joel.</margin>
Joel makes it manifest when he says: "Let the nations arise and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat: for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about. Put in the sickles, for the harvest is ripe; come and come down, for the press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is multiplied" <note>See Joel 3:12-13. The Valley of Jehoshaphat was traditionally identified as the site of the Last Judgment.</note>. Behold how the two witnesses of truth agree with one another, announcing the final judgment with a harmonious voice. For each takes the harvest in a good sense and the vintage in a bad sense. It is clear that this happens to both respectively; otherwise, one would not understand the cluster of grapes as evil but as good, since wine frequently signifies spiritual doctrine.

And it should be noted that the final preaching is designated by sickles, not by swords. A sickle, though it cuts, nonetheless gathers many things together into one. In other times, the axe placed at the root of the tree threatened judgment with many

<column-break/>

blows and delayed the end. But in that final time it is not so; rather, the severity of judgment follows the threat, and both will happen almost simultaneously. This is what is meant by: "In the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be finished" <note>See Revelation 10:7.</note>. Therefore, this harvest of both the reprobate and the elect is to be completed under the sixth angel,
<margin>Practice.</margin>
after which there is no more time for repentance. Instead, each person will immediately receive according to what they have done: either the "reward of error" for the impious, or the "fruit of patience" for the pious. ### Abbot: Part of the Exposition

They embrace one another <note>The "they" refers to the virtues discussed in the preceding context.</note> so that if one of them is missing from someone, the other cannot remain whole in him. For indeed, virtue is produced through itself equally: the virtue of humility, the virtue of faith, the virtue of hope, and the virtue of charity, and any similar to these. Yet no one can have true and perfect faith if he does not also possess patience, humility, charity, and hope; nor can one have true charity if he lacks patience, faith, humility, and hope. Know, therefore, that He who knows all things realizes how vain it is to possess any good works without these virtues. How worthy it is for the "inner man" <note>The "inner man" (interiorem hominem) is a Pauline concept referring to the spiritual soul or the mind renewed by God.</note> to be fortified by such illustrious virtues. 

Thus, in His five special works which He performed in the world—and in the coming of the Holy Spirit whom He sent for this purpose from heaven—He exhibited a completion. Through what He Himself did, He intended to show what ought to be done in us morally, and in the Church typically and allegorically. You may ask: what are these works? They are so solemn among many others that no Catholic man can exist to whom these are not fully known and precious. 

The first work is the **Nativity**; the second, the **Passion**; the third, the **Resurrection**; the fourth, the **Ascension**; and the fifth, the **Coming of the Holy Spirit**. Finally, in this last one, a limit in number was preserved, so that the number of mysteries would correspond to the mystery of the number. On the third day, He rose from the dead, so that the Resurrection would be noted as the third work. On the fortieth day, He ascended into heaven, so that the Ascension would be understood as the fourth work. On the fiftieth day—the Passover, which in Greek is called *Pentecost*—the Holy Spirit was sent to the apostles, so that this foremost solemnity would be shown to belong to the fifth work.

Therefore, just as there are four living creatures and one throne <note>A reference to the vision in Revelation 4, where four "beasts" surround the throne of God.</note>, so this fifth part is general in respect to the four preceding ones. But just as the first part is assigned to the first living creature—that is, the **Lion**—because it deals with Christ and the pastors; the second to the **Calf**, because it deals with the martyrs; the third to the **Man**, because it deals with the teachers; the fourth to the **Flying Eagle**, because it deals with the virgins and hermits; so this fifth part, which we have now begun to discuss, must be assigned to the **Throne** of Almighty God. This is surely because He is seen to rule those especially 
<margin>Psalm 133</margin>
of whom it is said: *Behold how good*

<column-break/>

*and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity!* <note>original: "Ecce quā bonum et qm iocundum habitare fratres in vnum." A quote from Psalm 133:1.</note> In the primitive Church, there were pastors and evangelists; there were teachers and virgins, each having special gifts, just as there are special members of the body of Christ. Yet that ointment which was poured out from the head of Christ <note>A reference to the anointing of the Holy Spirit descending from Christ (the Head) to the Church (the Body).</note> did not come to them alone, but to all those of whom it is said: *The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul.* Those former groups are "special orders," but this one is general. Each of those orders in the four periods of time had a conflict with their own specific adversaries. This group, in the fifth period—which is its own—acts generally. 

And indeed, since there are seven angels who proceed from the temple, it is manifest that the zeal of God is poured out upon the impious through each of the seven times. However, since this fifth part of the book treats this order, it is clear that in the fifth time, that which is discussed in this part is fulfilled more generally. For thus (as we have often said), the "specials" are to be considered in such a way that the impulse of the Spirit is directed toward a "general" intuition. For it is one thing that happens according to the *species* (the specific type) in individual times, and another that is acted out according to the *genus* (the general category) in certain times. It is like the difference between making a memory of the Lord’s Resurrection on every Sunday during the weeks of Lent, and observing the entire week of Easter solemnly once a year (even if for the same purpose). 

Therefore, as the place requires, a discourse follows concerning that which is general. Wherefore (and it is not absurdly asked in this fifth part of the book rather than in any of the preceding ones) the **vials of the wrath of God** <note>The OCR reads "secūdie," likely a misreading of "iracundie" (wrath), which appears in the vocabulary list.</note> are poured out upon the earth. And why these same vials were spoken of last, the author has stated: because in them the "wrath of God is consumed." I would hope (as I believe) that we are helped in explaining all these things—not to labor in a few words, but to diligently insert various testimonies of the Scriptures so that some things may be understood from others. 

Moreover, although the intention and will of the saints may be common in their devotion, and all are unanimously zealous where zeal is required and merciful where mercy must be shown, it is not in vain that more zeal is given to some and more clemency to others. For not all times are fit for zeal, nor all for clemency. Furthermore, because to those who love more...

### Joa. Fifth [Part] on the Apocalypse

...he zeals more: how to the order of the spirituals <note>original: "ordini spiritualium." In Joachim's theology, the "spiritual men" represent a new monastic order that would lead the Church in the final age of history.</note>, by a certain special prerogative of love, zeal has been granted. As far as God permits, we shall attempt to reveal this. The four previously described orders, which through four special periods had conflicts with their adversaries—namely, the **Apostles**, the **Martyrs**, the **Confessors**, and the **Virgins**—and how they were perfected by the Lord’s Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, we have sufficiently shown in the four preceding parts.

Truly, the fifth order, which we are now discussing, gathered in honor of the Holy Spirit, shows itself by its way of life to be that of which the Psalmist speaks:
<margin>Psalm</margin>
-> Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity. <-

It is like the ointment on the head that descends onto the beard, the beard of Aaron. We ask, however, what this ointment signifies, or that with which the kings among the people of Israel were anointed; and we find it written in the Acts of the Apostles:
<margin>Acts</margin>
God the Father anointed the man Christ Jesus with the Holy Spirit; just as the Psalmist had long ago predicted:
<margin>Psalm</margin>
-> God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. <-

Moreover, that the zeal of God belongs to this oil is clearly demonstrated by that mysterious anointing of Jehu <note>Jehu was a king of Israel (9th century BCE) who was anointed to destroy the house of Ahab and the worshippers of the pagan god Baal.</note>, by which he was anointed by one of the sons of the prophets sent by Elisha. For he was anointed as king over Israel for this purpose: to destroy the house of Ahab and kill the priests and worshippers of Baal. Therefore, it is clearly evident that the zeal of God belongs to the Holy Spirit and His outpouring. This zeal is also called "wrath"—without a doubt—because of those whom He justly destroys from the earth. But this must be investigated much more deeply: for what reason is this zeal of God, which belongs to the Holy Spirit, believed to be consummated in the final plagues? This is so that no one, losing the time of grace, should be consumed by mercy <note>The author warns against abusing God's mercy to the point where judgment becomes inevitable.</note> for an infinite duration. For the just Judge does not sustain the sins of the reprobate forever; nor did He decree that every sin should be punished with equal weight or dismissed everywhere, but as it is written: "Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to men, but the spirit of blasphemy is forgiven neither here nor in the future." And

<column-break/>

again: "Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but he who speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither here nor in the future." But who is this "Son of Man" if not He who is also the "Son of God"? Why, then, is it more venial to sin against the Son than against the Holy Spirit? Is it because—God forbid such a thought from the hearts of the faithful—He is greater than the Son, from whom the Holy Spirit Himself proceeds? Far from it. But because the Son of God alone was incarnate; and while He was seen by men, to believe Him to be God—He who appeared to men as one of the mortals, capable of suffering—it belonged to His goodness to forgive those who did not easily believe His words. This is because both the good and the evil often speak their words in a similar way. But when, having seen the miracles and the powers of the Holy Spirit, they blasphemed that same Holy Spirit, saying: "In Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out demons," then they had no excuse for their sin. For He said: "They have seen and hated both me and my Father." It should be noted indeed that just as it is said the Father made all things through the Word, so also the Son works in the Holy Spirit, so that there is believed to be one operation of the Three and one power, although the Father is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. But if this is so, why are signs and miracles specifically ascribed to the Holy Spirit, so that the Scripture says: "Power went out from Him" (that is, from the Son) "and healed all"? It is so that the person of the Holy Spirit might be understood in the power of miracles, just as the person of the Son is understood in the power of words, and the person of the Father in the manufacture of the entire world. For there are three things that make men marvel: the eminence of works (the Creator), the depth of wisdom, and the power of miracles. These three, although they are common to the three persons—because in all these things there is one operation of the three—nevertheless, by the property of the mystery, the first is ascribed to the Father, the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit. Moreover, the sons of men seek to imitate these three, and to very few is it given to achieve the 
<margin>Three wonders.</margin>
imitation of the second; but toward the imitation of the third...

### Abb. Part Exposition

...[belief is for] very few. For doing some good work is for many; speaking wisdom is for a few. Furthermore, to show signs and miracles, just as it happens to the rare few, so it is a sin unto death and a great iniquity not to believe those showing them, but on the contrary to heap blasphemy upon the Spirit (who is the author). And therefore those who do this have no excuse for their sin, because without a doubt hatred is the cause, which is more serious than any crime and any sin.

Wherefore God himself speaks to Moses, saying:
<margin>Exodus</margin>
I am a strong and jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. <note>original: "Ego sum deus fortis: & zelotes..." A reference to the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20.</note>

Therefore, regarding one doing good in truth, not to believe that his work is good is a sin, but not a mortal one; for there are many hypocrites who work, not for the sake of God, but for the sake of temporary glory, of whom it is said: "Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward." <note>original: "receperunt mercedem suam." A quote from Matthew 6:2 regarding those who perform religious acts for public praise.</note>

In the same way, regarding one speaking wisdom in truth, not to believe that his words are true is entirely a sin; for the Savior says to the teachers: "He who hears you, hears me; and he who despises you, despises me." Indeed, even the Queen of the South is praised by the Lord because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. <note>original: "Regina Austri." The Queen of Sheba, often used as a model of the seeker of truth.</note>

Yet, because there are some sterile wise men, of whom the Truth says: "For they say and do not do," and indeed because there are many who have plausible words that are nevertheless full of lies and deceits, those who hear and do not believe have some excuse for their sin, especially because of what John says: "Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see if they are from God." <note>original: "Nolite credere oi spiritui." From 1 John 4:1.</note>

Truly, not to believe one showing signs—signs which he does not show to others—but to heap blasphemy [upon him], is a sin against the Holy Spirit, which is not forgiven in this age nor in the future; for without doubt such blindness proceeds from the malice of hatred, which, unless it departs from the heart of man, does not allow him to perceive the truth. But if an objection is raised concerning false prophets, it is written: "By their fruits you shall know them." But still it must be sought more diligently:

<column-break/>

Why is it that he who speaks a word against the Son of Man is forgiven, but he who speaks against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven, neither in this age nor in the future? This is primarily so that it may be understood why, in this fifth part, he deals with the pouring out of the wrath of God and the final plagues, rather than in any of the preceding parts, and why the wrath of God is "consumed" or completed in these more than in the others.

The four works of Christ mentioned above do indeed judge sinners and vehemently accuse them; yet the wrath of God is not consumed in them, because a remedy still remains in the gift of the Holy Spirit, which, just as it saves the one who is converted from his sins, so it excludes the unconverted from the assemblies of the elect.

Because the Son of God was made man, he showed an example of **humility**. Because he was made the calf <note>original: "vitulus." In medieval symbolism, the ox or calf represents sacrifice and the Passion of Christ.</note> on the altar of the cross, he offered an example of **patience**. Because he rose from the dead, he strengthened the hearts of believers with the fortitude of **faith**. Because he ascended on high, he raised the eagerness of **hope** into heaven. Because he sent the Holy Spirit in the appearance of fire, he inflamed the hearts of the faithful to **love** him.

Therefore, in the fifth place, the perfection of holiness is given to the elect, just as, on the contrary, the consummation of iniquity is given to the wicked. For just as patience follows humility, and the fortitude of faith follows patience, and hope follows the fortitude of faith, and the love of God (which is divine fire) follows hope; so too, impatience accompanies the pride of the heart, the weakness of faith accompanies impatience, despair follows the weakness of faith, and hatred follows despair—which is the sin unto death. For he who hates God is already dead, and while still living in the flesh, he is buried in hell.

Many hear this and wonder why this was said specifically about the guilt of hatred, thinking there are many other more serious sins. Now, therefore, let him who wishes to be a disciple of truth hear the truth. It has been said that he who sins against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven, neither in this age nor in the future. Why is this? Because the Holy Spirit himself is the love of God; and he who does not have love cannot have the Holy Spirit, for love seeks love, and charity seeks charity. But he who [hates] the Holy Spirit...

### The Fifth Exposition on John

...does not have: he does not have life remaining in himself. For I speak not of a similar thing, but of a dissimilar one: as the human soul is the life of the body, so the life of the soul is the grace of the Holy Spirit. Wherefore it is also said by the apostle:
> The first Adam was made into a living soul. The second, however, into a life-giving spirit. <note>original: "Factus est primus Adam in animam viventem..." A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:45, contrasting the natural life of Adam with the spiritual life granted by Christ.</note>

If indeed it is the Spirit who gives life to the soul, then that Spirit is love; since love cannot exist where there is hatred, how can that soul live which does not have within itself the life-giving Spirit of God, who is love? Therefore, hatred rooted in the heart is a sin unto death, and is nonetheless a sin against the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit is love: what sin is contrary to love, if not hatred? Now John says:
> Little children, I command this to you that you do not sin; but even if you do sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins. <note>1 John 2:1-2.</note>

But there is (he says) a sin unto death, for which I do not tell you that anyone should pray. That this sin is certainly hatred appears clearly from the same epistle. Wherefore he also takes Cain as an example, who, driven by the sting of hatred's envy, slit his own brother's throat. <note>A reference to 1 John 3:12 and the story of Cain and Abel.</note> Nor is it a wonder if the crime of hatred is punished with such a great penalty. For if the fulfillment of the law is charity <term>charitas<gloss>divine love or selfless care for others</gloss></term>, what can hatred be but the fulfillment of all sins? But it is not to be understood as if one should not pray for those who hate, since Christ says:
> Pray for your enemies. <note>Matthew 5:44.</note>

But one is not to pray for it in the same way as for any other vice—such as the passion of anger, or gluttony, the lust of the eyes, and similar things; which, even if they are committed daily by enemies, are yet believed to be easily forgiven through prayer. For sometimes men sold under sin are drawn to this by the law of the flesh, even against their will. I say that one must not pray for hatred as for another passion, because whether someone hates willingly or unwillingly (which sometimes happens as a result of the guilt of previous offenses), as long as he hates, he remains in death; and unless he ceases to hate, he cannot have life at all. Wherefore the Savior also says: "If you

<column-break/>

offer your gift before the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you: leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother, and then coming, offer your gift." <note>Matthew 5:23-24.</note>

If, however (as Truth itself witnesses), an offering is not accepted because of discord, it remains that the sin of hatred—which is the root of discord—is worse than every sin, and in it is the fulfillment of God's wrath. Nor is it a wonder if the sin of hatred is so execrable before God, since even among men nothing is more wicked, nothing more hateful. For however wicked and troublesome a brother may be to you, as long as you do not doubt his love, you endure him with composure, you bear with him. But if you know you are held in hatred by him, you can hardly endure it; and with however many services he may flatter you, you despise those flatteries as if they were dung. We pray, therefore, for those who hate and slander us, so that God, who can do all things, by visiting their hearts, may snatch them from the chain of impiety and call them back to the path of charity and peace. 

But we do not pray that they may be saved while remaining in hatred, because it is written:
> Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer; and every murderer does not have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. <note>1 John 3:15.</note>

And it should be noted that if someone hates his neighbor <note>The OCR reads 'primum', but context strongly suggests 'proximum' (neighbor).</note> as if he were an enemy of God, thinking him a heretic or a schismatic—just as Paul once hated Christ and his disciples, being a zealous follower of his ancestral traditions—he does not commit that sin for which one must not pray, because ignorance excuses him, just as Paul himself says:
> I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly. <note>1 Timothy 1:13.</note>

Wherefore the Savior, placed on the cross, said of some:
> Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. <note>Luke 23:34.</note>

And this indeed refers to those who, thinking good to be evil, zealously persecute the good, having a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. But he who knowingly hates God and his members, he is the one who commits that sin which is against the Holy Spirit, which [is] not...

# Part of the Exposition

[The sin] is forgiven neither in this age nor in the future <note>original: "remittitur in hoc seculo: neque in futuro." This refers to Jesus’ warning about the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit in Matthew 12:32.</note> (as the Lord said). 
> They have seen and hated me and my Father: now they have no excuse for their sin. <note>John 15:23–24.</note>
Hence, regarding the Lord's Passion, the evangelist says: "Pilate knew that they had handed him over because of envy." Therefore, the sin of hatred (which is called by another name, **iniquity**) is the very sin against the Holy Spirit and the "sin unto death," of which John speaks: 
> There is a sin unto death: I do not say for that one that anyone should pray. <note>1 John 5:16. The author is identifying hatred and "iniquity" with this ultimate, unforgivable sin.</note>
And as if it were asked what that sin was, he added and said: 
> All iniquity is sin: and there is a sin unto death. <note>1 John 5:17. Note the original Latin: "Omnis iniquitas peccatum est."</note>
Behold, it is clearly stated here that **iniquity** is a sin unto death. If this is so, what is it that he had said earlier? 
> Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity: and sin is iniquity. <note>1 John 3:4.</note>
And again: 
> Everyone who remains in him does not sin; and everyone who sins has not seen him. <note>1 John 3:6.</note>
And likewise: 
> Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin. <note>1 John 3:9.</note>
How can we understand this, unless we realize he is speaking of that specific sin which is named **iniquity**? Otherwise, how will that which he said earlier stand? 
> If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. <note>1 John 1:8.</note>
and 
> If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us. <note>1 John 1:10.</note>
Who, therefore, could understand these words unless he who bound them together were to explain them? For if he who sins is not of God, how is it that "if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves," unless we understand what he himself taught us to understand at the end: 
> He who knows his brother to be committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life shall be given to him for the one sinning not unto death. <note>1 John 5:16.</note>
But what is it that he adds? 
> There is a sin unto death: I do not say for that one that anyone should pray. 
Does he not mean for us to understand that sin which he immediately explains by adding: 
> All iniquity is sin: and there is a sin unto death. 
It remains, therefore, to ask: is hatred the sin of iniquity for which 

<column-break/>

he says one should not pray, since to no one who confesses and repents should forgiveness be denied, even at the very last moment of life? Let us see, therefore, whether he explains himself in what is written above and reveals what he wanted to intimate to us. 
> If we confess (he says) our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. 
And he added: 
> If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us. 
But if iniquity is a sin unto death, for which no one is permitted to pray, what is it that he says? 
> If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. 
This must mean that the sin of iniquity itself is the *refusal* to let go of and confess one's sins. For who is it that does not want to be free of sin, except the one who is in despair and, like a brute animal, is ready for every iniquity? Hence, concerning this sin, it is said through the Psalmist: 
> The unjust man said that he might transgress within himself. <note>Psalm 36:1 (Vulgate 35:2). The author interprets "within himself" as a private, stubborn rejection of God's mercy.</note>
He transgresses within himself who kills himself by despairing. And why is this? 
> Because (he says) he acted deceitfully, so that his iniquity might be found unto hatred. 
And what follows there? 
> The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit: he did not wish to understand so as to do well: he meditated on iniquity in his bed: he stood upon every path that was not good; but he did not hate malice. 
Behold—this is **iniquity**. If you say in your heart: "I have done many evils; I have committed many iniquities; there is no reason for me to repent in vain; why should there be hope by which I might be reconciled to God? Even if I withdraw far from the fear of God and do whatever occurs to me to do, I will rejoice while I live, though I am to be tortured in the end—or rather, I will not be tortured, for all that they say is false; there will be no life after this life is finished." This is the iniquity that the unjust man has meditated upon in his bed. Therefore, one should not pray for him in such a way that his sins are forgiven as they are for one who confesses and repents; for unless he repents from the heart, he cannot deserve indulgence. Only this can prayer do for him, and for...

But for the one who confesses, all Christians should pour out prayers before the merciful God: that the Lord, in His kindness, might forgive him that which he cannot pay according to his own will due to his weakness. **Charybdis** <note>In Greek mythology, a dangerous whirlpool; used here as a metaphor for a sin that drags a soul into an inescapable abyss.</note> which pulls a man into the deep, is to be feared; for once it entangles someone, it suffocates and kills. Out of fear of this whirlpool, the leaders of the churches overlook many things and endure very many errors of those under their authority. They bear with infancy; they endure adolescence; they tolerate youth. But even when they find no fruit except bad fruit, they rightly begin to be indignant, yet with internal mercy and a certain modesty. If, however, they are not converted even then to the fruit of repentance, but—what is worse than this—they even incite others to evil and provoke them to sinning, what remains except that sentence which the vine-dresser imposed, who prayed for the fig tree? 
> If indeed (he said) it bears fruit [well]; but if not, in the future you shall cut it down. <note>Luke 13:9.</note> 
Nevertheless, often in any given age, like a certain seed of weeds, a person runs more quickly to the summit of malice, even at a younger age; so that, just as [some] boys—

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

—some boys, pricked by divine inspiration, transcend themselves and, before reaching their years of puberty, produce the "gray hairs" of perfection <note>original: "canos perfectionis." A common medieval trope describing a young person who possesses the wisdom and virtue of an old man.</note>, so some, inflated by a diabolical spirit, omit no depravity even in their childhood, so much so that they surpass many old men in the cunning of their iniquity. Therefore, whether it be those who slip gradually and over time into worse crimes, or those who produce the fruit of the wickedness of iniquity, the Church ought not to endure them any longer. For although they should be deferred to for a time, in case the Lord should visit them and snatch them from the bond of Satan by which they are held captive, nevertheless, those in charge should not seem to consent [to the sin]. If they mercifully endure every enormity, it is better that one should perish than that many should be endangered by one; especially since their salvation is doubtful, while the clear damages caused by him are not few. For who is ignorant of how many virgins might be violated by one wicked man whom the Church tolerates in the hope that he might be converted? Is it therefore just that while the leader fears to strike one lest he die, he allows many more innocent ones to be dragged to death? Therefore, for a time, we ought to consult the sinner's salvation mercifully and kindly, in a spirit of gentleness, repeatedly exhorting the one who wanders, as long as (as I have said) we are able to tolerate his misery without harm to many others. But if we make no progress, he ought finally to be rebuked with zeal—as if in the "fourth year" <note>An allusion to the parable of the fig tree, which is given four years to bear fruit before being cut down.</note>—so that perhaps, being provoked, he might return to his heart and repent of his wicked works; but in the fifth year, if he is not corrected, the "iron of the blade" must be used <note>original: "ferro incisionis." Likely a metaphor for excommunication—cutting the member off from the body of the Church to save the rest.</note>. But why this? Because a person cannot remain in the same state for long: but either proceeds from good to better, or falls from bad to worse. For just as the good progress toward the better, so the wicked advance toward the worse. The former add patience to their faith, humility to patience, hope to humility, and charity to hope. The sons [of the wicked] add impatience to their unbelief, pride to impatience, and to pride...

# Part of the Exposition

**Column 1**

despair: for despair is hatred. And so it happens: just as the elect, in the fifth place, receive the divine fire—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "donum spiritus sancti"</note>—so the reprobate, as if in a fifth apostasy, fall into hatred, which is the opposite of charity. Because of this, they sin mortally beyond measure, because they sin against the Holy Spirit and fall into that most wicked crime which is not forgiven men, neither in this age nor in the future. 

And it should be known that the Lord sustains the sinner through to the third precipice, sparing and pitying the delinquent. In the fourth, He threatens terribly; He does not "turn" toward them in the three, but in the fifth, there is no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the future. Hence it is said through the prophet: "Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of the people, and for the fourth, I will not turn him." <note>A reference to Amos 1:3. The author interprets the biblical phrase "I will not turn" as God ceasing to offer the grace of conversion.</note> For he who is not converted in the third, the Lord says He will not turn him over the fourth. Because he who adds impatience to the sin of infidelity, and pride to impatience, and is not converted, already over the fourth the hope that he can be converted is taken away. This is because the despair that succeeds in the fourth place is close to the sin which is "unto death"; and he returns to life with much greater difficulty the further he recedes from the heat of faith by despairing. 

And yet, if he still can, let him be converted and live; lest perhaps He who raised the four-day-dead <note>original: "quatriduanum," referring to Lazarus, who had been dead for four days (John 11:39).</note> from the deceased, and He who threatened the fig tree <note>original: "ficulnee," referring to the parable of the barren fig tree in Luke 13:6–9.</note> but was moved by the prayer of the gardener, might show mercy even now, though He says He will no longer show mercy. 

But let us see regarding the three crimes: why is hope not taken from them, or <margin>John</margin> why is it taken from the fourth more than from the three? First, however, it is necessary to say briefly that just as in the order of the four animals <note>The "four living creatures" from Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4, often associated with the four Evangelists.</note>, sometimes the "man" is prescribed first—as in the prophet Ezekiel—and sometimes the "lion"—as in this book—so sometimes we begin from humility, which pertains to the man, or from the pride which is its opposite; sometimes from faith or infidelity. For both faith and humility are "first" according to different perspectives. Therefore, if sometimes we begin from faith, and sometimes

<column-break/>

from humility, it is not due to carelessness, but to authority. For both are permitted, and therefore we hold to both. 

However, to address what was asked, it is known to all Catholics that the first cause of perdition is the sin of pride. The only-begotten Son of God, wishing to destroy this at the very front when coming to redeem the world, did not wish to come in His majesty and show the power of His might. Instead, He who was God was made man; He who was great was made small; He who was rich was made poor; and He who was Lord became a servant. This was so that, according to His name and glory, His praise would be to the ends of the earth, and so that He might demonstrate that the good of humility—which the proud creatures had looked down upon—is precious and worthy of God, showing this by action rather than by speech. 

Whoever, therefore, is not afraid to be proud after this, commits a very great crime, sinning especially against Christ Himself, who was made small and humble. To touch upon a few points out of many: he who, knowing the poverty of his King, is ashamed to be in need—does he not offend Christ, who was placed in a manger? He who is ashamed to ride the humble animal of Christ <note>The donkey.</note> and seeks for himself the arrogance of a spirited horse—does he not offend his King, whom he remembers sat upon an ass? He who disdains to serve his equals—does he not offend his Lord, who washed the feet of His disciples? 

Therefore, he who is not ashamed to be proud in the Church of God after the humility of Christ, and goes on defiantly against His precept, commits a crime worthy of damnation. But truly, we have learned (by the witness of Truth itself) that things which are impossible for men are not impossible for God <note>original: "impossibilia deo," reference to Matthew 19:26.</note>. He who refuses to be converted out of love for temporal glory is often touched by the Lord in that which he loves most; so that while the iron chain by which he was bound is broken, at least through being struck, he might be converted to God. 

But behold, a second enemy rising up as if from the side, seeks to subvert the work of God and to add his iniquity...

# John's Fifth [Book] on the Apocalypse 181

**Column 1**

through iniquity. For a person, spurred on by the Devil, begins to grumble under the lashes <note>The "lashes" or "scourges" (flagella) refer to divine discipline or hardships intended to correct a sinner.</note> of punishment: and to burst out with his voice against the Lord: not knowing, or caring little to weigh the matter according to the work of Christ, which He endured for our sake—He who did no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth. <margin>Sin against Christ</margin> Therefore, he sins who thus grumbles against the suffering Christ, who suffered not for His own fault, as we do, but for our crimes. Yet the Lord endures even this second crime, still seeking to turn the sinner back. For He who raised His Christ from the dead also raises the afflicted person from the miseries of his punishments: so that, having received mercy, he may be comforted and live. If, however, once he is freed from the lashes, he does not believe that the Lord struck him and healed him for this purpose—that henceforth he might live in justice and not in sin—but instead attributes <margin>Fortune</margin> both [the punishment and the healing] to fortune, he does not seek the things of God, but the things of the world. In this, he commits as it were a third crime, sinning against Him who died for our sins and rose for our justification. <note>original: "pro propter peccata nostra: 7 resurrexit propter iustificationes nostras"</note> But very often, when the pious Physician <note>A common medieval metaphor for God or Christ treating the "sickness" of sin.</note> sees that the lashes have not benefited the man, He seeks to call him back to Himself with kindnesses, lifting him up on high with Him and making all things happen prosperously for him beyond his hope: if in any way the man might reflect and consider the long-suffering of God's patience, and seek to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Whoever is converted, even in this way, will still find salvation. But he who is not converted even in this way, so as to believe in Him who makes poor and makes rich, who humbles and lifts up—but because <margin>Fortune</margin> fortune seems to smile on him (as he himself thinks, and as some say)—his hope is deprived of the desire for future blessedness, and he begins to hope for the fleeting riches and honors of this life. By this, he deserves all the more the indignation of Him without whom not even a sparrow falls to the ground; for he returns to the one who made him neither through the adversity of the lashes, nor through the prosperity of this life, but walks through the ways of his own desires. Therefore, regarding the fourth crime, the Lord does not turn

<column-break/>

him back: but leaves him according to the desires of his heart, lest perhaps if a true plague touches him, he should again begin to blaspheme. Yet He still sends His messengers to him, who may open His ways to him from the beginning even to the end: whether by comforting him in adversity, or by deterring him in prosperity: lest perhaps he should excuse himself on account of the ignorance or laziness of the preachers. If perhaps at the very end the word of God becomes a weariness to him, and he not only refuses to receive correction, but even begins to mock and hate the preacher as a messenger of evil—scorning both the one who was sent and the One who sent him—what remains but that the bad tree be cut down and cast into the fire? For on account of our diverse weaknesses, God wanted there to be diverse orders of preachers in His church—not just one who might happen upon one person—so that he who does not hear the first may at least hear the second. And indeed, he is praiseworthy who corrects himself at the voice of the bishop <note>original: "episcopi"</note> speaking generally in the church and commanding the mandates of God, or forbidding the contrary, as one having authority; mindful of that which the Apostle says: *He who resists authority, resists the ordinance of God.* <note>original: "Qui resistit potestati: dei ordinationi resistit." A reference to Romans 13:2.</note> But he who is so hardened that he refuses to obey the bishop unless he knows that what he commands is a mandate of God, let him at least hear the deacon reading the Gospel of God, and let him be converted and live. If, however, he says he does not understand, let him hear the priest <note>original: "sacerdotem"</note> who has the office of teaching and who explains the words of God to him daily. If, perhaps because that priest's life appears contemptible, such a person scorns him, let him hear the preaching of the hermit, who has nothing in common with the world. But if he rejects them all and scorns them all—and even, so to speak, Elijah <note>original: "Helyam"</note> himself—what is expected from Elisha <note>original: "Helyseo"</note> but the pouring out of the vessel of God's wrath? Understand this concerning any wicked man who is unwilling to act well. 
Now let us see concerning the multitude of worldly people (whose case is similar). Although it was said only for the sake of the elect

This zeal of God is fitting for special men in many ways, and not in one way only—namely those designated by **Elijah** <note>Helyas</note> or **Elisha** <note>Helyseo</note>. This is because the one who loves more is set on fire with a greater zeal against those who commit offenses, and also because it is more fitting for those whose lives are irreproachable and to whom the manifestation of the Spirit bears witness to be zealous. Most often these men rebuke the faults of offenders through words, or letters, and commands; but for those who are incorrigible, they threaten their souls with total death.

# Joachim [of Fiore], Fifth Part on the Apocalypse

...rebukes among the peoples. And this indeed God works in the holy ones. But what does the evil spirit work in the **children of distrust**? <note>original: "filijs diffidentie"; a reference to Ephesians 2:2, often translated as 'children of disobedience'</note> As long as holy preachers stroke and soothe their wounds, they honor and revere them—just as **Herod** revered **John** <note>John the Baptist</note> before he rebuked him concerning his brother’s wife. But if, after many exhortations and the sweet words of the saints—by which the sinner is nourished but not corrected—there comes suddenly to him another in the spirit of **Elijah** and **Elisha** <note>Prophets known for their sternness and miraculous judgments</note>, he is either corrected by his word (if he is to be corrected), or, having become worse because of the correction, he soon despairs. And what is worse than that: he begins to persecute and hate the physician, who loves that man’s health more than his own life; so much so that the physician does not cease to speak to him in the power of God, even for fear of death, if in any way he might be able to free him from death and loose him from the chain of his captivity. 

This, therefore, is the reason why the severe rebuke of the saints is called the "last plague," and why the wrath of God is fulfilled in it. Truly, it is because in the other words of the saints, the impulse of God's wrath is held back for a time, because the saints pretend <note>original: "simulēt"; here meaning they moderate or soften their tone</note> to speak harsh words to sinners so that they do not fall into the pit of despair. But in these [last plagues], because it is the time of judgment, no attention is paid to what may follow: either the sterile tree must produce fruit, or it is cut down so that it may wither and be cast into the fire. 

Therefore, this is a **great and wonderful sign** <note>Refers to Revelation 15:1</note> that was seen in heaven (that is, in spiritual understanding). Men wonder at this enough when they begin to see what they once did not see, and to understand certain hidden judgments which they did not understand. Among their number, this was great and wonderful enough: namely, why some saints spared ungodly men and endured them until death, while others punished and killed them; and why some speak to sinners humbly and kindly, as if to their brothers who are sick unto death, while others speak in zeal as if to the enemies of God—and yet both do good, and both act for the sake of life, following the one Lord? For this itself is a great and wonderful sign, and therefore it signifies something else, which is greater

<column-break/>

than itself. And what is that? The **Coming of the Redeemer and Judge**. Jesus Christ is one person, yet both God and man. He came first as a man in a spirit of gentleness; He is to come a second time as God in a spirit of judgment and fire. He had come first to redeem the world; He is to come a second time to judge the human race. In the first coming, sinners were given life; in the second, even the just shall fear. He, therefore, who so flatters himself regarding mercy that he does not fear judgment is a fool, because the Lord is both: namely, merciful and just. 

Behold, this is the sign of this matter. And although this sign—which was shown in the six or seven angels—does not pertain specifically to anything but the Day of Judgment, yet because those plagues of the angels are called the "last," it is understood that other times and other plagues have preceded them, in respect to which these are called the last. All these things had to be recorded as a kind of beginning, so that by comparing them, the sign itself might be understood. For the number five is not spoken of simply in itself, but in relation to the four preceding it. 

For through three times (as we have already said) the **fig tree** was expected; in the fourth it was altogether to be cut down by the Lord’s command. But the Lord of the vineyard abounded in mercy, so that He might patiently endure it in the fourth year—to be cut down without doubt in the fifth year if it should by no means produce fruit in the fourth. <note>A variation on the Parable of the Barren Fig Tree in Luke 13, adapted here to fit a five-stage historical scheme.</note> Regarding how this reaches the five parts of this book, and by what grace of reason the pouring out of the vials corresponds to the fifth order, enough has been said (as we believe). We are bound to cross over to other depths and to examine the rest that follows. <margin>Psalms</margin> For **deep calls unto deep** <note>original: "Abyssus enim abyssum inuocat"; Psalm 42:7</note>, because the depth of one scripture invites another depth; and the more things are said, the more things remain to be said. ...rebukes among the peoples. And this indeed God works in the holy. # Part of the Explanation by the Abbot

...the **bronze sea** <note>original: "mare eneum"; a reference to the large washbasin in Solomon’s Temple used by priests for purification (1 Kings 7:23).</note> in which the priests, once it was filled with water, would wash themselves. 
<margin>The law among the people</margin> 
However, this **glassy sea** <note>original: "mare vitreum"; from Revelation 15:2.</note> mixed with fire was shown in the spirit to the seeker of heavenly mysteries. This is because the baptism of the Old Testament was able to wash away external filth—just as water does—but it could not wash away internal filth. Only the **divine fire** consumes the impurities of the inner man. Furthermore, that fleshly people of old could hear the words of the Law sounding out (like the bronze sea), but to see "through a mirror darkly" <note>original: "videre autem per speculum in enigmate"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12, meaning to see spiritual truths indirectly.</note> is the proper gift of the faithful of Christ. Again, because this gift is not given to all whom the wave of baptism purifies by washing, and because we do not so despise the baptisms of the former Testament that we would also reject our own baptism, we may more fittingly understand the **priestly life** in the bronze sea and the **monastic life** in the glassy sea. Truly, the priestly life ought to be loud with preaching, while the life of monks—who are called to this—ought to be clear and transparent in contemplation. For in the water, the **Word** is signified; in the fire, the **gift of the Spirit**. In the water is the teaching of the letter, which is not apart from faith; in the fire is the spiritual and life-giving understanding. And that former teaching, if we use it healthily, cleanses the more serious crimes; but this spiritual fire diligently dries up the spiritual vices. Finally, the former instructs the soul in the virtue of humility, while the latter sets the humbled soul on fire with the flame of charity. However, the following words manifest that this sea does not belong to just any of the faithful, but to the **perfect** alone, when it is added:
<margin>Chapter 3</margin> > ¶ And I saw those who had conquered the **beast** and its **image**, and the **number of its name**, standing upon the glassy sea.

If the "beast" signifies the multitude of infidels persecuting the Church of God, the "image" signifies the doctrine of that beast, and the "number of its name" signifies the great multitude of vices, then we say those who have conquered these three are better 

<column-break/>

than those of whom **Augustine** says: "I have found none better than those who have made progress in monasteries." <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of the Western Church.</note> Finally, that same man, in his book on the Psalms, commends **three orders**: the first of the **laity**, the second of the **clergy**, and the third of the **monks**. Indeed, from the first of these (the laity), the victory over the **beast** is specifically required. From the second (the clergy), the victory is required not only over the beast but also over its **image**. From the third (the monks), the victory is required not only over the beast and the image, but also over the **number of its name**. 

For it is enough for a layman to manfully keep his faith and fight for it even unto death, provided he does not remain in mortal sin. But for a clergyman, it is not enough to keep the faith; because the clergyman ought to be the "mouth" of the layman when someone asks about the **doctrine of Christ**. He has a necessity to stand in the battle line on the day of conflict against the snares of heretics and to confound those who rise up against the faith from the opposite side, just as it is written concerning the blessed **Stephen**: "Certain men from the synagogue rose up disputing with Stephen, and they could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit that spoke through him." <note>Acts 6:9-10. Stephen was the first Christian martyr.</note> 

For if the laity are questioned about their faith, they either simply profess themselves to be Christians, or they say they believe in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But if they are asked for the **reason** <note>original: "ratione"; the logical or theological justification.</note> of this faith, they respond: "It is not for us to give a reason for this, because we are **laymen**, unlearned <note>original: "ydiote"; meaning those without formal theological training.</note>, and ignorant of the law of God; but we have our teachers among us, from whom you can inquire about these things, who may respond sufficiently to all your questions." For this is the usual excuse of the laity to those who question them about their faith. But if this is so, how will the faith of the laity stand if the clergy fail in the responses of doctrine? It is necessary, therefore, that the clergy be such that they overcome both the beast and its image by the constancy of their faith and the purity of their doctrine, so that neither their members fail in torments (except with the palm of victory), nor their words fail in response, as long as the power and faculty of speaking remains in them. Truly, the victory over this beast, which remains in the multitude of those sins which—if by others...

### Joachim’s Fifth Part on the Apocalypse

<margin>Augustine</margin>
...may be judged as venial; yet by perfect men, they are avoided as if they were mortal. These things are avoided by true monks who are worthy of God, who are permitted to live as they choose—being guided by the Spirit—rather than having it demanded of them by others. This is not to say that there have not been many in the order of the laity or the clergy who, under the guise of a layman or a cleric, observed monastic perfection; just as, on the contrary, many who wear the monk’s habit are far from that perfection which the habit represents. But private examples do not negate the general rule, nor does a hidden grace undo the order of a manifest gift. For, to pass over other matters:
<margin>To what purpose one enters the religious life.</margin>
to what purpose does any religious person enter the cloister—from which he is not permitted to leave without a command, nor even to look out—except so that he may turn away his eyes so as not to see vanity? He enters so that he may restrain his ears from hearing the songs of harlots and the words of the children of this world, for which the prophet groaned that he was "of unclean lips" <note>original: "immundum labijs"; a reference to Isaiah 6:5, where the prophet feels unworthy before God due to the worldly talk he has participated in.</note>. He enters to abstain from idle words and from the superfluous desire for food, as well as from every gift or the private ownership of anything without a specific command. And—what is greater than all these—he enters to turn away from his own individual will, so that by trampling underfoot such diverse "material for vice," he may conquer the vices themselves without difficulty. For it is very difficult to conquer vices where the material for those vices is abundant and strong. It is a great thing, and to be held as great, if someone lives in the world in such a way that the enemy does not prevail over him. Yet, simply because someone is not defeated, it does not mean they are immediately to be considered a victor. It is one thing to resist the enemy and stand continually in the battle line to avoid being conquered; it is quite another thing to remain in tranquility once the enemy has been utterly defeated. The former is indeed to be crowned because he fights manfully and does not cease fighting until death; but the latter is raised up on high to sit on the **throne of Christ**, because he has fought and he has conquered. Therefore, those who conquered the beast through faith—despising the kingdom of the world, which belongs to the beast—and conquered its image through the wisdom which is from heaven—not receiving any doctrine other than that which the **Roman Church** preserves and preaches—and conquered the number of its name through prayer, fasting, and other spiritual exercises; these were seen to stand upon the **glassy sea**, which is mixed with fire. This is because the contemplative life belongs to them alone,

<column-break/>

and they alone feel the ardor of the charity of God, for it is granted to them to triumph manfully over these three wars. But who are those who truly excel, if not those who leave behind not only their possessions, but even themselves, desiring to grasp the height of that precept where it is said: *Unless anyone renounces all he possesses, he cannot be my disciple*? <note>Luke 14:33.</note> For he who is called a monk is not necessarily a monk, just as not every cleric is truly a cleric, nor is everyone who is called a Christian truly a Christian. He, therefore, who is a true monk, considers nothing to be his own except his **zither** <note>original: "cytharam"; a stringed instrument often used in the Middle Ages to symbolize the harmony of the soul or the body’s discipline.</note>—that is, the "new man" who is created according to God, or the work of the Holy Spirit, in which three general strings resonate. Of these, the Apostle says: *Now abide faith, hope, and charity, these three.* <note>1 Corinthians 13:13.</note> For a heart cannot purely praise God if it is occupied by the images of kings and the anxieties of the world. *Where your treasure is, there also is your heart.* <note>Matthew 6:21.</note> For we sing sweetly in our hearts through faith, hope, and charity only if no love of worldly desire occupies the heart. Thus, it is not without reason that the victors over those three things are described as having the "zithers of God." For those who keep their hearts empty of worldly desires are worthy to be filled with the gifts of heaven. Conversely, those who think little of stripping off the "old man" <note>A Pauline concept (Ephesians 4:22) referring to the sinful, worldly nature of a person before spiritual renewal.</note> are unworthy to put on the "new man," and those who do not refuse the gifts of the world are unworthy to have the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He, therefore, who wishes to have the zither, must strive to overcome not only the beast and the image, but also the number; for he cannot receive the way of life of Christ who imitates the footsteps of the first man through the works of the flesh. But he who overcomes those three things pursues the zither of the three strings, which the Lord grants. For he who is not broken by the terror of threats into obeying the beast, nor deceived by the pretense of its doctrine into falling away from the hope he has in Christ Jesus, nor soothed by the presence of carnal love into deserting the love of God (which he received through the pouring out and infusion of the Holy Spirit), is proven to have the gifts of the plectrum <note>The tool used to pluck the strings of the zither, here symbolizing the active application of faith.</note> of faith, hope, and charity. Without these, we are unable to praise God with heart and soul, and in these, the praise of God is made whole and perfect.

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual rigors of the monastic life as a path to "perfection," comparing the internal discipline of monks to a "zither" with three strings: Faith, Hope, and Charity. It emphasizes that true victory over the world requires renouncing not just possessions, but one's own will and carnal desires.</summary>

### Part of the Exposition by the Abbot

<margin>the psalms.</margin>
...and it remains. 
> "Praise him," he says, "with the psaltery and the harp." <note>original: "psalterio & cythara"; a reference to Psalm 150:3.</note>

But why with the psaltery? Because 
<margin>The Law among the people</margin>
the fullness of the Law is contained in the psaltery. Truly, the ten strings signify the ten commandments of the Law, in which the fullness of justice is contained. But because it was a long journey to run through all the commandments, and the multitude of rules actually provided more opportunities for sinning, another prophet was sent to say: 
> "The Lord will perform a shortened word upon the earth." <note>original: "Verbum breuiatum"; a reference to Isaiah 10:23 and Romans 9:28, suggesting that the complex Old Testament Law is condensed into a simpler New Testament message.</note>

What this "shortened word" might be, the Apostle makes clear when he says: 
> "Now abide faith, hope, and charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." <note>original: "fides: spes: charitas"; 1 Corinthians 13:13.</note>

Hence it is that in this book, the saints rejoice with harps <note>original: "cytharis"; often translated as lyres or zithers.</note>; for the Lord, coming in the flesh, did not wish to frighten the hearts of the disciples with the expression of many commandments, but after some things pertaining to faith and hope, He said: "This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you." But now let us see and hear what those who have received such gifts sing, and whose song it is said to be that they were worthy to sing. For he says:

<margin>Chapter 15.</margin>
**H**aving the harps of God, he immediately added and said: And singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying:

For you alone are holy; for all nations shall come and worship in your presence, for your judgments have been made manifest." <note>This is the "Song of Moses and the Lamb" from Revelation 15:3-4.</note>

¶ This song, as far as the literal wording goes, is found explicitly neither in the words of Moses nor in the words of the Lamb. Therefore, what is said to be common to Moses the lawgiver and the Lamb the giver of grace,

Thus it is seen to belong both to fear (pertaining to the servant) and to love (pertaining to the son), according to that saying of the Psalmist: 
<margin>psalm.</margin>

For those who say:

show that they themselves fear the one whom they preach and teach should be feared. And those who immediately add: 
> "For you alone are holy," <note>original: "pius"; here used in the sense of the divine holiness and mercy shown in Revelation 15.</note>

surely show that they love the one whom they confess to be holy. And it should be noted that the cause of fear is contained in the preceding words, in which it is said: 
> ¶ "Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages." 

The cause of love is in the following words, in which it is said: 
> "For all nations shall come and worship in your presence, for your judgments have been made manifest."

For they say, "Great and wonderful are your works," which Moses wrote that you performed. "And just and true are your ways," by which you showed mercy to a few and judgment to many. Who, considering these things, will not fear you—especially one who is ignorant of the very ways of your judgments? And because now, at the end of the ages, you so abound in holiness <note>original: "pietate".</note> that you receive for salvation the nations which you once cast away, and because the judgments that were once obscure—why you had struck the Gentile people with blindness—have now been made manifest to the world to your knowing and understanding servants, showing that you struck them in order to heal them: who will not glorify you and magnify your name? ¶ For to "magnify" belongs to the one who loves, rather than to the one who fears. 
<margin>Luke.</margin>
> "My soul magnifies the Lord,"

# John's Fifth Vision on the Apocalypse

...because He is just in judgment and pious in His mercy. But why do they sing this to the praise of God? It is because those who commit spiritual fornication <note>original: "fornicantur a deo"; meaning those who turn away from God for worldly idols or sins</note> against God howl and blaspheme, accusing the judgments of God which they feel within themselves. They act as if the judgments by which they are condemned were not made manifest, even though God is so pious and merciful that He even spares the unfaithful nations who seek to be converted to Him and to come out of the darkness into His admirable light. For if He receives the unfaithful nations who are outside into salvation, it follows that it is not His will that any of those who are inside should perish; rather, they despair of themselves so that they do things that are not fitting and provoke their Savior to anger. It follows:

<margin>Text 4</margin>
**And** after this I saw: and the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven was opened: and the seven angels came out of the temple. <note>Revelation 15:5-6</note>

**In** the fourth part, John says that the temple of God was opened in heaven and the ark of the testament was seen in it. But here he says that the "temple of the tabernacle of the testimony" was opened in heaven, and seven angels came out of the temple having the seven plagues. It is asked, therefore, whether both things were said of one temple, or whether there are two specific temples about which these things are said. In the Old Testament, the tabernacle of the testimony was placed from the beginning in Shiloh <note>A major religious center of Israel before the Temple was built in Jerusalem.</note> in the tribe of Ephraim; but in the course of time, the temple was built in the tribe of Judah. That the tabernacle was rejected and the temple was built signified that the old things pass away and the new things succeed them. But it is not so in this place, where mention is first made of the temple, and afterwards of the temple of the tabernacle—especially since he says that it is "in heaven." For both temples are shown to remain in heaven: both that one mentioned in the fourth part and this one treated in this fifth part. Thus, it is understood that that one is one thing and this is another, just as under the Old Testament the temple was one thing and the

<column-break/>

tabernacle <note>The Tabernacle was the portable tent used by the Israelites in the wilderness, while the Temple was the permanent stone structure in Jerusalem.</note> was another; yet they are written in a reversed order in this book. But perhaps they are written in a reversed order in this book so that it would not be thought that he was writing about that physical temple or tabernacle, which were shadows of things to come, but rather about the spiritual temples that exist in heaven. For these temples are in heaven and not on earth, because whatever is said about them is to be understood in the spirit and not according to the letter. 

Therefore, according to allegory, these two mystical temples signify the two Testaments. In the first of these, the letter of the New Testament lay hidden, like an ark in a temple, or like a wheel within a wheel <note>original: "rota infra rotam"; a reference to the vision of Ezekiel 1:16, often used in the Middle Ages to describe how the New Testament is concealed within the Old.</note>, so that at some time it might be seen to emerge from it—just as virginal chastity emerges from the married life. Nevertheless, from the second temple, spiritual understandings have gone forth, according to the fact that there are many—that is, these seven angels and the seven spirits of the Lord sent into all the earth. 

But why is it called the "temple of the tabernacle"? Is it because the first believers had only the Old Testament, while the latest—that is, ourselves—have the Old and the New together? For we know that the temple of God is founded on the earth, in which it is fixed as if having roots; but the tabernacle could pass from place to place like a mobile thing, easy to carry. This is because the Old Testament was once given to an earthly people, and in them it solidified its roots to confirm the promises of the fathers; but the New Testament was issued in circumcision <note>Meaning it began among the Jewish people.</note> in such a way that it immediately passed over to the Gentiles. Yet it did not pass over in such a way as to desert the holy Apostles who were of the circumcision; rather, they themselves, who were of the seed of Abraham, passed over to the Gentiles with the doctrine of both Testaments. They presented themselves to the faithful as a "temple of the tabernacle," in which those who have entered in spirit may meditate on the law of the Lord day and night. Finally, even the stones of the temple which seemed more precious than the rest, and the vessels and columns, were transferred to the Gentiles—to the injury of the Jews—so that it might be a sign of the "living stones" <note>A reference to the faithful believers as building blocks of a spiritual church (1 Peter 2:5).</note> who were to pass from Judea to the Gentile people, so that the sanctuary might be built in them...

<summary>This page explores the symbolic transition from the Old Testament (the Tabernacle/Ephraim) to the New Testament (the Temple/Judah), explaining why John sees a "temple of the tabernacle" in heaven. The author argues that while the Old Testament was rooted in one people, the New Testament is a mobile, spiritual truth that passed through the Apostles to all nations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Revelation, Chapter 15.
