### Abbot’s Part of the Exposition

...of the Lord. And it is right that this temple is called the "tabernacle of testimony" <note>original: "tabernaculum testimonij"</note>: because by the very fact that the words of the testament—whether of the Old or the New—are mystical and spiritual, they bear testimony to the truth. Even beyond those things written according to the letter, they bear testimony themselves; for which reason they are called testaments. For we know that the testaments of the dead are the testimonies of the living; and while those legal testaments are handed down in writing because of those who have passed away, these spiritual testaments are delivered by the living voice of those who bear witness. This is because the "letter," which is said to "kill," was given as a testimony to the faithful; and the "spirit," which is said to "give life," bears witness to the truth outside and above the letter. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note> Therefore, the New Testament was given to the Gentile people—both the New together with the Old—and many, by continually reading it, have entered into it so that they might perceive a spiritual understanding. Yet they could not go out except at the appointed times, when, through those works of the Lord which have been completed, the testament itself is opened part by part. This is done so that those who are outside (though sometimes to their own harm) may see and understand what is being said.

<margin>Genesis</margin>
In this way, the two angels staying in the house brought Lot—who was waiting before the doors—in to themselves; and soon, having closed the door, they struck those who were outside with the darkness of blindness. <note>See Genesis 19:10-11. The author uses the story of Lot in Sodom as a parallel to spiritual protection and judgment.</note> These same angels, when they went out through the opened door, poured out upon them the wrath of their indignation, raining down fire and sulfur upon them to destroy their memory from the earth. Just so, these seven angels, who remain inside through contemplation, do not wish to go out to pour their bowls until the temple is opened. Once the mysteries are made manifest, they may reproach the unbelievers for their works and rebuke them for the hardness and blindness of their hearts—so that they might either be converted with their whole heart (if they are the elect) or, if they are the reprobate made worse, they might receive the full reward of their dissent. For just as Phinehas <note>A priest in the Old Testament known for his zeal; see Numbers 25.</note> was zealous for the Lord, and as one of the sons of the prophets anointed Jehu <note>Jehu was anointed king of Israel to execute judgment on the house of Ahab; see 2 Kings 9.</note> as king of Israel to carry out judgment on a wicked people, so even now, from the spiritual temple, the seven angels go out to exercise judgment upon spiritual sinners.
<meta>catchword: s</meta>

<column-break/>

men: concerning whom [it is said]: **And the seven angels went out of the temple, having the seven plagues.** These angels are said to have "plagues" because they burn continually with divine love; when they see God held in contempt and blasphemed by a wicked people, they are vehemently wounded <note>original: "sauciant," meaning to wound or strike</note> in their breasts. Unable to endure this out of grief, they pour out the wrath—which they receive from the fire of the spirit—upon unrepentant sinners. They themselves grieve first, but finally they inflict plagues upon others, so that once their zeal is acted upon, those who are zealous may be healed from their grief. But lest any should be unequal to the task, or perhaps ignited by the sting of mere passion as they pour out their zeal, the text shows how great their perfection is (or ought to be) to whom this task is given, when it adds:

## ¶ Clothed in pure and bright stone, and girded around their breasts with golden sashes.

There is no doubt that those who, by the gaze of divine love, deprive themselves of temporal things and their own desires, are clothed in that "pure and bright stone" of which the Apostle says: *But the Rock was Christ.* <note>original: "Petra autem erat Christus," quoting 1 Corinthians 10:4. While most Bibles say "clothed in linen," this manuscript uses a version reading "clothed in stone" (lapide), symbolizing Christ.</note> But we must remember here that the woman (whose sign we read of above, and understood through the gift of the Spirit) is shown to be "clothed with the sun" <note>The Woman of the Apocalypse from Revelation 12.</note>—namely, Christ. Just as the devotion of those who live spiritually in the wilderness is equal to those who live specifically for God in monasteries <term>cenobijs</term>, so too in the figures pertaining to them, a similarity is maintained. The reason why one is "clothed"—whether with the sun or with stone—is suggested by the Apostle when he says to the faithful: *Strip yourselves of the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of this world, and put on the new man who is created according to God.* <note>Ephesians 4:22-24.</note> As for the golden sashes <note>original: "zonis aureis"</note> girded around their breasts, what shall I say, except that they signify purity of mind? It is not necessary to speak much of them, for the difference between golden and leather sashes, and between girding the loins or the breasts, was sufficiently discussed (I believe) in the first part of this book. However, let him who does not have a golden sash beware...
<meta>catchword: not have</meta>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Book of Revelation, Chapter 15. [The text begins mid-sentence] ...not [girded] at the breasts: lest he be kindled with an indiscreet zeal <note>original: "indiscreto zelo"</note> against his neighbors, and strike delinquent brothers while being himself someone who ought to be struck by another. Instead, let him first search diligently the secrets of his own heart; and if he finds anything in himself worthy of being struck, let him learn to have humble mercy on the faults of others, just as he knows himself to be in need of mercy. This is so that he is not judged by the Lord in the same way he judges his neighbor. 

Indeed, many have "leather belts" <note>original: "zonas pelliceas"</note> around their loins, but few have "golden belts" around their breasts. This is because there are many who keep the continent life of the flesh <note>Refers to physical chastity or asceticism</note>, but it belongs to few to possess purity of mind. For the leather belt suffices for the chastity of the body, because the mortification of the flesh tames the insolence of lust. But here, the golden belt is necessary: because we can in no way keep the mind from dissolving into impure desires unless we bind it incessantly with a special kind of meditation. This is so that while the mind does not cease to meditate on good things, it does not happen to think upon the things of others, even for an hour. 

Almighty God incites such men to zeal, and leads them out like war-horses <term>dextrarios; these were heavy medieval chargers used in battle</term> from his stables to the fight. For the pastors of the church, who announce the words of God to the people in a spirit of gentleness, are like palfreys <term>palafredi; gentle, steady riding horses</term> carrying the King; they represent him to the people by preaching with constant thought. However, spiritual men who devote themselves to silence, hearing that the people have not turned away from those who strike them, are kindled with zeal. Like noble war-horses, snorting with the fury of their nostrils, they throw themselves more freely against the impious in the time of necessity, the more they have conceived this with a greater desire over a long time. It follows:

<margin>Lecture 6</margin>
**And one** of the four living creatures <note>original: "animalibus," referring to the four winged beings around God's throne</note> gave to the seven angels seven golden vials <note>or bowls</note>, full of the wrath of the living God, who lives forever and ever.

If the prophetic word had simply stated which of the four living creatures gave the golden vials to the seven angels, we might perhaps solve the other

<column-break/>

mysteries with less labor. But if the Holy Spirit wished to bind these and many other "sacraments" <note>In this context, "sacraments" refers to hidden divine mysteries or symbols</note> so that they cannot be solved without labor, it ought not to appear burdensome that we often make a digression so that we may grasp through other things those which cannot be grasped on their own. 

I recall having already said in certain places that the prophet Elijah <note>original: "Helyam"</note> designated the order of contemplatives (that is, the hermitic order). When he, kindled with zeal, had killed the prophets of Baal and fled from the face of Jezebel—who sought him for evil—and had come to Horeb, the mountain of God, he made a plea to God (who was speaking to him) against the sons of Israel, saying: "I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant. They have thrown down your altars, Lord; they have slain your prophets; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life to take it away." <note>1 Kings 19:10-14</note> 

When he had spoken thus in the sight of the Lord, the voice of the Lord came to him, saying: "Go and return on your way through the desert to Damascus. And when you arrive there, you shall anoint Hazael <note>original: "Azahel"</note> to be king over Syria; and you shall anoint Jehu the son of Nimshi to be king over Israel. And Elisha <note>original: "Helyseum"</note> the son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint to be prophet in your place. And it shall come to pass, that him that escapes the sword of Hazael shall Jehu slay; and him that escapes from the sword of Jehu shall Elisha slay." 

Behold, Elijah, performing the work of zeal, left his place to Elisha (at the Lord's command); and what Elijah touched upon in part, Elisha—through himself and through the kings who were his contemporaries—fully completed. Here it must be noted with great care: that although Elijah is commanded to anoint the kings, he nevertheless did none of these things himself. This is to be understood like the saying about the fig tree: "Cut it down, then." <note>Luke 13:7</note> Indeed, after three years the Lord threatened the unfruitful fig tree, yet at the prayers of the dresser of the vineyard, he let it be; but in such a way that the very tiller who had prayed for it would give the sentence against it, saying: "And if it bears fruit, well; but if not, then in the future you shall cut it down." 

Therefore, just as Elijah was zealous for the Lord, yet he himself was not permitted to pour out his zeal by his own hand upon the house of the impious king and the people...

### Abbot Erpo’s Part

...unjust: but it is just for Elisha <note>original: "Helyseum," referring to the prophet Elisha, successor to Elijah</note> to prevail in following the prophet in what he himself had conceived in his mind: he explores it diligently. Thus, the fourth animal—that is, the hermitic order <note>the "heremiticus ordo" refers to the tradition of desert-dwelling monks</note>—could not have failed to be zealous against the errors and impurities of those who have played the harlot away from God, and especially in the Greek <note>original: "Greco," likely referring to the Greek Church or region</note> context. But because the general time had not yet arrived in which there would be no excuse, a monastic order was established by them which could endure longer, and to which He could commit His turn in performing the zeal of the Lord at the opportune time. This was done lest divine moderation should seem to have too little long-suffering and patience if, before the sentence was given, He were to pass over other great men who would threaten this ruin (unless they were overturned) in the beginning. 

Therefore, the order itself went before, having prepared bowls <term>phyalas; these are the "vials" or ritual bowls mentioned in Revelation 15:7</term> delivered to it by the just God. Yet the order did not pour them out itself, but handed them over to others to be poured out at the time when sins would be completed. For those bowls are indeed pious traditions, by which they might instruct perfect disciples, teaching them to work justice and to be zealous for it, so that "their light might shine before men who see their good works" <note>Matthew 5:16</note>. For that is the true religion in the sight of God which both shines outwardly through example and is kindled inwardly by the heat of justice. 

Hence, these same bowls are shown not only to be golden but also full of the wrath of God: because both that which is shown outwardly from their life is bright and precious, and the love that lies hidden within cannot fail to avenge the injury of its God. For these two find themselves together: namely, a holy life and the zeal of God, so that one cannot please God without the other. For if a man is still proven to be subject to many vices, with what face or by what reason shall he be zealous against the sins of offenders? He who (his conscience being witness) knows himself to be one of those who are worthy of death, doing the same things that he condemns in others. Whence also the apostle says: "You are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who judges. For in that in which you judge others, you condemn yourself. For you do the same things that you judge" <note>Romans 2:1</note>. Therefore, he who finds himself to be so miserable that...

<column-break/>

...unless God has mercy on him, he is worthy of wrath: let him have mercy on offenders rather than show zeal, unless perhaps he also collectively reproves himself and those whom he knows to be sharers in guilt, according to that saying of the Psalmist: "We have sinned with our fathers: we have acted unjustly: we have committed iniquity" <note>Psalm 106:6</note>. 

In other cases, however, it is necessary to both lead a holy life and have manifest signs of holiness if one wishes to exercise the zeal of God upon sinners, so that there is no one who can criticize his life and say: "Cast out first the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye" <note>Matthew 7:5</note>. And that other saying: "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justices, and take my testament into your mouth?" <note>Psalm 50:16</note>. 

Hence, when the Lord was zealous and said: "It is written: For my house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves," the Jews answered and said: "What sign do you show us, because you do these things?" <note>John 2:16-18</note>. It is as if it were said through a rebuke: "We know that doing this belongs to the saints and to those whose life is unlike human life. But you, who live among sinners as one of us, and eat and drink with the same sinners—we do not see how this pertains to you, unless you show an open sign, through which we may understand you to be such a person whom we can all rightly obey." 

It is clear, therefore, that he who wishes to perform the zeal of his God must lead a holy life, because the Holy Spirit—to whom this zeal belongs—does not rest in a body subject to sin, the Lord saying: "If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter" <note>John 14:15-16</note>. For we read that the spirit of Moses was propagated, yet only upon those who were of good testimony and appeared to be more just among the whole multitude of the children of Israel. The spirit of Elijah <note>original: "Helye"</note> rested upon another man, yet upon him who had left all things for the sake of God. Therefore, Elisha <note>original: "Helyseus"</note> received from Elijah both the holy life designated by the garment and the spirit of the zeal of God: because...

### John Quinta on the Apocalypse

...if one were to precede, the other would by no means follow. Hence it is that the bowls <term>vials; sacred bowls used for pouring offerings, here containing divine judgment</term> which one of the four living creatures <note>original: "animalibus," referring to the four beings around the throne of God described in Revelation 4 and 15</note> handed to the seven angels—and which are said to be golden and full of the wrath of God—represent the institutions that the fathers of the monks received from spiritual men. They were seen to have the brilliance of the most precious gold in their teaching of morals, and a most fervent zeal in the love of God. This is not only because they taught in this way, but because, through a certain power of "fired" words, they were able to hand both down to those who were obedient to them. 

And it is well said that "one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God," adding: "of Him who lives forever and ever." For just as it belongs to one who dies to be judged, so it belongs to one who lives to judge; and just as it belongs to one who dies to suffer injury, so it belongs to one who lives to exact vengeance. For in those saints who patiently endure all things, the image of the dead Christ is seen—crucified by wicked men in the weakness of our flesh. But in those who carry out His zeal, He shows Himself to be living "forever and ever," and that He will come from heaven in the glory of His Father to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. 

Hence it is said by the Apostle: *It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.* <note>Hebrews 10:31</note> It also seems that the water in which Christ first came—to mortify our members—resembles something dead, or flowing toward death; whereas the fire in which He is to come the second time resembles something ever-living and remaining forever and ever. The first pertains to patience; the second to the zeal of God. Just as the Holy Spirit first appeared as a dove <note>a symbol of peace and patience</note> and finally in fire <note>at Pentecost, symbolizing zeal and judgment</note>, so the time of patience will be followed without delay by the time of judgment. It follows:

<margin>Text: 7</margin>
**And the temple was filled with smoke from the majesty of God and from His power; and no one could enter the temple until the seven**

<column-break/>

**plagues of the seven angels were completed.**

The angels go out from the temple to pour out the wrath of God upon the earth, and the temple is filled with smoke so that no one can enter it until the seven plagues are finished. This belongs to the just and strict judgment of God: when spiritual men—whose proper place is to remain inside—are compelled to go outside to enact the zeal of God, none of those who are outside are permitted to enter within until judgment is passed on the wicked men whose desperate madness is incurable. 

But why can no one enter the temple? Because, it says, it is "filled with smoke from the majesty of God and His power." Smoke offends the eyes so that they cannot see; likewise, divine indignation blinds the eyes of the minds of wicked men, so that they do not see the truth, just as it is written: *The wicked shall deal wickedly, and none of the wicked shall understand.* <note>Daniel 12:10</note>

<margin>Isaiah 6</margin>
Hence, in the person of the Almighty God, it is said to Isaiah: *Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest perhaps they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.* <note>Isaiah 6:10</note> 

But why is the temple said to be filled with smoke "from the majesty of God and from His power," except because just as humility and weakness pertain to redemption, so majesty and power pertain to Christ as Judge? Is it not because there is security where there is the smallness of Christ, but fear where there is His majesty? For just as He once showed Himself as small in order to enlighten the humble and the meek of the earth, so after His ascension into heaven, residing with the Father on the throne of His glory, He shows Himself ineffably great. Thus, by pouring out the darkness of His judgment, He strikes those who walk in pride with blindness, lest they ever (it says) "see with their eyes and hear with their ears."

# Abbot: Part of the Explanation

...temple <note>original: "templum"</note> until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished. This is the place for us to ask: why seven plagues and seven angels? We stated above that the pouring out of the bowls <term>vials; sacred bowls used for pouring offerings, here containing divine judgment</term> properly belongs to the fifth period of the church, and we have sufficiently expressed the reasoning for why this should be held.

<margin>Note wherever</margin>
And yet, as has often been noted: the individual parts of the book have their own specific times assigned to them, although all times are common to all parts, according to what we took care to suggest in the "doorway" of this work under the figure of the five peoples. Therefore, even if the proper time for those pouring out the bowls of God’s wrath is the fifth—just as the first is the time of the Apostles, the second of the Martyrs, the third of the Doctors, and the fourth of the Virgins—nevertheless, all times are common to all. Thus, every single period from the first to the seventh has within itself something pertaining to the pastors and something pertaining to the other orders; clearly, because each of these orders continues through succession from the first period until the seventh. Because these successions of individual orders vary through each period, it happens that each order is distinguished into seven portions. And although the order itself is one, it receives multiplicity through succession.

<margin>Common rule</margin>
For this reason: just as the first part—under the appearance of the seven angels of the seven churches—and the third part—under the appearance of the seven angels sounding trumpets—touches upon the sevenfold nature of the church uniformly, so the fifth part does so under the appearance of the angels pouring out the seven bowls, with individual angels assigned to individual times. For in each period, it was necessary for patience to precede, followed by zeal. This zeal is seen to be lacking in no one who felt that things should not be tolerated for the time being but punished in the end—just as with any man who, having been waited for over a long time, thinks little of grasping discipline. This, therefore, is the reason why there are said to be seven angels who went out of the temple to pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God. And why are they written to have seven bowls or seven plagues, when they are all of one order and one power? From this sense, that which the Lord says through Moses does not differ: *I will strike you seven times for your sins* <note>original: "Percutiam vos septies ppter peccata vestra"; see Leviticus 26:21</note>. Clearly, there are seven periods—or rather six, but with a double sixth—which are given for the repentance of the people of God. In these periods, the elect are struck so that they may be perfected, and the reprobate are struck so they may have no excuse for their sin, and so that their completed malice may be revealed in the charity of the just.

<column-break/>

Or perhaps zeal for justice is not born of charity? That zeal which corrects, which rebukes, which scourges, and (to mention that which is more severe) which kills? Was it not moved by this same burning zeal that Peter temporally killed Ananias and Sapphira <note>Referring to the story in Acts 5:1-11 where Peter rebukes a couple for lying to the Holy Spirit, and they fall dead</note>? Far from it. For who is more angry at the foolishness of a youth than a father, who loves him more? Who is more indignant at the levity of a girl than her bridegroom, who is bound to her by exceeding love? It is not, therefore, because the Lord hates His people that He strikes them with these plagues, which are harder than the rest, but so that they may be converted and live—even if impious men always progress toward the worse and hate Him without cause who loved them, snatching them from the power of the prince of darkness and redeeming them in His own blood. Therefore, whether the reprobate like it or not, it is necessary for the elect of God to perform the zeal of God, and to rebuke more harshly those who refuse to be converted, pouring out upon them the bowls of the wrath of God. For there follows:

->And I heard a great voice out of the temple, saying to the seven angels: "Go, and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth."<-

A great voice was heard from the temple, saying to the seven angels that they should pour out the seven bowls of God's wrath upon the earth. This has a manifest meaning from both Testaments: that spiritual men ought to pour out the zeal of Jesus upon those who are worldly <note>original: "terreni," literally "of the earth"</note> even unto the end, and who lust after earthly things—even if some of them, according to a false appearance, seem to be heavenly. For because of the diversity of the orders in which carnal men are known to lie to God through a false habit <term>monastic clothing</term> or tonsure <term>the practice of shaving the top of the head to indicate clerical or monastic status</term>, it is written in the following sections that the bowls of certain angels are poured out upon the sea, and upon the fountains of waters, as well as upon the sun and the air...

<summary>This page explains that while the "seven bowls" of judgment specifically characterize the fifth age of the Church, the themes of divine discipline and zeal apply across all seven historical periods. It justifies God's wrath as an act of parental or marital love intended to spur repentance, comparing it to Peter's harsh judgment of Ananias and Sapphira.</summary>

# Joachim: Fifth Part on the Apocalypse

...or that any celestial men were designated by the air. Here it is said not to just one of the angels, but to all generally: "Go and pour out the seven bowls of God's wrath upon the earth" <note>original: "Ite & effundite phyalas ire dei in terram"</note>. And it is well said: "Go," because those who are moved by zeal for God from the tranquility of their souls seem to "go" there where they were not before. And again, he who—after the quiet of his silence and while the love of his God flourishes—goes out to speak the word and rebuke delinquents, is said to "go." For unless he leaves a little of what he was holding onto—to go toward the height where he was not before—he can do nothing but what he did before: keep silent, read, sing psalms, and pray constantly to his God. But it is necessary that he go eventually, because the "great voice" heard from the temple does not permit him to rest. Therefore, the angels go because the heard voice compels them, and they each pour out their bowls <term>vials; sacred bowls used for offerings, here containing divine judgment</term>, every one in his order and in his time. For there follows:

### Concerning the first angel pouring out the bowl.

<margin>Text 2</margin>
<margin>Chapter 16 Text 1</margin>
And the first angel went and poured out his bowl upon the earth, and there came a sore and grievous wound <term>ulcer; a painful, festering sore</term> upon the men who have the mark of the beast, and upon those who worshipped its image.

¶ The primitive church, which was gathered in Judea from the "Circumcision" <note>original: "circuncisione"; referring to Jewish converts to Christianity</note>, is called the "earth," as we have already written elsewhere—either because it was gathered from an earthly people, or because it, embracing the earthly commands of Moses, was unwilling to rise up everywhere to celestial words. Because of this, the spiritual men who were in it took up zeal for the name of God against it, reproaching it for its hardness, as can be weighed from the words of Paul’s letters and the book of the Acts of the Apostles. Among these is what Paul says to those same people: "on account of the false brothers brought in, who came to spy on our liberty" <note>original: "propter itroductos falsos fratres qui venerunt explorare libertatem nostram"</note>

<column-break/>

"and in perils among false brothers," and in another place: "Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision" <note>original: "Videte canes: videte malos operarios: videte concisionem"; Paul's play on words regarding circumcision</note>. Thus, while spiritual men were zealous against that church which is called the Circumcision, a "sore and grievous wound" was made in the men who had the mark of the beast and worshipped its image. This happened because those who wanted to be called Christians—yet in such a way that it was permitted for them to live carnally and walk according to the desires of this life (which is to have the "mark of the beast," that is: the will of the flesh, which is contrary to the word of the cross, and to observe the doctrine of the Pharisees, which is to "worship its image")—could not bear the correction of the righteous and were wounded by a sore and grievous wound of grief. Thus, for those same carnal men, turned as if into madness and fury, their plague became incurable. So much so that some, having entirely abandoned the faith of Christ, returned to Judaism like "dogs to their own vomit" <note>a reference to Proverbs 26:11 and 2 Peter 2:22</note>, segregating themselves from the companions of Christ as if from the unclean and uncircumcised, and associating themselves again with the blasphemous men who had consented to His death and were partakers with those who shed His blood. For we said above, when we were dealing with the "beast" so often written about, that it began from the first Herod who killed the innocent children, and its first head was the Synagogue of the Jews. Those false Christians are rightly accused of having received the mark and worshipped the image of that beast, who, having left the liberty which is in Christ Jesus, accepted its carnal examples and pestilential doctrine.

# Part of the Exposition, Page 400

...tiles. Moreover, this is compared to the **sea** because of the **bitterness of the heart** and the **fluctuation of infidelity** <note>original: "infidelitatis"; referring here to the lack of faith among non-Christians</note> in which they had been held for a long time: that is, from the days of **Japheth** <note>Japheth was one of the sons of Noah; in medieval theology, his descendants were traditionally identified as the peoples of Europe and the Gentile world</note> until the time of **Christ**. However, by the blessing of the Lord—just as the formerly blessed land of **Israel** had brought forth fruit-bearing trees—so too this sea, at the voice of those preaching the **word of the cross**, brought forth a **copious multitude of chosen fish**. Concerning this, the Lord said to the first preachers:

> **"Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men."** <note>original: "Uenite post me : & faciam vos fieri piscatores hominum"; a reference to Matthew 4:19</note>

Truly, even in that very gathering of the faithful, there were many who followed **Nicholas**—one of the first seven deacons, from whom the sect of the **Nicolaitans** <term>an early Christian sect mentioned in Revelation 2, often accused by early Church Fathers of promoting licentiousness</term> was propagated. There were also those who returned, like a **washed sow to wallowing in the mud**—such as **Julian the Apostate** <note>The Roman Emperor Julian (r. 361–363) who famously rejected Christianity to return to Roman paganism</note>—and those who would believe for a time but fall away in a time of temptation, just as many failed during the persecutions. There were also those who wished to keep the faith of Christ while still living in impurity, like the **Gentiles who do not know God**. In the house of God, there could not be a lack of **spiritual men** who, seeing such abominations, would pour out their zeal upon the people—either because the reprobate themselves refused to be corrected of their sins, or because the chosen were being defiled by them, enduring and ignoring their iniquities. For the blessed **Paul** had predicted that such men would be in the church of God, saying:

> **"I know that after my departure, grievous wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves, men will arise speaking perverse things, to lead away disciples after them."** <note>original: "Ego scio qp intrabunt post discessionem meam lupi graves..."; a quote from Acts 20:29-30</note>

And **Peter**, too, in his epistle, foretold something similar, saying:

> **"There were false prophets among the people, just as there will be teachers of lies among you, who will introduce sects of perdition; and many will follow their luxuries, through whom the way of truth will be blasphemed; and in greed, they will trade in you with fabricated words."** <note>original: "Fuerunt in populo pseudo prophete..."; a quote from 2 Peter 2:1-3</note>

And these things, along with many other

<column-break/>

events that happened afterward, were predicted by the holy **Apostles** in the spirit of prophecy, so that the chosen would not be scandalized <note>offended or led into doubt</note> when they saw these things being carried out in reality. Furthermore, the great multitude of those who stood in the faith—and how quickly they turned back from what had been handed down to them by the holy commandment—is testified by the one who wrote the **Church History** <note>referring to Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History"</note> in that section where he begins to discuss the persecution of **Diocletian** and **Maximian** <note>Roman Emperors who led the "Great Persecution" against Christians starting in 303 AD</note>, saying:

> **"When, through great liberty, our habits were spoiled by too much indulgence, and our discipline was corrupted—while we envied one another and detracted from one another; while we bit and accused each other in turn, and the pile of evils swelled among individuals—Divine Providence, seeing the loss of discipline inflicted upon its people from too much peace and excessive laxity, first began to gently restrain those who were slipping."**

And a little later:

> **"But since no understanding of His mercy was returned by the people—instead, like those who do not know God, they thought things were done without Divine Providence, and through this they persisted even more in their evils—even those who seemed to be leaders of the people and princes of the divine mandate became unmindful of it. They were inflamed against each other with contentions, zeal, envy, pride, enmities, and hatreds, so much so that they believed themselves to be exercising a tyranny rather than a priesthood."**

Then at last, according to the voice of **Jeremiah**:

> **"The Lord has darkened the daughter of Zion in his anger, and has cast down the glory of Israel from heaven; nor did he remember his footstool in the day of his wrath."** <note>original: "obscurauit dominus in ira filie syon..."; a quote from Lamentations 2:1</note>

And after some other remarks:

> **"It is not for us to describe how many kinds of injuries were heaped upon the priests of God, just as we did not think it our task to explain in detail how great the madness of dissension <note>original: "rabies discensionis"</note> previously burned among Christians."**

It was only permitted to hand this much down to history: that by the **just judgment of God** and necessary correction, we felt the **divine hand**. For it does not matter what the remedy...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Seven Vials of Revelation 16. The author is transitioning from a general discussion of persecution to a specific interpretation of the second vial poured into the sea, which represents the world or the Gentile church.</meta>

Joa. Fifth Vision on the Apocalypse.
Aa 4

...to bear those for whom either the whirlwind of persecution was brought in, or those whom—and how many—the storm of lack of faith <note>original: "infidelitatis procella"</note> has submerged. But I shall commemorate those things which edify either us as we speak or others as they listen; and so forth. As for those who were much more numerous, whom fear oppressed and whom terror alone struck down before the conflict even began: I think it better to pass over them. Truly, it was pleasing to commemorate this so that we might know that fault was not lacking among the Christian people even in the time of the holy martyrs. Because of this, spiritual men would not have been undeservedly right to pour out upon them the **vial of the wrath of God** <note>original: "phyalam iracundiæ dei"</note>; let no one think that all the faithful of that time stood firm in persecution, or that all were holy and just before the persecution simply because one reads of many being crowned with the glory of martyrdom during the persecution of the pagans. Therefore, because not only the people but also the clergy transgressed in many ways, the vial of the wrath of God was poured out upon them, so that those who refused to be converted from the errors of their ways might know by experience what it was that the Apostle said to the Gentile: **"If God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you."** <note>A reference to Romans 11:21, where Paul warns the Gentile converts not to become arrogant toward the Jewish "branches" who were broken off.</note> For it follows:

<margin>Text 4</margin>

# And it became blood like that of a dead man, and every living soul died in the sea.

Some people, when they are rebuked, grieve if they either fear to avenge themselves or are unable to do so. And this especially happens to those who have **zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.** <note>A reference to Romans 10:2, describing those who are religious but lack true spiritual understanding.</note> But those who wish to be honored among the people—such as some of the clergy—if they are ever publicly rebuked for their vices and sins, or even for whatever errors they refused to correct when warned more privately: their heart dies within them out of confusion and shame. The warmth of hope completely recedes from them as they fail within themselves and cast the fear of the Lord out of their sight. And because there were many

<column-break/>

in that course of time who confessed that they were not God <note>likely meaning they confessed they were not "of God" or were merely human</note>, but denied it by their deeds: when spiritual forces began to rebuke them for their errors, a certain **blood of sloth** <term>accidie: a state of spiritual apathy or "sloth," one of the seven deadly sins, often described as a "dryness" of the soul</term> was produced in their hearts, through which every soul that was living in the sea died. Why is this? Because **worldly men** <note>original: "homines animales"; literally "soulish" or "animalistic" men, referring to those driven by natural instincts rather than the Holy Spirit</note> who thought they were doing something great because they had withdrawn from the worship of idols, yet did not want to withdraw from vices and sins, were soon scandalized when spiritual men rebuked them. They said: "If we cannot be saved in the Christian faith, what did it profit us to have withdrawn from the worship of idols?" Therefore, **every living soul died in the sea**, because worldly men who do not know the things of the Spirit of God, if they are compelled to desert that which they love, lose even that little bit of faith, hope, and devotion which they have toward God. Whence, by a fitting judgment, they were handed over to temptation; so that those who, in a time of peace, boasted of faith without the work of justice, might be proven to have had a **dead faith** in the time of temptation.

And it should be noted that this universal term "every" or "all" is not always to be understood in the Divine Scripture as "the whole," but for the "greater part." Just as, conversely, the word "no one" does not always carry the meaning it seems to, but another. For if the word "no one" were always to be taken for "not a single person," then when **John the Baptist** says in the Gospel concerning **Christ**: **"And no one accepts his testimony,"** <note>original: "Et testimonium eius nemo accipit"; John 3:32</note> he would by no means add: **"But he who has accepted his testimony has certified that God is true."** And if this universal term ("All") always looked to the entire universe, the Lord would by no means say: **"And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself,"** <note>John 12:32</note> but rather "some things." Therefore, what John says in this place—**"Every living soul"**—is not to be understood as the entire community of believers, but as the vast multitude of those who failed in faith during their time. It follows:

<summary>This page interprets the second vial of Revelation (the sea turning to blood) as a spiritual judgment on worldly Christians and clergy who abandoned their faith during trials because their devotion was superficial. The author also provides a lesson on biblical language, explaining that "all" often refers to a majority rather than every single individual.</summary>

->Exposition of the Abbot<-

### Concerning the third angel pouring out the vial

<margin>Text 5</margin>
**And the third Angel poured out his vial upon the rivers, and upon the fountains of waters: and they became blood.** <note>This refers to Revelation 16:4.</note>

In the third period, which began with Constantine <note>Constantine the Great (r. 306–337 AD), the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity.</note>, the state of the church was changed: because of the peace and dominion given to it, and because permission was given to Christians to teach their children freely. Thus, with the clergy ordained and disciples multiplied, there appeared in various places—to irrigate the hearts of the faithful—what seemed to be rivers and springs of water. These no longer brought forth the bitterness of worldly wisdom, by which Christ was lost (as the sea water did previously), but rather the sweetness of that wisdom which descends from heaven. 

But although this was not lacking, human iniquity remained; for those who were not called back to the right path even by this mercy deserved to be punished. For some of those who appeared to be teachers among the people, presuming from their own hearts, brought forth certain falsehoods among the many truths they seemed to teach. In these errors, they began to have not only many followers from that same multitude of clergy, but even defenders of their heresies. This reached such a point that a schism <note>A formal split or division within a religious body.</note> occurred among the clergy and the people of God: some standing for the truth, while others defended a lie as if it were the truth. 

And when holy men rebuked them with peaceful words, seeking to call them back to the right path, the heretical priests grew so powerful (as one reads in ecclesiastical history) that many were killed by their counsel, and were crowned with a new martyrdom after the victories over the pagans. Therefore, it came to pass that the third angel poured out his vial upon the rivers and the fountains of waters: that is, upon those bishops and priests who were infected with the Arian error <note>Arianism: A 4th-century heresy named after Arius which taught that Jesus Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father but was a created being.</note>. And it became blood: because when spiritual men were zealous against these wicked teachers, there was produced in their hearts a drink of mortality, regarding which the Apostle says:

<column-break/>

"The letter kills, but the spirit gives life." <note>original: "Litera occidit: spiritus autem viuificat." From 2 Corinthians 3:6.</note> For then, when heretics are rebuked for their doctrine (which they understand only in a carnal or literal sense), they harden their hearts and "stop their ears like an asp" <note>A reference to Psalm 58:4.</note> so that they refuse to ascend to spiritual understanding. They claim that those who introduce a meaning other than what is written in the literal text of the books are the ones who are heretics. 

But it was done by the just judgment of God that those who shed the blood of Catholics to defend their error should themselves soon drink such a potion of carnal doctrine—that which stays only in the literal "letter"—being ignorant of what is written: "It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing." <note>original: "Spiritus est qui viuificat: caro autem non prodest quicq̄." From John 6:63.</note> Whence it is added immediately:

<margin>Text 6</margin>
**And I heard the Angel of the waters saying: You are just, who are, and who were, the holy one, who have judged these things: because they shed the blood of saints and prophets: and you have given them blood to drink, as they are worthy. And I heard another Angel from the altar, saying: Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments.** <note>Revelation 16:5-7.</note>

The "Angel of the waters" designates those great and spiritual teachers who opposed the heretics for the sake of the true faith, showing that the heretics' understanding was "bloody" and carnal. Concerning this, the Lord said to Peter: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed it to you." <note>Matthew 16:17. Here "blood" is used as a metaphor for human, non-spiritual reasoning.</note> 

And because some wonder at the judgments of God, complaining to one another and saying, "If we believe a falsehood which we think is true, what is our fault? Or what iniquity is in us?" The reason why their hearts were so blinded is demonstrated when it is said: "Because they shed the blood of saints and prophets: and you have given them blood to drink, as they are worthy." For it is human to fall sometimes into error; but to persecute car... <note>The text ends mid-word; the catchword "nal" suggests the next page continues "carnaliter" (carnally) or "carnem" (the flesh).</note>

<summary>This page interprets the third vial of Revelation as the Arian heresy during the reign of Constantine. It explains that the "rivers" are the clergy, and their "turning to blood" represents a fall into literalist, non-spiritual interpretations as punishment for persecuting faithful Christians.</summary>

...Catholics <note>original: "tholicos", likely referring to those who turned against the orthodox faith</note> for the defense of error: and to shed their blood (as the Arians did) is diabolical. Thus it is: that when corrected by spiritual men, they were not worthy to receive discipline, but rather hardened their necks so that, having despised spiritual doctrine, they chose for the defense of their error to hold an understanding which brings death to those who taste it. And he says well: that they shed the blood of saints and prophets, because the Arian persecution <note>Arianism was a major 4th-century heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ. The Arian emperors and kings often violently persecuted those who held to the Nicene Creed.</note> involved not only pious priests and bishops, but truly also monks and hermits, among whom were some possessing the spirit of prophecy—as we read concerning Saint John the Anchorite and Saint Benedict—since even Catholic teachers may be called "prophets" because they predict future things. And the angel says well, *You are just: because you were holy*: for in the Old Testament He showed Himself to be holy and just, giving retribution to the proud; and in the New Testament likewise. Truly, the Angel who responded from the altar and said, *Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are your judgments*, I think designates the Catholic bishops gathered in councils <note>Ecumenical councils, like Nicaea or Chalcedon, where bishops gathered to define orthodox doctrine and condemn heresy.</note>, who, confirming the Holy Scriptures, condemned the heretical teachers. For an altar is made of stones set apart from others and joined together in one place. In this way, the holy bishops are set apart in some measure from the rest of the multitude of the faithful, so that they who are the elders in the Church might discern, when gathered in councils, what is to be rejected and what is to be held. It is as if the angel responded from the altar, saying: *Even so, Lord God Almighty: true and righteous are your judgments*: when from that very order of bishops some are gathered in councils, who, condemning heretical depravity, testified both that God Almighty is a just judge and that those men fell into the "judgment of blood" by their own fault, since they themselves shed blood. ¶ Concerning the fourth angel pouring out the vial.

<margin>Text 7</margin>
### And the fourth Angel poured out his vial upon the sun; and it was

<column-break/>

given to him to afflict men with heat and fire. <note>Revelation 16:8.</note>

¶ By the sun, as we have already said, are designated the "contemplatives": <term>contemplatores</term> <note>Those dedicated to the "contemplative life," such as monks or mystics, who focus on the direct vision of God.</note> whose proper role is to leave all things behind to gaze upon the face of God and see Him who made us. This "order" <note>Referring to the monastic or contemplative order of the Church.</note> had a conflict in the fourth period with the beast that ascended from the sea: because the former preaches chastity, while the latter preaches luxury. The former preaches contempt of the world, while the latter preaches temporal glory and worldly honors. But because in that state, through hidden pride, a desire for vain praise often creeps in where manifest religion marks out a reputation for holiness, even in an order so illustrious there could not be lacking something to be rebuked by holy men. For truly, all religion is vain which is not solidified and founded on the root of humility, even if by its excellence it seems to transcend the stars of heaven. Hence it is written: *The joy of the hypocrite is but for a moment: though his pride mount up to the heavens, yet he shall perish like a dung-heap in the end.* <note>A paraphrase of Job 20:5-7.</note> Therefore, even upon such men, if they refuse to be corrected in time, the vial of God's wrath is poured out just as upon the others. For those who are of this sort must be rebuked all the more harshly because their sin touches God more than it touches men. Truly, because they think themselves holy and just and more worthy than others, they are ignited with anger when rebuked by someone, as they think nothing of the lives of others who—as they themselves estimate—presume to rebuke them with reckless habit. Those who are of this sort are also accustomed to complain to those who flock to them, explaining their life to them so they may believe they are being rebuked out of the zeal of envy and the bitterness of hatred. Whence it often happens that they afflict men with heat and fire, and begin to seethe with great heat; because there is nothing that so offends the hearts of the carnal, and which so drives them to despair, as when they hear those whom they venerate as saints being rebuked by others whom they think are good men, but yet unequal in merit. And from this same rebuke, among those whom they believed to be holy...

<margin>hypocrites</margin>

<margin>Text 8</margin>

With a great heat, as I have already said, men are scorched when they hear those whom they have long testified to be holy among men being rebuked as lost souls. Because of this, they turn to the injury of those who say they are hypocrites; they blaspheme the Spirit of the Lord, who has power over these plagues and who gives power to men to perform judgment, so that they might feel the spiritual plagues which they refused to resist when they were able. It follows:

<margin>Text 9</margin>
**Neither did they do penance, so as to give Him glory.**

Since hypocrites are rebuked because they seek glory from men—to whom they are bound by certain familiarities and carnal friendships—and refuse to be converted, it would be necessary for those very men who were deceived by them to do penance. This is because the glory they ought to have paid to God alone, they instead paid to mortal men. But because they are ashamed to desert those they once began to venerate (truly, because they are merely men), they not only do not do penance to give glory to God—to whom alone it is due—but having become even worse, they break out into these very blasphemies, saying: "These men who hate and persecute the pious saints are not from God." For they must be believed to blaspheme none other than the Holy Spirit himself, whom they blaspheme because he rebukes and, as it were, persecutes the hypocrites whom they consider to be holy, spiritual men. For even those whom the Lord rebuked for having incurred the spirit of blasphemy did not blaspheme the Holy Spirit with open insults; rather, they said: *He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.* <note>original: "in belzebub... principe demonum ejicit iste demonia". A reference to Matthew 12:24, where Christ’s miracles were attributed to the devil.</note> It follows:

### Concerning the fifth angel pouring out the vial.

<margin>Text 10</margin>

Just as in the four previous periods of time the four living creatures <note>A reference to the four "animals" or "living creatures" from Revelation 4, which Joachimite theology often links to different historical eras or types of religious orders.</note> shone forth, and yet in each rank many abused the grace and mercy of God under a false appearance of religion, so in the fifth period the general church shone forth, which is the seat of God—specifically the order of clerics and monks <note>original: "clericorum & conuentualium"</note>. From this order, these seven angels have gone forth to perform judgment. As Augustine says: <note>referring to St. Augustine of Hippo, a foundational Church Father.</note> *I have found none better than those who have improved in monasteries, so I have found none worse than those who have failed in monasteries.* And because those who are of this sort desire beyond measure to reign over their brothers, they are not undeservedly taken away from the kingdom of the humble King; they pass into his kingdom of whom the Scripture says: *He is king over all the children of pride.* <note>A quote from Job 41:34, traditionally interpreted as referring to the Devil or the Antichrist.</note> Therefore, whatever canonical orders or monasteries have been conquered...

### John: The Fifth [Vial] in the Apocalypse

the beast: either by his image, or by the number of his name: they are made the seats of the beast, because he rejoices more in such people as these, saying:

They do not consider that the religious habit does not help, but rather hinders, if the outward clothing is at odds with their way of life. For those who endure being argued against patiently and justly are confessing their faults. A little later: if they persevere in patience, and grace comes upon them, they find consolation; and having been consoled, they bless the Lord, who saves those hoping in Him. against the Creator. Whence it is added here:

Moreover, they blasphemed Him because of their pains and wounds; for if concupiscence <note>Inordinate or sinful desire.</note> is not resisted from the beginning while there is time for repenting, at the end, when the pains are multiplied because one is not allowed to do what one likes, it happens that
<margin>Note: Death</margin>
the inner parts of the heart are wounded by the arrows of temptation. Whence the Truth <note>The "Truth" refers to Christ.</note> says through Himself: "Strive to enter through the narrow gate; for many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able." <note>Luke 13:24.</note> It follows:

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Seven Vials of the Apocalypse. Having previously discussed the fifth vial poured on the seat of the beast, the author now interprets the sixth vial, which is poured over the river Euphrates, and the appearance of the "three unclean spirits like frogs." The text draws a direct connection between the biblical Babylon and the Roman Empire of the author's era.</meta>

### [Abbreviated] Part of the Exposition

...they cannot feel the wounds of a heavier plague. For we know that the river Euphrates once flowed into that city called Babylon; and it is said later in this book: that the many waters upon which the harlot sits are many peoples. <note>Revelation 17:15.</note> But if the waters of this river called Euphrates are the peoples, nations, and tongues that obey the Roman Empire—since the city of Rome itself is the new Babylon—what does it mean that its waters are dried up at the pouring of the vial? It means that because those in charge do not accept correction, by the just judgment of Almighty God, He weakens their strength, so that with their armies failing, there is no one to resist the kings and tyrants who, as is more fully contained in the sixth part, are to come to strike the kingdom of Babylon itself. As for the one who is said to come **from the rising of the sun**: I think it should be understood literally: that tribulation will begin from the eastern region, as has indeed happened; that is, from that province where (to touch upon the spiritual meaning) the true Sun arose, and from where the light of evangelical preaching shone forth to the western parts of the world. It follows:

<margin>Text 3</margin>
> **AND I saw coming out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits in the manner of frogs. For they are the spirits of demons performing signs: and they go forth to the kings of the whole earth to gather them for battle on the great day of God Almighty.**

¶ After the desolation of the Roman Empire, that <term>iniquitous one</term><note>The Antichrist.</note> will be revealed, who is extolled and opposes everything that is called God or that is worshiped. Moreover, he will have in his company an army of lost men, designated as the beast that ascends from the sea; and a crowd of false clerics, which, as if of his prophets, is designated as the beast that ascends from the earth—namely, the beast which is called

<column-break/>

<margin>Apoc.</margin>
<margin>Bas.</margin>
the **false prophet**. And from their mouths will go forth the spirits of demons to perform signs, so that they may summon the infidel kings to empty out the kingdom of Christ; so that he who holds the place of the dragon may be worshiped by men and thought to be God—and be worshiped by men as if he were God himself. And indeed, their intention, purpose, and will shall be such. Nevertheless, all are to be gathered for the **great day of the Lord**: because the day of the Lord will be near, near and very swift, in which the infidels shall also blush for all their errors. But as for saying **in the manner of frogs**, he wished to express their uncleanness and falsehood, so that the elect may know what kind of spirits they will be, through whom lost men are to perform those signs, and not be scandalized by their offense. For when a frog is inflated, it pretends to be what it is not. So too, those signs will be lies, having nothing of truth or utility. But from that time when these things happen, the day and hour when the Lord comes will be unknown. More so than before the <term>son of perdition</term><note>A title for the Antichrist used by St. Paul.</note> is revealed, for the Lord is not to come for judgment yet. Not only does the Apostle testify to this in the Epistle to the Thessalonians, but he even begs that they not be deceived by anyone or believe this, saying: "We ask you, brothers, regarding the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, that you be not quickly moved from your sense, nor terrified, either by spirit or by word or by letter as if sent by us, as if the day of the Lord were at hand. Let no one seduce you in any way; for unless the falling away comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and is extolled above all that is called God or that is worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God." <note>2 Thessalonians 2:1-4.</note> Therefore, it is clearly evident that before the son of perdition is revealed, the Lord will not come for judgment. But after he is revealed, the day and hour will be uncertain when He will come like a thief to render to each according to his works. Whence also it is added here:

# John’s Fifth Book on the Apocalypse

<margin>Chapter 14 <note>This likely refers to a specific section in the commentator's source or a cross-reference to Revelation 14.</note></margin>
¶ **“Behold, I come as a thief. Blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame.”** <note>Revelation 16:15.</note>

¶ In this passage, John does not continue his own narration; instead, the Lord himself speaks, interjecting with an unfinished and interrupted speech, saying: *Behold, I come as a thief.* This "stealthiness" of his arrival designates his coming as sudden and terrible—a coming that no one knows except the Father alone. For it was not John's task to say at what time or what hour the Lord would come to judgment; rather, while John was speaking and forewarning the faithful about the evils that are to come near the end of the age, the Lord himself speaks and says: *Behold, I come as a thief.* We are to understand by this that when we see the words John speaks in this chapter being fulfilled, the day of the Lord and the arrival of his majesty will be near. From 그 hour onward, the elect must remain in suspense and prepared for the arrival of the Judge, not knowing on what day or at what hour he will come to judgment—just as happened in the days of Lot and the days of Noah. Therefore, only those will be blessed who, having set aside all worldly cares, keep watch and guard the commandments of God, weaving for themselves garments of justice and taking care that they do not appear naked of good works in the presence of such great majesty. They must not be put to shame like Adam, with everyone seeing their foulness and the filth of their sins. For "foulness" is sin uncovered—sin that is not covered by the garment of salvation.

<margin>Psalm</margin>
It is that very garment of which the Psalmist says: *Let your priests be clothed with justice.* <note>Psalm 132:9.</note> Therefore, blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and

<margin>Psalm</margin>
whose sins are covered. <note>Psalm 32:1.</note> Blessed are those who, through the worthy fruits of penance, recover the garment of justice which they had lost. On the other hand, woe to those whose hearts are weighed down with carousing, drunkenness, and the cares of this life, for that day will find them suddenly. This example, which was spoken by the Lord regarding the Flood, should be understood more as referring to the preceding judgment which will occur during the

<column-break/>

destruction of Babylon. This is similar to what the Apostle said in the previous letter to the Thessalonians: *When they say "peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pains upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape.* <note>1 Thessalonians 5:3.</note> It follows:

<margin>Text 15</margin>
¶ **“And he gathered them together into a place which is called in Hebrew, Armageddon.”** <note>Revelation 16:16.</note>

¶ Having completed the words of the Lord saying, "Behold, I come as a thief," John resumes what he had left unfinished and says: *And he gathered them into a place called in Hebrew, Armageddon.* It should be noted that he does not say "they [the kings] gathered," but rather "He gathered." For although it belongs to the unclean spirits to gather those kings of the earth for battle against the Lord and 

<margin>Psalm 2</margin>
against his Christ, it nevertheless belongs to Christ himself to gather them into a narrow place—which they themselves are entirely ignorant of—so that he may do battle 

<margin>Zechariah</margin>
against them, according to that word of the prophet Zechariah: *as he fought in the day of battle.* <note>Zechariah 14:3.</note> I believe the name of the place, which is called *Armageddon* in Hebrew, is symbolic, just like the "Valley of Jehoshaphat." However, an interpretation of this name that I could trust—so that I might know how it translates into our own language—has not yet occurred to me. If it should occur to anyone else before it does to me, I believe they might gain a full understanding of how it applies to this matter from the interpretation of the name itself. It follows:

### Concerning the seventh angel pouring out the vial.

<margin>Text 16</margin>
¶ **“And the seventh angel poured out his vial into the air, and a great voice came out of the temple from the throne, saying, 'It is done.'”** <note>Revelation 16:17.</note>

During the six preceding pourings, the world persisted in its malice; it remained invincible and hardened, refusing to accept discipline. But at this seventh strike, the world will wither away within itself and cease to exist.

...fear of death: whether so that they themselves or others may understand that the Lord is about to do something new upon the earth. ## And the great city was divided into <margin>E. 18</margin> three parts.

It is written in the Gospel: **"Every kingdom divided against itself will be brought to desolation."** <note>original: "Omne regnum in seipsum diuisum desolabitur"; a quote from Matthew 12:25.</note> Therefore, to show that the desolation of the kingdom is approaching—a kingdom that was once one and contiguous—as the sixth period approaches, it begins to be divided into three parts. # Joachim’s Fifth Part on the Apocalypse

...it shall be in Egypt: a work that makes the head and the tail, bending and restraining; and I will cause the Egyptians to fight against the Egyptians; and man shall fight against his brother, and man against his friend. <margin>Chapter 19</margin>
¶ **And the cities of the nations fell.**

¶ Why did they fall? Because the earthquake that shattered the great city also overthrew them. I think, however, that by these "cities," we should understand the Greek churches <note>Joachim refers to the Eastern Orthodox churches, which he considers to be in schism from Rome</note>. Regarding these, in the specific likeness of the court situated outside the temple, it was spoken of terribly under the sixth angel sounding the trumpet: "Cast out the court which is outside the temple, and do not measure it, for it has been given to the nations" <note>quoting Revelation 11:2</note>. If, however, the churches that are contained within this "court" were given to the nations, they are not without reason called "cities of the nations," since they are possessed by them as an inheritance. For so that we might understand the future through the present: a no small population remains in Alexandria that keeps the faith of Christ even to this day, just as in Syria and other places; yet, if one discusses their morals—whether they are truly Christians or Saracens <note><term>Saracens</term>: a medieval term for Muslims</note>—it is open to doubt. Therefore, these kinds of cities were "given to the nations," and have in a way become "of the nations," yet they still appear to stand in the faith. But when it reaches the ears of those who so stand that the solidity of the Christian people is dissolving, do you think they will be able to stand among their enemies? Indeed, even in the Old Testament, there were certain peoples mixed with the seed of Israel, called Samaritans: they kept only the Law of Moses, yet nonetheless sacrificed to their idols; they called themselves Israelites only as long as prosperity favored the Jews. They stood in the profession of the one God only as long as they hoped for peace with the children of Israel because of that confession. Otherwise, as they believed for a season, so in the time of temptation they fell away. So also several...

<column-break/>

...[several] Greek churches (as has already been proven by many experiences) very easily pass from the right to the left <note>from righteousness to error, or from the Church to its enemies</note>—without a doubt because they have retreated from the unity of that church of which Christ said to Simon Peter: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" <note>quoting Matthew 16:18</note>. But why all these things? Is it without cause? Heaven forbid! It is so that the strength of the Roman Empire <note>Joachim often identifies the "Roman Empire" with the Latin Christian world</note> may be weakened on account of its sins, and vengeance may be taken upon the apostate nation. Wherefore it is immediately added:

¶ **And great Babylon came into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath.**

¶ In all past times, the Lord has seemed to ignore the sins of those who fail, so that He might be thought to have forgotten judgment. But when the years of patience are completed and that great day comes in which the city mentioned above is to be judged, that which seemed forgotten will be recalled to memory; for not even one sin can be hidden for which a vengeance worthy of its merits is not taken. For God will give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of His wrath, so that she may feel the bitterness of the passion <note>suffering</note> with which she herself forced the martyrs of Christ to drink, pursuing them from city to city. We do not say this, however, as if the entire multitude of the wicked—who after the resurrection of the dead are to be cast into the furnace of fire—is to be gathered together in the "sixth time" <note><term>Sixth Time</term>: in Joachim's theology, the penultimate age of the world, marked by the arrival of the Antichrist</note> to receive the reward of their error all at once; rather, it refers to that part of the universal Babylon which will be present during the sixth time. For it is the custom of the Holy Scriptures that a part of a thing is often taken for the whole, and what happens to a part is referred to the whole. Why is this? Because even if the circumstances differ according to the time, the will of all the wicked is one, just as is the will of the elect. The children of the rejected Jews hear their fathers spoke of Jesus of Nazareth as a deceiver and an enemy of the Law; and the zeal of their fathers pleases

# Sixth [Part] on the Apocalypse

...of their own: so much so that they themselves crucify him by their will, even when they are unable to pursue him through their actions. And for this reason, if the opportunity were granted, they would most gladly persecute the members of his body; thus they do not seem to be immune from that work. For just as there is one man and he has many members, and yet through individual members he who is one is said to act—for the same person is said to see, though sight belongs to the eyes alone, and to hear, though hearing belongs to the ears alone, and so it is with the other members—so too the entire multitude of the reprobate <note>The "reprobate" refers to those whom Joachim believes are rejected by God, contrasting them with the "elect" or chosen ones.</note>, or of the elect, is seen to perform different works in one part or another, and at different times, earlier or later. Yet they all relate back to a single unity for this reason: that a single will makes those things which are diverse in the members to be shared in common.

<margin>Topic 20</margin>
Therefore, even if at the end there will be one furnace of fire in which the multitude of the reprobate (which is called Babylon) <note>Joachim uses "Babylon" as a symbol for the corrupt, worldly society, and "Jerusalem" for the spiritual Church.</note> shall be tortured without end, in this temporal life it does not happen to everyone in the same way. Rather, some are permitted to prosper until the very end, while others are judged by the Lord in this present life. And this indeed often happens so that the children of men do not forget the judgments of God, and so that malice does not multiply upon the earth. Generally, however, throughout five periods of time, God has endured patiently; He has allowed Babylon to reign in her delights, while the children of Jerusalem are afflicted by the persecuting children of Babylon—those who are born according to the flesh persecuting those born according to the spirit—until the justice of the former and the wickedness of the latter are fulfilled. But in the sixth period, which is near, an end will be placed upon the pride of the former and the affliction of the latter. This is not because tribulation against the elect by the unfaithful peoples outside the Church will cease (even to the death of the flesh), but because internal envy—which leads to the ruin of the heart—shall end. This alone is what those who love God truly desire. For the elect of God do not groan because they see Christians being slaughtered by the sword of pagans; they read that God did not wish to spare even the holy apostles and martyrs in this regard. Rather, they groan because the children of Babylon—who call themselves Christians but are

<column-break/>

not—corrupt good morals through evil conversations <note>original: "corrumpūt mores bonos colloquia malis" — a reference to 1 Corinthians 15:33</note>, and because they always torture the souls of the righteous with their wicked works, and because the righteous hear the name of the Lord blasphemed and are unable to avenge the injury done to their God. Hence, they do not desire to be spared from the death of the flesh, but they desire that the silver and the lead be cast together into the furnace, so that once the dross is universally consumed, that which was precious may become even more precious. Wherefore, when Isaiah said: "I will visit evils upon the cities, and their iniquities upon the wicked," he immediately added: "A man shall be more precious than gold, and a human more than pure gold" <note>quoting Isaiah 13:11–12</note>. Therefore, in the sixth period, there will be a threshing of the general floor and a winnowing fan in the hand of the Lord to purge his threshing floor, so that the wheat may be gathered into his barn, but the chaff burned with unquenchable fire. 

It follows:

<margin>Topic 21</margin>
->**And every island fled, and the mountains**<-
->**were not found.**<-

This has already been mentioned in the second part, regarding the opening of the sixth seal—something I have often said: that in this book, things are touched upon specifically which are contained more fully in a general sense. The **islands** are the episcopal churches <note>The administrative seats of bishops</note> which, surrounded on all sides by the waves of this world, suffer the greatest loss of their saints. The **mountains**, however, are the monasteries in which a narrow and difficult life of innocence is preserved by the servants of Almighty God. In that earthquake, therefore, which will be so powerful on that day—namely, when all the kingdoms of the nations shall be gathered into one and shall rise like the waves of a light sea against the daughter of Babylon—the monasteries shall flee from their places to hide themselves in secret places from the face of the storm. And many churches shall cease to exist, their defenders having been scattered or killed. For that day will not be a day of mercy, but a day of His wrath, just as it is said through the prophet: "Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation and wrath and fury, to destroy the land into a wilderness and to crush its sinners out of it" <note>quoting Isaiah 13:9</note>. Wherefore, the following is added here in a terrible manner.
