# Part of the Explanation by the Abbot

<margin>Topic 22</margin>
**And** great hail like a talent <note>original: "talentum." A talent was a massive ancient unit of weight, suggesting stones weighing nearly 100 pounds.</note> descended from heaven upon men: and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail: for it was made exceedingly great.

The earth being moved and shattered by such a terrible earthquake: it was necessary for the hearts of men to be crushed with fear: and to be split in many ways toward repentance: which those whose hearts are healthy will indeed do (as is shown in the opening of the sixth seal) when it is said: Every slave and free man will hide themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains: and they will say to the mountains and rocks: Fall upon us: and hide us from the face of the one sitting upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb: because the great day of their wrath is coming: and who will be able to stand? But as for those whose hearts are blind: and turned away from the truth: so that they do not wish to see the light which comes into the world: they shall fall into the judgment of the wrath of God (just as the apostle says).

<margin>Romans</margin>
The wrath of God is revealed from heaven upon all the impiety and injustice of those men who hold back the truth of God in injustice: because that which is known of God is manifest to them. And the hail (he says) was great like a talent and descended from heaven upon men. From heaven descends the rain: from heaven the snow: from heaven the hail. From the mouth of the righteous—whose holy gathering is not undeservedly called "heaven"—descends preaching to moisten the hearts of the faithful: there descends a cold threat to restrain the heat of vain and foolish joy: and there also descends a hard rebuke to crush the hardness of impious men: so that they might either return to their heart and perform penance for their crimes: or the unbeliever (as the apostle says) if he departs, let him depart. For what if they are scandalized by the word of judgment and, being destined to perish, they perish? Ahab, the king of Israel, was scandalized by the word of the prophet Micaiah: and he became worse than he was before. Zedekiah, scandalized by the word of Jeremiah, handed him over into custody: But should the

<column-break/>

witnesses of truth have remained silent regarding the truth simply because the sin of those people might be increased by their contempt for the word? For what is harder than the word of Peter saying to Simon Magus: May your money 

<margin>Acts</margin>
be with you in perdition? For it was necessary for the great hardness of the heart to be struck by the great blow of a hard word: not so that he might be scandalized: but so that, having been struck more harshly by the master, he might be stripped of such great negligence. He, however, was not corrected <note>original: "puer sus" (likely a scribal error or contraction for "profectus" or similar, here rendered as "corrected" based on context).</note> but utterly subverted: and he became a persecutor of the one who had struck him for his own salvation. But even now, what do the children of falsehood expect the disciples of truth to say to them? Perhaps soft and pleasing words? If they hope for this, they hope in vain: because it is not the time. If it is a scandal to them, it is unjust: because it is necessary that they preach for the salvation of many that which they know most certainly is to come. But why is this hail, which descends from heaven in the manner we described above, said to be as large as a talent: except that a talent is heavier than many other weights which it contains within itself? And this word which is written concerning the **ruin of Babylon** <term>Babylon: For Joachim, this represents the corrupt, worldly society or the "carnal" church.</term> is heavier than many other words by which so many calamities of the world are expressed. For this reason: carnal men who love the world and the things that are of the world are unable to bear it patiently when they hear that what they love is to perish universally: thinking that nothing is more pleasant than this present life. They blaspheme the Lord who is the author of such a harsh sentence: each one saying to his neighbor: "If it is to be thus, why did He who knows all things before they happen create them to be consumed by such a horrific end, unless those who say He is merciful and a lover of justice are merely flattering Him?" For this is that blasphemy which is proven in the one thief who hung on the cross, saying to the Lord of all who was likewise crucified: "If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us." Indeed, that thief who was hanging on the wood of the cross to the left (as it is thought) signifies the carnal people who, while they live and walk according to the flesh, must sometimes be handed over into the hands of the nations for their crimes. But they blaspheme the Lord, saying: "If you are the Son of God..."

# John’s Sixth [Book] on the Apocalypse

"Save yourself and us!" <note>original: "salua temetipsum & nos." This refers to the taunt of the thief on the cross in Luke 23:39.</note> This is the cry of a carnal people who do not know the things that are of God, but only those of the world. They mutter against Him during their punishments. Since Christ, who was without any sin, hung on the cross for the salvation of all, they respond and ask: "What necessity was there for him to suffer these things? If he is all-powerful and merciful (as the Scripture says), he neither should have suffered this himself, nor should he have condemned us to suffering." For they believe he could have saved the human race without his own suffering and the insults he endured, and simply transferred humanity from the transitory joys of the world to the eternal joys of heaven. This will be their blasphemy then, even as it is already in the mouths of many now. It is in the hearts of all who do not know what the Apostle says: *The word of the cross is indeed foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved, it is the power of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 1:18.</note> It follows:

<margin>Chapter 17 Text 1</margin>
**And there came one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls, and he spoke with me, saying: "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication, and those who inhabit the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her prostitution."**

Regarding the angels having the bowls, much was said in the preceding part of this book. However, the one who comes to John here is the **sixth angel**. It is said to him—more so than to the five preceding him—to uncover hidden sacraments <note>original: "sacramenta," here meaning "mysteries" or "sacred secrets."</note>. The angel comes to John so that John may go toward the angel who calls him, and so the angel may show him the judgment of the great harlot. For unless spiritual men approach the Word of preaching given to the disciples of truth, those same disciples can by no means approach those mysteries through the understanding of the heart, nor see the judgment of the great harlot who sat, and still sits, upon many waters. It is useful to see her judgment, for he who does not know what she is destined to suffer for her errors is easily deceived by the signals of her eyes. This "great one"—

<column-break/>

<margin>Rome</margin>
—the Catholic Fathers have said is **Rome**. They do not mean this in regards to the Church of the just, which has lived as a pilgrim within her, but in regards to the multitude of the reprobate <note>term: "reprobate" (reproborum). In medieval theology, this refers to those rejected by God for their persistent wickedness, as opposed to the "elect."</note>, who blaspheme and attack that same pilgrim Church with their iniquitous works. Nevertheless, if she is to be understood as the principal example, it nonetheless refers to the entire multitude of the reprobate, especially those with the greatest capacity and will for sinning—those who lead a luxurious life full of madness, rejoicing when they have done evil and exulting in the worst things. Therefore, the location of this most infamous harlot is not to be sought in only one kingdom or one province; but just as the wheat of the elect is diffused throughout the whole field of Christianity, so the chaff of the reprobate is dispersed through its entire breadth. As for what the "many waters" signify, the angel speaks of it here and explains it further down. <margin>Prelates</margin> Truly, the **kings of the earth** are said to be the **prelates** <note>term: "prelates" (prelati). High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots who held significant administrative and spiritual power.</note> to whom the governance of souls was committed to help the people avoid sin. Some of these commit fornication with Babylon; to please men, they think little of and neglect the mandate of God. Otherwise, if we were speaking of the princes of this world, they are simply those who reign in Babylon, and there is no difference between the head and the body. But in this place—just as in that passage where it is said of Christ that He is the *Prince of the kings of the earth*—the kings must be understood as the prelates. Except there, the "kings" refer to good prelates (the simple and humble of heart), while here they refer to the proud, the fearful, and those wise only in doing evil. These fornicate with the great harlot in the same way the sons of Israel once did with the Midianites: when they set aside the care of their people and seek day and night to please the princes of this world, even fighting for them until death if allowed. <margin>Genesis</margin> This was well-signified in **Genesis**, where it says: *The sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.* <note>Genesis 6:2.</note> For who can more appropriately be called the "sons of God" than those set in the governance of souls, holding the place of the sons of God? And who are the "daughters of men" if not the most wealthy cities? And if some desire to become bishops for the sake of the elect who live among them, they are free from this infamy. But if it is for the sake of riches and profit—

# Abbreviated Part of the Exposition

...[those] of the world should know that they commit "fornication" with those things which they choose for themselves in order to become rich. As the Lord says: *If your eye is simple, your whole body will be bright. But if the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness?* <note>Matthew 6:22-23. The "eye" represents the intention behind an action.</note> This is to say: if your intention is good, the work that follows that intention is good. But if the intention is depraved, it is inevitable that whatever is built upon it will be depraved. Therefore, for someone who desires the office of a bishop <term>episcopatum; the position of a high-ranking church overseer</term>: if he desires it only so that he may be a "father to orphans and a judge for widows" (according to the Apostle), he desires a good work. <note>1 Timothy 3:1.</note> But if he does so to become a friend of the rich and a relative of the powerful, let him know that he is among those of whom the Psalmist speaks:

<margin>Psalms</margin>
*You have destroyed all who are unfaithful to you.* <note>original: "Perdidisti omnes qui fornicatur abs te." Psalm 73:27. In Latin, "fornicating away from God" is a common metaphor for idolatry or worldliness.</note> What follows—*And those who inhabit the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her prostitution*—refers generally to all people who are poor in possessions but not in spirit. Even if they cannot be rich because "fortune" (as they say) is against them, they nevertheless snatch what they can of the pleasure of Babylon, so that at least at certain hours or days they are intoxicated by the wine of her prostitution. For although they cannot overflow with wealth as the harlot can, they still get drunk from the torrent of her pleasure, so that they are forced to forget the pleasure and "drunkenness" of the house of the Lord, with which those people are to be intoxicated of whom the Psalmist says:

<margin>Psalms</margin>
*They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house; and you shall make them drink from the torrent of your pleasure.* <note>Psalm 36:8.</note> For Christ also has a cup which he offers to the chosen, but it is very bitter; because the medicine by which the sick are healed must be bitter. If the bitterness of the Passion <term>Passion; the suffering and death of Jesus</term> is represented by the wine of Christ’s cup, what is meant by the wine that the harlot offers if not the sweetness of her worldly pleasure? Although all sins committed voluntarily are to be understood by the name of "fornication," the principal vice of Babylonian corruption is indeed lust. It is the vice that most dominates the children of this world, even if they have no power, possess no honors, and are

<column-break/>

supported by no riches. For there are some who cannot have beautiful or rich wives (because they themselves are poor in resources and weak in power), and yet they "inhabit the earth" through their heart's desire. Not only that: they are intoxicated by the wine of the harlot Babylon’s prostitution at least through the sight and memory of the wicked deed—by that love and ardor for luxury that reigns in the rich of this world, for whom, in this criminal way of life, whatever they desire is often permitted. It follows:

> $\P$ **And the angel carried me away into the wilderness in the spirit.** <note>Revelation 17:3.</note>

Leisure for reading, peace, and silence are necessary if you wish to understand what you read. But even when these are present, it is necessary that you pass from the literal sense of the words to a spiritual understanding. For if you always take what you read exactly as it is written, a carnal <term>carnal; fleshly or non-spiritual</term> understanding often leads you to something unsuitable. Hence Truth itself says: *It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.* <note>John 6:63.</note> Therefore, if you wish to see what end the kingdom of the world will reach, allow yourself to be carried by the angel into the wilderness, imitating Abraham, who went out from his land and from his kin and from his father’s house. In the same way, pass from the "letter" to a spiritual understanding; then you will be able to perceive what the children of this world cannot foresee. "In this your day," says the Lord, "the things that belong to your peace; but now they are hidden from your eyes." <note>Luke 19:42.</note> It follows:

### John: Sixth Part on the Apocalypse
BB 3

<margin>Text</margin> [clothed in purple] and scarlet, and gilded with gold, and with precious stones and pearls; having a golden cup in her hand full of abomination and the uncleanness of her fornication.

Those who are carried away by spiritual men into the desert—meaning they move from the literal sense of the text to a spiritual understanding—behold with the eyes of the mind a likeness of a woman. They see that most famous city, which was once the "lady of kingdoms," and to whom many nations, wild in their rituals and beastly in their customs, were once subjected. <note>The "lady of kingdoms" refers to Rome, which the author identifies with the Babylon of the Apocalypse.</note> Indeed, much has been said about this beast in the preceding sections, and some things still remain to be said in their proper place.

<margin>The fall of the world</margin> However, not only present things are visible to spiritual eyes, but also past and future things. Therefore, they see both for themselves and for others how great the glory of the Roman Empire once was, how that city was enriched with wealth, and how many worldly delights and carnal pleasures she was intoxicated by. They also see what is to come afterward, so that the chosen of God may learn not to envy evildoers nor be jealous of those who work iniquity. <note>original: "nolle emulari in malignantibus neq; zelari facientes iniquitatem." A reference to Psalm 37:1.</note> It should be known that in this sixth part, the discourse is mixed: some things are to be understood literally, and some according to allegory. This is because from the "sixth time" <note>The author uses a historical framework where the "sixth age" or "sixth time" represents the current era leading toward the end of the world.</note> that which is partial begins to pass away, and that which is perfect begins to come. Thus, the chosen no longer seek to see through a mirror dimly, as before, but begin to see face to face, now that the book and its seven seals have been clearly opened. This is why the angel speaks to John in this sixth part and opens the hidden mysteries to him, so that those who are "slow of heart to believe" <note>Luke 24:25.</note> everything the prophets have spoken may know that this is the appointed time of which the angel spoke to Daniel:

<margin>Daniel</margin> *Go, Daniel, because the words are closed and sealed until the appointed time; many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be manifold.* <note>Daniel 12:4, 9.</note>

<margin>Text</margin> Therefore, when John says: *And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious*

<column-break/>

*stones and pearls,* he wished this to be understood as follows: that by the name "woman" we should understand a "prostituted city" <term>fornicariam ciuitatem; a city that has abandoned God for worldly power</term>. Because of these kinds of ornaments, she has committed fornication with living men. This is especially true since the Apostle says:

*Greed is the service of idols,* <note>Colossians 3:5. The author equates the love of wealth with the worship of false gods.</note>

and it is written in the Gospel:

*Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation.* <note>Luke 6:24.</note>

For where there is an abundance of riches, there is an enormity of vices. Whence it is immediately added:

*having a golden cup in her hand, full of abomination and the uncleanness of her fornication.*

Precious vessels are not enough for the wealthy of this world to display their vain glory; they must also continually pour out exquisite wines in them, in which there is the "abomination of drunkenness" and the "uncleanness of luxury." Through these things, the Holy Spirit is excluded from the hearts of many, as the Apostle says:

*Do not be drunk with wine, in which is luxury, but be filled with the Spirit.* <note>Ephesians 5:18.</note>

Hence it is also said through the Prophet:

*Woe to you who are powerful at drinking wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness.* <note>Isaiah 5:22.</note>

<margin>Text 5</margin> And on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: Babylon the Great, the mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth.

The children of Jerusalem <note>A metaphor for the righteous or the Church.</note>, when they offend in deed or word, feel great shame. They diligently seek how they might hide their guilt both before men and before God—lest perhaps men be scandalized and perish, or God, being indignant, should punish the delinquents. They "hide" their guilt when they perform penance, showing themselves to be different people through good works than they were through their sin. They do not deny they are sinners, but seek to take hold of the garments of justice, so they are not among the number of those of whom it is said:

<margin>Psalms</margin> *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.* <note>Psalm 32:1.</note>

In contrast, the children of Babylon are ashamed to confess their sins to the priests of Christ, and...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation 17. The author is expanding on the character of the "Great Harlot" (Babylon), transitioning from her physical description to her symbolic role as the "confusion" of the wicked throughout history. The previous page discussed her worldly wealth; this page discusses her shamelessness and her persecution of the saints.</meta>

# Part of the Explanation

...they do not blush to boast of these things and of the public matter, preaching them before the multitude of lost men, just as the prophet says: *They have proclaimed their sins like Sodom, and they have not hidden them.* <note>original: "Peccata sua predicaverunt sicut Sodoma: nec absconderunt." A quote from Isaiah 3:9.</note> So, so is this harlot: she has written on her forehead a name of mystery: *Babylon the great, the mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth.* Surely, it is because she does not hide her own confusion <note>The word "confusion" (Latin: *confusio*) is used here to mean shame or disgrace.</note>, but rejoices to make it known. She is not confounded by it, but glories in it, according to what the prophet says of certain people: *They were confounded with confusion; or rather, they were not confounded.* <note>original: "Confusione confusi sunt: quin potius: non confusi." From Jeremiah 6:15.</note> What does it mean, "They were confounded, yet rather not confounded," except that those who are desperate are indeed greatly confounded by the very act of their shame, yet they blush to feel the blush of repentance, even though they are worthy of confusion and shame? Hence it is said through the same prophet: *A harlot’s forehead is made for you; you refused to blush.* <note>original: "Frons meretricis facta e tibi: noluisti erubescere." From Jeremiah 3:3.</note>

**O**n account of this cause especially, Babylon is called the "mistress of kingdoms," so that she is understood not so much as *having* confusion, but as being confusion itself, and as it were the "shame of the whole earth." Indeed, **Babylon** is interpreted as **confusion**. <note>The author uses a standard medieval etymology where the name Babylon is linked to the Hebrew word for "to mix" or "to confuse," referencing the Tower of Babel.</note> Moreover, that name is written on her forehead because the reprobate continually find an example in this name, so that they are not ashamed to act wickedly, saying: "Those people do this, and those people do that; we also shall be like one of them." It follows:

<margin>Text 5</margin> **And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.**

**A**s I have already said, the city of the reprobate, which is called Babylon, is not to be considered only as the city of Rome—or (God forbid) as Rome in its entirety—but as the whole multitude of wicked men born according to the flesh. Of these, the Apostle says: *Just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the spirit, so it is now.* <note>original: "Sicut tunc qui scđm carnem natus fuerat: persequebatur eum qui secundũ spirituz: ita ꝛ nunc." A reference to Galatians 4:29.</note> This city, therefore, is drunk with the blood of the saints who have been killed since the beginning of the world, because she, with her children, thirsted for their blood, and it was poured out

<column-break/>

in her midst; and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus, who were killed in the New Testament for his faith. It follows:

**And I wondered, when I had seen her, with great admiration.**

**T**hose who are transported into the desert by the Spirit for this purpose—that they might seek to understand spiritually the mysteries of previous ages—begin first to feel that some things are written here to signify something other than what they literally are. Then, when things occur that seem too secret, they wonder with great admiration, especially at those images which are entirely unusual: such as this kind of woman, and the beast that carries her, having seven heads and ten horns. They wonder because they know these things designate something, yet they are unable to arrive at the knowledge of them by themselves. But because all things have their time, lest the disciples of truth wonder too long at the pattern of those things through which many mysteries (which until now lay hidden in the letters of both Testaments) must be opened in the sixth age: John, who had already been transported into the desert, still speaks and says:

**And the angel said to me: "Why do you wonder? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns."**

**I**n the Divine Page <note>The "Divine Page" (*divina pagina*) is a traditional term for the Holy Scriptures.</note>, the word **sacrament** <note>original: "sacramentum." While we usually think of "sacraments" as church rituals, in Latin it also means a "sacred secret" or "mystery."</note> is usually taken in a positive sense. For it is called a "sacrament" as if it were a "sacred mystery" and a sign of a sacred thing. However, here "sacrament," as I judge, is to be taken for a simple mystery—unless perhaps "sacrament" does not refer to the woman and the beast, but to the sacred counsel of God which he says he will refer to, which covers these things for a time and opens them entirely when he wills. It should be noted, however, that the angel who spoke to John did not open this mystery in such a way that it would be fully reached at that time...

### John [on the] Sixth [Age] in the Apocalypse

<margin>Biblical Text</margin>
...just as it was to be: for the knowledge of the human race. However, it held a symbolic pattern <note>original: "typum tenuit." The author argues that the text is not a literal history but a "type" or symbol of spiritual realities.</note>—as I have already said—of spiritual men, who were to reveal [the truth] to the perfect disciples in the sixth age. Otherwise, if these words do not yet require a spiritual explanation in truth, then the seven mountains must be considered seven literal heads of the beast—and the beast itself would not be a kingdom of impious men, but a four-footed animal of the forest. This would be absurd and contrary to the faith. That other angel who spoke to Daniel—if indeed he is another and not the same one—<margin>Daniel</margin> clearly reveals this when he says: *The fourth beast will be the fourth kingdom in the world, which will be greater than all kingdoms, and will destroy the whole earth and crush it.* <note>A reference to Daniel 7:23, used to prove that "beasts" in prophecy represent empires, not literal monsters.</note> Therefore, as we are about to set down the words themselves which are said to be explained, let us hear what that same angel said.

### Part of the Explanation

But the angel had said: **The beast which you saw was and is not**; but now he says: **The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits.** But if the beast was and is not, how does he say the heads are mountains, unless because it is the custom of the Holy Scriptures that sometimes the present tense is put for the past and the future? Therefore he puts "are" for "were," just as we ourselves are often accustomed to do. Furthermore, who these mountains were was both stated in the "door" <note>original: "ianua"; refers to the preface or introduction of the book.</note> of this book and, if I am not mistaken, more carefully repeated in the fourth part.

The first head was the kingdom of Herod and his successors. The second was the empire of the Romans until Diocletian. The third, fourth, fifth, and sixth were the four kingdoms of the Arians <note>Arianism was a major Christological heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ; the author views Arian rulers as a collective series of "heads" or persecutors.</note> mentioned in this work. The seventh head is the kingdom of the Saracens <note>original: "sarracenorum"; a medieval term for Muslims.</note>. But also concerning the five kings who have fallen <note>The OCR reads "crediderunt" (believed), but the biblical text of Rev 17:10 is "ceciderunt" (fallen). The author is likely correcting or commenting on the status of these five preceding powers.</note>, it has been said in those same places who they were. 

However, it was not said: "And in those seven heads there are seven kings," as if each individual head had one of those seven (especially since the ten horns are designated as ten kings); but it says: **And there are seven kings**, so that the seven kings are understood to rise not individually through individual heads, but in another way—that is, through the individual seven periods of time, about which we have spoken frequently and at length in this work. For the seven heads of the beast did not arise individually through individual periods, but as it is better shown in Daniel: the first head in the first period; the second in the second; the fourth in the third; and the seventh in the fourth. From then on, the seventh head continues until the sixth period, in which it will also fail—or rather, it will seem to fail, only to rise after a little while so as to disappear into eternity. 

Therefore, the seven kings were to be assigned not through the seven heads but through the seven periods; and for that reason he says: **And there are seven kings.** The first of these (as we have already written) was Herod with his successors. The second was Nero with his successors. The third was Constantius the Arian with his successors. The fourth was Muhammad—or rather Chosroes, King of the Persians <note>Chosroes II (d. 628) was a Sassanid king who captured Jerusalem, often linked by medieval writers with the rise of Islam.</note> 

<column-break/>

with his successors. The fifth is he who first, in the western regions, began to harass the Church regarding the investiture of churches <note>A reference to the "Investiture Controversy," a power struggle between the Papacy and the Holy Roman Empire (starting with Henry IV) over the right to appoint bishops.</note>, for which reason many schisms and tribulations have arisen in the Church of God since that time. 

The sixth king, however, of whom it is said: **And one is**, is that eleventh king in the book of Daniel <note>Referring to the "Little Horn" of Daniel 7:8, commonly identified as the Antichrist.</note>, in whose time this revelation is to be clearly opened, and the "new Babylon" <note>In this context, a corrupt or worldly ecclesiastical hierarchy.</note> is to be struck by that same king and his accomplices; after its striking, he shall be killed. The seventh head of the beast [is struck] as if unto death, and tranquility shall be given to the Church of Christ. 

Furthermore, between the sixth persecution and the other which will be under that king of whom it is said: **And the other has not yet come**, there will be a brief space of time for the breathing of the faithful, as the empire of Babylon (which is within) and the empire of the beast (which is without) fail in persecution, because both shall die. Nevertheless, though Babylon is extinguished, the beast shall yet rise again as if by a demon; for it is to ascend from the abyss, so that it may carry out yet one more persecution as if in the eighth place, and immediately it will go into destruction, from which it shall not rise again. Whence he also soon adds:

> **And the beast that was and is not,**
> **even he is the eighth, and is of the seven,**
> **and goes into destruction.**

If this beast had eight heads, it would not be said: "He is the eighth and is of the seven," but only: "He is the eighth." For he would be called the eighth in an eighth head, in which alone he would remain. But because the seventh head of the beast will die and rise again, and also from the remnants of the errors of the other heads they will appear together, that most wicked gathering will indeed be the eighth both in time and succession; yet it will be "of the seven" because in it will be the collection of all errors which were shown in the seven heads, while that seventh king reigns, who will be the fountain of malice and the vessel of error, in whom the fullness of iniquity and the origin of wickedness shall rest. This is so that when iniquities have increased, all things which are written may be fulfilled. Meanwhile, under the sixth king, Babylon shall be struck by the beast and by the kings.

...if they were of only one order, they could not provide an entire and perfect testimony to such sublime matters. This is why some are described as having gone out from the temple which is in heaven, while others are simply narrated to have descended from heaven. Why is this? Because some go out from the communal <note>original: "conuentuali," referring to monks or clergy living in a community.</note> and designated order in the temple; others from the solitary and contemplative life designated in heaven. And those angels who went out from the temple are many, because in the communal life—just as diverse members assigned to diverse actions come together into one body—they are designated in one temple, from which these angels went out to pour the phials <note>The "bowls" or "vials" of God's wrath from Revelation 16.</note> of the wrath of God. But the one who is said to have descended from heaven is written of as being alone, and he is one, because that "one thing" pertains to the contemplative life, of which the Lord spoke: **Truly, one thing is necessary.** <note>Luke 10:42. Joachim links the singularity of the angel to the singular focus of the contemplative life, which prioritizes spiritual devotion over external activity.</note> But those other angels are not said to have descended, but only to have gone out from the temple; this angel, however, is described as descending from heaven because in the order of those in community, the active life is constantly present. And when someone among the brothers is converted and speaks the words of God, he is said rather to "go out" than to "descend," because he often speaks common words with them among which he occasionally speaks the words of God. But the contemplative life, which entirely requires solitude, is like a kind of heaven, towering higher than human affairs. When someone occasionally goes out from it to speak to men, he "condescends" <note>In the medieval sense of stooping down from a higher state to a lower one to help others.</note> enough to those to whom he speaks, even if it is the word of God, because it is alien to his purpose and life; and so that he may thus have compassion for men, nothing but a great and evident necessity can occasionally wring this from him. This preacher, whether he appears alone or with companions, is going to have great power of his own brightness in speaking the word of God, just as it is written of our Lord: **He spoke as one having power, and not as their scribes and pharisees.** <note>Matthew 7:29.</note> But the earth will also be illuminated by his glory; just as under the sixth angel with the trumpet sounding—I know not whether it was said of this one or another—because not yet in a dark

<column-break/>

riddle <note>original: "enigmate," referencing 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."</note>, as of old, but as if with the brightness of the sun, he will announce the truth to men, saying and announcing clearly that the ruin of the proud city is absolutely imminent. And, gathered in hell, let it become a habitation of demons and a haunt <note>original: "custodia," meaning a place of guarding or a cage/prison.</note> of every unclean spirit (that is, diabolical) and a haunt of every unclean bird (that is) of whatever soul is assigned to eternal punishments; and hateful, because of the confusion of its nakedness—she who was once clothed in purple and fine linen, adorned with pearls and precious stones. But why she suffers this is shown when it is immediately added below:

---

->**And all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication: and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her: and the merchants of the earth have grown rich by the power of her delicacies.**<- <note>Revelation 18:3.</note>

Regarding what he says: "Of the wrath of her fornication all nations have drunk," I recall having explained this in the fourth part of the book, in that place where, after the angel to whom the eternal gospel was given, another angel followed who said what this angel says in this place: **Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen,** etc. <note>Revelation 14:8.</note> Wherefore, because in the book of these things a recapitulation has been made again and again, I judge that this is that angel who is said to have descended from heaven under the sixth angel with the trumpet sounding, and who speaks toward the end of the fourth part, as I have already said, and says: "Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen, she who made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication." But whether he himself is one of those men who are to come—what opinion can be held in the meantime—let what was said in those same parts suffice. Indeed, the "kings of the earth" are the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials, such as bishops or abbots, whom Joachim often criticized for worldly corruption.</note> of the churches, some of whom commit fornication with Babylon, as was said above. # Joachim’s Sixth Book on the Apocalypse 199

...the kingdom of God: they gape after temporal gains and seek to please the rich of this world with deceitful words. Their strength lies in the delights of the flesh, so that they themselves may become wealthy and be able to live in luxury hereafter, observing how never-ending revenues of delights have been established for them. Thus, by bestowing much, it always turns out that they have more to bestow, and that which is to be given never fails. For this is the "power of the delights of Babylon," by which the merchants of the earth become rich. Furthermore, he who participates in her delights for a time—yet grieves and groans over this very thing—can, if he wishes, withdraw from her company and return to his King who redeemed him. This is so that, if he stays with her for long, he is not forced to participate in her great sins and, when the hour of vengeance arrives, receive her plagues. In such a case, the Lord punishes in him that which he himself neglected to punish in his own soul. For what follows is:

<margin>Text 1</margin>
<margin>Text 3</margin>
> And I heard another voice from heaven saying: "Go out of her, my people, and be not partakers of her sins, and you shall not receive of her plagues; because her sins have reached even unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities."

<margin>Jeremiah</margin>
In this place, as in many others in Divine Scripture, the Church is designated by the name "heaven." Indeed, this voice is heard within her because this very thing was already written, though in different words, in the book of Jeremiah <note>referring to Jeremiah 50:8 and 51:6-9</note> saying: *Depart from the midst of Babylon, and go forth out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be like the kids before the flock. For behold, I will stir up and bring against Babylon a great congregation of nations from the north country; and they shall be prepared against her, and from there she shall be taken. Their arrow, like that of a mighty man, a killer, shall not return empty. And Babylon shall be a spoil; all that waste her shall be filled, says the Lord.* Therefore, what is said here is heard "as if from heaven," because whatever is seen to be written 

<column-break/>

concerning that historical Babylon which was struck down is to be understood entirely according to the spirit <note>meaning allegorically or spiritually</note> regarding this current Babylon. This is the one which those kings we spoke of above are destined to strike. This is especially true since the ancient Babylon is said to have been struck by a single King of the Medes, whereas Jeremiah prophesied that not just one king, but many and terrible ones, would come against Babylon. 

But by what means can the people of the Lord "go out" from Babylon, since it is well known that her kingdom is spread throughout almost the entire world? And how does one depart from her if he was never physically in her? If, however, he who is commanded to go out is still within her, how can he avoid being a partaker of her sins? It must be noted that it is necessary for a person to receive her plagues if he remains in her until the hour of her striking. This applies even if he is one of the "elect," just like that thief who was hung with Christ on the cross and, because of his good confession, deserved to hear: *Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.* <note>Luke 23:43. Joachim suggests that spiritual "exit" is a matter of conversion and character rather than physical travel.</note> 

Therefore, he who does not wish to be a partaker of her scourges should either ascend the mountain with Abraham <note>Genesis 22</note> toward the spiritual life, or at least pass over in his conduct into Segor <margin>Genesis</margin> <note>original: "Segor," the city of Zoar where Lot took refuge during the destruction of Sodom; see Genesis 19:22-23.</note> and keep himself therein, producing in the meantime worthy fruits of penance. Otherwise, because God no longer tolerates the arrogance of Babylon, it is necessary, as I said, that he who neglects to anticipate the hour of her desolation be scourged along with her. 

But why does God, who has been patient until now, no longer endure her? Because, he says, "her sins have reached even unto heaven." For it is not enough for the children of Babylon that they continually persecute the members of Christ; they even set their mouths against heaven. Whenever anything adverse happens to them, they do not fear to blaspheme the Only-Begotten of God, who hung on the cross for the salvation of all, and to speak a word against the living God, who makes His sun to rise upon the good and the bad, and rains upon the just and the unjust. And because, in His exceeding patience, He seemed to have consigned to oblivion all the injuries of this great harlot in which she has been engaged since ancient days, when He begins to strike her with an incurable and unheard-of plague, it will seem...

# Abbot’s Part of the Exposition

...regarding that which was immediately added there: **"And the Lord remembered her iniquities."** Of which iniquities? Of those which she committed in persecuting the children of Jerusalem, to whom it is also said:

<margin>Revelation 18</margin>

## Render to her, as she herself has rendered to you: and double to her double according to her works. In the cup in which she mixed for you, mix for her double.

It is a wonder how it is now said to the elect: **"Render to her, as she herself has rendered to you,"** as if the judgment were being handed over into their hands, or as if it were in their power to determine how much this ancient harlot <note>original: "antiqua meretrix," referring to the corrupt city of Babylon</note> ought to be punished. This is especially striking since it seems contrary to the word of the Lord saying: **"Pray for those who persecute and slander you."** <note>Matthew 5:44</note>

But it must be understood that the Lord does not always command us to pray for enemies, especially if they are enemies of God. Rather, one prays according to the season and for a time—that is, up to the appointed time in which, after the day of patience, the day of judgment follows. This is the time of the saints, in which the Lord will begin to judge the world and render to each according to their works. Otherwise, if one must always pray for the wicked, then one would have to do so even in the future life. Indeed, we pray for the impious and the wicked as long as there is hope that they can be converted, lest perhaps one who is thought to be a reprobate is actually one of the elect. 

However, when the iniquity of the impious reaches even to heaven, and even to the blasphemy of the Holy Spirit, and it is certain that the sentence has gone forth and the just God wishes to take away evil from the earth, who would dare—contrary to the sentence of John—to pray for those committing a sin unto death, and for those hating and blaspheming Him who redeemed us with His blood? 

Therefore, on 그날 [that day], the children of Jerusalem will render to the fornicating city according to what she rendered to them. They will "double her double" according to her own works because, in accordance with the taunts and injuries they suffered from her, they will mock her. They will even double the shame on her face, they who were themselves shamed by her, when the 

<column-break/>

day of her calamity arrives. For we know that "the children of this world are wiser than the children of light in their generation," <note>Luke 16:8</note> and that the weak, ignoble, and contemptible things of the world which God chose for their simplicity have been handed over to the dominion and power of those who seem to be stronger in this age. 

And this indeed happens not by any chance, but by the permission of God, the just judge, who once handed over the children of Israel to the power of the Egyptians so that they might learn not to be high-minded, but to "consent to the humble." <note>Romans 12:16</note> Thus, even in this time, He willed for the children of Babylon to have dominion and power, and for the children of Jerusalem to be subjected to servitude, so that through many tribulations and injuries they might reach the kingdom of God, into which He makes the poor rich, while the rich enter with difficulty. 

There are indeed some rich—though very few—who have many households, male servants, and female servants, and yet they reach the kingdom of God; these are they who rule those under them not in a worldly way, but serve them as fathers to children, and strive to show them the same indulgence they themselves desire to obtain from the Almighty Lord. But the rest are not so. Instead, when those subject to them, weighed down by the burden of servitude, murmur against them—not considering that the Creator of the whole world chose such people—they return heavy injuries to them for a small and trivial word. They call them wicked, rustic, and perjured servants, covering their faces with ignominy, and expelling them from their sight with great confusion and fear. 

Therefore, these humble ones, when their time comes, will also cover the face of Babylon with confusion and fear, saying: "Behold, this is that Babylon, the city of the proud, which oppressed the humble in her power; now she has become like the mud of the streets and like the dung of the earth, full of all ignominy and everlasting confusion." Thus, the elect will render to her "double," as it were, by reproaching them with the misery of their calamity. They will shame her face not only for the temporal injuries they incurred—returning like for like—but even more for the hellish pains <note>original: "tartareis," a reference to Tartarus or hell</note> in which she is assigned for eternity. Wherefore it is immediately added:

# Sixth Book of Joachim on the Apocalypse

<margin>Text 5</margin>
**As much as she has glorified herself and lived in luxuries, so much give to her torment and mourning; because she says in her heart: "I sit as a Queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall see no mourning." Therefore, in one day her plagues shall come: death, and mourning, and famine, and she shall be burned with fire.**

The children of this world glorify themselves because they are noble, because they are powerful, because they are wealthy, and because they are enriched by the goods of others. But entirely ignoring the word of the cross <note>original: "verbum crucis"</note> and its virtue, they spend their days in good things and abound in many luxuries, just like that rich man who was buried in hell <note>A reference to the parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16</note>. Furthermore, on that day when the elect—who are now despised by those unwilling to receive their correction—shall reproach them with these things, torment and mourning will be stirred up within them. They will see themselves utterly hemmed in and unable to return to the accustomed luxuries and worldly honors they have lost. For they do not take these things to heart before they arrive so that they might bear them more lightly when experienced; therefore, their mourning will be intolerable and the affliction of their torments beyond remedy.

Because she says (he says) in her heart: "I sit as a Queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall see no mourning," therefore in one day her plagues shall come: death, and mourning, and famine, and she shall be burned with fire. The multitude of proud men glories in the kingdom of the world, which seems to them to have been handed over to them; and they feel as if they sit like a queen, commanding the humble and the poor of the earth. She also says she is not a widow because she trusts in the strength of the earthly princes who rule in her, so much so that she does not believe she will see mourning in all the days of her life, nor feel any of the various plagues written in this book—according to that word of the Gospel: "In this your day, the things that belong to your peace are now hidden from your eyes." <note>Luke 19:42</note> Therefore (he says), in one day—that is, at one time—her plagues shall come: death, mourning, and famine. For these are the spiritual plagues of the reprobate <term>reprobate: those rejected by God or destined for damnation</term> from the day of their death. They die an eternal death, and therefore eternal mourning follows. And because they do not die in such a way as to cease to exist, they shall hunger without end; and

<column-break/>

what is worse: those who hunger shall themselves be food for the eternal fire. A sufficiently just recompense! For a glorious life, death; for foolish joy, mourning; for luxuries, famine; for refreshment, fire. And as if one were to ask about the one who is to do this, and who might be of such great power as to be able to do this—since no power is seen on earth that equals His strength—he added and said:

**Because strong is the God who will judge her.**

<margin>Text 6</margin>
For it is as if it were said: if a mortal man were to take up war against them, and the indignation of Almighty God—whose wrath no one can resist—were not the cause, perhaps they might, as they have until now, presume upon their own strength. But because He fights against them who says through the prophet: "The day of vengeance is in my heart," <note>Isaiah 63:4</note> it is in vain that they contend to resist their enemies. For it is the will of the Lord that they be conquered by those whom He uses as vessels of death <note>original: "vasa mortis"</note>, just as the Lord Himself says of the people of Assyria through the prophet Isaiah: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury, and the staff of my indignation; I will send him into my wrath against a deceitful nation." <note>Isaiah 10:5</note> But what is a deceitful nation except one that pretends to be what it is not—one that confesses it knows God but denies Him by its deeds? Nevertheless, even if his judgment is partially carried out here, it will not reach its total consummation with the death of the flesh. Rather, it will be like a certain demonstration of the judgment to come. It follows:

**And all the kings of the earth shall weep and bewail themselves over her, who have committed fornication with her and lived in her luxuries.**

<margin>Text 7</margin>
These are the kings of the earth and the rulers of souls <note>original: "rectores animarum," referring to the clergy or bishops</note> who, for the sake of the luxuries of Babylon that come into their hands—as their works also testify—rejoice that they are the prelates of the churches. They do so to such an extent that they would rather offend the Vicar of the Chief Shepherd <note>The Pope</note> than the princes of the world and of Babylon. They will not be able to keep from wailing on that day when they see that which they loved so sweetly dragged away, never to return. And if, through the very harsh judgment they will endure, they are forced in this life to understand its eternal punishments, then they should strive to distance themselves from her way of life for fear of her torments. For there follows:

# Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

<margin>Text 8</margin> ¶ **When they shall see the smoke of her burning, standing afar off for fear of her torments.**
¶ If the battle of the ten kings <note>In Joachim’s theology, the "ten kings" are often associated with the forces of the Antichrist or worldly powers that turn against the corrupt Church.</note> were not material, we could understand this lower burning as only a spiritual punishment. But because it will indeed be material, the temporal fire can simply designate the punishment she is to suffer. A distinction is recognized between the smoke and the fire: smoke is often seen from a distance, even by those who cannot see the burning itself; for often groves of trees and obstructing hills prevent the fire from being seen. But whether the fire is large or small is understood by the outpouring of smoke. The burning of Babylon, therefore, designates the torment she will suffer on that day; the smoke, however, signifies her fame <note>original: "fama"</note>, which will fly further abroad. They shall stand afar off for fear of her torments because they will not dare to prepare themselves for battle, but will instead turn to mourning. And (it says) all the kings of the earth shall wail over her—those who have committed fornication with her and lived in her luxuries—when they see the smoke of her burning, standing afar off for fear of her torments, saying:

<margin>Text 9</margin> ¶ **Alas, alas, that great city Babylon, that mighty city: for in one hour your judgment is come.**
¶ These are people who, in the day of peace, do not consider how all temporal things that can pass away are as nothing. They do not consider the glory of the princes of this world, whom they strive to cling to so that they may be equally honored. When they suddenly see what has happened—which they previously did not believe when told—they will weep most bitterly because of the love by which they were bound to them. They will mourn, being stunned by the novelty of this transformation and by the fear of her torments, receding as far as possible. And because they cannot be present with her, they shall say in their hearts, both wondering and grieving: "Alas, alas, that great

<column-break/>

city: that mighty city, which once, in the greatness of its people and the strength of its military, subjugated the world; how has it been so suddenly swallowed up and reduced to nothing, so that not even a trace remains in memory of its greatness?" Wherefore the Lord also says through the prophet: *And Babylon, that glorious one among kingdoms, famous in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be even as when the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,* etc. <note>Joachim is quoting Isaiah 13:19</note>. It follows:

¶ **And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man shall buy their merchandise anymore.**
¶ The merchants of the earth are those who were mentioned above. They are the priests of Baal <gloss>who</gloss> do not know the things of God; they are animalistic priests <gloss>who</gloss> <note>original: "sacerdotes animales," referring to those driven by fleshly instincts rather than the Holy Spirit</note> are given over to the outer court so that they may "eat the sins of the people," who sell prayers and masses for coins, making the house of prayer into a shop of trade, making it a public hearth and a den of thieves. They shall grieve and weep over her because no one will buy their merchandise anymore; for they are not so struck with remorse that they blush at their own crime, but like animalistic and carnal men, they are forced to weep only for this: that they have lost what they loved, for there will be no one to whom they may sell their wares. Indeed, the zeal for selling will fail because the crowd of buyers will have passed away. Only a deluded and confused greed will remain, which, having its material for pleasure taken away, will break out into the voice of weeping; for now what was pleasing is not permitted, and that which was their own and familiar will be lacking. How precious this merchandise is—which they sell for carnal gain by abusing God’s gift—is revealed in what follows.

¶ **The merchandise of gold and silver, and precious stones, and pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner of vessels of ivory, and all manner of vessels of stone...**

# John’s Sixth Vision in the Apocalypse

...of precious stones, and brass, and iron, and marble; and cinnamon, and amomum <note>original: "amomum" — an aromatic spice plant from the ginger family, used in ancient perfumes</note>; and odors, and ointments, and frankincense; and wine, and oil, and fine flour; and wheat, and beasts of burden, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and the souls of men.

<margin>Text 10</margin>
All these things and those like them, when understood spiritually, have been entrusted to the priests and the clergy, not so that they might be traded for carnal things, but for spiritual things: that is, for the souls of the faithful and for good works. But what has happened? Was there not from the beginning a Simon <note>This refers to Simon Magus (Acts 8), who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit from the Apostles. The sin of "Simony"—buying or selling sacred things—is named after him.</note> who, having offered money to Peter and John, demanded that the gift of the Holy Spirit be sold to him? But at that time, though there was one who would buy, there was no one who would sell; instead, there was one who spoke against such a wicked buyer. Now, however, even if the buyer were slow to purchase, the seller is ready at hand, soliciting the souls of the miserable—not so that they might humbly obtain grace, but so that they might unhappily buy it; not so that they might be strengthened by a heavenly gift, but so that they might fall along with those who are already falling. Finally, to some has been entrusted the "gold" of wisdom and the "silver" of eloquence for the benefit of the Church; yet, because of these gifts, they do not seek to build up the elect of God (who are often despised), but rather to cling to the rich of this world, so that they might speak pleasing things to them and be honored by them. They are like the false prophets of old in Jerusalem who deceived the people with the promise of peace, saying "Peace, peace," when there was no peace. To others have been entrusted the divine sacraments, symbolized by "pearls and precious stones," for the salvation of the living and the dead; and yet they refuse to give them to anyone unless they either receive something in return or hope to receive it.

<margin>The merchant priest</margin>
<margin>Text 11</margin>
To others it has been given to be able to perform works of justice, symbolized by "fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet"; yet through these things they seek to please secular men more than God, making light of that which the Lord said:

<column-break/>

"Take heed to yourselves, that you do not perform your justice before men to be seen by them." <note>A reference to Matthew 6:1.</note> To others have been entrusted the necessary skills to perform what is good with their own hands, just as the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul, who worked as a tentmaker.</note> used to do; these are symbolized by "thyine wood <note>original: "ligno thimo" — a fragrant, high-quality wood used in luxury furniture and temples</note>, and vessels of ivory, and vessels of precious stone," as seen in the building of basilicas, the construction of monasteries, and the transcribing of books. But they are unwilling to do these very things unless there are those who offer with a generous hand from their abundance, or unless they are rewarded in this present life. To others have been entrusted physical labors which pertain to daily use, symbolized by "brass and iron and marble," so that they might work with their hands and have something to give to those in need; yet, they not only refuse to give anything of what they produce for God’s sake, but they even strive to extort higher prices for the most worthless things. To others are given spiritual exercises symbolized by "cinnamon and amomum, and odors, and ointments, and frankincense"; yet they do not fear to receive the praise of men for them, neglecting that which is written: "Amen I say to you, they have received their reward." <note>Matthew 6:2.</note> To others it is given to be able to refresh the hearts of the faithful with all spiritual doctrine, symbolized by "wine and oil, and fine flour, and wheat"; yet, lifted up in pride, they only aspire to public recognition. To others have been entrusted the faithful souls themselves, symbolized (according to the diversity of understanding) by "beasts of burden and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and the souls of men," so that they might guard them for salvation. Yet, although they ought to instruct them in the fear of the Lord so that they might please God alone, they teach them to please men in ways they should not, so that they might obtain temporal gain from them—not knowing that which is written: "The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please men; they are confounded, because God has despised them." <note>Psalm 53:5.</note> Behold, all these are the "merchants of the earth," who trade the gifts of God for temporal things and fleeting affections—or rather, for things that provoke God. They are the children of Babylon who claim to be faithful but are not; instead, they are the "synagogue of Satan." For we know that there is no nation or people in the entire multitude of those who are reckoned by the Christian profession...

### Part of the Explanation

...are seen: although she exists in great crimes, they nonetheless seek to have churches, priests, and clergy, and even sometimes to participate in the sacred rites; although he who participates unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:29, warning that taking the Eucharist in a state of sin leads to divine judgment.</note>. But because the children of Jerusalem <note>Symbolizing the true, spiritual Church.</note> are usually poor and despised, and the children of Babylon <note>Symbolizing the corrupt, worldly world or church hierarchy.</note> are all glorious, to whom do you think those people more willingly cling who—not for the sake of God, but for the sake of honor and profit—do not so much receive as usurp and seize the priestly dignity? Is it not rather to the children of Babylon, who have existed for a long time, rather than to the children of the poor little woman <note>original: "paupercule" — refers to the Church, often personified as a humble woman or widow in medieval commentary.</note> shaken by the storm? And since both are blind, both fall equally into the pit.

Nevertheless, because the cause of such great crimes remains principally in the fornicating city, it belongs to the just examination of the supreme Judge that that great harlot <note>original: "meretrix" — the "Whore of Babylon" from Revelation, interpreted here as a corrupting influence.</note> who provokes others to sin should be judged first; while those who were seduced by her are left to mourning, seeing taken away from them the joy and the worldly gladness which they loved. For carnal minds cannot easily forget those things which they have loved, especially since they have no consolation from heaven, nor do they think the joys of heaven are anything compared to earthly things, as the scripture testifies which says: *The natural man does not perceive the things of the spirit of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:14.</note> But because he carefully noted the profits of the merchants, it was also necessary for the blessed John, having changed the person of the speaker, to express the delights of Babylon—that is, those delights for which the same merchants are seen to have brought all their merchandise to the markets of Babylon itself, once an exchange was made between both types of goods. For it follows:

<margin>verse 12</margin>

> And your fruits of the desire of your soul have departed from you: and all fat and splendid things have perished from you. And the merchants who were made rich by her shall find them no more.

These wares of the wicked merchants are spiritual; but the wares of Babylon are carnal: because, clearly, carnal wares seem too sweet to their carnal priests. They also hand over 

<column-break/>

precious things for the greed of the throat: and for the sake of base gain, they exchange spiritual things for carnal things, imitating Judas the traitor, who sold the Lord for thirty pieces of silver. In these three types, however, the lust of the throat <note>original: "concupiscentia gule" — gluttony or carnal appetite.</note> principally remains: in fruits, in fat things, and in drinks of wine. But these and all similar things will pass away from Babylon, and there will no longer be anyone to sell, even if there is no lack of those seeking to buy. Whence, regarding these same merchants, now frustrated in their hope, it is added consequently:

> They shall stand afar off for fear of her torments, weeping and mourning and saying: "Woe, woe, that great city which was clothed in fine linen <note>original: "bysso" — a high-quality flax or silk-like fabric used for priestly and royal garments.</note> and purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stone and pearls: because in one hour such great riches have been brought to nothing."

These words of the mourning merchants are not to be understood spiritually, but rather according to the custom of mourners, who are used to taking word for word <note>meaning: "literally" or "at face value."</note>; so that through what is said—that she was clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and gilded with gold and precious stone and pearls—it may be understood that she was very wealthy, glorious, and noble. It follows:

> And every shipmaster, and all who sail to a far place, and sailors, and those who work on the sea, stood afar off and cried out, seeing the place of her burning, saying: "What city is like this great city?"

It is said "No one" <note>original: "Nemo"</note> in the divine page is not always to be taken universally: because often one thing is to be taken for many, and another for few. For as to what the Lord says: *All as many as came before me were thieves and*... <note>John 10:8: "All who came before me were thieves and robbers." The author is explaining that biblical terms like "all" or "none" often refer to specific groups rather than every single person in existence.</note>

## Sixth [Lecture] on John in the Apocalypse

...others: this is not to be understood generally of everyone, but of many. And what Saint John the Baptist says of Christ, "and no one accepts his testimony," <note>original: "Et testimonium eius nemo accipit" — a reference to John 3:32.</note> is not to be understood to mean that even the holy apostles did not receive it, but that those who received His word were few in comparison to those who did not. We know, however, that not only are many bishops and priests entangled in the business of Babylon in order to become rich, but also many abbots, monks, and various other religious—or rather, not those who truly are religious, but those who merely seem to be. For by the name "pilots," <margin>T. 13</margin> we should understand the prelates <note>Ecclesiastical leaders or superiors of a religious house.</note> of monasteries, because monasteries themselves are "spiritual ships." Since the voyage of these ships is long, some monks seek to distance themselves by fleeing to stay in solitude; and yet, in the end, they return to the banquets of Babylon, unable to abstain from her cursed delights. However, we should not lazily interpret what he says: "every pilot and all who sail to a distance," and he added, "and the sailors who work at sea." For we know there are some sailors who do not sail far, and some who work in the sea but never sail, such as fishermen; [similarly] some monks remain in cities, and some are even permitted to hold parishes. But all of these were mourning and will weep <margin>T. 14</margin> over the destruction of Babylon, which they loved for a time, "seeing," he says, "the place of her burning." For they will see the most noble cities desolated and the most fortified towns without an inhabitant. And because carnal men know not how to think of anything except the glory of the flesh, nor do they believe the things written in this book about the holy city Jerusalem, they are going to say to one another on that day what is written in this place: "What city is like this great city?" They are going to say this word when they see the desolation of such an innumerable multitude and such a great kingdom; though they may read of this now in the canonical books, they either understand it poorly themselves, or they cannot provide 

<column-break/>

faith to those who understand it fully. And because they are strongly attached in heart and mind to that which is falling—not knowing or not willing to live without her banquets—they cannot soothe their grief at her ruin, seeing and eventually recognizing that everything they loved has perished at once. For there follows:
<margin>T. 19</margin>
> And they cast dust upon their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning, saying: "Woe, woe, that great city, in which all who had ships in the sea were made rich from her prices, for in one hour she is desolated." <note>A translation of Revelation 18:19.</note>
Just as oil signifies joy, so dust designates sadness. Therefore, they "cast dust on their heads" who vehemently afflict their own minds. They cry out, weeping and mourning, while they clearly demonstrate that they grieve beyond measure. They grieve for those things, but even more because they have irrecoverably lost the "matter of their lust," <note>The physical objects or wealth that fueled their worldly desires.</note> according to that saying of the Apostle: "Men shall be lovers of themselves." <note>2 Timothy 3:2.</note> But if those people bewail her ruin and were her intimates, will the saints—who were killed by her and driven from the earth, fleeing from house to house and city to city—weep for her? Far from it. For there follows:
<margin>T. 20</margin>
> Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you holy apostles and prophets, for God has judged your judgment upon her. <note>Revelation 18:20.</note>
The "Church of the saints" is called "Heaven." Furthermore, the "holy apostles" are all the holy prelates, and the "prophets" are the teachers who predict future things. All of these are commanded to rejoice together over the destruction of Babylon, mindful of the things they suffered from her all the days of their pilgrimage. It follows:
> And a mighty angel took up a stone, as it were a great millstone, and cast it into the sea, saying: "With such violence shall Babylon, that great city, be thrown down, and shall be found no more at all." <note>Revelation 18:21.</note>

# Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

¶ If this is spoken as an example, this is how it should be understood. But if it is a mystery, it signifies one of the kings of the world, whom a single strong angel shall cast down into the abyss. It may happen in that same order, or a similar one, by which King Theodoric <note>Theodoric the Great (d. 526), an Arian king of the Ostrogoths who imprisoned Pope John I; medieval legend claimed he was thrown into a volcano as divine punishment.</note> of old was thrown into the pot of Vulcan <note>original: "olla vulcani", referring to the volcanic crater of the Lipari islands</note> by Pope John—as a manifest judgment on a most impious king—so that the wicked multitude might recognize what they deserve. Truly, she <note>Babylon, representing the worldly city</note> who has ruled in the world until now shall be submerged into Tartarus <note>original: "thartarũ", a classical term for the deepest pit of hell</note>, perishing in this age and remaining in eternal punishment. Neither shall she be found any longer, nor shall those things she loved find her. For the pleasure shall pass away in an hour, and the punishment for that pleasure shall remain forever. Joys will cease, and weeping and wailing shall not end. For there follows:

<margin>T. 18</margin>
¶ And the voice of harpers and musicians, and of those playing the flute and trumpet, shall be heard in her no more; and no craftsman of any art shall be found in you any more; and the light of the lamp shall shine in you no more; and the voice of the bridegroom and the bride shall not be heard in you anymore.

¶ Behold what kind of portion belongs to those who prefer the joys of this life to the life to come. It would have been better for them to reach joy through mourning than to pass from temporal joys to eternal torments. And if only it were enough for them to enjoy transitory joys in such a way that they at least left other men in peace—if they allowed their fellow servants and equals to be held as companions, and did not subject them to servitude by force, power, and their own character. But not only do they not fear to do this out of pride, but what is worse, they lead those they have subjugated into error. Wherefore it is immediately added:

<margin>T. 20</margin>
¶ Because your merchants were the princes of the earth; because by your sorceries <note>original: "ueneficiis", referring to deceptive or corrupting influences</note> all nations have erred.
¶ It should be noted that he spoke above concerning the kings and the traders of the earth: one of whom

<column-break/>

are the princes of the earth, and the others, if not princes, are nevertheless wealthy. But now he describes the merchants of Babylon as being the princes of the earth. It seems to me that the discourse here concerns different merchants than those mentioned before. Regarding those merchants who agree with the ones we spoke of above, and who think they can buy spiritual things with their carnal goods <note>This refers to simony, the buying or selling of church offices or spiritual favors</note>: as for what he says, *Because in your sorceries all nations have erred*, it is as if it were said: because you were placed in a more eminent position where you could be seen by everyone, your inventions were made all the more grievous; for by your example all the nations that were subject to you have erred. For where the head leads, there the members follow. There follows:

<margin>T. 24</margin>

And whoever has been unjustly killed, it was done either by her or through her. <meta>This page transitions from the fall of the worldly city (Babylon) in Revelation 18 to the heavenly celebration in Revelation 19.
