->### John: Sixth [Vision] in the Apocalypse<-

...of sin can be present in all: but most especially
in the second and third [parts]. These things having
been mentioned both effectively and necessarily
at the entrance of this seventh part—which we
have begun to treat—let us turn our words
to the order of the exposition. As
<margin>Augustine</margin> Augustine says in the book *The City of God*: 
certain people have thought, on the occasion
of this passage, that a period of a seventh age
of a thousand years is preferred, in which it
would be necessary for Christ to reign with
the saints after the resurrection: six thousand
years from the beginning of the world having 
first been completed. They added certain other
things which are altogether contrary to the 
Christian faith; to whose opinion [Augustine] seems
to agree in part and to resist in part: for indeed 
part of the opinion was true, and part was empty 
and vain. For they did not call that time which 
is to come after the above-written battle a 
seventh age and a Sabbath; in this their opinion
was true—or rather, not so much an opinion 
as a most serene understanding. 
However, that they gave a seventh millennium 
to that same seventh age is proven to be false 
in every way, both among the Greeks and 
among the Latins. For the former claim to have 
more years, and we far fewer; and we feel this 
to be entirely discordant from the path of truth. 
Furthermore, what they said—that the Lord 
would spend time with the saints in carnal 
feasts for a thousand years after the 
resurrection—is entirely turned away from 
the faith. It is most certain that this proceeded
not from spiritual minds, but from carnal ones. 
"Food for the belly, and the belly for food: 
but God will destroy both this and these." 
<note>original: "Esca enim ventri: & venter escis: deus autem & hunc & has destruet." Quoting 1 Corinthians 6:13.</note> 
But why different men have said different things 
about this place—and perhaps before the 
appointed time it behooves us also to set forth 
our opinion—the urgency of the time itself 
presses us rather than a curiosity for writing. 
We said above, when treating the fourth part 
concerning the seven heads of the dragon, 
that his individual heads are conquered in 
individual parts; but two are to be conquered 
at the same time in the sixth period. 
From this fact, it happened that according 
to one of his parts, [Satan] was imprisoned 
from that time in which Christ overcame him 
on the day of His death; but according to 
 the whole of his heads, [he is bound] from 
that day or hour in which the beast and 
the false prophet are sent

<column-break/>

into the lake of fire. And by this, in the 
thousand years is designated all the time 
that runs from the Resurrection of the Lord 
until the end of the world: especially on 
account of that great mystery of the Sabbath, 
by which we said the seventh age was begun 
simultaneously with the sixth; yet they are 
not to be consumed together. Just as John, 
who was called by Christ at the same time 
as Peter, yet did not pay the debt of death 
at the same time as him, but remained 
in this life for a long time after the death 
of Peter. For we have said that this pertains 
to the mystery of the Trinity; specifically, 
to show that the Holy Spirit—in whom 
freedom is given to men as yet to come—proceeds 
from the Father and the Son. One of them 
manifestly imposed labor upon the men of 
the Old Testament; the other upon the men 
of the New; yet not one without the other. 
In this way, the Father, having completed 
the labor which was under the servitude 
of the Law, might give to men the 
<term>spirit of adoption</term> <note>original: "spirituz adoptionis." A reference to Romans 8:15, signifying the transition from the "slavery" of the old law to the "freedom" of grace.</note> 
in which there is Sabbath and liberty; 
and the Son might give it more abundantly, 
this laborious time having been finished. 
Not that the Father gave it without the Son, 
or that the Son is to give it without the 
Father, since their essence is one; but

The words written above seemed clear enough, as they were brought down in an orderly sequence from the beginning of the book without any obstacle until a fitting conclusion—not only regarding the ages of the Church, but also the six parts of the book. But now, having heard that Satan is to be bound and released again, the understanding of many is dulled by this, as it seems far removed from common opinion. Indeed, this would be more distressing if the number "a thousand years" were not to be referred, by way of recapitulation, to the whole time of the Church. <note>Joachim uses "recapitulation" to mean that the 1,000 years isn't a new chronological period at the end of time, but a symbolic retelling of the entire history of the Church.</note> This is because the opinion of those who think these thousand years must refer to a literal Sabbath has been removed from our midst; rather, it should be understood according to its significance for the whole duration of the Church. Even if a certainty on this matter cannot be produced, a reasonable opinion that is not against the faith can still be offered. For behold, both the dragon and the beast are said to have seven heads; and we have written in this work regarding the seven periods <note>original: "septem capita et tempora"</note> that seven times were to be completed. # Joachim’s Sixth Part on the Apocalypse

...of sin might be present in all: but especially in the second and third. Having pre-discussed these things as effectively as they are necessary at the beginning of this seventh part—which we have begun to treat—let us turn our words toward the order of the exposition. As some have thought <margin>Augustine</margin> on the occasion of this passage: that the thousand years represent the time of the seventh age in which it is necessary for Christ to reign with the saints after the resurrection, after six thousand years from the beginning of the world have first been completed. They add certain other things that are entirely contrary to the Christian faith. It seems we should agree with their opinion in part and resist it in part; for indeed, part of the opinion was true, and part was empty and vain. For they said that the time which is to come after the battle described above is to be considered the seventh age and the Sabbath; their opinion in this was true—or rather, not so much an opinion as a most serene understanding. However, in how they assigned the seventh millennium to that same seventh age, it is established as being false in every way, both among the Greeks and among the Latins. For the Greeks claim to have more years, and we have far fewer; we feel this disagrees entirely with the path of truth. Furthermore, regarding their claim that the Lord would spend those thousand years with the saints in carnal feasts after the resurrection: this is entirely turned away from the faith. It is most certain that this did not proceed from spiritual minds, but from carnal ones. For "food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food, but God will destroy both this and those." <note>original: "esca enim ventri: et venter escis: deus autem et hunc et has destruet." This is a quote from 1 Corinthians 6:13, used here to argue against "chiliasm"—the belief in a literal 1,000-year kingdom of physical pleasures on earth.</note> Because various people have said various things about this place, and perhaps before the appointed time we must also set forth our own opinion, the urgency of the time itself is more vigorous than a mere curiosity for writing something. <margin>Seven heads</margin> We said above, when treating the fourth part concerning the seven heads of the dragon, that the individual heads were defeated in his individual parts; but two are to be conquered together in the sixth time. And for this reason it happens that, according to some part of himself, he was imprisoned from that time when Christ overcame him on the day of his death; but according to the totality of his heads, from that day or hour in which the beast and the false prophet are sent

<column-break/>

into the lake of fire. And through this, the thousand years designates all the time that runs from the resurrection of each individual <note>Joachim refers here to the spiritual resurrection of the soul through faith.</note> until the end of the world: especially because of that great mystery of the Sabbath in which we said the seventh age was begun together with the sixth. Yet they are not to be finished together, just like John: who was called by Christ at the same time as Peter, yet did not pay the debt of death at the same time as him, but remained in this life for a long time after the death of Peter. For we have said that this pertains to the mystery of the Trinity; namely, to show that the Holy Spirit—in whom freedom was given to men and is still to be given—proceeds from the Father and the Son. One of them [the Father] clearly imposed labor on the men of the Old Testament; the other [the Son] on the men of the New; yet one was not without the other. This was so that the Father, once the labor which was in the servitude of the Law was completed, might give to men the Spirit of adoption in which there is Sabbath and liberty; and the Son might give it more abundantly once this laborious time is finished. This is not because the Father gave it without the Son, or the Son is to give it without the Father, since their essence is one; but so that through the distinct and evident signs of the times, it may be clearly understood that He proceeds from both. Therefore, since at the end of the first state, liberty was given to the faithful regarding the servitude of the Law, and at the end of the second it is to be given more amply and perfectly regarding the narrowness of sufferings—since it consists in liberty, which the Apostle says belongs to the Sabbath where the Spirit of the Lord is—it is clear that the seventh age (in which that great Sabbath is to be) began in part from that Sabbath in which the Lord rested in the tomb; and it begins in its fullness from the ruin of the beast and the false prophet. Therefore, even if that which is written about the imprisonment of Satan must be perfectly completed from that point in time, nevertheless the beginning of the thousand years was initiated from the resurrection of the Lord. This is not because "a thousand years" should be estimated simply [literally], but because the number one thousand is most perfect and designates a great fullness of years. But even if the kingdom is taken from the Devil at that time in which it began in the human...

### Part of the Exposition

<margin><unclear>Handwritten note: Sander?</unclear></margin>
...the divine spirit rules in this way: whom we say is that angel who descends from heaven to capture the spirit of iniquity. This is the Holy Spirit <note>original: "spiritu sanctum"</note> who alone, by the presence of his heat, can suppress the "spirit of the north." This is according to what is said in the Song of Solomon: *Awake, O north wind; and come, O south wind; blow upon my garden, and let its spices flow.* <note>Song of Solomon 4:16. In medieval theology, the North wind often symbolized the devil or coldness of heart, while the South wind symbolized the Holy Spirit.</note> 

Now, the fact that this same angel is said to have the **key of the abyss** is not to be understood in the same way as the passage regarding the sixth angel sounding the trumpet: *And I saw a star fall from heaven unto the earth: and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit. And he opened the bottomless pit; and there arose a smoke out of the pit, as the smoke of a great furnace.* Instead, it should be understood according to what our Lord says: *And I have the keys of death and of hell.* <note>Revelation 9:1-2 and 1:18.</note> To that first angel, the key was given so that he might open the pit of the abyss, allowing locusts to ascend to punish those men who do not have the seal of the living God. But *this* angel has the key so that he may shut within it the king of those same locusts, so that he may no longer seduce the nations until the appointed time.

If the "abyss" (as we have already noted above) signifies the population of unbelievers, what is meant by its "key" if not a certain power <term>potestas|The legal or divinely granted right to exercise authority</term> to carry out his works among those unbelievers? The devil, possessing this power for some time, uses it wickedly until the time of his imprisonment. Ultimately, however, the Holy Spirit will possess it by right of victory—He who, through His exceeding goodness, conquers the malice of Satan, taking away his kingdom and power so that he is henceforth imprisoned and shut up within the remnants of that people who are called the "abyss." 

In this way, the virtue of the Spirit will suppress the spirit of darkness in the hearts of the unfaithful, so that he does not dare to stir them up to persecute the faithful. For when the cause of the sin ceases, the punishment will be removed; and when no one is found to be lashed, the whip will be taken away. For indeed, although many things are still permitted to the devil, he cannot contain himself or remain quiet in the hearts of his followers; he even leads forth with him multitudes of armed men and does not cease to disturb and persecute the kingdom of Christ. He does this because he still has the power to open the pit of the abyss and bring forth from

<column-break/>

it the beasts and creeping things of the earth because of the sins of those wicked men—specifically, those who profess to know God but deny Him by their deeds. 

Truly, on that day, that great power <note>original: "prās" / "potestas"</note> which the devil has possessed since the origin of the world will be taken from him and given into the hand of Christ, who says: *All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth;* and into the hand of the "people of the saints of the Most High," in whom the Holy Spirit is to reign. Thus, it will not be permitted for the devil to go out to persecute the elect as before; instead, he shall be silent and waste away in the prison of the unbelieving people. These people are still left in the furthest corners of the earth (as will appear below) so that he may seduce them at the appointed time; for it is necessary that he be released for a short time, so that he may be lifted up high one last time, only to fall forever.

Therefore, the key of the abyss having been taken from the devil, the angel is said to hold it: because on that day, the Holy Spirit will exercise His power not only among the chosen men, but even among the people of unbelief. Thus, what was once a source of strength for the devil’s kingdom shall henceforth be his prison and a punishment of pain. 

And this same angel is blessed to have a **great chain** in his hand, because great is the power of concord <note>original: "concordie"</note> which the Holy Spirit holds in His power to preserve the hearts of the faithful in the **bond of peace**. This concord is the only chain by which the devil is held bound, for he can find no part by which to enter to do harm, nor any place to thrust in his head to pour out his poison as he usually does. 

*And he seized,* it says, *the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss.* The Holy Spirit has already bound the devil in part, and He will bind him more fully on that day, until the time signified by the "thousand years" is completed. This spans from the time of the Lord’s resurrection until the time of the devil's release, enclosing him in the hearts of the <unclear>Scythian?</unclear> <note>original: "syrhicarz" - likely Scythian or pagan</note> nations against his own will. It is not that the Spirit wishes to dwell within them, but that the devil will no longer be permitted to deceive the nations everywhere or to destroy the soldiers of Christ in battle.

<summary>Abbot Joachim explains that the angel binding Satan in Revelation 20 represents the Holy Spirit, who uses the "key" of divine power and the "chain" of Christian harmony (concord) to imprison the devil within the hearts of unbelievers during a period of peace.</summary>

# Joachim’s Sixth Book on the Apocalypse

...nor to pass across: so that he might rage beyond the established boundaries. Whence it is rightly added: **And he closed and sealed over him: so that he might not seduce the nations further until the thousand years are completed.** This certainly means that for all those wavering in the faith of Christ, through the coming grace of the Holy Spirit, they shall be converted as if into a wall and into a fortified rampart. Thus, they may continually stand opposed to his pestiferous suggestion, being unable to resist him except by the <term>sign of the holy light<note>original: "signo sancti luminis". This refers to the seal of God or the light of grace that protects the soul from demonic influence.</note></term> with which the elect shall be sealed. However, it is not said "He sealed over him" in the same way that it is said in the fourth Psalm: *The light of your countenance, O Lord, is sealed upon us.* <note>Psalm 4:6 (Vulgate numbering). Joachim distinguishes between the "seal" of God's favor on humans and the "seal" of restraint placed upon the devil.</note> Rather, it is to be understood as if he said: He closed and fortified him with his own seal, which no one is permitted to loosen except He who binds him. Truly, where God has so ordained something that it cannot be changed, there is no one who can resist His will. Then, indeed, the Church of Christ will be able to enjoy true peace, when those nations—and the devil within them—shall be so bound by the power of the Holy Spirit that it is no longer permitted for them to do whatever they please; instead, they shall remain wasting away in their iniquities. 

But lest anyone should estimate that this was said concerning that eternal peace which will be in the <term>eighth age<note>Joachim’s theology divided history into "ages" or "states." The eighth age represents the eternal Sabbath of Heaven after the end of the world.</note></term>, it is immediately added: **And after these things he must be released for a short time.** Therefore, after the ruin of the <term>seventh head<note>The seventh head of the dragon/beast, often identified with the final Antichrist.</note></term> there will be peace, and after that peace, the persecution designated by the "tail." <note>In Joachim's imagery, the "tail" of the dragon represents the final outburst of evil at the very end of time (Gog and Magog).</note> In the meantime, however, that which the Apostle says concerning Christ must be fulfilled: **He must reign until he puts all his enemies under his feet** <note>1 Corinthians 15:25.</note>—namely the Jews and the Gentiles. For there follows:

<margin>some</margin>
<margin>Text 2</margin>
> **AND I saw thrones, and they sat upon them: and judgment was given to them: and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God: and who did not worship the beast nor his image, nor received his mark on their foreheads or in their hands: and they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were completed.**

These words, if understood soundly, are found

<column-break/>

written in Daniel, where it says: *I saw that the power of the other beasts was taken away: and times of life were appointed to them until a time and a time.* <note>Daniel 7:12.</note> And after some other things: *And the judgment shall sit, that the power may be taken away*—understand "of that king"—*and it shall be destroyed forever; but the kingdom and the power and the greatness of the kingdom, which is under all the heaven, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom: and all kings shall serve him.* <note>Daniel 7:26-27.</note> For it is necessary that the **souls of those beheaded** (that is, of the holy martyrs and other just people who did not worship the beast and his image, nor received his mark on their foreheads or in their hands in the unspeakable execration of [sinful] work) should live and reign apart from the others whose merits are not equal. This is so that they may reign first with Christ before the end of the world comes. 

And he rightly commemorates that the souls of the beheaded and of the other just ones have lived; for just as the life of bodies consists in souls, so the **life of souls** consists in the vision of God. This is indeed granted to certain of the just from the very hour of their death, just as it is believed to have been granted to him who said: *I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.* <note>Philippians 1:23.</note> To others, who have something less than true perfection, it is granted at the end. And this kingdom of blessed vision and peace—which according to its fullness will be given to the multitude of the just after the ruin of the seventh king—received its beginning from the very time of the Lord’s Resurrection. It is rightly said to remain for a **thousand years**, so that the same time may be understood for the incarceration of the dragon and the reign of the saints, because the one is known to be the cause of the other. 

However, the **rest of the dead** do not live with Christ until the thousand years are completed, because it pertains to the just and omnipotent judgment that those who are <term>sluggish in battle<note>original: "segnes sunt ad prælium". Joachim refers to Christians who were lukewarm or avoided the hardships of spiritual struggle/martyrdom.</note></term> and refuse to suffer for Christ—even if they are otherwise considered worthy of mercy—shall nevertheless suffer the loss of the happiness of that kingdom, at least until the fitting end of the years, paying the debt of their sins in the meantime. And because there are many who do not strive, thinking it sufficient for themselves if they do not lose the gifts of mercy at the very last moment, [the author] knowing how heavily such people are to be rebuked, follows up and says:

### Part of the Exposition of the Abbot

<margin>Text 3</margin> ¶ **This is the first resurrection: blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection.** And as if the reason were being asked, he says: **over these the second death has no power.**

¶ For what is more fortunate for a just man than to be granted thus to pass from this <term>pilgrimage<note>original: "peregrinatione". A common medieval metaphor for earthly life as a journey toward the heavenly homeland.</note></term> to his homeland, so that no debt of sin remains for him after death? Thus he is not compelled, even for a time, toward the **second death**—which is the punishment of the soul—nor can he be subjected to its power. **Over these**, he says, **the second death has no power.**

¶ **But they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and they shall reign with him for a thousand years.**

¶ But this reign exists in part from the time of the Lord’s resurrection; however, from the ruin of the <term>seventh king<note>Joachim’s theology of history often divided time into periods marked by "kings" or "ages." The seventh king usually refers to the final Antichrist figure of the current age.</note></term> it exists in its entirety until the time of **Gog and Magog**. ¶ And so it follows:

<margin>Gog</margin>
<margin>Text 4</margin> ¶ **And when the thousand years are finished, Satan shall be loosed from his prison, and he shall go out and seduce the nations that are upon the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog: and he shall gather them for battle, whose number is as the sand of the sea.**

¶ **Satan shall be loosed from his prison**, so that he may be permitted once more to seduce the nations as he did before, and to complete every plan of his wickedness, so that neither in great matters nor in small may he be seen to have any excuse. He **shall go out**, however, because appearing once more, manifest in that <term>lost man<note>original: "perdito homine". Joachim refers to the final human vessel of the Antichrist, whom Satan will "assume" or possess.</note></term> whom he shall take up, he will fight against the camp of the saints. And perhaps he will no longer be marked by obvious lies as before, but will appear as if in the glory of majesty; thus he might lie by making himself seem similar in all things and through all things to the Most High, whose rival he always is.

<margin>Ezekiel</margin> ¶ It should be noted that in the prophet Ezekiel, in the same manner as in this book, a brief discourse was held concerning the resurrection of the dead,

and afterwards concerning the coming of Gog, to whom it is said: ¶ **After many days you shall be visited; in the final years you shall come to the land that has returned from the sword.** And after a few verses: **In the final days you shall be.** It seems, however, that both [John and Ezekiel] agree with the Apostle Paul who says: ¶ **The dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive, who remain...** <note>1 Thessalonians 4:16-17.</note> except that here John says **the rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were finished.** Unless, perhaps, we understand that the saints, immediately after their resurrection—without the examination of that terrible judgment and without an interval of days—shall enter into true life, while the others do not enter immediately, but only after the completion of the judgment. 

But how are we to understand this if it is certain that nations are still to be seduced? Is it right to believe that even after the resurrection of the dead, some nations must be left behind to be seduced by the devil? Let it be understood, therefore, in the way stated above, or let us leave it until the Lord comes, who **will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and manifest the counsels of hearts.** <note>1 Corinthians 4:5.</note> But whichever way this may be, it remains entirely certain that near the end of the world, the devil will seduce these nations and lead them against the Church of the elect—which will be as beloved to Christ as <term>Rachel was to her husband<note>A biblical reference to the love Jacob held for Rachel (Genesis 29), symbolizing Christ's deep affection for the Church.</note></term>—so that he may bring upon them and upon himself a temporal and eternal judgment, and no longer have a time or place for persecuting the Church. ¶ Item, it follows:

<margin>Text 5</margin> ¶ **And they came up upon the breadth of the earth, and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.**

### Part of the Abbot’s Exposition

<margin>Text 3</margin>
**This is the first resurrection: blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection.** <note>original: "Hæc resurrectio prima est" - Joachim is quoting Revelation 20:5-6.</note> And as if the reason were being asked, he says: **over these the second death has no power.**

For what could be happier for a just man than to be granted the transition from this pilgrimage to the fatherland in such a way that no debt is left to him after death? By this debt, he might otherwise be compelled, even for a time, to be subject to the power of the "second death," which is the punishment of the soul. **Over these** (he says) **the second death has no power.**

**But they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and they shall reign with him for a thousand years.**

But this reign exists from the time of the Lord's resurrection according to one part; however, from the ruin of the **seventh king** <note>In Joachim’s view of history, the "seventh king" is a major Antichrist figure whose fall marks the beginning of a golden age of the Spirit.</note> according to the whole, it continues until the time of **Gog and Magog**. For it follows:
<margin>Gog</margin>

<margin>Text 4</margin>
**And when the thousand years are finished, Satan shall be released from his prison and shall go out and seduce the nations that are over the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog: and he shall gather them for battle, whose number is like the sand of the sea.**

Satan shall be released from his prison so that he may be permitted to seduce the nations once more as he did before, and to fulfill every counsel of his wickedness, so that neither in great things nor in small may he be able to have any excuse whatsoever. He shows, however, that appearing once more, manifest in a lost man whom he shall take up, he will fight against the **camp of the saints**. Perhaps he will no longer be distinguished by lies as before, but will appear as if in the glory of majesty, so that in all things and through all things he may lie, claiming to be like the Most High, whose rival he always is.

<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
It should be noted that in the prophet **Ezekiel**, in the same way as in this book, speech was first held concerning the resurrection of the dead,

<column-break/>

and afterwards concerning the coming of **Gog**, to whom it is said: *After many days you will be visited; in the final years you will come to the land that has returned from the sword.* And after some other things: *In the final days you shall be.* It seems that both the prophet and the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> agree when he says: **The dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive, who are left behind**; except that here John says: **The rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years were finished.** Perhaps we should understand that the saints, immediately after their resurrection—without the examination of that terrible judgment and without an interval of days—will enter into true life, while the others will not enter immediately, but after the consummation of the judgment. 

But how are we to understand this if it is certain that nations are still to be led out? And is it right to believe that even after the resurrection of the dead, some nations must be left behind to be seduced by the devil? Therefore, let it be understood in the way stated above, or let us leave it until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and manifest the counsels of hearts. But whichever way this may be, it remains entirely certain that near the end of the world the devil will seduce these nations and lead them against the Church of the elect, which will be as beloved to Christ as **Rachel** was to her husband. This is so that He may judge a temporal and eternal judgment upon them and upon himself, and that he may no longer have time or place to persecute the Church. For it follows:

**And they ascended over the breadth of the earth, and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.**

At that time, there will be <term>monastic communities<note>original: "cenobia monachorū". As is aptly shown in Ezekiel, there will be peace then in the world, and men will suspect no evil. And because God loves them, He will immediately judge Gog and his army. For it follows:

**And fire descended from God out of heaven and devoured them.**

### Part of the Exposition

<margin>g.</margin> Its initiation has already preceded along with the **sixth age**; <note>In the author's theology, historical ages overlap. The "seventh age" of peace begins even as the "sixth age" of conflict is still concluding.</note> however, the joy of the consolation of the righteous will not be brief, for the Lord says: *But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you.* <note>Quoting John 16:22.</note> Finally, the **second age** was of such brevity compared to the first that **Noah**, who had already lived six hundred years before the flood, is recorded as having remained until the end of that age and the beginning of the third. And perhaps this very fact pertained to the matter at hand: for just as in that first age—specifically up to the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life—the seven ages of the world were signified, so in the remainder of Noah’s life, the **seventh age** is signified, in which, once the floodwaters cease, there will be peace and a Sabbath for those who love God. Therefore, just as six parts of the book pertain to **Martha**, who is troubled about many things, so the seventh part pertains to **Mary**, who sits simply at the feet of the Lord Jesus. <note>original: "pertinent ad Martham... ad Mariam." A common medieval allegory where Martha represents the active, laboring life (the first six ages) and Mary represents the contemplative, peaceful life (the seventh age).</note> And just as the **sixth age** is contained within the seven laborious times designated by the six weeks of **Lent**, <note>original: "quadragesime." The forty-day fast before Easter.</note> so the seventh age was contained in the one time of peace designated by the **Easter season**; although (as I have already said) the dawn of the seventh age has shone upon this world from the beginning of the era—a matter we remember having sufficiently untangled in this work. One must not overlook, however, that because the **Latin people** were chosen for the honor of the **Son** by the property of the mystery, and the **Greek people** for the honor of the **Holy Spirit**, it is not to be believed to have happened by chance that it was handed down to the Greeks by their ancestors to solemnly sing **Alleluia** during the time of Lent, while it was handed down to us by our ancestors to remain silent from that same song until the Easter season. <note>The author interprets liturgical differences between the Western and Eastern Churches as divinely ordained symbols of the different Roles of the Trinity in history.</note> This was done so that in this very act it might be clearly understood that from the time Christ came into the world, it was handed down to God’s elect not only to receive and embrace the word of the cross—which belongs to

<column-break/>

**Christ** and to the **sixth age**—but also, in no small part, the joy of the contemplative life, which belongs to the **Holy Spirit**, concerning whom it is written by the Apostle: *Where the spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.* <note>Quoting 2 Corinthians 3:17.</note> Indeed, even if we say that blessed time, which is reckoned as a **Sabbath**, belongs entirely to the **Holy Spirit**—to whom belongs all spiritual joy and gladness with which the Lord was anointed above his fellows—it is not, however, in the same way as that future world. That future world was designated on the last day of the festival (that is, on the day of **Pentecost**), when the apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit in a way they had not been filled before; not even when they were baptized in Christ, nor when on Easter day the Lord breathed on them and said to them: *Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven, and whose sins you retain, they are retained.* <note>Quoting John 20:22-23.</note> Finally, in the prophet **Ezekiel**, after the ruin of **Gog** and his army is treated, it is immediately added: *I will set my glory among the nations, and all nations shall see my judgment which I have done, and my hand which I have laid upon them. And the house of Israel shall know that I am the Lord their God from that day forward.* <note>Quoting Ezekiel 39:21-22.</note> And after some other things: *And I will not hide my face from them, because I have poured out my spirit upon all the house of Israel.* <note>Quoting Ezekiel 39:29.</note> But just as **John**, after the ruin of Gog and Magog and with a few things interposed, begins to treat the glory of **Jerusalem**, so also Ezekiel treats a certain building that flourished to the south. <meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the "Seventh Age" and the end of the world. ### Sixth Part on the Apocalypse

...from whose face the earth and heaven fled: and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing in the sight of the throne, and books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the **book of life**: and the dead were judged from those things which were written in the books according to their works. <note>original: "a cuius conspectu fugit terra..." This is a direct translation of Revelation 20:11-12, describing the Great White Throne Judgment.</note>

---

Taking up the Lord’s parable of the noble man who went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and then return, <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents or the Pounds in Luke 19 and Matthew 25.</note> he indicated that he would come to settle the account with his servants at an hour they did not expect; he would reward the good servants, but punish the wicked for their laziness. Then, when he had spoken further, he added and said: *When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he will sit upon the seat of his majesty: and all nations will be gathered before him: and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. And he will place the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.* <note>Quoting Matthew 25:31-33.</note> Therefore, after the Lord comes in his majesty, he will sit upon the seat of his majesty so that he may separate the good from the evil. However, whether this happens immediately as he arrives, or after many or several days, is uncertain.

If, according to the opinion of the Church Fathers, a space of time remains after the fall of the **Antichrist** (though that time is unknown to men), it is clear that if the Lord then comes to judge the Antichrist—according to the opinion of **Jerome** <margin>Jerome</margin> on that passage of Paul’s letter to the Thessalonians: *Whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming* <note>original: "spiritu oris sui." This refers to 2 Thessalonians 2:8, suggesting the Antichrist is defeated by a mere word or "breath" from Christ.</note>—some time must intervene. This interval is called the "last day," <margin>Augustine</margin> according to the opinion of **Augustine**: it is the middle period between his arrival and the day in which <margin>Sal.</margin> he will sit on the seat of his majesty to divide the good from the bad, placing the good on his

<column-break/>

right and the bad on his left. If, however, he does not come in person to judge the Antichrist, but rather the **Archangel Michael** <note>In some medieval traditions, based on Daniel 12:1, Michael is the one who physically strikes down the Antichrist on Mount Olivet.</note> performs this according to the opinion of some, then it seems that "that day"—that is, the period called the **Judgment** <term>iudicij</term>—will begin indeed from the fall of the Antichrist. This is the time when the **false prophet** and the **beast** are cast into the lake of fire; but to bring that day to a close, the Lord would come toward the end. As soon as he arrives, he would sit upon the throne of his majesty to command the impious to go into eternal fire, and the righteous into eternal life.

If this is how it will be, what can be thought of what the Apostle says regarding the Antichrist: *Whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming*? Perhaps it means that on the day when **Satan** is imprisoned, he is understood to have been overcome by the **Holy Spirit**; and at the very end, when the Lord comes, he is destroyed entirely, at which point he is also cast into the lake of fire, where the beast and the false prophet already are.

But if, according to **Jerome**, the Lord himself comes in person to destroy the Antichrist—since Scripture records that he will come in fire—it seems that fire is the one which **Peter** mentions. <note>Referring to 2 Peter 3:10, describing the world being dissolved by fire.</note> It is said that **Gog** <note>A symbolic enemy of God's people; in Revelation 20, Gog and Magog represent the final rebellion before the last judgment.</note> and his army are to be slain, so that what is said regarding his judgment may be understood to pertain specifically to those who were found in this life to be "members of the Devil," who must be punished by that terrible fire even in a temporal sense.

Truly, amidst these narrow straits and ambiguous opinions, what else can we admit except what the Lord says: *Of that hour no one knows, except the Father alone*? For if Scripture spoke openly about the coming of the Son of God—so that it were written in its proper order like many other things—then the Son himself would not have said "Of that hour no one knows," nor would we suffer such "narrow straits" in trying to explain the manifestation of his coming. But because it is intended that no one should know the end, we are squeezed by divine authorities that seem to contradict one another.

### Part of the Exposition by the Abbot

its initiation has already preceded together with the sixth: yet the joy of the consolation of the righteous will not be brief; as the Lord says: *But I will see you again: and your heart shall rejoice: and no one shall take your joy from you.* <note>original: "Iterum autem videbo vos: & gaudebit cor vestrum: & gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis." A liturgical song of praise.</note> during the time of Lent: but to us by our ancestors there is silence from that same song during the same time, namely until the Paschal time: so that in this very thing it might be clearly understood: that from that time in which Christ came into the world: it was not only handed down to the elect of God to receive and embrace the word of the cross: which pertains to

<column-break/>

Christ and to the sixth age: but also, in no small part, the joy of the contemplative life: which pertains to the Holy Spirit: concerning whom it is written by the Apostle: *Where the spirit of the Lord is: there is liberty.* <note>original: "Vbi spiritus domini: ibi libertas." A quotation from 2 Corinthians 3:17.</note> Nevertheless, we say that the blessedness which is reckoned as the Sabbath pertains entirely to the Holy Spirit: to whom belongs all spiritual joy and gladness, with which the Lord was anointed above his fellows: yet not in the same way as that future world which is designated in the last day of the festival (that is) on the day of Pentecost: when the apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit in such a way as they had not been filled before: not even when they were baptized in Christ: nor when, on the day of Easter, the Lord breathed on them and said to them: *Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven: and whose you shall retain, they are retained.* <note>original: "Accipite spiritum sanctum: quoru[m] remiseritis peccata..." A quotation from John 20:22-23.</note> Finally, in the prophet Ezekiel: after the ruin of Gog and his army is dealt with: it is immediately added: *I will set my glory among the nations: and all nations shall see my judgment that I have done: and my hand which I have laid upon them. And the house of Israel shall know that I am the Lord their God from that day and forward.* <note>A paraphrase of Ezekiel 39:21-22.</note> And after some other things: *And I will not hide my face from them, because I have poured out my spirit upon all the house of Israel.* <note>Ezekiel 39:29.</note> But just as John, after the ruin of Gog and Magog <note>Gog and Magog are biblical figures symbolizing the final enemies of God's people who are defeated before the last judgment.</note> with a few things interposed, begins to deal with the glory of Jerusalem: so also does Ezekiel, concerning a certain building that flourished toward the south. But now the sails of the discourse, having been held back for a little while as if in a certain whirlpool, must be released: so that we may speak of that terrible day, which will be after the final time, as God shall grant. For after those things which were written by him, and in whatever way expounded by us, the holy evangelist John says:

**AND** I saw a great white throne and him sitting upon it

### Joachim: Sixth Book on the Apocalypse

<margin>John</margin>
> From whose presence the earth and heaven fled: and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing in the presence of the throne, and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged from those things which were written in the books according to their works. <note>original: "a cuius conspectu fugit terra et cælum..." This is a direct translation of Revelation 20:11-12.</note>

The Lord, taking up the parable of the nobleman who went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return, indicated that he would come to settle accounts with his servants at an hour when they did not expect it; he would reward the good servants, but punish the wicked for their idleness. <note>This refers to the Parable of the Talents or Minas in Luke 19:12-27.</note> Then, when he had spoken further, he added and said: *But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he shall sit upon the seat of his majesty: and all nations shall be gathered before him: and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on his left.* <note>A translation of Matthew 25:31-33.</note> Therefore, after the Lord comes in his majesty, he will sit upon the seat of his majesty to separate the good from the wicked; but whether he will do so as soon as he arrives, or after many or several days, is uncertain. For if, according to the opinion of the Fathers, there is a remaining space of time after the fall of the Antichrist <note>term: **Antichrist** (Antichristus); the ultimate enemy of Christ expected to appear before the end of the world.</note> (though unknown to men), it is clear that if the Lord comes then to judge the Antichrist, <margin>Jerome</margin> according to the opinion of Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was a scholar and priest known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> on that passage of the Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians: *Whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming,* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:8.</note> it is necessary that some time intervenes. This interval is called the "last day" <margin>Augustine</margin> according to the opinion of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note>—a middle period between his arrival and the day on which he will sit on the throne of his majesty to divide the good from the bad, placing the good on the

<column-break/>

right and the wicked on the left. If, however, he does not come in person to judge the Antichrist, but rather the Archangel Michael comes according to the opinion of some, then it seems that "that day"—that is, the period called the time of judgment—will indeed begin from the fall of the Antichrist. This would be from that time when the false prophet and the beast are cast into the lake of fire; <note>Referencing Revelation 19:20.</note> yet, to complete that day, the Lord is expected to come near the end. As soon as he arrives, he will sit upon the seat of his majesty to command the impious to go into eternal fire, and the righteous into eternal life. If this is how it will be, what can be thought of what the Apostle says concerning the Antichrist: *Whom the Lord Jesus shall slay with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming*? It must be understood that on that day in which Satan is imprisoned, he is overcome by the Holy Spirit, and in the end, when the Lord comes, he is destroyed entirely, at the time when he is also cast into the lake of fire where the beast and the false prophet already are. But if, according to Jerome, the Lord comes in person to destroy the Antichrist, since Scripture records that he will come in fire, it seems that this fire is the one mentioned by Peter <note>Likely referring to 2 Peter 3:10-12, describing the world being dissolved by fire.</note> when it is said that Gog and his army are to be slain. <note>term: **Gog**; a symbolic leader of the forces of evil in Ezekiel and Revelation.</note> Thus, what is said specifically about his judgment should be understood to pertain to those who are found in this life to be members of the Devil, to be punished by that terrible fire, which is also a temporal punishment. Truly, between these narrow straits and ambiguous opinions, what else can we confess except what the Lord says: *Of that hour no one knows, except the Father alone*? <note>Matthew 24:36.</note> For if Scripture spoke openly about the coming of the Son of God—so that it were written in its proper order (like many other things)—the Son himself would not have said, "Of that hour no one knows," nor would we suffer such difficulties in explaining his coming. But because it is his purpose that no one should know, we are squeezed by divine authorities that seem to contradict one another.

The author weighs the opinions of Jerome and Augustine regarding the "last day" and concludes that the exact timing remains a divine mystery.</summary>

equally in this part: we are dulled and overwhelmed, and we fail, knowing that which is written: *Dark water in the clouds of the air.* <note>original: "Tenebrosa aqua in nubibus aeris" from Psalm 18:11. This suggests that divine mysteries are often hidden behind a veil of obscurity.</note> It remains, therefore, that having discussed the other parts of the book and designated them distinctly by their times, we should remain silent regarding the hidden arrival of the Judge. Let us say only this, as freely as it is certain: that after the end of the **seventh age**, about which we have spoken much, the Lord will sit upon the seat of his majesty to separate the wicked from the elect and to render to each according to his works. How glorious that seat will be! It is the church of the just, in which the Lord shall sit on that day—great in merits and white with the brilliance of justice. From the presence of this place it is revealed when it is said: **And I saw a great and white throne.**

When he says, **And one sitting upon it, from whose face the earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them,** it is not to be understood so lazily as to think that heaven and earth literally flee from the sight of Christ. Rather, it means that all the ornamentation of heaven and earth will be considered as nothing and empty in respect to the glory of Christ and his saints, according to what is said by the prophet: *The moon shall be ashamed and the sun confounded when the Lord of hosts shall reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and shall be glorified in the sight of his elders.* <note>original: "Erubescet luna: z confundetur sol..." from Isaiah 24:23.</note> For just as the stars of heaven seem to fade at the sight of the sun—not because they cease to cease being what they are, but because the clarity of their brightness vanishes and becomes void—so while heaven and earth remain in their order, the decor and appearance of their beauty will be hidden. There will be no place or value for them among those things which the Lord has prepared for those who love him.

As for what follows—**And I saw the dead, great and small, standing in the sight of the throne**—the apostle Paul also makes this manifest when he says: *We must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.* <note>2 Corinthians 5:10.</note> Thus it is well added: **And the books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from those things written in the books according to their works.** This should be understood according to what is said in another place by the apostle: *Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes...*

<column-break/>

*...who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the secrets of hearts.* <note>1 Corinthians 4:5.</note> Indeed, the **closed books** are the hidden hearts of men, whose intentions and desires are known only to him who is Life. He who now keeps them closed and hidden will make them known on that day, and he will open the "book of justice" of his own heart to separate from the company of the wicked those whom he has always held written in his eternal memory. This is according to the word of the apostle: *The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his.* <note>2 Timothy 2:19.</note>

It should be noted that in this judgment, those of whom it was said above, *They lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years,* will themselves be judges alongside Christ. This fulfills the promise of the Lord, who said: *You who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* <note>Matthew 19:28.</note> Therefore, even if the apostle says, *We must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ,* it is not to be understood that the sins for which the elect were already judged in this life by the **vicars of Christ** <note>Referring to priests or bishops acting in the sacrament of penance.</note> and were forgiven, must be brought up again on that day. Rather, the good will stand so that the good they have done may be reported to the confusion of the wicked; and the wicked, even if unwillingly, will stand so that their evils may be reported to the honor of the good. For just as the wicked will be judged by the works of the good, so the elect will be magnified by the works of the wicked.

For this reason, I do not think the name "the dead" in this passage should be taken simply to mean all who have died, but rather **sinful men** who are dead in their offenses. However, some of these were repentant and willing to face their guilt—even if they did not perform enough penance to merit immediate pardon after the death of the flesh. They shall follow after **purgatorial punishments** <term>purgatorias: refers to the cleansing process of Purgatory where souls are purified of the remains of sin before entering heaven</term> and obtain indulgence, as David says of them in a certain place: *Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, for you have multiplied your mercy, O God.* <note>Psalm 36:6-7.</note> So much for these people. But what of those who reign with Christ?

<margin>Psalm</margin> ...a thousand years <note>original: "mille annis"</note> before they reach eternal life. "The children of men," it says, "shall hope under the cover of your wings. The author uses this to describe the reward of the righteous.</note> Just as the saints of God will not stand before the tribunal of Christ to recount the evil works that they have already confessed before priests—as if they were standing even now before Christ's tribunal, having already obtained pardon through worthy satisfaction for those deeds—so also John says here: **The dead were judged from those things which were written in the books according to the works of the impious.** <note>A reference to Revelation 20:12.</note> This is not to be understood as if forgiven iniquities are to be brought back to judgment, but rather it refers to the evil works for which they did not do penance in their life, and the good works which they are proven to have done with an eye toward piety. For those whose names the Son of God writes in the **book of his heart** through his own satisfaction will be received into the company of the elect after the necessary punishments for their sins, obtaining pardon on that day. <margin>Text 7</margin> ¶ **And the sea gave up the dead who were in it; and death and hell gave up the dead who were in them; and they were judged, every man according to their works. And hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This second death is the lake of fire.**

¶ **And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.**

¶ If we understand the "lake of fire" to be that place which is commonly nicknamed "hell," by what logic are death and hell said to be cast into the lake of fire, unless one thing is to be understood according to the letter, and another in the spirit?

In the fourth part, where it was said that he who sat upon the pale horse was called **Death**, and another followed him who was called **Hell**, we said that by the name of Death, we should understand the **false prophet of the Saracens** <margin>Saracens</margin> <note>original: "pſeudo prophetam Sarracenoꝝ." This means that the world will no longer be able to hold those whom it possessed for a long time as its own people—namely, those called "worldly"—but they shall rise from the dead and come to judgment. And those whom these figures (one called Death, the other Hell) possess as their own in their retinue, according to that saying of the prophet Ezekiel: **Pharaoh saw them and was comforted.** <note>original: "Vidit eos Pharao z cōſolatus eſt" from Ezekiel 32:31. ¶ It is necessary, whether they will or no, for them to come to judgment to be judged individually according to their works. Moreover, Death and Hell shall be cast into the lake of fire as the principals, where they are believed to have been before, along with all who were on their side: namely, those who are called the **Beast** and the **False Prophet**, who are even reported to have been sent alive into the lake of fire.

¶ But if, before this hour of the great and final judgment comes, they are to be sent alive into the lake of fire, why are they called back again to judgment? Is it not so that they may recount their evil works, so that those who were previously hardened by a hidden judgment might see, on that day, not only the judgment itself but also the manifest justice of its cause? Nevertheless, even if they descend alive according to the letter (which is nonetheless doubtful) into hell (as we read happened to **Dathan and Abiram** <margin>Dathan</margin> <note>Dathan and Abiram were biblical figures who rebelled against Moses and were swallowed alive by the earth (Numbers 16).</note>), one should not therefore believe that their souls are not to be separated from their bodies—as if they neither die in their bodies nor rise again—for even if they descend alive into hell like the others...

### Abbreviated Part of the Exposition

And it should be known that the "first resurrection" of the blessed is the "second resurrection," but the "second death" of the unhappy is the "first death." <note>The author is playing with the theological numbering of life and death: the spiritual "resurrection" from sin is the "first," making the bodily one the second; similarly, spiritual death is the "second" and more permanent death.</note> Why is this? Because the first resurrection pertains to the glory of the saints, but the second death pertains to the eternal punishments of the rejected. # John’s Sixth [Book] on the Apocalypse, Page 216

...that which John himself says in the Gospel: **"But as many as received him"**—that is, Christ—**"he gave them power to become the sons of God. Who were born, not of bloods, nor of the desire of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."** <note>original: "Quotquot autem receperunt eum... non ex sanguinibus... sed ex deo nati sunt." See John 1:12-13.</note> For we know that everyone who is born is said to "descend" from the one whose child they are: not indeed through a loss of status, but through the process of birth. Whence the only-begotten Son of God is called "the Truth," because he willed to descend from heaven so that he might honor the one who sent him. For he is truthful who confesses the truth, and who does not disdain to be subject to the one from whom he comes. In contrast, it is said of the "father of lies" <note>Satan</note> that he **"did not stand in the truth,"** because he wished to make himself equal to the Most High who created him.

And it is right that the city of Jerusalem is said to descend from God out of heaven: because by this very fact she is understood to be born of God. Through the impulse of humility, she "descends" from the glory of her calling; for although she understands herself to be a daughter of the most high God through grace, she does not call herself a daughter, but a handmaid. She knows that which is written: **"The Lord is high, yet he regards the lowly."** <note>Psalm 1138:6 / 137:6 in the Vulgate</note> And again: **"God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble."** She is called the **"New Jerusalem"** so that she is not mistaken for that "old" Jerusalem which is in slavery with her children. Whence she is also said to be **"prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,"** so that she may be understood as that Queen of whom the Psalmist speaks in the spirit to Christ the King:

<margin>Psalm 44</margin>
**"The queen stood,"** he says, **"at your right hand in clothing of gold, surrounded by variety."** <note>Psalm 44:10 in the Vulgate, corresponding to Psalm 45 in modern bibles. The "variety" refers to her multifaceted virtues.</note> But what kind of ornaments are hers believed to be? Are they visible or man-made? Far from it! For what can external finery contribute to the glory of those who are merely hired servants? For even <term>Babylon</term><note>In this context, Babylon represents the world or the corrupt city, contrasting with the holy Jerusalem.</note> is written to be gilded with gold and precious stones—and yet this is not to her glory, but to her shame. Furthermore, Jerusalem is always prepared for the marriage of Christ, taking care that nothing of deformity appears in her through the defilement of vices which might offend the eyes of her husband. She adorns herself daily with the ornament of virtues, as if with certain necklaces or precious

<column-break/>

stones, knowing that her husband by no means seeks external beauty, but internal beauty. It follows:

<margin>Text 3</margin>
> ¶ **AND I heard a great voice from heaven saying: Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them. And they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them as their God. ¶ The "throne of God," the "city of God," and the "people of God" are often to be understood interchangeably for the same multitude of the elect. However, when these terms are placed together, each one designates something specific and distinct for its part. Indeed, the **"throne of God"** in this place signifies the order of <term>prelates</term><note>High-ranking church leaders or elders who guide the community.</note> through whom God, who presides, carries out his judgments daily, and will carry them out more manifesty on that final day. From the throne of God, however, a voice was heard saying of the city of Jerusalem, which is the Church of the saints: **"Behold the tabernacle of God with men."** This is because the pastors of the Church have testified to that which we ourselves believe regarding the future glory of Holy Mother Church: namely, that she is the true <term>tabernacle</term><note>A "tabernacle" is a dwelling place or tent; here it refers to God's presence living within the community of believers.</note> of God. This is not a humble and transitory one like the tabernacle of Moses, at whose door multitudes of sheep, goats, bulls, and calves were gathered to be slaughtered upon its altar as a symbol of things to come. Rather, it is a tabernacle not made by hands, in which are gathered the crowds of men who were created in the image of God, so that they themselves might be his people and the sheep of his pasture. <margin>Text 4</margin>
**And he who sat on the throne said: "Behold, I make all things new."**
¶ A new heaven, a new earth, a new 
<margin>Song of Songs</margin>
Jerusalem. For now (as it says in the Song of Songs): **"Winter has passed; the rain is over and gone."** <note>original: "hyems transijt: ymber abijt & recessit" — Song of Solomon 2:11. The commentator uses the change of seasons as a metaphor for the transition from the "winter" of mortal life to the "summer" of eternity.</note> For how does summer appear in comparison to the winter time? Almost everything that appears beautiful to the eyes seems to possess the quality of novelty. It follows:

<margin>Text 5</margin>
**And he said to me: "Write, for these words are most faithful and true."**
¶ "Write," he says, these things with the "pen of the tongue" in the hearts of the faithful, lest anyone think these words are frivolous and, by not believing—since they are most faithful—repeatedly neglect to come to the wedding feast. Well, then, follows:

<margin>Text 6</margin>
**And he said to me: "It is done."**
¶ This phrase, **"It is done,"** signifies completion. He says this so that it might be understood not as something for the future, but as something already present; 
<margin>Psalms</margin>
since **"a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday that has passed."** <note>original: "mille anni ante oculos tuos tanquam dies externa quae preterijt" — Psalm 90:4. This suggests that from God's eternal perspective, the prophecy is already accomplished.</note> Whence also the mystery of that word which is written at the head of the book:

<margin>Text 7</margin>
**"I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end."**
¶ A repetition is made so that men might believe in the completion of things with the same ease with which they cannot doubt the beginning of creation. For if a mortal man, when he begins some good work that is either useful or dear to him, is saddened and ashamed if he cannot bring it to effect, how much more shameful would it be for the living and true God to begin a work in vain

<column-break/>

that he could not finish? But yet there are many who hear and do not believe, and therefore neglect to receive and possess the kingdom of God. He who redeemed us in his blood still speaks, and opening up the inexpressible treasure of his goodness and mercy, he protests and says: **"To the thirsty I will give from the fountain of the water of life freely"**—that is, from the grace of the Holy Spirit. And he added:

¶ **"He who overcomes shall possess these things, and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. But for the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and fornicators, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulfur, which is the second death."**
¶ The words of this chapter require warning, not explanation. For what is sweeter to the face of the just man than to enjoy the gift of the Holy Spirit and to possess the joys of Jerusalem, as if he were himself a son of God—that is, an heir of God the Father and a co-heir with Christ? And what is more bitter to the face of the wicked than to have a portion in the infernal lake burning with sulfur and fire? He calls those "fearful" who are afraid to leave behind present things for the sake of the future; who fear those who kill the body, and not rather Him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna <note>a term for Hell, derived from the Valley of Hinnom</note>. It follows:

**And there came one of the seven angels having the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues, and he spoke with me, saying: "Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb."**
¶ A little earlier he had said that he saw the New Jerusalem descending from heaven, and now he says he is called by one of the seven angels, saying to him: "Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb." Therefore, either summarizing by way of repetition... <meta>catchword: replicauit (repeated/folded back)</meta>

It contrasts the inheritance of the 'sons of God' with the 'second death' reserved for those who fear worldly loss more than spiritual judgment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the New Jerusalem from Revelation 21. The previous section established the city's identity as both a present reality (the Church on earth) and a future glory (the Church in heaven). The author now moves into the vision of the mountain and the symbolic materials of the city.</meta>

### Sixth Part on the Apocalypse of John

<margin>Exposition 1</margin>
He repeated what he had said to express the order of the vision, or more truly—as is believed—he said that first part regarding the one journeying on earth, but added this part regarding the one reigning in heaven. For he saw the former through himself, but the latter through another. Much has been written about the glory of the present church, which is called Jerusalem; these things could not only be read and understood according to the letter by disciples of truth, but indeed seen with the eyes and heard with the ears. However, that Jerusalem which is above—which is nonetheless built from the stones of this earthly one, there is no doubt—cannot now be seen with the eyes, nor is it found fully expressed in scripture as it truly is. Therefore, a spiritual teacher was necessary to draw perfect disciples to an <term>anagogical intellect</term> <note>anagogical intellect: From the Greek 'anagoge' (leading upward), this refers to the highest level of biblical interpretation, which explains how earthly things point toward eternal, heavenly realities.</note>. Through those things known in scripture regarding the city journeying on earth, they might be snatched up toward a spiritual vision of that city which triumphs in heaven. Thus, what follows is added:

<margin>Text 11</margin>
**And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain.**

This great and high mountain is that of which the Psalmist speaks: **"Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?"** <note>original: "Quis ascendet in mōtem domini: aut quis stabit in loco sancto eius?" — Psalm 24:3.</note> This mountain is the spiritual heaven, which those who wish to contemplate heavenly things must ascend. It is the anagogical intellect itself, which is truly great and high because it encompasses great and sublime things. Ultimately, the <term>literal intellect</term> <note>literal intellect: The basic, historical meaning of the text.</note> points to things that are transitory and earthly. The <term>typical intellect</term> <note>typical intellect: Also called the 'allegorical' sense; seeing how Old Testament figures prefigure the Church or Christ.</note> points to the state of the journeying church, which moves in a certain way between earth and heaven. But the anagogical, which is superior, points to the state of that city which is in the heavens. Yet, both there and here, Jerusalem is said to **descend from heaven from God**, because in both the present age and the future, she knows how to stoop to the humble. Thus, she always descends, yet she is always with God from whom she descends. Just as a river always flows from its source and from a higher place, descending to the depths, and yet is always where it flows and where it flows from; so too that heavenly Jerusalem, always remaining in heaven, always and without end descends through humility.

<column-break/>

Because the more she continually feels humble things about herself, the more firmly she remains in glory; she descends not by a change of location, but by humility. What follows:

<margin>Text 12</margin>
**And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven from God, having the glory of God; its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal.**

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
Because she is not lifted up in pride like the one who said: **"I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne"** <note>original: "In celum ascendam super astra celi: exaltabo solium meuz" — Isaiah 14:13. The commentator contrasts the city's humble descent with Lucifer's prideful attempt to ascend.</note>; but on the contrary, she descends from heaven (that is, from the glory given to her) through humility. She is made worthy to have the brightness of God, just as the moon has the brightness of the sun, so that she herself may shine like the sun in the kingdom of her Father. But why is her light said to be like a jasper stone and like crystal, when jasper and crystal are of different colors? It is because both faith and contemplation are the light of souls; one of these is designated by the jasper, the other by the crystal. For a person first receives the light of faith, which gives life to the soul; then the light of knowledge, which magnifies the soul that has been given life. For as the Apostle says: **"Those whom he foreknew, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also magnified."** <note>original: "Quos enim prescivit: hoc & vocauit: & quos vocauit hos & iustificauit: quos autem iustificauit: illos & magnificauit." — Romans 8:29-30. Note that the Latin 'magnificauit' (magnified/glorified) links to the idea of the stones' brilliance.</note> He justified them indeed through faith, designated by the **jasper**, which is green in color; surely because "the just shall live by faith." <note>A reference to Romans 1:17. In medieval symbolism, green (jasper) represented the life and vigor of faith.</note> He magnifies them through knowledge, designated by the **crystal**, whose splendor is like the brightness of the moon; specifically because the moon is said to be similar to crystal. It follows:

<margin>Text 13</margin>
**And it had a great and high wall, having twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written on them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel. On the east three gates. On the north three gates. On the south...**

<sig>EE</sig>

The jasper is identified with the life of faith, while crystal represents the clarity of spiritual knowledge.</summary>

### Abbreviated Part of the Exposition

...three gates. On the west, three gates.
The wall of the city is the army of the saints, which has been raised up to higher things; it is devoted to the perfection and defense of the church. "I heard," he says, "the number of those who were sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand, from every tribe of the children of Israel," <note>original: "Audiui... numerū signatoꝝ centū. 44. milia..." referencing Revelation 7:4.</note> and the rest that follows. And below: "I saw a great multitude which no one could number." <note>original: "Vidi turbā magnā..." referencing Revelation 7:9.</note> That great multitude, along with those named as being sealed under a specific number, is the wall of the city. Concerning the gates of the city and the corners, it will be spoken of later. It follows:

<margin>Lesson 14</margin>
**And the wall of the city had twelve foundations: and in them the twelve names of the twelve apostles, and of the Lamb.**

How it is that there is one stone of which the scriptures speak—upon which the foundations of the church were cast—is testified by Truth itself, which says: **"Upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."** <note>original: "Super hanc petram edificabo ecclesiam meā..." referencing Matthew 16:18. "Truth itself" is a common medieval title for Jesus Christ.</note> Now, the Lord said this to Peter, who is one and the first of the twelve foundations; "His foundations," he says, "are in the holy mountains." <note>original: "fundamēta eius in montibus sanctis" referencing Psalm 87:1.</note> The holy mountains are the twelve apostles in whom the foundations of Jerusalem are contained. Indeed, that the twelve foundations are the twelve apostles is testified by their very names and their works. For just as those twelve were founded upon the firm rock, which is <term>Christ</term> <note>original: "xps," a common abbreviation for the Greek 'Christos'.</note> Jesus, so the multitude of the faithful is founded upon their faith. It follows:

<margin>Lesson 15</margin>
**And he who spoke with me had a measure, a golden reed, to measure the city and its gates and its wall.**

The golden reed which the angel has in his hand is the consideration of reason, which is granted to spiritual men for estimating the measure or order of that most beautiful city. This is for those who know and understand that He who created all things in wisdom wished to maintain measure and number in His works, lest anything in them appear disordered

<column-break/>

or anything appear deformed or unseemly; but especially lest they should seem dissimilar to the image of God and of spiritual virtues. This is also rightly shown to be a golden reed because the contemplation of the saints is pure, like gold, and has nothing of falsehood mixed within it. It follows:

**And the city is laid out in a square; its length is as great as its width. And he measured the city with the golden reed, twelve thousand stadia. Its length, width, and height are equal.** <note>A 'stadium' (plural 'stadia') was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>

He measured the city with the golden reed because those who know how to contemplate with the truest spiritual consideration of reason can comprehend the state and order of the heavenly citizens. Whence it is also rightly added: **By twelve thousand stadia**; because these are the twelve troops of holy martyrs who were chosen and sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel—all one hundred and forty-four thousand together. Yet this must be understood in spirit, as we have already said, besides that great multitude which no one can number; all of these, through the perfection of their faith, belong to the walls of the city. If this sacred number is weighed with careful consideration, it shows not only that the length, width, and height of the city are equal, but also clearly reveals why this is so. For if we divide that multitude of heavenly legions into four parts and turn those same legions into the shape of a city in an orderly way, we are able to investigate how the length, width, and height are equal by a certain ratio of the <term>number six</term> <note>The number six was considered a "perfect number" in medieval mathematics because its factors (1, 2, and 3) add up to itself (1+2+3=6).</note>, which signifies general perfection, since that same number is found clearly and whole in those three prescribed dimensions.
