<meta>This page continues from the previous page's mathematical and architectural analysis of the New Jerusalem. Having established the dimensions of the city, the author now interprets the symbolic meaning of its wall, its measurement, and the specific gemstones that form its foundation, linking them to the Apostles and the nature of the "sealed" elect.</meta>

<header>The Abbot's Part of the Exposition</header>

<margin>Verse 17</margin>
¶ And he measured its walls, one hundred forty-four thousand: by the measure of a <term>cubit</term><note>An ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, about 18 inches.</note>, the measure of a man which is that of an angel.

<margin>the breadth of the whole world</margin>
¶ Truly, the 12,000 <term>stadia</term><note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note> designate as many great legions. Because the 144,000 cubits are nothing other than the 144,000 of the "sealed" <note>original: "signatorum"; referring to the 144,000 chosen ones mentioned in Revelation 7.</note>, their moderate multitude is distinguished by twelve boundaries according to their own characteristics. For indeed, John was about to say: "From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand were sealed," and so on for the rest; but first he said: "I heard the number of those who were sealed: 144,000 sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel." It is as if, therefore, for every thousand people, a single cubit is to be understood, so that the perfect number in the gatherings of the saints appears to be the same as the measure of the cubits in the wall's dimensions. As for what is added in that same passage—"the measure of a man which is that of an angel"—this seems to pertain to the opinion held by the saints: namely, that there is one single measure for angels and for the elect among men, according to what is written: "He set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God" <note>Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Septuagint/Old Latin tradition.</note>. Or certainly, that very measure of a cubit is said to belong to both man and angel because human mysteries are ordered according to the logic of spiritual things, just as the Lord said to his servant Moses: "See that you make all things according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain." It follows:

<margin>Verse 18</margin>
¶ And the structure of its wall was of jasper stone; but the city itself was of pure gold, like clear glass.

¶ We know by both word and example that there are two perfect lives within the Church: the life and the teaching of the saints. To some is given the strength of faith, so that they might act manfully even unto death; to others is given the clarity of contemplation, so that by observing the things of God, they might become clearer than gold proved by fire. Because the color of jasper (which has the appearance of the greenness of herbs and is known to be suitable for carving) designates the "greenness" of faith <note>original: "fidei viriditatem"; in medieval symbolism, green often represented the vitality and freshness of faith.</note> and perseverance, it is rightly said that the structure of the wall of Jerusalem is made of jasper stone. Surely this is because the holy martyrs conquered kingdoms through faith and worked

<column-break/>

righteousness, and they obtained the promise.
Hence it is also said through the prophet: "And I will make your bulwarks of jasper." And because the appearance of pure gold is like clear glass, it designates the purity of heart of the saints who, in the peace of the Church, fought against the vices of the flesh; it also designates the most serene clarity of their spirit. Thus the city itself is rightly said to be like pure gold and clear glass, for it is written specifically of them: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." These things are said in a general sense concerning that entire heavenly city and the multitude of saints, which is as innumerable as the stars of heaven which cannot be counted for their multitude. Concerning those things which are specifically spiritual, the following is added:

¶ The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone.

¶ For what virtue was not found in each of the holy apostles, who while still living in the flesh received the firstfruits of the Spirit? Nevertheless, although each of them was a sharer in all these gifts, a specific prerogative of some grace was nonetheless given to each, so that a certain difference of gifts appeared to be present in each individual. Hence, it is immediately added:

¶ The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, chalcedony; the fourth, emerald; the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, topaz; the tenth, chrysoprase; the eleventh, hyacinth; the twelfth, amethyst.

¶ The colors of these twelve stones designate the specific virtues which were undoubtedly present in the individual apostles, according to how each has his own gift from God—one in this way, another in that. However, we do not presume to fit these stones to specific apostles one by one, because the same order of description is not maintained uniformly among all the Evangelists, though some writers have attempted it.

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the New Jerusalem's foundations, specifically linking the twelve gemstones mentioned in Revelation 21 to the individual merits and lives of the twelve Apostles.</meta>

# John, Sixth [Part] on the Apocalypse

[...recorded] with one, who are enrolled with others: there is no doubt that their merits are believed to be equal. However, the very first foundation is most rightly said to be **jasper**, which signifies **true faith** <note>original: "veram fidem"</note>; because **Peter**, the first of the apostles, is commended for the strength of his faith. The second foundation is **sapphire**; this stone is like the serene sky, and when struck by the rays of the sun, it emits (as they say) a burning glow. The color of this stone signifies the vision by which we are carried away to heavenly things: namely, when provoked by the words of Christ (who is the true sun), we begin to be set on fire by the rays of His charity. Thus **Andrew**, who for the love
<margin>T.19</margin>
of the heavenly homeland left the world and followed John the Baptist; as soon as he stayed with Christ for two days, touched by the rays of His love, he clung to Him and became His disciple. The third foundation is **Chalcedony**. This stone is like a pale fire, almost like a lamp; and it shines more in the open air than inside a house. The appearance of this stone signifies the **humble heat of charity**: which sometimes remains hidden within, but at last is brought into the light through works; and what they were able to be before is revealed when the time requires it. We can, moreover, ascribe this virtue
<margin>f.10</margin>
to **James**, the brother of John: who, to show how much charity lay hidden in his breast, was the first among all the apostles to endure the Passion. Hence, he resists those wishing to engrave the stone itself <note>The author suggests that unlike Peter or Paul, James did not "engrave" his legacy through long writings, but through swift martyrdom</note>: because he was not like some who seemed to have demanded the field of battle so that they might leave certain patterns of perfection to their descendants through their "engravings" (as did Peter and Paul), but rather he wished to be quickly dissolved and to be with Christ. The fourth foundation is the **Emerald**. This stone is of the highest greenness, having the color of the purest oil. The color of this stone signifies that **perfect faith** which works through charity, poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. This virtue we can

<column-break/>

ascribe to the blessed **John**, whose book this is: who was more abundantly filled with that spiritual oil with which the Son of God was anointed above his companions. Whence also we read that he was cast into a vat of oil <note>Refers to the legend of John being cast into boiling oil at the Latin Gate in Rome, from which he emerged unhurt</note>, so that like a kind of emerald he seemed to profit from the oil. The fifth foundation: **sardonyx**. This stone is said to be black at the bottom, white in the middle, and red at the top. The appearance of this stone signifies that **progress of virtues** <note>original: "profectum illum virtutum"</note> which the Psalmist notes in some, when he says: "They shall go from virtue to virtue." Indeed, the black color noted in it signifies ignorance; yet that very ignorance is turned into the virtue of humility, which is great and useful above all virtues. This variety of colors can be ascribed to **Philip**, who, being ignorant at the beginning of the great goodness of God, preached that Christ was the son of Joseph from the city of Nazareth; from there he was led to the whiteness of truth, when Peter said: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God"; and at last he was led to the crown of martyrdom. The sixth foundation is the **sardius** <note>also known as sard or carnelian</note>. This stone has the color of blood only, and signifies the complete **perfection of martyrdom**. For on the sixth day the Lord suffered and snatched the human race from death, redeeming it with His blood. This perfection of martyrdom can be ascribed to **Bartholomew**, who, having been flayed by the infidels, endured a harsh passion. The seventh foundation is **chrysolite**. This stone shines like gold, and emits sparks like burning coals. It signifies the **wisdom of God**, from which proceed flaming words to set on fire the hearts of the listeners toward the love of God. This virtue is to be ascribed to **Matthew**, the first among the four Evangelists, who, writing the truth of the Gospel, left behind a virtue set on fire by spiritual and fiery words according to the literal sense, which proceed from that same virtue. The eighth foundation is **beryl**. This stone, if it is placed in a hexagonal shape, shines as if struck by the sun. It is also said to be of such great heat that it warms the hand of the one holding it. The nature of this stone signifies the **perfection of work**, of which the Lord says: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who...

### Illustration II. Part of the Exposition

is in the heavens. There is nothing that so warms the cold hearts of weak men as the example of a good work; for by this alone can those who are merely physical in their understanding be provoked toward the good. We can ascribe this virtue to **Thomas**, who was sent to preach in India; by the example of his good works, he converted the greatest part of that province’s physical-minded men to the faith. The ninth foundation is **Topaz** <note>original: "Topacius"</note>, which is said to be very precious. This stone is like the purest gold and the most serene sky, shining far more than other stones, especially when it is touched by the brightness of the sun. The appearance of this stone signifies the **contemplative life**, which is clear enough in itself, but is made even clearer by the vision of God. We can ascribe this virtue to **James, the brother of the Lord** <note>Often called James the Less to distinguish him from James, son of Zebedee</note>, who was held in high regard among the great apostles. After the death of James, the brother of John, he was preeminent in counsel; but he was far more illustrious because he was specially worthy to be called the "brother of the Lord."

The tenth foundation is **Chrysoprase** <note>original: "Chrisoparus," a variant of chrysoprasus</note>. This stone is purple in color, speckled with little drops of gold. The appearance of this stone designates the **nobility of justice** shining with the sentences of wisdom. This virtue can be ascribed to **Jude**, the brother of the aforementioned James, who among the other words of his teaching also wrote the epistle that is numbered among those called "canonical." The eleventh foundation is **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Jacinctus"</note>. The color of this stone changes with the air. It signifies that **grace of charity** which the Apostle describes when he says: *Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.* We might perhaps ascribe this to **Simon**, who is surnamed **the Zealot**; he is indeed listed before Jude according to Luke, but after him according to Matthew. If we were to find anything specific written about him, we would use it, but because other properties have been assigned to others, we can perhaps assign this one to this holy apostle. The twelfth foundation is **Amethyst** <note>original: "amertitus"</note>. This stone is purple, having a likeness 
<sig>c</sig>

<column-break/>

to the violet and the rose, and it seems to pour out certain little flames from itself. It signifies the **nobility of true and perfect justice**, which is consummated by the shedding of blood for the sake of a brother's salvation; as John says regarding this: *If God laid down his life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.* This virtue can be ascribed to **Matthias**, who, by the merit of his virtue and grace, was numbered with the eleven and made a companion of the apostles.

These things have been said by us in whatever way possible so that we would not seem to pass over the names of the twelve apostles (which are written in the foundations) in silence; we give this opportunity to those with leisure so they may learn to contemplate greater things through the smallest. 

Since such happy and glorious things have been said by John regarding the glory of the foundations, it remains for him to speak of the **gates**, in which are written the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel. Regarding these gates, one might rightly ask why they are written of after the foundations; but we know clearly that the twelve tribes, who were the first in faith, were made the last in the election, as the Lord said: *The first shall be last, and the last shall be first.* The divine word follows, saying:

-> **And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate made of a single pearl.** <-

What he had said above—that the city had a wall great and high, and twelve angels at the gates—he repeats again in this place, saying: *The twelve gates are twelve pearls, one for each; and the individual gates were made of individual pearls.* The exception is that previously he said nothing of pearls, but here he expresses that the gates and the angels <note>The text here says "angulos" (corners/angles) but refers to the gate structure</note> are made of pearls. <meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the New Jerusalem, moving from the foundations of the city (associated with the Apostles) to the construction of the walls and gates, which Joachim of Fiore links to the progression of sacred history through three "states" or ages.</meta>

Joachim, Sixth Book on the Apocalypse

<column-break/>

[The builder] places: first he finds a location in which it may be built; then, digging deep around the perimeter, he prepares the trenches in which the foundations may be laid; then, once the foundations are cast, the walls are built; finally, once the city is situated, the site is established and the furrows are dug. Second, the foundations are placed and the walls are built. Third, the gates are established and the houses are constructed. The first of these belongs to the **first state**; the second to the **second state**; the third to the **third state**. <note>Joachim of Fiore’s theology divides history into three "states" (status): the Age of the Father (Old Testament), the Age of the Son (New Testament), and the Age of the Holy Spirit (a future age of spiritual perfection).</note> For in the first period, the people of Israel were chosen so that the preparation for this most noble city might be made in them. Second, at the coming of the Lord, twelve apostles were chosen to be the foundations of the city; and after them, their "sons" and "grandsons" in faith from the people called the **Gentiles** <note>original: "gentilis," meaning the non-Jewish nations</note>, who were themselves made spiritual children of the patriarchs, just as the Apostle says: *If you belong to Christ, then you are the seed of Abraham.* <note>Galatians 3:29</note> They, too, were chosen so that they might pass into the walls of Jerusalem, for which they suffered mockeries and beatings in their bodies, even to the point of not loving their own lives unto death. However, when that time arrives of which the Apostle speaks—*Blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the nations has entered; and then all Israel shall be saved* <note>Romans 11:25–26</note>—it will be necessary for the gates to be established in the walls. 
<margin>E. 41</margin> 
Through these gates, the entire faithful people shall enter the city, rendering their vows to the Lord and offering the sacrifice of praise. Whether the men designated by the gates are to be chosen from the Jewish people, or rather from the Gentiles, or commonly from both, is uncertain. Yet from wherever they are chosen, they shall be bright with the whiteness of **pearls** <note>original: "margaritarum"</note>, because the chastity of that time will be great; and like the lilies among rose blossoms, they shall follow the purple crowns of the martyrs in their brilliance. Truly, the twelve pearls for each of the gates—which together make **one hundred and forty-four**—will be the helpers of those men in the preaching of the gospel, of which the Lord says: *And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in the whole world as a witness*

<column-break/>

*to all nations.* <note>Matthew 24:14</note> But one asks why there are one hundred and forty-four—that is, seventy-two and seventy-two—when **Moses** is recorded to have designated only seventy-two elders, and our Lord **Jesus Christ** seventy-two disciples. <note>Joachim refers to the 70 or 72 elders in Numbers 11 and the 70 or 72 disciples in Luke 10; manuscript traditions varied on the exact number.</note> For if in the first state, after the twelve patriarchs of the sons of Israel (in whose place twelve princes were appointed for each tribe in the desert), seventy-two elders were likewise chosen by Moses; and nonetheless, after the election of the twelve apostles, seventy-two disciples were chosen by Christ; it would seem more appropriate that in this third state, seventy-two men should likewise be called by the Holy Spirit, rather than one hundred and forty-four (that is, seventy-two and seventy-two), so that a perfect equality might be seen in each state. But it should be noted that **Job**, restored to his former health, obtained seven sons in place of those he had lost—that is, simple for simple—but he received all other things **doubled**. <note>Job 42:10–13</note> Thus, in the first state of the world, the Lord received, as it were, "simple" things from the people of Israel; likewise simple things in the second from the people called Gentiles; but in the third, truly doubled things, because the elect shall be gathered from both peoples. And while the simple likeness is maintained in the twelve persons across all three states, a multiplicity is found in the rest in that state which, as we have often said, belongs by its own nature to the **Holy Spirit**. For this same Spirit is simple in substance, yet becomes multiple in action and wealthy in gifts. This is why **Elisha** prayed that a "double portion" of the spirit of **Elijah** might be in him. <note>2 Kings 2:9</note> Hence the Apostle says of Christ: *Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.* <note>Ephesians 4:8</note> Therefore, the twelve pearls seen in the gates of the city are a type of the preachers of evangelical truth, so that *he may convert the hearts of the fathers to the children.* <note>Malachi 4:6</note> They shall be attached to the twelve gates just as the seventy-two disciples were to the twelve apostles of Jesus Christ. Regarding these gates, it has already been said above: three of them face the east, three the north, three the west, and three the south.

### 614 Part of the Explanation

Why is this? So that in every single part of the city the mystery of the Trinity may shine forth. Not only there, however, but in the body of the city itself, including the added suburbs and villages. Why, then, in five parts rather than in six or seven? We have assigned the reason more fully in our work, *The Psaltery of Ten Strings*. <note>original: "ī ope psalterij decē cordaꝝ" refers to Joachim of Fiore’s treatise *Psalterium Decem Chordarum*, which uses the ten-stringed instrument as a map for mystical and historical structures.</note> As for the fact that some gates are described as being on the east, others on the west, others on the south or midday: this must be referred to the diversity of graces. For to one is given the word of wisdom through the Spirit, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, and similar gifts. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12.</note> For some gates are on the east because to some of the Saints is given the prerogative of faith, in which is the rising of the true light and the showing of radiance. Others are on the North <note>original: "Aquilone," the north wind often associated with cold or evil in medieval allegory</note> because to some is granted the virtue of patience, by which they might resist the most wicked spirit of the north, so that even when struck for a long time they are not bent, but fight against him, persevering in patience until the end. Others are on the west because some, looking upon the fall of the world and the setting of this light, despise the present world and its glory. Others are on the south because many, touched more fully by the heat of the true Sun, exult in the joy of the Lord their God. Therefore, that there are three gates on each side <note>original: "ternæ & ternæ"</note> refers to the sacred mystery of the Trinity. That they are on four sides has been explained as the mystery of the four quarters of the world. Finally, the city itself, with its suburbs and villages, contains nothing less than this same mystery. It follows:

<margin>Chapter 21</margin>
> **And the streets of the City were like pure gold, as transparent glass.**

He had already said this above concerning the city itself, to which these specific streets belong, in contrast to the walls which are raised up high. For to the walls, which go around the perimeter, belongs the perfection of action. To the streets, which are within, belongs the

<column-break/>

integrity of contemplation. <note>In medieval theology, "action" refers to the outward work of the Church (preaching, charity, building), while "contemplation" refers to the inner spiritual vision of God.</note> Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: *Behold the bed of Solomon, sixty strong men surround it, of the strongest of Israel, all holding swords and most learned in war, because of the fears of the night.* <note>Song of Songs 3:7–8. The author treats the "bed" as a symbol for the peaceful, interior life of the city.</note> Truly, the bed of Solomon is the city itself; the strong men who surround it are the walls which are given on the outside for the defense of the city. And rightly are the streets of the city compared to pure gold, like transparent glass, because the hearts of those contemplating God are pure and clear, as the Lord says: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* <note>Matthew 5:8</note> It follows:

> **And I saw no temple in it: for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb.**

Therefore (he says) I saw no temple in that Jerusalem, because the Father and the Son are its temple. For in the temple made by hand, which Solomon built, there were High Priests and Priests appointed to teach the people the law of the Lord, and to offer Sacrifice for them, both for offense and for sin. Similarly—though much more worthily—that venerable headship <note>original: "capitulum," likely referring to the Apostolic See</note> which was founded at Rome in place of the Temple has been established in the Church, so that from it the faithful may receive the decrees and laws of the Christian life. In this place, he who presides as the Supreme Pontiff <note>original: "summus Pontifex," the Pope</note> acts in Christ's stead on earth, until He who is the High Priest Himself comes to seek His sheep and visit them, just as a Shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep. In that city which is above, however, neither a man-made Temple is necessary, nor an assembly of Priests to teach the people the way of God again, because the Almighty Lord with His Son is everything in

### Abb. Part of the Exposition

...only those who are written in the lamb’s book of life.

¶ It is understood: just as when Babylon still reigned in her waters, and Jerusalem itself—living as a pilgrim near her in some of its parts—was held captive, and while the tares were still mixed with the wheat in the field of the world; only those who are written in the lamb’s book of life, that is, they alone, will be the ones to imitate [the Lamb]. It follows.

<margin>Chapter 22, Text 1</margin>
¶ **And he showed me a river of water of life, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb in the middle of its street.**

<margin>John</margin>
¶ Do you ask what this river is? "He who thirsts," says the Lord, "let him come and drink: and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly." <note>original: "Qui sitit... veniat & bibat: & flumina de ventre eius fluent aquæ viuæ." Quoting John 7:37-38.</note> Moreover, he said this concerning the **Spirit** which those believing in him were about to receive. It should be noted, however, that by the name "Spirit," we should not always understand that person of the Trinity who is called the **Holy Spirit**; sometimes it is to be taken as the person himself, and sometimes as one of his gifts, according to that saying of Elisha: "I pray that your spirit may be made double within me." <note>original: "Oro ut fiat spiritus tuus duplex in me." A reference to 2 Kings 2:9, where Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit.</note> So also in this place: the river that proceeds from the throne—just like the rivers flowing from the belly of the believer—must be referred to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which were given to the Church so that they might belong to her. This is true even though the Spirit himself, who is God and one person in the Trinity, is said to be given to us, as the Apostle says: "The love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us." <note>original: "Charitas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum Sanctum qui datus est nobis." Quoting Romans 5:5.</note> Moreover, the river of living water proceeds from the throne of God because, outside of the Catholic Church, the gift of the Holy Spirit is not given to anyone; and because when holy men bring forth words that set the hearts of the faithful on fire, those who hear them are inflamed to the love of God and neighbor through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is written in the Acts 

<column-break/>

of the Apostles: "While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word." <note>original: "Adhuc loquente Petro cecidit Spiritus Sanctus super omnes qui audiebant verbum." Quoting Acts 10:44.</note> And it is rightly claimed that this river is "water of life," because "it is the Spirit," says the Lord, "who gives life; the flesh profits nothing." <note>original: "Spiritus... est qui viuificat: caro autem non prodest quicquam." Quoting John 6:63.</note> And the Apostle says: "The first Adam was made into a living soul; the second Adam into a life-giving spirit." <note>original: "Factus est primus Adam in animam viuentem: secundus Adam in spiritum viuificantem." Quoting 1 Corinthians 15:45.</note> For this reason, the same river is said to be **bright as crystal**, because where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is brightness; where he is not, there is blindness of the soul and a darkening of the mind. Indeed, the river is said to be "in the middle of its street" because, although the Lord gives all the Saints to drink from the torrent of his pleasure, he does so more abundantly for those who sit at the feet of the Lord and rest, concerning whom it is said: "Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." <note>original: "Maria optimam partem elegit: quæ non auferetur ab ea." Quoting Luke 10:42. This contrasts the active life (Martha) with the contemplative life (Mary).</note> Moreover, the Angel showed this river of living water to John, just as he showed many other good things, because spiritual men show spiritual words to perfect and capable disciples—not to the imperfect and <term>animal men</term> <note>original: "animalibus." In this context, "animal" refers to the "natural man" (psychikos) who lives by his senses or lower soul rather than by the Spirit.</note> who know nothing except the flesh. For the "animal man," it says, "does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God, for it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand because it is spiritually examined." But the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one. It follows.

¶ **And on both sides of the river was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.**

¶ The **Tree of Life** is Christ: simple indeed in himself, yet manifold in his branches or even in his offspring. Moreover, let him remain on both sides of the river, as if on the right and on the left: because those who are more or less pleasing to God through the **active life** remain as if on the left, while those who please through the **contemplative life** remain on the...

The author emphasizes that spiritual understanding is reserved for those within the Church who have moved beyond a purely physical or "animal" mindset.</summary>

# Sixth Book on the Apocalypse

...and yet in both <note>Likely referring to the active and contemplative lives, or the inner and outer man.</note> the new man lives and remains, in which they are also clothed: in both, the life of Christ dwells and reigns in them. It is well that it also brings forth twelve fruits throughout each month: because there were twelve (as I have already said in this work) principal churches designating the future generations of the faithful: and through each one Christ brought forth the fruit of the spirit and of good works: according as each one has his own gift from God: one indeed in this way, but another in that. But also the leaves of that tree are for the salvation of the nations: because through the words of Christ which proceed from the mouth of the faithful, those who have been converted and believed from among the nations are made safe: as the Apostle says: *Faith comes from hearing, but hearing through the word of Christ.* <note>Quoting Romans 10:17.</note> It follows.

<margin>Text 3</margin>
> ¶ **And there shall be no more curse.**

¶ It is understood: just as formerly when Ishmael and Isaac still remained in one house, and the chaff had not yet been separated from the Lord's wheat to be burned. <note>An allegory for the current world where the wicked (chaff/Ishmael) and the righteous (wheat/Isaac) live together until the final judgment.</note> In that which follows:

<margin>Text 4</margin>
> ¶ **And the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it; and his servants shall serve him: and they shall see his face: and his name shall be on their foreheads: and night shall be no more: and they shall not need the light of a lamp nor the light of the sun, because the Lord God will illuminate them: and they shall reign for ever and ever.**

¶ Who is it that would seek an explanation where the Spirit speaks so openly that he speaks no proverb? <note>The author suggests the meaning here is literal and clear.</note> However, the service in that city will be none other than filial: that is, not for those still laboring, but for those praising, as it is written: *Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever*

<margin>Psalm</margin>

<column-break/>

*they shall praise you.* <note>original: "Beati qui habitant in domo tua Domine: in secula seculorum laudabunt te." Quoting Psalm 84:4 (Vulgate 83:5).</note> But also the foreheads on which the names will be written are to be understood in the spirit rather than in the flesh. For the forehead is the front part of the head: and in it is understood the **memory** <term>memory (memoria): the author interprets the forehead as the seat of the mind's ability to retain and recall the presence of God</term> with which a person remembers their God and rejoices in him. And since that joyful name of the Lord by which we are made blessed in him is Christ—from whom the name "Christian" comes, which signifies that joy of which the Psalmist says: *God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions*—rightly is that name said to be written on the foreheads of the elect: because while they are always mindful (as I have already said) of the name of their God, they exult with joy in their heart, as it is written: *I remembered my God, and I was delighted.* <note>original: "Memor fui Dei: & delectatus sum." Quoting Psalm 77:3 (Vulgate 76:4).</note> After this Saint John follows and says:

<margin>Psalm</margin>

<margin>Text 5</margin>
> ¶ **These words are true and most faithful: and the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his Angel to show his servants what must happen soon.**

¶ This has already been said above, lest anyone think what is said to be frivolous, being ignorant of the power of **allegory**, in which there are multiple and spiritual meanings. Whence he also well says: *And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must happen soon*: because he who once gave his gifts to the prophets so that they might foreknow what was to be fulfilled at the coming of the Savior into the world, now himself sends spiritual men who, through spiritual understanding, may open the hidden mysteries and show to their own people what must happen soon. After this follows the word of the Lord, saying:

<margin>T. 6</margin>
> ¶ **Behold, I come quickly. Blessed is he who keeps the words of this book.**

¶ Now the Lord says this through himself, so that he who does not believe the disciple may at least believe the Lord the master. It follows.

## ¶ And I, John, who heard and saw these things.

¶ Understand: I say and testify: these things by themselves, I myself have said the Savior. <note>The commentator explains that John is emphasizing his role as a direct eyewitness to the divine revelation.</note>

<margin>Z. 6.</margin>
## ¶ And after I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the Angel who showed me these things. And he said to me: See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant, and of your brothers the prophets: and of those who keep the words of this book: worship God.

¶ The angel had already said this earlier, whether it was this same angel or another, near the end of the sixth part <note>A reference to Revelation 19:10.</note>; except that there it says: *Of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus.* <note>original: "Fratrum tuorum habentium testimonium Iesu"</note> Here, it is inserted: *Of your brothers the prophets.* You should understand that the former statement refers to the martyrs, while this one refers to the confessors <note>In the early church, "confessors" were those who suffered for the faith or lived it out through holy teaching without being killed, whereas "martyrs" died for it.</note>; for some have testified through faith, and others through the canonical doctrine. Both groups apply works of piety, without which faith is dead and doctrine is useless, just as it is written: <margin>Psalms</margin> *But to the sinner God said: Why do you declare my justices and take my covenant in your mouth?* <note>Quoting Psalm 50:16 (Vulgate 49:16).</note> And that other passage: <margin>James</margin> *Faith without works is dead.* <note>Quoting James 2:26.</note> Nevertheless, John falls at the feet of the angel to worship him, but the angel himself forbids this to be done, saying that he is John’s fellow servant rather than a superior, and commands that God be worshipped, who works all things in all people. For it is fitting that perfect disciples show reverence to spiritual men through whom mysteries hidden from the world are brought to light; and it is unworthy for those who have nothing they did not receive to allow themselves to be shown singular reverence by men, rather than giving it to Him alone, by whose gift and grace they are what they are. It follows:

<margin>Text 7</margin>
## ¶ Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book: for the time is near.

<column-break/>

¶ He who once heard a voice saying to him, *Seal the things which the seven thunders have spoken,* <note>A reference to Revelation 10:4.</note> now again hears the angel saying to him: *Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.* Why is this? Because that earlier command was to be attributed to certain secret words—represented by the cloth <note>original: "sudario"</note> that had been over the Savior’s head—while this command refers to those things which were to happen to the human race in their own times. Or certainly, the former refers to the time of the sixth angel sounding the trumpet, while this refers to the beginning of the seventh. Wherefore also in that same place, the book which was closed from the beginning in the hand of a certain angel appeared open. And in Daniel it is written: *The words are closed and sealed until the appointed time.* <note>Quoting Daniel 12:9.</note> Indeed, from the time the book is opened, the time begins to be near, so that He whom the faithful expect may come, saying: *Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.* Rebuking those who persecute the elect because they cannot believe the words of God which are written in this book, he adds through a reproach:

## ¶ He who harms, let him harm still; and he who is in filth, let him be filthy still; and the holy, let him be sanctified still; and the just, let him do justice still.

¶ And what then?

## ¶ Behold (he says), I come quickly: and my reward is with me: to render to everyone according to his works.

¶ Good things to the good, and likewise evil things to the evil. Moreover, he repeats for a third time what he has already said a second time:

## ¶ I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last: the beginning and the end.

¶ The text in two places is positioned in such a way that this voice seems to belong to the whole Trinity equally; but here, it prevails that it belongs to the Son. *Behold, I come quickly.* But because the unity of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit is so great, that in <unclear>...</unclear>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final chapter of Revelation. This page explores the Trinitarian nature of Christ’s final declarations and the ethical requirements for entering the New Jerusalem.</meta>

<header>Joannes. Sixth Book. On the Apocalypse. 223</header>

Often, what seems to be said of one person is understood of all three [persons of the Trinity]: as when it is said of God the Father that he alone has immortality; yet, in this place, the Father and the Holy Spirit are not excluded from what the Son is seen to say of himself: **I am the Alpha and the Omega,** <note>original: "Ego sum A. et ω."</note> just as was added subsequently at the beginning of this book: **Who is, and who was, and who is to come.** <note>Quoting Revelation 1:8.</note> However, in this third instance where the repetition is made, we are to understand that we must arrive at a full knowledge of the Deity through three solemn steps: here, the revelation of the Holy Spirit was made in three turns and three ways, and the promise was fulfilled in certain people. First, in the **dove** [at Christ's baptism]; this is similar to the gift given daily to those baptized in Christ. Second, in the **breathing** <note>original: "insufflatione" — referring to John 20:22 when Jesus breathed on the disciples.</note> [of Christ upon the Apostles]. Third, in the **fire** [at Pentecost]. What follows:

<margin>J[...] / Ban</margin>
<margin>Chapter 10</margin>
**Blessed are they who wash their robes, that they may have power in the tree of life, and may enter through the twelve gates into the city. Outside, however, are dogs, and sorcerers, and the unchaste, and murderers, and those serving idols, and everyone who loves and makes a lie.**

<margin>Egl</margin> <note>Likely an abbreviation for a specific commentator or authority used by the author.</note>
How great the glory of that city is has been sufficiently shown; he rightly calls those "blessed" who, through profession [of faith] and true penance, wash their robes from the pollution of sins, so that they may deserve to enter the city through the twelve gates. For the **robes** with which we are clothed are our works of justice; however, these are very often polluted as if by "dead blood," because among those good works we perform, we also commit many evils daily which pollute them. But whoever washes them through confession and strives to remain in the holiness of purity begins to have the power to partake of the **tree of life**, provided he receives the body of Christ not for judgment and condemnation, but for the attainment of eternal life. For it is written in both ways: namely, that he who eats—it is understood "as is fitting"—has eternal life; and he who eats unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself. <note>The author is harmonizing John 6:54 and 1 Corinthians 11:29 regarding the Eucharist.</note> Moreover, those who wash their robes enter the city through the twelve gates; not that everyone enters through all twelve gates, but because some enter in a certain way

<column-break/>

through the gates of the east, others through the gates of the north, others through the gates of the west, and others through the gates of the south; each according to the grace given to him and his work of justice. For just as before the Lord's advent there were those who were called "christs" <note>original: "christi" — meaning "anointed ones," such as kings or prophets.</note> and high priests as a type of him who is the High Priest and the true Christ, so from the time Christ came into the world, there has been no lack of holy men who were truly to be reckoned as the "gates of the city," showing the way of life to the faithful. And those indeed who are worthy enter the city in this manner through the twelve gates—that is, through the **holy doctrine**. **But those who suffer hunger like dogs, they are scattered; the sorcerers also, and the unchaste, the murderers, the greedy, those who serve idols, and all who love and make a lie, shall be left outside; because in no way do they deserve to enter the city by their will, nor after the end of the age in reality; but their part shall be (as was said above) in the lake of fire, which is the second death.** And lest anyone should yet presume to doubt the manner of the revelation, it follows in what he says: "Behold, I come quickly," and subsequently he says:

<margin>Chapter 11</margin>
**I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches.**
The man Christ Jesus sent his angel; and the Holy Spirit sent spiritual men who testify these things in the prayers of the elect. And let not the Lord Jesus, who says these things, be thought by the Jews to be an imposter.

<margin>Chapter 12</margin>
**I am (he says) the root and the offspring of David, the bright and morning star.**
As if he were saying: Let not the Jews falsely claim that a Messiah is yet to come from the seed of David according to the flesh—namely, him of whom Balaam said: **A star shall rise out of Jacob** <note>Quoting the prophecy in Numbers 24:17.</note>—so that when he comes he may announce all truth to men: for I am he who speaks to you. And he is rightly called the "bright and morning star": because he is a **star** according to his humanity, but the **sun** according to his divinity. And just as the morning star precedes the coming of the sun, so the revelation of his humanity preceded the showing of his majesty; for he is truly man and truly God. After Christ Jesus said, "I am the root and the offspring of David, the bright and morning star," he added and said:

<margin>Chapter 13</margin>
**And the Spirit and the bride say [Come].**

It also identifies Christ as the fulfillment of the "Star of Jacob" prophecy, asserting his dual nature as both human (the star) and divine (the sun).</summary>

...and let him who hears say: Come; and let him who thirsts come; and whoever will, let him take the water of life freely. <note>original: "accipiat aquam uitae gratis" — quoting Revelation 22:17.</note>
¶ That is: Not I alone invite men to eternal joys, but also the Spirit who testifies that these words are true, and my bride—the Church—to whom I have given the Spirit so that He may remain with her forever. Therefore, both say, "Come," to the one who hears the words of this book: the Spirit speaks through spiritual understandings, and the Church through words. For the Spirit breathes where He wills by Himself, and the Church, by speaking spiritual words, teaches and persuades concerning the kingdom of God. Wherefore, he who hears with the ears of the heart is bound to call his neighbor to the eternal joys of heaven, so that he might strive to share with others what he has received from others. "He who hears," he says, "let him say: Come; and he who thirsts, let him come;" <margin>psal.</margin> <note>Referring to Psalm 36:8: "they drink their fill from the abundance of your house; you give them drink from your river of delights."</note> it is understood that they come to drink from the torrent of His own delight. And lest someone should perhaps complain about the price, "he who wills," he says, "let him receive the water of life freely." This was also said long ago <margin>Esa.</margin> <note>Isaiah 55:1.</note> by the prophet: **All you who thirst, come to the water; and you who have no money, hurry, buy and eat. Come, buy wine and milk without money and without any exchange.** Thus far the Lord Jesus has spoken. But lest the blessed John—knowing that carnal men <note>original: "aiales hoies" (animales homines) — a term for those governed by worldly instincts rather than the spirit.</note> might be scandalized by the words of this book because they do not understand the high mysteries and deep meanings within it—might think it a work of piety to add to the text in some places, or indeed to take away something from God so that it might appear clearer (as heretics do in other chapters of the scriptures), he threatens those who would presume to do this, saying:

<meta>This page concludes the sixth book of the Abbot Joachim’s commentary on the Apocalypse. Following the line-by-line interpretation of the Book of Revelation, the author now addresses his audience and the Church authorities, offering his work for correction and reflecting on the dangers of misinterpretation in the "dangerous times" he believes are approaching.</meta>

<header>Joachim’s Sixth Book on the Apocalypse</header>

<margin>C. 25</margin>
...[to the] wicked and lazy [servant]: because he hid the money he received. <note>Joachim is referencing the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25.</note> "Wicked and lazy servant: you knew that I reap where I do not sow, and gather where I have not scattered: therefore you ought to have entrusted my money to the bankers, so that upon my return I would have received what is mine with interest." <note>original: "Serue male & piger... cum usuris." quoting Matthew 25:26-27.</note> Regarding this, I also beseech you, O faithful ones: just as I have undertaken the labor of so great a burden for your salvation, desiring to give you a sign so that you might flee from the face of the bow <note>A metaphor for escaping divine judgment or the arrows of tribulation.</note>, so also you should reach out a hand to me. Thus, if in this very work, or in other
<margin>word</margin>
of my short works, I have erred in anything as a man—which, although I do not have it on my conscience, I neither deny nor excuse—may He who is good grant indulgence by His mercy, for He knows my humility. If there is one who might piously correct me while I live, I am ready to receive the correction, 
<margin>Psal.</margin>
humbly imitating him who said: "Let the righteous man correct me in mercy: but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head." <note>original: "Corripiet me iustus in misericordia... non impinguet caput meum." quoting Psalm 141:5.</note> But if the swift calling of the Lord should withdraw me from this light <note>Meaning, if he dies before the work is reviewed.</note>, let the Roman Church—to whom universal
<margin>C. 16</margin>
teaching authority is given, and by whose mandate and permission I have written these things—command them to be presented in the presence of her high office. Thus, let her command authority to those things which are worthy; but if she suspects any things to be unworthy, I beseech her to deign to amend them. For if

<column-break/>

that supreme Apostle <note>St. Paul.</note> brought his writings to his predecessors, the apostles, lest perhaps he should run, or had run, in vain <note>Reference to Galatians 2:2.</note>, how much more I, who am nothing, do not wish to be my own judge, but rather the Supreme Pontiff, who judges all and is judged by no one? Be glad, even if in some places certain things are lacking, and through this they might be dragged by rivals toward an illicit understanding. Let the defender of truth search diligently in other places of our short works, and he will find clearly enough in one place what brevity perhaps made dark in another. For if there were not lacking iniquitous men who distorted (as Peter testifies) the letters of Paul; and if Jannes and Mambres <note>Traditional names for the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in Exodus.</note>, those impious men, resisted Moses: how much more is it necessary that what the apostle testifies will happen regarding the subverters of the truth be fulfilled? Especially since we see those "dangerous times" pressing upon us, in which he wrote that these very things and many others would come to pass.
<margin>because</margin>

<meta>The previous page provided was from a commentary on the Apocalypse by Joachim of Fiore. However, this page belongs to a different work: the *Seminarium Philosophicum* (Philosophical Seminary) by John Baptist Bernard. It is a philosophical encyclopedia or lexicon. This specific entry defines the term "seorsum" (separately or apart) using Aristotelian logic and physics.</meta>

### John Baptist Bernard’s Philosophical Seminary

...that it might be free from pledges <note>legal or financial obligations</note> or other impediments; and to receive it, as if someone possesses it by themselves, matters little; but it applies to things belonging to others, where someone applies some thing to another person: for he who has a thing apart from himself <note>original: "seorsum à seipso"</note> is said to possess it. However, he who does not have the thing with him, but refers it to another, is said to be in that person’s power. Thus, each thing is said to be "apart" <term>seorsum: a Latin term meaning "separately," "individually," or "on its own"</term> without any relation to another, so that it is free and unhindered.

We do not, however, focus on this specific definition in this place. Instead, we speak here of what is said of itself and as a **singular** thing; as it is contrasted with that which is **in common**. For that which is in common is not said to be "apart," since it belongs to many; but what belongs to one alone is said to be "apart." Therefore, we define this term in this way: it is the same as saying that something is called "apart" when it stands for the singular and not for the common.

<margin>Topics, chapter 4</margin>
Aristotle discusses this in the 1st book of the *Topics*, chapter 4, where he says that things are taken "apart"—that is, so that each thing exists by itself—and thus it is used for the **singular** in this passage.

<margin>On the Motion of Animals, chapter 1</margin>
Aristotle also uses this mode in the book *On the Motion of Animals*, chapter 1, while he says that it is necessary to have something within itself that remains still, by which that which is moved may indeed be moved. For otherwise there will be no mover; for nothing would move unless something stood "apart" and immovably. Thus, this name "apart" is used to suggest something fixed, firm, and singular, such as the earth is in respect to the animals walking upon it; for while the earth stands immobile, the animals themselves move. Thus, for an animal to move, it must have something at rest within itself.

<margin>On the Soul, book 3, chapter 9</margin>
Aristotle says the same in the 3rd book of *On the Soul*, chapter 9: that it is necessary for everything that is moved to have something fixed "apart" from which the motion may begin. This way of speaking does not differ from the previous one, because that which is fixed is singular and exists by itself; and every way of speaking by which a thing is said to be "apart" is reduced to these two headings.

Therefore, to understand what has been said, it should be noted that elsewhere "apart" is used for that which is **outside**.

<margin>Physics, book 4, chapter 3</margin>
Regarding this, Aristotle speaks in the 4th book of the *Physics*, chapter 3, and the 5th book, chapter 4, where those things are said to be "apart" which are in different places. For this, see the entry under **Outside**.

<column-break/>

Therefore, concerning these sayings, it should be known that although in the 2nd book of the *Metaphysics*, chapter 12, "apart" <note>original: "seorsum"</note> and "commonly" are opposites—about which Aristotle says there that there are no things outside the soul "apart" from singular things—it is nevertheless used there for **common universals**, such as the Platonic Ideas.

<margin>Metaphysics, book 2, chapter 12</margin>

<margin>On the Motion of Animals, chapter 2</margin>
Nevertheless, Aristotle in the book *On the Motion of Animals*, chapter 2, uses this word "apart" where it is said that two bodies cannot be "apart"—as if one wished to say that two bodies cannot be in the same place at once.

<margin>Physics, book 8, chapter 11</margin>
And in the 8th book of the *Physics*, chapter 11, where he says that if there were something else that was moved by itself "apart," then that would be the **prime mover**. Thus, by this word he understands something **absolute** and **separated** from others, and it signifies nothing else. This is relevant to our purpose, since a thing taken for itself and by itself is said to be "apart." However, see this reasoning more fully in the entry under **Separation** and **By Itself**; and for this, see also the entry for **Solitary**.

## ¶ Here begins the preface to the Psaltery of Ten Strings by Abbot Joachim.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated woodcut initial 'A' depicting a seated figure (possibly King David) playing a stringed instrument (psaltery), surrounded by ornate foliage and set within a square frame.</image-desc>

Through the **Ancient** tradition of the Fathers, it has been passed down even to the people of today: that the singing of psalms is of great reward, and that it pertains to that verse of the forty-ninth psalm: *A sacrifice of praise shall honor me: and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.* <note>original: "Sacrificium laudis honorificabit me..." From Psalm 49:23 (Psalm 50 in modern bibles). Joachim emphasizes that ritual praise, not just intellectual study, opens the path to God.</note> And indeed, many who desire wisdom have devoted themselves to study and persisted in learning; yet they were not permitted to reach the very marrow <note>The inner, spiritual meaning</note> of the text because they did not believe they should enter through grace, but rather through their own free will—which has never profited those who relied upon it from the beginning. For they did not find the **key of David**, <note>A biblical metaphor for the power to open what is shut; here, the ability to unlock the secret meanings of scripture.</note> nor him who opens it for those who love it. Therefore, groping around the outside, they were unable to find the entrance, according to that word of the Apostle: *Always learning and never reaching the knowledge of the truth.* <note>original: "Tota die addiscentes & nunquaz ad scientiam veritatis peruenientes." From 2 Timothy 3:7.</note> As we have heard this, so have we seen it; we have proven both, and unless I am mistaken, we have learned it by experience. I was once myself anxious regarding the words of God, and I sought to reach the knowledge of truth through the exercise of reading. But when I burned with desire to advance toward it through the study of reading, the truth took to itself wings like an **Eagle** and flew further away from me. However, when I was placed in a state of final fervor and began to love the singing of psalms for God’s sake, many things in the divine scripture began to be opened to me as I sang in silence—things which I had previously been unable to track down by reading. Not only before, but even then I began to feel the meaning of what is written in another psalm: *Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever and ever.* <note>original: "Beati qui habitant in domo tua domine..." From Psalm 83:5 (Psalm 84 in modern bibles).</note> But while I (as it then seemed) was becoming a dweller of that heavenly city in my thoughts

<column-break/>

and eagerness, enjoying a significant vision of peace according to the inner man, it happened—as it happens to many (who complain, though in vain, that it has happened)—that the care for the church and the management of the household forced me to be entangled in the business of the monastery. Whether these affairs are truly secular or almost secular in nature, I was compelled to cry out again with a groan of the heart and not without fear: *Woe is me, for my exile has been prolonged; I have dwelt with those who inhabit Kedar; my soul has been long a sojourner.* <note>original: "Heu mihi q᷑ incolatus meus prolongatus est..." From Psalm 119:5-6 (Psalm 120). 'Kedar' symbolizes a place of spiritual darkness or worldliness.</note> And also: *My life is cut off as if by a weaver; while I was yet beginning, he cut me off.* <note>original: "Præcisa est velut a texente vita mea..." From Isaiah 38:12.</note> While this kind of groaning was turning over in my mind, it happened after some years, when I was at the Monastery of **Casamari** <note>A famous Cistercian abbey in Italy where Joachim stayed while writing this work.</note>—the venerable man Gerald, Abbot of that house, and his brothers detaining me there and binding me to them with an unbreakable bond of charity—that a solemn day arrived: the day in which the gifts of the Holy Spirit were poured out upon the holy apostles, and they were infused with that spiritual oil with which the only-begotten of God was anointed above his peers. <note>Pentecost, the celebration of the Holy Spirit descending on the Church.</note> Because I was not entirely without an understanding of the holy oil, and I knew that the "sacrifice of praise" pertained to this very thing, I felt grieved that I had been without the grace of such a great benefit for so long. I decided within myself to recite some psalms to myself on that day in honor of the Holy Spirit, out of reverence for the solemnity of the day, hoping that something might be given to me on that day by Him who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach. Meanwhile, as I entered the oratory and worshipped Almighty God before the holy altar, a certain hesitation occurred within me regarding the faith of the **Trinity**; as if it were difficult to understand or believe that all the Persons are one God, and one God is all the Persons. When this happened, I prayed fervently; and being greatly terrified, I was compelled to invoke the Holy Spirit, whose sacred solemnity was at hand, that He might deign to show me the sacred mystery of the Trinity, in which

# Preface to the Psaltery of Ten Strings

f 2

...truth has been promised to us by the Lord. Saying these things, I began to sing psalms, so that I might reach the intended number. Without delay, there occurred to my mind the form of the **Psaltery of Ten Strings**, and in it the mystery of the holy **Trinity** was so clear and open that I was immediately compelled to cry out: *Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who works wonders.* <note>original: "Quis Deus magnus sicut Deus noster? Tu es Deus qui facis mirabilia." From Psalm 77:13-14.</note> And also: *Great is our Lord God, and great is his power: and of his wisdom there is no number.* <note>original: "Magnus dominus Deus noster... sapientie eius non est numerus." From Psalm 147:5.</note> Therefore (by His gift), while staying in that same monastery, I soon began and partially finished the first book of the work written below. The second and third books, however, were not written there, nor at that same time, but roughly two years later. Indeed, this work is divided into three books, just as there are three persons of the Godhead, in whom the beauty of our faith consists. And although after the work on the *Harmony* <note>Referring to Joachim's "Concordia Novi et Veteris Testamenti" (Harmony of the New and Old Testaments), which compared historical eras.</note> which we first began—

<column-break/>

And the *Exposition of the Apocalypse*: which (while I was completely ignorant of how the matter would turn out) by some providence of God proceeded by being born from that same first work—we decided to dedicate this third little work to the **Holy Spirit**, who also gives what we offer. Nevertheless, among created things, nothing is so attributed to one person of the Trinity that it is separate from the kingdom and operation of the other two; yet it is not unfitting that the mystery of the **Trinity** shines forth in this very structure. Thus, the first book, which deals with the **musical vessel** <note>The physical structure of the ten-stringed psaltery, which Joachim used as a diagram for the Father.</note> itself, is attributed by the property of high mystery to the **Father**, from whom all things come. The second book, which deals with the **number of the psalms**, is attributed to **Divine Wisdom** <note>The Son/Word</note>, through whom all things are made. The third, which deals with the **manner of singing psalms** and the instruction of the singers, is attributed to that same **Holy Unction** <note>The Holy Spirit; "unction" refers to the anointing of the Spirit.</note>, in whom all things exist. Since this Spirit is the joy and exultation of the Most High God, He makes those whom He fills with sacred gifts happy and joyful.

<meta>This page follows the visual introduction of the Ten-stringed Psaltery diagram. Abbot Joachim. Book of the Psaltery.

The tradition of the ancients, who toiled mystically <note>original: *mysterialiter*</note> within these forms, suggests that there are many types of figures and that they are most useful. However, the experience of many shows it is common for the vain—indeed, not without punishment—exhibition of moderns to sometimes occupy themselves in these matters to no end. Although these forms are numerous and known to many, none has received so solemn a name as the **ten-stringed psaltery**. This is because no other instrument, no matter how many there may be, is either placed before it or considered its equal in sacred mysteries <note>original: *sacramentis*; here meaning hidden spiritual truths</note>. 

For the vessel itself, which is called the **Psalter**, is excellent and famous among all, or above all musical instruments. Yet, the **Lyre** <note>original: *Lythara*; often used interchangeably with the harp or lute in medieval texts</note> is almost equal to it in divine mysteries, as **David** says of them in the Book of Psalms: *Take up a psalm and bring the timbrel; the pleasant psaltery with the*
<margin>Psalm 150</margin>
*Lyre.* And in another psalm: *Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with the psaltery and the harp.* Why is the harp <note>original: *cythara*</note> joined to the psaltery, if not because that greatest commandment, which is "Love God," must necessarily be joined to the other commandment, which is "Love your neighbor"? 

Therefore (as I have already said), the musical vessel is a work—namely a regulated one—having ten strings across its face; it is beautiful in form, slender in sound, and sweet in its melody. Since it is entirely mystical by art and divinely invented, nothing in it can be barren, nothing empty, nothing that does not sound and resound with a spiritual mystery. Indeed, so great is the sweetness of its melody that while the external sound itself strikes with a golden ringing, it greatly ravishes the souls of the listeners to an ecstasy of mind, and soothes them to the point of pouring out tears of contrition. But all external melody is silent when the internal song is perceived, and physical sweetness is despised when spiritual joy is found. For what can be sweeter than divine contemplation? To come to the contemplation of him who made all things, through those things which were made in the wisdom of God?

<column-break/>

For so it was written by the Apostle: *For his invisible things are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made from the creation of the world; also his eternal power and divinity; so that they are without excuse.* <note>Romans 1:20</note> If this is so, then some excuse themselves in vain regarding the slowness of their intellect, claiming it is impossible and extends beyond the measure of human capacity to reach an understanding even of the Creator. This would certainly not be the case if that which Scripture testifies were not true, saying: *The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:10</note> 

But what depths! Are they not the depths which we hold by faith? Not at all. For who, by any intellect or any genius of subtlety and insight, could imagine the living God—and not as **Three and One**—unless the entire face of the Scriptures sounded the same thing in harmony? Unless the two Testaments concurred together in that very thing? To set aside other testimonies of the truth which are spread far and wide: what does that voice of the **Seraphim** crying out in **Isaiah**, and the four living creatures in the **Apocalypse**, intend to show, if not that every tongue should confess God as one and three? That is, three persons of one substance, or three persons as one substance: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. 

For so says the Prophet **Isaiah**: *I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and the whole earth was full of his majesty. And those things that were under him filled the temple. **Seraphim** stood above it; each one had six wings; with two they covered his face, and with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried to one another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.* **John**, also agreeing in this same thing, testified that he saw and heard four living creatures having six wings, crying day and night (that is, in prosperity and adversity): *Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and* <insert>who is, and who is to come.</insert>

<summary>Joachim argues that the ten-stringed psaltery is the supreme instrument for representing divine mysteries, linking its strings to the commandments of love. He explains that through the Holy Spirit and the harmony of the Old and New Testaments, humans can contemplate the "depths of God" and the mystery of the Trinity.</summary>

### John I: The Ten Strings

...who is, and who is to come <note>original: "qui est : et qui venturus est"; a reference to the description of God in Revelation 1:4</note>. This is the frequent voice of the saints: the constant and common confession of the elect. No one can be a holy living being unless they uselessly ignore the excellence of this profession. For who among all Catholics—unless he fruitlessly ascribes the name of **orthodox** to himself—would fail to say this or fail to cry it out? Who would not confess God as one and three? All confess this with one voice and one confession. For God is **one** without confusion of the persons, and **three** in persons without division of the substance. He is always that which he is; nor can he ever be anything but three and one. He cannot be changed, he cannot be divided, nor suffer, nor be diminished, nor increased; but as it is written: *With whom there is no change nor shadow of turning.* <note>James 1:17</note> He is no greater in three persons than in each individual person, because there can be no greater power, wisdom, or charity than that by which the Father is powerful, wise, and loves; nor greater than that by which the Son is powerful, wise, and loves; nor greater than that by which the Holy Spirit is powerful, wise, and loves. This substance which is God is one, and supremely one, and more simple <note>In medieval theology, "simple" means "not composed of parts."</note> than can be said, and of one nature. Nor do we deny the Trinity in the confession of one substance; rather, we shudder at the cutting into parts which the carnal intellect imagines for itself. For we most truly, piously, and faithfully confess the three persons to be this one thing, and this one thing to be the three persons: the Father from none, the Son from the Father, and from both the Comforter <note>original: *paraclitum*; the Holy Spirit</note>. Only the Son is born from the Father alone; truly the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Therefore, the three are one, and the one is three; not divided by nature like earth, water, and fire; not by a separation of persons like three men of the same nature; not by the location of places like a lake and a river derived from it; but not at all like all things which are created. For the work cannot be equal to the maker, nor the thing made equal to its factor; nor can a sign subsist by its own operation in him who fashioned it. Yet, because his invisible things—which exhaust all sense—cannot be contemplated by the infirmity of our captivity <note>Joachim refers to the human condition after the Fall as a state of "captivity" or limited understanding.</note> except through visible things, let man at least study himself when he 

<column-break/>

desires to speak of that Majesty. Let him extend himself to contemplate the nobler creatures, such as light in visible things, and in invisible things the soul itself which thinks on this. If a man can comprehend himself, he will find in himself a **likeness of God**. If he cannot even comprehend himself, let him study to believe without hesitation those spiritual men to whom the Spirit was given—the Spirit who searches all things, even the depths of God. Let him restrain his imprudence from such temerity. For it is unjust to equate the uncircumscribed Light <note>original: *incircumscriptum lumen*; light that cannot be bound by limits or space</note> to corruptible bodies, to which it is foolish to even compare the soul or an angel. He is unfaithful and wicked who, not knowing how to discuss his own self, trusts his reason to be able to comprehend God, who is above him, exactly as He truly is. Therefore, you should not think of the divine substance, or the one God whom you hear is three, as being divided into three persons in such a way that you judge them to be three separate things, like an olive, a myrtle, and a palm—which are different in nature and kind. Nor should you think of them as three olives, which are of one nature but separated by the property of their bodies. Nor as three branches fixed to one root—judging the substance to be the root and the three branches to be the <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: *ipostases*; a Greek term for the distinct persons of the Trinity. Joachim is critiquing a specific theological model here.</note> according to the false belief of some. This would be to introduce a **Quaternity** <note>Joachim was famously accused of heresy for suggesting that if God’s "essence" was a thing distinct from the Father, Son, and Spirit, then God would be four things (a Quaternity) rather than three.</note>. But if, forced by some necessity, a visible figure must be accepted, let us at least take that which is nobler among things lacking reason. Let us take this **Light**, which it is established possesses some kind of image of that true Light—which does not so much illuminate the exterior eyes of rejected men as it illuminates the hearts 
<margin>John 1</margin>
of the elect. From this Light always flows that light which *illuminates every man coming into this world*, and from it proceeds that heat which gives life to all things. For from the light which is called the **Sun**, the **Ray** is ceaselessly born, and the **Heat** tirelessly proceeds. These reach the earth in such a way that they do not withdraw from the source from which they come. Without doubt, in the type <note>In this context, a "type" is a symbolic foreshadowing or earthly parallel to a divine reality.</note> of the Son we recognize the rays descending without withdrawing from the Father who sent them; and in the type of the Holy Spirit, who is given to us equally with Him, lest anyone should fall numb from the cold, He warms us with His fire...

<summary>Abbot Joachim defines the Trinity as three persons in one simple substance, rejecting physical analogies like "three branches on one root" to avoid the error of a "Quaternity." He proposes the analogy of the Sun (Father), Ray (Son), and Heat (Spirit) as the most noble way for the human mind to grasp the divine nature.</summary>
