### Abba. Book of the Psaltery

...to kindle the flame of charity for loving; so that in the light which is Christ, we may see what must be done, and in the heat of the Holy Spirit, we may be empowered to perform what we know. You have, therefore, in a single sun the mystery of the Trinity; you have it much better here than in three separate bodies. Yet, you are further from that purity—which the Creator alone reveals when he says: *The Father is in me and I am in the Father* <note>John 14:10</note>; and *He who loves me will keep my word: my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him* <note>John 14:23</note>—than the east is from the west. For while the sun cannot come with its own ray <note>The author distinguishes between the physical sun's limitations and God's omnipresence.</note>, the Father comes with the Son, undoubtedly in the Holy Spirit. For no one can be a Father without a Son, nor a Son without a Father, nor the Holy Spirit [without them]. Because the Father is everywhere, the Holy Spirit is everywhere; and the Son is entirely in the Father, and the Father in the Son; the Holy Spirit is entirely in both, and in him are the Father and the Son, because they are one. Whence He is simply said to be **One**, He who is truly the **Triune God**. For the three persons are truly such that one is in the others, and none can ever be divided from the others. Since if the ray and the heat of the sun are so truly two that they can by no means be partitioned, what great blindness is it to be unable to believe in the Triune God unless the truth of His unity is distanced from faith? You cannot make a cut between heat and splendor, and yet you do not doubt that they are two; yet you wish to rend the divine substance so that you can believe in a Triune God. Likewise, what is twice as wicked: I know not what three "new things" your invention has presumed to assign beyond the substance, so that in one the Unity is shown and in the other the Trinity. It is as if, when we say that the fiery substance in the sky, the ray born from it, and the heat are **one sun**, we were assigning some fourth thing by the name of "sun," rather than avoiding the division of those three while showing the unity in which they remain undivided. For what have you seen

<column-break/>

in the sun except those three things? Or what can we show there by saying they are the sun, or one substance, unless we show the whole of what those three were? O human audacity! How blind and how much an enemy to human piety is always such presumption. If you have so estimated the simple divine substance <term>substance: the "stuff" or essence of what God is</term> that you have thought of it as separate from the persons, you have cloaked Sabellius <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century heretic who taught "Modalism"—the idea that Father, Son, and Spirit are just different roles or "masks" played by a single person.</note> under Arius. If you separate the persons from the substance, you do not escape Arius <note>Arius was a 4th-century priest who taught that the Son was a created being, lesser than the Father.</note> under the cloak of Sabellius. The holy animals <note>The "living creatures" from the visions of Ezekiel and Revelation, often associated with the four Evangelists.</note> do not cry this out; David does not sing this on his ten-stringed psaltery; nor did the Seraphim whom Isaiah saw see this. Rather, a carnal sense composed these things. We have heard what the holy animals sing, but let it not be wearisome to hear again the secret of the words which always delights the saints of God to say and to hear: **Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.** <note>The "Trisagion" or "Thrice-Holy" hymn from Revelation 4:8.</note> This testimony of faith is better contemplated by the soul than pronounced by the mouth. If one seeks to discuss it, faith is blunted, and our impoverished capacity is not sufficient to preserve the purity of this Word in such a discussion. Sabellius wanted to explain it, and his ship ran aground on dry land. Arius sought to avoid this and was cast down into the mud of the deep. For Sabellius said that God was one person according to his own will: being Father, and being Son, and being Holy Spirit. Arius, detesting this, made three persons—which is a wickedness to say—distinguished in essence and majesty. They intended to praise God, but they fell away, because they had nothing in common with the holy animals; they spoke from their own [ideas], and thus they fell from the faith, just as Truth itself says: *When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and the father of lies.* <note>John 8:44</note> Because the holy animals cry out that God is Three and One, praise him on the psaltery and the harp as they have learned in the Psalms: *Give thanks to the Lord on the harp; on the ten-stringed psaltery [sing to him].* <note>Psalm 33:2</note>

<summary>Joachim uses the analogy of the sun—composed of the solar body, its light, and its heat—to explain the Trinity's simultaneous unity and tri-personality. He warns against the "audacity" of the heresies of Sabellius and Arius, which fail to balance God's oneness with His threeness.</summary>

# Joannes Gerson: First Part on the Ten-Stringed Psaltery

->sing praises to Him. Sing to Him a new song: play well to Him with a loud voice: because the word of the Lord is right and all His works are in faith. By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm: and by the breath of His mouth all their power. He spoke and they were made. He commanded and they were created.<- <note>original: "psallite illi... Ipse mandauit & creata sunt." These are verses from Psalm 32:2–9 (Vulgate numbering).</note> Why we have chosen to set forth these verses of the psalm will be shown in what follows. But now, as much as the divine majesty—of whom we desire to speak—has granted, let us examine the sacred mysteries of the **ten-stringed psaltery** <note>The <term>psalterium decem cordarum</term> (ten-stringed psaltery) was a common medieval musical allegory for the Ten Commandments or the perfection of the soul.</note>, which is the specific subject at hand. For it must not be believed that this instrument received such a famous name for no reason, or that the Book of Psalms would take its title from it, if some great <term>sacramentum</term> <note>In this context, a "sacrament" refers to a hidden, sacred mystery or symbol of faith.</note> of faith did not lie hidden in that same vessel. Indeed, it is well known that even the smallest things—and those which often tire the listener—contain mysteries, of which there is an infinite number. It is necessary, therefore, that this instrument be preferred over many other mysteries, since this book, which claims the name for itself, is preferred over many others. Indeed, it is the Book of Psalms which not only reports divine things, but through which a way is prepared for the Divinity, so that He may descend, when invited, into the inner chambers of our heart. 

Let us therefore sing praises to Him, not dishonorably, but as we are commanded—if we are able—wisely. And we must sing not only upon the **ten-stringed psaltery** <note>original: "decacordo psalterio"</note>, in which the <term>decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> of the commandments and the sum of the whole faith are contained, but also upon the **lyre** <note>original: "cythara"</note>. For the lyre itself is quite famous in the divine pages, and it is found in the sacred volumes no less than the psaltery. Yet we cannot be ignorant of how much the two differ if we vigilantly weigh their deep mysteries. The **lyre** clearly designates the "new man" who is created according to God, along with his body, which is the Church. The summit of its mystery consists of three over-extended strings and a hollow cavity. What is the hollow of the lyre, let us hear: *Unless one renounces all that he possesses, he*

<column-break/>

*cannot be my disciple.* <note>Luke 14:33</note> And again: *Do not store up for yourselves treasure on earth: for where your treasure is, there also is your heart.* <note>Matthew 6:19-21</note> When you have done this correctly and held to it, then you may trust that you belong to the number of the elect, when you assiduously praise your God with the three spiritual strings of the heart. Of these, the **first string** is action; the **second** is reading; the **third** is psalmody. Or certainly: the **first** is faith; the **second** is hope; the **third** is charity <note>The "theological virtues" of <term>fides</term>, <term>spes</term>, and <term>charitas</term>.</note>; and this is especially true when it is written as "alone," as in the Book of Revelation. 

Therefore, do not use the lack of learning as an excuse, or for this reason delay converting to God day by day. What you have heard is quite brief and can be learned by almost everyone: *Sell all that you have, and give to the poor* <note>Matthew 19:21</note>; and keep these strings as is fitting, and they can suffice for your eternal salvation. However, because a distinction must be made between "perfect" and "perfect," it is clearer than light that there is one perfection which belongs to the **active life** <note>original: "vita actiua"; the life of work and service to others.</note> and another which belongs to the **contemplative life** <note>original: "vita contemplatiua"; the life of prayer and meditation.</note>. These two "vessels" <note>The Psaltery and the Lyre.</note>, which are written of together, are to be understood such that in the one called the **Psaltery**, we receive that justice which properly belongs to the **love of God**; and in the other, which is the **lyre**, that which looks toward the **love of neighbor**. 

If, therefore, the contemplation of God delights you, and you desire and are able to be suspended in speculation, receive the more secret **ten-stringed Psaltery**. Enter into the hidden mysteries within the cellars of your heart; there, perhaps, you will begin to behold *what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:9</note> Nor is it a wonder if such a great prerogative of mystery remains in the Psaltery, because through it a way is prepared for the **Paraclete** <note>original: "paraclyto"; the Holy Spirit as "Comforter" or "Advocate."</note> to come to us. The Spirit Himself, as the Apostle testifies, *searches all things, even the deep things of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 2:10</note> Now, we said above, and it must often be said, that regarding that simple nature which is God—whose wisdom, as the Psalmist says, has no number, and whose greatness has no end—it cannot be described with certain likenesses in human words...

# Abba: The Book of the Psaltery

...[likeness] <note>The text likely completes the word "similitudo" from the previous page.</note> can be adapted: for it is necessary that quantity yield to that greatness which has no quantity, and visible form to the invisible nature, and the comprehensible body to the incomprehensible deity. For if He is so great that His immensity cannot be contained, and if He is so subtle and invisible that His appearance cannot be seen, what figure can there be that can be suitably adapted to Him? What then? Do we judge that we should desist here entirely, lest the discourse be understood otherwise? If it is so expedient, let us now confess that the scriptures were written in vain; that they were placed in the divine books of both the Old and New Testaments to signify things in vain. But if we fear that food, even when carefully cooked, might harm the stomach, we should fear much more if it is served raw; let that be far from us. Not at all, as I believe, would **Sabellius** <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century priest who taught "Modalism," the idea that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different "modes" or faces of one single person, rather than three distinct persons.</note> deny the Trinity if he truly understood the word of truth saying: *I and the Father are one.* <note>original: "Ego & pater vnum sumus." From John 10:30.</note> And *Hear, O Israel: your God is one.* He would by no means tear apart the faith of unity. **Arius** <note>original: "Arcius." This is a variant or OCR error for Arius, the 4th-century priest who taught that the Son was a created being, lower than the Father.</note> would not do so if he felt the substance of the Trinity to be of one nature. So, so it is that he who poorly understands what the Lord says—*I and the Father are one*—can easily fall into the error of Sabellius. And he who poorly understands what **John** says—*There are three who give testimony on earth: the Spirit, the blood, and the water; and there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Tres sunt qui testimonium dant..." From 1 John 5:7-8.</note>—is easily joined to a third group; some of whom denied the Trinity and others, as we have said, denied the Unity. But we, with God's help and walking the paths of the holy orthodox Fathers—in whose explanation many have endured great labors—let us confess: God is one, and supremely one. Let us confess Him as triple and truly triple: the Father from none; the Son from the Father, not made, not created, but begotten; the Holy Spirit from both, not made, not created, not begotten, but proceeding. Let us confess that He proceeds from the Son in such a way that the Son himself has this from the Father, from whom He is: not by a gift of grace, but by the simple truth of nature. The Son shows this where He says: *When the Paraclete* <term>Paraclete: A title for the Holy Spirit meaning 'Advocate' or 'Comforter'</term> *comes, whom I will send to you*

<column-break/>

*from the Father.* ¶ From the Father, He says, because just as He is from the Father, so also He has the Holy Spirit from the Father; because just as the Father could never be without being what He is, so neither could the Son, nor the Holy Spirit. For we do not say the Son is from the Father and the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son because we admit anything to be "prior" or "posterior" <note>Meaning "before" or "after" in time.</note> in the Trinity; rather, we confess all three persons to be **co-eternal** and **co-equal** to one another. We sing psalms regarding this on the **ten-stringed psaltery** <note>original: "decacordo psalterio."</note>, by faith rather than by intellect and voice. For we can understand something without being able to know *how* it is, yet we can believe *that* it is. We said above that there is no likeness that can be sufficiently adapted to such great majesty, and that there are so many mysteries which He established for us to investigate, according to that noted above which is said through John: *There are three who give testimony on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood.* And: *Let us make man in our image and likeness.* <note>original: "Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram." From Genesis 1:26.</note> And many other things of which there is no place to make mention at present. Therefore, among the works of the Lord which exhibit the mysteries of the Trinity, the **ten-stringed psaltery** holds a great place. For it is, as we have said: one musical vessel; and even if it can be divided into parts because it is a physical body, yet for it to be the ten-stringed psaltery, it is never divided. If it is divided into parts, it ceases to be what it was. Therefore, it is a measured vessel, but it is **triangular**, consisting in three corners in a marvelous way. Indeed, the unity possesses three divided corners in such a way that the three are seen to be one, and the one to be three—which can be better discerned in the figure itself than explained to you in fitting words. Do not any of the three, if you wish to contemplate any of them totally (that is, in the quantity of two lines that meet in one distinct angle), occupy its own part and touch something apart from the other two? But they are in one...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the ten-stringed psaltery as a symbol for the Holy Trinity. # John I: On the Ten Strings

...the aforementioned <note>original: "fa" likely completing "praefata" from the previous page.</note> **likeness of the substance** wonderfully suffices for these three: so much so that in any one of them, the two are necessarily included. Therefore, if a tangible thing can hold any trace of a likeness for contemplating the unity of that supreme essence—which is not a body but a spirit—the skillful man will easily understand that this is to be preferred above many other things. For it is not the physical body itself that serves this sacrament, but rather the **form**.

Indeed, in this **heavenly instrument** <note>The author refers to the psaltery as a "celestial organ" or instrument of divine praise.</note>, one does not deal with three dissimilar things—such as bread, wine, and oil; or water, blood, and spirit—in which the mystery of the Trinity is found only in a certain respect. Instead, one deals with the **form** itself, which is threefold, yet simple and indivisible; that is, the very figure or frame which is called the **psaltery**. He who does not understand this will, I fear, hardly be able to understand what follows. 

A **ship** is a single vessel, yet it is not made of a single piece of wood, but of a great quantity of timber, diligently constructed by the hand of a craftsman. It cannot be doubted by any wise person that the ship signifies the **Orthodox Church**. I ask: where is this figure? You will answer: in the ship. I ask: what is the ship? You will show me its **form**, I believe, not merely a forest of timber. For the logs themselves from which the ship is composed are not naturally a "ship," just as they are naturally logs; rather, that vessel is said to be a ship because it is composed of them. 

It is the same as how stones or mortar are not a "wall" in and of themselves, but that which is composed of them is a wall. We could provide a thousand such examples; however, a few suffice for the faithful, while even many are not enough for the unfaithful. In this way, consider the heavenly instrument with discernment, and you will be able to behold that wonder which we seek.

Therefore, the **three horns** <note>The "horns" (cornua) refer to the corners or the projecting structural points of the triangular/trapezoidal psaltery.</note> are to be understood as the likeness of the **three Persons**. This must not be done in a confused way—as if you could refer whatever you like to the Father, or to the Son, or to the Holy Spirit—but distinctly, as the matter requires, each in the mystery of its own property. Yet the whole vessel itself represents the likeness of the **Divine Substance**, which is the single substance of the three, not divided into parts, but entirely whole at once. This is because the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father; the Father and the Spirit are in the Son;

<column-break/>

and the Father and the Son are in the Holy Spirit: because they are **one** <note>original: "vnum" (neuter). In Latin theology, the neuter "one" refers to one essence or substance, rather than one individual person.</note>. For we do not dare to say "they are one person" <note>original: "vnus" (masculine).</note>, but "they are one thing," except when the word "God" is added. For when we say "they are one," we understand one substance of the three in this "one," just as Truth itself says: *I and the Father are one.* <note>original: "Ego & pater vnum sumus." From John 10:30. The "Truth" here refers to Christ.</note>

Thus, the three horns designate the **Trinity**, while the integrity of the psaltery designates the **Unity**. And pay attention to this with wonderful diligence: the word "One" <note>original: "vnus"</note> sounds like one thing, and "Unity" <note>original: "vnitas"</note> sounds like another. For "One" can be said absolutely only of one person. "Unity," however, cannot properly be spoken of except regarding at least two. For when we are commanded to stand together in unity, it should not be believed that this refers to a single isolated person. Rather, it refers to a people, an assembly, or a congregation. 

When one says absolutely, "He is one" <note>original: "vnus est"</note>, either here or there, and he is the only one in that place, I understand it without hesitation to mean one person. But when one says, "There is unity in that place," we certainly understand nothing else than that there is "one heart and one soul" among many; that is, **one will** and **one consent**. 

If, however, it is said "He is one in that place" in such a way that you immediately add a qualifier, "one" can be understood as a collection of many, such as "one people" or "one populace." Thus, when we say "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit," we do not dare to say "they are one person" <note>original: "vnus sunt"</note>, unless the word "God" is added immediately after. Therefore, if we say "the three Persons are one [thing]," it is a Catholic confession. And if we say "the three Persons are one God," it is a Catholic confession. But he who says "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one [person]" is proved to be an assertor of the **Sabellian heresy** <note>Sabellianism was the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons, but merely three different roles or "modes" played by a single God.</note>.

It is established, therefore, that neither "Trinity" nor "Unity" can be said simply of one person. Rather, "Trinity" is said of the three Persons, and "Unity" of the one substance—not the substance of one person, but of those three Persons themselves. In this matter, it should be noted that we do not understand the Persons simply in the word "Trinity," nor the Substance simply in the name "Unity." Rather, we understand them to be Persons by the very fact that we understand them to be **three**, and we understand it to be Substance by the very fact that we understand it to be **one**. This is because we can conceive of some "three" that are not Persons, and some "one" that is not a Substance—such as three hours of the night making up one night.

<summary>This page uses the structural form of the psaltery, along with analogies of a ship and a wall, to explain the Catholic doctrine of the Trinity: three distinct Persons sharing one divine Substance. It highlights the linguistic and theological distinction between the terms "One" and "Unity" to refute the Sabellian heresy.</summary>

# Abba. Book of the Psalter

But when those things which have been mentioned are added,
be they three or one: then we understand what 
those three are and what that one is: namely, three
**persons** and one **essence** <note>original: "persone et vna essentia"</note>. Although in the divine 
discourses of both Testaments, the name of 
"person" or "substance" may be a foreign term, 
nor can any name be found in the 
Prophets and Apostles by which the one essence 
of the Trinity is demonstrated except "God" and "Lord"; 
<margin>Exodus</margin> or something similar, like that which was said by the Lord to Moses: 
**"He who is has sent me to you"**; nor is there any name 
by which the three persons are understood, except in this: 
**"God, God, God; Holy, Holy, Holy,"** 
and if there be anything similar. For they are not 
called persons simply because they are three, nor is it 
called substance because it is the one of the three. 
For they would be called persons even if they were not three, 
and it would be called substance even if it were not 
one. Therefore, when it is asked how many persons there are? 
We answer "three"; lest anyone think that the 
Father is the same person as the Son and the Holy Spirit, 
and thus preach a **singularity of persons**, which 
is false, rather than a plurality. 
And when one asks about the divine substance: we say 
it is one; lest someone estimate those three persons to be 
unequal or divided, being ignorant of the word of the Lord 
saying: **"I and the Father are one."** For "Trinity" 
is said in relation to one thing, and "Unity" to another. 
**Trinity** is used to avoid the singularity of a person. 
**Unity** is used to guard against the division of a single substance. 
For Unity brings one thing; Singularity another; 
Plurality another. Trinity, as I have already said, 
is spoken of regarding the communion of several; 
it is not about one person alone, because where there is singularity, 
there cannot be unity. Singularity, however, is said of any 
one person who is alone; plurality of two 
and above: and as I have already said: not where there is 
singularity, but where there is plurality, there is unity. Because 
therefore three persons are there, and not just one, and they are 
inseparable from themselves: it is right that there be unity there; and 
in that unity, plurality—not singularity—is 
preached. We believe therefore that this substance, which is one, 
consists of three persons and not just one, lest singularity— 
as happened with **Sabellius** <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century heretic who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just three "masks" or modes of a single person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>—should occur in place of unity; 
and that in the three persons there is one substance, nor should 
division be thought to exist in those three persons. We believe one

<column-break/>

person is called the Father, because he has a Son; 
another is called the Son, because he has a Father; another is 
called the Holy Spirit, because he is breathed by both 
(that is) because he proceeds from both and is 
given by both; or if anything more worthy can be believed, 
it is fitting to be adapted to this holy name. 
Therefore, the Trinity was handed down to us by the holy 
and Catholic Fathers, so that through this name we might 
truly understand one God to be three persons. 
The name of **Unity** is used so that we may confess those 
three persons to be of one substance: (that is) 
that we may believe them to be undivided and inseparable 
from themselves, so that they are supremely one, and 
truly three. Furthermore, when we say that God 
is **Wisdom, Life, Charity, Justice, Truth**, 
and similar things: it must be understood according to his 
substance. Similarly, the name of "person" must be 
accepted according to substance: yet in such a way that when 
we say God the Father, God the Son, God the 
Holy Spirit—yet not three gods, but one God— 
we may say the person of the Father is the substance, 
the person of the Son is the substance, the person of the Holy 
Spirit is the substance; yet not three substances, but 
one substance. The **Sabellians** do not believe this 
because they do not know how to consider the invisible things 
of God through the visible things of the world, 
nor to contemplate sublime things through humbler and 
smaller matters. For we see 
one **fire** adhering to iron or coals; 
we see the **flame** generated from it, which 
is nothing other than a fiery splendor thickened from its 
expressing substance. We feel in both the **effulgence** <note>original: "effulorem," likely a misspelling of "effulgorem," meaning brightness or glow.</note> 
which proceeds unfailingly from the fire and the flame alike; 
yet there are not three fires in these 
three things we perceive, but one fire. 
Previously, however, the Fathers disputing against **Arius** <note>Arius taught that the Son was a created being and not co-eternal with the Father.</note>, 
who denied the eternity of the Son, gave the flame to 
this likeness of the Father's fire, and light to the Son, who 
is co-eternal with the Father. I, however, as if 
speaking to the faithful and not the unfaithful, would more 
fittingly give fire to the Father and flame to the Son, 
especially because that flame of the bush which appeared to 
Moses bears a likeness to the Son; and every 
flame that appears manifest through wood or straw— 
whereas it was hidden before—appears thus in wood 
in a tangible and earthly substance, just as the Son 
appeared in the prison of the flesh...

# Joachim I: On the Harmony

...[likeness]; however, the heat is the Holy Spirit. Again, in that comparison where we say: these three are one fire, and one fire is these three: if that light is understood only as that which is spread further out beyond the flame, then the likeness of the light itself cannot be so fittingly given in the second place as that of the flame, which is the fire itself. This is especially true since the **begotten Wisdom** <note>original: "sapientia genita"; referring to the Son, Jesus Christ</note>, whose likeness is in the flame, is one thing, and the **Spirit of Wisdom**, who is one of the seven gifts, is another. The likeness of the Spirit is rightly found in that light diffused further abroad, inasmuch as it is not the flame itself but proceeds from the flame. Nor should it disturb anyone that the flame, which is materially hidden in the fire, is not revealed at the same time as the fire from the beginning; for the Son did not wish to be revealed to men from the beginning, but remained in hiding until the appointed time, just as <margin>Isaiah</margin> it is said through the prophet: **"Lord, who has believed our report? and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?"** <note>Isaiah 53:1</note>. And it should be noted that not only is the flame covered by ashes, but also the fire, though the flame more so. For in the words of the Old Testament, the Father himself is often hidden, but even more often the Son, who is the Word of the Father, is hidden in the images of things. Yet, if these images are wiped clean by a certain breath of spiritual understanding, there soon appears not only the Father, who is designated by the fire, but also his Wisdom, which is Christ, <margin>John 1</margin> who **enlightens every man coming into this world.** <note>John 1:9</note> This is truly argued against Sabellius <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely three "modes" or names for one person.</note>, who preached <margin>Augustine</margin> only empty names and not also **subsisting persons** <note>original: "subsistentes personas"</note>, which the Greeks call **hypostases** <term>hypostasis: a Greek term for the underlying reality or "personhood" of the Trinity, as opposed to mere appearance</term>. Hence Augustine says in the book *The City of God*: "We do not call the nature of the Supreme Good 'simple' because there is only a trinity of names there without the substance of persons, as the Sabellians thought; but because it is what it has, except for what each person is called relatively to the other." <margin>Jerome</margin> And that this is to be understood in a fourfold way, Jerome teaches when writing to Pope Damasus

<column-break/>

regarding those who speak of "hypostases" but do not understand them correctly. "Let us ask," he says, "what they think three hypostases means; they say they understand three subsisting persons. We answer," he says, "that we also believe this, but this meaning does not suffice for them." Why does this meaning not suffice for them? Because they were trying to express something else in this word, through which they might try to assert either a singularity of person or a plurality of substance. But wherever they may be led by that spirit, in whatever sense, we profess three persons according to substance, not according to empty voices. Thus the holy and <margin>Bernard</margin> venerable father, Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, in his book *On Consideration* writing to Pope Eugenius, says: "For the names are not empty, nor are the voices hollow without significance." For if someone asks how this can be: let it suffice for him to hold that it is so; and this is not clear to reason, nor is it ambiguous to opinion, but it is persuaded by faith. This is a **great sacrament** <note>original: "sacramentum hoc magnum est"</note>, and indeed one to be venerated, not scrutinized. How is there plurality in unity, and this unity itself in plurality? To scrutinize this is rashness; to believe it is piety. Therefore, it is right to believe that the three persons are not hollow voices or empty names; and yet there is one substance of the three, the divine nature itself which is called **essence** <note>original: "essentia"</note>, so that no one should suspect anything divided or separable there. And therefore, though "three persons" is said according to substance, and the "essence of the persons" is said according to substance, there is yet this difference: the name "person" uttered in the plural number indicates plurality, while the name "substance" retains the singularity of the deity and its unity, admitting no scission or division. Although, I say, the persons are spoken of according to substance, and although the essence is spoken of according to substance, there is this difference: the name "person" admits the plural number, so that three are said to be; the one essence in all ways loathes division. It is not that this name has this quality in its own property, but that it was so placed by the Fathers so that there would be a way for us to answer heretics who ask us: "What three?" or "What one?" It would be better for us to ask: "How are the three one, and the one three?" rather than asking "What are the three and what is the one?" for there is not one thing there and another thing three; but they relate to each other. I did not say "another thing," but...

# Abba. Book of the Psaltery

...in relation to another: that these three persons are themselves one: and this "one" is itself the three persons. Yet, "three persons" is said in one sense, while "one substance" or "essence" is said in another. The former is spoken so that the three may be understood; the latter so that it may be understood that these three are not divided from one another by any cutting of parts. For there is no "part" there, just as in the example of a tree: the root, since it comes from no one, represents the Father; another part, the shoot, is the Son, who ascends from the root in which he also remains; and another is the Holy Spirit, like the bark <note>original: "cortex"; the outer layer of the tree, used here to represent the Holy Spirit's relationship to both Father and Son</note> which belongs to both. No physical image can fully express that supreme unity in which there is nothing less in the individuals than there is in the three together. However, if those three parts expressed by their own names are not three trees, but one tree, is it any wonder if the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called three persons, and yet one God, one essence, one nature? For where there is unity, there is joy; and where there is division, there is sorrow. Therefore, if that joy is beyond estimation, it follows that the unity must be beyond description.

But if the trinity of persons is designated in the "horns" <note>The "horns" or prongs of the ten-stringed psalter (instrument) were used by Joachim to map out the divine persons</note>, where is the unity? For there is a great difference between the designation of the trinity and the designation of the unity; both are not demonstrated with the same weight of reason. For I do not find any fourth thing that I can show to someone asking why we show those three. Therefore, we find it necessary to lead the eyes of the mind back to those three persons in whom we have designated the trinity, and to say that those three are one: they are one substance, one God. To use an example of things that are not identical but similar: the tribe of Judah, the tribe of Benjamin, and the tribe of Levi—which remained with the sons of David and the temple of the Lord—are called "one people" together. For when I say "one people," I am not designating a fourth thing, but I am saying that unity exists in those three, because they were not cut off or divided from the house of David as the other ten tribes were. Since this is the case, what can I show when I am asked about the unity, except that the vessel itself in which the three horns exist is one? And yet, to be "one" is different from being "divided," since these two are opposites of each other; they seem, in a certain way,

<column-break/>

these two contraries seem to fight against those three: while pure unity wants those three to be joined (to speak colloquially), a fit division seeks to cut and part them. Therefore, neither by saying something is "one" nor by saying something is "divided" is a specific substance denoted. Rather, these are certain intellectual terms by which it is hinted that some substance is divided, or that some substance is simply undivided. Thus, neither "being one" nor "being divided" denotes something substantive; they are intellectual terms by which it is hinted that a certain substance is one, or that a certain substance is diverse. Arius <note>Arius (c. 256–336 AD) was a priest whose teachings—Arianism—claimed that the Son was a created being, distinct from and subordinate to the Father, rather than being of the same substance</note> held to this "one" [division], while the Catholics hold to the other. For the very voice of Arius sounded of a cutting or division, which could be noted in three separate corners, distinct from one another.

Not incongruously, beneath those three horns of the psaltery, a certain round figure is usually made, so that in that very roundness we may understand the truest unity of substance. Therefore, that round figure which remains in the middle between the three horns is not to be accepted as if it were a substance itself, because it is not. For the substance is the whole vessel; rather, it is like a material expression <term>materialis vox: a physical representation or "voice" used to communicate a spiritual concept</term> proclaiming the unity of the whole vessel (that is, of the substance), so that no one, when they hear "trine," thinks it means "divided." Therefore, even if the three horns proclaim the Trinity and the circle proclaims the Unity, the little circle does not designate a "fourth thing" in the same way the three horns designate three persons—as if the divine essence were some fourth thing. Rather, it only hints at the unity of the three persons, and such a great unity as cannot be found in any similar thing. And yet, in those horns, something similar can be noted, if that which is at their tip or sharp point is taken as the material expression, so that neither in...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Trinity using the "Psaltery of Ten Strings" as a visual and conceptual model. The author is defending the co-equality and consubstantiality of the Trinity, arguing that the unity of God does not imply a "fourth" essence standing apart from the persons, but rather describes the relationship of the three. # Joachim: First [Book] of the Ten-Stringed [Psaltery]

...nor in that which is called three, which is one; nor in that which is called one, which is three, should the truth suffer harm. For this reason, although there are three persons, they are called one substance, just as those three horns <note>The "horns" refer to the three pointed corners or prongs of the ten-stringed psaltery, which Joachim uses as a diagram for the Trinity.</note> are one thing, one substance, and one vessel. However, as I have said, this is by way of a likeness and not by way of a cause; for it is one thing to provide an image, and another to express the cause. Therefore, wherever it occurs that such words as "how" or "just as" are placed, let them be taken as the one who writes understands them: because (as the most serene man <margin>Hilary</margin> Saint Hilary says in his book *On the Trinity*) "reality is not subject to speech, but speech is subject to the reality." <note>original: "non sermoni res; sed rei est sermo subiectus"</note> For it is necessary for the reader to examine the intention of the writer, rather than the impropriety of a word, which can scarcely be avoided in such high matters due to a poverty of language.

For if the divine essence were some fourth thing, the holy animals <note>Reference to the four living creatures in the Book of Revelation (4:8).</note> would not say: "Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty," but they would say at once "O three Holy Ones," and afterward they would add: "Lord God Almighty," because those are three and that one is one. But because God is called "one" for the reason that the three persons are not divided—just as the three horns of this vessel are not divided—"Holy" is said once for the Father, once for the Son, and once for the Holy Spirit. At the end, the reason is given why they did not dare to say "O three Holy Ones," when "Lord God Almighty" is added at the finish.

Therefore, through the horns of the psaltery themselves, the three are distinguished, and yet all three possess the whole together, so that nothing is to be raised up outside of them; rather, the whole must be confessed and acknowledged: that the three are one. Yet the extremities of them are seen, just as a circle seems to be material voices <note>Joachim suggests that the physical edges of the instrument represent the distinct "voices" or persons of the Trinity.</note>; so that just as the extremities indicate the three horns and the roundness of the vessel indicates its integrity, so these three extremities are seen to cry out: "Holy, Holy, Holy," while the roundness cries: "Lord God of Sabaoth." This is because that which is sharp <note>original: "acutum"; referring to the points of the triangle.</note> indicates a person, while that which is round indicates not one person, but the

<column-break/>

true and simple unity of those three persons themselves.

For we know that in a circle there is no difference of angle, but a circle is, in a certain way, the highest unity. If this could be said of anything other than God, it would be because a round thing seems to be entirely uniform within itself, and there is nothing in it that is shown to be divided by angles or horns. If, therefore, God were one in substance in such a way that He was not three in persons (which is false), certainly the figure of a single stroke <note>original: "vnius virgule"; a single vertical line.</note>—and neither a round nor a triangular figure—would befit so great a mystery. And if He were three in such a way that He was not also one God, a figure of three strokes would befit Him, such that neither a triangular nor a round figure would be suitable.

But because He is three in persons and one in substance, it is recognized that neither a single stroke, nor three greatly unequal and disjointed ones, befit Him in this mystery; but rather the triangular and the round together. This is according to the testimony He provides for Himself in the Book of Revelation, saying: "I am the Alpha and the Omega." <note>original: "Alpha & ω"</note> According to this, the form of the ten-stringed Psaltery is shown to have the shapes of both these elements: **A** and **Ω**. <margin>Revelation</margin> Therefore, whether we speak of the extremities of the three horns, or the triangular element which in Greek is called "Alpha" (A)—it sounds nothing other than "Holy, Holy, Holy." And whether it is that roundness which is carved between the three horns, or the round element which is "O" (Ω)—it resounds nothing other than "Lord God Almighty, to You is the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen." <margin>Revelation</margin>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument that the Trinity’s unity is not a separate "fourth" essence, but an ineffable bond of one substance. The author uses analogies of light (candle vs. sun) and the communal unity of the early Church to explain how three distinct persons are one God.</meta>

# Father. Book of the Psaltery

...to be able [to do so]: we must return to examples. For that which is written concerning human affairs is far different from divine ones; it is foreign to faith to rise to the knowledge of the creator through dissimilar similarities <note>original: "dissimiles similitudines" — Joachim argues that while we use earthly metaphors to understand God, they are fundamentally "dissimilar" because God's nature is infinitely higher than His creations.</note>; nor is it contrary to reason to assign something to distant things which is true in a far higher way when it is asserted of the creator. For if the light of a candle, which fails in a moment, can in any way be called "light," how much more truly is this said of the light of the Sun, which is so incomparably greater, and does not perish in an hour like the light of a candle, but remains continuous? Thus, if a creature is said to be something that is good and happy, it is necessary that this be said more truly of Him who—without quality or quantity <note>This means God does not possess goodness as an added "quality," but is goodness itself by His very nature.</note>—is good and happy, possessing essentially in Himself that which He communicates in time to His chosen ones, as if through His image and likeness, and by the bounty of His grace. 

For this reason, because He Himself is three in unity, He has always sought and will seek that more men and diverse peoples should meet in one, knowing that there can be no happiness where there is division and diversity. For "every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste." <note>A reference to the Gospel of Luke 11:17.</note> It is for this reason that the Son prays for His chosen ones that they may be one in the likeness of His and His Father’s unity, saying:

<margin>John</margin>

"Holy Father, keep them in your name whom you have given to me, that they may be one as we are." <note>John 17:11</note> And this he said concerning the Apostles. Then, after a few more things he reported, he added and said: "I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one; as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us." And a little later: "I have given them the glory which you gave me, that they may be one as we are one." <note>John 17:20–22</note>

Certainly, we have heard from the Word of Truth how the Son wishes us to be one in the image and likeness of that unity by which He and the Father are one. Yet this unity is in the spirit, according to that which is written in the Acts of the Apostles: "Now the multitude of those who believed was of one heart and one soul." 

<margin>Acts</margin>

According to this mode of unity, we must understand what the Apostle says: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit [with Him]." <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note> Augustine used this likeness

<column-break/>

in assigning the unity between the Father and the Son, saying: "Let it be said 'God from God,' so that this name 'God' applies to each one." But why did Augustine add this, if not because just as there is a great difference between unity and conjunction <term>conjunction: the joining together of separate things</term>, so there is a great difference between the joining of diverse natures and that natural unity of those things which have neither a diverse nature, nor a substance <term>substance: the underlying reality or "essence" of a thing</term>, or an essence divided by the splitting of parts. 

Therefore, when division itself is treated in the first place, conjunction in the second, and simplicity in the third, it is clear that a split creates division, while conjunction creates unity—yet not as simple in one thing as in another, nor in the same way in physical things as in spiritual things. For who could join the body of one man to the body of another in the way that fire is joined to fire, so that as long as it remains so joined, no division appears to be there? How much more, however, does spirit thus adhere to spirit, so that it is one spirit? How much more ineffably <note>ineffably: in a way that cannot be expressed in words</note> are they one substance and one spirit, since God is a spirit, namely the persons of the Godhead, who are not joined in time, but always remain together and undivided within themselves in that unity in which they exist. 

Therefore, because there is an ineffable unity in the Trinity, so that the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son, and in them their equal Spirit proceeding from both, it belongs to the likeness of that very unity that whatever is said there according to substance—that is, whatever is said there regarding some substance, either in the Father, or in the Son, or in the Holy Spirit—as Augustine says: "In that substance, whatever can be thought is substance, and there is nothing in God that is not God." For there is a substance begotten and a substance unbegotten, and vice versa; and nonetheless, let the unbegotten substance not be seen as different from the begotten, so that because of the supreme unity, one is called one person, and...

-># Joachim, First Book of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery<-

...unbegotten substance: another begotten: another proceeding: yet so that the three persons are not three substances at the same time: but one substance. Let us sing of this upon the heavenly vessel: let us see what is stored within it concerning so great a mystery. The Psaltery (as we have often said) is one instrument: and yet in it there are three corners; not one. <note>original: "cornua" — literally "horns," referring here to the three corners or points of the triangular psaltery instrument.</note> However, these three corners are not inserted or carved into it in such a way that the Psaltery is one thing and its three corners another: but they are the selfsame thing. How the selfsame? Because the whole Psaltery is the whole of the three corners: and the whole of the three corners is the whole Psaltery: and one corner contains as much as the three do together. Truly, even if the substance itself—which is called the Psaltery—is one in three, yet each individual corner possesses its own property in some way; neither does the unity imply a solitary singularity, nor does the singularity of any of the three exclude the unity. Why? Because the boundary and distinction of each individual corner cannot be found except in the fullness of the others. Therefore, unity is granted to the whole of the Psaltery: while to each person belongs the singularity of one of the three. I say "singularity," however—not (heaven forbid!) so that any person should be understood as being solitary there, since what belongs to one there belongs to all (as the Lord says): "And all mine are thine, Father, and thine are mine" <note>A reference to John 17:10.</note>—but rather to distinguish the unity (that is, of the one substance of the three persons). This is so that no one (heaven forbid!) takes the one essence of the three persons in the same way they take the essence of any [human] person; for there, by the name of "essence," we understand the unbegotten, the begotten, and the proceeding all at once, whereas here [in a human context] we understand only the Father, or only the Son, or only the Holy Spirit. For when I say "one substance," I embrace all three corners together in one vessel, as if I were naming one Psaltery and one substance. When, however, I say "three persons," I do not make a division of the unity because I name three persons, but I distinguish what pertains to each individual person. Next, if I seek to distinguish those three corners within myself...

<column-break/>

...I am not able: because to speak of it as it truly is is not easy. I behold those three things individually, and yet the three are one, and the one is three; and two are in one, and one is in two, and one is in another; so that the three together are no more than the one, nor is the one less than the three. He who can grasp it, let him grasp it. <note>original: "Qui potest capere capiat" — a common scriptural idiom from Matthew 19:12.</note> But he who does not grasp that which is below and can be seen with the eyes of the body, how will he be able to grasp that which cannot be seen? Nevertheless, lest anyone excuse themselves because of the difficulty, we shall strive to our best ability to make easy those things that threaten difficulty. Although Almighty God is great without quantity <note>Joachim means God’s "greatness" is a matter of His nature/essence, not a physical size or measurable dimension.</note>, it is necessary that the things by which we seek to understand Him through comparison be bounded by quantity. Otherwise, the figures themselves would be incomprehensible, just as He Himself is incomprehensible; He exceeds the sharpness and capacity of our senses because He is an uncircumscribed spirit, while we are localized and circumscribed. Therefore, every thing that is enclosed by a boundary must be considered in terms of the quantity of its space: such as a city within walls, a vineyard surrounded by a stone fence, and similar things. Now, therefore, we must consider the figure often described, which we have said is triangular, and what kind the points of its corners are, and by what space they must be bounded. For perhaps in this figure I have called those three corners "necessary" in the same way that the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit are called "three persons" by the Fathers out of the necessity of speaking, since they could not find a common name that would apply to them in the plural. <note>Joachim explains that "person" is a limited human term used because we lack a perfect word to describe the plurality of the Trinity.</note> Do not, therefore, understand those three things I called corners as if you should consider only their tips, but rather as much as two lines running forward together from opposite sides take up at the angle. Therefore, if you look carefully, starting from the primary corner, at the quantity of the corner itself which widens downward to its limit, you will see that the corner itself occupies the whole [space] which you see belongs to the three; and no harm occurs to the others that meet it, since they are no less equally that which they were. # Father. The Book of the Psaltery

...[so that one] may be able: we must return to examples. For that which is written concerning human affairs is far different from divine ones: it is foreign to the faith to ascend to a knowledge of the Creator through dissimilar likenesses; nor is it contrary to reason to assign something in distant things that is true in a far different way when it is asserted of the Creator. For if the light of a candle, which fails in a moment, can be called "light" in any way at all, how much more truly is this said of the light of the Sun, which is so much greater beyond comparison, and does not perish in an hour like the light of a candle, but remains continuous? 

So, if it is said of a creature that it is "good" and "happy," it must necessarily be said more truly of Him who—without quality or quantity—is good and happy, having essentially in Himself what He communicates in time to His chosen ones, just as through His own image and likeness, as if by His generous bounty.

### John [Joachim], Book One of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery

[one sub]stance is unbegotten, another begotten, and another proceeding; yet in such a way that the three persons are not three substances, but one substance. Let us sing of this upon the "celestial vessel" <note>A metaphor for the Psaltery as a spiritual instrument.</note> and see what is stored within it concerning so great a mystery. The Psaltery (as we have often said) is one instrument, and yet within it there are three horns <note>original: "cornua." In this context, Joachim refers to the three corners of the triangular-shaped psaltery.</note>, not just one. However, these three horns are not inserted or carved into it in such a way that the Psaltery is one thing and its three horns another; rather, they are the very same thing. How are they the same? Because the whole Psaltery is the whole of the three horns, and the whole of the three horns is the whole Psaltery; and one horn contains as much as the three do together. Nevertheless, the substance itself, which is called the Psaltery, is one in three in such a way that each individual horn possesses its own property in some respect. Unity does not introduce "singularity" <note>In medieval theology, "singularity" often implied being solitary or isolated, which would deny the relationship between the persons of the Trinity.</note>, nor does the singularity of any of the three exclude unity. Why? Because the boundary and distinction of each horn cannot be found except in the fullness of the others. Therefore, unity is given to the totality of the Psaltery, while singularity is given to any of one of the three persons. I do not say "singularity" (God forbid) as if any person were understood to be solitary there, since that which belongs to one belongs to all (as the Lord says): "And all mine are yours, Father, and yours are mine." <note>John 17:10.</note> This distinction is made to preserve the difference within the unity—that is, the one substance of the three persons—lest anyone (God forbid) should misunderstand one of the three persons. For when we speak of the name of the "Essence," we understand the Unbegotten, the Begotten, and the Proceeding together; but here we speak only of the Father, or only of the Son, or only of the Holy Spirit. For when I say "one substance," I embrace all three horns together in one vessel, as if I were naming one psaltery, one substance. But when I say "three persons," it is not because I am naming three persons that I create a tearing of the unity, but rather I am distinguishing what pertains to each individual person. Furthermore, if I seek to distinguish the three horns by my mind,

<column-break/>

I am not sufficient for the task. Because it is not easy to say things exactly as they are, I perceive those three to be individual, and yet the three are one, and the one is three; and two are in one, and one is in two, and one in the other; so that the three together are no more than the one, nor is the one less than the three. "He who can grasp it, let him grasp it." <note>A common scriptural refrain, notably from Matthew 19:12.</note> For if a man cannot grasp that which is below and can be seen with the eyes of the body, how shall he be able to grasp that which cannot be seen? Nevertheless, lest anyone excuse themselves because of the difficulty, we shall labor to the best of our ability to make easy those things which threaten us with difficulty. Although Almighty God is great without quantity <note>A philosophical concept: God is "large" or "great" in power and essence, but does not have physical dimensions or size.</note>, it is necessary that the things by which we seek to understand Him through comparison be limited by quantity; otherwise, the figures themselves would be incomprehensible, just as He Himself is incomprehensible. He exceeds the sharpness and capacity of our senses because He is an uncircumscribed spirit, while we are local and circumscribed. Every thing, therefore, that is encircled by a boundary must be considered in terms of the quantity of its space, such as a city within walls, a vineyard surrounded by a stone wall, and things similar to these. Now, therefore, we must consider the figure often described, which we have said is triangular, to see what kind of "horns" emerge from it and by what space they are to be bounded. For perhaps in this figure, I have called those three horns "necessary" in the same way that the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit are called "three persons" by the Fathers out of the necessity of speaking, since they could find no common name that would apply to them in the plural. Therefore, do not understand those three which I have called "horns" in such a way that you think only their extremities are to be considered; rather, consider how much the two lines occupy when running together from opposite sides toward an angle. Wherefore, if you begin from the principal horn and watch vigilantly how the quantity of that horn dilates downward even to its limit, you will see that this horn occupies the whole space which you see belongs to the three—incurring no prejudice to the others as they run in, since they themselves are equally what they were. ### Here ends the second Distinction. The third begins.

What has been handed down to us by the Catholic and Orthodox fathers concerning that simple nature which is God must be considered with subtle scrutiny: how, in the deity of the Trinity, whatever is powerful, whatever is eminent, whatever is glorious or blessed, is all said to be, believed to be, and understood to be of whichever person you choose. Thus, the very fullness of divine sublimity is no less in the individuals than in the three; indeed, what is said to belong to the three is not divided into parts among the individual persons, but is entirely the whole of each individual—except for what is proper to the Father to be the Father, to the Son to be the Son, and to the Holy Spirit to be the Holy Spirit. For if each individual is the same as the three <column-break/> together because of the ineffable bond of unity, how could the three together have anything greater there than the individuals? To speak of something from human experience: if some King were to take into the partnership of his Kingdom (as could happen) his son and grandson, or someone else of his own blood, and were to give them the full entirety of power in all things—so that the three together would be venerated with equal honor by everyone—in what way would one be less honored than the three together? Or how much more could the three together do in the Kingdom than each one of them individually, when one would rule there with the same power as the three together, and one would enjoy the same honor as the three together? 

However, if different things are brought together, there is a great difference between bodily things and incorporeal or spiritual things. Surely, if you go to a chest to carry wheat, or to a winepress for wine, or finally to a spring to draw water, you are not without reason concerned and anxious for yourself, lest perhaps you bring back less than the situation or necessity demands if the vessel is small. But if you seek to carry burning coals of fire to light straw or wood, do you not worry about the quantity in vain? For there is as much power in one coal as in three, and it does not burn any more from three than from each individual coal, even if what is seen by the eyes appears larger in three than in one. For the bodily quantity of a thing is not to be compared to God, but rather the quantity of power <note>The author distinguishes between "magnitude" (size) and "virtue" or "power." God is "great" in power, not in physical volume.</note>. Otherwise, if you wish there to be some difference between three coals and one, let us also use that for the persons of the deity, and let us say that the three persons are "more" than two; and yet they are not of greater power or virtue, because each individual person can do what the three can do together. But if there is such inequality between water and fire, how great an inequality do you think there is between fire and God? Especially since each one [of the persons] is great without quantity, and a Creator without material substance. For if the three were something greater than each individual of the three, then the limitlessness of each would likewise have an end—and thus none would be almighty. But if each...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Trinity, moving from the geometric metaphor of the ten-stringed psaltery to a deep philosophical and scriptural analysis of the "simplicity" and "equality" of the three Persons. It addresses the classic paradox of how three infinite Persons do not add up to a "larger" God than one Person alone.</meta>

# Joachim. First Book of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery.

If each of them is great without physical quantity <note>The author is using "quantity" in the Aristotelian sense—spatial size. Since God is spirit, His "greatness" is not about being big in size, but about infinite perfection.</note>, how can the three together be anything greater than each one of them individually? For each is as great in himself as that magnitude than which nothing greater can be; indeed, that is the nature of divine **simplicity**, in which there is no division of parts or of wills, but rather the highest unity and indivisible majesty. 

To return from those heavenly heights to our own lowliness: it has always and everywhere been the nature of unity to make that which belongs to individuals common to the many. If, however, unity acts through this good so that the individual possesses what all possess, what can all possess that the individual does not? Truly, this may be the case among men, but in God, it is not something that is *acted* upon; rather, He **is** that which He **is**. 

The rational creature <note>This refers to human beings, who are defined in medieval theology as creatures endowed with reason.</note> was formed in the likeness of this highest good—not taken up into the fullness of majesty, but raised to His image through the participation of grace. 

Yet, so great is the unity in that highest Trinity that the individual Person possesses the same majesty that the three possess together; the individual can do what the three can do. The exception is that the Father has this from no one; the Son has it from the Father; and the Holy Spirit has it from the Father and the Son <note>original: "spiritus sanctus a patre z filio." This refers to the "Filioque" doctrine, a central tenet of Western Christianity stating the Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son.</note>. This is not by a gift of grace, but by the truth of a simple nature. 

For the Father did not beget the Son because He "willed" to (in the same way He made all things He willed in heaven and earth); rather, just as He Himself always is, so the Son with the Holy Spirit is always with Him. Therefore, the Son is preached as the Father’s equal, because just as the Father is eternal, the Son is **co-eternal**. 

Because the same Son, with the Holy Spirit, is not separated from the Father, but always remains with Him and in Him in perfect unity, the Father could not lose what He gave to the Son and the Holy Spirit. Nor can they fail to have what is seen to have remained in the Father’s "property"—if indeed any "giving" or "property" <note>In theology, a "property" is a defining characteristic unique to one Person of the Trinity, such as the Father being "unbegotten."</note> can exist in that eternal unity, unless one understands how it can be so according to what the most serene 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine clearly explains. For the Son says of himself: *“As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.”* 
<margin>John</margin>
And concerning the Holy Spirit: *“He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine.”* 

<column-break/>

How these and similar passages are to be understood, Augustine explains through many lengthy words. Regarding those "properties" which here seem to belong specifically to individuals, so that they may then be found to remain in common among the three: both he and others have spoken much. 

Indeed, some, following those three things by which all things are perfected—namely: **Power**, **Knowledge**, and **Will**—have attributed **Power** to the Father, according to that passage in the book of 
<margin>Job</margin>
Job: *“God does not cast away the powerful, since he himself is powerful.”* And that saying of the most holy Mother of the Lord: *“Because he who is powerful has done great things for me.”* 

They attribute **Wisdom** to the Son, of whom 
<margin>Paul</margin>
Paul says: *“We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.”* 

They attribute **Will** or **Love** to the Holy Spirit, which they wish to be understood where it is said by the 
<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
Psalmist: *“Further in his will.”* And where it is said through 
<margin>John</margin>
John: *“In this the charity of God appeared among us, because God sent his only begotten Son into the world that we might live through him.”* 

And it should be noted that the Spirit is called the "Wisdom and Strength of God," the "Charity of God," and the "Love or Delight of God." These and similar terms are often found in divine discourse, and through them the Holy Spirit is understood. 

I do not recall having read the phrase "Power of God" in this specific way elsewhere; but if I have read "Powerful" or "Omnipotent," let it not be that the Son or the Holy Spirit is understood as "subject" to it—just as the Son is understood by the name "Wisdom of God" and the Holy Spirit by the name "Love of God." 

If, however, the studious reader finds this very thing in the Holy Scriptures, let him know that by the name "Power," the Son is to be understood. For where our impulse now tends, we are altogether prepared to say and prove that whatever is said in that simple Trinity according to **substance** <note>Substance (essentia) refers to the one Godhead that the three Persons share equally.</note>—and seems to be "proper" to one specific Person—must be understood as being proper to that Person in such a way that it is nonetheless shown to be common to the whole "genus" [of the Godhead]. 

For example: The Father is called **Power** because, in executing judgment upon sinners, He always shows Himself unconquered. The Son is called **Wisdom** because He did not wish to conquer by power, but by humility. The Holy Spirit is called...

**Column 1**

...is love: he who fully loves someone gives both himself and all that is his to the one he loves. For this reason, indeed, the Holy Spirit is both the gift and the giver: because he gave himself and his own, although one of these may seem to refer more to the Father and the Son, who gave him. And if this can be said in a Catholic <note>original: "catholice"; here meaning in accordance with universal Church doctrine</note> sense, it is not because he sent himself by giving himself, as some rave; for "mission" <note>In medieval theology, "mission" refers to the process of one Person of the Trinity being "sent" into the world, such as the Incarnation of the Son or the descent of the Spirit.</note> belongs only to him who sends another or something else, but "donation" can belong both to him who is sent and to him who sends. Concerning the Son alone can it be understood that he sent himself and was sent by another, on account of the substance of his dual nature, by which he is true God and true man. For any man, because he consists of two parts, is said to "emit" his spirit when the soul leaves the mortal body; for this reason, it is the interior man who is emitted and the exterior man who emits. Therefore, some strive in vain to assert in a simple substance what is assigned by Catholic men to a dual substance. But more on this elsewhere. However, to summarize what has been proposed: Behold, the Father is called Power, the Son Wisdom, and the Holy Spirit Charity <note>original: "charitas"; divine love</note>, because of those things said above, or whatever other worthy expressions might suit this great meaning. And yet, the whole Trinity is perfect Power, the whole Trinity is perfect Wisdom, and the whole Trinity is perfect Charity; otherwise, no person would be perfect. But if, according to what Augustine <margin>Augustine</margin> teaches in the pattern of memory, reason, and love, each one is power, wisdom, and love, it follows that each individual is nothing less than the three together. Well, then, in that triangulated figure <note>Joachim refers to his specific diagram of the Trinity, often depicted as three overlapping circles or a triangular psaltery, where the center and the corners represent the shared essence and the distinct persons.</note>, one corner contains as much as the three together, because the three Persons together are not greater nor do they have more than each of the three individually, nor is each individual less than the three together. Lest that which has been proven by reason seem impossible—not indeed to those who can grasp reason itself, but to those who are stronger in understanding—one must consider at least how much difference there is between the creature and the Creator, so they may know what can differ...

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

...between human and divine things: between the internal nature and the Creator of all good things who lacks nothing. Augustine relates this himself in the book *The City of God*. A piece of iron was applied to a certain stone <note>Joachim is describing a magnet or lodestone, used here as a scientific marvel to explain divine mysteries.</note>, and soon the power of the stone attracted the iron to the stone and joined it to itself, so that the two seemed to be bound together by a very strong union. The iron was then moved away from the stone and applied to other iron, and that same power was found to be in the iron which had been in the stone, in no way diminished in the stone. Moreover, the iron that had touched the stone was applied to another piece of iron, and the same power was found in that iron, even in a third degree; I believe even in a fourth and a fifth. If, therefore, the power of the stone itself is so great that it is not diminished by being shared—even though this is not a perfect image of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but rather a likeness of the gift of the Holy Spirit which is granted to the holy Church of God—how much more so if the Father is great without quantity <note>Meaning without physical size or spatial extension.</note>, the Son great without quantity, and the Holy Spirit great without quantity, so that each individual is not, nor has, anything less than the three together. Because wisdom is not lacking to him, nor power to prove what he is, let him who is able ascend in understanding to contemplate the beauty of this magnitude. Let him who cannot do so admire the power and believe, even if he can understand less clearly, saying continually with the Psalmist: "Great is our God and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number." <note>Psalm 147:5</note> "Great is the Lord and highly to be praised; of his greatness there is no end." <note>Psalm 145:3</note>
