# Joachim [of Fiore], First Book of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery

**Column 1**

...God the Father is to be understood as another [Person]: from whom the Son and the Holy Spirit [receive their being]; the one by being born <note>original: "nascendo"; refers to the "generation" of the Son</note>, the other by proceeding <note>original: "procedendo"; refers to the "procession" of the Holy Spirit</note>; they received their existence, which is what he himself is. This "principal" Person, therefore, is designated in the principal horn of the psalter <note>The "horns" are the structural corners of the triangular medieval psalter instrument, used here as a map for the Trinity.</note>: because he is seen as the "principal principle" of the two. For there (as we said above) remains the beginning of the whole vessel: and like water flowing from a fountain, he is dilated into certain wide seas. Therefore, that very horn which is principal is seen to be somewhat dissimilar from the other two. This certainly seems to suggest that just as the Father is from no one, so it is never read that he was "sent" to men: as one who did not have a beginning from whom he might be sent. 

But the Son, along with the Holy Spirit—flowing into that celestial city and filling it with his grace—saved the nine orders of angels, and like the force of a river, flowed down to the lower regions to save the human race. For he came to seek what was lost: and to perfect the lower string <note>In Joachim’s music theory, the lower strings of the instrument represent humanity or the earthly realm.</note> (in which, according to the arrangement of the strings, the whole art is terminated) to show the riches of his goodness toward the human race.

If the Father, because he is from no one, is thus never read as having been "sent," yet the Son and the Holy Spirit—one in the substance of flesh, the other in the dove and fire—were sent by him who is sent by no one: and they were so sent to men that they did not leave him who sent them, but remained in him and with him without end. It is fitting that the first place is ascribed to the first horn, with the two [others] concurring on this side and that; this is no less marvelous than it is clear. 

The Catholic Fathers also hand down to us that the Father is the principle <note>original: "principium"; meaning the source or origin</note> of the Son, and the Son with the Father is the principle of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the Father is a principle; the Son is a principle—a principle, I say, from the Father as principle—yet there are not two principles, but one principle. Similarly, the Holy Spirit is a principle; yet there are not three principles, but one principle. But of what do we confess the Holy Spirit to be the principle? The principle of all good things which are from him...

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

...the principle of all creatures: which, as Almighty God, he created for his own glory. <margin>Augustine</margin> Concerning this, Augustine says in the fifth book of *On the Trinity*: "If whatever remains in itself and begets something, or works, is a principle for that thing which it begets or for that which it works, we cannot deny that the Spirit is also rightly called a principle, because we do not separate him from the title of Creator." And it is written of him: that he works all things in all <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:6.</note>, and remaining in himself, he works in both. For he does not change or turn himself into any of those things; he is seen as the one who works. "To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for their benefit; to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit," etc. And a little later: "But one and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each one his own gifts as he wills" <note>1 Corinthians 12:7-11</note>—and in both cases, just as God does. For who can work such great things except God? 

If, however, the Holy Spirit is rightly called the principle of all that he works, who would dare to deny that he is the principle of the man Christ Jesus? Just as the Father who made all things, and the Word who was from eternity, through whom all things were made. Lest anyone should think this a matter of doubt, that entire "operation" of the New Man is shown to be attributed to the same Holy Spirit, when it is said: "Mary was found having [a child] in her womb from the Holy Spirit," and "that which is born in her is from the Holy Spirit." And in the Gospel, the angel says to Mary: <margin>Luke</margin> "The Holy Spirit (he said) shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you." And in the Creed: "I believe in Jesus Christ his Son: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary." 

O wondrous mysteries! <margin>Acts 3</margin> The only-begotten Son of God, visiting the world, so took up human nature into the unity of his person, that he who was already the Son but not yet man, was made the Son as man. And yet Scripture does not say this, though it is so clearly and transparently true; rather, it wished more to say that which—unless it is understood in the spirit—does not appear how it is true. Because...

**Column 1**

...for by this reasoning, he [Christ] is said to have been conceived of the Holy Spirit, though according to neither of his natures is he the "son" of the Holy Spirit. For according to his divine nature, he is in only one way the Son of God the Father; and according to his human nature, he is the son of Abraham, of David, and of the others whom Sacred Scripture commemorates for the most part. 

But this is easily resolved if we remember the words of the Apostle <note>Paul the Apostle, specifically 1 Corinthians 15:45</note> saying: "The first Adam was made into a living soul; the second Adam into a life-giving spirit." <note>original: "Factus est primus Adam in animam viventem. Secundus Adam in spiritum vivificantem."</note> Behold, look: Adam is the earthly man; Christ the heavenly. Adam is the natural man; Christ the spiritual. Why? Because to the former [Adam] was given a soul which would make him living and acting. To the latter [Christ], not only was a soul given, but also the Spirit of the living God. Not only, I say, a soul that was empty or void, but one full of the grace of the sevenfold Spirit <note>Refers to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord.</note>. Truly, just as the soul gives life to the body, so—I speak of a thing not similar but dissimilar—the Holy Spirit vivifies the soul created in the image of God. One of these was given to the first man, the other to the second; so that we, who were made animate according to the image of the first man, being vivified according to the image of the second, may glory in the beauty of the glory of the children of God. 

You have it written in Isaiah concerning the 
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
new man, Christ Jesus: "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding," etc. <note>Isaiah 11:2</note> However, the Holy Spirit did not rest upon him in such a way that he should be believed to have created him first and later entered into him; rather, the Spirit came before, because Christ was made a vessel for him. And therefore it is not without merit said of him that he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, because grace was present first in the mind of the Virgin before he was conceived in the mother's womb. Yet the Holy Spirit did not enter into him as he does into other elect who are conceived in sin; but from the beginning, he was present there together with the Word <note>The "Word" or "Logos" refers to the second person of the Trinity before the Incarnation.</note>, and he prepared that sacred little vessel of God for himself according to his own will. For this reason, he was never not full of the Spirit, just as he was never not united to the Word of God. And if, for the sake of the mystery, it was so performed that not when he was conceived of the Virgin, but when he was baptized by John, the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove upon him and remained over him—this was for the sake of those, namely, upon whom the Spirit descends when they are baptized in Christ.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

Therefore, it is not incongruously said that Christ specifically comes from the Holy Spirit. His body was not wrought by impure lust, but by divine power, filling it with sevenfold grace at the very beginning of its conception, so that he might rightly be called the heavenly man, the new man, the special man—as if he were not flesh, but spirit. For indeed, in a wondrous way the Son of God came in the flesh, yet not so that he might impose the law of the flesh, but that he might destroy it. I do not mean that law <note>The Torah or Mosaic Law</note> which he came not to destroy but to fulfill. But rather that law of which the Apostle says: "I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive into the law of sin." <note>Romans 7:23</note> 

And we have said this so that we may know that the Holy Spirit is the "principle" <note>term: principle (principium); in this context, it means the origin or source of a thing's existence.</note> of the man Christ Jesus; though, according to his being God, Christ himself is the principle of the Holy Spirit, being one with the Father as a source. And it must be known that if the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Word alone and not from the Father, it would seem somewhat less absurd that the same Son, the man Christ Jesus, should be said to be "sent" by the Holy Spirit, or even anointed by the Holy Spirit, or to have received the promise of the Holy Spirit, and the like. Because he who was once assumed by the Word into the unity of person could not then fail to have him [the Spirit] who proceeds essentially from the Word itself. 

But because the same Spirit, who principally proceeds from the Father, is called the Spirit of God the Father—according to that word of the Gospel: "For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you" <note>Matthew 10:20</note>—he is also called the Spirit of the Son, according to that word of the Apostle: "God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba [Father]." <note>Galatians 4:6</note> Correctly, then, the same Son is said to be sent by the Spirit of the Father, as that same Son says in the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." <note>Isaiah 48:16</note> So that the same Spirit may be understood as essentially "sending" him, because he proceeds from the Father. Thus, therefore, the Father is the principle of the Son; the Son, with the Father, is the principle of the Holy Spirit, according to his being God—but not according to his being man. Indeed, as he is man, he is not the source of the Holy Spirit, but rather the Holy Spirit is his principle, just as he is the source of all things that have been created. Not however...

# John’s First Book of the Decachord

the sacrament of faith <note>original: "sacramentum fidei"</note>: just as it was not necessary for any other person of the one true God to know himself, but it was necessary for us, lest perhaps some suspicion should arise in us that the Holy Spirit is not equal to the Begetter <note>The Father</note> and the Begotten <note>The Son</note>; and by this, we would be less "Catholic" <note>meaning "universal" or "orthodox" in the faith</note> if we did not worship God as is proper. For whoever attributes less devotion or faith to one person than another, preferring one to the other, errs criminally and nurtures heresy in his mind, even if he does not yet speak it with his mouth. But so that we may contemplate these things which we hold by faith again and again, we must still dwell upon the decachord psalter <note>A ten-stringed musical instrument used here as a mathematical and theological diagram</note> and return to its mysteries. For if the vessel itself is explained in such a way that its principal "horn" <note>a corner or projecting point of the instrument's frame</note>, which is ascribed to the Father, faces the rising sun <note>the East</note>; then surely that horn which faces the North must be ascribed to the Son; and that which faces the South to the Holy Spirit. And this is quite fitting. For to whom is the eastern part more suitable than to that person from whom the "Sun of Justice," Christ, was forever born, and from whom "all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named"? <note>A reference to Ephesians 3:15</note> Or to whom the northern part more than to him who entered the province of the North to fight against the prince of this world <note>Satan</note>, and who, through the "left hand" of the Passion which he voluntarily sustained for a time, overcame and conquered? To whom, indeed, does the southern part better belong than to him of whom it is said in the Canticles <note>The Song of Solomon 4:16</note>: "Come, south wind, and blow through my garden, and let its aromatics flow"? Certainly, God the Father is the principle of the Son; the Father and the Son together are the principle of the Holy Spirit. One can recognize this in the figure so often described. Begin writing from the upper part and strike all the lines that are depicted in the place of the strings, and you will surely find in the principal horn the primary principle <note>source</note> both for that which is ascribed to the Son and for that which is ascribed to the Holy Spirit. For you begin writing from there. But when you begin from the principal horn in such a way that through each individual line below you begin from that side which looks toward the North, then in a marvelous way both horns—that is, both the one pertaining to the Father and the one pertaining to the Son—appear to be together one principle for that which pertains to the Holy Spirit. This is better seen by the eyes of contemplation

<column-break/>

than can be sufficiently explained by the word of the mouth (as it is). Furthermore, if one asks about the writing of the Hebrews, who, beginning from the right side, end on the left, it must be believed that even this is not without a perfect mystery. This is undoubtedly because of what the Apostle says concerning the Word of God: "Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in human habit as a man." <note>Philippians 2:6-7</note> However, as we said above, his principle is the Holy Spirit, in that he is man, not according to his nature as man; and for this reason, in a fitting mystery, the Hebrews, beginning from the right, arrive at the left, establishing their end where we Gentiles <note>Latin-speakers/Westerners</note> establish our beginning—not indeed regarding the horn that pertains to the Father, but regarding that which is seen to pertain to the Son. But why does the Hebrew people, who were the first, begin from the right, unless because among them the Son was humbled so that he might receive from the Holy Spirit through the Virgin Mary? Thus he himself said 
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
concerning the Holy Spirit and himself: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me." <note>Isaiah 61:1</note> But the fact that the Christian people, beginning from the left, proceed to the right, designates what the Lord himself 
<margin>John</margin>
says: "Unless I go away, the Counselor <note>The Holy Spirit</note> will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you." <note>John 16:7</note> For it is as if he were saying: "Therefore I do not send the Holy Spirit to you now while I remain in the humility of the flesh, because it is not my role to show men the form of the one giving gifts, but of the one receiving them, until I complete the course of my humiliation; and I teach you to be listeners from the beginning so as to receive the understanding of greater things, rather than wishing to impart your own little bit of knowledge to others with impudence." 
<margin>John</margin>
Hence, concerning the same Master of Humility, John says: "The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified." <note>John 7:39</note> Therefore, the reason the Hebrews begin from the right and the Gentiles from the left is a clear mystery regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit, whose majesty is one with the Father, to whom be honor and glory with them forever and ever. Amen.

### ¶ The fifth distinction begins.

The upper horn <note>The corners or points of the triangular frame of the psaltery</note> is not sharp like the two lower ones: but is somewhat wide and visible compared to those two: so that the two remaining horns which are below may appropriately be seen to draw their origin from that one. Nor is this surprising. For God the Father, born of no other god: possesses in himself wisdom and love: namely, the Son and the Holy Spirit: through whom he reconciles to himself every chosen creature: whether it be in heaven: or on earth. For it is not in the same way that the Son and Holy Spirit send the Father: or that the Son alone without the Father sends the Holy Spirit according to the deity: or that the Holy Spirit alone without the Father sent the Son: according to the fact that the Son is man: so that in all things which are said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: a single likeness might be held. And therefore the first horn of the psaltery ought to be dissimilar from the two: so that where the origin <note>original: "principium"</note> is: one may understand it by that which is dissimilar in the vessel. Furthermore, both the Son has the Holy Spirit in himself: just as the Father does: but the Son has this very thing from the Father: as the Son himself demonstrates when he says: "When <margin>John</margin> the Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father." <note>John 15:26</note> And in another place: "As the Father has life in himself: so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself." <note>John 5:26</note> Moreover, the Father gave this to the Son: not as if by his own will or by a bounty of grace: but by the inheritance of nature. Since these things are so: the principal horn rightly lacks narrow sharpness <note>original: "astritudine," likely meaning the pointedness of a corner</note> compared to the two lower ones: because from it the Son and Holy Spirit proceed and are sent. I have called the two lower horns "lower": not as if they were unequal: but as if seeking lower things: to designate that which the Lord says: "He who speaks from himself: seeks his own glory. But he who seeks the glory of him who sent him: he is truthful: and there is no injustice in him." <note>John 7:18</note> And concerning the Holy Spirit: "For <margin>John</margin> he shall not speak from himself," he says: "but whatever he hears, he shall speak: and he will announce to you the things that are true." <note>John 16:13</note> Therefore, the principal horn does not begin from a narrow point, lest the Father be thought to have been alone in the beginning. But the two lower ones end in a point: so that one

<column-break/>

Son may be understood who is born of the Father: and one Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son. For the reverse is not true, that the Son or the Holy Spirit sends the Father: nor does the Father proceed or is he sent from the Son or the Holy Spirit: as is the case in all those things for which we establish an origin: but in these we understand only the primary origin <note>original: "principale principium"</note>: and in other things we understand them to end in a completing point: surely because there is one Son and one Holy Spirit. Otherwise, there would be two from any of them: so that just as the Son and Holy Spirit are from the Father: so the Father and Holy Spirit would be from the Son: or the Father and Son from the Holy Spirit: as if we were to establish a deserving origin in any of the three: or an origin in one and an end in two: lest anyone look for a fourth or fifth person in that threefold Trinity: in which one is from one: and one is from two. And because the Father and the Son are together the origin of the Holy Spirit: so that the Son has this from the Father from whom he also sends him: it was not necessary for the second horn to have a dissimilarity from the third because of this: except only in this, that it begins to write on the lower line: both in Greek and Latin: according to what was said above: because it is one thing to be the primary origin: another to be an origin from an origin: and one thing to be one origin for one person: and another to be two together as one origin for one: and it is so that one has this from the other: and together has this with that one from whom he has it. For although the Son is himself the origin of the Holy Spirit: because he himself is also from the Father: and has it from the Father that he is the origin of the Holy Spirit: not apart from the Father: but with him: nor so that they are two origins: but one origin: that horn which holds the mystery of the Son should not be entirely similar: nor that which holds the mystery of the Father: lest both seem to be the primary origin since this pertains to the Father alone: but the two horns themselves are to be joined together: so that both together may be seen to be one origin for this one <note>The Holy Spirit</note>: just as the Father and the Son are one origin of the Holy Spirit.

Rightly, therefore, the two lower horns end in a **point** <note>original: "acumine"; referring to a sharp tip or peak</note> because both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father and not from any others: but they themselves are only two. There is, however, another **sacred mystery** <term>sacramentum: here meaning a hidden theological truth revealed through symbols</term> that should be carefully considered in this matter. That which is sharp in any mystical figure signifies either a beginning or an end. If it were a beginning, it would designate that from which the art began; if an end, that in which it is finished. Since, however, it is established that an initial point signifies a **temporal beginning** <note>a beginning that occurs within time, rather than in eternity</note>: namely, in created things which were created by Him—who is the Beginning without beginning—not from any already existing thing, but entirely out of nothing: the same principal horn <note>representing the Father</note> rightly lacks the height of a point. Because God the Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, lacks a beginning of times and days: for He did not at some time begin to be, but was always that which He is. For if the principal horn started from the height of a point, it would seem to be similar to those things which began to be made out of nothing. But so that Almighty God may always be known as the Beginning without a beginning, that horn appropriately remains without a point; as if it cried out with fitting words, saying: "In the eternity of Almighty God, one must not seek a beginning of being; but He always was what He is." For we even presume to say in our common profession: <italic>As it was in the beginning, and now, and always.</italic> <note>original: "Sicut erat in principio & nunc & semp"</note>
<margin>Revelation</margin>And John the Evangelist in the Book of Revelation: <italic>Who was and who is and who is to come.</italic> <note>original: "Qui erat & qui est & qui venturus est"</note> And in the very beginning of his Gospel: <italic>In the beginning was the Word.</italic>
<margin>John 1</margin>Appropriately, therefore, the principal horn of the psaltery, which is compared to the Father, lacks the height of a point: because that eternity which was in God before the ages of the world is entirely unsearchable to us, who began to exist within time. By whatever hidden counsel He willed to create within time that which was not from eternity, the wisdom of men is dulled; sense and intellect fail. Thus, therefore, He was just as He is. He alone, without a beginning, is this pious [one], with the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are in Him and proceed from Him. <meta>This page continues the technical and mystical description of the Psaltery of Ten Strings. The previous page explained why the "principal horn" (representing God the Father) lacks a sharp point: because the Father has no beginning. This page extends that metaphor to the concepts of "Beginning and End" and how the Son and Spirit relate to temporal limits.</meta>

# Abba. The Book of the Psaltery

[...an eternal] beginning without end. For God is the beginning: because from Him are all things which have been created. But for this reason Almighty God is called the "beginning": because all things that exist are from Him and began to be. Is He therefore called the "end" <note>original: "finis"</note> because things cease to exist in Him? Far from it! But because the works which began from Him reach their perfection <term>perfectionem: in a medieval sense, this means reaching a completed or fully realized state</term> through Him: and in Him, who is the highest goodness, they will receive their completion. In this way, then, He is the beginning and the end. But because in the beginning there were no creatures—for whom and with whom time began to be—and neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit had yet assumed any created form, we who speak of the living and true God within time cannot properly say "He was" in the sense of how He existed or "He began to be" in that eternity. To say so would be entirely impious and wicked. We say "He was and is" because the word "was" can properly be said of a thing that has ceased to be what it was—as if we said "that man was good," but he ceased to be what he was—or it is said of a thing that at one time did not exist and now is. Since, therefore, Almighty God neither began to be nor ceased to be,

<margin>John</margin>
nor did "was" happen to Him, nor did He begin to be, but He either "was" [eternally] or "is." For the Truth <note>referring to Christ</note> said this to the Jews who were gasping to destroy Him: "Before Abraham was made, I am" <note>original: "Antequā abraam fieret: ego sum"; see John 8:58</note>. He did not say "I was" or "I began to be," but "I am." And when they said to Him, "Who are you?" He replied: "The beginning, who also speaks to you." If therefore it is true that God did not begin to be but always is, then rightly the principal horn—which refers to the Father, who is from no one and from whom proceed the Son and the Holy Spirit—lacks the narrowness of a point. This is so that He does not appear to have begun, but to always be that which He is. However, concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, we cannot speak in the same way—not because they were to have an end in terms of their essence (just as the Father did not), but because they themselves held a beginning of deity [from the Father]. For the Son had an end to this temporal life in His assumed flesh, according to what He himself said: "Those things which are written of me have an end." Or certainly, He is to have an end in the completion of His body, which is us [the Church]. And the Holy Spirit is to have an end in the pouring out of His gifts. For it was said

<margin>Psalms</margin>
in the figure <note>original: "typo"; a symbolic representation or foreshadowing</note> of the sun concerning Christ: "The sun knows its setting" <note>Psalm 104:19</note>. Truly, in the figure of the gift of the Holy

<column-break/>

Spirit which He pours into the hearts of the elect, the vessels were filled as much as they could hold. Like that widow woman who cried out to Elisha <note>referring to the miracle in 2 Kings 4, where a small jar of oil miraculously fills many vessels</note>: although that little bit of oil she was seen to have was multiplied and grew as it was poured through many vessels, yet when the vessels ran out, the oil stopped, and at last that pouring and infusing had an end. The Apostle speaks of that true pouring out which this miracle signifies: "The charity of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us" <note>Romans 5:5</note>. This is that virtue which is the mother of all virtues; without it, to gather the remaining virtues is like carrying empty, hollow stalks to a dismal threshing floor. For just as the humanity of Christ is set over all creatures, so the virtue of charity is set over all virtues. And just as John the Baptist was the forerunner of Christ, so the virtue of humility is thought to be the forerunner of charity. Concerning this charity, which is the chief gift of the Holy Spirit, the Psalmist says: "I have seen the end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad" <note>Psalm 119:96</note>. And the Apostle: "The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned" <note>1 Timothy 1:5</note>. Although the man Christ Jesus is great above all men, and the virtue of charity is great above all virtues, neither of these is great without "quantity." <note>The author is distinguishing between God's infinite nature and the "measured" nature of Christ's humanity and human virtues</note>. For nothing is made or placed without some limit being set—not so that it ceases to exist, but so that it receives a limit of quantity according to the measure of the worker. Divinity alone is great without quantity, and good without quality; alone, by its very nature, it is immense without the variation and changeability of time. Because that eternity which was before the beginning of the world is entirely inscrutable—since in it there were no creatures to remain in it—we do not know how far or near before the establishment of the world the orders of angels were created. Rightly, then, the principal horn is shown to lack a beginning, so that it may be seen to represent the "Beginning without a beginning," according to how God the Father was with His Son and Holy Spirit before the ages had begun. But the Son and the Holy Spirit are not, and will not be, inscrutable to us in that same way.

It highlights charity (love) as the supreme virtue, using the biblical story of Elisha’s oil as a metaphor for the Holy Spirit.</summary>

He is contrasting the eternal nature of the Father with the temporal missions of the Son and the Holy Spirit, associating the Father with the Old Testament and the Son/Spirit with the New.</meta>

# John I: On Harmony
### 239

...holy in His works: if indeed those works themselves are blessed in that future age in which we shall be children of God through the Son himself. But our understanding will be perfected in the revelation of those works, just as the Son himself says concerning himself and the Holy Spirit:

<margin>John</margin>
"I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; but when that Spirit of truth comes, He will teach you all truth." <note>John 16:12-13. Joachim uses this to show that full understanding comes later in time.</note> Therefore, since neither a temporal birth belongs to the Father <note>In traditional theology, the Father is "unbegotten" and has no beginning in time</note>, nor does a temporal mission or outpouring belong to the Father—except in the sense that there is a single operation of the three persons because of the ineffable bond of the Godhead—nothing belongs properly to the person of the Father that is not eternal. Rightly, then, the **principal horn** <term>cornu principale: the top point of the triangular psaltery, representing God the Father</term> is broader than the other two; for truly the eternity of the Father is common to both the Son and the Holy Spirit, but the temporal actions of the Son and Holy Spirit which we have described are proper to them alone. 

That eternal aspect is inscrutable so that it may be feared; this temporal aspect is knowable so that it may be loved. For the former belongs to servants, while the latter belongs to lovers. In the former, He willed to be incomprehensible; in the latter, to be comprehended and recognized. Therefore, in the former there is no beginning of times, because divinity lacks a beginning; here, however, in the Son and the Holy Spirit through the creatures they assumed, they willed to be comprehended by men as a "limit to the beginning." 

Because after the completion of His works—through which they deigned to be revealed in the humble form of the assumed creature—there follows an eternity of ages. This eternity is itself inestimable, but according to how the disposition of hearts demonstrates its beginning and its end, we providently note its integrity and its differences. It appears that the "width" itself which lies between the two lower horns is opposite to the summit of the principal horn. For just as in the principal horn the Father is seen to have begun His works (though they are not without the Son and Holy Spirit), so although they are not without the Father, the Son and Spirit are shown together in the **two horns** to complete those works at the end of the ages. From this, it follows that the **Old Testament** seems to belong properly to the Father, and the **New Testament** to the Son and the Holy Spirit. And just as that eternity of God which existed before the ages had no beginning but *was* the beginning, so that eternity which is to come after the end of time shall have no end 

<column-break/>

of ages. Rightly, the beginning and the end of the psaltery lack "sharp points" <note>original: "acuminibus". Joachim argues that if the instrument had points at the bottom, it would imply that the life given by the Son and Spirit eventually "runs out" or expires.</note>; this is so that the Son and Holy Spirit—who are shown to have "completing ends"—are not falsely thought to have "consuming ends" <term>fines consumptozios: an end that destroys or finishes a thing, rather than perfecting it</term>. Truly, in the amplitude of the space at the wider exit, it designates the abundance of God’s goodness which He shows us in the Son and the Holy Spirit. He had previously shown Himself as a terrifying Lord in Himself; but now, not only does that incomprehensible and eternal nature remain what it is without end, but even the ranks of the elect will remain without end with Him. 

And it is well that the completion of the entire work is given in the two horns: because it was only at the end of the ages that the Son and the Holy Spirit were visibly sent by the Father to redeem the human race. Though the Son was sent in one way and the Spirit in another, it was so that the terror He had shown in Himself might be mercifully mitigated in them, saving us through His clemency, because we could not be saved by our own works. Who with the same Son and Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

The common order of prayer, which is customarily performed daily in the Church of Christ, is not foreign to the aforementioned mystery. Whenever the solemnities of praise are completed, we ask for His clemency. For we have always provided that the first invocation be made to the Father—except when something occurs for which an invocation should be made to the Son, such as during His Advent, or when some reasonable cause or specific property demands this be done. I say that it is not outside the order of reason that this is done so frequently in the Church of Christ, nor is it without the mystery of true faith that we invoke the Father personally at the beginning, adding near the end: *Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son*, and at the very end: *In the unity of the Holy Spirit*. <note>original: "Per dominum nostrum... In unitate spiritus sancti". This refers to the standard Trinitarian conclusion of Catholic collects/prayers.</note> For the divinity of the Father, which presides over all things, would never allow this to be done in so many Catholic churches if the mystery of great faith and pious worship were not within it. Therefore, so that the secret of such great faith may shine forth, let us determine, if it pleases...

# The Book of the Psaltery
### Abbot Joachim

...the first mode of the prayer’s beginning: **Almighty eternal God** <note>original: "Omnipotens sempiterne deus"</note>. "We beseech you, almighty God" <note>original: "Quesumus omnipoteis deus"</note>; and things similar to these. Then, following the lines of the strings <note>The "strings" here represent the lines of the prayer as it is recited across the symbolic musical instrument</note> through the specific form of the prayer, reaching the last of the strings in the final ten, we bring forth the final verse. We do this in such a way that we begin at the **second horn** <term>cornu: a corner or point of the triangular psaltery</term> saying: "through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son" <note>original: "p dominū nostrū iesuz christū filium tuuz"</note>, and at the **third horn** where it concludes at the end: "in the unity of the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "in vnitate spiritus sancti"</note>. 

Thus, with the prayer completed, the confession of the orthodox faith—in which lies the salvation of all—is made. Who will claim this is a frivolous matter, unless we fortify these simply spoken words with greater authority? Throughout all the scriptures of the Old Testament and in that sequence of time which ran for a long span of years from Adam until John the Baptist, the Divine Name is found to have been solemnly known by faith to the patriarchs, prophets, and all the faithful of those times. Yet, the manifest tradition never revealed concerning the co-eternal Son of God that He was God (just as the Father is), nor did it ever reveal this concerning the Holy Spirit—except only in this, our **fullness of time** <note>A reference to Galatians 4:4, meaning the era of Christ</note>, in which the Son of God deigned to visit the world through Himself, and through the Holy Spirit whom He gave to us to complete the things He Himself began. 

For although God was always one and triune, nevertheless, whether He was triune was known only to a few perfected individuals from the beginning. The name of the one person—that is, God the Father—was announced to all, both to servants and to friends. It was announced to the children who were called the people of God, lest that people (still unrefined for that time) should be unable to grasp the mystery of the Trinity, and the plurality <note>meaning multiple persons</note> should turn the Jews away from the worship of the one God. Therefore, one must consider that the infinite multitude of the faithful—who, having rejected the plurality of gods, said that the one living and true God must be worshipped—did not err in their confession of the one God and Lord, even if they could not yet grasp the mystery of the Trinity. For truly, the one Almighty is pious, holy, and true, having in Himself the holy seed and the true life: namely, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning these, no manifest speech was made to the ancients that would call each of them "God," lest they should fall, as I have already

<column-break/>

said, into a plurality of gods. For if the confession of the Trinity were proposed to those people (who were still children for that time), they could in no way grasp it except as something divided; they would believe in three divided beings rather than in one true God, nor could anyone suggest otherwise to them through persuasive speech. 

Therefore, in that confession, it was indeed a matter of imperfection—but not of error—to believe in one God the Father from whom all things come, while not knowing that He has a Son and a Holy Spirit. However, to speak of "three gods" is wicked. Since it is not possible for pure senses to possess the discernment of reason between the **unity** <note>the oneness of God's essence</note> and the **trinity** <note>the three distinct persons</note>, the foundation of faith was placed for them, as if for children, in one God. To us, however, as those who are older in age, the hidden mystery of the Trinity has been opened. This was not from the beginning, but in this "elderly" fullness of time, when God sent His Son into the world to enlighten those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace. 

This, therefore, is the reason why through so many past centuries only one person, and not the whole Trinity, was known to those earthly and "animal" people <note>Joachim uses "animal" in the sense of "natural" or "unspiritual," following St. Paul's distinction</note>: lest they be forced to believe not in one God, but rather in three gods—especially since the worship of the pagans rejoiced in a great number of deities. But the faithful of that time are not to be thought to have worshipped God the Father alone because they were ignorant of the hidden mystery of the Trinity; for even in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are present, since the substance of the three is one. Indeed, it was very frequent among the Hebrews for the Trinity itself to be called **Adonai** and **Elohim** <note>Joachim suggests these Hebrew titles for God implicitly contain the plurality of persons</note>. But the confession of the Father was manifest then, while that of the Son and Holy Spirit was hidden. 

Isaiah expresses this clearly concerning the Son, saying: *Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?* And he says, *He shall grow up like a tender plant before God, and like a root out of thirsty ground.* <note>Isaiah 53:1-2. Joachim interprets the "arm of the Lord" as a metaphor for the Son.</note> Thus, in the beginning without beginning, God the Father existed with the Son and the Holy Spirit. However, He did not wish to reveal His "arm" and His love from the beginning of the world, but wished to hide the inestimable riches which He had within Himself until the fullness of time...

He uses the structure of the "Psaltery of Ten Strings" to map out how the names of the three Persons conclude the prayers of the faithful.</summary>

# Joachim: The First Book of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery

...of times and the ends of the ages: His Son, who is His power and His wisdom, and the Spirit of His mouth, who is His love and His goodness. He deigned to reveal these truths only to the prophets, who spoke much concerning them through riddles <note>original: "per enigmata"</note> in their own volumes. Indeed, whoever wished to collect those oracles from the prophets would require a massive volume. But it is not necessary, because this has been compiled by many others. Yet, however great that manifestation was, it seemed as nothing compared to the one made in its own proper time. For then, who the Son of God was and who the Holy Spirit was was known only to some—not to all who seemed to hold the faith of the one God. But now, the revelation of these persons has been made generally to everyone. It was made, as I have already said, through visible creatures, so that through those things which were made visible, we might come to know their invisible natures. To these visible creatures, assumed for a time by the Son and the Holy Spirit, the work was brought to completion—which, as I said, is symbolized by the **sharp horns** <term>cornua: the three corners or points of the triangular psaltery instrument, representing the three Persons of the Trinity</term>. Indeed, it was fitting for the horns to be "sharp," as they designate the distinct identities of these two persons. We must distinguish between the first horn and the other two; let us enter into what the truth holds, as the Truth itself has granted. The first and principal horn seems so proper to itself that, as we said above, it appears as a common fountain and origin of the other two. The other two horns are proper to themselves, as their very extremities testify; for surely God the Father is what He is in such a way that He deigns to send forth from Himself the co-eternal Son and the co-eternal Holy Spirit to the elect through creatures. But the only-begotten Son of God is what He is in such a way that He does not send His own "begetter" <note>the Father</note> to anyone; nor does the Holy Spirit send the Father from whom He proceeds, nor the Son whose Spirit He is—except in the fact that the Son himself is a man. For truly, the Father is God in such a way that He is from no one; the Son is God in such a way that the Father is not from Him, but He is from the Father; and the Holy Spirit is God in such a way that the Father and the Son are not from Him, but He is from both. And though the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, one Lord, and one co-eternal 

<column-break/>

majesty, only the Father is the Begetter, only the Son is Begotten, and only the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Only the Father sends the Son and the Holy Spirit in such a way that He is sent by no one; therefore, the eternal divinity of the Father is common to the Son and the Holy Spirit. However, the Incarnation of the Son is proper only to the Son. The taking of the form of a dove or of fire is proper to the Holy Spirit, even if the operation of the three is one.
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Concerning this, Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity*: 
"Although the Father begat the Son, and therefore He who is the Father is not the Son; and the Son was begotten by the Father, and therefore He who is the Son is not the Father; and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, Himself co-equal to the Father and the Son and belonging to the unity of the Trinity—nevertheless, we do not say that this same Trinity was born of the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven, but only the Son. Nor do we say that the same Trinity descended in the likeness of a dove upon Christ when He was baptized, or on the day of Pentecost after the Lord’s ascension, when a sound came from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind and divided tongues like fire appeared, but only the Holy Spirit. 
<margin>Matthew</margin>
Nor do we say that the same Trinity spoke from heaven, saying: 'You are my beloved Son,' whether when He was baptized by John, or on the 
<margin>Matthew</margin>
mountain when the three disciples were with Him, or when the voice sounded saying: 'I have both glorified it and will 
<margin>John</margin>
glorify it again' <note>original: "Et clarificaui & iterum clarificabo"</note>; rather, it was only the Father's voice spoken to the Son, even though the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable in essence, so they work inseparably." 
Therefore, the paternal name which belongs principally and properly to the Father does not exclude the Son and the Holy Spirit from itself, because the Son can also be called "father" in that both are the Creator; <note>The text repeats "nunq̃ ter dici potest: qz vterqʒ creator" likely due to a scribal or printing error</note>. And I will bring forth a sufficiently similar example: because the dignity of the **patriarchate** <term>patriarchatus: the status of a 'first father' or tribal leader</term>, which would have been fitting for Adam had he not sinned, was given to Abraham. Thus, Abraham is to be accepted as the first of the patriarchs, as if he did not have a human father, so that he might serve as a type...

<meta>This page continues Joachim of Fiore’s exposition on the Trinity as symbolized by the ten-stringed psaltery. # Abba: The Book of the Psaltery

...the property of God the Father seems to be held above all others. For instance, consider the first patriarch, Abraham: he is not considered the son of any patriarch, and thus he represents what we are seeking <note>That is, the unbegotten source</note>. However, we should not say that Isaac is "not the son of a patriarch" in the same way Abraham was; rather, Isaac is called the son of a patriarch, yet he is also called a patriarch himself—and likewise Jacob, just like Isaac and Abraham. In this exact way, God the Father alone is Father because He is from no one. The Son, however, is not only called "Son," but also "Father"—though in a different sense—for He is the father of us all <note>Through spiritual regeneration</note>. Similarly, the Holy Spirit is also to be called "Father," because it is through Him that we are born again. Therefore, as far as it concerns created beings, there is one God, one Father: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But as far as it concerns the Godhead, neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is "the Father"; only the Father is the Father of the Son—one Father of one Son—and neither of them has an equal. For this reason, we must consider that in all the sequence of ages, in which the one God who is the Father of all was preached as the one to be worshipped, not only did the person of the Father remain in the worship of that ancient people, but also the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, one does no injury to the Son or the Holy Spirit by invoking the Father in the first place, or in a special way.

As we have laboriously explained, whatever is offered to the Father's majesty under this faith is also offered to the Son, who is consubstantial <term>consubstantialis: sharing the same divine essence or "stuff"</term> with the Father, and to the Holy Spirit, who is "persubstantial" <note>original: "persubstantialis," a term Joachim uses to emphasize the Spirit's role in the shared essence</note> with both. When we add the phrase near the end of our prayers, *Through our Lord Jesus Christ Your Son, who lives and reigns with You in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God* <note>original: "Per dominum nostrum iesum christum filium tuum..."</note>, we are recalling those specific things concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit that became clear at the end of time. We do this so that even in that invocation which we make to the Father, we may distinguish the divine excellences, confessing ourselves to be His useless servants worthy of punishment, until at last, comforted in Christ—who first deigned to become one of us—and ultimately in the Holy Spirit, we may rejoice that we are to be set free and made truly free through them.

<margin>John 8</margin>
For this is what the Truth <note>Christ</note> says of Himself: *If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.* For who is he who remains in the word of the Lord, except the one who patiently waits until the Truth teaches him? This Truth is the 

<column-break/>

wisdom of the Father, and through it, he may reach the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle <note>Paul</note> says: *Where the Spirit is, there is liberty.* But where is there liberty, if not where there is love? For God is good and pious, lovely and sweet; and because of this, those who recognize Him, love Him. And those who love are set free from fear, because *perfect love casts out fear.* For it is written concerning "fear" and "wisdom" in the Book of Psalms: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.* In ancient times, the word "fear" was used out of reverence for God Himself; as when Jacob said to his father-in-law Laban: *Unless the God of my father Abraham and the Fear of Isaac had been with me, perhaps you would have sent me away empty-handed.* and a little later: *Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.* <note>Genesis 31:42, 53. In Hebrew tradition and Joachim’s exegesis, "The Fear" (Pachad) is used as a name for God</note> This "Fear" is also spoken of in the Psalm: *Come and see the works of the Lord; He is terrible in His plans for the children of men.* If "Fear" is understood as a name for Power, or as a title for the Lord, then God the Father is properly intended. If "Wisdom" is the name for the Son, then we rightly confess that "Fear" is the beginning of "Wisdom," since the Father is the "beginning" <note>original: "principium" or source</note> of the Son. Just as we understand the Father by the name of "Fear" and the Son by the name of "Wisdom," so we understand the Holy Spirit by the name of "Love" <note>original: "charitas"</note>. Concerning Love, the Apostle says: *The fullness of the law is love.* If this is so, then the "beginning" of wisdom is in Fear, but its "end" or fulfillment is in Love. Yet these three names belong to all three Persons, so that not only the Father is to be called "Fear," but also the Son and the Holy Spirit—for not only the Father is to be feared, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, not only the Son is "Wisdom," but also the Father and the Holy Spirit. Nor is only the Holy Spirit "Love," but also the Father and the Son. Although this is a deep question, it was not for nothing that it was said above that by a certain property of reason, the Father is called "Fear," the Son "Wisdom," and the Holy Spirit "Love" in the Scriptures. Thus, when it is said, *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom*, and that which was said further up, let us not only understand the Son and the Holy Spirit, but also the Father when "the Wisdom of God" is mentioned...

He uses the patriarchs and liturgical formulas to show how the "Fear of Isaac" (the Father) is the source or "beginning" of Wisdom (the Son).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Joachim of Fiore’s theological exploration of the Trinity. Having established the unique roles of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit through the figures of the patriarchs, he now examines the specific "properties" or names attributed to each—Fear, Wisdom, and Love—and how these names relate to the shared nature of the Godhead.</meta>

# John I: The Ten-Stringed Psaltery

...not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit: but only let us understand the Son. And when it is said, "God is Love," <note>original: "Deus charitas est"</note> we should not think of the Father or the Son, but only the Holy Spirit—even though these three names are common to all three Persons and perfectly suit each one of them. 

Now let us see the reason for these specific attributions. God the Father, who created all things from nothing, wishing to show His power and strike **terror** into men so they would not sin, did not wish to correct transgressors gently from the beginning. Instead, by punishing many with terrible severity, He struck the hearts of many with excessive fear. Thus it happened that among the ancients, who knew no other name for Him, He was called **"Fear"**; for indeed, they were drawn to the knowledge of Him through fear and trembling. 

But the only-begotten Son of God is specifically called **"Wisdom,"** because He did not wish to defeat the proud through the fear of power, but rather, through the teaching of wisdom and through humility, He trampled upon the necks of the proud. 

And the Holy Spirit is called **"Love"** <note>original: "charitas"</note> because He Himself inspires in us the love of God and neighbor, so that when fear is cast out, we may rejoice in being free and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. Therefore, because we are compelled by fear in the Father like servants, educated and instructed in the Son like disciples of the truth, and snatched from the lash in the Holy Spirit like entirely free and faithful friends, the name of **Fear** is not inappropriately ascribed specifically to God the Father. For He, through the many judgments He exercised before the Son came into the world, showed Himself as a terrible Lord to all mortals. 

Truly, the name of **Wisdom** seems to be placed in those passages where it concerns the Son, as if it comes from a wise person—though He Himself is Wisdom by His very nature. In this, an analogy of "flowing forth" <note>The Latin term *manatio* refers to the theological concept of emanation or the "procession" of the Persons</note> is to be understood. Just as water flowing from a source might be called a "river" or a "stream"—not because of what the water is essentially, but because of the fact that it flows or is diverted through fields to water the meadows. For not all water is a river, but only water that flows; and in flowing, it waters not the higher ground, but the lower places. This is surely because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Therefore, if flowing water signifies the Wisdom which is Christ, and water naturally seeks not the higher ground but the 

<column-break/>

lower, it is clear that where there is humility, there also is wisdom; and where there is pride, there also is insult. Hence, where "water" is written as a <term>type</term> <note>A symbolic representation or foreshadowing in scripture</note> of Christ, mention is often made of "descending," so that His humility may be understood. <margin>Psalms</margin> This is according to the words of the Psalter: *He shall descend like rain upon a fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth.* <note>Psalm 72:6</note> <margin>Isaiah</margin> And in Isaiah, speaking with the voice of the Father: *As the rain and snow descend from heaven and soak the earth, making it sprout... so shall my word be that proceeds from my mouth.* <note>Isaiah 55:10-11</note> 

Furthermore, where His birth from the Virgin is signified, "ascending" is used rather than "descending," according to the book of Genesis: <margin>Genesis</margin> *A fountain ascended from the earth, watering the entire surface of the ground.* <note>Genesis 2:6</note> For it has been handed down to us by the ancient interpretation of the Fathers that the only-begotten of God is signified by this fountain. 

The Holy Spirit is also called **"Love"** <note>original: "Charitas"</note> by a certain specific property because Love is not properly said of one person, but of many. For everyone who loves well loves another, not himself; for Love cannot exist between fewer than two persons—even if it is said improperly of some, *There shall be men who are lovers of themselves.* For even if this seems to be said in some way regarding fleshly love, it is not said of that Love by which He is distinguished. And the meaning of the Apostle is manifest, where he says of this affection which is called Love: *Love seeks not its own.* <note>1 Corinthians 13:5</note> This Love, therefore, tends toward another; and in that it tends toward another, it proceeds from one to another. 

Just as the Son is named in relation to something else—namely "Wisdom"—because He was sent by the Father to teach men the faith of God and to enlighten every man coming into this world; <margin>John 1</margin> so also the Holy Spirit is called **"Love"** by a specific property. This is that Love by which He was sent to us to make us also lovers [of God], according to the words of the Apostle: *The love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.* <note>Romans 5:5</note> 

Otherwise, regarding His own essence, not only the Son, but also the Father and the Holy Spirit can substantially be called "Wisdom." And "Love" can be called substantially not only the Holy Spirit, but also the Father and the Son...

# Abba: The Book of the Psaltery

Even if those who are taught and those who love did not exist, God would nonetheless always be, in Himself, eternal **Love** <note>original: "charitas"</note> and eternal **Wisdom**. However, because man must toil for a long time under the **spirit of servitude** <note>original: "spiritu servitutis," a biblical concept describing a state of obedience driven by fear rather than love</note> before being imbued with wisdom and reaching the **freedom of love**, the name of the Father—to whom **fear** specifically belongs—was made known to human creatures long before the names of the Son and the Holy Spirit. This was so the Son of God would not be sent to redeem those under the Law before the **fullness of time** <note>A reference to Galatians 4:4, the appointed time for Christ's birth</note> had passed, and so that the gifts of the Holy Spirit would not be given to men until, being founded in the virtue of humility, they had learned to agree with the humble.

¶ Certainly, three commands of virtue have been given to us, as many as we who are called to perfection by God’s command. We have already mentioned this above, but since the opportunity of this mystery arises here, it must be discussed more fully. This is either because the likenesses of these virtues belong to that supreme Trinity which works all in all according to the counsel of His will, or because these three instruments suit, one by one, the **three orders of the elect** <note>Joachim often divided history and society into three "status" or orders: monks, clerics, and laypeople</note> who were created in the image of God. The first of these is the **work of the hands**. The second is the **study of reading**. The third is the **devotion of singing psalms and praying**. In the mastery of action: **fear of the Lord**. In the study of reading: **wisdom**. In prayer and the declaration of works: **love**. We are bound to obey because of fear, which is the Father. We are bound to read because of wisdom, which is Christ. We are bound to sing psalms and pray because of love, which is the Holy Spirit. For in work, it is necessary to fear; in reading, to be wise; in psalm-singing, to love. Through the study of reading, we are joined to the Son. Through devoted psalm-singing, we cling to the Holy Spirit—provided that our understanding does not remain focused on lower things, but returns to the things above. Finally, in fear we kiss the **foot**; in reading, the **hand**; in psalm-singing, the **mouth**. For it is only there that the faithful Isaiah is free to say:

<margin>Song of Sol. 1</margin>
**"Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth."** In our actions, we embrace the feet, because through this we piously and faithfully demonstrate that we are servants of God. In reading, we kiss the hand, because through it we behold the works of God performed in

<column-break/>

wisdom. In contemplation, we kiss the mouth, because through it we are joined to Almighty God in the **kiss of peace**, from whose mouth the sweetness of the Spirit drips down upon us. Therefore, in action, we acknowledge our servitude. In reading, we ponder the great works of the Lord with admiration. In contemplation, our sense is directed toward God Himself, from whom all things come, so that we may be able to love Him more as we feel the sweetness of His love. For it is not enough for us that He offers His feet to be kissed; it is not enough that He extends His hand; rather, let Him kiss me (she says) with the kiss of His mouth. A good beginning is in the kiss of the feet; better is perseverance in the kiss of the hand; the best perfection is in the kiss of His mouth. Just as the work of the hands alone is not enough for perfection, so too reading alone is not enough unless psalmody is added. Certainly, in sacred reading, Christ becomes near to you, He who is the Word of God and the Wisdom of the Father, and who illuminates you with His teaching so that you may know what is to be avoided and what is to be done. But remember that He said to His disciples: *"Unless I go away, the Counselor will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you."* <note>John 16:7</note> Unless you free your mind from the study of meditating on those things which pertain to the knowledge of things—which, as the Psalmist says, **"were made in wisdom"**—you will not be able to feel the sweetness of the love of God, which is usually infused into entirely free minds by the presence of the Holy Spirit. It is also written: **"Be still and see that the Lord is sweet."** <note>original: "Uacate & videte qm suauis est dñs," a variation of Psalm 46:10 and 34:8</note> Just as one can only progress in the Scriptures and knowledge if one vigilantly shakes off the cares of earthly things, so one cannot sufficiently contemplate that simple Essence which is God through the coming of the Holy Spirit unless one rests from the noise of created things and the actions of whatever words pertain to the knowledge of the Scriptures, and turns the study and devotion of one’s intention toward Him who made all things. Certainly, those things written about Adam and Moses, about Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, are authentic words; they are to be read with pious faith and revered by the faithful. But if they are authentic and worthy of memory, is it the same thing to think of them as it is to contemplate God? To pray and praise Him through whom all things were made? This is to offer voluntarily the **sacrifice of praise**. "Voluntarily," He says...

Joachim uses the allegory of the "Three Kisses" from the Song of Songs to describe the soul's progression from fearful service to divine union.</summary>

...I will sing to you: and I will praise your name because it is good. For it is one thing to look back at what is holy; it is another to contemplate Him who made what was made. Just as it is one thing to know something so that it may be known, and another to know it so that it may be loved. In the former, there is **knowledge** alone, which often "puffs up." In the latter, there is **wisdom** with **charity**, which "builds up." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 8:1: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up."</note> Although a certain unity, by which they take hold of one another, seems to be present in these three: because in work, not only is **power** necessary, but also **knowing** and **willing**; and in choice, not only is **knowing** necessary, but also **power** and **willing**; and in the singing of psalms, not only is **willing** necessary, but also **knowing** and **power**. It is as if they were seen to cry out clearly with their own voices: but to create some understanding, let one Person be called **Power**, another **Wisdom**, and another **Charity**. <note>Joachim associates Power with the Father, Wisdom with the Son, and Charity/Love with the Holy Spirit.</note> Nevertheless, in simple truth, this must be felt and held, as a certain one of the holy fathers said against a certain heretic: "It is not common to three or two, nor is it the property of each individually." <note>This likely refers to the unique yet unified nature of the Trinity, where the essence is shared but the Persons are distinct.</note> Furthermore, it must be known that a person baptized in Christ does not immediately pursue perfect **freedom** after the grace of baptism; that freedom is only to be hoped for in the **homeland**. <note>original: "patria"; a common medieval term for Heaven, the true home of the soul.</note> Instead, for a long time before, one is consumed in labor, so that at last, with the fruit of works, one may arrive at the grace of freedom. To this pertains what the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> says: "For as long as the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all: but is under tutors and governors until the time appointed by the father." <note>Galatians 4:1-2</note> So also we, when we were children, were serving under the elements of this world. And when the fullness of time came, God sent His Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. "When," he says, "the fullness of time came." For indeed, in **five ages**, servile fear persisted in the world. But in the **sixth** and **seventh ages**, filial fear and love are present: one of which pertains to the Son, the other to the Holy Spirit. According to this, as the holy Pope Gregory <note>Gregory the Great</note> teaches, the ages of a single man are to be observed and weighed; and this grace of the Holy Spirit is not bound by human law. For according to the law of Moses, the sons of Levi are commanded to minister in the tabernacle until the fiftieth year; from then on, they are to rest from the ministry and become guardians of the holy vessels that were in the tabernacle. <margin>Psalms</margin> This is to receive the kingdom of holy souls. Truly, it is written in the psalm: "The days of our

<column-break/>

years are seventy years." <note>Psalm 90:10 (89 in the Vulgate)</note> That old man is of a sufficiently faint hope who, the closer he is to the time of his calling, does not insist all the more worthily and assiduously on contemplation or prayer, saying with the Psalm: "Lord, make me know my end, and what is the number of my days, <margin>Psalms</margin> that I may know what is lacking to me." <note>Psalm 39:4</note> Behold how many things have been said, and in all of them a uniform authority and equal testimony is found to be given: so that from a long delay of servitude, one comes gradually to freedom. But regarding those things said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: by what reason was it necessary for the Father's name to be manifested to the children of men from the beginning of the world, while the Son and the Holy Spirit were only manifested in the fullness of times? We have shown this figured in the three-fold work of the **psaltery**, distinguishing between the **principal horn**, which is the beginning of the whole art, and the **two other horns** which look toward the lower parts, in which the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are designated. <note>The "psaltery of ten strings" was a triangle-shaped instrument. Joachim uses its three corners (horns) to symbolize the Trinity.</note>

### The End of the Sixth Distinction. The Beginning of the Seventh Distinction.

**B**ecause up to this point enough has been said (as I believe) concerning the **three horns**, we must now come to the **ten strings**, from which the work not fruitlessly took its surname. For so the "Psaltery of Ten Strings" is spoken of, as if one said: the God of the Hebrews, the God of Christians, the God of men and angels. As I mentioned at the start of this work, it was spoken regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit: "By the word of the Lord <margin>Psalms</margin> the heavens were established, and all the power of them by the spirit of his mouth." <note>Psalm 33:6</note> If, however, by the name of "heavens," angels and holy men are to be understood, they themselves are designated in the **ten strings**. What is this? It is that the ten strings themselves are firmly bound on this side and that to the two lower horns; this is because all the faithful adhere to their head, Christ Jesus (whose body they are), by an insoluble knot of connection; and no less to the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle says: "He who adheres to God is one spirit." <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note> The same Apostle says: "We are one body in Christ, and we have all been made to drink of one Spirit." Therefore, not without merit, the ten strings, beginning from the first, are fastened here and there by the two horns: because by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power was established. For they were made firm by the **Word** through whom they were made, and solidified by the virtue of the **Spirit** through whom <margin>Psalm 148</margin> they were created. He said—that is, God the Father—"I spoke and they were made; he commanded and they were created." <note>Psalm 148:5</note>

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Trinity, moving from the philosophical concepts of Power, Wisdom, and Love to a visual and musical analogy using the ten-stringed psaltery. It specifically addresses how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cooperate in creation and judgment, while refuting ancient heresies that misunderstood their unity.</meta>

### Father. The Book of the Psaltery

The Father is not excluded—He who spoke and things were made, who commanded and they were created <note>original: "dixit et facta sunt: mandavit et creata sunt," a reference to Psalm 33:9</note>—from whom the Word and the Holy Spirit proceed. If anyone notes that something is done through the first Word, or something through the Holy Spirit, it is so that no faithful person should doubt that the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, is the Creator. This is according to what the Son Himself says: "For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father." <note>John 5:22-23</note> Regarding this judgment, He examines by Word and Wisdom; and we know that the Son is the Word and Wisdom. Hence, He Himself says in the Gospel: "The word that I have spoken, that will judge him" (that is, the unfaithful man) "on the last day." <note>John 12:48</note> Truly, that judgment is also given to the Holy Spirit by the Father and the Son can be proven by many authorities. When the prophet spoke concerning Christ, he said: "By the spirit <note>original: "Spiritu," often translated as 'breath' in this context</note> of his lips shall he slay the wicked." <note>Isaiah 11:4</note> And the Apostle says of that same Antichrist whom Christ is to judge: "And then that wicked one shall be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus shall kill with the spirit of his mouth and destroy with the brightness of his coming." <note>2 Thessalonians 2:8</note> Since these things are so, it is a delight to contemplate this in the **ten-stringed psaltery**, <note>The "decacordo psalterio" is a musical instrument often used by medieval theologians to symbolize the Ten Commandments or the Trinity.</note> where the purity of this sacred mystery is contained in a work so clear that it is better seen than described.

**W**e have in the principal horn <note>In this context, the "horns" refer to the points or corners of the triangular psaltery instrument.</note> of the psaltery the image of the Begetter [the Father]. Although He is the Beginning in the Godhead, we read that He did nothing by Himself alone, as if the Word were excluded; rather, He did all things from Himself through the Word, with the Holy Spirit cooperating in all things, of whom it is said:

<margin>Psalms</margin> "And by the spirit of his mouth all their power." <note>Psalm 33:6</note> Because of this, no strings belong uniquely to that same principal horn; instead, they belong only to the two horns on either side. Yet, because those two horns proceed from the principal one, He possesses the whole in Himself through them, and possesses no less than the two. For, as was said above, there is a certain unity in the three that is beyond what can be expressed; so much so that if one seeks rightly, nothing less is found in each individual than in the three together. These strings sound in the presence of God, but through the Son and the Holy Spirit. They sound because they praise, and God hears their resonance. For this psaltery has openings in its center through which the sound of the strings is conducted to the interior, as if through ears,

<column-break/>

reaching the inner chambers of the musical vessel. And it is written of the Almighty who is the Creator of all: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the just, and his ears are open to their prayers." <note>Psalm 34:15</note> It is fitting that these openings are in the middle of the vessel: for just as what is done by one Person belongs equally to the three, so also what one hears, the three hear together. Because just as their glory is one, so too is their will nothing less than one. Therefore, the strings sound when they praise God humbly with the spirit of the few. But the Almighty Lord does not accept the praises of those who, like the Jews, worship only God the Father apart from the Son and the Holy Spirit; nor of those who, with Arius, <note><term>Arius</term>: A 4th-century priest who taught that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father, thus "splitting the substance" of the Trinity.</note> split the substance and divide the unity of the Godhead in the Trinity, or confound the unity within the unity. These openings are in the middle (that is, between the three horns) so that there should be no leaning toward any side where it would be permitted to depart from unity; for he who deserts unity utterly destroys himself. But perhaps Sabellius <note><term>Sabellius</term>: A 3rd-century heretic who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were just different "modes" or faces of a single person, rather than three distinct Persons.</note> held the truth because he preached "one"? Not at all. For Sabellius did not teach unity, but "singularity," as if one horn were alternating within itself, appearing now as this, now as that. But the roundness of the instrument cries out against this with its own voice; the unity and trinity of the sacred vessel encompass this. For the horns are not located at common extremities, but within the roundness. This is because it does nothing for a prayer directed to one Person to either exclude the Lord like the Jew, or find Him "lesser" like Arius, or to think one is heard by one Person and not another. This is what usually happens to those who, when the memory of the Godhead occurs to them, imagine the faces of three images running by, or like three kings sitting in their chariots, distinct in glory and power. (Which is false: for the Trinity is God and man—not flesh, but the Holy Spirit.) They fear their prayer cannot reach the ears of the Divinity. For the Father is not appeased by one who does not honor the Son in the confession of faith just as he honors the Father; then he likewise venerates the Holy Spirit; and he who confesses not multiple kingdoms but one single Kingdom, believes in the Father and the Holy Spirit. For even if...
