# John the First: The Ten-Stringed [Psaltery]

...kings but one king: and yet the Father is king: the Son is king: the Holy Spirit is king: the Son, I say, is of the King: He is the Son: just as light from light: God from God: and yet not two gods but one God. But Sabellius <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century priest who taught "Modalism," the idea that the Father, Son, and Spirit are not distinct persons but merely three modes or "faces" of a single person. This was declared a heresy.</note> calls upon neither, for he denies the Trinity and has not learned to maintain its roundness <note>original: "rotunditatem," likely referring to the perfect, circular unity of the Godhead</note> but rather a singularity: he suspects that as if one very sharp horn were fixed into something. Therefore, the faithful confession of that man penetrates the ears of the Divinity: who indeed recognizes and worships three persons: but yet with the eye of the mind perceives the unity: since he thinks of the persons distinctly, not divided: and does not imagine the substance of the persons to be singular, but one. Such a voice of the strings quickly penetrates the ears of Majesty. Such praise from the living creatures reaches even to the third heaven. He who thus prays and sings psalms, praising and calling upon his God, should know his voice reaches the ears of the Most High: if yet his works are not contrary to his voice. He exceeds man, steps above the angel: he rests in God. There he looks back upon wondrous mysteries; there what the eye has not seen nor the ear heard; there are the secret words <margin>13.</margin> which it is not lawful for man to speak: because, he says, the natural man <note>original: "animalis homo," referring to 1 Corinthians 2:14, describing a person operating only on a physical or intellectual level without the Holy Spirit</note> does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God. <margin>For now.</margin> Both Christ and Him crucified must be preached. For not all have equal virtue: nor is this power one and the same: because the voice of the strings is not one: nor is their position the same. One is higher than another: another is more plentiful: and that which is higher sounds higher and sharper: and yet is smaller in length: while that which is lower sounds deeper and more humble, and yet is greater in length. But what is to be contemplated in all these things except that distinct multitude of orders: which God governs with such art and such providence: that distinguished by diverse mansions: (that is) by dignities and honors, He adorns that heavenly court: as if with diverse flowers or colors: and those who are greater are fewer: lest there Leah should still emulate Rachel; <note>A reference to the biblical sisters in Genesis; Leah was fertile but less loved, while Rachel was beloved but initially barren.</note> and those who are more numerous are inferior: lest they overwhelm those who are fewer, as Peninnah, once fertile, did by despising Hannah. <note>From 1 Samuel; Peninnah mocked the childless Hannah, though Hannah was the preferred wife.</note> But even this is not done by physical distance (so to speak), with boundaries placed between them: as if between princes and clients there were no middle order: otherwise, as far as

<column-break/>

regards common judgment: some would despise others: and some would envy others. But while one, as it were, presides as a bishop over several priests; while priests over many deacons: while deacons [preside] over subdeacons: subdeacons over acolytes: acolytes over exorcists: exorcists over lectors: lectors over porters <note>The "ostiarius" or porter was the lowest of the minor orders in the medieval church, responsible for guarding the doors.</note>: the greater are set over their inferiors as if from nearby: the diversity of honors wonderfully adorns that holy and heavenly homeland: and the moderation of unity excludes the injury of spite: and indeed, although grace may work peace there, yet wisdom is also necessary there: so that not only by the power of the spirit the heavens may seem perfect there: but also strengthened and solidified by the word of the Lord: lest that seem to be lacking in that city which the Psalmist admires in the works of God, saying: <margin>Ps.</margin> "In wisdom you have made all things, O Lord." <note>Psalm 104:24</note> The strings are short: as I have already said: those which are closer to the principal horn: because the apostles, whom the Lord appointed as princes over all the earth, were very few. But if the fathers were few, are the children therefore few? Did that grain which descended from heaven wish to fall into the earth and die in vain, and not rather that it might bring forth much fruit and fill the granaries to the top? <margin>Apo.</margin> "I heard" (says John) "the number of those who were sealed, a hundred and forty-four thousand": and after them: "A great multitude which no one could number" of whom it is said in what follows: "These are they who have come out of the great tribulation and have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb." <note>Revelation 7:4, 9, 14</note> Because, by a certain property, martyrs belong to Christ, just as contemplative virgins belong to the Holy Spirit. Something similar was said of the virgins in the same book. <margin>Apo.</margin> "I saw the Lamb standing upon Mount Sion, and with Him a hundred and forty-four thousand." And a little later: "These are they who have not been defiled with women: for they are virgins." <note>Revelation 14:1, 4</note> Let us now place, if it please you, in the first place the Apostles. Second, the Prophets and Evangelists. Third, the Doctors. Fourth, the Contemplatives. ->Abba. The Book of the Psaltery<-

...of rank: fewer who are more worthy: so that those who are inferior may yield to the happiness of the fewer; and those who are higher should not despise the multitude of the inferior: but let all be of one mind and bound by a wondrous charity; and let each one rejoice to be that which he is, with all impious jealousy and envy removed. Thus, for a time, whoever wishes may remain on the throne with the Father and be honored by all; may almighty God grant me, through patience and purity of mind, to have a portion with this multitude of saints. And what should be said of these things? I do not know what certain thing I might write about them; I am ignorant of which of these I should prefer or set aside, because I frequently find those who are inferior in rank to be more blessed according to the rewards of grace. I would wonder at these things if I did not know that the mother of someone—in the sense that she is a mother—is preferred by maternal dignity over her own son, and if I did not see that the King of Heaven chose a humble woman for himself as a mother. It remains, therefore, that he who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child shall not enter into it. An honest man will be well able to judge this, for he would judge that there is no art to the ten-stringed <term>psaltery</term> <note>A stringed instrument, similar to a harp or lyre, often used in the Bible to symbolize divine harmony.</note> if there were only one sound in the whole vessel, or if there were one and the same melody in all the strings. For God did not wish there to be differences of rank because He loved some more than others—since we see that John was loved more than Peter and his successors—but rather he was subject to his posterity just as he himself did not disdain to be subject to his mother. Instead, it is so that by bringing forth distinct sounds with the heart, they might gladden that holy City of God with the sweetness of melody, in which there is a dwelling place for all who rejoice. May Jesus Christ, the Son of God, lead us to this city; He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

### Here ends the first book of the ten-stringed psaltery concerning the contemplation of the trinity. Here begins the Second book concerning the number of the Psalms: and concerning the perfection or significance of that very number.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring ornate white foliate and scroll-work patterns against a dark, textured rectangular background.</image-desc>

Among the other sounds and numbers which Holy Scripture mentions, the number one hundred and fifty is most sacred, inasmuch as the entire collection of the <term>Psalter</term> <note>The Book of Psalms.</note> is contained in its total. Certainly, the arrangement of the psalms was established by King David to be presented to the living God—or rather by the Holy Spirit who was directed into him and who prepares the way for himself to visit the hearts of the faithful. As it is written from the voice of that Spirit in the forty-ninth Psalm: *The sacrifice of praise shall honor me: and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.* <note>original: "Sacrificiū laudis honorificabit me..." (Psalm 50:23 in modern numbering).</note> The proportions of this sacred number invite us—who have received adoption through the grace of that same Spirit—in many ways to contemplate the invisible things of God and His ineffable works. Surely, the three fifties <note>original: "tres quagenarij" - groups of fifty.</note> indicate that the works of the Trinity are perfect; and the five thirties show that the Triune God is present everywhere; and the eleven tens <note>original: "undecim denarij"</note>, which pertain to eleven steps, demonstrate that the mystery of the holy faith is perfect everywhere. Thus, we sing psalms wisely as we are commanded, if we understand the sacrament <note>In this context, "sacrament" refers to a hidden or sacred mystery.</note> of the psalms: namely, what they wish for: the one hundred and fifty psalms, the songs of the steps, or the fifteen steps themselves, and the ten strings. We weigh these things with subtle investigation so that, having vigilantly discussed all these matters, we may be able to reach an understanding of spiritual psalmody. For that we may begin from those very steps by which one must ascend to the contemplation of higher things—since the number ten is perfect in its kind—it reaches the fifteenth ten by three groups of five tens. It is free to consider what the number three means within the number five, and how both need perfection, especially for a Christian who, having left all things, seeks to be perfect. Certainly, from the twenty-fifth year the law of the <term>Levites</term> <note>Members of the Hebrew tribe of Levi who served as assistants in the Temple.</note> begins to serve in the temple, and from the fiftieth year they cease from service and become guardians of the sacred vessels. And this has its place in three states...

# Joa. Primus Bececordaz

<columns>

It seems that human life is distinguished by certain <term>lustra</term> <note>original: "lustris"; while a "lustrum" usually refers to a five-year period in Roman tradition, the author here redefines it as a twenty-five-year span to fit his theological numerology.</note> such that twenty-five years are ascribed to each of them: according to which <margin>Luke</margin> Luke writes seventy-five generations in his gospel. For there is a reasoning that seems to be contained within this: he who would wish to begin from smaller things and gradually come to perfection with the passage of time, ought to be a layman for twenty-five years, working with his hands at what good he can, until he sees whether he can remain a continent man or not. For another twenty-five years, he should serve the Lord in the office of the <term>clergy</term> <note>The state of being a cleric or ordained minister.</note>. And again, for another twenty-five years, up to the seventy-fifth, he should be free for prayers and psalms, waiting daily and prepared for the hour of his calling. For whatever he survives beyond this is, as it were, beyond the rule; <margin>Pla. 44</margin> <note>Likely a reference to Plato or a specific legal "platea," discussing the natural limits of human life.</note> and thus it is not so much conducted by human law as it is moderated by divine dispensation. He, therefore, who walks thus, does so as if with certain gentle steps, and completes his course as if in fifteen days; because fifteen days seem, not incongruously, to designate as many *lustra*. But he who from childhood itself has run toward three things equally—that is, toward the work which is proper to laymen, toward the doctrine which belongs to clerics, and toward the jubilation <note>A term often used in medieval theology to describe wordless praise or the ecstatic singing of monks.</note> of the monks—this indeed is laudable; all for the sake of the words of the Lord saying: "Watch therefore, for you know not the day nor the hour." He has run, as it were, in five *lustra* and completed his journey. And this indeed is said of those who, whether late or suddenly, convert from the vanity of the world to the service of God. Nevertheless, there are also other *lustra* greater than these, designated in the days of <term>Pentecost</term> <note>The fifty days following Easter, here used as a symbolic timeframe for spiritual maturity.</note>, which absolutely suit the three orders of the elect: according to how each one has his own observers until the end, and each observes what is commanded to him according to his own property. But regarding these, more will follow. Truly, according to the ages of character which are especially to be emulated by any Christian, we can—in five general virtues pertaining individually to the Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of the Lord, and the Advent of the Holy Spirit—assign those three states of human life quite fittingly; because those virtues are not given to all to be possessed equally, nor are they so rooted in them

<column-break/>

who are <term>neophytes</term> <note>original: "neophiti"; meaning "newly planted," referring to those new to the faith or a religious order.</note>, unless perhaps some by a miracle of imitation of the "right hand of the Most High," by which they are made whole and perfect. For he ascends those fifteen steps of Christianity who כך disposes in his heart the Nativity of the Lord, His Passion, Resurrection, and His Ascension into heaven, as well as the Advent of the Holy Spirit, like certain ascents. In individual works or virtues which He signified in them, he should study to preserve three certain modes: by which, by beginning, perfecting, and consuming, he may be able to reach the summit of their perfection. For to these five works must be referred those five <term>trigenaries</term> <note>original: "trigenarij"; groups of thirty, likely referring to the thirty years of Christ's hidden life before His ministry.</note> which are contained in them in spirit: the sum of our perfection. Why in these more than in others? Because in these we are seen to have received those gifts which were given to us for our sake, so that through them we might please God, and being pleasing, might be able to inherit eternal life. For by Christ’s Nativity we are taught to consent to the humble; by Christ’s Passion to act patiently; by Christ’s Resurrection to be strong in faith; by His Ascension to be long-suffering in hope; and by the ascent of the fire <note>The Holy Spirit appearing as tongues of fire.</note>, to be kindled by the fervor of charity. Each one of these is carried forward as if through certain steps so that it may be borne toward perfection, so that in the first it is judged small, in the second middling, and in the third complete. For someone is in the first step of humility when he humbles himself to his superiors, like a servant to a master. In the second, when he humbles himself to an equal. In the third, when he is humbled to inferiors, like a master to a servant. One is in the first step of patience when he suffers lashes for his own sins. He is in the second when he suffers for friends. He is also in the third when he suffers for enemies. And this is indeed regarding two virtues which always look upon humbler things and acquire exaltation for their observers. Concerning faith also, which is the substance of things to be hoped for, something similar must be felt. For someone is in the first step of faith when he believes that those who act well are remunerated by a just God with temporal goods, according to that which is written: <margin>Psalms</margin> "I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread." And that other: "Seek first the kingdom of God and His justice, and all these things shall be added unto you." But they reach the second step when they believe...

</columns>

# Abba. The Book of the Psalter

<columns>

...firmly: in the resurrection of the dead; and that the elect of God lack all the groans of this life. Furthermore, to reach the **third step** is to believe in the future and eternal company of the angels, to dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem and to see Christ the King as he is; to be inebriated by the abundance of the house of the Lord and to drink from the torrent of his delight: that is, to have those gifts of the Holy Spirit of which the Apostle says: *Eye has not seen, O God, without you, what you have prepared for those who love you.* <note>A paraphrase of Isaiah 64:4, famously quoted by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> In the same way, one is said to be in the **first degree of hope** when he hopes, like the children of Israel, for a temporal reward—not based on his own works. He is in the **second degree** when, after the labor of this present life, he hopes that by passing away he will reach the true life; and after the hardships of the world, cross over to rest. Also, to have a new body in the resurrection of the just. He is in the **third degree** when he hopes to enjoy the vision of his God; to remain in that heavenly city of Jerusalem with those blessed ranks of angels; to participate with them in the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and to be counted among the sons of God. Also, one is in the **first degree of charity** when, according to God, he loves his own flesh, parents, namely his relatives—or what is more worthy—his neighbors and friends. He is in the **second degree** when he loves strangers and pilgrims. He is in the **third degree** when he loves his enemies. These are those fifteen steps by which one ascends into the temple of God: because indeed, for him who wishes to go from virtue to virtue and see the God of gods in Zion, it is not enough for him to maintain humility among his elders, unless he also maintains it among his peers and equals; and what is greater than that, among subordinates and servants. Nor is it enough for him to suffer for himself and for his friends, unless his justice abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees: so that, if it is necessary, he undergoes suffering for the salvation of his enemies; so that while showing them the clearest affection of charity, he makes them, as much as in him lies, friends instead of enemies. Nor is it enough to believe that a reward of this present life is given to the worshipers of truth: but also of the future life, and of that homeland which is in the heavens. Nor is it enough to hope for temporal goods from the Lord, unless he also hopes that a new body will be given to him...

<column-break/>

...and the joy of the future life: otherwise we would hope only for the body, and not also for the homeland where there is the vision of peace; as if we were returning to misery again, not to beatitude. Nor is it enough for anyone to love neighbors and friends unless he loves his enemies, as Truth itself <note>In medieval theology, "Truth" is often used as a proper name for Christ.</note> testifies, saying: *If you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? But love your enemies and do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.* <note>Matthew 5:44-46.</note> These are truly those steps by which one ascends into the temple of God: I do not mean that temple which was built by Solomon, King of Jerusalem, and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon; but that temple not made with hands, which is in heaven, to which one arrives by spiritual steps of the mind, as if by **three sets of fifteen** <note>original: "tres quinarios"; referring to the 15 "Songs of Ascents" (Psalms 120–134) which were traditionally sung on the fifteen steps of the Temple.</note>, or rather by **three sets of fifty** <note>original: "tres quinquagenarios"; referring to the 150 Psalms of the Psalter.</note>. For unless someone begins to set a foot in any of these virtues—to go, in a way, and to run—he cannot arrive at their summit and perfection. For it belongs to children to enter these virtues in the **first degree**; to young men in the **second**; to the elderly in the **third**. For the Christian religion has its own ages, which are distinguished not so much by the number of years, but by differences in life.

### ¶ Concerning the three general orders of the elect, and that the fifteen steps and the number of one hundred and fifty psalms pertain to them.

These steps can also be assigned in another way; indeed, they can be assigned in a far higher and more worthy manner in the three orders of the elect, if we take care to venerate their venerable mysteries with the diligence we can manage. First, however, let us disentangle ourselves from other questions that arise here and there, so that we may pass more freely to scrutinize these matters more diligently. Let us proceed more quickly with what has been begun.

# Joachim the First: On the Concordance

<columns>

...it is their place to be in the first degree of the aforementioned virtues; for the clergy to be in the second; and for the monks to be in the third. For it is not permitted for anyone from the order of monks to return to the life of the clergy, just as many pass from the life of the clergy to the life of monks. 

For this reason, the number ten <note>original: *denarius*</note> seems to belong to the married in some way; the number twenty <note>original: *vicenarius*</note> to the clergy (these are two tens together); and the number thirty <note>original: *trigenarius*</note> to the monks (that is, three tens together). And why is this? Because a cleric was originally a layman among laymen, and in the following stage, he began to be a cleric without the status of a layman. Similarly, the monk who reaches this life by degrees: from the beginning, he is a layman among laymen; in the next stage, a cleric with the clergy; and at last, a monk with the monks. 

And although this might sometimes happen otherwise for the sake of another mystery—which is also great—this order is nonetheless more fitting. For indeed, a layman might be received as a monk in the same way as a cleric; however, because a layman is rarely found who knows the sacred letters, the psalms, and everything belonging to the divine office as well as a cleric does, there is a great difference between the two. One is recognized as being more suited for one thing than the other, since one is received more for action <term>action: the active life of service and work</term> and the other for contemplation <term>contemplation: the life of prayer and study</term>. They are like Martha and Mary <note>A reference to the sisters of Lazarus in Luke 10:38–42, traditionally representing the active and contemplative paths of Christian life.</note> dwelling in one house: one after the other, they meet the one Redeemer.

### Why a single "ten" is not assigned to each of the three orders, but rather ten to the first, twenty to the second, and thirty to the third.

It might perhaps seem more fitting to someone that a single "ten" should be assigned to each of the orders—namely, the laity, the clergy, and the monks—because of the mystery of the Holy Trinity. This way, just as three persons are one God, those things belonging to these orders would be equally reduced to the highest point and gathered into one. But this would be most aptly said if psalmody <note>The singing or reciting of the Psalms.</note> belonged equally and in common to all; if we were not dealing here with psalmody alone, but

<column-break/>

commonly with those three exercises, each of which belongs specially to its own order while also being practiced in common. 

Because indeed, psalmody claims the monks for its own, just as the exercise of work claims the married, and doctrine claims the clergy, the likeness of the Trinity is not to be sought in the psalms in that [equal] way, but in another. And indeed, in these three orders, three often-recorded perfections are to be sought, undoubtedly in the mystery of the Trinity: because **work** in a certain way pertains to the Father from whom are all things; **doctrine** to the Son through whom are all things; and **jubilation** <note>original: *iubilatio*, referring here to the joyful singing of praise.</note> to the Holy Spirit in whom are all things. 

Therefore, the functions of all are divided, and yet in some sense, each belongs to all. The Father creates; the Master teaches; Charity gladdens. And yet the Father works all these things, the Son works them, and the Holy Spirit works them, because the operation of the three is one and the same. 

Hence it is that the individual orders need these three: namely, work, doctrine, and praise. And yet, for the first order [the laity], work belongs in the first place, doctrine in the second, and jubilation in the third. For the second [the clergy], doctrine in the first place, with work and jubilation in the second and third. For the third [the monks], jubilation in the first place, reading <note>original: *lectio*, specifically spiritual reading.</note> in the second, and work in the third.

This then is done rightly according to order and reason: if the layman indeed works threefold, if the cleric reads threefold, and if the monk is exercised threefold in the psalms. Indeed, the layman who wishes to approach God with devotion must have a "ten-fold" perfection in divine praises, a "twenty-fold" in doctrine, and a "thirty-fold" in manual work. It is necessary for the devout cleric to have a "ten-fold" perfection in manual work, a "twenty-fold" in psalmody, and a "thirty-fold" in doctrine. But also the true monk must have a "ten-fold" perfection in work, a "twenty-fold" in doctrine, and a "thirty-fold" in psalmody. 

Since, therefore, these three things belong to the three orders, and are so common to all three that nonetheless each belongs specially to each by merit: I would say that the "ten" of psalms is assigned to the laity, the "twenty" to the clergy, and the "thirty" to the monks. For just as a threefold work belongs to the laity, so a threefold psalmody belongs to the monks. For the monks <note>The text here contrasts the freedom of the religious orders with the secular obligations of the laity.</note> can devote themselves equally to God, whereas [the laity] are debtors to wives and children, to parents and kinsmen.

</columns>

Likewise, someone is in the first degree of charity <term>charity: in this context, "caritas" or divine love, the highest of the virtues</term> when, according to God's will, he loves his own flesh, his parents: namely, both relatives or—what is more worthy—neighbors and friends. He is in the second degree when he loves strangers and pilgrims. He is in the third degree when he loves his enemies. These are those fifteen steps <note>original: "quindecim gradus." Referring to the fifteen "Psalms of Ascent" (120–134) sung by pilgrims going up to the Temple.</note> by which one ascends into the temple of God; for truly, he who wishes to go "from virtue to virtue" and "see the God of gods in Zion," it is not enough for him to maintain humility among his superiors, unless he also maintains it among his peers and equals; and what is even greater, among his subordinates and servants. Nor is it enough for him to suffer for himself and for his friends, unless his righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees: so that, if necessary, he undergoes suffering for the salvation of his enemies; so that as a leader, he shows them the most evident affection of charity, making—as much as in him lies—friends out of enemies. Nor is it enough to believe that a reward in the present life is given to the cultivators of truth, but also a reward in the future life: and of that homeland which is in the heavens. Nor is it enough to hope for temporal goods from the Lord, unless he also hopes for a new

<column-break/>

body and the joy of the future life; otherwise, if we hoped only for this time, and not also for the homeland which is the "vision of peace" <note>original: "visio pacis," a traditional etymological definition of the name Jerusalem.</note>, it would be as if we returned again with the reprobate to misery, rather than to blessedness. Nor is it enough for anyone to love relatives and friends, unless he loves his enemies, according to the testimony of Truth itself <note>A title for Christ.</note> which says: *If you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this? But love,* He says, *your enemies and do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven.* <note>Matthew 5:44-46.</note>

These are truly those steps by which one ascends into the temple of God: I do not mean that temple which was built by Solomon, King of Jerusalem, and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon; but into that temple not made with hands, which is in heaven, to which one arrives by the spiritual steps of the mind—as if by three groups of five <note>original: "tres quinarios," referring to the 15 steps.</note>, or rather by three groups of fifty <note>original: "quinquagenarios," referring to the 150 Psalms divided into three sets of 50.</note>. For unless someone begins to set his foot in any of these virtues, and to go forward and progress, he cannot arrive at their summit and perfection. For it is the part of "little ones" to have these virtues in the first degree; of "youths" in the second; and of "elders" in the third. For these are the ages of the Christian religion, which are distinguished not so much by the number of years, but by the difference in one's way of life.

### On the three general orders of the elect, and how the fifteen steps and the number of one hundred and fifty psalms pertain to them.

These steps can also be assigned in another way; indeed, they can be assigned in a far higher and more worthy way among the three orders of the elect <note>The three orders usually refer to the Married, the Clergy, and the Monks.</note>, if we take care to investigate their venerable mysteries with the study we are able to provide. First, however, we must disentangle ourselves from other questions that arise here and there, so that we may more freely pass over to scrutinizing these things more diligently. But let us carry out what has been begun more swiftly.

->Joachim, Book One: The Ten-stringed Psalter<-

it is proper for them <note>The laypeople discussed on the previous page.</note> to be in the first degree of the aforementioned virtues; the clergy in the second; and the monks in the third. For it is not permitted for anyone from the order of monks to return to the life of the clergy, just as many pass from the life of the clergy to the life of monks. For this reason, the number ten <note>original: "denarius"</note> seems to pertain to the married according to one measure; the number twenty <note>original: "vigenarius"</note> to the clergy (these being two tens together); and the number thirty <note>original: "trigenarius"</note> to the monks (that is, three tens together). And why is this? Because a cleric was at first a layman among laymen, and in the following stage he began to be a cleric among the clergy. Likewise, the monk who reaches this life by degrees is at the start a layman with laymen, in the next stage a cleric with the clergy, and finally a monk with the monks. And although this sometimes happens otherwise for the sake of another mystery—which is also great—this order is nevertheless more fitting. Indeed, a layman may be received as a monk in the same way as a cleric; however, because a layman is only rarely found who knows the sacred scriptures and psalms and whatever pertains to the divine office as well as a cleric, there is a great difference between the two. Each is known to be suited to a different way: for one is received more for action, the other for contemplation; so that, like Martha and Mary remaining in one house, one after the other they may meet the one Redeemer. <note>Joachim references the sisters Martha and Mary from Luke 10:38–42, traditional symbols of the "active" life of work and the "contemplative" life of prayer.</note>

### ¶ Why a single ten is not ascribed to each of the three orders, but rather ten to the first, twenty to the second, and thirty to the third.

Perhaps it might seem more fitting to someone that a single ten be ascribed to each of the individual orders—namely, of laypeople, clergy, and monks—because of the mystery of the Holy Trinity; so that just as the three persons are one God, so those things which pertain to these orders might be reduced equally to the highest and collected into one. But this would be most aptly said if psalmody <term>psalmody: the act of singing or chanting the Psalms as a spiritual exercise</term> belonged equally to all in common, and if we were not dealing here with psalmody alone, but generally

<column-break/>

generally with those three exercises, each of which belongs specifically to its own order. But because psalmody claims the monks as its own as properly as the exercise of labor claims the married, and teaching claims the clergy, the likeness of the Trinity is not to be sought in the psalms in that way, but in another. And indeed, in these three orders, three often-written lessons <note>original: "plectiones," likely referring to spiritual readings or sections of the Law.</note> are to be sought, without doubt because in the mystery of the Trinity, labor in a certain way pertains to the Father from whom are all things; teaching to the Son through whom are all things; and jubilation <term>jubilation: a form of wordless or ecstatic singing in praise of God</term> to the Holy Spirit in whom are all things. Thus, these things belong to everyone, and yet according to a certain measure, each belongs to each. The Father creates, the Teacher <note>The Son/Christ</note> teaches, and Charity <note>The Holy Spirit</note> makes one joyful. And yet the Father works all these things, the Son works them, and the Holy Spirit works them, for the operation of the three is one and the same. Hence it is that the individual orders need these three things: namely, labor, teaching, and praise. Yet for the first order <note>laypeople</note>, labor pertains to them in the first place, teaching in the second, and jubilation in the third. For the second order <note>clergy</note>, teaching in the first place, then labor and jubilation in the second and third. For the third order <note>monks</note>, jubilation in the first place, reading in the second, and labor in the third. This is then rightly done according to order and reason: if the layman indeed works in a triple measure; if the cleric reads in a triple measure; and if the monk is exercised in the psalms in a triple measure. Indeed, it is necessary for the layman who wishes to draw near to God in devotion to have a ten-fold perfection in divine praises, a twenty-fold in teaching, and a thirty-fold in the labor of his hands. It is necessary for the devoted cleric to have a ten-fold perfection in the labor of hands, twenty-fold in psalmody, and thirty-fold in teaching. But it is also necessary for the true monk to have a ten-fold perfection in labor, twenty-fold in teaching, and thirty-fold in psalmody. Therefore, since these three belong to the three—and are so common to all three—yet specifically each belongs to each by merit: I would say that the ten of the psalms is ascribed to the laypeople, the twenty to the clergy, and the thirty to the monks. For just as triple labor belongs to the laypeople, so triple psalmody belongs to the monks. For they <note>the laypeople</note> cannot be equally free for God, since they are debtors to wives and children, parents and kinsfolk.

Monks are assigned the number 30 for psalmody because their life is dedicated most fully to the "jubilation" of the Holy Spirit, free from worldly ties.</summary>

## Why a single ten is not ascribed to each of the three orders, but rather ten to the first, twenty to the second, and thirty to the third.

Perhaps it would seem more fitting to someone that a single "ten" be ascribed to each of the orders—namely, the laypeople, the clergy, and the monks—because of the mystery of the Holy Trinity. This would be so that, just as three persons are one God, those things which pertain to these orders might be reduced equally to the highest point and gathered into one. But this would be most aptly said if <term>psalmody</term> <note>The act of singing or reciting the Psalms</note> pertained equally to everyone in common, and if we were not treating specifically of psalmody here, but commonly...

<column-break/>

...commonly of those three exercises, each of which specially pertains to its own order. Because psalmody claims the monks so properly for itself, just as the exercise of work claims the married and doctrine claims the clergy, the likeness of the Trinity must not be sought in the psalms in that way, but in another. And indeed, in these three orders, the three aforementioned perfections are to be sought, without doubt in the mystery of the Trinity: because work in some way pertains to the **Father**, from whom are all things; doctrine to the **Son**, through whom are all things; and jubilation <note>original: "iubilatio," referring to the joyful singing of God's praise</note> to the **Holy Spirit**, in whom are all things. Therefore, they belong to the Lord of all, and yet, in a certain sense, each belongs to each. The Father creates; the Teacher teaches; Charity brings joy. And yet are not all these things one work? The Father works, the Son works, and the Holy Spirit works, because the operation of the three is one and the same. Hence it is that the individual orders need these three things: namely, work, doctrine, and praise. Yet, for the first order <note>The laypeople</note>, work pertains in the first place, doctrine in the second, and jubilation in the third. For the second order <note>The clergy</note>, doctrine in the first place, then work and jubilation in the second and third. For the third order <note>The monks</note>, jubilation in the first place, reading in the second, and work in the third. This is then done rightly according to order and reason: if the layman works three-fold, if the cleric reads three-fold, and if the monk is exercised three-fold in the psalms. Indeed, it is necessary for the layman who wishes to draw near to God in devotion to have a "ten-fold" perfection in divine praises, a "twenty-fold" in doctrine, and a "thirty-fold" in the work of his hands. It is also necessary for the devout cleric to have a ten-fold perfection in the work of his hands, a twenty-fold in psalmody, and a thirty-fold in doctrine. But the true monk must also have a ten-fold perfection in work, a twenty-fold in doctrine, and a thirty-fold in psalmody. Therefore, since these three belong to the three, and are so common to the three that each specifically belongs to its own by merit: I would say the "ten" of psalms is ascribed to the laypeople, the "twenty" to the clergy, and the "thirty" to the monks. Because just as a three-fold work belongs to the laypeople, so a three-fold psalmody belongs to the monks. For those who are debtors to wives and children, to parents and kinsmen, cannot be equally free for God...

### Abbot. Book of the Psalter <note>original: "Abba. Liber Psalterii," referring to the *Psalterium Decem Chordarum* (Psalter of Ten Strings) by Joachim of Fiore</note>

...whatever they [the laypeople] have from the labor of their hands or live by their own expenses. Along with these are those sustained by the offerings of the faithful, by tithes and firstfruits <note>In the medieval church, "firstfruits" were the first agricultural produce of a season given as an offering</note>; nor are these clerics themselves, who are bound to minister to the churches and give back to those from whom they receive offerings, to be compared with those who have left fathers and mothers and all things for the sake of sacred devotion, if they should take up a more powerful path. For it is also said by the Apostle: "He who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided." <note>original: "Qui at̄ cū vxore est: sollicitus est que sunt mūdī quō placeat vxori z diuisus est"; citing 1 Corinthians 7:33-34</note> But what then? Are all to be compelled to leave everything and become monks? Especially those who not only cannot, but even if they could, do not wish to; for the less they acknowledge, the less they love?
**Abstinence.** <note>original: "Abst̄." This likely marks a response or a distinction regarding asceticism</note> This is not a matter of necessity, but of will. Rather, some are so bound in that lower life by the bond of necessity <note>Refers here to the legal and moral bond of marriage</note> that even if they wish to change their life and leave their wives, it is not permitted, lest something worse happen. But what shall they do? Let them do what they can: let them walk with a slower step, lest being too burdened they fail on the way. But even those who, by their way of life, are to be considered "youths" <note>original: "adolescentes"; in this context, spiritual beginners or those not yet ready for the rigors of the monastery</note> are not to be forced to a higher grade, to sell everything and give to the poor to enter the fellowship of those serving God; but only if they knock [at the door] should they be encouraged, lest perhaps being offended—like that young man we read of in the Gospel—they turn backward; and not only fail to do what they are advised, but even shrink away from their accustomed way of life. Nor should it be admitted that the past way of life of that young man could not have sufficed for eternal life, since Truth itself <note>A common medieval title for Jesus</note> gave testimony to him, saying: "Do this and you shall live." <note>Luke 10:28</note> But clearly it was not sufficient for *perfection*—I mean that perfection which the Lord indicated a little later, saying: "You who have followed me will sit upon twelve seats judging the twelve tribes of Israel." <note>Matthew 19:28</note> There is a difference, however, between those who wish but cannot, and those who do not wish, even if the power is granted. For those who wish but cannot, being held back by some just necessity, though they are not monks in their <term>habit</term> <note>The distinctive clothing of a religious order, signifying their status</note>, they are so in mind and will; and therefore they should not despair of participating in 그 glory which the Lord showed when he said: "If you wish to be perfect, sell all and give to the poor and come, follow me." But those who are able and do not wish to: even if they are not to be despaired of regarding their life because of their

<column-break/>

keeping of the other commandments; if indeed the kingdom of God is open to them too, they are nonetheless apart from that glory designated in the City; because he who does not want the lot of the peasants here <note>Referring to the humble status of a monk or the "poor in spirit" in this world</note> cannot be counted among the nobles within the protection of the walls there. Nor should it trouble you that the Lord says: "It is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven," <note>Matthew 19:23</note> because "the kingdom of heaven" is not always to be understood as that eternal homeland in which all the elect will be; but rather a certain private glory and blessedness of the saints which is granted only to those who strive lawfully, as John says in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. [Concerning] the Beast and the image and the number of its name. Indeed, they conquer the Beast who are prepared to die first for the faith rather than obey the wicked man (so as to desert their faith). They conquer the image who, just as they claim to know God with words, prove it with works, abstaining from those sins called "criminal" <note>Mortal or grave sins</note>. They conquer the number of its name who strive to abstain from that multitude of sins called "venial" <note>Lesser sins that do not fully separate a person from God's grace</note>; judging to be significant among perfect men that which the common folk judge as venial or trivial. So that John might show how much difference there is between these and those, and to whom the kingdom chiefly pertains, he says: "I saw thrones and they sat upon them, and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and who did not worship the beast nor its image, nor received its mark on their foreheads or in their hands; they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years." <note>Revelation 20:4</note> Concerning those who suffered for Christ or strove lawfully for the Trinity, it is said they live and reign; but of the others this is not said; then "books were opened, and another book was opened which is the book of life, and the dead were judged from what was written in the books according to their works." <note>Revelation 20:12</note> Note what John says: "And they were judged according to their works," and compare it with the words of the Lord saying: "You who have followed me will sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel," recognizing that only the saints judge with Christ, while the others are to be judged, according to what is written in the Psalms: "He has called..." <note>Psalm 50:4</note>

### Joachim, First Book on the Harmony <note>original: "Joa. Primus De Cōcordaz," referring to Joachim of Fiore’s *Liber de Concordia Novi et Veteris Testamenti* (Book on the Harmony of the New and Old Testaments)</note>

from above and from the earth to distinguish His people from people. Indeed, we say this to show, according to the judgment of truth, how great a distance there is between those devoted Christians who do not wish to leave themselves and their possessions, and those who, leaving all things under a shepherd who holds the place of Christ, live in community. One of these is of a lower or middle righteousness; the other is integral and consummate. Therefore, the faithful laity and clergy are not to be compelled to live for God by leaving all things, but rather warned—at least if that evening hour has not yet arrived in which the righteous Lot is compelled by angels to leave <margin>Genesis</margin> Sodom and Gomorrah, and that hour in which the Lord commands a flight to the mountains. Finally, Lot himself passed from Sodom into Segor, and from Segor he ascended into the mountain, fearing to remain any longer in a place not commanded but merely permitted to him. But if anyone recognizes that this hour is pressing, he is not to be rebuked if he compels some, desiring to hide them from the face of Him who sits upon the throne and to make them safe from the hour of temptation that is to come upon <margin>Apocalypse</margin> the whole world, to tempt and oppress those dwelling on the earth. Otherwise, each of these three groups has its own perfection, though not equal; rather, each has what is designated in the Gospel in that place where the Truth says: "One thirty-fold, another sixty-fold, another a hundred-fold." <note>A reference to the Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13:8). Joachim interprets these numbers as the three orders: 30 for the laity, 60 for the clergy, and 100 for the monks.</note>

### ¶ How the order of the laity is to be likened to children, the clergy to youths, and monks to elders.

It is not absurd that the order of the laity, which is also called the "conjugal" order <note>The state of being married</note>, is likened to little ones in Christ; the clergy, who retain their own property, to youths; and those who live in community <note>monks</note> to older men. For just as the ages of bodies are distinguished by years, so the ages of souls are to be distinguished by their character. Yet the order of the clergy has its distinct perfection, as I have said, in the number twenty, just as the laity have that perfection which pertains to the number ten; for indeed ten is a perfect number. Hence not only is the Father together with the Son and Holy Spirit one perfect God, but even both Father and <margin>Abbot</margin> Son together, or the Holy Spirit; thus also the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone. For just as we are compelled by

<column-break/>

Christian truth to confess each person individually as God or Lord, so we are forbidden by the Catholic religion to say there are three gods or lords. For quantity is not to be considered in figurative things, but perfection. For God in each person lacks "quantity," and for this reason—as we have already said in the previous book—one person is not something less than three together. But this must also be noted: those who were baptized with the baptism of John the Baptist (who publicly preached the Son of God), when asked by Paul if they had received the Holy Spirit upon believing, <margin>Acts</margin> responded: "But we have not even heard if there is a Holy Spirit." <note>Acts 19:2</note> The Pharisees too, when asked about Christ, whose son He was, responded: "David's." When the Lord objected to them: "How then does David in the spirit call Him Lord, if He is the son of God?" <note>Matthew 22:43-45</note> they did not know how to answer, because as unlearned people and "little ones" <margin>Psalms</margin> they did not know that God has a Son equal to Himself. For what if they read: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," if they did not understand what they read? So also the Apostle rebukes certain people baptized in Christ, calling them "little ones" and "carnal," saying that the "animal man" <note>or "natural man" (1 Corinthians 2:14)</note> does not understand the things of the Spirit of God. For what if those baptized had received the Holy Spirit? Did not the disciples of Christ also receive the Holy Spirit because they were baptized in Christ? And yet of this John says: <margin>John</margin> "The Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified." <note>John 7:39</note> We say this to show that in the first time there was a manifest revelation of the Father alone; in the second, of the Son; in the third, of the Holy Spirit. From this, it is also shown that the carnal people who were under the Law until John the Baptist were permitted to come to the knowledge of one God, but were not permitted to come to the knowledge of His Son, except for certain patriarchs and prophets to whom the Spirit of God revealed this. The Christian people, by the very fact that they know the Son, also know the Father. This follows the form of reason. Indeed, when we see a barbarian man, we doubt whether he is a father or not; because we do not perceive him to be a father simply because we believe him capable of procreating, for we see many such men who do not have sons. But if we see a child wandering...

# Abbot. The Book of the Psalter <note>original: "Abba. Liber Psalterii," likely referring to the *Psalterium Decem Cordarum* (Psaltery of Ten Strings) by the 12th-century mystic Joachim of Fiore.</note>

...those who live by the labor of their hands or at their own expense. Along with those who are sustained by the offerings of the faithful, tithes, and first-fruits; nor should the clerics themselves, who are held to minister to the churches, return possessions to those from whom they receive offerings: if sacred devotion chooses better things, it should be compared with those who have left fathers and mothers and all things. Whence the Apostle says: 
> "He who is with a wife is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided." <note>original: "Qui autem cum uxore est: sollicitus est quae sunt mundi quomodo placeat uxori et divisus est." See 1 Corinthians 7:33-34.</note>

But what then? Must all be forced to become monks by leaving everything? Especially those who not only cannot, but even if they could, do not wish to, because the less they know, the less they love? **Far be it.** This is not a matter of necessity, but of will. Rather, some are bound in that lowlier life by the bond of necessity: so that even if they wished to change their life by leaving their wives, it would not be permitted, lest something worse should follow. What then shall they do? Let them do what they can; let them walk with a slower step, lest being too heavily burdened they fail on the way. But even those who, by their way of life, are to be considered youths <note>referring to those new or young in the spiritual life</note>, are not to be forced to a higher grade—that having sold everything and given to the poor, they should enter into the company of those serving God—yet if they knock, they are to be encouraged: lest perhaps, being offended like that young man of whom we read in the Gospel, they turn back, and not only fail to do what they are advised, but even shrink from their accustomed way of life. Nor must it be said that the previous way of life could not have sufficed for that young man for eternal life, since Truth itself bears witness to him, saying: 
> "Do this, and you shall live." <note>original: "Hoc fac et vives." See Luke 10:28.</note>

But clearly it was not sufficient for him for perfection—I mean that perfection which the Lord indicated a little later, saying: 
> "You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel." <note>original: "Vos qui secuti estis me sedebitis super sedes duodecim iudicantes duodecim tribus israel." See Matthew 19:28.</note>

Yet there is a difference between those who wish for perfection but cannot, and those who do not wish it, even if the power to do so is granted. For those who wish but cannot, being held back by some just necessity, though they are not monks in their habit, they are so in spirit and will: and therefore they are not to be despaired of regarding a participation in that glory which the Lord showed when He said: 
> "If you wish to be perfect, sell all things and give to the poor, and come, follow me." <note>original: "Si vis perfectus esse vende omnia et da pauperibus et veni sequere me." See Matthew 19:21.</note>

But those who can and do not wish it, even these are not to be despaired of in this life, on account of their keeping of the other

<column-break/>

commandments; for indeed the kingdom of God also proceeds from them. They are, however, partially excluded from the glory designated in the city <note>referring to the New Jerusalem</note>: for he who does not wish to have a part of the common folk <note>original: "rusticorum," referring to the laity or the unlearned in a spiritual sense</note> here, cannot be numbered among the nobles there within the protection of the wall. Nor should that saying move us when the Lord says: 
> "It is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." <note>original: "Difficile esse divitem ingredi in regnum caelorum." See Matthew 19:23.</note>

Because the "kingdom of heaven" is not always to be understood as that eternal homeland in which all the elect shall be, but rather as a certain private glory and blessedness of the saints, which is granted only to those who "strive lawfully," as John says in the Apocalypse: 
> "The beast and its image and the number of its name." <note>original: "Bestiam et imaginem et numerum nominis eius." See Revelation 15:2.</note>

Truly, they overcome the beast who are prepared to die first for the faith, rather than obey the unjust commands of the impious (so that they might desert their faith). They overcome the image who, as they know God in words, so also profess Him in works, abstaining from those sins which are called "criminal" <note>referring to mortal or grave sins</note>. They overcome the number of his name who choose to abstain from that multitude of sins which are called "venial" <note>referring to minor or pardonable sins</note>: judging it proper for perfect men to be counted by name, while what is judged among the common crowd is venial and very small. But so that John might show how much difference there is between the former and the latter, and to whom the kingdom properly belongs: "He saw," he says, 
> "thrones, and they sat upon them; and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus, and for the word of God, and who had not worshiped the beast nor his image, nor received his mark on their foreheads or in their hands; they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years." <note>original: "sedes et sederunt super eas..." See Revelation 20:4.</note>

Of these who suffered for Christ or strove lawfully with perseverance, it is said that they "live and reign"; but of the others, this is not said, but only that "the books were opened, and another book was opened which is the book of life: and the dead were judged from those things written in the books according to their works." <note>original: "aperti sunt libri..." See Revelation 20:12.</note> Pay attention to what John says: "And judgment was given to them according to their works," and combine this with the words of the Lord saying: 
> "You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel," <note>Matthew 19:28</note>

and you will recognize that only the saints judge with Christ; the others, however, are to be judged according to that which is written in the Psalms: "He called..."

## ¶ That the order of the laity should be likened to children, the clergy to youths, and the monks to the elderly.

**Not** without reason, the order of the laity—which involves the marital state—is to be likened to little children in Christ. The order of the clergy, who retain their own property, to youths. But the order of those who live in common <note>the monks</note>, to the elderly. For just as the ages of bodies are distinguished by years, so the ages of souls are to be distinguished by their character. Nevertheless, the order of the clergy has its own distinct perfection, as I have already said, in the number twenty; just as the laity's perfection pertains to the "denarius" <note>the number ten</note>, because the denarius is a perfect number. For not only is God perfect as Father together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, but also both together—Father <margin>Abbot.</margin> and Son, or Holy Spirit—and even the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone. For just as we are compelled by Christian truth to confess each person individually as God or

<column-break/>

Lord, so we are prohibited by the Catholic religion from saying there are three gods or lords. For quantity is not to be considered in things that are likenesses, but rather perfection. For God, in each individual person, lacks quantity, and because of this—as we have already said in the previous book—one person is not anything less than the three together. But it should also be noted that those who had been baptized with the baptism of John <note>John the Baptist</note>, who publicly preached the Son of God, were asked by Paul if they had received the Holy Spirit <margin>Acts</margin> when they believed. They replied: "We have not even heard if there is a Holy Spirit." The Pharisees also, when questioned about Christ, whose son he was, replied: "David’s." When the Lord countered them, "How then does David in the spirit call him Lord <margin>Psalms</margin> if he is the Son of God?" they did not know what to answer, because as unlearned people and "little children," they did not know that the Son was equal to God. For what if they read, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," if they did not understand what they read? So too the Apostle rebukes certain people baptized in Christ, calling them "little children" and "carnal," saying that the "animal man" <note>original: "animales hominem," the natural or soulish man who lacks spiritual insight.</note> does not understand the things that are of the Spirit of God. For what if those baptized had received the Holy Spirit? Did not the disciples of Christ also receive the Holy Spirit when they were baptized in Christ? <margin>John</margin> And yet John says of him: "The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified." We say this for this reason: to show that in the first period, a manifest revelation of the Father alone was made; in the second, of the Son; in the third, of the Holy Spirit. # Father. Book of the Psalter <note>original: "Abba. Liber Psalterij." "Abba" is the Aramaic word for Father, often used in the New Testament to denote an intimate relationship with God.</note>

When we hear an infant <note>original: "lactentem," literally a "suckling"</note> at its mother's breasts, or when we look at a child playing, we recognize that he must have—or must have had—a father. Thus, upon hearing the voice of a boy, we are accustomed to ask whose son he might be, judging by his appearance that he has a father. Indeed, it would be most absurd to ask about someone "whose father he is" <note>This is a logical point: we identify a child by their source (the father), but we don't define the existence of a child by asking who the father's "father" is in the same way.</note>. Furthermore, it is asked whether one has a son; and if it is established that he does, one does not ask whose father he is, but rather who his son is, by the same logic.

The new people who are called "Christians," by the very fact that they know Christ is called the "Son of God," necessarily understand that he has a Father; for he who has no father cannot be called a son. However, it does not follow that because one knows Christ was made flesh, one can immediately understand the things that are of the Spirit of God; for, as it is said, "the natural man <note>original: "animalis homo," a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:14</note> does not understand the things of the Spirit of God." For the Holy Spirit himself was not made flesh like the Word <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to Jesus Christ</note>, so as to be able to be perceived by carnal men.

But, <margin>John</margin> as it is written: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, the Spirit of Truth, whom this world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you shall know him, because he will abide with you and will be in you." <note>A translation of John 14:16-17</note> But if this same Spirit is the gift of God, how can we possess the gift if we do not first recognize the one to whom the gift belongs? For this reason, the promise was spoken: "Behold," he says, "I send the promise of my Father upon you." <margin>John</margin> Who says this? Jesus Christ. For he gave the Spirit of promise to those who had recognized that the Father had sent him.

From all these things, it is clearly gathered that the **First People** <note>The people of the Old Testament</note> were led to some measure of knowledge of God the Father; the **Second People** <note>The Christians of the New Testament</note> to a better knowledge of the Father and the Son; and the **Third People** are to be led more fully to the knowledge of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the entire Trinity. It is not that the Son was not expected to come from the beginning, but that the Jews did not know whether Christ, whom they expected, was the Son of God. Likewise, many Christians often speak of the Holy Spirit, yet they do not know the greatness of his goodness, and they are

<column-break/>

ignorant of his power and the gifts of his graces. Nevertheless, because the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Son alone, but from the Father and the Son <note>This refers to the "Filioque" doctrine, a major point of theology regarding the Trinity</note>, he ought to have become known to that people to whom the Son-made-man became known—though perhaps not as fully or solemnly as he will be to that people who shall be the **Third** from the first. This Third People pertains more specifically to the Holy Spirit than the other two. Truly, as these three steps are noted in the three orders written above, he who receives more ought to rejoice more; and he who recognizes God more fully ought to sing psalms and praise him more abundantly.

### Again, on the likeness of the three orders, and the perfection of the number written above; also concerning the numbers five and seven.

The Book of Psalms, which is the focus of our current discussion, reaches its fulfillment, as it were, in three Jubilees <note>A "Jubilee" here refers to a grouping of fifty. The Book of Psalms contains 150 psalms, which Joachim divides into three sets of 50 to represent his three ages.</note>; for the entire collection of psalms consists of three fifties. Blessed is he who can possess what the first fifty signifies. More blessed is he who obtains what the second designates. Most blessed is he who is not excluded from what the third signifies.

Perfect God is the Father; perfect is the Son; perfect is the Holy Spirit. However, he who believes and fears, but does not understand, is led as if to the knowledge of the Father alone, which among the ancients was called "Fear." Hence it is said: "Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac." <note>A reference to Genesis 31:53</note> And it was fitting that among that people, God was called "Fear," because at that time he <note>the people</note> was still a small child; for it is characteristic of small children to dread and tremble, as they are ignorant of the fairness of judgment and do not understand what they read.

But those who believe and understand are led, as it were, to the knowledge of the Father and the Son, because the Son is the Wisdom of the Father; and this indeed belongs to young men <note>original: "adolescentulorum," referring to the second stage of spiritual growth</note>. But those who believe, understand, and find delight, having the knowledge of the Father and the Son, are known to have reached the understanding of the Holy Spirit; for he himself is the delight and love of God—he is the "honey from the rock" and "oil from the hardest stone." <note>References to Psalm 81:16 and Deuteronomy 32:13</note> He is, I say, the honey from the rock; he is the spiritual joy with which the Psalmist exulted for it to be given to him, saying...

# Joachim’s First Book on the Ten-Stringed Psalter <note>original: "Joa. Primus Decēcordaz." Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202) was a mystic and theologian known for his theory of three ages of world history.</note>

<margin>psal. 50</margin>
"To my hearing you will give joy and gladness, and the bones that were humbled shall exult." <note>original: "Auditui meo dabis gaudiū & letitiā & exultabunt ossa humiliata," quoting Psalm 51:8 (Psalm 50 in the Vulgate).</note> And if the first of these belonged to children, and the second to youths, it is clear that the third belongs to the elderly: those who, for God’s sake, feel nothing of the flesh, desire nothing foul, and covet nothing earthly or fleeting. If, therefore, you wish to refer these three stages to those three ages in which the works of God are especially to be consulted, you will find that the first "man" <note>The "first man" here refers to a stage of human development or a specific era of history.</note> belongs to that time which was under the Law. The second belongs to the time of Grace, lasting until the conversion of Israel. The third belongs to the time of fuller grace, which will exist from that time until the very end. For in the first period, the people were under the oldness of the letter, seeking to learn the Law of Moses and to walk according to the flesh in its commandments. In the second, having been freed from the slavery of the Law, they were occupied with the truth of the Gospel. In the third, freed from the labor of suffering, it will be granted to them to devote themselves to prayer and to be free for divine praises. In this matter, one must consider how great the perfection of the number fifty <term>quinquagenarius; the number fifty</term> is. It is not without reason that the year of remission <note>The "Year of Jubilee" described in Leviticus 25.</note> occurred through cycles of fifty years, signifying that great Jubilee which is to come at the very end of the age—following the two others which, as God grants, will be discussed in the writings below. For if it is divided by ten, it is known to have five decades. If indeed it is divided by seven, with the unit <note>original: "monade"</note> subtracted, it is proven to contain seven weeks within itself. However, it cannot easily be explained in speech how much perfection lies in the numbers five and seven, which when joined together rise to the number twelve. Nevertheless, as God provides, we shall speak of this in what follows. But in the present place, among the many things to be said about the perfection of the number five, I do not wish to pass over this in silence: although there are many gifts of God distributed among the faithful people for their benefit, none are so necessary to everyone in common as those five virtues about which we shall say much, and have already spoken somewhat above: namely, humility, patience, faith, hope, and charity. Because each individual person of the Trinity is perfect God—

<column-break/>

—for the Father can do nothing that the Son and the Holy Spirit cannot do equally—there are for us three sets of fifty psalms under the same significance. This is not so that a "multiplicity" is understood to exist in God, but so that the Trinity of persons is not denied. For just as it is not one Christ who is signified in Isaac, another who is signified in Solomon, and another who is signified in John the Baptist—but he is one and the same who is signified in these three, as in many others—so also the virtues designated in the first fifty psalms are not different from those in the second or third sets. Rather, they are the very same virtues signified in all three, inspired not by the Father alone, or the Son, but simultaneously by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If this is so, what does this threefold significance of the same virtues confer? Should I say "significance" or "bestowal"? If we say both, it is true. For this reason, the Holy Spirit, who had been given to the apostles so that they might believe in Jesus, is recorded as being given again and again. If it is asked: what benefit is there in being given again what has already been given? I ask: what benefit is there for scarlet cloth <note>original: "cocco"</note> to be dipped in the dye and pulled out, and dipped in it again, until it reaches the perfect color? Is it because that liquid is different? Not at all. It is because it did not receive the tint perfectly the first time. So it is with those people who were taught by Moses; they recognized the Almighty God, but not as perfectly as the Christian people who were taught by Christ Jesus, according to that doctrine which befits "little ones" in Christ. But even these are not as perfect as the spiritual people among whom holy men speak wisdom. As I have already said, the capacity of children is one thing, that of youths another, and that of the elderly another; children progress in virtues in one way, youths in another, and the elders in yet another. So too is the order of the married: the more one seeks to please a wife and to raise children, the less one can be intent on the things that are of God—unless it happens that someone is so prevented by grace that, having a wife, he is as if he had none, and possessing many things, he is as if he possessed nothing. Truly, the order of the clergy is less burdened in this—

# Abba. The Book of the Psalter <note>original: "Abba. Liber Psalterij"</note>

...is more capable in the spiritual life; yet less so than monks because of parents and friends to whom they are joined by affection. Indeed, what is more, because of the people committed to them, the overseer has taken up the care of a physician for those with diseased morals. Truly, the order of monks ought not to be a boy or a small child in their senses; in "senses," I say, not in "malice." Rather, by the very right of their name, 
<margin>Gregory</margin>
they should be whole and perfect. They should not be a boy or a child who has need of milk and not of solid food, but advanced and an elder, according to that saying of the holy Pope Gregory, which he wrote concerning the venerable man Benedict, saying: "From the very time of his childhood, bearing the heart of an elder, he gave his mind to no pleasure." <note>original: "Ab ipso pueritie tempore cor gerens senile: nulli animum dedit voluptati." A famous quote from St. Gregory the Great’s *Life of Saint Benedict* describing Benedict’s early maturity.</note> Truly, from the time of his childhood: because, unless (says the Lord) "you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." <note>Matthew 18:3</note> For he who is an elder among men is a child before God, and vice-versa. 

But to come to the sum of the matter: the **number ten** <term>denarius; the number ten, often symbolizing the Ten Commandments or the basic level of faith</term> pertains to the **layman** in his knowledge of the deity. In this, he clings to the "letter" of the Old Testament by imitating the Patriarchs in the procreation of children. This "letter," if we understand it healthily, possesses the image of the Father, who is Unbegotten Wisdom. 

The **number twenty** pertains to the **clerics** in this: that knowing and venerating the letter of the Old Testament, they cling much more to the letter of the New Testament by imitating the Apostles, who were together with the holy women and those coming continually into the Church. This "letter" was indeed propagated from the letter of the Old Testament, having itself the image of the Only-Begotten God, who is Begotten Wisdom. And as Saint Augustine says: 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
"Wisdom from Wisdom." <note>original: "Sapientia de sapientia."</note> 

The **number thirty** <term>trigenarius; the number thirty, representing the Trinity and the highest spiritual grade</term> pertains to the **monks** in this: that knowing and venerating the letter of the Old and New Testaments in the Patriarchs and Apostles (whom they know to be chosen and holy), they cling to the **spiritual understanding** <term>intellectui spirituali; the deep, mystical meaning of scripture beyond the literal text</term> which proceeds from both "letters." -> ¶ According to the perfection of the number discussed, the celestial Jerusalem may be built. <-

The Truth <note>i.e., Christ</note> testifies that there were five wise virgins: because that heavenly city, Jerusalem, is placed in a certain land so that it is written to have walls on four sides (that is, from the East and from the West, from the North and the South). But what is said there concerning the perfection of the walls? "From the East," it says, "three gates; from the West, three gates; from the North, three gates; from the South, three gates." <note>A reference to the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:13.</note> Behold, in the four walls there are twelve gates; by the perfection of ten, like the "ten-ness" of the Psalms, there are twelve of them, making **one hundred and twenty**. <note>12 gates x 10 = 120. But if each of the four parts has three perfections, what remains except that a fifth part be known as distinct by the same reasoning (that is, in the city itself, in the suburbs, and the villages)? For if even the fifth part of the city is divided into three sections—according to how the whole world is known to be divided into Asia, Europe, and Africa—there are assigned in them, and fittingly, the three "tens" <note>denarijs</note> which remained to reach the fifteenth number and perfection.

I believe the most blessed man **Benedict** contemplated these venerable mysteries when he established that twelve Psalms were to be said on feast days, marking them by connecting canticles from the Prophets. And he believed that he who is the **Abbot** <note>original: "Abba"</note> must be blessed: because just as the twelve Psalms seem to pertain to those orders designated in the gates, so the three canticles pertain to those orders designated in the city, the suburbs, and the villages: that is, to those orders which...
