# Joachim the First: The Ten-Stringed Psaltery <note>original: "Ioa. Primus Decêcorday." This refers to Joachim of Fiore’s work *Psalterium Decem Chordarum*, where he uses the ten-stringed instrument as a metaphor for divine order.</note>

...live under a rule or an abbot. Indeed, in the present church, we recognize four spiritual orders, and a fifth general one. The spiritual orders are: the apostles, the martyrs, the confessors, and the virgins. The general order, however, consists of those living in the common life <term>common life; "communi vita," referring to the general body of the faithful or secular clergy who do not follow a strict monastic rule</term>. And these things are indeed so.

### ¶ Why the mystery of the Trinity is repeated five times.

Now, why should the mystery of the Trinity be repeated or reiterated five times, since there are only three persons of the Godhead? It would seem that any three mystical things would suffice for their significance. I see no reason for this unless it is because, even if the one God is a Trinity, He is nevertheless spoken of and understood in multiple ways. This is just as if one man were called a "soldier" because he holds a military belt, a "teacher" because he has disciples, a "father" because he has sons, a "lord" because he has servants, and many such things. According to this, five relative names—spoken in relation to something else—seem to suit the Triune and one God, just as there are five parts of the city, and each part has its own property. 

For the name of "Father" seems to belong to the eastern part; the name of "Lord" to the northern part; the name of "Teacher" to the western part; the name of "Friend" or "Spouse" to the southern part; and the name of "Judge" or "King" to the body of the city itself. In saying this, however, we do not mean to say that in that heavenly city there is fighting, terror, or harsh discipline; rather, we mean that while it is placed in this earthly pilgrimage, it is named thus in its various parts. 

Hence the Apostle says: "To each one of us grace is given according to the measure of the gift of Christ." <note>Ephesians 4:7</note> For which reason he says: "Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men." And he himself gave some indeed to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, and so on. <note>Ephesians 4:8, 11</note> And this is indeed while we are in this life. In the fatherland <note>original: "in patria," a standard medieval term for Heaven, our true home</note> it is not so, yet it is "as if" it were so; for even if the battle ceases, each person will nevertheless be placed in a dwelling suitable for them, so that they may receive their own reward according to their labor <note>original: "sm suum laborem" (secundum suum laborem)</note>: that is, apostles with apostles, 

<column-break/>

martyrs with martyrs, doctors with doctors, virgins with virgins, and community members with community members. 

But to begin from the eastern part, following the order of the four living creatures <note>The "four animals" from the visions in Ezekiel and Revelation, traditionally associated with the four Evangelists</note>: the first relation is of the Father to the Son. The second is of the Lord to his servants—or, to express the service itself, to his soldiers. The third is of the Teacher to the disciples. The fourth is of the Spouse to the bride—or of a friend to friends. Truly, the fifth relation is of the King to the kingdom, or of the Judge and Ruler to the people. For it belongs principally to Him who created the people to judge them, just as Paul says: "We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ." <note>Romans 14:10</note> And it is His right to choose from that same family those whom He may make judges of others. 

Therefore, since the almighty God is Father, Lord, Teacher, Friend (or Spouse), and Judge, he is rightly spoken of and understood in multiple ways even though He is one—not as He is in Himself, but in relation to others. 

But if one asks why there are three names in each gate or part of the city instead of just one, it is because not only must the Father be called "Father" in relation to his adopted sons—
<margin>Psalms</margin>
concerning which it is said: "I have said, you are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High" <note>Psalm 82:6</note>—but the Son and the Holy Spirit must also be called so. And not only the Father must be called Lord, or Teacher, or Friend, or Judge, or King, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit. For just as 
<margin>Revelation</margin>
Abraham alone was not called the patriarch and father of the children of Israel, but also Isaac and Jacob, so the Father alone is not to be called the Father of Christians and of all the faithful, but also the Son and the Holy Spirit. 

That is why the four living creatures, which signify these four orders, cry out with one voice: "Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty," because in each of the four parts of the city the entire Trinity has worked and is working its deeds while the city still journeys as a pilgrim on the earth: imparting to some the prerogative of faith, to others the word of wisdom, to others the word of knowledge, and similar gifts. It was not said of the Throne, however, that it also cried out "Holy, Holy, Holy" like the four animals, because that is revealed...

For it remains within it: because since the city contains both the urban and the rural areas, it remains in each of the four parts. In every order of the righteous, there are some who are more capable in works, others who excel in doctrine, and others who are more capable in prayer and the singing of psalms. Because those who are more capable in good works possess in a special way the image of the Father; those in doctrine, the image of the Son; and those in prayer, the image of the Holy Spirit.

If, therefore, there are five troops of the righteous who constitute that heavenly city of Jerusalem—namely, four special groups and one general group—there is a certain distinction in each by which one can discern between the general part and the other parts of the city by the property of their gifts. In this way, the likeness of the Trinity distinguishes between the various groups. It is clear then that there are fifteen <note>original: "undecim"; the OCR likely misread "xv" (15) as "xi" (11), as the text immediately follows with the fifteen Gradual Psalms.</note> perfections of this city, according to the fifteen Gradual Psalms <note>The "Psalms of Ascent" (Psalms 120–134), traditionally associated with the fifteen steps of the Temple.</note> and the fifteen steps. These fifteen perfections are compressed into five portions, just as the entire Psalter is comprised of five groups of thirty psalms <term>trigenarijs; sets of thirty psalms, which Joachim uses to divide the 150 Psalms into symbolic units</term>. And since five perfections are seen to pertain to the Father by way of likeness, five to the Son, and five to the Holy Spirit, it is clear that one "fifty" <term>quinquagenarius; a group of fifty psalms</term> of the psalms is to be ascribed to the Father, another to the Son, and another to the Holy Spirit.

### On the properties of the gifts which are bestowed upon each of the orders.

<margin>og</margin> But there still remains a question: why in the eastern part does God work as Father; in the western part as Teacher; in the north as Lord; in the south as Friend; and in the main body of the city as Judge? In the eastern part, which pertains to the elders and prelates of the churches—who are also called the "fathers of Christians"—God is rightly to be esteemed as Father. This is not only because He is the Father of His Only-Begotten Son, but because He is the Father of us all, and because from Him all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named <note>A reference to Ephesians 3:15.</note>.

<column-break/>

Indeed, it is written: *I have said, "You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High."* <note>original: "Ego dij estis et filij excelsi omnes" (Psalm 82:6).</note> And therefore, as I have already said, He alone is to be called "Father" in respect to the elect; yet so too are the Son and the Holy Spirit, because we do not believe in the Father alone, but also in the Son and the Holy Spirit. Nor were we baptized in the name of the Father alone, but in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the Apostles could not be called "fathers of Christians" if they themselves were not principally sons of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. 

And because this rank is the first (according to what we have written above), the Lord and God rightly presents Himself in this part as Father. For those who are already elders by age and character are worthy of confidence, not fear, and of veneration rather than insult, as the Apostle says: *Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father.* <note>original: "Seniorem ne increpa sed obsecra vt patrē" (1 Timothy 5:1).</note> And because these same prelates and elders are the few among the people of God, that part of the city pertaining to them is rightly said to be placed in the East; for the East is, in a sense, the beginning of the world, and from there they await the light of heaven.

However, just as the eastern part belongs to the Apostles and prelates of the churches, so the southern part belongs to the deacons and martyrs. Rightly in that part must the Lord be esteemed as one to be venerated and feared, lest by the violence of the scourge <note>A reference to persecution or divine discipline.</note> faith be lost, truth be lost, or love be lost, and the Triune and one God be denied—He who "is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna." <note>original: "qui potest animas et corpus perdere in gehennā" (Matthew 10:28).</note> Because He strikes with fear, He shows Himself to be the Lord; and He is indeed "terrible in His counsel over the sons of men."

The western part, however, pertains to the Teachers, because the highest humility is necessary for them. True humility is to look back at the lowliest things and to feel the opposite of the man who sees only what is sublime. For they cannot nourish the little ones with milk unless they are strengthened for the weak, so that they themselves become like little ones in their midst, not measuring what they owe or what they can do against those little ones. That the prelates <note>OCR: "p̄lares"</note> might know this—they upon whom these duties fall—He made Himself such a one, who by the will of the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit was made a little one, though He was great.

# Abba. Book of the Psaltery

### Column 1

<margin>Genesis</margin>
One must be said to be closer to the goal rather than simply the one who runs more. Take **Jacob** for instance: <note>referring to Jacob receiving the blessing in Genesis 27</note> not because he ran more, but because he was nearby. He quickly did what his mother commanded, and thus received the blessing. It is clear, then, that he who **contemplates** is closer to God than he who works externally. For the more profoundly someone proceeds in following and carrying out the business of the world, the further he is distanced from Him who is present to free minds. When a man is **baptized**, he seems to be as if a hundred and fifty days’ journey from the fatherland. When he is made a **cleric** (if indeed he is worthy), he is as if a hundred days away. When he is made a **monk**, he is as if fifty. 

Therefore, the first is distant by **three jubilees** <note>original: "tribus iubileis"; a jubilee is a period of fifty years</note>. The second by two. The third by one. Yet, sometimes one who stands in the first grade runs so swiftly that he outstrips the others to reach the palm of victory, leaving behind those who seemed to be ahead, and arriving first in the kingdom of God. This does not always happen with the clergy, but sometimes. For the former is a special case, while the latter is the general rule; and those things which are special in no way prejudice the general rules. But who is it that runs thus, if not the one who is seen to be in the first grade and is quickly snatched from it to the third, everywhere progressing and perfecting a good work, knowing not—if I may put it this way—how to delay in his going? 

Regarding those who are joyful, if we speak of those who are hindered by the bonds of the world, yet strive by vow and desire to enter through the **narrow gate** and acquire a place for themselves in the city: we say that those **married persons** who are of such a kind are "monks in the first grade" and "clerics in the world." Only those, however, who <margin>Note</margin> are called such in the third grade <note>meaning the monastic order</note>. In this matter, it is appropriate to look more diligently at what is signified in the three jubilees of years regarding the times of the **three states**, about which we shall speak in what follows as God grants. We see that the people of the **first state**, who flourished in the married life and were not sufficiently adorned with spiritual wings, are represented by a hundred and fifty years—that is, fifteen "pennies" of years <note>original: "denariis annorum"; likely referring to the reward given to workers in the vineyard in Matthew 20</note> according to what they signify. It is necessary for them to wait to reach that final day in which all the elect will generally reach the kingdom of God. The order of clerics, according to some

<column-break/>

part of itself, remains in this **second state**—shining in chastity—for roughly a hundred years. This is two jubilees, which make ten "pennies" on the journey. It is necessary for this order to pass through the **third state** before they see that day. 

Truly, the **order of monks**—and I do not speak of those who have run until now alongside the order of clerics for the sake of another mystery, but of those whose life began in some part of the world with a more perfect life, or will soon begin when **Israel is converted to God**—finds that only a third part of the journey remains. I do not say this according to the literal number of years, but according to the **mystery** <note>original: "fm misterium"; referring to the symbolic or allegorical meaning</note>. For if it is consumed in a short time, it will fulfill many ages. It is necessary for him to work threefold; so that what the first order completed in three jubilees, this one, like a man, completes devotedly in one. 

Moreover, there are seventy years of life, the time of the **Babylonian migration** <note>the 70-year exile of the Israelites in Babylon, used here as a symbol for the soul's exile from heaven</note>; the Church observes the mystery of **Septuagesima** <note>the seventy-day period of penance before Easter</note> to signify this. For those years signify the same as these days. Therefore, we ought to estimate fifty days here as the fifty years of **Pentecost** <note>original: "penthecosten"</note>; that is, fifteen and fifteen days as if they were ten times ten years, so that we might arrive at the likeness of the mystery. 

But someone might say: "If I belong to the men of my order and not to the city, what is it to me whether it is morning, noon, or evening in the city, since my possession was given to me in the **villages** and not in the city?" But if this is the case, there is no question. If you do not wish to be a **citizen of Jerusalem** according to the dignity of God rather than a common fatherland—even if one had a portion among the soldiers—it is of no consequence to the cause. But we are discussing those who want, desire, and sigh for it; those who, having gladly sold all things, seek **Christ**, but are nevertheless detained by certain obstacles. Concerning them, it was asked whether those who have left everything can have something in common with them. It was asked in what way this is possible, provided they persist in the same will and do what they can, or what is judged possible for many.

# Joachim, First Book of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery 150
### IJ 2

It has been shown: For we said that he who is a monk in the third grade is distant from the city <note>The "city" refers to the New Jerusalem or the state of spiritual perfection.</note> by about fifty days' journey; he who is in the second grade by about a hundred; and he who is in the first, by about a hundred and fifty. We are not speaking here of that rare perfection of the saints which is granted to very few—those who used to recite the whole psalter in a single day—but rather of what is common to many. Indeed, to complete the whole psalter in one day is, in any age of life, to be converted to the Lord and then, without delay, to be dissolved and be with Christ. 

Therefore, even if this number [150] is so celebrated and so perfect in that heavenly city of Jerusalem, it is nonetheless also found in this pilgrimage, distinguished by certain boundaries of the ages according to the course of time and years. We must run and act according to this measure so that we might reach that heavenly Jerusalem, where it is not the one who is born first or begins first, but the one who runs faster according to God who obtains the first place; thus many who are first there shall be last, and the last shall be first. 

But more shall be said of these things in what follows. Regarding the perfection of these numbers, however, it must not be overlooked that just as the number thirty <note>original: "tricenarius"</note> pertains to the Trinity which is God, so the number one hundred and fifty pertains to the fulfillment and fullness of those virtues which are to be understood from that highest source. This is true whether they are considered in relation to the names of the Persons [of the Trinity] or essentially. Specifically, the total sum of this number [150] is contained within fifteen perfections, which are designated by groups of ten <note>original: "denarii"; Joachim is explaining that 150 is 15 times 10.</note>. And since there are, as we have often said, five general virtues, the Trinity of God must be invoked in them five times, so that He who is the supreme teacher may work **humility** in us; He who is the great Lord may work **patience** in us while we fear Him more than the torments of the executioners; He who is the true Father may work **faith** in us; He who is the kind friend may work **hope** in us; and He who is the just judge may work His **zeal** in us, making us hate vice and love virtue. Therefore, the number thirty, which consists of three decades <note>3 groups of 10</note>, pertains to the faith of the Trinity; 

<column-break/>

but the one hundred and fifty, which consists of fifteen decades, pertains to the perfection of virtues. 

If, however, according to what we wrote above, the number ten pertains to the order of the laity, twenty to the order of the clergy, and thirty to the order of the monks, what does it mean to complete the Psalter in fifteen decades <note>15 groups of 10</note> except to ascend step by step and with deliberation from virtue to virtue? It is to go, in a sense, from Egypt into the desert, and to move without the space of delay from the desert (as the Scripture says) into the desirable land flowing with milk and honey. 

Furthermore, **Abraham** did not do this. Instead, as soon as he departed from Egypt, he went up into the mountain, signifying those who pass from a secular life directly to the monastic life. However, the fact that the **children of Israel** went up from Egypt into the wilderness and stayed there for some time, and from the wilderness went to the fertile land situated among the lush mountains, signifies those who pass from the secular state to the clergy, and from the clergy to the monastic life. 

Moreover, the fact that Abraham, from the time he went up from Egypt, always remained in the mountains, signifies those who are dedicated to the Lord from their childhood and, in a sense, compress three days' journey into one. Therefore, how laudable and lovable it is for someone to reach this grade <margin>Genesis</margin> can be understood from what has been said. He who cannot reach this one, but can reach perfection in the second grade, should not think little of it or neglect it; for he who serves well acquires a good grade for himself. But he who cannot even do this should remain at least in the first, so that he may have a part, even if late, in the first resurrection. <margin>Revelation</margin>

->Abbot. The Book of the Psaltery<-

...moved by [these] questions: it seems to belong to the weight of the same question. What should be thought of those laypeople or clerics who do not have the will to leave all things and follow Christ, but rather to do the good they can within their own <term>orders</term> <note>original: "ordinibus" — referring to the social and religious categories of the time: laity, clergy, and monks.</note>? For to them belongs none of those perfections which are granted only to those who desire and often sigh for them; for he who does not seek, does not ask; he who does not knock, does not consider; he who does not desire, makes himself almost a stranger to the jubilation of the psalms. But what then? Are those who are like this to be despaired of regarding salvation? Far from it.

### ¶ On the difference of merits.

For there is one cause that makes a difference between the reprobate and the elect; another between those who will be judged and those who will be saved; and another between those who will not only be saved, but will even be <term>judges</term> <note>In medieval theology, the "perfect" (apostles and those who followed their lifestyle of poverty) were believed to sit in judgment alongside Christ at the end of time.</note>. There is another cause that makes a distance between judges and judges, so that each may receive his own reward according to his labor. For the cause of glory is not equal for him who has served God in a <term>monastery</term> from childhood, and him who comes to it only when the world has already been <note>original: "crucifixus est mundus" — crucified to him; a reference to Galatians 6:14, meaning the world no longer holds any attraction or use for him.</note> out of necessity—unless the converted child lives proudly and negligently, while the converted old man begins to be humble and submissive, returning to the simplicity and innocence of children. But this happens sometimes, even if rarely. How can the zeal for life be equal for him who comes in the morning, and those who come at midday or in the evening? Does not he who came in the morning retain the first place? The second he who came at midday? The third he who came in the evening? Therefore, all come together to one <term>banquet</term> <note>original: "conuiuium" — a reference to the heavenly feast.</note> for which all have sighed; but he who desired more, ran and arrived first, and he finds the seat empty of a sitter. But the others who followed him sat in the order in which they arrived. For merits must be great to prefer a younger person to one who came before, according to that saying: *He who humbles himself like this little child, he is greater in the kingdom of heaven.* Whether, therefore, a man fulfills in childhood that exhortation

<column-break/>

of which it is said: *If you wish to be perfect, sell all you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me*; whether in youth or in old age, nothing stands in the way of obtaining that blessedness of which it is said: *Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, shall find watching. Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself and make them sit down at table, and passing by, he will serve them.* Nothing, I say, stands in their way to obtaining this blessedness; but nevertheless, the Lord is just, so that he who labors more worthily in watching may receive more reward at his coming. All, therefore, will be in one dwelling place, as many as are of one vow and one purpose; yet each, as I have already said, will receive his own reward according to his labor, whether he comes first or not.

Furthermore, if we deal with those who always wish to remain in the <term>secular world</term> <note>original: "seculo" — literally 'the age', referring to life outside of a monastery.</note> and be subject to God like the faithful with their wives and children; or those clerics who do not wish to enter the community of those who live in common <note>This refers to the "Canons Regular," clerics who lived a communal life similar to monks.</note>, but wish to use their freedom, to acquire things they do not have and to possess simply what they do have, and yet to live well according to their order: the aforementioned sentence of Truth is manifest regarding them, which says: *You know the commandments; keep them and you shall live. You shall not kill; nor commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness,* and so on, which follow there. 

But if it is asked what is the difference between such married people—who live chastely but still do their own will and have private property—and those who have left everything and themselves to follow Christ? I confess that the difference is as great as that between <term>peasants, burgesses, and citizens</term> <note>original: "rusticos et burgenses et ciues" — Joachim uses the social hierarchy of the 12th-century city-state to explain spiritual ranks: from the rural serf to the free town-dweller to the ruling elite.</note>—that is, the difference between those who are subject to servitude, those who are free but have no servants, and those who, by the nobility of their lineage, rule over servants and families. And indeed, it is a great thing to be a citizen of Israel and to rule among the children of the kingdom and reign with Christ; but nevertheless, in respect to those who are outside, it is blessed to remain even in his courts. For it is written that in her [Jerusalem], through all her streets, there shall be sung a [song of praise]... <note>The text likely continues with "Alleluia."</note>

...who desire to change their lives and pass to that "best part" which Mary chose <note>A reference to Mary of Bethany (Luke 10:42), who sat at Jesus' feet, representing the contemplative life, while Martha represented the active life.</note>. However, being held back by their duty toward fathers, mothers, or sisters who perhaps have no other means of support, they delay going quickly toward that which they love, lest they abandon those whom they naturally love into great misery. For it is one thing to remain for a time in a lower order and reach the more worthy ranks step by step; it is quite another to remain in a lower state until death so that one does not even seek to pass to another. Therefore, if we treat these three groups together, each has its own specific characteristic. For, as we have often said, the study of labor belongs to the **laity**; the exercise of doctrine to the **clergy**; and the jubilation of psalmody to the **monks**. In this context, by the name "clergy," we should understand those clerics who are permitted to remain as they are and to hold property. This does not include those who live communally and canonically according to the rules of Saint Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD). His "Rule" became the basis for many religious communities.</note> with the humble purpose of charity. For Saint Augustine himself calls these men "monks," as they are "of one mind," the firmest lovers of unity, according to the voice of that Psalm which says: *Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity.* <note>original: "Ecce qd bonum & qd iocudum habitare fratres in unum" — Psalm 133:1.</note> Furthermore, if we carefully examine these three orders, we see that there is as much distance between the life of clerics and monks as there is between the lives of the laity and the clergy. For if we speak of continence <note>The practice of self-restraint, particularly regarding marriage or physical desires.</note>, it is granted to all laity to have wives, unless a vow or a firm purpose is the cause. To the clergy, it is granted in part, or rather permitted what is granted and inhibited in part, so that this order appears to be a middle step between the two. For monks, however, it is judged unlawful always and everywhere among all men. But as we have already said, two of these orders have their own duties: to work and to teach. Thus, one of them feeds the bodies of the needy, while the other refreshes the minds of those who beg for truth. Furthermore, we said that the jubilation of the psalms is the proper duty of monks, and it was asked whether this belongs to any of the laity or clergy, or if it belongs solely to the monks—

<column-break/>

—in such a way that it does not also belong to other faithful who desire to be praisers of their God, but who are hindered by certain circumstances and cannot do so in an absolute and total way. It should be known, therefore, that every one of the faithful ought to praise God according to their ability. Yet, one cannot do so worthily unless the Holy Spirit inspires a sense of devotion. To some, this feeling is given for an hour, but it cannot remain with them for long because it is choked and extinguished by the love of lust or of profit, so that it cannot stay with them. However, there are some who have wives more for the sake of offspring than for lust, and are held back in the cares of the world more by necessity than by will. And there are some clerics who are held back more by love for their people and for the sake of bearing fruit in the word of God than for the sake of "filthy lucre" <note>original: "turpis lucri" — a common biblical phrase for dishonest or greedy gain.</note>. Thus, even if they are physically "outside," they may live with an integral mind among those who live spiritually. There is no doubt about these people: the jubilation of God belongs to them, and they are considered worthy in the eyes of God to be counted among his praisers. Nevertheless, because married people cannot be equal with the clergy, nor the clergy with the monks who have left their belongings and their all for Christ, I might not improperly say that a "ten-fold" <note>original: "denarium" — referencing the Roman coin, but here used to denote a numerical grade or reward of 10.</note> number of psalms should be attributed to these types of pious laity; a "twenty-fold" <note>original: "vicenarium"</note> to the clergy; and a "thirty-fold" <note>original: "tricenarium"</note> to the monks. For the first are monks by devotion; the second by devotion and continence; but the last by devotion, continence, and the renunciation of their possessions. According to this, it seems there are three kinds of monks in this world: one by will and deed; another by will even if not by deed; and a third somewhere in between. Certainly, there are three special things that make a monk: the vow, continence, and the renunciation of one's possessions and oneself. For other virtues can be held even by those outside the monastery. But a married person staying with a spouse, even if they wish to, perhaps cannot live continently.

Joachim’s First [Book] on the Harmony
Ii 4

...nonetheless, he desires to be released from these earthly bonds and to pass into the blessed life; he says, indeed, that he **desires to be released from these and to be with Christ** <note>original: "cupit... dissolui & eē cū Christo"; a reference to Philippians 1:23</note>. For this, he should praise God, who opened the eyes of his mind so that he might know **how kind and sweet the Lord is** <note>Psalm 34:8</note>. 

Furthermore, the cleric who is still in the world, but burns with an equal desire, is recognized as already having two "pennies" in that he desires this and lives continently. From this, he is able to sing, as it were, twenty psalms to God. However, he has not yet reached the third "penny," which is: **Sell everything and give to the poor and come, follow me** <note>original: "Vende omnia & da pauperibus & veni sequere me"; the command of Jesus to the rich young man in Matthew 19:21.</note>. But he who adds to the desire he had to serve Christ the vow of continence, voluntary poverty, and obedience until death—this man is truly a monk; he has reached the thirty-fold perfection.

### How those things which were said of the three orders are mystically designated in Leviticus.

If one asks what follows from devotion where the work of devotion differs from necessity, it is demonstrated in another way through the clear mysteries in Leviticus <note>The Third Book of the Torah/Old Testament, focused on priestly laws.</note>. We said above that the **city** pertains to those religious persons designated by the **Levites** <note>The tribe of Israel dedicated to divine service.</note>; the **suburbs** and **villages** pertain to the remaining multitude of God’s elect. Some, however, think that the Levites specifically designate the clergy; but it is not so, for they reflect one another as kings to kings, pontiffs to pontiffs, and Levite to Levite. 

According to a specific understanding, the kings and princes signify the rulers; the pontiffs of the New Testament signify the soldier-clerics who live under them; the priests signify the rectors of monasteries; and the Levites signify the monks, who are also called cenobites <note><term>cenobite</term>: a monk living in a community rather than as a hermit.</note>. Thus, the property of the "city" pertains to those whom the Levites designate, and the property of the "suburbs" to the clergy; while the property of the men who are outside pertains to the remaining mul-

<column-break/>

titude of those to be saved, as will appear from what we write below regarding Leviticus. Yet again, because we intend to show the fruit of the reward for those who, while still remaining in the world, live among the monks in thought and eager desire, we must begin there. 

**If someone sells** (it says) **a house within the walls of a city, he shall have the liberty to redeem it until one year is completed.** **If he has not redeemed it, and the circle of a year has passed, the buyer shall possess it, and his descendants forever; and it cannot be redeemed even in the Jubilee.** **But if the house is in a village that has no walls, it is considered by the law of the fields. If it has not been redeemed, it shall return to the owner in the Jubilee.** **However, the houses of the Levites which are in the cities can always be redeemed. If they have not been redeemed, they shall return to the owners in the Jubilee, because the houses of the Levite cities are held as possessions among the children of Israel. But their suburbs shall not be sold, because it is an everlasting possession.** <note>Joachim is paraphrasing Leviticus 25:29–34. He uses these ancient property laws as metaphors for the permanence or fragility of a person's spiritual state.</note>

Surely you have heard what a difference Moses—or rather the Holy Spirit through him—made between the Levites and the other tribes of the children of Israel. For he says that the houses of the Levites within the walls, if sold, can always be redeemed, while the houses of others cannot be redeemed unless it be within a year. From this, it is clearly understood that the rest of the children of Israel could have houses within the city walls. 

The life of monks is a narrow path: a sublime, arduous, and contemplative happiness. Yet there are some, as I have said—whether laity or clergy—who, while remaining in the body among secular people, are among the monks in vow and spirit. These, therefore, are not Levites, but they possess houses in the city together with the Levites. They must be careful not to sell them for temporal gain; or if they do sell them, let them redeem them as quickly as possible. For a person "sells the house" he possessed in the city when, having abandoned his way of life and intention, he begins to grow cold in his devoted love and starts to live like the others who are outside. Another then "buys his house," and he himself becomes a stranger to it, while another person is shaped by his former examples...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the three orders of the Church—laity, clergy, and monks—by mapping them onto the laws of property and redemption found in the Old Testament Book of Leviticus. Abba. The Book of the Psaltery

...the deeds that the other was doing, seeking with all his strength the things of God. It happens quite often—and it must be said without fear—that while one person strives to draw near to God through prayer, another strives to make progress in temporal gains through work. One may emulate the practice of the other to such an extent that, through a mutual exchange, the one who has relaxed his way of life returns to the practice of labor, and the other, having despised temporal gain, turns to the study of prayer. This reciprocal emulation—where one is shaped by the other toward that which he does not have—is like a kind of sale. For each of them, having made an exchange of their way of life, deserts what he held and takes hold of what belonged to the other. 

If, therefore, the circle of the year has turned—that is, if the end of his life has arrived—and has not found him (the one who thus "sold" his glory) performing penance while he is healthy for his "first charity" which he lost <note>original: "charitate sua prima"; a reference to the Church of Ephesus in Revelation 2:4 which "lost its first love."</note>, and yet he is found in other good studies pertaining to the **suburbs and villages** <note>original: "suburbana vicos"</note>—that is, to the **active life** <term>active life: the "vita activa," characterized by external works of mercy and labor, contrasted here with the "suburbs" of the holy city.</term>—he will indeed be among the number of those to be saved. However, he will forever lack that honor of which he allowed himself to be defrauded. 

Furthermore, the **house** which that man sold is possessed by the buyer and his descendants forever; this is because the one who emulated him now possesses that acquired mansion of **contemplative sublimity** <term>contemplative sublimity: the "vita contemplativa," the highest form of spiritual life focused on prayer and the vision of God.</term>, and so do those who, shaped by his example, imitate him through a kind of spiritual succession until the end of the age. But if both repent, both return to their prior state, having let go of what they exchanged. If only one of them is of such a character, and that "house" is so spacious, then by a certain harmony of a single will it may hold both of them; it is a blessed thing for two to remain in it together rather than one. 

Certainly, the **houses of the Levites** can always be redeemed. That this was decreed by a dispensation of piety is revealed when it is said: *The houses of the cities of the Levites are for possessions among the children of Israel. But their suburbs they shall not sell, for it is an eternal possession.* <note>Joachim is quoting Leviticus 25:32-34 to explain the permanent status of the clergy and monks.</note> It is as if it were said: just as their own possession is for those who 

<column-break/>

are outside—the active life—so for those who are inside, it is the contemplative life. For it is considered unworthy among the kings of the earth that, however sluggishly a soldier might act (perhaps weighed down by some infirmity), the common honor which soldiers are accustomed to have should be taken from him. For if he were deposed from his honor and placed among the shield-bearers, it would be for him as if he were expelled from the kingdom. He would no longer be able to lift his eyes before his fellow soldiers, nor join the choir of those rejoicing in their joy. 

However, the case is not the same for one who seeks to become a soldier as it is for one who is already a soldier and then repents. So it is with the man who desired to become a monk and afterward made little of it, yet still performs what other good works he can. Even if there is some shame for him before the angels of God because he grew cold toward such a worthy aspiration—since he did not yet make a formal vow or fully know the life—that shame will not lead to damnation, nor should he be cast out from the number of the elect. 

But he who has vowed and begun to "render" <note>An allusion to Psalm 76:11: "Make vows to the Lord your God and fulfill them."</note>, being strengthened by grace and blessing, is counted in the number of **Christ’s soldiers** <note>original: "christi milituz"; the "militia Christi" was a common metaphor for the monastic life.</note>. What would it be for him to be separated from their society, if not to be rejected from the kingdom of God? For it is written: **Draw near to God and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded** <note>original: "Accedite ad deum & illuminamini & facies uestre non confundentur"; Psalm 34:5.</note>. 

Rightly, then, does it say: *But their suburbs they shall not sell, for it is an eternal possession.* This is because even if a monk cannot remain continually in his "novice fervor" regarding those things that pertain to the contemplative life, at least he ought not to cease from the effort of maintaining it. Indeed, that possession is eternal to him, and he ought not to alienate or lose it for any reason. 

Therefore, for the laity and the clerics, hope is reserved that they may be able to return to their possessions which are "outside the city" until the **Jubilee** <term>Jubilee: In the Old Testament, a year of restoration; Joachim interprets this as the "last day" or the end of time.</term>—that is, until the final day. And for the monks, the hope remains for those things which are "inside the city." And yet, blessed is he who holds fast, who does not seek back what he lost, but firmly preserves what he has acquired. Truly, strength is necessary.

...that they have houses outside the city: except that no one is to be forced into those high precepts <note>original: "alta illa precepta"; referring to the strict ascetic requirements of the monastic life</note> which only He who wishes to impose them can command. He alone is able to pour in the affection of devotion to fulfill them, so that he does not, perhaps, thoughtlessly and against the Apostle <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:35, where Paul says he does not wish to "cast a snare" or "place a noose" (laqueum) over the neck of the faithful.</note> seem to place a snare upon a person's neck. For just as some monks, burdened by physical infirmity, are unable to work with their hands alongside the laborers, or because they were not instructed by teachers, they cannot teach alongside the instructors—and yet they can still be good monks in the observance of their own part—so too many of the laity and clergy, hindered by the occupations of the world, are unable to persist in prayers and the singing of psalms. Yet, they can still be good laity as long as they provide alms from the things they produce by work; and those others can be good clergy as long as they labor well in the word of God, especially because of that which is written: **"Give alms, and behold, all things are clean to you."** <note>Luke 11:41</note>

### ¶ What the difference is between those who are converted from childhood to the service of God, and those who delay until old age.

<margin>Psalms</margin>
In order that we may be able to explain the three-part cause of the questions raised above, we must first attend to what properly belongs to the laity, what to the clergy, and what to the monks. Next, we must see what the difference is between those who begin to keep watch from childhood, yet delay and carry over their perfection until the time of their old age, and those who—whether in childhood, youth, or old age—awaken from the sleep of death and, upon awakening, immediately seize the life of perfection. As we have often said, it is the property of the laity **to work**, of the clergy **to teach**, and of the monks **to praise**. All these are good and necessary in the house of the Lord, because not only was gold accepted in the construction of the temple of the Lord—which signifies the life of those contemplating and praising the Lord—nor only silver—which signifies the doctrine of the words of the Lord, as it is written: **The words of the Lord**—

<column-break/>

**are pure words: silver examined by fire.** <note>Psalm 12:6</note> But also bronze <note>original: "es" (aes); often translated as bronze or brass, signifying common or durable labor.</note>, which signifies the work of hands for the sustenance of the needy. Indeed, through this work bodies are nourished; through the doctrine signified by silver, the minds of those who are infants in Christ are refreshed. Both of these pertain to the love of neighbor, because man—consisting of two needy substances <note>body and soul</note>—subsists by these two. Furthermore, the third of these, which is signified by gold, belongs to the love of God, which is the greatest and first commandment. 

¶ For this reason, it is written concerning Solomon—who was the second king from David and the third from Saul—that in the days of Solomon, silver was not accounted for. <note>1 Kings 10:21</note> It is as if it were said: In the days of Saul, who was chosen by the Lord to signify the people of the **first state** <term>first state: the first age of the world, associated with the Father and the Old Testament laity.</term>, work (bronze) was accounted for. In the days of David, who was also chosen by God to designate the **second state**, bronze was not accounted for because of the abundance of silver. But in the days of Solomon—whom the Lord loved and raised up to the kingdom as a type (without doubt) of the people of the **third state** <term>third state: the coming age of the Holy Spirit, characterized by monastic contemplation and "gold-like" love of God.</term>—<margin>1 Kings 10</margin> because of the excessive abundance of gold given to him, even silver itself was not considered to be anything of value in comparison to it. 

Truly, if we speak of those three orders: first, the order of the **married** <note>the laity</note> shone forth in Abraham and Isaac, to whom through prayers an eternal progeny was given. Second, the order of the **clergy** in Moses and Aaron. Third, the order of the **monks** in Elijah and Elisha. For after those two patriarchs, many patriarchs followed. And after Moses and Aaron, the order of the Levites shone forth. And after Elijah and Elisha, the order of the sons of the prophets, who lived in Bethel and Jericho. But this is only according to their part. According to the fullness of each: the order of the married, which began with Adam, flourished from Abraham. The order of teachers, initiated by Moses—and in another way by the prophet Isaiah—flourished in Christ and the Apostles. The order of monks was initiated by Elijah, or rather—

### Abba. Book of the Psalter

...as the reasoning of time demands from Saint Benedict, <note>Saint Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547 AD), the founder of Western monasticism.</note> now, by God’s favor, it is time for it to come to the light, so that it may shine for everyone who is in the house. For what is the light of a Christian but the work of justice? Thus the Lord says: **"Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven."** <note>Matthew 5:16</note> Because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, it was necessary for the second state <note>Joachim's "Second State" refers to the age of the New Testament/the Son, which followed the "First State" of the Old Testament/the Father.</note> to have contemplatives just as it had teachers. For just as the order of teachers, by the property of the mystery, belongs to Christ, so the order of contemplatives belongs to the Holy Spirit. However, their initiation, performed by Elijah and Isaiah, <note>original: "Helye & Esaia"</note> will clearly appear near the end of this little work, where the generations are to be discussed. Because that same Spirit proceeds from the Son, it was necessary for the third state to have its own order, which would nevertheless be one with the preceding one for the honor of the Creator—the Spirit whose initiation preceded in Saint Benedict, the institutor of Western monks.

Perhaps men hear these things and are scandalized. "The monks," they say, "attribute silver and brass to us, but they apply gold to themselves." It is no wonder: for Paul, caught up into the third heaven—which signifies the life of contemplatives—says that he heard secret words that it is not lawful for a man to speak. But for how long? Surely not forever? Far from it. Rather, until the predefined time. For just as Moses placed a veil over his face so that the children of Israel would not gaze upon him, so too Paul in this place seems to have placed a veil over his face. But just as that veil was removed in Christ, so also this one is removed in the Holy Spirit. For the first heaven was the Old Testament, which was established in the Patriarchs. The second heaven is the New Testament, which was established in the Apostles. The third heaven is spiritual understanding, which teaches us to depart from the Egypt of the present age and to pass through the narrow way of the desert that leads to life, and to go into the Jerusalem above. To depart from the synagogue of the Jews: this belongs to those Christians who are Egyptians in their habits and "carnal Jews" <note>A term used to describe those who interpret scripture only literally rather than spiritually.</note> so that—

<column-break/>

—just as the Apostles and their successors, through the many tribulations of those times, reached the point where they obtained the Roman Empire. Indeed, from the days of Saint Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (reigned 314–335 AD), associated with the conversion of Emperor Constantine.</note> until the present, Peter the Fisherman is known once to have ruled in Rome; so also let us pass through many tribulations to the celestial empire—or even, temporally, to that blessed vision which will be in the third state of the age: to that peaceful kingdom of which the angel speaks to Daniel: **"The kingdom which is under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High."** <note>Daniel 7:27</note> Now, therefore, because it is time for the veil to be removed, let man cease to be [merely] man, and it will be permitted to hear. For why does man murmur and grow angry? If he wishes to be a beast by following earthly things, or a "man" by being partly here and partly in heavenly things, let him fear; but in his perfection, there will no longer be fear. For it is written: **"Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, according to how you have multiplied your mercy, O God."** <note>Psalm 36:6–7 (Vulgate 35:7–8)</note>

Why is he indignant if I prefer celibacy to marriage, or contemplation to labor? If I say of those who follow the Son of Man: **"The children of men shall hope in the covering of your wings; they shall be inebriated by the abundance of your house, and you shall give them to drink from the torrent of your pleasure."** <note>Psalm 36:7–8 (Vulgate 35:8–9)</note> Does it not seem just to you that he who despises soft garments for the sake of God should be considered worthy to be covered by God's own wings? And he who lacks the abundance of living should perceive the abundance of the Spirit? And he who casts away from himself the pleasure of the flesh should be given to drink from the torrent of God's own pleasure? But if you are evilly envious, hear the sentence of Truth against you, which says: **"If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the hell of fire."** <note>Matthew 5:29</note> If, however, you are well-disposed in your emulation, enter in. Who will prohibit you from entering? The banquet of King Ahasuerus <note>A reference to the feast in the Book of Esther, used here as a metaphor for the spiritual feast of the Third Age.</note> has come and is prepared; behold, it is prepared in the orchard. From now on, no one is prohibited from entering, from the least to the greatest. If, however, you serve... and yet are hindered by some chain...

# ¶ That the order of monks itself, which has left the world in heart and body to follow Christ, consists of three kinds.

While we were dealing in this little work with the three orders of the elect, the discourse was drawn to this point: that it happened to treat those married people and clerics who—because they know the joys of Jerusalem less through the feeling of inspiration—desire to reach it less; rather, they even weep for their friends who are passing into it. But now we have spoken of those married people and clerics who, knowing what they have lost, lament and say: *How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land? If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten.* <note>Psalm 137:4–5. This refers to the spiritual exile of the soul longing for the "New Jerusalem" or heaven.</note> And if we remember well when we were dealing with those laity and clerics who were called "men and beasts" <note>original: "homines & iumenta" – a reference to Psalm 36:6. In Joachim’s theology, "men" often represent the spiritual-minded and "beasts" those who are more focused on physical or carnal labor.</note> in the third degree, we dealt with monks—not indeed those who are monks in name alone and not also in fruit, but those who wish to be pilgrims and sigh daily for their homeland.

Wishing, however, in the second place to deal with monks alone, we find that there are three kinds of monks: two in hope, and one in reality. <note>original: "duo in spe: vnū in re" – a distinction between those aspiring to the ideal and those actually living it.</note> But even this monastic life which we say is "in reality" is distinguished into three species. For some pass to this life from childhood; others wake up in youth, staying until the "second watch"; <note>A reference to the watches of the night in Luke 12:38, used here as a metaphor for stages of life.</note> while others do so in old age. And what is to be said of these? It has already been said above: *He who labors more will receive more of a reward.* <note>1 Corinthians 3:8</note> For everyone will receive their own reward according to their labor.

For those who, from childhood, force themselves into a mature way of life and attain the perfection of the elders, it is as if they gained three talents of gold every year for thirty years. But those who take up the sweet yoke of Christ in their youth, learning from Him that He is meek and humble of heart, it is as if they did that same thing from their tenth year until their thirtieth—that is, for twenty continuous years. But those in old age, as

<column-break/>

if from their twentieth until their thirtieth. Yet it sometimes happens that the humility and prudence of those who arrived late outweighs the sloth <term>accidie: a spiritual apathy or "noonday-demon" often discussed in monastic life</term> of those who came before; thus they not only receive a reward like the others, but the "last become first," both in this world and in the one to come. For it is not he who is *called* a monk who has the prize, but he who *is* a monk.

And it must be known that if death prevents maturity <note>original: "preueniens meretatem" – likely a shorthand for death coming before one reaches the "late hour" of old age.</note> in those who are converted in childhood, it does not take away their merit. For since God Himself imposes necessity in such moments, each person is judged not so much by the fruit of their works as by their heart. For one does not receive the sacred habit to serve the Lord for an hour or a moment, but so that it may be forever. If the one who lives [God] takes pity on his labor and says to him in his vineyard: "Rest," does the mercy of God take away his reward? <note>Alluding to the Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16), where those who start late receive the same pay as those who started early.</note> These things were mentioned as if on a journey and placed before our mind's eye, lest we seem to leave untouched those questions that might be raised. Otherwise, the force of our intention was and is directed toward those three orders who live reasonably, as far as human fragility permits.

# ¶ Likewise, concerning the three orders often written about.

For if Christians live as they truly ought, it is necessary for each of the three orders to have those three things designated by gold, myrrh, and frankincense. <note>The gifts of the Magi from Matthew 2:11, here interpreted as virtues.</note> **Gold**, namely, is the obedience of doing what is good, just as the Apostle commands. **Myrrh** is brotherly compassion, which resists the rot of sin. **Frankincense** is the devotion and praise to be confessed to Almighty God.

However, as I have already said, it is more incumbent upon the layman to work than the other two; more upon the clerics to persist in doctrine; and more upon the monks to insist on prayer and to be free for divine praises. For the more a vessel of a man is emptied... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the bottom of the column.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Three Orders" (Married, Clergy, and Monks). Joachim is explaining how different life paths relate to the timing of spiritual rewards and their proximity to God, using biblical figures like Abraham and John the Baptist as archetypes for these different states of being.</meta>

<header>Joachim [of Fiore], First Book of the Ten-Stringed Psalter</header>

...are directed downwards. And this is just enough. For the justice that belongs to the earth: its reward is stretched out over a long duration. But that which is enacted (so to speak) between earth and heaven: it walks in the middle between both. Yet the justice that is of heaven soon leads to the kingdom of God. Certainly, we have learned that there are three times in which these three orders will reach their fulfillment. For behold, that ancient people who persevered in faith until John the Baptist awaits its reward from the Lord in the future resurrection. Similarly, the following people who believed in the coming of Christ. And similarly, the third people who are to believe at the end of time. Behold how far off that first group is, and how near this last is! For examples of this mystery <term>mystery: in this context, a hidden spiritual truth revealed by God</term> are not lacking, if we seek them carefully in the divine scriptures. 

For we read that Abraham fathered a child in his old age; that John the Baptist preached when he was thirty years old, just like the prophet Ezekiel, and just like the mediator between God and men himself, Christ Jesus. We read that Benedict, the true father and leader of monks, just like many others, was consecrated to God from his childhood. From their evident mystery, it is given to be understood more clearly than light that the life of the married is of longer duration in order to receive the fruit of their reward; the life of the cleric is of shorter duration; and the life of the monk is of the shortest duration of all. For the further someone recedes from God through the desires of this life, the more slowly they are led before His face; and the more one approaches Him through the affect of love, the more quickly they are established in His sight. 

Therefore, those who are bound by carnal embraces by occasion of the marriage bond can scarcely bring forth the fruit of good work competently until the final stage of their life, when at least failing old age commands the good of continence. However, those who, out of love for their kin, scarcely in middle age release themselves from those ropes to take up divine possessions. Hence it is that children were given to the patriarchs in their old age, as we have already said, when they came together with their wives more out of love for offspring than for lust. Hence it is that, by the example of the Lord, one ought to be at least thirty years old who undertakes the mystery of

<column-break/>

preaching—that is, when a person can now use the judgment of reason freely, so that they have discretion between the holy and the profane, and know how to reject the evil and choose the good. 

But those who, from their childhood, having despised all that they possess, adhere to God, can serve Him more freely to the extent that they trample upon the pestilential necessities of this sort which importunely press upon mortals, and which place a stumbling block for the elect of God <margin><note>original: "Plat." - likely a scribal error or OCR misreading of "Psal." for Psalm 139:6.</note> Psalms</margin> along the way; they feel little or nothing of carnal affection. Thus, the first of these is proper to the married; the second to the clergy; the third to the monks. Truly, because just as not all monks are equal in merit, so neither are all clerics, nor all laypeople equal; leaving aside what these or those do according to their own desires, let us hold as an example what those who wish to be blessed *ought* to do—or rather, what many do whose memory is held in blessing.

### Concerning the three exercises, each of which
### belongs to one of the three orders.

Three exercises have often been written and commended to us in the three aforementioned orders, pertaining to the image of the Trinity: work, doctrine, and praise. <note>original: "opus doctrina & laus" — Joachim aligns the three orders with these three spiritual activities, which in turn reflect the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> Yet because the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father, and the Father and the Holy Spirit are in the Son, and the Father and the Son are in the Holy Spirit, nothing is so attributed to the image of one person that the likeness of the other two is not immediately found in it. Therefore, the likeness of the Trinity is held in work alone, in doctrine alone, and in psalmody <note>psalmody: the singing or reciting of psalms as an act of worship.</note> alone. For it is one thing to work for one's own benefit, another for the support of one's neighbors, and another for the glory and praise of God. Similarly, this must be observed in doctrine. For it is one thing to read for one's own benefit, another for the edification, institution, and instruction of one's neighbors, and another for the glory and praise of God. Similarly in psalmody: it is one thing to sing psalms for one's own consolation, another for the salvation of neighbors, and another for the glory and

# Abbot. The Book of the Psalter

...the praise of God. For we are seen to work for **our own benefit** when we provide the provisions for temporal <note>Refers to earthly, time-bound life as opposed to eternal life.</note> life from those things we do; we do something for the **benefit of our neighbors** when we minister to those who have need among those over whom we are set. But a person works for the **glory of God** when they expend care on the building of churches <note>original: "basilicarum"</note>, so that God may be honored in their magnificence. In the same way, we read for our own benefit when we build ourselves up, seeking in the divine pages what is necessary for our own salvation. We read for the benefit of our neighbors when we prepare ourselves to respond to those who ask us about the words of God, so that hearing from us a word of comfort, they may be built up so that they might be saved. We read, nevertheless, for the glory of God when we seek to understand His mercies and remember His judgments which are from of old. 

And we are proven to sing psalms for both our own and our neighbors' benefit when, singing in the presence of the Most High, we pray for our own failings <note>original: "excessibus"</note>, saying:
<margin>Psalm [6:1]</margin>
> O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath.
And also:
<margin>Psalm [40:12-13]</margin>
> My iniquities have overtaken me, and I could not see. They are multiplied more than the hairs of my head, and my heart has failed me. May it please you, O Lord, to deliver me; Lord, look down to help me.
Why do I say this, when nearly a third of the psalms seem to be a prayer for sins? Hence it is that we are accustomed to say psalms for our own and others' sins, praying for both our own and our neighbors' salvation. But what is greater: we ought to sing and chant without ceasing for the glory and praise of God, saying every day with the Psalmist:
<margin>Psalm [34:1-2]</margin>
> I will bless the Lord at all times; His praise shall ever be in my mouth. In the Lord my soul shall be praised.
And things similar to these. Behold how distinctly what we predicted to be held has been proven—namely, that there are three modes in each of the three <note>Three modes (self, neighbor, God) within three categories (work, reading, singing).</note>. And it should be known that the first of each belongs properly to the people who were under the Law <note>The Jewish people of the Old Testament.</note>, who sought their own benefit rather than that of other peoples. The second 

<column-break/>

[belongs] to the Christian people, who are commanded to give themselves over in order to gain more people. The third belongs more to the **spiritual people** <note>Joachim’s "Spiritualis Intellectus" or the monastic order of the final age.</note> who will be of the third state. When peace and joy have been given to all, they will be converted more than usual to the praise of God, saying continually with the Psalmist:
> You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have cut off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness. So that my glory may sing to you and I may not be sorrowful; O Lord my God, I will confess to you forever. <note>Psalm 30:11-12</note>
Since these things are so, it is clear that in work and teaching, just as in testimony, the mystery of the Trinity is found—namely, through the **ten-stringed psalter** <note>A symbolic musical instrument Joachim uses to represent the harmony of the Law and the Trinity.</note>; just as we also wrote in the first book [concerning its] triangular shape, so that the mystery of the Trinity in Unity and Unity in Trinity may be seen to be cried out and expressed by certain natural voices. ### That the number five is of such great perfection that all perfection of the mysteries of God is contained under it. And that the same number is distinguished into three, five, and seven; and that this is the cause of such great perfection.

Some things have been said about the fifteen steps <note>Refers to the 15 "Psalms of Ascents" (120–134) traditionally sung on the 15 steps of the Temple.</note> and about that heavenly city of Jerusalem according to the number of the fifteen decades of psalms; but still other things have been preserved until this hour of light until now, so that the shadows which the lesser light <note>Usually a metaphor for the Old Testament or the moon.</note> had partially put to flight might be more resplendently erased by the rising sun of higher understanding. So that this may be done, the numbers **three, five, and seven**—which, joined together, constitute the number fifteen—must be considered in many ways, as will appear below: whether in the same sense as thirty, fifty, and seventy, which show the very same thing. # Joachim’s First Book of the Ten-Stringed Psalter

I think it should be understood for the rest in this way: so that those things of which we speak may be perfectly understood in their essence. But we shall deal with these matters in what follows. For it is necessary that we show in their proper place and sequence in what ways the **fifteen steps** <note>original: "quindecim gradus"; a reference to the fifteen "Psalms of Ascent" (120-134), which Joachim links to spiritual progression.</note> are to be understood, according to the many levels of understanding through which these and other things must be received. Now, therefore, we must contemplate the numbers themselves in that **celestial city**, so that from there we may be raised up to contemplate Him who made all things. For since we are examining what belongs to God, we must seek and hold to it with a more subtle diligence, as it is certain that God Himself is the end of our inquiry and our desire. Indeed, in Him and with Him remains that happiness of which the Scripture says: *Eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what things you have prepared for those who love you.* <note>A paraphrase of Isaiah 64:4 and 1 Corinthians 2:9.</note> Therefore, so that the eye of our mind may be raised in that holy city of which glorious things are spoken, to contemplate Him who alone is to be loved and venerated, the numbers themselves which are being discussed must be assigned—or rather, revealed as they have been assigned by God.

Just as the number **three** (*ternarius*) pertains to the whole of that city, so do the numbers **five** (*quinarius*) and **seven** (*septenarius*). First, three things must be considered: the districts beneath the city and the city itself; then, in the structure of the walls, twelve parts are to be considered, which are distinguished by gates and foundations. For it is manifest that the number twelve consists of **five** and **seven**; when **three** are added to these, they complete the number **fifteen**. There is a difference, however, between the first three and the following twelve: the first three are general, while the twelve are specific.

Furthermore, so that it may be clear that all this was made in the **image of the Deity**, it is now pleasing to consider more clearly how the mystery of the Deity is contained in these three numbers, and how they seem sufficient for everything. For the number **three** pertains to the three properties of the Persons <note>Refers to the unique characteristics of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>, by which each Person is understood to subsist through Himself and not be another. The number **five** pertains to the **five relations**. <note>In medieval theology, these are the five "notions" or relations that distinguish the Persons: innascibility, paternity, filiation, common spiration, and procession.</note> The number **seven** pertains to the **seven modes** by which God is spoken of in relation to Himself. Indeed, through the three properties, we understand the three distinct Persons.

<column-break/>

Through the **five relations**, we understand *who* is from *whom*, or *who* is from *which ones*. Through the **seven modes** by which the Persons are spoken of in relation to themselves, we understand the perfection of each individual Person, and the most perfect unity of two or three. And this indeed possesses an **Anagoge** <note>Anagogical: The highest of the four levels of medieval biblical interpretation, dealing with the spiritual ascent to heaven or eternal truths.</note>.

**Morally**, however, the number **three** pertains to those three exercises belonging to the three orders described above. The number **five** pertains to the **five virtues** of which we made mention earlier. The number **seven** pertains to the **seven natural virtues of the soul**. But concerning this, more will follow.

First, however, it must be shown how the number **three** (or rather thirty) pertains to the Trinity; the number **five** (or fifty) to the five relations; and the number **seven** (or seventy) to the seven modes by which God is spoken of in relation to Himself. This is done so that the path to reaching the perfection of the Catholic confession may be shown to us through the fifty psalms, and that we may enter the **Holy of Holies** through the fifteen steps mentioned in this work. Amen.

Therefore, first, the Trinity itself must be established in the foundation of our faith: He who is what He is, the **God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob**, as signified in those three angels who appeared to Abraham. This means that, before all else, we should believe there are three perfect Persons—not divided, but distinct by their own properties. Then, that there is one Person from one <note>The Son from the Father.</note>, and another from two <note>The Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.</note>, and from those three, the **seven spirits** of the Lord Himself are sent into all the earth, as the following treatise and diagrams teach regarding what is contained in the five relations. Then, that each individual Person is true God; two together are one God; and the three together are equally one God. Therefore, the place is set so that, while treating the number three and having set forth the appropriate figures, we may direct the eye of the mind toward the understanding of the three Persons—seeking to understand the invisible through visible things, and the **Creator of all things** through created things.

### On the mystery of the trinity.

<margin>Genesis</margin>
While Abraham was sitting under the tree in the heat of the day, three men appeared to him, as the scripture says. Now, it had stated earlier that God appeared to Abraham, but when describing the manner of the appearance, it added that three men appeared. Because he was illuminated from within, he saw and understood. He saw three, and those same three—appearing as three and yet as one—he adored. But since we generally hold that those three whom Abraham saw were celestial spirits clothed in bodily form (as God knows best), why were they not called angels from the beginning, but "men"? Finally, one of them who stood on the mountain was called not an angel, but "the Lord." The two who descended to Sodom were first called "angels," and then "the Lord." This was done because where they are called "three men," it was intended to signify the unity and equality of the Persons. Where two of them are called "angels" (which translates as "messengers"), it was clearly intended to make known that the Son and the Holy Spirit were to be sent by the one Father for the salvation of the human race. And where the one who is called "the Lord" is said to have stood on the mountain, from whom the two were sent, it is shown that God the Father has no father, nor is there a beginning for Him from which He might be sent. And where the two who descended are called "the Lord," it clearly became known that they remain in the unity of the paternal dominion and the majesty of divine glory. Whence it is also blessed in that place: *It rained from the Lord out of the Lord* <note>original: "Pluit domino a domino"</note>, because the Son and the Holy Spirit are the one Lord who rains, and the Father alone is the one Lord from whom it rains. Therefore, in this figure, the trinity of persons is aptly shown. But because the Trinity itself says in the Apocalypse: *I am Alpha and Omega* <note>original: "Ego sum Alpha & ω"</note>—and that "O" is written in two ways 
<margin>1 Apocalypse</margin>
among the Greeks, which we shall speak of scattered and distinctly in what follows so that what is said may be more clearly grasped—it is exhibited summarily and more distinctly in these three figures. For behold, in the first figure which is called **Alpha**, it is openly shown that God is three persons; and in those three persons who appeared to Abraham, and in their deeds, it is openly shown that the Son and Holy Spirit are 

<column-break/>

sent by the one Father. In the second figure, however, with the three small rods raised, one looks higher to the three patriarchs <note>Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob</note>; the last of whom, having gone out from the two, went away into Aram <note>ancient Syria/Mesopotamia</note> while the two remained in the mountains of Israel. By this it is clearly hinted that the one Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and from the Son. Furthermore, in the third figure, which is round, it is signified that there is one God and one Lord. And it is well represented as one through the surrounding line, but a double figure so that the relation and unity of the persons may be designated. For by that which we understand—that the Son is always begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds boundlessly from both—it is necessary to understand a perfect unity in that place; for that which proceeds from another not once but always is not separated from the one from whom it never ceases to go forth.

### On the five relations of the persons

Although both the relations and the unity of the persons are shown in the aforementioned figures, we have treated more fully the number three (which properly pertains to the Trinity), but very little concerning the five relations and the five ways in which they are expressed. This is the place for us to discuss these relations a little more diffusely, hinting at the whole of God: how one person is spoken of in relation to another, or two persons to one, or to two, or all three to the subject creature. For the Father has a certain property and relation to the Son alone, because He is the one Father of the one Son; and the Son has a certain property toward the Father alone, because He is the one Son of the one Father; and there is one where the Father and Son relate to the one Holy Spirit, because there are only two there who send the Holy Spirit; and a certain one where the Father and Holy Spirit relate to the one Son, because there are only two there who are <insert>associated with the mission</insert> from the Father; and a certain one where all three relate to every creature, because those three persons are the only one Creator, of whom the Apocalypse says: *From Him and through Him and in Him are all things; glory and empire forever and ever.* <note>A paraphrase combining Romans 11:36 and Revelation 1:6</note> Should anyone perhaps understand this less clearly, he may investigate the figure more easily from the present description.
