¶ In the same way, if not exactly similarly, we can say that one Abraham has a relation to one Isaac; and one Isaac to one Abraham; and again Abraham and Isaac to one Jacob, because that one [Jacob] comes from those two; and Isaac and Jacob together to one Abraham, because those two come from that one. And all three together to the whole people of the children of Israel, because that whole people comes from those three patriarchs. And there is still something more in this same mystery which requires a slightly sharper understanding: because no person is exempt from this common relation, for either one has a relation to two, or two to one, or three to something else. In this mode of relation, however, the "mission" <note>In theology, a "mission" refers to how a Person of the Trinity is sent into the world, such as the Son becoming flesh.</note> remains the primary cause. For indeed, it is one who sends two, and there are two who send one, and there are two who are sent from one, and one who is sent from two. <margin>Revelation</margin> And there are three who give testimony in heaven, from whom proceed the seven spirits sent into all the earth. Because truly, in no way would two proceed boundlessly from one, or one from two, if the two were not one, and the one with the two were not one. So that these things may be more easily grasped, we must return to the "images" prepared by God; so that what might appear obscure through a bare word might become clear and manifest when held up to the mirror of light. We seek to understand how sometimes the Father is to be understood alone when he is said to "send" the Son and the Holy Spirit; or how the Holy Spirit is understood alone when he is said to be sent by the Father and the Son; or how the Father and the Son are believed to be together one God when they are said to send the Holy Spirit together; or how the Son and the Holy Spirit are believed to be together one God when they are said to be sent from the one Father; or how if

<column-break/>

<margin>Revelation</margin>
all three together are believed to be one God when they are said to send "seven spirits into all the earth" to bless the creature which he himself founded—lest (heaven forbid!) anyone should think two together are greater than one alone, or one alone is less than two or three together. Truly, to designate the excellence of so secret a mystery, five venerable men were chosen at the very beginning of the Old Testament by the Creator himself of whom we speak: in these five, those five relations were noted in an ineffable way, so that nothing is left out or lacking from the perfection of the mystery. These men are: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Ephraim. Truly, Abraham is accustomed to being understood more specifically as "the Father" than the other fathers, as a designation for God the Father. Isaac is sometimes a designation for the Father (as in the place where he blesses his son Jacob) and sometimes a designation for the Son. Jacob is sometimes <margin>Genesis</margin> a designation for the Father (as in the place where he blesses Manasseh and Ephraim) and sometimes a designation for the Son (as in the place where he moved the stone from the mouth of the well); and sometimes a designation for the Holy Spirit, as when it is said: <margin>Genesis, Exodus</margin> "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Joseph also sometimes signifies the Son (as in the place where he was sold by his brothers) and sometimes the Holy Spirit <margin>Genesis</margin> (as where he tried to move the right hand of his father over Manasseh). Furthermore, Ephraim, whose name is interpreted as "fruitfulness," signifies the Holy Spirit who bore fruit among the nations, <margin>Genesis</margin> just as Manasseh signifies the Only-begotten of God. Therefore: Abraham signifies the Father, Isaac signifies the Son, and Jacob the Holy Spirit. Again: Isaac signifies the Father, Jacob the Son, and Joseph the Holy Spirit. Again: Jacob signifies the Father, Joseph the Son, and Ephraim the Holy Spirit—according to what is more clearly demonstrated in this figure.

Consider, reader, these three-fold triple figures, and learn why the Church sings the three-fold triple "Lord, have mercy" <note>original: "Kyrieleiſon"</note> before Mass, even though those who are invoked are only three. Indeed, from this figure are gathered those five modes of relations, since it is clearly shown therein: that in Abraham alone, the Father is designated. In Isaac alone, the Father and Son are designated together. In Jacob alone, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In Joseph alone, the Son and Holy Spirit. In Ephraim alone, the Holy Spirit. But why is this? It is to show that the Father alone is not something less, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, than the entire Trinity; nor are the three together something more than each of the three individually. Rather, God is so perfect—whether as God alone begotten, or unbegotten, or proceeding—just as the whole Trinity is one God. Most importantly, this more clearly demonstrates the truth of the relations within the Godhead: namely, how one sends two; how two are sent by one; how two send one; and how one is sent by two. Together, the three have a relation to the seven spiritual gifts, which are called the seven spirits of the Lord sent into all the earth.

<margin>Revelation</margin>
Certainly, there is no reciprocal relation from these seven spirits back to the three Persons according to an equality of persons; for there are only three Persons of the Godhead from whom those seven gifts come, just as all other things do. For these divisions of graces are not of the substance of the divine nature itself; rather, the Holy Spirit is truly one, who, remaining whole in each individual, gives from his own gifts—not as much as those in whom he remains might wish, but as he himself wills. For when the Apostle said, "There are varieties of graces, but the same Spirit," and added, "To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge," etc., he further added and said: "All these things are worked by one and the same

<column-break/>

spirit, dividing from his own to each as he wills." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:4-11.</note> For even the Prophet, when speaking in the singular, said: "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him"; he immediately added and said: "The spirit of wisdom and understanding," etc., so that both the one Spirit and his many gifts might be understood. <note>A reference to Isaiah 11:2.</note> The Scripture also calls these gifts "spirits," as John does in the Apocalypse: "And from the seven spirits (he says) who are in the sight of his throne." <note>A reference to Revelation 1:4.</note> Therefore, the likeness of the Father is in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The likeness of the Son is in Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. The likeness of the Holy Spirit is in Jacob, Joseph, and Ephraim. For in this way—through these five perfections and the five vowel letters—the secret of this sacred mystery is contained. It clearly shows what pertains specifically to the Father or to the Holy Spirit, what belongs commonly to the Father and Son, or to the Son and Holy Spirit, and what belongs commonly to all three together. Abraham signifies the Father alone, because the Son and Holy Spirit are sent by the Father alone. Ephraim signifies the Holy Spirit alone, because only the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son, from whom he also proceeds. Isaac alone signifies two—the Father and the Son—yet not two gods, but one God; for those two, who are the one God designated in Isaac, send the one Holy Spirit. Joseph alone similarly signifies two together—namely the Son and the Holy Spirit—yet not two, but one God; for those two, who are the one God designated in Joseph, are sent together by the one Father. This does not refer to that visible mission in which the Son of God became man, nor is this a discourse about that; rather, it refers to that spiritual mission by which he is sent daily to bless and enlighten holy souls.

# John: The First [Book] of the Ten-Stringed Psaltery

...which enlightens every man coming into this world. <note>original: "illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum," a reference to the Gospel of John 1:9</note> But also, Jacob alone signifies the three together—namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—yet not as three gods, but as the one God who is the creator of all good things, both visible and invisible. From him are all things, through him are all things, and in him are all things, because he himself is the creator of every visible and invisible creature. To these five modes of relations belong those five virtues of which we spoke above. This will appear more clearly if we adapt these same five relations to their own five periods of time.

### On the difference of the five times.

<margin>The first time</margin> In the first time, which was before the Law, God took up Abraham and established him as the father of many nations. Abraham (who we read did something no patriarch before him had done) was extremely—and almost excessively—anxious about an heir, saying to the one who had led him out of his own land: "Lord <margin>Genesis</margin> God, what will you give me? I shall go without children, and the son of the steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus." And Abraham added: "To me you have given no seed, and behold, my servant shall be my heir." God showed such great kindness to this same Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—the three patriarchs—that he was thought of not so much as their Lord, but as their Father, in respect to the dignity of the other patriarchs who were burdened by the weights of the Law. But also, such clear judgments of truth were revealed to them by the Lord that they could not doubt God's promise; instead, they believed firmly in the one promising, and it was credited to them as righteousness. <note>original: "reputaret eis ad iustitiā"</note> And although this phrase was written about Abraham alone, there is no doubt <margin>The second time</margin> that it must be accepted as applying to all the faithful.

In the time that was under the Law, having led the people out of Egypt, the Lord brought them into the desert, and it was said that the Angel of the Lord preceded Israel. This very angel appeared to the children of Israel after the death of Joshua and said to them: "I led you out of Egypt and brought you into the land for which I swore to your fathers; and I promised that I would not make my covenant with you void forever, provided that you did not strike a bargain

<column-break/>

with the inhabitants of this land; yet you would not hear my voice." Behold how great this Angel of the Lord was! He says that he himself led the people of Israel out of Egypt and brought them into the land for which he had sworn to their fathers. In the books of Moses, the one true God ascribes this to himself, and he himself testified that he had sworn this. Who then was this Angel, if not the one of whom the Father says: "And presently the Lord whom you seek shall come to his holy temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire"? <note>This identifies the "Angel of the Lord" in the Old Testament as the pre-incarnate Son of God, citing Malachi 3:1.</note> Hence it is that in the history of Samson, he is called both God and Angel. It appears, moreover, that from the time God spoke to his servant Moses, the Son—who is the true Lawgiver and Master Lord—began to show his majesty under a hidden enigma, under the appearance of an Angel, to perform judgments among the nations and rebukes among the peoples, and even among those who were called his own people, to show himself to be, together with the Father, the Lord of the whole earth.

The third time <margin>The third time</margin> followed under the kings and prophets from the days of Samuel the prophet, in which time Jerusalem was built and kings were anointed to preside over that people. It was said to the first of them, namely Saul, that when he should see the company of prophets, the Spirit of the Lord would leap upon him and he would prophesy. Regarding David, the <margin>1 Kings <note>In the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note></margin> Scripture says that Samuel anointed him in the midst of his brothers, and the Spirit of the Lord was directed into him on that day and thereafter. Therefore, from that time, Scripture has spoken more clearly and more frequently than usual about the Spirit of the Lord beginning to be revealed and becoming known in kings and prophets. For although Scripture speaks of the Spirit of the Lord in the time of the judges and from the very beginning, it did not wish to give such certain signs of itself then as it did from the time of the prophets and kings. During that same time also, the two royal and Levitical tribes—while others departed from the house of David—became one tribe, so that there might be in Jerusalem and Judah a perfect mystery of the Trinity, in which many prophets of the Lord...

<summary>This page outlines the first three of five historical "times," mapping the revelation of the Trinity from the Patriarchs (Father), through the Law and the Angel of the Covenant (Son), to the era of Kings and Prophets (Holy Spirit).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological exposition of history divided into distinct periods (the "Five Times"), focusing on how the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—reveals itself progressively through biblical events. It transitions from the time of the Prophets to the Incarnation (the Fourth Time) and looks forward to the present age (the Fifth Time).</meta>

# Abba. The Book of the Psaltery

...began to be multiplied: those who, when the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon them, spoke openly about the faith of the Trinity. They prophesied with a single voice both concerning the coming of the Son in the flesh and the pouring out of the Holy Spirit; and what they saw and predicted, they left behind for us. Therefore, because in the **first period** God the Father revealed himself as he willed and to those fathers he chose who lived before the Law; in the **second period**, there was added the manifestation of the Son in the "Angel of the Lord," <note>In medieval theology, the "Angel of the Lord" in the Old Testament was often interpreted as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ.</note> who was called both God and Lord; and in the **third period**, there followed the showing of the Holy Spirit speaking through kings and prophets. It appears that in this third period—though under a veiled mystery <note>original: "sub obscuro enigmate"</note>—the entire Trinity, which is one God, showed itself working together. It showed that God was not just one person, but Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Consider now, if you can with the eyes of your mind, what that time was like in which there was no Law; what that time was like in which the Law was given; and what that time was like in which the prophets appeared—that is, the time of the patriarchs, the time of the judges, and the time of the prophets and kings—and you will recognize how great a difference there was between one time and another. And rightly, in the "body of the city," <note>Likely referring to the "City of God" or the community of the faithful.</note> God is to be esteemed as both King and Judge: because King David, who held His place, was appointed by Him over Zion, His holy mountain; and not long after there followed Elijah, who, kindled with the fire of God's zeal, afflicted the whole land of Israel with drought and heat, and even burned up the proud with the fire of judgment. 

<margin>The fourth time</margin> 
But we must pass on to the **fourth period**: in which the Son and the Holy Spirit, who had not been so openly revealed in past times as the Father had been, appeared so clearly that the one (the Son) worked his deeds openly until his Ascension, and the other (the Spirit) worked for a long time through the apostles—though not one without the other, just as they do not work without the Father. They continue to work even unto the present, to complete the works they began. In this matter the reader must be warned—and lest he fall asleep because he has been warned elsewhere, he must be diligently urged—that whenever one Person is said to be working, he must not (God forbid!) understand that 

<column-break/>

Person to be working alone. Nor should he think that I have ever meant this, even if it is not noted by me in some places. For I am speaking not to unbelievers, but to the faithful. It would be very tedious to note the same point in every single place—once, twice, and a third time, again and again at every moment. Rather, it must be clearly understood and held as follows: that Scripture remains silent about two Persons and speaks of one for the sake of the specific place and time, so that the work being discussed may be ascribed to that Person by the "property of the mystery." <note>This is a technical term meaning that while all three Persons of the Trinity act together, certain actions are "appropriated" to one Person to help us understand their unique character.</note> This is done so that the reader understands that the Person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another.

In this **fourth period**, regarding the things written above, the Son and the Holy Spirit were shown working together. For the Son himself was baptized by John so that he might sanctify the waters, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove. They wished themselves to be understood as one God, and that both were sent by the Father to redeem the human race. Indeed, if we speak of humility, what is more humble than for the Son of God to appear in the flesh, and the Holy Spirit in the form of the simplest bird, which is not even accustomed to hurting the smallest worms? 

Why, however, did he appear in the form of a dove and not, as he did later, in the form of fire? Was it not because the dove signifies what was then beginning and appearing, while the fire signifies what was yet to come? This is why James and John, wishing to imitate the zeal of Elijah, heard from the Master of humility himself: "You do not know of what spirit you are; the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them." <note>Luke 9:55-56</note> Therefore, the Son and the Holy Spirit were sent together by the Father at the same time, as the Angel said to Mary: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you," <note>Luke 1:35</note> so that it might appear that both proceed from one Father. "I," says the Son, "proceeded and came from God." <note>John 8:42</note> And here is the difference: everyone who is born proceeds, but not everyone [who proceeds] is "turned back." <note>A complex point of Trinitarian theology regarding the different "processions" or origins of the Son and the Spirit.</note> 

But now we must deal with the **fifth period**, in the beginning of which we now stand: in which it is necessary for the Holy Spirit, sent by the Son, to still perform his works—much more deeply than he has worked until now.

The author emphasizes that while specific Persons are highlighted in different eras (like the Spirit in the present "Fifth Time"), the Trinity always acts as a single, unified Godhead.</summary>

# John [Joachim], The First [Book] of the Ten-Stringed [Psaltery]

...everyone should learn to honor the Holy Spirit just as they honor the Father and the Son. In this, there is no doubt that it is found in his Gospel. For he who is not submissive and devoted does not honor him as is fitting when he receives his Gospel. And what is his Gospel? It is that of which John speaks in the Book of Revelation: <note>original: "Apocalypsis"</note> *I saw an angel of God flying through the midst of heaven, and the eternal gospel was given to him.* <note>Referencing Revelation 14:6. For Joachim, the "Eternal Gospel" is not a new book, but a spiritual understanding of the New Testament that would characterize the coming third age.</note> What is his Gospel? It is that which proceeds from the Gospel of Christ. For *the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.* <note>2 Corinthians 3:6</note> For this reason, Truth itself <note>referring to Christ</note> says: *When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.* And to show that he would take from the Gospel of Christ and from his scripture—and, changing it as if from water into wine, would intoxicate the elect—he added and said: *For he will not speak of himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things to come. He will glorify me because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you.* Therefore, the Holy Spirit will perform this work in us: by teaching us all truth, he may raise our minds to heavenly desires and make us look forward to that day for which all the saints sighed, and to glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. For it is necessary for him to transform our minds—which he can do when he wills and as he wills, since he is God—and to transfer our hearts from carnal desires to the love of heavenly things, so that in a certain way we are not what we were, but begin to be something else. Behold, if we remember those things which have been said:

*   In the **first period**, God worked **faith**.
*   In the **second**, **patience**.
*   In the **third**, **zeal**.
*   In the **fourth**, **humility**.
*   In the **fifth**, **hope**.

However, because in this life the kingdom is not in its full truth but is in exile <note>original: "exiliuz"</note>, nor must one work in judgment as Elijah did, but in gentleness as Jesus taught, that which was said about the middle time—that is, about the time of the Kings and Prophets—

<column-break/>

was done more for the demonstration of those things which will exist in our heavenly homeland after the end of the world, rather than to be believed that the cause of so great a mystery was completed back then. Therefore, it is to be consummated in the future age: when all the wicked have been judged by Almighty God in the fire of his zeal, with the judges also sitting upon their thrones, he alone will reign in Jerusalem and will fill the hearts of all the people living in it with joy and gladness, just as it is said: *The dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.* <note>Psalm 87:7</note>

Now, so that we may compare these mysteries with the things that truly happened:

**One Abraham** signifies the **Father alone**, because he, the one Father, sends the Son and the Holy Spirit.

**One Isaac** signifies the **Father and the Son together**, because together the Father and Son are one God, and they two equally send the Holy Spirit.

**One Jacob** signifies the **three persons together**, because those three persons are one God. And from that one God, who is triune and one, "seven spirits" <note>Symbolizing the fullness of the Holy Spirit's gifts.</note> were sent into all the earth.

**One Joseph** signifies the **Son and the Holy Spirit together**, because together those two are one God, and they were sent together by the one Father.

**One Ephraim** signifies the **Holy Spirit alone**, because he, the one Holy Spirit, is sent by the Father and the Son.

In a wondrous way, God the Father has, in a different reality, something similar to the Holy Spirit. The Father and Son [share something] with the Son and Holy Spirit. But the Trinity itself has nothing to which it is similar, because it is itself and not some other thing. For the one Father has the role of sending the Son and the Holy Spirit. The one Holy Spirit has the role of being sent by the Father and the Son. The Father and the Son together have the role of sending the Holy Spirit. The Son and the Holy Spirit together have the role of being sent by the Father. Truly, the three together have the role of giving and sending their gifts to make the elect blessed, making them participants in their fullness.

Since we have seen in the first section the mystery of the Trinity, and in the second section the five relationships by which one person is distinguished from another person, or even the Trinity itself from the things created by it, it is now worthy of praise to treat the seven modes <note>Joachim refers to the seven ways we can speak of God: as three individual persons, three pairs of persons, and the three together as one.</note> in which whatever is called "God" is spoken of in relation to Himself: whether it be worshipped as a single person, two together, or three at once. But so that this may be more easily grasped, we must similarly turn to examples.

¶ In what ways the persons of the deity are spoken of in relation to themselves: whether individually, two together, or three at once.

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
It is the custom of the Holy Scriptures that the word "flesh" is understood to mean "man," as in that saying: *And all flesh shall see the salvation of God together.* <note>Isaiah 40:5 and Luke 3:6. Here "flesh" is a synecdoche, where a part represents the whole human being.</note>

<column-break/>

From Leviticus also and from other places in the scriptures, it can be shown that all relatives are "one flesh," <note>referring to the laws of kinship and marriage, such as in Leviticus 18:6 or Genesis 2:24</note> just as husband and wife are. Because this is so, not only is the flesh of one man to be called "one flesh," but also, at the same time, the flesh of husband and wife, the flesh of father and son, the flesh of uncle and nephew, and so on for the rest. Therefore, Abraham alone is "one flesh." Isaac alone is "one flesh." Jacob alone is "one flesh." Then, Abraham and Jacob together are "one flesh"; Abraham and Isaac together are "one flesh." Isaac and Jacob are likewise "one flesh," and at the same time all three themselves are "one flesh." This is surely said and understood, even if the unity of flesh stands far apart from the unity of spirit—and especially of that Spirit whose wonder is found in everything that exists. For if anything that is good and lovable can be said of the lowest things <note>meaning earthly or physical realities</note>, how much more so of the Lord!

...from God almighty, the creator of all good things. How truly lovely it is for men to have their own <term>flesh</term> <note>original: "carnez suam". In this context, "flesh" refers to a biological heir or blood relative.</note> as an heir, rather than

<column-break/>

a stranger: this can be proven by the example of Abraham himself, who desired and received one.

Therefore, to use the words of Augustine speaking of that majesty which exceeds all speech in his book *On the Trinity*: <note>St. Augustine’s "De Trinitate" is the foundational Western theological text on the nature of the Triune God.</note> "And the Father individually is one God; and the Son individually is one God; and the Holy Spirit individually is one God. But Father and Son together are one God. Father and Holy Spirit together are one God. Son and Holy Spirit together are one God. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are one God." Whether, therefore,

<column-break/>

he is called God, or Wisdom, or Goodness, or anything similar, it is to be understood in the same way. And under these seven confessions <note>The "seven confessions" refer to the seven possible ways of grouping the three Persons (3 individual, 3 pairs, 1 trio) as shown in the diagram above.</note> it must be condensed with an equal judgment. In this, you must also watchfully observe: that in a similar way, one must understand whatever is said of God in relation to his creatures, such as God as creator, almighty, king, shepherd, teacher, and even "Father" when it is spoken in relation to creatures. For if it is established throughout that it is not only God the Father who is to be called the Father...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the Trinity, moving from the definitions of the persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) to their "missions" or how they act within time toward humanity, referencing St. Augustine’s theology.</meta>

# Abba. Book of the Psaltery

...of the faithful peoples: indeed, even the Son and the **Holy Spirit** are called "father" <note>In the sense of being the source or creator of the faithful.</note>; although in this specific way, neither should the Father alone be called "Father," nor should the three together be called "three fathers," but rather each person is Father, and all three together are one Father. 

But when the word "Father" is used relatively to the Son, then He alone is to be called Father, just as the Son alone is to be called Son. Let it not be a burden to repeat what has been said regarding these relationships, so that what we expressed less fully before may be added to. The Son and the Holy Spirit are sent by the Father alone, because they are sent by Him from whom they have their being. 

According to this, God the Father is spoken of relatively: not only in relation to the Son, but also to the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, both the Father and the Son are spoken of relatively to the Holy Spirit in the sense that they send and give Him. But the Son and the Holy Spirit together are also spoken of relatively to the Father, because they are sent by Him. Similarly, the Holy Spirit is spoken of relatively to the Father and the Son, because He is sent and given by them. For indeed, he who is sent by someone has a relationship to the one who sends him. 

Furthermore, all three persons together have a relationship to those **seven gifts**: which are called the "seven spirits of the Lord sent into all the earth" <note>A reference to the gifts of the Holy Spirit mentioned in Isaiah 11:2 and Revelation 5:6.</note>, and to every chosen creature, but more specifically to all His messengers. These <term>missions</term> <note>In theology, a "mission" refers to the way a person of the Trinity "proceeds" into the world or into a soul.</note> began to exist in time, starting from the moment the creatures to whom they were sent began to exist. This is because the Son and the Holy Spirit were sent, and by them also those seven gifts were sent—the "seven spirits of the Lord sent into all the earth"—and all who are sent from on high for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation. 

Hence they are also called holy angels. In these relationships, one should not understand the eternal birth of the Son or the eternal proceeding of the Holy Spirit, but rather that which began in time. This is not—God forbid—because that Nature is changeable (for with Him "there is no change or shadow of turning" <note>James 1:17</note>), but because there were now creatures for whose sake all these things were said. 

Nor should it be understood that the Son, who is the **Word of God**, and the Holy Spirit, who is the **Love of God**, pass from place to place like physical creatures do, or even as spiritual creatures <note>Such as angels or human souls.</note> do, who approach or depart from here or there by their thoughts;

<column-break/>

and although the Son and the Holy Spirit are everywhere, just as the Father is, through the presence of their divinity, they are not everywhere through <term>indwelling grace</term> <note>The specific way God "lives" within a person who is in a state of grace.</note>. 

This is much like if a blind man were placed in the sun: he would not see the light present there, nor would a sick man feel the heat; yet it would be said that the power of the sun "came" to them when the blind man’s eyes are opened and the sick man's coldness passes away. 

Therefore, even if these relationships were temporal, they are neither dissimilar nor foreign to those which are eternal, because the eternal ones are the cause of the temporal ones. The temporal ones occur according to the pattern of the eternal. For because the Father and the Son produce the Holy Spirit from themselves (if I may speak this way), they both send Him who proceeds from them without end. 

Because the Son and the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father—though the Son in one way and the Holy Spirit in another—both were sent to redeem the human race. Thus the angel said to Mary: "The Holy Spirit," he said, "shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you" <note>Luke 1:35</note>. It is well said that both act together, yet only one person was born of the Virgin: because only one was always begotten of the Father. And because there is only one Spirit who proceeds from the Father, He proceeds nonetheless from the Son; and by both the Father and the Son, He is sent to men and given as a gift. 

Together in themselves, all three persons have the power to give the "seven spirits," which are the seven gifts of that same Spirit; they send them into all the earth—that is, into every creature chosen by the Lord. Thus, eternal relationships became, in a sense, temporal through the Lord acting as the cause, though this followed the pattern and likeness of the eternal state. 

Finally, those five virtues we spoke of above are temporal in regards to their labor, even if they are eternal in regards to their fruit. For in the afterlife, there will be no labor of humility, no pain of patience, no argument of faith, no failing of hope, nor the heat of zeal by which the just man is tested. And yet, the "fruit" of these virtues will remain forever. For surely in that heavenly homeland, no one will be proud, no one impatient, no one unfaithful, no one despairing, and no one bitter...

Joachim uses the metaphor of a blind man in the sun to explain how God can be "present" in new ways through grace without moving or changing His eternal nature.</summary>

# Joachim’s First [Book] on the Ten-Stringed [Psaltery]

...perfection. But for this reason all those things will cease: because they will have obtained those states of blessedness for which they have long struggled. Although **charity** is not transitory in the same way as the other four; for even if its temporal exercise does not remain forever, its essence does. Therefore, these **five virtues** <note>Faith, Hope, Charity, Humility, and Patience.</note> have something in common with those five <term>relations<note>In Trinitarian theology, "relations" (relationes) refer to the ways the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished by their relationship to one another (e.g., Paternity, Filiation).</note></term>: just as the **seven gifts of the Holy Spirit** relate to those seven modes by which the persons of the deity are spoken of toward themselves—whether each one individually, or two or three together. This is done so that—just as the Son is from the Father and not from the Holy Spirit—one might not think there are certain gifts from the Father alone or the Son alone that do not also come from the Holy Spirit. Otherwise, just as the Son is the Word of God and the Son of the most high Father, so too the Holy Spirit...

Therefore, these seven gifts are sent and given by the entire Trinity, even if they are properly ascribed to the Holy Spirit—just as charity is—because they are distributed by him to individuals. But if you ask how this is, or how the same Spirit is said to "distribute from his own as he wills," or how God the Father or the Son is said to "give of the Holy Spirit," or how that word of the Psalmist is understood—*You have received gifts among men* <note>original: "Accepisti dona in hominibus" from Psalm 68:18.</note>—this is not the time to discuss it. This much we know: that the Holy Spirit himself is the supreme gift of God, namely of the Father and the Son, in whom and under whom all these gifts are contained, along with many others. And it must be noted that just as each person of the Trinity is understood differently when spoken of in relation to the others...

<column-break/>

...is truly the Spirit of the Father and the Son: so these seven gifts belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And it should be noted that of those virtues written above, the two lower ones seem to pertain to the **humanity of Christ**: namely, **Humility** to the soul and **Patience** to the flesh; the remaining three pertain to the Trinity itself (which is God): namely, **Faith** to the Father, because she is the foundation of the virtues, just as the Father is the Principle in the deity; **Hope** to the Son, who, coming into the world, promised us the kingdom and the future life; and **Charity** to the Holy Spirit, who was given to us so that charity itself might be poured out into our hearts. Whoever is rooted in these five virtues is considered worthy by God to receive those seven special gifts, which are the "seven spirits of the Lord sent into all the earth."

---

...differently than when spoken of toward themselves: so it is with these gifts. For indeed, in relation to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they are called "gifts"; but in relation to themselves, they are called "seven spirits" or even "seven virtues."

It appears that just as those five virtues pertain in some way to those five relations, so these seven pertain to those seven modes by which God is spoken of toward Himself. However, this is more a matter of intellectual likeness than a specific cause. Truly, as in the higher understanding—which is called <term>anagogical<note>A method of spiritual interpretation that looks toward the eternal or heavenly fulfillment of a text.</note></term>—the three <term>denaries<note>original: "denarij," referring to groups of ten. # Abba: The Book of the Psaltery

...of the persons of the deity to themselves: so too in contemplative understanding: the **three denarii** <note>original: "tres denarij". Here, Joachim uses "denarii"—literally Roman coins—as symbolic units or rewards representing theological concepts.</note> designate those three exercises which we mentioned above: namely, **prevenient grace**, **cooperating grace**, and **perfecting grace**. The **five denarii** represent the five virtues written above; the **seven denarii** represent the **seven gifts of the Holy Spirit**. But so that this may be more easily understood, it is necessary for us to insert something into this little work concerning the fullness of the special spiritual meanings <note>original: "intelligentiarum". In Joachim's system, an "intelligence" is a specific method or level of interpreting the Bible.</note> themselves. Thus, the reader who has the time may presume to explain even the greatest things from the few we have noted in the faith of that Supreme Master who holds the **Key of David** <term>Key of David<note>A biblical symbol (Isaiah 22:22) for the authority to open or shut the meaning of God's word; Joachim attributes this "unlocking" of history to the Holy Spirit.</note></term>. We have as our helper the Holy Spirit himself, the administrator of these meanings, in whom this promise was made to us; a promise which must be fulfilled according to its fullness in its own time. For this is not from any prophet or apostle, but from the Truth itself <note>A reference to Jesus Christ.</note> who says: *when that Spirit of Truth comes, he will teach you all truth.* <note>John 16:13.</note>

### On the fullness of the spiritual meanings which are contained in the numbers three, five, and seven.

In these things which we have treated until now under the Lord's protection, the hidden mysteries of the Most High God have been shown—to whom belongs everything that is best. We have shown how the **thirty psalms** pertain to the knowledge of the Holy and Indivisible Trinity; the **fifty** to the five relations by which the persons are spoken of in relation to other persons; and finally, those same three persons to their own gifts. The **seventy** pertain to the seven modes by which the persons of the deity are spoken of toward themselves: whether each one individually, or two and two together, or even all three together. Now, however, something must be said about the fullness of those spiritual meanings themselves, according to what has been said so far, so that with the testimonies of truth multiplied, people may be converted with their whole heart and whole faith to Him who called us out of darkness into his admirable name. Indeed, it should be known that there are **twelve special spiritual meanings** flowing in a miraculous way from the triple source of the "letter" <note>The "letter" refers to the literal text of the Bible, which Joachim sees as a fountain for deeper spiritual layers.</note>—not indeed from the whole scripture of the New or Old Testament, but from that

<column-break/>

part which is written as history: and even this only in part. For not all spiritual meanings can be assigned in all places of the histories, but they can be in many. The "source of the letter" itself is what we call the Trinity: the Old and New Testaments, and the institutions of the Holy Fathers, among which is contained the ministry of the Church. This ministry is manifold, instituted by apostolic men to designate something great. Therefore, from this **triple letter**, twelve spiritual meanings proceed. Of these, some are lower and more humble, and yet through them, a more abundant fruit is found in the human race.

The first of these is the **historical sense**, where something is taught to have been instituted according to the example of history: as when an abbot is sent to a new monastery with twelve monks, following the example of Christ and the Apostles. The second is called the **moral sense**, because through it, morals are composed; as when vices and virtues are signaled by visible things, both good and evil. But we can better show the properties of each—namely the historical and the moral—which we have brought forth in bare words, by using examples of things. 

Imagine a certain man who has a talkative and lascivious wife; not wishing to make her sad, he agrees with her in all things, following her will. If a priest seeks to rebuke this man over his confusion, he says the man is a "miserable Adam" who followed Eve. He calls him a "miserable and weakened Samson" who, through the love of an impious woman, was deprived of that singular strength of his, and then deprived of his eyes. There is also another good man who has a chaste wife, fearing God, humble and faithful; he guards her more for the love of God than for lust, just as Joseph guarded Mary. Yet, because she is a woman, he—as a man—disdains to follow her will in any strong matter. To this man it must be said that he should learn to be toward his wife in such a way that he regards her as a Sarah—a prudent woman who fears God. But if an Abbot should consider it, he should know that in order to cast out the handmaid and her son, Abraham did not follow his own will, but that of his wife <note>A reference to Sarah demanding the expulsion of Hagar and Ishmael (Genesis 21), which was confirmed by God.</note>, just as...

# John First [Book] On Harmony

...wishing to bless Esau, Isaac was overcome by his wife so that he would bless Jacob; he was deceived by the pious deception of a pious wife. For Isaac loved the one whom the Lord did not love <note>Isaac favored Esau, while God had chosen Jacob (Malachi 1:2-3).</note>. Rebecca, however, loved the one whom the Lord loved. And for that reason she prevailed, as her will was one with God's in her loving. There is no doubt that she was inspired by the divine Spirit.

Let us speak of this more clearly, so that it may be more easily understood. Sarah was called not only the wife but also the sister of Abraham. Now, there may be some good man who has a sister who does not want a husband, but rather chooses to live in chastity, so that she might be (according to the Apostle) free and holy and serve God in mind and body <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:34.</note>. Seeing his sister’s devotion, he does not wish to hand her over to a husband against her vow—one who would feed and rule her—but he himself decides to be bound to her in all things for her life. She, seeing at last that it is beneficial, advises her brother to take a wife and procreate children. But because she herself has no carnal son, she seeks a way to have a special one (with her brother nonetheless willing) and him agreeing in all things. For he sees some orphan and pities him; taking him into his house, he and his sister together adopt him as a son and fear God. 

However, it often happens that the one born of the wife begins to envy this adopted son (if perhaps the latter is wiser than him) and seeks to oppress him and subject him to himself, as if in play, while the mother sees and agrees. This is how he who is born according to the flesh from servile work <note>Ishmael, born of the bondwoman Hagar.</note> persecutes him who is born according to the spirit <note>Isaac, born of the free woman Sarah.</note>. It then belongs to the virgin of God to take her side on behalf of the spiritual son and say to her brother: 
<margin>Genesis</margin>
"Cast out this bondwoman and her son" <note>original: "Ejice ancillam hanc ꝛ filiū eius." From Genesis 21:10.</note>. That is: hold a wife and a son born to you according to the flesh in your outward work, but nonetheless ordain that this one who lives spiritually should remain alone in your interior affairs; for this one is the heir more than the other, and to him more than the other is the inheritance of the righteous father owed. 

Therefore, examples of this kind and similar ones are to be ascribed to **historical understanding** <term>historical understanding<note>Also called the literal sense; interpreting the Bible as a record of events that serve as moral examples for behavior.</note></term>. It also belongs to this understanding to console the faint-hearted in times of affliction by proposing examples of the righteous who suffered similar things. This is done rightly if, 

<column-break/>

for one suffering exile through the envy of relatives, Joseph is called to memory. If one is fleeing from the face of an enemy, let the examples of Jacob, Moses, David, and Elijah be proposed, so that he may learn, if he is good, to have trust in Him who does not desert those hoping in Him, saying daily in his prayers: "If the Lord is my helper, I will not fear what man can do to me" <note>original: "Si dominus mihi adiutor est: non timebo quid faciat mihi homo." From Psalm 118:6.</note>. If he is scourged by God, let him look to Job. If afflicted by subordinates, to Moses and Aaron. If deposed from dignity, to Samuel the prophet. If worn down for the sake of justice, let him look to those who suffered for justice's sake. Therefore, this kind of teaching, which is assigned to the surface of the historical letter, is so named because, by likening the matters at hand to similar ones, it shows simple people through these examples what they ought to desire and what they ought to avoid.

<margin>Second intelligence</margin>
The **second understanding**, which is called **moral**, is not conducted only in outward things like the historical—although even the historical sometimes touches upon internal matters—but walking as if between both, it embraces now internal things, now external. It is not to be assigned to many different persons as the historical is, but in another, more subtle way. 

For example: Abraham had two sons, one from a bondwoman and one from a free woman. We ask what these things signify according to moral understanding, and we find it signified 
<margin>Genesis</margin>
in **Abraham**: a man recently converted from the vanity of the age to the service of God. And the legitimate wife of this man is the "good conduct" which he has chosen. The bondwoman, however, is "carnal anxiety," which the Lord forbids in the Gospel, saying: "Do not be anxious, saying: what shall we eat? or what shall we drink? or with what shall we be clothed?" <note>original: "Nolite solliciti esse dicentes: quid manducabimus..." From Matthew 6:31.</note>. And the Lord indeed forbids this, who also says elsewhere: "Be you therefore perfect, even as your heavenly Father is perfect" <note>original: "Estote ergo vos perfecti..." From Matthew 5:48.</note>. But because this anxiety mostly accompanies a man (as if by necessity) when he is ascending out of "Egypt" <note>Joachim uses "Egypt" as a symbol for the worldly, sinful life the convert is leaving.</note>—due to the sterility of the spiritual wife who does not yet deserve to see the fruit of her labor—she must be tolerated for a time and made fruitful with offspring, so that at least her work may benefit those using it for salvation. But because the fruit of this kind of exercise is not well accustomed... <meta>catchword: ...to play (lus)</meta>

# Father. Book of the Psalter

...to proceed with the fruit of a spiritual way of life inspired by God; for certainly the utility of temporal convenience seeks to subject and trample the utility of the eternal. Therefore, Scripture must be heard, which speaks freely in part, saying: *Cast out this bondwoman and her son; for the son of the bondwoman shall not be an heir with the son of the free woman* <note>original: "Ejice ancillam hanc z filium eius..." from Genesis 21:10 and Galatians 4:30. In this allegory, Hagar/the bondwoman represents the Law or worldly cares, while Sarah/the free woman represents Grace or the spiritual life.</note>. What does it mean that the son of the bondwoman shall not be an heir with the son of the free woman, if not that which the Apostle says: *No one soldiering for God entangles himself in secular business* <note>original: "Nemo militās deo implicat se secularibus negotijs" from 2 Timothy 2:4.</note>. And Sarah spoke this well at that time when she rejoiced that she had received a legitimate heir; because then anyone can be secure in that promise of the Lord saying: *Look at the birds of the air: they do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they?* <note>A quote from Matthew 6:26, emphasizing trust in divine providence over worldly anxiety.</note> For just as your heavenly Father [provides], because here all things are needed. Light from long conversation in spiritual exercise: now he considers himself to have attained the fruit from the Lord. And this is indeed for the sake of example.

<margin>A showing</margin> Having shown the foundations, he who feeds the little ones with the **milk of history** <note>The "historical sense" is the literal meaning of the Bible, considered basic nourishment for beginners.</note> has two understandings: the first instructs the youths by the examples of the fathers; the second, by the **butter of mystical words**, fattens the young men progressing toward God. One must then pass to those understandings which require a spiritual elder, because in them is contained the fullness of faith and the sublimity of the knowledge of the sacraments of God.

<margin>Certainly</margin> Certainly, in these things that have been assigned, everything that has been said—or can be said—pertains to the instruction of human life. In the remaining ten, however, the great works of the Lord are shown, sought out according to all His wills; and what is greater than these: even the invisible mysteries of God. However, it must not be overlooked that these two understandings remain in the number of the others until the completion of the **fifteen steps** <note>Likely referring to the fifteen "Psalms of Ascent" (Psalms 120-134), used here as a metaphor for spiritual progress.</note>; or to the fulfillment of the number of twelve, where to the forty days or the seventy elders, two and two were added; and yet the forty days and the seventy elders are written rather than forty-two or seventy-two, so that for the sake of one mystery they are outside, while for the sake of another they seem to be present. Nor is it a wonder if these two understandings are separated from the number of the [other] ten.

<column-break/>

For in His birth, Christ Jesus—to whom the **moral understanding** pertains—and in His passion—to which the **historical understanding** pertains—wished to appear in this way: rejected in the midst of the Jews, so that He might show Himself more as a man than as God. Just as He could not deny Himself in His signs <note>His miracles.</note>, because He is the Truth; nevertheless, because "soulish" men <note>term: "animales homines" - people who live according to natural instincts or the "flesh" rather than the Spirit.</note> were only able to weigh what they saw, they thought Him a mere man and killed Him, so that those things written in the Law and the Prophets about Him might be fulfilled.

Those things concerning the woman were to teach us to consent to good things; He suffered on the cross so that He might show an example of one who suffers. And while in the **historical understanding**, patience is strengthened by the examples given; in the **moral**, humility is solidified. Indeed, the Resurrection, the Ascension, and the coming of the Holy Spirit—to which the higher understandings pertain—were separated from this law; for He who was already dead had completed the Law, He who, having received the vinegar on the cross, had said: *It is finished.*

These pertain to three things: those three paths, as we have often said, which the Apostle commemorates saying: *Now there remain: faith, hope, and charity, these three* <note>1 Corinthians 13:13.</note>. Namely: **faith** for the resurrection, **hope** for the ascension, and **charity** for the advent of the Holy Spirit. And not only charity itself, but also other gifts with it, according to what both the things seen and the authorities testify. For not only, he says, *the charity of God is poured out in the hearts of the faithful through the Holy Spirit who was given to them* on that day; but also the gifts were made proper to individuals, about which the Prophet predicted long before: *You have ascended on high, You have led captivity captive, You have received gifts among men* <note>Psalm 68:18.</note>. And the Apostle: *Ascending on high, He led captivity captive, He gave gifts to men* <note>Ephesians 4:8.</note>. And soon it follows: *And He gave some to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.*

# John I. The Ten Strings 264

...until we all meet in the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ <note>original: "occurramus oēs in vnitatem fidei & agnitionem filij dei..." from Ephesians 4:13</note>. Therefore, He did not give just one gift to the faithful, but many: of which, however, seven are special. It is for this reason that the solemnity of this feast is celebrated for seven days in the Church: so that the sacred solemnity might correspond to the showing of the tongues and the authorities <note>This refers to the "tongues of fire" at Pentecost and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note>. Wherefore, if faith, hope, and charity are commended to us in those three works, and the dispersion of tongues occurred at that very hour when the Holy Spirit came to the apostles: it is clear that His seven gifts, which Scripture so solemnly commends to us, make ten virtues. These ten virtues pertain to the Paschal season, according to the ten strings of the psalter <note>term: "ten strings of the psalter" (decem cordae psalterii). In medieval theology, the ten-stringed lyre mentioned in the Psalms was often used as a symbol for the Ten Commandments or, as here, a combination of the three theological virtues (Faith, Hope, Charity) and the seven gifts of the Spirit.</note>, upon which one must not rightfully play except in a time of joy, provided that the long chants of lamentation and mourning are completed. However, the fact that psalms are also said at other times at the beginning of joys—which pertain to the time of joy according to a part—must be noted. For although there are fifteen virtues belonging to the fifteen steps <note>A reference to the "Psalms of Ascent" or "Gradual Psalms" (120–134), often associated with steps of spiritual progress.</note>, there are nevertheless ten of them that belong to the ten strings: Faith, Hope, Charity, and the seven gifts of the Spirit designated in the tongues. And as we have seen regarding the two understandings which pertain to patience and humility, for the instruction of the outer and the inner man—since the historical pertains to the outer, and the moral to the inner—not in every case entirely, but in part: it remains for us to see, as God grants, the ten "intelligences" <note>term: "intelligences" (intelligentijs). Here, the author uses the word to mean levels of reading or interpreting the Bible.</note> that belong to the ten strings.

<margin>Genesis</margin>
### ¶ Of the ten intelligences which belong to the ten strings of the psalter.

We said above that in Hagar, according to the historical understanding, a woman is signified; in Sarah, a woman fearing God, free from marriage, who serves the Lord with a perfect heart. According to the moral understanding, however, the "maidservant" signifies the anxiety for fleshly things, while the "free woman" signifies a pious conversation and a will directed toward the good. Now let us look at the remaining understandings as God shall grant.

### ¶ Of the tropological intelligence.

The tropological intelligence <note>term: "tropological" (tropologica). The "moral" sense of scripture, specifically how the words of the Bible should change one's behavior or "mode" of living.</note> is that in which the various modes of the words of God

<column-break/>

are specifically treated. This rightly exceeds the moral level by one degree, because in that level the focus is on the flesh and the soul, but in this one it is on the letter and the spirit; in that level, on things that are below; in this one, on things that are above. For *Tropos* in Greek is "mode" in Latin, and *logos* is "speech." Hence, "tropology," because according to it we deal with the different modes of the words of God. Moreover, in this species, Abraham signifies the doctor <note>In a medieval context, a "doctor" is a formal teacher of the Church or a master of theology.</note> of the Church, whose legitimate wife is spiritual understanding, but whose concubine is the literal letter—which must sometimes be cast out along with her sons. For the sons of the literal letter are carnal senses, but the sons of spiritual understanding are spiritual meditations.

### ¶ Of the contemplative intelligence.

After this follows the contemplative intelligence, which is the fourth from the historical, and the second from the tropological. It also exceeds the tropological by one degree because it desires the spiritual more than the former, containing both worlds—both the things of the world and those extending toward the things of the Spirit of God. This is according to that word of the Apostle: *The spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one* <note>original: "Spūalis qui iudicet omnia..." from 1 Corinthians 2:15.</note>; who eats butter and honey so that he may know how to refuse evil and choose good; or who knows how to providently withdraw himself from a lesser justice so that he may grasp a more powerful one. According to this understanding, Abraham signifies the spiritual man: for example, a perfect monk or a hermit. The maidservant signifies the active life. Sarah signifies the contemplative life <note>The "active life" involves physical works of mercy, while the "contemplative life" focuses on prayer and the study of God.</note>. The sons of the maidservant are bodily exercises; the sons of the free woman are spiritual virtues. However, although it is a good work to feed the hungry, to give drink to the thirsty, to clothe the naked, and things similar to these, nevertheless all bodily exercises are to be considered as nothing in respect to spiritual virtues. For the Lord said, *The poor you will always have with you, but me you will not always have* <note>John 12:8</note>; and that Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her <note>Luke 10:42</note>. Because bodily exercise is useful for a little, but piety is useful for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come <note>1 Timothy 4:8</note>.

# ¶ Concerning the Anagogical Sense

<margin>It is called anagogical because no other understanding exists above it. Truly, "anagogy" <note>original: "anagogen"</note> is interpreted as the higher intellect. For what can be higher than God?</margin>
**T**he fifth intelligence—the third being the tropological <term>tropological: the "moral" sense of Scripture that teaches us how to act</term>—is properly called the Anagogical <term>anagogical: the "heavenly" sense of Scripture that points toward the afterlife and the final union with God</term>. According to this understanding, Abraham signifies God the Father; the handmaid signifies the earthly Jerusalem, who was cast out with her children; but the Free Woman <note>Referencing Sarah from the Book of Genesis</note> signifies that Jerusalem which is above—that is, the perfect vision of peace—for which the souls of the elect sigh. Her children neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven; they are the children of God, being children of the resurrection. These are the three intelligences that pertain to faith, hope, and charity. Indeed, the tropological pertains to faith, because "faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ." The contemplative pertains to hope, because we seek to see that which we love and hope for. The anagogical pertains to charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) means divine love</term>, because through it we seek God. God is Charity; and whoever has charity possesses in it everything they seek at once. For if the gifts of the Holy Spirit—which were given to the elect on the day of Pentecost and are to be given to all the elect on the last day—are designated in the son of the free woman, and the first and highest of those gifts is charity itself: it is clear that just as charity is the "end of the commandment," so the anagogical intelligence is the end of the five intelligences prescribed here, because there is none higher. Now, so that it might not be a burden to produce the "keys" to these five prescribed intelligences: it must be known that the first of them, called the historical, is properly designated in the two sons of Terah—namely, Abraham and his nephew Lot—who went out with him from Ur of the Chaldeans to come into the land of Canaan, though Terah himself only reached Haran and died there. The second, called the moral, is designated in the two wives of Abraham. Abraham reached the land of promise because at this intelligence, the spiritual understandings begin to emerge.

<column-break/>

For in Hagar is signified the state of servitude, and in Sarah the liberty that is in faith, through which Abraham was made certain. The third, called the tropological, is designated in the two sons of Isaac: the younger of whom <note>Jacob</note> received the blessing of the elder <note>Esau</note>. For Esau signifies carnal doctrine, which is according to the "letter that kills," while Jacob signifies spiritual doctrine, which is not made by human hands but inspired by mother grace. The fourth, called the contemplative, is designated in the two wives of Jacob: the first, named Leah, signifies the life of contemplative monks. The second, named Rachel, signifies the hermit's life <note>original: "vitam heremitariam"</note> where they gaze upon divine solaces. The fifth, called the anagogical, is signified in the two sons of Joseph: the first, named Manasseh, signifies temporal life <note>The name Manasseh was traditionally interpreted as "forgetting," here implying forgetting worldly things</note>. The second, named Ephraim, signifies that blessed heavenly life enjoyed by the holy angels and the souls of the righteous—not now "through a mirror darkly," but in the perfect vision of God. The recorded lineage of this holy progeny ends with Ephraim, who was the fifth from Abraham; this matches the ascent of these intelligences, the last of which is the fifth from the historical, and is the superior intellect. A truly wonderful thing happens in these mysteries: the men and women correspond to each other in turns. In the first step, two men lead; in the second, two women follow; in the third, two men; in the fourth, two women; in the fifth, two men. Why is this, if not because the moral and contemplative intelligences are better suited to those who seek to be "built up"—the subordinates who need instructors—rather than the leaders? Furthermore, in the first, third, and fifth steps, a "masculine" significance is necessary: for the married man, to whom the "history" applies, keeps his wife and family under discipline; and the "tropological" applies to the teacher, who holds the Church under his doctrine to form it; and he who, departing from the world, goes to the fatherland of those who renounce the world, begins in a way to be a father. Therefore, these intelligences are mixed together, and contemplative rest works—

Joachim: First Book of the Harmony <note>original: "Joa. Primus Dececorday" is a corrupted OCR transcription of "Joachim: Primum De Concordia," referring to Joachim of Fiore’s major work *De Concordia Veteris et Novi Testamenti* (The Harmony of the Old and New Testaments)</note>

...be argued by the diligence of those working: if by chance laziness is sometimes the cause: let the diligence of the workers in the first and third grades be tempered by the leisure of those who contemplate. Enough has been said about these matters according to the place. We must come, however, to typical understanding <term>typical understanding: also known as typology, this is a method of Bible interpretation where people or events in the Old Testament are seen as "types" or "foreshadowings" of things in the New Testament</term>: which we have said has seven types: which the seven spirits sent from heaven work upon the earth.

### ¶ Concerning the seven types of typical understanding.

In the first type of typical understanding, Abraham signifies the high priests of the Jews; Hagar signifies the Israelite people; Sarah signifies the tribe of Levi, which was established to live from the labor of the sons of Israel. In the second, Abraham signifies the bishops; Hagar the church of the laity; Sarah the church of the clergy. In the third understanding, Abraham signifies the prelates <note>leaders or abbots</note> of monasteries; Hagar the church of the converts <term>converts: "conversi," or lay brothers who joined monasteries later in life to perform manual labor</term>; Sarah the church of the monks. Furthermore, each of these churches has its own children similar to itself: namely, those who are instructed by them. In the fourth type, Abraham signifies the high priests of the Jews and the bishops of the Greeks; Hagar the synagogue of the Jews; Sarah the church of the Greeks. Hence it is said by the apostle: "The power of God is the gospel for the salvation of everyone who believes: to the Jew first and then to the Greek." In the fifth understanding, Abraham signifies the high priests of the Jews and the bishops of the Latins; Hagar signifies the synagogue as above; Sarah the church of the Latins. According to this understanding, that word of the apostle must also be accepted: "For these are the two testaments." I think, moreover, that he wished to say for this reason that the church is twofold: so that these two understandings might be formed according to a likeness; or rather so that in created things, the likeness of the Creator and the perfect mystery might be fulfilled. In the sixth understanding, Abraham signifies the prelates of the second and third status <term>status: Joachim’s famous historical stages. The Second Status is the age of the Son (Clergy), and the Third is the age of the Holy Spirit (Monks)</term>. Hagar signifies the church of those laboring, which is present. Sarah signifies the church of those resting, which is future in the third status: when the "Sabbath-rest" <note>original: "sabbatismus"</note> shall be given to the people of God. For it is necessary that what is signified by Peter should pass away, and what is signified by John should remain.
<meta>catchword: John</meta>

<column-break/>

For whatever is called "rejected" <note>original: "reprobum," meaning cast aside or superseded</note> cannot be called rejected in its entirety, but only in part. Otherwise, if the fact that the synagogue of the Jews (which gave birth in servitude) is said to be rejected must be taken in its entirety and not rather (as the apostle says) in part, what shall we say of the patriarchs and prophets, who themselves gave birth in servitude according to the time? Rather, the preceding thing, which was good in part, is set aside so that the subsequent thing, which is more perfect, may be established. It is not that those who served well in their time do not receive their reward in the kingdom; rather, it is so that the imitation of those things which were good in their own time may cease, so that as the lesser good passes away, that which is greater may be established immediately. To offer something by way of example: the house of God had to be built and decorated with bronze, silver, and gold; so much so that bronze held the first place in it, silver the second, and gold the third. These three were equally necessary. But how was the order imposed on things? If those who were accustomed to offer bronze offered enough and received their reward and returned joyfully to their own homes: why would those who come after them, invited to offer silver, still seek to offer bronze again, whose work is finished and has reached its rest? Or why should those who succeed in the third turn offer silver again when its work is finished, and not rather gold and precious stones, which are necessary in their own place and time? Therefore, the bronze that was placed in the temple is not rejected; rather, the *offering* of bronze is rejected when it is not offered in its proper time. Those offering bronze were rejected because silver was required from them. Nor is the silver that was placed in the temple rejected; but its offering must cease, lest the work of gold (which is necessary at the end) be neglected. For this cause, it is fitting that servitude and liberty be understood according to time and time <note>i.e., according to their specific eras</note>: just as if servitude were ascribed to iron in respect to bronze, to bronze in respect to silver, and to silver in respect to gold. Doubtless, this is because each thing is used more according to how common it is, and is guarded in the best place according to how precious it is.

->Abba. Book III of the Psaltery<-

For these three things are concerned with what the six species of typical understanding signify, which were noted above. For the first three of them are simply understandings: each one in its own state: yet in such a way that a threefold offering <term>threefold offering: "oblatio trina," likely referring to the different spiritual contributions of the three ages of history</term> is deemed necessary according to more or less in individual states: provided that the second state is more splendid than the first; the bronze <note>original: "ere," meaning bronze or brass</note> of the first more splendid [in its own way], and the bronze of the third more splendid than the second. Similarly, silver is generally considered such that it is not judged to be rejected silver in the time of the second or third state, but rather the silver of the first. Nor is silver generally rejected in the time of the third state: but rather the silver of the second. For—let us touch upon the cause (heaven forbid)—lest we say that in the second state the married life was rejected, in which the first parents lived; but what is clearly rejected in this part is the imitation of Abraham, who had two wives at once, and Jacob, who had two sisters as his concubines and two concubines likewise, and David, who had many wives and concubines at the same time and used a bill of divorce <note>original: "libellum repudij"</note>, and any similar thing. But perhaps in the Church, the Apostle did not allow this: because if God were to pour in grace—indeed, he does pour it in—he will pour it in more fully as something to be preferred: so that many might be found among the Christian people who take wives not for the sake of lust, but for the sake of offspring: having wives as if they did not have them <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:29</note>, so that they are refreshed not by the pleasure of the flesh but by the pleasure of the spirit, and serve the Lord with a perfect heart. If this seems impossible to men, it is not so to God. Let them wait a little while until Babylon is struck: because a human being will be more precious than gold, and more refined than pure gold <note>original: "mu[n]do obrizo"</note>. 

Let the **seventh species** be added, in which is the end of all things: and in it, the highest peace, because it embraces silver and gold together, creating a unity: so that there is no schism between them, because each one is necessary in its own place. Therefore, according to this species, the patriarch **Abraham** signifies God the Father with all the prelates <note>high-ranking church leaders</note> who have existed from the beginning of the age until the end. According to this understanding, in the **Handmaid** <note>Hagar</note> is designated the whole Church of the elect from the beginning to the end. In the **Free Woman** <note>Sarah</note> is designated that Jerusalem which is above, which is our mother. For as in the fourth and

<column-break/>

fifth understanding the Church is joined to the Synagogue, and in the sixth the church of clerics is joined to the church of monks: so in the seventh, the pilgrim Church is joined to that Jerusalem which is above: whose children are the children of the resurrection: just as those of the Church which pilgrimages on earth are reborn of water and the Holy Spirit. Nor should it be thought that this is the contemplative life itself, which is one of the five [types of life]: because the consideration that the saints have concerning that city is one thing, but the city itself is another. For there, it is shown what the life of those who think about that city is like; here, it is shown what that city itself is like, which is our mother.

¶ Likewise, according to this species, the patriarch **Abraham** signifies all the prelates from the beginning of the age until the end. The **Handmaid** signifies the Synagogue together with that part of the Church of the second state which pertains to **Peter**. The **Free Woman** signifies that part which pertains to **John** with the whole Church of the third state, which itself likewise pertains to John. For in the first state, there was only the Church of those who labor. In the third, there will only be the Church of those at rest. In the second, one part is of those who labor, and the other truly of those who are at rest.

¶ These are the **twelve understandings** <term>twelve understandings: Joachim often links the senses of Scripture to the twelve tribes of Israel or the twelve apostles</term> which proceed in a marvelous way from the triple fountain of the literal sense, in which I think an end has been placed upon our labors: provided, however, we are sufficient to assign them where it is necessary: since no one can be sufficient for even the smallest of these things by himself: but only according to how God divides to each a measure of grace, granting to individuals as he wills.

¶ Now that the twelve understandings have been assigned in the letter of the Old Testament—which in like manner could be assigned again and again in the letter of the New, in a higher and nobler way—we see them in **Zechariah** the priest, and his wife **Elizabeth**, and the mother of the Lord **Jesus**. It remains that in these fifteen steps and ten strings <note>Referring to the 15 "Songs of Ascents" in the Psalms and the 10-stringed Psaltery</note>, honor is not the focus of the assignment, but rather the number. For the steps of the Lord are not in a [fixed] good place because one is higher than another, but because he passes through them and, by his own progress, becomes greater every day. Indeed, there are fifteen steps; there are fifteen ways in which he speaks...
