<meta>This page continues Joachim’s intricate symbolic analysis of the genealogy of the Kings of Judah. Having previously established the "ten strings" of the psaltery as a map of sacred history, he now explains why certain kings were omitted from the Gospel of Matthew's lineage of Jesus, arguing that their "carnal" nature disqualified them from representing the divine mystery, which instead passed to spiritual figures like the priest Jehoiada and the prophet Elisha.</meta>

# ->Father. Book of the Psaltery<-

Indeed, the history of these kings leads to the salvation of many (by a just judgment) even down to this Ahaziah <note>Ochozias; King of Judah, son of Jehoram</note>, who was almost extinguished in his seed, so that "all flesh might not glory in His sight." Therefore, in this fourth degree <note>Joachim divides history into "degrees" or stages of growth</note>, the wicked King Ahaziah does not carry the image of the Father; rather, the just priest Jehoiada, who was his contemporary, does. Nor is Joash <note>Johas</note>, the son of Ahaziah, the image of the Only-Begotten of God <note>The Son/Christ</note>; but rather Zacharias, the son of that same Jehoiada, whom that same Joash made a martyr. For undoubtedly, Joash—who was born according to the flesh—persecuted him who was born according to the spirit. 

Nor does Amaziah <note>Amasias</note>, the son of Joash, signify the Holy Spirit; rather, Elisha <note>Helyseus</note> the prophet does. It was through Elisha that the opportunity was given for Ahaziah and Jehu <note>Hyeu</note> and his son, even to the third generation, to prevail over the kings of Judah. Nor is it a wonder if the zeal of a just man, who signifies the Holy Spirit, was kindled against those who gloried in the flesh—claiming to have David as their father while refusing to imitate his works—walking according to the flesh and not according to the spirit. For as Paul says: *The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.* <note>original: "Caro percupiscit aduersus spiritum; spiritus autem aduersus carnem"; a reference to Galatians 5:17</note> 

Precisely because Jehu seemed to obey the prophet in some way—signifying those who claim to obey the spirit more than the flesh—it was granted to him to conquer the impious kings and humble those who walked according to the flesh. Indeed, these signify those who prefer carnal nobility to spiritual nobility, and earthly justice to that justice which is from heaven. 

<margin>Kings</margin> For although Jehu had been anointed as prince over Israel to destroy the house of King Ahab <note>Achab</note>, the king of Judah was nevertheless punished together with the king of Israel. For even if the iniquity had come forth from the house of Ahab, it had nonetheless reached the kings of Judah at that time through their marriage alliance. 

Therefore, when the impious king was dead, the just man—who was the true king—lifted up his head; and although he could not prevail in all things, he taught and demonstrated the good things he could. And it should be noted that none of the kings of Judah from David until Josiah was killed by the sword, except for these three whom Matthew omits <note>In Matthew 1:8, the genealogy skips from Joram to Uzziah, omitting Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah</note>. This was done so that, by the same logic of the mystery, they might be understood as omitted in the New Testament for the same reason they are recorded as being slain in the Old Testament. 

Therefore, at the beginning of the fifth degree, the Spirit is seen to have prevailed more than at the beginning of the fourth; for in the former, Samuel was rejected by the people, whereas here the prophet Elisha 

<column-break/>

was made a judge among judges. In the former case, the venerable mystery of the Trinity was separated from the law of the flesh in a single person (namely, in Samuel the prophet); but here, it is in two: in Jehoiada and in Elisha. 

For neither Jehoiada the high priest nor Elisha the prophet were in the [genealogical] line that was written according to physical birth—which proceeds smoothly—and neither was Zacharias. For one was the son of Jehoiada, and the other was not. This is the reason for both: why we confess only the Son to be born of the Father, and not the Holy Spirit as well. 

In this place, the law of the flesh began to be weakened, and the law of the spirit, which was to be fully revealed in its own time, began to be secretly revealed. And it should be known that from this place, or thereabouts, the Trinity which is contemplated does not appear in the line of generations, but the line of generation itself is one. For it must be considered in one way according to how it pertains to the Old Testament, and in another way according to how the New Testament is initiated in or around that same place. 

For because in all these things there is a likeness of that supreme Trinity, it was predestined so that some of its beauty—or at least some likeness of it—might be seen by the mortal race of men, specifically the elect. From this place, or around it, [the New] seems to proceed from the same line, as if from the same trunk two shoots grew here and there; as these grow and spread, the summit of the trunk itself reaches its end. 

And because the brightness of the ancients is disregarded in comparison to the moderns—due to the imperfection that the people had under the Old Testament—that illustrious likeness of the Trinity, which pertains to the "joyful psaltery," <note>The "joyful psaltery" refers to Joachim's vision of a perfected spiritual understanding of the Trinity in the coming "Age of the Spirit."</note> seems to leave the old line as far as the Old Testament is concerned, in order to carry itself over to the New. The very change of persons and lines teaches this most aptly. Therefore, on the whole journey, one must adhere to two paths: one which seems to belong to the Son, and the other to the Spirit. 

The reason why this has been confirmed in this work is for the sake of harmony. However, let it not be entirely silenced that the New Testament was initiated by King Hezekiah, under whom the Son and the Holy Spirit were clearly revealed to men. And because the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son in the same way that the Son proceeds from the Father alone, it was shown that he also proceeds from the Father in such a way that both parts of the mystery were opened to men in time.

He uses the metaphor of a tree trunk with two branches to describe how the New Testament (the Son and Spirit) emerges from the Old (the Father).</summary>

# ## Joachim: The Second [Book] on the Ten Strings ##

...to His own [works], He willed to perform His works in wisdom <note>original: "sapientia"</note> so that the needy creature could not contemplate within them what is seen by pious faith in the secret chamber of the soul concerning the majesty of such great sublimity. Therefore, leaving aside from this place what seems to pertain to the Old Testament, we must approach the New by two paths, so to speak—or rather, not by two paths but by one path in two modes. One mode is considered in what pertains to the Son, and the other in what pertains to the Holy Spirit. But what can pertain to one that does not pertain to the other, since all things are common to them? I think that this property should not be considered in the thing itself, but rather in the **image** of the thing <note>Joachim’s "Theology of Images": historical figures act as symbols or "icons" of divine Persons</note>; for indeed, in some things, a likeness of the Father is more readily found, in others a likeness of the Son, and in others a likeness of the Holy Spirit. 

Let this be a general rule for you, reader: wherever anything is said to be attributed specifically to one of the Persons, [look for that likeness]. Therefore, according to the first definition which pertains to the Holy Spirit: Jehoiada <note>Ioiada</note> is to be taken for Ahaziah <note>Ochozia</note>; Zechariah for Joash; and Elisha <note>Amelyseus/Helyseus</note> for Amaziah. In these three is the likeness of the psaltery and the likeness of the Trinity. 

The names of those who signify the **ten strings** <note>The "ten strings" of the biblical psaltery are interpreted here as ten generations of leaders</note> are these:
1. **Uzziah** <note>Ozias</note>
2. **Jotham** <note>Iohathan</note>
3. **Ahaz** <note>Achaz</note>
4. **Hezekiah** <note>Ezechias</note>
5. **Manasseh** <note>Manasses</note>
6. **Amon**
7. **Josiah** <note>Iosias</note>
8. **Jehoiakim** <note>Ioachim</note>
9. **Jeconiah** <note>Iechonias</note>
10. **Shealtiel** <note>Salatiel</note>

In this Shealtiel, the kings of Judah ceased, and princes began to rule in their place, just as it was in the beginning. Thus, as the kingdom of the flesh failed, the kingdom of the spirit was strengthened. Since all the final kings who were born during the Babylonian exile <note>original: "transmigratione babylonis"</note> were most wicked in the sight of the Lord, three holy men were chosen in the spirit of prophecy: **Jeremiah**, who was like a father; **Ezekiel**, who was the heir of his prophecy; and **Daniel**, to whom heavenly secrets were revealed. Among these, Jeremiah was the father of Ezekiel in prophecy, not in the flesh; because Ezekiel’s prophecy was seen to depend on similar words from the prophecy of Jeremiah, who had preceded him in prophesying.

<column-break/>

For both prophesied about the ruin of the city; both predicted future evils—one indeed in Jerusalem, the other in Babylon—to a people who did not believe but contradicted them. 

Now, just as two of the men who appeared to Abraham descended to Sodom, but one did not descend but remained on the mountain <note>A reference to Genesis 18, where three visitors represent the Trinity; only two go to destroy Sodom</note>, so **Jeremiah** alone did not descend into Babylon. **Ezekiel** and **Daniel**, however, did descend into it. Do you ask the reason? *Adonai* <note>The Lord</note> and Jerusalem signify the Kingdom of Heaven; Sodom and Babylon signify the kingdom of the world. We know that the Father is never described as being "sent," but only the Son and the Holy Spirit <note>In traditional theology, the Father is the "Unsent Sender"</note>. But to whom were they sent? Was it to the children of Babylon? Far from it! Rather, they were sent to the children of Jerusalem—and with the children of Jerusalem—who for a time and even until now sit mourning and weeping *by the rivers of Babylon*. <margin>Psalm [137]</margin>

Therefore, **Jeremiah** carries the type of the Father; **Ezekiel** the type of the Son; and **Daniel**—a most chaste and honored man, whom even the proudest kings venerated—carries the type of the Holy Spirit. This is also recognized and proven by the difference in their speech or revelations. Indeed, Jeremiah’s speech is written almost without order, and because of this, it grows dark with excessive obscurity compared to the other two. Ezekiel’s speech is indeed obscure, but it is accomplished in part and with a direct order. Daniel not only preserves order, but he even adds an explanation to the things he saw. And these things, for the most part, are lucid and clear. 

In that time, indeed, when "God spoke to the fathers in the prophets in many and various ways" <note>A quote from Hebrews 1:1</note> to those who served Him with servile fear—because they were still men of their time and carnal—it was not given to them to know what their Lord was doing. But in the following time, when the only-begotten Son of God came into the world, He made known to His friends all things that He heard from His Father. Yet, they were made known in such a way that some things still remained, of which He said: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; <margin>John [16]</margin> however, when that **Spirit of Truth** comes, He will teach you all truth." Lest anyone say these things were completed generally on the day of Pentecost, let them hear those who were still disputing after that day...

<meta>This page continues Joachim of Fiore’s explanation of the "spiritual" genealogy of the Kings of Judah. He is explaining why Matthew’s Gospel omits three kings—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah—and argues that they were replaced by spiritual figures (Jehoiada, Zechariah, and Elisha) who better represent the Trinity.</meta>

->Abba. The Book of the Psaltery<-

<column-break/>

Nay, it reached to the salvation of many (by a just judgment) even unto this Ahaziah <note>original: Ochoziaz</note>; he was nearly wiped out in his seed, so that **"no flesh might glory in His sight"** <note>quoting 1 Corinthians 1:29</note>. Therefore, in this fourth rank <note>original: gradu; Joachim’s term for historical epochs or generations</note>, the wicked king Ahaziah does not carry the image of the patriarch; rather, **Jehoiada** <note>Ioiada</note> the just priest does, who was his contemporary. Nor does Joash, the son of Ahaziah, represent the Only-begotten Son of God; rather, **Zechariah** does, the son of that same Jehoiada, whom Joash made a martyr. For indeed, he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the spirit. 

Nor does Amaziah, the son of Joash, signify the Holy Spirit; rather, **Elisha** <note>original: Helyseus</note> the prophet does. Through him, the occasion was given for Ahaziah and Jehu <note>original: Hyreu/Heu</note> and his son to be slain, even unto the third generation, so that they might prevail over the kings of Judah. Nor is it a wonder if the zeal of a just man—who signifies the Holy Spirit—was kindled against those who gloried in the flesh, saying they had David as their father, yet were unwilling to imitate his works, walking according to the flesh and not according to the spirit. For as Paul says: **"The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh"** <note>original: Caro pcupiscit aduersus spūz; quoting Galatians 5:17</note>.

Because Jehu <note>original: Heu</note> seemed in some way to obey the prophet—signifying those who pretend to obey the spirit more than the flesh—it was granted that he should conquer the impious kings and humble those who walked according to the flesh. Indeed, they signify those who prefer carnal nobility to spiritual nobility, and earthly justice to that justice which is from heaven. For although Jehu was anointed as prince over Israel to destroy the house <margin>Kings</margin> of King Ahab, he was nevertheless punished together with the king of Israel, as was the king of Judah. For even if the iniquity had come forth from the house of Ahab, it had nonetheless reached the kings of Judah at that time through a mediated affinity <note>intermarriage between the two royal houses</note>.

Therefore, when the impious king died, the just man—who was the true king—raised his head. And although he could not prevail in all things, he nevertheless taught and demonstrated the good things he could. And it should be noted that none of the kings of Judah from David until John <note>John the Baptist</note> was slain by the sword, except for these three whom Matthew omits. Thus, by the same logic of the mystery, they are understood to be omitted in the New Testament for the same reason they are recorded as being slain in the Old Testament. 

Therefore, at the beginning of the fifth rank, the Spirit seems to have prevailed more than at the beginning of the fourth. For there, Samuel was rejected by the people, but here Elisha

<column-break/>

the prophet was made the judge of judges. In the former case, the venerable mystery of the Trinity was separated from the law of the flesh in one single person—that is, in Samuel the prophet. In this case, it is in two: that is, in Jehoiada and in Elisha. For Jehoiada the high priest and Elisha the prophet were not part of the lineage that was so solemnly written according to carnal birth; nor was Zechariah. But because one was the son of Jehoiada, and the other was not, there is a reason for both: that we profess only the Son to be born of the Father, and not the Holy Spirit as well. 

Therefore, from this place, the law of the flesh began to be weakened, and the law of the spirit—which was to be fully revealed in its own time—began to be revealed, as if by stealth. And it should be known that from this place, or around it, there is a triad <note>original: triniū</note> that must be considered in the line of generations, even though the line itself is but one. For it must be considered differently insofar as it pertains to the Old Testament, and differently insofar as the New was initiated from or around that same place. 

Because in all these things the likeness of that supreme Trinity is at stake, so that the mortal race of men (at least those elect predestined for life) might be seen to possess some of its beauty through some likeness, it seems to proceed from this place—or around it—from the same line. It is as if two shoots <note>original: furculi</note> grow out from one trunk, here and there; as they grow out and grow forward, the summit of the trunk itself reaches its end. And because of the imperfection which that people had under the former testament, the brightness of the old things is disregarded in respect to the new. That excellent likeness of the Trinity, which pertains to the **joyful psaltery**, seems to leave the lineage of the Old Testament and transfer itself to the New, which the change of the persons and the lines themselves most aptly teaches. 

Therefore, having left one path, we must adhere to two tracks. One is the reason why this harmony was initiated in this work. Lest it be entirely silent, let it be known that from this place the New Testament was initiated, under which the Son and the Holy Spirit were clearly revealed to men. And because the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son alone in the same way the Son proceeds from the Father alone—since He also proceeds from the Father in such a way—both aspects of the mystery might be opened to men in [due] time.

# Joachim the Second, On Concordance
### Dd 3

...by His [works], He willed to perform His works in wisdom, so that the needy creature could not contemplate in them what is seen through pious faith in the sanctuary of the mind concerning the majesty of such great sublimity. Therefore, setting aside from this point what seems to belong to the Old Testament, we must approach the New by two paths, as it were; or rather, not by two paths but by one path in two ways: one by which it is considered, which pertains to the Son; the other by which it is kindled, which pertains to the Holy Spirit. But what can pertain to one that does not pertain to the other, since all things are common to them? I think this property should not be considered in any actual thing, but rather in the image of the thing; for certainly, in some things a likeness of the Father is found more clearly; in others, the Son; in others, the Holy Spirit. And let this be your general rule, reader: wherever something is said to be specially attributed to one of the Persons of the Trinity. Therefore, according to the first definition which pertains to the Holy Spirit: **Jehoiada** <note>original: Josaia; likely a scribal variant for Jehoiada/Ioiada, the priest mentioned on the previous page</note> is to be taken for Ahaziah <note>Ochozia</note>; **Zechariah** for Joash; **Elisha** <note>Helyseus</note> for Amaziah. The names of those who signify that which is "ten-stringed" <note>the ten kings who followed the first three</note> are these:

First, **Uzziah** <note>Ozias</note>; second, **Jotham** <note>Jothathan</note>; third, **Ahaz**; fourth, **Hezekiah**; fifth, **Manasseh**; sixth, **Amon**; seventh, **Josiah**; eighth, **Jehoiakim** <note>Joachim</note>; ninth, **Jeconiah** <note>Jechonias</note>; tenth, **Shealtiel** <note>Salatiel</note>. In this Shealtiel, the kings of Judah ceased, and they began to be princes for them, just as in the beginning. This was so that, while the kingdom of the flesh failed, the kingdom of the spirit might be strengthened; for indeed all the last kings, who were born during the Babylonian captivity, were most wicked in the sight of the Lord. Thus, three holy men were chosen in the spirit of prophecy: **Jeremiah**, who was like a father; **Ezekiel**, who was the heir of his prophecy; and **Daniel**, to whom the celestial secrets were revealed. Jeremiah was the father of Ezekiel in prophecy, not in the flesh; because the prophecy of Ezekiel appeared to hang upon similar words from the prophecy of Jeremiah, who had preceded him in prophesying. For both

<column-break/>

prophesied concerning the ruin of the city; both predicted future evils—the one in Jerusalem, the other in Babylon—to a people who did not believe but rather spoke against them. Just as two of the men who appeared to Abraham <note>referencing the three angels at Mamre in Genesis 18</note> descended to Sodom, but one did not descend but remained on the mountain, so Jeremiah alone did not descend into Babylon. Ezekiel and Daniel, however, did descend into it. Do you ask the reason? Zion and Jerusalem signify the kingdom of heaven. Sodom and Babylon signify the kingdom of the world. For we know that the Father is never read to have been "sent," but only the Son and the Holy Spirit. But where were they sent? Surely not to the sons of Babylon? Far from it. But to the sons—and with the sons—of Jerusalem, who for a long time and even <margin>Psalm [137]</margin> until now sit mourning and weeping by the rivers of Babylon. Therefore, Jeremiah bears the type of the Father; Ezekiel, of the Son; Daniel—a most chaste and honored man, whom even the most proud kings venerated—bears the type of the Holy Spirit. This is also recognized and proven by the difference in their speeches or revelations. Indeed, the speech of Jeremiah is written almost without order; and for this reason, it grows dark with excessive obscurity compared to the other two. Ezekiel’s speech is indeed obscure, but it is completed partly in a direct order. Daniel not only preserves the order but even adds an explanation to the things which he saw. And these things, for the most part, are lucid and clear. Indeed, in that time when **"God spoke in many portions and many ways to the fathers through the prophets"** <note>quoting Hebrews 1:1</note>, to those who had served him then in a servile manner (because at that time men were still carnal), it was not given to them to know what their Lord was doing. But in the time that followed, when the only-begotten Son of God came into the world, He made known all things which He heard from His Father to His friends; yet they were made known in such a way that some things still remained, concerning which He said: **"I have many things to say to you, but <margin>John [16]</margin> you cannot bear them now; but when that Spirit of Truth comes, He will teach you all truth"** <note>quoting John 16:12-13</note>. Lest anyone say these things were completed in a general sense on the day of Pentecost, let him hear what was still being disputed after that day...

-># Abba. The Book of the Psaltery<-

[...the] apostle saying, "For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away." <note>original: "Ex parte enim cognoscimus...". A quote from 1 Corinthians 13:9-10.</note> It is necessary, therefore, for there to be a time in which the **Holy Spirit** speaks to us more openly, so that those things which we have hitherto seen as through a glass darkly, we may begin to see face to face. Therefore, **Jeremiah** is to be taken in the place of **Joachim**; **Ezekiel** and **Daniel**, who went together into Babylon, in the place of **Jeconiah** and **Shealtiel**. Now, the names of those who signify that which belongs to the <term>ten-stringed</term> <note>Referring to the "decem corde" or ten-stringed psaltery, which Joachim uses as a mathematical key to correlate different periods of history.</note> are these: first, **Zerubbabel**; second, **Abiud**; third, **Eliakim**; fourth, **Azor**; fifth, **Zadok**; sixth, **Achim**; seventh, **Eliud**; eighth, **Eleazar**; ninth, **Matthan**; tenth, **Jacob**. This Jacob, the father of **Joseph**, the husband of **Mary**, is a contemporary, or nearly a contemporary, of the aged **Zechariah**, the father of **John the Baptist**, under whom the royal priesthood began in the tribe of Judah, according to what was said by the Father's voice to Christ the King in the Book of Psalms: <margin>Psalm [110]</margin> *You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.* <note>original: "Tu es sacerdos in eternum sm ordinem Melchisedech."</note> Now, however, one ought to marvel at the changing of the mystery and the diversity of the sacrament in a similar matter, because the mysteries required enough worthy memory for this very thing to happen. For from the beginning, when men still saw this time to be carnal, He did not wish to be likened to any of them; or rather, He deigned to do so because men were not yet spiritual as they have been from the time Christ came into the world. For "the first man," as the apostle says, "is of the earth, earthly; and as is the earthly, such are the earthly." <note>1 Corinthians 15:47-48.</note> Wherefore John the Baptist, than whom no one is greater among those born of women, spoke of himself as a <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future spiritual reality.</note> of that people, saying: "He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks of the earth." <note>John 3:31.</note> Or, to show us the affection of His kindness, He did not disdain to be likened to those men who either fathered children in sin or were born in sin—even in this very fact, that they either fathered in sin or were conceived from impure seed—which among the other great wonders of God is quite marvelous indeed. Yet, in the process of time, in certain good men among whom there was not so much a propagation of the

<column-break/>

flesh as a design of the will for the propagation of virtue, it was done so that no one should think the married life should not only be made equal to celibacy, but even preferred to it. Therefore, through the advancements of the times, so that He might show what pleased Him more, He introduced spiritual things by gradually removing the carnal images, as if they were already speaking with open voices in that time: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit." <note>John 3:6.</note> Nor was this done suddenly, as if by initiating all things new, He would utterly dissolve the old; rather, He did so lest one should think that better things subsist from good things (which is true), but that entirely good things subsist from evil things (which is false). Nor, because the Lord persuaded us toward a chaste life, should He be believed to have condemned the marriages which began from Adam. Just as when He says to that man who was seeking the perfect life: "Sell all you have and give to the poor," <note>Matthew 19:21.</note> He does not therefore condemn those who wish to possess what is their own and manage it for themselves. But clearly, He showed that **Mary’s** part was to be preferred when He said: "Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." <note>Luke 10:42.</note> And He showed virginity to be better than marriage when He dedicated a Virgin Mother for Himself as if for a temple. For from what else should we know that one of these is good and the other better? Distinguish, then, between the fruit of the womb of the married **Elizabeth** and the fruit of the virginal womb of **Mary**; then you will recognize that marriage is a great good, and yet it differs from celibacy as much as the difference between flesh and spirit, and no less than between heaven and earth. For this [married] life is common to men and beasts; the other belongs to men; the third belongs not to men, but to angels. The things pertaining to this [carnal] life are manifest to all and well-known; but concerning that [spiritual] life, there are secret words which it is not granted to man to speak. Therefore, it is not because this life is secret that the other is rejected; rather, it is honored because the virginity that proceeds from marriage has decorated that life just as the beauty of flowers decorates the naked face of the earth. And this happens when the frost has been cast off at the beginning of spring, in the vicinity of summer. Therefore, the humility of life was not to be stretched out [forever], but because the blessed and happy eternal age was near, its face was to be adorned with the flower of virginity, so that the good which it did not deserve to have in itself might proceed from another and be supplied. But concerning these things, elsewhere...

-># Joachim, Second Book of the Ten Strings<-

We must return to **Uzziah** <note>original: "Oziam". Also known as Azariah.</note> so that we may follow the line of the fathers as it pertains to the likeness of the Son. We said that from **Ahaziah** the line was to be considered in two ways: concerning the generations on account of the Son and the **Holy Spirit**. As it pertains to the **Holy Spirit**, three generations were to be changed; as it pertains to the Son, they were neither to be changed nor established, but were to be excluded from the number of the others.

<margin>
The
fifth
degree.
</margin>

And this fifth degree is to be begun from **Uzziah**. This **Uzziah** was good at the beginning, both he and his son **Jotham**. Now, **Uzziah** remains at the root of the New Testament according to its initiation, just as **Adam** was at the root of the former [Old Testament]. Whence **Uzziah** bears the image of the Father in this part, just as his son **Jotham** <note>original: "Joathan"</note> governed his house in the image of the Son, who is the ruler and redeemer of the Church. For the fact that **Uzziah** was struck with leprosy and cast out of the temple signifies the plague in the hearts of the Jewish priests, on account of which they were expelled from their own house and remain secluded until the day of their death—that is, until the illicit zeal for the Law fails in them, so that they may die in that part in which they live badly in their sin.

Meanwhile, however, the priests of **Christ**, who were chosen from the gentile people, take the place of **Christ**; they rule the house of the Church, disposing all things according to God, beginning from **Christ** and from **Peter**, the prince of the apostles. They remain thus until that people [the Jews] fails in that part where it lives in the leprosy of its own uncleanness. Finally, when that people reaches its end in such a way of life, **Jotham** shall begin, in a certain sense, to reign; 

<margin>Daniel</margin>

because "the kingdom that is under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High." <note>A reference to Daniel 7:27.</note> However, just as **Adam** did not lose the likeness of either the Father or the Son through sin (no wonder, since the likeness of fatherhood is one thing, and the likeness of guilt is another), so **Uzziah**—not in the fact that he was struck with leprosy—signifies God the Father, but in the fact that he was established in that place in the line where the New Testament was initiated. Truly **Isaiah**, who prophesied in their days and even after their days, signifies the **Spirit** who spoke through the prophets in the time of the "First Status," <term>Status</term> <note>Joachim's "Status" are the three great ages of history: the Father (Old Testament), the Son (New Testament), and the Holy Spirit (The coming age of spiritual understanding).</note> and spoke through the apostles and doctors in the days of the second, and speaks nonetheless in the third. 

<column-break/>

Just as in the first degree **Abel** had to be accepted for one generation so that a recapitulation could always be made from the tenth generation—that is, from the tenth, the twentieth, the thirtieth, the fortieth, and the fiftieth—so also here, so that harmony <note>original: "concordia". Joachim's primary method of matching Old and New Testament events.</note> may be maintained. The prophet **Isaiah**, who began to prophesy from the days of **Uzziah**, is to be taken as one generation. For, as I have already said, King **Uzziah** remains at the root of the New Testament, just as the first-formed **Adam** was at the root of the Old.

Therefore, the names of the men who signify that which belongs to the <term>ten strings</term> <note>Referring to the "Decem Chordae," the ten-stringed psaltery which Joachim uses as a mathematical framework for history.</note> are these:
First, **Ahaz**;
second, **Hezekiah**;
third, **Manasseh**;
fourth, **Amos**; <note>likely referring to Amon.</note>
fifth, **Josiah**;
sixth, **Jehoahaz**; <note>original: "Joachiz"</note>

eighth, **Shealtiel**; <note>original: "Salatiel"</note>
ninth, **Zerubbabel**;
tenth, **Abiud**.

Therefore, **Zerubbabel**—those three generations having been removed which are to be segregated from the others for the reason written above—is the fiftieth in the number of the fathers, according to the truth of history. Under him, or around his time, the histories of the Old Testament are summed up, and under him liberty was given to the people of Israel, so that the "Great Jubilee" might be shown there. This is especially true since from **Adam** to **Cyrus** are found seventy "weeks" of years, which is forty-nine [Jubilees]. <note>Joachim's complex chronology aligns the end of the Babylonian exile with the 50th generation (the Jubilee) to symbolize spiritual liberation.</note> It was that forty-ninth year in which the land kept its Sabbaths, according to the prophecy of the prophet **Jeremiah**. When that was finished and the fiftieth was begun, liberty was given by **Cyrus** to the Jewish people to go up from **Babylon** into **Jerusalem**, in the year (as it is thought) in which all of Babylon was destroyed and the empire of the Chaldeans was ended. 

There, therefore, is the end of the first "Great Jubilee"; there was fulfilled what is signified by the fiftieth Psalm. <note>Psalm 51 (50 in the Vulgate), the *Miserere*.</note> Now, it is believed that **Shealtiel**, by whose surname the "Just Son" was called, was a good man and one fearing God; for we never read of just men being surnamed by the names of their fathers unless the fathers were also such as deserved to be named alongside such great men. Hence it is that **Hezekiah** and **Josiah** were not called the sons of those who begat them in the first degree (whom it is certain were wicked), but were called "Sons of **David**." Therefore, **Shealtiel** bears the type of God the Father, and **Zerubbabel** the type of the Son; for the former strove to build the house of the Lord made with hands, and the latter does not cease to build the one not made with hands even until now. Furthermore, **Abiud** bears the type of the **Holy Spirit**; **Jozadak**... <note>original: "Joſedech". The text cuts off as it moves to the next figure.</note>

degree.

**Nathan** <note>original: "Nathan". In the Gospel of Matthew, this is Matthan.</note>; eighth, **Jacob**; ninth, **Joseph**; tenth, **Christ**. Truly, in this degree which was the seventh from the first: **Zechariah** the priest, who rejoiced that he might have an heir, designates God the Father. **John** [the Baptist], who did not wish to be a father, designates the only-begotten of God. But the only-begotten Son of God himself, the man **Christ Jesus**—who on earth had neither father nor son according to the flesh—holds the type of that person in the Trinity who is neither father nor son: namely, the **Holy Spirit**, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore, in **Christ**, the line of the flesh failed entirely; specifically, in that degree which was the seventh from the first. There, what had preceded in figure was shown in truth. For even after his birth from the Virgin, a likeness has not been and will not be lacking until the final judgment. **Christ** is the end of the law for salvation to everyone who believes.

But it should now suffice for us to have thus far numbered the "strings" and to have assigned the mystery of the **Psaltery** <note>The Book of Psalms, often used by Joachim as a blueprint for the ages of the world.</note> up to the seventh degree. It is time that, leaving these things aside, we ought to sing and play the psaltery. For it is difficult and laborious to seek that same thing in the New Testament through each decade of generations; yet I estimate it is not lacking. It is enough for us to know that in four decades of spiritual generations—within the space of a brief enough time—the course of this second state must be completed, as if in seven weeks of forty days, or as if in forty days.

Those generations which are joined to those ten that began from **Cyrus**, we shall find according to Pentecost (that is, the fiftieth) and according to the Jubilee. In this time, the **New Babylon** is to be struck down, and Mother Church, which is the **New Jerusalem**, is to be liberated from its tyranny. For just as the **Old Babylon** was struck down then, so too must the **New Babylon** be struck here, as it is written in the **Book of Revelation**, where it is treated under the appearance of the **Great Harlot**.

<column-break/>

In the exposition of this, almost all teachers are known to agree. Although, regarding the day and the hour: "It is not yours nor mine to know." <note>A paraphrase of Acts 1:7 and Matthew 24:36.</note> Do you seek the nearness of the time? Know that from **Abiud**, the son of **Zerubbabel** (under whom the **Old Babylon** was struck), forty-nine generations have been completed, and the greater part of the fiftieth—which is the present one—is here. If, however, this very generation is the fiftieth, I advise those who remain in the midst of **Babylon** to flee from her center.

But just as the memory of the Passion of **Christ** is celebrated at the end of forty days, so at the end of forty generations, the faithful must fear "the face of the bow." <note>A biblical metaphor for impending divine judgment or war.</note> For the first tribulation will destroy the empire of **Babylon**. The second will chastise the sins of the delinquent Church. From then on, what remains of time—like the period from Easter to Pentecost—will consume the work of God in approximately five decades of spiritual generations.

And here, through fifteen "steps" <note>original: "gradus". Likely a reference to the fifteen Psalms of Ascent.</note> or decades, we shall enter into the Holy of Holies. Thus, the **Psalter** is contained in one hundred and fifty Psalms, and the university of all time is contained in one hundred and fifty generations: that is, from **Adam** until the consummation of the age.

Yet, take care that you do not propose a long space of years for yourself in these final five decades of generations. For certainly, from **Adam** to **Shem** there are ten generations, and from **Shem** to **Abraham** there are likewise ten generations; and yet the number of years between those two ages is so disparate that the single generation of **Noah** was greater than that entire age of ten generations from **Shem** (son of **Noah**) to **Abraham**. Therefore, whether these future generations are of days, or months, or years—and how many months or years there were in each—those who will be there will know. For now, however, know that the matter of the three generations which were numbered in the discussion is a great mystery; specifically, that those three generations exceeded the number of decades, which is nothing other than what was signified in the one hundred and fifty-three fish caught [by the Apostles]. <note>Reference to John 21:11, often interpreted numerically in medieval exegesis.</note>

<meta>This page continues Joachim of Fiore’s symbolic analysis of the Trinity using musical and numerical metaphors. Having previously discussed the generations of Christ, he now applies the structure of the 150 Psalms (divided into three groups of 50) to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</meta>

-># Joachim, Third [Book of the] Ten-Stringed [Psaltery]<-

...and of the final fishing of Peter <note>A reference to the 153 fish caught in the miraculous haul in John 21:11, which Joachim interprets through numerical symbolism.</note>: for it is designated that one [person] presides over each group of fifty: the reason for this logic is open and clear. For there is one God the Father, to whom the first fifty belongs. There is one God the Son, to whom the second fifty belongs. There is one God the Holy Spirit, to whom the third fifty belongs. And because there is one almighty God who presides over all in three persons—Father, Son, and Spirit are one—and so too is the people of God from the beginning until the end: and one Book of Psalms, which contains in itself three groups of fifty. Indeed, not only one but many ten-stringed psalteries are written to have been made by David and Solomon for praising the Lord: it is clear that according to the number of steps and tens of psalms, fifteen ten-stringed psalteries <note>15 ten-stringed psalteries equal 150, the total number of Psalms.</note> are to be understood under the one book of psalms: so that, namely, each mansion of the righteous may likewise sing in its own order: which we distinguished above when we made mention of that heavenly city. Five, therefore, belong to the first state: five to the second: five to the third. And in the smaller division, the likeness of the Trinity is most evident (as I have already said). If, therefore, we wish and are able; if we desire and are permitted to sing well to our God: then let us know that we are heard by Him; then let us know that the sacrifices of our praises are made acceptable in His sight: if we praise Him as He is: if we understand what praise is owed to the individual persons and to the three in common: this the Psalmist exhorted the chosen of God, when he said: *God is King of all the earth: sing praises with wisdom.* <note>Psalm 47:7</note>. Oh, how wickedly **Sabellius** <note>A 3rd-century heretic who taught Modalism—the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons but merely three "modes" or "masks" of one God.</note> sang; who, understanding nothing, chanted only a single ten-count <note>original: "denarium". This refers to the number ten, representing the perfection of a single person in Joachim's system.</note>, saying: "God is one person—the Father when he wills, the Son when he wills, the Holy Spirit when he wills." Oh, how perversely **Arius** <note>A 4th-century priest who taught that the Son was a created being subordinate to the Father, rather than co-eternal.</note> organized [the song], who, giving one ten-count to the Father, made a smaller portion for the Son and the Holy Spirit, saying: "The Father is greater, the Son is lesser, the Holy Spirit is the least and the minister of the two." For it was as if he offered a ten-count to the Father, a five-count to the Son, and a lower number to the Holy Spirit. Oh, how per-

<column-break/>

-versely in all ways he amended both [views] who said that there was one substance as a certain supreme thing common to the three persons, and that each individual person was that substance. For it is as if you were to put the number one hundred for the substance, but for the persons three ten-counts: or if he does not wish to say that the substance is greater than any person, it is as if three ten-counts were put for the persons and a fourth ten-count for the substance: as if God were not a Trinity but a Quaternity <note>Joachim was famously accused of teaching a "Quaternity" (four-ness) by Peter Lombard's followers, because his diagrams of the Godhead sometimes appeared to show the "Divine Essence" as a fourth element above the three Persons.</note>. But those who strive to cloak this madness in such a way as to say that each person is that substance, speak as if they were saying that three ten-counts are one ten-count, and one ten-count is three: and both are wrong. But one ten-count belongs to the Father, one ten-count to the Son, one ten-count to the Holy Spirit: and the three-count together belongs to the Trinity. Now, if you say: "Therefore, the three together are something more than two or one": that is false. If you say: "They are more [in number]": that is true. For here the individual is noted, and there the three are noted together. Yet it is not "more" or "less," because each person is great without [the category of] quantity. Therefore, the ten-number is placed to designate the perfection of the person, not to signify quantity. The three-number is to designate the Trinity, not to signify quantity: where there is no end, no [limited] signification can be given. And look: If I ask, "How many persons are there?" you will safely answer, "Three." If I ask about quantity, you will fail. For *Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of His greatness there is no end.* <note>Psalm 145:3</note>. Therefore, three ten-counts designate three persons, each of whom is perfect God. One thirty-count, which is the collection of ten-counts, [represents] the Trinity of one substance: because the Trinity is perfect God, and each of the persons is perfect God. Look at the conclusion of the question in that sacred name of God, which is: **JEUE** <note>Joachim's transliteration of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton (YHWH). He divides it into syllables to represent the Trinitarian persons.</note>. **IE** is one name and refers to the Father. **EU** is one name and refers to the Son. **UE** is one name and refers to the Holy Spirit. **JEUE** is indeed one name: but not so that it can simply be referred to the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone: but to the three together: unless perhaps it contains that which the Apostle says: *From Him, and through Him, and in Him* <note>Romans 11:36</note>: insofar as here in the three [parts] of the proportion...

<summary>Joachim uses the 150 Psalms and the number ten (the "denarius") to explain the co-equality of the Trinity, refuting the heresies of Sabellius and Arius. He concludes by breaking down the divine name JEUE (YHWH) into three parts to represent the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</summary>

## Here begins the Third Book on the training of those who sing psalms.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'Q' containing a man's face looking upwards, framed by leafy decorative flourishes.</image-desc>

Because of the true and eternal God—who is wonderful in his saints and far more wonderful in himself—in his inaccessible and inexpressible majesty in which he alone always glories and reigns as God, Three and One: according to the measure of our capacity, or rather by the gift of his grace, contemplating those things which we were permitted to grasp of his glory, and also of his great works sought out (as the 
<margin>Psalms</margin>
Psalmist says) in all his purposes. In the two previous books, we took care to record with subtle diligence of style; it is necessary for us in this third book to deal briefly and succinctly with the method of psalmody <note>The practice of singing or chanting the Psalms during worship.</note> and the training of those who sing: so that we may sing to him whom we know to be the great King (as we read) wisely. But what is it to sing "wisely," if not to utter the very words of the psalms with discernment and intention? For it is better to offer a few

<column-break/>

psalms in an orderly way than many in a disorderly fashion and without the guard of discipline: because it is not a large quantity of words, but rather affection and devotion that are commended by God. Therefore, if different things are sought by different people, the affection of devotion must nonetheless be in all. Otherwise, if strength does not suffice, one should yield rather to quantity. Since strength is not equal, and it is not possible for everyone to be equally free for it, we know that the fathers have left behind various traditions of examples for their successors. Thus, it is even doubted by many which path should be imitated; for some are fervent in age but raw in devotion, and while they wish to grasp the height of perfection, they presume something beyond their strength that will not last until the end, thinking it impossible for others to do what they themselves cannot strenuously achieve. To these, that saying is rightly thrown: *If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you.* Among the ancient fathers who led the hermit’s life individually, the whole Psalter <term>Psalter: the Book of Psalms used in daily prayer</term> was completed by each one. Others truly did less, but did what their holy devotion, inspired by the Divine, suggested to them, wishing to fulfill in this way what is written in the same book: *I will add to all your praise.* And this was indeed enough. But for us, as our father Benedict <note>St. Benedict of Nursia, the 6th-century author of the Rule for monks, which set the standard for Western monastic life.</note> says, who know these things and do not do them, it is a cause for shame. But because not only the hundredfold and sixty-fold fruit is accepted by the Truth, but he also commends the one who brings forth thirty-fold <note>A reference to Jesus’ Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13:8), where different people produce different amounts of spiritual "fruit."</note>. And because the Lord is good and seeks the heart more than gifts, he prefers the offering of a poor woman to the abundance of the rich. Therefore, because of various events and other cares of occupation that unexpectedly emerge for us, it is said to be of no small devotion for a monk to say fifty psalms daily in honor of the Holy Trinity, over and above the required and customary hours <note>The "Divine Office" or "Liturgy of the Hours," the set times of prayer monks are required to observe.</note>, so that in such a perfect number faith may be fortified with intention and a reward found in fulfilling them. But it is also a mark of inherent devotion for a cleric to say twenty in a day: for as a monk is held to the third level in this regard, a cleric is held to the second. But if a literate man from the order of the laity <note>Non-clergy members of the church.</note>, desiring also himself to praise his Lord, should be zealous toward those who are free for reading...

...with [prayers] and psalms: however, for the sake of family business, he may not have promised to imitate him <note>Likely referring to a spiritual mentor or the ideal monk.</note> fully in the zeal he possesses. This also seems good to us: that as much as he is able, he should fulfill in three days what those who are devoted to the monastic life strive to fulfill in one day; so that they might at least study to complete in fifteen days what I believe was designated—and not without reason—by those fifteen steps by which one ascended into the Temple. For it is truly written for all the elect:
<margin>Psalms</margin>
**The sacrifice of praise** <note>original: "Sacrificium laudis," from Psalm 50:23</note> **shall honor me: and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.** For singing psalms and praising does not pertain to monks alone, because it was not said of them alone: *The sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtle-dove a nest.* And: *Blessed are they who dwell
<margin>Psalm 83</margin>

Thus, even if he arrives late, he may at least in his later years, as he reaches the end of this transitory life, finish and complete his course.
<margin>James</margin>
Every Christian ought to love the singing of psalms: especially since, just as the service of manual labor belonged to the first state, and the study of doctrine to the second, so the jubilation of the psalms—which draws a person toward the contemplation of God—is proper to the **third state**, which is at the very doors. This psalm-singing is the **key of David** <note>A reference to Revelation 3:7, symbolizing spiritual authority and access to divine mysteries.</note> by which an open door is given to the angel of Philadelphia, such that without this key it is difficult to enter the **Holy of Holies** in any other way. Whether it be ten psalms, in the manner described in the previous book, which refers mystically to the laity; or fifteen or twenty, which refers mystically to the clergy; or thirty, which refers mystically to the monks: let it be pleasing to each one according to his rank to offer them when he is free and his strength suffices, or in another way as God shall inspire him. We warn you to take great care in this: that no one should hold this or any other arrangement of psalms as if it were a debt of servitude to be paid, but rather out of the freedom of the spirit and the affection of devotion, because it is written: **Where the spirit of the Lord is,**

<column-break/>

**there is liberty.** <note>2 Corinthians 3:17</note> And in another place: **There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.** <note>1 John 4:18</note> If, therefore, a devoted brother—who has decided to apply himself to this or another method of private psalm-singing as far as he is able and willing—is perhaps weighed down by some bodily infirmity, or is frequently subject to joint pain <note>original: "dArthe," likely referring to arthritis or gout.</note> or hindered by the burden of some administrative duty: if he either cannot do it at all, or cannot finish what is advised without the suffering of weariness, let him not judge himself as if he were a criminal because he cannot pay the debt. Instead, let him merely reprove himself as being less devoted, since he loses the fruit of so great a reward through negligence. For we do not read that the Lord condemned the disciples because their eyes were heavy with sadness and they were unable to pray; but rather that he only warned them, saying: **Watch and pray that you enter not into temptation.** <note>Matthew 26:41</note> Just as when an illness occurs, one must be touched with gentle encouragement, and not driven out from a wretched mind by a spirit of fear; lest perhaps the old strength cannot endure a new strain, and by **sewing a patch of new cloth onto an old garment**, a greater tear is made. Therefore, let no one think that what is advised must be performed out of sadness or out of necessity, but as one gifted with liberty, let him praise and glorify his God. And whether he praises more or less, let him believe himself saved through the mercy of God, for which reason he is bound to sing and praise in every way. For sometimes the one who praises more with his mouth is less able to praise with his heart, and he who praises more with his heart praises less with his mouth, because perhaps labor and occupation do not permit what the affection suggests. Since this is so, what remains but for us to confess that the Lord is good to all who hope in him? Neither should one presume less of the reward when one praises with the mouth, nor should one despair of mercy when it is granted that one can do less; rather, one must fear what is said of certain people:
<margin>Isaiah</margin>
**This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.** <note>Isaiah 29:13</note> But we must truly presume upon that which is written: **The sacrifice
<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
to God is a troubled spirit: a heart con-** <note>Psalm 51:17 in modern numbering: "A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."</note>

# The Abbot's Book of the Psalter

...**a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.** <note>original: "tritum et humiliatum deus non despicies," from Psalm 51:17.</note> For the mind cannot be free to sing psalms in the same way in a time of mourning and labor (even if it is no less necessary then) as it is in a time of prosperity and joy; as the Apostle says: *Is anyone among you sad? Let him pray with an even mind and sing.* <note>James 5:13. Joachim is emphasizing that prayer is a tool for all emotional states.</note> Therefore, even in a time of gloom, a useful brother ought to apply a little force to himself and bless the Almighty God in his tribulations. Thus, not only in the day of joy, but also in the night of sadness, he may praise and glorify his God, remembering what is written in that same book:
<margin>Psalm</margin>
**In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places and bless the Lord.** <note>Psalm 134:2.</note> But this must also be observed above all—which is well-suited to pious minds and approved by divine authorities—that is, to sing and make melody in our hearts to God. For to speak and cry out with an open voice and the clatter of lips is a matter of action; to pray and sing psalms with silence is a matter of contemplation. Nor should anyone think these are contrary: that which is observed solemnly in the church is a matter of fear <note>Meaning "reverence" or "awe" before God's majesty.</note>, while this is a matter of love; that is a matter of debt <note>Duty or obligation.</note>, while this is a matter of devotion. Although fear is necessary there and love here, so that the one (so to speak) might be tempered by the other, as the Psalmist admonishes, saying:
<margin>Psalm</margin>
**Serve the Lord in fear: and rejoice in him with trembling.** <note>Psalm 2:11.</note> And in another place:
<margin>Psalm</margin>
**Mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord.** <note>Psalm 101:1.</note> However, where there is debt, there is fear; but where there is no debt, there is the love of free men. Therefore, that public prayer ought to be open, but this other should be secret. We must profess our God in the open by the service of the voice for the sake of those who are outside; but in secret, by his gift, we enter the inner chambers of our heart. There, without the noise and sound of the voice, we offer to him alone a **sacrifice of praise**, just as was said of Saint Hannah, the future mother of Samuel:
<margin>1 Kings</margin>
**Moreover, she spoke in her heart, and only her lips moved: and her voice was not heard at all.** <note>1 Samuel 1:13. In the Latin Vulgate, 1 & 2 Samuel are called 1 & 2 Kings.</note> And to that same Samuel, the Lord’s voice said:
<margin>Kings</margin>
**Man sees those things that appear; God, however, looks at the heart.** <note>1 Samuel 16:7.</note> He who watchfully inspects these and similar places in the Scriptures does not think it sufficient for himself to pay what he clearly owes by law and common debt, unless he has something secret that he may offer privately to his God, lest he fail to be—

<column-break/>

—proven a friend rather than a servant. For he is a servant if he does not offer something spontaneously from his own vow, but pays only what is entirely forced and demanded of him. Therefore, all good things that a Christian does must have a good intention as their beginning, so that they are not done absurdly or in vain. But first and principally, they should be for the praise and glory of God, who is the author of all good things; then for the remedy and forgiveness of his own sins; for conquering the passions of the flesh which war against the soul; and for obtaining the grace of the Spirit. Therefore, so that the affection of devotion may always be more fruitful in those who spend their time in psalms and prayers, it is a very good and laudable thing to apply oneself to the singing of psalms in such a way that, through that which is brought forth outwardly by the mouth, the mind is illuminated inwardly; and that what is done discretely on the outside may be revealed and grow in our inner knowledge. For this reason, for those who desire to praise their God on a **ten-stringed psaltery** <note><term>ten-stringed psaltery</term>: A musical instrument used as a metaphor for the Ten Commandments or spiritual perfection.</note>, I would not think it vain to recommend the **number thirty** <note><term>tricenarium</term>: The number 30. Joachim uses "30" to represent the Trinity (3) acting through the Law (10).</note>. For it is clearer than light, as was said above, that three tens pertain to the perfection of the Persons, while the thirty itself pertains to the unity of the Trinity. 
<margin>James</margin>
For there is **one God, one Lord, one King, one Creator, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning.** <note>James 1:17.</note> We believed it pertained to His glory and praise to thus divide the whole Psalter: whether in five ascents <note>Cycles of 30.</note> through thirty psalms, or in fifteen steps <note>Gradual psalms.</note> through ten psalms, so that a useful distinction is made through every ten psalms. Thus, each of the three decades <note>Groups of ten.</note> may be paid to the honor and reverence of each Person: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And because, as noted above, certain persons precede each of the three decades of generations as a "type" <note>A symbolic foreshadowing.</note> of the most reverend and excellent Trinity, so that this venerable mystery might be maintained for the sake of faith (just as it was shown in the generations of the ages and in the secret payment of the psalms), **nine psalms** are to be taken from the body of the Psalter. These are called "threes," and they are used as threes in each confession, to the honor of the Holy Trinity.

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual distinction between vocal, public prayer (driven by duty) and silent, heart-centered prayer (driven by love). Joachim also introduces the mystical significance of the number thirty in organizing the 150 Psalms to honor the Trinity.</summary>

### Joachim's Third Book: On the Ten-Stringed Psalter

...namely, that the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father; the Father and the Holy Spirit are in the Son; and the Father and the Son are in the Holy Spirit. Nothing is attributed to one person by the property of the mystery <note>The "mystery" here refers to the Trinity; Joachim is explaining that while we name three persons, their essence is shared.</note> that is not equally and indifferently common to the three. Therefore, these nine psalms are to be said three by three through each of the three decades <note>A "decade" refers to a set of ten; Joachim is organizing the recitation of the 150 Psalms into spiritual groups.</note>—that is, before the decades are completed—and at the last, a commemoration of the holy and indivisible Trinity shall be made after the melody of the thirty psalms. Indeed, trust for completing this must be placed in Him who promises to fulfill it in us; without doubt, in these times, He speaks through Zechariah the prophet, saying among other things: *In that day I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem, and I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and prayers.* <note>original: "In die illa queram perterere omnes gentes... et effundam... spiritum gratie et precum." From Zechariah 12:9-10.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'D' within a square frame, featuring intricate foliate and vine scrollwork.</image-desc>
An explanation of the fifteen signs of the Day of Judgment. Note that while a brother lector <note>A "lector" was a formal teacher within the Franciscan order.</note> of the convent of the Friars Minor at Toulouse was reading the decretals <note>Church laws or letters containing a papal ruling.</note> to the scholars of Toulouse during the Christmas holidays (as is the custom), he called upon Brother Gerard Odonis. This Gerard later became the Minister General of the entire Order of Friars Minor <note>The highest-ranking official of the Franciscans; Gerard Odonis held this office from 1329–1342.</note>, a Master at Paris, and a most excellent man who produced and gave many writings on the decretals. He stated that in various separate books of theology in the University of Paris, he had found these things concerning the Day of

<column-break/>

Judgment—namely, in Daniel and in the eighth book of Joachim. However, he did not assert them to be true, but rather that he had found them written thus: that some things will happen before the Day of Judgment, some during the Day of Judgment, and some after the Day of Judgment. Before the Day of Judgment, there will be five wars: 

¶ **The first war** will be between the peasants and the clergy; the peasants will defeat the clergy, and the Roman Church will be so trampled underfoot that the clergy will not dare to wear their tonsure <note>The practice of shaving the top of the head to indicate clerical status.</note>, nor will people even call them clerics. 

¶ **The second war** will be between the laity and the Church, such that neither the Pope nor the cardinals will dare to appear in public. 

¶ **The third war** will be between the peasants and the nobles; the peasants will defeat the nobles, and at that time all shall be equal. 

¶ **The fourth war** will be between the Christians and the Saracens <note>term: "Saracens" - a common medieval term for Muslims.</note>; the Christians will be defeated and will pay tribute to the Saracens for a long time. 

¶ **Afterward**, two Christian kings will be born: one in Greece and the other in Italy. They will be faithful Christians and will wage war against the Saracens; just as the Christians used to pay tribute to the Saracens, so the Saracens who remain will pay tribute to the Christians. This will be a true war. 

¶ When this is done, those two kings will appoint eight other kings with the people, and there will be ten kings in total. They and all the Christians will appoint one Roman Emperor. This faithful Emperor will make a shield upon which two men will be painted, and above them he will place another man, to denote that he himself is Lord over those kings and over all Christians. 

¶ Afterward, that Emperor, as a faithful Christian, and other Christians will take up the cross of Christ and go to Jerusalem. There the Emperor will make his dwelling, and thus the whole world will be at peace. 

¶ And all things shall be one, and one shall love the other as a father loves a son. This shall last for a long time; afterward, the Antichrist will be born.

### Abbot. Book of the Psalter

¶ Here begins the hymn of the same Abbot Joachim concerning the heavenly homeland. <note>original: "patria celesti." This refers to the spiritual home of the soul in Heaven, a common theme in medieval mystical writing.</note>

**O** happy kingdom of the celestial homeland: in which the hosts of saints rest; all things decorated with much glory in eternal peace.
It is not for the writing pen to mark, nor for the eloquent man to narrate, how much the eternal God has prepared for those who will reign in you.
The lost offspring of the human race <note>A reference to humanity after the Fall of Adam.</note> sighs for you, lost in the first parent; but redeemed by the death of the Redeemer sent from heaven.
Rightly does it sigh, subjected to darkness, which, deprived of the joys of paradise, lost the light which the heavenly citizens always enjoy.
For the blind crowd of youth is deceived by the splendor of the present light; thinking that to be joyful which fills the world with eternal weeping.
What can a mortal man do but weep for miserable ruins; and mourn his habitation of brief lineage?
He is indeed wretched and very unhappy who, while he lives, does not know he is an exile; who does not sigh for the happiness of that kingdom.
¶ If anyone could feel the banquets of that kingdom in the palace of his heart, he would despise all the things which this present life falsely claims are joyful.
It is no wonder if the work is noted, distinguished by the merit of the creature; prepared as threefold for the good, the evil, and those in the middle. <note>This "threefold" division likely refers to the medieval conception of Heaven, Hell, and Earth (the "middle").</note>
For heaven, earth, and the underworld, considered together, show each thing; while in respect to each other, every single thing is weighed.
The underworld <note>original: "Inferus"</note> is a place of darkness below; above is the heaven of eternal light; the dry land remaining in the middle, common between both.
The underworld does not include angels; the heavenly kingdom contains the blessed spirits; the earth contains the human race wounded by the mouth of the serpent. <note>The "serpent" refers to the devil in the Garden of Eden.</note>
Now if the status of each were asked: both the abyss and paradise; he who contemplated these two diverse things would believe the world [is also separate].
For in respect to the place of darkness, this world is believed to be a pleasant place; but in respect to heaven, it is thought of as a pit—and rightly so.
For this is called the Valley of Tears, which, offering tears to our first parents, compelled the whole crowd of their children to weep.

<column-break/>

Why indeed does the pilgrim man not weep? He who, sitting by the river of Babylon, <note>A reference to Psalm 137: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." In medieval thought, Babylon represents the world, and Zion represents Heaven.</note> remembers the mother from whose sight he has been deprived for a long time.
¶ Truly, the heavenly city is our mother; to you, faithful souls sigh, who taste the cups of your dew sent down from heaven.
Your brightness is eternal brightness: honor and beauty are in your towers; and through the walls, all things are joyful, with songs of praise.
Your stones are choice stones: pure gold is your beauty; every gate consists of pearls.
The structure of precious stones: the individual foundations bloom; and through the streets rises the tree of manifold fruit.
O happy tree which is watered by the wave of the eternal fountain that flows from the throne; by whose force the city of God is always made joyful.
Nor of your praise, joyful city: no tongue can resonate; indeed, the sense of the human heart does not suffice to explore it.
Since if we think more broadly: how great is the glory of the just for you; who remain crowned by you before the throne of the eternal King.
They never labor; they never hunger; they always exult, rejoice, and sing psalms; for indeed no festive times close those joys.
For now the rain will pass and the winter; flowers will bloom everywhere on the earth; and the new songs of the exulting turtledove <note>The turtledove's song was a traditional herald of spring, often allegorized as the voice of the Holy Spirit or the Church.</note> call out.
The voice of the rejoicing Bridegroom <note>The "Bridegroom" is a traditional title for Christ.</note> will be heard: "Arise, you who sleep, hasten, my beloved: and come to receive the crown prepared for you."
Now the fruitful union of the marriage calls forth the joyful instruments of the musicians; let the joyful chorus of the harpers strike together.
At whose voices the earth also resonates: the choirs of saints exult together; and the hearts of the singers are filled with unheard-of joys.
But this sight shows only small things: of that Bridegroom, King, and Master; who rules and reigns over all, one and the same.
How wonderful is his glory: majesty: goodness: immense brightness; whose splendor illuminates all the ages.
Therefore, having despised the glory of the deceptive world... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the column.</note>

### Here begins his clear and most 
### wonderful vision concerning the glory of paradise.

**O**f a vision from a wonderful history I shall begin; I shall write succinctly of the one of happy memory. A certain religious man, not unknown by fame, wrote of a thing he saw while placed in a state of stillness. Led by an ecstasy of the mind, he walked through trackless places. No open fields or passable locations were available to him. On the first day, having set out, he fell among thieves. Bound in tight places, his life almost failed him. There, twice released, the second light <note>The second day</note> finds him half-dead. Not to be cared for, but to be slaughtered by the stings of scorpions. On the third day, having been twice freed, he is surrendered to misery. He makes his way destitute of the counsel of men. He suffers no less danger on the fourth day: wasted by hunger, thirst, and the heat of the wilderness. On the fifth, a wild beast mangles him with its claws and frequently tears him with the bites of animals. But he considers himself to have endured all this until, on the sixth day, he enters the ultimate misery. On one side lynxes, on the other hyenas and the ferocity of griffins <note>original: "grisonum"</note> forbid him from proceeding further on the paths. On this side lions, on that side dragons threaten destruction; asps and basilisks create a dismal hissing. Crushed by their teeth, he is compelled to lay down the burden of his distressed flesh, by which weight he is oppressed. Yet in this very hour in which he is released from the body, he sees a river surging with fire and foul sulfur. There a bridge is established, narrow in its passage <note>The "Bridge of Judgment" is a common motif in medieval visions; only the righteous can cross its narrow, slippery surface without falling into the fires below.</note>, through which the souls of the miserable pass unwillingly. Those who do not know the narrow way fall from the peak of the bridge; tumbling into the deep, the river swallows them. But happy are those who prune themselves from the luxury of the world and studiously restrain themselves from the allurements of the flesh; who crucify themselves along with the vices of nature, and clothed in the wings of life, fly away from these dangers.

<column-break/>

There, secure and swift as if they were light eagles, they cross the narrow bridge into the leading-way of the homeland. Moreover, there was a huge wall placed next to the river, and at the summit of the wall was a most pleasant field. The wall itself displayed the appearance of bronze, established without hands by the Supreme Architect. But also, a path was arranged through windings by which one could ascend to the heights of the fields. Therefore, when the aforementioned man passed through there in spirit, he saw the crowds of the blessed, divided into three ranks. In the first hour, beyond the river at the top of the wall, he was drawn into an immense boundary of space. <meta>catchword: cem.</meta> There were spacious places illustrated by light, and in them a blessed people enjoying the rest of peace. There were forests there, dense with various trees; all bear fruit of sweet flavor. They are very tall, exceeding other species; their shade provides a pleasant tempering of the heat. The snake is absent, the frog is absent, the evil beast is absent. All is beautiful, all is safe, all is full of glory. Walking for many days near a turbid year <note>meaning a long duration of time</note>, he sees on one side the punishment of the guilty, and on the other the reward of the just. Having surveyed these things in these places and returning to the first, he seeks to pass further so that he might know the land. But when he had wandered much toward the base of the summit of a high mountain, whose rock-wall is of silver, he saw a ladder raised above the mountain’s peak, by which he climbs and contemplates the appearance of the just. And there he looks out upon a spacious plain, displaying the charms of a beautiful vision. Among the species of herbs, the green meadows smell of the fragrance of lilies and roses. There, many rushing streams divide, which flow from the fountain of life in a thousand channels. They also flow into and irrigate the places described below, and they make fertile everything within the circuit of the wall. Truly, above are most beautiful trees bearing nectar, decorated with leaf and flower, and most abundant with fruit. Yet he seeks the source of the water through the depths of the meadows, and is led to the beginnings of a higher mountain. Then he ascends, given the aid of a garment, and perceives himself established in the palace of the King. Its walls were constructed of green jasper and every kind of precious stone. Its roof was of pure gold over clear glass, and in it was a shining throne from which a flame <note>likely the Holy Spirit, often symbolized by fire</note> goes forth...

The vision features classic medieval motifs like the narrow bridge of judgment, a silver-walled mountain, and a jasper-walled divine palace.</summary>
