# Abba: The Book of the Psaltery

The throne itself glows with precious stones,
And it glitters with wondrous rows of gems.
Set on high, it surpasses the rays of the sun,
And illuminates the ranks <note>original: "cuneos," meaning battalions or wedges; a common medieval term for the organized rows of saints</note> of the elect situated below.
Around this throne: many seats,
And upon these the elders <note>The twenty-four elders described in the Book of Revelation</note> decree judgments.
There the beautiful Church resides above the moon,
Like a bride surrounded by her husband's glory.
Before the throne thousands of children assisted,
Whose clothes were pearls and whose crowns were lilies.
They play the harp and sing the song of songs,
And they made joyful the three-fold ranks of the elect.
Of the one sitting upon the throne, it is not easy to speak:
He surpasses not only sight but even the sharp edge of the mind.
But when he <note>the visionary</note> sought understanding of the three-fold mansion,
He was taught what he ought to proceed through.
In the first level are contained the populations of the elect,
Professing faith in the Triune and one Lord.
Who in a more humble life please God with their gift,
Of praise and offering and faithful work.
Whose married life carries the value of copper <note>original: "eris" (aes), meaning bronze or copper. In Joachite thought, metals represent the three states of humanity: copper for the laity, silver for the clergy, and gold for the monastics</note>,
Through which the servants of the house fulfill their ministry.
It stands of a green color, through which faith is known.

<column-break/>

To designate in what way whoever joins himself to God lives.
In the second level remain those who, through holy studies,
Build up the ranks now by word and now by example.
The life of these is believed to be signified by silver.
The brightness of this gives splendor to the certainty of the saved.
In the highest level remain those who, having despised worldly glory,
Sought only to see the King in the fatherland <note>original: "patria," a common term for Heaven as the true home of the soul</note>.
Whose life is esteemed as similar to pure gold,
And the ornaments of their virtues are precious stones.
Therefore there are three venerable branches <note>original: "germina," meaning sprouts or offspring</note> of the elect,
Established in the villages, the suburbs, and in the city <note>Joachim uses these locations as metaphors for the three spiritual states: the "villages" of the married, the "suburbs" of the clergy, and the "city" of the contemplatives</note>.
With a three-fold voice they sing together unheard-of songs,
And they praise the King of heaven who made all these things.
To the Triune God, the three-fold crowd of the elect
Sings poems and exults through eternal ages.
->Amen. The End.<-

# Abbot Joachim’s [Book of] the Ten Strings
## Here begins the Table of Contents for the first book of the Psaltery of Ten Strings.

How in the physical shape of the Psaltery, the three sets of fifty psalms <note>The 150 Psalms of the Bible, traditionally divided into three groups of fifty</note> are shown: representing the three persons of the Deity and the three statuses of the world. folio 226, column 1.

Concerning how the ten strings of the psaltery itself are physical and contain all the generations of the world from Abraham until the last of the elect, as Holy Scripture teaches. folio 226, column 1.

Concerning the fact that the first and upper corner of the psaltery is not sharp like the other two lower ones: because the Father, remaining at the summit of majesty, is not recorded as having been "sent"; rather, only the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent from the Father himself to our narrow straits. folio 226, column 1.

Concerning man being set above even all the orders of Angels because of the Word of the Father assuming human flesh: so that he might restore the tenth rank of the string (which fell). <note>Joachim refers to the medieval belief that humanity was created to fill the void left by the fallen tenth choir of angels</note> folio 226, column 1.

Concerning the first of the ten strings: it begins with fear and ascends even to the height of charity. folio 226, column 1.

Concerning how, through the stature and the connections of the wheels described by Ezekiel, the four "intelligences" or senses of Holy Scripture are understood: and each of them is divided into different types: Note this and keep it with you. folio 226, column 2.

How it has been brought forth from the ancient tradition of the fathers down to the moderns: that psalm-singing is of great reward; and that the verse from Psalm 49 pertains to it: "The sacrifice of praise will honor me: and there is the path by which I will show him the salvation of God." folio 227, column 1.

Concerning many who, desiring wisdom, devoted themselves to the study of reading, persisting in doctrines; yet they did not arrive at its marrow <note>original: "medullam," meaning the core or inner essence</note> because they did not judge the entrance to be through grace, but rather through art; whose freedom likewise did not profit those striving over it from the beginning. folio 227, column 1.

<column-break/>

Concerning the aforementioned who, searching in such a way: did not find the Key of David <note>A biblical metaphor for the authority to interpret Scripture</note>, nor Him who opens for those who love Him. folio 227, column 1.

Concerning the author: he himself was once anxious regarding the words of God and sought to reach the knowledge of God’s truth through the exercise of reading; and as he burned to hasten toward it through the study of reading, by taking on burdens like an eagle, he receded further from it. folio 227, column 1.

Concerning the author: placed in a new fervor, he began to love psalm-singing for God’s sake; whence many things in Holy Scripture began to be revealed to him while singing, which he had previously been unable to track down through reading. folio 227, column 1.

Concerning the author: on the holy day of Pentecost, out of reverence for such a great solemnity, he decided to recite several psalms in honor of the Holy Spirit, hoping that something would be given to him by Him on that day. folio 227, column 1.

Concerning the author: while he was praying and singing psalms before the holy altar on the aforementioned day: the form of the ten-stringed psaltery occurred to his mind, and in it such a clear and open mystery of the Holy Trinity, that he was immediately compelled to cry out: "Who is a great God like our God? etc." <note>original: "Quis deus magnus sicut deus noster"</note> and thus he began to compile the first book of the work written below. folio 227, column 1.

Concerning how the author dedicated the work on *Concordance* <term>Concordia: Joachim's theory of the harmony between the Old and New Testaments</term> to God the Father; the work on the *Apocalypse* to the Son; and the little work on the *Psaltery* to the Holy Spirit; and how the second proceeds from the first, and the third from both. folio 227, column 2.

Concerning the said work being divided into three books according to the three persons of the Deity in whom the beauty of our faith consists. folio 227, column 2.

Concerning how, in the first book of this work, it deals with the "musical vessel" <note>The instrument itself</note>, which by the property of a high mystery is attributed to the Father, from whom are all things; in the second, it deals with the number of psalms of divine wisdom: through which are all things; in the third, it deals with the manner of psalm-singing: and the instruction of those singing to the same Holy Unction; in...

# Table [of Contents] for the Exposition on the Psaltery.

...whereby all things: since it is the joy and exultation of the Most High God: it makes those whom he fills with sacred gifts happy and joyful. folio 223, col. 2.

Concerning the fact that the psaltery is excellent and distinguished among all and above all musical instruments, to which nonetheless the kithara <note>original: *cythara*; a stringed instrument similar to a lyre</note> is nearly equal in divine mysteries. folio 228, col. 2.

Concerning why the kithara is thus joined to the Psaltery: because to that greatest commandment which is "Love God," another must necessarily be joined, which is "Love thy neighbor." folio 228, col. 2.

Concerning the Psaltery: or musical vessel, which is a regulated work having ten strings before its face, beautiful in form, slender in sound, sweet in melody, entirely mystical in its art, and divinely invented. folio 228, col. 2.

Concerning how there is such sweetness of melody in it: that while the sound itself strikes the outer ears with its ringing, it often carries away the minds of the listeners to an ecstasy of the spirit, and by its soothing, compels them even to the shedding of tears. folio 228, col. 2.

Concerning how all outer melody ceases when the inner song is perceived: and physical sweetness is despised when spiritual joy is found; for what is sweeter than divine contemplation, and through those things which were made, to arrive at the Maker. folio 228, col. 2.

Concerning how some excuse themselves in vain for their slowness of intellect, saying that it is impossible and beyond the measure of human capacity to extend oneself to the understanding of the Creator: since Scripture bears witness, saying, "The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." <note>original: *Spiritus scrutatur omnia & etiam profunda dei*; a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:10</note> folio 228, col. 2.

Concerning how the work cannot be equaled to the craftsman, nor the thing made to its maker: nor can a sign be raised up by its own operation against the one who formed it. folio 229, col. 1.

Concerning how the invisible things of God, which surpass all sense, cannot be contemplated by the weakness of our captivity except through visible things. folio 229, col. 1.

<column-break/>

Concerning how man, when he desires to speak of the divine majesty, ought to extend himself to contemplating the nobler creatures: so that through visible things, [the light of] invisible things might be made proper to what the soul thinks; and if a man can comprehend himself, he will find in himself the likeness of God. folio 229, col. [1].

Concerning how if a man cannot comprehend himself, in whom the image of God shines: let him be careful not to hold inconstantly to spiritual men, to whom the Spirit is given, searching all things, and even the deep things of God. folio 229, col. [1].

Concerning how he is sufficiently unfaithful and wicked who, not knowing how to examine himself, trusts that he can comprehend God (who is above him, as He truly is) by reason. folio 229, col. [1].

Concerning how from the nature and property of the sun, the mystery of the Trinity is arrived at and known. folio 229, col. [1].

Concerning how he should not grow weary of hearing again and again that which it always delights the elect of God to speak and to hear. folio 229, col. [1].

How Sabellius and Arius <note>Sabellius and Arius were famous early Christian heretics; Sabellius taught that the Father, Son, and Spirit were just different "modes" of one person, while Arius taught that the Son was a created being subordinate to the Father.</note> erred: for Sabellius, wishing to speak of the Trinity, ran his ship onto the dry land; Arius, seeking to avoid this, was cast down into the mud of the deep. folio 229.

Concerning how it should by no means be believed that the instrument called the psaltery would have received such a celebrated name—so that from it, the Book of Psalms should take its title—unless a great sacrament of faith lay hidden in that same vessel. folio 230.

Concerning how often even the smallest things, which the learned themselves often loathe, are found to contain mysteries: the number of which is infinite. folio 230.

Concerning how the Book of Psalms not only reports those things which are divine: but truly a path is prepared for the Divinity itself, so that he may descend into the inner chambers of our hearts: let us therefore sing psalms, etc. folio 230.

Concerning the fact that one must play music not only on the Ten-Stringed Psaltery—in which the Ten Commandments <note>original: *preceptorum Decalogus*</note> and the sum of the whole faith is contained—but also upon the Kithara <note>original: *Lythara*; a ancient stringed instrument similar to a lyre</note>, because it too is celebrated enough in the divine pages and is found in the sacred volumes no less than the Psaltery. They differ, however. See folio **230, col. 1**

Concerning how the Kithara designates the "new man" who is created according to God, together with his body, which is the Church. The height of its mystery consists in three over-stretched strings and its hollow cavity. folio **230, col. 1**

Concerning the cavity of the Kithara, which is according to that saying of Christ: "Unless one renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple," and "Do not store up for yourselves treasure." See folio **230, col. 1**

Concerning how you may trust that you belong to the elect even now, when you diligently praise your God with three special strings: the first is work <note>or "action"</note>, the second is reading, and the third is psalmody; or certainly: the first is Faith, the second is Hope, and the third is Charity. folio **230, col. 1**

Concerning how the Psaltery pertains to the contemplative life and the love of God, while the Kithara pertains to the active life and the love of one's neighbor <note>original: *amorẽ primi*; likely referring to the first or nearest person</note>. folio **230**

Concerning how, if the contemplation of God delights you, take up the secret Ten-Stringed Psaltery and enter into the hidden mysteries within the cellars of your heart; there perhaps you will begin to observe "what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9 regarding the joys of heaven</note>. Nor is it a wonder, for through this instrument a path is prepared for the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit as "Advocate" or "Helper"</note> to come to us. folio **230, col. 1**

Concerning the fact that there is no likeness that can be sufficiently adapted to the divine majesty of the Trinity, although there are many mysteries which He established for the sake of investigating Himself. Note: folio **230, col. 2**

Concerning the three divine persons named by the holy fathers—Father, Word, and Holy Spirit—(by the necessity of speaking) because they could not find a common name that would suit them in the plural. folio **234, col. 1**

That which is handed down to us by the Catholic fathers concerning that simple nature which is God must be weighed with subtle scrutiny: that in the deity of the Trinity, whatever is powerful, eminent, glorious, or happy is said to be the whole; it is believed and understood to belong to whichever person, so that there is no less in each individual than in all three together. folio **234, col. 2**

### Index to the Exposition on the Psaltery

[Ma]gnitude is great in itself: than which nothing greater can be. folio 235, column 1.

$\P$ Some, following these three things by which all are perfected—namely power, knowledge, and will—attribute power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and will or love to the Holy Spirit. folio 235, column 2.

$\P$ The Father is thus called "Power" because, in executing judgment upon sinners, he always shows himself to be unconquered. The Son is also called "Wisdom" because he did not wish to conquer through power, but through humility. The Holy Spirit is truly called "Love" because whoever fully loves someone gives to the one he loves both himself and all that he owns. folio 235, column 1.

$\P$ Regarding the Son alone can it be said (insofar as he is both God and man) that he sent himself and was sent by another—namely, from the Father—likening him to any man when he dies. See folio 235, column 2.

$\P$ Iron was applied to a certain stone <note>the magnet or lodestone</note>, and immediately the power of the stone drew the iron to itself; that iron then received the same power, and thus another piece of iron touching it received that same power, which Augustine relates having seen in *The City of God*. <note>original: *Augustinus in de civitate dei*</note> folio 235, column 2.

$\P$ For the reason that the Father is from no one <note>he is "unbegotten"</note>, it is never read that he was sent to men, since he had no beginning from which he might be sent, unlike the Son and the Holy Spirit. folio 236, column 1.

$\P$ The Holy Spirit is the principle <note>or source</note> of the man Christ Jesus, and in what way: just like the Father, because that entire work of the "new man" is shown to be attributed to the same Holy Spirit, because he was conceived of the Holy Spirit. folio 236, column 1.

$\P$ If the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Son alone and not from the Father, it would seem most absurd; the reasons for this are provided. folio 236, column 1.

Why the Hebrews begin to write from the right side and end on the left; this is not without a mystery. folio 237, column 1.

$\P$ Attributing greater devotion or

<column-break/>

honor and similar things to one divine person more than another is a mortal sin; indeed, such a person nurtures heresy in their mind. folio 237, column 1.

$\P$ That eternity which was in God before worldly times is entirely unsearchable to us (who began to exist within time). The wisdom of men is dulled, and sense and intellect fail, regarding by what secret counsel he willed to create at that time which was not from eternity. folio 238, column 1.

$\P$ The Father was revealed to men more in the first time; then the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that they too might appear more manifest in their own times: namely, the Father in the first state of the world, the Son in the second, and the Holy Spirit in the third state, etc. <note>This refers to Joachim's famous "Three Ages" of history.</note> folio 238, column 1.

$\P$ Charity <note>or Love</note> is the mother of all virtues, without which gathering the remaining virtues is like carrying empty and useless stalks to a sad threshing floor. folio 238, column 2.

$\P$ Just as the humanity of Christ is set above all creatures, so is the virtue of Charity above all other virtues. And just as John the Baptist was the precursor of the Christian, the virtue of humility is the precursor to Charity, which is the chief gift of the Holy Spirit. folio 238, column 2.

How he explains regarding Charity: "I have seen the end of all perfection; <note>original: *omnis confirmationis* (likely a variant of *consummationis* from Psalm 119:96)</note> your commandment is broad indeed." folio 238, column 2.

$\P$ Divinity alone is great without quantity and good without quality; it alone, by its very nature, is immense without the variation and volatility of time. folio 238, column 2.

See in the revelations of Amadeus the Minorite <note>Amadeus of Portugal (c. 1420–1482), a Franciscan mystic whose "Apocalypsis Nova" was often associated with Joachite thought</note>, who asserts that the orders of Angels were created long before, in the first "rapture" of the second revelation and in the second "rapture."

$\P$ We do not know how far or near before the constitution of the world—or if in the very beginning of the world—the orders of Angels were created. Therefore, the "main horn" of the psaltery rightly lacks a beginning, so that it appears to represent a "beginning without a beginning." Noted on folio 238, column [1].

$\P$ There is one operation of all three persons in divine matters because of the ineffable bond of the deity. folio 239, column 1.

$\P$ The Old Testament seems to pertain to the Father, while the New [Testament] pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit. folio 239, column 1.

$\P$ Why in the church we have become accustomed to making the first invocation to the Father in prayers, and toward the end to add "through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son," <note>original: *per dominum nostrum Jesum Christum filium tuum*</note> and at the conclusion "in the unity of the Holy Spirit." <note>original: *in unitate spiritus sancti*</note> folio 239, column 1.

$\P$ How the Catholic Church (with divine majesty governing) ordains that prayers be said as mentioned above. folio 239, column 1.

$\P$ According to the sequence of prayer: namely, that the beginning pertaining to the Father is located at the highest corner of the psaltery; and "through our Lord Jesus Christ" at the second corner; and "in the unity of the Holy Spirit" at the third. folio 239, column 2.

$\P$ Although God was always one and three as he is, nevertheless, whether he was three was known only to a few perfected individuals in the Old Testament from Adam until Christ; however, the name of one person—namely, the Father—was announced to all of them, both servants and friends: that is, those who were called the people of God. folio 239, column 2.

$\P$ Therefore, the mystery of the Trinity was not yet revealed to that unrefined people during that time, lest, not being capable [of it], they might turn the worship of one God into a plurality of gods. folio 239, column 2.

$\P$ The beginning of wisdom is in fear, but the end is in charity <note>or love</note>; see where. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ What was the cause that through so many past ages only one person, and not also the whole Trinity, was known to that earthly and unspiritual <note>original: *animali*, referring to the "natural man" in contrast to the "spiritual man"</note> people; instead, like children, the foundation of faith in one God was laid for them, but for us, as for elders and perfected ones, the mystery of the Trinity has been opened. folio 239, column 2.

$\P$ God the Father is so much that which he is, that he deigns to send from himself the Son and the Holy Spirit, co-eternal with himself, to chosen creatures; however, neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit sends the Father. folio 240, column 1.

$\P$ The dignity of the patriarchate, which would have been fitting if Adam had not sinned, was given to Abraham; and thus Abraham is to be accepted as the first of the patriarchs, as if he had no human father. folio 240, column 1.

$\P$ How through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob the Trinity of persons in divine matters is figured and declared. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ As far as it concerns us, the creatures, the Father as well as the Son and the Holy Spirit are to be called "Father"; however, it is not so regarding the deity, where only the Father is the Father—namely, of the Son. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ No injury is done to the Son or the Holy Spirit when, in praying and in any way, the Father is invoked in the first place and as if specially; because whatever is offered under this faith to the paternal majesty is also offered to the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are consubstantial with the Father and are fathers to us, as mentioned above. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ When in prayer toward the end there is added: "through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who lives and reigns in the unity [of the Holy Spirit, one] God," <note>original: *per dominum nostrum Jesum Christum filium tuum: qui vivit et regnat in uni. f. f. deus*</note> we recall those special things which became clear concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit at the end of times. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ The Father is understood by the name of fear and power; the Son by the name of wisdom; and the Holy Spirit by the name of charity and love. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ How it is declared that fear is the beginning of wisdom; for through fear is understood the Father, who is the principle of the Son, who is his wisdom; and through charity [is understood] the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the beginning of wisdom is in fear, and the end in charity, although these three names are common [to all three persons]. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ What is the cause of the property of the three aforementioned names; and whether the Father is called fear, and the Son wisdom, and the Holy Spirit charity. folio 240, column 2.

$\P$ Where there is humility, there is wisdom; and where there is pride, there is insult. folio 241, column 1.

# Index of the Commentary on the Psaltery

...we are called to: which correspond to the three orders of the elect who were created in the image of God: namely, the work of the hands, in which are restraint and the fear of the Lord; the second is the study of reading, in which is wisdom; the third is the singing of psalms and the devotion of prayer. Note: folio 241.

We are bound to obey because of fear, which is the Father; to read because of wisdom, which is Christ; and to sing and pray because of charity, which is the Holy Spirit. In fear, we kiss the foot; in reading, the hand; and in psalmody, the mouth. There is a good beginning in the kissing of the feet, better perseverance in the kissing of the hand, but the best completion in the kiss of His mouth. folio 241, column 2.

Just as one cannot progress in the knowledge of the scriptures unless he vigilantly shakes himself free from the worry of earthly things, so too he is not capable of contemplating that simple essence which is God through the coming of the Holy Spirit, unless he rests from the noise of created things, of actions, and of whatever words, and turns the study of his intention and devotion to Him who made all things. folio 241, column 2.

It is one thing to look back at what was made, and another to gaze upon Him who made what was made; just as it is one thing to know something so that one may know, and another to know so that one may love. For in the former, there is knowledge alone, which often "puffs up"; in the latter, with wisdom, is charity, which "builds up." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 8:1: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up."</note> folio 242, column 1.

In the five ages of the world, servile fear persists in the world; but in the sixth and seventh, filial fear and love are present. One of these pertains to the Son, the other to the Holy Spirit; and according to this (as Pope Gregory teaches) the ages of a single man are to be observed and weighed—a beautiful note. folio 242, column 2.

According to the law of Moses, the sons of Levi are commanded to serve in the tabernacle until the fiftieth year; from then on, they are to rest from ministry and become guardians of the sacred vessels. This also signifies receiving the kingdom of holy souls. folio 242, column 1.

That old man is of a sufficiently weak hope who, the 

<column-break/>

closer he feels the time of his calling to be at hand, does not insist on contemplation and prayer as worthily and assiduously as the Psalmist: "Make known to me, O Lord, my end," etc. <note>original: *Notum fac mihi domine finem meum* (Psalm 39:4)</note> folio 242, column 1.

By the ten strings of the psaltery are understood the faithful and holy men. folio 242, column 1.

The prayer and confession of that faithful person penetrates the ears of the Divinity when he acknowledges and venerates the three persons, yet with the eye of the mind sees the unity of substance; when, for instance, he thinks of the persons as distinct but not divided, and does not imagine the substance of the persons to be singular <note>Meaning "isolated" or "solitary," as Joachim argues for a collective unity of the three persons.</note>, but one. folio 243, column 1.

In the first rank are placed the apostles; in the second, prophets and evangelists; in the third, teachers; in the fourth, contemplatives; in the fifth, clergy and monks; in the sixth, the continent and the multitude of all the faithful. folio 243, column 1.

Although in heavenly glory there are diverse mansions and ranks of saints and blessed ones, they are nevertheless all of one mind and connected by a wonderful charity; and each one rejoices to be what he is, with all impious zeal and envy removed. folio 243, column 2.

# The Ten Strings [Psaltery] of Abbot Joachim

[Of] the ten strings: we weigh them with subtle investigation, for through these very steps one must ascend to the contemplation of heavenly things. <note>Joachim relates the ten-stringed psaltery mentioned in Psalm 33:2 and 92:3 to the mystical structure of the universe and the Trinity.</note> folio 243, column 2.

Concerning how human life is distinguished in three states: and to each of them are ascribed twenty-five years. folio 244, column 1.

He who would wish to come gradually from lesser stages to perfection with the passage of time: he ought to be a layman for twenty-five years and serve God for as many in the office of the clergy; and for another 25 up to 75 [years old] devote himself to prayers and psalms, waiting daily in readiness for the hour of his calling. Whatever anyone lived beyond this: is as if outside the rule; note. <note>Joachim suggests a life divided into three 25-year segments, mirroring his theology of the Three Ages of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> folio 244, column 1.

Concerning the moral ages: which are to be especially emulated by every Christian: we can assign these three states of human life in five general virtues pertaining specifically to the birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension of the Lord, and the coming of the Holy Spirit. folio 244, column 1.

Concerning how one ascends those fifteen steps <note>Original: "quindecim gradus." These refer to the fifteen "Psalms of Ascent" (Psalms 120–134) sung by pilgrims.</note> in order: who, through the said works or virtues signified in them, as if through certain ascents, disposes in his heart how he may reach the height of their perfection by beginning, progressing, and completing. folio 244, column 1.

Concerning how five sets of thirty psalms are to be referred to the five aforesaid works: because in them is contained, in spirit, the sum of our perfection; for in them we are seen to have received those gifts given to us for our sake, so that through them we may be blessed with eternal life. folio 244, column 1.

Concerning how from the birth of Christ we are taught to agree with the humble; from His passion to act patiently; from Christ’s resurrection to be strong in faith; from His ascension to be long-suffering in hope; and by the manifestation of fire <note>The fire of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.</note> to be kindled with the fervor of charity. folio 244, column 1.

Concerning how someone is in the first step of humility when he humbles himself to his superiors; in the second when he humbles himself to his equals; in the third when he humbles himself to a social inferior. folio 244, column 1.

<column-break/>

Concerning who is in the first step of patience: when he suffers lashes for his own sins; in the second with friends; in the third when for his enemies; and this indeed concerning two virtues <note>Humility and patience.</note> which always look upon humbler things and acquire exaltation through their observance. folio 244, column 1.

What it means to believe in the first, second, and third degree of faith and similarly of hope. folio 244, column 1.

Concerning how he is in the first step of hope who hopes for temporal reward; and in the second when, after the labor of this present life, he hopes to reach that heavenly homeland; and in the third when he hopes to enjoy the vision of God. folio 244, column 2.

Concerning how one is in the first step of charity: when, according to God, he loves his own flesh, parents, and relatives; or what is more worthy, neighbors and friends; and in the second when he loves strangers and pilgrims; and in the third when he loves enemies. folio 244, column 2.

Concerning how the aforesaid steps of virtues are those fifteen steps by which one ascends into the temple of God: namely through the three steps of humility, patience, faith, hope, and charity; note. folio 244.

Concerning how through these steps one does not ascend to a temple made by hands, which Solomon built, but to that not made by hands which is in heaven, by the spiritual steps of the mind. folio 244, column 2.

Concerning how it belongs to the little ones to have these virtues in the first degree; of the younger ones in the second; of the elders in the third degree; note. folio 244, column 2.

Concerning how the Christian religion has its ages, which are distinguished not by the number of years, but by the difference of life. folio 244, column 2.

Concerning how there are three general orders of the elect: namely, laity, clergy, and monks, to whom belong the fifteen steps and the number of one hundred and fifty psalms. folio 244, column 2.

Concerning how it belongs to the laity to be in the first degree of the aforesaid virtues, to whom the number of ten pertains; in the second to the clergy, to whom twenty; in the third to the monks, to whom thirty. <note>These numbers refer to the mathematical/mystical divisions of the 150 Psalms (10, 20, 30 multiplied by five virtues).</note> folio 245, column 1.

Concerning how into the monastic life and rule, some are received into the active life with Martha; some to the contemplative life with Mary. <note>Martha and Mary from the Gospels are the traditional symbols for the life of work/service and the life of prayer/contemplation.</note> folio 245, column 1.

# Index to the Exposition on the Psalter

To the married specifically pertains the exercise of work; to the clergy, doctrine; and to monks specifically, psalmody <note>The practice of singing or reciting the Psalms as a spiritual discipline.</note>. folio 245, column 1

To the Father pertains, in a certain way, work, from whom are all things; to the Son, doctrine, through whom are all things; and to the Holy Spirit, jubilation <note>original: "iubilatio"; here referring to a state of wordless spiritual joy or melodic singing</note>, in whom are all things. folio 245, column 1

The Father creates; the Master (that is, the Son) teaches; until Charity (that is, the Holy Spirit) gladdens; and yet all these are the works of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together. folio 245, column 1

Each individual order requires these three: work, doctrine, and praise. However, for the first [laypeople], work pertains in the first place, then doctrine, and thirdly jubilation. For the second [clergy], doctrine is first, then work and jubilation. For the third [monks], jubilation is first, then doctrine and work. folio 245, column 1

The aforementioned things are done rightly according to order if the layman works three-fold, if the cleric reads [studies] three-fold, and if the monk sings the psalms three-fold. folio 245, column 1

If a layman wishes to draw near to God through devotion, he must have a ten-fold <note>original: "denariam"</note> perfection in divine praises, a twenty-fold in doctrine, and a thirty-fold in manual labor; and so it is for the cleric and monk in their own manner. see folio 245, column 1.

Those who are debtors to children, parents, and kinsfolk (such as laypeople) cannot devote themselves to God in the same way, nor can the clergy who are bound to serve the churches and give back to those from whom they receive offerings; unlike the monks, who have left parents and all things for the sake of Christ. folio 245, column 1

How that saying from the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> concerning the worship of the beast, its image, and the number of its name is explained. folio 245, column 2

Spiritual men strive to abstain not only from criminal [mortal] sins, but even from venial ones, judging that among perfect men something is considered a crime which among the common crowd is judged as venial and very small. folio 245, column 2

Great is the difference between those devout Christians who do not wish to leave themselves and their possessions, and those who, leaving all things, live together in a community under a shepherd who holds them with Christ. folio 246, column 1.

<column-break/>

The order of laypeople, which is also called the married state, is to be likened to children in Christ; that of the clerics who retain property for themselves to youths; but the order of those who live in common to elder men. For just as the ages of the body are distinguished, so must the ages of the soul be distinguished by their character. folio 246, column 1

The first people (that is, the Jews) were led as far as some knowledge of God the Father. The second (that is, the Christian people) to a more powerful knowledge of the Father and the Son. But the third is to be led more fully to the knowledge of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the entire Trinity. folio 246, column 1 and 2

Because from the beginning that [first] people expected the Christ, they did not know, however, whether he was the Son of God; just as many Christians often speak of the Holy Spirit, yet they do not know his goodness and are ignorant of the gifts of his graces and his power. folio 246, column 2

Although the Spirit is known to the Christian people, he is not known as fully or as solemnly as he will be by that third people who are to come; for that time belongs to the Holy Spirit by a certain unique property. folio 246, column 2

The whole of the Psalms consists of three sets of fifty; <note>The Book of Psalms contains 150 songs, which Joachim divides into three groups of fifty to represent spiritual growth.</note> and blessed is he who can have what the first fifty signify; more blessed is he who obtains what the second designates; but most blessed is he who is not excluded from what the third signifies. folio 246, column 2

To fear belongs to children; to dread and tremble belongs to those who are ignorant of the fairness of judgment and do not understand what they read. However, those who believe and understand are led to the knowledge of the Father and the Son, and this belongs to youths. Those who see, understand, and are delighted, having knowledge of the Father and Son, have come to the greatness of the Holy Spirit. folio 246, column 2

Of those things which have been said: the first stage belongs to infants, the second to youths, the third to elders (who, through the gift of grace, [consider] nothing... <note>The sentence cuts off as a catchword for the next page.</note>

# The Ten-Stringed Psaltery of Abbot Joachim <note>original: "Decem chordaz Abbatis Joachim"</note>

¶ Those who will be judged and saved; and those who will not only be saved but will also be judges; and the other factors that create a distance between judges and those they judge, so that each may receive his own reward. folio 251, column 2.

¶ The grounds for glory are not equal for one who serves God from childhood and for one who comes to that service only when the world has already been crucified to him by necessity <note>meaning someone who only turns to God in old age or at the end of life when they can no longer enjoy worldly pleasures</note>: note. folio 250, column 2.

¶ When it is said in this place that "the exercise of doctrine pertains to the clerics," it should be understood as referring to those who are permitted to remain as individuals and to have personal property, and not those who live commonly and canonically according to the rule of Saint Augustine in the first purpose of charity; for Saint Augustine calls these latter ones "monks." folio 251, column 2.

¶ There is as much distance between the life of clerics and monks as there is between the life of the laity and the clerics: see in what manner. folio 251, column 2.

Regarding clerics, it is partially permitted and partially forbidden to have wives; for monks, it is entirely prohibited. folio 251, column 2.

Some married laity are "monks" in their devotion and will; among the clerics, some are also so by devotion and <term>continence</term> <note>the practice of refraining from sexual relations</note>. True monks, however, are so by devotion, continence, and the renunciation of their goods and of their very selves. folio 251, column 2.

There are three special things that make a monk: a vow, continence, and the renunciation of one’s goods and one’s self. folio 251, column 2.

A married layman who is a monk in desire and will holds a "penny" <note>symbolizing a unit of spiritual reward</note> of monastic perfection and psalmody; however, a cleric who lives continently holds two pennies. folio 252, column 2.

According to the <term>concordance</term> <note>original: "concordiam"; Joachim's method of matching Old Testament figures with New Testament counterparts</note>, kings reflect kings, priests reflect priests, and Levites reflect Levites between the Old and New Testaments, looking at one another with mutual faces. folio 252, column 1.

According to the spiritual understanding: the Kings and princes of the Old Testament signify the <term>pontiffs</term> <note>high-ranking prelates or bishops</note> of the New; the soldiers signify the clerics who live under them; the priests signify the directors of monasteries; and the Levites signify the monks, who are also called <term>cenobites</term> <note>monks who live in a community rather than as hermits</note>. folio 252, column 1.

<column-break/>

If a monk cannot continually remain in his initial fervor regarding those things that pertain to the contemplative life, at the very least he must not cease from the "study of attainment" <note>the effort to maintain spiritual progress</note>, which is for him an everlasting possession that he should by no means alienate or lose. folio 252, column 2.

What the difference is between those who are converted to the service of God from childhood and those who delay until old age. folio 253, column 1.

Gold signifies the contemplative life and those praising the Lord. Silver signifies the doctrine of the Lord’s utterances. And bronze signifies the work of the hands for the support of the needy: note. folio 253, column 1.

Through work, bodies are nourished; through doctrine, the minds of the "little ones" in Christ are refreshed; and both of these look toward the love of neighbor. But the third, which is signified by gold—namely, the contemplative life—looks toward the love of God, which is the first and greatest commandment. folio 253, column 1.

In the days of King Saul, who was chosen by the Lord to signify the people of the <term>First State</term> <note>Joachim’s "Status," or Ages of history; the First State is the Age of the Father</note>, bronze was highly regarded. In the days of King David, who was also chosen by the Lord to signify the people of the <term>Second State</term> <note>The Age of the Son</note>, bronze was not regarded because of the abundance of silver. And in the days of Solomon, who represents the <term>Third State</term> <note>The Age of the Holy Spirit</note>, because of the excessive abundance of gold, even silver was not regarded as anything. folio 253, column 1.

The order of the married, which began with Adam, shone forth in Abraham; the order of clerics, initiated by Moses, shone forth in Christ and the apostles; the order of monks, initiated by Elijah, is even now (by God’s favor) at the time where it should come to the light, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. folio 253, column 1.

The initiation of the Third State, pertaining to the Holy Spirit, began in Saint Benedict, the founder of the Western monks; it will, however, shine forth fully in its own time. folio 253, column 2.

...and Levites signify the monks who are also called <term>cenobites</term> <note>monks who live in a community rather than as hermits</note>. folio 252, column 1.

If a monk cannot continually remain in his initial fervor in those things pertaining to the contemplative life, at least he ought not to cease from the study of perseverance: because it is an everlasting possession for him, which he ought not to alienate or lose for any reason. folio 252, column 2.

What the difference is between those who are converted from childhood to the service of God and those who delay until old age. folio 253, column 1.

**Gold** signifies the contemplative life and those praising the Lord. **Silver** signifies the doctrine of the Lord's words. And **Bronze** signifies the work of hands for the support of the needy: note. folio 253, column 1.

Through work, bodies are nourished; through doctrine, the minds of the "little ones in Christ" are refreshed; and both look toward the love of neighbor; but the third, which is signified by gold—namely, the contemplative life—looks toward the love of God, which is the first and greatest commandment. folio 253, column 1.

In the days of King Saul, who was chosen by the Lord to signify the people of the **First State** <note>the Age of the Father and the Old Testament</note>, bronze was esteemed. In the days of King David, who himself was chosen by the Lord to signify the people of the **Second State** <note>the Age of the Son and the Gospel</note>, bronze was not esteemed because of the abundance of silver. And in the days of Solomon, who represents the **Third State** <note>the Age of the Holy Spirit and Monasticism</note>, because of the extreme abundance of gold, even silver was not esteemed as anything. folio 253, column 1.

The order of the married, which was begun by **Adam**, shone forth in **Abraham**; the order of clerics, initiated by **Moses**, shone forth in **Christ** and the apostles; the order of monks, initiated by **Elijah**, is now, by God's favor, at the time where it should come to the light, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. folio 253, column 1.

The initiation of the **Third State**, pertaining to the **Holy Spirit**, was in **Saint Benedict**, the founder of the Western monks; but it will shine forth in its own time. folio 253, column 2.

# The Ten-Stringed Psaltery of Abbot Joachim
<note>Joachim’s work *Psalterium Decem Chordarum* uses the ten-stringed harp mentioned in the Psalms as a mathematical and musical model for the Trinity.</note>

¶ That there are three exercises belonging to the three orders—namely the laity, the clergy, and the monks—which also correspond to the image of the Trinity: namely, **work**, **doctrine**, and **praise** (that is, psalmody). folio 255, column 1.

¶ That it is one thing to work for one’s own benefit, another for the assistance of neighbors, and another for the glory and praise of God. And similarly regarding doctrine and psalmody. Note. folio 255, column 1.

¶ That nearly a third part of the Psalms consists of prayer for sins; and for this reason, we are accustomed to recite the psalms praying for our own salvation and that of our neighbors. folio 255, column 2.

¶ That psalmody properly belongs to the people of the **Third Status** <note>Joachim’s "Third Age" of the Holy Spirit, a future era of spiritual contemplation and monastic peace</note> which will be at the end of the age; when, with peace and joy granted to Christians on all sides, the people will turn by habit to the praise of God, saying continually with the Psalmist: *“Thou hast turned my mourning into joy for me,”* etc. <note>original: "Convertisti planctum meum in gaudium mihi"</note> folio 255, column 2.

¶ That the number **fifteen** is of such great perfection that within it is contained every perfection of the mystery of God. folio 255, column 2.

¶ That the said number is divided into the numbers **three**, **five**, and **seven**. <note>3 + 5 + 7 = 15. Joachim uses these subdivisions to categorize different divine and natural attributes.</note> folio 255, column 2.

¶ That the glorious God is the end of our inquiry and our desire. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That the numbers three, five, and seven pertain to that entire heavenly city. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That in the heavenly city, three things are to be hoped for: namely, the villages, the suburbs, and the city itself. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That the mystery of the Godhead is contained in the aforementioned three numbers. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That the number **three** (the ternary) pertains to the three properties of the Persons <note>The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note>, according to which each Person is understood to exist by Himself and is not the other. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That the number **five** (the quinary) pertains to the **five relations** <note>In scholastic theology, these are the logical ways the Persons of the Trinity relate to one another: paternity, filiation, spiration, procession, and innascibility.</note>. And the number **seven** (the septenary) to the seven modes by which God is spoken of in relation to Himself: note: folio 256, column 1.

¶ That morally: the number three pertains

<column-break/>

to the three exercises: namely work, doctrine, and psalmody, of the three aforementioned orders. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That the number five pertains to the five virtues as mentioned above; and the number seven to the seven natural virtues of the soul. folio 256, column 1.

¶ How in the **one hundred and fifty psalms**, the way of reaching the perfection of the Catholic confession is shown to us. And in the **fifteen steps** (in this work): a memorial of entering the approach to the Holy of Holies. <note>Joachim links the 150 Psalms to the 15 "Gradual Psalms" sung when ascending the Temple steps.</note> folio 256, column 1.

¶ That first: in the foundation of our faith, the Trinity must be established: so that, before all things, we believe there are three perfect Persons, not divided, but distinct by their own properties. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That second: we ought to believe in one Person from one <note>The Son from the Father</note>, and another from two <note>The Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son</note>; and from these three themselves, the **seven spirits** of the Lord himself, sent into all the earth. folio 256, column 1.

¶ That third: it should be believed that each individual Person is true God; and two together; and three equally together are one God. folio 256, column 2.

¶ That **Alpha** is written in two ways among the Greeks: $\alpha$ and $\omega$. <note>The text likely refers to the Alpha and Omega symbols</note>. And how through these figures an exposition is made for the Trinity itself: Note. folio 257, column 2.

¶ How the Father has a certain proper relation to the Son; and conversely the Son to the Father; and both to the Holy Spirit. And simultaneously the three to every creature. folio 257, column 2.

¶ That to designate the excellence of so secret a mystery—namely, the **five relations** in divine matters—five venerable men were chosen at the beginning of the Old Testament: namely, **Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Ephraim.** folio 258, column 1.

¶ How the said men are sometimes understood as the Father and as the Son; and how this happens in different respects; and sometimes for the Holy Spirit. folio 258, column 1.

¶ Consider, reader, the **thrice-threefold figure**; and for a long time... <note>The entry cuts off, referring to one of Joachim's famous complex diagrams or 'figurae'.</note>

# The Ten Strings of Abbot Joachim

...calls the doctor of the Church: whose lawful wife is spiritual understanding. Truly, the "letter" <note>the literal or surface meaning of scripture</note> is a concubine, which must sometimes be cast out along with her children. folio 264, column 1.

¶ The children of the "letter" are carnal senses; truly, the children of spiritual understanding are spiritual meditations. folio 264, column 1.

¶ The fourth level of understanding, namely the **contemplative**, exceeds the **tropological** <note>the moral or figurative interpretation</note> by one degree: oh, how much more than that [level] it desires a spiritual man who is continent regarding the world and the things of the world, and who extends himself toward the things that are of the Spirit of God. folio 264, column 1.

¶ Abraham’s handmaid <note>Hagar</note> signifies the active life; Sarah signifies the contemplative life. folio 260, column 1.

¶ The fifth level of understanding is called **anagogical** <note>the spiritual interpretation relating to the afterlife or the end of time</note>, above which no other is found: for it is superior to all others. "Anagoge" <note>original: "Anagogen"</note> is interpreted as "superior understanding." folio 264, column 2.

¶ The **tropological** understanding pertains to faith, because faith comes from hearing; the **contemplative** to hope, because we seek to see that which we love and hope for. The **anagogical** to charity <note>love</note>, because the God whom we seek through it is charity; and he who has charity has everything at once that he seeks. folio 264, column 2.

¶ The **historical** understanding is properly designated in the two sons of Terah <note>original: "Thare"</note>, namely Abraham and Lot. The **moral** in the two wives of Abraham. The **tropological** is designated in the two sons of Isaac. The **contemplative** in the two wives of Jacob. The **anagogical** in the two sons of Joseph: in whom concludes the twin marking of this holy lineage, specifically Ephraim, who was the fifth from Abraham. folio 264, column 2.

¶ In the anagogical level of understanding, the ascent of understandings ends; it is the fifth from the historical, and the superior understanding. folio 264.

¶ It is marvelous what happens in these mysteries: that men and women succeed each other in turn, so that in the first degree there are two men; in the second, two women; in the third, two men; in the fourth, two women; and in the fifth, two men. Note the reason and the correspondence of the levels of understanding within them. folio 264, column 2.

¶ It is necessary that the significance of **Peter**—that is, the clergy—passes away, and the significance of **John**—that is, the monks—remains. folio 265, column 1.

¶ In the Law of Grace <note>the era of the New Testament</note>, the custom of the Old Testament concerning two wives joined to one man at the same time—as in Abraham, Jacob, and David—is rejected, and [the law] creates a "bill of divorce." folio 265.

¶ In the time of the **third state** <note>Joachim’s predicted future age of the Holy Spirit</note>, after the striking down of Babylon, many will take wives not for the sake of lust, but for offspring; and they shall be as if they had no wives, so that they are not refreshed by the pleasure of the flesh, but by the Spirit, and they may serve the Lord with a perfect heart. ¶ The seventh species of typical understanding is the last, in which is the end of all things. folio 265, column 2.

In the free woman <note>Sarah</note> is that Jerusalem above, which is our mother. folio 265, column 2.

# Table of the Commentary on the Psalter

Regarding the beginning of the Second State <note>The Age of the Son, or the era of the New Testament</note>, when the Son of God came into the world. folio 266, column 1.

¶ Just as there were fifteen men and patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and his twelve sons; and similarly, there were fifteen in the beginning of the Second State, namely: Zacharias, John the Baptist, the man Christ Jesus, and his twelve Apostles; so also in the beginning of the Third State <note>The Age of the Holy Spirit, which Joachim believed was beginning in his own time</note>, fifteen similar to them are to come. folio 266, column 1.

¶ **Historical understanding** is when something is done or recognized to have been done in the likeness of those things ordained by God, so that while the likeness is maintained, the merits [of the action] are sought after. folio 266, column 2.

¶ Following the example of the twelve patriarchs and the twelve apostles, the custom was established that twelve regular monks should be sent to a new monastery, which even the blessed Benedict did in twelve monasteries. folio 266, column 2.

¶ **Morally**, Abraham signifies the "outer man" <note>the physical or worldly self</note>; Isaac the "inner man" <note>the spiritual self</note>; Jacob signifies the free choice of the will. His five sons who were patriarchs represent the five external senses; the remaining seven represent the seven motions of the mind by which the soul is moved to obtain the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. folio 266, column 2.

¶ The seven motions are like seven aptitudes by which the gifts of the Holy Spirit themselves can be grasped, just as light or a word is received by the eye, and so on. folio 266, column 2.

¶ In the five patriarchs who were sons of Jacob are signified five general gifts: namely, humility, patience, faith, hope, and charity <note>love</note>. folio 267, column 1.

¶ In the seven remaining patriarchs who were sons of Jacob are signified seven special gifts, that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit <note>Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Fortitude, Knowledge, Piety, and Fear of the Lord</note>. folio 267, column 1.

¶ Seven communities or monasteries will shine brightly during the time of the Third State, in the likeness of the seven Churches of Asia. And this will happen when that which Peter signifies—following God with his Cross—has passed through.

<column-break/>

folio 267, column [1]

¶ In the fifteenth and final degree of the "understandings" themselves, which is "Generation" <note>original: "generatio"</note>—so called because it gathers the whole human race into one—Abraham signifies the prelates <note>church leaders</note> of the First State; Isaac the prelates of the Second; and Jacob the prelates of the Third State, etc. Note. folio 267, column [1].

¶ In those three great women—Sarah, Rebecca, and Rachel—are designated three specific things in each of the aforementioned fifteen degrees of understanding, for the most part. folio 268, column [1].

¶ At the beginning of the Third State (which is to come soon), the remnants of the Jews and the Gentiles shall be called and converted to the faith. folio 268, column [1].

¶ How the "first sheep" of understanding are not among the number of the twelve, but are added to them historically and morally, by which we ought to be instructed in what to do or what to avoid. folio 269.

¶ In **moral understanding**, one deals with the battle against physical vices; and in **tropology** <note>figurative moral interpretation</note>, with the battle against heresies. In **contemplation**, however, one deals with the battle against the spiritual attackers of the devil. folio 270.

¶ The battle pertaining to moral understanding is designated by the crossing of the Red Sea; that which pertains to tropology by the temptation in the desert; and that which pertains to the contemplative by the bitter wars against the Philistines. folio 270.

¶ He keeps the Sabbath best who, having left behind the vanity of the world, turns himself entirely to the service of God. This is according to the moral understanding. folio 271.

¶ According to **tropology**, the Sabbath is kept by ceasing from the observation of the Law according to the "letter" <note>literal, ritual law</note> and keeping the Law according to the Spirit. folio 271.

¶ **Contemplatively**, to keep the Sabbath is to pass from a life of toil and action to a life of quiet rest through the perfection of life. **Anagogically** <note>relating to the afterlife</note>, however, he keeps the Sabbath who, released from the weight of the flesh, rests in peace. folio 271.

Under him [Zerubbabel] or around his time, the histories of the Old Testament were completed. folio 276, column 1

☞ Under Zerubbabel <note>The leader of the first group of Jews to return from the Babylonian Captivity</note>, liberty was given to the people of Israel: so that there might be shown the completion of the "great jubilee," especially since seventy groups of years <note>original: "septuagenarij annorum," referring to the 70 years of exile</note> are found completed from Adam until Cyrus. folio 276, column 1

☞ In the year that Babylon was struck and the empire of the Chaldeans fell: there was the end of the first great jubilee: and that which the first fifty psalms signify was fulfilled. folio 276, column 1

☞ In the second group of fifty and the second jubilee, the "New Babylon" <note>In Joachim's thought, this often refers to the corrupt institutional Church or worldly power</note> is to be struck, just as the old one was struck by Cyrus: of which it is treated in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> in the likeness of the Great Harlot, as all the Doctors of the Church agree. folio 276, column 2

the sins of the remaining Church: and thereafter what remains of time: the work of God will be completed: and thus through fifteen stages or decades we shall enter into the Holy of Holies. folio 276, column 2

☞ Just as the Psaltery is contained in one hundred and fifty psalms, so the totality of time is contained in 150 generations: that is, from Adam until the completion of the age: yet beware lest you imagine a long space of years for yourself in these final five decades of generations. folio 276, column 2

☞ Whether the generations that remain in the future are of days, or of months, or of years: and how many years or months per individual generation, those who will be present there will know. folio 276, column 2

☞ Then let us know that we are heard by God and the sacrifices of our praises are made acceptable in his sight: if we praise him as he is: and if we understand what praise is owed to each person individually and to the three in common. folio 277, column 1

**T**hat to sing psalms wisely to God is to utter the very words of the psalms with discernment and intent. folio 277, column 2

**T**hat it is better to offer a few psalms in an orderly way than many in a disorderly fashion and without the guard of discipline, because it is not so much the numerous quantity of words as the affection and devotion that is commended by God. folio 277, column 2

**T**hat even if the quantity [of psalms] differs among different people, the affection of devotion ought to be the same in all of them; otherwise, if strength is not sufficient, one should trust in quantity <note>Likely meaning to rely on the prescribed amount for one's station</note> because virtue is not equal in everyone. folio 277, column 2

**T**hat there are some who are fervent in will but unrefined in devotion who, while they wish to seize the peak of perfection, presume something beyond their strength which they will not persevere in to the end, thinking that impossible for others which they themselves cannot strenuously complete. folio 277, column 2

**T**hat the great fathers who led the hermit life individually paid out the whole psalter every single day; others truly more or less, according to what holy devotion inspired by God suggested to them, wishing to grasp in this way what is written in the same book: *I will add beyond all your praise.* <note>original: "Adijciam super omnem laudem tuam," from Psalm 71:14.</note> folio 277, column 2

**T**hat for us (as Saint Benedict <note>The founder of Western monasticism</note> says), because we know these things and do not do them, it is a blush of confusion; yet not only the hundredfold and sixty-fold, but even—

**T**hat because the Lord is good and pious, he seeks hearts more than gifts, preferring the offering of the poor woman to the abundance of the rich. <note>A reference to the biblical story of the Widow’s Mite.</note> folio 277, column 2

**T**hat it does not seem to be of small devotion for a monk to say thirty psalms daily beyond the owed or canonical and customary hours, in honor of the Holy Trinity, and especially those who are detained and bound by various accidents and constant cares of occupations (which emerge unexpectedly). folio 277, column 2

**T**hat for a cleric to say twenty psalms daily is not of a sluggish devotion; for just as it is for monks to hold the third rank in this regard, so it is for clerics the second. Moreover, if any devout secular <note>term: "secularis," meaning a layperson living in the world rather than in a monastery.</note> wished, he too could imitate them and say ten. folio 277, column 2

**T**hat what the monks, being at leisure, strive to fulfill in one day—namely, the whole psalter—seculars should study to complete at least in fifteen days, because it is truly written for all the elect: *The sacrifice of praise shall honor me: and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God.* <note>Psalm 50:23</note> folio 278, column 1

**T**hat it does not belong to monks alone to sing psalms and praise, but to all Christians, and all Christians ought to love the singing of psalms. folio 278, column 1

<meta>This page continues the index for Book 3 of Abbot Joachim of Fiore's "Exposition on the Ten-Stringed Psaltery." The previous page introduced the concept of singing the psalms with proper intent and the differing requirements for various spiritual ranks. This section delves into the specific mystical numbers—tens and thirties—that structure the prayer life of monks and clergy, and the importance of silent, contemplative prayer over mere vocal recitation.</meta>

# The Ten-Stringed Psaltery of Abbot Joachim

...that [the number twenty] pertains to the clergy and thirty refers to the monks, so that each person, according to their rank, may offer as they please when they have leisure and their strength is sufficient. folio 278, column 1.

**S**ometimes he who praises more with his mouth is less able to praise with his heart, and conversely: he who praises more with his heart praises less with his mouth; for perhaps labor and occupation do not permit what the affection of the heart suggests. folio 278, column 1.

**T**he mind cannot be free to sing psalms in the same way during a time of groaning and labor (even if it is no less necessary then) as in a time of prosperity and joy; for as the Apostle says: *Is any among you sad? Let him pray with a steady mind and sing.* <note>Joachim is quoting James 5:13, though he refers to "the Apostle."</note> And therefore, at such a time, a brother ought to apply force to himself. folio 278, column 2.

**B**efore all things, it must be observed—as has been established for pious minds and approved by divine authorities—that we should sing and make melody in our hearts to God more than with an audible voice and the clashing of lips; for speaking and shouting belong to action, while praying and singing with silence belong to contemplation. folio 278, column 2.

**I**n public, we ought to confess our God with the service of our voice for the sake of those who are outside; but in secret, by His gift, we should enter the inner chambers of our heart, and there, without the noise and sound of the voice, offer the sacrifice of praise to Him alone, just as Hannah did. <note>original: "Anna"; Joachim refers to Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:13, who prayed in her heart while only her lips moved—a model for medieval contemplative prayer.</note> folio 278, column 2.

**H**e who vigilantly inspects the Holy Scriptures does not think it sufficient for himself to pay what he clearly owes by law and common duty, unless he has some secret thing to offer privately to his God; lest he be proved not a friend but a servant, if he offers nothing spontaneously by his own vow, but only under compulsion. folio 278, column 2.

**A**ll the good things a Christian does ought to have a good intention as their beginning. First, for the praise and glory of God; then, for the remedy and forgiveness of their sins; for conquering the pas-

<column-break/>

sions of the flesh; and for obtaining the grace of the Holy Spirit. folio 278, column 2.

**S**o that in those who have leisure for psalms and prayers, the feeling of devotion may always become more fruitful: it is a good and praiseworthy thing to give effort to psalmody in such a way that, through what is brought forth outwardly by the mouth, the mind may be illuminated inwardly. folio 278, column 2.

**T**hree <term>denarii</term> <note>original: "denarij." While this usually means coins, in Joachim's mathematical theology, it refers to groups of ten psalms, representing the Ten Commandments or "strings" of the psalter.</note> of psalms pertain to the perfection of the persons; the number thirty pertains to the unity of the Trinity. folio 278, column 2.

**T**he entire Psalter pertains to the glory and praise of God, whether divided into thirty psalms through five "ascents," or into fifteen "steps" of ten psalms each; so that a distinction is made for every ten psalms, paid for the honor and reverence of each, namely: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. folio 278, column 2.

**E**ach decade of generations is preceded by three certain persons as a type of the most excellent Trinity, as has been shown. folio 278, column 2.

**I**n the private recitation of the psalms, nine psalms are also to be taken from the body of the Psalter; these are called "the threes," and are used in groups of three in individual confessions to the honor of the Holy Trinity. folio 278, column 2.

**T**he aforementioned nine psalms are to be said in groups of three through each of the three decades—that is, before the decades are completed—and at the end, a commemoration of the indivisible Trinity should be made after the melody of the thirty psalms. folio 279, column 1.

**T**rust for completing [this task] must be placed in Him who promises to fulfill it in us (without a doubt); which He says in these times through Zechariah, among other things: *In that day I will seek to destroy all the nations,* etc., *and I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace.* <note>Quoting Zechariah 12:9-10.</note> folio 279, column 1.
